topic: A witness is questioned about a conversation they overheard in a company hallway
text:
Q: Mr. Delgado, you were in the hallway on the third floor on March 15th, correct?

A: I was in a hallway, yes.

Q: The third floor hallway. Near the executive suite.

A: If you say so.

Q: I'm asking you, Mr. Delgado. Do you recall being near the executive suite?

A: I was walking to the bathroom. I don't memorize which floor I'm on every time I need to use the facilities.

Q: But you do recall overhearing a conversation that day, don't you?

A: I recall hearing people talk, sure. People talk in offices. That's generally what happens.

Q: And one of those voices belonged to Rebecca Thornton, the CFO?

A: Could have.

Q: Could have or did?

A: I wasn't checking IDs. A woman was talking. It might have been her.

Q: You told your supervisor it was her. On March 16th. The very next day.

A: Then I guess I was more certain then than I am now, sitting here with you.

Q: So your memory was better the day after than it is today?

A: My memory is fine. My patience for guessing games is what's deteriorated.

Q: Mr. Delgado, did you or did you not hear Rebecca Thornton say the words "bury the report"?

A: I heard someone say something about a report. Whether it was "bury" or "hurry" or something else, I couldn't swear to it under oath. Which, as you may have noticed, I am.

Q: You seemed quite sure when you reported it.

A: And you seem quite sure you know what I heard better than I do.

---

topic: A witness is questioned about a conversation they overheard in a company hallway
text:
Q: You were employed as an administrative assistant in March of this year?

A: That's correct.

Q: And your desk was located near the hallway connecting the legal department to the main conference room?

A: Yes.

Q: On March 22nd, did you observe anyone in that hallway around 4 p.m.?

A: I saw several people throughout the day.

Q: I'm asking about 4 p.m. specifically.

A: I don't sit there with a stopwatch, counsel.

Q: Let me rephrase. Did you, at any point in the late afternoon, see David Chen and Margaret Holloway speaking in that hallway?

A: I may have.

Q: You may have. That's your testimony?

A: I'm being careful. You should appreciate that.

Q: What I appreciate, Ms. Yuen, is a direct answer. Did you see them or not?

A: I saw two people talking. I believe one was David Chen. The woman could have been Margaret Holloway. I wasn't staring.

Q: But you were close enough to hear what they said?

A: Pieces of it.

Q: And what pieces did you hear?

A: Something about a deadline. Something about signatures.

Q: Something about signatures. Can you be more specific?

A: No.

Q: No, you can't, or no, you won't?

A: No, I can't, because that's all I heard. I'm not going to invent testimony because you're standing there looking at me like I'm hiding something.

---

topic: A witness is questioned about a conversation they overheard in a company hallway
text:
Q: State your name for the record.

A: Thomas Whitfield.

Q: Mr. Whitfield, you've worked at Hensley Manufacturing for six years?

A: Six years in August.

Q: And you were present in the building on the afternoon of April 3rd?

A: I was.

Q: Where specifically?

A: I'd just left the supply room on the second floor. I was heading back toward my workstation.

Q: And as you walked, you passed by the operations manager's office?

A: I passed by several offices.

Q: Did you happen to hear a conversation taking place inside or near one of those offices?

A: I did hear voices, yes.

Q: Can you describe what you heard?

A: Two men. Sounded like they were disagreeing about something.

Q: Did you recognize either voice?

A: One of them was definitely Gary Pruitt. He's got a distinctive way of talking. Loud.

Q: And the other?

A: I couldn't say for certain.

Q: What were they disagreeing about?

A: Something about shipping records. Gary said something like "that's not what the numbers show."

Q: What else?

A: The other man—whoever he was—said they needed to "make it work" or "make it right." Something along those lines.

Q: Which was it? "Make it work" or "make it right"? Those mean very different things.

A: I'm aware they mean different things. I'm telling you I don't remember exactly. I wasn't taking notes. I was carrying a box of printer paper.

Q: A box of printer paper.

A: Yes. It's a real object. We use it for printing.

---

topic: A witness is questioned about a conversation they overheard in a company hallway
text:
Q: Ms. Patel, I want to be very clear about the timeline here. You've previously stated you were in the east corridor at approximately 2:15 p.m.?

A: That's my best estimate, yes.

Q: And you've stated you heard two individuals speaking in raised voices?

A: I said I heard a conversation. I don't know that I'd call them raised voices.

Q: Your written statement to HR says, quote, "they were speaking loudly enough that I could hear them clearly from fifteen feet away." Does that refresh your recollection?

A: That's not the same as raised voices. That's just... audible.

Q: Fine. They were audible. From fifteen feet away.

A: Correct.

Q: And one of the speakers was Brian Kendrick?

A: Yes.

Q: The plaintiff in this case.

A: I'm aware of who he is.

Q: Just establishing the record. And the other speaker?

A: I believe it was someone from HR. A woman.

Q: You believe, or you know?

A: I believe. I didn't see her face.

Q: But you could hear the conversation clearly from fifteen feet away.

A: I could hear some of it.

Q: What did you hear Brian Kendrick say?

A: He said something about being set up. That someone was trying to make him look bad.

Q: "Make him look bad." Those were his words?

A: Words to that effect.

Q: Ms. Patel, I need his actual words, not your interpretation.

A: And I'm giving you what I remember, counsel. I'm not a recording device. If you want exact transcription, you should have installed microphones in the hallway.

---

topic: A witness is questioned about a conversation they overheard in a company hallway
text:
Q: Good afternoon. You are James Okonkwo, currently employed in the IT department?

A: That's correct.

Q: On February 8th, you were in the fourth floor hallway near the server room?

A: Yes, I was doing scheduled maintenance checks.

Q: And during that time, did you happen to witness a conversation between any employees?

A: I did.

Q: Between whom?

A: Sandra Liu and another person. I didn't recognize the other individual.

Q: Male or female?

A: Male.

Q: Can you describe him?

A: Tall. Gray suit. I didn't get a good look at his face.

Q: What were they discussing?

A: I only caught a portion. Something about accounts. Offshore accounts, I think.

Q: You think, or you know?

A: I'm fairly certain the word "offshore" was used.

Q: And what was the context?

A: I don't know the context. I heard maybe thirty seconds of conversation while I was walking past.

Q: In those thirty seconds, what exactly did you hear Sandra Liu say?

A: She said they needed to move quickly. Before the audit.

Q: Before the audit. You're certain of that phrase?

A: Yes.

Q: And the man's response?

A: I didn't hear his response. I had already passed them.

Q: Convenient.

A: Excuse me?

Q: I said that's convenient. You heard the incriminating part but not the explanation.

A: I heard what I heard. I wasn't lingering to eavesdrop. I had work to do. If you're suggesting I'm fabricating this, counsel, I'd invite you to say so directly instead of making snide remarks.

Q: I'm not suggesting anything. I'm exploring your testimony.

A: Then explore it without the editorializing.

topic: A warehouse supervisor is deposed about safety protocols that were allegedly ignored
text:
Q: Mr. Hernandez, who was responsible for conducting the weekly safety inspections in Warehouse C?

A: That would be me. I conducted them. Every week.

Q: Every week without exception?

A: I—yes. I mean, there were times when—look, I conducted them on a regular basis, as required.

Q: I'm asking about every week. Did you conduct an inspection every single week in the six months prior to the accident?

A: I don't have the records in front of me. I can't say with absolute certainty about every single week without seeing the documentation.

Q: Would it surprise you to learn that we have only eleven inspection reports for a twenty-six week period?

A: I'd have to see those records. I'm not saying that's wrong, I'm just—I conducted inspections. Whether every single one got logged properly, I can't speak to that right now.

Q: So inspections occurred that weren't documented?

A: That's not—I didn't say that. I said I'd need to review the records.

Q: Mr. Hernandez, either inspections happened or they didn't. Which is it?

A: Inspections happened. Okay? They happened. If the paperwork doesn't reflect every single one, then there's a paperwork issue, but the inspections happened.

Q: Who else would have knowledge of whether these inspections actually occurred?

A: I don't—there were people around. Shift workers. I don't keep a list of witnesses to my inspections.

Q: But you just testified the inspections occurred. Surely someone can corroborate that?

A: I'm telling you they occurred. I'm telling you that under oath. I don't know what else you want from me.

topic: A warehouse supervisor is deposed about safety protocols that were allegedly ignored
text:
Q: Let's discuss the forklift training program. You oversaw that program, correct?

A: I coordinated it, yes. HR had involvement too.

Q: When a new operator was hired, walk me through the certification process.

A: Okay. So. The new hire would complete classroom training, usually about four hours. Then they'd do a practical assessment with either myself or a certified trainer. Then paperwork gets filed with HR.

Q: And Marcus Webb—did he complete this process?

A: I believe so, yes.

Q: You believe so.

A: I'm confident he did.

Q: Are you confident, or do you know?

A: I know he was trained. I know he was operating equipment. You don't operate equipment without being trained, that's the rule.

Q: But you don't have a specific memory of Mr. Webb's training?

A: I've trained probably two hundred people over the years. I don't have a photographic memory of each one. But there's a system. The system was followed.

Q: Let me show you what's been marked as Exhibit 14. Do you recognize this document?

A: It's a certification log.

Q: Is Marcus Webb's name on that log?

A: ...I'm looking.

Q: Take your time.

A: I don't see it on this particular page, but that doesn't—this might not be the complete record.

Q: This is the complete record for 2022, Mr. Hernandez. Your signature is at the bottom of each page.

A: Then there's been some kind of filing error. I'm not saying the system was perfect.

Q: The system you just told me was followed?

A: I said the system was followed. I didn't say the paperwork was perfect.

topic: A warehouse supervisor is deposed about safety protocols that were allegedly ignored
text:
Q: The accident report references something called a "near-miss" that occurred approximately three weeks before the incident. Are you familiar with what I'm referring to?

A: I am.

Q: Tell me about it.

A: A pallet shifted during transport. No one was injured. We documented it and moved on.

Q: That's all? A pallet shifted?

A: It fell. From about eight feet. It fell, it hit the ground, nobody was underneath it. That's a near-miss.

Q: And what action was taken following this near-miss?

A: We reviewed stacking protocols with the team. Standard procedure.

Q: Was there any investigation into why the pallet fell?

A: We looked at it. The strapping was—there was a strapping issue.

Q: A strapping issue.

A: The load wasn't secured properly.

Q: Who secured that load?

A: I don't recall specifically.

Q: You documented a near-miss, reviewed protocols with your team, but you don't know who was responsible for the improperly secured load?

A: We addressed it as a team issue, not an individual issue.

Q: Is that standard practice? Not identifying the responsible party?

A: It's how we handled it.

Q: I'm asking if that's standard practice, Mr. Hernandez.

A: Sometimes, yes. Look, the goal was to prevent it from happening again, not to—the goal was prevention.

Q: Three weeks later, a pallet fell and struck Thomas Chen. Was that the same type of strapping issue?

A: I don't—I can't say definitively—the investigation is still—I don't know.

topic: A warehouse supervisor is deposed about safety protocols that were allegedly ignored
text:
Q: Good afternoon. How long have you served as warehouse supervisor?

A: Yes.

topic: A warehouse supervisor is deposed about safety protocols that were allegedly ignored
text:
Q: Who is responsible for maintaining the incident reporting system?

topic: An employee is deposed about a coworker's termination they believe was retaliatory
text:
Q: Ms. Torres, how long had you worked alongside Daniel Okonkwo before his termination?

A: Four years. A little over four years, actually. He started about six months after I did.

Q: And during that time, would you say you had occasion to observe his work performance?

A: I did. We were on the same team. I saw how hard he worked. Every day, I saw it.

Q: Let's talk about the period leading up to his termination. Were you aware that Mr. Okonkwo had filed a complaint with Human Resources in February of last year?

A: Yes. He told me about it. He was... he was really torn up about whether to do it, actually. He asked me what I thought.

Q: What did you tell him?

A: I told him he should do what he felt was right. That the company had policies for a reason. That he shouldn't be afraid to use them.

Q: Do you know what the complaint concerned?

A: He said it was about safety violations in the warehouse. Equipment that wasn't being maintained. He'd reported it to his supervisor twice and nothing happened.

Q: Take your time if you need to. What happened after he filed that complaint?

A: Things changed. The way people talked to him changed. And I watched it happen, and I didn't—I should have said something sooner than I did.

Q: What do you mean by "the way people talked to him changed"?

A: Little things at first. Being left off meeting invites. His supervisor stopped saying good morning. Then bigger things. Write-ups for things nobody else got written up for. Being late by two minutes. Taking too long at lunch. Things that had never mattered before suddenly mattered for Daniel and only Daniel.

Q: Did you ever discuss these changes with Mr. Okonkwo?

A: Many times. He'd come to my desk sometimes, and he'd just stand there, and I could see it was weighing on him. I tried to tell him it wasn't his fault. That he'd done the right thing. But I don't know if that helped. I don't know if anything I said helped.

Q: Ms. Torres, I want to be clear—you're not on trial here. I'm just trying to understand what you observed.

A: I know. I know. I just think about whether I could have done more. He was a good person who tried to do the right thing, and look what happened to him.

Q: When you say "look what happened to him," you're referring to his termination?

A: Yes. Three months after his complaint. After eleven years with the company. They said it was performance-related, but I was there. I saw his performance. It wasn't performance.

---

topic: An employee is deposed about a coworker's termination they believe was retaliatory
text:
Q: Mr. Hassan, I'm going to ask you some questions about the events leading up to Karen Whitfield's termination. You understand you're under oath?

A: Yes.

Q: How would you describe your working relationship with Ms. Whitfield?

A: Professional. Friendly. We weren't close outside of work, but inside, we worked well together.

Q: Were you aware that Ms. Whitfield had raised concerns about billing practices in your department?

A: I was.

Q: How did you become aware?

A: She told me. She came to me because she trusted me, I think. She was worried about what she'd found.

Q: What specifically did she tell you?

A: That she'd found discrepancies. Invoices being duplicated. She thought it might be intentional, but she wasn't sure. She wanted to know if I'd seen anything similar.

Q: Had you?

A: I hadn't looked closely before. After she mentioned it, I started paying more attention.

Q: Mr. Hassan, I notice you're speaking carefully. Is there something about this topic that makes you uncomfortable?

A: I'm trying to be accurate. Karen's not here to speak for herself, so I want to make sure I get it right. She deserves that.

Q: That's understood. After Ms. Whitfield raised these concerns, what happened next?

A: She went to compliance. I told her she should. I said the company would want to know. I believed that at the time.

Q: Do you believe it now?

A: I believe the company should have wanted to know. Whether they actually did—I'm less sure about that now.

Q: Why do you say that?

A: Because two weeks after she reported it, she was on a performance improvement plan. And I'd worked next to her for three years. Her performance was never a problem before. Not once.

Q: Did you ever speak with management about your concerns regarding the timing?

A: I tried. Once. I was told it wasn't my business and to focus on my own work. So I did. And I've thought about that conversation a lot since then.

---

topic: An employee is deposed about a coworker's termination they believe was retaliatory
text:
Q: State your name for the record.

A: Patricia Vaughn.

Q: Ms. Vaughn, you were James Delacroix's direct supervisor, correct?

A: I was, yes.

Q: For how long?

A: Two years and three months.

Q: And you were his supervisor at the time of his termination?

A: I was not involved in that decision.

Q: That wasn't my question. Were you his supervisor at the time?

A: Technically, yes. But they didn't consult me. They didn't ask my opinion.

Q: Who is "they"?

A: HR. Upper management. I found out the same day James did.

Q: How did that make you feel?

A: It made me feel like I'd failed him. He was my employee. I should have been able to protect him.

Q: Protect him from what?

A: From what was coming. I could see it building after he testified at that OSHA hearing. The way leadership talked about him changed. He became a "problem" overnight.

Q: When you say "problem," can you elaborate?

A: Suddenly everything he did was scrutinized. I had regional managers asking me for weekly reports on his productivity. In two years, no one had ever asked me for that before. Not for any employee.

Q: Did you provide those reports?

A: I did. I thought if I could show them the numbers—show them he was a good worker—maybe they'd leave him alone. I documented everything. Every positive thing I could find.

Q: Did that help?

A: No. It didn't matter what I put in those reports. The decision was already made. I just didn't want to see it.

Q: Ms. Vaughn, do you need a moment?

A: No. I'm fine. I just—he had a family. A new baby. He'd shown me pictures the week before they let him go. I keep thinking about that.

---

topic: An employee is deposed about a coworker's termination they believe was retaliatory
text:
Q: Mr. Reeves, did there come a time when you became aware of allegations that Marcus Chen had been terminated in retaliation for protected activity?

A: I heard about the lawsuit, if that's what you mean.

Q: Before the lawsuit. During your employment, did you have any concerns about the circumstances of Mr. Chen's termination?

A: Look, I don't want to get anyone in trouble.

Q: I understand that. But you're under oath, and I'm asking what you observed.

A: Yes. I had concerns.

Q: What were they?

A: Marcus had filed that EEOC charge, maybe two months before? About the promotion he didn't get. Then suddenly he's being written up for things that made no sense. Coming back from lunch three minutes late. Not having his badge visible. Stuff that happens to everyone, every day.

Q: Did you ever witness other employees receive write-ups for similar infractions?

A: Never. And I've been there nine years. Never once saw anyone get written up for a badge violation until Marcus.

Q: What was your reaction when you learned Mr. Chen had been terminated?

A: I felt sick about it. Honestly. He'd worked there longer than me. He was good at his job. Everyone knew he was good at his job.

Q: Did you say anything to anyone at the company about your concerns?

A: I wanted to. I started to, once, with my supervisor. But I have kids. I have a mortgage. And I saw what happened to Marcus when he spoke up. So I stopped myself.

Q: Do you regret that?

A: Every day. He didn't deserve what happened to him. And I think about the fact that I could've said something and I didn't. I have to live with that.

Q: Mr. Reeves, I know this is difficult. Just a few more questions. In your view, based on everything you observed, do you believe Mr. Chen's termination was related to his EEOC charge?

A: I can't say what was in anyone's head. But if you're asking what it looked like from where I was standing—it looked like they wanted him gone, and they found a way to make it happen.

---

topic: An employee is deposed about a coworker's termination they believe was retaliatory
text:
Q: Ms. Yuen, you've testified that you considered Diane Hartley a friend as well as a colleague.

A: That's right. We were close.

Q: I want to ask you about a conversation you had with Ms. Hartley approximately two weeks before her termination. Do you recall that conversation?

A: I remember a lot of conversations with Diane. Could you be more specific?

Q: Of course. I'm referring to a conversation in which Ms. Hartley discussed her decision to report sexual harassment to Human Resources. Do you remember that?

A: Yes. I remember.

Q: Can you tell me what she said?

A: She said she'd made up her mind. That she was going to report what had been happening with Mr. Graves. She said she couldn't stay quiet anymore, even if it cost her.

Q: Did she say she was afraid it might cost her?

A: She knew. She wasn't naive about it. She'd seen what happened to other people who complained. But she said she couldn't look at herself in the mirror if she didn't say something.

Q: What was your response?

A: I told her I was proud of her. I told her I'd back her up if she needed me to. I meant it.

Q: Did she ask you to speak to HR on her behalf?

A: She didn't have to ask. I volunteered. I went to HR myself, the day after she filed her report. I confirmed what I'd seen. The comments, the way he looked at her, how uncomfortable she was.

Q: What happened after you made that statement to HR?

A: Nothing. For about a week, nothing at all. Then Diane was called in and told she was being terminated for "restructuring." Except no one else was let go. Just her.

Q: How did you learn about her termination?

A: She called me. She could barely get the words out. I just listened. I didn't know what else to do.

Q: Ms. Yuen, after Ms. Hartley's termination, did you continue working at the company?

A: For three more months. But it was different after that. I couldn't stop thinking about what they'd done to her. What I'd helped them do, in a way, by encouraging her to come forward.

Q: Do you believe you bear responsibility for what happened to her?

A: I know I don't. I know that rationally. But she trusted me, and I told her to do the right thing, and the right thing destroyed her career. So yes. Some nights, it feels like my fault.

topic: An accountant is deposed about transactions they processed on behalf of a client
text:
Q: Mr. Harrington, you processed the wire transfers at issue in this litigation, correct?

A: I did. All seventeen of them, over a fourteen-month period, each one documented, verified, and reconciled within twenty-four hours of execution.

Q: I was just asking if you processed them.

A: And I'm giving you the complete picture. You'll find that my work speaks for itself.

Q: Let's focus on the March 2022 transfer. The $2.3 million to the Cayman account.

A: March 14th, 2022, executed at 2:47 PM Eastern, confirmation number ending in 4471. I have the documentation here if you'd like to see how thoroughly it was prepared.

Q: That won't be necessary at this moment. Who authorized that transfer?

A: Mr.Elden authorized it in writing, per the protocol I personally designed for his accounts. Three-step verification. Most firms use two. I implemented three.

Q: Did you have any concerns about the destination account?

A: I conducted due diligence that exceeded—and I want to be clear about this—exceeded what any regulatory body requires. Beneficial ownership verification, source of funds documentation, compliance cross-checks. All clean.

Q: So your answer is no?

A: My answer is that I did my job correctly. Better than correctly.

Q: Mr. Harrington, I'm asking a yes or no question. Did you have concerns?

A: No. Because I had already eliminated any basis for concern through proper procedure.

Q: Who else reviewed these transfers?

A: No one else needed to. I've been doing this for twenty-two years without a single compliance violation. Not one.

Q: That wasn't my question.

A: The answer is no one. Because when you do the work right the first time, you don't need someone looking over your shoulder.

topic: An accountant is deposed about transactions they processed on behalf of a client
text:
Q: Ms. Castellano, I want to walk through your methodology for flagging unusual transactions. Take your time.

A: Of course.

Q: You developed a screening system for the Moreau portfolio, is that right?

A: I did.

Q: And this system—help me understand—this caught the discrepancy in the October disbursements?

A: It did. Three days before the internal audit would have.

Q: Three days before. Now, when you identified that discrepancy, what was your process?

A: I isolated the transaction, traced it back through four layers of subsidiary accounts, identified the coding error, and prepared a corrective memorandum.

Q: All of that yourself?

A: All of that myself. By the end of the same business day.

Q: That's remarkable efficiency. The corrective memorandum—you still have it?

A: I keep records of all my work product. Seven years, organized by client, date, and transaction type.

Q: Very thorough. Did Mr. Moreau ever acknowledge this catch?

A: He did. In writing. I can provide that as well if it would assist your understanding.

Q: It would. Now, after October, did you modify your screening parameters?

A: I refined them. The original system was already effective, but I improved the sensitivity thresholds. Since then, zero discrepancies have gone undetected.

Q: Zero. In how many months?

A: Eighteen months. Four hundred and twelve transactions.

Q: Ms. Castellano, that's an exceptional record.

A: I'm aware.

topic: An accountant is deposed about transactions they processed on behalf of a client
text:
Q: The QuarterPoint software—you used it for the Brennan account?

A: No findings. No penalties. No follow-up.

Q: Were you surprised?

A: I was not.

topic: An accountant is deposed about transactions they processed on behalf of a client

topic: An accountant is deposed about transactions they processed on behalf of a client

topic: A store manager is questioned about a customer slip-and-fall on their premises
text:

A: Yes.

Q: How many, approximately?

A: I don't know. A few. Maybe five or six. These things happen in retail.

Q: These things happen. Is that what you tell your employees?

A: I tell them to follow the safety protocols. That's what I tell them.

Q: Were the safety protocols followed on October 14th?

A: I believe so. I wasn't on the floor when it happened.

Q: Who was on the floor?

A: Derek. Derek Simmons. He was the shift lead that afternoon.

Q: Did you speak with Derek after the incident?

A: Of course I did.

Q: What did he tell you?

A: He said a bottle of olive oil broke in aisle seven. He said he was getting the wet floor sign when the customer fell. He was getting it. He wasn't standing around.

Q: How long does it take to get a wet floor sign?

A: I don't know. A minute. Maybe two. Look, I've been through this with your office, with our insurance people, with corporate. Derek did what he was supposed to do. It just... it wasn't fast enough, I guess. Sometimes that's how it goes.

topic: A store manager is questioned about a customer slip-and-fall on their premises
text:
Q: Ms. Patterson, I'm going to show you what's been marked as Exhibit 4. Do you recognize this document?

A: ... I would assume so.

Q: But you don't know if they were there before?

topic: A store manager is questioned about a customer slip-and-fall on their premises
text:
Q: Let's talk about the maintenance log for that day.

topic: A store manager is questioned about a customer slip-and-fall on their premises
text:
Q: Mr. Okonkwo, you mentioned earlier that you reviewed the security footage after Mr. Brennan's fall.

A: I did.

Q: And what did you observe?

A: I observed Mr. Brennan walking through the garden center. I observed him stepping on a puddle of water near the potted plants. I observed him falling.

Q: Did you observe where the water came from?

A: One of the overhead sprinkler lines had a leak. Small leak. It had been dripping.

Q: For how long?

A: I can't say exactly. The footage only goes back four hours.

Q: So at minimum, four hours?

A: At minimum, yes.

Q: Was there any signage warning customers about the leak?

A: No.

Q: Any cones? Barriers?

A: No.

Q: Any employee stationed nearby to warn customers?

A: No. No, there was nothing like that.

Q: Why not?

A: Because no one knew about it. Or if they knew, they didn't report it. Either way, it didn't get to me.

Q: Is it your testimony that a leak can drip for four hours in your store without anyone noticing?

A: That's not my testimony. That's just... that's what happened. I'm not going to pretend otherwise. We missed it. The system broke down somewhere, and we missed it.

Q: What system are you referring to?

A: The system where employees are supposed to report hazards. The system that's supposed to prevent exactly this. It didn't work that day. I'm not going to sit here and tell you it did.

topic: A store manager is questioned about a customer slip-and-fall on their premises
text:
Q: Let's discuss the condition of aisle three on the morning of the incident.

topic: A building inspector is deposed about a structural assessment they signed off on
text:
Q: Mr. Delacroix, how long have you been a licensed building inspector in this state?

A: Thirty-two years this past March. I was in the first cohort to receive certification under the revised structural integrity protocols in 1992. There were forty-seven of us who passed that examination. I can still name most of them.

Q: And you conducted the assessment of the Meridian Tower on June 14th, 2023?

A: I did. Personally. From foundation to rooftop mechanical room. Eight hours on site, which I should note is double what most inspectors allocate for a building of that square footage.

Q: The report indicates you found no structural deficiencies. Is that accurate?

A: That's an oversimplification of what my report indicates. What I found was a building in substantial compliance with all applicable codes, with three minor notation items that I documented in appendix C, all of which were remediated within the fourteen-day window I specified.

Q: Did anyone accompany you during the inspection?

A: I brought Marcus Webb, one of our junior inspectors. Training opportunity. I believe in hands-on mentorship—it's how I learned, and it's how the next generation should learn. He observed my methodology throughout.

Q: What methodology is that, specifically?

A: The Delacroix Protocol, as some in the department have taken to calling it. My own systematic approach. I developed it over two decades of fieldwork. Visual inspection grid, load-bearing member assessment, connection point verification. I've trained over sixty inspectors using this framework.

Q: Is this protocol documented anywhere?

A: I authored a training manual in 2015. The department adopted it officially in 2018. Would you like me to have my attorney provide a copy? It's quite comprehensive—two hundred fourteen pages.

Q: That won't be necessary at this time. When you examined the east support column—

A: Column E-7. I remember it specifically because it presented an interesting case study. Hairline surface crazing that an inexperienced inspector might have flagged. But I recognized it immediately as cosmetic settling consistent with the building's age. I used it as a teaching moment for Marcus.

Q: You were confident in that assessment?

A: Counselor, I've examined over four thousand structural columns in my career. I know the difference between a cosmetic imperfection and a structural concern. That column was sound. I would stake my reputation on it—and in fact, I did, by signing that report.

topic: A building inspector is deposed about a structural assessment they signed off on
text:
Q: Ms. Okonkwo, please describe the sequence of your inspection on September 3rd.

A: I arrived at approximately 8:15 a.m. Checked in with the site manager. Reviewed the previous inspection file. Then proceeded systematically through the structure.

Q: Systematically how?

A: Floor by floor. Basement to roof.

Q: And what did you observe in the basement level?

A: Nothing outside normal parameters.

Q: Can you be more specific?

A: Foundation walls intact. No visible water intrusion. Mechanical systems properly secured. Support columns showed no signs of stress or deterioration.

Q: You noted in your report that you observed "minor efflorescence" on the north wall. What does that mean?

A: White mineral deposits. Indicates past moisture presence. Common in buildings of that vintage. Not a structural concern.

Q: How do you know it wasn't a structural concern?

A: Because I've been doing this for eleven years and I know what structural concerns look like.

Q: Fair enough. Now I'd like to turn to the third floor—

A: You're moving past the basement rather quickly.

Q: Excuse me?

A: I spent two hours in that basement. Documented everything. If you have questions about my basement assessment, I'd suggest you ask them now rather than circling back later and wasting everyone's time.

Q: I appreciate your... thoroughness. Let's discuss the third-floor cantilever.

A: What about it?

Q: You signed off on it as structurally sound.

A: Because it was structurally sound. I measured the deflection myself. Well within tolerance.

Q: What was the measurement?

A: Three-sixteenths of an inch under static load. Code allows up to three-quarters. I documented this with photographs, measurements, and timestamp data. It's all in my file.

topic: A building inspector is deposed about a structural assessment they signed off on
text:
Q: Mr. Huang, I want to be very precise here. When you signed the assessment form on line 47, what were you certifying?

A: That in my professional judgment, the structure met applicable safety codes.

Q: Your professional judgment.

A: Yes.

Q: And how long did you spend forming that professional judgment?

A: Approximately four hours on site.

Q: Four hours for a twelve-story building. Would you say that's adequate?

A: I would say—and I've said this in training seminars I've conducted—that inspection quality is not measured in hours. It's measured in expertise and attention. Some inspectors could spend twelve hours and miss what I identify in one.

Q: That's quite a claim.

A: It's not a claim. It's documented. I identified the Canton Street facade failure in 2019 during what was supposed to be a routine compliance check. Twenty-minute walkthrough. I saw the mortar degradation pattern that three previous inspectors had missed over five years. The building was evacuated that afternoon. It partially collapsed six days later.

Q: I'm familiar with that incident. But we're here to discuss the Parkview Commons assessment.

A: Then let's discuss it. What specifically would you like to know?

Q: The lateral bracing on floors eight through ten—

A: Original to the 1987 construction. Steel moment frames with bolted connections. I inspected each connection point personally. No signs of fatigue, corrosion, or loosening.

Q: How many connection points are we talking about?

A: Forty-seven per floor. One hundred forty-one total. I have photographs of each one time-stamped in my documentation. The building's engineer was present and verified my observations.

Q: And yet the building experienced lateral movement during the November windstorm.

A: Within designed tolerances. Buildings are supposed to move, counselor. That's how they survive. The Parkview Commons performed exactly as it should have. I reviewed the accelerometer data afterward. Textbook response.

topic: A building inspector is deposed about a structural assessment they signed off on
text:
Q: Let's talk about your qualifications, Ms. Reeves.

A: Certainly. Bachelor's in civil engineering from—

Q: Actually, let me stop you there. I'm more interested in your practical experience with pre-war construction specifically.

A: Ah. Well. The Blanchard Building was constructed in 1928, so I understand your focus. I've inspected... let me think... perhaps fifteen or twenty buildings from that era.

Q: Fifteen or twenty. Out of how many total inspections in your career?

A: Several hundred. I'd have to check my records for an exact number.

Q: So pre-war buildings represent a relatively small portion of your experience?

A: A smaller portion, yes. Though I did complete a specialized certification in historic structural assessment through the National Trust program in 2020.

Q: A certification program. How long was that?

A: It was a forty-hour course.

Q: Forty hours.

A: With an examination. And a practical component. I had to—

Q: Let's move on. The Blanchard Building's steel frame—you noted it was in "satisfactory" condition. What does satisfactory mean to you?

A: It means meeting the applicable standards for continued occupancy with no immediate safety concerns.

Q: And you felt qualified to make that determination based on forty hours of coursework?

A: I felt qualified based on my engineering degree, my eight years of field experience, my specialized training, and my thorough examination of the structure. The coursework was supplementary to an already established foundation of knowledge.

Q: Did you consult with any specialists in pre-war construction before signing off?

A: I consulted the building's original architectural drawings, the 1952 renovation plans, and three subsequent inspection reports. I also—

Q: That wasn't my question. Did you consult with any living specialists?

A: I... no. I did not feel it was necessary given my own assessment.

Q: Thank you. That answers my question.

A: But I should note that my assessment has since been validated by the structural engineering firm that conducted the post-incident analysis. They found no errors in my methodology or conclusions.

topic: A building inspector is deposed about a structural assessment they signed off on
text:
Q: Dr. Vance, you've testified in seventeen building failure cases. Is that correct?

A: Nineteen, actually. Your colleague's research may be slightly outdated.

Q: Nineteen. And in how many of those cases were you testifying in defense of your own inspection work?

A: This is the first.

Q: The first. So this is different for you.

A: The circumstances are different. My testimony is the same. Factual. Professional. Based on thirty-one years of structural engineering experience and twelve years as a certified inspector.

Q: Let's discuss the Heritage Plaza parking structure. You conducted the assessment on April 2nd of last year?

A: April 2nd and 3rd. It was a two-day inspection due to the facility's size.

Q: And you concluded the structure was sound.

A: I concluded the structure met all applicable safety standards and was suitable for continued use with recommended maintenance items as noted in my report.

Q: One of those recommended maintenance items was re-coating the rebar exposure points on level three.

A: Correct.

Q: How urgent was that recommendation?

A: I categorized it as a twelve-month maintenance item. Standard timeline for that type of remediation.

Q: The collapse occurred eight months later.

A: On level two. Not level three. The rebar exposure I noted was unrelated to the failure point.

Q: How can you be certain of that?

A: Because I reviewed the forensic engineering report in detail. The failure initiated at a post-tensioned cable anchorage that showed no external signs of distress during my inspection. Internal corrosion. Undetectable through visual assessment.

Q: Undetectable.

A: By any visual inspection methodology currently in use. I've since co-authored a paper recommending ultrasonic testing protocols for post-tensioned systems in coastal environments. It's being considered for adoption by three state licensing boards.

Q: So you're saying no inspector could have caught this?

A: I'm saying I didn't miss anything that was possible to see. And I'm saying I've spent the last eight months working to ensure no inspector faces this situation again. My paper has been cited fourteen times already. The methodology is sound. It will save structures. It will save lives.

topic: An HR director is questioned about a harassment complaint that was filed and closed
text:
Q: Ms. Delgado, you received the written complaint from Ms. Thornton on March 3rd, correct?

topic: An HR director is questioned about a harassment complaint that was filed and closed
text:

topic: An HR director is questioned about a harassment complaint that was filed and closed

topic: An HR director is questioned about a harassment complaint that was filed and closed

topic: A doctor is deposed about informed consent procedures before a surgery
text:
Q: Dr. Hernandez, let's talk about the informed consent process for Mrs. Patterson's knee replacement surgery on March 15th. Can you walk me through what occurred?

A: Absolutely. I met with Mrs. Patterson three days before the procedure, on March 12th, in my office. We spent approximately forty-five minutes together. I explained the nature of the surgery, the expected outcomes, the risks involved, and the alternatives available to her, including non-surgical options.

Q: Forty-five minutes. That's a substantial amount of time.

A: It is, and I find that's what's needed. Joint replacement is a significant decision. Patients deserve the opportunity to ask questions, to process the information, and to feel confident in their choice. I don't rush these conversations.

Q: What specific risks did you discuss with her?

A: Infection, blood clots, nerve damage, the possibility of implant loosening over time, the chance that the procedure might not fully eliminate her pain, and the risks associated with anesthesia. I also discussed the expected recovery timeline and the physical therapy requirements.

Q: Did you document this conversation?

A: I did. I dictated a detailed note that same afternoon, and it's in her chart. I can tell you that my practice is to be thorough in documentation because I believe the record should reflect exactly what was communicated.

Q: And the consent form itself—when was that signed?

A: The morning of surgery, March 15th. But I want to be clear: the form is a formality that memorializes the discussion. The actual informed consent happened in my office three days earlier.

Q: Did you speak with her again before she signed the form?

A: I did. I visited her in pre-op, asked if she had any new questions, reviewed the key points, and confirmed she still wished to proceed. She told me she'd discussed everything with her daughter over the weekend and felt ready.

Q: How would you characterize her understanding of the risks?

A: Excellent. She asked thoughtful questions during our initial consultation—particularly about infection rates and what signs to watch for afterward. That told me she was engaged and processing the information appropriately.

Q: Is this your standard practice, Doctor, or did you do something different for Mrs. Patterson?

A: This is exactly how I approach every surgical patient. I developed this process over twenty-two years because it works. Patients who understand their procedures tend to have better outcomes and more realistic expectations.

topic: A doctor is deposed about informed consent procedures before a surgery

A: The note is brief, but the conversation was thorough.

A: The note summarizes. I don't transcribe every word of every patient encounter.

topic: A doctor is deposed about informed consent procedures before a surgery
text:
Q: Let's discuss Mr. Franklin's cardiac catheterization. You were the attending cardiologist?

A: That's right.

Q: And you handled the informed consent?

A: Personally, yes.

Q: Some physicians delegate that to residents or nurses. You don't?

A: No. I believe the physician performing the procedure should be the one explaining it. That's been my philosophy for my entire career, and I think it serves patients well.

Q: Walk me through what you told Mr. Franklin.

A: I explained that we'd be inserting a catheter through his femoral artery to visualize his coronary arteries. I told him we might find blockages, and if we did, we could potentially treat them during the same procedure with angioplasty and stenting.

Q: So you discussed the possibility of intervention?

A: Extensively. I told him that if we found significant blockages, I'd recommend treating them then rather than bringing him back for a second procedure. He agreed that made sense.

Q: What risks did you cover?

A: Bleeding at the access site, arterial damage, reaction to the contrast dye, heart attack, stroke, kidney injury from the dye, and death—though I emphasized the mortality risk is very low, less than one percent for diagnostic catheterization.

Q: You mentioned kidney injury. Did you know Mr. Franklin had reduced kidney function going in?

A: I did. His creatinine was mildly elevated. That's precisely why I discussed contrast-induced nephropathy specifically. I told him we'd use the minimum amount of dye necessary and hydrate him well before and after.

Q: Did he express any concerns about that?

A: He asked if there were alternatives that didn't require dye. I explained that CT angiography also uses contrast, and that stress testing had already been inconclusive. He understood catheterization was the most reliable diagnostic option.

Q: Was his wife present for this conversation?

A: She was. She asked several questions herself, particularly about recovery time. I appreciated her involvement—it often helps patients to have a family member there.

Q: How did the conversation conclude?

A: Mr. Franklin said he wanted to move forward. He signed the consent form that afternoon, and the procedure was scheduled for two days later.

topic: A doctor is deposed about informed consent procedures before a surgery
text:
Q: Dr. Okonkwo, isn't it true that you spent less than five minutes discussing risks with Ms. Delgado before her hysterectomy?

A: That's not accurate.

Q: How long did you spend?

A: Our consultation was approximately thirty minutes, and a significant portion addressed the risks, benefits, and alternatives.

Q: But you don't have any documentation of exactly how long, do you?

A: I don't record timestamps within a consultation. What I have is a detailed note reflecting the content of our discussion.

Q: Let me ask about something specific. Did you tell Ms. Delgado that she might experience bladder injury during surgery?

A: Yes.

Q: Those exact words?

A: I told her that injury to the bladder or ureters is a known risk of hysterectomy, occurring in a small percentage of cases, and that if it happened, we would repair it during the same surgery.

Q: You're certain you said that?

A: I am. I discuss these risks with every hysterectomy patient because they're specific to this surgery. It's part of my standard consent discussion.

Q: And you remember this particular patient specifically?

A: I do, because she asked several questions about her anatomy. She'd had multiple C-sections and was concerned about scar tissue. I explained that adhesions from prior surgery could make the procedure more challenging, which is exactly why I mentioned the risk of injury to adjacent structures.

Q: Did you tell her the risk was higher because of her surgical history?

A: I told her that adhesions can increase complexity. I didn't quote her a specific percentage because the literature doesn't support that level of precision for an individual patient.

Q: Wouldn't that information have been relevant to her decision?

A: I gave her the relevant information—that her history created additional considerations. She understood that.

Q: Did she ask about alternatives to hysterectomy?

A: She did. We discussed endometrial ablation and hormonal management. She had tried hormonal therapy without relief and wasn't a candidate for ablation given her fibroid size.

Q: So hysterectomy was the only option?

A: It was the best option. She made an informed choice.

topic: A doctor is deposed about informed consent procedures before a surgery
text:
Q: Dr. Whitmore, I want to understand your general practice regarding informed consent before we discuss Mr. Yates specifically. Fair enough?

A: Certainly.

Q: How do you typically approach informed consent for spinal surgery?

A: I use a structured approach that I've refined over the years. First, I ensure the patient understands their diagnosis and why surgery is being recommended. Then I explain the procedure itself, the anticipated benefits, the material risks, and the alternatives—including doing nothing.

Q: When you say material risks, what do you mean?

A: Risks that are either common enough that a reasonable patient would want to know, or serious enough that even a small chance would affect decision-making. For spine surgery, that includes infection, bleeding, nerve damage, spinal fluid leak, failed back surgery syndrome, and the possibility that symptoms won't improve.

Q: Do you use any visual aids?

A: I do. I have a spine model in my office, and I often draw diagrams. Patients find it helpful to see what I'm describing.

Q: Let's turn to Mr. Yates. He underwent a lumbar fusion on November 12th. When did you first discuss the surgery with him?

A: At his consultation on October 28th.

Q: Two weeks before surgery.

A: That's right. I want patients to have time to think, to do their own research, to discuss with family.

Q: What do you recall about your discussion with him?

A: He was nervous—appropriately so. Spine surgery is significant. I spent considerable time explaining why I believed fusion was necessary given the instability at L4-L5, what the surgery would involve, and what he could realistically expect afterward.

Q: What did you tell him about the recovery?

A: That it would be gradual. That he'd likely have restrictions for several months. That physical therapy would be essential. I told him fusion isn't a magic fix—it's about stabilizing the spine to prevent further deterioration and reduce pain, but some discomfort might persist.

Q: Did he seem to understand?

A: He asked good questions. He wanted to know about the hardware, whether he'd set off metal detectors, how long until he could golf again. Those practical questions told me he was engaged.

Q: How did the conversation end?

A: He told me he wanted to go home and talk to his wife, and he'd call my office. He called three days later and scheduled the surgery.
