A: Yes. Eventually.

Q: How long did you wait before moving toward it?

A: I didn't wait. I finished processing what I'd heard and then I walked over. Maybe ten seconds.

topic: A witness is questioned about events at a party where an assault allegedly occurred
text:
Q: You testified earlier that you'd had three drinks by 10 p.m. Is that accurate?

A: That's what I said.

Q: Mr. Calhoun, I want to make sure we're being precise here. Three drinks in what time span?

A: I arrived around eight. So two hours.

Q: What were you drinking?

A: Whiskey and Coke.

Q: Singles or doubles?

A: I wasn't pouring them myself. I don't know.

Q: You don't know whether you were drinking single or double pours of whiskey over a two-hour period?

A: Someone handed me drinks. I drank them. I didn't interrogate the bartender.

Q: Were you intoxicated by 10 p.m.?

A: No.

Q: Not at all?

A: I said no.

Q: Three whiskeys in two hours and you weren't feeling any effects whatsoever?

A: I didn't say I felt nothing. I said I wasn't intoxicated. There's a difference. Do you need me to explain it?

Q: I need you to answer the question. Were your perceptions impaired at the time you witnessed the events in question?

A: My perceptions were fine.

Q: You had no difficulty seeing, hearing, or remembering what occurred?

A: None.

Q: Mr. Calhoun, you understand you're under oath.

A: I'm aware of where I am and what oath I took. I've answered your question three times now. Would you like me to answer it a fourth?

topic: A witness is questioned about events at a party where an assault allegedly occurred
text:
Q: Ms. Yuen, did anyone at the party appear to be in distress that night?

A: I noticed Brianna seemed upset at one point.

Q: When was this?

A: I don't know exactly. Sometime after eleven.

Q: And what did you observe that led you to believe she was upset?

A: She was crying.

Q: Where was she?

A: In the bathroom. The door was open a little.

Q: Did you speak with her?

A: Briefly.

Q: What did she say?

A: I asked if she was okay. She said she wanted to go home.

Q: Did she say anything else? Did she say why she wanted to go home?

A: No.

Q: Nothing at all?

A: She said she wanted to go home. That's what she said.

Q: Ms. Yuen, I'm going to ask you to think carefully. This is a serious matter.

A: I understand it's serious. You don't need to tell me that.

Q: Did Brianna mention the defendant's name at any point?

A: Not that I recall.

Q: Not that you recall, or no?

A: I said what I said. I don't recall her mentioning his name. If you want me to manufacture a different answer, I can't do that.

Q: No one is asking you to manufacture anything.

A: Good. Then we understand each other.

Q: Did she have any visible injuries?

A: Her mascara was running. I didn't see injuries. I wasn't looking for injuries. I was trying to help her.

topic: A witness is questioned about events at a party where an assault allegedly occurred
text:
Q: How well do you know the defendant?

A: We've met a few times.

Q: Through what context?

A: We have mutual friends. I've seen him at maybe four or five parties over the past year.

Q: Would you describe yourself as friendly with him?

A: I would describe myself as someone who has exchanged words with him in social settings. I wouldn't call us friends.

Q: Have you ever seen him behave aggressively toward anyone?

A: No.

Q: Never?

A: That's what "no" means.

Q: And on the night of March 15th, did you observe any confrontation involving the defendant?

A: I saw him arguing with someone near the garage.

Q: Who was he arguing with?

A: I didn't recognize the other person.

Q: What did you observe about this argument?

A: They were speaking loudly. The defendant had his hands up like this—palms out.

Q: The record can't capture gestures, Mr. Okonkwo. Can you describe it verbally?

A: I'm aware of how depositions work. His palms were facing outward, at chest height. A defensive posture.

Q: How do you know it was defensive?

A: Because I have eyes and I've been a human being for thirty-four years. That's how people stand when they're trying to de-escalate.

Q: You're offering your interpretation.

A: You asked what I observed. I observed his posture. The interpretation is common sense.

Q: Did this argument become physical?

A: Not while I was watching.

Q: How long did you watch?

A: Long enough to see it didn't escalate. Then I went back inside because it wasn't my business.

topic: A witness is questioned about a fire they discovered in a neighboring unit
text:
Q: Let's talk about the evening of March 14th. You were home that night, weren't you?

A: I was.

Q: And at some point you became aware of a fire in unit 4B, correct?

A: That's what I'm here for, isn't it?

Q: I'm asking the questions, ma'am. Did you become aware of a fire in unit 4B?

A: Yes.

Q: What time was that?

A: Around 9:15, 9:20. Somewhere in there.

Q: Which is it? 9:15 or 9:20?

A: I didn't exactly check my watch while the building was burning down, counselor.

Q: So you don't know what time it was.

A: I said around 9:15 to 9:20. That's my answer.

Q: How did you first become aware of the fire?

A: Smoke. Coming through the vents.

Q: You smelled smoke through the vents?

A: That's what I said.

Q: And what did you do when you smelled the smoke?

A: What do you think I did? I went to investigate.

Q: Did you call 911 first?

A: No.

Q: Why not?

A: Because I didn't know there was a fire yet. I smelled smoke. For all I knew someone burned their dinner.

topic: A witness is questioned about a fire they discovered in a neighboring unit
text:
Q: Mr. Okonkwo, you've lived at 2847 Whitmore Lane for how long?

A: Eleven years this coming August.

Q: And in those eleven years, you've come to know your neighbors fairly well, I assume?

A: Some of them. I keep to myself mostly.

Q: But you knew the Delgados in unit 6, didn't you?

A: I knew who they were.

Q: Did you have any disputes with the Delgados?

A: No.

Q: No disagreements at all? In eleven years?

A: We weren't close enough to have disagreements.

Q: Let me ask you this directly, Mr. Okonkwo. Isn't it true that three weeks before this fire, you complained to building management about noise from the Delgado unit?

A: I filed a noise complaint, yes. That's not a dispute. That's using the proper channels.

Q: I see. The proper channels. And when you discovered the fire started in their unit, what was your first thought?

A: My first thought was that I needed to get out of the building.

Q: Nothing else?

A: I'm not sure what you're fishing for here.

Q: I'm not fishing, Mr. Okonkwo. I'm asking what you thought.

A: And I told you. I thought about getting out alive. Is that suspicious to you?

Q: I haven't suggested anything is suspicious.

A: Haven't you?

topic: A witness is questioned about a fire they discovered in a neighboring unit
text:
Q: When you opened your apartment door, what did you observe in the hallway?

A: Heavy smoke. Thick. Gray. Coming from the direction of 4B.

Q: Could you see flames at that point?

A: Not from where I was standing, no.

Q: Did you proceed toward unit 4B?

A: I took a few steps in that direction.

Q: Why?

A: Because Mrs. Patterson lives alone and she's eighty-three years old.

Q: So your concern was for Mrs. Patterson?

A: Of course it was. What else would it be?

Q: I'm simply establishing the facts. Did you reach her door?

A: No. The heat was too intense. I could feel it from maybe fifteen feet away.

Q: At fifteen feet. You're sure about that distance?

A: Give or take.

Q: Give or take how much?

A: I don't know, a few feet? I wasn't measuring.

Q: So it could have been ten feet?

A: It could have been. Sure.

Q: Or twenty?

A: Are you going to ask me about every possible distance, or do you have an actual question?

Q: My question is whether you can reliably estimate how close you got to unit 4B.

A: I got close enough to know I couldn't get closer. That's what I can reliably tell you.

topic: A witness is questioned about a fire they discovered in a neighboring unit
text:
Q: You called 911 at 10:47 p.m., correct?

A: If that's what the records show.

Q: I'm asking what you recall.

A: I recall making the call. I don't recall looking at a clock.

Q: Fair enough. Now, in that call, you told the dispatcher—and I'm reading here—"I think it started in the corner unit." Do you see that?

A: I'll take your word for it.

Q: You don't remember saying that?

A: I remember the call. I don't remember my exact words.

Q: Well, let me ask you this: why did you think the fire started in the corner unit?

A: Because that's where the smoke was coming from.

Q: Did you see the fire start?

A: No.

Q: Did anyone tell you it started there?

A: No.

Q: So this was just an assumption on your part?

A: It was an observation. Smoke was pouring out from under their door. Not my door. Not anyone else's door. Their door.

Q: But you didn't actually witness the origin of the fire?

A: Asked and answered.

Q: Excuse me?

A: I said no already. Twice. Do you need me to say it a third time, or can we move on?

topic: A witness is questioned about a fire they discovered in a neighboring unit
text:
Q: Describe what you did after you exited the building.

A: I went to the parking lot across the street and waited.

Q: Did you speak with anyone?

A: A few people. Other residents.

Q: Do you recall who?

A: Tom from 2A. Maria something, I don't know her last name. A couple others.

Q: What did you discuss?

A: What do you think we discussed? The building was on fire.

Q: I'm asking specifically what was said.

A: I don't have a transcript. People were scared. People were talking.

Q: Did anyone mention how the fire might have started?

A: There was speculation.

Q: What kind of speculation?

A: The usual kind. Someone said electrical. Someone else said a candle.

Q: Did you offer any theories?

A: No.

Q: You had no opinion at all about how the fire started?

A: I had plenty of opinions. I kept them to myself because I don't know what happened. Unlike some people, I don't pretend to have answers I don't have.

Q: I'm not suggesting you should pretend anything, Mr. Reeves.

A: Good. Then we understand each other.

Q: Did anyone mention the tenant in 4B by name?

A: Probably. I don't remember specifically.

Q: You don't remember, or you'd rather not say?

A: I said I don't remember. If you're going to call me a liar, counselor, just do it directly.

topic: A witness is questioned about a conversation they overheard in a company hallway
text:
Q: Ms. Fernandez, I'd like to direct your attention to March 14th of this year. Were you present at the Kendrick Technologies office that day?

A: I was.

Q: And at approximately 2:30 in the afternoon, where were you located within the building?

A: I was in the hallway. Third floor. Near the copy room.

Q: What were you doing there?

A: Waiting for a print job. The machine was slow that day. It's always slow, but that day especially.

Q: While you were waiting, did you observe anyone else in that hallway?

A: Mr. Trent and Ms. Okonkwo came out of the conference room. They were talking.

Q: Did you hear what they were saying?

A: Some of it. I wasn't trying to listen. But they weren't exactly whispering.

Q: Tell me what you heard.

A: Mr. Trent said something about the quarterly numbers. That they needed to "adjust the timeline" before the board meeting.

Q: Those were his exact words? "Adjust the timeline"?

A: Yes. I remember because I thought it was a strange way to put it.

Q: What did Ms. Okonkwo say in response?

A: She asked if that was really necessary. And he said—look, I've gone over this before. He said it was either that or they'd have to explain the discrepancy.

Q: You've gone over this before with whom?

A: With your colleagues. With the internal investigators. With my own supervisor. I've told this same story probably five or six times now.

Q: I understand. But I need to hear it directly.

A: I know. I know you do. He said they'd have to explain the discrepancy. That's what I heard.

topic: A witness is questioned about a conversation they overheard in a company hallway
text:
Q: Mr. Huang, you were employed as a facilities coordinator at Bellmer & Associates in October of last year, correct?

A: That's correct.

Q: On October 9th, did you have occasion to be on the fourth floor of the main office building?

A: I did. There was an issue with one of the thermostats. Someone had complained.

Q: What time was this?

A: Late afternoon. Maybe 4:00, 4:15.

Q: And while you were addressing this thermostat issue, did you hear a conversation taking place nearby?

A: There were two people talking in the hallway. I was inside the supply closet working on the panel.

Q: Could you identify the voices?

A: One was definitely Mr. Sorrell. I've worked there long enough to know his voice.

Q: And the other?

A: A woman. I didn't see her face. I couldn't say for certain who it was.

Q: Fair enough. What did you hear Mr. Sorrell say?

A: He was talking about a contract. Something about making sure the dates lined up with what they'd submitted.

Q: "Making sure the dates lined up." Is that a direct quote?

A: I think so. Or close to it. Does it matter at this point?

Q: I'm just trying to establish—

A: No, I understand. You're trying to establish what I heard. I heard him say something about dates lining up. Whether those were his precise words, syllable for syllable, I can't swear to.

Q: Did the woman respond?

A: She said okay. Just "okay." That was it.

Q: Did they say anything else?

A: If they did, I didn't hear it. The panel was giving me trouble and I was focused on that.

Q: Let's move on.

A: Fine by me.

topic: A witness is questioned about a conversation they overheard in a company hallway
text:
Q: Ms. Trotter, how long have you worked for Meridian Consulting?

A: Seven years this past June.

Q: In your role as executive assistant, you have regular access to the sixth floor, is that right?

A: That's right.

Q: I want to ask you about an incident that allegedly occurred on January 22nd. Does that date mean anything to you?

A: You're going to have to be more specific.

Q: Were you present on the sixth floor that day?

A: Probably. I'm there most days.

Q: Do you recall overhearing a conversation between Mr. Ashworth and another individual in the hallway outside his office?

A: I recall being asked about this already, yes.

Q: And what's your recollection of the conversation itself?

A: I heard voices. Mr. Ashworth and someone else. I wasn't paying close attention.

Q: You weren't paying close attention.

A: No. I had my own work to do.

Q: But you heard something.

A: I heard Mr. Ashworth say that the inspection report needed to be "handled carefully." That's what I remember.

Q: "Handled carefully."

A: Yes.

Q: Did he elaborate on what he meant by that?

A: Not that I heard.

Q: Who was he speaking with?

A: I believe it was Mr. Decker, but I didn't see them. I was at my desk around the corner.

Q: Did you hear Mr. Decker respond?

A: He might have. I don't remember what he said, if anything.

Q: Ms. Trotter, I'm going to ask you to think carefully here—

A: I have thought carefully. I've had months to think about it. I heard what I heard. I didn't hear what I didn't hear. I'm not going to invent something just because you keep asking the same question in different ways.

Q: I'm not asking you to invent anything.

A: Then we're finished with this part, aren't we?

topic: A witness is questioned about a conversation they overheard in a company hallway
text:
Q: Let's talk about what you observed on August 3rd. You were in the building that day?

A: Yes.

Q: What brought you to the second floor?

A: I was returning a stapler to Accounting. Janet Liu had lent it to me.

Q: A stapler.

A: A stapler. I know it sounds trivial. That's what it was.

Q: I'm not suggesting otherwise. What happened when you got to the second floor?

A: I walked past the break room and heard Mr. Garrison talking to someone. The door was open partway.

Q: Did you see who he was talking to?

A: I saw the back of someone's head. Short hair, gray jacket. I didn't recognize them.

Q: What were they discussing?

A: Mr. Garrison was saying something about the client files. That they needed to pull certain records before anyone came looking.

Q: Before anyone came looking. Those were his words?

A: That's what I heard.

Q: What did you take that to mean?

A: I didn't take it to mean anything. I dropped off the stapler and went back to my desk.

Q: You didn't find it unusual?

A: Counselor, I've been doing this job for twelve years. People say all kinds of things. I don't make it my business to interpret everything I overhear.

Q: But you remembered it.

A: I remembered it because you're asking me about it now. And because other people asked me about it before you.

Q: Did you report what you heard to anyone at the time?

A: No.

Q: Why not?

A: Because I didn't think it was my place. And honestly, I still don't. But here we are anyway.

topic: A witness is questioned about a conversation they overheard in a company hallway
text:
Q: Mr. Padilla, you've stated that you were walking through the east corridor at approximately 11:00 a.m. on the morning in question.

A: That's correct.

Q: And you heard voices coming from somewhere nearby?

A: From the alcove near the stairwell. There's a little nook there where people sometimes take phone calls.

Q: How many voices?

A: Two. Both male.

Q: Did you recognize either of them?

A: I recognized Mr. Whitmore. The other one I wasn't sure about at the time.

Q: But you've since learned who it was?

A: People have told me it was probably Mr. Choi. I never confirmed it myself.

Q: What did you hear them saying?

A: Mr. Whitmore was talking about a shipment. He said something like, "We can backdate the invoice and no one's going to check."

Q: "No one's going to check."

A: That's what he said.

Q: And the other man—Mr. Choi, allegedly—what did he say?

A: I don't remember exactly. Something like "if you say so" or "if that's what you want." Something noncommittal.

Q: Did you stop walking when you heard this?

A: No. I kept going. I had a meeting.

Q: So you didn't hear the rest of the conversation.

A: No.

Q: Do you wish you had stopped?

A: Counselor, I've asked myself that question a hundred times already. I don't have a good answer for you. I didn't stop. I kept walking. That's what happened.

Q: I understand.

A: Do you? Because I'm not sure anyone really does at this point. It was just a hallway. I was just passing through.

topic: A witness is questioned about a conversation they overheard in a company hallway
text:
Q: Please state your name for the record.

A: David Chen. And I have to say, I've been waiting to talk about this because I think it's really important that someone finally hears what actually happened.

Q: Mr. Chen, I'm going to direct your attention to March 15th of this year. Were you present at Meridian Technologies' corporate office that day?

A: Absolutely. I was there all day, actually. I remember it perfectly because it was the day everything changed—the day I heard what Mr. Thornton and Ms. Reeves were really planning behind closed doors. Well, not behind closed doors, which was their mistake.

Q: Let's slow down. Where exactly were you when you overheard this conversation?

A: Third floor, east hallway, right by the water cooler station. There's this little alcove there—you probably haven't seen it, but it's got a bench and some plants—and I was sitting there eating my lunch because the break room was too crowded. I eat there a lot, actually. It's quieter. And from that spot, you can hear everything that happens near the corner office suite.

Q: And what time was this?

A: 12:47 PM. I know because I had just checked my phone to see if my wife had texted me back about dinner plans—she hadn't—and then I heard the voices approaching. I looked right at the time stamp when they started talking because something in Mr. Thornton's voice made me think I should pay attention.

Q: What did you hear?

A: Oh, this is the part that matters. Mr. Thornton said—and these are his exact words, I wrote them down afterward—he said, "We need to move the Hendricks account offshore before the audit committee starts asking questions." And Ms. Reeves, she laughed, and she said, "Finally, someone with a spine around here."

Q: You wrote this down afterward?

A: Immediately! I went right back to my desk and typed it into a Word document. I even emailed it to myself so it would have a timestamp. I still have it. I can get you a copy. I've been keeping meticulous records ever since because I knew—I just knew—this was going to come out eventually.

Q: Did either Mr. Thornton or Ms. Reeves see you?

A: No, no, they had no idea. The plants in the alcove, they're these big ferns, and they completely block the view. I've tested it. I went back the next day and had my coworker stand where they were standing and he couldn't see me at all. So I know for certain they thought they were alone.

Q: Did you report what you heard to anyone at the company?

A: I reported it to HR on March 18th. And to my direct supervisor. And I called the ethics hotline. I have records of all of those too. Nobody did anything, which is exactly why we're sitting here today, isn't it?

Q: What was the response from HR?

A: Janet Miller—she's the HR director—she told me she would "look into it." That was it. Four words. I followed up three times over the next two weeks. I have the emails. Want to know what she finally said? She said the matter had been "addressed internally" and that I should "focus on my own responsibilities." Can you believe that? This is exactly the kind of cover-up I was worried about from the start.

topic: A witness is questioned about a conversation they overheard in a company hallway
text:
Q: Ms. Patterson, you've testified you were in the fourth-floor hallway on October 3rd.

A: Yes.

Q: Excellent. Now, this is where it gets interesting. Can you describe the layout of that hallway for us?

A: It's a long hallway. Offices on both sides. Carpet.

Q: Carpet, right, right. And the acoustics in that hallway—would you say sounds carry? Would you say voices travel in a way that someone might overhear things they weren't meant to hear?

A: I suppose.

Q: You suppose! But you did hear something, didn't you? You heard a conversation that I think is going to be very illuminating for this case.

A: I heard two people talking.

Q: Two people talking—and not just any two people. This was Marcus Webb, the CFO, and Diana Corso, the head of procurement, correct?

A: I believe so.

Q: You believe so, or you know so? Because Ms. Patterson, what you heard could be absolutely critical. This could be the key to everything.

A: It sounded like them.

Q: It sounded like them. Their voices. Voices you'd recognize because you'd worked with both of them for how long?

A: Three years.

Q: Three years! So you knew their voices well. Very well. And what were these voices saying on that October afternoon? What did Marcus Webb say to Diana Corso?

A: He said something about vendor contracts.

Q: Something about vendor contracts—can you be more specific? This is important. Really important.

A: He mentioned Triton Industries.

Q: Triton Industries! The same company that received $2.3 million in contracts over the following quarter. What exactly did he say about Triton Industries?

A: I don't remember exactly.

Q: You don't remember exactly—but you remember some of it, surely. The gist, the substance, the thrust of it?

A: He said they should make sure Triton got the Westfield bid.

Q: "Make sure Triton got the bid." Those were his words?

A: Something like that.

topic: A witness is questioned about a conversation they overheard in a company hallway
text:
Q: State your full name.

A: Robert James Mulligan.

Q: Mr. Mulligan, on June 22nd, you were employed as a security guard at Vance & Associates?

A: That's right.

Q: Where were you stationed that day?

A: Front desk, main lobby. Same as always.

Q: Did there come a time when you left the front desk?

A: Yeah, around 2 PM. Had to do my rounds.

Q: Describe your rounds, please.

A: Walk each floor, check the stairwells, make sure nothing's out of place. Takes about forty minutes.

Q: During these rounds on June 22nd, did you observe anything unusual?

A: I heard people arguing. Second floor.

Q: Who was arguing?

A: Two men. I didn't see their faces at first.

Q: What did you hear?

A: One guy said, "This is fraud, plain and simple." Real loud.

Q: Did you recognize the voice?

A: Not right away. But then the other one said, "Keep your voice down, Steven." So I knew it was Steven Hartley. He's the operations manager.

Q: And the other man?

A: I came around the corner and saw it was Mr. Vance himself. The owner.

Q: What happened when you came around the corner?

A: They stopped talking. Mr. Vance looked at me and just nodded, like nothing was wrong. Then they walked off in different directions.

Q: Did you hear anything else before they saw you?

A: Mr. Hartley said something like, "The inspectors are going to find out." That's when I came around the corner.

Q: Did you report this to anyone?

A: I told my supervisor at the end of my shift.

topic: A witness is questioned about a conversation they overheard in a company hallway
text:
Q: How long have you worked at Brennan Medical Supply?

A: It's been—oh gosh—eleven years this past April. I started in the mail room, if you can believe it, and worked my way up to executive assistant. Eleven years of my life in that building.

Q: On January 9th, where were you at approximately 3 PM?

A: Third floor. I was coming back from delivering some documents to Legal, and I had to pass by the conference room corridor. That's the one with the glass walls, you know, though there are blinds. The blinds were closed that day, but the door was open just a crack.

Q: Did you hear anything as you passed?

A: Did I ever. I wasn't trying to eavesdrop—I want that on the record—but voices carry in that hallway. It's the ventilation system or something. Everyone knows about it.

Q: What did you hear?

A: I heard Dr. Preston—he's our medical director—telling someone that the testing data had been "adjusted for presentation purposes." Those exact words. "Adjusted for presentation purposes." I stopped walking because I couldn't believe what I was hearing.

Q: Did you hear who he was speaking to?

A: I did! Because she responded. It was Karen Wells from regulatory affairs. She said—and I remember this because it horrified me—she said, "The FDA doesn't need to see the preliminary numbers."

Q: What did you do?

A: I stood there for a moment, frozen honestly. My heart was pounding. Then Dr. Preston said something I couldn't quite make out, and I heard footsteps coming toward the door, so I hurried away. I didn't want them to know I'd heard.

Q: Did you tell anyone about this conversation?

A: I told my husband that night. I was so upset I could barely eat dinner. I told him everything, exactly what I heard, and he said I should write it all down while it was fresh.

Q: Did you write it down?

A: I did. In my journal. I can show you the entry—it's dated January 9th, and I described the whole thing. I even drew a little diagram of where I was standing relative to the door because I thought it might matter someday. I guess I was right about that.

Q: Did you report this to anyone at the company?

A: I wanted to, I really did, but I was scared. Dr. Preston has a lot of power at Brennan. But I did eventually contact the compliance hotline—anonymously—about three weeks later.

topic: A witness is questioned about a conversation they overheard in a company hallway
text:
Q: You've indicated you were in the west wing hallway on September 8th.

A: That is correct.

Q: What time?

A: Late afternoon. Perhaps 4:30.

Q: What brought you to that hallway?

A: I had a meeting in Conference Room W-7. I was early.

Q: What, if anything, did you observe?

A: I saw two individuals speaking near the elevator bank.

Q: Did you recognize these individuals?

A: Yes. Lawrence Chen, the regional director, and a woman I later learned was Patricia Simmons from accounting.

Q: You say you "later learned"—you didn't know her at the time?

A: Correct. I asked a colleague afterward.

Q: Why did you ask?

A: The conversation seemed significant.

Q: Let's talk about that! What made it seem significant? What caught your attention?

A: Their body language, initially. Mr. Chen was leaning in close and speaking quietly.

Q: And you could hear them despite the quiet speaking?

A: The hallway was empty. I was perhaps fifteen feet away.

Q: Fifteen feet—that's close enough to hear. What exactly did you hear that was so significant?

A: Mr. Chen said something about "moving the numbers before the quarterly close."

Q: Moving the numbers! And what else? What did Ms. Simmons say?

A: She seemed uncomfortable. She said, "Larry, I don't think I can do that."

Q: She resisted—but then what? Did he push her?

A: He said, "You've done it before."

Q: "You've done it before"—implying this was an ongoing practice?

A: That was my interpretation.

Q: Your interpretation, yes, but based on his words. Did you hear anything else? Anything that might tell us more about the scope of this?

A: Ms. Simmons saw me. She stopped talking and walked away quickly.

Q: She walked away quickly—perhaps because she knew what they were discussing was improper?

A: Objection, calls for speculation.

Q: Withdrawn. What did Mr. Chen do after Ms. Simmons walked away?

A: He looked at me, then took the elevator.

Q: Did he say anything to you?

A: No.

Q: Did his expression tell you anything? Did he seem concerned that you might have overheard?

A: I couldn't say.

topic: A building inspector is deposed about a structural assessment they signed off on
text:
Q: Mr. Harmon, you conducted the structural assessment of the Meridian Tower parking garage on June 14th, 2022, correct?

A: I conducted an assessment on that date, yes.

Q: And you signed off on that assessment, indicating the structure was sound?

A: I signed the report, yes. The report reflected my findings at that time based on what was observable.

Q: What was observable. Let's talk about that. Did you observe the support columns on level B2?

A: I— yes. I observed the columns.

Q: All of them?

A: I conducted a visual inspection of the columns that were accessible.

Q: How many columns are on level B2, Mr. Harmon?

A: I'd have to look at the drawings to give you an exact number. I don't want to misspeak.

Q: Approximately?

A: I believe— I think there are fourteen. Fourteen or fifteen.

Q: And how many did you actually inspect?

A: The ones that were accessible. As I said.

Q: How many, Mr. Harmon?

A: I don't recall the specific number. Several were obstructed by vehicles. There was equipment stored— look, this was a standard inspection. I followed protocol.

Q: I'm just asking how many you inspected.

A: I don't have that number in front of me.

Q: Would it surprise you to learn that the collapse originated at column B2-7, one of the columns you may or may not have inspected?

A: I'm not— I can't speculate on what may or may not surprise me. I conducted the inspection according to standard procedures.

---

topic: A building inspector is deposed about a structural assessment they signed off on
text:
Q: Ms. Castellano, I want to be very clear about what happened on September 3rd. You arrived at the Wexford Commons site at what time?

A: Approximately 8:30 a.m.

Q: And you were there how long?

A: Maybe two hours. Two and a half.

Q: Two hours to inspect a six-story mixed-use building?

A: That was a follow-up inspection. The initial assessment had already been completed.

Q: By whom?

A: By me. I had been there the previous month.

Q: So this was your second visit. And in two hours, you determined the structure was safe for occupancy?

A: I determined that the issues identified in the initial inspection had been adequately addressed by the contractor.

Q: The cracking in the foundation wall—

A: Had been repaired.

Q: You're certain?

A: The contractor provided documentation. I observed the repair. It appeared— it was consistent with the specifications.

Q: "Appeared consistent." That's interesting phrasing.

A: That's accurate phrasing. I'm not going to sit here and say I have x-ray vision. I saw what I saw.

Q: Did you request any core samples?

A: That's not standard for a follow-up of this nature.

Q: That's not what I asked. Did you request core samples?

A: No.

Q: Did you use any diagnostic equipment at all?

A: I used the equipment appropriate to the scope of the inspection.

Q: Which was?

A: Visual inspection. Measurement tools. The standard equipment.

Q: Ms. Castellano, twelve families lost their homes when that foundation wall gave way.

A: I'm aware of that. I'm very aware of that.

---

topic: A building inspector is deposed about a structural assessment they signed off on
text:
Q: Let's go back to the report. Page four. You see where it says "no significant structural deficiencies observed"?

A: I see that.

Q: You wrote that?

A: That's my language, yes.

Q: Mr. Okonkwo, I need to understand something. Help me understand. You write "no significant structural deficiencies," and yet three months later, an entire balcony detaches from the building. How does that happen?

A: Are you asking me to explain the collapse?

Q: I'm asking you to explain your report.

A: The report reflects what I observed during my inspection. I'm not an engineer. I don't— I perform code compliance inspections.

Q: You're a licensed building inspector.

A: Yes.

Q: With seventeen years of experience.

A: Yes.

Q: And you saw nothing wrong with those balcony connections?

A: I saw the balconies. I noted the visible conditions. If you're asking whether I pulled apart the facade to examine the anchorage system— no. That's not what an inspection entails.

Q: What does an inspection entail, in your view?

A: I've explained this. Visual assessment. Code compliance verification. Documentation review.

Q: Let me ask it differently. What would you have needed to see to flag a deficiency?

A: Visible deterioration. Obvious code violations. Displacement. Cracking. Signs of water damage affecting structural elements.

Q: And you saw none of that?

A: Not— no. Not to the degree that would warrant a deficiency notation.

Q: "Not to the degree." What degree did you see?

A: I don't recall specific— I don't recall.

---

topic: A building inspector is deposed about a structural assessment they signed off on
text:
Q: The timestamp on your report says 2:47 p.m. Do you see that?

A: Yes.

Q: And the building permit office closes at 3:00 p.m., doesn't it?

A: I believe so.

Q: So you completed this inspection and filed the report within— what— thirteen minutes?

A: I don't know how long the filing took.

A: Correct.

Q: How long were you there?

A: An hour. Maybe a little less.

Q: Did you note which areas you couldn't access?

A: I noted what I inspected.

Q: Would have. Did you?

A: I'd have to look at my notes.

A: It varies.

Q: This inspection was eleven months ago.

A: I understand that.

---

topic: A building inspector is deposed about a structural assessment they signed off on
text:
Q: You testified earlier that you were familiar with the building code requirements for seismic reinforcement. Is that right?

A: I testified that I apply the relevant code sections during my inspections.

Q: The Riverside Lofts building—

A: Which building are we discussing now?

Q: Riverside Lofts. The subject of this lawsuit.

A: Fine. Go ahead.

Q: That building was constructed in 1987 and retrofitted in 2019. You inspected the retrofit work?

A: I signed off on the final inspection, yes.

Q: Did you verify that the retrofit met current seismic code requirements?

A: I verified that the work matched the approved engineering plans.

Q: That's not the same thing, is it?

A: I'm not the engineer. I don't design the retrofit. I verify the work was done according to the plans that were approved by the engineering department.

Q: So if the plans were deficient—

A: That's not my determination to make.

Q: —you would have signed off anyway.

A: I would have verified the work matched the approved plans. Which is my job. That's what I do.

Q: Did you personally review the seismic calculations?

A: No.

Q: Did you compare the retrofit specifications to the current code?

A: That's engineering review. That happens before the plans reach me.

Q: You relied entirely on other people's work.

A: I relied on the approved plans, counselor. The plans that went through your client's own engineering department. The same department that's now trying to— never mind.

Q: No, finish your thought, Ms. Park.

A: I've answered your question.

topic: A witness is questioned about a fire they discovered in a neighboring unit
text:
Q: Please state your name for the record.

A: Thomas Bradshaw.

Q: Mr. Bradshaw, you resided at 4412 Willow Creek Drive, Unit B, on the night of March 15th, correct?

A: That's correct.

Q: And Unit A, the unit where the fire originated, shares a wall with your unit?

A: It does. The eastern wall of my living room is adjacent to their kitchen.

Q: Tell me what you observed that evening.

A: I was reading in my living room at approximately 9:47 p.m. when I first noticed the smell. Electrical burning—distinct from wood smoke or cooking. Within two minutes, I observed smoke seeping through the baseboard along that shared wall. I called 911 at 9:49 p.m. exactly. I have the call log if you need it.

Q: That's quite precise timing.

A: I looked at my phone when I made the call. The timestamp is the timestamp.

Q: Did you attempt to alert the occupants of Unit A?

A: I pounded on their front door for approximately thirty seconds before retreating to the parking lot. No response. The smoke was already visible from their front window by that point.

Q: You didn't try to enter?

A: The door was locked, the smoke was thick, and I'm not a firefighter. I made the appropriate decision.

Q: Did you see anyone exit Unit A?

A: No. The unit was unoccupied. I'd seen both residents leave around 6 p.m. Neither vehicle had returned.

Q: How can you be certain of that?

A: Because I park directly behind them, Counselor, and I notice when I can pull straight in versus when I have to angle around their Subaru. The spot was empty all evening.

Q: Fair enough. Did you observe anything unusual about Unit A in the days leading up to the fire?

A: I observed Mr. Hernandez carrying in what appeared to be space heaters on two occasions that week. The older kind, with the orange coils.

---

topic: A witness is questioned about a fire they discovered in a neighboring unit
text:
Q: You discovered the fire at what time, Ms. Patterson?

A: It was... I believe around ten? Maybe a little after?

Q: Can you be more specific?

A: I'm sorry, I didn't check a clock. I was watching the news, and the late broadcast had started, so probably between ten and ten-fifteen.

Q: That's fine. Now, the fire was in Unit 7, and you live in Unit 9. Walk me through exactly what drew your attention.

A: Well, I heard what I thought was a car backfiring. Twice. Then maybe a minute later, I saw this orange flickering through my kitchen window.

Q: You're certain it was flickering, not a steady light?

A: Absolutely. It had that uneven quality—bright, dim, bright again. Like flames. I've seen enough campfires to know what firelight looks like.

Q: What did you do next?

A: I stepped out onto my back patio to get a better look. That's when I saw the smoke coming from the back of Unit 7. Thick, dark smoke. I ran back inside and called 911.

Q: Did you approach Unit 7 at any point?

A: No. I stayed on the line with the dispatcher until the trucks arrived. She told me to stay back.

Q: In your estimation, how large was the fire when you first saw it?

A: When I first saw the glow? I couldn't tell. When I went outside, maybe two or three minutes later, the flames were coming through what looked like a back bedroom window. Maybe four feet high, visible above the windowsill.

Q: Did you see anyone near Unit 7 before, during, or after you noticed the fire?

A: Before, no. During, no. After—once the fire department arrived, I saw Mrs. Chen from Unit 8 standing in the parking lot in her bathrobe. But nobody from Unit 7.

Q: Did you know the occupants of Unit 7?

A: Only to wave at. A younger man, lived alone I think.

---

topic: A witness is questioned about a fire they discovered in a neighboring unit
text:
Q: Mr. Okonkwo, let's talk about what you smelled that night.

A: What I smelled?

Q: Yes. You mentioned in your initial statement to investigators that you noticed an unusual odor.

A: I said I smelled something chemical. Sharper than regular smoke.

Q: Could you describe it further?

A: Like... I don't know how to describe it better. Chemical. Acrid. It wasn't like burning wood or paper.

Q: Have you ever smelled gasoline burning?

A: I'm not going to speculate about what it was.

Q: I'm not asking you to speculate. I'm asking if you've ever smelled gasoline burning.

A: Yes.

Q: At a gas station, a car fire, somewhere else?

A: My brother-in-law restored cars. I've been around burning fuel before.

Q: Did the smell that night resemble burning gasoline?

A: It might have. I can't say for certain.

Q: But it's possible?

A: I said it might have. That's all I can tell you.

Q: Let's move on. You called 911 at 10:23 p.m. according to the records. Does that sound right?

A: If that's what the records say.

Q: Before making that call, did you attempt to investigate the source of the smell yourself?

A: I opened my front door and looked toward Unit 4. I saw smoke. I closed my door and called 911. I didn't investigate anything.

Q: You didn't walk over to Unit 4?

A: No.

Q: You didn't knock on the door?

A: I just answered that.

Q: Why not?

A: Because there was smoke pouring from under their door, Counselor, and I'm not in the business of opening doors to active fires.

---

topic: A witness is questioned about a fire they discovered in a neighboring unit
text:
Q: Mrs. Yamamoto, good morning. I want to take you through the sequence of events carefully. You've done this before in your written statement, so this should be familiar territory. Ready?

A: Yes.

Q: Excellent. What were you doing at approximately 8:30 p.m. on the evening of January 12th?

A: I was preparing dinner. Cutting vegetables at my kitchen counter.

Q: And your kitchen faces which direction?

A: East. Toward the neighboring unit.

Q: Unit 14, where the fire occurred?

A: That's right.

Q: From your kitchen, can you see into Unit 14?

A: Parts of it. Their living room window is visible from my kitchen window.

Q: And on that night, did you happen to look out your kitchen window?

A: I did. Several times while I was cooking.

Q: What did you see during those times?

A: Early on, nothing unusual. Lights on in their living room. The TV flickering—I could see the blue glow.

Q: What time did things change?

A: Around 8:45. I looked over and the lights seemed brighter. Then I realized it wasn't the overhead light, it was something else. Something lower, near the floor maybe.

Q: Did you immediately recognize it as fire?

A: No. I thought maybe they had a fireplace going. It wasn't until I saw the smoke about five minutes later that I understood.

Q: When you saw the smoke, what did you do?

A: I turned off my stove, grabbed my phone, and went outside. I called 911 from my front porch.

Q: Did you attempt to warn the occupants of Unit 14?

A: I shouted toward their door. I didn't go close because I could already see flames through the window by then.

Q: Did anyone respond to your shouting?

A: No. No one came out.

---

topic: A witness is questioned about a fire they discovered in a neighboring unit
text:
Q: State your full name.

A: Derek Alan Whitfield.

Q: Mr. Whitfield, how long have you lived at the Cedarbrook Townhomes?

A: Eleven years this past April.

Q: So you're familiar with the property, the layout, the other residents?

A: Very. I've served on the HOA board for six of those years.

Q: On the night of the fire, August 8th, where were you?

A: In my unit, 22C, watching the Olympics. Swimming finals.

Q: When did you first become aware something was wrong?

A: When I heard glass shatter. Loud. Close.

Q: What time was this?

A: 11:15, give or take two minutes. The women's 200 medley had just ended.

Q: What did you do when you heard the glass?

A: Muted the television. Listened. Then I heard what sounded like a whooshing noise—hard to describe. Like a strong wind, but contained. I went to my back door and opened it.

Q: What did you see?

A: Unit 22B, directly adjacent to mine, had flames coming out of the back bedroom window. The window was broken out. Fire was climbing the exterior wall.

Q: How high were the flames?

A: Reaching the roofline already. Moving fast.

Q: What was your immediate reaction?

A: I grabbed my phone, dialed 911, and began pounding on doors down the row. Units 22A, 22D, 22E. Got everyone out into the parking lot.

Q: Did you attempt to enter 22B?

A: Their back door was already warped from the heat. Even if I'd wanted to, it wasn't opening. And I could feel the heat from six feet away.

Q: You mentioned the fire was moving fast. In your eleven years there, have you ever seen a fire spread that quickly?

A: I've never seen a fire there at all. But no, I've never seen any fire behave like that. It was unnatural.

Q: Unnatural in what way?

A: It spread too fast for an accident. That's my observation. Draw your own conclusions.

topic: A neighbor is questioned about noise complaints and a confrontation they witnessed
text:
Q: State your name for the record.

A: Patricia Wellman. 4217 Crescent Drive. I've lived there for nineteen years, since before the subdivision was even finished.

Q: Ms. Wellman, you submitted a noise complaint to the HOA on March 14th of this year?

A: I submitted seven complaints between January and April. March 14th was the third one. I have copies of all of them if you need them.

Q: Let's focus on March 14th. What did you hear that night?

A: Music. Bass-heavy, the kind that vibrates through the walls. It started at 11:47 PM. I know because I looked at my phone when it woke me up.

Q: And how long did this continue?

A: Until 2:23 AM. Two hours and thirty-six minutes.

Q: Did you attempt to address this directly with the defendant before filing the complaint?

A: I walked over there at 12:15. Knocked on the door. Rang the bell twice. Nobody answered, even though I could see people moving around through the front window.

Q: You could see inside the house?

A: The blinds were open. The living room was lit up. There were at least eight people in there that I could count.

Q: Did you call the police?

A: I called the non-emergency line at 12:40. They said they'd send someone. An officer arrived at 1:15, stayed maybe ten minutes, and left. The music got quieter for about twenty minutes, then went right back up.

Q: How would you characterize the volume when it resumed?

A: Identical. Maybe louder. I measured it at 58 decibels from inside my bedroom with a sound meter app.

Q: You measured it?

A: I've been measuring it since February. I have a log.

Q: Ms. Wellman, isn't it possible you're being overly sensitive to normal neighborhood sounds?

A: Normal neighborhood sounds don't register at 58 decibels through two walls at one in the morning. I know what normal sounds like. I lived next to the Hendersons for fourteen years before they sold. Never had a single issue.

topic: A neighbor is questioned about noise complaints and a confrontation they witnessed
text:
Q: Mr. Okonkwo, you were present during the confrontation on April 2nd?

A: Yes.

Q: Tell me what you observed.

A: She said something to the younger guy. I couldn't hear what.

A: I saw Mr. Reeves step forward. Point his finger. The other guy knocked his hand away.

Q: He knocked his hand away. Describe that motion.

A: A slap. Quick. Knocked the arm to the side.

Q: Did Mr. Reeves react?

A: He stepped back. Said something I couldn't hear. Then he walked back toward his house.

Q: Did the defendant pursue him?

A: No.

Q: Did you observe any injuries to either party?

A: No.

Q: Did you speak to Mr. Reeves afterward?

A: I asked if he was alright. He said he was fine. That was it.

topic: A neighbor is questioned about noise complaints and a confrontation they witnessed
text:
Q: How long have you lived on Maple Court?

A: Three years in September.

Q: And you know both parties involved in this dispute?

A: I know Mrs. Brennan pretty well. We walk our dogs together sometimes. The Chows I've only spoken to a few times.

Q: Let's talk about what you witnessed on the evening of May 19th.

A: Okay.

A: On my back deck. Grilling.

A: I heard Mrs. Brennan yelling. Not words at first, just—her voice was raised.

Q: Were they both yelling?

Q: What was Mrs. Brennan saying?

Q: Was there music playing at that time?

A: There was music coming from the Chow house, yes. Not crazy loud though.

Q: When you say "not crazy loud"—

A: I mean I could hear it from my deck, but I could also hear Mrs. Brennan clearly from the same distance. So it wasn't drowning her out.

Q: Did you form an opinion about whether the music was unreasonably loud?

topic: A neighbor is questioned about noise complaints and a confrontation they witnessed
text:
Q: You've known Dale Reeves for how long?

A: I don't know Dale Reeves. I know who he is. I've seen him around.

Q: Fair enough. You've seen him around the neighborhood?

A: Yes.

Q: Would you describe him as a confrontational person?

topic: A neighbor is questioned about noise complaints and a confrontation they witnessed
text:
Q: Ms. Vance, I want to be very precise about the timeline here. You stated you heard raised voices at approximately 9 PM.

A: Between nine and nine-fifteen. I wasn't looking at a clock.

Q: But you're certain it was after nine?

A: The news had just started. I watch the nine o'clock news. So yes, after nine.

Q: And the raised voices—whose voices were they?

A: Two men. I assumed it was Mr. Harding and whoever lives in 4B. Turns out I was right.

Q: How did you confirm that?

A: I opened my door and looked. Mr. Harding was standing in the hallway outside 4B.

Q: Was the door to 4B open or closed?

A: Open. The other man was standing in the doorway.

A: Mr. Harding was telling him to keep it down. That there'd been complaints. That it was every weekend and people were fed up.

A: He told Mr. Harding it was none of his business. Asked who appointed him building manager.

Q: Did Mr. Harding respond to that?

A: He said everyone in the building had the same right to quiet enjoyment. Those were his exact words—quiet enjoyment. I remember because I thought it sounded like something from a lease.

Q: Did you observe any physical contact?

A: No.

Q: Did either man raise a hand toward the other?

A: No.

Q: Did either man step toward the other aggressively?

Q: How did the confrontation end?

Q: Did you speak to Mr. Harding afterward?

A: I said "good luck with that." He just shook his head. That was all.

topic: A pharmacist is deposed about a prescription that was filled with the wrong dosage
text:
Q: Please state your name and occupation for the record.

A: Dr. Raymond Chen. I've been a licensed pharmacist for twenty-three years, the last fourteen of which I've spent as pharmacy director at Westbrook Medical Center. I also serve on the State Board of Pharmacy's disciplinary committee and have published extensively on medication error prevention protocols.

Q: I only asked for your name and occupation, Dr. Chen.

A: I understood the question. I'm providing context so the record reflects who is offering testimony today.

Q: Let's discuss the prescription at issue. On March 14th, a prescription for metoprolol was filled at your pharmacy, correct?

A: A prescription was filled, yes. Whether it was filled incorrectly is precisely what we're here to examine, and I'd note that our pharmacy has a verification system I personally designed that has reduced dispensing errors by sixty-two percent since implementation.

Q: The prescription called for 25 milligrams. The patient received 100 milligrams. Do you dispute that?

A: I dispute the characterization that this was a simple error. The prescriber's handwriting was evaluated by three separate pharmacists using our protocol. I can walk you through each step if you'd like.

Q: A yes or no will suffice. Did the patient receive 100 milligrams instead of 25?

A: The patient received what our trained professionals reasonably interpreted from an ambiguous prescription. If you want a yes or no, you'll need to ask a question that permits one.

Q: Who filled this prescription?

A: One of my staff pharmacists. But every prescription passes through my verification system, and I stand behind the process we followed.

Q: What is the pharmacist's name?

A: Linda Marsh. Fifteen years of experience, impeccable record. She followed every protocol I've established.

Q: Did you personally review this prescription before it was dispensed?

A: I was not on duty that day. However, my system was. And my system works.

Q: Your system dispensed the wrong dosage, Dr. Chen.

A: Your characterization, not mine. My system flagged the prescription for secondary review. It received that review. The protocols functioned as I designed them. What failed was the prescribing physician's penmanship—but I don't suppose he's being deposed today.

topic: A pharmacist is deposed about a prescription that was filled with the wrong dosage
text:
Q: Ms. Holloway, you were working the afternoon of June 8th?

A: Yes.

Q: Walk me through exactly what happened when Mr. Tennant's prescription came in.

A: It came in electronically around 2:15. I pulled it up, verified the patient information, checked for interactions against his profile, and proceeded to fill it.

Q: The prescription was for lisinopril, 10 milligrams?

A: That's what appeared in our system, yes.

Q: But you dispensed 40 milligrams.

A: I dispensed what the electronic record showed. I want to be very clear about that—I did not misread anything. If there was a discrepancy, it originated before the prescription reached my screen.

Q: You're suggesting the electronic system was wrong?

A: I'm stating that I filled precisely what was in front of me. I've been doing this for nine years without a single verified dispensing error. Not one. I check and double-check because that's who I am as a pharmacist.

Q: The prescribing physician's records show he ordered 10 milligrams.

A: Then I'd suggest examining what happened between his office and our system. Because I filled 40 milligrams only if the system told me 40 milligrams. I don't invent dosages.

Q: Is it possible you saw 10 and pulled the wrong bottle?

A: No.

Q: You sound very certain.

A: I am certain. I've built my entire career on precision. Ask anyone I work with—I'm the one who catches other people's mistakes.

Q: Yet a patient received four times his prescribed dose.

A: A patient received exactly what our system instructed me to dispense. I did my job correctly. Whatever went wrong, it wasn't in my hands.

Q: Do you feel any responsibility for what happened to Mr. Tennant?

A: I feel terrible that he was harmed. But responsibility? That belongs wherever the error originated. And it did not originate with me.

topic: A pharmacist is deposed about a prescription that was filled with the wrong dosage
text:
Q: Mr. Patterson, I want to acknowledge your pharmacy's strong safety record before we proceed.

A: Thank you. We've worked hard to build that. Twelve years without a reportable incident until this.

Q: That's exactly why I find this situation so puzzling. Help me understand how this happened.

A: I wish I could. Honestly. I've gone over it a hundred times.

Q: Your system has redundancies specifically designed to catch dosage errors?

A: Triple verification. Patient profile check, pharmacist review, and final count confirmation. I implemented it myself based on best practices from Johns Hopkins.

Q: And somehow a 500-microgram Digoxin prescription was filled as 500 milligrams?

A: A thousandfold error. It shouldn't be possible. It goes against everything I've built there.

Q: Yet it happened.

A: It happened. And it happened on my watch. Under a system I created and trusted absolutely.

Q: Who was the dispensing pharmacist?

A: I was.

Q: You personally filled this prescription?

A: I did. And I have to sit here and tell you I don't remember making any error. I've replayed it in my mind constantly. I followed my own protocols. But somewhere, somehow, I must have—

Q: Take your time.

A: I've trained dozens of pharmacists. I've lectured on error prevention. I genuinely believed my system was the best in the region. And now I have to reconcile that with a patient who coded in her kitchen.

Q: Has this changed how you approach your work?

A: It's made me question everything I thought I knew. Which I suppose was necessary. Because apparently what I knew wasn't enough.

topic: A pharmacist is deposed about a prescription that was filled with the wrong dosage
text:
Q: You conducted the internal review after this incident, correct?

A: I led the review team, yes.

Q: Tell me what you found, and please—I want details. This is clearly an area where you have significant expertise.

A: We traced the error to a point-of-entry mistake. The technician who received the verbal order transposed the numbers. The prescription called for 0.125 milligrams, but it was entered as 1.25 milligrams.

Q: A tenfold error.

A: Exactly. And I have to say, our team's analysis was thorough. We mapped every touchpoint, interviewed every staff member, reviewed the audio recording of the verbal order.

Q: There was an audio recording?

A: We implemented that system two years ago. I advocated for it specifically because verbal orders are high-risk. Having that recording allowed us to pinpoint exactly where the breakdown occurred.

Q: Impressive foresight.

A: Patient safety requires anticipating failure modes before they materialize. That's always been my philosophy.

Q: So the technician made the error. But shouldn't your pharmacist have caught it?

A: She should have, yes. The dosage was outside normal parameters for the patient's age and weight. Our system flagged it, but she overrode the alert.

Q: Why would she do that?

A: Override fatigue. Too many alerts that don't require action, so staff become desensitized. It's an industry-wide problem I've written about extensively. We're currently piloting a smarter alert system of my design.

Q: After the horse left the barn.

A: I'd characterize it as continuous improvement informed by outcome data. But I understand your point.

Q: A child was hospitalized, Mr. Weiss.

A: I'm aware. And my team's analysis will prevent it from happening again. That's what rigorous review processes achieve.

topic: A pharmacist is deposed about a prescription that was filled with the wrong dosage
text:
Q: How long did you say you've worked in this pharmacy?

A: Fourteen months.

Q: That's not very long.

A: Long enough to know my job. I graduated top of my class from State, completed a residency at University Hospital, and passed my boards on the first attempt. I know what I'm doing.

Q: Then explain to me how Mrs. Delacroix received Warfarin 10 milligrams when her prescription clearly stated 1 milligram.

A: The prescription didn't clearly state anything. Have you seen the original? The physician's one looked like a zero. Anyone would have read it as ten.

Q: Anyone? Your colleague testified she would have called to verify.

A: My colleague has the luxury of hindsight. In the moment, with the volume we were handling, the notation appeared unambiguous.

Q: Volume. You were rushed?

A: I was efficient. There's a difference.

Q: A patient nearly bled to death. Was that efficient?

A: That's not a fair characterization of—

Q: Answer the question, please.

A: I made a judgment call based on the information in front of me. The handwriting was poor. I interpreted it reasonably. Other pharmacists in this region deal with the same prescribers and the same illegible scripts daily.

Q: But they didn't send Mrs. Delacroix to the emergency room.

A: And I've filled thousands of prescriptions without incident. Thousands. One ambiguous script from a physician who should have been using electronic prescribing, and suddenly my entire competence is being questioned.

Q: I'm not questioning your competence generally—

A: Yes you are. And I'm telling you, I did what any capable pharmacist would have done with that prescription. The error began with the prescriber. I simply didn't catch it. That's not the same as causing it.

Q: Did you consider calling to verify?

A: I considered it. The office was closed. The patient needed her medication. I made a decision. It was the wrong one. But it wasn't a reckless one.

topic: A witness is questioned about events at a party where an assault allegedly occurred
text:
Q: Ms. Thornton, you were present at the residence on Maple Drive on the night of September 14th, correct?

A: Yes.

Q: And approximately how many people were at this gathering?

A: I don't know. Thirty, maybe. Forty. It's hard to say.

Q: You didn't count?

A: No. I didn't count.

Q: Fair enough. Now, at some point during the evening, did you observe an altercation between two individuals?

A: I saw something, yes.

Q: Can you describe what you saw?

A: Two men arguing. It got physical. That's what I saw.

Q: Which two men?

A: I only knew one of them. Derek. The other one I'd never seen before.

Q: Derek Mullins, the defendant?

A: If that's his last name, then yes.

Q: You don't know his last name?

A: I knew him as Derek. We weren't close. I'd seen him at a few things. That's the extent of it.

Q: Alright. When you say it "got physical," what do you mean by that?

A: I mean what everyone means. Pushing. Then a punch. I don't know what else you want me to say about it.

Q: I want you to say what you observed.

A: I just did.

Q: Did you see who threw the first punch?

A: No. I looked over when I heard shouting, and by then they were already—it was already happening. I didn't see how it started. I've said this before.

---

topic: A witness is questioned about events at a party where an assault allegedly occurred
text:
Q: Mr. Reeves, let's talk about the layout of the backyard. There was a pool, is that right?

A: I don't know. Thirty feet. Fifty. I'm not good with distances.

A: It wasn't close.

A: Some. A few. People were moving around.

Q: So when you say you saw Mr. Decker strike the plaintiff, you were observing this from fifty feet away, through a crowd.

A: Then yes. Those were the conditions.

Q: Was it well-lit in that area?

A: There were string lights. Some kind of patio light near the door. It wasn't dark.

Q: But it wasn't bright either.

A: I suppose not.

Q: And you'd been drinking.

A: I'd had two beers over the course of several hours. I wasn't impaired.

Q: I didn't say you were. I'm just establishing the facts.

A: Then we've established them.

topic: A witness is questioned about events at a party where an assault allegedly occurred
text:
Q: Ms. Okonkwo, I want to ask you about the moments just before the altercation. Where was the plaintiff standing?

A: Not at first.

A: I don't remember exactly. A few minutes in, maybe. The music was loud and I wasn't really paying attention to them.

A: I noticed because it cut through. That's what made me look over.

topic: A witness is questioned about events at a party where an assault allegedly occurred
text:
Q: Let's move on to something else. You mentioned earlier that you left the party around midnight.

A: No. I'm sorry. I know that's not helpful.

A: I understand.

Q: Did you speak with either Mr. Garza or the plaintiff that evening?

A: I said hello to Chris—Mr. Garza—when I arrived. That's it.

A: Okay.

topic: A witness is questioned about events at a party where an assault allegedly occurred
text:
Q: Mr. Pratt, you've now given three different accounts of where you were standing when this happened.

A: I've given one account. You keep asking me the same question in different ways.

A: There aren't any. I was near the garage. I've said that each time.

Q: In your initial statement to police, you said you were "by the side gate."

A: I could see the patio. I could see people standing around. I saw two guys get into it.

Q: What kind of noise?

A: Shouting. Then something breaking—a glass, maybe. I don't know.

Q: And after you looked over?

A: One of them was on the ground. That's what I saw. I already told the police this. I already told your colleague. I'm telling you now. It's the same answer. It's going to keep being the same answer.

topic: A former employee is deposed about discriminatory remarks made by a supervisor
text:
Q: Ms. Fernandez, you worked under Mr. Haddad for approximately two years, correct?

topic: A former employee is deposed about discriminatory remarks made by a supervisor

topic: A former employee is deposed about discriminatory remarks made by a supervisor

Q: Mr. Choi, you've stated that Ms. Patterson made discriminatory comments about your age. When did these comments begin?

topic: A former employee is deposed about discriminatory remarks made by a supervisor
text:
Q: Dr. Anand, I want to return to the conversation you had with Mr. Reilly in his office on July 8th.

topic: A store manager is questioned about a customer slip-and-fall on their premises
text:
Q: Please state your name and position for the record.

A: James Whitfield, Store Manager at Greenleaf Grocery on Fifth Avenue. Been there six years now, actually just celebrated my anniversary last month.

Q: Mr. Whitfield, can you tell me about the incident on March 14th?

A: Absolutely! So I was in the back office reviewing inventory when Sarah—she's my assistant manager—came running back to tell me a customer had fallen in aisle seven. I immediately dropped what I was doing and headed straight out there.

Q: What did you observe when you arrived?

A: The customer, Mrs. Patterson, was sitting on the floor near the dairy section. There was a puddle of what turned out to be milk—about, I'd say, two feet in diameter, maybe a little more. I could see the broken container about three feet away from where she was sitting.

Q: How long had the spill been there before the fall?

A: Great question. We actually have a system for this! Our employees do floor sweeps every fifteen minutes, and according to the log—which I pulled immediately after the incident—the last sweep was completed at 2:47 PM. Mrs. Patterson fell at approximately 3:02 PM.

Q: So the spill could have been there for fifteen minutes?

A: Theoretically, yes, but I can tell you that based on the temperature of the milk and the spread pattern, our safety consultant estimated it had been on the floor no more than three to five minutes. I was really pleased we had that data available.

Q: Did anyone witness the milk being spilled?

A: Yes! A customer named Rodriguez—first name Carlos, I believe—saw a child knock the container off the shelf and told his mother, who was actually on her way to find an employee when the fall occurred.

Q: What is the store's policy for handling spills?

A: Oh, I'm glad you asked. We have a comprehensive protocol. Any employee who spots a spill must stay with it and radio for cleanup. We provide cones, we have mops stationed at three locations throughout the store, and I personally train every new hire on this during their first week.

Q: Were there any warning signs or cones near the spill at the time of the fall?

A: No, there weren't yet, and I want to be completely transparent about that. The spill had just occurred. But I'm proud to say we've since implemented an additional measure—overhead announcements for active spill zones.

Q: You seem quite prepared to discuss these details.

A: I take safety very seriously. After the incident, I conducted a full internal review. I have documentation, timestamps, everything. I want to make sure we learn from this and that the facts are crystal clear.

topic: A store manager is questioned about a customer slip-and-fall on their premises
text:
Q: You were working the day this happened, correct?

A: Yes.

Q: Walk me through what you did that morning before the incident.

A: I opened the store at 6 AM. Checked the registers. Did a walkthrough.

Q: And the walkthrough—you checked the floors?

A: Yes!

Q: Now I'm getting somewhere. Tell me exactly what you saw during that walkthrough.

A: Everything was clean, dry, organized. I personally checked every single aisle, and I want you to know that I take this responsibility incredibly seriously. The floors were immaculate at 6 AM.

Q: What time did the plaintiff fall?

A: 11:43 AM.

Q: Five hours later. A lot can happen in five hours, can't it?

A: It can, which is exactly why we have protocols! Every hour, my team does a full floor inspection. I have the logs right here—well, not physically here, but they exist and they're thorough.

Q: How many employees were working that morning?

A: Four on the floor, plus myself. Adequate coverage, I assure you.

Q: Who found the plaintiff after she fell?

A: Derek Martinez, one of my best employees. He responded in under thirty seconds—I timed it on the security footage myself.

Q: You reviewed the security footage?

A: Multiple times! I wanted to understand exactly what happened. I can tell you the plaintiff entered the store at 11:31 AM, proceeded directly to aisle four, and the incident occurred when she turned to reach for a product on the lower shelf.

Q: What caused her to fall?

A: There was a small amount of cooking oil on the floor. Approximately a quarter-cup, based on the residue pattern.

Q: And where did that oil come from?

A: A bottle with a defective seal on the shelf above. We've since contacted the manufacturer, filed a product complaint, and instituted new inspection procedures for all bottles before shelving.

topic: A store manager is questioned about a customer slip-and-fall on their premises
text:
Q: How would you describe the condition of your store's floors on a typical day?

topic: A store manager is questioned about a customer slip-and-fall on their premises
text:
Q: State your role at the store, please.

A: I'm the manager. I oversee operations.

Q: How long have you held this position?

A: Three years.

A: Yes.

Q: Prudent because the previous location was dangerous?

A: Prudent because I wanted to prevent future incidents.

topic: A store manager is questioned about a customer slip-and-fall on their premises
text:
Q: Good morning. Let me start by saying I appreciate your time here today. How are you feeling?

A: Fine, thank you.

Q: I understand you've been with the company for twelve years. That's remarkable! You must know every inch of that store.

A: I know it well.

Q: I'm sure you do. Now, on November 15th, a customer named Harold Greene fell in your store. You remember that day?
