topic: A daycare worker is deposed about an injury a child sustained while in their care
text:
Q: Please state your name and your position at Little Stars Learning Center.

A: Absolutely! I'm Miranda Chen, and I'm the lead toddler room teacher. I've been there for six years now—actually, six years and four months if we're being precise—and I just love what I do. Every single day with those kids is a gift.

Q: Were you working on March 14th of this year?

A: I was! I remember that day really well, actually. We had just started our new spring curriculum, which I designed myself, and the children were so engaged with the butterfly life cycle stations I'd set up.

Q: At some point that day, did something happen involving Tyler Rennick?

A: Yes, and I have to say, I responded exactly as I was trained to do. The moment I saw Tyler trip near the block corner, I was there in seconds. I mean, our safety protocols are top-notch, and I take so much pride in how quickly our team reacts.

Q: Can you describe what you observed?

A: Of course! So Tyler was walking—well, more like that adorable toddler waddle-run they do—toward the block corner, and his shoelace, which his mother had tied in the morning because we always check, must have come undone, and he went down. I was already moving before he even hit the ground, honestly.

Q: What happened when he fell?

A: He bumped his forehead on the edge of the block shelf. But I want to be really clear here—we had just installed those new foam corner guards two weeks prior. I actually picked them out myself from a catalog because they had the highest safety rating. So the impact was significantly cushioned.

Q: Did Tyler cry?

A: He did, briefly, but I scooped him right up and used our calm-down techniques. I've done extra training in child comfort responses—I took a weekend seminar on my own time—and Tyler settled within maybe ninety seconds. I timed it because I always document these things.

Q: Did you notice any visible injury?

A: There was a small red mark, about the size of a quarter. I immediately got the first aid kit, applied a cold compress with our little penguin ice pack—the kids adore that penguin—and filled out an incident report. I actually developed the current incident report template we use!

Q: Who else was present in the room?

A: My assistant teacher Jade was there, and she'll tell you the same thing—we handled it perfectly. We work together like a well-oiled machine. Our room has the lowest incident rate at the whole center, which I'm really proud of.

Q: Did you contact Tyler's parents?

A: Immediately! Well, within four minutes of the incident. I called Mrs. Rennick personally because I believe in that direct communication. I gave her every detail, offered to send a photo, and invited her to come check on him if she wanted. That's just how I operate.

Q: What did you tell her specifically?

A: I told her Tyler had a minor tumble, that he was already smiling again, that we'd applied ice and documented everything, and that I would personally keep an extra close eye on him for the rest of the day. Which I did! I barely let him out of my sight.

topic: A daycare worker is deposed about an injury a child sustained while in their care
text:
Q: How long have you worked in childcare?

A: About three years.

Q: Three years at Sunshine Days Academy specifically?

A: Yes.

Q: Excellent. Now, let's talk about the playground. I understand the facility recently upgraded the outdoor equipment, correct?

A: We got new swings last fall.

Q: New swings! And I imagine the children were thrilled. Tell me about the safety surfacing under those swings.

A: It's rubber mulch.

Q: Rubber mulch—the industry standard, very good. Now, on June 7th, were you assigned to outdoor supervision?

A: I was one of the supervisors, yes.

Q: One of how many? I want to make sure I understand the staffing picture completely here.

A: Three of us.

Q: Three supervisors for how many children? Take your time, I want to get the exact number.

A: I think around twenty.

Q: Around twenty! So better than the required ratio, would you say?

A: I guess so.

Q: You guess so—well, let's be precise. The state requires one-to-eight, and you had one-to-seven, approximately. That's commendable. Now, where exactly were you positioned when Emma Fitzgerald fell from the swing?

A: Near the slide.

Q: The slide. And how far would you estimate that is from the swings?

A: Maybe twenty feet.

Q: Twenty feet—so well within visual range. Could you see the swings clearly from that position?

A: Yes.

Q: Wonderful. So tell me what you actually observed when Emma fell.

A: She was swinging and then she wasn't holding on and she fell backward.

Q: She fell backward onto the rubber mulch surfacing you described?

A: Yes.

Q: The rubber mulch that's specifically designed to cushion falls?

A: Yes.

topic: A daycare worker is deposed about an injury a child sustained while in their care
text:
Q: State your name for the record.

A: Derek Williams.

Q: How long have you been employed at Growing Minds Daycare?

A: Two years, maybe a little more.

Q: On February 3rd, were you responsible for the infant room?

A: I was working in the infant room, yes. I wasn't the only one responsible.

Q: Who else was working with you?

A: Patty Molina was the lead caregiver. I assist.

Q: Fine. Tell me about the changing table incident involving Baby Doe.

A: I didn't see exactly what happened because I was on the other side of the room warming a bottle.

Q: So you didn't see the child roll off the changing table?

A: No, I heard Patty call out and I turned around and the baby was already on the floor.

Q: The baby was on the floor. Meaning Patty was changing the baby and the baby fell?

A: I wasn't watching Patty, so I can't tell you exactly what Patty was or wasn't doing. I just know the baby ended up on the floor and then I came over to help.

Q: You came over to help. What did you observe when you reached the changing table?

A: The baby was crying. There was a red mark on the side of her head. Patty was picking her up.

Q: Did Patty say anything about what happened?

A: She said the baby rolled faster than she expected.

Q: "Faster than she expected"—those were her exact words?

A: That's what I remember her saying, yes. But you should probably ask Patty what she meant by that.

Q: I'm asking what you heard. Did Patty seem surprised?

A: I guess. I mean, babies roll. It happens. I'm not going to characterize Patty's emotional state for you.

Q: I'm not asking you to characterize anything. I'm asking what you observed.

A: I observed Patty picking up a crying baby and looking concerned. That's what anyone would do and feel.

Q: Were the changing table straps being used?

A: I wasn't standing there watching the changing process. I was across the room. I've already told you that.

Q: Is it facility policy to use the changing table straps?

A: Yes.

Q: Were they used on this occasion?

A: I don't know. I wasn't there. You keep asking me about things I've told you I didn't see.

topic: A daycare worker is deposed about an injury a child sustained while in their care
text:
Q: Ms. Porter, I'd like to focus on the afternoon nap routine. Walk me through it.

A: Sure. Around 12:30, we start transitioning the kids to their cots. Lights go down, we play soft music, the kids lie down with their rest items from home.

Q: Rest items—blankets, stuffed animals, that type of thing?

A: Right. Whatever the parents send that comforts them.

Q: And on April 22nd, did anything unusual happen during nap time?

A: Yes, Marcus had a seizure.

Q: Tell me about that.

A: I noticed he was making unusual movements on his cot. At first I thought he was just fidgeting, but then I realized something was wrong. His arms were jerking and his eyes looked strange.

Q: What did you do?

A: I called for my co-teacher to watch the other kids and went straight to Marcus. I turned him on his side like we're trained to do, made sure nothing was near his face that he could hurt himself on, and called 911.

Q: Had Marcus ever had a seizure at the facility before?

A: Not that I know of. His file didn't indicate any seizure history. I actually double-checked after the paramedics took him, because I wanted to make sure I hadn't missed something.

Q: So as far as you knew, this was a new medical development?

A: Right. His parents were shocked when I called them too. Apparently it was his first one ever. Just one of those scary things that happens sometimes with kids—nobody's fault, just a medical event.

Q: Did Marcus injure himself during the seizure?

A: He bit his tongue a little, and he had some minor bruising on his arm from the jerking movements. But given what could have happened, I'm really relieved I noticed when I did and knew what to do. Those first aid certifications really pay off in moments like that.

Q: How long did the seizure last?

A: I'd estimate about two minutes, maybe two and a half. It felt longer, honestly. But I kept my composure because that's what Marcus needed from me in that moment.

Q: Did you stay with Marcus until the paramedics arrived?

A: Absolutely. I talked to him the whole time, kept him calm, held his hand once the convulsions stopped. I wasn't going to leave that little boy alone for a second. That's just not who I am.

topic: A daycare worker is deposed about an injury a child sustained while in their care
text:
Q: You were the director on duty on September 9th, correct?

A: That's correct.

Q: Let's talk about the field trip permission forms. Riveting topic, I know, but necessary. Who was responsible for collecting them?

A: The lead teacher for each classroom collects the forms and submits them to the front office. Then I review them before any trip.

Q: And for the zoo trip on September 9th, did you review the forms?

A: I did.

Q: Did you have a signed permission form for Connor Bradley?

A: We had a form on file, yes.

Q: On file. Was it signed for this specific trip?

A: We use a blanket permission form that covers all field trips for the semester. The Bradleys signed that form in August.

Q: A blanket form! How efficient. So one signature covers multiple trips?

A: That's our policy, yes. Parents appreciate not having to sign ten different forms.

Q: I'm sure they do. Now, at the zoo, Connor was stung by a bee and had an allergic reaction, correct?

A: That's what happened, yes.

Q: Tell me about the facility's medical information procedures. I find these systems fascinating—really the backbone of child safety.

A: Each child has a file that includes emergency contacts, medical conditions, allergies, and physician information.

Q: And Connor's file—did it indicate a bee allergy?

A: No, it did not.

Q: It did not! So this was unknown to you and your staff?

A: Correct. The parents hadn't disclosed any allergies.

Q: Because they didn't know themselves, or because they didn't disclose it?

A: I can't speak to what the parents knew or didn't know.

Q: Fair enough. But your forms—they specifically ask about allergies, I assume?

A: Yes, there's a section for allergies and medical conditions.

Q: And that section was left blank on Connor's enrollment paperwork?

A: It was marked "none known."

Q: "None known"—so the parents affirmatively represented that there were no known allergies?

A: That's what the form indicates, yes. We rely on parents to provide accurate medical information. We're educators, not physicians.

topic: A store manager is questioned about a customer slip-and-fall on their premises
text:
Q: Could you please state your name and position for the record?

A: Certainly. My name is David Chen, and I serve as the general manager of the Westbrook Shopping Plaza location.

Q: And how long have you held that position, Mr. Chen?

A: It will be six years this coming March.

Q: Thank you. Now, I'd like to direct your attention to the afternoon of September 14th. Were you working that day?

A: I was, yes. I arrived at approximately 7:30 in the morning and remained on-site until we closed at 9 PM.

Q: At some point that afternoon, were you made aware of an incident involving a customer?

A: I was. One of my floor associates, Marcus, came to find me in the back office around 2:15 or so. He informed me that a customer had fallen near the produce section.

Q: What did you do after receiving this information?

A: I walked to the location of the incident. I didn't run—I've found that creates unnecessary alarm among other customers—but I walked there promptly.

Q: And what did you observe when you arrived?

A: I saw a woman, who I later learned was Mrs. Patterson, seated on the floor near the banana display. One of our employees was already with her, and she appeared to be holding her left wrist.

Q: Was there anything on the floor in that area?

A: There was some moisture on the tile. A small amount. It appeared to be water, though I couldn't say definitively what it was at that moment.

Q: Did you take any action regarding that moisture?

A: I did. I asked Marcus to retrieve the wet floor caution sign and the mop from the supply closet. He returned within a minute or two, and I had him section off the area while I attended to Mrs. Patterson.

Q: Had you received any reports of a spill in that area prior to the incident?

A: No, I had not. I reviewed our incident log afterward, and there was no notation of any reported spill in produce that day prior to approximately 2:15.

Q: Is it your testimony that no employee was aware of the wet floor before Mrs. Patterson fell?

A: That is my understanding based on the information available to me. I spoke with each employee who had been working in or near that section, and none of them reported having seen or been informed of any liquid on the floor prior to the incident.

---

topic: A store manager is questioned about a customer slip-and-fall on their premises
text:
Q: Mr. Okonkwo, let's talk about your store's inspection procedures. Does your store conduct regular safety inspections of the floor?

A: We do.

Q: How often?

A: Every hour during operating hours. Sometimes more frequently in high-traffic areas or during inclement weather.

Q: Who performs these inspections?

A: The floor supervisor on duty, or in their absence, a designated team lead.

Q: And these inspections are documented?

A: They are.

Q: I'm going to show you what's been marked as Exhibit 7. Do you recognize this document?

A: Yes. This is our floor inspection log for November 3rd.

Q: I notice there's an entry at 10:00 AM and then not another until 12:15 PM. That's more than two hours. Can you explain that gap?

A: I can. We experienced a delivery issue that morning—a truck arrived with damaged freight that required immediate attention from our supervisory staff. The 11:00 inspection was delayed as a result.

Q: So the inspection schedule wasn't followed that morning?

A: The 11:00 inspection was delayed, yes. It was completed at 12:15.

Q: And Mrs. Franklin fell at approximately 11:40 AM, correct?

A: That is the time recorded in the incident report, yes.

Q: So at the time of her fall, it had been an hour and forty minutes since anyone had inspected aisle seven?

A: If the inspection times recorded on that log are accurate, then that would be correct.

Q: Do you have any reason to believe they're not accurate?

A: I have no reason to believe they're inaccurate, no.

Q: Mr. Okonkwo, whose decision was it to delay the 11:00 inspection?

A: I don't know that anyone made a conscious decision to delay it. The situation with the delivery simply required immediate attention, and the inspection didn't occur at its scheduled time as a result.

---

topic: A store manager is questioned about a customer slip-and-fall on their premises
text:
Q: Walk me through what you saw when you first arrived at the scene of the fall.

A: I came around the end of aisle four and saw Mr. Dominguez on the ground. He was on his back, maybe partially on his side. His shopping cart had tipped over next to him.

Q: Where exactly in the aisle was he?

A: There was a clear liquid. Looked like water. Maybe a four-foot area, roughly.

Q: Four feet in diameter?

A: I'd say so. Maybe a bit less. I'm estimating.

Q: That's understood. Did you determine where the liquid had come from?

A: Not at that moment, no. My priority was assisting Mr. Dominguez.

Q: Did you later determine the source?

A: We found a leaking water bottle on the shelf nearby. One of the gallon jugs. It had a crack along the bottom seam.

Q: When you say "we found," who do you mean?

A: Myself and Janet Reeves. She's our assistant manager.

Q: How long after the fall did you discover this cracked bottle?

A: Perhaps twenty minutes. We were looking for the source once Mr. Dominguez had been attended to.

Q: Had any customer or employee reported that leaking bottle before the fall?

A: Not to my knowledge, no.

---

topic: A store manager is questioned about a customer slip-and-fall on their premises
text:
Q: Ms. Whitfield, you mentioned earlier that you have cameras throughout the store. Were any cameras positioned to capture the area where the plaintiff fell?

Q: But on the afternoon of January 8th, during what I understand was a rainy day, there was no sign in the entrance vestibule?

topic: A store manager is questioned about a customer slip-and-fall on their premises
text:
Q: Let me ask you about training. What training do employees receive regarding spill response?

A: All new hires complete a safety orientation during their first week. Spill response is one of the modules.

Q: What does that module cover?

A: The basics. Identify the spill, secure the area, clean it up or contact maintenance if it's beyond what a mop and bucket can handle. Document it in the log.

Q: How long is this training module?

Q: And after that initial training, is there any refresher?

Q: The employee who discovered the spill that Mr. Bauer slipped in—had that person completed their annual refresher?

A: I'd have to check the training records to answer that precisely.

Q: Do you recall who that employee was?

A: Brittany Saunders.

Q: Had Ms. Saunders been employed at your store for more than a year?

A: She had. Approximately eighteen months, I believe.

Q: So she would have completed at least one refresher course?

A: In the ordinary course, yes. But I'd want to verify the records before testifying to that definitively.

Q: That's fair. When Ms. Saunders discovered the spill, what did she do?

A: She went to the supply closet to get a mop and a caution sign.

Q: Did she stay near the spill to warn customers?

A: It's my understanding she did not. She left briefly to retrieve the supplies.

Q: And that's when Mr. Bauer fell?

A: The incident occurred while she was getting the supplies, yes.

Q: How far is the supply closet from aisle twelve?

A: Approximately sixty feet. Perhaps a bit more.

Q: And how long would it take to walk there and back?

A: A minute. Maybe ninety seconds, depending on whether the closet is occupied or if she had to locate the items.

topic: A pharmacist is deposed about a prescription that was filled with the wrong dosage
text:
Q: Please state your name and current position for the record.

A: Dr. Rebecca Thornton. I'm the pharmacy director at Westlake Medical Center, a position I've held for eleven years.

Q: And you were working on the evening of March 14th when Mrs. Patterson's prescription was filled?

A: I was on duty, yes. I should clarify—I wasn't the dispensing pharmacist that evening, but I was supervising.

Q: Walk me through your standard verification protocol.

A: Gladly. Every prescription goes through a three-step verification process. First, the technician enters the prescription into our system. Second, the pharmacist reviews the original prescription against what's been entered. Third, before dispensing, there's a final visual check of the medication against the label.

Q: And this protocol was followed on March 14th?

A: It was. I've reviewed our logs extensively.

Q: Yet Mrs. Patterson received 100 milligrams instead of 10 milligrams. How do you explain that?

A: I can explain exactly what happened. The prescribing physician's handwriting was ambiguous. The numeral one followed by what appeared to be two zeros. Our pharmacist interpreted it as written. We have the original prescription, and I'd invite you to examine it yourself.

Q: Are you suggesting the error was the physician's fault?

A: I'm stating a fact about the prescription as it was written. I'm not here to assign blame—that's your job. I'm here to tell you what our records show and what our procedures are.

Q: Has your pharmacy ever made a dispensing error before this incident?

A: In eleven years, we've filled over two million prescriptions. Our error rate is 0.003 percent, which is significantly below the national average. I have those statistics documented if you'd like to see them.

Q: That wasn't my question. Has your pharmacy made errors before?

A: Every pharmacy has. The relevant question is whether we followed protocol, and we did.

---

topic: A pharmacist is deposed about a prescription that was filled with the wrong dosage
text:
Q: Mr. Okonkwo, how long have you been a licensed pharmacist?

A: Three years.

Q: And on June 8th, you personally filled the prescription for Daniel Reeves?

A: Yes.

Q: The prescription called for 25 micrograms of levothyroxine. What did you dispense?

A: 250 micrograms.

Q: That's ten times the prescribed dose, correct?

A: Yes.

Q: Tell me what happened.

A: I... the prescription was electronic. The dosage field showed 250. I filled what I saw on the screen.

Q: Did you check the original electronic prescription against what you dispensed?

A: I thought I did.

Q: You thought you did?

A: I reviewed the screen. The order said 250. I matched the pills to 250.

Q: Let me show you Exhibit 4. This is the electronic prescription log from your system. Do you see where it says "25 mcg" right there?

A: I see it now, yes.

Q: So the system showed 25, not 250.

A: It appears that way in this document.

Q: There's no ambiguity there, is there, Mr. Okonkwo? Twenty-five micrograms. Plain as day.

A: Looking at this document, no.

Q: You simply misread it.

A: It was a busy evening. We were short-staffed. The screen—

Q: I'm not asking about staffing. I'm asking whether you misread a clear electronic prescription. Yes or no?

A: ...Yes.

Q: And no one else checked your work before Mr. Reeves walked out with a potentially lethal dose?

A: There should have been a second check.

Q: But there wasn't.

A: No.

---

topic: A pharmacist is deposed about a prescription that was filled with the wrong dosage
text:
Q: Dr. Yamamoto, you've testified as an expert witness in pharmacy malpractice cases before?

A: Seventeen times, yes. For both plaintiffs and defendants.

Q: You reviewed the records in this case?

A: Thoroughly. The prescription records, the pharmacy logs, the inventory documentation, and the depositions of both the dispensing pharmacist and the pharmacy technician.

Q: And you've formed an opinion about whether the pharmacy met the standard of care?

A: I have.

Q: Before we get to that—the pharmacy's counsel has argued that their verification system is industry-leading. Do you agree?

A: I'd say it's adequate on paper. Many pharmacies use similar three-step verification protocols. The question isn't whether the system exists. It's whether it was followed.

Q: Was it followed here?

A: No. And the evidence is unambiguous.

Q: Explain.

A: The timestamp on the verification log shows the second check occurred seven seconds after the first entry. Seven seconds. That's not verification—that's clicking a button without looking. I've timed this process in multiple pharmacy settings. A genuine verification takes a minimum of forty-five seconds to two minutes depending on the medication.

Q: Could there be another explanation for the seven-second gap?

A: I've considered alternatives. None of them hold up. The system wasn't malfunctioning—I reviewed the IT logs. The pharmacist wasn't verifying a simple refill where she might already know the dosage—this was a new prescription. Seven seconds means she didn't look.

Q: The defense will argue you can't know what she actually did in those seven seconds.

A: They can argue whatever they like. The laws of physics and the documented workflow make their position untenable.

Q: What should the pharmacist have caught?

A: The prescription was for methotrexate, 2.5 milligrams weekly. What was dispensed was 25 milligrams daily. Any pharmacist paying attention would recognize that 25 milligrams of methotrexate daily is a chemotherapy-level dose, not a rheumatoid arthritis maintenance dose. It's not a close call.

---

topic: A pharmacist is deposed about a prescription that was filled with the wrong dosage
text:
Q: Ms. Franklin, take me through what you remember about filling the Henderson prescription.

A: It was a Tuesday. Mid-afternoon, probably around 2 or 2:30. We'd had a rush earlier but things had calmed down.

Q: What do you recall about the prescription itself?

A: It was for oxycodone. The doctor—Dr. Patel—had written for 5 milligram tablets, quantity of sixty.

Q: And what did you dispense?

A: That's what I dispensed. 5 milligram tablets. Sixty of them.

Q: The plaintiff alleges she received 50 milligram tablets.

A: Then the plaintiff is mistaken.

Q: You're certain?

A: Completely. I remember this prescription specifically because of the quantity and because controlled substances require additional documentation. I pulled the 5 milligram stock, I counted sixty tablets, I verified the NDC number against the prescription, and I documented everything in our controlled substance log.

Q: You have a specific memory of checking the NDC number?

A: I do, because the 5 milligram and 50 milligram bottles are different colors in our system. The 5 milligram is a white label. The 50 milligram is orange. I pulled a white-label bottle.

Q: That was seven months ago. You remember the color of a label?

A: I remember it because the next day, Mrs. Henderson called claiming she'd been given the wrong medication. So yes, I went back and replayed it in my head. Multiple times. I remember exactly what I did.

Q: Is it possible—

A: No.

Q: I haven't finished my question.

A: You were going to ask if it's possible I'm misremembering or confusing this with another prescription. The answer is no. I've been a pharmacist for fourteen years. I know what I dispensed.

Q: The pills Mrs. Henderson brought back to the pharmacy were 50 milligram tablets.

A: Then someone switched them. Those weren't the pills I put in that bottle.

---

topic: A pharmacist is deposed about a prescription that was filled with the wrong dosage
text:
Q: You were the technician who entered the prescription into the system, correct?

A: That's right.

Q: And the pharmacist then reviews what you enter?

A: That's the process, yes.

Q: So if you entered the wrong dosage, the pharmacist should have caught it?

A: Well... yes. That's the whole point of the verification step.

Q: Let's look at what you entered. Exhibit 7, please. Do you see the entry for the warfarin prescription?

A: Yes.

Q: What dosage did you enter?

A: It says 5 milligrams.

Q: And the original prescription from Dr. Morrison—that's Exhibit 8—what does it say?

A: Um. 0.5 milligrams.

Q: Point-five milligrams. Not five milligrams.

A: The decimal point was... it wasn't clear.

Q: Wasn't clear?

A: It looked like a speck. Or a stray mark. I've seen doctors make stray marks before.

Q: So you made a judgment call.

A: I... yes.

Q: Did you ask anyone about it?

A: No.

Q: Did you flag it for the pharmacist to review more carefully?

A: I should have.

Q: But you didn't.

A: No.

Q: And then the pharmacist, Ms. Chen, approved your entry. She didn't catch the discrepancy either.

A: She must not have looked at the original.

Q: That's her job, isn't it? To compare your entry against the original?

A: Yes. That's what she's supposed to do.

Q: So the system failed at two points. Your entry, and her verification.

A: I can only speak for myself. I made an honest mistake with a prescription that wasn't clearly written. What Ms. Chen did or didn't do—you'd have to ask her.

topic: A supervisor is deposed about performance reviews given to an employee who was later fired
text:
Q: Mr. Patterson, you conducted the annual performance review for Diane Kershaw in March of 2022, correct?

A: I did.

Q: And you gave her an overall rating of "meets expectations"?

A: That's what the form says, yes.

Q: Is that not accurate?

A: No, it's accurate. That's what I gave her.

Q: Can you explain to me how someone who "meets expectations" in March is terminated for performance issues in September?

A: Look, I've been through this with HR, I've been through it with legal, and now I'm going through it with you. The March review reflected where she was in March. Things changed.

Q: What changed?

A: Her performance. Her attitude. The quality of her work product declined.

Q: But you didn't document any of that between March and September, did you?

A: No.

Q: No written warnings?

A: No.

Q: No performance improvement plan?

A: No. We should have. I know that. I've said that.

Q: So you're acknowledging the company failed to follow its own progressive discipline policy?

A: I'm acknowledging that I didn't do what I should have done. Whether that means the company failed to follow policy, that's for you and whoever else to sort out. I'm just telling you what happened.

Q: What did happen, Mr. Patterson?

A: I gave her too much benefit of the doubt for too long, and then when it became clear it wasn't working, we moved forward with separation. That's what happened. I'm not going to dress it up for you.

---

topic: A supervisor is deposed about performance reviews given to an employee who was later fired
text:
Q: Ms. Okonkwo, how long did you supervise Brian Teller?

A: A little over two years. From when I took over the department in January 2021 until his termination.

Q: And during that time, how many formal performance reviews did you conduct for him?

A: Two. One each year.

Q: Let's talk about the first one, in 2021. What rating did you give him?

A: Satisfactory. Across the board, I believe.

Q: You believe, or you know?

A: I'd have to look at the document to give you the exact ratings in each category, but my recollection is that he was satisfactory overall.

Q: Fine. And the 2022 review?

A: The same.

Q: Also satisfactory?

A: Yes.

Q: Ms. Okonkwo, I have to ask you—if Mr. Teller was satisfactory for two consecutive years, what justified his termination three months after that second review?

A: I understand why you're asking. I do.

Q: That's not an answer.

A: I know it's not. The answer is that the reviews don't tell the whole story. They never do.

Q: Then why give them?

A: Because we're required to. Because HR has a form and a deadline and we fill it out.

Q: So these reviews are meaningless?

A: I didn't say meaningless. I said they don't tell the whole story. There's what goes on the form and what you actually deal with day to day.

Q: And what were you dealing with day to day with Mr. Teller?

A: Lateness. Missed deadlines. Complaints from other team members that I couldn't put in writing because he'd file a grievance every time anyone looked at him sideways. It wears on you. It wore on all of us.

Q: But none of that appears in these reviews.

A: No. It doesn't.

---

topic: A supervisor is deposed about performance reviews given to an employee who was later fired
text:
Q: The performance improvement plan was issued on June 15th, correct?

A: If that's what the document says.

Q: I'm asking if you remember.

A: It was mid-June. I don't remember the specific date, but mid-June sounds right.

Q: And Mr. Garrett was terminated on August 3rd?

A: Approximately, yes.

Q: That's less than two months.

A: Yes.

Q: The company handbook indicates that PIPs should run for a minimum of 90 days. Were you aware of that?

A: I was aware that was the general guidance.

Q: General guidance or policy?

A: I'm not going to parse words with you, counsel. I knew it was supposed to be 90 days.

Q: Then why was it cut short?

A: Because there was an incident.

Q: What incident?

A: He sent an email to a client that was... it was unprofessional. It undermined a project we'd been working on for months.

Q: One email?

A: One email that did significant damage, yes.

Q: Did you consult with HR before terminating him?

A: I did.

Q: And what did they say?

A: They said it was my call.

Q: That's it? They just said it was your call?

A: More or less. They asked if I was sure, I said I was sure, and we moved forward. I don't know what else you want me to tell you. We made a decision. Maybe it was the wrong one. I'm here, aren't I? We're doing this. So maybe it was the wrong one.

---

topic: A supervisor is deposed about performance reviews given to an employee who was later fired
text:
Q: I want to direct your attention to the comments section of the 2023 review. Do you see where you wrote, "Sandra continues to be a valued member of the team"?

A: I see that, yes.

Q: Did you write that?

A: I did.

Q: Did you mean it?

A: At the time, I suppose I did.

Q: You suppose?

A: Counsel, do you want me to explain how these reviews actually work, or do you want to keep asking me questions like I wrote a love letter?

Q: I want to understand how you could write that someone is "valued" and then support her termination four months later.

A: Because "valued" doesn't mean "perfect." Because "valued" doesn't mean "immune from consequences." Because I was trying to be encouraging in a review that's supposed to be constructive.

Q: So you were being generous.

A: I was being professional. I was being a manager.

Q: Would you write the same thing today, knowing what you know now?

A: No. Obviously not. I would have been more direct about the areas of concern.

Q: Why weren't you more direct at the time?

A: Because nobody wants to be the bad guy. Because HR tells you to sandwich criticism between compliments. Because I thought she might turn it around.

Q: But she didn't.

A: No. She didn't. And here we are.

Q: Here we are.

A: Yes.

---

topic: A supervisor is deposed about performance reviews given to an employee who was later fired
text:
Q: How would you characterize your working relationship with Mr. Dean?

A: Professional.

Q: That's all? Just professional?

A: What are you looking for? We weren't friends. We weren't enemies. I was his supervisor. He reported to me. Professional.

Q: Did you ever have any personal conflicts with him?

A: Define "personal conflicts."

Q: Disagreements that went beyond work performance.

A: We had disagreements. Whether they went beyond work performance, I honestly couldn't tell you. It all bleeds together after a while.

Q: After a while?

A: After two years of managing someone who doesn't want to be managed.

Q: Is that how you would describe Mr. Dean? Someone who didn't want to be managed?

A: I would describe him as someone who had his own way of doing things and didn't appreciate feedback.

Q: Did you document that?

A: Some of it.

Q: In his performance reviews?

A: In the reviews, in emails, in notes I kept.

Q: Where are those notes now?

A: I don't know. I left that job eighteen months ago. Whatever was in my desk, I assume it was thrown out or archived. I don't have it anymore.

Q: So we just have the formal reviews.

A: I guess so.

Q: And those reviews don't reflect any of these concerns you're describing.

A: They reflect some of them. Not all. I've already told you how this works—you try to be balanced, you try to be fair, and then something like this happens and everybody wants to know why you weren't harsher. I don't know what to tell you. I did what I thought was right at the time. It wasn't enough. I understand that now.

topic: A store manager is questioned about a customer slip-and-fall on their premises
text:
Q: Mr. Hendricks, you were the store manager on duty the morning of March 14th, correct?

A: Yes.

Q: And can you describe for me the general condition of the floors in the produce section that morning?

A: They were... they were fine. Normal. I don't know what else you want me to say about floors.

Q: I'm asking what you observed.

A: I observed floors. Tile floors. They looked the way they always look.

Q: Were they wet?

A: Not that I saw.

Q: Were they dry?

A: I just said they weren't wet.

Q: Mr. Hendricks, I'm asking you to affirmatively state whether the floors were dry.

A: Yes. Fine. The floors were dry when I saw them. Is that—can we move on?

Q: When did you first become aware that a customer had fallen?

A: Someone came and got me. One of the stock clerks.

Q: What time was that?

A: I don't know. Midmorning. Maybe ten, ten-fifteen. Somewhere in there.

Q: And what did you do when you were informed?

A: I walked over there. To the produce section. Looked at the situation.

Q: What did you see?

A: A woman on the floor. Some employees standing around. A grape. Can we take a break soon?

Q: We'll take a break when we finish this line of questioning. You said a grape?

A: Yes. A grape. On the floor. Near her.

topic: A store manager is questioned about a customer slip-and-fall on their premises
text:
Q: Ms. Thornton, how long have you been the manager at the Greendale location?

A: A little over four years now.

Q: And in that time, have you received any training on how to handle slip-and-fall incidents?

A: Yes, we do annual training. There's a module on it.

Q: A module. Okay. What does the module cover?

A: Incident response, documentation, securing the area, notifying corporate. The basics.

Q: Does it cover prevention?

A: It covers... I mean, yes, there's a section on prevention. Keeping aisles clear, spill response, that sort of thing.

Q: Spill response. Let's talk about that. What's the protocol when an employee discovers a spill?

A: They're supposed to stay with the spill and radio for cleanup, or if they can't stay, they put out a wet floor sign and then radio.

Q: On September 8th, the day Mrs. Patterson fell, were there wet floor signs in the area?

A: I don't recall specifically if there were signs out before the incident. There were signs out after, I know that much.

Q: You don't recall. Is that because you didn't check, or because you checked and don't remember?

A: I think I looked. I must have looked. But I'm not going to sit here and invent a memory I don't have.

Q: That's fair. Do you have any documentation from that day about the floor conditions prior to the fall?

A: I'd have to look at the incident report. I don't have it memorized.

Q: We'll get to the incident report. I'm asking what you personally remember.

A: Then no. I don't remember. It was eight months ago.

topic: A store manager is questioned about a customer slip-and-fall on their premises
text:
Q: Let me ask you about staffing levels on the day in question.

A: Okay.

Q: How many employees were on shift in the morning?

A: I'd have to check the schedule to give you an exact number.

Q: Your best estimate.

A: Maybe... twelve? Fifteen? It was a weekday. We run lean on weekdays.

Q: Run lean. What does that mean?

A: Fewer people than weekends.

Q: Okay. And of those twelve to fifteen, how many were assigned to floor maintenance?

A: We don't have people assigned specifically to floor maintenance. Everyone's responsible for keeping an eye on things.

Q: Everyone. Meaning no one specifically.

A: Meaning everyone. That's what I said.

Q: So if there's a spill in aisle six and everyone's at the registers—

A: Then whoever sees it calls it in. That's the system.

Q: Alright. Did anyone call anything in before Mrs. Delgado's fall?

A: No.

Q: How do you know?

A: Because I pulled the radio logs. After.

Q: After you were notified of the lawsuit?

A: ...Yes. After that.

Q: Let's move on. Tell me about the lighting in the frozen foods section.

A: What about it?

Q: Was it adequate?

A: I've never had complaints about the lighting. It's standard commercial lighting. It's fine.

topic: A store manager is questioned about a customer slip-and-fall on their premises
text:
Q: I want to direct your attention to the incident report, which has been marked as Exhibit 4. Do you recognize this document?

A: Yes.

Q: You prepared this?

A: I did.

Q: The time stamp shows 11:47 a.m. The fall allegedly occurred at approximately 10:15 a.m. Why the gap?

A: I was dealing with the actual situation first. Making sure the customer was okay, talking to her, calling for medical, all of that. The paperwork came after.

Q: An hour and a half after.

A: These things take time. I wasn't going to leave an injured woman sitting on the floor so I could fill out a form.

Q: Understood. Now, in the section marked "Floor Condition at Time of Incident," you wrote "appeared dry." Do you see that?

A: I see it.

Q: What does "appeared dry" mean?

A: It means... it looked dry. When I got there.

Q: You didn't touch the floor?

A: No.

Q: You didn't test it in any way?

A: I looked at it.

Q: So "appeared dry" is a visual assessment only.

A: Correct.

Q: Could there have been a thin layer of liquid you didn't see?

A: I suppose anything is possible.

Q: Is that a yes?

A: It's a "could there have been something I didn't see, that's not something I can answer, that's the nature of not seeing things."

Q: Let me rephrase. Based on your visual inspection—

A: —it appeared dry. Which is what I wrote. Which is what I've now said three times.

topic: A store manager is questioned about a customer slip-and-fall on their premises
text:
Q: Mr. Okonkwo, walk me through what happened after you arrived at the scene of the fall.

A: Sure. I came over, I saw the customer on the ground, I asked if she was hurt. She said her hip. I told Marcus—one of my guys—to call for medical assistance. Then I cleared the area, moved some of the shopping carts back.

Q: Did you take any photographs?

A: Yes. Eventually.

Q: Eventually. How long after you arrived?

A: I don't know exactly. Ten minutes, maybe fifteen.

Q: What were you doing for those ten to fifteen minutes?

A: Helping. Talking to the customer. Waiting for the paramedics. We only have so many hands.

Q: When you took the photographs, what did you photograph?

A: The floor. The area where she fell. The shelf nearby. I got maybe six or seven shots.

Q: Did you photograph any substance on the floor?

A: No, there wasn't any substance when I took the pictures.

Q: But there was a substance earlier?

A: There was something wet. One of the employees wiped it up.

Q: Before you photographed?

A: ...Yes. Before I photographed.

Q: Who made that decision?

A: I don't know. It just happened. People were trying to help.

Q: So the substance that may have caused the fall was cleaned up before it could be documented.

A: When you put it that way—look, nobody was thinking about lawsuits. We were thinking about a woman who was hurt.

Q: I understand. Just a few more questions and we can break. Did anyone collect whatever was used to wipe up the substance?

A: No. I don't... no.

Q: Do you know what the substance was?

A: Someone said it looked like yogurt. Pink. Probably from the dairy case.

Q: But you didn't see it yourself.

A: No. It was already gone when I got there.

topic: A contractor is questioned about delays that caused a construction project to fail
text:
Q: Mr. Harmon, you were the general contractor on the Riverside Commons project, correct?

A: I was the general contractor, yes. Though I'd point out that my scope was modified three times before we even broke ground.

Q: I'm asking about your role. You were the general contractor?

A: Yes. I just said that.

Q: And the project was scheduled for completion on March 15th of last year?

A: That was the date in the original contract. Which, as I mentioned, was modified.

Q: Was March 15th the completion date or not?

A: It was *a* completion date. The original one. Before the owner made changes that fundamentally altered the timeline.

Q: So you're saying you weren't responsible for meeting that deadline?

A: I'm saying the deadline became meaningless when they added 4,000 square feet to the second floor in November.

Q: Mr. Harmon, I'm going to ask you to answer my questions directly. Were you contractually obligated to complete the project by March 15th?

A: Under the original contract, yes. Under the modified scope, no. Which version would you like to discuss?

Q: Let's discuss why the project wasn't completed until September.

A: All right. Would you like the full explanation, or are you going to interrupt me again?

Q: Just answer the question.

A: You haven't asked one. You made a statement.

Q: Why wasn't the project completed until September?

A: Because you cannot add six months of work to a project and expect the original deadline to hold. That's not how construction works.

Q: Is it your testimony that every day of delay was caused by the owner's changes?

A: I'm testifying that the delays had causes. Multiple causes. If you want to discuss them individually, I'm happy to do that. If you want me to accept blame for things outside my control, I won't.

---

topic: A contractor is questioned about delays that caused a construction project to fail
text:
Q: You submitted a schedule update on October 3rd, didn't you?

A: I'd have to see the document to confirm the exact date.

Q: I'm showing you what's been marked as Exhibit 14. Is that your signature?

A: Yes.

Q: And the date?

A: October 3rd.

Q: This schedule shows substantial completion by February 28th. Do you see that?

A: I see that, yes.

Q: But you didn't reach substantial completion until August. That's six months late.

A: Approximately, yes.

Q: So this schedule was wrong.

A: The schedule was accurate when I submitted it.

Q: How can it be accurate if you missed it by six months?

A: Because a schedule is based on assumptions. When those assumptions change, the outcome changes.

Q: What assumptions changed?

A: The assumption that the structural engineer's drawings were correct, for one.

Q: You're blaming the engineer?

A: I'm explaining what happened. You asked what changed.

Q: When did you discover the engineering problem?

A: November. Around the 15th, I believe.

Q: And you didn't notify the owner until January?

A: That's not accurate.

Q: I have an email here dated January 8th—

A: That's the formal RFI. I notified the owner's representative verbally in November and sent a written summary on November 22nd. I have that email if you'd like to see it.

Q: We'll get to your documents. I'm asking about the formal notice.

A: And I'm telling you the formal notice wasn't the first notice. Those are different things.

---

topic: A contractor is questioned about delays that caused a construction project to fail
text:
Q: How many subcontractors did you have on this project?

A: Yes.

Q: Did you issue written warnings?

A: Yes.

Q: How many?

A: Three, I believe.

Q: Over what period?

A: About five weeks.

Q: And then you terminated them?

A: Then I terminated them and brought in a replacement, yes.

Q: How much time did that replacement process cost?

A: Three weeks, roughly.

---

topic: A contractor is questioned about delays that caused a construction project to fail
text:
Q: Mr. Dillon, I want to ask about the concrete pours in December.

A: All right.

Q: There were three scheduled pours that month, correct?

A: I don't recall the exact number without looking at the schedule.

Q: Does three sound right?

A: It might. I'd want to verify.

Q: Let's say three. How many were actually completed?

A: Again, I'd need to check the records.

Q: You don't remember?

A: I remember there were weather delays. I don't remember the specific count off the top of my head.

Q: You were the project manager and you don't remember whether you completed your concrete pours?

A: I was project manager on a fourteen-month project that ended two years ago. I'm not going to guess at numbers when I can give you accurate information from the records.

Q: Fair enough. Let me show you Exhibit 22. Does this refresh your recollection?

A: Yes. Two pours were completed in December. One was pushed to January.

Q: Why was it pushed?

A: Weather. It says right there—temperatures dropped below the threshold for proper curing.

Q: Couldn't you have used heating blankets?

A: On a pour that size? The cost would have been significant, and the owner had already declined that option.

Q: The owner declined it.

A: Yes.

Q: When?

A: At the project meeting on December 4th. It's in the minutes.

Q: So the delay was the owner's decision.

A: The delay was caused by weather. How we responded to it was a joint decision, and the owner chose the less expensive option, which meant waiting.

---

topic: A contractor is questioned about delays that caused a construction project to fail
text:
Q: Let's talk about the HVAC installation.

A: Okay.

Q: That was significantly behind schedule, wasn't it?

A: It was behind, yes.

Q: How far behind?

A: At one point, about eight weeks.

Q: Eight weeks is significant on a twelve-month project.

A: It is.

Q: Whose fault was that?

A: I'm not sure I'd characterize it as anyone's "fault."

Q: Someone was responsible.

A: Several factors contributed.

Q: Such as?

A: Equipment lead times were longer than quoted. The manufacturer had supply chain issues.

Q: Did you account for supply chain issues in your original schedule?

A: I accounted for standard lead times based on the manufacturer's quotes.

Q: But not additional contingency?

A: There was contingency built in. Just not eight weeks of it.

Q: Why not?

A: Because if I built eight weeks of contingency into every trade, the project would take three years and no one would have hired me.

Q: So you took a risk.

A: I made a reasonable assumption based on industry standards.

Q: And it didn't work out.

A: The assumption was wrong, yes. But it wasn't unreasonable when I made it.

Q: The owner might disagree with that.

A: The owner is welcome to. That doesn't change whether it was reasonable.

Q: Did you consider alternative suppliers when the delays became apparent?

A: I did. The alternatives were either more expensive or had even longer lead times.

Q: So you just waited.

A: I communicated the issue to the owner, presented options, and we made a decision together. That's not "just waiting." That's managing a problem.

topic: A driver is deposed about the events leading up to a multi-vehicle collision
text:
Q: Mr. Hernandez, let's talk about the moments before the collision. You were traveling northbound on Route 9, correct?

Q: It changes?

A: Yeah, it—there's a section where it goes up to fifty-five, and then it drops back down. I don't know exactly where the signs are. I drive it every day but I don't, you know, memorize where each sign is.

Q: So you're not certain what the posted limit was at the point of impact?

A: I'm saying I thought it was fifty. If you're telling me it's forty, then I guess it's forty. I'm not arguing with you. I just don't have a picture of the sign in my head.

Q: Fair enough. Now, when did you first become aware of the vehicle in front of you?

A: Which vehicle?

Q: The silver Honda that you struck.

A: Okay, but I didn't—I struck the pickup. The pickup hit the Honda. I think. That's how I remember it.

Q: You struck a pickup truck?

A: The red one. Yes.

Q: Let me check my notes here. You're saying you made contact with a red pickup truck, not the silver Honda?

A: That's what I've been saying since the accident. I don't know where the Honda is coming from. I mean, I saw it, but I didn't hit it. Did I?

Q: I'm asking you, Mr. Hernandez.

A: Then no. I hit the pickup.

---

topic: A driver is deposed about the events leading up to a multi-vehicle collision
text:
Q: Ms. Okonkwo, you were driving a white Nissan Altima on the date in question?

A: Yes, that's correct.

Q: And you were traveling westbound on Miller Avenue?

A: I was, yes.

Q: At approximately what time?

A: Around five-thirty. Maybe a little after. I'm not certain of the exact minute.

Q: Were you in the left lane or the right lane?

Q: And at some point, you applied your brakes?

A: Yes.

Q: Why?

A: Because—well, wait. Are you asking why I braked at a specific moment, or are you asking why I was braking generally in stop-and-go traffic?

Q: Let's start with the specific moment before the collision.

A: Okay. Then I braked because the car in front of me braked. That's what happens in that kind of traffic.

Q: Did you notice anything unusual about how the car in front of you braked?

A: Unusual how?

Q: Did it brake suddenly? Gradually?

A: I don't—I mean, it braked. I braked. I don't know how to quantify that for you. It was traffic. Everyone brakes.

Q: Did you come to a complete stop?

A: Before the impact?

Q: Yes.

A: I think so. I think I was fully stopped or almost stopped. It happened very fast.

Q: Almost stopped or fully stopped?

A: I want to say fully stopped, but I can't swear to it. I'm trying to be accurate here.

---

topic: A driver is deposed about the events leading up to a multi-vehicle collision
text:
Q: Let's go back to the intersection. You said the light was green when you entered?

Q: A solid green, not a green arrow?

A: Yes.

---

topic: A driver is deposed about the events leading up to a multi-vehicle collision
text:
Q: Tell me what happened after you heard the first impact.

A: After I heard it?

A: Maybe one. Maybe less. I'm not going to give you a number I'm not sure about.

Q: I appreciate that. Were you able to see the driver of the vehicle that struck you from behind?

A: Not at that moment. Later. At the scene.

---

topic: A driver is deposed about the events leading up to a multi-vehicle collision

topic: A former employee is deposed about discriminatory remarks made by a supervisor
text:
Q: Ms. Patterson, I want to direct your attention to the meeting on March 14th. You were present?

A: Yes.

Q: And Mr. Hendricks was there as well?

A: Yes.

Q: During that meeting, did Mr. Hendricks make any comments about the female employees on the marketing team?

Q: What did he say?

A: He said something along the lines of... look, I've been over this in my written statement, in the EEOC filing, in the interview with HR. He said the women on the team were "too emotional to handle client-facing work." That's the quote.

A: I just did.

Q: Let me ask you again. Did you see him fall?

A: I just answered that. I saw him on the floor. I did not see the fall itself.

Q: You heard a crash and turned around?

A: Correct.

Q: How long between the crash and when you turned?

A: I couldn't tell you precisely. A second? Two seconds? I wasn't timing myself.

Q: But you never reported this incident to your supervisor, did you?

A: Other people were already responding. Jennifer Cho was on the radio immediately. There were four or five people around David within thirty seconds. I didn't see what additional value my report would add to the five reports presumably already being made.

Q: So you made an assumption that others had reported it?

A: It wasn't an assumption. I watched Jennifer pick up the radio.

Q: Did you hear what she said into the radio?

A: No.

Q: Then you don't actually know she was reporting the incident, do you?

A: I suppose she could have been ordering a pizza, counselor, but that seems unlikely given the context.

topic: A witness is questioned about a workplace injury they observed but did not report
text:
Q: When you saw Mr. Patterson's hand get caught in the conveyor belt, what did you do?

A: I froze for a second. Then someone hit the emergency stop.

Q: Someone. Who?

A: I don't know. Someone closer to the button.

Q: You don't know. You were standing right there and you don't know who hit the emergency stop?

A: There were probably eight people in that area. I was focused on Derek's hand, not on who was pressing what button.

Q: Let's slow down. Let's slow way down. You're telling me you witnessed a serious injury—

A: Yes.

Q: —and you can't identify a single other person who was present?

A: I didn't say that. You asked about the button specifically. I can tell you who else was working that line. You want the full list?

Q: I want to understand why you didn't fill out an incident report.

A: Because Terri Marsh filled one out. She told me she was handling it.

Q: Did you see her fill it out?

A: Did I watch her physically write on the form? No. She told me she was handling the paperwork.

Q: And that was enough for you?

A: Terri's the line supervisor. That's her job.

Q: Your company policy states that any witness to a workplace injury—

A: I know what the policy states.

Q: —shall complete an independent incident report within twenty-four hours.

A: I'm aware of the policy.

Q: And yet you didn't follow it?

A: I relied on my supervisor's instruction. If that was wrong, it was wrong. But I did what I was told.

topic: A witness is questioned about a workplace injury they observed but did not report
text:
Q: Mr. Okonkwo, thank you for being here today.

A: Of course.

Q: I understand you've worked at Rayburn Manufacturing for six years?

A: Six and a half, yes.

Q: And you have an excellent safety record yourself, is that fair to say?

A: I've never had an incident, if that's what you mean.

Q: That is what I mean. So you understand the importance of safety protocols?

A: I do.

Q: Good. Then help me understand something. On July 19th, you witnessed Angela Reyes sustain a back injury while lifting a crate without assistance, correct?

A: I saw her lift a crate. I saw her react like she'd hurt herself.

Q: React how?

A: She straightened up suddenly and put her hand on her lower back. Her face— she looked like she was in pain.

Q: Did she say anything?

A: She might have. I was about fifteen feet away. The machinery is loud.

Q: Did you go to check on her?

A: I finished what I was doing—securing a pallet—and then yes, I walked over. Maybe ninety seconds later.

Q: And when you reached her?

A: She said she'd tweaked something but she was fine.

Q: "Tweaked something." Those were her words?

A: Something like that.

Q: Did you encourage her to report the injury?

A: She said she was fine.

Q: That wasn't my question.

A: No, I didn't specifically tell her to file a report.

Q: You didn't think a potential back injury warranted documentation?

A: She said she was fine. Angela's been doing this work longer than I have. I'm not going to tell a senior employee how to handle herself.

Q: Even though you just testified you understand the importance of safety protocols?

A: I understand them. I also understand that people are adults.

topic: A witness is questioned about a workplace injury they observed but did not report
text:
Q: I'm going to ask you one more time, Ms. Chen. You saw the shelf unit collapse?

A: I've answered this three times now. Yes.

Q: And you saw it strike Ricardo Vega?

A: I saw him go down. I couldn't tell you the exact point of contact.

Q: But you saw him go down.

A: Yes.

Q: Was he unconscious?

A: I don't— I couldn't tell from where I was standing.

Q: You couldn't tell if a man was conscious or unconscious?

A: He wasn't moving. Whether that means unconscious or stunned or just trying to figure out what happened, I couldn't say.

Q: Did you call for help?

A: Other people were already responding.

Q: That's not what I asked. Did you personally call for help?

A: No.

Q: Did you personally render any assistance?

A: No.

Q: Did you personally report the incident to management?

A: No.

Q: Did you personally do anything at all?

A: I stayed out of the way so that people who actually knew first aid could get to him.

Q: That's your explanation?

A: That's what happened.

Q: You're trained in first aid, aren't you, Ms. Chen?

A: Basic first aid. The certification course the company makes everyone take.

Q: So you do know first aid.

A: I know how to put a bandage on a cut. Ricardo had a shelving unit on top of him. What exactly would you have liked me to do?

topic: An accountant is deposed about transactions they processed on behalf of a client
text:
Q: Mr. Hartwell, let me take you back to the wire transfer dated March 15th, 2021. You processed that transaction, correct?

A: I processed hundreds of transactions in March 2021. You'll need to be more specific.

Q: I'm referring to the $2.3 million wire to Coastal Ventures LLC.

A: If you're showing me Exhibit 14, then yes, I see my initials on that form.

Q: So you processed it?

A: My initials are on the form. That's what I just said.

Q: Did you have any concerns about that transaction at the time?

A: Define "concerns."

Q: Did anything about the transaction strike you as unusual, irregular, or worthy of additional scrutiny?

A: Every transaction over $1 million received additional scrutiny. That was standard protocol. So in that sense, yes, it received scrutiny. In the sense you're implying, no.

Q: I'm not implying anything, Mr. Hartwell. I'm asking questions.

A: Then perhaps you could ask them more precisely.

Q: Did you flag this transaction for compliance review?

A: I followed the procedures that were in place at the time.

Q: That's not what I asked. Did you personally flag this transaction for compliance review, yes or no?

A: No.

Q: Why not?

A: Because it didn't meet the criteria for flagging. The recipient was a known vendor, the amount was consistent with prior payments, and I had authorization from the client. I'm not sure what else you want me to say.

---

topic: An accountant is deposed about transactions they processed on behalf of a client
text:
Q: Ms. Chen, how long did you serve as the accountant of record for Whitmore Holdings?

A: Approximately four years. From 2019 to 2023.

Q: And in that time, you became familiar with their typical transaction patterns?

A: Yes, reasonably familiar.

Q: Let's talk about the payments to something called "Apex Consulting Group." Do you recall those?

A: I recall the name, yes.

Q: How many payments did you process to Apex Consulting Group?

A: I don't have that number memorized. If you have records, I'm happy to review them.

Q: I'm asking what you remember.

A: And I'm telling you I don't have a specific number in my memory. There were several. More than five, fewer than fifty. That's the best I can do without documentation.

Q: Did you ever meet anyone from Apex Consulting Group?

A: No.

Q: Did you ever verify that Apex Consulting Group performed actual services for Whitmore Holdings?

A: That wasn't my role.

Q: Whose role was it?

A: The client's. I processed payments based on invoices I received. I wasn't hired to audit their vendors.

Q: So you just processed whatever invoices came across your desk?

A: I processed invoices that were approved by authorized representatives of my client, consistent with my engagement letter. That's what accountants do, Counselor.

Q: Did it ever occur to you that these payments might not be legitimate?

A: No. And frankly, I'm not sure what basis you have for suggesting otherwise.

---

topic: An accountant is deposed about transactions they processed on behalf of a client
text:
Q: Mr. Okonkwo, I want to ask you about the December 2022 transactions.

A: All right.

A: Not specifically, no.

Q: Let me show you what's been marked as Exhibit 7. Take your time.

A: Thank you. Yes, I see the transfers you're referring to.

A: That's what it says.

Q: Had you ever processed payments to Meridian Capital Partners before December 2022?

A: Not that I recall.

A: New vendors and partners are established all the time. Business relationships evolve. I had no reason to question it.

Q: Who instructed you to make these payments?

A: I would need to check my records. Presumably Mr. Whitmore or someone with signatory authority.

Q: You don't remember?

A: No. I've answered that.

---

topic: An accountant is deposed about transactions they processed on behalf of a client
text:
Q: Ms. Petrov, you testified earlier that you maintained detailed records of all transactions.

A: That's correct.

Q: Meticulous records, I think you said.

A: Yes.

Q: Then why can't you locate any documentation for the $175,000 payment to Larkspur Industries?

A: I didn't say I couldn't locate it. I said it wasn't included in the materials I was asked to bring today.

Q: You were asked to bring all records related to your work for Mr. Davenport.

A: I brought seventeen boxes of documents, Counsel. If something is missing, it's an oversight, not a conspiracy.

Q: I didn't suggest it was a conspiracy.

A: The tone of your questions suggests otherwise.

Q: Let's stay focused on the documents. When can you produce the Larkspur Industries records?

A: When I return to my office and have adequate time to search for them. Presumably within a week.

Q: Did the Larkspur payment concern you at the time you processed it?

A: No.

Q: Not at all?

A: Asked and answered. No.

Q: $175,000 to a company with no apparent connection to Mr. Davenport's business, and you had no concerns?

A: I wasn't aware of any lack of connection. Mr. Davenport had diverse business interests. I processed what I was instructed to process with proper authorization.

Q: You keep saying "proper authorization." What did that authorization look like?

A: A signed payment request from Mr. Davenport or, in some cases, a verbal instruction followed by written confirmation. Standard practice.

Q: Do you have the written confirmation for the Larkspur payment?

A: As I said, I'll need to check my records.

---

topic: An accountant is deposed about transactions they processed on behalf of a client
text:
Q: Let's discuss the quarterly payments to Brennan & Associates.

A: Fine.

Q: You processed those payments for approximately two years, correct?

A: Sounds about right.

Q: Always the same amount?

A: No. They varied.

Q: Ballpark it for me.

A: I'd rather not guess when you presumably have the actual figures in front of you.

Q: Were the Brennan & Associates invoices detailed?

A: They included descriptions of work performed, yes. Whether that meets your definition of "detailed," I couldn't say.

topic: A former employee is deposed about discriminatory remarks made by a supervisor
text:
Q: Ms. Patterson, I'd like to ask you about a meeting that took place in March of 2022. Do you recall a department meeting where Mr. Hendricks discussed the promotion cycle?

A: Yes, I remember that meeting.

Q: Who was present?

A: Myself, David Chen, Raquel Simmons, and I believe Tom Forester was there as well. And Mr. Hendricks, of course.

Q: During that meeting, did Mr. Hendricks make any comments about employees in the department?

A: He made several comments. Could you be more specific about what you're asking?

Q: Of course. Did he make any comments that referenced the age of any employees?

A: Yes. He said that the promotion track was really designed for people who still had, and I'm quoting here, "enough runway left to make it worthwhile."

Q: And what did you understand that to mean?

A: I understood it to mean that older employees shouldn't expect to be promoted because they'd be retiring before the company saw a return on the investment.

Q: Did anyone respond to that comment in the meeting?

A: No. The room was quiet. I remember David shifted in his chair, but no one said anything.

Q: Did you say anything?

A: I did not.

Q: Was there any other occasion where Mr. Hendricks made similar remarks?

A: There were several occasions, yes.

Q: Let's take them one at a time. Can you describe the next instance you recall?

A: About two weeks later, he stopped by my desk and asked when I was planning to "wind things down." I was forty-seven at the time.

Q: What did you say in response?

A: I told him I wasn't planning to wind anything down. He laughed and walked away.

---

topic: A former employee is deposed about discriminatory remarks made by a supervisor
text:
Q: Mr. Okonkwo, how long did you report directly to Diane Fessler?

A: Approximately fourteen months. From when I joined the team in January 2021 until she was reassigned in March 2022.

Q: During those fourteen months, did you ever hear Ms. Fessler make comments about employees' national origins?

A: I did.

Q: Tell me about the first time you heard such a comment.

A: It was during a team lunch. We were discussing a project delay, and she said something to the effect that she wasn't surprised because—and I want to get this right—she said, "That's what happens when you hire people who learned English as a second language. Everything takes twice as long."

Q: Who was she referring to?

A: I assumed she meant Priya Sharma. Priya had been leading that project.

Q: Was Priya present at this lunch?

A: No, she was not.

Q: How did you react when you heard this?

A: I didn't react outwardly. I continued eating.

Q: Did you report this comment to anyone?

A: Not at that time, no.

Q: Why not?

A: I'd been with the company for less than two months. I wasn't sure what the protocol was, and frankly, I wasn't sure anyone would take it seriously.

Q: Did there come a time when you did report Ms. Fessler's comments?

A: Yes. After the third or fourth incident, I spoke with HR.

Q: Approximately when was that?

A: August of 2021.

Q: And what was the result of that report?

A: I was told they would look into it. I never heard anything further.

---

topic: A former employee is deposed about discriminatory remarks made by a supervisor
text:
Q: You mentioned that Mr. Vaughn made a comment during the holiday party. Let's slow down there. What month was this party?

A: Correct.

Q: Where was the party held?

A: At the Marriott on Congress Street. They'd rented out a ballroom.

A: I was standing near the bar area with a small group.

Q: Who else was in that group?

A: Janet Liu, Marcus Reed, and Sarah—I don't recall her last name. She was a contractor.

Q: Was Mr. Vaughn part of your group, or did he approach?

A: He approached. He'd been making the rounds, talking to different clusters of people.

Q: What did he say when he joined your group?

A: He made small talk at first. Asked about the holidays, that sort of thing.

Q: And then?

A: And then Janet mentioned she was hoping to take extended leave in the spring for her wedding. Mr. Vaughn said, "Another one bites the dust," and then he said—he looked at me and Marcus—he said, "You two better pick up the slack. You know how it goes once the ring goes on."

Q: What did you understand him to mean?

A: That Janet would become less committed to her work after getting married. That her priorities would shift.

Q: Did you respond?

A: I said something like, "Janet's one of the hardest workers here." He just shrugged and moved on to another group.

---

topic: A former employee is deposed about discriminatory remarks made by a supervisor
text:
Q: I want to be precise about the timing. You said this conversation with Mr. Ellis happened in his office. Was anyone else present?

A: No, it was just the two of us.

Q: And this was after your performance review?

A: I had asked about the timeline for the senior analyst position. Whether I should apply.

A: I understood him to be referring to my being a single mother.

topic: A former employee is deposed about discriminatory remarks made by a supervisor
text:
Q: Mr. Tanaka, you've testified that you overheard a conversation between Ms. Rourke and another manager. Let's go through that carefully. Where were you when you heard this conversation?

A: I was in the copy room. It's adjacent to Ms. Rourke's office.

Q: Was the door to her office open?

A: It was partially open. Maybe six inches.

Q: Could you see the people speaking?

A: Not clearly. I could see movement through the gap, but I couldn't make out faces.

Q: How did you know it was Ms. Rourke speaking?

A: I recognized her voice. I'd worked with her for three years.

Q: And the other person?

A: I believe it was Greg Harmon, but I'm less certain. The voice sounded like his.

Q: What did you hear Ms. Rourke say?

A: She was talking about the new hires. She said something like, "I don't know why corporate keeps pushing diversity hires on us. Half of them can barely do the job."

A: Yes.

A: She was a junior project coordinator. She'd been hired about two months before this conversation.

A: He laughed. I heard him say, "You're not wrong."

Q: Did you report what you overheard?

A: I did, about a week later. I reported it to the ethics hotline.

Q: Did anyone follow up with you?

A: Yes. I received a call from someone in HR about ten days after I made the report. They took a statement and said they'd be in touch. That was the last I heard of it.

topic: A building inspector is deposed about a structural assessment they signed off on
text:
Q: Mr. Harrell, you signed the structural assessment for 4200 Commerce Street on March 14th, 2022, correct?

A: Yes.

Q: And that assessment indicated the building was structurally sound?

A: That's what the report says.

Q: I'm asking what you concluded, Mr. Harrell.

A: I concluded what's in the report. Structurally sound.

Q: Did you personally inspect the basement foundation walls?

A: I inspected the accessible areas of the basement, yes.

Q: That's not what I asked. I asked about the foundation walls specifically.

A: And I'm telling you I inspected the accessible areas. Some of those areas included foundation walls. Some areas were obstructed.

Q: Obstructed by what?

A: Storage. Equipment. The usual. You want me to list every box?

Q: I want you to answer my questions directly. What percentage of the foundation walls would you estimate you actually observed?

A: I don't carry a measuring tape for walls I can't see, Counselor.

Q: Give me your best estimate.

A: Sixty percent. Maybe. I'm not going to guess beyond that.

Q: So forty percent of the foundation walls were not inspected, yet you certified the structure as sound?

A: I certified based on what was observable and consistent with standard practice. Which it was.

topic: A building inspector is deposed about a structural assessment they signed off on
text:
Q: Ms. Delgado, how long have you worked as a building inspector for the city?

A: Eleven years this past June.

Q: In those eleven years, approximately how many structural assessments have you completed?

A: I couldn't give you an exact number. Hundreds. Possibly over a thousand.

Q: And in your experience, what does a thorough structural assessment require?

A: Visual inspection of load-bearing elements, foundation, roof structure, connections, signs of water damage or settling, documentation of any deficiencies—

Q: Let me stop you there. Documentation of deficiencies. You mentioned that.

A: Yes.

Q: Your report for the Greenway Tower property lists no deficiencies. None at all.

A: That's correct.

Q: A forty-year-old building with no structural deficiencies whatsoever?

A: I documented what I observed. If I didn't observe deficiencies, I didn't document them.

Q: Ms. Delgado, I'm going to ask you again. A forty-year-old commercial building. Exposed to weather, use, time. And you found nothing?

A: Asked and answered. I documented what I observed.

Q: Were you aware that the previous inspection in 2019 noted crack propagation in the eastern stairwell?

A: I was not provided the 2019 report.

Q: You didn't request prior inspection records?

A: That's not standard procedure for the scope I was assigned.

Q: Whose procedure? Yours?

A: The city's. Read the municipal code if you'd like. Section 11.4.3.

topic: A building inspector is deposed about a structural assessment they signed off on
text:
Q: Mr. Okonkwo, did you observe any water infiltration during your March inspection?

A: There was some minor staining on the lower level ceiling tiles.

Q: Minor staining. Can you describe what you mean by minor?

A: Discoloration. Consistent with past moisture exposure. Nothing active.

Q: You touched the ceiling tiles?

Q: Which areas?

A: I don't recall the specific tiles. It's been over a year. I touched several.

A: And I'm not the one asking questions I already know the answer to.

A: Yes.

Q: How many photographs?

A: I'd have to review my file to give you an exact count.
