topic: A building inspector is deposed about a structural assessment they signed off on
text:
Q: When you arrived at the property on September 8th, who let you into the building?

A: The property manager. A woman. I don't recall her name.

Q: Did she accompany you during the inspection?

A: For portions of it.

Q: Which portions?

A: She walked me through the first and second floors. Then she had other obligations.

Q: So you were unaccompanied for the remainder of the inspection?

A: That's correct.

Q: How long were you on site in total?

A: Approximately two hours.

Q: Two hours for a six-story building?

A: Yes.

Q: Mr. Fontaine, I want to make sure I understand. Two hours for six floors, a basement, and a rooftop inspection?

A: I said approximately. It may have been slightly longer.

Q: How much longer?

A: I didn't— I wasn't watching the clock. Two to two and a half hours.

Q: That's roughly twenty minutes per floor.

A: If you want to do the math that way, sure.

Q: Is twenty minutes sufficient to conduct a thorough structural assessment of a commercial floor plate?

A: It depends on the floor. It depends on the conditions. It depends on what you're looking for.

Q: What were you looking for?

A: Structural integrity. Signs of failure. Exactly what I was hired to assess.

Q: And you felt two hours was adequate to make that determination with confidence?

A: I made the determination I was qualified to make in the time I was there. If you have a different opinion about how long it should take, you're welcome to get your own inspector's license.

topic: A building inspector is deposed about a structural assessment they signed off on
text:
Q: Dr. Reeves, you indicated in your report that the support columns on the third floor showed no signs of compromise.

A: That's correct.

Q: What does "no signs of compromise" mean in practical terms?

A: No visible cracking, spalling, deflection, or rust staining that would indicate reinforcement corrosion.

Q: Visible being the key word.

A: Excuse me?

Q: You said visible. You're describing what you could see with your eyes.

A: That's what a visual inspection is, yes.

Q: Did you conduct any testing beyond visual inspection?

A: That was outside my scope of engagement.

Q: Who determined that scope?

A: The client. Wexford Property Holdings.

Q: So the building owner told you what to look for, and you looked for that and nothing more?

A: The client engaged me for a Level One assessment. Level One is visual. If they wanted invasive testing, they would have requested Level Two.

Q: Did you recommend they pursue Level Two?

A: I don't recall if I made a specific recommendation.

Q: Your report doesn't mention any such recommendation.

A: Then perhaps I didn't make one.

Q: Even though you knew a visual inspection has limitations?

A: Every inspection has limitations. Every methodology has limitations. I conducted the assessment I was engaged to conduct. I documented my findings accurately. If counsel is suggesting I should have done someone else's job in addition to my own, I'd appreciate him saying so directly.

Q: I'm simply trying to understand what you did and didn't do, Dr. Reeves.

A: Then I suggest you read the report more carefully. It's quite clear.

topic: A neighbor is questioned about noise complaints and a confrontation they witnessed
text:
Q: Mr. Hartley, you live at 4412 Crescent Drive, is that correct?

topic: A neighbor is questioned about noise complaints and a confrontation they witnessed
text:
Q: You called the non-emergency police line on September 14th, correct?

A: That's correct.

Q: What time did you place that call?

A: I believe it was around 11:45 p.m.

Q: You believe, or you know?

A: I didn't write it down. Somewhere between 11:30 and midnight.

Q: Fine. What did you report during that call?

A: I reported excessive noise from 4414 Crescent.

Q: Was this your first noise complaint about that address?

A: No.

Q: How many previous complaints had you made?

A: I don't have an exact count.

Q: Estimate.

A: Maybe four or five over the past year.

Q: Four or five. And were those complaints about music as well?

A: Some were music. Some were parties. One was about his dogs barking at three in the morning.

Q: Let's get back to September 14th. After you called the police, what did you do?

A: I went to bed. Tried to, anyway.

Q: Did you witness any physical altercation that night?

A: I saw pushing. Through my window.

Q: Who pushed whom?

A: I couldn't tell who started it. They were both—it happened fast.

Q: But you saw pushing. Did you see anyone fall?

A: Mrs. Chen stumbled. I don't know if she fell completely.

Q: You don't know. Did you continue watching?

A: I called 911 at that point.

topic: A neighbor is questioned about noise complaints and a confrontation they witnessed
text:
Q: Ms. Hartley, describe your relationship with Linda Chen prior to September 14th.

A: We were friendly. Are friendly. We'd chat at the mailbox, that sort of thing.

Q: And your relationship with the defendant?

A: Cordial. Barely cordial, if I'm being honest.

Q: Why barely cordial?

A: He's not the most considerate neighbor. The noise, the parking, the general attitude.

Q: Let's focus on the confrontation. You stated you were on your porch. Why were you on your porch at 11:30 at night?

A: Because the bass was rattling my windows and I couldn't sleep.

Q: So you went outside to do what, exactly?

A: To sit. To get some air. To see if anyone else was as fed up as I was. Do I need a reason to be on my own porch?

Q: I'm simply trying to establish—

A: I was on my porch. That's where I was. That's why I saw what I saw.

Q: What did you see?

A: I saw Linda walk up to Marcus's door. I saw him come out. I saw them argue. I saw him grab her arm.

Q: He grabbed her arm?

A: Yes.

Q: Which arm?

A: Her left arm. He grabbed it right above the elbow and yanked her toward the steps.

Q: Are you certain it was her left arm?

A: I just said it was her left arm. Yes. I'm certain.

Q: Then what happened?

A: She pulled away, lost her balance, and fell onto the lawn. He went back inside and slammed the door.

Q: Did she appear injured?

A: She was holding her wrist when she got up. She was crying.

topic: A neighbor is questioned about noise complaints and a confrontation they witnessed
text:
Q: How far is your porch from Mr. Webb's driveway?

A: I don't know exactly. Maybe forty feet? Fifty?

Q: And there's lighting in that area?

A: There's a streetlight. Marcus has a porch light. It was bright enough.

Q: Bright enough for what?

A: Bright enough to see what was happening.

Q: Could you see facial expressions from that distance?

A: I could see enough to know they were angry.

Q: That's not what I asked. Could you see facial expressions?

A: Not in detail, no.

Q: Could you hear the specific words being exchanged?

A: Some of them.

Q: Which words specifically?

A: I heard Marcus say "get the hell out of here." I heard Linda say something about calling the police.

Q: Something about calling the police. What exactly?

A: I don't remember the exact phrasing.

Q: You remember "get the hell out of here" exactly, but not what Mrs. Chen said?

A: He was louder. He was shouting. She was more—her voice didn't carry the same way.

Q: I see. Now, you mentioned in your police statement that Mr. Webb was intoxicated. How did you determine that?

A: He was stumbling. Slurring.

Q: You could hear slurring from forty or fifty feet away?

A: When he was shouting, yes. The words were running together.

Q: Have you ever seen Mr. Webb intoxicated before?

A: A few times.

Q: So you're familiar with how he presents when intoxicated?

A: Unfortunately, yes.

topic: A neighbor is questioned about noise complaints and a confrontation they witnessed
text:
Q: Prior to September 14th, had you ever spoken to Mr. Webb directly about the noise?

A: Once. Maybe twice.

Q: Which is it?

A: Twice.

Q: When?

A: Once was last summer. Once was a few months before the incident.

Q: And how did those conversations go?

A: About how you'd expect.

Q: I don't know what I'd expect, Ms. Hartley. That's why I'm asking you.

A: He wasn't receptive. The first time he said he'd keep it down and didn't. The second time he told me to mind my own business.

Q: Those were his exact words? Mind your own business?

A: Words to that effect.

Q: Were there any witnesses to these prior conversations?

A: My husband was there for the second one.

Q: Anyone else?

A: No.

Q: Getting back to the 14th—

A: Can we take a break soon? I've been here for two hours.

Q: We're almost finished with this line of questioning. On the 14th, after Mrs. Chen fell, did anyone else come outside?

A: The Morettis across the street turned their lights on. I don't think they came out.

Q: Did you approach Mrs. Chen after she fell?

A: I walked over to check on her, yes.

Q: What did she say to you?

A: She said he'd grabbed her. She said he'd been drinking. She asked me if I'd seen what happened.

Q: And what did you tell her?

A: I told her I saw everything.

topic: A witness is questioned about a workplace injury they observed but did not report
text:
Q: Mr. Delacroix, you were present on the loading dock on September 14th of last year, correct?

A: I was.

Q: And at some point that afternoon, you observed an incident involving a forklift?

A: I observed Marcus Chen get his left foot run over by a forklift operated by Dave Simmons. That happened at approximately 3:15 p.m., about forty feet from where I was standing near Bay 7.

Q: You seem to have a detailed recollection.

A: I do. I've worked that dock for eleven years. I know what I saw.

Q: Fair enough. Now, after this incident occurred, what did you do?

A: I walked over to check on Marcus. His boot was torn. He was on the ground. Dave had stopped the forklift and was just sitting there looking pale.

Q: Did you call for medical assistance?

A: No.

Q: Did you report the incident to a supervisor?

A: No, I did not.

Q: Why not?

A: Because Marcus told me not to. He said he was fine, said he didn't want Dave to get written up. I respected his wishes.

Q: You respected his wishes over company safety protocol?

A: I made a judgment call. Marcus was conscious, talking, and explicitly asked me to stay quiet. So I did.

Q: Do you regret that decision now?

A: I understand why you're asking that. The answer is I did what I thought was right at the time, and I'd make the same call again under the same circumstances.

topic: A witness is questioned about a workplace injury they observed but did not report
text:
Q: Ms. Patterson, I want to direct your attention to the afternoon of March 3rd. You were working in the fabrication area?

A: Yes.

Q: And you witnessed an accident involving one of the hydraulic presses?

A: I... yes, I saw something happen.

Q: Something happen. Can you be more specific?

A: Linda Okonkwo got her hand caught. Just for a second. She pulled it out.

Q: Just for a second. Was she injured?

A: I don't know. I wasn't close enough to see.

Q: How far away were you?

A: Maybe fifteen feet? Twenty?

Q: Fifteen to twenty feet. That's close enough to see someone's hand get caught in a hydraulic press, wouldn't you agree?

A: I saw her hand go in and come out. That's what I saw.

Q: Did you see blood?

A: I don't remember.

Q: You don't remember whether you saw blood when someone's hand was caught in a hydraulic press?

A: I'm telling you what I remember. I'm not going to make things up to satisfy your questions.

Q: I'm not asking you to make anything up. I'm asking what you observed.

A: And I've answered that. Three times now.

Q: Let's move on. Did you report this incident?

A: No.

Q: Any particular reason?

A: Linda went right back to work. If she was hurt, she didn't show it. I figured if something needed reporting, she'd report it herself.

topic: A witness is questioned about a workplace injury they observed but did not report
text:
Q: You've been employed at Westfield Manufacturing for how long?

A: Seven years this April.

Q: And in your role as quality control inspector, you move throughout the facility?

A: That's correct.

Q: So you have occasion to observe work being performed in various departments?

A: Yes.

Q: On or about June 18th of last year, did you observe anything unusual in the packaging department?

A: I observed an injury, if that's what you're getting at.

Q: Tell me about that.

A: Tommy Reeves was operating the band sealer. The heating element malfunctioned—or he positioned his arm wrong, I'm not sure which—and he got a significant burn on his forearm.

Q: How significant?

A: The skin was blistered. Red. Maybe three inches long.

Q: What happened next?

A: Tommy went to the bathroom. Came back with wet paper towels wrapped around his arm. Kept working.

Q: And you?

A: I kept doing my inspections.

Q: You didn't report the injury to anyone?

A: I did not file a report, no.

Q: Even though you just described blistered skin and a three-inch burn?

A: Counsel, I'm going to be direct with you. I've seen a lot of minor injuries in seven years. Cuts, burns, bruises. Most of them don't get reported by the person they happen to. It wasn't my injury to report. That was my thinking.

topic: A witness is questioned about a workplace injury they observed but did not report
text:
Q: Now, Mr. Huang, I want to be very careful here. I want to make sure we understand exactly what you saw.

A: Okay.

Q: On November 11th, you were working in the warehouse?

A: Yes.

Q: What were your duties that day?

A: Inventory. Scanning items, checking them against the manifest.

Q: At some point, you observed an incident involving a coworker?

A: Yes.

Q: Walk me through it, please. Take your time.

A: Sure. Jerome—Jerome Washington—was up on one of the rolling ladders pulling stock from the upper shelves. The ladder shifted, and he fell. Maybe five feet. He landed on his side.

Q: Did he cry out?

A: Yeah, he made a sound when he hit.

Q: What did you do?

A: I went over to him. Asked if he was okay. He sat up after a minute, said he'd knocked the wind out of himself.

Q: Did he appear injured?

A: He was holding his ribs. Wincing.

Q: Wincing and holding his ribs. Did you offer to call someone?

A: I offered to get the supervisor. Jerome said no, don't bother, he was fine.

Q: And you accepted that?

A: He's a grown man. He said he was fine. I wasn't going to argue with him.

Q: Did you have any concerns about his condition afterward?

A: I noticed he moved slower the rest of the shift. But he finished his work and clocked out like normal.

topic: A witness is questioned about a workplace injury they observed but did not report
text:
Q: Let's cut right to it, Ms. Tran. You saw Derek Mullins get hurt on August 8th, didn't you?

A: Yes.

Q: What happened?

A: He was adjusting the tension on a conveyor belt. The wrench slipped, and his hand went into the rollers.

Q: Into the rollers. Was the conveyor running at the time?

A: It was moving, yes.

Q: So his hand went into moving machinery?

A: Briefly. He pulled it out immediately.

Q: Was he injured?

A: His knuckles were scraped up. There was blood.

Q: There was blood. What did Mr. Mullins do after that?

A: He wrapped his hand in a shop rag and finished the adjustment.

Q: He finished the adjustment with a bleeding hand wrapped in a shop rag?

A: That's what happened.

Q: And you were standing there watching this?

A: I was present, yes.

Q: Did you offer assistance?

A: I asked if he needed help. He said he had it under control.

Q: Did you report this to a supervisor?

A: I did not.

Q: Did you report it to safety personnel?

A: No.

Q: Did you fill out an incident report?

A: No.

Q: Did you document this in any way whatsoever?

A: I'm going to answer the same way I've answered the last four questions, Counsel. No. I did not. Derek handled it himself, and I let him handle it. If you want to ask me the same thing a fifth way, you can, but my answer isn't going to change.

topic: A business partner is deposed about financial records they were responsible for maintaining
text:
Q: Mr. Halverson, you were responsible for maintaining the accounts receivable ledger for the partnership, correct?

A: Yes.

Q: And that responsibility included ensuring all client payments were properly recorded?

A: Yes.

Q: So when a payment came in from Thornton Industries on March 15th of last year, you would have recorded it?

A: If a payment came in, I recorded it. That was my job.

Q: I'm asking specifically about the Thornton payment.

A: And I'm telling you I recorded every payment that came across my desk. Every single one.

Q: Then why does the ledger show no entry for March 15th?

A: Maybe because there was no payment on March 15th.

Q: We have the wire transfer confirmation, Mr. Halverson. Eighty-seven thousand dollars.

A: Then maybe you should ask the bank why it didn't hit our account until later. Maybe you should ask someone at Thornton why their confirmation dates never match actual transfer dates. Maybe you should do a little more homework before you sit here and suggest—

Q: I'm not suggesting anything. I'm asking you a question.

A: No, you're suggesting I didn't do my job. You've been suggesting it for the last hour.

Q: Let me rephrase. Did you ever see a payment from Thornton Industries for eighty-seven thousand dollars?

A: I saw a lot of payments. I maintained records for a partnership that did twelve million in revenue. So you'll have to be more specific.

Q: I'm being as specific as I can, Mr. Halverson.

A: Then we have a problem, don't we?

---

topic: A business partner is deposed about financial records they were responsible for maintaining
text:
Q: Ms. Chen, I want to turn to the quarterly reconciliation process.

A: Alright.

Q: Who was responsible for reconciling the operating account each quarter?

A: I was.

Q: And did you perform that reconciliation for Q3 of 2022?

A: I did.

Q: Walk me through how that process worked.

A: I would pull the bank statements, compare them against our internal ledger entries, identify any discrepancies, and document them in a reconciliation report.

Q: Did you identify any discrepancies in Q3?

A: A few minor ones. Timing differences mostly.

Q: What about the eighteen thousand dollar discrepancy on September 12th?

A: I don't recall that specific amount without looking at the documents.

Q: Let me refresh your recollection. Exhibit 14.

A: Okay. I see it.

Q: Does that refresh your memory?

A: It shows a variance, yes.

Q: Eighteen thousand, four hundred, and twelve dollars. That's not a "timing difference," is it?

A: I would need to see the supporting documentation to characterize it accurately.

Q: You prepared this report, Ms. Chen.

A: I prepared hundreds of reports. I'm not going to sit here and guess about something I can't fully recall just to make your job easier. If you want to show me the backup, I'm happy to review it.

Q: That's exactly what we're going to do. Exhibit 15.

A: Fine. Let's do that then.

---

topic: A business partner is deposed about financial records they were responsible for maintaining
text:
Q: Did you keep backup copies of the expense reports?

A: We've been over this.

Q: I'm asking again.

A: And I've already answered. Twice.

Q: Then answer it a third time for the record.

A: Yes. I kept backup copies. On a shared drive. Which I've told you. Which I told your colleague last month. Which I put in writing in response to your discovery requests.

Q: The shared drive that was wiped in January?

A: The shared drive that IT wiped during a routine server migration, yes.

Q: Convenient.

A: Excuse me?

Q: I said the timing seems convenient.

A: I'm sorry, is there a question there, or are you just making accusations now?

Q: Did you instruct IT to wipe that drive?

A: Absolutely not.

Q: Did you know the wipe was going to happen?

A: I knew there was a migration scheduled. I didn't know the specific date.

Q: You didn't think to make copies beforehand?

A: I thought IT was handling the transfer. That's what they told us. That's what the company-wide email said. Do you want me to find that email for you, Counselor? Because I'd be happy to.

Q: That won't be necessary.

A: I think it might be.

---

topic: A business partner is deposed about financial records they were responsible for maintaining
text:
Q: Mr. Okonkwo, let's discuss the petty cash fund.

A: Sure.

Q: You managed that fund personally?

A: I oversaw it, yes. Sandra usually handled the day-to-day.

Q: But final responsibility was yours.

A: Correct.

Q: The fund was supposed to maintain a balance of five thousand dollars.

A: That was the policy.

Q: When's the last time you verified the actual balance?

A: I couldn't give you an exact date.

Q: Ballpark.

A: Maybe... October? November of last year?

Q: So you went at least four months without checking?

A: It wasn't my only responsibility. I had a department to run.

Q: I understand. But this was also your responsibility, wasn't it?

A: One of many, yes.

Q: And when you finally did check, in February, what did you find?

A: There was a shortfall.

Q: How much?

A: Twenty-three hundred, approximately.

Q: Twenty-three hundred dollars missing, and you have no idea when it disappeared or who took it?

A: I have ideas. I just don't have proof.

Q: That's not what I asked.

A: Well, that's my answer.

---

topic: A business partner is deposed about financial records they were responsible for maintaining
text:
Q: I want to be very clear about what you're saying, Ms. Drummond.

A: I've been clear.

Q: You're testifying that you never saw the amended partnership agreement?

A: That's correct.

Q: Never saw it, never signed it, never discussed it with Mr. Farrow?

A: Asked and answered.

Q: This is your signature on page fourteen, is it not?

A: It looks like my signature.

Q: "Looks like?"

A: I didn't sign that document.

Q: So someone forged your signature?

A: I didn't say that.

Q: Then what are you saying, Ms. Drummond? Because we have a document with your signature on it, and you're telling me you never signed it. Those two things cannot both be true.

A: What I'm telling you is that I don't recall signing any amended agreement. If that's my signature, then I was clearly misled about what I was signing.

Q: Misled by whom?

A: You know exactly by whom.

Q: I need you to say it for the record.

A: Marcus. Marcus Farrow. Your client. Who handed me stacks of documents every week and said "sign here" and "initial there" and never once explained what half of them actually were.

Q: So your testimony is that you signed without reading?

A: My testimony is that I trusted my partner. Clearly, that was a mistake.

topic: A supervisor is deposed about performance reviews given to an employee who was later fired
text:
Q: Mr. Hartley, you conducted Ms. Vance's 2022 annual performance review, correct?

A: I did.

Q: And in that review, you rated her "meets expectations" in all six categories?

A: That's what the document shows.

Q: I'm asking if that's the rating you gave her.

A: Yes. I gave her those ratings.

Q: So in your professional judgment, as of March 2022, Ms. Vance was meeting expectations?

A: As of that review period, based on the criteria we use, that was my assessment at that time.

Q: That's a yes?

A: I just answered the question.

Q: Mr. Hartley, seven months later, you recommended her termination. Help me understand how an employee goes from "meets expectations" to terminated in seven months.

A: Performance can change. Circumstances can change. I don't know what you want me to say beyond that.

Q: I want you to identify what changed.

A: Her attendance became a problem. Her attitude with the team shifted. There were incidents.

Q: Incidents. Were any of these incidents documented before the termination recommendation?

A: Some were. Some were addressed verbally.

Q: Which ones were documented?

A: I'd have to see the file to give you specifics. I'm not going to guess and have you tell me later I got a date wrong.

Q: We can look at the file together. I have it right here.

A: Fine. Then let's do that.

---

topic: A supervisor is deposed about performance reviews given to an employee who was later fired
text:
Q: You were Ms. Vance's direct supervisor for how long?

A: About two and a half years.

Q: During that time, how many formal performance reviews did you give her?

A: Two. They're annual.

Q: Let's talk about the first one, in 2021. You wrote that she was—and I'm quoting—"a reliable team member who consistently produces quality work." Did I read that correctly?

A: You did.

Q: Did you believe that when you wrote it?

A: I wouldn't have written it if I didn't believe it.

Q: So she was reliable?

A: At that time.

Q: She consistently produced quality work?

A: At that time, yes.

Q: And the following year, same ratings, "meets expectations" across the board?

A: Correct.

Q: Ms. Vance was terminated four months after that second review.

A: I'm aware.

Q: Were you aware, when you gave her that "meets expectations" review, that she would be terminated four months later?

A: Of course not.

Q: So something significant must have happened in those four months.

A: Things happened, yes.

Q: What things?

A: I've already explained this. There were performance issues that developed.

Q: Developed in four months.

A: I don't know why you keep repeating the timeframe like it's impossible. Things change. People change. Work situations change. Four months is four months.

Q: I'm just trying to understand the timeline, Mr. Hartley.

A: And I'm trying to give you an answer, but you keep asking the same question different ways.

---

topic: A supervisor is deposed about performance reviews given to an employee who was later fired
text:
Q: Did you ever place Ms. Vance on a performance improvement plan?

A: No.

Q: Was that ever discussed?

A: In what sense?

Q: In any sense. Did you ever discuss with HR or anyone else whether to place her on a PIP?

A: I don't recall a specific conversation about that.

Q: You don't recall.

A: No.

Q: Is that something you would typically remember?

A: I supervise eleven people. I've had a lot of conversations with HR over the years about a lot of employees. I'm not going to sit here and manufacture a memory I don't have.

Q: I'm not asking you to manufacture anything.

A: Then I've answered your question. I don't recall.

Q: Let me ask it differently. Was there any reason Ms. Vance was not placed on a PIP before being terminated?

A: I'd have to defer to HR on the procedural piece.

Q: I'm asking about your recommendation. Did you recommend a PIP?

A: I don't believe I made a formal recommendation either way on that.

Q: Why not?

A: Because by the time we were having serious conversations about her performance, the issues were—look, a PIP is for situations where you think improvement is achievable. That's not where we were.

Q: When did you reach that conclusion?

A: I couldn't give you an exact date.

Q: A month? A range?

A: I said I couldn't give you a date. I don't have one.

---

topic: A supervisor is deposed about performance reviews given to an employee who was later fired
text:
Q: I want to ask about the comments section of the 2022 review. You wrote, quote, "Lisa continues to be an asset to the team and has shown improvement in client communication skills." Correct?

A: If that's what the document says, then yes, I wrote it.

Q: Is that accurate? Was she an asset?

A: At the time of the review, I believed she was contributing positively.

Q: "Continues to be." That suggests an ongoing state, not a one-time occurrence?

A: Sure, I suppose that's how language works.

Q: So up through March 2022, Ms. Vance was, in your words, "an asset"?

A: In the context of that review period, yes.

Q: Mr. Hartley, do you understand why I'm asking these questions?

A: I assume because you're looking for inconsistencies you can use.

Q: I'm looking for the truth.

A: Then we want the same thing.

Q: Good. Then let me ask: How does an "asset" become a liability in four months?

A: I've answered this. Multiple times now. Performance declined.

Q: In what specific way?

A: Missed deadlines. Errors in reports. Attitude problems in team meetings.

Q: Were the missed deadlines documented?

A: Some of them.

Q: Were the errors documented?

A: They were corrected.

Q: That's not what I asked. Were they documented?

A: I corrected them and moved on. That's how supervision works. You don't write up every single mistake or you'd never get anything else done.

---

topic: A supervisor is deposed about performance reviews given to an employee who was later fired
text:
Q: Who else provided input into Ms. Vance's performance reviews?

A: Just me. I was her direct supervisor.

Q: No one from HR?

A: HR has a template. They don't tell me what ratings to give.

Q: Did anyone review your ratings before they were finalized?

A: My manager signs off on them.

Q: That would be David Chen?

A: Yes.

Q: Did Mr. Chen ever express any disagreement with your ratings for Ms. Vance?

A: Not that I recall.

Q: Did he ever suggest the ratings were too high?

A: No.

Q: Too low?

A: No.

Q: So he agreed with your assessment that she met expectations?

A: He didn't disagree.

Q: That's not the same thing.

A: Isn't it?

Q: No, Mr. Hartley, it's not. Silence isn't agreement.

A: He signed the review. That's agreement.

Q: Did he read it before signing?

A: You'd have to ask him that.

Q: I'm asking what you know.

A: I know he signed it. I don't stand over people's shoulders while they read documents.

Q: Do you have any reason to believe he didn't read it?

A: I have no idea what David does or doesn't read. I gave him the review. He signed it. I filed it. That's the process.

Q: Every time?

A: Every time I've ever submitted a review, yes.

topic: A store manager is questioned about a customer slip-and-fall on their premises
text:
Q: Mr. Harmon, you were the manager on duty the morning of February 14th, correct?

A: I was.

Q: And you're aware that a customer, Mrs. Patricia Vance, fell in aisle seven that morning?

A: I'm aware she claims she fell, yes.

Q: She claims she fell. Did you see her on the floor, Mr. Harmon?

A: I saw her sitting on the floor when I arrived at the aisle. Whether she fell or simply sat down, I couldn't tell you.

Q: Was she injured?

A: She said her hip hurt.

Q: Did you call an ambulance?

A: No.

Q: Why not?

A: Because she didn't ask for one, and she walked out of the store under her own power fifteen minutes later.

Q: Let's talk about the floor in aisle seven. Was there liquid on the floor?

A: There was a small amount of moisture near the base of a refrigeration unit. Condensation. Normal for that equipment.

Q: Normal. So this was a known condition?

A: It's a known property of refrigeration, Counselor. Things get cold, moisture forms. That's physics, not negligence.

Q: Was there a wet floor sign posted?

A: There was a mat.

Q: I asked about a sign, Mr. Harmon.

A: And I'm telling you there was a mat, which addresses the condition. You want to talk about what was actually there, or what you wish had been there?

---

topic: A store manager is questioned about a customer slip-and-fall on their premises
text:
Q: How long have you worked at Greenleaf Market?

A: Six years this August.

Q: And in those six years, how many slip-and-fall incidents have occurred in the store?

A: I don't have that number memorized.

Q: More than five?

A: Possibly.

Q: More than ten?

A: I said I don't have it memorized.

Q: We can come back to exact numbers. Let's discuss your training. Were you trained on how to respond to spills?

A: Of course.

Q: What does that training involve?

A: Identifying the spill, blocking the area, cleaning it, documenting it.

Q: In that order?

A: Generally, yes.

Q: On March 3rd, when Mr. Okonkwo fell, had the spill in the produce section been blocked off?

A: The area was being actively cleaned when he walked through it.

Q: That's not what I asked. Was it blocked off?

A: An employee was standing right there with a mop.

Q: Was there a cone? A sign? Caution tape?

A: There was an employee. Holding a mop. In the spill area. Most people understand that means don't walk there.

Q: So your testimony is that a person holding a mop constitutes adequate warning?

A: My testimony is that a reasonable person sees someone mopping and doesn't walk through the wet spot. Yes. That's my testimony.

---

topic: A store manager is questioned about a customer slip-and-fall on their premises
text:
Q: Ms. Chen, I want to understand the store's inspection procedures. How often are aisles checked for hazards?

A: Every hour, documented on our safety logs.

Q: Every hour. And who performs these checks?

A: Floor staff. Whoever is assigned to that zone.

Q: On the day in question, November 19th, who was assigned to the zone that included aisle four?

A: I'd have to check the schedule.

Q: You don't remember?

A: It was eight months ago. Do you remember who was working in your office eight months ago on a random Tuesday?

Q: I'm not the one being deposed, Ms. Chen. Let's move on. The inspection log for November 19th—

A: Which you have in front of you.

Q: Yes, I do. It shows the last inspection of aisle four occurred at 9:15 a.m. The fall happened at 10:45. That's ninety minutes.

A: I can do math.

Q: So the hourly checks weren't happening hourly?

A: They were happening. That log shows checks at 9:15 and then again at—if you flip the page—10:50.

Q: After the fall.

A: The fall occurred during the window. That doesn't mean procedures weren't followed.

Q: It means the hazard existed for ninety minutes unchecked.

A: It means someone could have dropped something thirty seconds before she walked through. You can't prevent every accident. We're not psychic.

---

topic: A store manager is questioned about a customer slip-and-fall on their premises
text:
Q: Let me ask you about the broken tile. When did you first become aware of it?

A: When did I become aware of it, or when was I told about it?

Q: Is there a difference?

A: There's a significant difference. I was told about it after the incident. I wasn't personally aware before.

Q: Who told you?

A: My assistant manager.

Q: And what did he say?

A: That a customer had tripped and that there was a cracked tile in the entryway.

Q: Had that tile been cracked before the day of the incident?

A: I have no way of knowing that.

Q: You walk through that entryway every day, don't you?

A: I walk through it. I don't conduct a forensic examination of the floor every time I enter the building.

Q: Is it your testimony that you never noticed the cracked tile?

A: It's my testimony that I don't recall noticing it, which is different from saying it wasn't there.

Q: So it could have been cracked for days? Weeks?

A: Anything's possible.

Q: Months?

A: Now you're speculating.

Q: I'm asking what's possible, as you said.

A: And I'm telling you I won't sit here and validate your guesswork. I didn't notice it. I can't tell you when it cracked. That's my answer.

---

topic: A store manager is questioned about a customer slip-and-fall on their premises
text:
Q: Mr. Patel, did you personally witness Mrs. Drummond's fall?

A: No.

Q: Where were you when it happened?

A: In my office, reviewing inventory reports.

Q: How did you learn about the incident?

A: Tanya—one of our cashiers—came and got me.

Q: What did she tell you?

A: That a lady fell down in the back of the store and was upset.

Q: Upset. Did she say the woman was hurt?

A: She said she was upset.

Q: When you arrived at the scene, what did you observe?

A: I observed Mrs. Drummond sitting in a chair that one of my employees had brought her. She was holding her wrist.

Q: Was she in pain?

A: She appeared uncomfortable.

Q: Did you ask if she needed medical attention?

A: I asked if she was okay. She said she wanted to call her husband.

Q: Did you examine the area where she fell?

A: I looked at it.

Q: And what did you see?

A: I saw the floor. Some merchandise that had been knocked over.

Q: Any liquid? Any substance?

A: There was hand lotion on the floor. A bottle had broken.

Q: Had that lotion been there before she fell?

A: How would I know? I wasn't there.

Q: Did you ask anyone?

A: I asked Tanya. She didn't know either. Nobody saw a bottle break. Nobody saw her fall. She was just on the floor, and there was lotion, and everyone's supposed to accept your client's version of how those two facts connect. I documented what I saw. That's what I can speak to.

topic: A project manager is questioned about deadlines they missed on a software contract
text:
Q: Mr. Holloway, let's talk about the March 15th milestone. Can you tell me what that milestone was supposed to deliver?

A: Absolutely. March 15th was our API integration completion date—and honestly, this was one of the most ambitious targets I've ever worked with. We were connecting to three legacy systems, a cloud infrastructure that was still being built out, and a proprietary database that the client's team had developed in-house. So when we talk about "API integration," we're really talking about a massive undertaking.

Q: Was that milestone met?

A: It was not met on March 15th, no. But I have to tell you, the work we did accomplish by that date was extraordinary. My team had completed integrations with two of the three legacy systems, and we had a working prototype of the cloud connection that was already passing preliminary tests.

Q: But the contract specified all three integrations by March 15th, correct?

A: Correct, but—and this is important—the contract was drafted before anyone fully understood the scope of what we were dealing with. I actually flagged this in our kickoff meeting. I said, "This timeline is aggressive, and I love that, but we need flexibility built in."

Q: Did you get that flexibility?

A: We did! That's the thing—Mr. Reeves from Datacorp, he sat in that meeting and nodded along. He understood. We were all on the same page about pushing boundaries here.

Q: Yet the deadline remained March 15th in the contract.

A: On paper, sure. But there was an understanding. Look, I've managed dozens of projects like this, and what I've learned is that the best outcomes happen when everyone stays adaptable. That's what we were doing.

Q: When did you actually complete the third integration?

A: April 2nd. Eighteen days later. And I'll tell you something—when that integration went live, it performed better than anyone expected. My lead developer, Sandra, she actually found a way to optimize the data handoff that reduced latency by forty percent. Forty percent! The client's own technical team said they'd never seen anything like it.

Q: Was there a penalty clause in the contract for missing the March 15th date?

A: There was language about liquidated damages, yes. But penalties aside, what matters is what we delivered. And what we delivered was exceptional work.

Q: I'm asking about the penalty clause, Mr. Holloway.

A: Right, right. Yes, the clause existed. I'm not disputing that. I'm just trying to give you context because the numbers on a page don't capture what actually happened here.

topic: A project manager is questioned about deadlines they missed on a software contract
text:
Q: Good morning, Ms. Tran. I want to focus on the user acceptance testing phase. When was that scheduled to begin?

A: Good morning. UAT was scheduled for June 1st.

Q: And when did it actually begin?

A: June 1st.

Q: So that milestone was met?

A: The start date was met, yes.

Q: But?

A: But UAT requires a functional build to test against.

Q: And you didn't have a functional build on June 1st?

A: We had a build. Whether it was fully functional depends on your definition.

Q: What's your definition?

A: My definition is that a functional build allows testers to exercise core workflows without encountering blocking errors. By that standard, we were about eighty percent there.

Q: So you started UAT with a build that was eighty percent functional. That's fantastic! That's still significant progress under the circumstances, wouldn't you say?

A: I... yes, I suppose that's one way to characterize it.

Q: Help me understand the circumstances. What prevented the build from being fully functional?

A: The payment processing module had unresolved defects. Three critical bugs that our QA team had identified but hadn't yet resolved.

Q: This is really helpful, Ms. Tran. Now, whose responsibility was it to resolve those bugs before UAT?

A: That was my team's responsibility.

Q: And how long had those bugs been known before June 1st?

A: They were logged on May 19th.

Q: Thirteen days. That's a substantial window! So your team had thirteen days to fix three critical bugs and didn't complete that work?

A: That's correct. Though I'd point out that during those same thirteen days, we also fixed forty-seven other defects.

Q: But not these three.

A: Not these three.

Q: And these were the ones that mattered for UAT, weren't they? The ones that really would have made a difference?

A: They were significant, yes.

Q: How long was UAT delayed because of these three bugs?

A: Testing on the payment module was delayed eleven days.

Q: Eleven days. Did that delay have downstream effects on the final delivery date?

A: It contributed to the final delivery date being pushed back, yes. Among other factors.

topic: A project manager is questioned about deadlines they missed on a software contract
text:
Q: Mr. Okonkwo, I'm going to show you what's been marked as Exhibit 14. Do you recognize this document?

A: Yes, this is a project status report I submitted on January 22nd.

Q: And on page two, there's a section labeled "Risk Assessment." Can you read the first item listed there?

A: "Resource constraint risk: current staffing levels may be insufficient to meet February deliverables."

Q: You wrote that?

A: I did. And I'm glad you're bringing this up because I think it shows exactly how proactive we were in identifying potential issues. Most project managers wouldn't put something like that in writing—they'd hide it, minimize it. But I believe in transparency. I believe in getting problems on the table early so we can solve them.

Q: Did you request additional resources?

A: I did, multiple times. I can walk you through each request if you'd like. The first was informal, a conversation with my director, Patricia Welch, on January 8th. Then I followed up in writing on January 12th. Then again on January 19th, which was three days before this report. I kept detailed notes on all of these conversations because I knew—I knew—that resourcing would be the make-or-break factor for this project.

Q: What was the response to your requests?

A: Patricia told me the budget didn't allow for additional headcount. But here's the thing—I didn't stop there. I proposed alternatives. I suggested we bring in contractors. I suggested we borrow developers from the maintenance team. I even offered to work weekends myself, and I did, by the way. I worked seven straight weekends in January and February.

Q: Despite these efforts, the February deliverables were late?

A: Some of them, yes. But not because of any failure on my team's part. We gave everything we had.

Q: I'm not asking about effort, Mr. Okonkwo. I'm asking about the deliverables.

A: And I'm telling you that the deliverables need to be understood in context. We completed the data migration module on time. We completed the reporting dashboard on time. The only component that slipped was the notification system, and that was because—

Q: How late was the notification system?

A: Three weeks. But those three weeks allowed us to deliver something truly robust. If we'd rushed it out the door, we would have been dealing with production failures for months.

Q: Was the three-week delay approved by the client in advance?

A: There were discussions.

Q: Was it approved?

A: Not formally, no.

Q: Thank you. Let's move on.

A: But I want to be clear—the client was kept informed at every step. There were no surprises here. Good project management means keeping stakeholders in the loop, and that's exactly what we did.

topic: A project manager is questioned about deadlines they missed on a software contract
text:
Q: Ms. Petrov, who was responsible for creating the project timeline?

A: I was.

Q: And who approved that timeline?

A: It went through several reviews. My director approved it. The client's project sponsor approved it.

Q: So multiple people signed off on the timeline you created.

A: Yes.

Q: In hindsight, was that timeline realistic?

A: In hindsight, there were elements that proved more challenging than anticipated.

Q: That's a very diplomatic answer.

A: It's an accurate answer.

Q: Let me try again. When you created the timeline, did you believe it was achievable?

A: I believed it was achievable with the assumptions we had at the time.

Q: What assumptions?

A: That requirements would be stable. That the client's legacy data would be clean and well-documented. That we would have access to the client's subject matter experts when we needed them.

Q: And those assumptions proved incorrect?

A: Some of them, yes.

Q: Which ones?

A: The legacy data was... not what we expected. There were inconsistencies that took significant time to resolve.

Q: How much time?

A: Approximately four weeks of additional effort.

Q: Did you build any buffer into your timeline for unexpected issues?

A: There was a two-week contingency buffer.

Q: But you needed four weeks.

A: Yes.

Q: So you were two weeks short.

A: Mathematically, yes.

Q: Is there another way to look at it?

A: I think the relevant question is whether the contingency buffer was reasonable given what was known at the time. And it was. Industry standard is ten to fifteen percent contingency. We had twelve percent.

Q: But it wasn't enough.

A: It wasn't enough for this particular situation, no.

Q: Did you communicate to the client that the timeline was at risk once you discovered the data issues?

A: I did.

Q: When?

A: March 3rd.

Q: And when was the final deadline?

A: March 31st.

Q: So you gave the client twenty-eight days' notice that you might miss their deadline.

A: I gave them notice as soon as the risk became apparent. That's the responsible approach.

topic: A project manager is questioned about deadlines they missed on a software contract
text:
Q: Let's talk about the security audit, Mr. Callahan. When was that scheduled?

A: August 15th.

Q: Walk me through what happened.

A: We brought in the third-party auditors on August 15th as planned. They conducted their assessment over three days. On August 18th, they delivered their preliminary findings.

Q: And what did those findings indicate?

A: They identified twelve items requiring remediation before the system could be certified.

Q: Twelve items. Were you expecting that?

A: We were expecting some findings. That's normal with security audits. Twelve was on the higher end of what I'd anticipated, but not dramatically so.

Q: How long did the contract give you to complete remediation?

A: Fourteen days.

Q: Did you complete remediation in fourteen days?

A: We completed eleven of the twelve items.

Q: What about the twelfth?

A: The twelfth item related to encryption protocols. It required a change to our authentication architecture that was more involved than the auditors initially realized.

Q: How much more involved?

A: It ended up requiring twenty-three days instead of the allotted fourteen.

Q: So you missed the remediation deadline by nine days.

A: For that one item, yes.

Q: Was there a certification deadline tied to this?

A: There was. September 1st.

Q: Did you meet that deadline?

A: We did not receive certification until September 12th.

Q: What was the consequence of that eleven-day delay?

A: The system couldn't go live until certification was received.

Q: And the go-live date in the contract?

A: September 1st.

Q: So the system went live eleven days late because of this one encryption issue?

A: That was the proximate cause, yes.

Q: Did anyone on your team flag the encryption issue as a risk before the audit?

A: Not specifically, no.

Q: Should they have?

A: That's a fair question. In retrospect, we might have benefited from a pre-audit assessment.

Q: But you didn't conduct one.

A: We did not.

topic: A supervisor is deposed about performance reviews given to an employee who was later fired
text:
Q: Ms. Hartwell, thank you for being here today. I'd like to start by giving you a chance to tell us a bit about your working relationship with Daniel Reeves.

A: Of course. Danny—Daniel—reported to me for almost four years. He started as a junior analyst and worked his way up. Honestly, he was one of those employees you root for, you know? Came in early, asked good questions, really wanted to learn the business.

Q: It sounds like you got to know him fairly well.

A: I did. I made it a point to check in with all my direct reports regularly, but with Daniel, those conversations just flowed more naturally. He'd stay after our one-on-ones sometimes and we'd talk about his goals, his family. He was proud of his kids.

Q: Let's turn to his performance reviews. You conducted those annually?

A: Yes, every January. And I want to be clear—I took those seriously. They weren't just box-checking for me. I saw them as a chance to really sit down and map out someone's growth.

Q: How would you characterize the reviews you gave Mr. Reeves over those four years?

A: Strong. Consistently strong. He received "exceeds expectations" in most categories, "meets expectations" in a few. Never below that. I was genuinely proud of the progress he made.

Q: I'm showing you what's been marked as Exhibit 14. Do you recognize this document?

A: Yes, that's Daniel's 2022 review. His last one before... before everything changed.

Q: Take your time. Can you read aloud what you wrote in the summary section?

A: "Daniel continues to be a valued member of our team. His attention to detail and collaborative spirit make him someone others look to for guidance. I have every confidence in his continued growth here." I meant every word of that.

Q: Ms. Hartwell, given what you wrote there, can you help me understand what happened between January 2022 and his termination in August?

A: I've asked myself that question more times than I can count. The directives came from above me. I was told the department was restructuring. But if you're asking whether Daniel deserved to lose his job based on his performance? No. He didn't.

Q: Thank you for your candor.

A: He deserved better. I should have fought harder.

topic: A supervisor is deposed about performance reviews given to an employee who was later fired
text:
Q: Mr. Okonkwo, you supervised Priya Shah in the customer success department, correct?

A: That's correct.

Q: For how long?

A: A little over two years. She joined my team in March 2021.

Q: And during that time, you conducted her performance reviews?

A: I did, yes. And if I may—I want to say upfront that Priya was a delight to work with. I know this is a legal proceeding and I should stick to the questions, but I think context matters here.

Q: I appreciate that, and I'd actually like to hear that context. What made her a delight?

A: She had this way of making everyone around her better. In team meetings, she'd lift people up—credit others for ideas, offer help before anyone asked. The kind of person who remembers birthdays and asks about your mother's surgery.

Q: That's quite a description.

A: It's accurate. I've managed a lot of people over the years. Priya stood out.

Q: Let's look at her mid-year review from 2022, marked as Exhibit 7. You wrote that she "demonstrates exceptional client rapport and has reduced churn in her portfolio by 12%."

A: That's right. Those weren't just numbers on a page—she worked incredibly hard for that. Called clients on her own time, really listened to their concerns.

Q: Yet four months after this review, she was placed on a performance improvement plan. Help me bridge that gap.

A: I wish I could. The PIP wasn't my idea. I was informed by HR that she needed to be put on one due to "shifting departmental standards." I pushed back. I told them her metrics were excellent.

Q: What was the response?

A: I was told the decision had already been made. I asked Priya to meet me for coffee that day, off-site. I wanted her to hear it from me first, not in some cold conference room. She deserved that dignity.

Q: How did she take it?

A: She was confused. Hurt. But she didn't complain—she asked me what she could do to improve. That's who she was. Even then, she was trying to make it work.

topic: A supervisor is deposed about performance reviews given to an employee who was later fired
text:
Q: You're familiar with the company's performance review criteria?

A: Very familiar. I helped draft the current version three years ago.

Q: Then you'll appreciate why we need to understand how those criteria were applied to Marcus Thompson.

A: I'll do my best to help you understand. Marcus was—look, I don't want to get emotional here, but Marcus was someone special on my team.

Q: Take whatever time you need.

A: Thank you. I'm okay. It's just that when you work closely with someone, watch them struggle through a difficult project and come out the other side better for it, you feel invested in their success.

Q: Can you tell me about a specific instance where you saw that in Mr. Thompson?

A: The Henderson account, without question. Client was ready to walk, had been mishandled before Marcus took over. He spent weeks—nights, weekends—rebuilding that relationship. Saved us probably $200,000 in annual revenue.

Q: Was that reflected in his performance review?

A: Absolutely. I made sure of it. I wrote a full paragraph about it and flagged it for the VP as well.

Q: I'm looking at Exhibit 22, his 2023 annual review. But I don't see that paragraph here.

A: What? Let me see that. This isn't—this has been edited. This isn't the version I submitted.

Q: You're certain?

A: I am completely certain. I keep copies of all my submitted reviews. The Henderson account was specifically mentioned. Someone removed it.

Q: Do you have any idea who might have done that?

A: No, but I intend to find out. Marcus worked too hard, cared too much, for his record to be rewritten like this. That's not right.

topic: A supervisor is deposed about performance reviews given to an employee who was later fired
text:
Q: Ms. Chen, let's discuss the performance evaluation system at Ridgeway Financial.

A: Sure. What would you like to know?

Q: In your experience as a supervisor, did you find the system adequate for assessing employee performance?

A: For most purposes, yes. It was fairly comprehensive—metrics, competencies, development goals. Pretty standard stuff.

Q: Did you use that system to evaluate James Whitfield?

A: I did. James was on my team for nearly three years.

Q: And how did you find him as an employee?

A: Exceptional, truthfully. He had a mind for numbers that I rarely see, but more than that, he had heart. Some analysts just crunch data—James understood there were real people behind the portfolios.

Q: That combination is rare?

A: In my experience, yes. You usually get one or the other. James had both, and he was generous with his knowledge. Spent countless lunch hours mentoring our junior staff even though no one asked him to.

Q: Looking at Exhibit 31, his final performance review before termination, you rated him "meets expectations" across all categories. That seems inconsistent with what you just described.

A: I know how it looks. But you have to understand—I was explicitly told by my director that no one in the department could receive higher than "meets expectations" that cycle. Budget reasons, she said. Didn't want to create expectations for raises or promotions.

Q: So this review doesn't accurately reflect your assessment of Mr. Whitfield's performance?

A: No, it doesn't. And I told James that at the time. I sat with him after the review and explained the situation. I told him his real rating, in my eyes, was outstanding.

Q: What did he say?

A: He said he understood. Then he thanked me for being honest with him. That was James—gracious even when he had every right to be angry.

Q: Did you document that conversation anywhere?

A: I didn't. I wish I had. I should have protected him better.

topic: A supervisor is deposed about performance reviews given to an employee who was later fired
text:
Q: Let's focus on the period between Ms. Rodriguez's final performance review and her termination.

A: All right.

Q: That was approximately six weeks?

A: Closer to seven, I think. Early September to late October.

Q: In that final review, you gave her high marks in nearly every category.

A: I did, because she earned them.

Q: Mr. Patterson, you've been doing this a long time. You've let people go before.

A: I have. It's never easy, but sometimes it's necessary.

Q: Was it necessary with Elena Rodriguez?

A: No. I want to be clear about that: no.

Q: Then why did it happen?

A: Politics. New leadership came in and wanted to clean house. Elena wasn't part of anyone's inner circle—she was just good at her job and kept her head down. That made her expendable to people who didn't bother to know her.

Q: You sound frustrated.

A: I am frustrated. Elena used to bring her grandmother's empanadas to our team potlucks. She'd stay late to help colleagues with their presentations even when she had her own deadlines. When her coworker had a baby, she organized the entire shower herself. That's the person we let go.

Q: Did you advocate for her?

A: I tried. I went to HR, I went to my VP. I brought her reviews, her client feedback, her metrics. They listened politely and then did what they'd already decided to do.

Q: How did you deliver the news to her?

A: I asked if I could do it myself. I owed her that much. I took her to the small conference room—the one with the window—and I told her the truth: that this wasn't about her performance, and that I was sorry. She hugged me when we were done. Can you imagine? She was the one who'd just lost her job, and she hugged me.

Q: Did she say anything?

A: She said, "Thank you for always being in my corner." I think about that a lot.

topic: A building inspector is deposed about a structural assessment they signed off on
text:
Q: Mr. Harmon, you personally inspected the foundation at 1847 Crescent Avenue on March 15th, correct?

A: I did.

Q: And you signed the structural assessment form that day?

A: My signature is on the document. You have it in front of you.

Q: I'm asking if you signed it.

A: I just answered that.

Q: You certified the foundation as structurally sound, yes?

A: That's what the form says, counselor. I assume you can read it.

Q: Mr. Harmon, I'm going to ask you to answer my questions directly.

A: I am answering directly. You're asking me to confirm what's already in evidence. I signed the form. The form says what it says.

Q: Were you aware that the east wall showed signs of horizontal cracking at the time of your inspection?

A: I documented everything I observed. My notes are attached to the assessment.

Q: That's not what I asked. Did you personally observe horizontal cracking?

A: If it's not in my notes, I didn't observe it. If it is in my notes, I did. That's how documentation works.

Q: So you're telling this jury you have no independent memory of what you saw?

A: I'm telling you I conducted a thorough inspection and documented my findings according to department protocols. Which I've been doing for nineteen years without a single complaint until your client decided to blame someone else for their problems.

Q: Move to strike everything after "protocols."

A: Strike whatever you want.

topic: A building inspector is deposed about a structural assessment they signed off on
text:
Q: Ms. Delgado, how long have you worked as a building inspector for the city?

A: Twelve years this coming August.

Q: And in those twelve years, approximately how many structural assessments have you completed?

A: I couldn't give you an exact number. Thousands, certainly.

Q: Would you say you're experienced in identifying foundation defects?

A: I would say I'm one of the most experienced inspectors in this region, yes.

Q: Then help me understand something, Ms. Delgado. The Whitfield Building collapsed eleven months after you certified it as structurally sound. How does that happen?

A: Buildings don't collapse because of foundation issues I was asked to assess. They collapse for many reasons—water damage, subsequent construction, seismic activity, deferred maintenance.

Q: So it's everyone's fault but yours?

A: I didn't say that. I said foundation assessments evaluate conditions at a specific moment in time.

Q: A moment in time. Interesting. So your certification was only good for that one day?

A: My certification reflected conditions as they existed during my inspection. I don't have a crystal ball, counselor. Neither do you.

Q: Did you review the soil composition reports before signing off?

A: I reviewed every document that was provided to me.

Q: That's not what I asked. Did you review soil composition reports?

A: If they weren't provided, I couldn't review them, could I? My job is to assess what's in front of me, not to chase down documents the property owner fails to supply.

Q: So you signed off without complete information?

A: I signed off based on the information required by code. If you have a problem with what's required, take it up with the state legislature.

topic: A building inspector is deposed about a structural assessment they signed off on

topic: A building inspector is deposed about a structural assessment they signed off on
text:
Q: You completed the assessment in under two hours, correct?

A: Approximately, yes.

Q: The building was 40,000 square feet.

A: Yes.

Q: That's roughly 333 square feet per minute.

A: I didn't realize you'd be testing my math skills today, counselor.

Q: Does that seem like adequate time to you?

A: It was adequate for that particular inspection, yes.

Q: How could you possibly—

A: Because I'm a professional. Because I know what to look for. Because not every square foot requires the same level of attention. Do you spend the same amount of time on every page of a legal brief, or do you focus on what matters?

Q: I'm not the one being deposed, Mr. Okonkwo.

A: No, but you are the one suggesting I don't know how to do my job.

Q: I'm trying to understand your methodology.

A: My methodology is sound. It's been sound for fifteen years. I've inspected buildings that are still standing perfectly fine decades later. One building has a problem and suddenly I'm incompetent?

Q: Did you inspect the basement level?

A: Of course I did.

Q: Your notes don't mention the basement.

A: My notes mention areas of concern. If the basement isn't mentioned, there was nothing concerning about it.

Q: Or you never went down there.

A: I went down there, counselor. I walked every level of that building. If you're calling me a liar, say it plainly.

topic: A building inspector is deposed about a structural assessment they signed off on
text:
Q: Ms. Hartwell, you initialed page seven of the structural assessment, indicating you reviewed the load-bearing calculations?

A: I did.

Q: And you found no issues with those calculations?

A: The calculations met code requirements at the time.

Q: At the time. Are you suggesting the code was inadequate?

A: I'm suggesting I enforce the code as written. That's my job. I don't write the code.

Q: But you have discretion, don't you? You can flag concerns even if something technically meets code?

A: I can. When concerns exist.

Q: And none existed here?

A: None that I observed, no.

Q: Ms. Hartwell, eight people were injured when that mezzanine collapsed.

A: I'm aware. I've thought about it every day since it happened.

Q: And yet you maintain you did nothing wrong?

A: I maintain I followed proper procedures based on the information available.

Q: What information was missing?

A: The contractor's revised drawings, for one. Which were never submitted to my office.

Q: Are you blaming the contractor?

A: I'm answering your question. You asked what was missing. I told you.

Q: Shouldn't you have demanded those drawings?

A: I can't demand what I don't know exists. My office received the original plans. We had no indication revisions were made. If you want to know why those drawings never arrived, I suggest you depose someone from Morrison Engineering. I've been sitting here for three hours answering for decisions other people made.

Q: We'll determine who else to depose, Ms. Hartwell.

A: I'm sure you will.

topic: A warehouse supervisor is deposed about safety protocols that were allegedly ignored
text:
Q: Mr. Delgado, how long have you been the warehouse supervisor at the Brennan Road facility?

A: I was aware it had been reported.

Q: But you do remember it was reported?

A: Yes. I just said that.

Q: And what did you do when it was reported?

A: I followed procedure. I submitted a work order.

Q: To whom?

A: To maintenance. That's how it works. That's how it's always worked. I submit the order, they handle the repair.

Q: Did you follow up on whether the repair was completed?

A: That's not my responsibility. Once the work order is in, it's in their queue.

Q: So the answer is no?

A: The answer is that I did my job. If you want to know why the repair wasn't done, you should be deposing the maintenance department.

topic: A warehouse supervisor is deposed about safety protocols that were allegedly ignored
text:
Q: Ms. Thornton, I'm going to ask you about the lockout/tagout procedures at the facility. Are you familiar with those?

A: Yes. I was told that.

Q: Had there been previous incidents involving lockout/tagout failures?

A: Define "incidents."

Q: Injuries resulting from failure to follow lockout/tagout procedures.

topic: A warehouse supervisor is deposed about safety protocols that were allegedly ignored
text:

topic: A warehouse supervisor is deposed about safety protocols that were allegedly ignored
text:
Q: Mr. Pearson, you've testified that the spill on aisle twelve was reported to you at approximately 2:15 PM. Is that correct?

Q: You believe. You're not certain?

A: I'm reasonably certain.

A: I assumed it was handled.

A: Asked and answered. I delegated it.

topic: A witness is questioned about events at a party where an assault allegedly occurred
text:
Q: Ms. Hernandez, you were present at the party on the evening of October 14th, correct?

A: I saw people moving around. I saw a lot of things.

Q: Ms. Hernandez, I'm asking specifically about an altercation. A physical confrontation.

A: And I'm telling you what I saw. People were moving. It was a party.

Q: Did you see Marcus Webb strike another individual that night?

A: I saw Marcus. I saw him talking to people. I saw him by the pool at some point.

Q: That's not what I asked. Did you see him strike someone?

A: I don't know what you want me to say. I didn't see him hit anybody. Is that clear enough?

Q: You sound frustrated, Ms. Hernandez.

A: I sound like someone who's been asked the same thing three different ways. Ask it a fourth way if you want. My answer's not changing.

Q: Were you drinking that evening?

A: I had a glass of wine. Maybe two. I wasn't impaired, if that's where this is going.

Q: I'm simply trying to establish the facts.

A: Then maybe try asking questions that let me give you facts instead of fishing for something I didn't see.

---

topic: A witness is questioned about events at a party where an assault allegedly occurred
text:

text:

topic: A daycare worker is deposed about an injury a child sustained while in their care

topic: A daycare worker is deposed about an injury a child sustained while in their care

topic: A daycare worker is deposed about an injury a child sustained while in their care

topic: An employee is deposed about a coworker's termination they believe was retaliatory
text:
Q: Mr. Thornton, how long did you work alongside Ms. Vega before her termination?

A: Four years. Four years and... I think three months, roughly.

Q: And during that time, would you say you came to know her professionally?

A: Yes.

A: She was... she was one of those people who stayed late not because anyone asked her to, but because she cared. She'd review other people's reports if they were struggling. She mentored two of the junior analysts. She remembered everyone's birthdays. I'm sorry, I know that's not what you're asking exactly.

A: Thank you.

A: It was October. October 14th. I remember because it was the day after my daughter's birthday and I'd brought in leftover cake. Elena—Ms. Vega—she came to my desk that morning and she just looked... she asked if we could talk somewhere private.

Q: What did she tell you?

Q: Mr. Thornton, I notice you're taking a moment. Do you need a break?

A: No. No, I'd like to finish. I just want to make sure I say this right. She deserved better than what happened to her.

topic: An employee is deposed about a coworker's termination they believe was retaliatory
text:
Q: Ms. Chen, you were present at the staff meeting on March 3rd, correct?

A: Correct.

Q: And that was the meeting where the reduction in force was announced?

A: Yes.

A: I thought... I thought it was strange that Marcus was the only one from our team.

Q: How would you characterize his demeanor when he said that?

A: He wouldn't look at me.

Q: Ms. Chen, in the weeks before the termination, had Mr. Webb done anything that might have drawn negative attention from management?

Q: And approximately how long before his termination was this complaint filed?

A: Sixteen days.

topic: An employee is deposed about a coworker's termination they believe was retaliatory
text:
Q: Let's move to the period immediately following Mr. Okonkwo's termination. You continued working at Hensley & Associates?
