topic: An employee is deposed about a coworker's termination they believe was retaliatory
text:
Q: You mentioned earlier that you and Mr. Park were hired the same year.

A: Same month, actually. We went through orientation together.

Q: Did you maintain a professional relationship throughout your time at the company?

A: Professional and personal. We carpooled for two years when we lived near each other. I was at his wedding.

Q: I see. So you would have been aware of any difficulties he was experiencing at work?

A: Yes.

Q: When did you first notice something had changed for Mr. Park?

A: After the OSHA incident.

Q: The incident being—

A: When he reported the forklift safety violations to OSHA because internal channels weren't responding.

Q: And management learned he had made that report?

A: Within days. It's a small facility. Word travels.

Q: What changed for Mr. Park after that?

A: His shift was changed from days to nights without explanation. He was moved to a workstation away from the rest of the team. His locker was reassigned to the far end of the building.

Q: Did he complain about these changes?

A: He filed a grievance. He did everything by the book, everything he was supposed to do.

Q: What came of the grievance?

A: It was denied. And then, about six weeks later, he was terminated for "repeated tardiness."

Q: Was Mr. Park frequently tardy, in your experience?

A: In eleven years, I saw Daniel Park arrive late exactly twice. Both times he called ahead. Once was because his son was in the emergency room.

Q: Mr. Nguyen, I'm going to ask you something difficult. Do you believe the termination was connected to the OSHA report?

A: ...I know it was.

Q: How do you know?

A: Because three days before they fired him, Supervisor Morrison told him—told him directly—that he should have "kept his mouth shut and let things work themselves out."

topic: An employee is deposed about a coworker's termination they believe was retaliatory
text:
Q: Dr. Franklin, you've testified that you supervised Ms. Holloway for approximately two years.

A: That's correct.

Q: During that time, did you ever have cause to discipline her?

A: No.

Q: Any written warnings?

A: None.

Q: Any verbal warnings?

A: Not a single one.

Q: So it's fair to say she was a satisfactory employee?

A: She was exceptional. I've supervised over forty researchers in my career. She was in the top five.

Q: That's high praise.

A: It's accurate praise.

Q: I understand. Now, at some point Ms. Holloway raised concerns about research data being altered. Were you aware of those concerns?

A: I was. She came to me first.

Q: What did you advise her to do?

A: I told her to document everything and go to the compliance office.

Q: Did she follow that advice?

A: She did exactly what I told her to do. And I have thought about that every day since.

Q: What do you mean?

A: I mean that I gave her advice that I believed was right, and it ended her career at this institution.

Q: Dr. Franklin, I need to ask—was there any legitimate performance-based reason for Ms. Holloway's termination?

A: None that was ever communicated to me.

Q: Were you consulted before the decision was made?

A: I was not. I learned about it the same day she did. I was called into a meeting and told that my input was "not required for this personnel matter."

Q: How did you respond?

A: I didn't respond. I should have. I sat there and I didn't say a word, and then I walked back to my office, and her desk was already being cleared out.

topic: A warehouse supervisor is deposed about safety protocols that were allegedly ignored
text:
Q: Mr. Hernandez, how long have you worked as a warehouse supervisor at Ridgeline Distribution?

A: Seven years. Give or take.

Q: And in that role, you're responsible for ensuring compliance with safety protocols, correct?

A: That's one of the things I do, sure.

Q: One of the things. What would you say is your primary responsibility?

A: Getting product out the door. Meeting shipment deadlines. That's what we get measured on.

Q: Were you aware that OSHA requires quarterly safety audits for facilities handling hazardous materials?

A: I've heard that, yeah.

Q: Did Ridgeline conduct quarterly safety audits in 2023?

A: I wouldn't know the exact schedule. That's more of a corporate thing.

Q: You wouldn't know. Even though you're the supervisor on-site?

A: They send people. I don't keep track of when.

Q: Do you recall an audit occurring in the three months before Mr. Deluca's accident?

A: Not specifically, no.

Q: Does that concern you?

A: I'm not sure what you want me to say to that.

Q: I want you to answer the question. Does the absence of a safety audit before a serious workplace injury concern you?

A: Things happen. We do what we can with what we've got.

Q: "Things happen." Is that Ridgeline's official position on workplace safety?

A: It's just what I said. I'm not a spokesperson.

topic: A warehouse supervisor is deposed about safety protocols that were allegedly ignored
text:
Q: Let's talk about the forklift inspection logs. Who's responsible for maintaining those?

A: The operators fill them out. I sign off at the end of the week.

Q: And when you sign off, do you review what they've written?

A: I look at them.

Q: You look at them. Do you read them?

A: I skim them, I guess. Make sure everything's filled in.

Q: I'm showing you what's been marked as Exhibit 14. Do you recognize this document?

A: That's one of the logs. Sure.

Q: Can you read the entry for March 3rd?

A: "Brake response sluggish. Reported to maintenance."

Q: And your signature appears at the bottom of that page, correct?

A: Looks like it.

Q: So you were aware the brakes on Forklift 7 were reported as sluggish eleven days before the incident?

A: I signed the page. I can't tell you if I specifically remember reading that line.

Q: Fine. Let me ask you this—what's the protocol when an operator reports a mechanical issue?

A: They're supposed to tag it out and notify maintenance.

Q: Was Forklift 7 tagged out after March 3rd?

A: I'd have to check the records.

Q: We've checked the records. It wasn't. Does that surprise you?

A: Not really. We only have four forklifts. You pull one, the whole floor backs up.

topic: A warehouse supervisor is deposed about safety protocols that were allegedly ignored
text:
Q: Ms. Tran, I'm going to ask you about the safety training records for temporary workers. Okay?

A: Sure.

Q: According to Ridgeline's employee handbook, all temporary workers must complete a four-hour safety orientation before operating machinery. Is that accurate?

A: That sounds right.

Q: Sounds right, or is right?

A: It's in the handbook. I assume it's right.

Q: Did Mr. Aguilar complete a four-hour safety orientation before he was assigned to the loading dock?

A: He went through orientation. I don't have a stopwatch on it.

Q: The sign-in sheet shows he arrived at 7:15 a.m. and was on the floor by 9:30 a.m. That's two hours and fifteen minutes.

A: Okay.

Q: So he didn't complete the required four hours?

A: I guess not, if you're doing the math.

Q: Why was the orientation cut short?

A: We were behind. Needed bodies on the floor.

Q: Who made that call?

A: I don't remember. Could've been me. Could've been someone else.

Q: Do you understand that Mr. Aguilar was injured operating equipment he may not have been properly trained on?

A: I understand that's what you're saying, yeah.

Q: Is there anything you'd like to add to clarify your answer?

A: Not really. It is what it is.

topic: A warehouse supervisor is deposed about safety protocols that were allegedly ignored
text:
Q: Mr. Okonkwo, let me direct your attention to the incident on September 14th. Where were you when the pallet collapsed?

A: In my office. Maybe twenty feet from the floor.

Q: Did you hear it happen?

A: I heard something. Didn't know what it was at first.

Q: What did you do when you realized there'd been an accident?

A: Went out. Saw the mess. Called it in.

Q: Called it in to whom?

A: Dispatch. Then corporate. Standard procedure.

Q: Walk me through what you observed when you reached the scene.

A: Pallets down. Product everywhere. Kendricks on the ground.

Q: Was he conscious?

A: Yeah. He was talking. Complaining about his back.

Q: Did anyone render first aid?

A: Someone grabbed the kit. I don't remember who.

Q: The investigation report suggests the pallets were stacked beyond the maximum height. Were you aware of that?

A: I've seen the report.

Q: Were you aware of it before the accident?

A: We stack what we need to stack. Space is tight.

Q: So that's a yes?

A: It's an acknowledgment of reality.

Q: Let me rephrase. Did you personally observe pallets stacked above the posted limit before September 14th?

A: Probably. I don't memorize every stack height I walk past.

topic: A warehouse supervisor is deposed about safety protocols that were allegedly ignored
text:
Q: How often did you conduct safety walkthroughs of the warehouse floor?

A: When I had time.

Q: Can you be more specific?

A: Once a week. Sometimes more, sometimes less.

Q: The company policy states daily walkthroughs are required. Were you aware of that?

A: I was aware of what the policy says.

Q: But you didn't follow it?

A: I followed it when I could.

Q: Let's move on. Next question. Were you familiar with the chemical storage requirements for the solvents kept in Section D?

A: Familiar enough.

Q: What does that mean?

A: I knew they needed to be in the caged area. Ventilated. Away from heat sources.

Q: On the day of the fire, were those solvents in the caged area?

A: Some of them.

Q: Some of them. Where were the others?

A: Staging area. Waiting to be moved.

Q: For how long?

A: I don't know. A day or two.

Q: The fire marshal's report indicates the ignition point was in the staging area where those solvents were located. Any comment?

A: I've read the report.

Q: That's not what I asked. Do you have any comment on that finding?

A: It's the fire marshal's finding. I don't have anything to add.

topic: A contractor is questioned about delays that caused a construction project to fail
text:
Q: Mr. Hardin, I want to direct your attention to the period between March and June of 2022. During that time, who was responsible for coordinating the concrete subcontractors?

A: I was.

Q: And were there delays in the concrete pours during that period?

A: Yes.

Q: How many days of delay would you estimate?

A: Forty-three days. Give or take.

Q: That's a specific number.

A: I've had time to think about it.

Q: What caused those forty-three days of delay?

A: Weather, mostly. Some material shortages. The rebar shipment from Consolidated was late by two weeks. The cement plant had a strike. Pick whichever one you want.

Q: I'm asking what you believe caused the delays, Mr. Hardin.

A: All of it. Every single one of those things. They just kept stacking up.

Q: Did you communicate these delays to the project owner?

A: I sent reports. Weekly reports, like the contract required.

Q: And what was the response?

A: There wasn't one. Not really. They'd say they received it. That was about it.

Q: Did that concern you?

A: At first.

Q: And later?

A: Later I just kept sending the reports.

topic: A contractor is questioned about delays that caused a construction project to fail
text:
Q: Let's talk about the HVAC installation, Ms. Correa. Your company was the general contractor, correct?

A: That's correct.

Q: And Briarwood Mechanical was your subcontractor for HVAC?

A: They were.

Q: When did you first become aware there were problems with Briarwood's performance?

A: October, maybe. Late October 2021.

Q: What kind of problems?

A: They weren't showing up. Their crew chief would send three guys when we needed eight. Units were sitting in the staging area for weeks.

Q: Did you take any action?

A: I called Dan Meyers. He was their project manager.

Q: What did Mr. Meyers say?

A: He said they were stretched thin. Other jobs. He said they'd get to it.

Q: Did they get to it?

A: Eventually. Three months later.

Q: Ms. Correa, did you consider terminating Briarwood and hiring a different subcontractor?

A: Sure, I considered it.

Q: But you didn't.

A: No.

Q: Why not?

A: Because by then we were already behind on electrical, behind on framing, behind on inspections. Switching HVAC contractors in the middle of winter wasn't going to save the project. Nothing was going to save the project by that point.

Q: So you just... continued with Briarwood?

A: I continued with Briarwood.

topic: A contractor is questioned about delays that caused a construction project to fail
text:
Q: Mr. Okonkwo, I've been doing this for twenty-two years. I've taken a lot of depositions in construction cases. So I'm going to ask you some questions, and I'd appreciate direct answers. Can you do that?

A: I'll do my best.

Q: The project schedule called for substantial completion by November 15, 2022. Is that your understanding?

A: That was the contractual date, yes.

Q: When did you first realize that date was not achievable?

A: Probably... probably around April.

Q: April 2022?

A: Yes.

Q: So seven months before the deadline, you knew you weren't going to make it.

A: I knew it was unlikely.

Q: Did you inform Heritage Development of that assessment?

A: Not in those terms.

Q: In what terms, then?

A: I told them we had schedule pressure. I told them we needed decisions faster. I told them the permit issues were killing us.

Q: But you didn't tell them the project was going to fail.

A: No one wants to hear that. You know that as well as I do.

Q: I'm not asking what they wanted to hear, Mr. Okonkwo.

A: No. I didn't tell them. I kept thinking maybe we'd figure it out.

Q: And did you?

A: We're sitting here, aren't we?

topic: A contractor is questioned about delays that caused a construction project to fail
text:
Q: I want to understand the change order process on this project. Who had authority to approve change orders over fifty thousand dollars?

A: The owner's representative. That was Jim Stratton.

Q: And how long did it typically take Mr. Stratton to approve a change order?

A: Typically? Or on this project?

Q: On this project.

A: Could be two weeks. Could be six. Once it took eleven weeks.

Q: Eleven weeks to approve a single change order?

A: Change order number twenty-three. Foundation reinforcement. Eleven weeks and two days.

Q: What happened to the project while you waited eleven weeks for approval?

A: We waited.

Q: You stopped work?

A: On that portion, yes. We couldn't pour the foundation without the reinforcement. We couldn't do the reinforcement without approval. We couldn't get approval.

Q: Did you escalate the issue?

A: To who? Stratton was the owner's representative. That was the chain of command.

Q: What about the owner directly? Heritage Development?

A: They told me to work with Jim.

Q: So you were stuck.

A: That's one word for it.

Q: What word would you use?

A: I'd say we were stuck. That's accurate enough.

topic: A contractor is questioned about delays that caused a construction project to fail
text:
Q: Mr. Paulsen, you mentioned earlier that labor shortages affected the project. Let's explore that. How many carpenters did your crew schedule call for during peak construction?

A: Thirty-two.

Q: And how many did you have on site during peak construction?

A: It varied.

Q: Give me a range.

A: Eighteen to twenty-four, most weeks.

Q: So you were operating at roughly sixty to seventy-five percent of your planned workforce.

A: If you want to put numbers on it, sure.

Q: What did you do to address the shortage?

A: What everyone does. Posted ads. Called the union hall. Offered overtime to the guys we had.

Q: Did any of that work?

A: Some of it. For a while.

Q: Mr. Paulsen, you've been in this industry for how long?

A: Thirty-one years.

Q: Have you seen labor shortages before?

A: Of course.

Q: How did this one compare?

A: It was worse. The whole industry was worse. Every contractor in the city was fighting for the same guys.

Q: Did you communicate the severity of this to Heritage Development?

A: I told them we were short-staffed. I told them everyone was short-staffed.

Q: What did they say?

A: They said they expected us to meet the schedule anyway.

Q: And what did you say to that?

A: What could I say? I said we'd do our best.

Q: Did you believe that when you said it?

A: I believed we'd do our best. Whether it would be enough... that's a different question.

Q: Did you know the answer to that different question?

A: I had my suspicions. Let's leave it at that.

topic: A witness is questioned about a fire they discovered in a neighboring unit
text:
Q: Mr. Delacroix, let's talk about the evening of March 14th. What time did you first become aware something was wrong in Unit 4B?

A: Around 9:15, 9:20. Somewhere in there.

Q: Which is it? 9:15 or 9:20?

A: I said somewhere in there. I wasn't staring at my watch waiting for something to happen.

Q: Did you smell smoke first, or did you see it?

A: Smelled it.

Q: And where were you in your unit when you smelled it?

A: Living room. On the couch.

Q: What did you do when you smelled smoke?

A: I got up. Walked around. Tried to figure out where it was coming from.

Q: How long did that take?

A: I don't know, a minute? Two minutes? I wasn't timing myself.

Q: Mr. Delacroix, I'm trying to establish a timeline here. Can you give me your best estimate?

A: And I'm giving you my best estimate. A minute or two. That's as precise as I can be. I wasn't conducting a scientific study, I was trying to figure out if my building was on fire.

Q: Fair enough. What did you do after you determined the source?

A: Called 911.

Q: Before or after you knocked on your neighbor's door?

A: Before. Obviously.

Q: Why obviously?

A: Because that's what you're supposed to do. Call emergency services first. I'm not going to bang on someone's door while their apartment burns down behind me.

Q: Did anyone answer when you knocked?

A: No.

Q: Did you try more than once?

A: Yes. Three times. Hard. Then I left because the smoke was getting thick and I'm not interested in dying for a deposition.

topic: A witness is questioned about a fire they discovered in a neighboring unit
text:
Q: Ms. Thornton, you stated in your written statement that you discovered the fire at approximately 8:45 p.m. Is that correct?

A: Yes.

Q: And you were returning home from where?

A: The grocery store. Millbrook Market on Fifth.

Q: When you entered the building, did you notice anything unusual in the lobby?

A: No, nothing in the lobby.

Q: What about the stairwell?

A: The stairwell, yes. There was a haze. Not thick, but noticeable.

Q: A haze. Could you describe—

A: Like I said. A haze. Gray. Thin. Hanging in the air around the second-floor landing.

Q: I'm going to ask you to let me finish my questions, Ms. Thornton.

A: I'm trying to be thorough.

Q: I appreciate that. Could you describe the smell associated with this haze?

A: Burning. Electrical, maybe. That sharp kind of smell, like when a wire overheats.

Q: You said electrical. Are you speculating about the cause of the fire?

A: No. I'm describing what it smelled like. You asked what it smelled like. I'm telling you what it smelled like.

Q: Did you proceed up the stairs despite the haze?

A: I live on the third floor. I needed to see what was happening.

Q: So your answer is yes?

A: My answer is I explained what I did and why I did it. Yes.

Q: What did you observe when you reached the second floor?

A: Smoke coming from under the door of 2C. Thicker than the stairwell. I could hear something crackling inside.

Q: Did you attempt to alert the occupant?

A: I knocked and yelled. Then I pulled the fire alarm in the hallway and called 911 from the third-floor landing.

topic: A witness is questioned about a fire they discovered in a neighboring unit
text:
Q: Tell me exactly what you saw when you opened your front door, Mr. Okonkwo.

A: Smoke. Thick smoke. And an orange glow coming from down the hall.

Q: An orange glow. From which direction?

A: From 7F. The Martindale unit.

Q: You're certain it was 7F?

A: I've lived in this building for eleven years. I know which unit is which.

Q: I'm not questioning your familiarity with the building. I'm asking how you determined, in a smoke-filled hallway, that the glow was coming specifically from 7F and not 7E or 7G.

A: Because I could see the door. 7F's door. The glow was visible around the frame. The edges. 7E and 7G were dark.

Q: Could the smoke have obscured your view?

A: The smoke was present. My view was not obscured to the point where I couldn't see a door fifteen feet from my own.

Q: Fifteen feet. You're certain of that distance?

A: Approximately fifteen feet. Do you want me to measure it? Would that help?

Q: That won't be necessary. What did you do after observing this glow?

A: I went back inside, told my wife to get our daughter, and we left via the east stairwell.

Q: Did you call 911?

A: My wife did. From the stairwell.

Q: Did you at any point approach unit 7F?

A: No.

Q: You didn't think to check if anyone was inside?

A: I thought to get my family out of a burning building. That's what I thought to do.

topic: A witness is questioned about a fire they discovered in a neighboring unit
text:
Q: Dr. Reyes, I want to go back to something you said earlier. You mentioned you heard a "popping" sound before you smelled smoke. Can you describe that sound in more detail?

A: I can try. It was— look, it's difficult to describe a sound after the fact with the kind of precision you seem to be looking for.

Q: Just do your best.

A: It was sharp. Irregular. Like— I don't know, like something bursting. Small bursts. Several of them in quick succession.

Q: How many?

A: I didn't count them.

Q: More than three?

A: Yes, probably.

Q: More than ten?

A: I have no idea. I wasn't cataloging the sounds. I heard popping, then I smelled smoke, then I looked out my window and saw flames in the unit below mine. That's the sequence.

Q: Let's talk about the flames. What color were they?

A: Orange. Yellow.

Q: Any blue?

A: I don't— possibly. At the base. I wasn't analyzing the color spectrum.

Q: Dr. Reyes, these details matter for determining the origin and cause of the fire.

A: I understand that. I'm telling you what I observed. I'm not a fire investigator.

Q: Did you see anyone in or near unit 3A before the fire?

A: I saw Mr. Huang leave around 6:00. That's it.

Q: You're certain it was 6:00?

A: I was making dinner. I always start at 6:00. So yes.

Q: Did he appear to be carrying anything?

A: A briefcase. Maybe a gym bag. Something under his arm.

Q: Which was it? A briefcase or a gym bag?

A: It was dark. It was under his arm. I'm not going to guess and have you hold me to a guess as if it were sworn testimony about the contents of his hands.

topic: A witness is questioned about a fire they discovered in a neighboring unit
text:
Q: Walk me through what happened after you called 911, Ms. Anderssen.

A: I waited on the line. Gave them the address. Told them there was a fire in unit 12.

Q: Did you provide any other information?

A: What other information?

Q: Did you tell them how large the fire was? Whether anyone was inside? Whether you had attempted to extinguish it?

A: I told them there was a fire and gave them the address. They asked if anyone was hurt, I said I didn't know. They said help was on the way. That's the extent of the conversation.

Q: Then what?

A: I grabbed my dog and left through the back entrance.

Q: Why the back entrance?

A: Because unit 12 is near the front entrance. I wasn't going to walk toward the fire.

Q: Did you see anyone else evacuating?

A: A few people. Mrs. Chen from unit 8. The couple from unit 15, I don't know their names.

Q: Was Mr. Baxter among them?

A: I don't know who that is.

Q: The occupant of unit 12.

A: I didn't see him. I didn't even know that was his name until just now.

Q: You lived in adjacent units and you didn't know his name?

A: I lived in unit 11. We shared a wall. That doesn't mean we shared holiday dinners. People keep to themselves in that building.

Q: Had you ever had any interactions with the occupant of unit 12?

A: I heard his television sometimes. Smelled his cooking. That's not an interaction.

Q: Did you ever hear anything unusual coming from that unit? Arguments? Loud noises?

A: I heard his television. I heard normal apartment sounds. I'm not in the habit of listening through walls and I'm not going to invent something to make your questions easier to answer.

topic: An accountant is deposed about transactions they processed on behalf of a client
text:
Q: Mr. Harmon, I'm going to direct your attention to a wire transfer dated March 15th of last year. Do you recall that transaction?

A: March 15th. I'd need to see the documentation to be certain which specific transfer you're referring to.

Q: It was for $847,000. To an account in the Caymans. Does that refresh your recollection?

A: I processed a number of international transfers for Mr. Dietrich. If you're asking whether I specifically remember that one, I—I would need to see the paperwork.

Q: You processed so many transfers to offshore accounts that you can't remember an $847,000 wire?

A: I'm not saying I don't remember it. I'm saying I want to be precise. You're asking me to testify under oath, and I want to give you accurate information.

Q: Fair enough. I'm handing you what's been marked as Exhibit 14. Take a moment to review it.

A: Okay. Yes. Yes, I see this now.

Q: You initiated this transfer?

A: I—the initials here are mine, so yes, it appears I processed it.

Q: "It appears"?

A: I processed it. Those are my initials.

Q: And what was the purpose of this transfer, as you understood it?

A: Mr. Dietrich told me it was for a real estate acquisition. An investment property.

Q: Did you verify that?

A: That wasn't—I mean, my role was to execute the transactions as directed. Client funds, client direction.

Q: So the answer is no?

A: The answer is that I relied on my client's representations. That's standard practice.

Q: Is it standard practice to wire nearly a million dollars offshore without any supporting documentation?

A: There was documentation. There was—Mr. Dietrich provided a purchase agreement.

Q: Do you have that purchase agreement?

A: I would have to check my files. I don't—I don't have it in front of me right now.

---

topic: An accountant is deposed about transactions they processed on behalf of a client
text:
Q: Ms. Tennant, how long have you served as the accountant for Ridgeline Properties?

A: Six years in September.

Q: And in that time, you've had access to all of their financial accounts?

A: Their operating accounts, yes. Not personal accounts of the individual partners.

Q: Let's talk about the operating accounts. You're aware of the payments made to Coastal Consulting?

A: I am.

Q: How many payments were made to Coastal Consulting between January 2022 and June 2023?

A: I believe it was fourteen. Fourteen or fifteen.

Q: You believe. You don't know?

A: Fourteen. It was fourteen.

Q: Totaling how much?

A: Approximately $1.2 million.

Q: Approximately. Can you be more precise?

A: One million, two hundred eighteen thousand dollars. And some cents.

Q: What services did Coastal Consulting provide in exchange for $1.2 million?

A: They were listed as consulting fees. Strategic consulting.

Q: Listed by whom?

A: By the partners. The payment authorizations came from Mr. Reeves.

Q: Did you ever see a contract between Ridgeline and Coastal Consulting?

A: No.

Q: Did you ever see an invoice from Coastal Consulting?

A: No.

Q: Did you ever meet anyone from Coastal Consulting?

A: No. But that's not unusual. I don't typically meet vendors.

Q: $1.2 million to a company with no contract, no invoices, and no apparent personnel—that didn't strike you as unusual?

A: I'm an accountant, not an investigator. I process what I'm given.

---

topic: An accountant is deposed about transactions they processed on behalf of a client
text:
Q: Let's move on. The quarterly payment to D&R Holdings—

A: I'm sorry, can we take a short break?

Q: We've only been going for forty minutes, Mr. Okonkwo.

A: I understand. I just—I'd like a moment.

Q: We'll take a break when we finish this line of questioning. The payment to D&R Holdings, it was $75,000 per quarter?

A: Yes.

Q: For what purpose?

A: It was categorized as a licensing fee.

Q: Licensing for what?

A: I don't know specifically.

Q: You processed $300,000 a year in licensing fees and you don't know what was being licensed?

A: Proprietary business processes. That's what I was told.

Q: By whom?

A: By Ms. Chen.

Q: Did Ms. Chen explain what these proprietary business processes were?

A: No.

Q: Did you ask?

A: I—no.

Q: No?

A: I had been instructed that certain matters were confidential. That I should process them without—without unnecessary questions.

Q: Who instructed you that?

A: Ms. Chen.

Q: So your client told you not to ask questions, and you just... didn't?

A: I followed the scope of my engagement. That's what I did.

---

topic: An accountant is deposed about transactions they processed on behalf of a client
text:
Q: I want to ask about an entry I noticed. Page forty-seven of the ledger, there's a notation that says "K.M. adjustment." What does that refer to?

A: I'd have to see the specific entry.

Q: It's right there in front of you. Page forty-seven.

A: Yes, I see it now. That would be an adjustment related to Kevin Marsh.

Q: What kind of adjustment?

A: A correction.

Q: A correction of what?

A: Of a previous entry that was made in error.

Q: What was the error?

A: I don't recall the specifics without reviewing the underlying documentation.

Q: The adjustment is for $340,000. That's a significant error.

A: Yes.

Q: And you don't remember what the error was?

A: These records are from three years ago. I've handled hundreds of transactions since then.

Q: Let me ask it a different way. Was the original entry too high or too low?

A: Too high.

Q: So the adjustment reduced Mr. Marsh's allocation by $340,000?

A: If that's what the entry shows, then yes.

Q: Why would Mr. Marsh's allocation need to be reduced by $340,000?

A: I would only be guessing.

Q: I'm not asking you to guess. I'm asking what you knew at the time.

A: At the time, I was told there had been a calculation error and I was asked to make the correction.

Q: Asked by whom?

A: By Mr. Marsh himself.

---

topic: An accountant is deposed about transactions they processed on behalf of a client
text:
Q: The disbursement account—let's talk about that. Who had signatory authority?

A: Mr. Franklin and Ms. Yee.

Q: Anyone else?

A: No.

Q: What about you?

A: I could initiate transfers, but I couldn't approve them.

Q: So you would set up the transfer and one of them would authorize it?

A: Correct.

Q: Every time?

A: Yes.

Q: Every single time?

A: That's what I said.

Q: I'm going to show you Exhibit 31. This is a transfer for $50,000 dated October 3rd. Whose authorization is on this transfer?

A: I'd need to look at it.

Q: Please do.

A: This is—the signature line is blank.

Q: The signature line is blank. So how did this transfer go through?

A: I don't know.

Q: You initiated it?

A: It has my initials, so yes, apparently I initiated it.

Q: And then what? It just... transferred itself?

A: There must have been a verbal authorization.

Q: A verbal authorization for $50,000?

A: It happened occasionally. If Mr. Franklin was traveling, he would call and authorize—

Q: Is there any record of that call?

A: I would have made a note.

Q: Is there a note?

A: I don't see one here.

Q: So we have a $50,000 transfer with your initials, no signature, and no documentation of verbal authorization. Is that correct?

A: That appears to be what the document shows, yes.

topic: A witness is questioned about a fire they discovered in a neighboring unit
text:
Q: Mr. Tanner, can you tell us what you were doing on the evening of March 14th when you first became aware of the fire?

A: Watching TV.

Q: What program were you watching?

A: I don't know. Something. News, maybe.

Q: And what first alerted you to the fire in Unit 7B?

A: The smoke alarm. Their smoke alarm.

Q: What did you do when you heard the alarm?

A: Looked out the window.

Q: And what did you see?

A: Smoke. Coming from their kitchen window.

Q: Did you call 911?

A: Yeah.

Q: Approximately what time was that?

A: I don't know. Eight? Eight-thirty? Somewhere in there.

Q: Did you attempt to alert the occupants of Unit 7B?

A: No.

Q: Why not?

A: Wasn't my business. I called 911. That's what you're supposed to do.

Q: Did you see anyone exit the unit?

A: I saw the guy come out the front eventually. After the trucks showed up.

---

topic: A witness is questioned about a fire they discovered in a neighboring unit
text:
Q: Ms. Vance, you've stated you discovered smoke coming from the adjacent unit at approximately 9:15 p.m. Is that correct?

A: That's my best estimate, yes. I wasn't checking the time obsessively.

Q: Fair enough. Now, prior to noticing the smoke, did you hear anything unusual?

A: Like what?

Q: Any sounds. Voices, banging, anything out of the ordinary.

A: I heard their TV. I always hear their TV. The walls are thin.

Q: Anything else?

A: Maybe some kind of thump. I don't know. Could have been anything.

Q: Let's move on. When you saw the smoke, what was your first action?

A: I grabbed my phone.

Q: To call emergency services?

A: To take a video, actually. Then I called.

Q: You recorded video before calling 911?

A: It was like ten seconds. Maybe fifteen. I figured it might be important later.

Q: Do you still have that video?

A: Somewhere. Probably. I'd have to look.

Q: We may request that. Now, did you know the occupants of the unit personally?

A: I knew their names. Chen, I think. We weren't friends or anything.

---

topic: A witness is questioned about a fire they discovered in a neighboring unit
text:
Q: State your name for the record.

A: David Alan Forrester.

Q: Mr. Forrester, you resided at 4412 Birchwood Lane on the date of the incident?

A: I did.

Q: Unit 3A?

A: Correct.

Q: The fire occurred in Unit 3B. That's directly next to yours?

A: It shares a wall, yes.

Q: Tell me what you observed.

A: I smelled smoke around nine. I went into the hallway. There was smoke coming from under their door. Thick, gray smoke. I knocked. No answer. I called the fire department.

Q: You knocked on the door?

A: I did.

Q: How many times?

A: Three or four times.

Q: Okay. Did you attempt to enter the unit?

A: No.

Q: Was the door locked?

A: I have no idea. I didn't try it.

Q: Any particular reason?

A: I'm not a firefighter. I'm a CPA. I reported it. That was the extent of my involvement.

Q: Right. Did you see flames at any point?

A: Through the window later. Orange glow. The firefighters were already there by then.

---

topic: A witness is questioned about a fire they discovered in a neighboring unit
text:
Q: Let's go through the timeline again, Mrs. Delgado.

A: We've been through it twice.

Q: I understand. Just a few more questions. You said you first noticed something wrong at 7:45?

A: Around then.

Q: And the something wrong was what exactly?

A: I told you. A burning smell.

Q: Right. Fine. What did you do after you noticed the smell?

A: I checked my own stove first. Then I went into the hallway.

Q: Did you see smoke in the hallway?

A: A little. Hazy.

Q: Okay. And then?

A: I knocked on Mrs. Patterson's door. She didn't answer. I called 911.

Q: You were concerned about Mrs. Patterson specifically?

A: She's elderly. Lives alone.

Q: Had you spoken with her that day?

A: No.

Q: The day before?

A: I don't remember. Probably not. We're neighbors, not family.

Q: Was there anyone else in the hallway when you were there?

A: The guy from 4C came out eventually. After I was already on the phone.

---

topic: A witness is questioned about a fire they discovered in a neighboring unit
text:
Q: Mr. Huang, I want to understand the sequence of events. You discovered the fire at what time?

A: It was late. After eleven.

Q: How did you discover it?

A: I was coming home. I saw the glow through their window from the parking lot.

Q: A glow?

A: Fire. Orange light flickering. It was obviously fire.

Q: What did you do?

A: Called 911 from my car.

Q: Did you approach the building?

A: Not right away. I waited for the fire department.

Q: You stayed in your car?

A: I moved my car, actually. Away from the building. In case it spread.

Q: That was your primary concern? Your vehicle?

A: It's a new car. And I could hear sirens already. What was I going to do, run inside with a garden hose?

Q: Did you see anyone else in the parking lot or near the building?

A: A couple people came out of the other units. I didn't talk to them.

Q: Did you know the tenant in the unit where the fire originated?

A: Barely. Young guy. Kept to himself.

Q: Had you ever had any interactions with him?

A: He borrowed a jumper cable from me once. That's it.

Q: Did he return it?

A: Eventually.

topic: A tenant is questioned about property damage they reported to their landlord
text:
Q: Mr. Hernandez, you reported a leak in the bathroom ceiling on March 14th, correct?

A: That's what my email says, yes.

Q: And you described this leak as "severe" in your communication to the landlord?

A: I described it as what it was. Water was coming through the ceiling.

Q: Coming through. You mean dripping?

A: I mean coming through. There's a difference.

Q: Help me understand that difference.

A: Dripping is a faucet. This was water actively running down my bathroom wall and pooling on the floor. I had to put down towels. Multiple towels.

Q: How many towels, specifically?

A: I didn't count them. I was trying to stop water from destroying my apartment.

Q: But you want me to accept that this was severe based on your characterization.

A: I want you to look at the photos I attached to that same email. Did you receive those in discovery?

Q: I'm asking the questions, Mr. Hernandez.

A: And I'm answering them. Accurately. With documentation.

Q: Let's move on. How long did you wait before reporting this leak?

A: I reported it the same day I noticed it. Within hours.

Q: Within hours. Not immediately?

A: I was at work when the leak apparently started. I came home, saw the damage, and sent the email that evening. Is there a faster timeline you'd prefer I had followed?

topic: A tenant is questioned about property damage they reported to their landlord
text:
Q: Ms. Chen, when did you first notice the mold in the bedroom?

A: It was... I want to say mid-January. Around the 15th or 16th.

Q: You want to say, or that's when it was?

A: That's when it was. I remember because I had just taken down my holiday decorations.

Q: And you're certain the mold wasn't present before that date?

A: I'm certain I didn't see it before that date.

Q: Those are two different things, aren't they?

A: I suppose they are. But I can only tell you what I observed.

Q: Fair enough. Now, you claimed the mold covered—and I'm quoting your complaint—"a significant portion of the wall."

A: That's what I wrote, yes.

Q: What does "significant" mean to you?

A: Maybe... two feet by three feet? Roughly?

Q: Roughly. Did you measure it?

A: No, I didn't get out a tape measure. I saw mold spreading on my bedroom wall and I contacted my landlord.

Q: But you felt comfortable using the word "significant" without measuring.

A: I felt comfortable using a word that any reasonable person would use when they see mold spreading across their wall where they sleep every night.

Q: Did you take photographs?

A: I did. Several.

Q: And those would show this significant coverage?

A: They show exactly what was there. You can measure the photographs yourself if precision is what you're after.

topic: A tenant is questioned about property damage they reported to their landlord
text:
Q: Tell me about the window, Mr. Okonkwo.

A: Which window?

Q: The one you reported as damaged.

A: The living room window. The frame was rotted and the window wouldn't close properly.

Q: Wouldn't close properly. Define that for me.

A: There was a gap. Maybe an inch, inch and a half. Couldn't get it to seal no matter what I did.

Q: Did you try to force it closed?

A: I tried to close it normally.

Q: That's not what I asked.

A: No, I didn't force it. I'm not going to break a window and then be blamed for breaking it.

Q: Has anyone blamed you for breaking it?

A: You're asking me if I forced it closed. Why would you ask that unless you were suggesting something?

Q: I'm just trying to understand the sequence of events. When did you report this issue?

A: November 3rd.

Q: And the window had been in this condition for how long before that?

A: A few days. I noticed it when the weather turned cold and I could feel the draft.

Q: A few days. More than three?

A: I don't have an exact count. It wasn't weeks, if that's what you're implying.

Q: I'm not implying anything, Mr. Okonkwo.

A: Then I'll take your questions at face value. Is there anything else about the window?

topic: A tenant is questioned about property damage they reported to their landlord
text:
Q: Ms. Patterson, your maintenance request mentions water damage to your personal belongings.

A: That's correct.

Q: Specifically, you listed a laptop computer.

A: Yes.

Q: Valued at two thousand dollars.

A: That's approximately what I paid for it, yes.

Q: Do you have a receipt for that purchase?

A: I have a credit card statement. I can provide it.

Q: That would be helpful. Now, this laptop—where was it located when the water damage occurred?

A: On my desk. In the second bedroom I use as an office.

Q: And the leak was directly above your desk?

A: The leak was in the ceiling of that room. Water came through and damaged the laptop along with several books and documents.

Q: So the laptop was directly beneath the point of the leak.

A: The water spread. It wasn't a single drip point—it was a section of ceiling that was saturated.

Q: I see. Had you considered moving the laptop once you noticed the leak?

A: I wasn't home when the leak started. I came home to find the damage already done.

Q: You didn't notice any warning signs before that day? Discoloration, bubbling in the ceiling?

A: If I had noticed warning signs, I would have reported them and moved my belongings.

Q: That's not quite an answer to my question.

A: The answer is no. I did not notice warning signs. The ceiling looked normal until it didn't.

topic: A tenant is questioned about property damage they reported to their landlord
text:
Q: Mr. Reeves, how would you describe your relationship with the property manager prior to this incident?

A: It was fine. Normal.

Q: Normal meaning what, exactly?

A: Meaning I paid rent on time, they responded to occasional maintenance requests. Nothing remarkable.

Q: And after you reported the HVAC failure?

A: After I reported it, things became... less cordial.

Q: Less cordial. Can you give me a specific example?

A: My emails started taking longer to get responses. Requests that used to be handled in days suddenly took weeks.

Q: Is it possible the property manager was simply busy?

A: It's possible. But the timing was notable.

Q: Notable to you.

A: Notable to anyone paying attention, I'd think.

Q: Let's talk about the HVAC failure itself. You reported it on August 8th?

A: Correct.

Q: In August. In Texas.

A: Yes.

Q: And you claim the unit was completely non-functional.

A: I don't claim it. It was. The compressor wouldn't turn on. No cold air whatsoever.

Q: Did you have anyone inspect it before contacting the landlord?

A: I'm not permitted to hire contractors to work on the unit. That's in the lease. I reported it to the people responsible for repairs.

Q: And how long did repairs take?

A: Sixteen days.

Q: During which time you remained in the apartment?

A: I had nowhere else to go. So yes, I remained in an apartment with no air conditioning in August in Texas for sixteen days.

topic: A paramedic is questioned about the response time and treatment at an accident scene
text:
Q: State your name and occupation for the record.

A: Michael Torres. Paramedic, twelve years. Can we move this along?

Q: We'll proceed at the pace necessary to get accurate testimony, Mr. Torres. You were the first paramedic on scene at the Riverside Boulevard accident on March 15th?

A: I was.

Q: What time did you arrive?

A: 4:47 PM.

Q: The 911 call came in at 4:31 PM. That's sixteen minutes.

A: Is there a question?

Q: Why did it take sixteen minutes to travel what I'm told is a four-mile route?

A: Traffic. Construction on Harbor. A stalled vehicle. Pick one.

Q: Did you try alternative routes?

A: We followed dispatch protocol. We took the route we were directed to take. I don't have a helicopter.

Q: When you arrived, what was the victim's condition?

A: Unresponsive. Significant blood loss from a head laceration. We initiated treatment immediately.

Q: Immediately. Meaning you didn't waste any time once you finally got there.

A: Counsel, I don't "waste time" when someone is dying in front of me. I did my job. The sixteen minutes getting there were outside my control, and if you're suggesting otherwise, you should say it plainly.

Q: I'm simply asking questions, Mr. Torres.

A: Then ask better ones.

topic: A paramedic is questioned about the response time and treatment at an accident scene
text:
Q: Ms. Okonkwo, walk me through the treatment protocol you initiated upon reaching the patient.

A: We assessed airway, breathing, circulation. Standard trauma protocol. Cervical collar, backboard, started an IV line, administered fluids.

Q: And how long did that assessment take?

A: Maybe ninety seconds. It's rapid by design.

Q: Yet according to the hospital records, the patient arrived with no IV fluids running.

A: That's not accurate.

Q: I have the intake form right here, Ms. Okonkwo. "IV: not present upon arrival."

A: Then someone at the hospital made an error, because I personally inserted that line and watched it running for the entire transport. Twelve minutes. Lactated Ringer's.

Q: So the hospital is lying?

A: I said they made an error. There's a difference. The line may have been dislodged during transfer. That happens.

Q: Convenient.

A: Excuse me?

Q: I said that's convenient, that the evidence of your treatment happened to disappear.

A: Counsel, I have been a paramedic for nine years. I have never—never—fabricated treatment records. My partner can confirm the IV. The run sheet documents it. If the hospital lost it, that's not on me.

Q: Your partner, who was driving?

A: Who checked on the patient twice during transport. Yes.

Q: We'll be deposing him as well.

A: Good. Do that.

topic: A paramedic is questioned about the response time and treatment at an accident scene
text:
Q: Let's discuss the time between your arrival at 2:15 PM and when you began CPR.

A: There was no delay. We began immediately.

Q: The fire department's incident report states CPR was initiated at 2:19 PM.

A: Four minutes. We had to extricate him from the vehicle first. The driver's side door was crushed.

Q: Four minutes is a long time when someone isn't breathing.

A: I'm aware of that. Intimately aware. Are you suggesting we should have started chest compressions while he was pinned inside a crumpled sedan?

Q: I'm trying to understand the sequence of events.

A: The sequence is: we arrived, we assessed, we determined he was trapped, we coordinated with fire rescue to pry open the door, we extracted him, we began CPR. Four minutes. Under the circumstances, that was fast.

Q: Under the circumstances.

A: Yes.

Q: Did you consider breaking the windshield to access him?

A: The windshield was already shattered. The angle didn't allow access. We're trained in vehicle extrication, counsel. This wasn't our first accident.

Q: But it was Mr. Patterson's last day alive.

A: ...Yes. It was.

Q: And you feel the response was adequate?

A: I feel that I did everything within my power and my training. That man was catastrophically injured. We gave him his only chance. Sometimes that's not enough. That doesn't mean we failed him.

topic: A paramedic is questioned about the response time and treatment at an accident scene
text:
Q: What medication did you administer on scene?

A: Epinephrine. One milligram IV push.

Q: Just the one dose?

A: Followed by a second dose four minutes later per ACLS protocol.

Q: And the naloxone?

A: What naloxone?

Q: Are you saying you didn't administer naloxone at the scene?

A: There was no indication for naloxone. This was a motor vehicle trauma, not an overdose.

Q: The toxicology report shows opioids in the victim's system.

A: Which I didn't have access to while I was doing chest compressions on the side of the highway.

Q: But the pinpoint pupils—

A: The patient had massive head trauma. Pupil response was abnormal for multiple reasons. There was no drug paraphernalia, no witness report of drug use, no track marks visible. We treat what we see.

Q: So you missed it.

A: We treated a trauma patient as a trauma patient. If you're going to sit there with a toxicology report that took a lab three days to produce and tell me I should have diagnosed it in three seconds—

Q: I'm asking whether different treatment might have changed the outcome.

A: And I'm telling you that's a question for a physician, not a paramedic being second-guessed with information he didn't have.

Q: Fair enough. Let's move on.

A: Let's.

topic: A paramedic is questioned about the response time and treatment at an accident scene
text:
Q: You've reviewed your incident report prior to today's deposition?

A: I have.

Q: And this is your signature on page three?

A: It is.

Q: The report states you arrived at 7:52 PM. Is that accurate?

A: Yes.

Q: Your unit was dispatched at 7:38 PM. Fourteen minutes for a six-minute drive.

A: We had another call.

Q: Another call.

A: We were completing transport on a cardiac patient to St. Vincent's when the dispatch came through. We cleared that call and proceeded directly.

Q: So this accident was not your priority.

A: The cardiac patient who was actively in our ambulance was our priority at that moment, yes. That's how emergency medicine works.

Q: And no other units were available?

A: You'd have to ask dispatch. We responded as soon as we were clear.

Q: The family believes those fourteen minutes cost their daughter her life.

A: I understand that. I understand their pain. But I cannot be in two places at once, and I will not apologize for not abandoning a seventy-year-old man having a heart attack.

Q: I'm not asking you to apologize.

A: Then what are you asking? Because it sounds like you want me to say I did something wrong, and I didn't. We followed protocol. We responded. We fought for that girl for thirty-one minutes. I'm the one who called time of death. So whatever you're looking for here, counsel, you should know that I carry that night with me. Every shift. Don't sit there and suggest I didn't care enough to drive faster.

Q: I have no further questions at this time.

A: Fine.

topic: A nurse is questioned about a patient fall that occurred during her shift
text:
Q: State your name for the record, please.

A: Linda Marchetti. Linda Ann Marchetti.

Q: Ms. Marchetti, you were the charge nurse on duty the night of October 14th, correct?

A: I was the charge nurse on the third floor, yes. The medical-surgical unit specifically.

Q: And you were assigned to Mr. Okonkwo's room that night?

A: I was assigned to several rooms. His was one of them. I believe I had six patients total that shift, maybe seven. I'd have to check the assignment sheet to be completely certain.

Q: That's fine. What time did your shift begin?

A: Seven p.m. 7:00 p.m. exactly. Well, I clocked in at 6:52, but the shift officially began at seven.

Q: When did you first see Mr. Okonkwo that evening?

A: I did initial rounds between—it would have been between 7:15 and 7:45, somewhere in there. I saw him during that time. I don't have the exact minute documented, but it was during that window.

Q: How would you describe his condition at that time?

A: He was—let me think. He was alert. Oriented. He was watching television, I believe. His vitals from the previous shift were stable. I reviewed those. His IV was intact. He didn't report any complaints when I asked.

Q: Did you assess him as a fall risk?

A: The fall risk assessment had been completed on admission. I reviewed it. He was—I believe he was scored as moderate risk. The yellow bracelet was on his wrist. The sign was posted. I verified both of those things during my rounds.

Q: What precautions were in place?

A: The bed alarm was—the bed alarm should have been activated. The call light was within reach. I positioned it myself. Side rails were up, both of them. Non-slip socks had been provided. I'm certain about the socks because I noted the color. They were yellow, which matched his risk level.

Q: You said the bed alarm "should have been" activated. Was it or wasn't it?

A: It was activated when I checked. I'm just—I'm being careful with my words because I can only speak to what I personally observed. I observed it activated. What happened after I left the room, I can't—I wouldn't want to speculate about that.

topic: A nurse is questioned about a patient fall that occurred during her shift
text:
Q: Nurse Delgado, how long have you worked at Riverside Memorial?

A: Eleven years.

Q: And in those eleven years, how many patient falls have you personally witnessed?

A: Witnessed? Maybe three.

Q: How many have occurred during your shifts, whether you witnessed them or not?

A: I don't know.

Q: More than ten?

A: I don't know. I haven't counted.

Q: Let's talk about Mrs. Patterson. What do you remember about finding her on the floor?

A: I heard a sound. A thump. I went to her room. She was on the floor beside the bed.

Q: What kind of sound exactly?

A: A thump.

Q: Loud? Soft?

A: Medium.

Q: Where were you when you heard it?

A: The hallway.

Q: Where in the hallway?

A: Near the nurses' station.

Q: How far is that from room 412?

A: I'm not sure exactly. Thirty feet maybe.

Q: Did you run to the room or walk?

A: I walked quickly.

Q: Was anyone else in the room when you arrived?

A: No.

Q: Was Mrs. Patterson conscious?

A: Yes.

Q: What did she say to you?

A: She said she was trying to get to the bathroom.

topic: A nurse is questioned about a patient fall that occurred during her shift
text:
Q: Let me make sure I understand your testimony. You're saying you checked on Mr. Briggs at 2:00 a.m.?

A: Approximately 2:00 a.m., yes.

Q: And the fall occurred at what time?

A: The fall was—I found him at 3:47. That's when it was documented.

Q: So nearly two hours passed between your check and the fall?

A: The rounding schedule was every two hours. That was the protocol for his risk level. I was following protocol.

Q: I'm not asking about protocol right now. I'm asking about the gap. Two hours is a long time, isn't it?

A: I—it's the standard interval. For moderate-risk patients.

Q: Were you busy with other patients during that time?

A: I had other patients, yes. I had a full assignment.

Q: How many?

A: Five that night.

Q: Any emergencies during that window?

A: There was a patient who needed—yes, there was a situation that required my attention.

Q: What situation?

A: A patient was experiencing chest pain. I was with her for—I don't remember exactly. Maybe thirty, forty minutes. The physician was paged.

Q: Did that delay your rounds?

A: It may have. I was prioritizing based on acuity.

Q: So it's possible you would have checked on Mr. Briggs sooner if not for the chest pain situation?

A: I don't know. I can't say what would have happened. I responded to the situation in front of me. That's what we do. We triage. I triaged.

Q: I'm just asking whether—

A: I understand what you're asking.

topic: A nurse is questioned about a patient fall that occurred during her shift
text:
Q: The bed alarm. Walk me through how it works.

A: It's a sensor pad. Under the mattress pad, on top of the mattress. When the patient's weight comes off it, it triggers the alarm at the nurses' station.

Q: Simple enough. So if Mr. Vance got out of bed, the alarm would sound?

A: In theory, yes. If it was functioning properly and positioned correctly.

Q: Was there any reason to think it wasn't functioning properly that night?

A: No. Not that I was aware of.

Q: Did you test it yourself?

A: We don't typically—the protocol doesn't require us to test it every shift.

Q: That wasn't my question. Did you personally test the bed alarm in Mr. Vance's room on the night of February 3rd?

A: No.

Q: When was the last time anyone tested it, do you know?

A: I don't know. That would be in the maintenance logs. Biomed handles that.

Q: Did you hear an alarm before Mr. Vance was found on the floor?

A: ...No.

Q: No alarm at all?

A: Not that I heard.

Q: Were you at the nurses' station?

A: I was—I had stepped away briefly.

Q: Stepped away to where?

A: To the supply room. We were low on IV tubing. I was restocking.

Q: How long were you in the supply room?

A: A few minutes. Five, maybe. I really don't—it wasn't long.

Q: Long enough to miss an alarm?

A: I don't know if the alarm even went off. I can't confirm that it did.

topic: A nurse is questioned about a patient fall that occurred during her shift
text:
Q: Ms. Yoon, in your incident report, you wrote that Mrs. Gladwell was quote, "found on floor beside bed, responsive and alert." Is that accurate?

A: Yes.

Q: You also wrote that she quote, "denied pain at the time of assessment." Correct?

A: That's what she told me, yes.

Q: But she later reported hip pain.

A: Later, yes. In the morning. Several hours later.

Q: And X-rays revealed a fracture.

A: That's my understanding, yes.

Q: Looking back, do you think your initial assessment missed something?

A: I documented what she reported to me. She denied pain. I asked her directly. Multiple times actually. I asked if anything hurt, and she said no.

Q: Did you palpate the hip?

A: I performed a visual assessment. I checked for obvious deformity. She was moving her legs. She didn't appear to be—she wasn't guarding.

Q: Did you palpate the hip, yes or no?

A: No. She was moving all extremities. She had full range of motion. I didn't—at the time, there was no indication.

Q: No indication to you.

A: To me, correct. Based on my clinical judgment at that moment.

Q: A fractured hip, and no indication.

A: She was elderly. Elderly patients sometimes don't—the pain presentation can be atypical. That's well documented in the literature. I'm not making excuses. I'm explaining that it's—it happens. It's a known phenomenon.

Q: I'm sure it is.

A: I did what I was trained to do. I assessed her. I documented accurately. I reported to the physician.

topic: A pharmacist is deposed about a prescription that was filled with the wrong dosage
text:
Q: Mr. Holloway, you were the pharmacist on duty the morning of September 14th, correct?

A: I was one of two pharmacists on duty, yes.

Q: And you personally filled the prescription for Mrs. Delgado?

A: I verified the prescription. The pharmacy technician physically counted and bottled the medication.

Q: So when you say "verified," what exactly does that mean?

A: It means I checked the prescription against what was dispensed. The drug, the quantity, the dosage, the patient information.

Q: You checked all of that.

A: That's what verification means, yes.

Q: And yet Mrs. Delgado received 50 milligram tablets instead of the prescribed 5 milligrams.

A: That's what I've been told occurred, yes.

Q: You've been told. You don't know?

topic: A pharmacist is deposed about a prescription that was filled with the wrong dosage
text:

topic: A doctor is deposed about informed consent procedures before a surgery
text:
Q: Dr. Patel, I'd like to ask you about the consent process for Mrs. Thornton's surgery. Can you walk me through what happened that morning?

A: Of course. Mrs. Thornton was scheduled for a laparoscopic cholecystectomy. I came to see her in pre-op around 6:15 in the morning. Her daughter was with her—I remember because Mrs. Thornton kept looking over at her while we talked.

Q: And what did you discuss with her?

A: I went through the procedure itself, the risks we'd discussed before in my office, and I asked if she had any questions. She'd had some time to think since our consultation, so I wanted to make sure nothing new had come up for her.

Q: Did she have questions?

A: She did. She asked me again about the recovery time because her grandson was graduating in three weeks. That mattered to her. So we talked through what she could realistically expect, what activities she'd need to avoid, that sort of thing.

Q: How long did this conversation take?

A: Maybe fifteen minutes. I don't rush these conversations. Patients are anxious before surgery—that's just the reality of it—and I've found that taking a few extra minutes helps them feel more settled.

Q: Did you discuss the specific risk of bile duct injury?

A: I did. I always discuss that risk with cholecystectomy patients because while it's uncommon, it's serious. I told her the risk was roughly one in two hundred to one in five hundred, depending on anatomy.

Q: What was her response?

A: She nodded. She said she understood. Her daughter asked a follow-up question about what would happen if that occurred, and I explained the potential need for additional surgery and the recovery implications.

Q: Did Mrs. Thornton seem to understand what you were telling her?

A: She did. She was alert, she was asking appropriate questions, and when I asked her to tell me back what she understood, she got it right. She was a sharp woman.

Q: You used the past tense just now.

A: Yes. I'm aware of how things turned out for her. I think about her quite a bit, actually.

topic: A doctor is deposed about informed consent procedures before a surgery
text:
Q: Dr. Marchetti, how many spinal fusion surgeries would you estimate you've performed?

A: Over the course of my career? Somewhere around eight hundred.

Q: And in each of those cases, you obtain informed consent?

A: Every single one.

Q: Let's talk about Mr. Davis specifically. Did you have a consent conversation with him?

A: I did.

Q: When?

A: Two occasions. Once in my office during the surgical consultation, and again the morning of the procedure.

Q: Why twice?

A: Because I believe patients need time to process what they're hearing. When someone first learns they need spine surgery, they're often frightened. They're not always absorbing everything. So I go through it once, give them materials to take home, and then we revisit it when they've had time to think.

Q: That's not required by hospital policy, is it?

A: No. It's just how I practice.

Q: During the consent conversation, did you discuss the risk of paralysis?

A: I did.

Q: What exactly did you tell Mr. Davis?

A: I told him that while paralysis is a rare complication, it is a known risk of the procedure. I explained that the risk was less than one percent but that it was real and that he needed to understand that before agreeing to surgery.

Q: How did he react?

A: He was quiet for a moment. Then he asked me if I'd ever had a patient become paralyzed. I told him I had not, but that I had colleagues who had, and that this was part of why we take every precaution we do.

Q: Did you feel he understood?

A: I did. Mr. Davis was a thoughtful man. He asked good questions. He took the consent form home and came back with it signed two days later. He'd clearly read it carefully.

Q: Dr. Marchetti, I have to ask these questions. I'm not suggesting you did anything wrong.

A: I understand. And I want to answer them thoroughly because Mr. Davis deserved excellent care, and I want his family to know exactly what happened.

topic: A doctor is deposed about informed consent procedures before a surgery
text:
Q: State your name for the record.

A: Dr. Yolanda Freeman.

Q: Dr. Freeman, you performed a hysterectomy on Sandra Bellamy on March 14th of last year, correct?

A: That's correct.

Q: Did you obtain her informed consent?

A: I did.

Q: Tell me about that process.

A: I met with Ms. Bellamy in my office a week before surgery. We discussed her diagnosis, the recommended procedure, alternatives to surgery, and the risks involved.

Q: What risks did you discuss?

A: Bleeding, infection, injury to surrounding organs, adverse reaction to anesthesia, and the permanence of the procedure—meaning she would no longer be able to bear children.

Q: Did she express any concerns?

A: She did.

Q: What were they?

A: She was thirty-four. She hadn't had children yet. Even though she understood the medical necessity, this was not an easy decision for her.

Q: What did you say to her?

A: I gave her time. I told her this was her decision and that I would support whatever she chose. I explained the alternatives again—medication management, less invasive procedures—and I was honest that none of them would address her condition as definitively.

Q: Did you pressure her to have the surgery?

A: No. Absolutely not. I told her to take as much time as she needed. She went home, talked to her family, and called my office four days later to schedule the procedure.

Q: When you saw her the morning of surgery, what was her demeanor?

A: She was emotional but resolved. She told me she'd made peace with it. She thanked me for giving her space to decide.

Q: Did you discuss the risks again that morning?

A: Briefly, yes. I always do. I asked if she had any last questions. She said she didn't. She signed the consent form, and we proceeded.

topic: A doctor is deposed about informed consent procedures before a surgery

Q: Dr. Huang, did you explain to Mr. Kowalski that he might lose his leg?

A: Yes.

Q: Those exact words?

A: I don't remember my exact words. But I absolutely communicated that amputation was a possibility if the bypass failed.

Q: You don't remember your exact words, but you're certain you communicated this?

A: I am certain.

Q: How can you be certain if you don't remember the exact words?

A: Because I have had this conversation hundreds of times in my career. I know what I say. I know how I explain it. And I documented the conversation in my note that same day.

Q: Let's look at your note, then.

A: All right.

Q: It says, "Risks, benefits, and alternatives discussed. Patient understands and consents."

A: That's correct.

Q: That's not very detailed, is it?

A: It's a summary. The conversation itself was much longer.

Q: How long?

A: At least twenty minutes, possibly longer. Mr. Kowalski had a lot of questions.

Q: What kind of questions?

A: He wanted to know the success rates. He wanted to know what his life would look like if the surgery worked versus if it didn't. He asked about rehabilitation, about prosthetics, about whether he'd be able to work again.

Q: And you answered all of those?

A: Every one. I sat with him until he told me he had no more questions.

Q: Did you sit with him, or were you standing?

A: I sat. I pulled up a chair and sat at his bedside.

Q: Why does that matter?

A: Because when you're standing over someone in a hospital bed, you're in a position of authority. When you sit, you're telling them you're there to talk with them, not at them. That matters, especially when someone is scared.

topic: A doctor is deposed about informed consent procedures before a surgery
text:
Q: Dr. Okonkwo, I want to understand the timeline here. When did you first discuss surgery with the Reyes family?

A: The day after Miguel was admitted. Once we had the imaging results and understood the extent of the tumor.

Q: Miguel was nine years old at the time?

A: Yes.

Q: So you discussed consent with his parents?

A: With his parents, yes. But I also talked to Miguel directly.

Q: Why?

A: Because it was his body. He was going to be the one going through this. I wanted him to understand as much as he could about what was happening.

Q: How do you explain brain surgery to a nine-year-old?

A: Carefully. I used simple language. I showed him pictures. I told him I was going to help fix something in his head that was making him sick, and that he would be asleep the whole time and wouldn't feel anything.

Q: Did he seem to understand?

A: As much as any child can. He asked if it would hurt afterward. He asked if his hair would grow back. Those were the things that mattered to him.

Q: What did you tell him?

A: I told him the truth. I said yes, there would be some soreness, but we would give him medicine to help. And yes, his hair would grow back.

Q: Let's talk about the consent conversation with his parents.

A: Of course.

Q: What did you tell them about the risks?

A: I told them this was a serious surgery. I explained the location of the tumor, the structures at risk, the possibility of neurological deficits, the risk of bleeding, infection, and the small but real risk that Miguel might not survive the procedure.

Q: How did they respond?

A: His mother cried. His father held her hand and asked me what would happen if they chose not to operate.

Q: What did you tell them?

A: I told them the tumor would continue to grow. That Miguel would likely have six months, maybe less. That the end would not be peaceful.

Q: That's a difficult thing to say to a parent.

A: It's the most difficult thing I ever have to say. But they deserved the truth. They needed it to make their decision. I wasn't going to take that away from them.
