A: Yes. Two adults. That's the ratio we're supposed to maintain.

Q: Where exactly were you standing when Marcus fell from the climbing structure?

A: I was—okay, I need to be very precise here because I've gone over this so many times. I was by the sandbox. Which is maybe fifteen feet from the climbing structure. Maybe twenty. I didn't measure it.

Q: Fifteen to twenty feet. And where was Ms. Cole?

A: She was—I believe she was helping one of the other children with their shoes. By the bench.

Q: So neither of you was within arm's reach of the climbing structure?

A: We can't be everywhere at once. I need you to understand that. We can't be within arm's reach of every piece of equipment simultaneously. That's not—that's not physically possible.

Q: I'm simply asking where you were positioned, Ms. Hernandez.

A: And I told you. I told you exactly where I was.

Q: Did you see Marcus begin to climb?

A: I saw him on the structure. I don't—I can't tell you the precise second he started climbing because I was scanning, I was watching all of them, which is what we're trained to do. We don't focus on one child. We scan.

Q: At what point did you realize something was wrong?

A: When I heard the sound. When I heard him—when he hit the ground. And I was there immediately. Immediately. I was right there.

topic: A daycare worker is deposed about an injury a child sustained while in their care
text:
Q: Let's talk about the incident report you filled out that afternoon.

A: Okay.

Q: You wrote here—and I'm reading—"Child was running in the hallway and collided with door frame." Is that accurate?

A: That's what I wrote, yes.

Q: Is that what happened?

A: To the best of my recollection at the time, yes.

Q: At the time. Has your recollection changed?

A: I'm just saying that's what I remembered when I wrote it. That day. While it was fresh.

Q: Mr. Patterson, I need to know what actually happened to this child.

A: And I'm telling you what I observed.

Q: Were you in the hallway when Emma fell?

A: I was in the doorway of the Butterfly Room.

Q: So you saw her running?

A: Yes.

Q: And you saw her hit the door frame?

A: I saw her fall. I heard the impact.

Q: Those are two different things. Did you see contact with the door frame or didn't you?

A: I—things happened very fast. She was running, and then she was on the ground, and there was blood. There was a lot of blood. Head wounds bleed.

Q: I understand. But you wrote definitively that she "collided with door frame." Were you guessing?

A: I was documenting what made sense based on where she was and where she ended up.

Q: So you didn't actually see the collision.

A: I saw enough to write what I wrote.

topic: A daycare worker is deposed about an injury a child sustained while in their care
text:
Q: Ms. Okonkwo, walk me through the diaper changing procedure at Little Explorers Academy.

A: We take the child to the changing station, check that all supplies are within reach, keep one hand on the child at all times during the change, dispose of the diaper properly, clean the child, apply any necessary cream, put on the fresh diaper, wash our hands, and sanitize the area.

Q: One hand on the child at all times?

A: That's the policy.

Q: Is that what happened on January 15th with Aiden?

A: Yes.

Q: Then how did he end up on the floor?

A: I don't—he moved very quickly.

Q: He moved very quickly while you had one hand on him?

A: Children move. They squirm. They're not—they don't stay still.

Q: So your hand wasn't on him when he rolled off the table?

A: My hand was—I was reaching for the wipes.

Q: The wipes that should have been within reach before you started the change?

A: They were. They just—I needed more than I'd pulled out.

Q: So you removed your hand from Aiden to reach for additional wipes?

A: For a second. One second. Not even.

Q: And in that second, he fell approximately three feet onto a tile floor?

A: Yes.

Q: Had anyone ever discussed with you what happens when you take your hand off a child during a change?

A: We know not to do that.

Q: But you did it.

A: I made a mistake. I made a mistake, and I have to live with that. Is that what you want me to say?

topic: A daycare worker is deposed about an injury a child sustained while in their care
text:
Q: Tell me about the supervision log for the infant room on August 8th.

A: What about it?

Q: Have you reviewed it recently?

A: My attorney showed it to me, yes.

Q: Good, so you'll recall that your initials appear at 2:15 p.m. for a routine check?

A: If that's what it says.

Q: I'm asking if you remember initialing at 2:15.

A: I initial when I do my checks. That's the protocol.

Q: And what does a routine check involve?

A: Visual confirmation that each infant is breathing normally, positioned safely in their crib, no signs of distress.

Q: Did you check on Baby Lily at 2:15?

A: I checked on all the infants.

Q: Including Lily?

A: Including Lily.

Q: And she was breathing normally?

A: Yes.

Q: Positioned safely?

A: On her back, yes.

Q: No signs of distress?

A: No.

Q: Then can you explain why, at 2:22—seven minutes later—she was found unresponsive and blue in the face?

A: I cannot explain that. I wish I could. I've gone over it a thousand times. She was fine at 2:15. She was fine.

Q: Seven minutes.

A: I know how long seven minutes is.

topic: A daycare worker is deposed about an injury a child sustained while in their care
text:
Q: How would you describe your training on allergen management, Ms. Reeves?

A: It was thorough. Very thorough.

Q: Define thorough for me.

A: We had a full module on it during orientation. Identifying allergens, reading labels, emergency protocols, EpiPen administration.

Q: EpiPen administration. You were trained to use an EpiPen?

A: Yes.

Q: On March 3rd, did the classroom have an EpiPen available for children with known allergies?

A: We had one for Sophie. It was in the cabinet.

Q: And when Sophie began showing signs of anaphylaxis, what did you do?

A: I called for help. I called for Ms. Drummond and I went to the cabinet.

Q: And?

A: And it wasn't there.

Q: The EpiPen wasn't in the cabinet.

A: It wasn't—I don't know where it was. It was supposed to be there. It's always supposed to be there.

Q: Whose responsibility was it to ensure the EpiPen was in that cabinet?

A: I check every morning.

Q: Did you check on March 3rd?

A: I—we were short-staffed that day and things were hectic when I came in—

Q: Did you check on March 3rd, yes or no?

A: I don't remember checking.

Q: You don't remember, or you didn't check?

A: I don't remember.

Q: Ms. Reeves, a five-year-old girl spent six days in the ICU. I need to know whether you checked that cabinet.

A: I understand what happened. I understand exactly what happened. And I don't—I cannot tell you with certainty that I checked, and I have to live with that for the rest of my life. But I don't remember. I truly don't remember.

topic: A witness is questioned about a workplace injury they observed but did not report
text:
Q: Mr. Hendricks, I want to direct your attention to the afternoon of March 14th. You were working in the warehouse that day, correct?

A: Yes.

Q: And at some point that afternoon, you observed an incident involving your coworker, Daniel Reyes?

A: I saw something, yeah.

Q: Can you describe what you saw?

A: He was up on one of the ladders. The rolling ones. And he came down off it in a way that... I don't know. It didn't look right.

Q: What do you mean, "didn't look right"?

A: Like he slipped or lost his footing. I wasn't standing right there. I was across the floor.

Q: How far away would you estimate you were?

A: I don't know. Thirty feet? Forty? I'm not good with distances.

Q: That's fine. Just your best estimate. So you saw Mr. Reyes slip or lose his footing on the ladder. What happened next?

A: He was on the ground. Holding his arm, I think. Or his side. I really... I saw it for a second, and then I had to get back to what I was doing.

Q: You had to get back to what you were doing?

A: We had a shipment going out. I was already behind.

Q: Did you approach Mr. Reyes to see if he was injured?

A: No.

Q: Did you call out to him?

A: No.

Q: Did you report what you saw to a supervisor?

A: ...No.

Q: Why not?

A: I figured someone else would. There were other people around. And like I said, I was in the middle of something.

topic: A witness is questioned about a workplace injury they observed but did not report
text:
Q: Ms. Thornton, how long have you worked at Greenleaf Processing?

A: It'll be six years in August.

Q: And in those six years, have you received training on workplace safety protocols?

A: We do the training every year. The videos, the sign-off sheets.

Q: So you're familiar with the procedure for reporting injuries?

A: I know what we're supposed to do, yes.

Q: Walk me through that. What are you supposed to do if you witness a workplace injury?

A: You're supposed to notify your supervisor. Or go to the safety office if it's serious.

Q: Okay. Let's talk about what you witnessed on October 2nd. You were in the break room?

A: Just outside of it. In the hallway.

Q: And what did you see?

A: Linda — Linda Marsh — she was coming out of the supply closet, and she was moving strange. Limping. And she had her hand pressed against the small of her back.

Q: Did she say anything to you?

A: She said something about the shelving unit. That something fell.

Q: What exactly did she say? As best you can recall.

A: She said, "Those damn brackets gave out again." Something close to that.

Q: What did you understand that to mean?

A: That something on the shelf fell and hurt her.

Q: Did you report this to anyone?

A: I didn't, no.

Q: You just testified that you're familiar with the reporting procedure. You saw a coworker injured. Why didn't you follow the procedure?

A: I... look, I don't have a good answer for you. I should have. I didn't. Linda said she was fine, said she'd handle it herself. I took her at her word.

Q: Did she handle it herself, to your knowledge?

A: I don't know what she did after that. I went back to my station.

topic: A witness is questioned about a workplace injury they observed but did not report
text:
Q: Let's go over this one more time, Mr. Paulson.

A: We've been over it twice already.

Q: I understand. I have a few more questions.

A: Fine.

Q: You stated that you saw Kevin Alderman fall from the loading dock.

A: I saw him go down. I didn't see the actual fall. By the time I looked, he was already on the ground.

Q: Alright. When you looked over, was anyone else in the vicinity?

A: There were people around. I couldn't tell you who.

Q: You couldn't tell me a single person who was in the area?

A: It was months ago. I don't have a photographic memory.

Q: I'm not asking for a photographic memory, Mr. Paulson. I'm asking if you recall anyone at all.

A: ...Maybe Tommy Weiss was on the forklift. Maybe. I'm not certain.

Q: Did Tommy Weiss see what happened?

A: You'd have to ask Tommy.

Q: Did you speak with Tommy about it afterward?

A: I don't think so.

Q: You don't think so, or you didn't?

A: I didn't.

Q: Did you speak with anyone about what you observed?

A: I don't... no. I kept my head down and did my work.

Q: And you didn't file a report.

A: No.

Q: Even though you witnessed a coworker injured on company property.

A: I didn't witness it. I saw the aftermath. There's a difference, and I've explained that difference to you now three times.

topic: A witness is questioned about a workplace injury they observed but did not report
text:
Q: Mrs. Delacroix, I just have a few questions about the incident on June 18th.

A: Alright.

Q: You were working in the packaging department that day?

A: Yes, same as every day.

Q: Can you tell me what happened with regards to the injury sustained by Marcus Webb?

A: I can tell you what I saw. Whether it's what happened, I can't say for certain.

Q: That's all I'm asking. What did you see?

A: Marcus was working the sealing machine. The one with the heat element. And he pulled his hand back very suddenly and made a sound.

Q: What kind of sound?

A: A pained sound. Like a yelp, I suppose.

Q: Did you see what caused him to react that way?

A: I assumed he touched the heating element. Burned himself. But I didn't see it directly.

Q: What did you do after you heard him make this sound?

A: I looked over. He was shaking his hand. Then he walked off toward the restroom.

Q: Did you follow him?

A: No.

Q: Did you check on him later?

A: I asked him if he was okay when he came back. He said it was nothing.

Q: Did you report the incident?

A: ...I thought about it.

Q: But you didn't.

A: No.

Q: Why not?

A: I don't know. He said he was fine. I had my own work to do. The day just... kept going.

Q: Is that typically how things are handled in your department? Someone gets injured, and the day just keeps going?

A: I'm not going to speak to what's typical. I can only tell you what happened that day.

Q: Fair enough. Let me ask it differently. Was there any reason you felt you shouldn't report it?

A: No, there was no reason like that. I just... didn't.

topic: A witness is questioned about a workplace injury they observed but did not report
text:
Q: Mr. Okonkwo, we've been at this for a while now, so I'll try to keep this portion brief.

A: I appreciate that.

Q: On April 3rd, you were working the second shift in Building C, correct?

A: Correct.

Q: At approximately 9 p.m., there was an incident involving a coworker named Janet Freely.

A: Yes.

Q: Tell me what you observed.

A: Janet was moving one of the chemical drums — the smaller ones, maybe fifty-five gallons — and it tipped. Some of the contents splashed onto her legs.

Q: What kind of chemical was in the drum?

A: I believe it was a cleaning solvent. Industrial grade.

Q: Did it cause a visible reaction? Burns, irritation?

A: She was wearing her coveralls, so I couldn't see her skin. But she was in distress. She went immediately to the wash station.

Q: Did you assist her?

A: I made sure the area was clear so no one else would slip. The floor was wet.

Q: That was good thinking. Did you do anything else?

A: I finished clearing the spill while she was at the wash station.

Q: Did you report the incident to a supervisor?

A: I did not.

Q: Why not?

A: Janet said she had it under control. She said she'd report it herself if it was serious.

Q: Do you know if she ever did?

A: I don't. We weren't on the same shift after that week.

Q: Looking back, do you think you should have reported it regardless of what Janet said?

A: ...Probably. Yes. But at the time, it didn't seem like my place.

Q: Let's leave it there.

A: Alright.

topic: A witness is asked about a car accident they saw from their front porch
text:
Q: Good morning. You were sitting on your front porch on the afternoon of March 12th, correct?

A: That's right.

Q: And from that position, you witnessed a collision between two vehicles?

A: I saw something happen, yes.

Q: Something happen. Can you describe what you saw?

A: Well, I heard it first. A loud noise. Then I looked up and there were two cars in the intersection.

Q: Which direction were you looking when you heard the noise?

A: I was... I had been reading. So I was looking down. At my book.

Q: So you didn't actually see the moment of impact?

A: I saw the cars afterward. They were stopped. Or—one was stopped, one was still moving a little. Rolling, I guess.

Q: Rolling in which direction?

A: Toward the curb. The one curb. On the east side? Or maybe that's west. I'm not—which way is Maple Street from where I sit?

Q: I'm asking you, ma'am.

A: Right. Sorry. I think it rolled to my left. If I'm facing the street.

Q: To your left. And the other vehicle?

A: It was just... there. In the middle of everything.

Q: In the middle of the intersection?

A: Or near it. There was a lot happening. The horn was going off, someone was yelling. I remember thinking I should call someone but I couldn't remember if you're supposed to call 911 for car accidents or if there's a different number.

---

topic: A witness is asked about a car accident they saw from their front porch
text:
Q: Mr. Patterson, how far is your porch from the intersection where this accident occurred?

A: I'd say about fifty feet. Maybe sixty.

Q: Fifty to sixty feet. And there's nothing obstructing your view?

A: There's a mailbox. And the Hendersons' truck, when it's parked there. But it wasn't that day.

Q: So you had a clear line of sight?

A: I had a clear line of sight to the intersection, yes.

Q: Good. Now, the vehicle that you've described as a "dark sedan"—

A: I said it looked dark. It could have been dark blue, could have been black. Could have been a very dark green, even.

Q: Let me finish my question, please.

A: Sorry.

Q: The vehicle you described as a dark sedan—was it traveling north or south on Birch Avenue?

A: It was coming from my right.

Q: Which would be which direction?

A: I don't... north? I think north is to my right when I'm facing the street.

Q: You think?

A: I've lived there eleven years and I've never had to testify about compass directions before.

Q: Fair enough. The car was coming from your right. What about the other vehicle?

A: From the left. A white SUV. Or off-white. Cream, maybe. It was definitely lighter colored.

Q: And which vehicle entered the intersection first?

A: That's what I can't—they both just appeared. At the same time, almost. I don't know who was there first.

---

topic: A witness is asked about a car accident they saw from their front porch
text:
Q: Let's go back to the traffic signals. You mentioned you could see the light from your porch?

A: I can see the light facing the east-west traffic.

Q: And what color was it when the collision occurred?

A: Green.

Q: Green for which direction of traffic?

A: For the cars going east-west.

Q: So it would have been red for north-south traffic?

A: That's how traffic lights work, yes.

Q: I'm just trying to establish—

A: I know. I'm sorry. Yes. If it was green one way, it was red the other way.

Q: Now, you've stated the pickup truck was traveling east, is that right?

A: I don't think I said that.

Q: In your statement to police—

A: I told the police officer I wasn't sure. He kept asking me to pick a direction. I said I thought maybe east.

Q: So you're not certain which direction the truck was traveling?

A: I know it came through the intersection from the side that should have had a red light.

Q: Should have had?

A: Did have. Had a red light.

Q: But you just told me the green light was for east-west traffic.

A: Right.

Q: And the truck was traveling east.

A: If east is... hold on. Which street runs east-west? I'm turned around now.

Q: Oak Street runs east-west.

A: Then I don't know why I said east. The truck was on Birch. Coming down the hill.

---

topic: A witness is asked about a car accident they saw from their front porch
text:
Q: How long have you lived at 247 Crescent Drive?

A: Six years this August.

Q: And in that time, have you witnessed other accidents at that intersection?

A: A few fender benders. Nothing like this.

Q: Nothing like this. What made this one different?

A: The speed, I guess. And the sound. It was loud.

Q: How fast would you estimate the vehicles were traveling?

A: I don't know. I'm not good at estimating speed.

Q: If you had to guess?

A: I'd rather not guess.

Q: The police report indicates you told Officer Daniels that one vehicle was "going way too fast."

A: Did I say which one?

Q: I'm asking you.

A: Because I remember thinking one of them must have been speeding, but sitting here now, I couldn't tell you which. They both just—it happened so fast. That's a funny thing to say, isn't it? It happened fast, but I don't know who was going fast.

Q: Take your time.

A: The red car. The red car seemed like it was going faster. But I also saw it longer because it spun afterward, so maybe that's why it seems that way in my memory.

Q: The red car spun after impact?

A: Rotated. Turned. I don't know the right word.

Q: How many times did it rotate?

A: Not all the way around. Maybe halfway? Less than halfway? It ended up facing the wrong direction.

---

topic: A witness is asked about a car accident they saw from their front porch
text:
Q: You've testified that you were on your porch when you heard brakes squealing, correct?

A: Yes.

Q: And then you looked up and saw the collision?

A: I looked toward the sound, yes.

Q: Toward the sound. Did you see the actual collision?

A: I saw the cars hit each other.

Q: Both of them? At the moment they made contact?

A: I... I'm not sure what you're asking.

Q: Were you looking at the intersection at the exact moment of impact?

A: I was looking in that direction.

Q: That's not quite the same thing.

A: No, I suppose it isn't.

Q: So let me ask again: did you witness the moment the two vehicles collided?

A: I believe I did.

Q: You believe you did.

A: Yes.

Q: But you're not certain?

A: I saw two cars hit each other. I don't know what else you want me to say.

Q: I want you to tell me what you actually saw, Mr. Novak.

A: And I'm trying to do that. But you keep asking the same question different ways like you're waiting for me to change my answer.

Q: I'm simply trying to understand your testimony.

A: Then understand this: I heard a noise, I looked up, I saw a collision. Whether my eyes got there a half-second before or a half-second after—I couldn't tell you. It was all one moment.

topic: A nurse is questioned about a patient fall that occurred during her shift
text:
Q: Nurse Delgado, I want to direct your attention to the morning of March 14th. You were assigned to Room 312, correct?

A: Yes.

Q: And the patient in Room 312 was Margaret Holloway?

A: Yes, that's correct.

Q: What time did you last check on Mrs. Holloway before the fall?

A: I believe it was—it was around 6:15 a.m. Approximately. I'd have to check the chart to be certain of the exact time.

Q: You'd have to check the chart.

A: I'm trying to give you accurate information. I don't want to guess.

Q: Fair enough. When you checked on her at approximately 6:15 a.m., was the bed alarm activated?

A: I— yes. Yes, it was. I remember checking it.

Q: You remember checking it.

A: I did check it. That's part of the protocol.

Q: And yet the incident report indicates the bed alarm was found in the "off" position after Mrs. Holloway was discovered on the floor. Can you explain that?

A: No. I mean—I can't explain it, but I know I checked it. I specifically remember checking it because I had just come from another room where there'd been an issue with—I remember checking it.

Q: Was anyone else in the room between 6:15 and when the fall occurred?

A: I don't know. I wasn't— I had other patients. I don't know.

Q: You don't know.

A: That's what I said.

Q: Let me ask it differently. Did you see anyone else enter Room 312?

A: I said I don't know. I was attending to other patients. I can't see every room at every moment.

---

topic: A nurse is questioned about a patient fall that occurred during her shift
text:
Q: How many patients were assigned to you on that shift?

A: Six.

Q: And is six patients a typical assignment on the orthopedic floor?

A: It depends. Sometimes it's five, sometimes seven. It varies.

Q: Let me ask you this—were you adequately staffed that night, in your opinion?

A: I'm not sure what you mean by "adequately."

Q: Did you have enough nurses on the floor to safely care for all patients?

A: We had the number of nurses that were scheduled.

Q: That's not what I asked.

A: I understand what you asked. I'm telling you we were staffed according to the schedule.

Q: Nurse Thompson, I'll ask once more. In your professional judgment, were there enough nurses on the floor that night to provide safe patient care?

A: I don't—I'm not comfortable making that determination here. That's an administrative question.

Q: You've been a nurse for eleven years, correct?

A: Yes.

Q: And in those eleven years, have you developed a professional judgment about safe staffing levels?

A: Counsel, I—

Q: It's a yes or no question.

A: Yes. I have professional judgment.

Q: Then use it. Were you adequately staffed?

A: We were—we were busy. It was a busy night.

Q: Were you adequately staffed, yes or no?

A: I would have preferred another nurse on the floor. Yes. I would have preferred that.

---

topic: A nurse is questioned about a patient fall that occurred during her shift
text:
Q: When did you first learn the patient had fallen?

A: When I heard the call light alarm, I think. Or—no, actually, I heard Mrs. Patterson in 308 calling out first. I went to check on her, and that's when I saw the light was on for 310.

Q: So you went to 308 first?

A: Yes.

Q: How long were you in 308?

A: A minute? Maybe two? She needed help adjusting her IV line.

Q: And then you went to 310.

A: Yes.

Q: Describe what you saw.

A: Mr. Okonkwo was on the floor, on his left side, between the bed and the window. He was conscious. He was saying something—I couldn't make it out at first.

Q: What did you do?

A: I called for assistance immediately. I didn't move him. I followed the protocol—I assessed him verbally, asked if he was in pain, checked for obvious bleeding.

Q: Did you find any?

A: There was a small laceration on his forehead. Not actively bleeding, but there was some blood on the floor. Maybe a tablespoon.

Q: Now, the fall was reported at 2:47 a.m. You were in Mrs. Patterson's room at—what time, you estimate?

A: I don't know the exact time. It was shortly before that.

Q: Shortly before. One minute? Five minutes?

A: I said I don't know the exact time. I was doing my job, not looking at the clock every thirty seconds.

Q: I understand. I'm trying to establish a timeline.

A: And I'm trying to answer accurately.

---

topic: A nurse is questioned about a patient fall that occurred during her shift
text:
Q: Had you received any specific instructions regarding fall precautions for this patient?

A: Yes, it was in his chart. He was flagged as a fall risk.

Q: What precautions were in place?

A: Bed in low position, call light within reach, non-slip socks, bed alarm, and he was supposed to call for assistance before ambulating.

Q: He was supposed to call.

A: That was the instruction, yes.

Q: But he didn't call.

A: Evidently not.

Q: Did you instruct him personally about the need to call for assistance?

A: I— yes. During my assessment at the start of the shift.

Q: What exactly did you tell him?

A: I told him he needed to press the call button if he wanted to get up, that he shouldn't try to walk on his own.

Q: And what did he say?

A: He said okay. He acknowledged it.

Q: Did he seem confused when you spoke with him?

A: No, he seemed—he was oriented. Alert.

Q: And yet three hours later he got up without calling. Does that suggest to you he didn't understand the instruction?

A: I can't speak to what he understood. I gave him the instruction clearly.

Q: Nurse Johannsen, isn't it true that patients with his medication regimen often experience confusion during nighttime hours?

A: Sometimes. Not always.

Q: But sometimes.

A: Yes, sometimes. I said that.

---

topic: A nurse is questioned about a patient fall that occurred during her shift
text:
Q: Let me back up. You mentioned you were on your break when the fall occurred?

A: I was returning from my break. I hadn't made it back to the station yet.

Q: Where were you, specifically?

A: Walking from the break room.

Q: And where is the break room in relation to Room 204?

A: It's at the other end of the hall. Past the elevators.

Q: So you were not on the floor.

A: I was on the floor. I was in the hallway, walking back.

Q: But you were not at the nurses' station.

A: No, I was walking back to the nurses' station.

Q: Who was covering your patients during your break?

A: Rachel—Rachel Yuen. She was covering.

Q: And where was Nurse Yuen when the fall occurred?

A: You'd have to ask her. I don't know exactly where she was at that moment.

Q: You don't know.

A: I was on my break. I was walking back. I don't know where Rachel was standing at that exact second.

Q: The fall occurred at 11:52 p.m. according to the incident report. What time did your break end?

A: 11:45.

Q: So seven minutes.

I told her—and I remember this clearly because I've thought about it many times since—I told her that in my experience, this company rewards people who speak up. That's what I believed. That's what my own career trajectory had demonstrated.

Q: Did you advise her to file a formal complaint?

A: I walked her through the entire process myself. Step by step. I even reviewed her written statement before she submitted it. Made sure it was airtight.

A: Richard Torres pulled me into his office two days after she filed. He asked me if I'd "coached her." His word, not mine. I told him I'd given her the same guidance I'd give any employee who came to me with a legitimate concern. He didn't like that answer.
