Q: State your name for the record, please.

A: Dr. Angela Morris.

Q: Dr. Morris, you were employed as a research scientist at Vertex Laboratories from 2019 to 2023?

A: That's correct.

Q: Tell me about your supervisor during that time.

A: Dr. Richard Hayes was the department head. He oversaw all the junior researchers, including me.

Q: How would you characterize your working relationship with Dr. Hayes?

A: Complicated. He was brilliant—there's no denying that. He'd been in the field for thirty years, published extensively. When I first joined, I was genuinely in awe of him. He took time to mentor me, review my work, push me to be better. I learned a great deal from him.

Q: But something changed?

A: Over time, I started noticing patterns in how he treated the women in the department versus the men. Small things at first. Interrupting us in meetings. Assigning us more administrative work. Questioning our findings more aggressively.

Q: Did he make any explicit comments that you would characterize as discriminatory?

A: Yes. There was an incident in November 2022 that I'll never forget. We were discussing a grant proposal, and I suggested a modification to the methodology. He looked at me and said, "Angela, this is hard science. Maybe you'd be more comfortable in a support role."

Q: How did you interpret that statement?

A: It felt like a punch to the gut, honestly. Because I knew—I knew—that if one of the male researchers had made the same suggestion, he would have engaged with it seriously. He'd said similar things to other women on the team. It was a pattern.

Q: I can see this still affects you. We can pause if you need a moment.

A: No, I'm okay. I want this on the record. I want people to understand what it was like.

Q: I appreciate your willingness to share this. Were there other women who experienced similar treatment?

A: Several. We actually started meeting informally—just to compare notes, support each other. It helped to know we weren't imagining things. There's a solidarity in that, you know? A comfort in being believed.

topic: A former employee is deposed about discriminatory remarks made by a supervisor
text:
Q: Mr. Tran, you've stated that you witnessed comments made by the defendant to your colleague, Rachel Odom. Is that right?

A: Yes, I was there.

Q: I appreciate you being willing to testify about what you observed. Can you tell me where this incident took place?

A: It was at the company retreat last October. We were at a resort in the Poconos, one of those team-building weekends. Friday night, there was a cocktail reception.

Q: And what did you witness during this reception?

A: Mr. Garrett—the regional manager—he'd had a few drinks. He was talking to Rachel by the bar. I was maybe ten feet away, close enough to hear.

Q: What did you hear him say?

A: He was commenting on her appearance. Saying she looked "exotic." Asking where she was "really from." She told him she was from Ohio, and he laughed and said, "No, but where are your people from?"

Q: How did Ms. Odom respond?

A: She tried to deflect. Made a joke about being from the exotic land of Cleveland. But I could see she was uncomfortable. Her smile didn't reach her eyes—you know what I mean? She was just trying to get through the conversation.

Q: What did you do?

A: I walked over. Made some excuse about needing to steal Rachel for a minute because our colleague was looking for her. Got her away from him.

Q: That was a kind intervention on your part.

A: It was the right thing to do. Rachel's a good person, a good friend. I wasn't going to just stand there and watch her squirm.

Q: Did you and Ms. Odom discuss the incident afterward?

A: Later that night, yes. She thanked me for stepping in. I told her she didn't have to thank me, that nobody should have to deal with that. We talked for a while, actually. She told me it wasn't the first time he'd said things like that to her. That meant a lot—her trusting me with that.

Q: Did she indicate whether she planned to report the behavior?

A: She was torn. She was worried about retaliation—Garrett's been with the company forever, knows everyone. I told her I'd support her whatever she decided, that she wouldn't be alone in this. I meant it then, and I mean it now.

Q: Is that why you agreed to provide testimony today?

A: Yes. Because Rachel deserves to have someone in her corner. And because what happened to her was wrong.

topic: A witness is questioned about events at a party where an assault allegedly occurred
text:
Q: I'd like to ask you about the party on the evening of March 15th. Can you tell me how you came to be there?

A: Sure. My friend Marcus invited me. He said it was going to be a small get-together, maybe fifteen people, and he thought I'd enjoy meeting some of his coworkers. I'd been going through kind of a rough patch, to be honest, and Marcus was trying to get me out of the house more. He's thoughtful like that.

Q: That's kind of him. And what time did you arrive?

A: Around eight, maybe a little after. I remember thinking I didn't want to be the first one there, you know how that can be awkward, so I waited until I saw a few cars in the driveway.

Q: When you went inside, can you describe what you observed?

A: It was really nice, actually. People were scattered around the living room, some in the kitchen. Someone had put together a cheese board—I remember that because I thought it was such a thoughtful touch, the little labels for each cheese. There was music playing, not too loud, the kind where you can still have a conversation. Everyone seemed relaxed.

Q: And did you know anyone else at the party besides Marcus?

A: I knew his girlfriend, Delia. She gave me a hug when I walked in. And I'd met his coworker Tom once before at a barbecue, so we nodded at each other. Everyone else was new to me, but people were friendly. A woman named Sandra introduced herself and asked about my work, seemed genuinely interested.

Q: Take your time with this next question. At some point during the evening, did you witness any kind of altercation?

A: I did, yes. It was later, probably around eleven or so.

Q: Can you walk me through what you saw, in as much detail as you're comfortable sharing?

A: Of course. I was in the kitchen getting a drink when I heard raised voices from the back patio. I went to the sliding door and saw two men facing each other. One of them—I later learned his name was Kevin—was backing away with his hands up, like this, palms out. The other man, who I didn't know, stepped toward him and shoved him hard in the chest.

Q: What happened after the shove?

A: Kevin stumbled backward into one of those patio chairs, the metal kind. He didn't fall completely, but he knocked the chair over and had to catch himself on the railing. A few people rushed over. Marcus got between them and was talking in this low, steady voice—I couldn't hear exactly what he said, but whatever it was, it seemed to help.

Q: Did you see what preceded the shove? What might have led to that moment?

A: I wish I could tell you more, I really do. I only caught the tail end of it. From what I gathered talking to people afterward, there had been some prior tension between them, something about a work situation. But I don't want to speculate beyond what I actually saw.

Q: I appreciate that. Is there anything else about that evening you think might be helpful for us to know?

A: Just that—and I don't know if this matters—but Kevin seemed pretty shaken up afterward. He sat in the kitchen for a while, and Sandra brought him a glass of water. A few of us stayed with him until he felt okay to drive home. I gave him my number in case he needed someone to talk to. I hope he's doing alright.

topic: A witness is questioned about events at a party where an assault allegedly occurred
text:
Q: State your name for the record, please.

A: Jennifer Okonkwo.

Q: Ms. Okonkwo, you were present at 445 Ridgeway Drive on November 8th of last year, correct?

A: That's right.

Q: How would you describe your relationship with the host, David Brennan?

A: We've been friends for about six years. We met through a book club, actually, and just hit it off. He's one of my closest friends. I was excited when he said he was hosting—he'd just bought the house and wanted to show it off a little, which I thought was sweet.

Q: Now, I understand there were approximately thirty guests that evening?

A: Something like that, yes. Maybe a few more. David knows a lot of people.

Q: I want to ask about a specific guest—a man named Richard Tully. Did you interact with him?

A: I did. We talked for quite a while, actually. He was standing by himself near the bookshelf when I noticed him, and he looked a little lost, so I went over and introduced myself. Turns out he's an architect, and we got into this whole conversation about how buildings shape the way people feel. It was fascinating.

Q: How did Mr. Tully seem to you during this conversation?

A: Thoughtful. A little reserved at first, but once he opened up, he had a lot of interesting things to say. He mentioned he didn't know many people there—he'd come with a coworker who had wandered off. I got the sense he appreciated having someone to talk to.

Q: At any point, did you observe Mr. Tully in a confrontation with another guest?

A: Yes, later in the evening. I'd stepped away to use the restroom, and when I came back to the living room, Richard was near the front door with another man. Their voices were raised.

Q: Do you know who the other man was?

A: I learned afterward his name was Gregory something. I hadn't spoken with him during the party.

Q: Describe what you witnessed, please.

A: Gregory was pointing at Richard, jabbing his finger in the air. Richard had his hands in his pockets and was sort of leaning back, like he was trying to create distance. Then Gregory grabbed Richard's shirt—right here, by the collar—and shoved him against the wall. The picture frame next to them fell and the glass broke.

Q: What did you do?

A: I called out—I think I said something like "Hey, stop!" David was already moving toward them. He got Gregory to let go and walked him outside. I went to check on Richard.

Q: How was Mr. Tully after the incident?

A: He was embarrassed more than anything, I think. He kept apologizing, which seemed so unnecessary—he hadn't done anything wrong from what I could see. I told him it wasn't his fault. We sat on the porch for a while until he felt ready to go home. I offered to drive him, but he said the fresh air was helping.

topic: A witness is questioned about events at a party where an assault allegedly occurred
text:
Q: You were at a party on July 22nd at the residence of Marie and Thomas Chen?

A: Yes.

Q: What was the occasion?

A: Their daughter's college graduation. Amy. She'd just finished at Georgetown.

Q: Congratulations to her. How do you know the Chen family?

A: I've lived next door for eleven years. Watched Amy grow up, really. I remember when she was learning to ride a bike in the driveway.

Q: That must have made the celebration feel special for you.

A: It did. Marie put so much effort into that party—the decorations, the food. She'd been planning it for months. She kept coming over to ask my opinion on little details, like whether the lanterns in the backyard looked right. I think she just wanted everything to be perfect for Amy.

Q: Let's talk about what happened later that evening. Did there come a time when you observed a physical altercation?

A: There was an incident, yes. I hesitate to call it an altercation—it happened so fast.

Q: Tell me what you saw.

A: I was sitting at one of the tables in the backyard. Amy's boyfriend—I think his name is Derek—was talking to another young man near the fence. I wasn't paying close attention at first, but then I heard a crash. When I looked up, Derek was on the ground and the other man was standing over him.

Q: Did you see what caused Derek to fall?

A: I saw the other man's arm moving, like he'd just swung at him. But I can't say for certain whether it was a punch or a push. It happened in my peripheral vision.

Q: That's fair. What happened next?

A: A few people ran over. Amy was crying—that's what I remember most, actually. She was so upset. Her mother was trying to comfort her while Thomas dealt with the situation. I felt terrible for them. This day they'd been looking forward to, and then this.

Q: Did you approach the scene yourself?

A: I did after a minute. I wanted to make sure Derek was okay. He had a cut on his forehead, not deep, but it was bleeding. I got some ice from inside and brought it out to him. Marie thanked me later—she had her hands full trying to keep things calm.

Q: Did you learn what precipitated the confrontation?

A: Not entirely. I heard fragments—something about a comment that was made, maybe a misunderstanding. But I don't want to relay secondhand information that might not be accurate.

Q: I understand. Is there anything else you observed that evening that you think is relevant?

A: Only that the family handled it with such grace. Thomas walked the other young man out quietly, no yelling, very dignified. And Amy—even though she was upset—she made sure to thank everyone for coming before we left. That's how she was raised, I suppose.

topic: A witness is questioned about events at a party where an assault allegedly occurred
text:
Q: Let's move to the early morning hours. You said the party continued past midnight?

A: Yeah.

Q: Were you still there at 1 a.m.?

A: I was.

Q: And by that point, how many guests remained?

A: Maybe ten.

Q: I'd like to understand the setting better. Can you describe the atmosphere at that hour?

A: Most people were pretty tired. Some folks were crashed on the couch. A few of us were still talking in the kitchen.

Q: You mentioned earlier that you were in the kitchen. Who else was there?

A: Let me think. Brianna, the host. A guy named Pete who I'd met that night. And Carla—she's Brianna's roommate.

Q: Anyone else?

A: This other guy came in at some point. I didn't catch his name.

Q: Can you describe him?

A: Tall. Dark hair. Wearing a denim jacket.

Q: What was he doing when he entered the kitchen?

A: Just getting a drink, seemed like. He opened the fridge, looked around.

Q: Did he interact with anyone?

A: He said something to Brianna. I didn't hear what.

Q: What was Brianna's reaction?

A: She kind of stiffened up. Took a step back.

Q: And then what happened?

A: Pete noticed. He asked if everything was okay. I think he was trying to help—he seemed like a decent guy, had been looking out for people all night. Earlier he'd made sure everyone had a safe ride home lined up.

Q: What did the man in the denim jacket do after Pete spoke?

A: He turned around fast and got in Pete's face. Said something like "mind your business."

Q: How did Pete respond?

A: He stayed calm. He put his hands up and said he didn't want any trouble. But the other guy shoved him anyway—hard—and Pete went backward into the counter.

Q: Was Pete injured?

A: He knocked some glasses over. One broke. He might have cut his hand, I'm not sure. I know Carla got him a towel afterward.

Q: What happened to the man in the denim jacket?

A: He left. Just walked out the back door. Brianna locked it after him.

topic: A witness is questioned about events at a party where an assault allegedly occurred
text:
Q: When did you first notice something was wrong?

A: Probably around ten-thirty? There was this shift in the energy, I guess you could say.

Q: What do you mean by a shift?

A: People had been dancing, having a good time. Then I noticed a small group forming near the hallway to the bedrooms. People were craning their necks to see something.

Q: Did you go to see what was happening?

A: Eventually, yes.

Q: What did you observe?

A: Two women were arguing. One of them—I later learned her name was Natalie—was crying. The other woman was speaking very sharply, lots of hand gestures.

Q: Did you hear what they were arguing about?

A: Something about a phone. Messages, I think. The second woman kept saying "I saw what you wrote."

Q: What happened next?

A: The second woman slapped Natalie across the face.

Q: How did Natalie react?

A: She just stood there for a second, holding her cheek. Then she ran toward the bathroom. A couple of women followed her—friends, I assume.

Q: Did anyone intervene with the woman who struck her?

A: The host, Marcus, came over. He was very measured about it, spoke to her quietly. She seemed to calm down a little, though she was still agitated.

Q: Did you have any interaction with either woman that evening?

A: I spoke with Natalie briefly earlier, actually. She'd complimented my earrings, and we got to talking. She was telling me about her sister's wedding coming up, how excited she was to be the maid of honor. She seemed genuinely happy.

Q: After the incident, did you see Natalie again?

A: I found her in the kitchen about twenty minutes later. She was holding a bag of frozen peas to her face. I asked if she was okay, if she needed anything. She said her friend was coming to pick her up.

Q: Did you stay with her?

A: I did, until her friend arrived. We didn't talk much—she seemed like she just wanted some quiet. But I didn't want her to be alone. When her friend got there, I walked her out to the car. She squeezed my hand before she got in. I think about that sometimes.

topic: A store manager is questioned about a customer slip-and-fall on their premises
text:
Q: Mr. Patterson, how long have you been the store manager at FreshMart on Oak Street?

A: Seven years.

Q: And in those seven years, you've received training on safety protocols, correct?

A: Yes.

Q: Including protocols for wet floors?

A: Yes.

Q: So you knew on March 15th that a wet floor without signage was a hazard?

A: I knew that wet floors should be marked, yes.

Q: Should be marked. But they weren't marked that day, were they?

A: I wasn't personally aware of the spill until after the incident.

Q: That's not what I asked you. Were there signs up or not?

A: No.

Q: No signs. And Mrs. Chen fell, didn't she?

A: Someone fell, yes.

Q: Someone. You mean the seventy-two-year-old woman who broke her hip in your store?

A: I don't have her medical records in front of me. I can't confirm what she broke.

Q: You saw her on the ground, didn't you?

A: I saw a customer on the ground. I called for assistance immediately.

Q: How noble of you. Let me ask you this—

A: I'm going to stop you right there. I don't appreciate the commentary. Ask your questions and I'll answer them.

Q: Mr. Patterson, in the fifteen minutes before Mrs. Chen fell, how many employees walked past the spill in aisle six?

A: I don't know.

Q: You reviewed the security footage, didn't you?

A: I did.

Q: Then you know exactly how many employees walked past it. Don't you?

A: Three.

topic: A store manager is questioned about a customer slip-and-fall on their premises
text:
Q: Ms. Hernandez, walk me through your morning routine on January 8th.

A: I arrived at 5:45 a.m. to open the store. I did a walkthrough of all aisles, checked the refrigeration units, reviewed the overnight delivery log, and unlocked the doors at 6:00 a.m.

Q: During your walkthrough, did you check the entrance mats?

A: Yes, I always do. It had been snowing overnight, so I made sure the mats were positioned correctly and that we had the floor dryer running near the front.

Q: You were aware that melting snow creates slip hazards?

A: Of course. That's why I took those precautions. That's why we have a wet weather protocol. I've worked in retail for nineteen years, Counselor. I understand how floors work.

Q: I'm just trying to establish—

A: You're trying to establish that I was negligent. I wasn't. I followed every protocol we have.

Q: Ms. Hernandez, I haven't accused you of anything.

A: The lawsuit accuses me. This whole process accuses me. So let's just get through your questions.

Q: Fine. At what time did Mr. Boyko fall?

A: Approximately 8:40 a.m.

Q: And where were you at 8:40?

A: In my office reviewing schedules.

Q: So you weren't monitoring the entrance?

A: I can't be everywhere at once. That's what employees are for. That's what training is for.

Q: Was anyone assigned to monitor the entrance that morning?

A: Yes. Derek Mullins.

Q: Where was Mr. Mullins at 8:40?

A: I don't know precisely. You'd have to ask him.

Q: I'm asking you. You're his supervisor.

A: And I don't install tracking devices in my employees. I assigned him a task. Whether he was doing it at that exact moment, I can't say with certainty. I'm not going to lie under oath to make your case easier.

topic: A store manager is questioned about a customer slip-and-fall on their premises
text:
Q: Let's talk about the maintenance log.

A: Okay.

Q: You do keep a maintenance log, correct?

A: We do.

Q: And spills are supposed to be recorded in that log?

A: When they're reported and cleaned, yes.

Q: I'm looking at the log from September 3rd. I see an entry at 9:15 a.m. and then nothing until 2:30 p.m. Does that seem right to you?

A: If that's what the log shows.

Q: Mr. Franklin, your customer fell at 11:45 a.m. There's no entry anywhere near that time.

A: Then I suppose the spill wasn't logged.

Q: You suppose?

A: I'm not the one who fills out every entry. Employees are trained to document incidents.

Q: So someone failed to follow the protocol you claim to enforce?

A: I didn't say they failed. I said it wasn't logged. Maybe they didn't see it before it happened.

Q: Or maybe no one was paying attention.

A: That's your characterization.

Q: Let me ask it differently. Does the absence of a log entry concern you?

A: Concern me how?

Q: Does it concern you that there's no record of anyone addressing the hazard that injured a customer?

A: What concerns me is sitting here being interrogated about a log entry when I've already explained how the system works.

Q: Mr. Franklin—

A: No, let me finish. I've answered your question. The log shows what it shows. I can't manufacture entries that don't exist.

Q: Are you finished?

A: I am.

Q: Good. Now, who was responsible for aisle nine that morning?

A: I'd have to check the floor assignment sheet.

topic: A store manager is questioned about a customer slip-and-fall on their premises
text:
Q: Ms. Okafor, I want to ask you about the cleanup supplies kept in the store.

A: Certainly.

Q: Where is the nearest supply closet to the pharmacy section?

A: There's one at the back of the store, maybe forty feet from pharmacy.

Q: Forty feet. And is it kept locked?

A: Yes, for liability reasons. Some of the chemicals—

Q: A simple yes or no is fine.

A: ...Yes.

Q: Who has keys to that closet?

A: Shift supervisors and management.

Q: How many people is that on a typical shift?

A: Two or three.

Q: So if someone spills something near the pharmacy, an employee would need to locate one of those two or three people, get a key, walk forty feet to the closet, retrieve supplies, and walk back to the spill?

A: Or they could use paper towels from the restroom nearby, or—

Q: I didn't ask about alternatives. I asked about the supply closet.

A: Then yes. That's the process.

Q: How long does that take, in your estimation?

A: It depends.

Q: Give me a range.

A: Three to five minutes if someone is readily available.

Q: And if they're not?

A: Longer.

Q: How much longer?

A: I don't know. Seven, eight minutes?

Q: Your customer slipped in cooking oil. How long does it take someone to walk through a puddle of cooking oil? Two seconds? Three?

A: I understand what you're implying.

Q: I'm not implying anything. I'm asking whether your system creates a window where a hazard exists and no one can address it.

A: We do the best we can with the resources we have.

Q: That wasn't my question.

A: It's my answer.

topic: A store manager is questioned about a customer slip-and-fall on their premises
text:
Q: Mr. Dreyer, you filled out an incident report after Mr. Salazar's fall, correct?

A: I did.

Q: I have it here. You wrote, quote, "Customer slipped on unknown substance near freezer aisle." Did I read that correctly?

A: Yes.

Q: Unknown substance. Did you ever determine what the substance was?

A: It appeared to be condensation from the freezer units.

Q: Appeared to be. So you're not certain?

A: I'm reasonably certain.

Q: Then why did you write "unknown"?

A: Because at the time I filled out the report, I hadn't confirmed it.

Q: Fair enough. Now, condensation from freezer units—that's not unusual, is it?

A: It can happen.

Q: It can happen, or it does happen?

A: It does happen.

Q: Regularly?

A: I wouldn't say regularly.

Q: How often?

A: I don't have a number for you.

Q: Once a week? Once a month?

A: Maybe once or twice a month in humid weather.

Q: And what do you do about it?

A: We mop it up when we see it.

Q: When you see it. So you wait until it's already on the floor?

A: The freezers are designed to minimize condensation. We can't prevent every drop of moisture.

Q: Mr. Dreyer, did you know that the door seal on freezer unit seven was damaged?

A: ...I was aware there was a maintenance request pending.

Q: Pending for how long?

A: I'd have to check.

Q: Let me help you. The request was filed six weeks before Mr. Salazar fell. Does that refresh your recollection?

A: If that's what the records show.

Q: Six weeks, Mr. Dreyer. Six weeks of a broken seal. Six weeks of condensation pooling on the floor. Does that sound like adequate maintenance to you?

A: We have dozens of equipment issues at any given time. We prioritize based on severity.

Q: And a fall hazard wasn't severe enough?

A: In hindsight, obviously it should have been addressed sooner.

Q: In hindsight.

A: That's what I said.

topic: A warehouse supervisor is deposed about safety protocols that were allegedly ignored
text:
Q: Mr. Harmon, I want to direct your attention to the forklift inspection logs for the month of October 2023.

A: Okay.

Q: Were you responsible for ensuring those logs were completed daily?

A: Yes.

Q: And were they completed daily?

A: To my knowledge, yes.

Q: To your knowledge. You didn't personally verify them?

A: I had other responsibilities. I delegated that to shift leads.

Q: So when you say "to your knowledge," you mean you trusted someone else to do it.

A: I mean I had seventeen other things happening at any given moment. The logs were one piece of a much larger operation.

Q: I understand. Let me ask it differently. Did you ever personally look at a completed forklift inspection log in October 2023?

A: I'm sure I did at some point.

Q: Can you recall a specific instance?

A: No. I can't recall a specific instance of looking at a specific log on a specific day, no.

Q: Fair enough. Were you aware that forklift unit seven had a documented brake issue on October 14th?

A: I was made aware of it after the incident, yes.

Q: But not before.

A: No.

Q: And if the inspection log had been reviewed by a supervisor, that brake issue would have been flagged, correct?

A: Counselor, I've answered this in three different ways now. I didn't see that particular log before the incident. I don't know what else you want me to say.

Q: I want you to answer the question. Would the brake issue have been flagged?

A: Yes. If someone had looked at it, yes.

topic: A warehouse supervisor is deposed about safety protocols that were allegedly ignored
text:
Q: Ms. Trujillo, how long have you worked as warehouse supervisor at the Eastgate facility?

A: Going on six years now.

Q: And in those six years, have you received training on OSHA requirements for aisle clearance?

A: I have.

Q: When was that training?

A: I want to say... 2019? Maybe early 2020. Before the pandemic, I remember that much.

Q: So approximately four years before the incident we're discussing today.

A: Give or take.

Q: Was there any refresher training between 2020 and the date of the incident?

A: There may have been. I don't recall specifically.

Q: You don't recall, or there wasn't?

A: I don't recall. There's a difference.

Q: Okay. Let me move on. On February 3rd, 2024, what was the standard protocol for maintaining clear aisles in the loading zone?

A: Thirty-six-inch minimum clearance, marked with yellow tape.

Q: And on that date, was the thirty-six-inch clearance maintained?

A: I wasn't on the floor at that exact moment.

Q: That wasn't my question.

A: Then I need you to ask it again, because I'm not sure what you're asking.

Q: Was the clearance maintained on February 3rd in the loading zone?

A: Based on what I learned afterward, no, it wasn't.

Q: Alright. Let's move to the next... actually, let me ask—did you conduct a walkthrough that day?

A: ...Yes.

Q: What time?

A: Morning. Maybe eight, eight-fifteen.

Q: And the incident occurred at what time?

A: Around two in the afternoon.

topic: A warehouse supervisor is deposed about safety protocols that were allegedly ignored
text:
Q: You mentioned earlier that safety meetings were held monthly.

A: That's correct.

Q: Every month without exception?

A: I believe so, yes.

Q: You believe so.

A: Yes.

Q: Mr. Denning, I'm showing you what's been marked as Exhibit 14. Do you recognize this document?

A: It's a calendar. Our internal scheduling calendar.

Q: And looking at August, September, and October of 2023, can you point to the scheduled safety meetings?

A: ...I see September here. And October.

Q: What about August?

A: I don't see one marked for August.

Q: So not every month.

A: Apparently not that month.

Q: Do you recall why August was skipped?

A: No, I don't. We were probably... I don't know. I don't remember.

Q: Were you short-staffed in August?

A: We're always short-staffed.

Q: I'll rephrase. Were you more short-staffed than usual?

A: I really couldn't say.

Q: Okay. Let's talk about what was covered in the September meeting. Do you have any recollection of that?

A: Probably the usual. PPE compliance, incident reports from the previous month, any new procedures.

Q: Probably.

A: I don't have the agenda in front of me. I'm doing my best here.

topic: A warehouse supervisor is deposed about safety protocols that were allegedly ignored
text:
Q: Let me take you back to the morning of the incident. What time did you arrive at the facility?

A: Five-thirty, maybe five-forty-five.

Q: That's early.

A: That's every day.

Q: Was there anything unusual about that morning?

A: No.

Q: Nothing at all?

A: Not that I recall.

Q: Did you receive any reports about the condition of the B-wing racking?

A: Not that morning, no.

Q: What about the week before?

A: ...I'd have to check the maintenance logs.

Q: I'm asking what you recall.

A: And I'm telling you I'd need to see the logs to give you an accurate answer. I'm not going to guess.

Q: That's fine. Let me ask about your general practice. When a racking issue was reported, what was the protocol?

A: Tag it, take it out of service, submit a work order.

Q: Every time?

A: That was the protocol, yes.

Q: Was the protocol always followed?

A: We made every effort.

Q: That's not what I asked.

A: I know what you asked. I'm answering as honestly as I can. We made every effort. Sometimes things fall through the cracks. That's reality.

Q: What kinds of things fell through the cracks?

A: Are we going to be here much longer? I've been answering these questions for four hours.

Q: We'll take as long as we need to, Mr. Okonkwo.

A: Fine. Ask your question again.

topic: A warehouse supervisor is deposed about safety protocols that were allegedly ignored
text:
Q: Ms. Chen. Can you describe the procedure for reporting a safety hazard at the Northfield warehouse?

A: Employee fills out a hazard report form, submits it to their shift supervisor, supervisor logs it in the system and determines priority level.

Q: And who reviews the logged hazards?

A: I do. Or I did, at the time.

Q: How often did you review them?

A: Daily. End of each shift.

Q: Without exception?

A: I made it a priority.

Q: I have here a log from March 2024 showing a hazard report submitted on March 7th regarding a liquid spill in aisle twelve. There's no notation of supervisor review until March 11th. Can you explain that?

A: ...No. I can't explain that sitting here today.

Q: Is it possible you missed it?

A: Anything is possible.

Q: Is it probable?

A: I don't know. I'm looking at a piece of paper four days after the fact, trying to remember one entry out of hundreds.

Q: So you reviewed hundreds of hazard reports.

A: Over the course of that quarter, yes.

Q: And this one slipped by.

A: Apparently.

Q: The incident occurred on March 9th.

A: I'm aware of the timeline.

Q: Two days after the report was submitted. One day before anyone reviewed it.

A: I understand the math, counselor.

Q: I'm just establishing the facts.

A: You're establishing something.

topic: A store manager is questioned about a customer slip-and-fall on their premises
text:
Q: Mr. Patterson, how long have you been the store manager at the Greenfield location?

A: Four years, eight months.

Q: And on the date in question, March 15th, were you working?

A: Yes.

Q: What were your duties that day?

A: The same duties I have every day. Managing the store.

Q: Can you be more specific about what "managing the store" entails?

A: Supervising employees, handling customer issues, overseeing inventory, making sure the store runs. The usual things a manager does.

Q: Were you aware of any spills in the store that day?

A: I was made aware of one, yes.

Q: When were you made aware?

A: After the incident.

Q: So not before the customer fell?

A: That's what "after the incident" means.

Q: Who informed you about the spill?

A: One of my employees. Jessica. She works the registers.

Q: And what exactly did Jessica tell you?

A: She told me a customer had fallen near aisle six and that there was liquid on the floor. I already said this in my written statement. It's all in there.

Q: I understand, Mr. Patterson. I'm asking you now, under oath, what you recall.

A: And I'm telling you. She said a customer fell, there was liquid on the floor. That's what I recall.

---

topic: A store manager is questioned about a customer slip-and-fall on their premises
text:
Q: Ms. Chen, let's talk about the store's spill response policy. You have one, correct?

A: Of course we do.

Q: Walk me through it.

A: If an employee sees a spill, they're supposed to stay with it or mark it with a wet floor sign, and call for cleanup over the radio.

Q: Every employee knows this policy?

A: They're trained on it when they're hired.

Q: That wasn't my question. Does every employee know this policy?

A: I can't be inside their heads. They're trained. They sign off on the training. What they retain is up to them.

Q: On February 3rd, the day of the incident, were there wet floor signs available in the store?

A: Yes.

Q: Where were they kept?

A: In the supply closet by the back entrance, and there's usually one near the registers.

Q: "Usually"?

A: There's supposed to be one near the registers. Yes.

Q: Was there one near the registers on February 3rd?

A: I don't specifically remember checking that morning whether a yellow plastic sign was in its exact designated spot. No.

Q: So you don't know.

A: I said I don't specifically remember. That's different from not knowing. The policy is that one is kept there. I had no reason to believe it wasn't there.

Q: But you can't confirm it was there.

A: I can confirm the policy. I can confirm the training. I can't confirm I laid eyes on that sign at 9 a.m. on a Tuesday three months ago.

---

topic: A store manager is questioned about a customer slip-and-fall on their premises
text:
Q: Mr. Davis, did you personally witness the plaintiff fall?

A: No.

Q: Where were you when it happened?

A: In my office. I was on a call with our regional distributor.

Q: How long were you on that call?

A: I don't know, maybe twenty, twenty-five minutes.

Q: And no one interrupted you during that call?

A: No.

Q: No one knocked on your door, no one radioed you?

A: No. I just said no.

Q: I'm just being thorough, Mr. Davis.

A: Right.

Q: After you finished the call, what happened?

A: Marcus came to tell me someone had fallen.

Q: Marcus is?

A: Stock associate. He'd been working the floor.

Q: What did Marcus say, specifically?

A: He said a lady slipped and fell in produce and that someone had called an ambulance. He asked if he should do an incident report.

Q: Had Marcus seen the fall?

A: You'd have to ask Marcus.

Q: I'm asking what he told you.

A: He didn't say whether he saw it or not. He just reported it.

Q: And you didn't think to ask him?

A: I was more concerned with getting to the customer, counsel. I wasn't conducting an investigation in that moment.

---

topic: A store manager is questioned about a customer slip-and-fall on their premises
text:
Q: Let's slow down for a second. You mentioned the floor gets mopped every morning before opening. Is that right?

A: That's right.

Q: Who's responsible for that?

A: Whoever's on the opening shift. It rotates.

Q: Do you know who mopped on the morning of April 22nd?

A: I'd have to check the schedule.

Q: You don't know sitting here today?

A: No. I don't have the schedule memorized.

Q: Fair enough. Now, after mopping, is the floor inspected?

A: What do you mean by "inspected"?

Q: Is there a walk-through to ensure the floor is dry, clean, free of hazards?

A: The opener walks the floor, yes.

Q: And documents that walk-through?

A: We have a checklist.

Q: Did you bring that checklist today?

A: I brought what your subpoena asked for.

Q: The subpoena requested all documents related to floor maintenance. Would the checklist fall under that category?

A: I suppose it would.

Q: So do you have it?

A: I have what our corporate office provided. If it wasn't included, I don't know what to tell you. I don't handle document production. That goes through legal.

Q: Understood. Let me ask this differently. Have you ever personally seen the checklist for April 22nd?

A: I don't recall seeing that specific date, no.

---

topic: A store manager is questioned about a customer slip-and-fall on their premises
text:
Q: Ms. Torres, I want to understand the timeline. The incident allegedly occurred at approximately 2:15 p.m. When did you first learn of it?

A: Maybe ten, fifteen minutes after.

Q: How did you learn of it?

A: Darren radioed me.

Q: What did Darren say over the radio?

A: Something like, "We've got a customer down in frozen foods, requesting manager."

Q: "Customer down." Those were his words?

A: I don't remember his exact words. That was the substance of it.

Q: What did you do when you received that radio call?

A: I went to frozen foods.

Q: Immediately?

A: Yes. Immediately.

Q: What did you observe when you arrived?

A: A woman sitting on the floor holding her wrist. Darren was there, and another customer was standing nearby.

Q: Did you observe anything on the floor?

A: There was some water. A small amount.

Q: How small?

A: I'm not sure what you want me to say. It wasn't a lake. It was some water.

Q: Could you estimate the size? A puddle the size of a dinner plate? A basketball?

A: Maybe... the size of a piece of paper? Letter-sized? I'm guessing. I wasn't measuring it.

Q: Did you take photographs of the water?

A: No.

Q: Why not?

A: Because my focus was on the injured customer, not on building a legal case. I didn't realize I'd need to be defending myself in a conference room six months later.

topic: A witness is questioned about a workplace injury they observed but did not report
text:
Q: Ms. Delgado, I want to take you back to the morning of September 14th. You were working the floor that day, correct?

A: Yes, I was.

Q: And at some point during your shift, you observed an incident involving Marcus Webb?

A: I saw what happened to Marcus, yes.

Q: Tell me what you saw.

A: He was up on the scaffolding—the temporary one they'd set up for the ductwork installation. And the guardrail, it just... it gave way. He grabbed onto the platform, thank God, but his shoulder—you could hear it. You could hear something tear or pop. I don't know how to describe it exactly. It was awful.

Q: What did Mr. Webb do after that?

A: He pulled himself back up. He was holding his arm close to his body, like this. His face was white. I've never seen someone look that pale and still be standing.

Q: Did you approach him?

A: I did. I asked him if he was okay, if he needed me to get someone. He said no, said he was fine, just tweaked it a little. But he wasn't fine. Anyone could see he wasn't fine.

Q: What made you think that?

A: The way he was breathing. Short breaths, like he was trying not to move too much. And he wouldn't look at me when he said he was okay. Marcus always looks you in the eye. That's just who he is.

Q: Did you offer to report the incident on his behalf?

A: I asked if he wanted me to tell the supervisor. He said please don't. He said it like that—please don't. So I didn't.

Q: Take your time with this next question, Ms. Delgado. Why do you think he asked you not to say anything?

A: ...Because he'd only been there four months. Because he was still in his probationary period and he was scared. His wife had just had a baby. He told me that the week before, showed me pictures on his phone. He was so proud.

Q: And that factored into your decision not to report?

A: I thought I was helping him. I thought if I said something, it might make things worse for him. I didn't want to be the reason he lost his job. I was trying to... I don't know. I was trying to look out for him.

Q: Do you feel differently about that decision now?

A: Every single day.

topic: A witness is questioned about a workplace injury they observed but did not report
text:
Q: Mr. Okonkwo, you've testified that you were present in the warehouse on November 3rd.

A: Correct.

Q: And you witnessed an injury to a coworker named Patricia Simmons?

A: I did.

Q: But you did not file an incident report.

A: No.

Q: You didn't tell your supervisor.

A: No, I did not.

Q: You didn't document it in any way.

A: That's correct.

Q: Help me understand why, Mr. Okonkwo. I'm not trying to place blame here—I genuinely want to understand what was going through your mind.

A: ...It's complicated.

Q: I'm sure it is. Take whatever time you need.

A: Patricia and I had worked together for six years. She was—she is—one of the hardest workers I've ever known. She came in early, stayed late. Never complained. When she fell that day, when that pallet shifted and knocked her down, the first thing she did was get back up and say she was embarrassed. Not hurt. Embarrassed.

Q: What happened after she got up?

A: She was limping. Badly. I told her she needed to sit down, that I would handle the rest of the unloading. She said absolutely not, that she wasn't going to leave me with all that work.

Q: Did she continue working?

A: For about an hour. Then she said she needed to use the restroom. She was gone for fifteen minutes. When she came back, I could tell she'd been crying.

Q: And still, you didn't report this.

A: She made me promise. She said if I was really her friend, I wouldn't say anything. She said she couldn't afford the time off, that she was already behind on her rent. She has two kids at home, Mr. Reeves. Two kids she's raising by herself.

Q: I understand.

A: Do you? Because I've been carrying this for eight months. I see her now, the way she walks, and I know that if I'd said something—

Q: Mr. Okonkwo, I want you to know that what you're telling me today matters. It matters a great deal.

A: I hope so. I really do.

topic: A witness is questioned about a workplace injury they observed but did not report
text:
Q: State your name for the record.

A: David Chen.

Q: Mr. Chen, on the afternoon of July 19th, you were working in the packaging area, correct?

A: Yes.

Q: And you observed an incident involving the conveyor system?

A: I saw Jenny—Jennifer Kowalski—get her hand caught.

Q: Describe what you observed.

A: The line was moving fast that day. We were behind on quota. Jenny was trying to clear a jam, and she reached in without hitting the stop, and the belt caught her glove and pulled her hand in. Just her fingers, but—it happened so fast.

Q: What did you do?

A: I hit the emergency stop. Ran over to her.

Q: What was her condition?

A: Her two middle fingers were—they were bent wrong. She was shaking. Not crying, just shaking all over, holding her hand against her chest.

Q: Did you call for help?

A: I was about to. I was reaching for the radio, and she grabbed my arm with her good hand. She said wait. Just wait.

Q: Why did she want you to wait?

A: She said she needed a minute to think.

Q: To think about what?

A: I don't know exactly. She kept saying she just needed to figure something out.

Q: And you gave her that minute?

A: I gave her more than that. I gave her twenty minutes. We sat behind the pallets where the cameras don't reach, and she cried, and I didn't know what to do except sit there with her.

Q: Did she explain why she didn't want the incident reported?

A: She said she'd already had two incidents on her record. She said a third one and she'd be out. I told her this wasn't her fault, that the line was running too fast, that we all knew it. She just kept shaking her head.

Q: Mr. Chen, I can see this is difficult for you to talk about.

A: Jenny's a good person. She was just scared. And I made a choice to protect her instead of doing what I was supposed to do. I'm not sure anymore if that was the right thing.

topic: A witness is questioned about a workplace injury they observed but did not report
text:
Q: You worked the night shift at the Riverside facility in March of last year?

A: That's right.

Q: And you were present when an employee named Roberto Vega was injured?

A: Yes.

Q: Tell me what happened.

A: One of the press machines malfunctioned. Roberto's foot got caught when the safety guard failed to engage properly.

Q: How serious was the injury?

A: His ankle was fractured. We didn't know that at the time, but it was clear something was very wrong. He couldn't put weight on it at all.

Q: What steps did you take after witnessing this?

A: I helped him to a chair. Got him some ice from the break room.

Q: Did you notify a supervisor?

A: No.

Q: Did you call emergency services?

A: No. Roberto asked me not to.

Q: Ms. Franklin, I want to ask you something, and I'd like you to really think about your answer. If you had it to do over again, would you make the same choice?

A: That's not a simple question.

Q: I know it isn't.

A: Roberto came to this country eight years ago. He's been working at that plant for five of those years. He sends money home to his mother every month. Every single month. When he asked me not to call anyone, he wasn't being reckless. He was being terrified.

Q: Terrified of what?

A: Of losing everything he'd built. Of the questions that would come. Of being seen as a liability.

Q: And you understood that.

A: I understood that in that moment, he trusted me. And I couldn't—I didn't want to betray that trust. Maybe I should have. I don't know anymore. But I knew what it would cost him if I did, and I couldn't be the one to do that to him.

Q: What happened after that night?

A: He kept working on it for three more weeks before he finally went to a doctor. By then, it had healed wrong. He still limps.

Q: I appreciate your honesty, Ms. Franklin.

A: For whatever it's worth now.

topic: A witness is questioned about a workplace injury they observed but did not report
text:
Q: Mr. Hassan, let's discuss what you witnessed on October 8th.

A: Okay.

Q: You saw an injury occur in the loading dock area?

A: I did.

Q: Who was injured?

A: Terry Blackwell.

Q: How did the injury happen?

A: A crate fell from the top shelf. It struck Terry on the back as he was bending over.

Q: Did you see the immediate aftermath?

A: I was the first one to reach him.

Q: What was his condition?

A: He was on the ground. He couldn't straighten up. He was trying to breathe but it was like his body wouldn't let him take a full breath.

Q: Did you assist him?

A: I helped him to his feet. Slowly. He leaned on me for a while until he could stand on his own.

Q: And after that?

A: After that, he asked me to help him get to his car.

Q: He wanted to leave?

A: He said he just needed to lie down. That he'd be fine.

Q: Did you try to stop him?

A: I told him he should see the nurse. That this could be serious. He said he knew his own body.

Q: But you didn't report this to anyone.

A: Terry looked at me and said—I remember exactly what he said—he said, "Amir, I've got eighteen months until retirement. Eighteen months. Please." And the way he said please...

Q: Take your time.

A: He was sixty-three years old. He'd been there since before I was born. I couldn't—how was I supposed to look at him and say no?

Q: I understand this puts you in a difficult position, Mr. Hassan.

A: I keep thinking about it. Whether I did right by him or whether I made everything worse. He's been on disability for six months now. His back never healed right.

Q: That's a heavy thing to carry.

A: It is. It really is. But I'd want someone to do the same for me, you know? If I was scared and hurting and asking for help, I'd want someone to just... be human about it.

Q: Thank you, Mr. Hassan. Let's take a short break.

topic: A daycare worker is deposed about an injury a child sustained while in their care
text:
Q: Please state your name and position for the record.

A: My name is Rachel Tenorio. I'm a lead caregiver at Sunshine Days Learning Center. I've been there almost seven years now.

Q: Ms. Tenorio, I understand this has been a difficult situation for everyone involved. Can you walk me through what you remember about the morning of March 14th?

A: I remember everything about that morning. Everything. Lily had come in a little earlier than usual—her mom had a meeting, I think. She was wearing a purple shirt with butterflies on it. She loved butterflies.

Q: Take your time. What happened leading up to the incident?

A: The children were doing free play. I was helping two of the younger ones with blocks near the window. Lily was on the climbing structure with Marcus and another little girl—Ava, I think. They were playing some kind of game. Lily was laughing. She had this wonderful laugh, you know? And then—I'm sorry. I'm sorry.

Q: Would you like a moment?

A: No, I want to finish. I want her parents to know what happened. She reached for the top bar, and her foot slipped. I was already moving toward her when she fell. I wasn't fast enough.

Q: How far away were you when she fell?

A: Maybe eight feet. Maybe ten. It felt like a mile. I keep thinking if I had been standing closer, if I had been watching her instead of helping with the blocks—but we had fourteen children that morning, and I was the only one in the room because Jessica had taken a child to the bathroom.

Q: The protocols say there should be two caregivers present at all times for that group size, correct?

A: Yes. And there were two of us. Jessica was only gone for a minute, maybe two. But that was the minute it happened. I've gone over it a thousand times.

Q: What did you do immediately after Lily fell?

A: I ran to her. I didn't move her—we're trained not to move them if there might be a neck or back injury. I talked to her. I told her she was going to be okay, that I was right there, that her mommy was coming. I held her hand. I stayed with her until the paramedics arrived.

Q: Did she respond to you?

A: She was crying. She kept saying her arm hurt. I told her I knew, that help was coming, that she was so brave. I wanted her to know she wasn't alone. I never let go of her hand. Not once.

Q: Thank you, Ms. Tenorio.

A: I just need her family to know—I loved that little girl. I love all of them. This job isn't just a job to me. What happened to Lily is the worst thing that's ever happened in my career. I think about her every single day.

topic: A daycare worker is deposed about an injury a child sustained while in their care
text:
Q: Mr. Okafor, how long had you been employed at Little Steps Academy before the incident on November 8th?

A: About fourteen months.

Q: And you were the caregiver directly supervising the toddler room that afternoon?

A: I was one of two. Dina Marchetti was also present.

Q: Can you describe the layout of the toddler room?

A: It's roughly thirty by twenty feet. There's a soft play area in one corner with foam mats, a reading nook, a table for crafts and snacks, and cubbies along the back wall where we keep the children's belongings.

Q: Where were you positioned when Caleb Porter was injured?

A: I was at the craft table with four children. They were finger painting.

Q: And where was Caleb?

A: He was in the soft play area with Dina. Or—he was supposed to be.

Q: What do you mean by that?

A: I mean I looked up and saw him near the cubbies. The cubbies have a low shelf attached, about eighteen inches off the ground. He had climbed onto it. Before I could get to him—before either of us could get to him—he fell backward.

Q: Did you call out to him?

A: I did. I said his name. I said "Caleb, sit down, buddy." But he was two. Two-year-olds don't always listen. They don't understand danger the way we do. They're just exploring their world.

Q: Are those shelving units secured to the wall?

A: They are now. They were supposed to be anchored before. I'd actually mentioned it to our director, that they seemed a little wobbly. About three weeks before this happened.

Q: Did you document that concern?

A: I told her verbally. I should have put it in writing. I should have followed up. I think about that a lot.

Q: What happened after Caleb fell?

A: He hit the back of his head on the floor. It's a carpeted floor, thin carpet over concrete. He started crying immediately. Dina got to him first. There was blood—head wounds bleed so much, even small ones. I called the front office for first aid and to notify his parents.

Q: How did Caleb seem to you in the moments after the fall?

A: Scared. He was so scared. I sat with him while Dina applied pressure to the cut. I sang to him—he loved "The Wheels on the Bus." I wanted him to focus on something familiar. He kept reaching for me, so I let him hold onto my finger. His grip was so tight for such a little guy.

Q: Is there anything else you want to add about that day?

A: Only that I wish I could undo it. I went into childcare because I wanted to keep kids safe while their parents couldn't be there. And I failed Caleb that day. I failed his mom and dad. That's something I have to carry.

topic: A daycare worker is deposed about an injury a child sustained while in their care
text:
Q: Ms. Whitfield, I'm going to ask you about the events of January 22nd. Before I do, I want to clarify—you're here voluntarily today?

A: Yes.

Q: And you understand you can take breaks if you need them?

A: I understand.

Q: Good. Let's start with your role at Bright Horizons Childcare.

A: I'm an assistant caregiver. I work primarily with the three-to-four-year-old group.

Q: How many children were in your care on January 22nd?

A: Twelve.

Q: And how many staff members?

A: Two. Myself and the lead caregiver, Donna Price.

Q: At approximately 2:15 PM, a child named Sophie Reeves sustained an injury. Is that correct?

A: Yes.

Q: Describe what happened.

A: Sophie and another child, Aiden, were arguing over a toy truck. Aiden pushed Sophie. She fell into the corner of the bookshelf.

Q: Did you witness the push?

A: I heard the argument. I was walking toward them to intervene when Aiden pushed her. It happened very fast.

Q: How severely was Sophie injured?

A: She had a cut above her eyebrow. It required stitches. Four, I think.

Q: What did you do immediately after she fell?

A: I went to Sophie first. I could see she was bleeding. I applied a clean cloth to the wound and had Donna call the office. I stayed with Sophie and talked to her the whole time. I told her she was going to be okay, that cuts on our face sometimes bleed a lot but it didn't mean it was serious, that her mommy was coming.

Q: What about Aiden? The child who pushed her?

A: Donna took him aside. He was very upset—I don't think he meant to hurt her. He's three. He doesn't fully understand cause and effect yet.

Q: Are you defending his behavior?

A: No. I'm—I'm explaining it. He's a child. He made a mistake. Sophie got hurt, and that's terrible, but Aiden isn't a bad kid. He was crying too. He kept asking if Sophie was okay. He didn't understand what had happened.

Q: That wasn't my question.

A: I know. But I need you to understand that these are small children. Both of them needed care in that moment. Sophie needed medical attention, and Aiden needed someone to help him understand what happened. That's our job—to take care of all of them.

Q: Let's move on. Were the Reeves notified promptly?

A: Yes. Within five minutes of the incident.

Q: And who made that call?

A: Donna did. I stayed with Sophie. I didn't leave her side until her mother arrived. I wanted to be the one to hand her over, so her mom would know exactly who had been with her, who had been watching over her. She deserved that.

topic: A daycare worker is deposed about an injury a child sustained while in their care
text:
Q: State your full name.

A: Thomas Andrew Chen.

Q: Your position?

A: Director of Tiny Treasures Learning Center.

Q: How long have you held that position?

A: Eleven years.

Q: Mr. Chen, on September 3rd of last year, a four-year-old named Marcus Williams broke his collarbone while attending your facility. Correct?

A: That's correct.

Q: Were you present when the injury occurred?

A: I was in my office. I was called to the playground within a minute of the incident.

Q: Tell me what you observed when you arrived at the scene.

A: Marcus was lying on the ground near the swing set. He was crying. One of my staff, Elena Vance, was kneeling beside him. She had already instructed the other children to move to the sandbox area with our second caregiver.

Q: What did you do?

A: I assessed the situation. Marcus was holding his shoulder and couldn't move his arm without significant pain. I suspected a fracture. I called 911 and then called his mother.

Q: Describe Marcus's demeanor.

A: He was in pain and frightened. He kept asking for his mom.

Q: What did you tell him?

A: I told him his mom was on her way. I told him he was being very brave. I sat down on the ground next to him—I didn't want to be standing over him, looking down. I wanted to be at his level. I told him the doctors were coming to help him feel better.

Q: Did you touch him?

A: I held his hand. He squeezed it very hard. I let him.

Q: Mr. Chen, according to incident reports, the injury occurred because Marcus was attempting to climb the support pole of the swing set. Is that accurate?

A: Yes.

Q: Is climbing the swing set poles against facility rules?

A: It is. But Marcus was four years old. Four-year-olds test boundaries. That's developmentally normal.

Q: So you're saying this was expected behavior?

A: I'm saying children don't always follow rules, no matter how many times you tell them. Elena redirected Marcus away from the poles twice before this happened. She was supervising eight children. She turned to help another child who had fallen in the sandbox—a minor fall, no injury—and in those few seconds, Marcus climbed again.

Q: Do you believe adequate supervision was provided?

A: I believe my staff did everything reasonable. I believe Elena followed every protocol. And I believe she has replayed that moment in her head every day since. I've watched her carry this. She's one of the best caregivers I've ever employed, and this incident has been devastating for her. That matters too.

Q: I didn't ask about Ms. Vance's feelings.

A: No. You didn't. But you're going to ask me whether we did enough, and I'm telling you—we did. And it still wasn't enough to prevent a little boy from getting hurt. That's the hardest part of this job. You do everything right and something still goes wrong. Marcus didn't deserve to be hurt. Elena didn't deserve to have this happen on her watch. His parents didn't deserve that phone call. None of it was fair.

topic: A daycare worker is deposed about an injury a child sustained while in their care
text:
Q: Ms. Patel, how would you describe the safety protocols at Happy Hearts Daycare?

A: They're thorough. We have protocols for everything—drop-off, pick-up, meals, nap time, playground supervision, illness, emergencies.

Q: And on April 17th, were those protocols being followed?

A: Yes.

Q: Then how did Emma Schultz end up with a concussion?

A: Because sometimes, even when you do everything right, children get hurt. That's not an excuse. That's just—that's reality.

Q: Walk me through what happened.

A: Emma was playing in the block area. She was building a tower with another child, Jayden. The tower got tall—maybe three feet. Jayden knocked it over, and one of the larger blocks struck Emma on the side of her head. She fell and hit her head again on the floor.

Q: Where were you?

A: Three feet away. Reading a book to two other children.

Q: Three feet away, and you couldn't prevent this?

A: No. I couldn't. It happened in less than a second.

Q: Did you see Jayden knock over the tower?

A: Yes. I saw it. I was already reaching for Emma when the block hit her.

Q: What happened next?

A: Emma started crying. I picked her up—I know we're supposed to minimize movement with head injuries, but she was reaching for me and she was scared. I held her. I checked her pupils. I felt her head for swelling. I called for backup.

Q: You held her.

A: Yes.

Q: Despite the protocol about minimizing movement.

A: She was frightened and in pain and she needed comfort. I made a judgment call. I'd make the same call again.

Q: Even knowing it might have worsened her injury?

A: I held her gently. I supported her head. And I talked to her the whole time. I told her I had her, that she was safe, that I wasn't going anywhere.

Q: What did Emma say?

A: She asked for her daddy. Over and over.

Q: How did that make you feel?

A: ...

Q: Ms. Patel?

A: How do you think it made me feel? She was three years old and she was hurt and all she wanted was her father and I couldn't give her that. I could only give her me. So I held her and I told her Daddy was coming as fast as he could, and I stayed with her in the ambulance because her parents couldn't get there in time, and I held her hand while they examined her at the hospital. I didn't leave her alone. Not for one second. Because that's what you do. That's what she needed.

Q: Thank you, Ms. Patel. I don't have further questions at this time.

A: I just want to say one more thing. For the record. Emma is okay now. She recovered fully. And I still think about her every day. I still wonder if I could have been faster, if I could have seen it coming. I'll probably always wonder. But I know I did my best to take care of her after it happened. I know that.

topic: A witness is questioned about a workplace injury they observed but did not report

topic: A tenant is questioned about property damage they reported to their landlord
text:
Q: Mr. Okonkwo, you submitted a maintenance request on March 15th regarding water damage in your unit, correct?

topic: A tenant is questioned about property damage they reported to their landlord

Q: Ms. Vance, I want to direct your attention to the incident report dated June 3rd. You wrote that you discovered mold in the bathroom. Is that accurate?

topic: A tenant is questioned about property damage they reported to their landlord
