topic: A doctor is deposed about informed consent procedures before a surgery
text:
Q: Dr. Patel, let's talk about your informed consent process. Can you walk me through what you do before a surgical procedure?

A: Oh, absolutely. I'd be happy to. So, my process is actually something I've refined over about fifteen years of practice, and I think it's quite thorough. I start with an initial consultation where we discuss the diagnosis, then I bring the patient back for a second visit specifically dedicated to consent—

Q: Let me just stop you there. A second visit specifically for consent?

A: Yes! This is actually something I implemented about eight years ago because I found that patients retain information better when they're not processing a new diagnosis at the same time. The research supports this approach. There was a study in the Journal of Patient Safety in 2018 that showed—

Q: I appreciate that, Doctor. Let's focus on the specific case at hand. Mrs. Thornton's surgery on March 15th.

A: Of course, of course. With Mrs. Thornton, I followed my standard protocol. We had our diagnosis conversation on February 28th, then she came back on March 8th for what I call the "consent conversation"—I actually have a handout I give patients, would you like to see it?

Q: We'll get to documents later. During this March 8th visit, what specifically did you discuss?

A: Everything. I mean, truly comprehensive. The nature of the procedure, the alternatives—and there were three realistic alternatives in her case—the risks, the benefits, recovery expectations. I even draw diagrams. I find visual aids really help patients understand what we're doing anatomically.

Q: Did you discuss the specific risk of nerve damage?

A: Yes, that's actually one of the first risks I mention with this type of procedure. I tell every patient—and I told Mrs. Thornton—that there's approximately a two to four percent chance of temporary nerve involvement and less than one percent chance of permanent damage. I remember being very clear about this because it's something I take seriously.

Q: How did Mrs. Thornton respond to that information?

A: She asked excellent questions, actually. She wanted to know what "nerve damage" would feel like, whether it would affect her ability to work—she's a pianist, you know—and I walked her through all of that. We probably spent twenty minutes just on that topic.

Q: Twenty minutes on nerve damage alone?

A: At least! This is exactly why I schedule the full hour for consent conversations. You can't rush this. Patient education is—well, it's fundamental to good medicine, in my view.

Q: And this was all documented in the chart?

A: Every bit of it. I dictate my notes immediately after these visits while everything is fresh. Would you like me to walk you through what I documented?

topic: A doctor is deposed about informed consent procedures before a surgery
text:
Q: State your name for the record.

A: Dr. Harold Vance.

Q: Dr. Vance, you performed surgery on Michael Reyes on September 3rd of last year?

A: I did.

Q: Before that surgery, did you obtain informed consent?

A: Yes.

Q: Tell me about that process.

A: I spoke with Mr. Reyes about the procedure. He signed the consent form.

Q: That's it?

A: That's the summary, yes.

Q: Walk me through the details—what did you actually tell him?

A: I explained the surgery, the risks, the alternatives.

Q: Which risks specifically?

A: The standard risks for a cholecystectomy. Bleeding, infection, bile duct injury.

Q: Now this is what I find fascinating about your practice, Doctor—your consent form lists seventeen separate risks. Did you discuss all seventeen with Mr. Reyes?

A: I discussed the material risks.

Q: But all seventeen are listed. So someone must have thought they were important enough to include, right? I mean, your hospital's form is actually more comprehensive than most I've seen—

A: The form is comprehensive by design. I discuss what's clinically relevant to each patient.

Q: And who decides what's clinically relevant? You?

A: The physician makes that determination, yes.

Q: So in your judgment—your expert medical judgment—bile leak wasn't worth mentioning to Mr. Reyes?

A: I didn't say that.

Q: Well, it's risk number twelve on your form. You said you discussed "material risks." So I'm curious—did bile leak make the cut?

A: I don't recall the specific wording of every conversation.

Q: Fair enough. But you keep records, don't you? Your chart note from that visit—can you read what you wrote about the consent discussion?

A: "Informed consent obtained. Patient verbalized understanding."

Q: That's the entire entry?

A: Yes.

topic: A doctor is deposed about informed consent procedures before a surgery
text:
Q: Dr. Kim, how long have you been practicing orthopedic surgery?

A: Nineteen years.

Q: And in those nineteen years, how many total knee replacements have you performed, roughly?

A: Somewhere around two thousand.

Q: Two thousand. That's remarkable. You must have your consent process down to a science by now.

A: I have a consistent approach, yes.

Q: Tell me about it!

A: I meet with the patient. We review the procedure, the expected outcomes, what could go wrong, and what the alternatives are, including doing nothing.

Q: And what about this specific patient, Mr. Holloway—what do you remember about your consent conversation with him?

A: I remember Mr. Holloway well. He was anxious about anesthesia.

Q: Anxious about anesthesia! Now that's interesting. What did you do about that?

A: I spent extra time explaining the anesthesia options. I also brought in the anesthesiologist for a pre-operative consultation, which isn't standard for this procedure but I felt it was warranted.

Q: You went above and beyond, it sounds like.

A: I addressed my patient's concerns.

Q: Did Mr. Holloway ask about any other risks?

A: He asked about infection.

Q: And what did you tell him?

A: The truth. That infection rates for total knee replacement at our facility are below the national average—about 0.8 percent—but that infection remains a real risk that can have serious consequences.

Q: Did you discuss the signs of infection he should watch for post-operatively?

A: At that visit, I discussed it briefly. We covered it in much more detail at the pre-op appointment and again at discharge.

Q: Multiple touchpoints, then?

A: Exactly. Informed consent isn't a single event. It's a process.

Q: I love that—"it's a process." Did you document all of these touchpoints?

A: I documented each conversation in the relevant visit note.

Q: Wonderful. We'll want copies of all of those.

A: My attorney has already provided them, I believe.

topic: A doctor is deposed about informed consent procedures before a surgery
text:
Q: Dr. Sandoval, let's turn to the consent form itself. Who prepares this document?

A: The hospital's legal department created the template. I review it with patients.

Q: Did you review it with Ms. Chen?

A: Yes.

Q: Page by page?

A: We went through the key sections together.

Q: Which sections did you skip?

A: I wouldn't say I skipped anything.

Q: But you said "key sections." That implies some sections aren't key.

A: There's standard language about hospital policies, HIPAA acknowledgments—administrative sections that don't relate to the medical risks of the procedure.

Q: Got it. So you focused on what—the medical risks?

A: Risks, benefits, alternatives, and the nature of the procedure itself.

Q: Did Ms. Chen ask any questions?

A: She did.

Q: What did she ask?

A: She asked about scarring. She was concerned about visible scarring because of her profession—she's a model.

Q: A model! That must have changed your approach to the conversation.

A: It informed which aspects I emphasized, yes. I spent significant time discussing the incision placement and what she could expect cosmetically.

Q: That's exactly the kind of individualized care patients deserve! How long did this conversation take?

A: Perhaps forty-five minutes.

Q: Forty-five minutes. And was anyone else present?

A: My nurse was in the room.

Q: Can your nurse corroborate what was discussed?

A: You would have to ask her, but she was present throughout.

Q: We will. Now, Dr. Sandoval, at any point did Ms. Chen express hesitation about proceeding?

A: She wanted time to think. I told her to take all the time she needed.

Q: How much time did she take?

A: She called my office three days later to schedule the surgery.

topic: A doctor is deposed about informed consent procedures before a surgery
text:
Q: Dr. Washington, you've testified that you explained the risks of the spinal fusion to Mr. Okonkwo.

A: Correct.

Q: Including the risk of paralysis?

A: Yes.

Q: How did you explain that risk?

A: I told him that any surgery near the spinal cord carries some risk of neurological injury, including, in rare cases, paralysis.

Q: "Rare cases." Can you be more specific?

A: The literature puts the risk of significant permanent neurological deficit at under one percent for this procedure.

Q: Did you give Mr. Okonkwo that statistic?

A: I don't quote statistics to patients as a general rule.

Q: Why not?

A: Because numbers can be misleading without context. A one percent risk sounds small, but if you're the one percent, it's one hundred percent of your outcome. I prefer to help patients understand risks qualitatively—what could happen, how likely it is relative to other risks, what we do to minimize it.

Q: That's a thoughtful approach, Doctor. Really thoughtful. Did you explain what you do to minimize the risk?

A: I did. I explained that we use intraoperative neurological monitoring, that the procedure would be performed with image guidance, and that I stop immediately if there's any signal change.

Q: Did Mr. Okonkwo seem to understand?

A: He did. He asked whether he'd be "awake enough" during surgery for the monitoring to work, which showed me he was following along.

Q: What a great question from him. How did you respond?

A: I explained that he'd be under general anesthesia but that the monitoring doesn't require him to be awake—it measures electrical signals in the nerves.

Q: After all this, did Mr. Okonkwo agree to proceed?

A: Not that day. He wanted to discuss it with his wife first.

Q: And then?

A: He came back the following week with his wife. We went through everything again. They both had questions. And then he signed the consent.

Q: Both visits are documented?

A: In detail.

topic: A pharmacist is deposed about a prescription that was filled with the wrong dosage
text:
Q: Mr. Harmon, let's go back to the afternoon of September 14th. You filled the prescription for Mrs. Delacroix yourself, correct?

A: I already answered that. Yes.

Q: And the prescription called for lisinopril 10 milligrams?

A: That's what I said in my previous answer. Ten milligrams.

Q: But the bottle you dispensed contained 40-milligram tablets, didn't it?

A: You have the pharmacy records in front of you. You know what they say.

Q: I'm asking what you know, Mr. Harmon.

A: Fine. Yes. The bottle contained 40-milligram tablets.

Q: So you dispensed four times the prescribed dosage to an 82-year-old woman with documented kidney disease?

A: I didn't have her complete medical history in front of me. We fill prescriptions based on what the physician sends us.

Q: You didn't think to verify?

A: I verify hundreds of prescriptions a day. Hundreds. Every single day. Do you have any idea what that workload looks like?

Q: I'm not asking about your workload generally. I'm asking about this prescription, this patient, this day.

A: And I'm telling you that the system we operate under makes it impossible to—you know what, the answer is no. I did not call the physician's office to verify.

Q: Because you were too busy?

A: Because I trusted the prescription as written. Which is what pharmacists do. That's the entire basis of the system.

Q: The entire basis of the system. And Mrs. Delacroix spent nine days in the ICU.

A: I'm aware of that. I don't need you to remind me.

---

topic: A pharmacist is deposed about a prescription that was filled with the wrong dosage
text:
Q: Ms. Vance, who else was working the pharmacy counter with you on March 3rd?

A: It was just me and the pharmacy tech, Brian.

Q: Brian Ostrowski?

A: Yes.

Q: And it's your testimony that Brian pulled the medication from the shelf?

A: That's correct.

Q: But you're the one who checked it before it went to the patient?

A: That's the protocol, yes.

Q: So when the 5-milligram methotrexate tablets went out instead of the 2.5-milligram tablets, you had already looked at that bottle?

A: I had looked at it, yes. I'm not denying that.

Q: Then help me understand something, Ms. Vance. The bottles are different colors, aren't they?

A: They are, but—

Q: Different colors. Different label sizes. And you looked at the bottle.

A: Counsel, I was working a twelve-hour shift. I had been on my feet since six in the morning. We had a line of customers out the door because corporate cut our staffing again, and I was doing the work of two pharmacists while also trying to administer flu shots in the back. So yes, I looked at the bottle. And no, I didn't catch it. And I have to live with that.

Q: You have to live with that.

A: That's what I said.

Q: Mr. Thornton has to live with weekly blood transfusions now because of the methotrexate toxicity.

A: I understand that.

Q: Do you?

A: Don't question whether I understand the gravity of what happened. Don't you dare do that.

---

topic: A pharmacist is deposed about a prescription that was filled with the wrong dosage
text:
Q: Dr. Reeves, I want to be very precise here. The prescription transmitted from Dr. Anand's office indicated oxycodone 15 milligrams?

A: According to the electronic record, yes.

Q: According to the electronic record. Is there some other record I should be looking at?

A: I'm simply being precise with my language, as you requested.

Q: The patient received oxycodone 80 milligrams instead. Correct?

A: That is what the investigation concluded.

Q: That's not what I asked. I asked whether it's correct.

A: Yes. It's correct.

Q: An 80-milligram extended-release tablet given to a patient with no opioid tolerance. Yes?

A: Yes.

Q: Walk me through how that happens.

A: I've explained this three times now in this deposition.

Q: Then explain it a fourth time.

A: The NDC numbers are similar. The automated dispensing system flagged nothing. The tablet was pulled, it was counted, it was dispensed.

Q: And you signed off on it.

A: I signed off on the prescription, yes.

Q: While a twenty-three-year-old patient went home with enough opioid to stop her breathing.

A: Is there a question, counsel, or are we just doing this for effect now?

Q: Here's my question: At what point in your process should someone have caught this?

A: At multiple points. And no one did. Including me.

Q: Including you.

A: That's what I said.

---

topic: A pharmacist is deposed about a prescription that was filled with the wrong dosage
text:
Q: Let's talk about the training you received on high-alert medications.

A: What about it?

Q: When was the last time you completed a module on insulin dispensing?

A: I don't remember the exact date.

Q: Approximately?

A: Maybe six months before the incident. Maybe longer.

Q: Would it surprise you to learn that your employer's records show no completed training on insulin protocols in the eighteen months preceding July 19th?

A: Those records are incomplete.

Q: Incomplete how?

A: The system doesn't always log everything. There were technical issues.

Q: So your testimony is that you completed training that wasn't recorded?

A: My testimony is that I completed training. What your records show is your problem.

Q: Mr. Castellan, do you understand that Mr. Boyajian received insulin glargine 100 units per milliliter when his prescription was for 50 units per milliliter?

A: I'm aware of what happened.

Q: And that he experienced severe hypoglycemia requiring emergency hospitalization?

A: I'm aware.

Q: You keep saying you're aware. I'm trying to understand whether you appreciate the severity—

A: I appreciate it just fine, counselor. What I don't appreciate is being blamed for a system that sets pharmacists up to fail and then wonders why errors happen. I was working alone. No tech. No backup. Twelve-hour shift, no meal break, corporate breathing down my neck about fill times. So yes, I am aware. More aware than you'll ever be sitting in that chair.

---

topic: A pharmacist is deposed about a prescription that was filled with the wrong dosage
text:
Q: Ms. Okoro, who made the decision to override the drug interaction warning?

A: I did.

Q: The system flagged a potential contraindication between the warfarin and the prescribed dosage of amoxicillin, correct?

A: It flagged an interaction. Those flags come up constantly. Ninety percent of them are clinically insignificant.

Q: So you overrode it.

A: I used my professional judgment.

Q: Your professional judgment.

A: Yes. Something pharmacists are trained to do.

Q: And in this case, your professional judgment resulted in a patient experiencing uncontrolled bleeding requiring a three-day hospital stay.

A: I'm not going to sit here and be cross-examined like a criminal. I made a judgment call based on the information available to me at the time.

Q: What information told you the interaction was insignificant?

A: The dosage was within normal range. The patient's age wasn't flagged as a risk factor in our system.

Q: The patient was seventy-eight years old.

A: And our system didn't flag that. You want to know why? Because the software is ten years out of date and corporate won't pay to upgrade it.

Q: So it's the software's fault.

A: I didn't say that.

Q: Then whose fault is it, Ms. Okoro?

A: It's a systemic failure. But you don't want to hear that. You want one person to blame so your client can collect a check.

Q: I want to understand how my client ended up in the hospital.

A: And I've told you. Repeatedly. Whether you choose to listen is up to you.

topic: A witness is questioned about a workplace injury they observed but did not report
text:
Q: Mr. Delacroix, you were working on the warehouse floor on September 14th, correct?

A: I was in the building, yes.

Q: In the building. Were you on the warehouse floor specifically?

A: I was in and out of several areas that day.

Q: Let me be more direct. Were you within visual range of the loading dock at approximately 2:15 p.m.?

A: I don't wear a watch that tells me exactly where I am every minute.

Q: Did you see Marcus Webb fall from the forklift?

A: I saw something happen near the forklift, yes.

Q: Something happen. Did you see Mr. Webb fall or not?

A: I saw movement. I heard a sound. I wasn't standing there with a clipboard taking notes.

Q: After you witnessed this "movement" and "sound," what did you do?

A: I continued with my work.

Q: You continued with your work. You didn't approach Mr. Webb?

A: Other people were already moving in that direction.

Q: Did you report what you observed to a supervisor?

A: There were plenty of people around who saw more than I did. I'm sure they handled it.

Q: That's not what I asked. Did you personally report the incident?

A: No.

Q: Why not?

A: Because I'm not the safety officer, counsel. I'm a forklift operator. I do my job. Other people are paid to do theirs.

topic: A witness is questioned about a workplace injury they observed but did not report
text:
Q: Ms. Thornton, I want to establish your location at the time of the incident. You were on the third floor, correct?

A: Yes.

Q: And from your workstation, you have a clear view of the stairwell landing?

A: I can see parts of it, depending on where I'm sitting.

Q: Were you sitting at your workstation when Patricia Okonkwo fell down the stairs?

A: I was at my desk, yes.

Q: So you saw her fall?

A: I saw her after she'd already fallen. She was on the landing. I heard the noise first.

Q: What did you hear?

A: A loud thump. Then some clattering. It sounded like something heavy hitting the stairs.

Q: Did you go to investigate?

A: I got up and looked through the window.

Q: You looked through the window. But you didn't go to the stairwell?

A: No.

Q: Did you call out to Ms. Okonkwo?

A: No, I—she was already getting up by the time I looked.

Q: She was getting up. Was anyone helping her?

A: Not that I could see. She was pulling herself up on the railing.

Q: And you watched this through the window?

A: For a few seconds. Then she walked off and I went back to my work. She seemed fine. People fall sometimes. It's not a crime to not run over every time someone trips.

topic: A witness is questioned about a workplace injury they observed but did not report
text:
Q: Let's talk about the reporting procedures at Hendricks Manufacturing. You're familiar with them?

A: Somewhat.

Q: Somewhat. Have you completed the mandatory safety training?

A: Yes.

Q: And that training covers the reporting of workplace injuries, does it not?

A: It covers a lot of things.

Q: Answer the question, please. Does it cover reporting of workplace injuries?

A: Yes, it mentions it.

Q: It "mentions" it? Isn't there an entire module devoted to incident reporting?

A: I don't memorize training modules, counsel. I complete them and move on.

Q: Fair enough. Do you recall being instructed that all witnessed injuries must be reported within 24 hours?

A: I recall something like that.

Q: Something like that. So when you saw Daniel Reeves get his hand caught in the press machine, you understood you had a duty to report it?

A: I understood that there's a process. I also understood that Daniel was screaming and six people came running, including the floor manager. It got reported. What exactly would I have added to that situation?

Q: That's not the question—

A: No, I think it is the question. You're asking me why I didn't fill out a form when the man's supervisor was standing right there watching him bleed. You want to talk about procedures? Talk to the people who wrote a policy that doesn't account for common sense.

topic: A witness is questioned about a workplace injury they observed but did not report
text:
Q: I'm going to ask you again, Mr. Yates, and I'd like a clear answer this time. Did you witness the incident involving Kevin Marsh on November 3rd?

A: I've already answered that question three times.

Q: Then answering it a fourth time shouldn't be difficult.

A: I saw Kevin on the ground. I didn't see how he got there.

Q: Where were you standing when you first saw him on the ground?

A: By the tool crib.

Q: How far is that from where Mr. Marsh was found?

A: Maybe thirty feet. Forty.

Q: And what was your first thought when you saw him?

A: Objection to the form. You can answer.

A: I thought someone should help him.

Q: Did you help him?

A: I started walking over, and then Ray—Ray Donahue—he was already there, so I stopped.

Q: You stopped.

A: That's what I said.

Q: Did you speak to anyone about what you observed?

A: I talked to Ray later. He said Kevin slipped on some hydraulic fluid.

Q: Did you report that information to management?

A: Ray's a shift lead. He is management.

Q: I'm asking if you personally filed a report or made a formal statement about the hydraulic fluid or the unsafe condition.

A: You know what, counsel? In fifteen years on that floor, I've never once seen a report change anything except who gets blamed. So no. I did not file a report.

topic: A witness is questioned about a workplace injury they observed but did not report
text:
Q: Ms. Yamamoto, we've established you were present in Lab C when the incident occurred. Now I want to understand what you did immediately after.

A: I stayed where I was.

Q: You stayed where you were. Dr. Hollins had just been burned by a chemical splash, and you stayed where you were?

A: The safety shower was on the other side of the room. He ran to it. I wasn't in his way.

Q: Did it occur to you to assist him?

A: I'm not trained in chemical burn response. I would have made things worse.

Q: Did you consider calling for help?

A: Someone had already hit the alarm. I could hear it.

Q: So you did nothing.

A: I did exactly what we're trained to do in a chemical exposure event, which is to not create additional chaos. Is there a question in here somewhere, or are you just going to keep implying I should have done something different?

Q: I'm trying to understand why no incident report bears your name, Ms. Yamamoto.

A: Because Dr. Hollins filed the report. He's the principal investigator. It's his lab. His chemical. His burn.

Q: Protocol requires all witnesses to file independent reports.

A: Then protocol has a problem, because in that lab, Dr. Hollins files the reports. That's how it works. That's how it's always worked. If you have an issue with that, I suggest you depose him.

Q: I'm deposing you.

A: And I've told you what happened. Whether you like the answer is not my concern.

topic: A doctor is deposed about informed consent procedures before a surgery
text:
Q: Dr. Harmon, you spoke with Mrs. Castellano the day before her hysterectomy, correct?

A: I did.

Q: And that conversation lasted how long?

A: I'd have to look at my notes.

Q: Your notes indicate eleven minutes.

A: Then eleven minutes.

Q: In those eleven minutes, you explained the risk of ureteral injury?

A: I explained all material risks, yes.

Q: I'm asking specifically about ureteral injury.

A: And I'm telling you I covered it.

Q: Do you have a specific recollection of saying the words "ureteral injury" to Mrs. Castellano?

A: I don't memorize every word of every conversation with every patient.

Q: So you don't specifically recall.

A: I recall covering the risks. Whether I said "ureteral injury" or "damage to surrounding structures including the tubes connecting the kidneys to the bladder"—I can't tell you which phrase I used that particular day.

Q: But you're certain you covered it.

A: I've been doing this for nineteen years. The conversation follows a pattern.

Q: A pattern. So you're testifying based on habit, not memory.

A: I'm testifying based on how I practice medicine.

topic: A doctor is deposed about informed consent procedures before a surgery
text:
Q: Dr. Phelps, walk me through your standard informed consent process.

A: Of course. I meet with the patient in my office, typically one to two weeks before any scheduled procedure. We discuss the diagnosis, the proposed intervention, alternative treatments including doing nothing, and the risks and benefits of each option. I ask if they have questions. I answer them. We then review the consent form together before they sign.

Q: That sounds very thorough.

A: I believe informed consent is foundational to ethical practice.

Q: And this is what happened with Mr. Bowen?

A: Yes.

Q: You met with him two weeks before the surgery?

A: I'd have to check the exact date, but approximately, yes.

Q: The records show you met with him the morning of the procedure. At 5:45 a.m. In pre-op.

A: Then there must have been a prior conversation that wasn't documented, or—

Q: Must have been.

A: I'm saying I wouldn't deviate from my standard practice.

Q: But you have no documentation of this prior conversation.

A: Not everything gets documented in real time.

Q: The consent form is signed at 5:52 a.m.

A: I see that.

Q: Seven minutes after you first spoke with him that morning, according to the records.

A: According to what's written, yes.

Q: Dr. Phelps, did you have a pre-operative informed consent conversation with Mr. Bowen before the morning of his surgery?

A: I believe I did.

Q: But you have no record of it and no specific memory of it.

A: That's correct.

topic: A doctor is deposed about informed consent procedures before a surgery
text:
Q: The consent form Mr. Dietrich signed—you have it in front of you?

A: I do.

Q: Turn to page two. Read the third paragraph aloud, please.

A: "Patient acknowledges that the risks of this procedure include but are not limited to bleeding, infection, nerve damage, and adverse reaction to anesthesia."

Q: Does that paragraph mention stroke?

A: Not in those specific words.

Q: Anywhere on that form—does the word "stroke" appear?

A: I'd have to review the entire document.

Q: Take your time.

A: ...No. The word "stroke" does not appear.

Q: Mr. Dietrich suffered a stroke during the procedure.

A: He did. A very unfortunate outcome.

Q: Did you verbally inform him that stroke was a risk?

A: The form says "not limited to." That language is specifically meant to indicate—

Q: I'm asking what you said. Out loud. To Mr. Dietrich.

A: I told him there were cardiovascular risks.

Q: Cardiovascular risks.

A: Yes.

Q: Did you say the word "stroke"?

A: I may have. I don't have a specific recollection.

Q: You may have.

A: I can't give you a verbatim transcript of a conversation from fourteen months ago.

Q: Dr. Kaplan, is stroke a known risk of this procedure?

A: It's a rare but recognized complication, yes.

Q: And you may or may not have mentioned it.

A: I covered cardiovascular risks. I consider that adequate.

topic: A doctor is deposed about informed consent procedures before a surgery
text:
Q: Dr. Muñoz, did you provide any written materials to Ms. Farrow about the lap-band procedure?

A: Yes, my office has a standard packet we give to all bariatric patients.

Q: What's in that packet?

A: An overview of the procedure, dietary guidelines for before and after, a list of potential complications, and frequently asked questions.

Q: May I show you what's been marked as Exhibit 14?

A: Please.

Q: Is this the packet your office used in 2022?

A: It appears to be, yes.

Q: The section on complications—page four—lists twelve risks.

A: Yes.

Q: Erosion of the band into the stomach wall. That's listed?

A: Let me check. ...I don't see it on this page.

Q: Is it elsewhere in the document?

A: I don't believe so, no.

Q: Is band erosion a known complication?

A: It occurs in a small percentage of cases.

Q: What percentage?

A: Studies vary. Perhaps one to three percent.

Q: One to three percent. And it's not mentioned in the materials you gave Ms. Farrow.

A: The document says "including but not limited to."

Q: You're the second physician this week to point me to that phrase.

A: I can't speak to other depositions.

Q: Dr. Muñoz, why wouldn't you include a one-to-three percent complication in your written materials?

A: The document is meant to be accessible, not exhaustive. I supplement it with verbal discussion.

Q: Did you verbally discuss band erosion with Ms. Farrow?

A: Yes.

Q: You're certain.

A: Yes, counsel. I am certain.

topic: A doctor is deposed about informed consent procedures before a surgery
text:
Q: Dr. Ashford, you're board certified in orthopedic surgery?

A: I am.

Q: How many total knee replacements have you performed?

A: Over my career? Approximately eight hundred.

Q: You performed Mr. Quinlan's knee replacement on March 3rd of last year.

A: That's correct.

Q: Before that surgery, did you discuss the possibility that he might have a leg length discrepancy afterward?

A: I discussed the general risks of the procedure.

Q: I'm asking about leg length discrepancy specifically.

A: I don't recall whether I used those exact words.

Q: Is leg length discrepancy a known risk?

A: It can occur. It's uncommon.

Q: How uncommon?

A: I don't have a percentage in front of me.

Q: Would you say it's rare?

A: I would say it's not typical.

Q: Mr. Quinlan's left leg is now one and a half centimeters shorter than his right.

A: That's what the post-operative measurements show.

Q: He says you never warned him this could happen.

A: With respect, patients don't always remember every element of a pre-surgical conversation.

Q: Is it possible you didn't mention it?

A: I suppose anything is possible.

Q: That's not what I'm asking.

A: Then ask it more precisely.

Q: Did you, Dr. Ashford, tell Michael Quinlan before his surgery that his leg might end up shorter than the other one?

A: I believe I covered it under the discussion of alignment and mechanical outcomes.

Q: That's not a yes.

A: It's the most accurate answer I can give.

topic: A project manager is questioned about deadlines they missed on a software contract
text:
Q: Mr. Hadley, the contract specified a delivery date of March 15th for the beta release, correct?

A: That's what the contract said, yes.

Q: And the beta was not delivered on March 15th, was it?

A: No.

Q: It was delivered on April 28th, wasn't it?

A: I'd have to check the exact date.

Q: I'm showing you Exhibit 14. Does that refresh your recollection?

A: Fine. April 28th.

Q: That's forty-four days late, Mr. Hadley.

A: I can do arithmetic.

Q: I'm sure you can. What I'm wondering is whether you can explain to this jury why your team missed the deadline by forty-four days.

A: There were factors outside our control.

Q: Factors outside your control. Let's talk about those factors. You had six developers assigned to this project initially, correct?

A: At the outset, yes.

Q: And by February, you had three. You personally reassigned three developers to a different project, didn't you?

A: That decision was made at the leadership level.

Q: You are leadership, Mr. Hadley. You're the project manager. You signed the reassignment orders.

A: I signed what I was directed to sign.

Q: So when you said "factors outside your control," you meant factors outside your control that you personally set in motion?

A: That's a mischaracterization and you know it.

---

topic: A project manager is questioned about deadlines they missed on a software contract
text:
Q: Let's turn to the milestone schedule. You're familiar with the milestone schedule attached to the contract?

A: Of course I'm familiar with it. I helped draft it.

Q: Good. Then you can tell me why Milestone 3 was completed nineteen days behind schedule.

A: I can tell you exactly why, if you'd actually like to hear the answer instead of cutting me off.

Q: Please. Enlighten me.

A: The client changed the authentication requirements on February 2nd. We documented this extensively. Your client's own IT director signed off on the change order, which added three weeks to the timeline. So when you say "nineteen days behind schedule," you're ignoring the fact that the schedule itself was amended.

Q: The original schedule was amended?

A: Yes.

Q: By whom?

A: By agreement of both parties. I have the emails if you'd like to see them.

Q: I'm asking the questions, Mr. Okonkwo. Was there a formal contract amendment signed?

A: There was a change order. Which, under Section 4.2 of the contract, constitutes a binding modification.

Q: You're a lawyer now?

A: I'm someone who reads contracts before I sign them. Perhaps your client should try it.

Q: Move to strike. Mr. Okonkwo, just answer the questions.

A: I am answering them. Accurately.

---

topic: A project manager is questioned about deadlines they missed on a software contract
text:
Q: Ms. Reeves, how many status meetings did you hold with the client between January and March?

A: I'd have to review my calendar to give you an exact number.

Q: Approximately.

A: I don't like to approximate in a legal proceeding.

Q: Would it surprise you to learn that we have records of only two meetings during that entire period?

A: It wouldn't surprise me that your records are incomplete, no.

Q: So there were more meetings?

A: There were phone calls, emails, Slack messages—constant communication. Your question assumes that a "meeting" is the only form of contact.

Q: I'm asking about formal status meetings, Ms. Reeves. Scheduled. Documented.

A: Then two sounds right.

Q: Two meetings in three months. On a project with a $2.3 million budget.

A: Is there a question?

Q: Did you believe two meetings were sufficient?

A: I believed—and I still believe—that the level of communication was appropriate given the client's own responsiveness.

Q: The client's responsiveness.

A: Yes. We sent fourteen requests for clarification on the API specifications. Your client responded to three of them. Three. Would you like to see those emails, or should I just keep answering questions that assume my team was the only party with obligations?

---

topic: A project manager is questioned about deadlines they missed on a software contract
text:
Q: When did you first become aware that the June 1st deadline was in jeopardy?

A: Probably mid-April. Maybe earlier. Things were getting tight.

Q: Getting tight. That's an interesting way to put it.

A: How would you put it?

Q: I'd put it as a deadline you were contractually obligated to meet, Ms. Chen.

A: And I'd put it as a deadline that became impossible when the scope tripled.

Q: The scope tripled.

A: Yes.

Q: Can you point me to any documentation of this tripling?

A: Can I point you to the 847 emails your client sent requesting additional features after contract signing? Yes. I can.

Q: Ms. Chen, let me be clear with you.

A: Please do.

Q: We're going to go through this timeline carefully. And every time you claim your client caused a delay, I'm going to ask you for documentation. And if that documentation doesn't exist—

A: It exists.

Q: Then we'll see, won't we?

A: Yes. We will.

Q: Let's start with April 15th. What happened on April 15th?

A: Your client's CTO called me directly and demanded we add biometric authentication to the login module. A feature nowhere in the original contract. That happened on April 15th.

---

topic: A project manager is questioned about deadlines they missed on a software contract
text:
Q: You sent an email on May 3rd to your supervisor. Exhibit 22. Do you see it?

A: Yes.

Q: Please read the highlighted portion.

A: "At this point, I'm not confident we can hit the deadline unless something changes."

Q: "Unless something changes." What did you mean by that?

A: I meant we needed more resources or a scope reduction.

Q: Did you get more resources?

A: No.

Q: Did you get a scope reduction?

A: No.

Q: So nothing changed.

A: Correct.

Q: And you missed the deadline.

A: Yes.

Q: Mr. Patel, did it occur to you to escalate this more forcefully?

A: I escalated it to my supervisor. As documented in that very email.

Q: And when your supervisor did nothing, did you go higher?

A: I did my job. I reported the risk. I can't force people to listen.

Q: So your testimony is that you warned people and they ignored you.

A: My testimony is exactly what's in front of you. I put it in writing. I sent it to the appropriate person. What they did with that information was beyond my authority.

Q: Beyond your authority.

A: Yes.

Q: Very convenient, Mr. Patel.

A: There's nothing convenient about any of this.

topic: A supervisor is deposed about performance reviews given to an employee who was later fired
text:
Q: Mr. Hendricks, you conducted performance reviews for Danielle Osman during her employment, correct?

A: Yes.

Q: How many reviews did you conduct for her?

A: Three. Annual reviews, each December.

Q: And in those reviews, did you ever rate her as "needs improvement" in any category?

A: I'd have to see the documents to be certain which categories—

Q: I'm asking what you remember, Mr. Hendricks.

A: Fine. Yes. I believe there were some categories marked that way.

Q: Which categories?

A: I don't have the reviews in front of me.

Q: We provided you copies this morning. Did you not review them?

A: I glanced at them. I review dozens of employees. I can't be expected to memorize every line item from three years of paperwork.

Q: Let's look at Exhibit 14, then. This is the December 2021 review. You see here under "Communication Skills" you marked "exceeds expectations"?

A: I see that.

Q: And yet four months later, the termination memo cites communication deficiencies. How do you explain that?

A: Things change. Performance changes. That's the whole point of ongoing evaluation.

Q: In four months?

A: Yes. In four months. People decline. It happens.

Q: Did you document any communication issues between December 2021 and her April termination?

A: I documented what needed documenting at the time it needed documenting. Can we move this along?

topic: A supervisor is deposed about performance reviews given to an employee who was later fired
text:
Q: Ms. Tran, when you gave Rachel Mendez her 2022 performance review, did you discuss areas for improvement?

A: Of course. That's standard practice.

Q: What areas did you identify?

A: Time management was one. There were concerns about meeting deadlines on the Kowalski project.

Q: Anything else?

A: Attendance, I think. There were some late arrivals.

Q: How many late arrivals?

A: I don't recall the exact number.

Q: More than five?

A: I couldn't say.

Q: More than ten?

A: Counsel, I said I don't recall. Asking variations of the same question isn't going to change my memory.

Q: I'm entitled to probe your recollection, Ms. Tran.

A: Then probe it with something useful. I've told you what I remember.

Q: Did Ms. Mendez receive any written warnings about attendance?

A: Not that I issued personally.

Q: Did anyone else issue written warnings?

A: You'd have to ask HR. I don't have access to every piece of paper that went into her file.

Q: But as her direct supervisor, you would have been informed of written warnings, wouldn't you?

A: Generally, yes. And generally, I don't recall any. There's your answer.

topic: A supervisor is deposed about performance reviews given to an employee who was later fired
text:
Q: Mr. Okonkwo, I want to talk about the rating scale used in your performance reviews.

A: Alright.

Q: The scale runs from one to five, correct?

A: Correct.

Q: And a three represents "meets expectations"?

A: That's right.

Q: In the eighteen months you supervised David Liang, did he ever receive a rating below three in any category?

A: I believe so, yes.

Q: In which review?

A: The second one. Summer of 2022.

Q: Which category received below a three?

A: I think it was... teamwork, maybe? Or collaboration? Those might be the same category, I'm not sure how it was labeled.

topic: A supervisor is deposed about performance reviews given to an employee who was later fired

topic: An employee is deposed about a coworker's termination they believe was retaliatory
text:
Q: Please state your name and your position at Meridian Technologies.

A: Sarah Chen. I'm a senior software engineer in the platform development group. I've been there for six years, and I worked directly alongside Marcus Webb for four of those years.

Q: You're aware that Mr. Webb's employment was terminated on March 15th of this year?

A: I'm aware that's the date the company claims he was terminated, yes. I'd characterize it as the date he was pushed out for doing the right thing.

Q: I'm asking about facts, Ms. Chen, not your characterizations.

A: And I'm giving you facts. The fact is Marcus filed a complaint about the billing discrepancies on February 28th. The fact is he was terminated fifteen days later. Those are facts.

Q: Were you present for any conversations between Mr. Webb and his supervisor regarding his job performance?

A: I was present for dozens of conversations. Would you like me to start with the performance review from January where Diana specifically praised his attention to detail? Or should I skip ahead to the conversations that happened after he raised concerns about the client overbilling?

Q: Let's focus on conversations after February 28th.

A: After February 28th, Diana stopped praising his attention to detail. Funny how that works.

Q: Can you describe a specific conversation?

A: March 3rd. Conference room B. Diana told Marcus his "communication style" had become "problematic." I was there because we were supposed to be discussing the Henderson project. Marcus asked her what specifically was problematic. She couldn't give him a single example. Not one.

Q: Did Mr. Webb respond to that criticism?

A: He asked for documentation. He asked for specific instances. He asked what he could do differently. Diana just kept repeating that there had been "concerns raised." When he asked who raised them, she said she couldn't disclose that.

Q: Did you ever discuss the billing discrepancies with Mr. Webb directly?

A: I was the one who first noticed them. I brought them to Marcus because he had more direct contact with the client accounts. He's the one who had the courage to escalate it. I should have been the one to file that complaint, and I'll have to live with that.

Q: Are you speculating about the reasons for his termination, or do you have direct knowledge?

A: I have direct knowledge that a exemplary employee with four years of outstanding performance reviews was suddenly labeled a "poor cultural fit" two weeks after he reported potential fraud. I have direct knowledge that three other people on our team saw the same pattern. I have direct knowledge because I documented every conversation, every meeting, every sudden shift in how he was treated. Would you like dates?

topic: An employee is deposed about a coworker's termination they believe was retaliatory
text:
Q: Mr. Patterson, how long did you work in the same department as Emily Okonkwo?

A: Yes.

A: They said it was a reduction in force.

A: I'm not sure how I sound. I'm just answering your questions.

Q: Let me ask it differently. Did you believe the reason given for her termination?

A: No.

Q: Why not?

A: Because five days before the "reduction in force," Emily filed a formal complaint about safety violations in the warehouse. And because she was the only person "reduced" from a team of twelve. And because they hired someone for her exact position six weeks later.

Q: How do you know about the safety complaint?

A: She told me she was filing it. She showed me the form. She asked me if I'd be willing to back her up if anyone asked, because I'd seen the same violations she had.

Q: Did you back her up?

A: Nobody ever asked me. Which I found interesting, given that HR supposedly investigated her complaint.

Q: You seem to have a detailed memory of these events.

A: I kept notes.

Q: You kept notes?

A: After what happened to Emily, I started documenting everything. Dates, times, who said what. I've got eighteen months of notes. I assumed someone would eventually want to see them.

Q: Were you told to keep these notes by anyone?

A: Nobody told me to. I'm not that brave. I just started doing it because I watched a good person lose her job for trying to keep people safe, and I didn't want to forget how it happened.

topic: An employee is deposed about a coworker's termination they believe was retaliatory
text:
Q: You testified earlier that you witnessed the meeting between Ms. Hendricks and the HR director. Let's revisit that. Who else was present?

A: Tom Schultz, the HR director. Janet Hendricks. And myself, though I don't think they realized I could hear through the partition.

A: I was sitting at my desk. The walls are thin. I didn't put myself there to listen. I was working.

Q: What did you hear?

A: I heard Tom tell Janet that her "attitude" had become a "liability."

Q: Those were his exact words?

A: Yes.

Q: You're certain?

A: I wrote them down immediately after.

Q: And what was this attitude he was referring to?

A: The attitude of expecting the company to follow OSHA regulations. The attitude of documenting when they didn't.

Q: Did he specifically reference her safety complaints?

A: He referenced her "constant complaints." When Janet asked which complaints specifically, he said—and again, I'm quoting—"You know exactly which ones, Janet."

Q: That could refer to any number of things.

A: It could. Except Janet hadn't filed any other complaints about anything. Ever. I've known her for three years. She's not a complainer. She's a worker.

Q: That's your characterization.

A: That's my observation based on three years of working beside her.

Q: Did you hear anything else in this conversation?

A: I heard Tom tell her that the company "values team players" and that she should "think carefully" about whether she wanted to "continue down this path."

Q: What path?

A: Presumably the path of reporting safety violations to OSHA after the company ignored her internal complaints. Which, I believe, is protected activity under federal law. But I'm not a lawyer.

Q: Did Ms. Hendricks respond?

A: She said she was just trying to keep people from getting hurt. Tom said that wasn't her job. She said she thought it was everyone's job. Then I heard her get up and leave.

topic: An employee is deposed about a coworker's termination they believe was retaliatory

topic: A building inspector is deposed about a structural assessment they signed off on

topic: A witness is questioned about a fire they discovered in a neighboring unit
text:
Q: Please state your name for the record.

A: The smell. Burning plastic and something else. Electrical, maybe.

Q: Did you attempt to alert Mr. Hartwell?

A: Of course I did. I'm not in the habit of watching my neighbors burn.

Q: How did you attempt to alert him?

A: I walked over and banged on his door. Loudly. For about thirty seconds. Then I called 911.

Q: And there was no response from inside the unit?

A: I already told you. No response. That's why I called 911.

Q: Did you try the door handle?

A: I touched it. It was hot. Would you like me to describe the specific temperature gradient, or can we move on?

---

Q: These are electronic timestamps—

A: I don't care if they're carved in stone. I know what time I saw smoke. Your electronic timestamps can say whatever they want.

Q: Let's move on. When you saw the smoke, what action did you take?

A: I left my unit and knocked on Unit 8's door.

Q: Did anyone answer?

A: No.

Q: What did you do then?

A: I called the fire department. What would you have done?

---

topic: A witness is questioned about a fire they discovered in a neighboring unit
text:
Q: Ms. Tran, I want to be very precise here. You've testified that you saw flames through the window of Unit 14-B.

A: Yes.

Q: Visible flames. Not just smoke.

A: Flames. Yes.

Q: And you were standing where exactly when you observed these flames?

A: On the walkway outside my unit. 14-A.

Q: How far from the window of 14-B?

A: Maybe fifteen feet.

Q: Fifteen feet. And it was nighttime?

A: It was 9 p.m. Yes.

Q: So it was dark outside.

A: There are lights on the walkway. And fire tends to be bright.

Q: I'm simply establishing the conditions, Ms. Tran.

A: And I'm simply answering your questions.

Q: The fire department report indicates the fire was contained to a back bedroom. The window you could see from the walkway faces the living room area. Can you explain how you saw flames?

A: I saw what I saw.

Q: That's not an explanation.

A: I'm not here to explain the fire department's report. I'm here to tell you what I witnessed.

Q: What you claim to have witnessed.

A: What I witnessed. If you want to call me a liar, counsel, go ahead and do it directly.

Q: I'm not calling you anything, Ms. Tran. I'm trying to reconcile your account with the physical evidence.

A: Then I suggest you try harder.

---

topic: A witness is questioned about a fire they discovered in a neighboring unit
text:
Q: Let's go back to the moment you first became aware of the fire.

A: Okay.

Q: You were in your living room?

A: Yes.

Q: Television on?

A: No.

Q: What were you doing?

A: Reading.

Q: And then what happened?

A: I heard glass breaking.

Q: From where?

A: From next door. The Palmers' unit.

Q: You heard glass break, and your first thought was fire?

A: My first thought was that something was wrong. I went outside to check.

Q: Immediately?

A: Yes. Immediately. Should I have waited?

Q: I'm just asking questions, Mr. Byrne. Did you see anyone outside when you went to check?

A: No.

Q: No one at all.

A: I said no.

Q: The Palmers weren't home?

A: Their car wasn't in the driveway. I assumed they weren't home.

Q: Did you assume, or did you know?

A: I assumed. I don't monitor my neighbors' schedules.

Q: But you knew their car. You knew to look for it.

A: I've lived next to them for six years. Yes, I recognize their car. Is that suspicious to you?

Q: I didn't say it was suspicious.

A: You're implying something. If you have an accusation, make it.

Q: I have no accusation. I'm gathering facts. You went outside, saw no one, and then what?

A: I saw smoke coming from their side window. I called 911. That's the whole story.

---

topic: A witness is questioned about a fire they discovered in a neighboring unit
text:
Q: Mrs. Delgado, how long have you lived at the Maplewood complex?

A: Eleven years.

Q: And in that time, have you had any disputes with the occupant of Unit 3?

A: I don't see what that has to do with anything.

Q: Please answer the question.

A: No. No disputes.

Q: No disagreements about noise, parking, shared spaces?

A: Nothing significant.

Q: So there were some disagreements.

A: I said nothing significant. Neighbors talk. Sometimes they disagree. That's not a dispute.

Q: Fair enough. On the night of the fire, where were you?

A: In my unit. Asleep.

Q: What woke you?

A: The smoke alarm in the hallway.

Q: The building's alarm, not your unit's?

A: Correct. The building alarm is much louder.

Q: And what did you do when you heard it?

A: I got up. I looked out my door. I saw smoke in the hallway.

Q: Coming from where?

A: From the direction of Unit 3.

Q: Did you see fire?

A: No. Just smoke.

Q: Did you investigate?

A: I evacuated. Like you're supposed to.

Q: You didn't check on your neighbor? The one you had no disputes with?

A: I'm seventy-three years old. I have a heart condition. I evacuated.

Q: I wasn't suggesting—

A: Yes, you were. You were suggesting something. I did exactly what I was supposed to do. I left the building and called 911 from the parking lot. If you're looking for someone to blame, counsel, look somewhere else.

topic: A doctor is deposed about informed consent procedures before a surgery
text:
Q: Dr. Halloran, let me take you back to the morning of March 14th. You met with Mrs. Delacroix before the laminectomy, correct?

A: I did.

Q: And at that meeting, you discussed the risks of the procedure?

A: That's what informed consent is, yes.

Q: I'm asking whether you did so in this instance.

A: And I answered. Yes.

Q: What specific risks did you communicate to her?

A: The standard risks. Infection, bleeding, nerve damage, adverse reaction to anesthesia, possibility of incomplete resolution of symptoms.

Q: Did you mention the risk of paralysis?

A: Nerve damage encompasses that.

Q: Does it? If I asked Mrs. Delacroix whether "nerve damage" and "paralysis" mean the same thing to her, what do you suppose she'd say?

A: I'm not in a position to speculate about what your client would say. I can tell you what I told her.

Q: Then tell me. Did the word "paralysis" come out of your mouth during that conversation?

A: I don't have a transcript of the conversation, counselor. I explained the risks in terms a patient could understand.

Q: That's not what I asked.

A: I'm giving you the most accurate answer I can. I explained that there were risks to nerve function, which could range from numbness to more significant deficits.

Q: "More significant deficits." That's the phrase you used with a sixty-three-year-old retired schoolteacher?

A: I used language appropriate to the patient in front of me. I've been doing this for nineteen years.

Q: I'm sure you have. Did you document the specific risks you discussed?

A: The consent form was signed.

Q: I've seen the consent form. It's a one-page hospital template. I'm asking whether you made any contemporaneous notes about what you personally discussed with her.

A: The form reflects that consent was obtained after discussion of risks, benefits, and alternatives. That is the standard documentation.

---

topic: A doctor is deposed about informed consent procedures before a surgery
text:
Q: Dr. Patel, who was present when you spoke with Mr. Andersen about the bypass surgery?

A: Myself, Mr. Andersen, and I believe one of the floor nurses. I'd have to check the chart for her name.

Q: You don't remember who was there?

A: I remember the conversation clearly. The specific nurse on duty that morning—there are several who rotate through.

Q: Fair enough. How long did this conversation last?

A: Fifteen to twenty minutes.

Q: That's fairly precise. Do you typically time your consent discussions?

A: I'm estimating based on my usual practice.

Q: So you don't actually know how long this particular conversation took?

A: I know approximately. That's what I said.

Q: During those fifteen to twenty approximate minutes, did you explain to Mr. Andersen that he could refuse the surgery?

A: Of course.

Q: Those words specifically? "You can refuse this surgery"?

A: I make sure patients understand they have a choice. Whether I used those exact words—

Q: Did you use those exact words or not?

A: I'm trying to answer your question. I explain that surgery is one option, that there are alternatives, and that proceeding is their decision. That conveys the same substance.

Q: I'm not asking about substance. I'm asking about what you said.

A: And I'm telling you I don't memorize my sentences. I've given testimony for six hours already today, counselor. I'm doing my best to be accurate.

Q: I appreciate that. Let's move on. Did you explain the mortality risk?

A: Yes.

Q: What did you tell him?

A: That with any cardiac surgery there is a risk of death, and that for a procedure like his, the risk was approximately two to three percent.

Q: Did you tell him what factors increased his particular risk?

A: His age, his diabetes, his history of smoking—yes.

Q: Did you tell him his personal risk was higher than two to three percent given those factors?

A: I told him the range and explained that his history placed him at the higher end.

Q: Did you give him a number for his personal risk?

A: I don't recall giving a specific percentage beyond the range.

---

topic: A doctor is deposed about informed consent procedures before a surgery
text:
Q: When you see here on the consent form where it says "risks and benefits discussed"—you signed that?

A: I did.

Q: And Mrs. Tran signed below your signature?

A: That's correct.

Q: So this form represents that a conversation occurred?

A: It represents that informed consent was obtained, yes.

Q: But you have no memory of this particular conversation, do you?

A: I have a general memory of meeting with Mrs. Tran. The specific details—it was eight months ago. I've seen hundreds of patients since.

Q: So when you say "informed consent was obtained," you're relying on this form, not your memory?

A: I'm relying on my standard practice, which is to have these conversations before every surgery I perform.

Q: Let me ask it differently. Sitting here today, you cannot tell me one single thing you said to Mrs. Tran about the risks of her hysterectomy?

A: That's not—

Q: Can you or can you not?

A: I can tell you what I always discuss. Bleeding, infection, injury to surrounding organs, complications from anesthesia—

Q: Dr. Yeun. I asked what you said to Mrs. Tran. Not what you say generally.

A: And I've explained that I follow a consistent protocol. That protocol includes discussing those risks.

Q: A protocol. Like a script?

A: Like a professional standard of care that I adhere to with every patient.

Q: Do you ever deviate from this protocol?

A: I tailor the conversation to the patient's questions and concerns.

Q: What were Mrs. Tran's questions and concerns?

A: I don't recall specifically.

Q: What about her concerns about future fertility—did that come up?

A: She was forty-seven. A hysterectomy was being performed for severe fibroids. Fertility would not have been—

Q: Did it come up, Doctor?

A: Not that I recall.

Q: Isn't it true that Mrs. Tran asked you specifically whether there were alternatives that would preserve her fertility?

A: If she had, I would have discussed them.

Q: Would you have documented that discussion?

A: ...It would depend on the circumstances.

---

topic: A doctor is deposed about informed consent procedures before a surgery
text:
Q: Dr. Weiss, I want to be very careful here because I know we've been going back and forth on this. The surgical consent form—who prepares that?

A: The surgical coordinator prepares the form. I review it with the patient.

Q: You review it with the patient. Every time?

A: Every time.

Q: And you reviewed it with Mr. Ogawa on January 9th?

A: Yes.

Q: Walk me through that review.

A: I go through the form section by section. The nature of the procedure, the risks, the benefits, the alternatives, and then I ask if they have questions.

Q: Section by section. How long does that take?

A: It varies. Five minutes, ten minutes, depending on questions.

Q: Does your chart reflect how long the consent discussion took?

A: No.

Q: Why not?

A: Because that's not something we document.

Q: Why not?

A: Because—look, the medical community doesn't time-stamp every interaction. We document that consent was obtained.

Q: Let me ask you something else. The "alternatives" section—what alternatives did you discuss with Mr. Ogawa?

A: Continued conservative management. Physical therapy. Pain management.

Q: Did you discuss the option of a less invasive surgery?

A: The procedure I recommended was the appropriate procedure for his condition.

Q: That wasn't my question. Did you discuss the option of a less invasive approach?

A: I discussed the options that were medically appropriate.

Q: Dr. Weiss, I'm going to ask you one more time, and I'd like a yes or no answer. Did you discuss the option of a microdiscectomy as an alternative to the fusion surgery you performed?

A: A microdiscectomy would not have addressed his instability. So no.

Q: No, you didn't discuss it? Or no, you didn't think it was appropriate?

A: Both. I didn't discuss it because it wasn't appropriate.

Q: But you made that judgment for him, didn't you?

A: I made a medical judgment. That's my job.

---

topic: A doctor is deposed about informed consent procedures before a surgery
text:
Q: Let's talk about what happened after Mrs. Feldman signed the consent form.

A: What do you mean, "what happened"?

Q: Did you have any further discussions with her about the surgery?

A: I may have seen her briefly before she was taken to pre-op. I don't recall a substantive conversation after the consent was signed.

Q: Why not?

A: Because the consent process was complete.

Q: So once the form is signed, you consider the matter closed?

A: I consider the formal consent process complete. If a patient has additional questions, I answer them.

Q: Did Mrs. Feldman have additional questions?

A: Not that I recall.

Q: Her husband testified that she was anxious that morning, that she asked a nurse to bring you back into the room.

A: I wasn't aware of that.

Q: No one communicated to you that your patient wanted to speak with you?

A: If they had, I would have gone.

Q: Are you saying that didn't happen, or that you weren't told?

A: I'm saying I have no knowledge of that request. I can't speak to what the nursing staff did or didn't communicate.

Q: Does it concern you that your patient may have wanted to speak with you before surgery and wasn't given that opportunity?

A: It concerns me if any patient's needs aren't met.

Q: That's a very general answer.

A: It's an honest answer. I don't know what happened. I can't respond to allegations about things I have no knowledge of.

Q: Let me ask you this. If Mrs. Feldman had wanted to withdraw her consent that morning, how would she have done so?

A: She would tell any member of the surgical team. We would stop.

Q: Would you have been notified?

A: Absolutely.

Q: And you weren't notified of anything unusual that morning?

A: No.

Q: Nothing at all?

A: Counselor, I've answered this question. No. I was not notified of anything unusual. If you have evidence to the contrary, I'd like to see it.

topic: A tenant is questioned about property damage they reported to their landlord
text:
Q: Mr. Hernandez, when did you first notice the water damage in your apartment?

topic: A tenant is questioned about property damage they reported to their landlord
text:
Q: Ms. Patterson, let's talk about the mold you reported. When did you first see it?

A: Oh, it must have been—let me think—probably around mid-January? Maybe the 15th or 16th? I remember because my sister was visiting and she has terrible allergies and she kept sneezing, and I thought it was just the dust, but then I looked behind the dresser and there it was, this dark greenish-black patch, and I just—

Q: Ms. Patterson. The date is sufficient.

A: I'm trying to give you context.

Q: I appreciate that. Mid-January. Where exactly was this mold located?

A: Behind the dresser. In the corner of the bedroom. Near the exterior wall.

Q: How large was the affected area?

A: Well, at first it was maybe—I don't know—the size of a dinner plate? But by the time anyone actually came to look at it, which took three weeks, by the way, it had spread to—

Q: I'm asking about when you first saw it.

A: Dinner plate. I just said that.

Q: Did you photograph the mold?

A: Yes. Multiple times. Want to see them?

Q: Those will be entered as exhibits. Did you report this to the landlord?

A: Of course I did. That same day.

Q: How did you report it?

A: Email and phone call. I like to document everything.

Q: Let's move on. The repair request—

A: —which was ignored for three weeks.

Q: Ms. Patterson, please wait for my question.

A: Then please ask questions I haven't already answered.

topic: A tenant is questioned about property damage they reported to their landlord
text:
Q: Mr. Chen, you submitted a maintenance request on February 8th, correct?

A: Correct.

Q: What was the nature of that request?

A: The bathroom floor was buckling.

Q: Buckling in what way?

A: The tiles were coming up. There was moisture underneath.

Q: How did you know there was moisture underneath?

A: Because when I pulled up one of the loose tiles, the subfloor was wet. And it smelled.

Q: You pulled up a tile yourself?

A: It was already loose. It practically came up on its own.

Q: But you physically removed it?

A: I lifted a tile that was already separating from the floor to see what was underneath. Yes.

Q: Did you have permission to do that?

A: Permission to look at my own bathroom floor?

Q: Did you contact the landlord before disturbing the flooring?

A: I contacted the landlord to report the problem. I didn't realize I needed authorization to investigate why my bathroom smelled like rot.

Q: I'm simply trying to establish the sequence of events, Mr. Chen.

A: The sequence is: floor buckles, I look, I report, nothing happens for two months. That's the sequence.

Q: Did anyone from property management eventually inspect the bathroom?

A: Eventually.

Q: When?

A: April 2nd.

Q: And what was their assessment?

A: That there was water damage. Which I had told them eight weeks earlier. Is there anything else you'd like me to tell you twice?

topic: A tenant is questioned about property damage they reported to their landlord
text:
Q: Ms. Williams, I want to direct your attention to the incident report dated October 12th. You reported a broken window, is that correct?

A: Yes.

Q: Tell me how the window came to be broken.

A: No.

A: No.

A: No.

A: Is that a question?

A: Interior.

Q: Let's move on to the temperature in your apartment. You also reported heating issues, yes? Same day?

topic: A tenant is questioned about property damage they reported to their landlord
text:
Q: Mr. Davis, you lived in unit 4B from 2019 to 2023, correct?

A: Yes.

Q: During that time, you reported a ceiling collapse. Let me find the date here. Bear with me.

A: July 14th, 2022.

Q: Thank you. What were the circumstances?

A: I was at work. My wife was home. Part of the living room ceiling came down.

Q: How much of the ceiling?

A: A section about four feet by three feet.

Q: Was anyone injured?

A: No. My wife was in the kitchen.

Q: What did you do when you learned of this?

A: I left work and came home immediately.

Q: And then?

A: I called the landlord. I called the fire department. I took photographs.

Q: In that order?

A: Does it matter?

Q: I'm trying to establish a timeline.

A: Landlord, fire department, photographs. Or maybe photographs first. It was a stressful day. A ceiling had just fallen into my living room.

Q: Had you noticed any warning signs prior to the collapse? Cracks, sagging?

A: Yes. I reported cracks two months earlier.

Q: Did you receive a response to that report?

A: I received a response saying someone would be out to look at it.

Q: And did someone come?

A: No.

Q: You're certain?

A: I think I would remember if someone had come to inspect the ceiling that later fell on my furniture.

Q: Mr. Davis, I have to ask these questions.

A: Then ask the next one.

topic: A financial advisor is deposed about investment decisions made on a client's behalf
text:
Q: Mr. Hartley, let's talk about the Meridian Growth Fund. When did you first recommend this fund to Mrs. Patterson?

A: I'd have to check my notes for the exact date.

Q: Approximately.

Q: And what was your basis for recommending a high-risk growth fund to a client who was sixty-seven years old?

A: I've already explained this in my written response to the complaint. The fund was appropriate given her stated objectives.

Q: I'm asking you now, under oath. What was your basis?

A: She wanted growth. She told me she wanted growth. I recommended a growth fund. That's how this works.

Q: Did you document that conversation?

A: Yes.

Q: Where?

A: In my client notes. Which you have.

Q: I'm asking you to tell me where in your records this conversation appears.

A: Page twelve. Or thirteen. It's in the section dated January 2021. I'm not going to recite my own files back to you.

Q: Did you explain the risks of this fund to Mrs. Patterson?

A: Of course I did.

Q: How?

A: Verbally. And I gave her the prospectus. Like I do with every client. Like I've done for twenty-three years.

Q: Did she sign anything acknowledging those risks?

A: She signed the standard disclosure forms. Again—you have all of this.

topic: A financial advisor is deposed about investment decisions made on a client's behalf
text:
Q: Mr. Okonkwo, I want to direct your attention to the rebalancing that occurred in Mr. Vance's portfolio in March of 2022.

A: Okay.

Q: Who made the decision to shift forty percent of the portfolio into energy sector ETFs?

A: I did, in consultation with Mr. Vance.

Q: In consultation. What does that mean, specifically?

A: It means I spoke with him. I explained my reasoning. He agreed.

Q: How long was that conversation?

A: I don't recall exactly.

Q: Five minutes? An hour?

A: Somewhere in between. Maybe twenty minutes.

A: That's not—look, you're characterizing this in a way that—

Q: I'm asking a question, Mr. Okonkwo.

A: Then let me answer it. He wasn't "convinced." He came to me concerned about inflation. He'd been reading articles. He asked me what we could do to protect against it. Energy was performing well. It made sense at the time.

Q: Did you discuss the possibility that energy prices might fall?

A: Yes.

Q: What did you tell him?

A: That there's always risk. That past performance doesn't guarantee future results. That we should revisit in six months.

A: We did.

topic: A financial advisor is deposed about investment decisions made on a client's behalf
text:
Q: The allocation in question—the one to the Stratford Real Estate Investment Trust—when was that made?

topic: A financial advisor is deposed about investment decisions made on a client's behalf
text:
Q: Tell me about the fee structure you used with the Delgado account.
