topic: A financial advisor is deposed about investment decisions made on a client's behalf
text:
Q: Ms. Thorne, you've testified that you believed the municipal bond allocation was appropriate for Mr. and Mrs. Kessler.

A: That's correct.

Q: Even though they told you they needed liquidity within eighteen months?

A: They mentioned that as a possibility. Not a certainty.

Q: Let me read from your own notes. Quote: "Clients anticipate needing approximately two hundred thousand dollars liquid within twelve to eighteen months for purchase of vacation property." End quote. Does that refresh your recollection?

A: Yes, I wrote that.

Q: So they did tell you they needed liquidity within eighteen months.

A: They told me they anticipated needing it. Anticipated. For a vacation home. Not a medical emergency. Not a fixed obligation.

Q: Does that distinction matter for purposes of selecting an appropriate investment vehicle?

A: Yes, it does. Considerably.

Q: Explain.

A: If someone says they might want to buy a vacation home, that's different from saying they have a closing date. I built in flexibility. The bonds had staggered maturities. If they needed the money, they'd have access to portions of it over time.

Q: But they couldn't access all of it when they needed it, could they?

A: Not without penalty, no.

Q: And they incurred a loss when they had to liquidate early?

A: They incurred a cost. Whether it was a loss depends on how you're calculating.

Q: How much did they lose, Ms. Thorne?

A: I don't accept the framing of that question.

Q: Then let me rephrase. How much less did they receive than they invested?

A: Approximately fourteen thousand dollars. Which I've already stated in my interrogatory responses. Which you've already read.

topic: A driver is deposed about the events leading up to a multi-vehicle collision
text:
Q: Good morning. Before we begin, can I get you some water or anything else? I know these things can go on for a while.

A: No, thank you, I'm fine. I appreciate you asking.

Q: Let's start with some background. How long have you been driving, roughly?

A: Oh, let's see—I got my license when I was sixteen, so that would be about twenty-three years now. My father taught me, actually. He was very particular about defensive driving techniques, and I like to think I've carried that with me.

Q: That's helpful context. Now, on the morning of March 14th, can you walk me through how your day started?

A: Of course. I woke up around six-thirty, which is typical for me. I made coffee, checked my emails—nothing unusual. I left for work around seven-forty-five because I like to give myself extra time. I've always been that way. My wife teases me about it, but I'd rather be early than rushed.

Q: Take your time with this next part. What route did you take that morning?

A: I took Maple Street to the highway entrance on Fifth, which is my usual route. I've been driving it for about eight years now, ever since we moved to the Westside. I know every pothole, honestly.

Q: And how were the road conditions that morning, as best you recall?

A: The roads were dry. Clear skies. I remember thinking it was a nice morning—the kind where you roll down your window a little, you know? Visibility was excellent.

Q: I understand. Now, as you approached the intersection at Fifth and Commerce, what do you remember seeing?

A: I saw the light was green for me. I was in the left lane. There was a white sedan ahead of me, maybe two car lengths. And I noticed a delivery truck in the right lane, slightly behind me. I always try to be aware of what's around me.

Q: That's very thorough. What happened next?

A: The sedan in front of me braked suddenly. I remember thinking—well, I reacted immediately, applied my brakes firmly but not—I didn't slam them. I'd been keeping a safe distance, so I was able to stop in time. But then I heard the truck's brakes behind me, that awful sound, and then the impact.

Q: I'm sorry you had to go through that. Are you okay to continue?

A: Yes, yes, I'm fine. Thank you for asking. I want to help get this sorted out properly.

Q: Just a few more questions. After the impact, what did you do first?

A: I checked myself—made sure I could move. Then I got out to check on the other drivers. The young man in the truck, he was shaken up. I stayed with him until the paramedics arrived. It felt like the right thing to do.

---

topic: A driver is deposed about the events leading up to a multi-vehicle collision
text:
Q: State your name for the record.

A: Michael Torres.

Q: Mr. Torres, you were driving a gray Honda Accord on the date in question, correct?

A: That's right.

Q: I want to ask you about the moments before impact. How fast were you traveling?

A: Maybe thirty-five, forty miles per hour. The speed limit there is forty.

Q: You say "maybe." Can you be more specific?

A: I wasn't staring at my speedometer. I was watching the road. But I know I wasn't speeding.

Q: Fair enough. I'm not trying to trip you up here—I just want to understand what you observed.

A: I get it. No, I understand. I was going with the flow of traffic.

Q: That's helpful. Were there other vehicles around you at that point?

A: There was a pickup truck to my right, a little ahead of me. And I could see a motorcycle in my rearview—he'd been behind me for a few blocks.

Q: What about the vehicle that struck you? When did you first become aware of it?

A: Honestly? Not until it was too late. I heard the horn first. Then I looked left and saw this SUV coming through the intersection. It was like—time slowed down, if that makes sense.

Q: It does. A lot of people describe it that way.

A: Yeah. I remember thinking, very clearly, "This is going to hurt." And then it did.

Q: Take a moment if you need it. There's no rush here.

A: I'm okay. Thank you.

Q: After the collision, were you able to exit your vehicle?

A: Not right away. My door was jammed. A bystander—a woman, I never got her name—she helped me get out through the passenger side. She was very kind about it. Kept telling me to take my time, that help was coming.

Q: Did you have any conversation with the other drivers at the scene?

A: The SUV driver came over after a few minutes. He was upset, crying actually. He kept saying he didn't see the light. I told him we'd figure it out, that the important thing was everyone was alive. I don't know why I said that. It just came out.

Q: That was generous of you, given the circumstances.

A: I don't know about generous. I just—everyone makes mistakes. I've made them too.

---

topic: A driver is deposed about the events leading up to a multi-vehicle collision
text:
Q: Ms. Chen, I'm going to ask you about your speed as you entered the intersection.

A: I've already told the police, and I'll tell you—I was going the speed limit.

Q: I understand you gave a statement. But I'd like to hear it directly from you today, if you don't mind.

A: Fine. I was doing thirty-five. Maybe thirty-seven. Right around the limit.

Q: And you're certain of that?

A: As certain as anyone can be without a dashcam pointed at their speedometer, yes.

Q: That's a fair point, actually. Did your vehicle have a dashcam?

A: No. I've thought about getting one after all this, though. Lesson learned, right?

Q: I imagine so. Now, you mentioned in your written statement that you saw the light turn yellow.

A: I did. It turned yellow when I was maybe—I don't know—twenty feet from the intersection? Close enough that stopping would have meant slamming my brakes.

Q: So you made the decision to proceed through?

A: I made the decision that was safe under the circumstances, yes.

Q: That's a reasonable way to put it. What happened after you entered the intersection?

A: Everything happened very fast. The minivan came from my left—I don't think she saw me. Or maybe she thought she could make it. I don't know what she was thinking.

Q: You said "she"—did you see the driver before impact?

A: Just for a split second. She had this look on her face—I'll never forget it. Just total surprise. She wasn't being reckless; she just didn't see me coming. I genuinely believe that.

Q: That's a kind interpretation.

A: It's the truth as I see it. There's no point in me sitting here demonizing someone. We were both just trying to get somewhere, and something went wrong.

Q: I appreciate your candor.

A: Well, I figure we're all here trying to figure out what happened. I'd rather be helpful than difficult.

Q: Just a few more questions, then. After the collision, did you speak with the other driver?

A: Briefly. At the hospital, actually. She came to check on me. We didn't talk about fault or anything—she just wanted to make sure I was okay. I thought that took courage, honestly.

---

topic: A driver is deposed about the events leading up to a multi-vehicle collision
text:
Q: You testified that you checked your mirrors before changing lanes.

A: I did.

Q: Both mirrors?

A: Rearview and side mirror, yes.

Q: And what did you see?

A: The lane was clear.

Q: Mr. Patterson, I'm trying to give you an opportunity to walk me through this in detail. The more specific you can be, the better this goes for everyone.

A: I understand. I'm trying to remember exactly. There was a sedan behind me in my original lane—a dark color, maybe blue or black. The lane I was moving into looked empty. I signaled, checked again, and started the lane change.

Q: How long would you say your signal was on before you began moving?

A: Three or four seconds. I'm not someone who just flicks it on and goes. My grandfather was a driving instructor—he drilled that into me.

Q: That sounds like good training.

A: It was. He'd be sitting in the passenger seat saying, "Mirror, signal, mirror again, then move." I can still hear his voice.

Q: It sounds like he made an impression on you.

A: He did. I think about him every time I drive, honestly. He passed a few years ago, but—sorry, that's probably not relevant.

Q: No, please—I asked. I'm sorry for your loss.

A: Thank you. Anyway. I did everything the way he taught me. I still don't understand how I didn't see the motorcycle.

Q: Tell me what you remember about first becoming aware of the motorcycle.

A: I heard the horn. Not a car horn—higher pitched. I jerked the wheel back into my lane, but by then there was contact. Just the side mirrors clipping, but enough to send him off balance.

Q: What did you do after that?

A: Pulled over immediately. Ran back to him. He was down, but he was conscious, talking. I stayed with him, kept him calm, told him not to move until the EMTs arrived. I've never been so scared in my life.

Q: That must have been difficult.

A: It was. But he's doing better now—I actually called to check on him last week. I hope that's okay to mention.

---

topic: A driver is deposed about the events leading up to a multi-vehicle collision
text:
Q: How would you describe traffic conditions at the time of the accident?

A: Moderate. It was around 10 a.m., so past the morning rush.

Q: And you were traveling northbound on Industrial Boulevard?

A: Correct.

Q: Ms. Okafor, tell me about the moments leading up to the collision.

A: I was approaching the intersection at Industrial and Seventh. I had a green light. I was going straight through. That's really all there was to it.

Q: Sometimes the simple accounts are the most accurate. What happened next?

A: A flatbed truck ran the red light coming from my right. I saw it too late to stop completely, so I tried to swerve. I clipped his rear end and spun into the median.

Q: Were you injured?

A: Bruised ribs, some whiplash. I was lucky.

Q: I'm glad it wasn't worse. Did anyone stop to help you?

A: Several people, actually. There was a man in a construction vest who was there almost immediately. He opened my door, helped me out, asked if I knew where I was and what day it was. I think he'd had some first aid training.

Q: Did you speak with the truck driver at the scene?

A: No. He stayed in his vehicle until the police came. I think he was in shock, honestly. Young guy. He looked terrified when they finally got him out.

Q: How did that affect your feelings about the situation?

A: You know, I was angry at first. Of course I was. But seeing him standing there, shaking—I just couldn't hold onto it. He made a terrible mistake, but he wasn't some monster. He was just a kid who messed up badly.

Q: That's a generous perspective.

A: I don't know if it's generous. It's just—what's the alternative? Stay furious forever? I'd rather put my energy toward healing than hating.

Q: Have you had any contact with him since?

A: His mother called me. She was in tears, apologizing over and over. I told her I accepted her apology, and I meant it. I hope he learns from this. That's all I really want.

topic: A paramedic is questioned about the response time and treatment at an accident scene
text:
Q: Please state your name and occupation for the record.

A: Michael Torres, paramedic with County Fire and Rescue, eleven years on the job.

Q: You responded to the accident on Route 12 on the morning of March 3rd?

A: I did. My partner and I were the first medical unit on scene.

Q: What time did you arrive?

A: 7:42 a.m. I noted it in my log the moment we stopped. We were dispatched at 7:34, so that's an eight-minute response time from a station that's 6.2 miles out on rural roads.

Q: And you believe that response time was adequate?

A: I don't believe it—I know it. Our county average for that district is eleven minutes. We beat it by three.

Q: When you arrived, what was the condition of the plaintiff?

A: She was conscious, alert, complaining of neck pain and tingling in her left arm. GCS of 15. I immobilized her spine within ninety seconds of making contact.

Q: Ninety seconds. You're certain of that?

A: I am. My partner was already pulling the board while I was doing the primary assessment. We've worked together for four years. We don't waste motion.

Q: Did you administer any medication at the scene?

A: No. She didn't meet the criteria for field analgesia, and I wasn't going to medicate someone who might need imaging. That's protocol, and it's also good medicine.

Q: So you made a judgment call to withhold pain relief?

A: I made a protocol-driven decision to prioritize her long-term outcome over short-term comfort. Yes.

Q: Has anyone suggested your treatment was deficient in any way?

A: No one with any standing to make that judgment has suggested it, no.

Q: What do you mean by "standing"?

A: I mean no physician, no medical director, no peer reviewer. The people who actually understand prehospital care have had no issues with anything I did that morning.

topic: A paramedic is questioned about the response time and treatment at an accident scene
text:
Q: How long have you been a paramedic, Ms. Chen?

A: Seven years, all with Metro EMS.

Q: And you were working on September 14th of last year?

A: I was.

Q: Tell me about the dispatch call.

A: Multi-vehicle collision on the interstate, mile marker 47. We got the call at 3:17 p.m., en route at 3:18.

Q: That's a fast departure.

A: We were already in the rig doing equipment checks. Timing worked out.

Q: Now, when you arrived at the scene, there were multiple injured parties?

A: Three vehicles, five patients. Two critical, two moderate, one walking wounded.

Q: Walk me through your triage decisions.

A: Certainly. Red tags on the driver of the sedan and the rear passenger of the SUV. Yellow tags on the sedan's passenger and the pickup driver. Green tag on the SUV driver who was ambulatory with minor lacerations.

Q: You made those determinations yourself?

A: I did. START triage. Takes about thirty seconds per patient when you know what you're doing.

Q: The plaintiff was the rear passenger of the SUV—one of your red tags.

A: Correct.

Q: She claims she waited nearly fifteen minutes before receiving any treatment.

A: That's not accurate.

Q: You're disputing her recollection?

A: I'm disputing her timeline. I have my field notes, timestamps, and radio traffic logs. She received her first intervention—supplemental oxygen and hemorrhage control—at 3:31. We arrived at 3:28. That's three minutes.

Q: Perhaps her perception of time was affected by the trauma?

A: That's entirely possible, and I'd expect it. But perception doesn't change the documented facts.

Q: You sound very sure of your documentation.

A: I am. I write my reports knowing they might end up in a room like this one.

topic: A paramedic is questioned about the response time and treatment at an accident scene
text:
Q: Let's talk about your training, Mr. Okonkwo.

A: What would you like to know?

Q: How many hours of continuing education have you completed in the past two years?

A: Ninety-six, which is double the state requirement.

Q: Is there a reason you've exceeded the requirement?

A: Yes. I want to be good at my job.

Q: Fair enough. Now, on the night in question, you responded to a single-car accident on Hillcrest Drive?

A: Correct. Vehicle struck a utility pole, driver unresponsive.

Q: What time was the 911 call placed?

A: 11:47 p.m.

Q: And you arrived when?

A: 11:59.

Q: That's twelve minutes. The plaintiff's family has suggested that was too long.

A: I understand they're grieving, and I have sympathy for that.

Q: But?

A: But the call came from a residence a quarter mile away. The witness heard the crash, went outside, found the vehicle, went back inside to call. That's several minutes right there before we were even dispatched.

Q: So you're saying the delay wasn't on your end.

A: I'm saying there was no delay on our end. We were dispatched at 11:52 and arrived at 11:59 from a station 4.8 miles away on winding roads at night. You do the math.

Q: When you found the driver, what was his condition?

A: Unconscious, agonal breathing, significant head trauma. I'm not going to sugarcoat it—it was a bad scene.

Q: Did you begin resuscitation efforts?

A: Immediately. Airway management, BVM ventilation, C-spine precautions. We had him packaged and en route to the trauma center by 12:11.

Q: Twelve minutes on scene for a critical patient?

A: Twelve minutes to extricate, assess, stabilize, and load a patient who was pinned against a crumpled dashboard. Yes. That's efficient work under difficult conditions.

topic: A paramedic is questioned about the response time and treatment at an accident scene
text:
Q: Ms. Reeves, I'm going to ask you some questions about the treatment you provided. Please listen carefully.

A: Of course.

Q: You administered epinephrine at the scene, correct?

A: Correct.

Q: On whose authority?

A: My own, under standing medical orders and direct communication with our medical control physician.

Q: You called for permission?

A: I called to report. The situation met the criteria for administration. I wasn't asking permission—I was keeping the doctor informed, which is protocol.

Q: Is that standard practice?

A: Yes. Paramedics aren't nurses waiting for orders. We have treatment algorithms and the training to execute them.

Q: Let me rephrase. Is it standard practice to administer epinephrine without explicit physician authorization?

A: Let me rephrase my answer. It's standard practice to follow evidence-based protocols that have already been authorized by our medical director. That's exactly what I did.

Q: The family believes their son had an adverse reaction to the epinephrine.

A: I've read their complaint.

Q: Do you have a response?

A: The patient was in anaphylactic shock. His airway was closing. Without epinephrine, he would have died in that parking lot. The medication I gave him is the reason he's alive to have a family that can file complaints.

Q: That's a strong statement.

A: It's an accurate one.

Q: Are you always this certain about your decisions?

A: When I've made the right call? Yes.

Q: And you believe this was the right call.

A: I know it was. Any paramedic, any ER physician, any allergist would tell you the same thing.

topic: A paramedic is questioned about the response time and treatment at an accident scene
text:
Q: Mr. Franklin, let's establish the timeline. What time were you dispatched?

A: 2:14 p.m.

Q: And arrival on scene?

A: 2:21.

Q: Seven minutes. That seems reasonable for the distance involved.

A: It is reasonable. It's actually quite good given the construction on Miller Avenue.

Q: You encountered traffic delays?

A: Minor ones. We used the siren and lights. People moved. But there's only so much you can do when a lane is closed.

Q: Now, the plaintiff, Mr. Harrison, was the driver of one of the vehicles?

A: He was.

Q: What treatment did you provide?

A: Initial assessment, oxygen therapy, wound care for facial lacerations, spinal immobilization as a precaution, IV access en route.

Q: He's alleged that you were dismissive of his complaints of chest pain.

A: That's incorrect.

Q: Tell me what happened.

A: He mentioned chest discomfort approximately four minutes into transport. I immediately performed a 12-lead ECG, which showed normal sinus rhythm. I increased my monitoring and documented his complaint. That's the opposite of dismissive.

Q: Did you consider the possibility of cardiac involvement?

A: Of course I did. That's why I ran the ECG.

Q: But you didn't divert to a cardiac facility.

A: Because the ECG was normal, his vitals were stable, and the receiving trauma center was eight minutes out with a full cardiac cath lab anyway. What would diversion have accomplished?

Q: I'm asking the questions, Mr. Franklin.

A: And I'm giving you the answers. The clinical answer is: nothing. Diversion would have accomplished nothing except delay his evaluation for his obvious traumatic injuries.

Q: Let's move on. Did you communicate the chest pain complaint to the receiving facility?

A: Word for word. It's on the recorded radio traffic. They were expecting it when we rolled in.

topic: A witness is questioned about a conversation they overheard in a company hallway
text:
Q: Good morning. Could you please state your name for the record?

A: Jennifer Mathis.

Q: Ms. Mathis, I'd like to ask you about an event that occurred on March 14th of this year. Were you working at Hendricks & Associates on that date?

A: Yes, I was.

Q: And at some point during that day, did you happen to overhear a conversation in one of the hallways?

A: I did, yes. It was in the afternoon, around two-thirty or so.

Q: Can you describe where you were positioned when you heard this conversation?

A: I was in the copy room. The door was open about halfway, and the hallway runs right past it.

Q: And who did you observe in the hallway?

A: I saw David Chen and a woman I didn't recognize. She was wearing a visitor badge.

Q: Were you able to hear what they were discussing?

A: Parts of it. They weren't whispering, but they weren't exactly loud either.

Q: What portions were you able to make out?

A: Mr. Chen said something about a shipment being delayed. He mentioned a date—I believe it was the twenty-second. The woman seemed concerned about documentation.

Q: When you say she seemed concerned, what gave you that impression?

A: Her voice went up slightly. She asked him twice whether the paperwork would be ready.

Q: Did Mr. Chen respond to that question?

A: He told her it would be handled. Those were his words—"It'll be handled."

Q: Did either of them appear to notice you in the copy room?

A: No. I was standing behind the door, and they moved on after about a minute.

topic: A witness is questioned about a conversation they overheard in a company hallway
text:
Q: Mr. Okonkwo, you've testified that you were on the third floor on the afternoon in question. Is that correct?

A: That's right.

Q: I'd like you to walk me through exactly what you heard. Take your time.

A: Sure. I had just come out of the restroom near the stairwell. Two people were standing maybe fifteen feet away, near the window by the elevator bank.

Q: Did you recognize either of them?

A: One was Sarah Levine from accounting. The other was a man in a gray suit. I'd seen him before but didn't know his name.

Q: What were they discussing?

A: Ms. Levine was talking about numbers. She said something like, "The figures don't add up, and someone's going to notice."

Q: What was the man's response?

A: He laughed. Not a big laugh—more like a chuckle. Then he said, "Let me worry about that."

Q: How would you characterize his tone when he said that?

A: Dismissive, I suppose. Like he wasn't particularly concerned with what she was telling him.

Q: Did Ms. Levine say anything further?

A: She lowered her voice. I couldn't make out the next part.

Q: Did you make any effort to hear more clearly?

A: No. I walked to the elevator and went back to my floor.

Q: At any point did either Ms. Levine or the man acknowledge your presence?

A: Ms. Levine glanced at me briefly. That was all.

Q: Did her expression change when she noticed you?

A: Not really. She just looked back at the man and kept talking.

topic: A witness is questioned about a conversation they overheard in a company hallway
text:
Q: You were deposed once before in a different matter, is that right?

A: About four years ago, yes.

Q: So you understand how this works. I ask questions, you answer truthfully.

A: I do.

Q: Good. Now, on October 9th, you were walking through the east corridor of Building C. Correct?

A: Correct.

Q: And you've previously stated you overheard a conversation between two individuals. I want to be very precise here. How far away were you from these individuals?

A: I'd estimate ten to twelve feet.

Q: Not closer?

A: No. The hallway is fairly wide there, and I was on the opposite side.

Q: Could you hear them clearly at that distance?

A: Clearly enough. The building was quiet—it was after six.

Q: Who were these individuals?

A: Mark Reeves and someone from legal. I believe her name was Patterson or Peterson.

Q: What did you hear Mr. Reeves say?

A: He was explaining that a client had requested certain files be removed from the server.

Q: Removed. That was the word he used?

A: Yes.

Q: Did the woman respond?

A: She asked if that was something they were authorized to do. Mr. Reeves said he'd already cleared it with someone upstairs.

Q: Did he specify who?

A: Not that I heard.

Q: Did you stop walking during this exchange, or did you continue past them?

A: I slowed down, but I kept moving. I didn't want to appear to be eavesdropping.

topic: A witness is questioned about a conversation they overheard in a company hallway
text:
Q: Ms. Vance, let's return to the conversation you mentioned in your initial statement. You said it took place near the break room?

A: Just outside the break room, yes. In the hallway.

Q: Who was present?

A: Linda Hoffman and a man I later learned was from the auditing firm.

Q: How did you come to learn he was from the auditing firm?

A: I saw him in a meeting the following week. Someone introduced him.

Q: What time of day did this hallway conversation occur?

A: Mid-morning. Maybe ten, ten-fifteen.

Q: Were you passing through, or did you stop?

A: I had stopped to check my phone. I was leaning against the wall near the vending machines.

Q: What did you hear?

A: Ms. Hoffman was telling him that certain inventory records had been adjusted.

Q: Adjusted. Did she elaborate on what that meant?

A: She said the numbers had been brought into alignment with projections.

Q: Were those her exact words?

A: As close as I can remember, yes.

Q: What was the auditor's reaction?

A: He didn't say much. He nodded a few times. Then he asked who had authorized the adjustments.

Q: Did Ms. Hoffman answer?

A: She said it came from the top. She didn't name anyone specifically.

Q: Did you report this conversation to anyone at the time?

A: No. I didn't think it was my place.

Q: But you're reporting it now.

A: I was asked. So I'm answering.

topic: A witness is questioned about a conversation they overheard in a company hallway
text:
Q: Let me direct your attention to January 7th. Were you at work that day?

A: I was, yes.

Q: And did something unusual happen that day?

A: I wouldn't call it unusual, but I did overhear a conversation that stuck with me.

Q: Why did it stick with you?

A: Because of who was involved and what they were talking about.

Q: Who was involved?

A: Thomas Briggs, our CFO, and a woman I didn't recognize. She might have been outside counsel.

Q: What makes you think she was outside counsel?

A: She had a briefcase, and she kept referring to "your company" rather than "our company."

Q: Fair enough. Where did this conversation take place?

A: In the hallway outside the executive conference room on the fifth floor.

Q: Were you supposed to be on that floor?

A: I was dropping off documents for Mr. Briggs's assistant.

Q: What did you hear?

A: Mr. Briggs said they needed to get ahead of the situation before the board meeting. The woman asked what exposure they were looking at.

Q: Did he answer?

A: He said, "Enough to cause problems."

Q: Did he quantify what he meant by "problems"?

A: Not in the portion I heard. They moved into the conference room shortly after.

Q: Did either of them see you?

A: I don't believe so. I was around the corner, near the elevator.

Q: And you didn't follow up or ask anyone about what you'd heard?

A: No. It wasn't my business.

topic: A neighbor is questioned about noise complaints and a confrontation they witnessed
text:
Q: Please state your name and address for the record.

A: Margaret Ellen Whitfield. I've lived at 4412 Crescent Drive for thirty-seven years. Since 1987.

Q: And you're familiar with the property at 4408 Crescent Drive?

A: Familiar? I've watched three different families come and go from that house. I know every change that's been made to it. The Hendersons put in the pool in '94, the Marshalls added the deck in 2003, and Mr. Reeves—well, we all know what Mr. Reeves has contributed.

Q: What do you mean by that?

A: Noise. Disruption. A complete disregard for the neighborhood standards we've maintained for decades.

Q: Can you describe the incident on the evening of March 15th?

A: I was the one who organized the neighborhood response, so yes, I can describe it in detail. At approximately 9:47 p.m.—I noted the time—the music from Mr. Reeves' property reached a level that I measured at 78 decibels from my own porch. I have the app on my phone. I can show you the screenshots if you'd like.

Q: That won't be necessary at this time. What did you do next?

A: I did what any responsible community member would do. I went to speak with him directly, as I've done on eleven prior occasions. I keep a log.

Q: You keep a log of your interactions with Mr. Reeves?

A: Of course. Dates, times, nature of the disturbance, his response. It's all documented. I was a legal secretary for twenty-two years at Morrison & Associates. I understand the value of documentation.

Q: What happened when you approached him on March 15th?

A: I walked across the lawn—my lawn, then his—and I knocked on the door. Firmly. He opened it and immediately became confrontational. I remained calm. I've handled far more difficult personalities in my career.

Q: What did Mr. Reeves say to you?

A: He used language I won't repeat, but I stood my ground. I informed him that I had already contacted the other affected homeowners, that we were unified in our position, and that this matter would be escalated if necessary. As it has been.

Q: Did he make any threatening gestures or statements?

A: He raised his voice and stepped toward me. But I didn't flinch. I've dealt with attorneys who bill eight hundred dollars an hour—I'm not intimidated by a man in a tank top holding a beer can.

Q: What happened after that exchange?

A: He slammed the door. The music continued for another forty-three minutes. I documented everything, contacted Officer Reynolds—who I know personally from the Citizens' Advisory Board—and filed the formal complaint the following morning. The process I initiated is why we're all here today.

topic: A neighbor is questioned about noise complaints and a confrontation they witnessed
text:
Q: How long have you lived at your current residence?

A: About four years now.

Q: And in that time, have you had any interactions with the residents at 7720 Maple?

A: Some, yeah. Normal neighbor stuff mostly. Until recently.

Q: Let's talk about what changed. When did you first become aware of issues between Mr. Thornton and the Garcias?

A: Maybe six months ago? The Garcias started having people over more. Cars on the street, music, you know.

Q: Did you personally witness any confrontations?

A: The big one, yeah. The one in September.

Q: Tell me about that.

A: It was a Saturday afternoon. The Garcias were having a birthday party for their kid—I think she was turning eight or something. There was a bounce house. Mr. Thornton came out of his house and walked right into their backyard.

Q: He entered their property?

A: Walked right through the side gate like he owned the place. I was in my driveway washing my car, so I had a clear view.

Q: Excellent. Now, what did you observe Mr. Thornton do once he entered the Garcia property?

A: He went straight to where the speakers were set up and just—unplugged them. Ripped the cord right out. There were like thirty people standing there, kids everywhere, and he just did it like it was his right.

Q: What was the reaction?

A: Mr. Garcia came over pretty fast. He was upset but—I mean, he kept his cool way better than I would've. He asked Thornton to leave. Said something like, "This is my daughter's birthday. Please leave."

Q: And did Mr. Thornton leave?

A: Not right away. He started going off about noise ordinances and property values and how long he'd lived in the neighborhood. Meanwhile there's an eight-year-old crying because the music stopped.

Q: Did the situation escalate physically?

A: Mr. Garcia put his hand on Thornton's shoulder to guide him out, and Thornton knocked it away. That's when Mrs. Garcia started recording on her phone.

Q: You observed Mrs. Garcia recording?

A: Yeah. I thought that was smart. I should've done the same.

topic: A neighbor is questioned about noise complaints and a confrontation they witnessed
text:
Q: Mr. Okonkwo, did there come a time when you intervened in a dispute between your neighbors?

A: There did. November 3rd of last year.

Q: Walk me through what happened.

A: I was coming home from my shift—I work nights at the hospital, I'm an RN in the cardiac unit—and I could hear yelling as soon as I got out of my car. It was about 7:15 in the morning.

Q: Where was the yelling coming from?

A: The Dalton residence. 558 Birchwood. Ms. Weston from 562 was standing on the sidewalk, and Mr. Dalton was on his porch.

Q: Could you hear what was being said?

A: Ms. Weston was saying something about the construction noise starting too early. Mr. Dalton had contractors working on his garage—they'd been there for a few weeks at that point.

Q: What was Mr. Dalton's response?

A: He was dismissive. Told her to go back inside if she didn't like it.

Q: What did you do?

A: I assessed the situation and made a decision to de-escalate. That's part of my training—recognizing when a situation is heading somewhere dangerous and intervening appropriately.

Q: How did you intervene?

A: I walked over calmly. I acknowledged both of them. I told Mr. Dalton that I understood he had work to complete, and I told Ms. Weston that I understood her frustration. Then I suggested a compromise—could the contractors start at 8 a.m. instead of 6:30?

Q: What was the response?

A: Mr. Dalton didn't like it at first, but I explained—calmly, without raising my voice—that the city ordinance actually supported Ms. Weston's position. I happened to know this because I'd dealt with a similar situation when I renovated my kitchen.

Q: So you referenced the municipal code?

A: I did. Section 11.4.3. Construction noise before 7 a.m. in residential areas. Once I cited the specific ordinance, Mr. Dalton's demeanor changed. He agreed to speak with his contractor.

Q: Did the situation resolve after that?

A: It did. Ms. Weston thanked me. Mr. Dalton went inside. The next morning, the work started at 8 a.m. Sometimes people just need someone who can communicate clearly and keep everyone focused on solutions.

Q: Were there any further incidents between them?

A: Not that I'm aware of. But I did give both of them my cell number in case anything came up. I told them to call me before it escalated. No one's called.

topic: A neighbor is questioned about noise complaints and a confrontation they witnessed
text:
Q: Did you witness the events of January 22nd?

A: Part of them.

Q: Tell me what you saw.

A: I saw the end of it. When the police arrived.

Q: Let's back up. Where were you when you first became aware something was happening?

A: Inside. I was cooking dinner.

Q: What drew your attention outside?

A: I heard a crash. Like something breaking.

Q: What did you do?

A: I looked out the window.

Q: And what did you see?

A: Mr. Patterson was standing in his driveway, and Mrs. Liu was on her porch. There was a broken flowerpot on the ground between the properties.

Q: Could you tell what had happened to the flowerpot?

A: No.

Q: Did either party say anything that you could hear?

A: It was muffled through the window.

Q: Did you open the window or go outside?

A: No.

Q: Why not?

A: It wasn't my business.

Q: But you're here today testifying about it.

A: I was subpoenaed.

Q: Fair enough. What happened next?

A: They argued for a few more minutes. I couldn't hear the words. Then Mr. Patterson went back inside, and Mrs. Liu called someone on her phone. The police showed up maybe fifteen, twenty minutes later.

Q: Did you speak with the officers?

A: They knocked on my door and asked if I'd seen anything. I told them what I saw.

Q: Which was what you've told me today?

A: More or less.

Q: Is there anything else you observed that you haven't mentioned?

A: No. That's it.

topic: A neighbor is questioned about noise complaints and a confrontation they witnessed
text:
Q: Now, I want to direct your attention to the specific language Mr. Hendricks used during this confrontation.

A: Okay.

Q: You mentioned earlier that he used profanity.

A: That's right.

Q: Can you recall the specific words?

A: I'd rather not repeat them.

Q: I understand, but for the record, we need to know exactly what was said.

A: He called her a—he used a gendered slur. And he said she should—I don't want to say this.

Q: Take your time.

A: He said she should go back where she came from. Those were his exact words.

Q: And what was Ms. Yamamura's response?

A: She stayed composed. More composed than I would've been. She said, "I was born in San Jose," and then she turned and walked back to her house.

Q: What did Mr. Hendricks do after she walked away?

A: He yelled something else after her. I couldn't make out the words from where I was standing.

Q: Where were you standing?

A: At the end of my driveway. I'd been getting the mail.

Q: How far is that from where the confrontation occurred?

A: Maybe forty feet? The Hendricks property is two houses down from mine.

Q: What made you stop and observe rather than going back inside?

A: At first I thought it was just a normal disagreement. Then his voice changed. Got uglier. And I realized this was something different.

Q: Did you say anything to either party?

A: After Ms. Yamamura went inside, I walked over to Mr. Hendricks. I told him what he said was out of line.

Q: What did he say to you?

A: He told me to mind my own business. Used some colorful language with me too.

Q: Did that end the interaction?

A: I told him this was my business. We've lived on this street for eleven years, and that kind of talk wasn't going to fly. Not while I was standing right there. He went inside after that.

Q: Did you have any further contact with Mr. Hendricks that day?

A: No. But I went to Ms. Yamamura's house afterward. Checked on her. Made sure she was okay.

topic: A pharmacist is deposed about a prescription that was filled with the wrong dosage
text:
Q: Mr. Hendricks, you were the pharmacist who filled prescription number 4471-B for Eleanor Castellano on March 14th, correct?

A: The prescription was filled under my supervision.

Q: Under your supervision. So someone else filled it?

A: We have pharmacy technicians who assist with the filling process. That's standard practice.

Q: And who was the technician that day?

A: I'd have to check the records to give you a specific name. I don't want to guess.

Q: You don't remember who you were working with four months ago on the day a patient received ten times her prescribed dosage?

A: I work with multiple technicians on rotating schedules. I want to be accurate.

Q: How convenient. Let me ask you this—whose initials appear on the verification line of that prescription label?

A: Mine do.

Q: So regardless of who physically counted the pills, you verified the prescription was correct before it left your pharmacy?

A: That's what my initials indicate, yes.

Q: That's what your initials indicate. Is that different from what actually happened?

A: I'm saying my initials are there. I'm not disputing that.

topic: A pharmacist is deposed about a prescription that was filled with the wrong dosage
text:
Q: Walk me through your standard procedure when you receive a prescription for a controlled substance.

A: We verify the prescription is valid, check the patient's history in the monitoring database, confirm the dosage against standard protocols, fill the prescription, and perform a final verification before dispensing.

Q: Every time?

A: Every time.

Q: No exceptions?

A: No exceptions. It's policy.

Q: Ms. Okonkwo, the prescription in question called for 2.5 milligrams of Warfarin. The bottle dispensed contained 25 milligrams. How does that happen with no exceptions?

A: I've been trying to understand that myself.

Q: Have you reached any conclusions?

A: Not ones I'm comfortable stating without more information.

Q: What information would you need?

A: I'd want to know whether someone accessed that prescription after my final verification. Whether anyone else handled it.

Q: Are you suggesting the prescription was tampered with?

A: I'm suggesting there are questions I don't have answers to.

Q: But you verified it personally, correct? You saw 2.5 milligrams on the label?

A: I verified a prescription that day. Whether what left the pharmacy was what I verified—that I cannot say with certainty.

Q: That's a remarkable distinction to draw, Ms. Okonkwo.

A: It's an accurate one.

topic: A pharmacist is deposed about a prescription that was filled with the wrong dosage
text:
Q: How long have you been a licensed pharmacist, Mr. Dahl?

A: Eleven years.

Q: And in those eleven years, how many prescriptions would you estimate you've filled?

A: I couldn't give you a meaningful number.

Q: Ballpark.

A: Hundreds of thousands, probably.

Q: Hundreds of thousands. And in all that time, have you ever made an error in dosage?

A: I'm human. There have been near-misses that were caught in verification.

Q: Near-misses. What about errors that weren't caught?

A: None that I'm aware of before this incident.

Q: Before this incident. So you're aware of one now?

A: I'm aware that an error occurred. I'm not certain it was my error.

Q: The prescription came from your pharmacy.

A: Yes.

Q: Filled on your shift.

A: Yes.

Q: With your verification stamp.

A: Yes, but—

Q: I'm sorry, I didn't hear the rest of that.

A: What I was going to say is that my verification stamp means I checked the prescription against the original order at that point in time. It doesn't account for what happened to that bottle in the forty-five minutes before the patient picked it up.

Q: What are you suggesting happened in those forty-five minutes?

A: I'm not suggesting anything. I'm stating what my stamp does and does not prove.

topic: A pharmacist is deposed about a prescription that was filled with the wrong dosage
text:
Q: Let's talk about the computer system at Greenway Pharmacy. When a prescription is entered, it generates a label, correct?

topic: A pharmacist is deposed about a prescription that was filled with the wrong dosage
text:
Q: Ms. Chen, do you recall a conversation with store manager David Wolfe on the afternoon of January 8th?

topic: A financial advisor is deposed about investment decisions made on a client's behalf
text:

topic: A financial advisor is deposed about investment decisions made on a client's behalf

topic: A building inspector is deposed about a structural assessment they signed off on
text:
Q: Mr. Hendricks, you conducted the structural assessment of 4200 Wexler Avenue on March 15th, 2022, correct?

A: That's what the report says, yes.

Q: I'm asking if you recall conducting it.

A: I conduct dozens of assessments every month. I'm not going to pretend I have some vivid memory of walking through that particular building on that particular day. The report is my record. That's how this works.

Q: Fair enough. The report indicates you spent approximately forty-five minutes on site. Does that sound accurate?

A: If that's what's logged, then that's what it was.

Q: Is forty-five minutes sufficient to assess a six-story commercial building?

A: It depends on what you're assessing. This was a routine five-year certification, not a forensic investigation.

Q: So you weren't looking for structural deficiencies?

A: I was looking for visible indicators of structural concern. That's the scope of a certification inspection. You understand there's a difference, I assume.

Q: I'm asking the questions, Mr. Hendricks.

A: Then maybe ask ones that reflect how inspections actually work.

Q: Did you access the basement mechanical room during your forty-five minutes?

A: Yes.

Q: Did you observe the support columns in that room?

A: I observed the visible portions of the columns, yes. The ones not behind equipment or cladding.

Q: And you noted no concerns?

A: I noted what's in the report. No visible indicators of concern. If you want me to have x-ray vision, I'm afraid you hired the wrong witness.

topic: A building inspector is deposed about a structural assessment they signed off on
text:
Q: Ms. Delgado, how long have you worked as a certified building inspector?

A: Eleven years this August.

Q: And in those eleven years, roughly how many structural assessments have you completed?

A: I couldn't give you an exact number. Several hundred, certainly.

Q: Would you say you're experienced in identifying load-bearing failures?

A: I'm experienced in identifying indicators of potential structural issues, yes.

Q: That's not what I asked.

A: With respect, counsel, it's a more accurate answer than the one you're fishing for. I'm not a structural engineer. I identify concerns that warrant engineering review.

Q: Let me rephrase. In your eleven years, have you ever identified a load-bearing failure?

A: I've identified conditions that were subsequently confirmed as load-bearing failures by engineers, yes.

Q: How many times?

A: Three. Possibly four.

Q: Out of several hundred inspections?

A: Correct.

Q: Does that strike you as a low number?

A: It strikes me as exactly the number it should be. Most buildings don't have load-bearing failures. That's why they're still standing.

Q: The Greenway Towers building at issue here—you signed off on it six weeks before the partial collapse. Correct?

A: I issued a certification based on my inspection, yes.

Q: And you identified no load-bearing concerns?

A: None were visible at the time of my inspection.

Q: None were visible. Is that your professional opinion, or is that your legal position?

A: I don't understand the distinction you're trying to manufacture.

topic: A building inspector is deposed about a structural assessment they signed off on
text:
Q: Let's go through this carefully, Mr. Okonkwo. You arrived at the Meridian Complex at what time?

A: Approximately 8:30 in the morning.

A: I said approximately because I don't have a timestamp in front of me. If you have one, I'm happy to confirm it.

Q: I'm simply asking.

A: And I'm simply answering. No.

Q: Mr. Okonkwo, is it possible you missed something during this inspection?

topic: A building inspector is deposed about a structural assessment they signed off on
text:
Q: Ms. Chen, I want to direct your attention to page four of your report. Do you have that in front of you?

A: I do.

Q: You wrote—and I'm quoting—"Minor hairline cracking observed in northwest stairwell, consistent with normal settling." Do you see that?

A: I see it.

Q: What made you conclude it was consistent with normal settling?

A: The pattern, the width, the location. Hairline cracks in stairwells are extremely common in buildings over twenty years old.

Q: But you're not a structural engineer.

A: We've established that.

Q: So how can you determine what's "normal settling" versus something more serious?

A: Training, experience, and professional judgment. The same way any licensed inspector makes any determination.

Q: Let me ask it differently. Did you measure the cracks?

A: I did a visual assessment.

Q: That's not what I asked. Did you measure them?

A: No.

Q: Did you photograph them?

A: The protocol doesn't require photographs for hairline cracks.

Q: I'm not asking about protocol. Did you photograph them?

A: No.

Q: Did you document their precise location?

A: I documented their general location. Northwest stairwell.

Q: General location. Not precise.

A: Counsel, do you understand how many hairline cracks exist in a typical twenty-year-old building? If I documented every one with GPS coordinates, inspections would take six months.

Q: So the answer is no.

A: The answer is I followed standard protocol for a routine inspection.

topic: A building inspector is deposed about a structural assessment they signed off on
text:
Q: Mr. Patterson, you've reviewed your inspection report in preparation for today?

A: I have.

Q: Good. Then you can explain to me why there's no mention of the east wing foundation in your assessment.

A: There's no mention because there was nothing to mention.

Q: You inspected the east wing foundation and found no issues?

A: I inspected the accessible portions and found no visible issues.

Q: The accessible portions. What portions were inaccessible?

A: Portions that were behind storage, equipment, standard obstructions you find in any basement.

Q: Did you ask to have the obstructions moved?

A: That's not part of a routine certification inspection.

Q: I'm asking if you asked.

A: No, I didn't ask. Because it's not part of a routine certification inspection.

Q: Mr. Patterson—

A: Counsel, I've answered the question twice now.

Q: Let me finish. Mr. Patterson, if you couldn't see the foundation, how could you certify it?

A: I certified that the visible portions of the structure met code requirements at the time of inspection. That's what the certification says. That's what every certification says.

Q: So the certification is limited.

A: Every inspection is limited. We're not demolishing walls to check what's behind them. If you'd like to propose a new inspection protocol, I suggest you take that up with the licensing board.

Q: I'm taking it up with you, since you signed this one.

A: And I've explained what my signature means. I can keep explaining it, if that helps.

topic: A witness is questioned about a workplace injury they observed but did not report
text:
Q: You were working in the warehouse on March 15th, correct?

topic: A witness is questioned about a workplace injury they observed but did not report
text:
Q: Let's talk about the safety meeting on February 3rd. You attended?

Q: That's a long time to serve a community. Could you walk me through what happened on the morning of March 14th when Mrs. Patterson's prescription came in?
