A: We dispensed 200 milligrams. I—I need to explain something, if I may. The way our system displays the numbers, the zero can sometimes appear to run together with the preceding digits. I'm not making excuses. I just want you to understand what happened.

Q: Please, go ahead.

A: Thank you. I reviewed the prescription, but I was also training a new technician that morning, and I didn't catch that the dosage had been entered incorrectly. That's on me. I should have caught it.

Q: You mentioned training someone. Can you tell me about that?

A: Her name was DeShawna. Bright young woman, very eager to learn. I was showing her how we verify the electronic prescriptions against what we pull from inventory. The irony isn't lost on me—I was teaching her to catch exactly this kind of error.

Q: What happened when you learned of the mistake?

A: I received a call from Mrs. Patterson's daughter on March 16th. She was upset, understandably so. I immediately pulled our records and confirmed what had happened. I called Mrs. Patterson myself that evening to apologize.

Q: You called her personally?

A: I did. I've known Eleanor—Mrs. Patterson—for eleven years. She was one of the first customers I served when I transferred to this location. I owed her that much, at least.

Q: What did you say to her?

A: I told her I was sorry. I told her we had failed her, that I had failed her. And I told her that whatever came of this, I wanted her to know that her wellbeing mattered to me. It still does.

topic: A pharmacist is deposed about a prescription that was filled with the wrong dosage
text:
Q: State your name for the record.

A: Michael Chen.

Q: Mr. Chen, you were working on January 8th, correct?

A: I was, yes.

Q: Tell me what you remember about filling the prescription for Daniel Okonkwo.

A: I remember it was a busy day. We were short-staffed because one of our technicians had called in sick, and there was a line at the counter most of the afternoon.

Q: I'm sure that was stressful.

A: It was. But I want to be clear—busy days happen. We have protocols for a reason. What happened to Mr. Okonkwo shouldn't have happened regardless of how many people were in line.

Q: What was the prescription for?

A: Metformin. The prescription called for 500 milligrams twice daily. Standard dosing for someone newly diagnosed with type 2 diabetes.

Q: And what was actually dispensed?

A: 1000 milligram tablets. So effectively, he was taking four times the intended dose.

Q: How did you discover the error?

A: Mr. Okonkwo's wife called three days later. She said he'd been experiencing severe nausea and diarrhea. I asked her to read me the label on the bottle, and I knew immediately what had happened.

Q: What did you do?

A: I told her to stop the medication right away and to take him to urgent care if his symptoms didn't improve within a few hours. Then I documented everything in our system and reported it to my district manager.

Q: Did you speak with Mr. Okonkwo directly?

A: I did, a few days later. He came into the pharmacy, and I stepped away from the counter so we could talk privately. He was gracious about it, honestly more gracious than I deserved. He said he understood that people make mistakes.

Q: How did that conversation end?

A: He shook my hand. Told me he'd still be filling his prescriptions with us because he trusted me to make sure it didn't happen again. I think about that conversation a lot.

topic: A pharmacist is deposed about a prescription that was filled with the wrong dosage
text:
Q: You've reviewed the dispensing records we marked as Exhibit 4?

A: I have.

Q: The prescription from Dr. Hartley was for hydrocodone, 5 milligrams, is that correct?

A: That's what the original prescription stated, yes.

Q: But the patient received 50 milligrams.

A: That is correct.

Q: Help me understand how that happens in a pharmacy with your experience level.

A: I wish I could give you a satisfying answer. The truth is, I looked at that prescription, I read it, and somehow my brain filled in a zero that the doctor never intended. It was a cognitive error, pure and simple.

Q: You're being very forthcoming about this.

A: There's no point in being anything else. A seventeen-year-old girl ended up in the emergency room because of my mistake. The least I can do is be honest about what happened and why.

Q: Tell me about Sophia. The patient.

A: She'd had her wisdom teeth removed. First time she'd ever needed prescription pain medication. Her mother dropped off the prescription that afternoon, and I filled it myself because we were slow and I thought—I thought it would be faster.

Q: What do you mean by that?

A: I mean I bypassed the double-check system we have in place. Normally, one of the technicians pulls the medication and I verify it. That day, I did both steps myself. I was trying to get Mrs. Reeves in and out quickly because she mentioned she needed to pick Sophia up from a friend's house.

Q: You were trying to help.

A: I was. And I nearly killed her daughter in the process. I've replayed that afternoon in my head hundreds of times. Mrs. Reeves thanked me for being so quick. I smiled and told her I hoped Sophia felt better soon.

Q: When did you learn what had happened?

A: The next morning. Sophia had taken two pills before bed as directed—well, as I had directed—and her mother found her unresponsive around 3 a.m. I didn't sleep for two days after I found out.

topic: A pharmacist is deposed about a prescription that was filled with the wrong dosage
text:
Q: I want to ask you about your training procedures. Is that all right?

A: Please, go ahead.

Q: When you started at MedFirst Pharmacy, what were you taught about verifying dosages?

A: We had a two-week onboarding process. The first week was all classroom—state regulations, company policies, that sort of thing. The second week was shadowing a senior pharmacist on the floor.

Q: And during that training, were you taught any specific technique for catching dosage errors?

A: We were taught the "three-point check." You verify the drug name, the dosage, and the patient name against the original prescription at three separate stages: when you pull the medication, when you count or pour it, and when you label the bottle.

Q: Did you perform the three-point check on Mr. Harriman's prescription?

A: I believed I did at the time. Looking back at it now, I honestly can't tell you whether I completed all three stages or whether I just thought I did because it had become so automatic.

Q: That's a fair answer. Tell me, how long had you been at MedFirst when this happened?

A: Eight months. I was still relatively new, though I'd been a licensed pharmacist for three years before that at a different chain.

Q: Did you feel adequately trained?

A: I thought I did. But the systems were different between the two pharmacies—the software, the layout, even the lighting over the dispensing counter. I've wondered since whether I'd fully adjusted.

Q: What do you mean about the lighting?

A: The old pharmacy had these bright fluorescent panels directly over the workspace. MedFirst uses softer overhead lighting, and in the late afternoon, there's glare from the front windows. It sounds like I'm making excuses again. I'm not trying to. You asked what I've thought about, and I've thought about everything.

Q: It sounds like you've done a lot of reflecting on this.

A: Mr. Harriman is seventy-four years old. He reminded me of my grandfather. When I found out what happened, I went home and sat in my car in the driveway for an hour before I could go inside and face my family.

topic: A pharmacist is deposed about a prescription that was filled with the wrong dosage
text:
Q: Dr. Patel, let me make sure I understand your role. You're the pharmacist-in-charge at the Waldon Avenue location?

A: That's correct.

Q: So any dispensing error at that location ultimately falls under your supervision?

A: It does. I take that responsibility seriously.

Q: I'm sure you do. I'm not here to suggest otherwise.

A: I appreciate that. I know how these things can go, and I want you to know I'm not going to try to shift blame onto anyone else. The buck stops with me.

Q: Tell me about the day in question. November 2nd.

A: It was a Wednesday. We typically see higher volume midweek because that's when a lot of the local physicians have their clinic days. The prescription for Ms. Thornton came in around 2 p.m.

Q: Warfarin, correct?

A: Yes. Blood thinner. The prescription was for 2 milligrams daily. What got dispensed was 12 milligrams.

Q: How does a 2 become a 12?

A: The prescriber's handwriting. The "1" in front of the 2 was actually a stray mark—we think it was from the pen skipping when Dr. Ansari started writing. But Keisha, my technician, read it as 12. And when it came to me for verification, I looked at the bottle, looked at the paper, and I saw what she saw.

Q: You're not blaming the technician?

A: Absolutely not. Final verification is my job. Keisha did exactly what she was trained to do—she flagged it as an unusual dosage because 12 milligrams is high. She brought it to me specifically because she wasn't sure.

Q: And what did you tell her?

A: I told her it was probably a loading dose. Some patients start on higher amounts before tapering down. I was wrong. I should have called the prescriber's office to verify.

Q: Why didn't you?

A: Because I was confident. Because I'd been doing this for sixteen years and I thought I knew better than a technician with eighteen months of experience. That confidence nearly cost Ms. Thornton her life, and it taught Keisha exactly the wrong lesson about trusting her instincts.

Q: Have you spoken with Keisha about this since?

A: Many times. I told her she was right to question it, and I was wrong to dismiss her concern. She's going to be an excellent pharmacist someday, and I won't let my mistake make her doubt herself.

topic: A witness is asked about a car accident they saw from their front porch
text:
Q: Please state your name for the record.

A: Margaret Holloway.

Q: Ms. Holloway, you've indicated you witnessed a car accident on the afternoon of September 14th, is that correct?

A: That's what I'm here for, isn't it?

Q: I need you to answer yes or no for the record.

A: Yes.

Q: Where were you when you observed this accident?

A: On my front porch. Like I already told the other lawyer. And the police. And the insurance people.

Q: I understand you've discussed this before, but I need your testimony today. What were you doing on your porch?

A: Sitting.

Q: Just sitting?

A: I was drinking coffee and reading the newspaper. Is that specific enough?

Q: What direction were you facing?

A: Toward the street. Obviously. That's how I saw the accident.

Q: And approximately what time did the accident occur?

A: Around two-thirty. Maybe two-forty. I wasn't staring at my watch.

Q: Did you see the vehicles before the collision?

A: I saw a blue sedan come through the intersection. Then I saw the pickup run the stop sign and hit it. That's the whole story. I don't know what else you're expecting me to add.

Q: I'm just trying to understand what you observed, Ms. Holloway.

A: And I'm telling you.

---

topic: A witness is asked about a car accident they saw from their front porch
text:
Q: Good morning. Could you describe your vantage point from your porch on the day of the accident?

A: Sure. My porch is elevated, maybe four feet up from the sidewalk. I've got a clear view of the intersection at Maple and Third. No trees blocking it or anything.

Q: How far would you estimate your porch is from that intersection?

A: I'd say about seventy, eighty feet? I'm not a surveyor, but it's close.

Q: You're not a surveyor. So you're guessing.

A: I said it's an estimate. You asked me to estimate.

Q: Let's try to be more precise. Could it have been a hundred feet?

A: It could have been. It could have been sixty. I don't carry a tape measure onto my porch.

Q: Mr. Devine, I'm simply trying to establish distances. Could it have been a hundred and fifty feet?

A: No. That's too far. I know my own property.

Q: But you just said you're not a surveyor.

A: I'm not. But I'm also not blind. The intersection is close to my house.

Q: Were you wearing your glasses that day?

A: I don't need glasses for distance. Only reading.

Q: So you weren't wearing them.

A: I just told you I don't need them for distance. Do you want me to explain how prescriptions work?

Q: That won't be necessary. Let's move on. What did you see first?

A: The white SUV approaching from the north, going too fast for that street.

---

topic: A witness is asked about a car accident they saw from their front porch
text:
Q: You've stated you were on your porch. Were you seated or standing?

A: Seated, in my rocking chair.

Q: For how long before the accident?

A: Maybe twenty minutes. I'd just gotten home from the pharmacy.

Q: What drew your attention to the roadway?

A: I heard the engine first. Someone was really gunning it. Then I looked up and saw the gray car speeding down Orchard.

Q: When you say speeding, what do you mean?

A: Going fast. Faster than you should on a residential street.

Q: Can you estimate the speed?

A: Forty, forty-five maybe.

Q: The speed limit on Orchard is twenty-five, correct?

A: I believe so.

Q: You believe so, or you know so?

A: I know so. I've lived there eleven years.

Q: I'm going to show you what's been marked as Exhibit 4. Do you recognize this photograph?

A: That's the intersection.

Q: Is this an accurate representation of your view from the porch?

A: More or less. This was taken from the sidewalk though. My porch is higher.

Q: But you'd agree the view is substantially similar?

A: I said more or less. That's my answer. I'm not going to say substantially similar if I don't know what you mean by that.

Q: Fair enough. Did you see the other vehicle before impact?

A: The minivan? Yes. It was already in the intersection when the gray car came through.

---

topic: A witness is asked about a car accident they saw from their front porch
text:
Q: Let me take you back to the moment of impact. Describe what you heard.

A: A loud crash. Metal on metal. Then the sound of glass breaking.

Q: Then what?

A: Then I stood up. I was going to call 911.

Q: Did you call 911?

A: Someone else already had. I could hear sirens within a couple minutes.

Q: So you didn't call.

A: No. I just said someone else did.

Q: What did you do after you stood up?

A: I walked to the edge of my porch to see better.

Q: And what did you see?

A: The two cars. The pickup was spun around, facing the wrong way. The sedan was up on the curb, the front end all smashed in.

Q: Did you see the drivers?

A: I saw a man get out of the pickup.

Q: Can you describe him?

A: Heavyset. Wearing a red shirt or jacket. He was walking around, seemed okay.

Q: Did you see the driver of the sedan?

A: Not at first. I couldn't see into the car from where I was.

Q: Did you at any point go down to the scene?

A: No.

Q: Why not?

A: Because there were already people there. Neighbors. And I'm seventy-three years old with a bad hip. I'm not running anywhere.

Q: I wasn't suggesting you should have run, Mr. Patterson. I'm simply asking what you did.

A: And I'm telling you. I stayed on my porch and watched until the ambulance came.

---

topic: A witness is asked about a car accident they saw from their front porch
text:
Q: Ms. Yuen, how long have you lived at 4512 Birchwood?

A: Six years this past April.

Q: And you're familiar with the traffic patterns at the intersection near your home?

A: Very familiar. Cars blow through that stop sign all the time. I've called the city about it.

Q: So this is something you've noticed before.

A: Multiple times. It's a known problem.

Q: On October 3rd, the day of the accident, were you actively watching traffic?

A: Not actively. I was on my porch doing a crossword puzzle. But when you hear a crash, you look up.

Q: So you didn't actually see the collision.

A: I saw the immediate aftermath. I looked up right when it happened.

Q: Right when it happened, or right after?

A: Does it matter? It was within a second.

Q: It matters for the record, Ms. Yuen. Did you see the actual impact or not?

A: I saw the cars collide. Whether that was the first millisecond or the third millisecond, I couldn't tell you.

Q: Let's be very clear. Did you see the vehicles before they made contact with each other?

A: I saw the black truck entering the intersection. I saw the other car already there. Then they hit.

Q: Which vehicle had the right of way?

A: The silver car. The truck had the stop sign.

Q: Did you see the truck stop at the sign?

A: No.

Q: Because you weren't watching, or because it didn't stop?

A: Both. I wasn't watching until I heard the noise, and by then he was already in the intersection. He clearly didn't stop.

Q: You're concluding he didn't stop based on where he was when you looked up.

A: I'm concluding he didn't stop because he hit another car in the middle of the intersection. That's what happens when you don't stop.

topic: An HR director is questioned about a harassment complaint that was filed and closed
text:
Q: Ms. Thornton, I'm going to direct your attention to the complaint filed by Rebecca Yates on March 14th. You were the one who closed that investigation, correct?

A: I was.

Q: And how long did that investigation remain open before you closed it?

A: I'd have to check the exact dates.

Q: Let me help you. The complaint was filed March 14th and closed March 19th. Five days. Does that refresh your recollection?

A: If that's what the document says.

Q: Is five days a typical duration for a harassment investigation at Meridian Corp?

A: It depends on the complexity of the allegations.

Q: I didn't ask what it depends on. I asked if five days is typical.

A: No.

Q: No, it's not typical. In fact, your own policy manual recommends a minimum of fifteen business days for investigation. Isn't that right?

A: The manual provides guidelines. They're not mandatory timelines.

Q: Guidelines. So when you closed Ms. Yates' complaint in five days, you were exercising discretion?

A: I was doing my job.

Q: Your job. Let's talk about what your job involved here. How many witnesses did you interview?

A: I interviewed the relevant parties.

Q: How many, Ms. Thornton?

A: Two.

Q: Two witnesses for a complaint involving conduct that allegedly occurred in front of an entire sales team. Did I get that right?

A: You got the number right. Whether you understand the context is another matter entirely.

Q: Then help me understand the context.

A: The complainant's account was inconsistent. The accused denied the allegations. There was nothing further to investigate.

---

topic: An HR director is questioned about a harassment complaint that was filed and closed
text:
Q: Good morning, Mr. Reeves. You've been HR Director at Blanchard Financial for how long?

A: Eleven years. Eleven years of doing this work, counselor, so I have some idea what I'm doing.

Q: I'm sure you do. I'm just trying to understand the process you followed with the Harrison complaint.

A: Then ask your questions.

Q: The complaint was filed by Daniel Chen on September 3rd. You received it that same day?

A: I receive every complaint that comes through the portal. Yes.

Q: And according to your notes, you spoke with Mr. Harrison the following morning. September 4th.

A: That's correct.

Q: Before you spoke with Mr. Chen.

A: I spoke with both parties within the same 48-hour window. There's no requirement about sequencing.

Q: I didn't say there was a requirement, Mr. Reeves. I'm just establishing the timeline. You spoke with the accused before you spoke with the complainant.

A: And I'm telling you that's a meaningless distinction. I treat both parties fairly.

Q: Let's look at what Mr. Harrison told you in that conversation. He said, and I'm quoting from your notes, "Chen has always had it out for me." Did he explain what he meant by that?

A: He provided context about their working relationship. Which is exactly what I would expect from an accused party.

Q: Context. Did you document that context anywhere?

A: It's in my notes.

Q: I've reviewed your notes, Mr. Reeves. I see the quote. I don't see any follow-up. Should I look again, or would you like to point me to the page?

A: I'm not going to sit here and have you tell me how to do my job.

---

topic: An HR director is questioned about a harassment complaint that was filed and closed
text:
Q: Dr. Okonkwo, the Lawson complaint—you concluded that the allegations were, quote, "unsubstantiated." Is that accurate?

A: That is the language in the closing memorandum, yes.

Q: What does "unsubstantiated" mean in this context?

A: It means that after completing the investigation, I did not find sufficient evidence to support a policy violation.

Q: And what evidence did you consider?

A: I reviewed the written complaint, interviewed the complainant and the respondent, and examined relevant communications.

Q: Did you interview any other employees who might have witnessed the alleged conduct?

A: I made a determination that additional interviews were not necessary given the scope of what was alleged.

Q: Who told you to close the investigation early?

A: Excuse me?

Q: It's a simple question, Dr. Okonkwo. Who instructed you to close this investigation?

A: No one instructs me to do anything. I am the director of this function.

Q: So it was entirely your decision to wrap this up in—let me check—six business days?

A: Counsel, I have been in this field for twenty-three years. I have handled investigations involving executives, involving litigation holds, involving matters that would make this complaint look like a parking dispute. I do not need instruction, and I certainly do not need it implied that I would take instruction to bury a complaint.

Q: I didn't use the word "bury."

A: You didn't have to.

Q: Let me rephrase. Did anyone express to you a preference for how this matter should be resolved?

A: No.

---

topic: An HR director is questioned about a harassment complaint that was filed and closed
text:
Q: Walk me through what happened when you received the Patterson complaint.

A: I received it through the standard intake process, logged it, and began the investigation.

Q: When you say "began the investigation," what was your first step?

A: I reviewed the complaint for completeness and then scheduled an intake interview with Ms. Patterson.

Q: How long after receiving the complaint did that interview occur?

A: I believe it was three days later.

Q: Three days. Was there a reason for the delay?

A: I had other matters on my desk. I handled it as promptly as circumstances allowed.

Q: Ms. Patterson's complaint alleged that her supervisor made comments about her body on multiple occasions in front of coworkers. You would agree that's a serious allegation?

A: All complaints are taken seriously.

Q: That's not what I asked.

A: Then perhaps you could ask what you actually mean, counselor, instead of trying to get me to perform for the record.

Q: I'm asking whether you recognized this as a serious allegation that warranted urgent attention.

A: I recognized it as a complaint that required investigation, which is what I did.

Q: Let's look at the outcome. You issued a written warning to the supervisor. No termination, no suspension, no reassignment of Ms. Patterson away from him.

A: The written warning was consistent with our progressive discipline policy.

Q: Consistent with policy. Ms. Patterson resigned two weeks later. Were you aware of that?

A: I was informed, yes.

Q: Did you do anything in response?

A: Her resignation was a separate matter. The investigation was closed.

Q: I see. The investigation was closed. So from your perspective, the system worked?

A: I followed the process. That's what I can speak to.

---

topic: An HR director is questioned about a harassment complaint that was filed and closed
text:
Q: Ms. Franklin, I want to ask you about the timeline of the Odom investigation.

A: Go ahead.

Q: You closed the investigation on November 15th. The complaint had been filed on October 28th.

A: If those are the dates in the file, I'll accept that.

Q: During that eighteen-day period, how many hours would you estimate you spent on this matter?

A: I don't track my time by complaint.

Q: Ballpark, Ms. Franklin.

A: I couldn't give you an accurate estimate. I'm not going to guess.

Q: Would it surprise you to learn that your calendar shows only two meetings related to this matter?

A: Much of investigation work doesn't happen in formal meetings. There are document reviews, phone calls, email exchanges.

Q: Let's talk about those email exchanges. I have a message from you to Gerald Simmons, the General Counsel, dated November 12th. Three days before you closed the investigation. Do you recall that email?

A: I communicate with the General Counsel regularly. I don't recall every email.

Q: Let me read it to you. "Gerald—following up on our conversation. I think we're aligned on the path forward. Will finalize this week."

A: I see the text.

Q: What path forward were you aligned on?

A: I don't recall the specific conversation that email references.

Q: You don't recall a conversation with the General Counsel about an open harassment investigation?

A: I said I don't recall the specifics. That's not the same as saying it didn't happen.

Q: What did Mr. Simmons tell you to do, Ms. Franklin?

A: Mr. Simmons doesn't tell me what to do. We consult. That's the nature of working with legal.

Q: And in this consultation, did he express any view about how this complaint should be resolved?

A: He may have provided input. I made the final determination.

Q: What input did he provide?

A: I've told you I don't recall the specifics.

Q: You closed the investigation three days after this email. You found no policy violation. And you don't recall what the General Counsel's "input" was.

A: Asked and answered, counselor. I'm not going to keep repeating myself because you don't like my response.

topic: A contractor is questioned about delays that caused a construction project to fail
text:
Q: Mr. Brennan, let's talk about the foundation pour that was scheduled for March 15th. That didn't happen on March 15th, correct?

A: No, it did not.

Q: When did it happen?

A: April 3rd.

Q: So nearly three weeks late.

A: That's—yes, that's the math.

Q: And during those three weeks, what was happening on site?

A: I'm sorry, what do you mean what was happening?

Q: Were there workers on site? Equipment? Activity?

A: Some days, yes. Some days, no. It depends on what you're asking about specifically.

Q: I'm asking generally. Was work being performed?

A: Work on what? Because there are multiple—I mean, we had framing crews doing prefab off-site, we had electrical doing conduit layouts in the staging area—

Q: On the foundation. Was work being performed on the foundation during those three weeks?

A: No. I thought that was—no. Not on the foundation itself.

Q: Why not?

A: We were waiting on the revised soil report. I've explained this in my written responses. The geotechnical engineer flagged the compaction tests. We couldn't pour until that was resolved.

Q: Who was responsible for obtaining that revised report?

A: The owner's geotechnical consultant. That's not—that was never under my scope.

Q: So you're saying the delay was entirely the owner's responsibility?

A: I'm saying I couldn't pour concrete onto soil that hadn't been certified. Whether that's "responsibility" in the way you mean it, I don't—I'm not sure what you want me to say.

topic: A contractor is questioned about delays that caused a construction project to fail
text:
Q: You mentioned earlier that there were issues with the HVAC subcontractor. Can you describe those issues?

A: They were behind schedule.

Q: By how much?

A: It varied. At different points, different amounts.

Q: Give me a range.

A: Two weeks to maybe six weeks, depending on which milestone you're measuring against.

Q: That's a significant variance. Two weeks to six weeks.

A: Right, well—

Q: Which is it?

A: I don't—it's not a single number. That's what I'm trying to tell you. If you're asking when they finished the rooftop unit installation versus when they completed the ductwork on the third floor, those are different timelines with different delays.

Q: Let's focus on the rooftop units. How late were those?

A: I'd need to look at the schedule. I don't have it memorized.

Q: Approximately.

A: I don't want to guess and have you hold me to a wrong number later.

Q: This is your project, Mr. Danes. You were the general contractor.

A: I'm aware of my role, counsel.

Q: Then surely you recall roughly how delayed a major mechanical installation was.

A: Roughly? Maybe four weeks. But I want the record to reflect I'm estimating.

Q: Noted. And why were they four weeks behind?

A: You'd have to ask them. Equipment shipping, I think. Supply chain. This was during—you know when this was.

Q: I'm asking what you knew at the time.

A: What I knew at the time was that the units weren't on site when they were supposed to be. That's what I knew.

topic: A contractor is questioned about delays that caused a construction project to fail
text:
Q: Ms. Tran, I want to direct your attention to the email you sent on June 7th, 2022. Do you have that in front of you?

A: I have a lot of emails in front of me. Which tab?

Q: Exhibit 14.

A: Okay. Yes.

Q: You wrote, and I'm quoting here, "We cannot continue at this pace without additional crew." Do you see that?

A: I do.

Q: What pace were you referring to?

A: The pace that was being demanded by the owner's construction manager.

Q: And what pace was that?

A: They wanted us to complete the exterior envelope in three weeks. We had originally scheduled five.

Q: Why the change?

A: I don't know. That came from their side.

A: David Kohl. The owner's CM.

A: He communicated that was the new expectation, yes.

Q: And you're saying that was impossible?

A: I'm saying it required more crew than I had allocated. Which is what the email says. I'm not sure what else you're looking for here.

Q: Did you get the additional crew?

A: Eventually. Not in time to meet their three-week target.

Q: So you missed the deadline.

A: We missed their revised deadline. We would have made the original deadline. There's a distinction.

topic: A contractor is questioned about delays that caused a construction project to fail
text:
Q: Let me make sure I understand the sequence here. The steel delivery was delayed. Correct?

A: Correct.

Q: That pushed back the structural framing.

A: Yes.

Q: Which in turn delayed the—help me out here—the exterior sheathing?

A: Well, no. Not directly.

Q: No?

A: No, the sheathing wasn't waiting on steel. The sheathing was waiting on the vapor barrier inspection, which was waiting on the framing, which was—okay, yes, I see what you're getting at. But it's not a straight line.

Q: I'm trying to trace the critical path here, Mr. Okonkwo.

A: Right, and I'm trying to explain that the critical path shifted multiple times during this project. What was critical in April wasn't necessarily critical in June.

Q: Because of the steel delay?

A: Because of several factors. The steel was one. The permit revision was another. The owner's hold on the storefront glazing was a third.

Q: Wait—there was a hold on the glazing?

A: Yes.

Q: When was that?

A: Early May? I believe?

Q: Why am I just hearing about this now?

A: I don't—I'm not sure how to answer that. It's in the project documentation.

Q: We've been through the project documentation.

A: Then I don't know what to tell you.

Q: Let's back up. Who issued the hold on the glazing?

A: The owner. Through their architect.

Q: For what reason?

A: Design change. They wanted a different mullion profile. I don't know the aesthetic rationale. I just know we couldn't order the glass until they finalized it.

topic: A contractor is questioned about delays that caused a construction project to fail
text:
Q: Did you attend the progress meeting on September 12th?

A: I don't recall specifically. Probably. I attended most of them.

Q: The minutes reflect you were present.

A: Then I was present.

Q: At that meeting, there was a discussion about the project being eight weeks behind schedule. Do you remember that discussion?

A: I remember discussions about schedule delays. Whether that specific number was used at that specific meeting, I couldn't say for certain.

Q: The minutes attribute a statement to you. "We need to have a realistic conversation about the timeline."

A: That sounds like something I would say, yes.

Q: What did you mean by "realistic"?

A: I meant that the original timeline was no longer achievable.

Q: Why not?

A: I've listed—there were multiple factors. You want me to go through them again?

Q: I want to understand what you meant at that moment.

A: At that moment, I meant that between the weather delays in July, the inspection failures on the fire stopping, and the owner's indecision on the interior finishes, we had lost time that couldn't be recovered without acceleration costs.

Q: And who was supposed to bear those acceleration costs?

A: That was in dispute.

Q: What was your position?

A: That the owner-caused delays entitled us to a time extension, not an obligation to accelerate at our own expense.

Q: And the owner's position?

A: You'd have to ask them. I'm not going to characterize their position.

Q: Fair enough. Did you ever get that time extension?

A: No. The project was terminated before it was resolved.

topic: A neighbor is questioned about noise complaints and a confrontation they witnessed
text:
Q: Mr. Delano, you live at 4517 Birchwood Lane, is that correct?

A: That's what I said in the paperwork, yes.

Q: And how long have you resided at that address?

A: Fourteen years. Fourteen years and three months, if you need it exact.

Q: The property at 4519 Birchwood Lane, that's immediately to your east?

A: I know where my neighbors live.

Q: On the night of September 14th, did you hear anything unusual coming from that property?

A: Define unusual.

Q: Loud noises. Yelling. Anything out of the ordinary.

A: There was yelling. There's been yelling from that house for two years. September 14th wasn't special.

Q: But you did file a noise complaint that specific night, didn't you?

A: I filed twelve noise complaints over eighteen months. You want to talk about all of them, or just the one that fits whatever story you're building here?

Q: I'm asking about September 14th, Mr. Delano.

A: Then yes. I called the non-emergency line at 11:47 p.m. I have the phone record if your client's attorney didn't bother to subpoena it.

Q: What specifically did you hear that prompted the call?

A: A man screaming. A woman screaming back. Something breaking. Glass, I think. Maybe ceramic. Hard to tell through walls.

Q: Could you make out any words?

A: I wasn't taking notes. I was trying to sleep. Some of us work in the morning.

---

topic: A neighbor is questioned about noise complaints and a confrontation they witnessed
text:
Q: You witnessed a confrontation on October 3rd, correct?

A: I saw two people arguing in a driveway, yes.

Q: And what time was this?

A: Around seven. Maybe seven-fifteen.

Q: Morning or evening?

A: Evening. Obviously evening. Who argues in their driveway at seven in the morning?

Q: I need you to be specific for the record, Ms. Thurman. What did you observe?

A: The man—Mr. Garrett, I assume—was standing by the garage. The woman was closer to the street. They were both talking loud.

Q: Talking loud or yelling?

A: What's the legal distinction? They weren't whispering.

Q: Were they shouting?

A: Yes. Fine. Shouting.

Q: Could you hear what was said?

A: Bits and pieces.

Q: Such as?

A: She said something about him never listening. He said she was crazy. Original stuff.

Q: Did you see any physical contact between them?

A: He grabbed her arm at one point.

Q: How would you characterize that contact?

A: I'm not a domestic violence expert. He grabbed her arm. She pulled away. That's what I saw.

Q: Did she appear to be in pain?

A: I don't read minds. She pulled away. She walked inside. I went back to watering my lawn.

---

topic: A neighbor is questioned about noise complaints and a confrontation they witnessed
text:
Q: Let's go back to the noise complaints. You made how many total?

A: I already answered this.

Q: For the record, please.

A: Four. I made four complaints.

A: June through November of last year.

A: Loud music. Parties. The usual.

Q: The usual. So this was a regular occurrence?

A: I just said I filed four complaints in six months. What do you think?

Q: I'm asking what you observed, Mr. Peralta, not what I think.

A: Music loud enough to rattle my windows. Cars parked on my lawn. People shouting at two in the morning. That answer your question?

Q: Did you ever speak directly with the residents about these issues?

A: Once.

Q: When was that?

A: August, I think. Early August.

Q: And what was said?

A: I asked them to keep it down. Politely. The man laughed and shut the door.

Q: Did you say anything else?

A: What was I supposed to do, force my way in? He shut the door. Conversation over.

Q: Is that when you began filing formal complaints?

A: No, I waited another month hoping they'd develop basic human decency. They didn't.

---

topic: A neighbor is questioned about noise complaints and a confrontation they witnessed
text:

topic: A neighbor is questioned about noise complaints and a confrontation they witnessed
text:
Q: Let me ask you again, Mr. Bashir. You're certain you saw Mr. Novak push his wife?

topic: An HR director is questioned about a harassment complaint that was filed and closed
text:
Q: Ms. Hartley, I'm going to direct your attention to a complaint filed on March 14th of last year. Do you recall that complaint?

A: I recall a number of complaints filed around that time. I'd need to see the specific document to confirm which one you're referring to.

Q: This would be the complaint filed by Denise Okonkwo against her supervisor, Mark Trellman. Does that refresh your recollection?

A: Yes. I remember that complaint.

Q: And you were the HR director responsible for handling that complaint, correct?

A: I was the HR director, yes. Whether I was solely responsible—I mean, there's a process. I oversaw the process.

Q: Who else was involved in that process?

A: Our HR coordinator, Janet Vance, conducted the initial intake. I reviewed her notes. Legal was consulted at various points. It's not—it wasn't just me making decisions in a vacuum, if that's what you're suggesting.

Q: I'm not suggesting anything, Ms. Hartley. I'm asking questions.

A: Fine. Then yes, I was involved.

Q: The complaint was closed within eleven days. Is that typical?

A: It depends on the nature of the complaint. Some matters resolve quickly. Others take longer.

Q: What factors made this one resolve quickly?

A: I'd have to review the file to speak to specifics. I don't want to misstate anything.

Q: You don't recall what factors led to closing a harassment complaint in eleven days?

A: I recall the matter was investigated and a determination was made. The specifics—dates, interviews, the exact sequence—I would need documentation to speak accurately.

Q: Ms. Hartley, did you interview Ms. Okonkwo as part of this investigation?

A: Janet Vance conducted the intake interview. I reviewed the summary.

Q: Did you personally speak with Ms. Okonkwo at any point?

A: I... I believe I did. Briefly. Toward the end of the process.

Q: What did you tell her?

A: I don't recall the exact words. I would have communicated the outcome.

---

topic: An HR director is questioned about a harassment complaint that was filed and closed
text:
Q: Mr. Buchanan, how many harassment complaints did your department receive in 2022?

Q: Ballpark.

A: I'd have to check the records.

A: It was a joint decision. HR and legal.

A: I did.

Q: And before you signed, did anyone express disagreement with closing it?

A: I'm not sure what you mean by disagreement.

topic: An HR director is questioned about a harassment complaint that was filed and closed
text:
Q: Let's talk about the Keating complaint. When did you first learn of it?

A: I remember we followed protocol. The specifics—the exact measures—I don't have committed to memory. That's why we keep records.

---

topic: An HR director is questioned about a harassment complaint that was filed and closed
text:
Q: Ms. Pratt, I want to be very clear about the timeline here. The complaint was filed on September 3rd. Correct?

A: If that's what the document says, then yes.

Q: And it was closed on September 19th.

A: Okay.

Q: Sixteen days.

A: If you say so.

topic: An HR director is questioned about a harassment complaint that was filed and closed
text:
Q: The complaint form—you have a standard form employees fill out?

A: Yes.

Q: And Jennifer Walsh filled one out?

A: She did.

Q: Describe the form for me.

A: It's—it's a simple form. Name, date, description of the incident or incidents, names of anyone involved, that sort of thing.

Q: How much space is there for the description?

A: It's a text box. There's no specific limit.

Q: Did Ms. Walsh's description fill the box?

A: I... I think so. It was detailed.

Q: Detailed. What details did she include?

A: She described multiple incidents over several months. Comments made to her. Conduct she found inappropriate.

Q: Comments of what nature?

A: I'd rather not characterize without the document in front of me.

Q: Were they sexual in nature?

A: Some of them, yes.

Q: And despite these detailed allegations, the complaint was closed as unsubstantiated?

A: The investigation did not find sufficient evidence to—

Q: I'm asking about your conclusion, Ms. Chen. Multiple incidents. Detailed descriptions. Sexual comments. And you closed it.

A: We followed our process.

Q: Did you believe her?

A: That's not—it's not about belief. It's about what can be substantiated.

Q: That's not what I asked.

A: I assessed the evidence according to our policy. That's what I did.

A: I took her complaint seriously. I investigated it. I reached a conclusion based on the available evidence.

topic: A witness is questioned about a conversation they overheard in a company hallway
text:
Q: Ms. Fernandez, I'd like to direct your attention to the afternoon of March 14th. Were you present in the third-floor hallway near the executive offices?

A: Yes.

Q: And what were you doing there?

A: Yes.

A: Mr. Aldridge and someone from HR. I think it was Mrs. Cho.

topic: A witness is questioned about a conversation they overheard in a company hallway
text:
Q: Mr. Okonkwo, you've indicated you were in the hallway outside Lab 4 on the evening in question. Is that correct?

A: That's correct, yes.

Q: And you've stated you heard Dr. Reeves speaking with another individual. Were you able to identify that other person?

A: It was Marcus. Marcus Delaine. He worked under Dr. Reeves.

Q: I'm sure you have. Did Mr. Delaine say anything else?

A: No.

Q: Thank you, Mr. Okonkwo. I have nothing further on this line.

topic: A witness is questioned about a conversation they overheard in a company hallway
text:
Q: Let's talk about what you heard in the hallway, Mr. Tran.

A: Alright.

Q: You were walking past the HR director's office when you heard voices?

A: That's right. The door was open partway. Maybe six inches, enough that I could hear clearly.

Q: And you recognized the voices?

A: One was Mr. Steadman. The HR director. The other was Janet Mosley, my supervisor.

Q: Your direct supervisor.

A: Yes.

Q: What were they discussing?

A: Janet was asking about her position. Whether it was being eliminated.

Q: And what did Mr. Steadman say?

A: He told her the decision had already been made. That there was nothing he could do. He said he'd tried, and I believe him, because his voice— he sounded like he meant it.

Q: I'm not asking you to characterize his sincerity, Mr. Tran.

A: You asked me what he said. I'm telling you how he said it.

Q: Fair enough. What else was said?

A: Janet asked about her team. About what would happen to us. And he said we'd be reassigned, that we'd be taken care of, but she just— she laughed. Not a real laugh.

Q: What do you mean, not a real laugh?

A: The kind of laugh when nothing is funny.

Q: Did you hear anything else?

A: She asked him for a moment. Said she needed a minute before she went back out. I left then. I didn't want her to come out and see me there.

Q: Did Ms. Mosley ever discuss this conversation with you directly?

A: No. She never mentioned it. And I never brought it up. What would I have said?

topic: A witness is questioned about a conversation they overheard in a company hallway
text:
Q: I want to be very precise about this, Ms. Huang. You were in the east hallway at approximately 4:15 p.m.?

A: I believe so, yes. I wasn't checking the time, but the shift change was about to happen, so it would have been around then.

Q: And you heard Mr. Castellan and Ms. Voorhees speaking?

A: Correct.

Q: Could you make out what they were saying?

A: Parts of it. They were speaking quietly. I think they were trying not to be heard.

Q: But you heard them nonetheless.

A: I wasn't eavesdropping, counselor. I was walking to the break room. They were in my path.

Q: I'm not suggesting anything, Ms. Huang. I'm simply trying to establish what you heard. Can you tell us what you were able to make out?

A: Ms. Voorhees was talking about her daughter. About the medical bills.

Q: Her daughter's medical bills.

A: That's right. She said she didn't know what she was going to do. With the insurance changes, she didn't know how she was going to— she didn't finish the sentence.

Q: Did Mr. Castellan respond?

A: He told her he wished he had better news. He said the company's hands were tied.

Q: Is that the phrase he used? "Hands were tied"?

A: Yes. I remember because Ms. Voorhees repeated it back to him. She said, "Hands are tied," like she was testing whether the words meant anything.

Q: And then?

A: Then nothing. Then it was quiet, and I kept walking. I didn't look at them when I passed.

Q: You didn't look at them.

A: No. I thought she deserved that much.

topic: A witness is questioned about a conversation they overheard in a company hallway
text:
Q: Mr. Baylor, you've testified you were near Conference Room C when you overheard the conversation in question.

A: I was in the alcove by the vending machines. The one across from the conference room.

Q: And the door to Conference Room C was open?

A: Partially. Maybe a third of the way.

Q: Who did you observe inside?

A: I didn't observe anyone. I wasn't looking in. But I recognized the voices.

Q: Whose voices?

A: David Chen, our CFO. And Richard Muñoz, the controller.

Q: What were they discussing?

A: The pension fund.

Q: Can you be more specific?

A: Mr. Muñoz was asking what they were supposed to tell people. Mr. Chen said they weren't supposed to tell anyone anything yet. That the announcement would come from legal.

Q: Did Mr. Muñoz say anything in response?

A: He said these were people's retirements. That some of them had been contributing for twenty, thirty years.

Q: What did Mr. Chen say?

A: He didn't say anything at first. Then he said, "I know, Rich."

A: Then he said something about how it wasn't supposed to happen this way. That no one thought it would actually come to this. His voice was— it was quiet. Not like he usually sounds in meetings.

Q: Not like he usually sounds.

A: No. He sounded like someone had taken something from him too.

Q: Did you hear anything else?

A: No. One of them closed the door after that.

topic: A former employee is deposed about discriminatory remarks made by a supervisor
text:
Q: Ms. Patterson, you were employed at Ridgeline Distribution from March 2019 until your resignation in August 2022, correct?

A: Yes.

Q: And during that time, your direct supervisor was Marcus Denton?

A: He was, yes.

Q: I'd like to ask you about a meeting that took place on June 14th, 2022. Do you recall a team meeting on that date?

A: I remember it.

Q: Can you describe what happened during that meeting?

A: ...We were going over quarterly numbers. There were seven of us in the room. Marcus was running the meeting.

Q: And at some point, did Mr. Denton make a comment about you?

A: He made a comment, yes.

Q: What did he say?

A: He said... he said that maybe the company should stop hiring people who needed to "run off to their villages" during harvest season. He was looking at me when he said it.

Q: How did you interpret that comment?

A: I'm sorry, I just... I need a moment. I'm sorry.

Q: Take your time.

A: He knew my family is from Guatemala. He knew I'd requested leave to visit my grandmother before she passed. He knew that. Everyone in the room knew what he meant.

Q: What happened after he made that statement?

A: Nothing. People laughed. A few of them, anyway. And then Marcus moved on to the next slide like it was nothing. Like he hadn't just...

Q: Did anyone say anything in your defense?

A: No.

Q: Did you report this incident to Human Resources?

A: I did. I reported it the next day. I filled out the form. I did everything I was supposed to do.

Q: And what was the result of that report?

A: Nothing. They said they'd look into it. No one ever spoke to me about it again. Not once.

---

topic: A former employee is deposed about discriminatory remarks made by a supervisor
text:
Q: Mr. Chen, how long had you worked in the accounting department before the incident you've described in your declaration?

A: Eleven years. Eleven years and four months, if you want to be exact about it.

Q: And in that time, you'd received positive performance reviews?

A: Every single year. I have the documentation. I kept copies.

Q: I'm not disputing that, Mr. Chen. I'm just establishing your tenure.

A: Fine. Eleven years.

Q: You've stated that on or about September 3rd, 2021, your supervisor, Diane Kowalski, made certain remarks during a one-on-one meeting. Is that correct?

A: That's correct.

Q: What were you meeting about?

A: She called me in to discuss my request for a religious accommodation. I needed to leave early on certain Fridays.

Q: For Shabbat observance?

A: Yes. Which I had explained. Which I had put in writing.

Q: What did Ms. Kowalski say?

A: She asked me if I "really needed to do all that." She said she didn't understand why I couldn't just be "normal about it" like everyone else.

Q: What did you understand her to mean by "normal about it"?

A: Counsel, I'd been at that company for over a decade. I'd worked weekends. I'd missed my daughter's piano recitals. I was asking for two hours on Fridays, and she wanted to know why I couldn't be normal. What do you think she meant?

Q: I'm asking what you understood—

A: I understood that my faith was a problem for her. I understood that clearly.

Q: Did you respond to her at the time?

A: I didn't know what to say. I'd never... in eleven years, no one had ever... I just sat there.

Q: What happened with your accommodation request?

A: Denied. I got the email the following Monday.

---

topic: A former employee is deposed about discriminatory remarks made by a supervisor
text:
Q: I want to be careful with you, Ms. Okonkwo. I understand this is difficult.

A: Thank you. I'm okay to continue.

Q: You mentioned in your written statement that there was an incident involving a nickname. Can you tell me about that?

A: Yes. David Marsh, my supervisor, he started calling me "the African Queen." It started maybe... March of 2020, I think.

Q: How often did he use this term?

A: In the beginning, maybe once a week. Then more. By the end, it was almost every day.

Q: Were other employees present when he used this term?

A: Sometimes, yes. Sometimes it was just the two of us.

Q: How did other employees react?

A: Most of them didn't react at all. Sandra from HR was there once. She just... she looked at her phone.

Q: Did you ever ask Mr. Marsh to stop?

A: I asked him three times. The first time, he said he meant it as a compliment. The second time, he said I was being too sensitive. The third time...

Q: What happened the third time?

A: He laughed and said if I didn't like it, there were plenty of other kingdoms I could go rule. Then he walked away.

Q: What did you do after that?

A: I went to the bathroom. I stayed there for a while. Then I went back to my desk and finished my shift.

Q: You continued working there for another eight months after that third conversation, correct?

A: I needed the job. I had a son in daycare. I had rent. I didn't have the luxury of...

Q: I'm not suggesting—

A: I know. I know you're not. I'm sorry. I just wanted you to understand why I stayed.

topic: A former employee is deposed about discriminatory remarks made by a supervisor

topic: A former employee is deposed about discriminatory remarks made by a supervisor
text:
Q: Mr. Reeves, I need to ask you about an incident that occurred during the December 2021 holiday party. I know you've given statements about this before.

A: I have.

Q: The woman who came forward with the initial complaint, Yolanda Simms, she was a friend of yours?

A: She was my friend, yes. We'd worked together for six years.

Q: And she's no longer with the company?

A: She's no longer with us at all. She passed away in March.

Q: I'm... I'm sorry. I wasn't aware of that.

A: It's in the file. Somewhere. I assume it's in the file.

Q: Mr. Reeves, if you need a moment—

A: I don't need a moment. I need someone to hear what happened to her. That's why I'm here.

Q: Can you tell me what you witnessed at the holiday party?

A: Raymond Schultz, our regional manager, he walked up to Yolanda in front of at least a dozen people and told her she was "pretty articulate for someone from her background." Those were his exact words.

Q: How did Ms. Simms respond?

A: She didn't respond. She just stood there holding her glass of wine. She'd been with the company for nine years. She had a master's degree. And he said that to her like it was some kind of gift he was giving her.

Q: Did anyone else respond to the comment?

A: People heard it. I know they heard it. But everyone just kept talking. Like nothing had happened.

Q: Did you say anything?

A: I should have. I think about that all the time. I should have said something right then. But I didn't. I found her later in the parking lot. She was sitting in her car with the engine off.

Q: What did she say to you?

A: She said she didn't understand why it still surprised her. After everything. She said she thought she'd gotten used to it by now.

Q: Did she file a complaint?

A: She filed a complaint. I supported her complaint. And then they let her go four months later for "restructuring." And now she's gone, and I'm the one sitting here, and Raymond Schultz is still regional manager.

topic: A warehouse supervisor is deposed about safety protocols that were allegedly ignored

topic: A tenant is questioned about property damage they reported to their landlord
text:
Q: Mr. Hernandez, let me direct your attention to the water damage you reported on March 3rd. You contacted your landlord that morning, is that correct?

A: No. Absolutely not. I didn't touch anything. I didn't want anyone to say I made it worse or—no, I didn't touch it.

Q: The photographs you mentioned—

A: Timestamped. They're timestamped. I can tell you the exact times if you need them.

Q: Did you notice any discoloration on the ceiling before March 3rd?

There might have been a slight yellowing, but I honestly can't say whether that was before or if I'm remembering it from that day. I want to be precise about this.

topic: A tenant is questioned about property damage they reported to their landlord
text:
Q: Mr. Okonkwo, I want to make sure I understand the timeline correctly. Bear with me here—these dates matter and I need to get them right.

topic: A tenant is questioned about property damage they reported to their landlord

topic: A tenant is questioned about property damage they reported to their landlord
text:
Q: Let's discuss the incident with the heating system, Ms. Reyes.

A: Alright.

Q: You reported that the radiator in the living room was malfunctioning.

A: It wasn't just malfunctioning. It was making sounds. Loud sounds. Banging.
