topic: A witness is asked about a car accident they saw from their front porch
text:
Q: Could you please state your name for the record?

A: Eleanor Vance. That's V-A-N-C-E.

Q: Ms. Vance, where were you on the morning of September 14th at approximately 8:15 a.m.?

A: On my front porch. I sit there every morning with my coffee. Have for thirty-two years. I know that intersection better than anyone on this street.

Q: And what did you observe that morning?

A: I saw the whole thing. Start to finish. The silver Honda was traveling northbound on Maple, and the blue pickup ran the stop sign coming off of Birch. I saw the driver of the pickup—he didn't even tap his brakes. Not once.

Q: How can you be certain the pickup didn't brake?

A: Because I was watching. I've seen hundreds of cars come through that intersection. I know what it looks like when someone slows down. That truck came through at full speed. Forty miles an hour, at least.

Q: You estimated forty miles an hour. Do you have any training in speed estimation?

A: I raised three sons who all drove too fast. I've been watching cars on that road since 1992. You learn to tell the difference between twenty-five and forty.

Q: Did you see the actual moment of impact?

A: Clear as day. The pickup struck the Honda on the driver's side door. I was already reaching for my phone before the glass finished falling.

Q: You called 911?

A: I was the first call. The dispatcher told me so when the officer arrived. I gave them the plate numbers for both vehicles before anyone else even came outside.

Q: Both plate numbers?

A: I have excellent distance vision. Always have. The pickup was Colorado plates, started with A-B-7. The Honda was local.

Q: Is there anything else you observed that morning that you haven't mentioned?

A: The driver of the pickup got out and looked at his phone first. Before checking on the other driver. I noted the time: 8:17. I keep a notebook by my chair for exactly this sort of thing.

---

topic: A witness is asked about a car accident they saw from their front porch
text:
Q: Mr. Denning, I want to take you through your observations carefully and precisely. Can you do that for me?

A: I'll try my best.

Q: Let's start with the basics. What drew your attention to the roadway that afternoon?

A: I heard tires squealing. I looked up from my book.

Q: And what did you see?

A: A red car and a white SUV. They collided in the intersection.

Q: Now, Mr. Denning, when you say you "looked up," how quickly did that occur after you heard the sound?

A: Immediately. Within a second.

Q: Within a second. So you would have seen the vehicles in the moment just before impact?

A: I saw them hit each other. I can't say what happened before that.

Q: That's a fair distinction. Now, the positioning of the vehicles at the moment of impact—can you describe that for me precisely?

A: The SUV was partway into the intersection. The red car hit it on the passenger side.

Q: Partway. Can you quantify that? Was the SUV one-quarter through, halfway through?

A: Maybe a third. The front third was past the crosswalk line.

Q: Excellent. That's exactly the kind of detail we need. Now, after the collision, what did you observe?

A: Both cars spun. The red car ended up on the sidewalk. The SUV stayed in the road.

Q: And you watched all of this unfold from your porch?

A: Yes.

Q: Mr. Denning, you've been remarkably precise in your recollections. The crosswalk line, the rotation of the vehicles. Did you take any notes after the incident?

A: I did not.

Q: So this is all from memory, three months later?

A: I remember what I saw. It was a significant event.

Q: It certainly was. And your memory has served us very well today.

---

topic: A witness is asked about a car accident they saw from their front porch
text:
Q: You were on your porch when this happened?

A: That's right.

Q: Doing what, exactly?

A: Watering my plants.

Q: So your attention was on your plants, not on the road?

A: I can do two things at once.

Q: I'm not suggesting you can't. I'm asking what you were focused on at the moment of the collision.

A: I was focused enough to see a black sedan blow through a red light and T-bone a minivan with two kids in the back.

Q: How do you know there were children in the minivan?

A: Because after the crash, I ran out to help. I was the one who kept those kids calm until the paramedics arrived. I held the little girl's hand for fifteen minutes.

Q: That must have been difficult.

A: It was necessary. Someone had to do it.

Q: Let's go back to the moment before impact. You said the sedan ran a red light. How do you know the light was red?

A: Because I could see it from my porch. I can see that signal clearly. I've watched it cycle thousands of times.

Q: And you're certain it was red for the sedan's direction of travel?

A: I am certain. It had been red for at least three seconds. I remember thinking the minivan was safe to go. Then that sedan came out of nowhere.

Q: Out of nowhere?

A: Fast. Too fast to stop. The driver wasn't paying attention. I could see him looking down, probably at his phone.

Q: You could see inside the vehicle from your porch?

A: I could see the angle of his head. That's enough.

Q: Is it?

A: It was enough for me to give a statement to the police, and it's enough for this.

---

topic: A witness is asked about a car accident they saw from their front porch
text:
Q: Ms. Thornton, I'm going to ask you some very specific questions about timing. I need you to be as accurate as possible.

A: Okay.

Q: When you first noticed the vehicles involved in the collision, where were they?

A: Um, the truck was... I think it was approaching the intersection? From the east.

Q: You think, or you know?

A: I'm trying to remember. It was a few months ago.

Q: Take your time. We want to get this right.

A: The truck was coming from the east. The motorcycle was already in the intersection, I think, making a left turn.

Q: Making a left turn. Did the motorcycle have a green arrow, do you know?

A: I... I couldn't see the signal from where I was sitting.

Q: That's fine. That's an honest answer. Now, the truck—was it speeding, in your estimation?

A: It seemed fast. But I'm not... I don't know how fast exactly.

Q: Faster than normal traffic on that road?

A: I think so. Yes.

Q: Good. That's helpful. Now, I want to be very precise here, because your testimony could be important. Did you see the truck make any attempt to stop before hitting the motorcycle?

A: I saw brake lights. I think. It happened so fast.

Q: You saw brake lights. That's a significant detail, Ms. Thornton. You should feel good about remembering that.

A: I'm just trying to tell you what I saw.

Q: And you're doing an excellent job. One more question: after the collision, did you see the truck driver exit the vehicle?

A: Yes. He got out and ran to the motorcycle. He was screaming for someone to call 911.

Q: Did you call?

A: Someone else already had.

---

topic: A witness is asked about a car accident they saw from their front porch
text:
Q: State your name, please.

A: Marcus Webb.

Q: Mr. Webb, you've indicated you witnessed a collision on October 3rd. Where were you at the time?

A: Front porch. I was having a cigarette.

Q: What did you see?

A: Gray coupe rear-ended a station wagon at the stop sign.

Q: The stop sign at Elm and Fourth?

A: That's the one.

Q: Did the station wagon come to a complete stop?

A: It did.

Q: How long was it stopped before the impact?

A: Couple seconds. Long enough that it was obvious the guy behind wasn't paying attention.

Q: The driver of the gray coupe—could you see what he was doing before the collision?

A: Nope.

Q: But you're certain he wasn't paying attention?

A: The station wagon was dead stopped. Brake lights on. If he was watching the road, he would've stopped too.

Q: That's an inference, Mr. Webb.

A: That's common sense.

Q: Fair enough. What happened after the collision?

A: Driver of the station wagon got out. Older woman. She was shaken up. The guy in the coupe stayed in his car for a while.

Q: How long?

A: Minute or two. Then he got out and started taking pictures of the damage to his own car. Not hers. His.

Q: Did you interact with either driver?

A: I walked over. Asked the woman if she was okay. Gave her a bottle of water from my cooler.

Q: That was kind of you.

A: It was the right thing to do. She was seventy years old and some idiot just slammed into her.

Q: Mr. Webb, I'm going to ask you to keep your characterizations neutral.

A: You asked what I saw. I'm telling you what I saw.

topic: A pharmacist is deposed about a prescription that was filled with the wrong dosage
text:
Q: Mr. Hendricks, you filled the prescription for Mrs. Patterson on the afternoon of March 14th, correct?

A: I filled a prescription that day, yes. Whether it was "the afternoon" specifically, I'd have to see the timestamp.

Q: The timestamp shows 2:47 PM. Does that refresh your recollection?

A: Then it was 2:47 PM. You have the document.

Q: And the prescription called for 10 milligrams of lisinopril, didn't it?

A: The prescription that Dr. Okonkwo wrote called for 10 milligrams, yes.

Q: But you dispensed 100 milligrams.

A: That's what's being alleged.

Q: That's not an allegation, Mr. Hendricks. That's what the pill bottle recovered from Mrs. Patterson's home contained. 100-milligram tablets. Are you disputing that?

A: I'm disputing that I personally made that error. Your question assumes facts that haven't been established to my satisfaction.

Q: To your satisfaction. I see. Let me ask you this: were you the pharmacist of record for that prescription, yes or no?

A: My name is on the label. That doesn't mean I physically counted and bottled every pill.

Q: So someone else made the error?

A: I didn't say that. I said the process involves multiple people.

Q: Who else touched that prescription?

A: I'd need to review the workflow logs.

Q: You've had four months to review the workflow logs, Mr. Hendricks. Who else touched the prescription?

A: I don't have those documents in front of me, and I'm not going to guess to make your job easier.

Q: Let's take a short break.

A: Fine by me.

topic: A pharmacist is deposed about a prescription that was filled with the wrong dosage
text:
Q: Good morning. Could you state your full name for the record?

A: Linda Marie Ashworth.

Q: And you're a licensed pharmacist in this state?

A: For twenty-three years, yes. Never a single disciplinary action until this.

Q: I didn't ask about disciplinary actions.

A: I thought you'd want the context, since you're here trying to paint me as incompetent.

Q: Ms. Ashworth, I'm here to ask questions. Can you do that? Just answer questions?

A: I can answer questions that are asked in good faith.

Q: On June 8th, you filled a prescription for Thomas Dwyer. Do you recall that?

A: I filled approximately ninety prescriptions that day. I don't have independent memory of each one.

Q: Do you recall being informed that Mr. Dwyer was hospitalized two days later?

A: I was informed, yes.

Q: And do you recall what you said when your supervisor told you about the dosage discrepancy?

A: I don't recall my exact words, no.

Q: Let me read from your supervisor's incident report. Quote: "Ms. Ashworth stated, 'That's impossible, I double-checked it myself.'" Does that refresh your recollection?

A: It refreshes my recollection that my supervisor has a habit of paraphrasing instead of quoting.

Q: So you deny saying that?

A: I deny that those were my exact words, yes.

Q: What were your exact words?

A: I don't recall. As I said.

topic: A pharmacist is deposed about a prescription that was filled with the wrong dosage
text:
Q: Can you walk me through your standard verification procedure?

A: Sure. I'd be happy to. The technician fills the order, then it comes to me at the verification station. I check the NDC number against the prescription, confirm the pill count, verify the patient information, and approve or reject.

Q: Every time?

A: Every time.

Q: Without exception?

A: I just said every time. Is there an echo in here?

Q: I'm trying to establish whether you followed that procedure on October 3rd.

A: And I'm telling you I follow it every time, which would include October 3rd.

Q: Then how do you explain the 50-milligram discrepancy?

A: I can't explain it. That's what I keep telling you people. I've been over it in my head a hundred times.

Q: You people?

A: You. Her lawyers. The board investigator. Everyone's asking me the same questions like I'm going to suddenly remember making a mistake I don't believe I made.

Q: You don't believe you made it.

A: That's what I said.

Q: But you acknowledge the patient received the wrong dosage.

A: Something went wrong. I'm not disputing that. I'm disputing that it was my error.

Q: Whose error was it?

A: I don't know. Maybe the wholesaler sent mislabeled stock. Maybe the technician pulled from the wrong bin. I don't know.

Q: Have you seen any evidence of mislabeled stock?

A: No. But I haven't been allowed back in the pharmacy to look, have I?

topic: A pharmacist is deposed about a prescription that was filled with the wrong dosage
text:
Q: You testified earlier that you were working alone that evening.

A: I did.

Q: No technician on duty?

A: Budget cuts. We'd been short-staffed for three weeks. I flagged it to management twice.

Q: In writing?

A: In writing and verbally. I have copies of both emails if you'd like them entered into evidence, assuming that's still how this works.

Q: I'll take that as a yes. So you were responsible for both filling and verifying the Kowalski prescription?

A: Technically, yes.

Q: Not technically. Actually.

A: Fine. Actually. I was actually responsible. Is that better?

Q: I'm not looking for better, Mr. Price. I'm looking for accurate.

A: And I'm giving you accurate. I was the only pharmacist on duty. I filled it, I verified it, and I dispensed it. What I am telling you is that I verified it correctly.

Q: The patient received double the prescribed dose.

A: So I'm told.

Q: You don't accept that?

A: I accept that's what she's claiming. I accept that's what her lawyers are claiming. What I don't accept is that I handed her the wrong pills, because I know what I checked.

Q: How can you be certain, three months later, about one prescription out of—how many did you say you fill per shift?

A: I remember because I remember. Some things stick.

Q: Why would this one stick?

A: Because she was rude to me, frankly. Stood there tapping her credit card on the counter the whole time I was trying to concentrate.

topic: A pharmacist is deposed about a prescription that was filled with the wrong dosage
text:
Q: Ms. Trujillo, I want to be very clear about the timeline. Very clear. You received the prescription electronically at 9:14 AM?

A: According to the system log, yes.

Q: And it was marked as filled at 9:31 AM?

A: Yes.

Q: Seventeen minutes.

A: That's the math, yes.

Q: Is seventeen minutes a typical turnaround time for a new prescription?

A: It depends on the prescription and how busy we are.

Q: That's not what I asked. I asked if seventeen minutes is typical.

A: For a straightforward fill on a slow morning, yes.

Q: Was November 12th a slow morning?

A: I don't recall the volume.

Q: Would the pharmacy records show the volume?

A: They might.

Q: You don't know?

A: I said they might. I'm not the IT department.

Q: Let me show you Exhibit 14. This is the transaction log for November 12th. How many prescriptions were filled between 9:00 and 10:00 AM?

A: I count... fourteen.

Q: Fourteen prescriptions in one hour. Does that seem slow to you?

A: It's not our busiest.

Q: But Mr. Reeves's prescription was filled in seventeen minutes. While you were also handling thirteen other prescriptions. Does that seem like adequate time to verify a dosage?

A: I verified it correctly.

Q: That wasn't my question.

A: Then maybe you should ask clearer questions.

topic: A witness is questioned about a fire they discovered in a neighboring unit
text:
Q: Ms. Delgado, you've stated you were home on the evening of March 14th. What time did you first become aware something was wrong?

A: Around nine-thirty. Maybe a little after.

Q: And what drew your attention to the situation?

A: The smell. Smoke. It came through the vents.

Q: What did you do when you noticed the smell?

A: I went to my door. Opened it. Looked into the hallway.

Q: What did you observe in the hallway?

A: Smoke. Coming from under 4B. Mr. Reiner's unit.

Q: Did you attempt to alert Mr. Reiner?

A: I knocked. He didn't answer. I knocked again. Nothing.

Q: How many times would you say you knocked?

A: I don't know. Three times. Four. It doesn't really matter now, does it.

Q: I'm just trying to establish the sequence of events, Ms. Delgado.

A: I know what you're trying to do. I knocked. He didn't answer. I called 911. That's what happened.

Q: Did you attempt to enter the unit yourself?

A: No.

Q: Why not?

A: Because the door was hot. And I'm not a firefighter. And none of this is going to change what happened to that man's apartment.

Q: I understand. Did you see anyone else in the hallway during this time?

A: No. Everyone else had more sense than to stand around breathing smoke.

topic: A witness is questioned about a fire they discovered in a neighboring unit
text:
Q: Mr. Okonkwo, let's go through this one more time. You were returning from the parking garage when you noticed the fire?

A: Yes. I've said this already.

Q: I know. Bear with me. What floor were you on when you first saw flames?

A: The third floor. I was walking past unit 312.

Q: And the flames were visible from the hallway?

A: Through the window. The window in the door. There's a small window.

Q: Approximately how large were the flames at that point?

A: I don't know how to answer that.

Q: Your best estimate.

A: They were... they filled the window. The part I could see. I'm not a fire investigator.

Q: I'm not asking you to be one. Just what you observed.

A: What I observed is that there was fire. Significant fire. I observed that I should not be standing there observing it.

Q: Fair enough. Did you have your phone with you?

A: Yes.

Q: Did you call 911?

A: Someone already had. I could hear the sirens by the time I got to the stairwell.

Q: So you proceeded to the stairwell. Did you alert anyone on your way?

A: I knocked on two doors. 310 and 308. No one answered. I kept moving.

Q: You didn't wait to see if anyone would answer?

A: Counselor, there was fire. I knocked. I moved. That's what a person does.

topic: A witness is questioned about a fire they discovered in a neighboring unit
text:
Q: Let's talk about what you heard that night, Mrs. Yamamoto.

A: All right.

Q: You mentioned earlier there was a sound that first caught your attention. Can you describe it?

A: A popping. Like something electrical.

Q: Popping. How many times did you hear this sound?

A: Several. I wasn't counting.

Q: More than five times?

A: Possibly. I really couldn't say with certainty.

Q: That's fine. We're just looking for your best recollection.

A: My best recollection is that it was several times. I'm sorry I can't give you the exact number you're looking for.

Q: No need to apologize. What did you do after hearing the popping sounds?

A: I muted my television. Listened. Then I heard what sounded like a small explosion.

Q: An explosion.

A: A whoosh. A loud whoosh. I don't know the technical term.

Q: And then?

A: Then I smelled it. The smoke.

Q: At that point, what action did you take?

A: I put on my shoes. I got my purse. I left.

Q: Did you investigate the source of the sounds before leaving?

A: No. I'm seventy-four years old. I don't investigate fires. I leave buildings when they're on fire.

Q: Of course. I'm simply trying to understand the timeline.

A: The timeline is that I heard sounds, smelled smoke, and left. I don't know what more you need from me.

topic: A witness is questioned about a fire they discovered in a neighboring unit
text:
Q: Mr. Brennan, I want to ask you about the condition of the hallway when you exited your apartment.

A: Okay.

Q: Was there visible smoke at that time?

A: Yes. Gray smoke. Not thick yet, but visible.

Q: Could you see the door to unit 7C from where you were standing?

A: Yes.

Q: Was there anything notable about that door?

A: There was smoke coming from the edges. The frame. Around the hinges.

Q: Around the hinges specifically?

A: And the bottom. The gap at the bottom.

Q: I see. Did you approach the door?

A: No.

Q: Why not?

A: Because there was a fire behind it.

Q: Did you consider trying to warn the occupant?

A: Mrs. Patterson wasn't home. Her car wasn't in the lot. I'd noticed earlier.

Q: So you made a judgment that the unit was unoccupied.

A: I made an observation. Her car wasn't there. It's a blue Camry. It's always in the same spot. It wasn't there.

Q: Let's move on. Did you pull the fire alarm?

A: I did.

Q: Where was the alarm located?

A: By the stairwell door. Maybe fifteen feet from my apartment.

Q: And after pulling the alarm, what did you do?

A: I left. I took the stairs. I went outside. I waited for the fire department. This has all been covered.

Q: I understand. We're just being thorough.

A: I know. We're being thorough.

topic: A witness is questioned about a fire they discovered in a neighboring unit
text:
Q: Ms. Chen, I'd like to understand the sequence of events from your perspective. You were in bed when you first became aware of the fire?

A: I was lying down. Not sleeping yet. Reading.

Q: What alerted you to the situation?

A: The alarm. The building alarm.

Q: Not smoke or sounds from the neighboring unit?

A: No. Just the alarm.

Q: And what did you do when the alarm sounded?

A: I got up. I put on my robe. I looked out into the hall.

Q: What did you see?

A: Other residents. Moving toward the stairs. And smoke, down at the far end, near the corner unit.

Q: Did you see flames at that point?

A: No. Just smoke.

Q: Did you speak with any of the other residents in the hallway?

A: Mr. Brennan. From 7A. He said there was a fire in 7C.

Q: Did he say anything else?

A: He said we should move. So we moved.

Q: Did you take any belongings with you?

A: My phone. I grabbed my phone.

Q: Nothing else?

A: What else should I have taken? Photo albums? Jewelry? There was a fire.

Q: I'm just asking what you took.

A: And I've told you. My phone. That's all. I'm sure there's some point you're building toward, but I don't know what it is, and I don't think I can help you get there any faster.

Q: We're almost finished, Ms. Chen.

A: I know. We're almost finished.

topic: An HR director is questioned about a harassment complaint that was filed and closed
text:
Q: Ms. Hartwell, you were the HR director at Crestview Industries in 2022, correct?

A: I was, yes.

Q: And you were responsible for overseeing the investigation into the complaint filed by Jennifer Morales?

A: I was responsible for a lot of things. That was one of them.

Q: The complaint alleged sexual harassment by a regional sales manager, Thomas Kendrick?

A: That's what it alleged.

Q: Can you walk me through what steps you took when the complaint first came across your desk?

A: I did what I always did. I logged it into our tracking system, I notified legal, I scheduled an intake interview with Ms. Morales. The standard protocol.

Q: And did you conduct that intake interview yourself?

A: I did.

Q: What did Ms. Morales tell you during that interview?

A: She told me what she'd put in the written complaint. Unwelcome comments. Some emails she found inappropriate. An incident at the holiday party.

Q: Did you find her credible?

A: I found her consistent.

Q: That's not what I asked.

A: Counselor, I've been doing this for nineteen years. I've learned that credibility determinations made in the first thirty minutes tend to be wrong. I documented what she said. I moved to the next step.

Q: The next step being?

A: Interviewing Mr. Kendrick. Interviewing witnesses. Reviewing whatever documentation existed.

Q: And at the end of all that, the complaint was closed with no finding of harassment. Is that accurate?

A: That's what the file says.

Q: Is that what you determined?

A: That's what the file says, and I signed off on the file.

topic: An HR director is questioned about a harassment complaint that was filed and closed
text:
Q: Mr. Patterson, how many harassment complaints did your department handle in 2021?

A: I'd have to check the exact number. Somewhere between forty and fifty.

Q: And the complaint filed by David Chen—that was one of those forty to fifty?

A: It was.

Q: Did anything about the Chen complaint stand out to you at the time?

A: They all stand out in their own way.

Q: I'm asking specifically about this one.

A: I understand what you're asking.

Q: Then please answer it.

A: Mr. Chen alleged that his supervisor made repeated comments about his accent. He provided dates, approximate times, names of people who might have overheard. It was detailed. Is that what you're looking for?

Q: I'm looking for whatever you actually remember.

A: Then that's what I actually remember. A detailed complaint. A complainant who seemed genuinely upset.

Q: Who conducted the investigation?

A: Sarah Brandt from my team.

Q: Not you personally?

A: I had forty to fifty complaints that year, counselor. I supervised. I didn't personally investigate every single one.

Q: Did you review Ms. Brandt's findings before the complaint was closed?

A: I signed off on it, so yes, presumably I reviewed it.

Q: Presumably?

A: I reviewed it. I don't have an independent recollection of sitting down and reading it, but I wouldn't have signed something I didn't review. That was my practice.

Q: And the finding was unsubstantiated?

A: That was the finding.

topic: An HR director is questioned about a harassment complaint that was filed and closed
text:
Q: Let's talk about the timeline, Ms. Okonkwo. The complaint was filed on March 3rd?

A: According to the documents, yes.

Q: And it was closed on March 17th?

A: If that's what the closing memo says.

Q: Two weeks seems fast for a harassment investigation, doesn't it?

A: Does it?

Q: I'm asking you. You're the HR professional.

A: Two weeks can be appropriate depending on the complexity of the matter and the availability of witnesses.

Q: Were witnesses available in this case?

A: I'd have to review my notes.

Q: You don't remember?

A: I remember this complaint, counselor. I remember Danielle Shaw sitting in my office. I remember her crying. I remember her asking me if anything was actually going to happen. What I don't remember, three years later, is the precise sequence of witness interviews.

Q: What did you tell her? When she asked if anything was going to happen?

A: I told her we would conduct a thorough investigation.

Q: Did you?

A: We conducted an investigation.

Q: That's not the same thing.

A: I suppose that's what we're here to determine.

Q: The accused in this case was Robert Frost, the CFO?

A: That's correct.

Q: Did his position affect how the investigation was conducted?

A: It shouldn't have.

Q: I didn't ask if it should have.

A: Then I don't have anything else to add to what I've already said.

topic: An HR director is questioned about a harassment complaint that was filed and closed
text:
Q: Walk me through the documentation process when a complaint is closed.

A: What specifically do you want to know?

Q: Everything. Start to finish.

A: The investigator prepares a summary memo. The memo includes a statement of the allegations, the evidence gathered, witness interviews, and a recommended finding. I review the memo. If I concur, I sign it. The complainant is notified of the outcome. The file is closed.

Q: And in the case of the Martinez complaint, you followed this process?

A: I did.

Q: The summary memo in our exhibit—Exhibit 14—that's three pages long.

A: If you say so.

Q: Does three pages seem thorough to you?

A: Thoroughness isn't measured in page count.

Q: How is it measured?

A: By whether the relevant questions were asked and answered.

Q: Were they? In this case?

A: I believed so at the time.

Q: What do you believe now?

A: I believe I'm sitting in a conference room answering questions about a decision I made four years ago, and I believe I followed the process that was in place.

Q: The process that was in place. Did you design that process?

A: I inherited most of it.

Q: But you could have changed it?

A: I could have done a lot of things.

Q: Did you ever raise concerns about the adequacy of your investigation protocols?

A: I raised a lot of concerns over the years, counselor. Some of them were addressed. Some of them weren't.

topic: An HR director is questioned about a harassment complaint that was filed and closed
text:
Q: When you closed the Franklin complaint, did you notify anyone in senior leadership?

A: I don't recall specifically. It would have depended on who the accused was.

Q: The accused was Mark Ellison, vice president of operations.

A: Then yes, I would have notified someone.

Q: Who?

A: Probably the CEO or the general counsel. Possibly both.

Q: Before or after you made your determination?

A: After.

Q: So they didn't influence your decision?

A: That's a very careful way of phrasing that question.

Q: I'm a careful person.

A: They didn't tell me what to decide, if that's what you're asking.

Q: Is there something else I should be asking?

A: I wouldn't presume to tell you how to do your job.

Q: Ms. Yates, did you feel pressure regarding the outcome of this investigation?

A: I felt the same pressure I always felt.

Q: Which was?

A: To get it right. To be fair. To protect the company. To not ruin someone's career over something unsubstantiated. To not dismiss someone's genuine experience of being harassed. Those pressures don't always point in the same direction.

Q: And when they conflict?

A: You do your best. You make a call. You write it down. You move on to the next one.

Q: And you moved on from the Franklin complaint?

A: I did.

Q: Any regrets?

A: Is that relevant to these proceedings?

Q: I'll withdraw the question. Let's move on.

topic: A neighbor is questioned about noise complaints and a confrontation they witnessed
text:
Q: Mr. Patterson, you live at 4417 Ridgewood Lane, correct?

A: I've lived there for twenty-three years. Longer than anyone else on that street, including the Delgados.

Q: I didn't ask about the Delgados yet, sir. I'm simply confirming your address.

A: And I'm giving you context. You want to understand what happened, don't you?

Q: Let's stick to my questions. On the night of September 14th, did you hear any loud noises coming from the Delgado residence?

A: I heard what I've been hearing for the past eighteen months. Music. Shouting. Car doors slamming at two in the morning. You want me to pick just one noise?

Q: I'm asking about September 14th specifically.

A: Fine. Yes. Music. Bass so loud my windows were vibrating. Is that specific enough?

Q: What time did this occur?

A: Started around eleven. Maybe ten-forty-five. I wasn't exactly sitting there with a stopwatch, but I know it was after the news ended.

Q: And did you witness a confrontation that evening?

A: I witnessed Mr. Delgado screaming at my wife. Is that what you're dancing around?

Q: I'm asking what you saw, Mr. Patterson.

A: I saw a grown man six inches from my wife's face, yelling about how we need to "mind our business." That's what I saw. You want more details, or are you going to twist those too?

Q: No one is twisting anything. What happened after that exchange?

A: I came outside. I told him to back away from her. He didn't like that much.

Q: What did Mr. Delgado do?

A: He shoved me. Right here. You can probably still see the bruise if the lighting's right, but I'm sure that's not in your little folder.

topic: A neighbor is questioned about noise complaints and a confrontation they witnessed
text:
Q: Ms. Chen, you were home on the evening in question?

A: I was.

Q: And you could hear the noise from your property?

A: Yes.

Q: Can you describe it?

A: It was a party. Music, people talking loudly, that sort of thing.

Q: "That sort of thing." Could you be more specific about the volume?

A: It was loud enough that I noticed it. I don't have a decibel meter.

Q: I'm not asking for a decibel reading. I'm asking whether it was loud enough to interfere with your normal evening activities.

A: I already said I noticed it. What more do you want from me?

Q: I want you to answer the question. Did it interfere with your activities?

A: I turned up my television. Satisfied?

Q: You also called the non-emergency police line that night. Why?

A: Because it was after midnight and I had work in the morning. People do that.

Q: Had you ever called about the Hendersons before?

A: Once. Maybe twice.

Q: Our records show seven calls over four months. Does that refresh your recollection?

A: Then your records know more than I do. I didn't keep a log.

Q: But you did step outside when the police arrived, didn't you?

A: I wanted to see if they were actually going to do something for once.

Q: And what did you observe?

A: I observed the officers talking to Mr. Henderson, and I observed Mr. Henderson pointing at my house like I was the problem. That's what I observed.

topic: A neighbor is questioned about noise complaints and a confrontation they witnessed
text:
Q: You were outside when the argument began?

A: I was checking my mail.

Q: At nine-thirty at night?

A: I work late. I check my mail when I get home. Is that a crime now?

Q: No one suggested it was. I'm establishing the timeline.

A: Then establish it. I was checking my mail.

Q: And from that position, what did you see?

A: The Martins were on their lawn. Mrs. Okafor came over from across the street. They were arguing about the party the Martins had the weekend before.

Q: Who was arguing?

A: Mrs. Martin and Mrs. Okafor. Mr. Martin was standing back, looking like he wanted to be anywhere else.

Q: What were they saying?

A: I wasn't close enough to hear every word.

Q: But you were close enough to see the confrontation clearly?

A: I could see them. I couldn't hear everything. Those are two different things.

Q: You told the police you heard Mrs. Okafor make a threat. Did you hear that or didn't you?

A: I heard her say something about "dealing with this another way." I don't know if that's a threat. You people seem to think it is.

Q: "You people"?

A: Lawyers. You twist everything into whatever fits your case. I'm telling you what I heard. What you do with it is your business.

Q: I'm simply trying to understand what happened.

A: Sure you are.

topic: A neighbor is questioned about noise complaints and a confrontation they witnessed
text:
Q: How long have the Burkes lived next door to you?

A: About three years.

Q: And in those three years, have you ever had any disputes with them?

A: No.

Q: No disagreements at all?

A: I said no.

Q: So when you made the noise complaint on July 8th, that was the first issue you'd ever had with the Burke family?

A: I didn't say that. You asked about disputes. I didn't consider it a dispute.

Q: What would you call it?

A: I'd call it me asking them to turn down their music.

Q: You called the police to ask them to turn down their music?

A: I called the police because they didn't turn it down when I asked.

Q: So you did speak to them first?

A: I spoke to their son. He laughed at me and went back inside.

Q: He laughed at you.

A: That's what I said. Do you need me to spell it?

Q: And this was the seventeen-year-old, Tyler Burke?

A: I don't know how old he is. I know he's old enough to know better.

Q: What happened after he went back inside?

A: The music got louder. So I called.

Q: And you witnessed the confrontation between Mr. Burke and Officer Reyes when police arrived?

A: I watched from my porch. Mr. Burke was upset. He was waving his arms around, getting in the officer's space.

Q: Did you hear what he said?

A: Something about harassment. Something about how his family was being targeted. The usual nonsense people say when they get caught.

topic: A neighbor is questioned about noise complaints and a confrontation they witnessed
text:
Q: Ms. Thornton, I want to be very clear about the timeline. You stated in your written complaint that the noise began at approximately 10 p.m.

A: That's correct.

Q: But the police report indicates officers arrived at 10:07 p.m. and observed no noise violation.

A: Then the police report is wrong.

Q: You're saying the officers were mistaken?

A: I'm saying by the time they got there, the Nguyens had turned everything off. They saw the police car coming.

Q: You observed them doing this?

A: I observed the noise stopping suddenly right when the car turned onto our street.

Q: So you didn't actually see anyone turn off the music?

A: I'm not going to sit here and play word games with you. The music was blasting. The police came. The music stopped. It doesn't take a detective.

Q: I'm asking what you directly observed.

A: And I'm telling you what happened. You can write it down however makes your client look better.

Q: My client isn't on trial here, Ms. Thornton. This is a deposition.

A: Really? Because it feels a lot like I'm the one being interrogated.

Q: Let's move on. You witnessed an altercation between your husband and Mr. Nguyen the following morning?

A: My husband walked over to have a conversation. Mr. Nguyen started screaming.

Q: Your husband walked onto the Nguyen property?

A: He walked to the edge of the driveway. He didn't storm the gates.

Q: And what did Mr. Nguyen say?

A: He told my husband to get off his property and that he was "done being harassed by racists." That's a direct quote.

Q: How did your husband respond?

A: He came home. Unlike some people, my husband knows how to walk away.

topic: A project manager is questioned about deadlines they missed on a software contract
text:
Q: Mr. Hardin, you were the project manager for the Vertex software implementation, correct?

A: Yes.

Q: And the original contract specified a delivery date of March 15th, 2023?

A: That's what the contract said, yes.

Q: The software was not delivered on March 15th, was it?

A: No.

Q: When was it actually delivered?

A: May 2nd.

Q: So nearly seven weeks late. Mr. Hardin, at what point did you first become aware that the March 15th deadline was in jeopardy?

A: I'd have to look at my notes to give you an exact date.

Q: Your best estimate.

A: Sometime in February. I don't remember the specific day.

Q: Early February? Late February?

A: Mid-February. Maybe the 12th or 14th. Somewhere in there.

Q: Did you communicate this to anyone at Vertex?

A: Of course I did.

Q: Who specifically?

A: Their project lead. Sandra Chen.

Q: And when you told Ms. Chen in mid-February that the deadline was in jeopardy, what was her response?

A: She asked what the issue was. I explained it. She said she'd need to discuss it with her team.

Q: Did she get back to you?

A: Eventually, yes.

Q: When?

A: I don't have dates memorized. I wasn't aware I'd need to recite a calendar from two years ago.

---

topic: A project manager is questioned about deadlines they missed on a software contract
text:
Q: Let me direct your attention to the integration module. That was your responsibility, wasn't it?

A: The integration module was one of approximately fourteen deliverables under my oversight, yes.

Q: I'm asking about the integration module specifically.

A: And I'm answering. Yes, it was among my responsibilities.

Q: The integration module was due November 1st. It wasn't completed until December 19th. What happened?

A: What happened is that the client changed the API specifications three times between September and November.

Q: Three times.

A: Yes. Three. I can provide the change request documentation if that would help clarify.

Q: We'll get to documents. Right now I'm asking for your testimony. Did these specification changes affect the timeline?

A: Obviously they affected the timeline. That's precisely why I'm mentioning them.

Q: Did you request a deadline extension?

A: I requested a scope review meeting. Which is the appropriate protocol.

Q: That's not what I asked. Did you request, in writing, a deadline extension?

A: I submitted a formal change impact assessment on October 3rd which outlined the timeline implications of their modifications.

Q: Mr. Patterson, did you request—yes or no—a deadline extension?

A: If you'd let me finish. The change impact assessment included a revised timeline. That is how extensions are requested in this industry. That is the standard practice. If you want to call it something else, that's your prerogative.

Q: I see. And this assessment—was it approved?

A: It was acknowledged. Approval is a different matter, which I suspect you already know.

---

topic: A project manager is questioned about deadlines they missed on a software contract
text:
Q: Ms. Reeves, the milestone for user acceptance testing was originally scheduled for what date?

A: July 8th.

Q: And it actually occurred when?

A: July 29th.

Q: Why the three-week delay?

A: There were several factors.

Q: Name them.

Q: Who reassigned the developers?

A: That decision came from above me.

Q: Who specifically?

A: David Chen. Our VP of Engineering.

Q: Did you object to that decision?

A: I raised concerns.

Q: To Mr. Chen?

A: To Mr. Chen, yes. In writing.

Q: What did he say?

A: He said the Millbrook project was the priority and we'd need to adjust.

Q: So you adjusted by missing your deadline.

A: I adjusted by working my team sixty-hour weeks for a month and still delivering a functional product. The delay was three weeks, not three months.

Q: But it was still a delay, correct?

A: Yes. I've already said that. It was a delay. I'm not disputing the calendar.

---

topic: A project manager is questioned about deadlines they missed on a software contract
text:
Q: Good afternoon, Mr. Okonkwo. I want to cover some ground efficiently here, so I'd appreciate direct answers. You were PM on the Ridgeline contract?

A: Yes.

Q: Total contract value?

A: $2.4 million.

Q: Final delivery was how late?

A: Sixty-two days past the original deadline.

Q: Sixty-two days. Let's break that down. The authentication module—late?

A: Yes.

Q: How late?

A: I believe around three weeks.

Q: The reporting dashboard—late?

A: Slightly, yes.

Q: How slightly?

A: Eleven days.

Q: The data migration component—late?

A: Yes.

Q: How late?

A: That one had the longest delay. Approximately six weeks.

Q: Why?

A: The client's existing data was in worse condition than their technical team had represented. We essentially had to rebuild their normalization schema from scratch.

Q: Did you document this?

A: Extensively.

Q: Before or after the deadline passed?

A: Both. We flagged the data quality issues in week two of the project.

Q: Week two. And the deadline still wasn't adjusted?

A: Ridgeline didn't want to adjust. They had a product launch tied to our delivery date.

Q: So you knew you couldn't meet the deadline and continued anyway?

A: We continued trying to meet it. That's what project management is. You don't surrender the moment something gets difficult.

Q: But you didn't meet it.

A: No. We did not.

---

topic: A project manager is questioned about deadlines they missed on a software contract
text:
Q: Ms. Tran, how many projects were you managing simultaneously during the relevant period?

A: I'd have to check the exact number.

Q: Approximately.

A: Four. Maybe five.

Q: You don't know if it was four or five?

A: Projects overlap. They phase in and out. At any given moment the number in active status varied.

Q: The Beacon project—that was one of them?

A: Yes.

Q: That project missed three consecutive milestones. You're aware of that?

A: I'm aware of what happened on Beacon, yes.

Q: Can you explain how a project misses three milestones in a row?

A: Can you be more specific about which milestones you're referring to?

Q: All of them. Start with the first one.

A: The requirements sign-off was delayed because the client kept adding scope.

Q: The second?

A: Design approval. Same issue. They wanted revisions that weren't in the original statement of work.

Q: Third?

A: Development completion. Which was downstream of the first two delays. We can't develop what hasn't been designed, and we can't design what hasn't been scoped.

Q: Did you raise these issues with your management?

A: Weekly. Sometimes daily.

Q: And?

A: And they told me to manage the client relationship.

Q: What does that mean?

A: It means they wanted me to make the client happy without telling the client no. Which is not actually possible when the client's expectations are unrealistic.

Q: So you're saying the deadlines were unrealistic from the start?

A: I'm saying they became unrealistic once the scope tripled and the timeline stayed the same. That's mathematics, not opinion.

Q: But you accepted the project under those original deadlines.

A: I accepted the project under the original scope. Those are two different things, and I think you know that.

topic: A financial advisor is deposed about investment decisions made on a client's behalf
text:
Q: Mr. Hartley, you placed approximately $2.3 million of Mrs. Chen's retirement funds into high-yield bonds in March of 2021, correct?

A: That's what the records reflect, yes.

Q: And you made that decision without consulting her first?

A: I made that decision consistent with the discretionary authority she granted me in writing. Which you have.

Q: I'm asking whether you picked up the phone and called her before you moved $2.3 million.

A: No.

Q: You didn't think a 74-year-old retiree might want to know her life savings were being moved into high-yield bonds?

A: The investment policy statement we developed together—which, again, you have—specified an allocation of up to 30 percent in fixed income with flexibility for yield optimization. I was operating within those parameters.

Q: That's not what I asked you.

A: Then perhaps you could rephrase.

Q: Did you think Mrs. Chen would want to know?

A: I think Mrs. Chen trusted me to manage her portfolio according to the guidelines we established. That's what discretionary management means. That's why clients grant it.

Q: So that's a no?

A: That's an explanation of how discretionary accounts function, Counselor. If you'd like a yes or no, the answer is: I didn't believe notification was required or expected for trades within policy guidelines.

Q: Within two months, those bonds had lost 18 percent of their value.

A: Some of them. Others held. The portfolio as a whole experienced a drawdown, yes.

Q: And you still didn't call her.

A: I sent a quarterly statement. As I always did. As she expected me to.

topic: A financial advisor is deposed about investment decisions made on a client's behalf
text:
Q: Let's talk about the Meridian Tech investment.

A: And I've told you I don't recall the specific words. It was four years ago. I had over two hundred clients. I can't reproduce conversations verbatim.

Q: Let me show you Exhibit 14. Do you see your signature at the bottom?

A: Yes.

A: ...I'd need a moment to review it.

Q: Take your time.

A: ...It doesn't appear to be in this document.

topic: A financial advisor is deposed about investment decisions made on a client's behalf
text:
Q: Ms. Pearson, walk me through your process for determining a client's risk tolerance.

A: We use a comprehensive questionnaire, a personal interview, and a review of their financial situation, time horizon, and stated objectives.

Q: And you conducted this process with Dr. Whitfield?

A: Of course.

Q: The questionnaire is Exhibit 7 in front of you. Can you turn to page three?

A: I'm there.

Q: Question 12 asks how the client would react to a 20 percent portfolio decline. What did Dr. Whitfield mark?

A: He marked "I would be very concerned and might want to change my investment strategy."

Q: That's the most risk-averse option available, isn't it?

A: It's one of the options.

Q: It's the most risk-averse option, yes or no?

A: Yes.

Q: Yet within six months, you had allocated 60 percent of his portfolio to emerging market equities and leveraged ETFs. How does that square with his answer here?

A: Risk tolerance is one factor. It's not the only factor.

Q: What other factor overrode his clearly stated discomfort with losses?

A: His return objectives. Dr. Whitfield was very clear that he wanted aggressive growth. He wanted to retire at 55.

Q: So you prioritized what he wanted to earn over what he could stomach losing?

A: I balanced both. That's the job. That's what I do every day. You take competing inputs and you build a portfolio that tries to serve all of them.

Q: And when the portfolio dropped 34 percent in 2022?

A: That was a market-wide event. Virtually every equity-heavy portfolio declined.

Q: He called your office eleven times in March of that year alone.

A: I'm not going to dispute the call log.

Q: Did you return those calls?

A: I returned some of them.

Q: Some of them.

A: Yes. Some of them. I had multiple clients calling during that period. Everyone was calling. I did my best.

topic: A financial advisor is deposed about investment decisions made on a client's behalf
text:
Q: You've been a financial advisor for nineteen years, is that correct?

A: It is.

Q: In those nineteen years, you've developed some expertise in evaluating speculative investments?

A: I'd like to think so.

Q: Then help me understand something. The Vantage Limited Partnership—what was the projected rate of return on that investment?

A: As I recall, the offering materials projected returns in the range of 18 to 24 percent annually.

Q: 18 to 24 percent.

A: That's what the materials stated, yes.

Q: Mr. Reeves, in your nineteen years, how often have you seen a private placement legitimately return 24 percent annually?

A: It happens. Rarely, but it happens.

Q: But it's rare.

A: Yes.

Q: What due diligence did you perform before placing the Ostrowski family's money in this rare opportunity?

A: I reviewed the offering memorandum. I spoke with the fund manager. I examined their track record.

Q: You spoke with the fund manager.

A: Yes.

Q: By phone?

A: Yes.

Q: For how long?

A: I don't have exact records. Perhaps twenty minutes. Maybe thirty.

Q: Twenty to thirty minutes of conversation, and you felt confident placing $1.2 million of your clients' money?

A: It wasn't my only source of information.

Q: What else?

A: I told you. The offering memorandum. Their track record.

Q: Which you got from whom?

A: From the fund.

Q: From the fund. So your due diligence consisted of reading what the fund told you about itself and calling the fund to ask if the fund was a good investment?

A: That's a reductive way of putting it.

Q: Then give me the complete picture, Mr. Reeves. What am I missing?

A: ...I also consulted with colleagues who had worked with similar structures.

Q: Which colleagues?

A: I'd have to check my notes.

topic: A financial advisor is deposed about investment decisions made on a client's behalf
text:
Q: Let's talk about the rebalancing in October 2019.

A: Fine.

Q: You moved Mrs. Patterson from a 60/40 equity-bond split to something closer to 85/15, is that right?

A: The allocation shifted, yes. I'd want to verify the exact percentages.

Q: Exhibit 22 is the quarterly statement from Q4 2019. Does that refresh your memory?

A: ...Yes. 83 percent equities, approximately.

Q: Why?

A: Why what?

Q: Why did you make that change?

A: Market conditions. Interest rates were low. Bonds weren't generating meaningful yield. Equities had momentum.

Q: Mrs. Patterson was 68 years old.

A: I'm aware of how old my client was.

Q: Conventional guidance suggests investors her age should be reducing equity exposure, not increasing it.

A: Conventional guidance is a starting point. It's not a mandate.

Q: Did you document your reasoning for departing from conventional guidance?

A: I'm sure I made notes.

Q: Do you have those notes?

A: Your discovery requests were extensive. I assume my firm produced what was available.

Q: We haven't seen any notes explaining this decision.

A: Then perhaps they weren't retained.

Q: Perhaps they weren't made?

A: I made notes. I always make notes. Whether they were preserved through two office moves and a system migration is beyond my control.

Q: So your position is that the notes existed but conveniently disappeared?

A: My position is that I followed my standard practices, documented my reasoning at the time, and cannot account for gaps in records that are five years old. That's my position.

topic: A witness is questioned about a fire they discovered in a neighboring unit
text:
Q: Please state your name for the record.

A: Thomas Whitfield.

Q: Mr. Whitfield, you lived at 4521 Crescent Avenue, Unit B, correct?

A: That's correct.

Q: And on the night of March 14th, you discovered a fire in the neighboring unit?

A: I discovered smoke. Then fire. Yes.

Q: What time was this?

A: Around 11:15 p.m. Give or take.

Q: Give or take how much, Mr. Whitfield?

A: I don't know, a few minutes? I wasn't exactly checking my watch while the building was burning down.

Q: I'm simply asking for your best estimate.

A: And I gave you one. 11:15.

Q: Were you alone when you discovered the smoke?

A: My wife was asleep.

Q: So that's a yes?

A: That's a "my wife was asleep," counselor. I was awake. Alone in the living room. Is that specific enough?

Q: What drew your attention to the smoke?

A: The smell. Then I heard something—a kind of crackling. I looked out the window and saw it coming from under their door.

Q: Did you attempt to alert anyone in Unit A before calling 911?

A: I banged on their door. No one answered. Then I called.

Q: How long did you bang on the door?

A: Long enough to know no one was coming.

---

topic: A witness is questioned about a fire they discovered in a neighboring unit
text:
Q: You were the first person to call 911 regarding the fire at 782 Delancey Street, is that right?

topic: A witness is questioned about a fire they discovered in a neighboring unit
text:
Q: Let's go back to the timeline, Mr. Huang. You said you first noticed something unusual at approximately 9:40 p.m.

topic: A witness is questioned about a fire they discovered in a neighboring unit
text:

topic: A witness is questioned about a fire they discovered in a neighboring unit
text:
Q: Mr. Okonkwo, I want to be very precise about what you observed. You've testified you saw the fire through a window.

topic: An employee is deposed about a coworker's termination they believe was retaliatory

A: Not specifically. I heard Darren mention something about the compliance report he'd filed with HR. I didn't catch Linda's exact words.

topic: An employee is deposed about a coworker's termination they believe was retaliatory

topic: A nurse is questioned about a patient fall that occurred during her shift
text:
Q: Good morning. I understand you've been working at Mercy General for quite some time now. Could you tell me a bit about your experience there?

A: Yes, of course. I've been with Mercy General for eleven years this past March. I started in the medical-surgical unit, then moved to the orthopedic floor about six years ago. It's been a wonderful place to build my career, honestly.

Q: Eleven years is substantial. And on the night of September 14th, you were working the overnight shift on that orthopedic floor, correct?

A: That's right. I came on at seven p.m. and was scheduled through seven the next morning.

Q: Can you walk me through how you first learned about Mrs. Patterson and her care needs when you started your shift?

A: Absolutely. During our shift change report, the day nurse—that was Rebecca—gave me a thorough rundown. She mentioned that Mrs. Patterson was two days post-op from a hip replacement, that she'd been a little restless during the afternoon, and that her pain management was being adjusted. Rebecca was really detailed about it, which I appreciated.

Q: That's helpful context. Now, at some point during your shift, Mrs. Patterson fell. I want to understand what happened, but first—can you tell me what her mobility status was supposed to be?

A: She was on assisted ambulation only. Meaning she shouldn't get up without a nurse or aide present. We had that clearly documented, and there was a sign on her door as well.

Q: And the bed alarm—was that part of the protocol for her?

A: Yes, it was. I checked it myself when I did my first rounds at eight o'clock. It was functioning properly. I remember testing it because I always do with my post-surgical patients. It gives me peace of mind, and it gives them peace of mind too.

Q: I appreciate you explaining your routine. So the alarm was set. What happened later that night?

A: Around 2:15 a.m., I was in another patient's room—Mr. Donnelly, two doors down—when I heard the alarm trigger from Mrs. Patterson's room. I excused myself immediately and went straight there.

Q: What did you find when you arrived?

A: She was on the floor beside her bed, on her left side. She was conscious and talking, a little disoriented but aware. I knelt down next to her and just talked to her calmly, made sure she didn't try to move until we could assess her properly.

Q: You said she was talking. Do you remember what she said?

A: She said, "I just needed to use the bathroom. I thought I could make it." And I told her—I said, "That's okay, we're going to take good care of you." I didn't want her to feel embarrassed. These things happen, and patients already feel so vulnerable.

Q: It sounds like you responded with care. After you found her, what steps did you take?

A: I called for assistance, and my colleague James came right away. We did a full assessment before moving her—checked for any obvious injuries, asked about pain, looked at her hip site. Then we used proper transfer techniques to get her back to bed, and I paged the on-call physician immediately.

Q: Thank you for walking me through that. Just one more question for now—looking back, is there anything you would have done differently?

A: I've thought about that a lot, honestly. I wish I could have been in two places at once. But I followed protocol, the alarm worked as it should, and I responded as quickly as I could. I just wish she hadn't felt like she needed to try on her own.

topic: A nurse is questioned about a patient fall that occurred during her shift
text:
Q: State your name for the record.

A: Linda Marsh.

Q: Ms. Marsh, you were the charge nurse on duty the morning Mr. Beltran fell, correct?

A: I was one of two nurses on the floor, yes. I wasn't charge that day—Dina Okonkwo was charge.

Q: I appreciate the correction. Let me ask you this: how many patients were you personally responsible for that morning?

A: I had six patients assigned to me, including Mr. Beltran.

Q: Six patients. And how many certified nursing assistants were available to help you?

A: Just one for the whole floor. We were short-staffed that day. Maria called in sick, and they couldn't find coverage.

Q: That must have stretched everyone thin.

A: It did. But we managed. We always manage. You figure out how to prioritize, how to be in the right place at the right time. That's just nursing.

Q: Tell me about Mr. Beltran. What do you remember about his condition that morning?

A: He was recovering from a mild stroke—his second one. He had some weakness on his right side, and he was a fall risk. We had him flagged in the system, yellow socks, the whole protocol. He was also—and I don't mean this unkindly—he was a proud man. Very independent before the stroke. It was hard for him to ask for help.

Q: Did you have any interactions with him before the fall?

A: I checked on him around 6:30 a.m. during my first rounds. He was awake, in good spirits actually. He made a joke about the hospital food—said his wife's cooking was worse, so at least he was used to it. We laughed together. I told him to call me if he needed anything, anything at all.

Q: What time did the fall occur?

A: The fall was reported at 7:47 a.m. I was in the medication room preparing the morning rounds.

Q: How did you learn about it?

A: Another patient's family member came running in, said someone had fallen in the hallway. I dropped everything and ran.

Q: What did you see?

A: Mr. Beltran was on the floor near the nurses' station. He'd made it about twenty feet from his room. He was trying to get up when I reached him, and I said, "Hold on, hold on, let me help you, let's do this together." I didn't want him to feel like he'd done something wrong. He was already upset with himself.

Q: Did he say anything about why he'd gotten up?

A: He said he wanted to walk to the window at the end of the hall. He wanted to see the sunrise. He said he used to watch the sunrise every morning at home.

topic: A nurse is questioned about a patient fall that occurred during her shift
text:
Q: Nurse Delgado, I want to focus on the documentation surrounding Mrs. Chen's fall. You completed the incident report, correct?

A: I did.

Q: What time did you document the fall as occurring?

A: 4:20 a.m.

Q: And what time did you actually complete the incident report?

A: I finished it around 5:15 a.m.

Q: So about an hour later. Why the delay?

A: Well, my first priority was the patient, making sure Mrs. Chen was stable, getting her examined, staying with her, contacting her family. The documentation is important, of course, but I wasn't going to leave her side to fill out paperwork while she was frightened and in pain.

Q: I understand. I'm not suggesting you should have. I'm just trying to establish the timeline.

A: Of course. I'm sorry if I sounded defensive. It's been a difficult few months.

Q: No need to apologize. You're doing fine. Let's talk about what you wrote in the report. You indicated that Mrs. Chen was found on the floor of her bathroom. Is that accurate?

A: Yes. She'd gotten up to use the toilet and lost her balance.

Q: The report also says the bed alarm was not activated at the time of the fall. Can you explain that?

A: Mrs. Chen had been continent and ambulatory for most of her stay. She was actually supposed to be discharged the next morning. The previous shift had discontinued the bed alarm per the physician's orders because she'd been doing so well.

Q: So the decision to remove the alarm wasn't yours?

A: No, it wasn't. But I want to be clear—it was a reasonable decision based on her progress. Everyone thought she was ready. These things are judgment calls, and sometimes... sometimes patients have setbacks that no one can predict.

Q: You sound like you've been thinking about this a great deal.

A: I have. Every day since it happened. Mrs. Chen was such a kind woman. She showed me pictures of her grandchildren. We talked about her garden. When I found her on that bathroom floor, it broke my heart. I keep thinking about what I might have noticed, what I might have done.

Q: I have to ask the difficult questions, but I want you to know—I can see how much you cared about her.

A: Thank you. I appreciate you saying that. I really do.

Q: Let's continue. In the report, you mentioned she had a small laceration on her forehead.

A: Yes. She'd hit the edge of the sink on her way down. It required three stitches.

topic: A nurse is questioned about a patient fall that occurred during her shift
text:
Q: You testified earlier that Mr. Franklin was confused when you found him after the fall.

A: That's correct.

Q: Confused how? Can you be more specific?

A: He didn't know where he was at first. He asked me if his daughter was coming to pick him up, even though it was three in the morning. He thought he was at a bus station.

Q: Was this level of confusion typical for him?

A: No, actually. Mr. Franklin had been sharp as a tack most of his stay. That's part of why the fall surprised me so much. He wasn't someone I expected to wander.

Q: Let me ask you something. You've been nursing for—how long now?

A: Eighteen years.

Q: Eighteen years. In your experience, when an elderly patient suddenly becomes confused like that, what might cause it?

A: It could be a lot of things. A urinary tract infection, medication reaction, dehydration, the beginning of sepsis, or sometimes just the stress of being in the hospital. We call it hospital delirium. It happens more than people realize.

Q: Did you notice any signs earlier in your shift that something might be off with Mr. Franklin?

A: I've asked myself that question a hundred times. When I checked on him at midnight, he seemed fine. Tired, but fine. He said goodnight to me. Called me "sweetheart," actually—he called all the nurses sweetheart, like we were his granddaughters. By three a.m., he was a different person.

Q: That must have been alarming.

A: It was. But you know, I sat with him after we got him back to bed. I held his hand and talked to him about his daughter, about his old job—he used to be a mail carrier, did you know that? Forty years. I just talked to him until he calmed down, until he remembered where he was.

Q: That wasn't in your incident report.

A: No, I suppose it wasn't. It didn't seem like the kind of thing you put in a report. It was just... it was just what he needed.

Q: I think it's worth noting. For the record.

A: Well, thank you for letting me share it.

topic: A nurse is questioned about a patient fall that occurred during her shift
text:
Q: Ms. Vasquez, let's talk about the fall protocol at your facility. You're familiar with it?

A: Very familiar. I helped write the current version, actually. I was on the patient safety committee for three years.

Q: Then you're the perfect person to ask. Walk me through what's supposed to happen when a patient is identified as a fall risk.

A: Of course. First, we complete a Morse Fall Scale assessment on admission and every shift thereafter. If the patient scores above 45, we implement our high-risk protocol: bed alarm, yellow non-slip socks, yellow wristband, a sign on the door, and we document it in the chart with a care plan.

Q: And for Mr. Yates, on the night in question—was all of that in place?

A: Everything except the sign on the door. The sign had fallen off at some point and wasn't replaced.

Q: Who was responsible for replacing it?

A: Honestly, anyone who noticed it was missing. It could have been me. It could have been the aide, the previous shift, housekeeping. We all share that responsibility.

Q: But on this night, you were his nurse.

A: I was, yes.

Q: And the sign was missing.

A: Yes. I noticed it was missing after the fall. I can't tell you how that made me feel—to realize I'd walked past that door multiple times and never registered that it wasn't there.

Q: Let me ask you this: do you think the missing sign contributed to Mr. Yates' fall?

A: I don't know. I honestly don't. Mr. Yates fell in his own bathroom, not in the hallway. The sign is mostly there to alert other staff and visitors. Whether it would have changed anything that night—I can't say for certain.

Q: That's a fair answer.

A: I try to be fair. And I try to be honest. What happened to Mr. Yates was awful, and I've lost sleep over it. But I also know that I did my best with what I knew at the time. We all did. Sometimes that's still not enough, and that's the hardest part of this job.

Q: Thank you for your candor.

A: Thank you for listening. Not everyone does.

topic: A building inspector is deposed about a structural assessment they signed off on
text:
Q: Mr. Hardin, you conducted a structural assessment of the Waverly Commons building on October 14th, 2022, correct?

A: That's what the date on the report says.

Q: And you personally inspected the load-bearing walls on the third floor?

A: I walked the building. Third floor was part of that.

Q: Did you observe any cracking in the concrete along the eastern wall?

A: There's always some cracking in buildings of that age. Minor surface cracking. Nothing structural.

Q: How did you determine it wasn't structural?

A: Experience. Visual inspection. The cracks were superficial.

Q: Did you measure the width of any of those cracks?

A: I don't recall if I took measurements that day specifically.

Q: Would measurements be reflected in your notes if you had taken them?

A: Probably. Maybe not. Depends on whether I thought it was worth noting.

Q: So if there are no measurements in your notes, you likely didn't take any?

A: Or I took them and they weren't significant enough to write down. Either way.

Q: Mr. Hardin, a building collapse occurred at that location four months later. Does that change your assessment of what you observed?

A: I documented what I saw when I saw it. What happened later happened later.

Q: Do you have any concerns, sitting here today, about the thoroughness of your October inspection?

A: I did my job the way I always do it. Same as every other inspection.

---

topic: A building inspector is deposed about a structural assessment they signed off on
text:
Q: Let's move to the basement level. You noted in your report that the foundation appeared sound. Do you see that notation?

A: Yes.

Q: What does "appeared sound" mean in your professional terminology?

A: It means I didn't observe evidence of failure or imminent failure.

Q: Did you conduct any testing of the foundation?

A: No.

Q: Is foundation testing something you're qualified to perform?

A: I'm qualified to recommend it if I think it's warranted.

Q: And you didn't think it was warranted here?

A: Correct.

Q: What would have made it warranted?

A: Visible settling. Significant cracking. Water intrusion patterns suggesting subsurface issues. Things like that.

Q: Did you observe any water staining in the basement?

A: Some. Older staining. Looked historical.

Q: How did you determine the staining was historical rather than ongoing?

A: It was dry. Discolored in a way that suggested age.

Q: Okay. Did you note the location of that staining anywhere in your documentation?

A: I don't believe so.

Q: Any particular reason?

A: It wasn't relevant to my structural findings.

---

topic: A building inspector is deposed about a structural assessment they signed off on
text:
Q: Ms. Thornton, how many inspections would you estimate you conducted in October 2022?

A: I'd have to check my records. Forty, fifty maybe. It was a busy month.

Q: So the Riverside Lofts inspection was one of approximately fifty that month?

A: Somewhere in that range, sure.

Q: How much time did you spend on site at Riverside Lofts?

A: The report should indicate my arrival and departure. I don't have independent recollection.

Q: The report shows you were on site for approximately ninety minutes. Does that seem accurate?

A: If that's what it says.

Q: Is ninety minutes sufficient time to conduct a thorough structural assessment of a six-story building?

A: Depends on the building. Depends on what you're looking for. Depends on a lot of things.

Q: What were you looking for at Riverside Lofts?

A: Whatever the scope of work specified. I'd have to review the engagement letter.

Q: You don't recall the scope of work?

A: I've done hundreds of inspections since then. I don't have specific recall of each one.

Q: Let me ask it differently. Generally speaking, what does a structural assessment include when you perform one?

A: Visual inspection of structural elements. Documentation of observed conditions. Professional opinion on structural integrity. The basics.

---

topic: A building inspector is deposed about a structural assessment they signed off on
text:
Q: I'm going to show you what's been marked as Exhibit 7. Do you recognize this document?

A: I'm not going to cite chapter and verse from memory. There are guidelines. I followed them.

topic: A building inspector is deposed about a structural assessment they signed off on
text:
Q: Ms. Castellano, prior to this inspection, had you ever assessed a building designed by Mercer & Associates?

A: Possibly. I don't track projects by architect.

Q: You're not aware that Mercer & Associates has faced multiple structural deficiency claims in the past five years?

A: I'm not here to discuss other projects.

Q: I'm asking whether you were aware of that history when you conducted your inspection.

A: No. And it wouldn't have mattered.

Q: Why wouldn't it matter?

A: Because I inspect the building in front of me. Not the architect's reputation.

Q: Fair enough. Let's talk about the building in front of you. You certified the roof trusses as structurally adequate. What did that assessment involve?

A: Visual inspection from the attic access point. Observation of truss connections and bearing points.

Q: Did you walk the entire attic space?

A: As much as was accessible.

Q: What percentage would you estimate was accessible?

A: I don't estimate percentages. I inspect what I can access and note any limitations.

Q: Did you note any access limitations in your report?

A: I'd have to look at the report.

Q: I'll represent to you that the report contains no mention of access limitations.

A: Then apparently there weren't any worth noting.

topic: A nurse is questioned about a patient fall that occurred during her shift

topic: A nurse is questioned about a patient fall that occurred during her shift
text:
Q: Nurse Chen, when did you first learn that Mr. Abernathy was a fall risk?

Q: Typically?

A: Yes. Typically.

Q: But you didn't test it?

A: I had fourteen patients that night, counselor. I checked what I could check in the time I had. The light was green. There was no alarm when he fell. You want me to explain why, but I don't have that answer. I wish I did.

topic: A nurse is questioned about a patient fall that occurred during her shift
text:
Q: Let's talk about the call light system. You're familiar with how it works?

A: If that's what the records say.

Q: But you don't specifically remember?

topic: A nurse is questioned about a patient fall that occurred during her shift
text:

topic: A nurse is questioned about a patient fall that occurred during her shift
text:

topic: An HR director is questioned about a harassment complaint that was filed and closed
text:
Q: Ms. Thornton, you were the HR director at Wellmark Industries in March of 2022, correct?

topic: An HR director is questioned about a harassment complaint that was filed and closed
text:
Q: Let's talk about the complaint filed by Sandra Okonkwo. You're familiar with that matter?

Q: How long was that interview?

A: Maybe twenty minutes. Long enough.

Q: Long enough for what?

A: To get the relevant information.

Q: Did she seem distressed during the interview?

A: She seemed like someone filing a complaint.

topic: An HR director is questioned about a harassment complaint that was filed and closed

topic: An HR director is questioned about a harassment complaint that was filed and closed
