topic: A witness is questioned about a fire they discovered in a neighboring unit
text:
Q: Please state your name for the record.

A: Michael Reeves.

Q: Mr. Reeves, you reside at 4521 Oakmont Drive, Unit B, is that correct?

A: Yes.

Q: And on the night of March 14th, you were home?

A: I was home, yes. I'd been home since about six, maybe six-fifteen. I remember because I'd picked up dinner on the way back and the receipt—well, I don't have the receipt anymore, but it was around that time.

Q: That's fine. I'm just establishing you were present. Now, at some point that evening, you became aware of a fire in the adjacent unit?

A: I became aware of—yes. Yes, I did.

Q: What time was that?

A: I don't—I want to say around nine? Maybe nine-thirty? I wasn't looking at a clock. I wasn't exactly checking my watch when I smelled smoke, if that's what you're asking.

Q: I'm simply asking for your best estimate.

A: Then nine. Or nine-thirty. Somewhere in there.

Q: How did you first become aware something was wrong?

A: The smell. It was—look, I've gone over this. The smell came first, then I heard what I thought was someone shouting, and then I looked out my kitchen window and saw the glow. Orange light. Flickering.

Q: You heard shouting?

A: I said I thought I heard shouting. I don't know if it was shouting or a television or—I don't know. I'm not going to say it was definitely shouting.

Q: Fair enough. What did you do after you saw the orange light?

A: I called 911. Immediately. I didn't—I called 911.

Q: Did you attempt to enter Unit A at any point?

A: No. No, I did not. I'm not—no.

Q: Did you see anyone exit Unit A?

A: I already told the investigator I didn't see anyone. I've said this multiple times.

Q: Mr. Reeves, I understand. I'm asking you now, under oath.

A: Then no. Under oath. No. I did not see anyone exit Unit A.

topic: A witness is questioned about a fire they discovered in a neighboring unit
text:
Q: You've testified you discovered the fire at approximately 10 p.m., correct?

A: Approximately, yes.

Q: And you were in your living room at the time?

A: I was in my living room.

Q: Doing what, specifically?

A: Watching television.

Q: What were you watching?

A: I don't remember.

Q: You don't remember what program was on?

A: No, I don't. Is that relevant?

Q: I'm trying to establish the circumstances. Were you alone?

A: Yes.

Q: Had you consumed any alcohol that evening?

A: I'd had a beer. One beer.

Q: When did you finish that beer?

A: I don't—maybe an hour before? I wasn't keeping track.

Q: So around 9 p.m.?

A: If you say so. Sure. Around nine.

Q: Ms. Thornton, let me be direct with you. The fire investigator's report suggests the fire may have been burning for some time before it was reported. I need to understand exactly when you became aware of it.

A: I've told you when I became aware of it.

Q: Let's try this again. What first drew your attention away from the television?

A: A sound. A popping sound.

Q: Popping?

A: Like—I don't know how to describe it. Like something cracking. Wood, maybe.

Q: And what did you do?

A: I muted the TV.

Q: Then?

A: I listened. And then I smelled it.

Q: Smelled what?

A: Smoke. What do you think?

topic: A witness is questioned about a fire they discovered in a neighboring unit
text:
Q: Mr. Aguilar, I want to focus on the moments immediately after you called 911. Can you do that for me?

A: I can try.

Q: After you made the call, where did you go?

A: I went outside. Through my front door.

Q: And what did you observe?

A: Smoke coming from under their door. The Hendersons' door. Unit 12.

Q: Thick smoke? Thin?

A: It was—I mean, it was smoke. I don't know how to quantify smoke for you.

Q: Was it difficult to see through?

A: I wasn't trying to see through it. I was backing away from it.

Q: Understood. Did you approach the door to Unit 12 at any point?

A: I went close enough to see the smoke. That's it.

Q: How close, would you say?

A: Maybe ten feet? I don't know. I wasn't measuring.

Q: Did you touch the door?

A: No.

Q: Did you attempt to open it?

A: No. I just said I didn't touch it.

Q: Did you call out to anyone inside?

A: I—yes. I yelled. I yelled to see if anyone was in there.

Q: What did you yell?

A: Something like "Is anyone there?" or "Hello?" I don't remember the exact words.

Q: Did anyone respond?

A: No.

Q: How many times did you call out?

A: Twice. Maybe three times. Then the smoke got worse and I moved back.

Q: Did you see any flames at that point?

A: Not yet. Just the smoke.

topic: A witness is questioned about a fire they discovered in a neighboring unit
text:
Q: State your name.

A: Patricia Yuen.

Q: Ms. Yuen, where do you live?

A: 88 Crescent Lane, Apartment 4C.

Q: And apartment 4D is directly adjacent to yours?

A: Yes.

A: No.

A: The smell was stronger. And there was—the door to 4D, the bottom of it, there was this sort of haze. Not smoke exactly. A haze.

A: Yes.

Q: How many times?

A: Three or four times. Hard.

Q: Any response?

A: Nothing.

Q: What did you do then?

topic: A witness is questioned about a fire they discovered in a neighboring unit
text:
Q: Let's go back to the timeline. You said you first noticed something was wrong around 8:45?

A: I said approximately 8:45. I'm not certain of the exact time.

Q: Fine. Approximately 8:45. You were in your bedroom?

A: Yes, I was getting ready for bed.

Q: Early evening for that, isn't it?

A: I wake up at 4 a.m. for work. Is that acceptable to you?

Q: I'm not questioning your sleep schedule, Mr. Okonkwo. I'm establishing the facts. You were in your bedroom, getting ready for bed. What happened next?

A: I heard my smoke detector go off.

Q: Your smoke detector? In your unit?

A: Yes.

Q: Not the one in Unit 7?

A: I can't hear their smoke detector from my bedroom. I heard mine.

Q: Why would your smoke detector activate if the fire was in Unit 7?

A: Because smoke travels, I assume. I'm not a fire scientist.

Q: Did you investigate the source of the smoke?

A: Of course I did.

Q: Tell me what you found.

A: I went into my hallway, and I could see smoke coming through—there's a vent. A shared vent between the units. Smoke was coming through the vent.

Q: What did you do?

A: I grabbed my phone, I grabbed my wallet, and I left my apartment.

Q: You didn't attempt to warn your neighbors in Unit 7?

A: The smoke was coming from Unit 7. What was I going to warn them about?

Q: Whether they were aware of the fire.

A: The building alarm went off thirty seconds after I got outside. Everyone was aware.

Q: But in that thirty seconds—

A: In that thirty seconds I was getting myself out of a building that was on fire. I'm sorry if that's not heroic enough for your purposes.

topic: A supervisor is deposed about performance reviews given to an employee who was later fired
text:
Q: Mr. Patterson, you conducted the 2022 annual review for Denise Watkins, correct?

A: I did, yes.

Q: And you gave her an overall rating of "meets expectations"?

A: That's correct.

Q: Now, six months later, she was terminated for performance issues. Help me understand how someone who "meets expectations" suddenly becomes a performance problem.

A: Well, I'm glad you asked that, actually. The annual review captures a snapshot in time. Denise's work was acceptable through most of 2022. The issues that led to her termination developed afterward—specifically in the first quarter of 2023.

Q: So nothing in the 2022 review period concerned you?

A: I documented two areas for improvement in that review. I have my notes if you'd like to see them. Timeliness on the Morrison project and communication with the Chicago team. Both flagged clearly.

Q: But those weren't significant enough to affect her overall rating?

A: They were developmental areas, not deficiencies. There's a distinction in our rating system. I applied it correctly.

Q: Who else reviewed your evaluation before it was finalized?

A: HR reviews all annual evaluations. Sarah Chen signed off on it.

Q: Did Ms. Chen raise any concerns?

A: She did not. The evaluation met all company standards.

Q: Looking back now, do you wish you had rated her more critically?

A: No. The rating was accurate for that period. What happened later was a separate trajectory. I stand by what I wrote.

Q: Thank you, Mr. Patterson.

A: You're welcome.

topic: A supervisor is deposed about performance reviews given to an employee who was later fired
text:
Q: Let's talk about the mid-year check-in you had with Mr. Okonkwo in July.

A: Okay.

Q: That was an informal review, correct?

A: We don't call it a review. It's a check-in. Development-focused.

Q: Fine. During that check-in, did you discuss any concerns about his performance?

A: I... I mentioned some things, yes.

Q: What things?

A: I'd have to look at my notes to be specific.

Q: Do you have those notes?

A: I believe they were produced.

Q: Let me show you what's been marked as Exhibit 14. Take a moment to review it.

A: Alright. Yes, these are my notes.

Q: Now, the first bullet point here—you wrote "strong Q2 numbers, exceeded target by 12%." Do you see that?

A: I do.

Q: The second bullet says "client feedback positive across the board." Correct?

A: Yes.

Q: Third bullet: "Recommend for leadership development program." That's your handwriting?

A: It is.

Q: Nowhere in these notes do you mention any performance concerns at all, do you?

A: The notes don't reflect everything we discussed verbally.

Q: So you're telling me you discussed concerns that you simply chose not to write down?

A: I... sometimes the conversations are broader than what gets documented.

Q: Mr. Kaplan, you recommended this man for a leadership program three months before he was fired. I'm just trying to understand what changed.

A: Things can change quickly.

Q: What changed, specifically?

A: I'd need to think about the timeline more carefully before answering that.

topic: A supervisor is deposed about performance reviews given to an employee who was later fired
text:
Q: You mentioned earlier that you supervised approximately fifteen employees in 2021?

A: Fourteen, actually.

Q: And you conducted performance reviews for all fourteen?

A: Yes.

Q: How would you characterize the review you gave to Jennifer Moss compared to the others?

A: Characterize it how?

Q: Was it more critical? More positive? About average?

A: It was... look, every review is individualized. I don't grade on a curve if that's what you're asking.

Q: I'm asking whether Ms. Moss's review stood out in any way.

A: It was thorough.

Q: They were all thorough, I assume?

A: They were.

Q: Let me try this differently. Did any of your other fourteen employees receive a "needs improvement" rating in 2021?

A: I'd have to check.

Q: Take your time.

A: Two others, I believe.

Q: And were those two employees terminated?

A: No.

Q: So Ms. Moss was the only employee you rated as "needs improvement" who was subsequently let go?

A: Within that review cycle, yes.

Q: Now, you testified earlier that termination decisions go through HR. Who in HR handled Ms. Moss's termination?

A: David Reilly.

Q: And did Mr. Reilly ever question why an employee with only one "needs improvement" rating was being recommended for termination?

A: We had discussions.

Q: What was the substance of those discussions?

A: He asked questions. I answered them.

Q: And ultimately, he approved moving forward?

A: He did. The process worked exactly as it should.

topic: A supervisor is deposed about performance reviews given to an employee who was later fired
text:
Q: Ms. Torres, how long had you supervised Brian Chen before his termination?

A: Eleven months.

Q: In those eleven months, how many formal performance reviews did you conduct?

A: One annual review, in March.

Q: And what rating did you give him?

A: "Partially meets expectations."

Q: That's the second-lowest rating in your company's system?

A: Correct.

Q: Now, who designed the rating categories your company uses?

A: I wouldn't know. They predate my time there.

Q: But you're trained on how to apply them?

A: We receive guidance, yes.

Q: What guidance were you given about the difference between "partially meets" and "does not meet"?

A: "Does not meet" is reserved for severe performance failures. Documented, ongoing issues that haven't responded to coaching.

Q: And you felt Mr. Chen's situation didn't rise to that level?

A: At the time of the March review? No. It was borderline, frankly.

Q: Borderline how?

A: Borderline in the sense that a reasonable supervisor could have gone either way. I chose the higher rating because I believed he could improve with support.

Q: Did he receive that support?

A: He did. I personally met with him weekly after that review.

Q: And yet he was terminated four months later?

A: He was.

Q: Ms. Torres, do you believe Brian Chen was treated fairly?

A: I believe the process was followed. That's what I can speak to.

Q: That's not what I asked.

A: Then I'll say this: I did my job correctly. What happened after the review was out of my hands.

topic: A supervisor is deposed about performance reviews given to an employee who was later fired
text:
Q: Let's turn to the written comments section of the review.

A: Okay.

Q: You wrote, and I'm quoting here, "Rachel demonstrates strong technical skills but struggles with collaborative projects."

A: That sounds right.

Q: What did you mean by "struggles with collaborative projects"?

A: She had difficulty working on teams. Taking feedback. That sort of thing.

Q: Can you give me a specific example?

A: There was an incident with the Hartman account. She disagreed with the team's approach and went around them to the client directly.

Q: When did that happen?

A: September, I think.

Q: September of 2022?

A: Yes.

Q: But this review is dated February 2022.

A: I... let me look at the date again.

Q: Take your time.

A: You're right. The review predates the Hartman incident.

Q: So the example you just gave me couldn't have been the basis for this comment.

A: There must have been earlier incidents I was thinking of when I wrote it.

Q: Can you recall any of those earlier incidents now?

A: Not specifically, no.

Q: So we have a written criticism in a formal review, and you can't identify a single incident that supports it from before the review was written?

A: I would have had a basis at the time.

Q: But you don't recall it now?

A: No.

Q: Thank you. Let's move on.

topic: A nurse is questioned about a patient fall that occurred during her shift
text:
Q: Ms. Thornton, you were the charge nurse on duty the night of October 14th, correct?

A: I was.

Q: And you were responsible for patient safety on the orthopedic floor that night?

A: I was responsible for overseeing the nursing staff, yes.

Q: That's not what I asked. Were you responsible for patient safety?

A: I just told you what my responsibilities were.

Q: Let me try again. Simple question. Yes or no. Were you responsible for patient safety on your floor that night?

A: In the sense that every nurse on the floor shares that responsibility, yes. I was one of many people responsible.

Q: How many patients fell on your floor that night?

A: One.

Q: And that was Mrs. Delaney?

A: You already know it was.

Q: I need your answer for the record, Ms. Thornton.

A: Yes. Mrs. Delaney.

Q: What time did that fall occur?

A: Approximately 2:15 a.m.

Q: Where were you at 2:15 a.m.?

A: I was at the nurses' station completing documentation, which is part of my job, in case you were planning to imply otherwise.

Q: I haven't implied anything, Ms. Thornton. I'm just asking questions.

A: Then ask them.

---

topic: A nurse is questioned about a patient fall that occurred during her shift
text:
Q: Nurse Patterson, walk me through the last time you checked on Mr. Garza before the fall.

A: I did my rounds at midnight. I checked his vitals, made sure his call button was within reach, confirmed the bed alarm was on, and asked if he needed anything. He said he was fine.

Q: And then you didn't check on him again until after he was found on the floor at 1:40 a.m.?

A: That's correct.

Q: An hour and forty minutes.

A: We had fourteen patients that night with two nurses and one aide. I was with another patient who was having a cardiac event. I documented all of this.

Q: Did Mr. Garza's care plan specify hourly checks?

A: It did.

Q: So you missed the 1:00 a.m. check.

A: I was preventing another patient from dying. Would you have preferred I left her?

Q: I'm asking about Mr. Garza's care plan.

A: And I'm telling you what was happening on that floor. You want to sit here and question my judgment, fine. But I had a patient coding and no backup because the hospital cut our staff again three months ago. Put that in your record.

Q: Did you notify anyone that you couldn't complete your scheduled rounds?

A: I notified the supervisor that we were understaffed before the shift even started. I have the text messages if you'd like to see them.

Q: That's not what I asked.

A: That's my answer.

---

topic: A nurse is questioned about a patient fall that occurred during her shift
text:
Q: You documented that the bed alarm was functioning at 11:00 p.m., correct?

A: Yes.

Q: But when Mr. Okonkwo was found on the floor, the alarm had not sounded.

A: That's what I was told afterward, yes.

Q: So either the alarm malfunctioned, or it was never actually turned on. Which was it?

A: I turned it on. I remember turning it on.

Q: You remember.

A: Yes. I remember.

Q: Do you remember, or are you reconstructing what you think you would have done?

A: I turned the alarm on.

Q: Then why didn't it sound when a 180-pound man got out of the bed?

A: I don't know. I've asked myself that every single day since it happened.

Q: Have you?

A: What is that supposed to mean?

Q: I'm asking if you've reflected on what went wrong that night.

A: I just told you I have. I don't know what more you want from me. I followed the protocol. I turned on the alarm. Something went wrong with the equipment. I've lost sleep over this. I've replayed it hundreds of times. So yes, counselor, I've reflected.

Q: Let's move on. What time did you first learn about the fall?

A: Around 3:15 a.m. when the aide found him.

---

topic: A nurse is questioned about a patient fall that occurred during her shift
text:
Q: How long had Mrs. Yuen been classified as a fall risk?

A: Since her admission on September 2nd.

Q: Twelve days before the incident.

A: Correct.

Q: And in those twelve days, how many times was she found attempting to get out of bed unassisted?

A: I'd have to check the chart for the exact number.

Q: Would three times sound right?

A: It might. I don't recall precisely.

Q: Three documented instances. And yet no one requested a sitter for her?

A: Sitters have to be approved by—

Q: I know the approval process, Nurse Chen. I'm asking why no one requested one.

A: I'm trying to explain if you'd let me finish.

Q: Go ahead.

A: Sitters have to be approved by the charge nurse and the bed manager, and we'd requested them multiple times that month. We were told there weren't any available due to budget constraints.

Q: So you did request a sitter for Mrs. Yuen specifically?

A: I requested sitters generally. For multiple patients.

Q: That's not the same thing, is it?

A: We work with what we're given. You want to know why she didn't have a sitter? Ask administration. Ask the CFO who cut the budget. I'm a nurse. I showed up for my shift, I did my job with the resources I had, and I'm sitting here being questioned like I personally failed this woman.

Q: Did you personally check on Mrs. Yuen the hour before her fall?

A: Yes. I did.

---

topic: A nurse is questioned about a patient fall that occurred during her shift
text:
Q: Ms. Reeves, you mentioned the patient's son visited that evening.

A: He did, yes.

Q: What time did he leave?

A: Around 9:30, I believe.

Q: Did he express any concerns to you about his mother's care before he left?

A: He asked if someone would be checking on her through the night.

Q: And what did you tell him?

A: I told him we'd be doing regular rounds.

Q: Regular rounds.

A: That's what I said.

Q: You didn't mention that the floor was short-staffed that night?

A: No.

Q: Why not?

A: Because that's not something we typically share with family members.

Q: Even though it might affect the level of care his mother received?

A: The level of care didn't change. We were short-staffed. We adapted. That's what we do.

Q: His mother fell and fractured her hip four hours later. Would you say you adapted successfully?

A: That is—I'm not going to sit here and let you characterize it that way.

Q: How should I characterize it?

A: You have no idea what that night was like. None. You're sitting in a conference room reading charts and you think that tells you something.

Q: I'm trying to understand what happened.

A: No, you're trying to assign blame. There's a difference.

topic: A neighbor is questioned about noise complaints and a confrontation they witnessed
text:
Q: Please state your name for the record.

A: Linda Marchetti.

Q: Ms. Marchetti, how long have you lived at 4512 Clearwater Drive?

A: Eleven years. Twelve in September, I guess.

Q: And you're familiar with the defendant, Mr. Harold Vance, who lives at 4508?

A: I know who he is.

Q: On the night of June 14th, did you hear any unusual noise coming from the Vance property?

A: There was music. Loud music.

Q: Can you describe it?

A: It was loud. I don't know what else you want me to say. Music.

Q: What time did you first notice the music?

A: Sometime after ten. I wasn't looking at a clock.

Q: Did you observe any confrontation between Mr. Vance and another neighbor that evening?

A: I saw two people in the driveway.

Q: Can you describe what you saw?

A: Two men standing in the driveway. One of them was Harold. They were talking.

Q: Were they arguing?

A: I don't know. I wasn't listening. They were talking loud enough that I could hear voices, but I didn't catch words.

Q: Did you see any physical contact between them?

A: I saw one of them—not Harold—wave his arms around. That's it.

Q: Did you do anything in response to what you witnessed?

A: I closed my window and went to bed.

---

topic: A neighbor is questioned about noise complaints and a confrontation they witnessed
text:
Q: Mr. Fenton, you've lived next door to the plaintiff for approximately three years, correct?

A: That's right.

Q: And you were home on the evening of March 22nd?

A: I was.

Q: Tell me what you remember about that evening.

A: I was in my garage working on my truck. I heard shouting from next door, maybe around eight, eight-thirty. I looked over, saw Dale—that's the plaintiff—and the other guy going at it in the front yard.

Q: Going at it how?

A: Yelling. Face to face. The usual.

Q: The usual?

A: Those two have been at it for months. I stopped paying attention after the third or fourth time.

Q: Did you hear what they were saying?

A: Something about a dog. Or the fence. I really couldn't tell you which.

Q: Okay. Did you see anyone throw a punch?

A: No.

Q: Any physical contact at all?

A: Dale shoved him once. Open palm to the chest. The other guy stumbled back a step. That was it.

Q: What happened next?

A: They kept yelling for another minute, then Dale went inside. I went back to my truck.

Q: Did you report this to anyone?

A: No. Why would I?

---

topic: A neighbor is questioned about noise complaints and a confrontation they witnessed
text:
Q: Mrs. Okonkwo, I'd like to ask you about the noise complaints filed against your neighbor at unit 7B.

A: Alright.

Q: How many times would you estimate you heard excessive noise from that unit between January and April of this year?

A: I really couldn't give you a number.

Q: More than five times?

A: Probably.

Q: More than ten?

A: Maybe. I work nights, so I'm not always home when other people are awake.

Q: When you were home, what kind of noise did you hear?

A: Music, mostly. Sometimes people talking loud. A party once.

Q: Did this noise disturb you?

A: I wear earplugs anyway. For my schedule.

Q: So it didn't bother you?

A: I didn't say that. I said I wear earplugs.

Q: Let me rephrase. Did the noise ever prevent you from sleeping?

A: Once or twice, maybe.

Q: Did you ever complain to building management?

A: No.

Q: Why not?

A: I figured someone else would handle it.

Q: Moving to April 3rd. Did you witness an altercation in the hallway outside your unit?

A: I heard something. I looked through the peephole, saw two people arguing, and went back to what I was doing.

---

topic: A neighbor is questioned about noise complaints and a confrontation they witnessed
text:
Q: You're testifying today about events on September 9th. Let's start with what time you arrived home that day.

A: Around six. Maybe a little after.

Q: And you live directly across the street from the Hendersons?

A: Correct.

Q: Fine. Now, at some point that evening, did you become aware of a disturbance?

A: Yes.

Q: Describe it.

A: There was yelling. A man and a woman. I assumed it was the Hendersons but I didn't go outside to check.

Q: You assumed. Did you eventually confirm who was involved?

A: I looked out the window after a few minutes.

Q: What did you see?

A: Mrs. Henderson was on her porch. A man I didn't recognize was standing in the yard, pointing at her.

Q: Pointing how?

A: With his finger. Like this.

Q: Let the record reflect the witness is extending his index finger. What was he saying?

A: I couldn't hear exact words through the glass.

Q: But he was yelling?

A: His mouth was moving like he was yelling. I had the TV on.

Q: Did you turn the TV off?

A: No.

Q: Did you consider going outside to intervene?

A: Not really. It wasn't my business.

---

topic: A neighbor is questioned about noise complaints and a confrontation they witnessed
text:
Q: Ms. Tran, let me direct your attention to the night of November 18th. You've stated previously that you witnessed an argument between two individuals. Who were they?

A: My neighbor Greg—I don't know his last name—and another man.

Q: Where were you when you observed this?

A: On my balcony. I was smoking.

Q: What time?

A: Late. After midnight.

Q: And what did you see?

A: Greg came out of his apartment and started yelling at someone in the parking lot. The other guy yelled back. They went back and forth for a while.

Q: How long is a while?

A: I don't know. Five minutes? I wasn't timing it.

Q: Did you hear what they were arguing about?

A: Something about noise. Greg kept saying "every night" and "I have to work." The other guy kept saying it wasn't that loud.

Q: Then what happened?

A: Greg walked toward him. The other guy backed up. Greg stopped. They yelled some more. Then the other guy got in his car and left.

Q: Did Greg say or do anything after the man left?

A: He stood there for a minute, then went back inside.

Q: Did you find any of this concerning?

A: Not especially.

Q: Did you report it to anyone?

A: No. People argue.

topic: A store manager is questioned about a customer slip-and-fall on their premises
text:
Q: Mr. Delgado, can you tell me what you personally observed on the morning of the incident?

A: I was in the back office when I heard someone call for help. I came out immediately, and I saw Mrs. Patterson on the floor near the produce section. She was... she was trying to get up, but she couldn't. Her face was very pale.

Q: What did you do when you saw her on the floor?

A: I went to her right away. I told her not to move, that we would get help. I held her hand because she was shaking. She kept apologizing, which—I remember that clearly because I thought, why is she apologizing? She didn't do anything wrong.

Q: Did you notice any liquid or debris on the floor near where she fell?

A: Yes. There was water. I could see it once I was standing there with her. It was maybe a two-foot area, not a huge spill, but enough. I felt terrible that we hadn't caught it sooner.

Q: Take your time. Had any employees reported that spill before the fall?

A: No. And I've thought about that a lot since it happened. If someone had just seen it five minutes earlier...

Q: I understand. What happened after you reached Mrs. Patterson?

A: I asked Maria—she's one of my cashiers—to call 911. I stayed with Mrs. Patterson the whole time. I didn't want her to be alone on that floor. I kept telling her help was coming.

Q: Did Mrs. Patterson say anything about how the fall happened?

A: She said she didn't see it. The water, I mean. She said one second she was walking, the next she was on the ground. She was scared. I could see it in her eyes.

Q: Did you take any photographs of the area after the incident?

A: I did, yes. After the paramedics took her away. I also... I wrote down everything I could remember while it was still fresh. I wanted to make sure there was a record, in case it could help her somehow.

Q: Mr. Delgado, did you visit Mrs. Patterson in the hospital?

A: I did. Twice. I know some people told me I shouldn't, but I couldn't just—she's a regular. She comes in every Thursday. I needed her to know that we cared about what happened to her.

topic: A store manager is questioned about a customer slip-and-fall on their premises
text:
Q: Ms. Tran, how long have you been the manager at this location?

A: About four years now.

Q: And you were on duty the day Mr. Whitmore fell?

A: I was, yes.

Q: Before we get into the details, I want you to know that I understand this may be difficult to discuss. These situations are never easy for anyone involved.

A: Thank you. I appreciate that.

Q: Can you describe the store's policy for floor inspections?

A: We do sweeps every hour. An employee walks the entire floor and checks for any hazards—spills, debris, anything like that. They sign a log when they complete it.

Q: Was a sweep completed in the hour before Mr. Whitmore's fall?

A: Yes. According to the log, it was done about forty minutes before.

Q: And in that sweep, was any hazard noted near the freezer aisle?

A: No, nothing was noted.

Q: I'm not trying to assign blame here, Ms. Tran. I'm just trying to understand what happened. Is it possible something was missed?

A: It's possible. I've asked myself that question many times. The employee who did the sweep, he's very thorough, but... things can happen quickly. A spill can occur right after someone walks by.

Q: When you arrived at the scene, what did you observe?

A: There was condensation on the floor near one of the freezer units. The seal had been failing—we had a repair scheduled, but it hadn't happened yet. When I saw Mr. Whitmore on the floor, my first thought was about that freezer. I knew.

Q: You knew what, specifically?

A: I knew we should have roped off that area until the repair was done. I'd thought about it, and I didn't do it. That's something I have to live with.

topic: A store manager is questioned about a customer slip-and-fall on their premises
text:
Q: State your name for the record.

A: Derek Simmons.

Q: Mr. Simmons, you're the general manager at the Greenfield Road location, correct?

A: That's correct.

Q: On January 14th, were you present when the plaintiff fell?

A: I was in the building, yes. I didn't witness the fall itself.

Q: Who informed you about what happened?

A: One of my assistant managers, Carla. She radioed me.

Q: What exactly did she say?

A: She said a customer had fallen near aisle seven and that it looked serious. She said the woman was crying.

Q: How did you respond?

A: I went straight there. Took me maybe thirty seconds.

Q: Describe what you saw.

A: An older woman—I later learned her name was Mrs. Okonkwo—was sitting on the floor with her back against the shelving. She was holding her wrist, and yes, she was crying. Not loudly, just... tears running down her face. She looked embarrassed more than anything, and that made it worse somehow.

Q: Made what worse?

A: Just seeing her like that. Sitting on a cold floor, hurt, surrounded by strangers staring at her. I asked everyone to give her space. I crouched down so I was at her level instead of standing over her. Nobody should have people towering over them in a moment like that.

Q: Did you ask her what happened?

A: I asked if she was okay first. The what happened part could wait. She told me her wrist hurt badly. I told her we'd get her help, and I asked if there was anyone I could call for her.

Q: Was there any substance on the floor?

A: Cooking oil. A broken bottle. I hadn't seen it before because the crowd was blocking my view. Once I noticed it, I had Carla get the caution signs and cleaning supplies.

Q: Did Mrs. Okonkwo say how the fall occurred?

A: She said she stepped on something slippery. She thought she was going to be fine, and then suddenly she wasn't. She kept saying she should have been watching where she was going. I told her this wasn't her fault.

topic: A store manager is questioned about a customer slip-and-fall on their premises
text:
Q: Mr. Reeves, you've stated that you completed the incident report, correct?

A: Yes.

Q: Let's go through that report together. It says here that the fall occurred at approximately 2:15 p.m. Is that accurate?

A: That's my best estimate based on the timestamps from our security system.

Q: And you wrote that the cause was, quote, "unknown liquid substance." Why didn't you identify what the liquid was?

A: Because I didn't know. It was clear. Could have been water, could have been something else. I wasn't going to guess on an official document.

Q: Fair enough. The report also indicates that Mr. Chen was transported by ambulance. Can you tell me about his condition when the paramedics arrived?

A: He was in pain. His ankle had already started swelling. I'm not a medical professional, but it looked bad.

Q: What was your interaction with Mr. Chen before the paramedics arrived?

A: I brought him a chair from the break room so he didn't have to stay on the floor. I got him some water. I stayed with him and talked to him—just to keep him calm, keep his mind off it.

Q: What did you talk about?

A: His grandkids, actually. He showed me pictures on his phone. He has three of them. The youngest one had just started walking. He was telling me about it right up until the ambulance arrived.

Q: The report doesn't mention the source of the liquid. Did you ever determine where it came from?

A: We found that a refrigerator case had a small leak. Maintenance records show it had been flagged two weeks prior.

Q: And why wasn't it repaired in those two weeks?

A: Scheduling issues. I wish I had a better answer than that. We were waiting on a part.

Q: You understand that Mr. Chen required surgery on his ankle?

A: I do. I sent flowers to his home after. The company didn't ask me to. I just—I felt it was the right thing to do.

topic: A store manager is questioned about a customer slip-and-fall on their premises
text:
Q: You're aware of why we're here today?

A: Yes. A customer was injured at my store.

Q: And you've had time to review the circumstances?

A: I have. I've reviewed everything.

Q: Then let me ask directly: in your opinion, could this accident have been prevented?

A: That's a difficult question.

Q: I'm not asking you to speculate about hypotheticals. I'm asking for your honest professional opinion, based on what you know now.

A: Yes. I believe it could have been prevented.

Q: How so?

A: The entrance mat was worn. It had curled up at the edge. We'd ordered a replacement, but it hadn't arrived yet. If I had removed the mat entirely rather than leaving it in place, Ms. Hartwell wouldn't have tripped on it.

Q: That must be hard to think about.

A: It is. Every day.

Q: Tell me about Ms. Hartwell's fall, as you understand it.

A: She was entering the store. It had been raining—her shoes were wet. The mat edge caught her foot, and she went down hard. She hit her head on the tile.

Q: Were you there when it happened?

A: No. I was in a meeting. But I saw the security footage. I've seen it probably a hundred times. She tried to catch herself, but it happened so fast.

Q: What happened after the fall?

A: My assistant manager, Paul, was first to reach her. He called 911 immediately. She was conscious but disoriented. There was blood.

Q: From her head?

A: Yes. A laceration above her eye.

Q: Have you had any contact with Ms. Hartwell since the incident?

A: I called her daughter to check on her recovery. I left my personal number and told them to call if there was anything—anything at all—that I could do. I know it doesn't change what happened. I just wanted them to know she wasn't just a claim number to us. She's a person who got hurt walking into my store, and I think about her often.

topic: A witness is questioned about events at a party where an assault allegedly occurred
text:
Q: Mr. Patterson, I'd like to turn your attention to the evening of March 15th. You attended a party at 442 Willow Creek Drive, is that correct?

A: That's correct.

Q: And approximately what time did you arrive?

A: Around 9:15, maybe 9:20. I remember because I'd just gotten off a shift that ended at 8:30, went home to change, and drove over.

Q: Now, at some point during the evening, did you observe an altercation in the backyard?

A: I did. I was standing maybe eight feet away when it started.

Q: Eight feet. That's quite close.

A: Close enough to see everything clearly. The lighting was good back there—they had those string lights up, and there was a porch light. I had an unobstructed view.

Q: Tell me what you observed.

A: Derek Mullins approached the plaintiff from behind. He grabbed his shoulder, spun him around, and threw the first punch. A right hook to the jaw. The plaintiff stumbled back into the patio table, knocked over several drinks, and before he could recover, Mullins hit him twice more.

Q: You saw Mullins throw the first punch.

A: Without question. The plaintiff's hands were at his sides. He was mid-conversation with someone else—I think it was the host's sister—and had no idea Mullins was coming.

Q: Were there any words exchanged before the physical contact?

A: Mullins said something as he grabbed him. I heard "You think you can talk to her like that?" or something very close to that.

Q: And what happened after the three punches you described?

A: Two other guests pulled Mullins back. The plaintiff was on the ground at that point, bleeding from his mouth. I helped him sit up against the side of the house while someone called 911.

Q: Did you see the plaintiff make any aggressive movements toward Mr. Mullins at any point that evening?

A: None. I'd been at that party for over two hours by then, and I never saw the plaintiff so much as raise his voice.

Q: Thank you, Mr. Patterson. That's helpful.

A: Of course.

---

topic: A witness is questioned about events at a party where an assault allegedly occurred
text:
Q: Ms. Vance, you were in the kitchen when you heard a commotion outside, correct?

A: I was in the kitchen, yes.

Q: What did you do when you heard it?

A: I walked to the sliding door and looked out.

Q: And what did you see?

A: Two men on the ground.

Q: Could you identify them?

A: Not at first.

Q: At some point you did identify them?

A: After a few seconds, yeah.

Q: Who were they?

A: I recognized Marcus—the guy who got hurt—because of his jacket. Red bomber jacket. The other one I didn't know by name.

Q: But you've since learned his name?

A: I've heard it, yeah.

Q: What is it?

A: Derek something.

Q: Mullins?

A: Maybe. I don't know him personally.

Q: Fair enough. Now, when you looked through the sliding door, describe the positions of these two men.

A: One was on top of the other.

Q: Which one was on top?

A: The one who wasn't Marcus.

Q: And what was he doing?

A: It looked like he was hitting him. Or had just finished. People were pulling him off.

Q: Did you see any punches land?

A: I saw his arm come down once or twice. I couldn't tell you exactly where it connected.

Q: Did you go outside?

A: No.

Q: Why not?

A: I don't get involved in things like that. I stayed inside until the ambulance came.

Q: Thank you, Ms. Vance. Let's move on.

---

topic: A witness is questioned about events at a party where an assault allegedly occurred
text:
Q: You testified a moment ago that you'd had "a few beers" by the time of the incident.

A: That's right.

Q: How many is a few?

A: Three, maybe four over the course of about three hours. I wasn't drunk, if that's what you're getting at.

Q: I'm simply trying to establish the facts. Would you say your perception was impaired?

A: No. I knew exactly what I was seeing.

Q: You sound certain.

A: I am certain, counselor. I've been to plenty of parties, had plenty of beers, and I know the difference between being impaired and being sober enough to trust my own eyes.

Q: Let's talk about what your eyes saw, then. You claim my client struck the plaintiff.

A: I don't claim it. I watched it happen.

Q: From what distance?

A: I was on the deck. Maybe fifteen feet.

Q: Fifteen feet, at night, after several drinks—

A: There were lights. Tiki torches, string lights, a spotlight over the garage. That backyard was brighter than this room.

Q: Was anyone standing between you and the altercation?

A: No one. I had a clear sightline because I'd just stepped outside to get some air. Most people were still inside.

Q: Is it possible you saw the plaintiff make a threatening gesture toward my client first?

A: It's not possible because it didn't happen. Your client walked up to a man who was minding his own business and attacked him. I watched the whole thing, start to finish.

Q: You seem very sure of the sequence.

A: I am very sure, because I was there, I was watching, and I remember exactly what I saw. Ask me again a hundred different ways—my answer won't change.

---

topic: A witness is questioned about events at a party where an assault allegedly occurred
text:
Q: Mr. Franklin, let's slow down for a moment. You said you heard shouting before you saw anything.

A: Yeah, I heard yelling coming from outside. That's what made me look.

Q: What did you hear specifically?

A: Couldn't make out words. Just loud, angry voices. Male voices.

Q: More than one voice?

A: Uh—I think so? It's hard to say.

Q: Take your time.

A: I want to say two voices, but I'm not a hundred percent sure. It could have been one person yelling and someone else responding normally. The music was pretty loud inside.

Q: That's fair. What happened when you went to look?

A: I walked toward the back door, and by the time I got there, I saw a guy on the ground.

Q: Just one person on the ground?

A: At that moment, yeah. Someone else was standing over him. Then other people kind of swarmed in.

Q: Did you see any physical contact between them?

A: Not directly. I mean, I saw the aftermath. The guy on the ground was holding his face.

Q: But you didn't witness a punch being thrown?

A: No, I—no. By the time I could see clearly, it seemed like it was already over.

Q: So you can't testify as to who initiated physical contact?

A: I can't, no. I only saw what came after.

Q: I appreciate your honesty, Mr. Franklin. Let me ask you about what happened next.

A: Sure, whatever helps.

---

topic: A witness is questioned about events at a party where an assault allegedly occurred
text:
Q: Ms. Chen, you were the one who called 911 that night, correct?

A: I was.

Q: What made you decide to make that call?

A: I saw a man on the ground who was clearly injured. There was blood on his face. It seemed obvious someone needed to call for help, and nobody else had their phone out yet.

Q: Where were you standing when you made the call?

A: I'd come outside through the side gate. I was maybe twenty feet from where he was lying.

Q: Did you witness the assault itself?

A: I saw the tail end of it.

Q: Describe what you saw.

A: A man—who I now know is the defendant—was being restrained by two other guests. He was trying to pull free, still shouting. The injured man was on his back near an overturned chair.

Q: What was the defendant shouting?

A: Something like "He had it coming" and "Get off me." He was very agitated.

Q: Did the injured man say anything?

A: Not that I could hear. He seemed dazed. Someone was kneeling next to him, telling him to stay still.

Q: After you called 911, what did you do?

A: I stayed on the line with the dispatcher and tried to keep people back. The dispatcher asked me questions about his condition, whether he was conscious, that sort of thing. I relayed what I could see.

Q: Did the defendant remain at the scene?

A: For a few minutes. Then he broke away from the people holding him and left through the back gate. Someone yelled after him, but he didn't stop.

Q: Did anyone try to follow him?

A: Not that I saw. Everyone was focused on the injured man.

Q: You've been very clear, Ms. Chen. Just a few more questions.

A: Take your time. I want to make sure you have everything you need.

topic: An accountant is deposed about transactions they processed on behalf of a client

topic: A supervisor is deposed about performance reviews given to an employee who was later fired

topic: An employee is deposed about a coworker's termination they believe was retaliatory
text:
Q: Ms. Chen, how long did you work alongside David Okonkwo?

topic: An employee is deposed about a coworker's termination they believe was retaliatory

topic: An employee is deposed about a coworker's termination they believe was retaliatory
text:

topic: An accountant is deposed about transactions they processed on behalf of a client
text:
Q: Good morning. Thank you for being here today. Could you please state your name and professional credentials for the record?

A: Of course. I'm Patricia Bellamy, CPA. I've been licensed in this state for twenty-two years, and I've had my own practice for the last fourteen. Happy to be here, though I know that sounds odd given the circumstances.

Q: Not odd at all. We appreciate your cooperation. Now, Ms. Bellamy, you handled the bookkeeping for Terrace Holdings from 2019 through 2022, is that correct?

A: That's right. They were one of my longer-standing clients. Gerald—Mr. Harmon—came to me originally because his previous accountant had retired, and he wanted someone who'd really take the time to understand his business. Which I tried to do.

Q: And in that role, you would have processed wire transfers on behalf of the company?

A: I did, yes. Though I should clarify—I prepared the documentation and verified the accounts, but Gerald or his office manager actually executed the transfers through their bank portal. I wanted to make sure you had the full picture there.

Q: That's helpful clarification. Do you recall a series of transfers in late 2021 to an entity called Coastal Meridian LLC?

A: I do remember those. There were four of them, I believe, between October and December. They stood out to me because the amounts were quite regular—$47,500 each time, if memory serves.

Q: Did you have any concerns about those transfers at the time?

A: You know, I thought about that a lot after everything came to light. At the time, Gerald told me it was for consulting services related to a coastal development project he was exploring. That made sense to me given his other investments. I documented it just as he described.

Q: Did you ever see a contract or invoice from Coastal Meridian?

A: I asked for supporting documentation—I always do, it's just good practice—and Gerald said he'd get it to me. He was usually very organized, so I didn't press too hard initially. Looking back, I wish I had followed up more persistently.

Q: I understand. These things are always clearer in hindsight. When did you eventually receive that documentation?

A: That's just it—I never did receive it. By the time I realized it was still outstanding, we were into tax season, and then... well, then the investigation started. I've felt terrible about that gap, honestly.

Q: Ms. Bellamy, no one is suggesting you did anything wrong. We're just trying to understand the sequence of events.

A: I appreciate you saying that. I've been in this profession a long time, and my clients' trust means everything to me. Gerald's situation has been difficult because I genuinely liked working with him.

Q: Just a few more questions. Did Mr. Harmon ever discuss the principals behind Coastal Meridian with you?

A: He mentioned a name once—I believe it was someone named Reeves or Reece. He spoke about this person as an old friend from his chamber of commerce days. That's all I recall specifically.

Q: Thank you. That's very helpful.

A: Of course. Whatever helps sort this out. I really do want to see things made right.

---

A: Almost nine years. Started with them in 2014, right when they were expanding from two dealerships to four.

A: It was. Busy for all of us. A lot of moving parts when you're scaling up like that. I remember a lot of late nights getting everything structured properly.

Q: I'd like to ask you about a specific account. The operating reserve account ending in 4471. Do you recall that one?

A: The 4471 account. Yes, that was their buffer account for unexpected expenses—equipment failures, that sort of thing.

Q: And you had signatory authority on that account?

A: I did. Thomas—Mr. Whitfield—added me as a signatory in 2016 because there were times he'd be traveling and something urgent would come up.

Q: Did you ever exercise that authority?

A: Twice. Once for an emergency HVAC repair at the Eastgate location. Once to cover a payroll timing issue when their main account had a hold placed on it by mistake.

Q: Both legitimate business expenses.

A: Absolutely. Both documented, both approved by Thomas before and after.

Q: What about the transfer on March 3rd, 2022? The one for $83,000 to Whitfield Family Trust?

A: I didn't authorize that transfer.

Q: The bank's records show your authorization code.

A: I understand that's what the records show. But I did not authorize that transfer. Someone used my credentials without my knowledge.

Q: Did you report this?

A: I reported it the moment I discovered it, which was March 7th. I called Thomas immediately. Then I called the bank. Then I contacted my professional liability carrier. I have records of all of those calls.

topic: An accountant is deposed about transactions they processed on behalf of a client
text:
Q: State your name.

A: Rebecca Chen.

Q: You worked for Hartley & Associates from 2018 to 2023?

A: I did.

Q: As a staff accountant?

A: I started as staff, yes. I was promoted to senior associate in 2020.

Q: Congratulations on that.

A: Thank you. I worked hard for it.

Q: I'm sure you did. Now, in your role as senior associate, you handled the Brennan Logistics account?

A: I was part of the team, yes. There were three of us assigned to that client.

Q: Who else was on the team?

A: David Park and our supervisor, Maureen Kowalski.

Q: How was the work divided?

A: David handled payroll and benefits accounting. I handled accounts payable and vendor payments. Maureen reviewed everything and handled client communications.

Q: So vendor payments were your area specifically.

A: That's correct.

Q: Ms. Chen, I want to take you through some of these carefully because I think your perspective is valuable here. There's no rush.

A: All right.

Q: In September 2022, Brennan Logistics began making payments to a vendor called TrueNorth Consulting. Do you remember those?

A: I do. They came through as approved invoices from the client's AP department.

Q: What was your process when you received an approved invoice?

A: I would verify that the vendor was in our system, confirm the invoice matched a purchase order or had appropriate authorization, then schedule the payment according to the client's payment terms.

Q: Was TrueNorth already in the system?

A: No, I had to add them. That's not unusual—businesses add new vendors regularly.

Q: What information did you have to add them?

A: The W-9 they provided, banking information for ACH payments, contact information.

Q: Did anything about TrueNorth give you pause?

A: Not initially. They had a professional invoice format, a valid tax ID, everything looked legitimate. It wasn't until January that I started noticing things.

Q: What did you notice?

A: The invoices were always round numbers. Always. And they were approved very quickly through the client's system—faster than typical invoices. It caught my attention.

Q: What did you do with that observation?

A: I brought it to Maureen. She said she'd look into it. Two weeks later, I was told Brennan Logistics had ended their engagement with our firm. A month after that, the subpoenas started arriving.

---

topic: An accountant is deposed about transactions they processed on behalf of a client
text:
Q: Good afternoon, Ms. Yee.

A: That's correct. I handled his personal financial affairs—tax planning, investment tracking, that sort of thing. His company had its own accounting department.

Q: How did Mr. Rhodes come to retain you?

Q: You helped him get organized?

A: I did. Over about six months, we got everything sorted. Accounts consolidated, a budget established, investment accounts properly allocated. He was a good student, actually. Asked a lot of questions.

Q: That brings us to the investment accounts. Specifically the brokerage account at Mercer Sachs, the one ending in 7829.

A: Yes, his primary investment account.

A: I've known him for four years. Some things you come to understand about a person. He's not cunning enough for what you're suggesting.

topic: A witness is asked about a car accident they saw from their front porch
text:
Q: Good morning. You were home on the afternoon of March 15th, is that correct?

A: Yes, sir, I was right there on my porch. Had my coffee, had my newspaper, and I had the best seat in the house for what happened next.

Q: Tell me what you observed.

A: Oh, where do I start? The red pickup—and I mean cherry red, beautiful truck actually—came barreling down Maple Street from the north. The sedan, that silver Honda, was pulling out of the Hendersons' driveway. Now, the Honda driver, she had her signal on, I noticed that specifically, she was doing everything right from what I could tell.

Q: How fast would you estimate the pickup was traveling?

A: Fast. Too fast for a residential street, I can tell you that much. I've lived on that street forty-two years, and I've seen people speed, but this guy was really moving. I'd say fifty, maybe fifty-five? The limit's twenty-five, so he was at least double.

Q: You mentioned the Honda's turn signal. What else do you recall about the Honda's movements?

A: She was easing out real careful, checking both ways—I saw her head turn, actually, left then right—and she'd just gotten her front end past the mailbox when the truck came over that little rise by the Patels' place. You know that rise? It's deceptive, hides cars coming from the north.

Q: Did you hear anything?

A: Did I hear anything! The brakes on that truck squealed like nothing I've ever heard. Then the crash, obviously. Glass breaking. And then—this is the part I keep thinking about—total silence for maybe three seconds before the woman in the Honda started screaming.

Q: What did you do after the collision?

A: I was off that porch faster than I've moved in years. Called 911 while I was running over. Gave them the whole description, stayed on the line like they told me, checked on the woman in the Honda first because her car took the worst of it.

Q: Did you speak with the pickup driver?

A: He was standing by his truck looking at his bumper, if you can believe it. I went over and asked if he was hurt, and he just kept saying "she came out of nowhere." I bit my tongue, but I wanted to say, sir, I watched the whole thing, and that is not what happened.

Q: Did you tell him that?

A: I did. I said, "I saw the whole thing from my porch." He didn't like that one bit.

topic: A witness is asked about a car accident they saw from their front porch

Q: State your name for the record.

A: No.

topic: A witness is asked about a car accident they saw from their front porch

Q: This is exciting—I've been looking forward to hearing from you. You're something of a key witness in this matter.

topic: A witness is asked about a car accident they saw from their front porch
text:
Q: You witnessed an accident on Birch Street on January 8th?

A: I witnessed what I would describe as a near-miracle that nobody was killed, yes.

Q: Describe what you saw.

A: Two cars, head-on, right in front of my house. The blue car crossed the center line—and I don't mean drifted, I mean crossed—and went straight into the path of the gray car coming the other direction.

Q: Why do you say it was a miracle?

A: Because the blue car must have been going forty, forty-five, and the gray car was going at least thirty, and the woman in the gray car walked away with a broken arm. That's incredible when you think about it.

Q: Let's focus on the moments before impact. You say the blue car crossed the center line?

A: By a good four feet at least. I was watching this happen thinking "no, no, no" the whole time.

Q: Could you tell what caused the blue car to cross over?

A: I've thought about this a lot. The driver was looking down. Not at the road, down, like at his lap. Phone, probably. I can't prove it was a phone, but what else would it be?

Q: You didn't actually see a phone?

A: I saw his head position. Chin down, eyes down. For several seconds before impact.

Q: Did the gray car take any evasive action?

A: She tried to swerve right, and that probably saved her life, honestly. If she'd been two feet more to the left, that would've been a direct driver's-door hit.

Q: Did you speak to either driver afterward?

A: I sat with the woman from the gray car until the ambulance came. She was shaking so badly. I held her hand and told her help was coming. She kept saying "I didn't see him until it was too late," and I told her, "Honey, this was not your fault."

Q: Did you tell her what you observed?

A: I told her exactly what I saw. I felt she deserved to know.

topic: A witness is asked about a car accident they saw from their front porch

topic: A contractor is questioned about delays that caused a construction project to fail
text:
Q: Mr. Hardin, I'd like to ask you about the six-week delay that occurred between April and mid-May of 2022. Can you tell me what happened during that period?

A: Yes. We lost our lead foreman, Tom Castellano. He'd been with me for eleven years.

Q: When you say "lost," you mean he left the company?

A: No, ma'am. He passed away. Heart attack on a Sunday morning. He was fifty-two.

Q: I'm sorry. Take your time if you need it.

A: Thank you. I'm alright. It's just—when you lose someone like that, it's not just the work that stops. It's everything. The crew, they looked to him. I looked to him.

Q: I understand. During those six weeks, what steps did you take to address the gap in leadership on the project?

A: I tried to step in myself at first. But I was already managing two other sites. And honestly, I wasn't in the best shape either. Tom and I came up together in this business.

Q: Did you communicate with Westbrook Development about the impact this would have on the timeline?

A: I called Daniel Reeves the day after the funeral. Told him we were in trouble. He said he understood. At least, that's what he said then.

Q: What was Mr. Reeves's response specifically?

A: He said, "Frank, do what you need to do. We'll figure out the schedule." Those were his words. I remember because I was grateful for them.

Q: Did you document that conversation in writing?

A: I didn't. I should have. But at the time, I was just trying to hold things together. For the crew, for Tom's family, for the project. I wasn't thinking about protecting myself legally.

Q: When you eventually brought in a replacement foreman, who was that?

A: Mike Serrano. Good man. But he needed time to learn how Tom ran things. Tom had his own systems, his own relationships with the subs. You can't just replace eleven years overnight.

Q: Did Mr. Serrano express any concerns to you about being able to meet the revised timeline?

A: He told me he'd do his best. And he did. He worked weekends, stayed late. The whole crew did. They were doing it for Tom as much as anything.

Q: Mr. Hardin, knowing what you know now, is there anything you would have done differently during that period?

A: I would have asked for more help sooner. I was trying to carry it all myself, and I couldn't. I know that cost us time. But when you're grieving, you don't always see things clearly. I suppose that's not much of an excuse.

Q: It's not an excuse I'm asking for. I'm just trying to understand what happened.

A: I appreciate that.

---

topic: A contractor is questioned about delays that caused a construction project to fail
text:
Q: Let's talk about the concrete pour scheduled for October 14th. That was delayed by eleven days, correct?

A: That's correct.

Q: And the reason given in your report was "weather conditions." Is that accurate?

A: That's what I wrote, yes.

Q: Was there more to it than that?

A: There's always more to it. The weather was part of it. But I also had a supplier issue I didn't put in the report.

Q: Why didn't you include that?

A: Because I was trying to protect someone. One of my material suppliers—he's a small operation, family-owned. His wife had been diagnosed with cancer that summer, and he was struggling to keep things running. His delivery was late, and I covered for him.

Q: You falsified a project report?

A: I didn't falsify it. The weather was a factor. I just didn't mention the other factor.

Q: Mr. Brennan, do you understand that distinction matters legally?

A: I do now. At the time, I was thinking about a man I've known for fifteen years who was watching his wife go through chemotherapy. I was thinking about how one bad report could cost him his contracts with every builder in the county.

Q: So you made a choice to prioritize your personal relationship over accurate documentation.

A: I made a choice to be a human being. Maybe that was wrong from a legal standpoint. But I've seen what happens when people in this industry turn on each other. I wasn't willing to do that to Ray.

Q: Did the eleven-day delay affect subsequent phases of construction?

A: It pushed back the framing start by about a week, once you account for curing time. So yes, it had a ripple effect.

Q: Were there other instances where you omitted information from reports to protect suppliers or subcontractors?

A: No. That was the only time.

Q: How can I be certain of that?

A: Because I'm telling you. And because I'm sitting here admitting to the one time I did it, which I didn't have to do. If I were in the habit of lying, I wouldn't have told you about Ray.

Q: Fair enough. Let's move on.

---

topic: A contractor is questioned about delays that caused a construction project to fail
text:
Q: Ms. Delgado, you were the project manager on the Riverside Commons development, correct?

A: I was, yes.

Q: And you reported directly to the defendant, Mr. Carver?

A: I reported to Mr. Carver, but I wouldn't use the word "directly." There were layers.

Q: Can you explain what you mean by "layers"?

A: I mean that when I raised concerns, they didn't always reach him. And when they did, they'd been filtered through people who had their own reasons for softening the message.

Q: Did you raise concerns about the project timeline?

A: Many times. Starting in March of 2021. I told anyone who would listen that we were understaffed for the scope of work.

Q: What response did you receive?

A: I was told to "make it work." That phrase exactly. More than once.

Q: That must have been frustrating.

A: It was exhausting. I had twenty-three workers trying to do the job of forty. Half of them were putting in sixty-hour weeks just to stay on schedule. I watched good people burn out. One of my best electricians—young guy, maybe twenty-six—he collapsed on site from dehydration because he'd been pushing himself so hard. That's when I really started making noise.

Q: What happened after that incident?

A: They brought in eight more workers. Temporary labor, not trained on our systems. It actually slowed us down for the first two weeks while we got them up to speed.

Q: Did you document your staffing concerns in writing?

A: I did. I have emails going back to March. I can provide them.

Q: We'd appreciate that. Ms. Delgado, do you believe Mr. Carver was aware of the conditions you've described?

A: I believe he should have been. Whether he chose to look closely enough to see them, I can't say. But I can tell you that the people between me and him knew. And they had a responsibility to tell him.

Q: Is there anything else you think is relevant to the delays on this project?

A: Just that the people who worked on that site gave everything they had. The failure wasn't theirs. They deserved better than what they got—from the company, from the client, from all of us who were supposed to be leading.

---

topic: A contractor is questioned about delays that caused a construction project to fail
text:
Q: Mr. Okonkwo, I want to ask about the change orders submitted between June and August. There were fourteen of them in that period. Is that typical?

A: No. That's high. Very high.

Q: What was driving so many changes?

A: The client kept revising the specifications. Every week, it seemed like there was something new they wanted.

Q: Did you push back on any of these revisions?

A: I tried. But you have to understand the position we were in. The client was threatening to pull the contract entirely. They had other bidders waiting. So we tried to accommodate.

Q: Even when accommodation meant delays?

A: Even then. Look, I have people who depend on this company for their paychecks. Families. If we lose a contract that size, I'm laying off fifteen, maybe twenty workers. These aren't just numbers to me. I know their names. I know their kids' names.

Q: So you accepted changes you knew would cause delays because you were afraid of losing the contract?

A: I accepted changes because I was trying to keep people employed while still delivering what the client wanted. It wasn't fear. It was responsibility.

Q: Did you communicate to the client that these changes would affect the completion date?

A: Every single time. In writing. I have the correspondence.

Q: And what was their response?

A: They acknowledged the delays in principle but disputed the extent. They always wanted to negotiate down the timeline extensions. "Can't you do it in two weeks instead of three?" That kind of thing.

Q: Did you agree to shortened timelines?

A: Sometimes. Probably more than I should have. But when someone's holding your livelihood over your head, you make compromises you wouldn't otherwise make. That's not an excuse. It's just the truth.

Q: Mr. Okonkwo, do you feel you bear responsibility for the project's ultimate failure?

A: I bear some, yes. But I also did everything I could to make it work, with the resources and constraints I had. I don't know what else I could have done differently, short of walking away. And walking away would have hurt a lot of people who didn't deserve it.

Q: I appreciate your candor.

A: I'm just telling you what happened.

---

topic: A contractor is questioned about delays that caused a construction project to fail
text:
Q: Mr. Fontaine, were you present at the August 3rd meeting where the decision was made to proceed despite the foundation issues?

A: I was.

Q: What was the response to her recommendation?

Q: Can you be more specific about where that pressure came from?

Q: I understand, but I need you to answer the question.

A: Alright. Victor Sloane, the development director, said we couldn't afford another delay. He said the investors were already asking questions. And Marcus Webb—he was the owner's representative—said the same thing, but more forcefully.

Q: What do you mean by "more forcefully"?

A: He raised his voice. Told Dr. Yee she was being overcautious. He asked her if she wanted to be the reason the project went under. That's a direct quote. I remember it because of the look on her face.

Q: How did Dr. Yee respond?

A: She held her ground for a while. She explained the risks, showed her data. But eventually she said she'd sign off if we agreed to additional monitoring during construction.

Q: Did you agree to that compromise?

A: The group did. I had reservations, but I didn't voice them strongly enough. That's something I've had to live with.

Q: Why didn't you voice your concerns?

A: Because I could see what it was costing Dr. Yee to fight alone. She was the only one in that room pushing back, and she was getting beaten down. I should have stood with her. Instead, I stayed quiet and let her carry the weight. I'm not proud of that.

Q: What happened with the east wing ultimately?

A: The settling got worse. We had to tear out four months of work and start over. Dr. Yee had been right.

Q: Did anyone acknowledge that she had been right?

A: Not to her face. But I sent her an email afterward. Privately. Told her I was sorry I hadn't supported her when it mattered. She wrote back two words: "Thank you."

Q: That's all she said?

A: That's all she needed to say.

topic: A nurse is questioned about a patient fall that occurred during her shift
text:
Q: Please state your name and current position for the record.

A: Rebecca Torres, RN, and I've been on the medical-surgical unit at St. Anne's for eleven years now—eleven years this past March, actually. I absolutely love what I do.

Q: Thank you. Now, directing your attention to the morning of September 14th—

A: The fall. Yes. I've been waiting to talk about this because there's so much context that matters here.

Q: Were you the nurse assigned to Mr. Garrett's room that morning?

A: I was, and I have to say, I was so glad I was his nurse that day. We'd built a real rapport over his three days on the unit. He trusted me. That matters with fall-risk patients—that trust, that communication.

Q: What time did you first see Mr. Garrett on September 14th?

A: 6:47 AM, right after shift change. I went straight to his room because I always prioritize my high-risk patients first thing. I've developed this whole system over the years—I call it my "sunrise round"—where I check bed alarms, positioning, call light access, all of it before the day gets chaotic.

Q: Was his bed alarm activated at that time?

A: Absolutely. I checked it myself. Tested the sensor pad, watched the green light confirm it was armed. I even documented it in my notes because I believe in thoroughness. Would you like me to walk you through exactly how those alarms work? The technology is actually fascinating—

Q: That won't be necessary. What happened at approximately 8:15 AM?

A: Oh, I can tell you precisely. I was in room 412, two doors down, administering IV antibiotics to Mrs. Chen, and I heard the alarm trigger. I dropped everything—well, secured the IV first, obviously, safety always—and I ran. I mean ran. Got to his room in maybe twelve seconds.

Q: And what did you find?

A: Mr. Garrett on the floor beside his bed. But here's what I want to emphasize—he was alert, talking to me, no visible head trauma. My training kicked in immediately. C-spine precautions, neuro check, called for assistance. The whole team responded beautifully.

Q: Had Mr. Garrett attempted to get out of bed unassisted before?

A: Twice during my shifts, yes, and I'd addressed it both times with patient education. That's actually something I'm really passionate about—fall prevention education. I've even submitted a proposal to our nurse manager about implementing a new teach-back protocol—

Q: I appreciate that. Let's stay focused on September 14th.

A: Of course, of course. I just think the bigger picture matters, you know?

topic: A nurse is questioned about a patient fall that occurred during her shift

Q: Did help arrive?

A: Not before the fall, no.

topic: A nurse is questioned about a patient fall that occurred during her shift

topic: A nurse is questioned about a patient fall that occurred during her shift
text:
Q: Walk me through your fall prevention assessment process for Mr. Kim.

A: Well, first I want to explain that fall prevention is something I take incredibly seriously. I actually just completed an advanced certification in it last month—forty hours of additional training, all on my own time.

Q: That's commendable. Let's talk about Mr. Kim specifically.

A: Absolutely. So when I got report from night shift, I was immediately concerned because his Morse Fall Scale score was 55, which puts him solidly in the high-risk category. I went to his room first—before I even looked at my other patients—because I wanted to assess the environment with fresh eyes.

Q: What did you observe?

A: Several things. His bed alarm was on, which was good. Side rails were in the proper configuration—two up, two down, per policy to prevent entrapment. But the call light had slipped down beside the mattress, so he couldn't reach it easily. I fixed that immediately.

Q: What else?

A: I noticed he seemed restless. Agitated, even. I asked him if he needed to use the bathroom, and he said no, but I could tell something was off. So I made a note to check on him more frequently than the hourly rounding would require.

Q: Did you document that plan?

A: I did. I wrote in my notes—I can quote it actually—"Patient appears restless, will increase monitoring frequency."

Q: What happened next?

A: I got pulled into an emergency in room 410. Code Blue. I had to respond—that's not optional. I was gone from the floor for about forty-five minutes.

Q: And the fall occurred during that time?

A: Yes. And I have to tell you, I've replayed it in my mind a hundred times. What could I have done differently? I've actually used this experience to advocate for better staffing ratios. I've spoken at two staff meetings about it. I submitted a formal safety report. Because if there had been adequate coverage—

Q: Nurse, I need to ask the questions.

A: Of course. I'm sorry. I just—this case matters to me. Patient safety matters to me. I want to help you understand what happened.

Q: I appreciate that. Let's continue.

topic: A witness is questioned about a fire they discovered in a neighboring unit

topic: A witness is questioned about a fire they discovered in a neighboring unit

topic: A witness is questioned about a fire they discovered in a neighboring unit

topic: A project manager is questioned about deadlines they missed on a software contract
text:
Q: Mr. Holloway, I want to turn your attention to the March 15th milestone. That was the deadline for the beta release, correct?

A: Of course.

topic: A project manager is questioned about deadlines they missed on a software contract
text:
Q: Ms. Quintero, you were the project manager for the Helios implementation, correct?

A: That's right.

Q: And you're aware that three of the seven contractual deadlines were missed?

A: I am. Painfully aware.

Q: Let's start with the first missed deadline—the requirements document, due October 1st. What happened there?

A: Honestly? I underestimated the scope. That's on me. The client's system architecture was more complex than what was represented in the initial meetings, and I should have built in more buffer time.

Q: You're saying you made an error in judgment?

A: I'm saying I made a mistake, yes. I'm not here to blame anyone else for that one.

Q: I see. And the second deadline—the integration testing phase?

A: That one was more complicated. We were dependent on API documentation from the client's legacy vendor, and it kept getting delayed.

Q: Did you escalate that dependency issue?

A: I did, multiple times. But I want to be careful here—the people at Meridian, their IT team, they were stretched incredibly thin. They'd just gone through layoffs. I watched their lead engineer, Tom, work eighteen-hour days trying to get us what we needed.

Q: You seem to have some sympathy for Meridian's team.

A: I have respect for people who are doing their best in a bad situation. Tom's not the reason this project went sideways.

Q: Then who is, in your view?

A: I think there's plenty of responsibility to go around, including mine. I'm just trying to give you an honest picture.

Q: That's all I'm asking for, Ms. Quintero. Let's move to the third deadline.

topic: A project manager is questioned about deadlines they missed on a software contract
text:
Q: Mr. Patel, I want to ask about the delay in delivering the user authentication module.

Q: That was due November 30th, and it was delivered December 14th, correct?
