A: Yes.

Q: What caused the delay?

A: There was a security vulnerability discovered in the framework we were using. It would have been irresponsible to deliver the module without addressing it.

Q: So you made a judgment call to delay delivery rather than deliver an insecure product?

A: I did.

Q: Did you discuss this with the client before making that decision?

A: I tried. I left two voicemails for Mr. Brennan and sent an email. I didn't hear back for three days.

Q: That must have been frustrating.

A: It was. But I also know Mr. Brennan was dealing with a lot at the time. His company was going through a merger. I don't think he was ignoring me; I think he was overwhelmed.

Q: You seem hesitant to criticize him.

A: I'm hesitant to criticize anyone who's doing their best. We were all under pressure. The situation didn't bring out the best in the process, but I don't think anyone acted in bad faith.

Q: Let me ask you directly: do you believe your team bears responsibility for the missed deadline?

A: I believe we made the right call on the security issue. If that means we bear responsibility for the delay, then yes, I'll own that. I'd rather be two weeks late than deliver something that puts people's data at risk.

Q: Fair enough, Mr. Patel. Let's talk about the documentation that accompanied that module.

topic: A project manager is questioned about deadlines they missed on a software contract
text:
Q: Ms. Chen, how long had you been managing software projects before the Vector account?

A: About six years at that point.

Q: So you were experienced.

A: I'd like to think so, yes.

Q: And yet the Vector project had significant delays. Four missed milestones.

A: That's correct.

Q: I'm not trying to make this adversarial, Ms. Chen. I'm genuinely trying to understand what went wrong.

A: I appreciate that. It's not a simple answer.

Q: Take your time.

A: The first delay—the architecture review—that was on us. We had a junior architect assigned who wasn't ready for a project of that complexity, and I didn't catch it early enough. I should have.

Q: What happened when you realized the problem?

A: I reassigned the work to a senior team member. But by then we'd lost two weeks.

Q: Did you consider asking for help? Additional resources?

A: I did ask. I was told the budget didn't allow for it. And I understood that—the company was going through a difficult quarter. People were worried about layoffs. I didn't want to push too hard and put anyone's job at risk.

Q: So you were trying to protect your team.

A: I was trying to do right by everyone. The client, my team, the company. Sometimes those interests don't line up neatly.

Q: It sounds like you were in a difficult position.

A: I was. But I'm not asking for sympathy. I'm just trying to explain what happened.

Q: I understand. Let's move on to the second missed milestone.

topic: A project manager is questioned about deadlines they missed on a software contract
text:
Q: Mr. Franklin, the deployment deadline was January 15th. Correct?

A: That's what the contract said, yes.

Q: And deployment actually occurred on February 2nd.

A: Correct.

Q: Eighteen days late.

A: I know the math.

Q: You seem frustrated.

A: I'm not frustrated with you. I'm frustrated with the situation. We did everything we could to meet that deadline, and we still fell short, and now we're here, and I have to explain it in a way that fits into a legal proceeding.

Q: I understand this isn't easy. Would you like to take a moment?

A: No. No, I'm fine. I just—I want you to understand that there were real people involved in this. My team worked through the holidays. One of my developers, Sarah, missed her daughter's first Christmas because she was debugging authentication issues at two in the morning. And I'm the one who asked her to do that.

Q: That's a significant sacrifice.

A: It is. And I carry that. So when we talk about deadlines like they're just numbers on a spreadsheet, I need you to know that there were costs. Human costs.

Q: I hear you, Mr. Franklin. I do.

A: Okay. Thank you.

Q: Let me ask—given those sacrifices, why was the project still eighteen days late?

A: Because the client changed the security requirements on January 3rd. We found out twelve days before the deadline that everything we'd built needed to be re-architected.

Q: Was that change documented?

A: It was in an email from their CTO. I can provide it.

Q: Please do. And Mr. Franklin—thank you for your candor today.

A: I'm just trying to tell the truth.

topic: A building inspector is deposed about a structural assessment they signed off on
text:
Q: Mr. Hendricks, you conducted the structural assessment of 445 Waverly Drive on March 14th of last year, correct?

A: Yes. That's correct. March 14th.

Q: And you signed off on that assessment, indicating the building was structurally sound?

A: I signed the assessment, yes. The report—it reflects my findings at the time of inspection.

Q: At the time of inspection. What do you mean by that qualifier?

A: I just mean—I mean that inspections are a snapshot. They reflect conditions as observed on that specific date. That's standard. That's how all inspections work.

Q: I understand. Let me ask you about the basement support columns specifically. You examined those?

A: I did. I examined them. I have notes. Do you want me to refer to my notes? I can refer to my notes if that would be helpful.

Q: That won't be necessary right now. Did you observe any cracking in those columns?

A: Minor surface cracking. Hairline. It's—you see that in poured concrete of that age. It's not necessarily indicative of structural compromise. I want to be clear about that.

Q: You want to be clear.

A: I just—yes. I want the record to reflect that hairline cracking is common and doesn't automatically suggest a problem. I followed protocol.

Q: Did you document the cracking in your report?

A: I would have to look at the report to confirm the exact language I used. I don't want to misstate anything.

Q: You don't recall whether you documented visible cracking in a structural assessment you signed?

A: I documented my findings. I'm certain I documented my findings. I'm just—I want to be precise about the specific language because the specific language matters, doesn't it?

Q: I'm asking the questions, Mr. Hendricks. Did anyone else accompany you during this inspection?

A: No. I was alone. That's standard. That's—we don't typically have two inspectors on routine assessments. It's not a budget item.

topic: A building inspector is deposed about a structural assessment they signed off on
text:
Q: Ms. Torres, how long have you worked as a building inspector for the city?

A: Eleven years this October.

Q: And in those eleven years, how many structural assessments would you estimate you've conducted?

A: Hundreds. Maybe three, four hundred. It's hard to give an exact number.

Q: The Greenfield Apartments on Sycamore—that was one of those hundreds?

A: Yes.

Q: You inspected that building on August 8th?

A: Yes.

Q: The entire building? Every floor?

A: Yes.

Q: Let me rephrase. You personally walked every floor of that six-story building on August 8th?

A: I—yes.

Q: You're certain?

A: I conducted a full inspection as required.

Q: That's not what I asked. I asked if you personally walked every floor.

A: Yes.

Q: Including the fourth floor?

A: Yes.

Q: The fourth floor where the east stairwell provides access?

A: I don't understand the question.

Q: The east stairwell. Did you use it?

A: I don't specifically recall which stairwell I used.

Q: Building records show the east stairwell was barricaded for maintenance on August 8th. The only stairwell providing fourth-floor access.

A: Then I would have—there must have been another access point. The elevator.

Q: The elevator was also out of service.

A: I inspected the building. I signed the assessment because I completed the inspection.

Q: So you found some other way to the fourth floor?

A: I must have. I don't recall the specific logistics of every inspection I conduct.

topic: A building inspector is deposed about a structural assessment they signed off on
text:
Q: Good morning, Mr. Chen.

A: Good morning.

Q: Let's talk about the Wellington Tower inspection from September of last year. You're familiar with that property?

A: I am.

Q: You conducted the initial inspection on September 3rd, correct?

A: Correct.

Q: But you didn't file your report until September 22nd. Almost three weeks later. Why was that?

A: Reports take time. There's analysis, documentation, review.

Q: Three weeks of analysis for a routine structural assessment?

A: It was thorough.

Q: Let me approach this differently—and I want to make sure I understand the timeline precisely. You inspected on September 3rd. You met with the property management company on September 10th. Then you filed on September 22nd. Is that accurate?

A: I don't recall meeting with—who told you I met with property management?

Q: Your calendar, Mr. Chen. Produced in discovery. "Wellington meeting, September 10th, 2PM, Meridian Property Group."

A: That could have been—that might have been about a different matter.

Q: A different matter involving the same property you were actively assessing?

A: I don't remember the substance of that meeting.

Q: You don't remember.

A: No.

Q: Did Meridian ask you to reconsider any of your preliminary findings?

A: I don't recall.

Q: Did your final report differ from your initial observations?

A: I'd have to compare documents. I can't speak to that without reviewing the materials.

Q: Your initial notes—handwritten, also produced in discovery—mention "significant water damage to load-bearing elements." Your final report calls it "minor moisture exposure." Can you explain that revision?

A: Terminology can be refined as analysis deepens.

Q: Is that what happened here? Refined terminology?

A: I believe so. Yes.

topic: A building inspector is deposed about a structural assessment they signed off on
text:
Q: Let's talk about the Parkview Commons inspection. You conducted that assessment?

A: Yes.

Q: What date?

A: February 2nd.

Q: What were your findings?

A: The building passed inspection. Structurally adequate.

Q: Structurally adequate. That's interesting phrasing. Is that a technical term?

A: It means what it says.

Q: Your report actually uses the word "sound." Structurally sound.

A: Then that's the term I used.

Q: But just now you said "adequate." Is there a difference in your mind?

A: No.

Q: No difference between adequate and sound?

A: I'm not playing word games with you, counselor.

Q: I'm not asking you to play games. I'm asking about your professional assessment of a building that partially collapsed six months later.

A: And I've told you—I conducted an inspection, I documented my findings, and the building passed.

Q: The southeast corner. Did you inspect that area specifically?

A: Yes.

Q: How long did you spend there?

A: I don't time myself room by room.

Q: An estimate.

A: I don't have one.

Q: Five minutes? Twenty minutes? An hour?

A: Sufficient time to complete my assessment.

Q: Your assessment of an area that would later experience catastrophic failure?

A: I can't predict the future. I inspect present conditions.

Q: And present conditions on February 2nd gave you no cause for concern?

A: My report reflects my findings.

Q: That's not an answer.

A: It's the only answer I have.

topic: A building inspector is deposed about a structural assessment they signed off on
text:
Q: Mr. Patterson, you've been doing this work for how long now?

A: Sixteen years.

Q: Sixteen years. So you've seen a lot of buildings.

A: I have.

Q: Seen a lot of problems too, I imagine.

A: Some.

Q: And you know what to look for—signs of structural distress, deferred maintenance, that sort of thing?

A: I do.

Q: The Millbrook address—1847 Millbrook—you inspected that property last April?

A: Yes.

Q: Tell me about the foundation.

A: What about it?

Q: What did you observe?

A: It was—it was a poured concrete foundation, typical for the era of construction. Some settling. Nothing outside normal parameters.

Q: Some settling.

A: Yes.

Q: Did you measure the settling?

A: We don't typically—I mean, yes, I took measurements. General measurements.

Q: Do you have those measurements?

A: They'd be in my file.

Q: They're not in your file, Mr. Patterson. We've reviewed your file extensively.

A: Then I—I may have recorded them elsewhere. Or they may have been preliminary notes that didn't make it into the final documentation.

Q: Preliminary notes that you discarded?

A: Not discarded. Just—not formalized.

Q: You testified a moment ago that you took measurements.

A: I said I believed I took measurements.

Q: No. You said you took measurements. "Yes, I took measurements." Those were your words.

A: I may have misspoken. I'm trying to be accurate.

Q: Are you? Because the homeowners are now looking at three hundred thousand dollars in foundation repairs, and your report said—

A: My report said what I observed. I can't—I stand by my report.

Q: Do you?

A: Yes.

topic: A neighbor is questioned about noise complaints and a confrontation they witnessed
text:
Q: Mr. Holloway, how long have you lived at 4412 Birchwood Lane?

A: Fourteen years. Fourteen years this past April.

Q: And the Delgado family lived next door to you that entire time?

A: Almost. They moved in about six months after I did. Maria brought over a casserole. A welcome casserole, she called it, even though I'd been there longer. That was just how she was.

Q: I'm asking specifically about the night of September 14th. Were you home that evening?

A: I was home. I'm always home now.

Q: Did you hear any unusual noises coming from the Delgado residence?

A: There was music. Loud music. The kind with the bass that you feel more than hear, you know? It comes up through the floor.

Q: What time did this begin?

A: I don't... maybe eight? Eight-thirty? I wasn't keeping track. I used to not mind their music. The kids would have birthday parties and there'd be music and I never once complained. Not once in fourteen years.

Q: But you did complain on September 14th, is that correct?

A: I went over there. I don't know if that's a complaint.

Q: What happened when you went over?

A: I knocked. I waited on the porch for a while. The concrete's cracked now. It wasn't when they first moved in.

Q: Mr. Holloway, I need you to focus on what happened next.

A: I'm sorry. I'm sorry. The son answered. Not Marco—the other one. The younger one. He looked at me like he didn't recognize me. I've known him since he was four years old.

Q: What did you say to him?

A: I asked if they could turn it down. That's all. I said please. I always say please.

Q: How did he respond?

A: He said something I couldn't hear over the music, and then Marco came to the door, and then... then it became something else.

Q: What do you mean by "something else"?

A: I keep thinking if I'd just stayed home. If I'd just put in earplugs like I usually do. Fourteen years and I never once went over there to complain. Not once.

topic: A neighbor is questioned about noise complaints and a confrontation they witnessed
text:
Q: Ms. Chen, I want to be very careful with you today. I understand this is difficult.

A: I can answer your questions.

Q: Of course. I just want you to know there's no rush.

A: I said I can answer them.

Q: You live at 7B in the Meridian Apartments, correct?

A: That's correct.

Q: And the incident took place in the hallway outside 7C?

A: Yes.

Q: What first drew your attention to the altercation?

A: The shouting. Walls aren't thick.

Q: Could you make out what was being said?

A: The man was yelling about the noise. The music. He said he worked nights and couldn't sleep.

Q: This was the plaintiff, Mr. Reeves?

A: I don't know his name. The older man. He lives alone down the hall.

Q: What did you do when you heard the shouting?

A: I opened my door. Just a crack. I have a chain.

Q: And what did you observe?

A: The older man was in the hallway in his bathrobe. He was pointing at the door of 7C. His hand was shaking. He looked... he looked like he hadn't slept in a long time.

Q: Was anyone from 7C present in the hallway?

A: The young man came out. He was laughing at first. Then he wasn't.

Q: Ms. Chen, I need to ask—and please, take your time—what happened next?

A: I've already told the police.

Q: I understand. For the record.

A: The young man pushed him. The older man, I mean. And he fell against the wall and kind of... slid down. And then everyone started yelling. And I closed my door.

Q: You closed your door.

A: I have a chain, but it's an old chain. And I'm alone too.

topic: A neighbor is questioned about noise complaints and a confrontation they witnessed
text:
Q: Let's go back to the noise complaints. You filed three separate complaints with building management before August, correct?

A: I did what anyone would do.

Q: I'm not questioning your judgment, Mr. Baxter. I'm establishing a timeline.

A: Fine. Yes. Three complaints.

Q: And what was the response from management each time?

A: They said they'd look into it.

Q: Did they?

A: I wouldn't know. Nothing changed.

Q: The music continued?

A: The music, the parties, the stomping around at two in the morning. I work. I used to work early shifts.

Q: Used to?

A: I don't see how that's relevant.

Q: I'm trying to understand the impact of the ongoing disturbances.

A: The impact. You want to understand the impact.

Q: Yes.

A: I haven't slept through the night in eight months. I lost my position at the warehouse because I couldn't focus. I fell asleep on a forklift. Do you understand what that means? Someone could have died. Someone could have died because I couldn't get four hours of peace in my own apartment.

Q: Mr. Baxter—

A: And then I go over there, I try to have a conversation like a human being, and that kid—he's maybe twenty years old—he looks at me like I'm dirt. Like I'm nobody. Like I haven't worked fifty-hour weeks for thirty years while he plays video games until sunrise.

Q: I need to ask about the specific words exchanged on the night of—

A: I know what you need to ask. Everyone has questions. Nobody has answers. I just wanted to sleep. That's all I ever wanted.

Q: Did you threaten Mr. Okonkwo that night?

A: ...I said things I shouldn't have said. I know that.

Q: What things?

A: I don't remember exactly. Isn't that convenient for you? I don't remember because I was exhausted. I am exhausted. I've been exhausted for a very long time.

topic: A neighbor is questioned about noise complaints and a confrontation they witnessed
text:
Q: Mrs. Patterson, you told the responding officer that you saw the entire confrontation from your kitchen window.

A: Most of it. I was doing dishes.

Q: What time was this?

A: Around nine. It was already dark.

Q: Describe what you saw.

A: The two men were on the driveway between the houses. The younger one—the tenant—he was holding his phone up like he was recording.

Q: And the older man, your neighbor Mr. Fitzgerald?

A: He was asking him to stop. To put the phone away. He had his hands up like this, palms out.

Q: Did Mr. Fitzgerald appear aggressive?

A: No. He appeared... no. He wasn't aggressive.

Q: How would you characterize his demeanor?

A: He was trying to explain something. He kept touching his chest, right here, when he talked. He does that. He's done it ever since his wife passed.

Q: I'm not sure that's—

A: You asked how he appeared. That's how he appeared. Like someone who was tired of not being heard.

Q: What was the tenant doing while Mr. Fitzgerald spoke?

A: Laughing. Moving the phone around. Making comments.

Q: Could you hear what was said?

A: Something about old people. Something about calling the cops on Black kids. I don't want to repeat it exactly.

Q: Did Mr. Fitzgerald respond to these comments?

A: He stopped talking. He just... stopped. He looked at the phone and then he looked at the ground and then he turned around and walked back to his house.

Q: He walked away?

A: Yes.

Q: Did he say anything else?

A: He said, "I used to know everyone on this street." That's what he said. And then he went inside and I didn't see him again until the ambulance came three days later.

Q: The ambulance is not related to this matter.

A: Isn't it?

topic: A neighbor is questioned about noise complaints and a confrontation they witnessed
text:
Q: Mr. Yates, let's try this again. You heard a noise at approximately 11 PM?

A: I heard several noises throughout the night. I noted the time at 11 because that's when I looked at the clock.

Q: And these noises were coming from the Whitmore residence?

A: They were coming from that direction.

Q: You seem reluctant to be more specific.

A: I'm trying to be accurate. There's a difference.

Q: Fair enough. When did you decide to go outside?

A: After the crash. The loud one.

Q: What did you think had happened?

A: I thought maybe someone had hit a garbage can with their car. Or the wind knocked something over. I didn't assume the worst.

Q: What did you find when you went outside?

A: The Whitmore boy was on the lawn. The father was standing over him.

Q: Standing how?

A: Just standing. His arms at his sides. The boy was sitting on the ground holding his face.

Q: Did you speak to either of them?

A: I asked if everyone was alright. The father said it was a family matter. He said thank you and goodnight.

Q: What did you do?

A: I went back inside.

Q: You didn't call anyone? The police?

A: No.

Q: Why not?

A: I've asked myself that. Many times. I've asked myself that question more times than you'll ask me anything today.

Q: Mr. Yates, I'm not trying to assign blame.

A: I know what you're trying to do. You're building a record. You're documenting who knew what and when. That's your job.

Q: That's correct.

A: The boy is nineteen now. I saw him at the grocery store last month. He didn't recognize me, or maybe he pretended not to. I watched the whole thing from thirty feet away and I went back inside and finished my drink and went to bed.

Q: Is there anything else you observed that night that you haven't mentioned?

A: The father stood there for a long time after I went in. I watched from the window. He didn't help the boy up. He didn't go inside. He just stood there on the lawn looking up at the sky like he was waiting for something that was never going to come.

topic: A project manager is questioned about deadlines they missed on a software contract
text:
Q: Mr. Brennan, let's talk about the March 15th deadline for the authentication module. That was missed, correct?

A: The original target date was adjusted, yes.

Q: I'm asking if it was missed.

A: I'd say it was revised based on factors that emerged during development. Factors, I should add, that I identified before anyone else on the leadership team had visibility into them.

Q: So that's a yes?

A: It's a yes with context that matters. I was the one who flagged the security vulnerabilities in the legacy integration layer. My team could have pushed something out by March 15th, sure. Would it have held up? No. And I made that call.

Q: You made the call to miss the contractual deadline?

A: I made the call to protect the client from a deployment that would have failed in production. That's what a project manager with fifteen years of experience does.

Q: Did you consult with Nextera Technologies before making that decision?

A: I consulted with my technical leads. The people who actually understood what we were building.

Q: That's not what I asked.

A: I'm giving you the relevant answer. I've managed over forty enterprise deployments. I know when something needs to breathe and when it can ship.

Q: Mr. Brennan, did you or did you not inform the client before the deadline passed?

A: I informed them when I had a complete picture to present. Not speculation. A complete picture. That's how I've always operated, and it's why clients come back to me.

Q: So the answer is no?

A: The answer is I used professional judgment that has been validated across a rather long career.

topic: A project manager is questioned about deadlines they missed on a software contract
text:
Q: Ms. Torres, I'm going to direct your attention to the payment processing module. The deadline was June 1st. When was it actually delivered?

A: June 23rd.

Q: Twenty-two days late.

A: Twenty-two days after the original date, yes.

Q: What caused that delay?

A: Resource constraints, primarily. We lost two senior developers in April.

Q: And whose responsibility was it to manage resource allocation?

A: Mine.

Q: So this falls on you?

A: The delay occurred under my management, yes.

Q: Now, I want to be very precise here, Ms. Torres, because I've reviewed your personnel records, and I see that despite these delays, you received a performance bonus in Q3. Is that accurate?

A: I'd have to see the document you're referencing.

Q: I'm asking if you received a bonus.

A: I believe there was a discretionary bonus, yes.

Q: For a project that was twenty-two days late?

A: For a project that, despite losing forty percent of its senior development capacity mid-cycle, still delivered a module that passed UAT on the first attempt. Zero critical defects. Do you understand how rare that is?

Q: I'm asking the questions, Ms. Torres.

A: And I'm providing the full picture.

Q: The bonus was approximately twelve thousand dollars?

A: I don't recall the exact figure.

Q: Would it refresh your recollection to know that I have the documentation right here confirming that amount?

A: If you have documentation, then you have documentation. I did my job. I did it well. The company recognized that.

topic: A project manager is questioned about deadlines they missed on a software contract
text:
Q: Let's discuss the testing phase delays. Mr. Okonkwo, you were the project manager responsible for QA timelines, correct?

A: That's correct.

Q: And the QA phase was supposed to be completed by August 10th?

A: That was the baseline date in the project charter.

Q: It wasn't completed until September 3rd.

A: Correct.

Q: That's a significant delay.

A: I suppose that depends on your frame of reference.

Q: Three and a half weeks doesn't strike you as significant?

A: It strikes me as the result of expanding scope that came directly from the client's change requests. Seven of them, if we're being precise.

Q: So you're blaming the client?

A: I'm describing what happened. The client asked for additional functionality. We delivered additional functionality.

Q: Did you push back on those change requests?

A: I documented the timeline impact in writing every single time. Every single time, Counsel. I have those emails if you'd like to see them.

Q: That's not necessary at this time.

A: Are you sure? Because I think they'd be quite illuminating.

Q: Mr. Okonkwo, I'll let you know what's necessary.

A: Of course. I just want to make sure the record reflects reality. The full reality.

Q: Let me ask you this—did you ever formally invoke the change control provisions of the contract?

A: I raised it with my director. She made the call to accommodate the client without formal change orders.

Q: So you passed the buck.

A: I followed the chain of command while creating a comprehensive paper trail. That's not passing anything. That's doing my job correctly.

topic: A project manager is questioned about deadlines they missed on a software contract
text:
Q: Ms. Whitfield, I want to discuss the API integration milestone. According to the contract, that was due October 15th. Do you recall that date?

A: I do.

Q: When was it actually completed?

A: November 8th.

Q: Who was responsible for that workstream?

A: I was.

Q: Can you explain the delay?

A: The client's existing infrastructure was… I'll be charitable and call it undocumented.

Q: Can you elaborate?

A: We were promised technical specifications in August. What we received were screenshots of a whiteboard from 2019 and a developer who'd been at the company for six months.

Q: Did you raise this issue?

A: Extensively.

Q: With whom?

A: My counterpart at Nextera, their IT director, my own leadership, and eventually their CTO.

Q: And what came of that?

A: We built the documentation ourselves. From scratch.

Q: Isn't that outside your scope?

A: Technically? Yes. But the project needed to succeed, and I wasn't going to let their disorganization become my failure.

Q: So you took on work that wasn't contracted?

A: I took initiative. I identified a critical gap, developed a solution, and executed it. That's what distinguishes adequate project management from exceptional project management.

Q: Some might say you overstepped.

A: Some might. They'd be wrong. The integration works. It works because of what my team built. If Nextera had held up their end, we'd have been early, not late.

topic: A project manager is questioned about deadlines they missed on a software contract
text:
Q: Mr. Reeves, let me take you back to the original project kickoff. You attended that meeting?

A: I led that meeting.

Q: And the timeline discussed—was it realistic, in your professional opinion at the time?

A: I raised concerns.

Q: What kind of concerns?

A: The kind of concerns that get noted in meeting minutes and then ignored by people who've never actually shipped software.

Q: You're referring to the Nextera executives?

A: I'm referring to the people who set a nine-month timeline for what should have been a fourteen-month project.

Q: So you knew from the start this would fail?

A: I knew it would be difficult. I also knew that if anyone could make it work, it was my team.

Q: But it didn't work, did it? You missed multiple deadlines.

A: We delivered a working product that is currently processing three million transactions a month without incident. I'd call that working.

Q: That's not what I asked.

A: No, you asked a question designed to reduce twelve months of complex work to a simple pass-fail metric. I'm giving you the answer that actually means something.

Q: Let me rephrase. Did you meet the contractual deadlines?

A: We met the final delivery deadline. The interim milestones were adjusted collaboratively.

Q: "Adjusted collaboratively." That's an interesting way to describe breach of contract.

A: It's an accurate way to describe professional adaptation to real-world conditions. Something I've been doing successfully for two decades. Shall I walk you through some of my other projects for comparison?

Q: That won't be necessary.

A: I didn't think so.

topic: A supervisor is deposed about performance reviews given to an employee who was later fired
text:
Q: Mr. Delgado, you conducted the annual performance review for Jessica Tran in March of 2022, correct?

A: I did.

Q: And you gave her an overall rating of "meets expectations," is that right?

A: That's what the form says.

Q: I'm asking if that's what you gave her.

A: If the form says "meets expectations," then yes, that's what I gave her. I don't have the form in front of me. You do.

Q: Let me show you what's been marked as Exhibit 14. Is that your signature at the bottom?

A: It is.

Q: And the rating?

A: "Meets expectations." As I said.

Q: Six weeks later, Ms. Tran was terminated for performance issues. Help me understand how someone goes from "meets expectations" to fired in six weeks.

A: I'm not sure what you're asking me to explain. I conducted the review. I didn't make the termination decision.

Q: You didn't recommend her termination?

A: I didn't say that.

Q: Did you or didn't you recommend her termination, Mr. Delgado?

A: I was consulted. I provided input. Whether that constitutes a "recommendation" is a question for someone with a law degree.

Q: What input did you provide?

A: That her performance had declined after the review period.

Q: Declined how?

A: I've already answered that in my written statement. I'm not going to sit here and repeat myself because you didn't read it.

---

topic: A supervisor is deposed about performance reviews given to an employee who was later fired
text:
Q: You were Ms. Chen's direct supervisor from January 2021 through her termination in August 2022, correct?

A: That's correct.

Q: During that time, you completed two formal performance reviews for her?

A: Yes.

Q: Let's talk about the first one. You rated her "exceeds expectations" in four out of six categories. Do you recall that?

A: I do.

Q: Was that an accurate assessment of her work at the time?

A: It was.

Q: And the second review, conducted roughly eleven months later, you rated her "needs improvement" in five out of six categories. What happened?

A: Her performance declined.

Q: In every category?

A: In most categories, yes.

Q: That's quite a fall. From exceeding expectations to needing improvement across the board.

A: Is there a question?

Q: I'm getting there. Was there a specific incident that triggered this decline?

A: It wasn't one incident. It was a pattern.

Q: A pattern you never documented in writing until this review?

A: I documented it in the review.

Q: But nowhere else? No emails? No memos? No written warnings?

A: Counseling doesn't always happen in writing, counsel.

Q: Convenient.

A: Objection. Is that a question or a comment?

Q: I'll rephrase. Isn't it true that there is no contemporaneous documentation of performance issues prior to this review?

A: I gave her verbal feedback. That's how I manage.

---

topic: A supervisor is deposed about performance reviews given to an employee who was later fired
text:
Q: Ms. Patterson, I want to be very precise here. The performance improvement plan was issued on June 3rd. Do you have that in front of you?

A: I do.

A: Because the issues were severe enough that we felt a shorter timeline was appropriate.

Q: Who is "we"?

A: HR and myself.

Q: And you made this decision together?

A: We discussed it.

Q: Did HR recommend the shortened timeline, or did you?

A: I don't recall who raised it first.

Q: You don't recall something that happened eight months ago?

A: I don't recall who said it first. We were in agreement.

Q: Were you in agreement, or did HR simply go along with what you wanted?

A: I'm not going to speculate about what was in other people's heads.

Q: I'm asking about the conversation.

A: And I'm telling you I don't remember who said what first. That's my answer.

Q: Fine. Let's talk about the "severe issues." What were they?

A: They're listed in the PIP.

Q: I want to hear it from you.

A: Then read the PIP into the record and I'll confirm it.

topic: A supervisor is deposed about performance reviews given to an employee who was later fired
text:
Q: The comments section of the October 2021 review—you wrote that Mr. Hassan "demonstrates leadership potential and should be considered for advancement." Your words?

A: Yes.

A: I addressed them verbally. In real time. Which is what supervisors do.

topic: A supervisor is deposed about performance reviews given to an employee who was later fired
text:
Q: Walk me through the rating scale your company uses.

A: One through five. One is unacceptable, five is exceptional.

Q: And you gave Ms. Patel a two in "teamwork."

A: Correct.

Q: What does a two mean?

A: "Needs improvement."

Q: Okay. And in the comments, you wrote—let me find it—"Does not collaborate effectively with peers." You see that?

A: I see it.

Q: Can you give me an example of her not collaborating effectively?

A: She didn't share information with the team. She worked in a silo.

Q: Didn't share information. Like what?

A: Project updates. Client communications.

Q: Was she required to share those things?

A: It was expected.

Q: Expected or required?

A: We expect people to function as part of a team. I shouldn't have to write a rule that says "tell your coworkers what's happening."

Q: But you didn't write it down anywhere.

A: No.

Q: So it's an unwritten expectation.

A: Yes.

Q: And you rated her poorly for failing to meet an unwritten expectation.

A: I rated her poorly for failing to function as a team member. Do you want me to write a rule that says "be a professional"? Should that be in the handbook too?

Q: I'm just trying to understand the basis for the rating.

A: And I've explained it. Twice now.

topic: A witness is questioned about events at a party where an assault allegedly occurred

topic: A witness is questioned about events at a party where an assault allegedly occurred
text:

topic: A witness is questioned about events at a party where an assault allegedly occurred
text:

topic: A witness is questioned about events at a party where an assault allegedly occurred
text:
Q: I'd like to ask you about the party on September 14th. You were present that evening, correct?

A: The defendant. He came up behind Marcus. There was no warning, no argument, nothing. Marcus didn't even see him coming.

A: He asked me not to leave. So I didn't. I stayed with him until the ambulance came. That's what you do, isn't it? You stay.

A: I'm ready. I want to help him however I can.

topic: A witness is questioned about events at a party where an assault allegedly occurred
text:

topic: A witness is questioned about events at a party where an assault allegedly occurred
text:
Q: Mr. Okonkwo, I want to be clear that you can take a break at any point if you need one. These questions may touch on some difficult moments.

topic: A witness is questioned about events at a party where an assault allegedly occurred
text:
Q: You were one of the hosts of this party, correct?

A: It was at my apartment, yes.

Q: So you felt some responsibility for what happened there?

Q: I'm not asking about your feelings of responsibility. I'm asking about what you witnessed.

A: I understand. I witnessed my friend get hurt in my home. That's what I witnessed.

Q: Let's be specific. You saw the defendant, Ryan Hollister, strike Marcus Webb?

A: Yes. I saw Ryan hit Marcus. I saw Marcus fall. I saw blood on my kitchen floor that I had to clean up the next day while my hands were still shaking.

Q: Ms. Patterson—

A: No, I'm answering your question. You want to know what I witnessed. I witnessed someone I invited into my home hurt someone else I cared about. I witnessed Marcus looking up at me from the floor like he didn't understand why this was happening. And I didn't have an answer for him.

Q: Did you attempt to intervene?

A: I tried to get between them after the first hit. Ryan pushed me aside. I'm not very big. I couldn't stop it.

Q: But you tried.

A: I tried. And then I sat with Marcus and I told him it would be okay, and I called 911, and I rode with him to the hospital because his family lives three hours away and I wasn't going to let him be alone.

Q: Were you injured when the defendant pushed you?

A: I had a bruise on my arm. It doesn't matter.

Q: It may matter to this case.

A: Fine. Then yes. I was bruised. But that's not why I'm here. I'm here for Marcus.

topic: A witness is questioned about events at a party where an assault allegedly occurred
text:
Q: You've indicated you were standing approximately ten feet from the altercation when it began.

A: Somewhere around there, yes.

Q: That's close enough to hear what was said between the two men?

A: I heard some of it.

Q: Tell me what you heard.

A: I heard Jay—the defendant—say something like "you don't get to talk to her." And then I heard Andre say he didn't know what Jay was talking about. Then Jay hit him.

Q: Just like that? No further exchange?

A: Maybe there was more. I don't remember every word. I remember Andre looked confused. He put his hands up like this—like he was trying to calm things down. And then he was on the floor.

Q: What did you do?

A: I froze. For a second, I just froze. Then I went to Andre because he was lying there and his eyes were closed and I didn't know if he was breathing.

Q: Was he breathing?

A: Yes. Thank God. He opened his eyes after a few seconds, but he didn't seem to know where he was.

Q: Did you stay with him?

A: I did. Someone handed me a jacket to put under his head. I talked to him. I just kept saying his name, asking if he could hear me. I didn't want him to slip away.

Q: Did he respond?

A: Eventually. He grabbed my wrist. He held on tight. I think he was scared.

Q: That must have been frightening for you as well.

A: It was. But I wasn't going to let him see that. He needed someone to be steady. So that's what I tried to be.

topic: A witness is questioned about a fire they discovered in a neighboring unit
text:
Q: Please state your name for the record.

Q: Mr. Brennan, I understand you want to be efficient. On the night of March 15th, what time did you first become aware of the fire?

A: Around eleven. Maybe 11:05. I've said this three times now in my written statement.

A: Is that seriously relevant?

A: I opened my door. Saw smoke in the hallway. Closed my door. Called 911. Do you need me to break it down into smaller steps?

A: No. Nothing. Are we almost done here?

topic: A witness is questioned about a fire they discovered in a neighboring unit
text:
Q: Ms. Vance, directing your attention to the evening of October 3rd. You discovered a fire in the unit adjacent to yours, correct?

A: That's correct.

Q: What time was this?

A: Approximately 8:30 in the evening.

Q: Approximately. Can you be more specific?

A: I didn't check my watch at that exact moment, so no, I cannot be more specific than approximately 8:30.

Q: Fine. What first alerted you to the fire?

A: The smoke detector in the hallway.

Q: The hallway smoke detector, not one inside your unit?

A: That's what I said.

A: Grayish. Medium thickness, I suppose. I wasn't conducting a scientific analysis. I was concerned about my safety.

Q: Did you approach unit 7C?

A: No. I went back inside and called the fire department.

Q: You didn't knock on the door to see if anyone needed help?

A: I'm not a firefighter. I did what any reasonable person would do.

---

topic: A witness is questioned about a fire they discovered in a neighboring unit
text:
Q: Mr. Okonkwo, let's talk about the fire. When did you first notice something was wrong?

topic: A witness is questioned about a fire they discovered in a neighboring unit
text:
Q: State your name.

topic: A witness is questioned about a fire they discovered in a neighboring unit
text:
Q: Dr. Hassan, I want to establish the timeline of events. You were home on the evening of July 7th?

topic: An HR director is questioned about a harassment complaint that was filed and closed
text:
Q: Ms. Hartwell, you were the HR director at Compton Industries when the complaint involving Marcus Chen was filed, correct?

A: That's correct. I held that position from 2018 through last year.

Q: And you were the person primarily responsible for handling that complaint?

A: I was, yes. The complaint came to me directly, and I oversaw the investigation from start to finish.

Q: Walk me through what happened when the complaint first arrived on your desk.

A: Certainly. I received the written complaint on March 14th, 2022. I reviewed it that same day, documented its receipt in our tracking system, and scheduled an intake interview with the complainant for the following morning.

Q: That would be Sarah Okonkwo?

A: Yes, Ms. Okonkwo.

Q: What did she tell you in that initial interview?

A: She described three separate incidents occurring between January and early March of that year. She felt that a coworker had made repeated comments about her appearance that made her uncomfortable in the workplace.

Q: Did she identify the coworker?

A: She did. She named DavidRessler, who worked in her department.

Q: And what steps did you take after that interview?

A: I interviewed Mr. Ressler, I interviewed two witnesses Ms. Okonkwo had identified, I reviewed email correspondence she had flagged, and I consulted with our legal department regarding appropriate next steps.

Q: How long did this process take?

A: The investigation was completed in eighteen days. I issued my written findings on April 1st.

Q: And the complaint was closed at that point?

A: It was closed following the implementation of the recommended remedial measures, yes. The file was formally closed on April 8th.

Q: What were those remedial measures?

A: Mr. Ressler received a written warning that was placed in his personnel file, he was required to complete additional harassment prevention training, and Ms. Okonkwo was given the option to transfer to a different team, which she declined.

---

topic: An HR director is questioned about a harassment complaint that was filed and closed
text:
Q: Mr. Patterson, I'd like to ask you about the investigation file for complaint number 2021-47.

A: Of course.

Q: You closed that investigation after eleven days. Is that typical?

A: It depends on the complexity of the matter. Some investigations require more time, some require less. Eleven days was appropriate for this particular situation.

Q: What made it less complex?

A: There were only two people involved, both were cooperative, and the documentary evidence was straightforward to review.

Q: When you say straightforward, what do you mean?

A: I mean the complainant had preserved the relevant text messages, there wasn't any ambiguity about what was communicated, and both parties agreed on the basic facts of what had occurred.

Q: They agreed on the facts but disagreed on something else?

A: They disagreed on whether the conduct constituted harassment under company policy.

Q: And you made that determination?

A: I did.

Q: What was your conclusion?

A: I concluded that the conduct did not rise to the level of harassment as defined in our employee handbook, but that it was nonetheless inappropriate and warranted a verbal counseling.

Q: Who received the counseling?

A: The respondent, Jennifer Walsh.

Q: Did the complainant accept your conclusion?

A: He expressed disappointment but did not appeal the decision within the ten-day window provided by our policy.

Q: Did you document his disappointment?

A: I noted in the file that he had been informed of the outcome and the appeals process.

---

topic: An HR director is questioned about a harassment complaint that was filed and closed
text:
Q: Let's talk about the timeline here, Ms. Reeves. The complaint was filed on September 3rd?

A: Yes.

Q: And it was closed on September 29th?

A: That's what the file reflects.

Q: Twenty-six days. That seems like a long time for what your report describes as an isolated incident.

A: I wouldn't characterize it that way.

Q: You wouldn't characterize it as an isolated incident?

A: No, I wouldn't characterize twenty-six days as a long time. The respondent was on approved medical leave during part of that period, which affected our ability to conduct his interview.

Q: How long was he out?

A: Nine days.

Q: So if we subtract those nine days, we're looking at seventeen days of actual investigation?

A: That's a reasonable approximation, yes.

Q: Is seventeen days typical?

A: It's within normal range. Every investigation is different.

Q: Let me ask you this. During those seventeen active days, how many interviews did you conduct?

A: I conducted four formal interviews and had several informal conversations that I documented in my notes.

Q: Four interviews for an isolated incident?

A: I believe I mentioned I wouldn't characterize it as isolated. The complainant raised concerns about a pattern. I investigated that pattern and found insufficient evidence to substantiate it, which is why my report describes a single incident.

Q: Fair enough. Who were the four people you interviewed?

A: The complainant, the respondent, and two colleagues who the complainant believed had witnessed relevant behavior.

---

topic: An HR director is questioned about a harassment complaint that was filed and closed
text:
Q: Ms. Thornton, I'm going to hand you what's been marked as Exhibit 14. Take a moment to review it.

A: Thank you. Yes, I recognize this document.

Q: What is it?

A: This is the closure memo I prepared for the Yamamoto complaint.

Q: You wrote this?

A: I did.

Q: The third paragraph states, and I'm quoting here, "Based on the foregoing, this office finds insufficient evidence to sustain the allegations." Do you see that?

A: I do.

Q: What did you mean by insufficient evidence?

A: I meant that after completing the investigation, I did not find enough evidence to conclude that a policy violation had occurred.

Q: Not enough evidence, or no evidence?

A: Those are different things, and I chose my words intentionally. There was some evidence. There was the complainant's account, which I found credible. But there was also contradictory evidence, and I could not reconcile the two sufficiently to make a finding.

Q: What was the contradictory evidence?

A: The respondent denied the allegation, two witnesses provided accounts that conflicted with the complainant's version, and the physical evidence was ambiguous.

Q: Physical evidence?

A: The complainant alleged that certain items had been left on her desk. When I examined the area, there was nothing there. That doesn't prove it didn't happen, but it didn't corroborate her account either.

Q: Did you believe her?

A: I found her credible, as I said. But credibility isn't the same as corroboration, and our standard requires both where possible.

Q: Did you explain that distinction to Ms. Yamamoto when you closed the file?

A: I explained my findings to her in detail. I'm confident she understood the basis for my decision, even if she disagreed with it.

---

topic: An HR director is questioned about a harassment complaint that was filed and closed
text:
Q: Mr. Gallegos, you've been doing this work for how long now?

A: I've been in HR for fourteen years. The last seven in a director capacity.

Q: In those seven years as a director, roughly how many harassment complaints have you personally handled?

A: I would estimate somewhere between eighty and one hundred.

Q: And this complaint, the one filed by Andrea Simmons, was that one of the eighty to one hundred?

A: It was.

Q: Tell me what stood out about it.

A: I'm not sure I understand the question.

Q: Was there anything unusual about the Simmons complaint compared to the others you've handled?

A: Every complaint has its own circumstances. I don't know that I would say this one was particularly unusual.

Q: The respondent was a vice president. Is that usual?

A: It's less common, but it's not unprecedented. I've investigated complaints against senior leadership before.

Q: Does the process change when the respondent is at that level?

A: The process remains the same. The participants are simply different.

Q: You don't involve the board, or outside counsel?

A: I involved outside counsel in this matter, yes. That's standard when executive-level employees are respondents. It protects the integrity of the investigation.

Q: And the board?

A: The board was notified that an investigation was underway. They were not involved in the investigation itself.

Q: Who notified them?

A: I did, through the general counsel's office.

Q: And when the matter was closed, did you notify them of that as well?

A: I provided a summary of the outcome to the general counsel, who communicated with the board as she deemed appropriate. I don't know exactly what she told them.

topic: A paramedic is questioned about the response time and treatment at an accident scene
text:
Q: Can you state your name and current position for the record?

A: Thomas Reilly. Paramedic with County EMS, fourteen years now.

Q: You responded to the accident on Route 12 on the evening of March 3rd?

A: I did.

Q: What time did dispatch receive the call?

A: 7:42 p.m.

Q: And what time did you arrive on scene?

A: 7:58 p.m.

Q: So sixteen minutes from dispatch to arrival?

A: That's correct.

Q: Is that within your department's target response time?

A: Look, the target is twelve minutes. We were over. I know we were over.

Q: What caused the delay?

A: It was—there was construction on Miller Road. We had to reroute. It added time.

Q: Did you radio dispatch about the delay?

A: Yes.

Q: And what was the condition of Mr. Hartley when you arrived?

A: He was unconscious. Significant blood loss from the leg wound. We started treatment immediately.

Q: Would those four extra minutes have made a difference in his outcome?

A: I've been asked that question a lot. By his family. By myself. I don't know. I genuinely don't know. We did everything we could once we got there, and I've gone over it a hundred times, and I still don't have a better answer for you than that.

Q: I understand. Let's move on to the treatment protocol you followed.

A: Fine.

---

topic: A paramedic is questioned about the response time and treatment at an accident scene
text:
Q: Ms. Vance, you were the lead paramedic on Unit 7 that night?

A: That's right.

Q: How long have you been a paramedic?

A: Eight years.

Q: The accident involved a single vehicle striking a pedestrian, correct?

A: Correct.

Q: When you arrived, where was the victim located?

A: She was on the sidewalk. Bystanders had moved her.

Q: They moved her before you arrived?

A: Yes. They were trying to help.

Q: Is that—should they have moved her?

A: Should they have? No. With a potential spinal injury, you don't move someone. But people panic. They see someone in the street, they want to get them somewhere safe. It happens.

Q: Did that complicate your treatment?

A: It meant we had to be more careful with spinal stabilization. We didn't know if there'd been additional injury from the movement.

Q: So it made your job harder.

A: It made it different. We adapted.

Q: Did you document that she'd been moved?

A: Yes.

Q: Did you speak to the bystanders about what they'd done?

A: No.

Q: Why not?

A: Because what was I going to say? Yell at them for trying to help? They didn't know any better. Most people don't. We just—we work with what we find when we get there.

Q: Fair enough. Let's talk about your assessment of her injuries.

---

topic: A paramedic is questioned about the response time and treatment at an accident scene
text:
Q: Mr. Okonkwo, I want to be clear about the sequence of events, so bear with me if some of these questions seem repetitive.

A: That's fine. Ask what you need to ask.

Q: Your unit was the second to arrive at the scene?

A: Yes, Unit 3 was already there.

Q: Why were two units dispatched?

A: Multiple victims. Dispatch protocol.

Q: How many victims were there?

A: Three. Two in the vehicle, one pedestrian.

Q: Which victim were you assigned to treat?

A: The driver.

Q: And his condition when you reached him?

A: Conscious but confused. Lacerations to the face and arms. Possible concussion.

Q: Was he trapped in the vehicle?

A: No. He'd gotten out on his own before we arrived.

Q: Where was he when you found him?

A: Sitting on the curb. About twenty feet from the car.

Q: Did he say anything to you?

A: He kept asking about the pedestrian. Over and over.

Q: What did you tell him?

A: That my colleagues were taking care of her. That he needed to focus on himself.

Q: Did he comply with your treatment?

A: Eventually. He was—he was pretty shaken up. It took some time to get him calm enough to assess properly.

Q: Did that delay his treatment?

A: By a few minutes, yes.

Q: Is there anything you would have done differently?

A: I've thought about that. Honestly? No. Some situations just are what they are.

---

topic: A paramedic is questioned about the response time and treatment at an accident scene
text:
Q: Let me ask you about the equipment on your unit that night.

A: Okay.

Q: You had a full complement of supplies?

A: We did.

Q: Including a defibrillator?

A: Yes.

Q: Was the defibrillator used on Mr. Chen?

A: No.

Q: Why not?

A: Because he was in PEA—pulseless electrical activity. The heart had electrical activity but no mechanical function. A defibrillator doesn't help with PEA.

Q: I see. So what did you do instead?

A: CPR. Epinephrine. Tried to address the underlying cause.

Q: Which was?

A: Hypovolemia. He'd lost too much blood.

Q: From the accident?

A: From the accident, yes.

Q: How long did you perform CPR?

A: Twenty-three minutes.

Q: And then?

A: And then he was pronounced at the hospital.

Q: Did you ride with him to the hospital?

A: I did.

Q: Were you still performing CPR in the ambulance?

A: My partner was.

Q: And you?

A: I was managing the airway.

Q: Mr. Reeves, let me ask you directly—

A: I know what you're going to ask. The answer is we followed protocol. Every step. It wasn't enough. Sometimes it isn't.

Q: That wasn't my question.

A: No, but it's the answer.

---

topic: A paramedic is questioned about the response time and treatment at an accident scene
text:
Q: You've been doing this a long time, Ms. Delgado.

A: Seventeen years.

Q: Seen a lot of accident scenes?

A: More than I could count.

Q: How would you characterize this one?

A: Chaotic. It was dark, raining, multiple vehicles involved. Bystanders everywhere. One of the more difficult scenes I've worked.

Q: Difficult how?

A: Just—everything at once. Trying to triage, trying to keep people back, trying to communicate with dispatch while treating patients.

Q: Were you adequately staffed that night?

A: We had two units. Four paramedics total.

Q: That wasn't my question.

A: I know.

Q: Were you adequately staffed?

A: We made it work with what we had.

Q: Ms. Delgado.

A: Counselor, I could tell you we needed more people. I could tell you I've been saying that for years. I could tell you exactly how many times I've filed reports about staffing shortages. But none of that changes what happened that night or what we did, so—what exactly do you want me to say?

Q: I want you to answer the question honestly.

A: I am answering honestly. We were understaffed. We're always understaffed. And we still did our jobs.

Q: Understood. Let's move on to the triage decisions you made.

A: Alright.

topic: A witness is questioned about a fire they discovered in a neighboring unit
text:
Q: Mr. Patterson, I want to direct your attention to the evening of March 14th. You were home that night?

Q: Mr. Patterson, I understand this is lengthy, but I need to establish the timeline. Were you asleep or awake when you first smelled smoke?

A: Somewhere in between. I don't know what you want me to say.

topic: A witness is questioned about a fire they discovered in a neighboring unit
text:
Q: Ms. Thornton, you lived at 442 Birch Lane in March of this year, correct?

A: Correct.

Q: Unit 4A?

A: Yes, 4A.

Q: And unit 4B was immediately adjacent to yours?

A: It shared a wall, yes.

Q: On March 14th, did something unusual occur?

A: There was a fire in 4B.

Q: Tell me about discovering that fire.

A: Well, I was in my kitchen. I heard my smoke detector go off, and at first I thought it was mine—you know, like maybe I'd burned something—but I hadn't been cooking. So I opened my front door to see if it was coming from the hallway, and that's when I saw the smoke.

Q: Okay. Let me slow down. You heard your smoke detector. What time was this?

A: Around ten-thirty.

Q: Ten-thirty p.m.?

A: Yes. At night.

Q: And you opened your front door. Was the smoke already visible in the hallway at that point?

A: Yes. I just said that.

Q: I'm clarifying the sequence, Ms. Thornton.

A: The sequence is I heard the alarm, I opened the door, I saw smoke. That's the sequence.

Q: How much smoke are we talking about?

A: Enough to see. A visible haze. It was coming from under their door and sort of... pooling near the ceiling.

Q: What did you do next?

A: I called 911.

Q: From your cell phone?

A: Yes. From my cell phone. What else would I use?

Q: Did you attempt to alert anyone in 4B?

A: I knocked on the door and yelled. Nobody answered.

Q: You knocked and yelled. How many times?

A: I don't know. Several. Three, four times. However many times it takes before you realize nobody's coming.

---

topic: A witness is questioned about a fire they discovered in a neighboring unit
text:
Q: Let's go back to the fire.

A: Okay.

Q: Actually, let's start earlier. What were you doing that evening before you discovered it?

A: Just... normal things. I'd made dinner. Watched some TV.

Q: What did you watch?

A: I don't remember. Something. Does it matter?

Q: I'm trying to get a sense of your evening.

A: My evening was unremarkable until there was a fire next door.

Q: Okay. When did you first notice something was wrong?

A: I heard a popping sound. Through the wall.

Q: A popping sound.

A: Yes.

Q: Can you describe it?

A: It was... I don't know how to describe a pop. It popped. Like something electrical, maybe. Or glass. I don't know.

Q: What did you think it was at the time?

A: I didn't think anything at the time. I just heard it.

Q: Did you investigate?

A: No. I figured it was nothing. Then I heard it again.

Q: A second pop?

A: More than one. A series of them.

Q: And then what?

A: Then I smelled smoke and I went out to the hallway.

Q: Okay. I want to make sure I have this right. You heard popping sounds—

A: We've been over this.

Q: —you heard popping sounds, then you smelled smoke, then you went to the hallway. Is that the correct order?

A: Yes. That's the order. I've said it three times now.

---

topic: A witness is questioned about a fire they discovered in a neighboring unit
text:
Q: Mr. Huang, I want to ask you about the condition of the hallway when you exited your unit.

A: Barely.

---

topic: A witness is questioned about a fire they discovered in a neighboring unit
text:
Q: Did anyone else come into the hallway after you?

A: Eventually, yes.

Q: Who?

A: Mrs. Donnelly from 4C. And I think someone from downstairs.

Q: Do you know who from downstairs?

A: No.

topic: A pharmacist is deposed about a prescription that was filled with the wrong dosage
text:
Q: Dr. Nguyen, I'm going to hand you what's been marked as Exhibit 14. Do you recognize this document?

A: Yes.

Q: Can you tell us what it is?

A: It's a prescription label.

Q: For what medication?

A: Metoprolol.

Q: And what dosage appears on that label?

A: 100 milligrams.

Q: Was that the dosage written on the original prescription from Dr. Harrison?

A: No.

Q: What was the prescribed dosage?

A: 25 milligrams.

Q: So there was a discrepancy between what was prescribed and what was dispensed, correct?

A: I believe I've already answered that question.

Q: I'm asking you to confirm it directly for the record, Dr. Nguyen.

A: Fine. Yes. There was a discrepancy.

Q: And you were the pharmacist who filled this prescription on March 3rd?

A: According to the system log, yes.

Q: According to the system log. Were you or were you not the pharmacist who filled it?

A: I don't have an independent memory of every prescription I fill in a day. I fill between 150 and 200 prescriptions per shift. The log says I filled it. I'm not disputing the log.

Q: Do you have any explanation for how a 25-milligram prescription became a 100-milligram dispensation?

A: I've answered this in my written statement. I don't know.

---

topic: A pharmacist is deposed about a prescription that was filled with the wrong dosage
text:
Q: Walk me through the verification process at your pharmacy, if you would.

A: Certainly. When a prescription comes in, whether electronic or paper, it's entered into the system by a technician. Then a pharmacist reviews the entry against the original prescription.

Q: And that pharmacist would be you, on the day in question?

A: That's correct.

Q: So you personally reviewed the entry before the medication was dispensed?

A: That's what the protocol requires, yes.

Q: That's not what I asked. Did you personally review it?

A: I— yes. I would have. That's the standard process.

Q: You would have, or you did?

A: I don't remember this specific prescription. I'm telling you what I do for every prescription.

Q: Every single one? Without exception?

A: Yes.

Q: Then help me understand something, Dr. Whitfield. If you reviewed every prescription without exception, and this prescription was reviewed by you, how did Mr. Garner receive four times the prescribed dose?

A: I... I can't answer that. I don't know.

Q: You don't know.

A: No. And I've been asking myself the same question for five months.

Q: Let's move on. Who else touched this prescription before it left the pharmacy?

A: The technician who entered it. Possibly another technician who pulled the stock. And whoever was at the pickup window.

Q: That's a lot of hands.

A: It's a normal workflow.

---

topic: A pharmacist is deposed about a prescription that was filled with the wrong dosage
text:
Q: Let's try this again. You testified that the pharmacy software has a built-in alert system.

A: That's correct.

Q: And this system is designed to flag dosage anomalies?

A: Among other things, yes.

Q: Did the system flag the prescription for Mrs. Delacroix?

A: I don't have that information in front of me.

Q: You don't recall whether there was an alert?

A: Counsel, I process hundreds of prescriptions a week. Each one may or may not generate alerts. I cannot recall whether this specific prescription generated an alert eight months ago.

Q: Fair enough. Let me show you Exhibit 22. Do you see the entry highlighted in yellow?

A: Yes.

Q: What does that indicate?

A: It indicates no alert was triggered.

Q: No alert. Despite the fact that the prescription was for 50 milligrams and the dispensed dosage was 200 milligrams?

A: That's what the record shows.

Q: Does that surprise you?

A: The system isn't perfect. No system is.

A: I didn't say that was an explanation. You asked if I was surprised. I answered.

Q: Let me ask you directly: Do you take any personal responsibility for what happened to Mrs. Delacroix?

A: I'm not going to answer that. That's— you can ask my counsel, but I'm not answering that.

---

topic: A pharmacist is deposed about a prescription that was filled with the wrong dosage
text:
Q: Mr. Okonkwo, how long have you worked as a pharmacist?

A: This incident.

A: I'm certain there were no others that were reported or that I'm aware of.

A: Define adequately.

A: Within guidelines.

Q: Mr. Okonkwo, did you feel you had enough staff to safely do your job that day?

A: ...No.

topic: A pharmacist is deposed about a prescription that was filled with the wrong dosage
text:
Q: I want to be very precise here. The prescription from Dr. Yamamoto specified lisinopril 10 milligrams once daily.

topic: A driver is deposed about the events leading up to a multi-vehicle collision
text:
