topic: A driver is deposed about the events leading up to a multi-vehicle collision
text:
Q: Ms. Okafor, you've stated you were traveling northbound on Route 9. What was your speed as you approached the Millbrook overpass?

A: Forty-five, maybe fifty. The limit is fifty there.

Q: And the weather conditions?

A: Clear. It had rained the night before, but the roads were dry by then.

Q: You're certain the roads were dry?

A: I am. I remember noticing that specifically because I'd been worried about it when I woke up.

Q: What made you worried?

A: I just... I check things. I check the weather, the roads. I'm a careful driver.

Q: Were you a careful driver on the morning of March 3rd?

A: I thought I was.

Q: You thought you were.

A: I checked my mirrors. I signaled. I did everything I was supposed to do.

Q: And yet.

A: I'm sorry?

Q: Let me rephrase. Despite doing everything you were supposed to do, three vehicles were involved in this collision, correct?

A: That's correct.

Q: One of those vehicles contained a family of four.

A: I know.

Q: You know.

A: I know who was in that van, counselor. I know their names. I know the children's ages. I know what hospital they were taken to. Is there something specific you'd like to ask me, or would you like to continue stating facts I'm already aware of?

Q: I'd like to ask if you've had any contact with the Patterson family since the accident.

A: I've tried. They don't... I understand why they don't want to speak with me.

---

topic: A driver is deposed about the events leading up to a multi-vehicle collision
text:
Q: Let's talk about the moments immediately before impact. You were in the left-hand lane, correct?

A: Correct.

Q: And Mr. Reeves' vehicle was where?

A: He was merging. Coming from the on-ramp.

Q: Did you see him merging?

A: I saw him.

Q: What did you do when you saw him?

A: I maintained my lane. I had the right of way.

Q: You maintained your lane.

A: That's what you're supposed to do.

Q: I'm not asking what you're supposed to do, Mr. Tran. I'm asking what you did.

A: I just told you.

Q: You made no effort to slow down?

A: There wasn't time.

Q: There wasn't time, or you didn't think you needed to?

A: I don't know how to answer that.

Q: Let me ask it differently. If you could go back to that moment—

A: Don't.

Q: Mr. Tran?

A: I've gone back to that moment every single day for eleven months. You don't need to ask me to do it here. I know what I would do differently. I know.

Q: What would you do differently?

A: I would have hit the brakes. I would have swerved. I would have done anything. I would have let him have the lane.

---

topic: A driver is deposed about the events leading up to a multi-vehicle collision
text:
Q: Mr. Fitzgerald, how long had you been driving commercially at the time of the accident?

A: Sixteen years.

Q: Sixteen years without incident?

A: I had a backing accident in 2019. Minor. A loading dock.

Q: But nothing like this.

A: No. Nothing like this.

Q: On the afternoon in question, you were hauling what kind of cargo?

A: Steel coils. Three of them.

Q: And they were properly secured?

A: They were inspected that morning. Signed off by the yard supervisor.

Q: I have the inspection report here. I see the signature. But I'm asking you—in your professional opinion, after sixteen years—were they properly secured?

A: I believed they were.

Q: That's not what I asked.

A: I know it's not.

Q: Mr. Fitzgerald?

A: One of the chains... after the accident, one of the chains had a weak link. It's in the report. You have the report.

Q: I do. I wanted to hear it from you.

A: Why?

Q: Excuse me?

A: Why did you need to hear it from me? You have the photographs. You have the engineering analysis. You know what happened when that coil came loose. Why do you need me to say it?

Q: Because you were there, Mr. Fitzgerald.

A: Yes. I was there.

---

topic: A driver is deposed about the events leading up to a multi-vehicle collision
text:
Q: Mrs. Delacroix, you were the first to call 911, is that right?

A: I was, yes.

Q: Can you walk me through what you observed immediately after the collision?

A: I had pulled over. I was shaking, I think. I couldn't... my hands weren't working properly with the phone.

Q: But you did manage to place the call.

A: Eventually. Yes.

Q: The transcript indicates you were on the line for approximately four minutes.

A: That sounds right.

Q: During that time, did you exit your vehicle?

A: I did. The dispatcher told me to stay in the car, but I couldn't just sit there.

Q: What did you see when you approached the other vehicles?

A: The sedan was... the front was completely compressed. And the SUV had rolled. It was on its side.

Q: Did you approach either vehicle?

A: I approached the sedan. The driver's side window was broken.

Q: Was the driver conscious?

A: She was.

Q: Did she say anything to you?

A: She asked about her son. She kept asking about her son.

Q: Was her son in the vehicle?

A: He was in the back seat.

Q: Mrs. Delacroix, take a moment if you need to.

A: Thank you. I'm sorry. I just... I held her hand until the paramedics arrived. That's all I could do. I just held her hand.

topic: A paramedic is questioned about the response time and treatment at an accident scene
text:
Q: Please state your name and occupation for the record.

A: David Chen, paramedic with County Fire Station 12. Eleven years.

Q: Mr. Chen, on the night of March 15th, you responded to a motor vehicle accident on Highway 9, correct?

A: That's correct.

Q: What time did you arrive on scene?

A: Our unit arrived at 11:47 p.m.

Q: And what time was the call dispatched?

A: I'd have to check the log, but I believe it was around 11:31.

Q: So sixteen minutes from dispatch to arrival?

A: If those times are accurate, yes. But I'm not certain about the dispatch time without looking at the actual record.

Q: Is sixteen minutes a typical response time for your station?

A: I'm not sure what you mean by "typical." Typical for what? That stretch of highway? That time of night? We have different response metrics depending on—

Q: Let me rephrase. Was there any delay in your response that night?

A: Delay compared to what? We responded immediately when the call came in. If you're asking whether something held us up, I'm not aware of anything, but I don't know what you're comparing it to.

Q: Were you the first emergency vehicle on scene?

A: No. Highway patrol was already there when we pulled up.

Q: How long had they been there?

A: I... couldn't tell you. I didn't ask them to timestamp their arrival for me. We had a patient to attend to.

Q: Fair enough. Who was the patient you treated first?

A: There was only one patient requiring treatment. The driver of the sedan. The truck driver was ambulatory and refused transport.

Q: And what was the sedan driver's condition when you reached her?

A: She was unresponsive, pinned behind the steering column. Significant trauma to the— look, are you asking me to reconstruct my medical assessment from memory, or do you have my incident report in front of you? Because I want to make sure I'm giving you accurate information here.

topic: A paramedic is questioned about the response time and treatment at an accident scene
text:
Q: Paramedic Okonkwo, you've been doing this job for how long?

A: Seven years this coming August.

Q: In your experience, when a patient is in cardiac arrest at an accident scene, what's the standard protocol?

A: Begin CPR immediately, prepare the AED, call for additional support if needed, and transport as quickly as safely possible.

Q: And did you follow that protocol on September 3rd with Mr. Hartley?

A: We did, yes.

Q: The hospital records indicate Mr. Hartley arrived at 4:52 a.m. You were on scene at 4:23 a.m. That's twenty-nine minutes. Why so long?

A: I'm sorry, where are you getting 4:23?

Q: From your own incident report.

A: Then I'd like to see it, because I don't recall that being the arrival time.

Q: Let me show you Exhibit 7. Is that your signature at the bottom?

A: It is. But this says 4:31, not 4:23.

Q: I apologize, you're right. 4:31. So twenty-one minutes on scene before transport. My question stands.

A: We were stabilizing him for transport. You can't just throw someone in cardiac arrest into an ambulance and floor it. There's a sequence of—

Q: But twenty-one minutes?

A: Are you asking me to justify the medical decisions I made, or are you asking what happened?

Q: I'm asking whether twenty-one minutes is consistent with your training.

A: My training tells me to stabilize the patient. Sometimes that takes five minutes. Sometimes it takes longer. Every scene is different.

Q: Was there anything unusual about this scene that extended your time?

A: The vehicle was on its side. Extraction was complicated. I put that in my report.

Q: The report mentions extraction took approximately eight minutes.

A: Then there's your answer. Eight minutes of extraction, the rest was medical intervention. I don't understand what you're suggesting took too long.

topic: A paramedic is questioned about the response time and treatment at an accident scene
text:
Q: Ms. Reeves, I want to focus on the medication you administered at the scene.

A: Okay.

Q: You gave the patient epinephrine, correct?

A: Correct.

Q: At what dosage?

A: 0.3 milligrams, intramuscular.

Q: Is that the standard dose for anaphylaxis?

A: Yes.

Q: And how did you determine the patient was experiencing anaphylaxis?

A: She had hives spreading across her chest and neck, her lips were swelling, and she was having difficulty breathing. Her friend told us she'd eaten something with peanuts.

Q: Wait— her friend told you? I thought the patient was alone.

A: No, there was a young woman with her. College age. She was the one who called 911.

Q: I have the dispatch record here, and it indicates the caller was a male who identified himself as a passing motorist.

A: Then... I don't know what to tell you. There was a woman at the scene who said she was with the patient. Maybe someone else called it in first?

Q: Did you get this woman's name?

A: I don't recall. We were focused on the patient. She might have given it to my partner.

Q: Your partner's report doesn't mention a female witness.

A: I don't know why that would be. She was definitely there. She was holding the patient's hand when we loaded her into the ambulance.

Q: She rode in the ambulance with you?

A: No. No, I don't think she did. I think she said she'd follow in her car. Or maybe— I'm sorry, I'm trying to remember, but this was months ago and we run dozens of calls a week.

Q: I understand. I'm just trying to establish who was present.

A: So am I. I know what I saw that night, but I can't explain why the paperwork doesn't match. It doesn't change the treatment I provided.

topic: A paramedic is questioned about the response time and treatment at an accident scene
text:
Q: Let's talk about triage decisions. You had two patients at the Fernwood intersection accident, correct?

A: Correct.

Q: How did you decide who to treat first?

A: The motorcyclist had obvious severe injuries—compound fracture, significant blood loss. The other driver was conscious, talking, ambulatory. Standard triage puts the more critical patient first.

Q: But the "ambulatory" driver, Mr. Petersen, collapsed forty minutes later from internal bleeding.

A: I'm aware of what happened to Mr. Petersen.

Q: Did you examine him at the scene?

A: I did a rapid assessment, yes.

Q: What did that consist of?

A: I checked his responsiveness, asked about pain, looked for obvious injuries, checked his pupils. He was alert, oriented, said he felt fine, refused transport.

Q: He refused transport.

A: Yes.

Q: Did you document that refusal?

A: Of course.

Q: Did you explain to him the risks of refusing?

A: I did.

Q: What specifically did you tell him?

A: I told him that internal injuries aren't always immediately apparent and that he should go to the hospital to be checked out. He said he felt fine and wanted to wait for his wife to pick him up.

Q: Did you consider overriding his refusal?

A: Overriding— I can't force a competent adult into an ambulance. That's not how this works.

Q: Did he seem competent to you?

A: He was answering questions appropriately, he knew where he was, he knew what had happened. What would you have had me do, exactly?

Q: I'm not suggesting anything, I'm just trying to understand the decision-making process.

A: The decision was his to make. I informed him of the risks. He declined transport. I documented it. That's the process.

topic: A paramedic is questioned about the response time and treatment at an accident scene
text:
Q: Paramedic Walsh, your unit was the second ambulance dispatched to the accident. Is that right?

A: We were dispatched second, yes. We arrived first.

Q: You arrived before the unit that was dispatched first?

A: That's what happened.

Q: How is that possible?

A: We were closer. Unit 7 was dispatched first because they were technically "next up" in the rotation, but we were finishing a call two miles away. Dispatch sent us as backup and we got there before they did.

Q: By how much?

A: I'd estimate four or five minutes.

Q: Did that create any issues with scene management?

A: I'm not sure what you're asking.

Q: Was there any— let me put it this way. When Unit 7 arrived, was there any discussion about who was in charge?

A: We'd already started treatment. They assisted. There wasn't a power struggle, if that's what you're implying.

Q: I'm not implying anything. I'm asking whether the unusual arrival sequence affected patient care.

A: Affected it how?

Q: In any way.

A: We treated the patient. Unit 7 helped. He was transported. I don't know what effect you're looking for me to identify.

Q: Were there any disagreements about treatment approach?

A: I mean... Tom from Unit 7 suggested a different IV access point. I disagreed. We went with mine. Is that a "disagreement"?

Q: Did that delay treatment?

A: The conversation took maybe ten seconds.

Q: So no delays.

A: No. No delays. We worked as a team. The patient received appropriate care. I genuinely don't understand what angle you're pursuing here, counselor, but I've answered it as best I can.

topic: A project manager is questioned about deadlines they missed on a software contract
text:
Q: Mr. Holloway, the contract specified a delivery date of March 15th for the first software module, correct?

A: Yes.

Q: And the module was not delivered on March 15th, was it?

A: No. It wasn't.

Q: When was it delivered?

A: April 3rd.

Q: That's nineteen days late.

A: Yes.

Q: Were you the project manager responsible for that deliverable?

A: I was. I was responsible.

Q: Did you communicate to anyone at Vertex Systems that the deadline would be missed?

A: I... yes. I sent an email on March 11th.

Q: Four days before the deadline.

A: Four days before. Yes.

Q: Why only four days?

A: I kept thinking we could make it. I kept thinking if we just... I thought we could still make it. I was wrong.

Q: You were wrong.

A: I was wrong about a lot of things on this project, counsel.

Q: Mr. Holloway, I'm just trying to establish the timeline.

A: I understand. I'm sorry. The answer is four days. I gave four days' notice. It wasn't enough.

Q: Did anyone on your team raise concerns before that point?

A: Sarah Chen did. In February. She told me we were understaffed. She was right. I should have listened to her. I should have done a lot of things differently.

topic: A project manager is questioned about deadlines they missed on a software contract
text:
Q: Let's talk about the testing phase, Ms. Reiner. The contract called for user acceptance testing to be completed by June 1st?

A: That's correct.

Q: And it was not completed by June 1st.

A: No.

Q: When was testing actually completed?

A: July 22nd.

Q: Almost eight weeks late.

A: Yes.

Q: Ms. Reiner, I want to understand what happened. Can you walk me through the delay?

A: We had... there were defects. More than we anticipated. Critical defects that couldn't be shipped.

Q: How many critical defects?

A: Forty-seven at peak.

Q: Forty-seven.

A: Forty-seven.

Q: And whose responsibility was it to ensure the code was ready for testing?

A: That was... the development team reported to me. So. Mine.

Q: Take your time if you need it.

A: I don't need time, counsel. I've had plenty of time to think about this.

Q: I'm not trying to—

A: I know what you're trying to do. I understand. You want to know who's responsible. I am. I was the project manager. The development team was understaffed and overworked and I knew it, and I told leadership, and when they said no to more resources I said okay. I said okay and I shouldn't have.

Q: You requested additional resources?

A: I requested. I documented. I followed up. And then I stopped following up. That's on me.

topic: A project manager is questioned about deadlines they missed on a software contract
text:
Q: Mr. Okonkwo, you became project manager on this contract in September of last year?

A: September 14th, yes.

Q: You inherited the project from Rebecca Marsh?

A: Yes.

Q: Why did Ms. Marsh leave the project?

A: She was reassigned.

Q: Reassigned. Was she reassigned because the project was behind schedule?

A: I don't know the reasons. You'd have to ask her. Or ask management.

Q: What was the status of the project when you took over?

A: We were behind.

Q: How far behind?

A: Two milestones. Roughly six weeks.

Q: Six weeks behind when you started.

A: When I inherited it. Yes.

Q: And by the time the contract was terminated, the project was how far behind?

A: Eleven weeks.

Q: So the project fell further behind under your management.

A: It did.

Q: Did you implement any recovery plans?

A: I tried. We worked weekends. We cut scope where the client would allow it. We brought in two contractors.

Q: But it wasn't enough.

A: No.

Q: Mr. Okonkwo, did you believe the project could be saved when you took it over?

A: I believed... I wanted to believe it could. I thought if we worked hard enough. If I worked hard enough.

Q: But you don't believe that now.

A: No. I don't believe that now. I think it was too late before I ever walked in the door.

topic: A project manager is questioned about deadlines they missed on a software contract
text:
Q: Ms. Castellanos, I want to direct your attention to the milestone payment schedule, Exhibit 14.

A: Yes.

Q: The second milestone payment was contingent on delivery of the integration module by October 30th, correct?

A: Correct.

Q: The integration module was not delivered by October 30th.

A: No.

Q: When was it delivered?

A: November 18th.

Q: And as a result, your company did not receive the milestone payment.

A: We received a reduced payment. Eventually.

Q: After negotiation.

A: After negotiation. After a lot of... yes. After negotiation.

Q: Ms. Castellanos, who was responsible for the integration module timeline?

A: Directly? David Park was the technical lead. I was the project manager overseeing the schedule.

Q: So you were responsible.

A: I was one of the people responsible.

Q: Did David Park report to you?

A: He did.

Q: Did he tell you the module would be late?

A: He told me there were risks.

Q: When did he tell you that?

A: Early October. Maybe late September.

Q: And what did you do with that information?

A: I... I escalated it. I sent emails. I had meetings.

Q: Do you have copies of those emails?

A: I provided everything I have.

Q: But nothing changed.

A: No. Nothing changed. We just... we kept going. We kept trying.

Q: You kept trying.

A: What else was I supposed to do, counsel? Tell me. What would you have done?

topic: A project manager is questioned about deadlines they missed on a software contract
text:
Q: Mr. Fitzgerald, the final delivery deadline was January 31st.

A: Yes.

Q: The software was not delivered on January 31st.

A: No. It was delivered February 28th.

Q: Nearly a month late.

A: Twenty-eight days. Yes.

Q: And by that point, the client had already sent a notice of breach.

A: They had.

Q: You received that notice on February 3rd.

A: I did.

Q: What was your reaction when you received it?

A: My reaction.

Q: Yes.

A: I don't know how to answer that.

Q: Did you think it was fair?

A: Counsel, I... I understood why they sent it.

Q: That's not what I asked.

A: I know it isn't.

Q: Was it fair?

A: We were late. We were late on multiple deliverables. They had every right to send that notice.

Q: Mr. Fitzgerald.

A: I'm not sure what you want me to say. We tried. We worked. My team worked nights and weekends for three months. Some of them missed holidays with their families. And it still wasn't enough. The notice was... it was within their rights.

Q: I'm not asking about their rights.

A: Then I don't know what you're asking.

Q: I'm asking how you felt when you read it.

A: I think you know how I felt, counsel. I think that's why you're asking.

topic: A building inspector is deposed about a structural assessment they signed off on
text:
Q: Mr. Delacroix, you conducted the structural assessment of the Pemberton Building on March 14th, 2022, correct?

A: I did.

Q: And you signed off on that assessment as satisfactory?

A: That's what the form says.

Q: I'm asking what you did, Mr. Delacroix.

A: Yes. I signed it.

Q: When you inspected the east stairwell supports, what did you observe?

A: I observed what I documented in my report. Concrete supports, some surface cracking consistent with the building's age, nothing that rose to the level of structural concern at that time.

Q: "At that time." You want to qualify that?

A: I'm not qualifying anything. I'm stating a fact. Inspections reflect conditions on a specific date. That's how inspections work. That's how they've always worked.

Q: Did you use any diagnostic equipment to assess the rebar integrity within those supports?

A: No.

Q: Is that standard practice?

A: It can be. It wasn't required under the assessment protocol I was working from.

Q: Did you consider requesting a more invasive evaluation?

A: I considered it.

Q: And?

A: And I didn't request it. The visual inspection didn't indicate it was necessary. If you want me to tell you I should have done something different, I can't give you that. I did my job the way I was trained to do it, the way I'd done it two hundred times before on buildings just like that one.

Q: Do you wish you had requested it?

A: I don't think that question has an answer that helps anyone in this room.

topic: A building inspector is deposed about a structural assessment they signed off on
text:
Q: Ms. Thornton, how many inspections had you conducted prior to the Ridgeway Commons assessment?

A: Somewhere around three hundred. Maybe more.

Q: So you were experienced.

A: I was experienced.

Q: And yet the load-bearing wall on the fourth floor—the one that collapsed—you rated it as structurally sound.

A: I rated it as meeting code requirements based on my inspection.

Q: Help me understand something. You noted in your report, and I'm reading here, "minor horizontal cracking observed, typical settling patterns." Do you see that?

A: I see it.

Q: What would it have taken for you to flag that as something more serious?

A: More significant displacement. Wider crack propagation. Evidence of active movement rather than historical settling.

Q: And you saw none of that?

A: I saw what I documented.

Q: Ms. Thornton, I'm going to ask you a direct question, and I'd appreciate a direct answer.

A: Alright.

Q: Looking at what you know now, did you miss something?

A: Counsel, I've been asking myself that question every day for eleven months. I've gone through my photographs. I've gone through my notes. I've gone through the code requirements line by line. What I can tell you is that on September 8th, 2021, based on what was visible, based on what I was trained to look for, based on twenty years of doing this work—I made the call I made.

Q: That's not a yes or no.

A: No. It isn't.

topic: A building inspector is deposed about a structural assessment they signed off on
text:
Q: Mr. Okafor, let's talk about the timeline. You received the inspection request on what date?

A: June 3rd.

Q: And when did you conduct the actual inspection?

A: June 19th.

Q: That's sixteen days. Is that typical?

A: We had a backlog.

Q: How large a backlog?

A: I don't remember exactly. Significant.

Q: More than fifty pending requests?

A: Probably.

Q: More than a hundred?

A: I don't know. Possibly. We were understaffed. We'd been understaffed for two years. Everyone knew it. I'd written memos about it. My supervisor had written memos about it.

Q: So when you finally got to the Crane Street property, were you rushed?

A: I spent the time the inspection required.

Q: How long was that?

A: About ninety minutes.

Q: Is that sufficient for a building of that size and age?

A: It was what I had.

Q: That's not what I asked.

A: I know what you asked. You want me to say I cut corners. I didn't cut corners. I worked within a system that—look, I'm not going to sit here and pretend the system was adequate. But I did my job within that system. That's all I could do. That's all any of us could do.

Q: Let's move on.

A: Fine.

Q: The foundation inspection—

A: I have the report in front of me. What do you want to know?

topic: A building inspector is deposed about a structural assessment they signed off on
text:
Q: Dr. Reyes, you were the senior inspector who reviewed and countersigned Mr. Patterson's initial assessment, is that right?

A: That's correct.

Q: What does that review process entail?

A: I examine the documentation, the photographs, the measurements. I compare them against the relevant codes. If everything appears to be in order, I countersign.

Q: Do you visit the site yourself?

A: Not typically, no.

Q: So you're relying entirely on the field inspector's work.

A: I'm relying on their documentation and their professional judgment, yes.

Q: Did anything in Mr. Patterson's report give you pause?

A: Not that I recall.

Q: You don't recall, or nothing gave you pause?

A: Counsel, I've reviewed hundreds of these assessments. I'm not going to sit here and claim I have a specific memory of my thought process on one particular file from three years ago. What I can tell you is that if something had concerned me, I would have flagged it. That's what the review process is for.

Q: Is it possible something should have concerned you but didn't?

A: It's possible. Yes. It's possible.

Q: Does that trouble you?

A: What do you want me to say? That I don't sleep well? That I think about the families? I countersigned a document. I followed procedure. And then seventeen months later, a parking structure collapsed. I don't know how to make those two facts fit together in a way that gives anyone closure. I've tried. If you figure it out, let me know.

Q: I have a few more questions about the specific documentation.

A: I assumed you would.

topic: A building inspector is deposed about a structural assessment they signed off on
text:
Q: Mr. Huang, the assessment checklist you used—was that the standard departmental form?

A: It was.

Q: Item 14 on that form asks about "visible signs of water infiltration or moisture damage." You checked "None observed."

A: I did.

Q: The post-collapse analysis found extensive water damage in the basement mechanical room. Rusted supports. Deteriorated concrete.

A: I'm aware of what the post-collapse analysis found.

Q: How do you reconcile that with your assessment?

A: The mechanical room was locked. I noted that in my report. "Access to basement mechanical room not available at time of inspection."

Q: You noted it. But you still checked "None observed" rather than "Unable to inspect."

A: There was no option for "Unable to inspect" on that form.

Q: So you chose "None observed."

A: I chose the option that seemed closest to accurate. I observed no signs of water damage in the areas I could access.

Q: Did you consider that misleading?

A: At the time? No. I was working with a form that didn't account for partial access situations. I made a judgment call. It's the same judgment call every inspector in the department made when they encountered a locked door or a restricted area. We all knew the forms were inadequate. We'd been saying so for years.

Q: To whom?

A: To anyone who would listen. Which wasn't many people. Not until afterward. Now everyone wants to listen. Now there are committees and reviews and new forms with better checkboxes. I'm glad. I mean that. I just wish it hadn't taken what it took.

Q: Did you ever follow up about gaining access to that mechanical room?

A: No. I moved on to the next building. There was always a next building.

topic: A project manager is questioned about deadlines they missed on a software contract
text:
Q: Mr. Hensley, the Meridian contract specified a delivery date of March 15th, correct?

A: That's what the contract states, yes.

Q: And the software was not delivered on March 15th, was it?

A: No, it was not.

Q: When was it delivered?

A: April 22nd.

Q: That's thirty-eight days late.

A: I—yes, if you're counting calendar days, that's—yes.

Q: I am counting calendar days, Mr. Hensley. Were you counting something else?

A: No. No, I was just—thirty-eight days, that's correct.

Q: At any point before March 15th, did you inform Meridian that you would miss the deadline?

A: We had communications with them, yes.

Q: That wasn't my question. Did you specifically tell them you would miss the March 15th deadline?

A: I believe we—look, there were multiple calls, multiple emails, and the situation was—it was evolving. I can't sit here and tell you the exact words of every communication.

Q: I'm not asking for every communication. I'm asking if you ever said the words "we will not meet the March 15th deadline."

A: I don't—I don't recall using those exact words.

Q: Do you recall using any words to that effect?

A: I recall discussing challenges. Timeline challenges.

Q: "Challenges." Did those challenges include the fact that you were going to be thirty-eight days late?

A: We didn't know it would be thirty-eight days. We didn't have—I mean, how could we know that specific number in advance?

topic: A project manager is questioned about deadlines they missed on a software contract
text:
Q: Let's talk about the milestone schedule. You prepared this document, Exhibit 14?

A: Yes.

Q: And it shows five delivery milestones between January and June of last year?

A: Correct.

Q: How many of these milestones were met on time?

A: One.

Q: One out of five. Which one?

A: The first one. The requirements documentation.

Q: And the other four?

A: They were delayed.

Q: By how much? Let's go through them. Milestone two, the architecture review—when was that due?

A: February 10th.

Q: When was it completed?

A: February 28th.

Q: Milestone three?

A: Due March 1st. Completed March 19th.

Q: Milestone four?

A: Can I—I have the document in front of me, I can just read them if that would be faster.

Q: I'd like you to answer from memory, please.

A: I don't understand why that matters.

Q: It matters because I'm asking. Milestone four—when was it due?

A: March 20th. Completed April 3rd.

Q: And milestone five, the final delivery?

A: April 15th, completed May 2nd.

Q: So after the first milestone, every single deadline slipped. Is that a fair characterization?

A: That's—yes, that's what happened.

Q: Whose responsibility was it to ensure these milestones were met?

A: That was—there were many factors outside my direct control. I was the project manager, but I didn't control staffing decisions, I didn't control the client's change requests—

Q: Mr. Okonkwo, I asked whose responsibility it was. Not what factors existed.

A: Mine. On paper, mine.

topic: A project manager is questioned about deadlines they missed on a software contract
text:
Q: Ms. Vasquez, when did you first realize the July deadline was in jeopardy?

A: Probably early June. Maybe late May.

Q: Which is it?

A: I can't give you an exact date.

Q: I'm not asking for an exact date. Late May or early June—those are different times.

A: Fine. Early June.

Q: What caused you to realize it in early June?

A: The integration testing was taking longer than we'd estimated.

Q: How much longer?

A: Significantly longer.

Q: Can you quantify that?

A: I don't have the numbers in front of me.

Q: Ballpark.

A: Maybe twice as long. Maybe more. I really—I would need to look at the actual logs.

Q: When you realized the deadline was in jeopardy, what did you do?

A: I escalated.

Q: To whom?

A: David Reinholt. My supervisor.

Q: What did you tell him?

A: I told him we had a problem with the integration phase and that the July date was looking unlikely.

Q: What did he say?

A: He told me to figure it out.

Q: Did he offer any resources? Additional staff?

A: No.

Q: Did you ask for additional resources?

A: I—yes. I asked.

Q: And?

A: And he said no. He said the budget was fixed. I told him what I could do with what I had, and I did it. I don't know what else you want me to say here.

topic: A project manager is questioned about deadlines they missed on a software contract
text:
Q: The deadline was December 1st.

A: Yes.

Q: You missed it.

A: Yes.

Q: By how long?

A: Eleven days.

Q: The contract contained a liquidated damages clause, didn't it?

A: I'm not—I was the project manager. Contract terms were handled by legal and the account team.

Q: But you were aware of the liquidated damages clause?

A: I became aware of it, yes.

Q: When?

A: After we missed the deadline.

Q: Not before?

A: Not specifically, no. I knew there were penalties of some kind. I didn't know the exact terms.

Q: So you were managing a project with financial penalties for late delivery, and you didn't know what those penalties were?

A: That's not—that's a very particular way of framing it.

Q: How would you frame it?

A: I would say I was focused on delivery. The financial and legal terms were not my area.

Q: Whose area were they?

A: Legal. Account management. As I said.

Q: Did anyone from legal or account management ever tell you what the penalties were?

A: Not in detail.

Q: In any detail?

A: I knew they were substantial.

Q: "Substantial." And knowing they were substantial, you still missed the deadline.

A: We did everything we could to meet it. Sometimes circumstances—

Q: I'm not asking about circumstances right now, Mr. Brennan. I'm asking whether you missed the deadline.

A: Yes. I already said yes.

topic: A project manager is questioned about deadlines they missed on a software contract
text:
Q: Let me ask you about the status reports you sent to the client.

A: Okay.

Q: You sent weekly reports, correct?

A: Correct.

Q: I'm looking at the report dated September 3rd. You wrote, and I'm quoting, "Project remains on track for October 15th delivery." Do you see that?

A: Yes.

Q: Was that true when you wrote it?

A: It was true based on what I knew at the time.

Q: What did you know at the time?

A: That we were on schedule according to our internal tracking.

Q: And a week later—September 10th—you wrote the same thing. "On track for October 15th."

A: If that's what it says.

Q: It is what it says. Was that still true?

A: I believed so, yes.

Q: September 17th, same thing.

A: Okay.

Q: September 24th, you wrote—still quoting—"Minor delays in testing phase; team working to recover schedule." What happened between September 17th and September 24th?

A: We encountered some issues.

Q: What kind of issues?

A: Technical issues. With the database migration.

Q: How serious were these issues?

A: They were—they required attention.

Q: Ms. Park, on October 15th, you delivered nothing. The actual delivery was November 9th. So I'm asking you: between September 17th, when everything was "on track," and September 24th, when you had "minor delays"—how did a project go from on track to twenty-five days late in one week?

A: It wasn't one week. The problems—look, the problems accumulated. They weren't all visible at once. That's how these things happen. I reported what I knew when I knew it. I didn't hide anything. I didn't lie in those reports.

Q: I haven't accused you of lying.

A: It certainly sounds like you're building to something.

Q: I'm asking questions, Ms. Park. That's all.

A: Then ask them.

topic: A store manager is questioned about a customer slip-and-fall on their premises
text:
Q: Please state your name and position for the record.

A: David Chen, General Manager of the Westbrook Plaza location. I've held that position for eleven years now, and I was actually the one who developed the safety protocol that's been adopted across all fourteen stores in our regional chain.

Q: Mr. Chen, were you present on the day of the incident, March 15th?

A: I was. I'm on-site six days a week, often seven. I believe in hands-on management.

Q: Can you describe the condition of the floor in aisle seven that morning?

A: Immaculate. I had personally walked the floor at 8:15 AM, as I do every morning before we open. I have a checklist system I created—would you like me to walk you through it?

Q: That won't be necessary. Were you aware of any spills prior to the plaintiff's fall?

A: There were no spills. My team knows that any liquid on the floor gets addressed within three minutes. That's our standard—my standard, actually. I implemented it in 2019, and we haven't had a single incident report until this claim.

Q: Yet the plaintiff alleges she slipped on a wet surface.

A: With respect, counselor, the plaintiff is mistaken. I reviewed the security footage myself within ten minutes of the alleged incident. The floor was dry. I know my store.

Q: Did any employee witness the fall?

A: Marcus Williams was nearby. He's one of my best—I trained him personally.

Q: What did Mr. Williams report to you?

A: That the customer appeared to lose her balance on her own. No external cause. He offered assistance immediately, exactly as I've trained my staff to do.

Q: Was a wet floor sign present in that area?

A: There was no need for one. But I'll tell you this—we have twelve signs stationed throughout the store at all times, ready for deployment. I ordered those myself when I took over. Prevention, counselor. That's how you run a safe operation.

Q: Did you document the incident?

A: Within the hour. I have a documentation system that the district manager has called "exemplary." I can provide those records if you'd like to see how a proper incident report looks.

topic: A store manager is questioned about a customer slip-and-fall on their premises
text:
Q: Good morning. You're the manager at Franklin's Hardware on Elm Street, correct?

A: Yes, ma'am.

Q: How long have you worked there?

A: About eight months now.

Q: And you were working on October 3rd of last year?

A: I was.

Q: Tell me about your training regarding floor safety hazards.

A: We had a video. Maybe an hour long. And some papers to sign.

Q: That's the extent of it?

A: Yes, ma'am.

Q: Now, I want to direct your attention to a rather impressive safety record your store has maintained. Zero reported incidents in the eighteen months prior to this fall—isn't that remarkable for a store with such heavy foot traffic?

A: I guess so.

Q: You guess so? That kind of record doesn't happen by accident, does it, Mr. Porter?

A: I don't know. I wasn't there for most of that time.

Q: But surely you've maintained those high standards since taking over?

A: I try to do my job.

Q: The previous manager must have established excellent protocols. Would you say you've upheld those protocols?

A: I follow the procedures I was given.

Q: The spill in question—it was in the plumbing aisle, yes?

A: That's what I was told.

Q: Told? You didn't see it yourself?

A: I was in the back doing inventory when it happened.

Q: So the exemplary safety culture at this store—that culture allowed a spill to go unaddressed for how long?

A: I don't know exactly.

Q: More than five minutes?

A: I really couldn't say.

topic: A store manager is questioned about a customer slip-and-fall on their premises
text:
Q: Ms. Hartwell, what procedures were in place for addressing spills on November 12th?

A: We had a comprehensive spill response protocol. I actually rewrote it myself when I became manager three years ago. The previous version was inadequate.

Q: What was inadequate about it?

A: Response times weren't specified. No clear chain of responsibility. I created a tiered system—I'm happy to explain it in detail.

Q: Just briefly.

A: Any employee who spots a hazard radios it in immediately. A designated responder has ninety seconds to arrive with appropriate materials. The area is cordoned off, cleaned, dried, and inspected before the cordon comes down. Average resolution time under four minutes.

Q: That's quite specific.

A: I track the metrics. I believe in accountability.

Q: Yet on November 12th, a customer fell.

A: She did.

Q: So the system failed.

A: No. The system worked exactly as designed.

Q: I'm not sure I follow. Someone was injured in your store.

A: The spill was reported at 2:47 PM. Mariana had the area blocked off by 2:48. The customer chose to step over the wet floor sign at 2:49. I have the timestamps.

Q: You're saying she ignored the warning sign?

A: I'm saying exactly what the footage shows. My team performed flawlessly.

Q: Do you have that footage?

A: Already provided to your office last month. I made copies the same day and secured the originals. Proper evidence preservation—another protocol I established.

Q: Did you speak with the customer after the fall?

A: Immediately. I offered first aid, called for medical assistance, and documented her statements while they were fresh. I also took photographs of the sign placement and her footwear, which had smooth soles, for the record.

Q: You photographed her shoes?

A: Thoroughness matters, counselor. Would you prefer a manager who cuts corners?

topic: A store manager is questioned about a customer slip-and-fall on their premises
text:
Q: State your name, please.

A: Robert Ansley.

Q: And your position?

A: Floor manager at Greenview Market.

Q: How long in that role?

A: Four years.

Q: Were you on duty on January 8th?

A: I was.

Q: Did you witness Mrs. Patterson's fall?

A: No. I heard about it after.

Q: Who informed you?

A: One of my cashiers. Delia.

Q: What did you do upon learning of the fall?

A: Went to the scene. Customer was on the ground near the dairy case. I helped her up.

Q: Did you investigate the cause?

A: There was a small amount of liquid. Looked like milk.

Q: How small?

A: Maybe... eight inches across? Not large.

Q: Do you know how long that milk had been on the floor?

A: No.

Q: More than five minutes?

A: I couldn't say.

Q: More than thirty minutes?

A: I don't believe so, but I can't be certain.

Q: Let me show you what's been marked as Exhibit 14—this is a schedule showing your staff positions that day. Do you see that there's a forty-minute gap where no one was assigned to monitor the dairy section?

A: I see that.

Q: How did that happen?

A: Jason called in sick. We were short-staffed.

Q: So your system broke down because one person was absent?

A: We have contingency procedures. They weren't followed correctly that day. That's on me. I should have caught it.

Q: You acknowledge the failure was preventable?

A: I do.

topic: A store manager is questioned about a customer slip-and-fall on their premises
text:
Q: Mr. Whitman, describe your store's floor inspection routine.

A: Inspections every thirty minutes. Logged and initialed.

Q: And on the date in question, August 22nd, were those inspections performed?

A: Yes.

Q: Every thirty minutes?

A: Every thirty minutes.

Q: I'm looking at your inspection log here. The 2:00 PM inspection is initialed, and then the next entry is at 3:15 PM. That's a seventy-five minute gap.

A: Let me see that.

Q: Of course.

A: That's... that's incorrect. That shouldn't have happened.

Q: But it did happen. On the day your customer was injured.

A: I see the gap. I can't explain it sitting here today.

Q: Who was responsible for the 2:30 inspection?

A: I'd have to check the assignment sheet.

Q: Let's do that. This is Exhibit 7—your assignment sheet for August 22nd. Who was assigned to floor safety between 2:00 and 4:00 PM?

A: It says Tyler Briggs.

Q: Is Mr. Briggs still employed at your store?

A: No.

Q: Why not?

A: He was terminated.

Q: When?

A: August 30th.

Q: Eight days after this incident. What was the reason for his termination?

A: I'd have to review his personnel file.

Q: Mr. Whitman, you terminated him. Surely you recall why.

A: Failure to follow safety protocols.

Q: This wasn't an isolated lapse, was it? This was a pattern with Mr. Briggs—a pattern you had documented and failed to address until someone got hurt.

A: We addressed it when we became aware of the extent.

Q: After the injury.

A: Yes. After the injury.

topic: A paramedic is questioned about the response time and treatment at an accident scene
text:
Q: Let's talk about the timeline that night. You arrived at the scene at what time?

A: Our unit arrived at 11:47 PM. That's documented in the run report.

Q: And the 911 call came in at what time?

A: 11:31 PM.

Q: So sixteen minutes from dispatch to arrival.

A: That's the math, yes.

Q: Is sixteen minutes a typical response time for your unit?

A: Define "typical."

Q: What's your average response time?

A: It varies. Depends on traffic, weather, distance from the station, whether we're already on another call. There's no single number I can give you that would be meaningful.

Q: I'm asking for an average. Surely you have some sense of that.

A: I don't carry statistics around in my head, counselor. What I can tell you is that we responded as quickly as conditions allowed that night.

Q: What conditions would those be?

A: Construction on Route 9. Single lane traffic for about a mile and a half. It's been that way for months. Anyone who drives that road knows it.

Q: Did you document the construction delay?

A: It's not standard practice to document every traffic condition we encounter.

Q: So no.

A: I just answered your question.

Q: Let me ask it differently. Is there anything in your written report that would explain a sixteen-minute response time?

A: The report documents our arrival time. It documents the care we provided. That's what a run report is for.

topic: A paramedic is questioned about the response time and treatment at an accident scene
text:
Q: When you reached the vehicle, what did you observe about the driver?

A: He was unconscious, slumped against the steering wheel. There was significant facial trauma, blood visible on the dashboard and windshield.

Q: What was your first action?

A: My partner stabilized his head and neck while I assessed his airway.

Q: And what did you find?

A: Airway was partially obstructed. Blood and what appeared to be a dislodged tooth.

Q: Did you suction the airway?

A: Yes.

Q: Immediately?

A: I'm sorry, what do you mean by "immediately"?

Q: Did you suction the airway right away, or did you do something else first?

A: We don't just start suctioning without assessment. There's a sequence. You assess, you position, you suction if indicated.

Q: How long did that sequence take?

A: I didn't have a stopwatch running. It was... efficient. We moved as quickly as the situation allowed while maintaining proper protocol.

Q: Would you say it took one minute? Two minutes?

A: I genuinely don't know. Under two minutes, I would estimate. Probably well under.

Q: You're estimating.

A: I am. Because that's all I can do without a timestamp, and there's no timestamp for every action we take.

Q: Is there any documentation of when you cleared the airway?

A: The run report notes that airway management was performed. It doesn't break down each individual step by the second.

Q: Would it surprise you if I told you the fire department's report indicates you were still assessing the patient four minutes after your arrival?

A: I'd want to see exactly what that report says and who wrote it before I commented on it.

topic: A paramedic is questioned about the response time and treatment at an accident scene
text:
Q: You've been a paramedic for how long?

A: Eleven years this past March.

Q: In your eleven years, have you ever had a patient die en route to the hospital?

A: Yes. It happens.

Q: How many times, roughly?

A: I couldn't give you an exact number. It's... part of the job. Some patients can't be saved regardless of what we do.

Q: I understand. I'm asking about frequency.

A: Maybe a dozen times? Fifteen? Over eleven years, working hundreds of calls a year.

Q: Does it become routine?

A: Excuse me?

Q: A patient dying. Does it become routine after eleven years?

A: No. It never becomes routine. I'm not sure what you're implying.

Q: I'm not implying anything. I'm asking about your state of mind.

A: My state of mind was focused on providing the best possible care to Mr. Hernandez that night. That's my state of mind on every call.

Q: Let's talk about the specific treatment decisions. You chose not to intubate in the field.

A: Correct.

Q: Why not?

A: Because I made a clinical judgment that BVM ventilation was adequate and that the faster we transported, the better his chances. Intubation in the field takes time. Time he didn't have.

Q: That's your judgment.

A: Yes. That's literally what you're asking me about.

Q: Other paramedics might have made a different call.

A: Other paramedics weren't there.

topic: A paramedic is questioned about the response time and treatment at an accident scene
text:
Q: I want to be very precise about this. You're saying the defibrillator was functioning properly?

A: Yes.

Q: No issues whatsoever.

A: It performed as expected, yes.

Q: Then can you explain why there's a maintenance log showing that same unit was flagged for battery issues two days later?

A: I can't explain what happens to equipment after I use it. I can tell you it worked when we needed it.

Q: It worked.

A: Yes.

Q: How do you know?

A: Because it analyzed the rhythm. It delivered the shock when indicated. It did exactly what it's supposed to do.

Q: Did you check the battery level before using it?

A: The unit runs a self-check when powered on. It indicated ready status. That's the protocol.

Q: Do you remember the specific battery indicator?

A: I remember it showing ready. I don't remember the exact percentage, if that's what you're asking.

Q: You don't.

A: No. I was focused on the patient, not on memorizing equipment readouts.

Q: How many shocks did you deliver?

A: Three.

Q: And after the third shock?

A: We achieved return of spontaneous circulation. His heart started beating on its own. That's a successful resuscitation, counselor.

Q: Which was then lost again in the ambulance.

A: He re-arrested during transport. It happens with severe trauma.

Q: I see. It happens.

A: It does. I'm not sure what else you want me to say.

topic: A paramedic is questioned about the response time and treatment at an accident scene
text:
Q: Your partner that night was Derek Simmons?

A: That's right.

Q: How long had you worked with Mr. Simmons?

A: About eight months at that point.

Q: Is that a long time in your field, or a short time?

A: It's... medium, I suppose. Long enough to know each other's rhythms.

Q: Did you and Mr. Simmons work well together?

A: Yes. We were a good team.

Q: No disagreements about treatment approaches?

A: Everyone has occasional differences of opinion. That's normal.

Q: On this particular call, did you have any differences of opinion?

A: Nothing significant.

Q: But something insignificant?

A: I didn't say that.

Q: You said "nothing significant." That implies there was something.

A: I meant there were no disagreements. I was trying to be precise and I misspoke.

Q: Let me ask you directly: Did Derek Simmons express any concern about any decision you made that night?

A: He asked if I wanted him to start a second IV line. I said we didn't have time.

Q: So he thought a second line was warranted, and you disagreed.

A: He asked a question. I made a call. That's how it works. One person has to be in charge.

Q: And you were in charge.

A: I was lead medic, yes.

Q: Have you spoken to Mr. Simmons about his recollection of that night?

A: No. I was told not to discuss the case with him once the lawsuit was filed.

Q: Before the lawsuit was filed?

A: We may have talked about it the way you talk about any difficult call. I don't remember the specifics of any conversation.

topic: A witness is asked about a car accident they saw from their front porch
text:
Q: Good afternoon. You were sitting on your front porch on the afternoon of March 15th, correct?

A: I was.

Q: And from that position, you had a view of the intersection of Maple and Third?

A: I did. Same view I've had for thirty-two years.

Q: Can you describe what you observed that afternoon?

A: The blue sedan ran the light. The pickup was already in the intersection. They collided. That's what happened.

Q: Let's slow down. When you say the sedan "ran the light," what exactly—

A: The light was red. The car went through it. I don't know how many different ways I can say it.

Q: I understand. I'm just trying to establish the sequence. How long had the light been red when the sedan entered the intersection?

A: I don't know. A few seconds. I wasn't counting.

Q: Would you say more than five seconds? Less?

A: I said I don't know. It was red. It had been red. That's all I can tell you.

Q: Fair enough. What color was the light for the pickup truck?

A: Green. Obviously.

Q: You saw the light for the truck's direction as well?

A: I can see both lights from my porch. I've been watching that intersection since before you were born, counselor. The truck had the green.

Q: After the collision, what did you do?

A: I went inside and called 911. Then I came back out. Then I waited. Then the police came and I told them what I told you. And now I'm here, telling you again.

Q: I appreciate your time, sir.

A: I'm sure you do.

---

topic: A witness is asked about a car accident they saw from their front porch
text:
Q: Ms. Patterson, you've stated you were on your porch at approximately 4:30 p.m.?

A: Around that time, yes.

Q: What were you doing on the porch?

A: Sitting. Having my coffee. Watching the street like I always do.

Q: And you witnessed a collision between two vehicles?

A: I saw it, yes.

Q: Okay. Let me ask you about the white SUV. Did you see it before the collision occurred?

A: I did.

Q: How long before?

A: Oh, I don't know. Maybe... maybe thirty seconds? It was coming down Maple from the east.

Q: And how would you describe its speed?

A: It was moving fast. Faster than it should have been.

Q: Can you estimate the speed in miles per hour?

A: I'm not... I really couldn't say a number. It just looked fast.

Q: Faster than the speed limit?

A: I assume so. I don't actually know what the speed limit is on that stretch. I probably should, shouldn't I?

Q: I'm just asking what you observed.

A: It looked fast. That's my observation. I'm sorry I can't give you more than that.

Q: That's fine. What about the other vehicle, the gray sedan—did you see it approaching?

A: Not until right before. It came from my left, from Third Street. I didn't really notice it until the SUV was already—until it was too late, I guess.

Q: Too late meaning—

A: Meaning they hit. The SUV hit the sedan. I'm sorry, I know you need details, but it happened so fast and I've gone over it so many times now.

Q: I understand. Just a few more questions. Did you hear anything before the collision?

A: The SUV's engine, I think. It was loud. Or maybe I'm just remembering it that way because I know what happened next.

---

topic: A witness is asked about a car accident they saw from their front porch
text:
Q: Mr. Dominguez, I want to focus on the moments immediately before the accident. You said you heard something that drew your attention?

A: A horn. Someone honked.

Q: Which vehicle honked?

A: I couldn't tell you.

Q: But you heard it clearly?

A: I heard a horn. Yes.

Q: Fine. And then what did you see?

A: Then I looked up and saw the cars collide.

Q: So you didn't actually see the vehicles approaching the intersection?

A: No. Not until the horn.

Q: Let me make sure I understand. Your testimony is that you only looked at the intersection after hearing the horn?

A: That's what I said.

Q: So you didn't see whether either vehicle ran a red light?

A: No.

Q: You didn't see the speed of either vehicle before impact?

A: No.

Q: Alright. Let's move on. After the collision—

A: Look, I know this isn't what you were hoping for. I've already told the police, I told the insurance people, I told your office when they called. I only saw the last second of it. I can't change that.

Q: Mr. Dominguez, I'm not suggesting—

A: I know what you're doing. You're trying to see if I'll remember something different this time. I won't. I heard a horn, I looked up, I saw the crash. That's the whole story.

Q: I appreciate your candor. Let me ask about what you saw after the impact.

A: Fine.

Q: Did either driver exit their vehicle?

A: Eventually. The man in the truck got out first. He was holding his neck.

---

topic: A witness is asked about a car accident they saw from their front porch
text:
Q: You mentioned the weather conditions earlier. It had been raining?

A: On and off all morning. By the afternoon it was just drizzle, really.

Q: Was the pavement wet at the time of the accident?

A: Yes. The roads were wet.

Q: Could you see the road surface clearly from your porch?

A: I could see it was shiny. Reflective. The way pavement gets when it's wet.

Q: Alright. Now, I'm going to ask you about something you mentioned in your statement to police. You said the red car "didn't even try to stop."

A: Did I say that?

Q: According to the police report, yes.

A: Then I suppose I did.

Q: Do you recall what you meant by that?

A: I meant... I don't know. I meant it didn't slow down. No brake lights that I remember.

Q: You watched for brake lights specifically?

A: I didn't watch for anything specifically. I just saw what I saw.

Q: But you don't recall seeing brake lights on the red car?

A: No.

Q: What about on the other vehicle?

A: The minivan? I think so. I think I saw the brake lights come on right before—yes. The minivan tried to stop.

Q: Let me ask this more directly. Is it your testimony that the red car made no attempt to avoid the collision?

A: I'm telling you what it looked like to me. From my porch. Fifty feet away. In the drizzle. I'm not an accident reconstruction expert. I'm a retired postal worker who happened to be sitting outside.

Q: I'm just asking what you saw.

topic: A witness is asked about a car accident they saw from their front porch
text:

Q: Alright. I think we've covered this ground. Let me ask about something else. Did you—

topic: A doctor is deposed about informed consent procedures before a surgery
text:
Q: Dr. Patel, I'd like to walk through your standard informed consent process. Can you describe what that looks like in your practice?

A: Certainly. I meet with the patient in my office, typically the week before surgery. We discuss the procedure itself, the expected outcomes, the risks, alternatives, and what recovery looks like. I answer any questions they have. Then we review the consent form together before they sign.

Q: And how long does that conversation usually take?

A: It varies depending on the complexity of the procedure and how many questions the patient has. For a surgery like the one we're discussing today, I'd estimate thirty to forty-five minutes on average.

Q: Do you document these conversations?

A: I do. I dictate a note after each pre-operative visit that summarizes what we discussed, including the specific risks I reviewed with the patient.

Q: Is that note part of the medical record?

A: Yes, it's incorporated into the patient's chart.

Q: Do you have a copy of that note for Mrs. Gutierrez?

A: I reviewed it before today. It's dated October 3rd, 2022.

Q: And what risks did you document discussing with her?

A: The note reflects that I discussed bleeding, infection, nerve damage, the possibility of incomplete symptom relief, and the risk of needing additional surgery.

Q: Did you discuss the specific risk of permanent numbness in her left hand?

A: That would fall under nerve damage. I explain to patients that nerve damage can present as numbness, tingling, weakness, or pain, and that in some cases it can be permanent.

Q: Do you recall whether you used the word "permanent" with Mrs. Gutierrez specifically?

A: I don't have an independent recollection of that specific conversation, but it's my standard practice to explain that nerve damage can be temporary or permanent, and my note reflects that I followed my standard practice.

Q: Fair enough. Does your consent form list permanent nerve damage as a risk?

A: It lists nerve damage. The form is a summary; the detailed discussion happens in person.

---

topic: A doctor is deposed about informed consent procedures before a surgery
text:
Q: Doctor, how do you typically explain surgical risks to patients who don't have a medical background?

A: I try to use plain language. I avoid jargon. If I need to use a medical term, I explain what it means. I also ask patients to repeat back their understanding so I know we're on the same page.

Q: You ask them to repeat it back?

A: When appropriate, yes. It's a technique called teach-back. It helps ensure comprehension.

Q: Did you use that technique with Mr. Holloway?

A: I don't recall specifically, but it's part of my routine.

Q: What risks did you discuss with him before his procedure?

A: The risks associated with lumbar fusion—infection, blood clots, hardware failure, adjacent segment disease, nerve injury, and the possibility that the surgery might not fully resolve his pain.

Q: Did you discuss the risk of paralysis?

A: Yes. With any spinal surgery, I discuss the risk of neurological injury, including the possibility of weakness or paralysis, even though it's rare.

Q: How rare?

A: The literature puts the risk of significant permanent neurological deficit at less than one percent for this type of procedure, and I share that with patients.

Q: Do you remember Mr. Holloway's reaction when you told him that?

A: I don't recall his specific reaction. Most patients are understandably concerned, but they proceed after weighing the risks against their symptoms.

Q: Did he ask any follow-up questions about paralysis?

A: I don't have a specific memory of that, no.

Q: Did anyone else witness your informed consent discussion with Mr. Holloway?

A: My nurse coordinator is typically present for these conversations. I believe Rebecca Tran was in the room.

---

topic: A doctor is deposed about informed consent procedures before a surgery
text:
Q: Let's talk about timing. When do you obtain consent relative to the surgery itself?

A: I have the detailed conversation in my office during the pre-op visit, usually one to two weeks before surgery. The patient signs the consent form at that visit. On the day of surgery, I see the patient again before we go back to the operating room.

Q: What happens during that day-of-surgery conversation?

A: I confirm they're still consenting to proceed. I ask if they have any last questions. I review what we're doing one more time. It's brief—five minutes or so—but it gives them a final opportunity to raise concerns.

Q: And if they raised a concern, what would happen?

A: We'd address it. If they wanted to postpone or cancel, we would respect that.

Q: Has that ever happened to you?

A: Once or twice over the years, a patient has gotten cold feet the morning of surgery. We postponed.

Q: Did Mrs. Chen raise any concerns on the morning of her surgery?

A: No. She confirmed she wanted to proceed and didn't have any additional questions.

Q: Do you document that day-of-surgery conversation?

A: The pre-op nursing note typically documents that consent was verified. My operative report confirms the procedure was performed with informed consent.

Q: But you personally don't write a separate note about that morning conversation?

A: That's correct. The nursing documentation and the signed consent form serve that purpose.

Q: Do you have any independent memory of speaking with Mrs. Chen that morning?

A: I remember her, yes. She was pleasant. She seemed prepared. Beyond that, the details blend together—I've done several hundred of these surgeries.

---

topic: A doctor is deposed about informed consent procedures before a surgery
text:
Q: Dr. Yamamoto, did you discuss alternative treatments with Mr. Franklin before recommending surgery?

A: I did. We had been managing his condition conservatively for about eighteen months before surgery became the recommendation.

Q: What conservative treatments had he tried?

A: Physical therapy, anti-inflammatory medications, two epidural steroid injections, and activity modification. He also saw a pain management specialist for a time.

Q: And those weren't effective?

A: They provided temporary relief, but his symptoms progressed. By the time we discussed surgery, he was experiencing significant functional limitations.

Q: When you say "functional limitations," what do you mean?

A: He could no longer work his job—he's a carpenter—and he was having difficulty with daily activities like walking more than a block or sitting for extended periods.

Q: Who made the decision to proceed with surgery?

A: Mr. Franklin did. I presented the options, gave him my recommendation, and he decided.

Q: What options did you present?

A: Continue with conservative management, pursue surgery, or seek a second opinion. I always offer patients the option of seeing another surgeon if they want a different perspective.

Q: Did he seek a second opinion?

A: Not to my knowledge.

Q: Did you encourage him to?

A: I mentioned it was available to him. I don't push patients in either direction on that.

Q: Is there anything in your records indicating he understood the alternatives?

A: My pre-operative note documents the discussion. The consent form he signed also includes a statement that alternatives were explained.

---

Q: But not a written checklist?

A: No. Some surgeons use them; I rely on my routine and my dictated notes.

Q: How do you ensure you don't miss anything?

A: Fifteen years of practice. The conversation is structured. I cover the same ground every time because that's how I was trained and how I train my residents.

Q: You have residents present during these conversations?

A: Sometimes. It's a teaching opportunity. They observe how to conduct informed consent properly.

Q: Was a resident present when you obtained consent from Ms. Barrera?

A: I'd have to check the note. I don't recall.

A: I have the note in front of me. No, there's no mention of a resident, so I likely conducted that visit alone.

Q: Does Ms. Barrera's consent form look standard to you?

A: It does. It's the form we use for all orthopedic procedures at the hospital.

topic: A doctor is deposed about informed consent procedures before a surgery
text:
Q: Doctor, I want to make sure I understand your testimony. You're saying you always discuss alternative treatment options with patients before surgery?

A: Always.

Q: Without exception?

A: Without exception.

Q: Then help me understand something. I've reviewed your records for Mrs. Patterson, and I see no mention anywhere—not in your notes, not in the consent form, not in any nursing documentation—of any discussion about non-surgical management of her condition.

A: The absence of documentation does not mean the conversation didn't occur.

Q: So you're asking us to just take your word for it.

A: I'm telling you what my practice is. My consistent, unvarying practice over two decades.

Q: Let's talk about what the records do show. Your pre-operative note says, and I'm quoting here, "patient consents to surgery." That's the entire note.

A: That was sufficient documentation at the time.

Q: Four words, Doctor? Four words to capture a discussion about a surgery that left this woman unable to walk without assistance?

A: I'm not going to sit here and be lectured about documentation standards by someone who—

Q: I'm going to stop you there. I'm asking questions, Doctor. That's all I'm doing. Now, did you or did you not discuss physical therapy as an alternative to surgery?

A: Yes. I did.

Q: Where is that documented?

A: It isn't.

Q: Did you discuss steroid injections?

A: Yes.

Q: Where is that documented?

A: It isn't. But I discussed it.

topic: A doctor is deposed about informed consent procedures before a surgery
text:
Q: Good afternoon, Doctor. Just a few questions about the consent process for Mr. Williams' cardiac catheterization.

A: I believe it was three days before. At his office visit on the 12th.

Q: And you discussed the risks at that time?

A: I did.

Q: Did you also discuss them on the day of the procedure?

A: I confirmed that he still wished to proceed and asked if he had any questions. He did not.

Q: So on the day of the procedure, you didn't go over the risks again?

A: I just told you what I did.

Q: I'm trying to understand, Doctor. Is that a no?

A: I confirmed consent. That is appropriate. That is what guidelines recommend. I don't need to read the same list of risks twice if the patient indicates understanding.

Q: Guidelines recommend. Which guidelines are those?

A: Are you seriously asking me to cite medical literature right now?

Q: I'm asking what you're basing that statement on.

A: My training. My experience. The standards of care in cardiology. Shall I go on?

Q: That would be helpful, actually.

A: I'm a board-certified cardiologist. I've performed over two thousand catheterizations. I know what appropriate informed consent looks like, Counselor, and I don't need you to explain it to me.

Q: No one's trying to explain anything to you, Doctor. I'm simply trying to establish what happened with this patient on this day.

A: Then perhaps we could do that without the insinuations.

topic: A former employee is deposed about discriminatory remarks made by a supervisor
