topic: A nurse is questioned about a patient fall that occurred during her shift
text:
Q: Can you walk me through what happened when you first entered Mrs. Delgado's room that morning?

A: I came in around 6:15 to check her vitals. She was awake, which surprised me a little because she'd had trouble sleeping the night before. She asked me if her daughter had called yet. I told her I hadn't heard anything, but I'd check at the nurses' station for her.

Q: And how did she seem to you at that moment?

A: She seemed... she was lonely, I think. She'd been with us for eleven days at that point, and her family lives about three hours away. She talked about her garden a lot. She missed being home.

Q: I understand. What happened next?

A: I finished her vitals, and she asked if she could sit in the chair by the window. She said she was tired of looking at the ceiling.

Q: What was your response?

A: I told her I'd help her, but I needed to get another staff member to assist because of her fall risk designation. She'd been marked as a fall risk since admission.

Q: Did you get that assistance?

A: I stepped out to find someone. Maria—Maria Okonkwo, one of our CNAs—she was finishing up in 412, and I asked her to come help me in just a minute.

Q: How long were you away from Mrs. Delgado's room?

A: It couldn't have been more than two, maybe three minutes. I know everyone wants an exact number, and I wish I could give you one, but it was very brief. I didn't even make it back to the nurses' station.

Q: And when you returned?

A: She was on the floor. She was on the floor next to the bed, and she was trying to push herself up, and I—I went to her immediately.

Q: Take your time if you need to.

A: Thank you. I'm sorry. I've gone over this so many times in my head. She was frightened. She kept saying she was sorry, that she just wanted to see outside.

Q: What did you do at that point?

A: I stayed with her. I held her hand and told her not to move, not to try to get up, that I was right there and she was going to be okay. Then Maria came in and we called for the charge nurse and initiated the fall protocol.

Q: Did Mrs. Delgado say anything else to you while you waited?

A: She asked me not to tell her daughter she fell. She didn't want her to worry.

topic: A nurse is questioned about a patient fall that occurred during her shift
text:
Q: Nurse Thornton, how long had Mr. Bauer been your patient prior to the incident?

A: Just that shift. I'd picked him up at 7 PM when I came on.

Q: Were you given any report about his condition or mobility status?

A: Yes, the day nurse told me he was ambulatory with assistance, that he'd been doing well with PT but he was stubborn about asking for help.

Q: Stubborn—that was the word she used?

A: Her exact word was "independent." She said he was very independent and that we should keep an eye on him.

Q: Did that concern you?

A: It made me attentive, yes. I've been doing this for fourteen years. You learn which patients need a little extra checking in.

Q: And did you check in on Mr. Bauer?

A: I rounded on him every hour, documented every time.

Q: Let's talk about the 11 PM round specifically.

A: At 11, I checked on him and he was asleep. The bed alarm was on, the rails were up on both sides, the call light was within reach.

Q: What about the 12 AM round?

A: I was delayed getting to his room.

Q: Delayed by what?

A: Another patient coded. Mrs. Patterson in 508. I was part of the response team.

Q: That must have been an intense situation.

A: It was. We lost her.

Q: I'm sorry.

A: Thank you. She was eighty-six years old and she'd been declining for days, but still. It doesn't get easier.

Q: When did you next see Mr. Bauer?

A: About 12:40. The code was called at 12:35, and I went immediately to check on my other patients. He was sitting in the bathroom doorway. The bed alarm hadn't gone off—we later found the battery was dead.

Q: What did you do?

A: I knelt down next to him and asked if he was hurt. He said his hip was "talking to him," which in Mr. Bauer's language meant he was in significant pain. I called for help and stayed with him.

topic: A nurse is questioned about a patient fall that occurred during her shift
text:
Q: State your name for the record.

A: Jennifer Morales.

Q: You were the RN on duty when the patient fell, correct?

A: I was one of three RNs on the floor, yes.

Q: Were you the nurse assigned to the patient's care?

A: I was.

Q: Tell me what training you received regarding fall prevention.

A: Annual competency training, plus the hospital's specific protocols. We also had an in-service about three months before this incident focused on high-risk patients.

Q: Would you describe the training as adequate?

A: I would describe it as standard for the industry.

Q: That's not what I asked.

A: Counselor, I'm trying to answer honestly. The training covered what we needed to know. Whether it was adequate depends on what you mean by adequate.

Q: Fair enough. Did you feel prepared to prevent falls?

A: I felt prepared to follow the protocols we had in place. No nurse can prevent every fall. We're not able to be in every room at every moment. What we can do is minimize risk, and I believe I did that.

Q: Let's talk about minimizing risk. What specific steps did you take with this patient?

A: Non-slip socks, bed in low position, call light in reach, bed alarm activated, toileting schedule, gait belt for any ambulation. She had a yellow wristband and a falling star sign on her door.

Q: All of that was in place?

A: All of it.

Q: And she still fell.

A: Yes. She still fell.

Q: How did you feel when you found her?

A: I don't understand how that's relevant.

Q: You can answer the question.

A: I felt terrible. I still do. Mrs. Chen was seventy-four years old and she'd come in for pneumonia and she ended up with a broken wrist. Do you think I don't replay that night? I do. I think about whether I could have checked on her five minutes earlier. Whether I should have requested a sitter even though staffing had denied it twice.

Q: Staffing denied a sitter request?

A: Twice. I documented both requests. I advocated for her.

Q: Why did you think she needed a sitter?

A: Because she was confused at night. Sundowning. And I knew—I knew she'd try to get up on her own.

topic: A nurse is questioned about a patient fall that occurred during her shift
text:
Q: You documented that you performed a safety check at 2:00 AM.

A: That's correct.

Q: And the fall occurred at approximately 2:47 AM.

A: Yes.

Q: What were you doing during that forty-seven-minute window?

A: I was administering medications to other patients, answering call lights, and completing charting.

Q: How many patients were you responsible for that night?

A: Seven.

Q: Is that typical?

A: It was typical for that unit at that time.

Q: Was it safe?

A: I'm not sure I'm qualified to answer whether staffing ratios are safe. That's a question for hospital administration.

Q: I'm asking for your opinion as a practicing nurse.

A: My opinion is that every nurse I know wishes they had more time with each patient. We do the best we can with the resources we're given.

Q: Mr. Hendricks was eighty-two years old and had documented dementia.

A: I'm aware of his history.

Q: Do you believe seven patients is an appropriate assignment when one of them has those risk factors?

A: I believe I provided the best care I could under the circumstances.

Q: That's not what I asked, Nurse Williams.

A: I know it's not. But I'm not going to sit here and say something that undermines the nurses who work beside me every night doing their absolute best. If you want to talk about staffing, talk to the people who make those decisions.

Q: Let's go back to Mr. Hendricks. When you found him after the fall, what was his condition?

A: He was disoriented. He had a laceration on his forehead. He kept asking for his wife.

Q: Is his wife living?

A: No. She passed in 2019. He asked for her every night.

Q: What did you tell him?

A: I told him she'd be there soon, and that I was going to take care of him until she came. Then I held a compress to his head and stayed with him until the doctor arrived.

topic: A nurse is questioned about a patient fall that occurred during her shift
text:
Q: Nurse Okafor, I want to understand the timeline as precisely as possible.

A: Of course. I want that too.

Q: The call light from Room 304 was activated at what time?

A: 8:14 PM according to the system log.

Q: And when did you respond?

A: I was in the room by 8:16.

Q: So two minutes.

A: Yes. Maybe a little less.

Q: What was the situation when you arrived?

A: Mr. Salazar was on the floor at the foot of his bed. His IV pole had fallen with him. The line was still attached, but there was some blood where the insertion site had pulled.

Q: Was he conscious?

A: He was. He was awake and alert. He said, "I just wanted to turn off the TV."

Q: The TV?

A: The remote had fallen on the floor. He didn't want to bother anyone so he tried to get it himself.

Q: Did you ask him why he didn't use the call light?

A: He said he felt bad. We were so busy. His words.

Q: How did that make you feel, hearing him say that?

A: It broke my heart, honestly. This man needed surgery on his hip, he was in pain, and he was worried about being a burden. I told him that's what we're there for. That he's never a burden. That next time, he should push that button no matter what.

Q: Did you have that conversation while he was still on the floor?

A: Yes. I didn't want to move him until we assessed him, so I got down on the floor with him and we talked while we waited for the team.

Q: You sat on the floor with him?

A: It didn't feel right to stand over him. He was already embarrassed enough.

Q: How long were you there with him?

A: Until transport came. Maybe eight minutes.

Q: What did you talk about?

A: His grandchildren, mostly. He has four. He was showing me pictures on his phone—he'd dropped it when he fell, but it wasn't broken. We just talked. It seemed to help him stay calm.

topic: A warehouse supervisor is deposed about safety protocols that were allegedly ignored

topic: A nurse is questioned about a patient fall that occurred during her shift
text:

A: In theory.

Q: What do you mean, in theory?

A: I mean the alarms go off constantly. Patients shift in their sleep. Patients reach for water. The alarm doesn't know the difference between someone rolling over and someone trying to climb out of bed.

Q: So the alarms are... unreliable?

A: I didn't say unreliable. I said they go off constantly. There's a difference.

Q: Was Mr. Okonkwo's bed alarm activated that evening?

A: According to the log, yes.

Q: According to the log. Do you have any independent memory of checking that it was activated?

A: I have a memory of doing my rounds. I have a memory of checking rooms. I don't have a specific memory of pressing a specific button on a specific bed, no. I'm sorry, I don't know what else you want me to say.

Q: I'm just asking what you remember.

A: And I'm telling you.

topic: A nurse is questioned about a patient fall that occurred during her shift
text:
Q: Nurse Delgado, how long have you been a registered nurse?

A: Eleven years this June.

Q: And you've been at St. Anne's for how long?

A: About... let me think. Six years? A little over six years.

Q: In your eleven years of nursing, have you ever had a patient fall during your shift before?

A: Yes.

Q: More than once?

A: Yes, more than once. Falls happen. We do everything we can to prevent them, but they happen.

Q: So when Mrs. Chen fell on the morning of April 2nd, that wasn't unusual to you?

A: Every fall is serious. I take every fall seriously.

Q: That's not what I asked.

A: Then could you ask it again? I want to make sure I understand what you're getting at.

Q: Was Mrs. Chen's fall unusual in any way?

A: She fractured her hip. That's always... that's a significant injury. Especially at her age.

Q: Were you the first to respond?

A: Yolanda—the nursing assistant—she found her. She called for me. I came.

Q: How quickly?

A: I came as quickly as I could given where I was and what I was doing at that exact moment.

Q: And where were you?

A: I was... I was in the break room. I had just sat down.

topic: A nurse is questioned about a patient fall that occurred during her shift
text:
Q: The incident report says the patient was found on the floor at 3:47 a.m.

A: If that's what it says.

Q: You filled out this report, didn't you?

A: I did.

Q: So 3:47 is accurate?

A: It's what I wrote at the time.

Q: Nurse Williams, I'm going to ask you to look at Exhibit 7. This is the hourly rounding log. According to this, you checked on Mr. Brandt at 3:00 a.m. Is that your signature?

A: Yes.

Q: So... 47 minutes passed between your check and when he was found on the floor.

A: Yes.

Q: Were you supposed to check on him more frequently than that?

A: The standard is hourly.

Q: The standard is hourly. But Mr. Brandt was post-surgical, correct?

A: Mm-hmm.

Q: Is that a yes?

A: Yes. Sorry. Yes.

Q: Were there any additional monitoring requirements for post-surgical patients?

A: It depends on the orders.

Q: What were Mr. Brandt's orders?

A: I don't have them in front of me.

Q: Okay. Let me find them. Bear with me. Just give me a moment here... I know I have them somewhere in this stack...

A: Take your time.

topic: A nurse is questioned about a patient fall that occurred during her shift
text:
Q: Nurse Thompson, you mentioned earlier that Mr. Reeves had been calling for assistance multiple times that night.

A: Yes.

Q: How many times, approximately?

A: I don't know. Several. He used the call button frequently.

Q: Frequently. Every hour? Every half hour?

A: I couldn't say exactly. The call logs would show it.

Q: Do you recall what he was calling about?

A: Different things. Pain. Needed to use the bathroom. Wanted his blanket adjusted.

Q: And you responded to these calls?

A: When I could. Sometimes the aide responded. Sometimes I was with another patient.

Q: The call that came in at 2:30 a.m.—the one immediately before his fall—who responded to that?

A: I... I don't know if anyone got there before...

Q: Before what?

A: Before we heard him fall.

Q: So no one responded.

A: I didn't say that. I said I don't know if anyone got there in time. We were... there were two codes that night. Two codes in three hours. I was in one of those rooms when... I was doing compressions on one patient while another patient was pressing a call button because he needed help getting to the bathroom. I'm not... I'm sorry. What was the question?

Q: I was asking whether anyone responded to Mr. Reeves' 2:30 call.

A: I don't believe so. No.

Q: Thank you.

A: Is there anything else?

topic: An accountant is deposed about transactions they processed on behalf of a client
text:
Q: Mr. Harmon, you prepared the quarterly wire transfer summaries for Colgate Holdings, correct?

A: I prepared summaries, yes. Quarterly, monthly, sometimes ad hoc depending on what was requested.

Q: And in the third quarter of 2022, you processed a wire transfer to an entity called Meridian Consulting Group?

A: I'd have to see the specific documentation you're referring to.

Q: I'm showing you what's been marked as Exhibit 14. Does this refresh your recollection?

A: This is a transfer authorization form, yes. I see my initials here.

Q: The amount shown is $340,000. Is that correct?

A: That's what the form indicates.

Q: Did you verify that Meridian Consulting Group had performed any actual consulting services for Colgate Holdings?

A: That wasn't my role. I processed transactions that were authorized by the client.

Q: So you simply processed whatever came across your desk without any independent verification?

A: I didn't say that. I said verifying the substance of a consulting arrangement wasn't within the scope of my engagement.

Q: What was within the scope of your engagement, Mr. Harmon?

A: Transaction processing, reconciliation, and maintaining accurate records consistent with the client's instructions.

Q: Did you ever meet anyone from Meridian Consulting Group?

A: No.

Q: Did you ever see an invoice from Meridian Consulting Group?

A: I don't recall one, but that doesn't mean one didn't exist.

Q: Doesn't it strike you as unusual to process a $340,000 payment without an invoice?

A: You're asking me to characterize something from two years ago without full context. What I can tell you is that I followed the procedures that were in place at the time.

topic: An accountant is deposed about transactions they processed on behalf of a client
text:
Q: Ms. Vaughn, how long were you the primary accountant for the Dellacroix Family Trust?

A: From March 2019 until they terminated our engagement in August of last year.

Q: During that time, who gave you instructions regarding disbursements from the trust?

A: Martin Dellacroix. Occasionally his assistant would relay information, but authorizations came from Martin.

Q: Always in writing?

A: Not always, no.

Q: How often would you receive verbal instructions?

A: I couldn't give you a percentage. It varied.

Q: Let me ask you about a specific transaction. In January 2023, there was a disbursement of $175,000 to something called "personal expenses." Do you recall that?

A: I recall disbursements to that category, yes.

Q: That's a rather large amount for a line item that vague, wouldn't you say?

A: I wouldn't characterize it as vague. It was a category the client established. Many family trusts use similar designations.

Q: Did you ask Mr. Dellacroix what those personal expenses were?

A: We had a conversation, yes.

Q: What did he tell you?

A: He said it was for family matters and preferred not to elaborate.

Q: And you were satisfied with that answer?

A: Counsel, I'm not sure what you mean by "satisfied." He was the trustee. He had authority over disbursements. I documented the transaction as directed.

Q: You documented it exactly as he wanted it documented?

A: I documented it accurately based on the information provided to me.

topic: An accountant is deposed about transactions they processed on behalf of a client
text:
Q: Mr. Okonkwo, I want to ask you about your relationship with Prestige Development LLC.

A: All right.

Q: You handled their accounts payable, is that right?

A: Among other functions, yes.

Q: Over what period?

A: I'd have to check, but approximately 2020 through early 2023.

Q: During that time, did you notice any patterns in how payments were made to subcontractors?

A: Patterns? You'll have to be more specific.

Q: Let me put it this way. Did certain subcontractors receive payments on an accelerated schedule compared to others?

A: Payment timing depended on contract terms and project milestones.

Q: That's the official explanation. What actually happened?

A: I'm not sure what you're implying, but I just gave you an accurate answer.

Q: Were you aware that Ryland Construction received payment within five days of invoice submission while other subcontractors waited sixty to ninety days?

A: I was aware of different payment timelines for different vendors, yes.

Q: Did you find that disparity noteworthy?

A: Noteworthy in what sense?

Q: In any sense, Mr. Okonkwo. Did you ever wonder why Ryland got preferential treatment?

A: I processed payments according to the instructions I was given. If you're asking whether I conducted an investigation into my client's business relationships, no, I did not.

Q: Did anyone ever tell you why Ryland was treated differently?

A: I was told they were a priority vendor. That was the extent of it.

topic: An accountant is deposed about transactions they processed on behalf of a client
text:
Q: Ms. Chen, let's discuss the offshore accounts you managed for Mr. Whitfield.

A: Managed is a strong word. I had limited visibility into those accounts.

Q: But you facilitated transfers into them?

A: I facilitated transfers that Mr. Whitfield authorized, yes.

Q: To accounts in the Cayman Islands?

A: Some, yes.

Q: Some. What other jurisdictions?

A: I believe there was an account in Luxembourg. Possibly one in Singapore. I'd need to review my files.

Q: You seem uncertain for someone who handled these transactions.

A: I handled many transactions for many clients over several years. I'm trying to give you accurate testimony rather than guess.

Q: Fair enough. Let me show you Exhibit 23. This is a transfer authorization dated April 4, 2022. Do you recognize it?

A: Yes, this appears to be my work.

Q: The beneficiary account is listed only by number, no institution name. Was that typical?

A: It wasn't atypical for certain clients who had privacy concerns.

Q: Privacy concerns. What kind of privacy concerns require hiding the name of a bank?

A: I wouldn't characterize it as hiding. The account number was sufficient for processing.

Q: Did you ever question why a client needed that level of anonymity?

A: It wasn't my place to question a client's legitimate financial arrangements.

Q: Who determined they were legitimate?

A: I relied on representations from the client and, where applicable, their legal counsel.

topic: An accountant is deposed about transactions they processed on behalf of a client
text:
Q: Mr. Fitzgerald, you mentioned earlier that you raised concerns with management about certain transactions. Let's talk about that.

A: All right.

Q: What specifically concerned you?

A: There were several instances where documentation seemed incomplete.

Q: Incomplete how?

A: Missing backup. Authorizations that came after the fact. That sort of thing.

Q: How often did this happen?

A: Often enough that I brought it up.

Q: And what was the response?

A: I was told not to worry about it. That everything had been approved at higher levels.

Q: Who told you that?

A: Diana Marsh, the CFO.

Q: Did that satisfy your concerns?

A: No.

Q: What did you do next?

A: I started keeping my own records. Dates, amounts, what documentation was present and what was missing.

Q: Why did you feel the need to do that?

A: Because I've been doing this for twenty-two years, and I've learned to protect myself when things don't add up.

Q: Did things add up at Vertex Capital, Mr. Fitzgerald?

A: I think you already know the answer to that, Counsel.

Q: I'm asking for your assessment.

A: My assessment is that I processed transactions I was instructed to process, I raised concerns through appropriate channels, and those concerns were dismissed. What you make of that is your business.

topic: A witness is asked about a car accident they saw from their front porch
text:
Q: Please state your name for the record.

A: Margaret Holloway.

Q: Ms. Holloway, you've already confirmed you were on your front porch on the morning of September 14th, correct?

A: Yes. I said that.

Q: And what time did you first notice the vehicles involved in this accident?

A: Somewhere around 8:15. Maybe 8:20. I wasn't checking my watch every thirty seconds.

Q: Can you describe what you saw?

A: The blue car ran the stop sign and hit the other one. I've explained this.

Q: I need you to walk me through it step by step. Where was the blue vehicle when you first observed it?

A: Coming down Maple. Fast.

Q: Fast meaning what, exactly?

A: Meaning faster than someone should be going on a residential street with a stop sign twenty yards ahead. Do you need me to guess the miles per hour? Because I'm not an engineer.

Q: I'm asking for your perception.

A: My perception is that it was going too fast. That's what I perceived.

Q: Did the blue vehicle slow at all before entering the intersection?

A: No.

Q: Not at all?

A: That's what "no" means.

Q: And the other vehicle—the silver sedan—where was it positioned?

A: In the intersection. Already in it. Because the driver had the right of way. Which I've also said.

Q: Did you see the driver of the blue vehicle at any point?

A: I saw a person behind the wheel. I didn't get a good look at their face. I was watching a car accident happen, not taking portraits.

topic: A witness is asked about a car accident they saw from their front porch
text:
Q: Mr. Dawes, how long have you lived at 414 Crescent Drive?

A: Going on twelve years now.

Q: And your front porch faces the intersection of Crescent and Bellwood?

A: That's right. I've got a clear view of the whole thing. Sit out there most mornings with my coffee.

Q: Were you on your porch on the morning of March 3rd?

A: I was.

Q: What time?

A: Oh, I'd say it was early. Maybe 7:30, 7:45. The sun was just coming up over the Hendersons' roof across the way—

Q: Let me stop you there. Did you witness a collision that morning?

A: Well, yes, that's why we're here, isn't it? I was getting to that. I was explaining the lighting conditions because I thought that might be relevant to whether I could see—

Q: We'll get to visibility. Just tell me: did you see the collision?

A: Yes.

Q: Which vehicle struck which?

A: The pickup hit the compact car. But if you'd let me finish, I was going to explain that the sun was in a particular position that morning, which is why I noticed the pickup in the first place—the glare off the windshield caught my eye.

Q: The pickup struck the compact car. Where in the intersection?

A: Middle of it. Dead center, more or less.

Q: Fine. Did you see what happened immediately before impact?

A: I saw the whole thing. I've been trying to tell you. If you'd just let me describe it in order—

Q: I'm asking specific questions, Mr. Dawes. Did the pickup stop before entering the intersection?

A: No. No, it did not. It rolled right through.

topic: A witness is asked about a car accident they saw from their front porch
text:
Q: You were sitting on your porch. What drew your attention to the street?

A: I heard the engine first. Someone accelerating hard.

Q: Which direction was this sound coming from?

A: From my left. That would be... eastbound on Delaney.

Q: Then what?

A: Then I looked up and saw the white SUV.

Q: How fast was it traveling?

A: I couldn't say exactly.

Q: Your best estimate.

A: I really couldn't say. I'm not good with that sort of thing.

Q: Faster than the speed limit? Slower?

A: Faster, I'd think. Based on the sound.

Q: You think, or you know?

A: I think. I said I think.

Q: Fine. What happened next?

A: The SUV entered the intersection.

Q: And?

A: And it collided with another vehicle.

Q: What vehicle?

A: A dark-colored car. Black or maybe dark blue.

Q: Where did the dark-colored car come from?

A: The cross street. Heading north.

Q: Did you see the dark-colored car before the collision?

A: Not until they were about to hit.

Q: So you didn't see whether that vehicle stopped at its stop sign?

A: No.

Q: You have no idea whether the driver of the dark car obeyed traffic signals?

A: I said no. I didn't see it until the last second.

topic: A witness is asked about a car accident they saw from their front porch
text:
Q: Ms. Tran, I want to make sure I understand your vantage point. Your porch is elevated?

A: Yes, we have three steps up from the walkway.

Q: And you were seated?

A: In my rocking chair, yes. The wooden one.

Q: How far is your porch from the intersection where this accident occurred?

A: Maybe forty feet? Fifty? I'm not certain of the exact distance.

Q: But you had a clear line of sight?

A: Yes, nothing was blocking my view.

Q: No trees, no parked cars?

A: There's a maple tree but it's off to the side. It doesn't block the intersection.

Q: Okay. You said in your statement that the red truck "flew through" the stop sign. Those were your words?

A: That sounds like something I'd say, yes.

Q: Did the truck stop at all?

A: No.

Q: Did it slow down?

A: Not that I could tell.

Q: Did you see brake lights?

A: I... I don't remember seeing brake lights.

Q: You don't remember, or there weren't any?

A: I don't remember. That's what I said. I can't tell you something I don't remember.

Q: Fair enough. After the impact, what did you do?

A: I went inside and called 911. Then I came back out.

Q: How long were you inside?

A: A minute, maybe two. Just long enough to make the call.

Q: Did anyone exit the vehicles while you were inside?

A: I wouldn't know. I was inside.

Q: When you came back out, where were the drivers?

A: Both standing outside their cars. The woman from the sedan was holding her neck.

topic: A witness is asked about a car accident they saw from their front porch
text:
Q: State your address for the record.

A: 2287 Orchard Lane.

Q: How long have you lived there?

A: Six years.

Q: You were home on the afternoon of July 19th?

A: Yes.

Q: On your porch?

A: Yes, I was reading.

Q: What were you reading?

A: Is that relevant?

Q: I'm establishing your state of attention. What were you reading?

A: A magazine. I don't remember which one.

Q: Were you engaged in your reading, or casually flipping through it?

A: I was reading it. I don't know how to quantify my engagement level for you.

Q: Were you paying attention to the street?

A: Not particularly. Not until I heard the noise.

Q: What noise?

A: Tires. Then the crash.

Q: So you heard it before you saw it.

A: Correct.

Q: What did you see when you looked up?

A: Two cars in the intersection. Already hit. The gray one was spun sideways.

Q: You didn't see the actual moment of impact?

A: No. I looked up right after.

Q: So when you say you "witnessed" this accident—

A: I saw the immediate aftermath. I heard the collision. I saw both vehicles and both drivers. I'd call that witnessing it.

Q: But you cannot testify to what occurred in the seconds before impact, correct?

A: I can testify to what I heard and what I saw immediately after. Whether that's useful to you is your problem, not mine.

Q: Did you see either vehicle approach the intersection?

A: No.

Q: Did you see either driver brake?

A: Asked and answered. No. I didn't look up until after.

topic: A witness is questioned about a workplace injury they observed but did not report
text:
Q: Mr. Delacroix, you were working on the second floor the morning of September 14th, correct?

A: I was.

Q: And you had a clear line of sight to the loading dock from your station?

A: Clear enough, I suppose.

Q: What does "clear enough" mean?

A: It means I could see what was happening if I looked. I wasn't always looking.

Q: But you did look at some point that morning?

A: Yes.

Q: And what did you see?

A: I saw Marcus slip. He went down hard. The forklift was still running.

Q: Was anyone else nearby?

A: A few people. Nobody moved right away.

Q: Did you move?

A: No.

Q: Did you call for help?

A: No.

Q: Did you report the incident to your supervisor at any point that day?

A: I did not.

Q: Why not, Mr. Delacroix?

A: Because I knew how it would go. I've been there eleven years. You report something, there's paperwork, there's questions, there's a target on you. Marcus got up eventually. I figured that was that.

---

topic: A witness is questioned about a workplace injury they observed but did not report
text:
Q: Ms. Thornton, let's talk about what happened after you saw Mr. Reeves fall.

A: Okay.

Q: You didn't go to him immediately, did you?

A: No, I didn't.

Q: You stayed at your workstation.

A: That's right.

Q: For how long?

A: I don't know exactly. A few minutes.

Q: And during those few minutes, did anyone else approach Mr. Reeves?

A: Eventually, yes. Jorge went over.

Q: But not immediately.

A: Not immediately.

Q: Ms. Thornton, I'm going to ask you something, and I want you to understand there's no trick here. Why didn't you go check on your coworker?

A: I just... I've seen people get hurt before. You learn that if you get involved, suddenly you're in meetings. You're explaining yourself. They start looking at your hours, your breaks. I needed my job more than Marcus needed me to walk over there. That's the truth.

Q: Did you feel any obligation to report what you saw?

A: I felt a lot of things. Obligation wasn't going to pay my rent.

---

topic: A witness is questioned about a workplace injury they observed but did not report
text:
Q: You testified earlier that you saw the accident occur.

A: That's correct.

Q: And you saw Mr. Huang's arm get caught in the conveyor mechanism.

A: I saw him pull back suddenly. I assumed that's what happened.

Q: You assumed.

A: Yes.

Q: Did you hear him cry out?

A: He made a sound. I couldn't tell you exactly what kind.

Q: But you knew something was wrong.

A: I knew something happened.

Q: Mr. Ellison, let me ask you directly. Did you report this incident to anyone?

A: No.

Q: To your supervisor?

A: No.

Q: To HR?

A: No.

Q: To safety personnel?

A: I did not report it to anyone.

Q: Can you explain why?

A: Look, I've been through this before. Not this exactly, but... you know. The company has ways of handling these things. They handle them their way. What I say doesn't change much.

Q: So you just went back to work.

A: I went back to work.

---

topic: A witness is questioned about a workplace injury they observed but did not report
text:
Q: Mrs. Okonkwo, I want to understand the timeline. You clocked in at 6 a.m.?

A: Yes.

Q: The incident occurred around 7:15?

A: Somewhere around there.

Q: And you clocked out at your normal time, 2:30?

A: Yes.

Q: So you worked a full shift after witnessing what happened to Ms. Guerrero.

A: I did.

Q: Did anyone ask you about it?

A: No one asked me anything.

Q: Did you volunteer any information?

A: No.

Q: Mrs. Okonkwo, I've been doing this a long time. I've sat across from a lot of witnesses. I'm not here to judge you. I just need to understand what happened and why.

A: I appreciate that.

Q: So help me understand. You saw a woman get hurt. You said nothing. Can you tell me what was going through your mind?

A: What was going through my mind is that I have three kids. What was going through my mind is that the last person who made noise about safety issues isn't here anymore. What was going through my mind is that nothing I do in this room or any room is going to change how that place operates. I'm sorry. I am. But that's all I have for you.

---

topic: A witness is questioned about a workplace injury they observed but did not report
text:
Q: Let's go back to the moment of impact, Mr. Sadowski.

A: If we have to.

Q: We do. You said you were approximately fifteen feet away.

A: Give or take.

Q: And you heard the crash before you saw it?

A: I heard a sound first, yes. Then I turned.

Q: What did you see when you turned?

A: Derek was on the ground. The shelving unit had come down. Boxes everywhere.

Q: Was Derek moving?

A: He was holding his leg.

Q: Was he saying anything?

A: He was making noise. I couldn't make out words.

Q: What did you do?

A: I stood there for a second. Then I went back to what I was doing.

Q: You went back to what you were doing.

A: Yes.

Q: Did it occur to you to call someone?

A: It occurred to me.

Q: But you didn't.

A: No.

Q: Mr. Sadowski, I have to ask these questions. It's my job. But I'll be honest with you—I'm not sure either of us is going to feel better by the end of this.

A: I could have told you that an hour ago.

Q: Fair enough. Let's keep going.

topic: An employee is deposed about a coworker's termination they believe was retaliatory
text:
Q: Ms. Patterson, I want to direct your attention to March 14th of last year. Were you present in the office that day?

A: I was.

Q: And did you observe any interaction between Derek Hollis and Supervisory Manager Crenshaw?

A: I observed several interactions. Could you be more specific?

Q: Let's start with the morning. Did anything unusual occur?

A: Define unusual.

Q: Out of the ordinary. Something that struck you as noteworthy.

A: There was a meeting. Derek was called into Crenshaw's office around ten. Maybe ten-fifteen. I don't know exactly.

Q: And what happened during that meeting?

A: I wasn't in the meeting.

Q: Did you observe anything before or after?

A: Before, Derek was at his desk. After, he came out and went to the break room.

Q: Did he say anything to you?

A: He said Crenshaw had written him up for the safety complaint he filed the week before.

Q: Those were his exact words?

A: I don't remember his exact words. That was the substance of it. Can we take a break soon?

Q: We'll take a break shortly. Did Derek seem upset?

A: Yes.

Q: And in your view, was the write-up connected to the safety complaint?

A: I'm not going to speculate about what was in Crenshaw's head. I told you what Derek said. That's what I know.

Q: Fair enough. Did you personally witness any other disciplinary actions taken against Mr. Hollis after the safety complaint?

A: I witnessed him getting called into offices. I witnessed him getting pulled off the Hendricks project. I don't know what else you want me to say. I've already gone over this with your colleague.

---

topic: An employee is deposed about a coworker's termination they believe was retaliatory
text:
Q: Mr. Okonkwo, how long did you work alongside Janelle Price?

A: About three years. A little over.

Q: Would you describe your working relationship as positive?

A: We got along fine. We collaborated on several accounts.

Q: Were you aware that Ms. Price had filed an internal complaint regarding wage discrepancies in September of 2023?

A: I was aware.

Q: How did you become aware?

A: She told me.

Q: What specifically did she tell you?

A: That she'd found out she was being paid less than Marcus Webb for the same role and that she'd brought it to HR.

Q: And what happened after she filed that complaint, to your knowledge?

A: Look, I've been sitting here for... what, four hours now? She filed the complaint. Then things changed for her. That's what I saw.

Q: Changed how?

A: Her assignments dried up. She got moved off the Peterson account, which she'd been running for two years. She started getting nitpicked on things nobody cared about before.

Q: Who was doing the nitpicking?

A: Sandra Vance. Her direct supervisor.

Q: Did Ms. Vance ever state a reason for the increased scrutiny?

A: Not to me.

Q: Did you ever discuss this with Ms. Price?

A: Yes.

Q: What did she say?

A: She said she was being pushed out. She said it was because of the complaint. I believed her. I still believe her. Is that what you needed?

Q: I'm just asking questions, Mr. Okonkwo.

A: Right.

---

topic: An employee is deposed about a coworker's termination they believe was retaliatory
text:
Q: Let's move on to the termination meeting itself. You were present?

A: Yes, I was asked to attend as a witness. HR policy.

Q: Who else was in the room?

A: Linda Marsh from HR. Tom Beckett. And Ryan, obviously.

Q: Ryan Chen, the employee being terminated?

A: Correct.

Q: Okay. Can you walk me through... actually, let me back up. What time did this meeting take place?

A: Late afternoon. Four-thirty, maybe five.

Q: And how long did it last?

A: Fifteen, twenty minutes.

Q: What was said at the beginning of the meeting?

A: Linda explained that Ryan's position was being eliminated due to restructuring.

Q: Was the word 'restructuring' used specifically?

A: I think so. Yes.

Q: You think so or you know so?

A: It was a year ago, counselor. I'm doing my best here.

Q: I understand. Let's just... take it step by step. After Ms. Marsh mentioned restructuring, what happened next?

A: Ryan asked why his position specifically. Linda said it was a business decision.

Q: Did Ryan respond to that?

A: He said it was because of his OSHA report. He said everyone knew it.

Q: What did Ms. Marsh say?

A: She said that wasn't accurate. She said the restructuring had been planned for months.

Q: And was that true, to your knowledge?

A: I... I really don't know what was planned and when. I wasn't part of those decisions. I was just there to witness. That's all I was there for.

---

topic: An employee is deposed about a coworker's termination they believe was retaliatory
text:
Q: Ms. Delacroix, I want to ask you about the weeks leading up to Mr. Aguilar's termination.

A: Okay.

Q: In early February, did you notice any changes in how Mr. Aguilar was being treated by management?

A: Yes.

Q: Please describe those changes.

A: He was being frozen out. Excluded from meetings he should have been in. Left off email chains.

Q: How do you know he should have been included in these meetings?

A: Because they were about projects he was leading. It was obvious.

Q: Did you raise this with anyone?

A: I mentioned it to my supervisor.

Q: And who is that?

A: Carol Wendt.

Q: What did Ms. Wendt say?

A: She said it wasn't my concern. She said staffing decisions were above my pay grade.

Q: Did she use those words? 'Above your pay grade'?

A: Yes. Those exact words.

Q: Now, you're aware that Mr. Aguilar had reported his supervisor to the ethics hotline approximately three weeks before this?

A: I'm aware.

Q: Did you believe there was a connection between the ethics report and the treatment you observed?

A: Counsel, I've been trying to answer your questions directly all day. Yes. I believed there was a connection. Others believed it too. It wasn't subtle.

Q: Who are these others?

A: I'd rather not name colleagues who might face... look, can you just ask me what you actually need to know? I'll answer. But I have a six o'clock flight and I've been here since eight this morning.

---

topic: An employee is deposed about a coworker's termination they believe was retaliatory
text:
Q: Mr. Sato. You still with me?

A: I'm here.

Q: Good. I want to ask about the conversation you overheard between Director Mills and Theresa Boykin on April 3rd.

A: Which part of it?

Q: Were there multiple parts?

A: It was a conversation. It had a beginning, middle, and end.

Q: Fair enough. Let's start with how you came to overhear this conversation.

A: I was in the copy room. The door to Mills' office was open. They were talking loudly.

Q: Could you hear them clearly?

A: Clearly enough.

Q: What did you hear Director Mills say?

A: He said—and I'm paraphrasing—that Theresa had made herself a liability by going to the board.

Q: 'Going to the board' meaning what?

A: Theresa had raised concerns about billing practices directly to two board members. Mills wasn't happy.

Q: Did he say anything else?

A: He said something like, 'We need to document everything from here on out.' He said HR would 'find a way to make it clean.'

Q: Those were his words? 'Make it clean'?

A: That's what I heard.

Q: And Ms. Boykin—what did she say?

A: She mostly listened. She asked if they should wait until after the audit. Mills said no.

Q: Mr. Sato, did you report this conversation to anyone?

A: I... no. No, I didn't.

Q: Why not?

A: Because I saw what happened to Theresa. She was gone two weeks later. I have a mortgage. I have two kids in college. You want me to explain it more than that?

topic: A witness is asked about a car accident they saw from their front porch
text:
Q: Good afternoon. I understand you were home on the day of the accident, is that right?

A: Yes, sir. I was sitting out on my front porch like I do most afternoons. It's my little routine—coffee, the paper, watching the neighborhood go by.

Q: That sounds like a nice way to spend an afternoon. Can you tell me what you remember seeing?

A: Well, I'd be happy to. The blue sedan—I remember it was blue because my late husband drove a similar one, a Buick, years ago—that car was coming down Maple headed east. Nice and steady, not speeding or anything like that.

Q: Take your time. What happened next?

A: The pickup truck came through the intersection. Just sailed right through. I remember thinking, oh no, oh no, and then the sound. You never forget that sound, the crunch of it.

Q: I'm sorry you had to witness that. Did you see the driver of the pickup before the collision?

A: I caught a glimpse. Young man, I think. He looked like he might've been looking down at something. I can't say for certain it was a phone, but his head was tilted that way.

Q: That's helpful. What did you do after the collision?

A: I set my coffee down—spilled half of it, honestly—and I went inside to call 911. My hands were shaking something awful, but I wanted to make sure help was coming.

Q: Did you go outside to check on anyone?

A: I did, after I made the call. My neighbor Bill, he's younger than me, he got there first. I just wanted to make sure those poor people knew someone was there, that help was on the way.

Q: That was kind of you. Did you speak with either driver?

A: The woman in the blue car, she was crying. I held her hand through the window and told her she was going to be just fine. I don't know if that was true, but it seemed like the right thing to say.

Q: It sounds like it was. One last question—did you notice what the weather was like that day?

A: Clear as a bell. Beautiful day, really. That's part of what made it so awful, I suppose. Nothing to blame but somebody not paying attention.

---

topic: A witness is asked about a car accident they saw from their front porch
text:
Q: Mr. Patterson, I want to make sure we get this right, so please stop me if any of my questions are unclear.

A: Alright.

Q: You were on your porch when this happened?

A: That's correct.

Q: And your porch faces the intersection of Maple and Third?

A: It does. I've got a clear view of the whole thing. Been living there thirty-two years.

Q: Thirty-two years. So you know that intersection pretty well, I imagine.

A: Better than most. I've seen plenty of close calls there. The city ought to put in a four-way stop, if you ask me, but nobody ever does.

Q: That's actually useful context. Before this accident, had you noticed any other problems at that intersection?

A: Oh, sure. Kids blow through there all the time. Delivery trucks too. I've called the city about it twice, maybe three times.

Q: And on this particular day, what drew your attention to the vehicles?

A: I heard the engine first. The truck was accelerating, you know, like he was trying to beat someone to the intersection. That caught my ear.

Q: What did you see when you looked up?

A: The truck entering the intersection at a good clip, and the other car—the Honda, I think—already in the middle of the turn.

Q: Did the Honda have a turn signal on, if you recall?

A: You know, I believe it did. Little blinking light on the left side. I remember because I thought, well, at least someone's following the rules.

Q: Mr. Patterson, you've been very helpful. Is there anything else about that day you think I should know?

A: Just that the woman driving the Honda—she was doing everything right. I hope she's okay. I've been thinking about her, if I'm being honest.

---

topic: A witness is asked about a car accident they saw from their front porch
text:
Q: State your name for the record.

A: Diane Okonkwo.

Q: Ms. Okonkwo, where were you on the afternoon of September 14th?

A: Home. On my porch, reading.

Q: Could you see the intersection of Maple and Third from where you were sitting?

A: Yes.

Q: What did you observe?

A: Two cars collided. A gray truck and a small red car.

Q: Can you describe how the collision occurred?

A: The red car was going through the intersection. The truck hit it on the passenger side.

Q: Did you see where the truck came from?

A: From the north, on Third Street.

Q: Was there a stop sign for vehicles traveling that direction?

A: There was.

Q: Did the truck stop at that sign?

A: It did not.

Q: Ms. Okonkwo, I appreciate you being here today. I know it's not easy to relive something like this. Did you happen to see the drivers after the accident?

A: I did. I walked over to help.

Q: That's understandable. What did you see when you got there?

A: The woman in the red car was conscious but confused. There was blood on her forehead. The man in the truck was already out, pacing around. He kept saying he didn't see her.

Q: How did that make you feel, if you don't mind my asking?

A: I minded my own feelings and focused on the woman. She needed someone calm.

Q: Of course. Thank you for your time today, Ms. Okonkwo.

A: You're welcome. I hope this helps her case.

---

topic: A witness is asked about a car accident they saw from their front porch
text:
Q: You've stated you had a clear view of the accident from your porch. How far would you estimate you were from the point of impact?

A: Maybe fifty feet, give or take. Close enough to see it all unfold.

Q: And you're certain about the color of the vehicle that ran the stop sign?

A: I am. It was white. A white SUV.

Q: Some witnesses have described it as silver. Could it have been silver?

A: Well, I suppose in certain light things can look different. But to my eyes, sitting where I was, with the sun where it was, that vehicle was white. I'm happy to walk you through my reasoning if that would help.

Q: Please.

A: The sun was behind me, coming from the west. The SUV was heading south, so the light was hitting it full on. No shadows, no glare. White as my kitchen cabinets.

Q: I appreciate you explaining that. What about the other vehicle?

A: A dark sedan. Navy blue, maybe black. Harder to say because of where it was positioned, but I'd lean toward navy.

Q: Did you see the driver of the SUV before the collision?

A: Just for a moment. A woman, I think. Dark hair. She was looking straight ahead, far as I could tell.

Q: Did she appear to be braking as she approached the intersection?

A: No, and that's what I keep coming back to. She never even slowed down. It was like she didn't know the stop sign was there at all.

Q: You've given this a lot of thought.

A: Well, you don't see something like that and just forget it. That poor man in the sedan—I think about him when I sit out there now. I hope he's recovering.

Q: As do we all. Thank you for your care in answering these questions.

A: Of course. I want to get it right for everyone involved.

---

topic: A witness is asked about a car accident they saw from their front porch
text:
Q: Let's go over the timeline again. What time did the accident occur?

A: Around four-fifteen, I'd say.

Q: How can you be sure?

A: My daughter calls me every day at four-thirty. The accident happened, I went inside, and I was on the phone with her about ten minutes later telling her what I'd just seen.

Q: So your estimate is based on that phone call.

A: That's right. I'm not just guessing.

Q: I understand. Now, you mentioned the truck was speeding—

A: I said it was going fast. I don't have a radar gun, so I won't say speeding in the legal sense, but it was going faster than it should've been for that street. Kids play out there.

Q: Fair enough. Did you see the truck before it entered your line of sight at the intersection?

A: I heard it first. Engine revving.

Q: What kind of engine sound?

A: Loud. Aggressive, like someone with their foot down.

Q: Did you form any impression of the driver's state of mind?

A: I'm not a mind reader, counselor.

Q: Of course. Let me rephrase—did anything about the driver's behavior strike you as unusual?

A: After the crash, he got out and just stood there. Didn't check on the other driver. Didn't call for help. Just stood there staring at the damage to his truck.

Q: Did that concern you?

A: It broke my heart, honestly. That woman in the other car was crying out for help, and he was looking at his fender. I was the one who went to her. Held her hand until the ambulance came.

Q: You stayed with her the whole time?

A: I did. No one should go through something like that alone.

topic: A witness is questioned about a conversation they overheard in a company hallway
text:
Q: Mr. Daniels, you've testified that you were in the third-floor hallway on the afternoon of March 15th. Is that correct?

A: That's what I said, yes.

Q: And you claim to have overheard a conversation between two individuals near the copy room?

A: I didn't "claim" anything. I told you what happened. I heard two people talking.

Q: Fine. You heard two people talking. Could you identify those individuals?

A: I identified one of them. Patricia Vance. I've worked with her for six years. I know her voice.

Q: And the other person?

A: I already told opposing counsel I didn't see him. It was a male voice. That's all I can say for certain.

Q: A male voice. So it could have been anyone.

A: It could have been any man in the building, sure. There are what, two hundred employees? I'm not going to guess.

Q: How far away were you standing from this conversation?

A: I was at the water fountain. Maybe fifteen feet. Maybe twenty.

Q: Fifteen to twenty feet. And there was a copy machine running?

A: I didn't say it was running.

Q: Was it running?

A: I don't recall. It might have been. The point is I heard what I heard clearly enough.

Q: Did you hear every word of the conversation, Mr. Daniels?

A: I heard enough of it.

Q: That's not what I asked.

A: No. I didn't hear every single word. I heard Patricia say "the auditors can't find out about the Springfield account." That part I heard clearly. Word for word.

topic: A witness is questioned about a conversation they overheard in a company hallway
text:
Q: Ms. Thornton, let's talk about what you remember from that afternoon.

A: Alright.

Q: You were walking past the executive wing around four o'clock?

A: Approximately, yes. I don't remember checking my watch.

Q: And you heard voices coming from inside Mr. Reeves' office?

A: From outside his office. The door was open partway. They were standing just inside.

Q: Who was standing inside?

A: Mr. Reeves and a woman I didn't recognize.

Q: You didn't recognize her. Had you ever seen her before?

A: I don't know. Possibly. A lot of people come through that floor.

Q: But you're certain it was Mr. Reeves?

A: I saw him through the gap in the door. Yes, I'm certain.

Q: What did you hear Mr. Reeves say?

A: He said something about making the numbers work. "We'll make the numbers work, don't worry about Chen."

Q: "Don't worry about Chen." Those were his exact words?

A: That's what I remember him saying. I'm not a recording device, counselor.

Q: I understand. I'm just trying to establish—

A: You're trying to establish whether I actually heard what I heard. I did.

Q: Did you stop walking when you heard this?

A: I slowed down. I didn't stop completely.

Q: So you heard this fragment of conversation while walking past an open door at normal pace?

A: At a slower pace, like I said. And it wasn't a fragment. It was a complete sentence. I understood what he meant by it.

topic: A witness is questioned about a conversation they overheard in a company hallway
text:
Q: Let me take you back to June 8th. You were on the fourth floor that morning?

A: Yes.

Q: What were you doing there?

A: Dropping off paperwork for HR. My insurance forms.

Q: And on your way to HR, you passed by the conference room?

A: I passed by several conference rooms. That floor has three of them.

Q: Conference Room B. The one adjacent to the stairwell.

A: Okay. Yes, I walked past that one.

Q: Was the door open or closed?

A: It was closed, but there's a window. A narrow one, in the door.

Q: Did you look through the window?

A: Not intentionally. I glanced in the direction of the door as I walked by. That's a normal thing to do.

Q: And what did you see?

A: I saw Mr. Hartley and Ms. Chen standing very close together. She had papers in her hand. He had his hand on her arm.

Q: On her arm. Could you describe that contact?

A: He was gripping her arm. Above the elbow.

Q: "Gripping." That's a strong word. How long did you observe this?

A: Two seconds, maybe three. I was walking.

Q: So in two or three seconds, while walking, through a narrow window, you determined he was "gripping" her arm?

A: I know what I saw. His knuckles were white.

Q: His knuckles were white.

A: Yes.

Q: From fifteen feet away, through a window, in two seconds?

A: The window is at eye level. It was right there. I don't know why you keep repeating what I'm saying like it's going to change.

topic: A witness is questioned about a conversation they overheard in a company hallway
text:
Q: Tell me about the conversation you overheard, Mr. Pak.

A: It was... I need to be careful here. I don't want to mischaracterize anything.

Q: Just tell me what you remember.

A: I was waiting for the elevator. I heard two voices around the corner, by the break room entrance.

Q: Did you recognize the voices?

A: I thought one of them was Derek Simmons. But I couldn't swear to it under oath—well, I mean, we're under oath now, but I can't be completely certain.

Q: What made you think it was Mr. Simmons?

A: He has a distinctive way of speaking. Very fast, clips the ends of words. I've worked with him on two projects.

Q: And the other voice?

A: Female. Younger, maybe? I really couldn't say. I'm not good with voices.

Q: What did they say?

A: That's the thing, I only caught pieces. Something about documents. And I think I heard the word "shredding" or maybe "shedding"? The elevator dinged and I lost the rest.

Q: Did you hear anything about the Morrison contract specifically?

A: I don't... I don't think so. Maybe? I don't want to put words in anyone's mouth that weren't there.

Q: Mr. Pak, you reported this conversation to your supervisor the next day. Why would you do that if you weren't sure what you heard?

A: Because what I thought I heard concerned me. I said "thought." I told her it might be nothing.

Q: But you still reported it.

A: Was that wrong? Was I supposed to just ignore it?

Q: I'm not asking what you were supposed to do. I'm asking what you actually heard.

A: And I'm telling you what I actually heard. Parts of a conversation. That's all.

topic: A witness is questioned about a conversation they overheard in a company hallway
text:
Q: Mrs. Okonkwo, you've stated that on November 3rd you overheard a conversation in the hallway outside the finance department.

A: Yes.

Q: Between whom?

A: Alan Marsh and someone on his phone. He was on a call.

Q: So this wasn't a conversation between two people present in the hallway?

A: It was a conversation. He was speaking to someone. I could only hear his side of it.

Q: Walk me through exactly what you heard.

A: He said, "The board doesn't need to know about this yet." Then something I couldn't make out. Then he laughed and said, "What they don't know won't hurt them."

Q: He laughed.

A: Yes.

Q: A casual laugh? A nervous laugh? An evil laugh?

A: I'm not going to characterize his laugh, counselor. He laughed. It's not my job to interpret what kind.

Q: Fair enough. Now, you said something was inaudible between those two statements?

A: Right.

Q: Could have been three seconds of mumbling? Could have been thirty seconds of context?

A: It was a few seconds.

Q: Could the context of that gap change the meaning of what you heard?

A: I suppose anything's possible.

Q: But you've already decided what it meant, haven't you?

A: Objection—argumentative.

Q: I'll rephrase. Mrs. Okonkwo, when you reported this to internal compliance, did you describe it as potential evidence of wrongdoing?

A: I described what I heard and said they should look into it. I let them decide what it meant.

Q: But you used the phrase "covering something up" in your written statement.

A: Because "what they don't know won't hurt them" sounds like covering something up. That's not interpretation. That's English.

topic: A building inspector is deposed about a structural assessment they signed off on
text:
Q: Mr. Harwood, you conducted the structural assessment of the Meridian Tower on March 15th, 2022, correct?

A: That's what my signature indicates, yes.

Q: And you personally inspected the load-bearing walls on the seventh floor?

A: I inspected the building according to standard protocol.

Q: That's not what I asked. Did you personally inspect the load-bearing walls on the seventh floor?

A: I... yes. I would have. That's part of the protocol.

Q: You would have, or you did?

A: I'm not sure I understand the distinction you're making here.

Q: It's a straightforward question, Mr. Harwood. Do you have a specific memory of inspecting those walls?

A: I inspect dozens of buildings. I follow the same procedure every time. So yes, I inspected them.

Q: Do you recall anything unusual about the walls on the seventh floor?

A: Unusual how?

Q: Cracks. Discoloration. Signs of water damage. Anything at all.

A: If there had been something unusual, it would be in my report. Is it in my report?

Q: I'm asking what you remember, Mr. Harwood.

A: Then no. Nothing unusual. Or I would have noted it.

topic: A building inspector is deposed about a structural assessment they signed off on
text:
Q: Ms. Vega, I want to direct your attention to page four of your assessment report. Do you have that in front of you?

A: I do.

Q: You wrote here that the foundation showed, quote, "no significant deterioration." Is that correct?

A: That's what it says.

Q: What does "significant" mean in this context?

A: It means deterioration that would compromise structural integrity.

Q: And how do you determine what compromises structural integrity?

A: Through visual inspection, measurements, comparing to code requirements—the standard methodology.

Q: Wait—visual inspection only? You didn't conduct any core sampling?

A: I didn't say only. I said visual inspection is part of it.

Q: So you did conduct core sampling?

A: On this particular building?

Q: Yes, on Meridian Tower.

A: I'd have to review my field notes. I don't have those in front of me.

Q: You signed off on the foundation's integrity but you can't tell me whether you took core samples?

A: I can tell you I followed proper procedure. Whether that included core sampling on this specific inspection—I'd need to check my notes. That's not an unreasonable answer.

topic: A building inspector is deposed about a structural assessment they signed off on
text:
Q: Mr. Okonkwo, how long did you spend on site during your March inspection?

A: Approximately four hours.

Q: Four hours for a twelve-story building?

A: That's correct.

Q: Is that typical?

A: It depends on the building. The scope of the assessment. What we're asked to evaluate.

Q: What were you asked to evaluate here?

A: I'd have to refer to the engagement letter, but my understanding was this was a standard pre-sale structural assessment.

Q: Your understanding. You don't recall specifically?

A: Counsel, I conduct over two hundred inspections a year. I remember this building. I remember walking the floors. I don't have the engagement letter memorized.

Q: Fair enough. In those four hours, did you access the mechanical room on sublevel two?

A: The mechanical room?

Q: Yes. Sublevel two. There's a mechanical room adjacent to the parking structure.

A: I'm not aware of a mechanical room on sublevel two.

Q: There isn't one?

A: Not that I—I mean, I inspected the sublevels. I don't recall a separate mechanical room. There was mechanical equipment, certainly.

Q: So you may have inspected it without realizing it was designated as such?

A: I suppose that's possible. I'm not sure what you're asking me to confirm.

topic: A building inspector is deposed about a structural assessment they signed off on
text:
Q: Dr. Patel, you've been a licensed structural engineer for twenty-three years, correct?

A: Twenty-four in August.

Q: And in those twenty-four years, have you ever signed off on an assessment that you later believed was in error?

A: I've revised assessments when new information came to light. I wouldn't characterize that as error.

Q: How would you characterize it?

A: As the nature of engineering. We work with available information.

Q: Let me ask this differently. The Meridian Tower assessment—do you stand by it today?

A: As of the date it was issued, based on the conditions I observed, yes.

Q: That's a lot of qualifications.

A: Those aren't qualifications. Those are the parameters of any structural assessment. I'm not sure what answer you're looking for.

Q: I'm looking for a yes or no, Dr. Patel.

A: Then you're asking an incomplete question. Stand by it under what conditions? With what hindsight? These aren't simple matters.

Q: The building's east stairwell collapsed eleven months after your assessment. Does that change your answer?

A: ...I assessed what I was able to assess. I can't account for what I wasn't shown.

Q: Wasn't shown? What do you mean by that?

A: I mean there were areas I wasn't given access to. That's in my report. Appendix C, if you'd like to look.

topic: A building inspector is deposed about a structural assessment they signed off on
text:
Q: Mr. Brennan, whose name appears on the Meridian Tower assessment as the supervising inspector?

A: Mine does.

Q: But you didn't conduct the physical inspection yourself, did you?

A: I supervised the inspection. Marcus Toller was the field inspector.

Q: So when you signed the report, you were relying on Mr. Toller's findings?

A: I reviewed his findings, reviewed the photographs, reviewed the measurements. That's what supervision means.

Q: Did you visit the site at any point?

A: I don't believe so, no.

Q: You don't believe so, or no?

A: No. I did not visit the site.

Q: Is that standard practice? To sign off on an assessment without visiting the site?

A: For a supervisory signature, yes. The field inspector does the on-site work.

Q: Let me make sure I understand. Your name is on this report. Your license number. Your signature. But you never set foot in Meridian Tower?

A: That's correct. That's how supervisory review works.

Q: In your twenty years of experience, Mr. Brennan—

A: Seventeen.

Q: I'm sorry?

A: Seventeen years. You said twenty.

Q: My apologies. In your seventeen years, have you ever had a field inspector's findings turn out to be materially wrong?

A: I'm not sure what you mean by materially.

Q: Substantially. Significantly. Wrong in a way that mattered.

A: I'd have to think about that. I can't give you a number off the top of my head.

Q: I'm not asking for a number. I'm asking if it's ever happened.

A: ...I suppose it's possible. I'd want to review specific files before answering definitively.

topic: A warehouse supervisor is deposed about safety protocols that were allegedly ignored
text:
Q: Mr. Delacroix, how long have you worked as a warehouse supervisor at Greenfield Distribution?

A: Seven years. Seven years and three months, if you need it exact.

Q: And in that role, you're responsible for enforcing safety protocols, correct?

A: I'm responsible for a lot of things. Safety is one of them.

Q: That's a yes?

A: Yes.

Q: Were you aware that forklift operators are required to complete a daily pre-shift inspection checklist?

A: Of course I was aware. I wrote the training manual for our location.

Q: You wrote it yourself?

A: With HR, yes. Is that surprising to you?

Q: I'm just asking questions, Mr. Delacroix. On March 14th of this year, do you know whether the pre-shift inspection was completed for Forklift Unit 7?

A: I'd have to see the logs.

Q: You don't recall independently?

A: I supervise nineteen operators and twelve pieces of equipment. No, I don't have March 14th memorized.

Q: Would it concern you to learn that no checklist was filed for Unit 7 that day?

A: If that's true, then yes, it would concern me. But I haven't seen evidence of that.

Q: I'm showing you what's been marked as Exhibit 14. Take a moment to review it.

A: I see a log sheet. I see that the Unit 7 line is blank. That doesn't tell me the inspection wasn't done—it tells me someone didn't fill out the paper.

Q: So your testimony is that the inspection may have occurred even though there's no record?

A: My testimony is that I don't know, because I wasn't standing next to that forklift at 6 a.m. on March 14th. That's my testimony.

---

topic: A warehouse supervisor is deposed about safety protocols that were allegedly ignored
text:
Q: Ms. Thornton, let's talk about the lockout-tagout procedures at the Riverside facility.

A: Okay.

Q: You're familiar with those procedures?

A: Yes.

Q: Who trained the floor employees on lockout-tagout?

A: We use a combination of online modules and hands-on training with shift leads.

Q: Did you personally conduct any of that training?

A: Some of it.

Q: Some of it. How much is "some"?

A: I couldn't give you a percentage.

Q: A rough estimate.

A: I don't want to guess and have you hold me to a number later.

Q: I'm not trying to trap you, Ms. Thornton.

A: Then let me answer carefully. I participated in training sessions, but I wasn't the sole trainer. I don't track my hours that way.

Q: Fair enough. Were you aware that on July 9th, a maintenance worker was injured while servicing Conveyor Line 3?

A: I learned about it afterward, yes.

Q: And were you aware that the conveyor had not been properly locked out?

A: That's what the incident report indicated.

Q: Did you investigate why?

A: Yes.

Q: And what did you find?

A: I found that the worker skipped a step. He admitted it.
