Q: The Rodriguez complaint from September—that's the one we're here to discuss—fell within your normal duties?

A: It did.

Q: Walk me through what happened after you received her written complaint on September 3rd.

A: I acknowledged receipt, opened a file, and began the investigation process.

Q: When you say "began the investigation process," what does that mean specifically?

A: I'm not sure what level of detail you're looking for.

Q: What did you actually do? Who did you speak to? What documents did you review?

A: I spoke to Ms. Rodriguez. I spoke to the accused employee, Thomas Whitfield. I reviewed her written statement and any relevant communications.

Q: Any relevant communications. What does that mean?

A: Emails. Text messages if they were provided.

Q: Were text messages provided in this case?

A: I don't recall specifically.

Q: You don't recall whether text messages were part of the evidence you reviewed?

A: There may have been screenshots. I'd have to look at the file.

Q: Let me show you what's been marked as Exhibit 7. Do you recognize this document?

A: This is... this appears to be a text message exchange.

Q: Between whom?

A: Between Ms. Rodriguez and Mr. Whitfield.

Q: Is this in your investigation file?

A: I don't... I'm not certain.

Q: You're not certain whether you've seen this before?

A: I'm saying I can't confirm whether this specific printout was part of my file without comparing it to my records.

Q: The timestamp on these messages is August 29th. Five days before the complaint was filed. Did you ever see messages from this date?

A: I need a moment to review this.

topic: An HR director is questioned about a harassment complaint that was filed and closed
text:
Q: You closed the Benson complaint as "unsubstantiated." That's the term in your final report?

A: That's correct.

Q: What does "unsubstantiated" mean in your terminology?

A: It means the investigation did not produce sufficient evidence to conclude that a policy violation occurred.

Q: Does it mean the conduct didn't happen?

A: No. It means we couldn't prove it happened.

Q: Is that distinction made clear to the parties?

A: We explain our findings to both the complainant and the respondent.

Q: Let me ask you about the interview with Mr. Cullen. He was the accused?

A: Yes.

Q: Your notes say he denied ever being alone with Ms. Benson. Is that accurate?

A: If that's what my notes say.

Q: I'm asking if you remember him saying that.

A: I remember him denying the allegations. I don't remember his precise words.

Q: But your notes are accurate?

A: I take careful notes, yes.

Q: Okay. Now, I have security footage logs from the building—this is Exhibit 14—showing Mr. Cullen and Ms. Benson both badging into Conference Room C on June 2nd. Alone. The room has a capacity of twelve, and only two badge-ins are recorded for that hour.

A: I see that.

Q: Did you review security logs during your investigation?

A: We don't typically pull badge records for every complaint.

Q: But this would have contradicted Mr. Cullen's denial, wouldn't it?

A: I suppose it would have shown they were both in the same room. Whether that contradicts—I mean, I don't know what he specifically denied.

Q: You said he denied being alone with her.

A: If that's what I wrote. I'm just trying to be precise about what the logs would actually prove.

Q: Would it have changed your conclusion if you'd seen this?

A: I can't speculate about hypotheticals. I made my determination based on the information I had.

topic: An HR director is questioned about a harassment complaint that was filed and closed
text:
Q: Dr. Yamamoto, let's talk about timeline. The Hollis complaint was filed February 1st?

A: Yes.

Q: And closed February 9th?

A: Let me check. Yes, that's the closure date.

Q: Eight days.

A: That's correct.

Q: In those eight days, what steps did you take?

A: I interviewed Ms. Hollis. I interviewed the subject of the complaint. I reviewed the department's email server for any relevant communications. I consulted with legal. And I prepared my final report.

Q: That's comprehensive work for eight days.

A: I'm sorry, is that a question?

Q: Did you feel eight days was sufficient time to thoroughly investigate these allegations?

A: I felt the investigation was complete when I closed it, yes.

Q: Were you under any pressure to resolve this quickly?

A: Pressure from whom?

Q: From anyone. Management. Legal. Anyone.

A: We always try to resolve complaints promptly. I wouldn't characterize that as pressure.

Q: The subject of the complaint, Daniel Farris—he was being considered for a promotion at this time?

A: I wasn't involved in promotion decisions.

Q: But you were aware he was up for VP of Operations?

A: I may have heard something about it.

Q: And the promotion announcement was scheduled for February 15th?

A: I didn't know the specific date.

Q: Six days after you closed the investigation?

A: If you're suggesting—

Q: I'm not suggesting anything. I'm establishing facts. Were you aware that a harassment finding would have disqualified Mr. Farris from the promotion?

A: That would depend on the nature of the finding.

Q: Company policy requires candidates for senior leadership to have no substantiated complaints in the previous twelve months. Isn't that correct?

A: I'd have to verify the exact policy language.

Q: You're the HR director and you'd have to verify that?

A: I want to be accurate. These policies have nuances.

topic: An HR director is questioned about a harassment complaint that was filed and closed
text:
Q: The complaint we're discussing was filed by someone named—let me find it—Jessica Tran. Is that right?

A: Actually, the complaint in question was filed by Jennifer Tran.

Q: I apologize. Jennifer Tran.

A: Yes.

Q: And she alleged—help me out here—what was the nature of her complaint?

A: She alleged that a coworker had made unwelcome advances over a period of several months.

Q: Unwelcome advances. Physical? Verbal?

A: Both, as I recall.

Q: You recall, or that's what's in the file?

A: That's my recollection, which is consistent with the file.

Q: Now, the coworker she accused—what was his position relative to hers?

A: They were at the same level. Neither supervised the other.

Q: But he had seniority?

A: I don't know what you mean by seniority.

Q: He'd been with the company longer?

A: Yes, that's accurate.

Q: And he was on the team that conducted her performance reviews?

A: He participated in peer reviews, as did several others.

Q: Wait—if he participated in her reviews, doesn't that give him some authority over her?

A: Peer review is a collaborative process. It's not a supervisory relationship.

Q: But negative input from him could affect her standing?

A: Input from anyone on the peer review team could theoretically affect outcomes. That's the nature of peer review.

Q: Did you consider that when evaluating her complaint?

A: Consider what, exactly?

Q: That she might face retaliation through the peer review process.

A: We have anti-retaliation policies in place.

Q: That's not what I asked. Did you consider it as a factor in this specific case?

A: I... I considered the totality of the circumstances, as I do with every complaint.

Q: But you closed the case and both employees remained on the same peer review team, correct?

A: Correct.

Q: Is that typical?

A: Every case is different. I don't know what you'd consider typical.

topic: A doctor is deposed about informed consent procedures before a surgery
text:
Q: Dr. Patel, I'd like to ask you about your informed consent practices. Can you walk me through how you typically approach that conversation with patients before surgery?

A: Of course. I actually enjoy that part of my work, if I'm being honest. It's a chance to really connect with someone who's often frightened or uncertain. I start by sitting down—always sitting, never standing over them—and I ask what they already understand about why they're there. That tells me where to begin.

Q: And how long do these conversations usually last?

A: As long as they need to. I know that sounds like a non-answer, but it's true. Some patients are ready in fifteen minutes. Others need an hour, or a second meeting. Mrs. Holloway—the patient in question—she had a lot of questions, and I was glad she did. It meant she was engaged.

Q: You remember her specifically?

A: I do. She reminded me a bit of my own mother, actually. Very sharp, very particular about understanding exactly what was happening to her body. I appreciated that about her.

Q: What do you recall discussing with Mrs. Holloway regarding the risks of the procedure?

A: We talked about the standard risks—bleeding, infection, adverse reaction to anesthesia. And then we spent quite a bit of time on the specific risks related to her anatomy and her age. She wanted to know percentages, which I provided where I could, and honest uncertainty where I couldn't.

Q: Did she express any concerns about proceeding?

A: She did, and I encouraged her to voice all of them. I remember telling her that no question was too small. She asked about recovery time, about scarring, about whether she'd be able to garden again by spring. We talked through each one.

Q: And did you feel she understood the information you provided?

A: I did. More than understood—she processed it thoughtfully. She asked me to repeat a few things, which I always take as a good sign. It means someone is really listening.

Q: Was there anything about the consent form itself that you reviewed with her?

A: Yes, I went through it line by line with her. Some doctors hand it over and let the patient read it alone, but I find that impersonal. I'd rather read it together, answer questions as they come up.

Q: Did she sign the form that day?

A: She did, but not until she was ready. I gave her the option to take it home, to think it over. She told me she appreciated that, but she'd made her decision. I believed her.

topic: A doctor is deposed about informed consent procedures before a surgery
text:
Q: Dr. Simmons, you performed the appendectomy on Mr. Rourke on March 14th, correct?

A: That's correct.

Q: Prior to that surgery, did you personally obtain informed consent from the patient?

A: I did.

Q: What time did that conversation occur?

A: It was approximately two hours before the scheduled surgery, around six in the morning.

Q: And Mr. Rourke had been in the hospital overnight at that point?

A: Yes, he'd been admitted through the emergency department the prior evening.

Q: Was anyone else present during your consent conversation with him?

A: His wife was there. Linda, I think her name was. She was sitting beside the bed, holding his hand.

Q: Tell me about that conversation.

A: Certainly. Mr. Rourke was understandably anxious—he'd never had surgery before. I pulled up a chair and explained what we'd be doing, why it was necessary, what could happen if we didn't proceed. I tried to speak slowly and clearly. His wife kept nodding along, which I think helped him feel more at ease.

Q: Did you discuss potential complications?

A: Yes. I explained the risks of infection, bleeding, injury to surrounding organs. I also mentioned the small possibility of conversion to an open procedure if laparoscopy wasn't feasible.

Q: How did he respond to that information?

A: He asked good questions. He wanted to know how often complications occurred in my experience specifically, which I appreciated. I gave him my personal statistics as best I could.

Q: And you felt he was competent to consent?

A: Absolutely. He was alert, oriented, asking appropriate questions. His wife was there as a second set of ears. I felt confident he understood what he was agreeing to.

Q: Did you document this conversation?

A: I did. I always make a point of noting the substance of consent discussions in my operative note. It's important to me that there's a record of what was said.

topic: A doctor is deposed about informed consent procedures before a surgery
text:
Q: State your name for the record.

A: Dr. Angela Morrison.

Q: Dr. Morrison, you were the attending surgeon for the knee replacement performed on Thomas Delaney?

A: I was.

Q: I want to ask you about the informed consent process. You're aware Mr. Delaney alleges he wasn't told about the risk of nerve damage?

A: I'm aware of the allegation, yes.

Q: And what's your response to that?

A: I discussed nerve damage with him. I discuss it with every knee replacement patient.

Q: You sound quite certain.

A: I am certain. I've done over four hundred of these procedures. The risk of nerve injury is part of my standard consent discussion. I wouldn't skip it.

Q: Help me understand how you can be so sure, given the volume of patients you see.

A: Because it's not something I improvise. I have a mental checklist I go through every time. Nerve damage is on that list. It's always on that list.

Q: Do you have any documentation of specifically discussing nerve damage with Mr. Delaney?

A: My consent note indicates that risks including nerve injury were discussed. That's my standard documentation.

Q: The note says "risks including nerve injury." It doesn't detail the conversation.

A: That's correct. My notes are summaries, not transcripts. But I can tell you what my practice is, and my practice is consistent.

Q: Mr. Delaney is a schoolteacher. He says he would have wanted to know the specific percentage risk of nerve damage. Did you provide that?

A: I typically quote a range of one to two percent for transient nerve symptoms, lower for permanent injury. I would have given him those numbers.

Q: Would have, or did?

A: Did. I follow the same process every time, Counsel. I understand you're doing your job, and I respect that. But I know what I told this patient.

Q: Fair enough. Did Mr. Delaney ask any follow-up questions about nerve damage?

A: Not that I specifically recall, but that's not unusual. Most patients don't. They're focused on the outcome, on getting back to their lives. I try to make sure they hear the important information even if they don't ask.

topic: A doctor is deposed about informed consent procedures before a surgery
text:
Q: Dr. Okafor, before we get into the specifics of the consent form, I want to understand your general philosophy around informed consent. Would you share that with me?

A: My philosophy?

Q: Yes. How do you approach it?

A: Well, I suppose I see it as a partnership. The patient brings their values, their fears, their hopes. I bring medical knowledge. Together, we make a decision. It's not me telling them what to do—it's us figuring out what's right for them.

Q: That's a thoughtful way to frame it.

A: Thank you. I didn't always see it that way, to be honest. Earlier in my career, I was more paternalistic. Experience has taught me that patients make better decisions when they feel genuinely heard.

Q: How has that philosophy shaped your practice specifically with Ms. Chen, the plaintiff in this case?

A: Ms. Chen was particularly invested in understanding her options. She came to appointments with printed articles, questions written in a notebook. I welcomed that. Some doctors find it challenging when patients do their own research, but I think it shows engagement.

Q: Did you feel her questions were reasonable?

A: Very much so. She asked about alternative treatments, about what would happen if she chose to delay surgery, about long-term outcomes. These are exactly the questions I want patients to ask.

Q: And you answered them fully?

A: To the best of my ability, yes. Where I didn't have data, I told her so. Where there was genuine uncertainty in the medical literature, I shared that uncertainty.

Q: How did she receive that honesty?

A: She seemed to appreciate it. She told me at one point that she'd seen another surgeon who had been dismissive of her concerns. She said talking to me felt different.

Q: Different how?

A: She said she felt like I was treating her as intelligent. I try to treat all my patients that way. They're trusting me with their bodies—the least I can do is trust them with information.

Q: Did she ultimately consent to the procedure?

A: She did, after our third meeting. She wanted time to discuss it with her family, which I encouraged.

topic: A doctor is deposed about informed consent procedures before a surgery
text:
Q: Dr. Brennan, I want to be precise about the timeline here. You met with Mr. Fitzgerald on January 8th to discuss the proposed cardiac surgery?

A: Yes.

Q: And the surgery was scheduled for January 15th?

A: Correct.

Q: During that January 8th meeting, did you discuss the risks of stroke?

A: I did.

Q: What specifically did you tell him?

A: I explained that stroke is a known risk of cardiac bypass surgery. I told him the risk was approximately two to three percent based on his age and health profile.

Q: Did you explain what a stroke might mean for his daily life?

A: Yes. I told him it could affect his speech, his movement, his cognition. I tried to be concrete about it because percentages can feel abstract.

Q: How did Mr. Fitzgerald react to that information?

A: He was quiet for a moment. Then he asked me what I would do if I were him.

Q: And what did you say?

A: I told him I couldn't answer that, because I'm not him. But I said that if the question was whether the risk was worth taking, I believed it was. His cardiac disease was progressing. Without surgery, his prognosis was poor.

Q: Did he seem to understand?

A: He did. He's a thoughtful man. He told me he'd been a carpenter for forty years, and he understood that every job has risks. He said he trusted me to do my job well.

Q: That must have meant something to you.

A: It did. It always does when patients place that trust in you. It's not something I take lightly.

Q: Was his wife present for this conversation?

A: She was. Margaret. She had questions of her own, mostly about recovery time and what kind of help he'd need at home. I could tell they were a team, the two of them.

Q: Did you feel you had adequately informed both of them?

A: I did. And I gave them my card, told them to call if anything else came up before the surgery date. Margaret called once, just to confirm a medication question. I was glad she felt comfortable reaching out.

topic: A supervisor is deposed about performance reviews given to an employee who was later fired
text:
Q: Mr. Hartwell, you conducted the 2022 annual performance review for Danielle Okonkwo, correct?

A: I did. November 14th, 2022, to be precise.

Q: And what overall rating did you assign Ms. Okonkwo in that review?

A: "Meets Expectations." The same rating I gave her in 2021 and 2020. Consistent performer.

Q: You have the review document in front of you?

A: I do, and I've reviewed it thoroughly in preparation for today.

Q: In the section titled "Areas for Improvement," you wrote—and I'm quoting—"Danielle should focus on developing stronger client-facing communication skills." Do you see that?

A: I see it because I wrote it. And I'd note that's a developmental suggestion, not a deficiency. Every employee in my department receives developmental suggestions. It's standard practice.

Q: Did you ever communicate to Ms. Okonkwo that her job was in jeopardy?

A: No, because it wasn't. Not under my supervision.

Q: When did you learn she was being terminated?

A: March 3rd, 2023. HR informed me that morning.

Q: Were you consulted before that decision was made?

A: I was not.

Q: Did that surprise you?

A: It did more than surprise me. I disagreed with it. I made that disagreement known in writing to HR Director Stevens that same day.

Q: Do you still have a copy of that communication?

A: I kept a copy specifically because I anticipated this conversation might happen someday.

topic: A supervisor is deposed about performance reviews given to an employee who was later fired
text:
Q: Let's talk about the metrics used in your performance reviews. What factors did you evaluate?

A: Well, there were several. Productivity numbers, obviously. Quality scores. Attendance. Team collaboration. Client feedback when applicable.

Q: Were these factors weighted equally?

A: Not exactly equally, no. Productivity and quality were weighted more heavily. I believe it was 30 percent each, then the others made up the remaining 40.

Q: You believe, or you know?

A: I know. I'm looking at the rubric right now.

Q: Good. Now, in Mr. Fitzgerald's final review, dated August 2022, what were his productivity numbers?

A: He was at 94 percent of target.

Q: And the departmental average?

A: Around 91 percent.

Q: So Mr. Fitzgerald exceeded the departmental average?

A: On that one metric, yes.

Q: What about quality scores?

A: 87 percent.

Q: Departmental average?

A: 89 percent.

Q: Two points below average?

A: Correct. Though I'd point out that a two-point variance is within normal fluctuation. I wouldn't characterize it as a significant gap.

Q: But you gave him an overall rating of "Needs Improvement." How do you reconcile that with numbers that were essentially average or above?

A: Because the numbers weren't the whole picture. The collaboration scores were low—several team members had raised concerns. And I documented those concerns extensively in the narrative section, which I'd encourage you to read in full rather than cherry-picking metrics.

topic: A supervisor is deposed about performance reviews given to an employee who was later fired
text:
Q: Ms. Patterson, how long have you supervised the accounts receivable department?

A: Seven years this past June.

Q: And in those seven years, how many employees have you recommended for termination?

A: I'd have to think. Maybe four? Five at most.

Q: Was Jerome Washington one of them?

A: No.

Q: You didn't recommend his termination?

A: I did not.

Q: Who made that decision?

A: I believe it came from upper management. Regional level.

Q: You believe?

A: Well, I wasn't in the room. I was informed after the fact. So I can only tell you what I was told.

Q: What were you told?

A: That Jerome was being let go for performance reasons.

Q: Did that align with your assessment of his performance?

A: I'm not sure how to answer that.

Q: Did you consider Jerome Washington a poor performer?

A: I considered him a developing employee. He'd only been with us fourteen months. There was a learning curve.

Q: His last performance review from you was in January. What rating did you give him?

A: "Meets Expectations."

Q: Not "Needs Improvement"?

A: No. "Meets Expectations." Because he was meeting them.

Q: Then help me understand—

A: I can only tell you what I observed and documented. What decisions were made above me, you'd have to ask the people who made them.

topic: A supervisor is deposed about performance reviews given to an employee who was later fired
text:
Q: Mr. Chen, I want to direct your attention to Exhibit 14. Do you recognize this document?

Second, there were accuracy issues with her data entry—error rate around 4 percent, and our threshold is 2 percent. Third, responsiveness to internal communications. Emails going unanswered for days at a time.

A: Not by me.

Q: By anyone?

topic: A supervisor is deposed about performance reviews given to an employee who was later fired
text:
Q: When you wrote—let me find the exact language—"Marcus demonstrates leadership potential that should be cultivated," what specifically were you referring to?

A: I was referring to several things. His mentorship of junior staff. The way he handled the Brennan account transition when that could have gone very badly. His willingness to take on additional responsibilities during the Q3 surge.

A: That's correct.

topic: A witness is questioned about a conversation they overheard in a company hallway
text:
Q: Please state your name for the record.

A: Margaret Chen. Senior Compliance Officer, eleven years with the company.

Q: Ms. Chen, directing your attention to March 14th of this year, where were you at approximately 2:30 in the afternoon?

A: I was walking back from the executive conference room on the fourth floor. I'd just finished presenting our quarterly compliance audit to the board. Received commendations, actually—but I assume that's not what you're asking about.

Q: What happened as you walked back?

A: I passed the alcove near the elevators—the one with the water cooler and the fake ficus—and I heard Mr. Brennan and someone else speaking. I recognized the voice as belonging to David Ostrowski from Legal.

Q: Did you stop?

A: I slowed. I didn't hide—I had every right to be there. I've been navigating that floor longer than either of them have been with the company.

Q: What did you hear?

A: Mr. Brennan said, and I'm quoting as precisely as I can because I have an excellent memory for these things, "The EPA doesn't need to know about the January readings. We bury it in the amended filing."

Q: You're certain of those words?

A: I documented compliance violations for over a decade. I know how to retain critical information. Yes, I'm certain.

Q: What did Mr. Ostrowski say in response?

A: He laughed—nervously, I thought—and said something like, "You're the boss." Rather spineless, in my assessment, but you didn't ask for my assessment.

Q: Did either of them see you?

A: Mr. Brennan glanced up as I passed. I didn't look away. I held his gaze and kept walking. I wasn't the one with something to hide.

Q: Did you report what you heard?

A: I drafted a memorandum that same evening. Timestamped, detailed, following the exact protocol I helped design for this company's whistleblower procedures. It's Exhibit 14 in your materials, I believe.

Q: Thank you, Ms. Chen.

A: You're welcome. I assume you'll want me available for additional testimony—I kept contemporaneous notes on several other conversations as well.

---

topic: A witness is questioned about a conversation they overheard in a company hallway
text:
Q: Good morning. You've done this before, haven't you, Mr. Isaacs?

A: Depositions? Once, yes.

Q: Then you know how this works. I'll ask questions, you'll answer truthfully. Simple.

A: I understand.

Q: Now, I've been looking forward to this particular conversation. You were present on the sixth floor of Meridian Tower on October 3rd, correct?

A: I was.

Q: And you happened to overhear a discussion between two individuals in the hallway outside suite 604?

A: That's right.

topic: A witness is questioned about a conversation they overheard in a company hallway
text:
Q: Mr. Tran, were you working late on the evening of July 19th?

A: Yeah, I was in the copy room until maybe nine, nine-thirty.

Q: Was anyone else on the floor at that time?

A: I thought I was alone. Then I heard voices coming from down the hall. Near Mr. Patterson's office.

A: One was definitely Mr. Patterson—I'd know that voice anywhere. The other took me a minute, but it was Angela Reyes from accounting.

A: I stayed in the copy room. Didn't want them to know I was there. I waited maybe fifteen minutes after they left.

A: I told my supervisor the next day. Mrs. Huang. She said I did the right thing coming forward.

topic: A witness is questioned about a conversation they overheard in a company hallway
text:
Q: State your position with the company.

A: I'm a facilities coordinator. Have been for three years.

Q: On February 8th, you were performing your regular duties on the third floor?

A: Yes.

Q: Describe what you observed.

A: I was checking the HVAC vents—we'd had complaints about cold air—and I heard two people around the corner. Near the break room.

Q: Did you recognize them?

A: I recognized Mr. Whitmore. The CFO. The other voice I didn't know.

Q: What were they discussing?

A: Money stuff. Numbers. I don't really understand finance.

Q: Try your best.

A: Mr. Whitmore said something about "keeping the auditors away from the Delaware accounts." The other person—a woman—said that was risky.

Q: What did Mr. Whitmore say to that?

A: He said, "Risk is my middle name." Then he laughed.

Q: He laughed?

A: Like a joke. But not really a joke, you know?

Q: Did you report this conversation?

A: No.

Q: Why not?

A: Who was I gonna tell? I fix air conditioners. Nobody asks me about Delaware accounts.

Q: So why are you here today?

A: Because someone finally asked. Took eight months, but someone finally thought to ask the guy who's actually in the building at all hours.

Q: Are you suggesting the investigation was inadequate?

A: I'm saying I could have told you all this in February. But facilities staff don't usually make it onto the interview list, do we?

Q: That's not—

A: It's fine. I'm here now. And I remember everything.

---

topic: A witness is questioned about a conversation they overheard in a company hallway
text:
Q: Ms. Okonkwo, you've testified that you were on the second floor mezzanine on April 4th.

A: That's correct.

Q: And you overheard a conversation between two people below you?

A: Yes. The acoustics in that atrium are actually quite remarkable—sound carries upward in a way the architects probably didn't intend. I've noticed it before.

Q: Who did you observe?

A: Thomas Crane and a woman I later identified as Jennifer Walsh, based on a company directory photo.

Q: You took the time to identify her afterward?

A: I thought the conversation warranted documentation.

Q: What did you hear?

A: Mr. Crane was explaining that certain safety inspection reports had been "adjusted" before submission to the state. Ms. Walsh expressed concern. He told her, "This is how it's done. Don't be naive."

Q: Did he use the word "adjusted"?

A: His exact word was "massaged," actually. I apologize—I should be precise. He said the reports had been "massaged."

Q: That's an important distinction.

A: I'm aware. Precision matters. That's why I wrote everything down within the hour, while my memory was fresh. I have the original notes if you'd like them entered into evidence.

Q: That won't be necessary at this time.

A: It's no trouble. I anticipated this deposition might go in several directions, so I brought supporting materials.

Q: We'll proceed with questions for now.

A: Of course. Though I should mention—I also have observations from two other occasions that may be relevant to your inquiry. Same individuals. Similar subject matter.

Q: We'll get to those if needed.

A: I'll be ready.

topic: A warehouse supervisor is deposed about safety protocols that were allegedly ignored
text:
Q: Mr. Dawson, how long have you worked as a warehouse supervisor at Kendrick Distribution?

A: Eleven years. Eleven years in March.

Q: And in those eleven years, you've been responsible for enforcing safety protocols?

A: That's part of it, yes.

Q: Part of it. What's the other part?

A: Making sure shipments go out. Making sure we hit our numbers. Keeping the floor running.

Q: Which of those responsibilities would you say takes priority?

A: I think you already know the answer to that, counselor.

Q: I'm asking what you would say.

A: The numbers. It's always the numbers. You learn that pretty quick.

Q: Did anyone explicitly tell you to prioritize shipment quotas over safety?

A: Nobody has to say it explicitly. You see what gets people promoted. You see what gets people called into the office.

Q: So it was implicit.

A: It was understood.

Q: On April 14th, were the forklift inspection logs completed before the morning shift began?

A: No.

Q: Why not?

A: Because we were short-staffed, and there were four trucks waiting at the dock. Same reason as always.

Q: Did you report the missed inspection to anyone?

A: I stopped reporting them about two years ago.

Q: Why?

A: Because nothing ever changed. You fill out the incident form, you send the email, you get a reply saying they'll look into it. Then you come in the next morning and it's the same thing all over again. After a while, you just... you do what you can and you go home.

---

topic: A warehouse supervisor is deposed about safety protocols that were allegedly ignored
text:
Q: Ms. Ferraro, I want to direct your attention to the safety training records for the overnight shift. Do you have those in front of you?

A: I do.

Q: Can you tell me when the last forklift certification training was conducted for overnight employees?

A: According to this, August of last year.

Q: August. So roughly fourteen months before the incident.

A: That's correct.

Q: OSHA requires recertification every three years, but your company policy calls for annual refreshers. Is that accurate?

A: Yes.

Q: So the overnight shift was overdue for a refresher.

A: Yes.

Q: Did you flag this for anyone?

A: I flagged it in September. And October. And again in January.

Q: To whom?

A: My regional manager, Dennis Kowalski.

Q: What response did you receive?

A: The first time, he said he'd get it on the schedule. The second time, he said budgets were tight and we'd have to wait until Q1. The third time, he didn't respond at all.

Q: He didn't respond.

A: No.

Q: Did you escalate beyond Mr. Kowalski?

A: I did, once. I called the corporate safety line.

Q: And?

A: And they transferred me to Mr. Kowalski's voicemail.

Q: I see. Let me ask you this, Ms. Ferraro—after January, did you continue to flag the training gap?

A: No. I figured I'd said what I could say.

---

topic: A warehouse supervisor is deposed about safety protocols that were allegedly ignored
text:
Q: Let's talk about the rack inspection schedule, Mr. Tran. How often were the storage racks supposed to be inspected for damage?

A: Weekly.

Q: Weekly. And were they?

A: Sometimes.

Q: Sometimes meaning what—half the time? Less?

A: I couldn't give you a percentage.

Q: Could you give me a general sense?

A: When we had the staff, we did them. When we didn't, we didn't.

Q: Fair enough. Let me try this differently. In the month before the collapse—October—how many rack inspections were completed?

A: I believe one.

Q: One inspection in four weeks.

A: Correct.

Q: Mr. Tran, I've been doing this for a long time. I've taken a lot of depositions in cases like this. The answers are usually the same. Short-staffed, behind schedule, no time. So let me just ask you directly: did you know those racks were damaged before they collapsed?

A: Yes.

Q: You knew.

A: I knew the second rack from the east wall had a bent upright. I put in a work order.

Q: When?

A: September 30th.

Q: Was it repaired?

A: No.

Q: Did you restrict use of that rack?

A: I tried. I put up tape. Someone took it down because they needed the space.

Q: Who took it down?

A: I don't know. Could have been anyone. We were storing pallets wherever we could find room.

Q: So you knew, you reported it, nothing happened, and you moved on.

A: I moved on. Yeah.

---

topic: A warehouse supervisor is deposed about safety protocols that were allegedly ignored
text:
Q: Mr. Okonkwo, were you present for the safety committee meeting on March 3rd?

A: I was.

Q: Can you describe what was discussed?

A: The usual. Incident reports from the previous month. Any open hazards. Training updates.

Q: Were the loading dock conditions discussed at that meeting?

A: They were.

Q: What specifically was said?

A: I raised concerns about the dock plates. Several of them were warped. One had a crack.

Q: How did the committee respond?

A: They added it to the action items list.

Q: Was any timeline set for repairs?

A: No.

Q: Was a budget allocated?

A: Not that I'm aware of.

Q: Mr. Okonkwo, how many times had you raised concerns about the dock plates prior to March 3rd?

A: At least three times. Maybe four.

Q: Over what period?

A: About a year and a half.

Q: Let me make sure I understand. You raised the same concern four times over eighteen months, and it remained on the action items list.

A: That's how it worked.

Q: That's how it worked.

A: You raise something, it goes on the list, the list gets reviewed, nothing gets funded, you raise it again next quarter. Eventually you stop expecting anything different.

Q: Did you stop raising it?

A: No. I kept raising it. I just stopped thinking it would matter.

---

topic: A warehouse supervisor is deposed about safety protocols that were allegedly ignored
text:
Q: Ms. Chen, I want to understand the chain of communication when a safety hazard was identified. Walk me through it.

A: Floor worker reports it to the shift lead. Shift lead reports it to me. I log it in the system and notify maintenance.

Q: And then?

A: And then maintenance either fixes it or they don't, depending on whether they have the parts and the time.

Q: What if it's not fixed?

A: It stays in the system as open.

Q: For how long?

A: As long as it takes. Some things sit open for months.

Q: Were you comfortable with that?

A: Comfortable? No. But I wasn't the one who decided what got fixed and what didn't.

Q: Who decided?

A: Maintenance had their priorities. Management had their budget. I just logged the tickets.

Q: On February 12th, a ticket was logged for a malfunctioning emergency stop on conveyor line three. Do you remember that?

A: I remember.

Q: That ticket was still open on March 8th when Mr. Reyes was injured.

A: I know.

Q: Did you follow up on it?

A: I followed up twice. The first time, I was told the part was on order. The second time, I was told they were waiting on approval for overtime to install it.

Q: Did you escalate it?

A: Escalate it to who? Everyone already knew. It was in the system. It was in the weekly report. It was on the board in the break room with all the other open items.

Q: So everyone knew, and nothing happened.

A: Counselor, I've been doing this job for seven years. I've logged hundreds of tickets. Some get fixed fast. Some take weeks. Some never get fixed at all, and eventually the equipment gets replaced or the building gets sold or someone gets hurt and then suddenly there's money. That's just how it is. I don't know what else to tell you.

topic: An accountant is deposed about transactions they processed on behalf of a client
text:
Q: Mr. Feldman, let's turn to the wire transfers initiated in March of 2021. You processed those personally, correct?

A: I did.

Q: All of them?

A: All the ones that came through my desk, yes.

Q: How many wire transfers are we talking about?

A: Fourteen. Fourteen outgoing wires that month.

Q: And the recipient accounts for those wires—you had that information?

A: I had the account numbers and the bank names. That's what was provided to me.

Q: Did you verify the ownership of those accounts?

A: No.

Q: Is that typical for your practice, Mr. Feldman? Not verifying account ownership?

A: Look, counsel, I've been doing this for twenty-two years. The client provides the account information, I process the transfer. That's how it works. That's how it's always worked. If you want me to tell you I should have done something different, I suppose we can sit here all day and I can agree with you, but that won't change what the standard practice was.

Q: I'm just asking what you did.

A: And I'm telling you. I processed what was given to me.

Q: The aggregate amount of those fourteen transfers—what was it?

A: Two point three million, roughly.

Q: Did that amount strike you as unusual?

A: It struck me as a large month. That's all.

Q: But you processed them anyway.

A: Yes, counsel. I processed them anyway.

---

topic: An accountant is deposed about transactions they processed on behalf of a client
text:
Q: Ms. Okonkwo, I want to ask you about the Bellevue Holdings account specifically.

A: Alright.

Q: You were the primary accountant on that account from 2019 through 2022?

A: That's correct.

Q: During that time, did you ever flag any transactions for internal review?

A: I flagged two. One in late 2020, one in early 2021.

Q: What happened to those flags?

A: They were reviewed and cleared.

Q: By whom?

A: By the compliance committee.

Q: Did you agree with their determination?

A: I'm not sure my agreement was relevant to the process.

Q: I'm asking whether you agreed.

A: I... no. I didn't agree with the second one.

Q: The early 2021 flag?

A: Yes.

Q: What was your concern?

A: The funds were being routed through three intermediary accounts before reaching the final destination. It seemed unnecessary. It seemed designed to obscure.

Q: You used the word "designed." That suggests intent.

A: It suggests a pattern. What the intent was—that's not something I could determine sitting at my desk.

Q: But you had a suspicion.

A: Counsel, I had a lot of things. I had a suspicion, I had a mortgage, I had a compliance committee that told me the transaction was fine. So I moved on to the next file.

Q: Fair enough. Let's talk about that next file.

A: Of course.

---

topic: An accountant is deposed about transactions they processed on behalf of a client
text:
Q: The quarterly reports you prepared for Stanton Capital—those went directly to Mr. Harding?

A: Yes, they went to Gerald.

Q: Every quarter?

A: Every quarter for six years.

Q: Did Mr. Harding ever question the figures in those reports?

A: Not the figures, no.

Q: What did he question?

A: The presentation, sometimes. He wanted certain line items... grouped differently.

Q: Grouped differently how?

A: Combined. Consolidated. He didn't like too many individual entries.

Q: Did that concern you?

A: I understood what he was asking for.

Q: That's not what I asked.

A: I know.

Q: Ms. Petrov, did the requests to consolidate line items concern you?

A: What would you like me to say, counsel? Yes, it concerned me. It concerned me and I did it anyway because Gerald was the client and the client wanted the reports formatted a certain way. Is that the answer you need for your record?

Q: I need the truthful answer.

A: Then yes. It concerned me.

Q: Did you document your concerns anywhere?

A: No.

topic: An accountant is deposed about transactions they processed on behalf of a client
text:
Q: Let's move on to the expense reimbursements.

A: Fine.

Q: You seem tired, Mr. Chen. We can take a break if you need one.

A: I don't need a break. Let's just get through this.

Q: The expense reimbursements submitted by Mr. Lowell in fiscal year 2022—you approved those?

A: I approved the ones that had supporting documentation.

Q: How many lacked supporting documentation?

A: Maybe a third of them. Maybe more.

Q: And those?

A: Those I sent back.

Q: Sent back to whom?

A: To Mr. Lowell's assistant. Then to Mr. Lowell directly when she stopped responding.

Q: Who in management?

Q: And then you processed them?

A: Then I processed them.

A: Counsel, I'm going to tell you the same thing I told the internal auditors, the same thing I told the board's investigator, and the same thing I'll apparently tell everyone else who asks. Once Davis approved something, it was approved. That was the system. I didn't build the system. I just worked in it.

topic: An accountant is deposed about transactions they processed on behalf of a client
text:
Q: Mr. Abrams, the transfers to the offshore accounts—let's be specific about dates.

A: I have the dates in front of me if that helps.

Q: It would.

A: The first was June 3rd, 2020. Then June 17th. Then there was a gap until August.

Q: Why the gap?

A: I don't know why the gap. I wasn't privy to the client's reasoning.

Q: Did you ask?

A: I might have. I don't recall.

Q: You don't recall whether you asked your client why there was a two-month pause in offshore transfers?

A: Counsel, there were forty-seven clients in my portfolio that year. I processed thousands of transactions. I'm doing my best to help you here, but I can't manufacture memories I don't have.

Q: Fair enough. After August, how frequently did the transfers resume?

A: Monthly. Sometimes twice monthly.

Q: Through when?

A: Through the end of my engagement. March 2022.

Q: When you were terminated.

A: When my services were no longer required, yes.

Q: Is there a difference?

A: Probably not. Not one that matters now.

Q: During those monthly transfers, did you ever contact the receiving banks directly?

A: No.

Q: Was there a reason?

A: The reason is that no one asked me to, and I had learned by then that questions I asked on my own initiative tended not to be appreciated.

Q: Appreciated by whom?

A: By anyone, counsel. By anyone at all.

topic: A witness is questioned about events at a party where an assault allegedly occurred
text:
Q: Mr. Delgado, you were present at the residence on Maple Court on the evening of March 15th, correct?

A: I was at a party that night, yes. I don't know the street name.

Q: But you were inside the house where the party took place?

A: At various points, sure.

Q: At various points. Were you inside the house at approximately 11:30 p.m.?

A: I didn't have a stopwatch on me.

Q: I'm asking for your best estimate.

A: I was probably inside around that time. I went in and out. People do that at parties.

Q: When you were inside, did you observe any physical altercation?

A: Define "physical altercation."

Q: Did you see anyone hit, push, grab, or strike another person?

A: I saw people bumping into each other. It was crowded. People were drinking.

Q: That's not what I asked. Did you see one person deliberately strike another?

A: I saw a lot of things that night. I'm not sure what you want me to say was "deliberate." I'm not a mind reader.

Q: Mr. Delgado, did you see the defendant make contact with Mr. Warren's face?

A: I saw them near each other at one point.

Q: Near each other. How near?

A: Close enough to have a conversation. Or an argument. Depending on your interpretation.

Q: Did you see a fist connect with Mr. Warren's jaw?

A: I saw movement. Fast movement. I wasn't staring at them the whole time. You're asking me to describe something that happened in a second, in a dark room, while I was three drinks in.

Q: So your testimony is that you can't say whether you saw a punch thrown?

A: My testimony is that I'm trying to be accurate instead of telling you what you obviously want to hear.

---

topic: A witness is questioned about events at a party where an assault allegedly occurred
text:
Q: Ms. Okonkwo, how long have you known the plaintiff, Jessica Trammel?

A: We've been friends since freshman year of college. About seven years now.

Q: Close friends?

A: Yes.

Q: And you attended this party at her invitation?

A: That's right.

Q: Now, you gave a statement to police three days after the party. Do you recall that?

A: I do.

Q: In that statement, you said—and I'm quoting—"I didn't see how it started."

A: That's correct.

Q: But in your declaration filed with this court, you state that you witnessed Mr. Booth grab Ms. Trammel by the arm "without any provocation." Those were your words. "Without any provocation."

A: Yes.

Q: How did you determine there was no provocation if you didn't see how it started?

A: I saw enough to know she didn't do anything to deserve being grabbed like that.

Q: That's not the same thing, is it, Ms. Okonkwo? Seeing "enough" and seeing "how it started"?

A: I saw her standing there talking, and then I saw him grab her. What more do you need?

Q: I need to understand the discrepancy. Were you watching them continuously before the grab, or weren't you?

A: I was watching them. Not every single second. But enough.

Q: Enough. You keep using that word. Let me ask it differently: is it possible something happened in the seconds you weren't watching?

A: Anything is "possible." But I know Jess. She didn't do anything.

Q: You know Jess. So this is based on your assessment of her character, not on what you actually observed?

A: It's based on both. I don't see why that's so hard to understand.

---

topic: A witness is questioned about events at a party where an assault allegedly occurred
text:
Q: You've testified you were standing near the kitchen doorway. About how far from Mr. Payne and Ms. Richter?

A: Maybe fifteen feet. Could've been a little more.

Q: And the music—was it loud?

A: It was a party. Yes, it was loud.

Q: Loud enough that you'd have to shout to be heard?

A: Probably, yeah.

Q: Yet you testified earlier that you heard Mr. Payne say, quote, "You're going to regret this." Is that still your testimony?

A: That's what I heard.

Q: From fifteen feet away. Over loud music.

A: There was a break in the song. One of those moments where everything gets quiet for a second. That's when I heard it.

Q: A convenient break in the music.

A: I'm sorry, is that a question?

Q: Let me rephrase. Are you certain the break in the music coincided exactly with Mr. Payne's alleged statement?

A: I'm certain of what I heard.

Q: What song was playing?

A: I don't remember.

Q: But you remember this precise gap in the music?

A: I remember it because of what I heard during it. That's how memory works. You remember the important parts.

Q: The important parts. Did anyone else react to this statement?

A: I don't know what other people heard.

Q: Did you see anyone else turn toward Mr. Payne? Look alarmed? Anything?

A: I wasn't watching everyone else. I was watching him.

Q: You were watching him specifically. Why?

A: Because something about the way he was standing made me pay attention. I can't explain it better than that.

---

topic: A witness is questioned about events at a party where an assault allegedly occurred
text:
Q: You stated earlier that you observed the defendant throw a bottle.

A: I observed him throw something. I believe it was a bottle.

Q: You believe.

A: It was dark, it happened fast. It looked like a bottle. A beer bottle, brown glass.

Q: Did you see where this bottle—or this object—landed?

A: It went toward the group standing by the back door.

Q: Toward them. Did it hit anyone?

A: I think it hit someone. There was a reaction.

Q: A reaction. What kind of reaction?

A: Someone yelled. The group scattered.

Q: Did you see anyone injured?

A: I saw someone holding their head afterward.

Q: Who?

A: I didn't know him. Some guy in a red shirt.

Q: The plaintiff is Mr. Nathaniel Torres. Do you know what he was wearing that night?

A: I have no idea.

Q: So you can't say whether the person holding their head was Mr. Torres?

A: I can't say for certain, no.

Q: Let me make sure I understand. You saw the defendant throw something that may have been a bottle, toward a group, and afterward someone you can't identify was holding their head. Is that accurate?

A: When you put it that way, it sounds like I didn't see anything. I know what I saw. I just can't fill in every detail you're asking for.

Q: I'm not asking you to fill in details, Mr. Yee. I'm asking you to tell me only what you actually observed.

A: And I am.

---

topic: A witness is questioned about events at a party where an assault allegedly occurred
text:
Q: Ms. Ashford, you've known the defendant for approximately two years?

A: About that, yes.

Q: And in that time, have you ever seen him become violent?

A: Never. Ryan isn't a violent person.

Q: He isn't a violent person. You're certain of that?

A: I've spent a lot of time with him. I've never seen him hurt anyone.

Q: Have you seen him angry?

A: Everyone gets angry sometimes.

Q: That's not an answer.

A: Yes. I've seen him frustrated, upset. Like anyone.

Q: How does he behave when he's upset? Does he raise his voice?

A: Sometimes, maybe. He's not a yeller.

Q: Does he throw things? Hit walls? Anything like that?

A: No.

Q: Never?

A: I've never seen that. No.

A: We were seeing each other, yes.

Q: I'll rephrase. Were you and the defendant in a committed romantic relationship in March of this year?

A: We were dating. I don't know what you mean by "committed."

A: I suppose, yes.

Q: And you're here today to testify that in two years, you've never seen any violent behavior from him whatsoever.

Q: I'm simply making sure you understand. Thank you. No further questions on this line.

topic: A neighbor is questioned about noise complaints and a confrontation they witnessed
text:
Q: Good morning, Mr. Holloway. I understand you've lived on Crescent Drive for quite some time now?

A: Oh, yes, going on eighteen years this October. Watched the whole neighborhood change, really. The Hendersons built that addition, the Pak family put in those beautiful rose bushes—you can probably tell I pay attention to these things.

Q: It sounds like you know your neighbors well.

A: I try to. I think that matters, don't you? Knowing the people around you. My wife and I, we make a point of it. Bring cookies when someone new moves in, that sort of thing.

Q: That's lovely. Now, regarding the evening of March 14th—

A: The night of all the commotion. Yes, I remember it clearly.

Q: Can you tell me what you first noticed that evening?

A: Well, I was out on my porch—I like to sit out there after dinner when the weather's nice, just to unwind. And I heard voices from the Brennan property. Not unusual in itself, people talk outside, but these voices had an edge to them, if you understand what I mean.

Q: When you say "an edge," could you describe that more specifically?

A: Raised, tense. Like people who are trying not to shout but aren't quite managing it. I've been married thirty-two years, I know what that sounds like.

Q: Did you recognize the voices?

A: Tom Brennan's, certainly. I'd know his voice anywhere. The other one took me a moment, but it was the young man from 412—I believe his name is Reeves? He's newer to the street, maybe two years now.

Q: And what did you do when you heard this exchange?

A: Honestly? I stayed right where I was. Not to eavesdrop, mind you, but I was concerned. Tom's getting older—he's seventy-four, I think—and I wanted to make sure things didn't escalate.

Q: That was considerate of you.

A: Well, you look out for people. That's what neighbors do.

Q: Did you hear any specific words exchanged between Mr. Brennan and Mr. Reeves?

A: Some. Mr. Reeves was saying something about his rights, his property, that sort of language. And Tom—Tom was trying to explain about the noise, about how it carries at night. He wasn't being unreasonable, I'll say that much. He was trying to be decent about it.

Q: And how did the conversation end?

A: Mr. Reeves walked off. Not storming, exactly, but not happy either. Tom stood there for a minute, then went inside. I almost went over to check on him, but I thought I'd give him his privacy. Called him the next morning instead. That seemed like the right thing to do.

topic: A neighbor is questioned about noise complaints and a confrontation they witnessed
text:
Q: Ms. Yuen, let's talk about your relationship with the Delgado family.

A: We're friendly. Not close friends, but we wave, we chat when we're both getting the mail. Normal neighbor things.

Q: Would you say you've had positive interactions with them?

A: Mostly, yes. Rosa—Mrs. Delgado—she helped me once when my car wouldn't start. Came right over with jumper cables without me even asking. That's the kind of person she is.

Q: That's helpful context. Now, on the night in question, June 8th, where were you?

A: In my kitchen. The window looks out toward their backyard.

Q: And what drew your attention outside?

A: The music, initially. They were having some kind of gathering—birthday, I think, for one of the kids. Perfectly fine, people are allowed to celebrate. But it had gotten quite loud by about ten o'clock.

Q: Did that bother you?

A: A little, honestly. But I wasn't going to make a fuss. One night of noise isn't the end of the world.

Q: What happened next?

A: I saw Mr. Patterson from across the street walk over to their yard. I couldn't hear what was said at first, but I could tell from his body language he was upset.

Q: How could you tell?

A: Arms crossed, leaning forward. You know how people stand when they're ready for a fight? It was like that.

Q: And how did the Delgados respond?

A: Rosa came out to talk to him. She had her hands up, palms out—trying to calm things down, I think. She's good like that, Rosa. Patient.

Q: Did Mr. Patterson's demeanor change?

A: Not really. He was pointing at their speakers, gesturing a lot. Rosa kept nodding, kept her voice low—I could tell even though I couldn't hear the words.

Q: Did anyone else get involved?

A: Mr. Delgado came out after a few minutes. He was calmer than I expected, actually. Put his hand on Rosa's shoulder, said something to Patterson. And then—this surprised me—he shook Patterson's hand.

Q: They shook hands?

A: They did. And the music went down after that. I thought that was the end of it, honestly. I thought they'd worked it out like adults.

topic: A neighbor is questioned about noise complaints and a confrontation they witnessed
text:
Q: State your name for the record.

A: David Chen.

Q: Mr. Chen, how long have you resided at 7845 Birchwood Lane?

A: Six years.

Q: And you're familiar with the ongoing disputes regarding noise in your neighborhood?

A: I'm aware of them.

Q: Could you be more specific?

A: There have been complaints. Several residents have had issues with noise late at night. I've heard about it.

Q: Have you personally witnessed any confrontations related to these complaints?

A: Define confrontation.

Q: Any direct interaction between neighbors regarding noise that you observed.

A: I saw one conversation. I don't know if I'd call it a confrontation.

Q: Tell me about that conversation.

A: It was between Mrs. Okonkwo and the tenant at 7852. I was walking my dog. They were on the sidewalk.

Q: Take your time. What did you observe?

A: Mrs. Okonkwo—she's a retired teacher, very dignified woman—she was explaining something. Her voice was steady, not raised. She had her hands clasped in front of her, like she was being very deliberate about staying composed.

Q: And the tenant?

A: He seemed agitated at first. Shifting his weight, looking away. But Mrs. Okonkwo just kept talking in that calm way she has, and after a minute or two, he sort of... settled.

Q: Settled?

A: Stopped fidgeting. Started actually listening, I think. She has that effect on people.

Q: Did you hear what she said to him?

A: Not all of it. Something about understanding that he was young, that she remembered being young herself. That she wasn't trying to ruin his life, she just needed to sleep.

Q: How did the conversation end?

A: He apologized. Actually apologized. I remember being surprised by that—he hadn't seemed like the apologizing type when it started. But Mrs. Okonkwo thanked him, touched his arm for just a second, and walked back to her house. I thought it was handled beautifully, actually.

Q: I appreciate you sharing that, Mr. Chen.

A: She deserves the credit, not me.

topic: A neighbor is questioned about noise complaints and a confrontation they witnessed
text:
Q: You've stated you were present during the incident on September 3rd, correct?

A: Yes.

Q: Walk me through what you saw.

A: I was coming home from work, maybe seven-thirty. I saw Janet—Mrs. Moreau—standing in her driveway, and the young man who lives in the rental, I don't know his name, was walking toward her.

Q: What was his demeanor?

A: He looked frustrated. Tense. His hands were in his pockets, but his shoulders were up around his ears, you know?

Q: What happened when he reached Mrs. Moreau?

A: He started talking. Fast, clipped. Something about being harassed, about how he had a right to live his life.

Q: And Mrs. Moreau?

A: She just stood there and let him talk. Didn't interrupt, didn't cross her arms or look defensive. Just... listened.

Q: For how long?

A: A minute, maybe two. He ran out of steam eventually, the way people do when no one's fighting back.

Q: Then what?

A: Janet said something like, "I hear you. I do." And she meant it—you could tell she meant it. She wasn't just saying words.

Q: How could you tell she meant it?

A: Her voice, I suppose. It was soft, unhurried. And she looked right at him, not past him or through him. Like he was a person, not a problem.

Q: What was his response?

A: He seemed thrown, honestly. Like he'd come ready for a battle and found something else instead. He stood there for a moment, and then he said, "Okay. Okay, maybe we can figure this out."

Q: Did they continue talking?

A: They did. Janet invited him onto her porch, offered him iced tea. I went inside at that point—felt like I should give them privacy.

Q: That was thoughtful.

A: Janet's been a good neighbor to me over the years. I didn't want to complicate things for her.

topic: A neighbor is questioned about noise complaints and a confrontation they witnessed
text:
Q: Let's return to the confrontation you witnessed on April 22nd. You testified earlier that you heard yelling.

A: I did.

Q: But then the situation changed. Can you describe that shift?

A: The Weston boy came outside. Must be seventeen, eighteen now. He'd been friends with Mr. Huang's son when they were younger—they used to ride bikes together, I remember.

Q: What did the Weston boy do?

A: He walked right into the middle of it. His father was red in the face, pointing at Mr. Huang, really going at him. And the kid just said, "Dad. Dad, come on."

Q: How did Mr. Weston senior respond?

A: He stopped mid-sentence. The boy put his hand on his father's arm—not pulling, just... there. And he said, "Mr. Huang used to fix my bike chain, remember? When I was eight?"

Q: What happened then?

A: It was like the air went out of the whole thing. Mr. Weston's shoulders dropped. He looked at Mr. Huang, really looked at him, and Mr. Huang nodded. Just once.

Q: Did anyone speak?

A: Mr. Weston said, "I'm sorry, Henry. I'm tired. The noise, it's been keeping me up, and I took it out on you."

Q: And Mr. Huang?

A: He said he understood. Said he'd make sure the music stopped at ten on weeknights. Then he asked about the boy—Marcus, I think his name is—asked if he was still playing baseball.

Q: They discussed baseball?

A: For several minutes, actually. Standing right there in the yard where they'd been shouting at each other. Mr. Weston even laughed at one point. It was something to see, honestly.

Q: How did you feel, witnessing that?

A: Hopeful, I suppose. People can surprise you, can't they? Even when you think things are too far gone.

Q: They can indeed. Thank you, Ms. Reilly.

A: Of course. I hope it helps.

topic: A tenant is questioned about property damage they reported to their landlord
text:
Q: Mr. Patterson, you submitted a maintenance request on March 15th regarding water damage in your unit, correct?

A: If that's what the form says.

Q: I'm asking what you recall.

A: I filled out a lot of forms. Sure, March 15th sounds right.

Q: Can you describe the water damage you observed?

A: There was water. On the ceiling. It was brown.

Q: How large was the affected area?

A: I don't know. Size of a dinner plate, maybe. I didn't measure it.

Q: Did you take any photographs?

A: Probably.

Q: Do you still have those photographs?

A: Somewhere on my phone, I guess.

Q: You guess?

A: I have a lot of pictures on my phone. I'm not going to scroll through three years of photos to tell you definitively yes or no right now.

Q: Did the water damage affect any of your personal property?

A: Not really.

Q: What do you mean by "not really"?

A: I mean I moved my stuff before it got ruined. So no.

Q: How long after you noticed the damage did you submit the maintenance request?

A: A few days. A week. Something like that. It wasn't urgent to me.

Q: Why wasn't it urgent?

A: It was a stain on the ceiling. The building's old. Things happen.

topic: A tenant is questioned about property damage they reported to their landlord
text:
Q: Ms. Vance, let's talk about the incident you reported on or around January 8th. What was the nature of the damage?

A: The bathroom floor had buckled. The linoleum was coming up near the toilet.

Q: And when did you first notice this?

A: Maybe a week before I reported it. Maybe a little longer. I wasn't keeping a calendar.

A: No.

Q: That's fine. What did the note say, to the best of your recollection?

A: Something like "bathroom floor is messed up, please fix." I wasn't writing a novel.

Q: Did anyone come to inspect the damage?

A: Eventually. Someone came by. Don't remember exactly when.

topic: A tenant is questioned about property damage they reported to their landlord
text:
Q: Mr. Diaz, I want to discuss the complaint you filed with management on September 3rd. You reported a broken window, is that right?

Q: Fair enough. Was the crack on the interior or exterior of the glass?

A: Exterior, I think. Does it matter?

Q: I'm just trying to establish the facts. Did you report this the same day you discovered it?

topic: A tenant is questioned about property damage they reported to their landlord
text:
Q: Let's turn to the mold issue you reported in October. When did you first become aware of mold in the unit?

topic: A tenant is questioned about property damage they reported to their landlord
text:
Q: Ms. Okonkwo, in your complaint dated June 22nd, you referenced damage to the kitchen cabinetry. Can you describe that damage?

topic: A paramedic is questioned about the response time and treatment at an accident scene
text:
Q: Please state your name and occupation for the record.

A: Michael Reeves. I've been a paramedic with County EMS for eleven years now.

Q: Mr. Reeves, I want to take you back to the evening of March 14th. You responded to a motor vehicle accident on Route 9, is that correct?

A: Yes, ma'am. That call—I remember it clearly.

Q: What time did dispatch contact your unit?

A: The call came in at 7:42 p.m. I know because I looked at the clock when we got the tone. My partner and I had just finished restocking from a previous run.

Q: And what time did you arrive on scene?

A: 7:58 p.m. Sixteen minutes. I wish it had been faster, but we were coming from the south station, and there was construction on Miller Road that forced us to detour.

Q: Sixteen minutes. Is that within your department's standard response time?

A: For that distance, yes, technically it falls within guidelines. But I want to be clear—when someone's hurt, guidelines don't mean much to them. Or to us, honestly. Every minute out there, you're thinking about whoever's waiting.

Q: When you arrived, can you describe what you observed?

A: Two vehicles. A sedan and a pickup truck. The sedan had significant front-end damage, driver's side. There was a young woman—she couldn't have been more than twenty—pinned behind the steering wheel. She was conscious. Scared. Calling out for her mother.

Q: What did you do first?

A: I went straight to her. Told her my name. Told her we were going to take care of her. Sometimes that's the most important thing you can do in those first moments—let them know they're not alone anymore.

Q: And medically? What was your initial assessment?

A: She had obvious trauma to her lower extremities. Possible internal injuries. We couldn't extricate her immediately—fire rescue was still en route with the jaws. So I stayed with her, monitored her vitals, kept her talking. Her name was Jessica. She told me she was a nursing student. She wanted to do what I do someday.

Q: I understand this is difficult, Mr. Reeves. Take your time if you need it.

A: Thank you. I'm alright. She deserves to have her story told properly.

topic: A paramedic is questioned about the response time and treatment at an accident scene
text:
Q: Paramedic Chen, how long have you been certified as an EMT-P?

A: Six years this coming September.

Q: On July 8th of last year, you responded to a workplace accident at Brennan Manufacturing, correct?

A: Correct.

Q: What was the nature of the emergency as communicated by dispatch?

A: Industrial accident. Male worker, possible crush injury. That's all we had initially.

Q: Your ambulance arrived at 2:47 p.m. according to the log. Does that sound right?

A: If that's what the log says, then yes.

Q: The call came in at 2:31 p.m. That's a sixteen-minute response time.

A: I'm aware.

Q: Is there a reason it took sixteen minutes to travel four miles?

A: There's always a reason. That day, we were returning from a transfer to Regional Medical when the call came in. We weren't at the station. We were seven miles out, not four, and we had to navigate through downtown during shift change at the automotive plant.

Q: The plaintiff's family believes a faster response could have prevented the amputation. What would you say to that?

A: I would say—and I mean this sincerely—that I think about Mr. Brennan often. I think about whether there was a different route, whether I could have pushed harder through that traffic. I've driven that path a hundred times in my head since then.

Q: That's not what I asked. I asked whether a faster response would have changed the outcome.

A: And I'm telling you that I don't have the luxury of certainty that you seem to want from me. What I know is that we did everything we could from the moment we arrived. His arm was already compromised. The tourniquet his coworker applied probably saved his life. I held that man's hand and told him he was going to see his kids again, and he did. He's alive.

Q: Did you follow proper protocol for a crush injury?

A: Yes. Every step. I can walk you through each one if you'd like, because I've gone over it a thousand times myself.

topic: A paramedic is questioned about the response time and treatment at an accident scene
text:
Q: Let's discuss the triage decisions you made that night. There were multiple victims, correct?

A: Three total. Two in the SUV, one in the other vehicle.

Q: Walk me through how you prioritized.

A: The driver of the SUV was unconscious, significant head trauma, GCS of 6. The passenger—a child, maybe eight years old—was alert but had a deformed left arm and was in obvious pain. The other driver was ambulatory, complaining of neck pain, but stable.

Q: You chose to treat the child before the unconscious adult?

A: My partner took the adult. I took the child.

Q: Why you specifically for the child?

A: Because she was alone and terrified, and I have a daughter about her age. I thought—I knew I could keep her calm while also assessing her injuries. Sometimes the medical and the human aren't separate things.

Q: Some might argue the unconscious patient required more urgent intervention.

A: He did require urgent intervention. That's why my partner, who has more trauma experience than I do, was with him immediately. We work as a team. We don't abandon one patient for another; we allocate resources.

Q: The little girl—what was her condition when you reached her?

A: She was crying, asking where her daddy was. Her left forearm had an obvious fracture—I could see the displacement through the skin. She was holding it against her chest, trying to protect it.

Q: What did you do?

A: I got down to her eye level. I told her my name was Sarah and that I was there to help her. I asked if she had a favorite animal. She said dogs. So I told her about my dog, Chester, while I splinted her arm. She stopped crying somewhere around when I described how he steals socks from the laundry.

Q: Is that standard protocol? Discussing your personal pet during treatment?

A: Protocol says to keep the patient calm and minimize psychological trauma. I'd say that's exactly what I did.

Q: Fair enough. What happened to the father—the unconscious driver?

A: He was transported first. He made it to surgery. I checked on him two days later. He was asking about his daughter.

topic: A paramedic is questioned about the response time and treatment at an accident scene
text:
Q: Paramedic Williams, you've reviewed the treatment log from October 3rd?

A: I have.

Q: The log indicates you administered epinephrine at 4:23 p.m. Is that accurate?

A: Yes, that's accurate.

Q: The patient's wife has stated that she told you about her husband's heart condition before you administered the epinephrine. Do you recall that conversation?

A: I recall Mrs. Patterson being present, yes. She was understandably frantic. Her husband wasn't breathing.

Q: Did she tell you about his heart condition or didn't she?

A: She may have. I want to be honest with you—when you have a patient in anaphylaxis, not breathing, there's a tremendous amount of information coming at you all at once. Family members are speaking, sometimes shouting. You're assessing, you're treating.

Q: So you don't remember.

A: I remember that my patient was dying in front of me. I remember that without epinephrine, he had minutes at best. I remember making the decision that giving him a chance at cardiac complications was better than watching him suffocate.

Q: The family is struggling with what happened, Mr. Williams. They're looking for answers.

A: I know. And I wish I had better ones for them. I wish I could tell them something that would make this easier. I've been doing this job for fifteen years, and I still don't have the words for when someone loses a person they love.

Q: Did you follow up with the family after Mr. Patterson's death?

A: I attended the funeral. I don't know if the family saw me—I stayed in the back. But I needed to be there.

Q: Why?

A: Because he mattered. They all matter. Every single one.

Q: Let's move on to the documentation. Can you explain why there's a gap in the timestamps between 4:23 and 4:31?

A: During that time, I was performing CPR. I wasn't looking at my watch. I was trying to bring him back.

topic: A paramedic is questioned about the response time and treatment at an accident scene
text:
Q: I'd like to understand the sequence of events after you arrived at the accident scene. Your unit was the second ambulance on site?

A: That's right. Unit 7 arrived approximately four minutes before us.

Q: And you took over care of which patient?

A: The rear passenger of the vehicle. A teenager. Seventeen years old.

Q: What was his condition?

A: He'd been ejected partially through the rear window. Severe lacerations to his back and shoulders. He was conscious but fading in and out.

Q: Conscious but fading. Can you elaborate?

A: He'd respond when I spoke to him directly, but his eyes would drift. He was losing blood. He kept saying one thing, over and over.

Q: What was that?

A: "Tell my mom I'm sorry." He said it maybe six or seven times while I was working on him.

Q: What were you doing during this time?

A: Packing the wounds, trying to control the bleeding. Establishing an IV line. And talking to him—telling him he could tell her himself, that we were going to get him to the hospital, that he needed to stay with me.

Q: Did you believe that? That he would make it?

A: I believed that as long as he was still breathing, he had a chance. And I believed that what I said to him mattered, whether he made it or not. No one should feel alone in those moments.

Q: The hospital records indicate he arrived in critical condition but survived. Were you aware of that?

A: I was. His mother actually found me a few months later. She came to the station.

Q: What did she say?

A: She said her son told her about the paramedic who kept talking to him, who wouldn't let him give up. She hugged me and she cried and she thanked me. I think about that when the hard days come. I think about Daniel.

Q: You remember his name.

A: I remember all of them.

topic: A witness is questioned about a conversation they overheard in a company hallway
text:
Q: Mr. Delano, I want to direct your attention to March 14th of this year. Were you present at the Westbrook Industries corporate office that day?

A: I was, yes.

Q: And at some point during that day, did you find yourself in the third-floor hallway near the executive conference room?

A: I—yes. I was in that hallway. I don't know if it was near the conference room specifically. There are several rooms along that corridor.

Q: But you were on the third floor?

A: Yes.

Q: And while you were there, did you overhear a conversation between two individuals?

A: I heard people talking, yes.

Q: Who was speaking?

A: I believe it was Mr. Hartwell and... I want to say it was someone from legal? A woman's voice. I didn't see her face.

Q: You didn't see her face. But you heard her voice clearly enough to identify her department?

A: No, I—that's not what I meant. I'm saying she sounded like she might have been discussing legal matters. That's why I assumed. I don't actually know who she was.

Q: What legal matters?

A: Something about a filing deadline? Or maybe it was a filing cabinet. I honestly couldn't tell you which. The words were similar and I wasn't—I wasn't trying to listen.

Q: You weren't trying to listen, but you stopped in the hallway?

A: I had stopped to check my phone. I was early for a meeting.

Q: How long did you stand there?

A: A minute? Maybe two? I genuinely don't know. I wasn't timing myself.

Q: In that minute or two, what did you hear Mr. Hartwell say?

A: He said something like "that's not how we're going to handle it" or "that's not how this works." One of those. Possibly neither. I'm doing my best here.

Q: Which is it, Mr. Delano? "That's not how we're going to handle it" or "that's not how this works"?

A: I don't know. I've told you what I remember. I can't manufacture certainty I don't have.

---

topic: A witness is questioned about a conversation they overheard in a company hallway
text:
Q: You've testified that you were walking toward the elevator bank on the second floor. Is that correct?

A: That's correct.

Q: And as you approached, you heard voices coming from around the corner?

A: Yes.

Q: Whose voices?

A: Tom Reiger was one of them. The other I didn't recognize.

A: Male.

Q: Off in what way?

A: I don't know what you mean.

Q: You said the shipment was "off." Off how? Missing items? Wrong items? Damaged?

A: I don't—I said I think they were discussing something being off. I didn't say I understood the specifics. You're asking me to characterize a conversation I caught maybe ten seconds of.

Q: I'm asking what you heard.

A: And I'm telling you. I heard Tom say something about numbers not matching. The other man said something I couldn't make out. Then Tom said—and I remember this part—"just make it work."

Q: "Just make it work."

A: Yes.

A: I have no idea what it meant. I'm telling you the words.

Q: Did you think it was unusual?

A: I didn't think anything. I was walking to an elevator. I pressed the button and I left.

Q: You didn't stop to listen further?

A: Why would I?

Q: I'm asking whether you did.

A: No. I did not.

---

topic: A witness is questioned about a conversation they overheard in a company hallway
text:
Q: Ms. Thornton, let me ask you about the afternoon of June 3rd.

A: Okay.

Q: You were on the fourth floor that afternoon?

A: I was.

Q: Near the break room?

A: At some point, yes. I got coffee.

Q: While you were getting coffee, did you hear a conversation taking place nearby?

Q: I'm not asking about the birthday thing. I'm asking—let me rephrase. Did you hear a conversation between Sandra Okonkwo and anyone else that afternoon?

Q: Let's say between two and four p.m.

A: Then... possibly? Sandra was there at some point. Whether I heard her having a conversation specifically—I mean, she talks to people. She's a friendly person.

Q: Do you remember her talking to David Marsh?

A: David Marsh.

Q: Yes.

A: I don't—wait, is he the one from facilities? Older gentleman?

A: No. Not that I recall.
