---

topic: A witness is questioned about a conversation they overheard in a company hallway
text:
Q: Mr. Yee, I want to ask you about something you mentioned in your previous testimony—a conversation you overheard outside the HR office on October 11th.

A: Yes.

Q: You said you heard two people talking. Who were they?

A: I said I believed it was Karen Moss and someone else. I couldn't identify the second person.

Q: Could you tell if the second person was male or female?

A: Female. I think.

Q: You think.

A: It sounded like a woman's voice. A lower register, but feminine. I could be wrong.

Q: And what were they saying?

A: Karen was saying something about—hold on. I want to be precise. She was saying something about "the complaint" and how it needed to be "handled internally."

Q: The complaint.

A: Yes.

Q: Did she identify what complaint?

A: No.

Q: Did the other woman respond?

A: She said—I think she said "that's not what I was told."

Q: Not what she was told by whom?

A: I don't know. Karen said something after that but I couldn't hear it. They'd moved further down the hall or lowered their voices or—I don't know. It got quieter.

Q: So you didn't hear the rest of the conversation?

A: I heard bits. "Documentation." I heard that word. And "timeline."

Q: In what context?

A: I don't—you're asking me to reconstruct something I caught fragments of. I'm telling you the words I heard. I can't give you context I don't have.

Q: Fair enough. After this conversation, did you see Karen Moss exit the hallway?

A: I saw her walk past me toward the stairwell. We made eye contact. She smiled, like normal. Then she kept walking.

Q: Did she seem unusual in any way?

A: She seemed like Karen.

---

topic: A witness is questioned about a conversation they overheard in a company hallway
text:
Q: Let's go back to January 22nd. You were in the north wing hallway near Mr. Levinson's office, correct?

A: I was near there, yes.

Q: And you heard a conversation through the door?

A: The door was open partway. I wasn't pressing my ear to it.

Q: I didn't suggest you were. What did you hear?

A: I heard Mr. Levinson. He sounded—he was speaking loudly. Emphatically.

Q: What was he saying?

A: Something like, "This wasn't supposed to come out yet."

Q: What wasn't supposed to come out?

A: I have no idea.

Q: Did he say anything else?

A: He said, "Who authorized this?" or maybe "Who approved this?" Something like that.

Q: And who was he speaking to?

A: I couldn't see into the room fully. I saw the back of someone's head. Dark hair.

Q: Man or woman?

A: I couldn't tell from the back of a head.

Q: Could you hear this other person respond?

A: Barely. They spoke quietly. I heard Mr. Levinson say "this is exactly what I was worried about." Then someone closed the door.

Q: Someone closed the door.

A: Yes. From inside.

Q: Did Mr. Levinson close it?

A: I don't know who closed it. The door closed. That's what I observed.

Q: And what did you do then?

A: I kept walking. I was on my way to the copy room. I wasn't going to stand there after the door closed. That would have been—I just kept walking.

Q: Did you mention this conversation to anyone afterward?

A: I mentioned it to—actually, no. I don't think I told anyone. Not until this whole thing started.

topic: A pharmacist is deposed about a prescription that was filled with the wrong dosage
text:
Q: Dr. Hendricks, how long have you been a licensed pharmacist?

A: Seventeen years.

Q: And during those seventeen years, you've filled how many prescriptions, approximately?

A: I couldn't give you an exact number.

Q: A rough estimate.

A: Thousands. Tens of thousands. I don't keep a running tally.

Q: Fair enough. Now, on March 14th of this year, you were working at the Walden Road CVS location, correct?

A: Yes.

Q: And you personally filled a prescription for metoprolol for a patient named Gerald Thornton?

A: The system shows my initials on the verification, yes.

Q: So that's a yes?

A: I just said my initials are on the verification. That means I verified it.

Q: The prescription called for 25 milligrams. Is that your understanding?

A: That's what the prescriber ordered, according to the records I've reviewed.

Q: But Mr. Thornton received 100-milligram tablets. How did that happen?

A: If I knew exactly how it happened, we wouldn't be sitting here, would we?

Q: I'm asking for your professional opinion.

A: My professional opinion is that an error occurred somewhere in the process. I've acknowledged that. I've said it to your client's attorneys, I've said it in written statements, and I'm saying it again now.

Q: Do you take responsibility for that error?

A: I take responsibility for my role in the verification process. Whether that constitutes sole responsibility is a legal question, not a pharmaceutical one.

topic: A pharmacist is deposed about a prescription that was filled with the wrong dosage
text:
Q: Let's talk about the workflow in the pharmacy on the day in question.

A: All right.

Q: How many pharmacists were on duty that afternoon?

A: Two.

Q: And how many technicians?

A: I believe three.

Q: You believe, or you know?

A: The schedule would reflect the exact number. I'm telling you my recollection is three.

Q: Would it surprise you to learn the schedule shows only two technicians?

A: Then it was two. I'm not sure why you asked if you already had the answer.

Q: I'm trying to understand your memory of that day.

A: My memory is that we were busy and understaffed. Whether that's two technicians or three doesn't change the fundamental situation.

Q: Were you feeling rushed that day?

A: We're always rushed. That's the nature of retail pharmacy.

Q: That's not what I asked. On March 14th specifically—

A: I don't have a specific recollection of feeling more rushed than usual on that particular date, no. It was seven months ago. I've filled thousands of prescriptions since then.

Q: Do you think being rushed contributed to the error?

A: I think it's possible. I'm not going to speculate beyond that.

Q: I'm not asking you to speculate. I'm asking for your professional assessment.

A: And I've given it. It's possible. That's my assessment.

topic: A pharmacist is deposed about a prescription that was filled with the wrong dosage
text:
Q: Walk me through the standard verification process at your pharmacy.

A: The technician fills the prescription, places the medication in a bag with the label, and it comes to the pharmacist for verification. The pharmacist checks the medication against the label and the original prescription.

Q: Every time?

A: That's the protocol, yes.

Q: I didn't ask about the protocol. I asked whether it happens every time.

A: I can't speak to what happens when I'm not the verifying pharmacist.

Q: When you're the verifying pharmacist.

A: When I'm the verifying pharmacist, I follow the protocol.

Q: Without exception?

A: I'm human. I'm sure there have been moments in seventeen years where I've been less thorough than I should have been. Is that what you want me to say?

Q: I want you to tell me the truth.

A: I am telling you the truth. I follow the protocol. I followed the protocol on March 14th. An error still occurred. Those two facts can coexist.

Q: How do you explain that?

A: The tablets are the same color. The same shape. The same manufacturer. The difference is a small number stamped on one side. If the lighting is poor, if you're looking at it for three seconds in the middle of a twelve-hour shift—

Q: So you're saying you only looked at it for three seconds?

A: I'm saying that's a realistic timeframe for a verification check, yes. I'm not saying that's what happened on this specific occasion because, frankly, I don't remember this specific prescription out of the hundreds I filled that week.

topic: A pharmacist is deposed about a prescription that was filled with the wrong dosage
text:
Q: Dr. Whitmore, are you familiar with your pharmacy's error reporting system?

A: Yes.

Q: How does it work?

A: When an error is discovered, we fill out an incident report. It goes to the pharmacy manager and to corporate.

Q: Did you fill out an incident report for the Thornton prescription?

A: Yes, I did.

Q: When?

A: The day after we were notified of the error. I don't recall the exact date.

Q: The error was reported to your pharmacy on March 19th. Does that refresh your recollection?

A: Then it would have been March 20th.

Q: The incident report is dated March 23rd.

A: Okay.

Q: That's four days later.

A: I said I didn't recall the exact date.

Q: Is there a reason for the delay?

A: I don't remember. It might have been my day off. It might have been that I was dealing with other responsibilities. I completed the report when I completed it.

Q: The report states, and I'm quoting here, "Root cause undetermined." Did you write that?

A: If it's in my report, I wrote it.

Q: You couldn't determine how 100-milligram tablets ended up in a bottle labeled 25 milligrams?

A: That's correct. The stock bottles were properly labeled. The prescription was properly entered. Somewhere between those two points, the wrong tablets were selected. I cannot tell you by whom or exactly when.

Q: Isn't that your job to determine?

A: My job is to report what I know. I reported what I knew.

topic: A pharmacist is deposed about a prescription that was filled with the wrong dosage
text:
Q: I want to ask about the pharmacy's inventory system.

A: Go ahead.

Q: The 25-milligram and 100-milligram metoprolol—where are they stored relative to each other?

A: They're in the same section of the shelf. Alphabetical by drug name, then organized by strength.

Q: So they're adjacent?

A: They would be near each other, yes.

Q: Has your pharmacy ever considered separating look-alike, sound-alike medications?

A: There are guidelines we follow from the Institute for Safe Medication Practices. We implement tall man lettering. We use shelf separators.

Q: But the bottles are still right next to each other.

A: They're in the same general area. I'm not going to agree that they're "right next to each other" if you're implying they're touching.

Q: I'm not implying anything. I'm asking about proximity.

A: And I've answered. They're in the same section.

Q: After this incident, did your pharmacy make any changes to how those medications are stored?

A: That would be a question for the pharmacy manager.

Q: You're not aware of any changes?

A: I didn't say I wasn't aware. I said it's a question for the pharmacy manager. She makes those decisions.

Q: Dr. Whitmore, I'm asking what you've observed.

A: I've observed that we now have an additional alert in the computer system when metoprolol is dispensed. I don't know whose decision that was or when it was implemented. I just know it exists.

Q: Anything else?

A: Not that I've noticed, no.

topic: A nurse is questioned about a patient fall that occurred during her shift
text:
Q: State your name for the record.

A: Rebecca Thornton, R.N.

Q: Ms. Thornton, you were the assigned nurse for Mr. Delacroix on the night of October 14th?

A: I was. Bay 4, bed 2. I had him from 1900 to 0700.

Q: Walk me through the last time you checked on him before the fall.

A: 2215. I completed a full round—vitals, IV check, pain assessment. He was resting comfortably, side rails up, bed in low position, call light within reach. I documented everything before I left the room.

Q: And you're certain about that time?

A: I am. I charted it at 2217. The timestamp is in the EMR.

Q: The fall occurred at approximately 2:45 a.m. That's over four hours later. Why such a gap?

A: It wasn't a gap. I rounded at midnight and again at 0200. Both documented. The 0245 fall happened approximately forty minutes after my last check, which is within standard protocol for a patient with his risk score.

Q: His risk score?

A: Morse Fall Scale. He scored a 35 on admission. That's low risk. It's in the intake assessment if you'd like to review it.

Q: I'm asking about your assessment.

A: And I'm telling you—I assessed him using the validated tool our facility requires. The score was 35.

Q: Did you consider increasing monitoring given his age?

A: Age alone doesn't dictate monitoring frequency. His cognitive status was intact, he was ambulatory with supervision, and he had no fall history. The protocol was appropriate. I followed it.

Q: You don't think anything could have been done differently?

A: I think I provided the standard of care. If you're asking me to speculate about hypotheticals, I'd need you to be more specific.

Q: Fair enough. Let's move on.

---

topic: A nurse is questioned about a patient fall that occurred during her shift
text:
Q: Nurse Patterson, the incident report indicates Mr. Huang was found on the floor at 0312. You found him?

A: Yes.

Q: Describe exactly what you observed.

A: He was on the floor, on his left side, approximately two feet from the bed. The bed alarm was sounding. His IV had pulled loose, and there was some blood on his gown from the insertion site.

Q: The bed alarm was sounding when you arrived?

A: That's correct.

Q: So the alarm was functioning?

A: It was functioning when I arrived, yes. It was set, and it triggered.

Q: Had you set that alarm yourself at the beginning of your shift?

A: I had verified it was set when I took over from day shift. It's part of my standard handoff check.

Q: You verified it. You didn't set it yourself?

A: The alarm was already active. I confirmed it was active. That's the protocol.

Q: Is there a difference?

A: There's a difference between initiating a setting and confirming one that's already in place. I confirmed it. It was working. Would you like me to explain how the alarm system functions?

Q: That won't be necessary. How long after the alarm sounded did you reach the room?

A: I was in the adjacent room with another patient. I heard the alarm and responded immediately—within thirty seconds, I would estimate.

Q: You would estimate?

A: I didn't have a stopwatch running, counselor. I responded immediately. That I know.

Q: What was Mr. Huang attempting to do when he fell?

A: Based on his position and what he told me afterward, he was trying to reach the bathroom.

Q: Had he used the call light?

A: He said he didn't want to bother anyone. That's a direct quote from him.

---

topic: A nurse is questioned about a patient fall that occurred during her shift
text:
Q: Let's talk about your training, Ms. Vance. When did you complete your fall prevention certification?

A: March of last year. We recertify annually.

Q: And that training covers bed alarm protocols?

A: Among other things, yes.

Q: Tell me what it covers.

A: Risk assessment using standardized tools, environmental modifications, patient education, proper use of bed and chair alarms, mobility assistance techniques, documentation requirements, and post-fall protocols. Do you want me to continue?

Q: That's sufficient. Now—the patient, Mrs. Okonkwo, she had been identified as a fall risk, correct?

A: Yes, she had a yellow wristband, a falling star on her door, and her Morse score was documented at 55.

Q: A score of 55 indicates what?

A: High risk.

Q: And for a high-risk patient, what's the monitoring protocol?

A: Hourly rounds at minimum, bed alarm activated, non-slip footwear provided, and patient education on calling for assistance.

Q: Did you complete all of those interventions?

A: Every single one. I can walk you through each if you'd like.

Q: That won't be necessary. The family has alleged the bed alarm wasn't functioning. How do you respond?

A: The bed alarm was functioning. It was tested at shift change, it was on when I left her room at 0100, and it alarmed at 0147 when she attempted to get up. That's how we knew to respond.

Q: So you're disputing the family's account?

A: I'm not disputing anything. I'm telling you what happened. The alarm worked. I heard it. I responded to it.

Q: Is it possible the alarm malfunctioned earlier and then started working again?

A: Anything is possible, counselor. But I tested it. It worked. It's documented.

---

topic: A nurse is questioned about a patient fall that occurred during her shift
text:
Q: Mr. Chen fell sometime between your 11 p.m. check and when he was discovered at 11:47. That's a forty-seven-minute window. Help me understand what you were doing during that time.

A: I was providing care to my other patients.

Q: How many patients were you assigned that night?

A: Six.

Q: Is six patients typical for your unit?

A: It's... on the higher end. We were short-staffed that night.

Q: Did you inform anyone you felt the patient load was unsafe?

A: I—I completed an ADO form.

Q: An ADO form?

A: Assignment Despite Objection. It's a formal documentation that I noted the staffing concern.

Q: So you had concerns about staffing levels?

A: I documented the ratio. Whether I had concerns—I followed the protocol for raising the issue.

Q: That wasn't my question. Did you feel the staffing was unsafe?

A: I felt that six patients was above our target ratio. I documented it. I still provided care to all of my patients to the best of my ability that night.

Q: Including Mr. Chen?

A: Including Mr. Chen. I assessed him at 2300. He was resting. His bed alarm was on. I moved to my next patient.

Q: Did you rush through your assessment because of the patient load?

A: No. I completed a full assessment. Vitals, pain level, orientation check, bed positioning. I didn't rush anything.

Q: You seem very certain about that.

A: Because I am. I know how I practiced that night, regardless of the circumstances.

---

topic: A nurse is questioned about a patient fall that occurred during her shift
text:
Q: You've been a nurse for how long?

A: Nineteen years. Twenty in February.

Q: And in those nineteen years, how many patient falls have you been involved with?

A: Involved with in what sense?

Q: Occurred on your shift.

A: I don't have an exact number. Falls happen. They happen in every hospital, on every unit, despite every precaution. It's a known risk of hospitalization.

Q: Would you say more than ten?

A: Over nineteen years? Certainly more than ten.

Q: More than fifty?

A: I wouldn't speculate on a number. I haven't counted.

Q: Let me ask it differently. Was there anything unusual about Mrs. Patterson's fall?

A: No. She was a post-surgical patient, day two, on pain medication that can cause dizziness. She'd been educated about calling for help. She chose to try to ambulate on her own. That's unfortunately common.

Q: You're saying she bears responsibility?

A: I'm saying she made a choice that contributed to what happened. That's not blame—that's describing the sequence of events.

Q: Did you bear any responsibility?

A: I followed every protocol. I documented appropriately. I educated her twice on my shift alone about using the call light. If you're asking whether I could have physically prevented her from making a decision while I wasn't in the room—no. No nurse can do that.

Q: You seem to have thought about this quite a bit.

A: I take my practice seriously, counselor. I've thought about every patient I've ever cared for.

Q: Is that a yes?

A: That's my answer.

topic: A contractor is questioned about delays that caused a construction project to fail
text:
Q: Mr. Hardin, you were the general contractor on the Riverside Commons project, correct?

A: That's correct.

Q: And the project was originally scheduled for completion by March 15th of last year?

A: March 15th, yes.

Q: It wasn't completed until September, was it?

A: September 3rd, to be precise.

Q: Nearly six months late. Now, during the project, you submitted delay claims related to weather, didn't you?

A: I did. Fourteen separate weather delay notices, each one documented with photographs, weather service data, and daily logs. Every single one submitted within the contractually required 48-hour window.

Q: And the owner rejected those claims?

A: Initially, yes. Every one of them. Which is why I'm particularly pleased that we're finally getting all of this on the record.

Q: Let's focus on my questions, Mr. Hardin. The owner's representative, Mr. Castellano, he communicated concerns about your crew sizes in April, didn't he?

A: He sent emails, yes. Emails that I responded to the same day, every time, with detailed explanations of why our crew sizes were appropriate given the conditions. I have copies of all of those responses if you'd like to see them.

Q: That won't be necessary at this time.

A: I'd be happy to walk you through them. The record should be complete.

Q: Mr. Hardin, isn't it true that you fell behind on the foundation pour by three weeks?

A: We adjusted the foundation schedule after discovering unmarked utilities that weren't on any of the drawings the owner provided. I notified them in writing within four hours of discovery. Would you like the date and time stamp on that notification?

Q: I have the documents.

A: Good. Then you can see we followed every procedure exactly as required.

Q: You're quite confident about your documentation.

A: I am. I've been doing this for twenty-two years, counsel. I know how these situations unfold. That's why I document everything.

topic: A contractor is questioned about delays that caused a construction project to fail
text:
Q: Ms. Thornton, you served as project manager for Bellamy Construction on the Oak Street Tower project?

A: I was the project manager, yes.

Q: The project experienced significant delays in the mechanical systems installation, correct?

A: There were delays, yes.

Q: About how long?

A: I'd have to look at the exact figures.

Q: Approximately?

A: I don't want to guess. The schedule documents would show the precise timeline.

Q: Fair enough. The mechanical subcontractor was Apex HVAC?

A: That's correct.

Q: And you selected Apex for this project?

A: The selection process involved multiple parties.

Q: But you recommended them?

A: I was one of several people who provided input on subcontractor selection.

Q: Ms. Thornton, I'm just trying to establish who made the decision to hire Apex. Did you recommend them or not?

A: I provided a list of qualified bidders. Apex was on that list. The final selection involved the owner's representative and our company's procurement department.

Q: Were there lower bidders than Apex?

A: I believe there were, yes.

Q: And yet Apex was selected?

A: Based on qualifications, past performance, and overall value. Not just price.

Q: Whose assessment of qualifications?

A: A collective assessment. As I said, multiple parties were involved in that determination.

Q: I see. And when Apex began falling behind schedule, who was responsible for addressing that?

A: That would depend on what you mean by "responsible." Could you be more specific about what aspect of the situation you're asking about?

topic: A contractor is questioned about delays that caused a construction project to fail
text:
Q: Mr. Okonkwo, let's talk about the change order process on the Meridian Hospital expansion.

A: Certainly.

Q: The owner issued a directive to add a fourth-floor surgical suite in October, correct?

A: October 14th, yes. And I want to say, this is exactly the kind of question I've been hoping we'd get to.

Q: You anticipated this line of questioning?

A: I anticipated that someone would finally look at how that directive was handled. Because the answer to most of your questions about delay is going to trace back to that decision.

Q: Tell me about the directive.

A: The owner's representative walked onto the site on October 14th with drawings—incomplete drawings, I should add—for an entirely new surgical suite that wasn't in the original scope. And he handed them to my superintendent and said, "We need this built."

Q: What was the timeline given?

A: "As fast as possible." Those were his exact words. No formal change order. No schedule analysis. No discussion of how this would affect every other trade on the project.

Q: Did you object?

A: Object? I did more than object. I sent a letter that same day outlining every impact this would have on the critical path. I requested a formal change order with appropriate time extension. I asked for a meeting to discuss sequencing.

Q: And the response?

A: "Proceed with the work. We'll sort out the paperwork later." That was the response. I have the email.

Q: So you proceeded?

A: What choice did I have? I'm not going to abandon a hospital project. But I made sure every single day of impact was documented. Every cost. Every delay to other work. All of it.

Q: And that documentation is available?

A: Absolutely. I've been waiting for someone to actually look at it.

topic: A contractor is questioned about delays that caused a construction project to fail
text:
Q: Now, Mr. Parsons, let me make sure I understand your testimony. You're saying the electrical rough-in couldn't proceed because of framing delays?

A: That's correct.

Q: And the framing delays were caused by what, exactly?

A: Late delivery of engineered lumber.

Q: Which was ordered by?

A: The framing subcontractor.

Q: Not by your company?

A: No.

Q: So it wasn't your responsibility?

A: The framing sub's procurement was their responsibility under their subcontract.

Q: Good. That's very helpful, Mr. Parsons. Let me shift topics slightly. The owner claims you failed to provide adequate supervision during the delay period. How do you respond?

A: I had a superintendent on site every day. Full time. Sign-in logs will confirm that.

Q: Every single day?

A: Every single working day, yes.

Q: Even during the period when, according to the owner, no meaningful work was being performed?

A: Correct. Because there was work being performed. Perhaps not the work the owner wanted to see, but necessary preparatory work, coordination meetings, material staging.

Q: This is exactly what I was hoping you could clarify. The owner's logs suggest the site was essentially dormant for three weeks in July.

A: Then the owner's logs are inaccurate.

Q: You're saying the owner is wrong?

A: I'm saying my daily reports, my superintendent's logs, and my time-stamped photographs will show consistent activity throughout that period. I welcome the comparison.

Q: We may take you up on that.

A: Please do.

topic: A contractor is questioned about delays that caused a construction project to fail
text:
Q: Ms. Chen, when did you first become aware there was a problem with the soil conditions at the Lakewood site?

A: When the excavation subcontractor hit water at eight feet.

Q: That wasn't anticipated?

A: Not based on the geotechnical report the owner provided during bidding.

Q: Did you request additional soil testing?

A: I did.

Q: And?

A: The owner denied the request. Said we should proceed based on the existing report.

Q: In writing?

A: Yes.

Q: So you proceeded?

A: I proceeded under protest. And I documented that protest in writing.

Q: Let me ask you something, Ms. Chen. Looking back, is there anything you would have done differently?

A: No.

Q: Nothing at all?

A: I followed every specification in the contract. I submitted every required notice. I documented every owner-caused delay. I communicated every concern in writing. So no, there's nothing I would have done differently.

Q: You seem very certain.

A: I am certain. I've had a lot of time to review our performance on this project while waiting for this deposition. And I'm confident that when all the evidence is examined—the actual evidence, not the owner's narrative—it will show that we performed exactly as the contract required.

Q: The owner disagrees.

A: The owner is welcome to present their evidence. I'm looking forward to that.

Q: We'll see what the documents show.

A: Yes, we will.

topic: A doctor is deposed about informed consent procedures before a surgery
text:
Q: Doctor, I'd like to turn your attention to the informed consent process for Mrs. Patterson's surgery. Can you describe your standard practice?

A: My standard practice. Okay. I meet with the patient, I explain the procedure, I explain the risks, I answer questions, and I obtain their signature on the consent form.

Q: How long does that process typically take?

A: It depends on the patient. Some patients have a lot of questions. Some don't.

Q: How long did it take with Mrs. Patterson?

A: I don't recall the exact duration.

Q: An estimate?

A: I really couldn't say. I see a lot of patients.

Q: More than five minutes?

A: Probably.

Q: More than fifteen?

A: I don't know. Maybe. I don't time these conversations.

Q: Do you have any documentation of what was discussed?

A: There's the signed consent form in the chart.

Q: Anything beyond the form itself? Notes about the conversation?

A: I may have... look, I document what's required. The form is the documentation.

Q: So no separate notes?

A: No.

Q: Doctor, did you specifically discuss the risk of nerve damage with Mrs. Patterson?

A: That risk is listed on the consent form. She signed it.

Q: I'm asking whether you verbally discussed it with her.

A: I go over the major risks verbally. That's one of them. So yes.

Q: You're certain?

A: I follow the same process every time. So yes.

---

topic: A doctor is deposed about informed consent procedures before a surgery
text:
Q: Good afternoon, Doctor. We've been at this for a while, so I'll try to keep this portion focused. When you met with Mr. Donnelly before his procedure, where did that conversation take place?

A: Pre-op area. Bed seven or eight, I think. One of those.

Q: And who else was present?

A: A nurse. I don't remember which one.

Q: Was Mr. Donnelly's wife present?

A: She may have been. There was a woman there. I assumed it was his wife.

Q: You assumed?

A: I don't check IDs, counselor.

Q: Fair enough. What did you tell Mr. Donnelly about the surgery?

A: I explained what we were going to do. Laparoscopic cholecystectomy. Remove the gallbladder through small incisions. Showed him on his abdomen where the ports would go.

Q: Did you discuss alternatives to surgery?

A: There weren't any realistic alternatives at that point. He'd already failed conservative management.

Q: Did you tell him that?

A: Yes.

Q: What about the option of doing nothing?

A: Doing nothing wasn't... his gallbladder was full of stones and he was having attacks. Doing nothing meant more attacks. Possible rupture. I told him that.

Q: The consent form references a risk of bile duct injury. Did you explain that to him verbally?

A: I explain all the material risks.

Q: That's not what I asked. Did you explain bile duct injury specifically to Mr. Donnelly?

A: Yes. I tell every patient that it's a known risk of the procedure.

Q: What words do you use?

A: What words do I use. I tell them that there's a small chance the bile duct can be injured during surgery, and if that happens, it requires additional surgery to repair.

Q: Every time? Those exact words?

A: The substance, yes. I'm not reading from a script.

---

topic: A doctor is deposed about informed consent procedures before a surgery
text:
Q: Dr. Reeves. Let's talk about consent. The form in the record is signed by your patient, correct?

A: Yes.

Q: And that's Ms. Thurman's signature at the bottom?

A: It appears to be, yes.

Q: Your signature is there as well?

A: It is.

Q: Now, this form is dated the morning of surgery. Is that when you obtained consent?

A: I spoke with her the day before. The form was signed the morning of.

Q: Why the delay?

A: It's not a delay. It's standard. We discuss in the office, they think about it overnight, they sign when they come in.

Q: So the actual consent conversation happened the day before?

A: That's what I said.

Q: Help me understand something, Doctor. If the conversation was the day before, how does the patient ask questions the morning of surgery if something occurred to them overnight?

A: They can ask me. I see them before we go back.

Q: For how long?

A: A few minutes.

Q: A few minutes.

A: Yes.

Q: That's sufficient time to address concerns about a four-hour spinal surgery?

A: Most patients don't have concerns at that point. We've already discussed everything.

Q: But if they did?

A: Then I would address them.

Q: Has that ever happened?

A: Has a patient ever asked a question the morning of surgery?

Q: Yes.

A: Of course.

Q: And you've postponed surgery because of it?

A: I... not that I recall specifically, no.

---

topic: A doctor is deposed about informed consent procedures before a surgery
text:
Q: Let me ask you about the risks you disclosed. You mentioned infection.

A: Yes.

Q: Bleeding.

A: Yes.

Q: Reaction to anesthesia.

A: Correct.

Q: What about stroke?

A: Stroke is a risk of any surgery involving general anesthesia. It's on the anesthesia consent.

Q: I'm asking about your consent. The surgical consent.

A: Stroke isn't typically listed as a specific risk of rotator cuff repair because it's not specific to that procedure.

Q: But it's a risk.

A: In the sense that it's a risk of being alive, yes.

Q: Doctor—

A: I'm being serious. You can have a stroke sitting at home. The question is whether a particular surgery elevates that risk in a meaningful way. For rotator cuff repair, it doesn't.

Q: Mr. Hensley had a stroke during your surgery.

A: I'm aware of that.

Q: And you didn't warn him that could happen?

A: I told him the risks of the surgery. Stroke is not a risk of rotator cuff repair. It's a risk of... of general anesthesia, of being a seventy-two-year-old man with hypertension. That's the anesthesiologist's domain.

Q: So it's someone else's responsibility?

A: I didn't say that. I said it's addressed on a different consent form by a different physician.

Q: Did you confirm that happened?

A: Did I confirm what happened?

Q: That the anesthesiologist discussed stroke risk with Mr. Hensley.

A: I don't supervise the anesthesiologist, counselor.

Q: That's not what I asked.

A: Then ask it more clearly.

Q: Did you, yourself, confirm that anyone discussed stroke risk with your patient before you operated on him?

A: No. I relied on the standard process.

---

topic: A doctor is deposed about informed consent procedures before a surgery
text:
Q: How many surgeries do you perform in a typical week, Doctor?

A: It varies.

Q: On average.

A: Twelve to fifteen, depending on complexity.

Q: And you obtain informed consent for each one?

A: Yes.

Q: Personally?

A: Yes.

Q: Let's talk about Mrs. Chen. Do you remember her?

A: I remember the case, yes.

Q: What do you remember?

A: Thyroidectomy. Total. She had papillary carcinoma.

Q: Do you remember the consent conversation?

A: Not specifically. It was two years ago.

Q: Then how can you testify about what you told her?

A: Because I follow the same process with every patient.

Q: Every patient for two years.

A: For twenty-three years.

Q: And you've never deviated from that process?

A: I'm sure there have been minor variations. But the substance is always the same.

Q: What's the substance?

A: I explain what the surgery involves. I explain why I'm recommending it. I explain what can go wrong.

Q: What can go wrong with a thyroidectomy?

A: Bleeding. Infection. Damage to the recurrent laryngeal nerve. Damage to the parathyroid glands. Hypothyroidism requiring lifelong medication.

Q: Did you tell Mrs. Chen she might lose her voice?

A: I told her there was a risk of nerve damage that could affect her voice.

Q: Those are different things.

A: I used the words I always use.

Q: Which are?

A: That there's a nerve that runs near the thyroid that controls the vocal cord, and if it's damaged, it can cause hoarseness or voice changes.

Q: Permanent voice changes?

A: I say it can be temporary or permanent.

Q: You're certain you said that to her?

A: I'm certain that's what I say.

topic: A financial advisor is deposed about investment decisions made on a client's behalf
text:
Q: Mr. Brennan, I want to direct your attention to the Whitfield account. You were the primary advisor on that account, correct?

A: Yes.

Q: And in March of 2021, you recommended a substantial position in Vertex Capital Partners, is that right?

A: I recommended it as part of a broader allocation strategy, yes.

Q: A broader allocation strategy. How much of the Whitfield portfolio did you place in Vertex?

A: I'd have to look at the exact figures.

Q: Approximately.

A: Somewhere around... I don't know, maybe thirty percent. Give or take.

Q: Give or take. That's a significant portion of a retirement portfolio, wouldn't you say?

A: It depends on the client's risk tolerance and investment horizon.

Q: Did Mrs. Whitfield indicate a high risk tolerance to you?

A: We discussed her goals. I explained the options. She agreed to the strategy.

Q: That wasn't my question.

A: Can you repeat it?

Q: Did Mrs. Whitfield indicate to you that she had a high risk tolerance?

A: She understood there were risks involved.

Q: Mr. Brennan, I'm asking whether she told you she was comfortable with high-risk investments. Yes or no.

A: I don't recall her using those exact words.

Q: What words did she use?

A: I don't remember specifically. It was three years ago.

topic: A financial advisor is deposed about investment decisions made on a client's behalf
text:
Q: Let's talk about the due diligence process at your firm. There is a due diligence process, correct?

A: Of course there is.

Q: Walk me through it.

A: Before recommending any investment product, we review the fund's prospectus, historical performance, management team, fee structure, and regulatory filings. We assess whether it aligns with our clients' stated objectives.

Q: And you performed this due diligence on the Meridian Growth Fund before recommending it to Mr. Castellanos?

A: Yes.

Q: Who else was involved in that review?

A: Typically it's myself and our compliance officer, Dana Wheeler.

Q: Typically. Was Ms. Wheeler involved in the Meridian review specifically?

A: I believe so, yes.

Q: You believe so.

A: Yes. I believe so.

Q: Is there documentation of her involvement?

A: There should be sign-off sheets in the file.

Q: We haven't received any sign-off sheets for Meridian.

A: Then I don't know what to tell you. They should be there.

Q: Did you actually perform due diligence on this fund, Mr. Okonkwo?

A: I just told you we did.

Q: Then where is the documentation?

A: I'm not the custodian of records. I don't know why you don't have what you're supposed to have. I did my job.

topic: A financial advisor is deposed about investment decisions made on a client's behalf
text:
Q: Ms. Reyes. The Andover account. When did you first recommend municipal bonds for that portfolio?

A: I'd need to see the account records to give you a precise date.

Q: We can mark this as Exhibit 14. Take a look at the second page.

Q: Yet by November, the account held nearly forty percent in high-yield corporate bonds. How does that align with capital preservation?

A: Yes.

Q: More than one?

A: I think so, yes. I'd have to... I mean, yes. We spoke multiple times.

Q: Are those conversations documented anywhere?

A: Some of them would be in my notes. Some were phone calls.

Q: Were the phone calls recorded?

A: I don't... I'm not sure of the firm's policy on that during that period.

Q: Fair enough. Let's move on. Who approved the shift to high-yield bonds?

Q: In writing?

A: I... I would have to check.

topic: A financial advisor is deposed about investment decisions made on a client's behalf
text:
Q: Mr. Patterson, how long have we been at this today?

A: Usually, yes.

topic: A financial advisor is deposed about investment decisions made on a client's behalf
text:
Q: Ms. Thornton, we've been through the Franklin portfolio and the Dubois portfolio. I want to turn now to the Nakata account.

topic: A contractor is questioned about delays that caused a construction project to fail
text:
Q: Mr. Delacroix, let's talk about the foundation pour scheduled for March 15th. That was delayed, correct?

A: Yes.

Q: By how long?

A: Eleven days.

Q: And what caused that delay?

A: Weather. We had rain for six consecutive days, then the site needed to dry.

Q: Six days of rain doesn't account for eleven days of delay, does it?

A: I just explained that. The site needed to dry. You can't pour concrete into mud.

Q: How many days to dry?

A: I don't have the exact figure in front of me.

Q: Approximately.

A: Three, four days. Maybe five.

Q: So six plus five is eleven. You're saying every single day of that delay was weather-related?

A: That's what I said, yes.

Q: No equipment issues? No crew availability problems?

A: I've answered this. Weather.

Q: Mr. Delacroix, I'm asking whether there were any other contributing factors.

A: And I've told you three times now. It was the weather. Would you like me to say it again?

Q: Were your crews fully staffed and ready to pour on March 21st when the site was dry?

A: Yes. Next question.

---

topic: A contractor is questioned about delays that caused a construction project to fail
text:
Q: When did you first notify Hartwell Development that the electrical rough-in would not meet the August deadline?

A: I'd have to check my records for the exact date.

Q: And you didn't tell your client while you were failing to solve it.

Q: A materials shortage that delays the project by three weeks is a hiccup?

A: That's not what I—look, I notified them as soon as I determined the delay was unavoidable.

topic: A contractor is questioned about delays that caused a construction project to fail
text:

topic: A contractor is questioned about delays that caused a construction project to fail
text:
Q: Ms. Vance, let's discuss the HVAC installation timeline.

A: All right.

Q: What was the primary cause?

A: Multiple causes. It's documented extensively.

Q: Give me the primary one.

A: We were waiting on ductwork. The manufacturer had backorder issues.

Q: When did you learn about the backorder?

A: September, mid-September.

A: Of course we did.

---

topic: A contractor is questioned about delays that caused a construction project to fail
text:

A: We produced everything that was requested.

Q: Let me ask again. Did you—

Q: Mr. Huang, I'm simply asking whether you have written documentation beyond the February 10th email.

topic: A daycare worker is deposed about an injury a child sustained while in their care

topic: A daycare worker is deposed about an injury a child sustained while in their care

topic: A daycare worker is deposed about an injury a child sustained while in their care

topic: A daycare worker is deposed about an injury a child sustained while in their care
text:
Q: The incident report says the injury occurred at 10:42 a.m. Do you see that?

A: I didn't need to consult it. I've been trained on it.

Q: Ms. Reyes, did anyone at the daycare take photographs of Tyler's injury before cleaning it?

A: No.

Q: Why not?

A: Because my priority was the bleeding child in front of me, not building a legal record.

---

topic: A daycare worker is deposed about an injury a child sustained while in their care
text:
Q: You mentioned you completed an incident report. I'm handing you what's been marked as Exhibit 7. Is this the report you prepared?

A: Yes.

Q: I notice the section titled "Witness Observations" is blank. Why is that?

A: Because no one witnessed the fall directly.

Q: No one saw a four-year-old fall off a bookshelf?

A: The bookshelf is in the reading corner. The children are allowed quiet independent time there.

Q: Allowed unsupervised time, you mean.

A: That's not what I said.

Q: But it's accurate, isn't it? No staff member was watching the reading corner.

A: We can't have eyes on every child at every moment. That's not—

Q: I didn't ask about every child. I asked about the reading corner.

A: The reading corner is within sightline of the main activity area.

Q: Within sightline. But no one was looking.

A: I can't account for where every staff member's eyes were pointed at every second.

A: I'm not going to speculate about hypotheticals.

Q: It's a simple question. Would a child be allowed to climb a bookshelf if a staff member were watching?

A: Obviously not.

topic: A tenant is questioned about property damage they reported to their landlord
text:
Q: Mr. Delacroix, you submitted a maintenance request on March 14th regarding water damage in your unit, correct?

A: I submitted a request about the ceiling falling apart, yes. Whether you want to call it "water damage" is your business.

Q: The form you filled out—Exhibit 7—uses the words "water damage." Those are your words, aren't they?

A: Those are the words on the dropdown menu your client's property management company makes tenants use. I didn't design the form.

Q: So you selected "water damage" from a dropdown menu?

A: That's what I just said.

Q: And when did you first notice this issue with the ceiling?

A: When chunks of drywall started landing on my kitchen table. Sometime in early February.

Q: Sometime in early February. Can you be more specific?

A: No, I cannot be more specific about the exact date I noticed my ceiling rotting. I wasn't taking notes for your deposition.

Q: But you waited until March 14th to report it?

A: I reported it verbally to the building super three times before that. He ignored me. So I put it in writing.

Q: You reported it verbally. To whom, specifically?

A: I just told you. The building superintendent. Carlos.

Q: And you have no documentation of these verbal reports?

A: I have Carlos's face every time I told him and he shrugged. Would you like me to describe it?

Q: Mr. Delacroix, I'm asking whether you have any written record, email, text message—

A: No. Because when your ceiling is falling in, you walk down the hall and tell somebody. That's what normal people do.

topic: A tenant is questioned about property damage they reported to their landlord
text:
Q: Ms. Okonkwo, let's discuss the photographs attached to your complaint. You took these yourself?

A: Yes.

Q: All of them?

A: Yes, all of them.

Q: The metadata shows these were taken on April 3rd. But your written complaint says you noticed the mold in mid-March. Why the delay in documenting it?

A: I wiped a wall. I didn't "alter" anything. The mold came back in two days.

Q: Ms. Okonkwo, isn't it possible that the mold was a result of your own failure to properly ventilate the bathroom?

A: The bathroom has no window and the exhaust fan has been broken since I moved in. I reported that in my first month.

Q: You reported a broken exhaust fan?

A: Yes.

Q: And do you have documentation of that report?

A: I have the same broken fan I've had for two years. Your client has the documentation. Ask him.

topic: A tenant is questioned about property damage they reported to their landlord
text:
Q: When you say the floorboards were "buckling," what do you mean by that?

topic: A tenant is questioned about property damage they reported to their landlord
text:
Q: You testified earlier that you smelled gas in the unit. When was this?

A: The first week of September.

Q: Can you narrow that down?

A: September 2nd or 3rd. I remember because it was right after Labor Day.

Q: And what did you do when you smelled gas?

A: I called the gas company and I called the landlord.

Q: In that order?

A: Yes.

Q: What did the gas company tell you?

A: They came out, found a leak in the line behind the stove, and shut off the gas to my unit.

Q: So the gas company resolved the issue?

A: The gas company found the leak. They didn't resolve anything. They turned off my gas and told me the landlord needed to hire someone to fix the line.

Q: And did the landlord arrange for repairs?

A: Eventually.

Q: How long did it take?

A: Eleven days.

Q: You were without gas for eleven days?

A: That's what I said.

Q: Did you communicate with the landlord during those eleven days?

A: Every single day.

Q: By what method?

A: Phone. Text. Email. Showing up at the management office. Pick one.

Q: And what responses did you receive?

A: "We're working on it." That was the response. Every time. "We're working on it."

Q: But ultimately repairs were made.

A: Ultimately, yes. After I'd been eating cold food and showering at my sister's house for a week and a half.

topic: A tenant is questioned about property damage they reported to their landlord
text:
Q: The damage report mentions a broken window in the bedroom. Tell me about that.

A: What would you like to know?

Q: How did the window break?

A: I don't know. I came home and it was cracked.

Q: You came home and it was cracked.

A: That's what I said.

Q: You have no idea how a window in your own bedroom cracked?

A: If I knew, I would tell you.

Q: Ms. Ferraro, isn't it true that you had a party at the unit on October 15th?

A: I had friends over. I wouldn't call it a party.

Q: How many friends?

A: Six or seven.

Q: And none of them broke the window?

A: No.

Q: You're certain?

A: I was there. The window was fine when everyone left.

Q: What time did everyone leave?

A: Around midnight.

Q: And when did you discover the crack?

A: The next afternoon.

Q: So something happened between midnight and the next afternoon.

A: Apparently so. I wasn't aware I needed to stand guard over my windows overnight.

Q: Did you report the broken window to the landlord?

A: Of course I reported it.

Q: And what was the response?

A: That it would be "assessed." Then nothing. It's been two months and I'm still taping plastic over the crack.

topic: A business partner is deposed about financial records they were responsible for maintaining
text:
Q: Mr. Hartwell, you were responsible for maintaining the accounts receivable ledger for the partnership from 2019 through 2022, correct?

A: That's what I did, yes.

Q: And in that role, you would have recorded all incoming payments from clients?

A: That was part of it.

Q: Was there some other part I'm missing?

A: I recorded payments. I reconciled accounts. I prepared monthly summaries. I flagged discrepancies. Do you want me to keep going, or is that sufficient?

Q: I'm just trying to understand the scope of your duties.

A: And I'm trying to answer your questions accurately.

Q: Let's look at the March 2021 ledger. You have Exhibit 14 in front of you?

A: I do.

Q: There's an entry here for $47,500 from Meridian Holdings. Do you see that?

A: I see it.

Q: Can you tell me what that payment was for?

A: It was a payment. From Meridian Holdings. For $47,500. Which is exactly what the ledger says.

Q: Mr. Hartwell, I'm asking what services or goods that payment corresponded to.

A: Then you should ask someone who handled the service agreements. I recorded what came in. I didn't negotiate the deals.

Q: Did you ever ask what Meridian Holdings was paying for?

A: No. That wasn't my job. My job was to make sure the numbers matched. They matched.

Q: Every single time?

A: Every single time I was given accurate information to work with, yes.

topic: A business partner is deposed about financial records they were responsible for maintaining
text:
Q: Ms. Delgado, I want to direct your attention to the quarterly expense reports you prepared.

A: All right.

Q: Specifically the Q3 2020 report. Do you recall preparing that document?

A: I prepared all the quarterly reports during that period, so yes, I would have prepared that one.

Q: Would have, or did?

A: Did. I did prepare it. I'm confirming what you already know.

Q: The report shows $12,000 in consulting fees paid to an entity called Blackstone Advisory. What can you tell me about that?

A: It was a consulting fee. Paid to Blackstone Advisory. For twelve thousand dollars.

Q: Ms. Delgado, who engaged Blackstone Advisory?

A: I don't know.

Q: You don't know, or you don't remember?

A: I don't know because I was never told. I received invoices. I logged invoices. I didn't conduct interviews about where they came from.

Q: Did you ever question why the partnership was paying $12,000 to a consulting firm you knew nothing about?

A: I questioned it exactly once.

Q: And what happened?

A: I was told to process the payment.

Q: By whom?

A: By Mr. Reeves.

Q: Did Mr. Reeves explain what Blackstone Advisory did for the partnership?

A: He said, and I quote, "Just process it, Diana." So I processed it.

Q: And you never followed up?

A: I followed up by doing my job, counsel. Which was processing payments. Not investigating my partners.

topic: A business partner is deposed about financial records they were responsible for maintaining
text:
Q: Mr. Chen, let's talk about the petty cash fund.

A: Fine.

Q: Who had access to that fund?

A: All three partners.

Q: Including yourself?

A: I just said all three partners. I'm a partner. So yes.

Q: How was the fund replenished?

A: When it ran low, one of us would write a check from the operating account.

Q: Was there a threshold? A specific amount that triggered replenishment?

A: Not formally, no.

Q: So anyone could replenish it at any time for any reason?

A: Within reason, yes.

Q: What does "within reason" mean?

A: It means we weren't idiots. If there was two hundred dollars left, nobody was writing a ten-thousand-dollar replenishment check.

Q: But there was no written policy?

A: There were three of us. We talked. We didn't need a manual for everything.

Q: Let me show you Exhibit 22. This is a check for $8,500 to replenish petty cash, dated June 3, 2021. Do you recognize it?

A: I see it.

Q: That's your signature, isn't it?

A: Yes.

Q: Why did the petty cash fund need $8,500?

A: I don't recall the specific circumstance.

Q: You don't recall writing a check for eighty-five hundred dollars?

A: I recall writing checks. I wrote many checks. I don't have a photographic memory of each one, counsel. That's why we kept records. Which you're holding.

topic: A business partner is deposed about financial records they were responsible for maintaining
text:
Q: I'm going to ask you again, Ms. Thornton. Where are the backup files for the 2020 fiscal year?

A: And I'm going to tell you again. I don't know.

Q: You were the partner responsible for financial record-keeping.

A: I was responsible for maintaining the primary records. The digital backups were handled by our IT contractor.

Q: Who was that contractor?

A: DataSafe Solutions.

Q: Did you ever verify that DataSafe was actually performing backups?

A: I received monthly confirmation emails.

Q: Did you ever independently verify the backups existed?

A: I'm not a technical person. I relied on the confirmations.

Q: So you never actually saw these backup files.

A: I saw the primary files. Daily. That was my responsibility.

Q: Ms. Thornton, the primary server crashed in February 2021, correct?

A: Correct.

Q: And when you contacted DataSafe to retrieve the backups?

A: They said there had been a system error.

Q: So the backups didn't exist.

A: Apparently not.

Q: Apparently not. And you're telling me you bear no responsibility for this?

A: I'm telling you what happened. Whether you like the answer is not my concern.

Q: Let me ask this differently—

A: Please do.

topic: A business partner is deposed about financial records they were responsible for maintaining
text:
Q: Mr. Patterson, walk me through how vendor payments were approved.

A: Invoice comes in, gets logged, gets reviewed, gets paid.

Q: Who reviewed them?

A: Depended on the amount.

Q: Explain that for me.

A: Under five thousand, any partner could approve. Over five thousand required two signatures.

Q: Always?

A: That was the policy.

Q: I'm looking at Exhibit 31. This is a payment to Cornerstone Supplies for $7,200. I only see one signature. Yours.

A: Okay.

Q: That violates the policy you just described.

A: It would appear to.

Q: You don't seem concerned about that, Mr. Patterson.

A: I'm not here to perform concern for you, counsel. I'm here to answer questions.

Q: Fine. Why does this check only have one signature?

A: I don't recall.

Q: Was this an oversight?

A: Possibly.

Q: Or did you intentionally bypass the two-signature requirement?

A: I did not intentionally bypass anything.

Q: Then how did it happen?

A: Things happen in a busy office. Checks get cut. Sometimes a step gets missed. It wasn't a pattern.

Q: Wasn't it? Because I have six more exhibits that show the exact same situation.

A: Then I guess you have more questions to ask me.

Q: I do, Mr. Patterson. I certainly do.

A: I'm sure you'll enjoy asking them.

topic: A daycare worker is deposed about an injury a child sustained while in their care
text:
Q: Ms. Hernandez, you stated earlier that you were the only staff member in the Butterfly Room between 2:00 and 2:30 that afternoon. Is that correct?

A: That's what the schedule showed, yes.

Q: I'm not asking about the schedule. I'm asking whether you were, in fact, the only adult present.

A: As far as I recall, yes.

Q: As far as you recall.

A: Yes.

Q: Would it surprise you to learn that the sign-in log shows another staff member, a Ms. Treadwell, entering the Butterfly Room at 2:14 p.m.?

A: I don't know what the sign-in log shows. I wasn't looking at it.

Q: But you would have noticed another adult entering the room you were supervising, wouldn't you?

A: Not necessarily. I was focused on the children. That's my job.

Q: Fourteen children, by your count. And one of them fell from a climbing structure hard enough to fracture his arm. But you didn't notice another adult walk into the room.

A: I didn't say I didn't notice. I said I don't recall. Those are different things.

Q: Help me understand the difference, Ms. Hernandez.

A: The difference is I'm being honest with you. I'm not going to say I remember something just because you want me to.

Q: I want you to tell me what happened to Marcus Williams.

A: He fell. I've told you that. I was across the room and I heard him cry out and I went to him.

Q: Across the room. How far, exactly?

A: I don't know. Fifteen feet. Maybe twenty.

topic: A daycare worker is deposed about an injury a child sustained while in their care
text:
Q: Can you describe the condition of the outdoor play area on the morning of June 3rd?

A: It was fine. We do a safety check every morning before the children go out.

Q: Who performed the safety check that day?

A: I did.

Q: And what does a safety check involve?

A: Walking the perimeter, looking for debris, checking the equipment, making sure the gate latches are secure.

Q: Did you document this safety check?

A: We're supposed to initial the log.

Q: Did you initial the log on June 3rd?

A: I believe so.

Q: You believe so, or you did?

A: I initialed it. Yes.

Q: The log we received in discovery doesn't have your initials for June 3rd. It has a blank space.

A: Then maybe I forgot that one day. It doesn't mean I didn't do the check.

Q: It just means you didn't document it.

A: Right.

Q: Ms. Patterson, the child was injured on a swing that had a cracked seat. Are you telling me you inspected that swing and didn't notice the crack?

A: I'm telling you I did my check the way I always do. I don't know when that crack happened. It could have happened during play.

Q: A crack that was four inches long.

A: I don't know what to tell you. I didn't see it.

topic: A daycare worker is deposed about an injury a child sustained while in their care
text:
Q: How long have you worked at Sunny Days Learning Center?

A: Coming up on six years.

Q: In those six years, have you received any disciplinary actions?

A: Why are you asking me that?

Q: I'm asking the questions, Mr. Franklin. Have you received any disciplinary actions?

A: One. A written warning.

Q: What was it for?

A: A disagreement with a parent.

Q: A disagreement. Can you be more specific?

A: A parent accused me of something that wasn't true, and I defended myself, and my supervisor thought I was too aggressive about it.

Q: What were you accused of?

A: This doesn't have anything to do with what happened to Lily.

Q: I'll decide what's relevant, Mr. Franklin.

A: You're trying to make me look like something I'm not.

Q: I'm trying to understand your employment history. What were you accused of?

A: Grabbing a child's arm too hard. Which I didn't do. The child had a bruise from falling at home and the parent blamed me.

Q: Was that investigated?

A: Yes. And I was cleared.

Q: But you still received a written warning.

A: For how I talked to the parent. Not for hurting anyone.

topic: A daycare worker is deposed about an injury a child sustained while in their care
text:
Q: Walk me through the moment you first realized Emma was injured.

A: She was crying. I went over to see what was wrong.

Q: Where were you when you heard her crying?

A: At the art table with some of the other kids.

Q: How far is the art table from the block corner?

A: I don't know exactly. Maybe ten feet.

Q: Were you facing the block corner?

A: No, I had my back to it.

Q: So you didn't see what happened.

A: No. I heard her cry and I turned around.

Q: What did you see when you turned around?

A: Emma was on the floor, holding her face. Another child, Dylan, was standing near her.

Q: Was Dylan holding anything?

A: A block.

Q: What kind of block?

A: One of the wooden ones. The rectangular ones.

Q: Did you ask Dylan what happened?

A: Yes.

Q: What did he say?

A: He said Emma took his block and he wanted it back.

Q: Did he say he hit her?

A: He's three years old. He didn't use those words.

Q: What words did he use?

A: I don't remember exactly.

Q: You remember the shape of the block but not what the child said immediately after the incident?

A: I remember he was upset. I remember Emma was hurt. I was focused on Emma.

topic: A daycare worker is deposed about an injury a child sustained while in their care
text:
Q: The incident report states that you discovered the injury at 4:15 p.m. Is that accurate?

A: That's what I wrote down, yes.

Q: When did the injury actually occur?

A: I don't understand the question.

Q: I'm asking whether 4:15 was when the injury happened, or when you noticed it.

A: When I noticed it.

Q: So you don't know when it actually occurred.

A: Correct.

Q: Could it have been 3:00?

A: I don't think so.

Q: Could it have been 3:30?

A: I really don't know.

Q: Ms. Chen, the child had a bruise the size of a golf ball on her forehead. How long would it take for a bruise like that to become visible?

A: I'm not a doctor.

Q: I'm asking for your experience. You've worked with children for how long?

A: Eleven years.

Q: In eleven years, you must have seen bruises form.

A: It depends on the child. Some bruise easily.

Q: This child. Did she bruise easily?

A: I wouldn't know. I'd only been in that room for two weeks.

Q: So there's a window of at least an hour, possibly more, during which this injury could have occurred, and you have no idea what happened during that time.

A: I know I was supervising the children. I know I was doing my job.

Q: And yet you didn't see a child get hurt badly enough to leave a golf-ball-sized bruise.

A: No. I didn't.

topic: A witness is asked about a car accident they saw from their front porch
text:
Q: Mr. Fontaine, you've stated you were on your front porch at approximately 4:15 p.m. on the day in question. Is that correct?

A: That's what I said, yes.

Q: And from that vantage point, you claim to have witnessed the collision between a silver Honda Accord and a red Ford F-150?

A: I don't "claim" anything. I saw it.

Q: Of course. Now, how far would you estimate your porch is from the intersection where the accident occurred?

A: Maybe sixty, seventy feet. Close enough.

Q: Close enough for what, exactly?

A: Close enough to see what happened. Which is why I'm here, I assume.

Q: Were you wearing your prescription glasses at the time?

A: I was. And before you ask, yes, my prescription is current, and no, I don't have cataracts.

Q: I hadn't asked about cataracts, Mr. Fontaine.

A: I've been deposed before, counselor. I know where these questions go.

Q: Let's stay focused on what you observed. Which vehicle entered the intersection first?

A: The Honda. The truck ran the stop sign. That's the whole story, unless you're planning to ask me about my hearing next.

Q: Did you see the truck's driver before the impact?

A: I saw enough to know he wasn't looking at the road. He was looking down at something. Phone, maybe. I'm not going to guess beyond what I saw.

Q: But you are guessing that it was a phone?

A: I said "maybe." You do understand what "maybe" means?

topic: A witness is asked about a car accident they saw from their front porch
text:
Q: Ms. Delacroix, I want to walk through the moments just before the collision. You said you heard something first?

A: Yes. Tires. That squealing sound, you know. I looked up from my book.

Q: And what did you see when you looked up?

A: The blue car—the Camry, I think they told me it was—it was already skidding. Like sideways, almost.

Q: Already skidding. So you didn't see what caused the driver to brake?

A: No, I just saw the skid and then the crash.

Q: Ms. Delacroix, I'm going to ask you to think carefully. In your written statement to police, you said you saw the Camry "flying down the street."

A: I don't remember saying "flying."

Q: I have the statement here. Would you like to review it?

A: I suppose I should, if you're going to quote it back to me.

Q: Take your time.

A: Okay. I see it. I guess I did say that. But I meant it was moving fast. Not literally flying, obviously.

Q: How fast, in your estimation?

A: I don't know. I'm not a speed gun.

Q: Faster than the posted limit of twenty-five miles per hour?

A: I couldn't say for certain. It seemed fast. That's all I can tell you.

Q: It seemed fast. But you can't say how fast.

A: No. I can't. Is there a question in there?

Q: Let me ask it differently. Did the Camry appear to be traveling at an unsafe speed for a residential street?

A: It seemed fast to me. I've answered this three times now.

topic: A witness is asked about a car accident they saw from their front porch
text:
Q: Mr. Okonkwo, how long have you lived at 414 Maple Street?

A: Eleven years this past March.

Q: And in those eleven years, have you witnessed other accidents at that intersection?

A: A few. Minor ones. Fender benders, mostly.

Q: So you're familiar with how traffic typically moves through there?

A: I'd say so, yes.

Q: On August 14th, you were sitting on your porch when the accident occurred. What drew your attention to the vehicles?

A: Nothing drew my attention. I was just sitting there and I saw it happen.

Q: You weren't reading, or on your phone, or—

A: I was watching the street. Is that unusual?

Q: I'm just trying to understand your state of attention at the time.

A: My state of attention was fine. I was watching the street, like I said.

Q: The black SUV—where was it when you first noticed it?

A: Coming down Maple, heading east. Maybe four houses away.

Q: And the motorcycle?

A: Coming from the cross street. Birch. I saw it a second or two before they hit.

Q: Only a second or two?

A: Maybe three. It was quick.

Q: In that second or two, did you see the SUV's brake lights?

A: No.

Q: You're certain?

A: I just said no. No brake lights.

Q: Mr. Okonkwo, is it possible you simply didn't notice them?

A: Counselor, I've been watching cars at that intersection for eleven years. I know what brake lights look like, and I know when they're not there.

topic: A witness is asked about a car accident they saw from their front porch
text:
Q: Mrs. Yamamoto, you mentioned in your initial statement that the weather was overcast. Do you recall that?

A: Yes, it was gray out. Not raining yet, but it looked like it might.

Q: Did the overcast conditions affect visibility in any way?

A: I don't think so. It was the middle of the afternoon. Plenty of light.

Q: Now, you've testified that the white sedan ran the red light. I want to make sure I understand what you actually saw.

A: I saw the light. It was red. The sedan went through it.

Q: Where exactly were you looking when the sedan entered the intersection?

A: At the intersection.

Q: At the light specifically, or at the vehicles?

A: Both. The whole area. I don't have tunnel vision, counselor.

Q: I'm trying to establish your precise line of sight. The traffic light—which one were you able to see from your porch?

A: The one facing the sedan's direction. Eastbound.

Q: And you're certain it was red and not yellow transitioning to red?

A: It was red.

Q: For how long before the sedan entered the intersection?

A: I don't know. A few seconds at least. I wasn't counting.

Q: But you were watching the light closely enough to know it was red, just not closely enough to estimate how long?

A: I know a red light when I see one. What exactly are you trying to get me to say?

Q: I'm not trying to get you to say anything, Mrs. Yamamoto. I'm trying to establish facts.

A: Then I've given you the fact. The light was red. He ran it. That's what I saw.

topic: A witness is asked about a car accident they saw from their front porch
text:
Q: Mr. Reeves, let me direct your attention to the pickup truck. You said it was green?

A: Dark green, yeah. Older model. Maybe a Chevy.

Q: Maybe a Chevy. You're not certain of the make?

A: I'm not a car expert. It was a green pickup truck.

Q: Did you happen to notice the license plate?

A: No.

Q: Any bumper stickers, decals, anything distinguishing?

A: Not that I remember.

Q: What about damage to the vehicle—before the collision, I mean. Any dents, rust, anything like that?

A: I wasn't studying it. I was just sitting on my porch and then suddenly there was a crash.

Q: Let's talk about "suddenly." How much time elapsed between when you first noticed the truck and when the collision occurred?

A: I don't know. Seconds.

Q: Five seconds? Ten? Two?

A: I said I don't know. Why does it matter exactly how many seconds?

Q: I'm trying to understand what you had time to observe.

A: I had time to see a truck run into a minivan. That's what I had time to observe.

Q: The minivan—did it have its turn signal on?

A: I think so. Yes.

Q: You think so, or yes?

A: Yes. Left turn signal.

Q: And the truck made no attempt to brake or swerve before impact?

A: None that I could see.

Q: Mr. Reeves, you seem quite certain about some details and quite uncertain about others.

A: I saw what I saw, counselor. I'm not going to make things up to fill in your blanks.

topic: A former employee is deposed about discriminatory remarks made by a supervisor
text:
Q: Ms. Patterson, I'd like to direct your attention to the meeting on March 14th of last year. You were present when Mr. Hendricks addressed the sales team, correct?

A: I was there, yes.

Q: And during that meeting, Mr. Hendricks made a comment about, quote, "women not having the stomach for this kind of work," end quote. Did you hear that statement?

A: He said something. I'm not sure those were the exact words.

Q: What words did he use, to the best of your recollection?

A: It was... he was talking about the quarterly push, and he said something about—I want to say it was about stamina? Or maybe it was—no, wait. He definitely mentioned women. But "stomach," I don't—I'm sorry, can you tell me where you're getting that quote from?

Q: I'm asking what you remember, Ms. Patterson.

A: Right, but I'm trying to remember, and I want to make sure I'm not mixing it up with something else he said another time. There were a lot of meetings.

Q: Let's stay with March 14th. Did Mr. Hendricks make any reference to women during that meeting?

A: Yes. I believe so. Yes.

Q: What did he say?

A: He said—okay, I think he said something like women on the team needed to toughen up. Or that the women—no, that's not quite it either. I'm sorry. I remember being uncomfortable. I remember that clearly. The exact phrasing is harder.

Q: Did anyone else react to the comment?

A: Karen looked at me. I remember that.

Q: Karen Volz?

A: Yes. She looked at me, and I looked at her, and we both just sort of—we didn't say anything. But we knew.

Q: You knew what?

A: That it was... that it wasn't right. What he said.

Q: But you can't tell me what he said.

A: I told you what I remember. I'm doing my best here.

---

topic: A former employee is deposed about discriminatory remarks made by a supervisor
text:
Q: Mr. Okonkwo, you reported directly to Diane Fleischer for how long?

A: Fourteen months.

Q: During those fourteen months, did Ms. Fleischer ever make comments about employees' national origins?

A: She made a lot of comments about a lot of things.

Q: I'm asking specifically about national origin.

A: I know what you're asking.

Q: Then please answer the question.

A: Yes. She did.

Q: Can you give me an example?

A: She asked me once where I was "really from."

Q: When was this?

A: Maybe June of 2022. Maybe July.

Q: What were the circumstances?

A: We were in her office. She was giving me feedback on a client presentation.

Q: And she asked where you were "really from" during a feedback session about a presentation?

A: That's what I said.

Q: Help me understand the context. How did the conversation move from presentation feedback to that question?

A: I don't know how to help you understand it. It happened. She said my communication style might be—she used the word "cultural." Then she asked where I was really from.

Q: Did she say anything else?

A: She said people from "over there" sometimes have trouble adjusting to American business norms. She said it like she was helping me.

Q: "Over there." Did she specify a location?

A: No. And I didn't ask. I was born in Cleveland.

Q: Did you tell her that?

A: I did.

Q: What was her response?

A: She said, "You know what I mean."

Q: Did you know what she meant?

A: I knew exactly what she meant.

---

topic: A former employee is deposed about discriminatory remarks made by a supervisor
text:
Q: Let's turn to the incident on September 8th. You were in the break room?

A: Yes.

Q: And Mr. Castellano was there as well?

A: Yes, him and two others.

Q: Who were the others?

A: I think it was Priya Sharma and—I want to say Devon? The new hire?

Q: Devon Albright?

A: Maybe. There's been a lot of turnover. I'm not certain.

Q: All right. What happened in the break room?

A: Mr. Castellano was telling a joke.

Q: What kind of joke?

A: A joke about—hold on. I want to get this right. It was something about... I think the setup was about a job interview? And the punchline involved an accent. An Asian accent. He was doing a voice.

Q: What did the voice sound like?

A: It was—like a stereotype. You know. The kind of voice people do when they're mocking—look, it was offensive. That's the point.

Q: Did anyone laugh?

A: Devon did. Priya didn't.

Q: What did you do?

A: Nothing. I left.

Q: You left the break room?

A: I wasn't going to stand there and—yes. I left. I went back to my desk.

Q: Wait—did you leave before or after the punchline?

A: After. I heard the whole thing.

Q: But you just said you left. I'm trying to understand the sequence.

A: I heard the joke. The whole joke. Then I left. That's the sequence.

Q: How long after the punchline did you leave?

A: I don't know. Immediately? A few seconds? I didn't have a stopwatch.

Q: I'm just trying to get the facts straight, Ms. Yuen.

A: And I'm trying to give them to you.

---

topic: A former employee is deposed about discriminatory remarks made by a supervisor
text:
Q: Mr. Pearce, you've testified that you overheard a conversation between Mr. Whitmore and Ms. Delgado. Is that correct?

A: Yes.

Q: Where were you standing when you heard this conversation?

A: I was in the hallway outside Mr. Whitmore's office.

Q: The door was open?

A: Yes.

Q: Could you see into the office?

A: Partially. I wasn't trying to eavesdrop. I was waiting to ask him about a supply order.

Q: Understood. Now—this conversation. It concerned Ms. Delgado's upcoming maternity leave?

A: Hold on—I don't think I said that.

Q: Page 34 of your declaration, Mr. Pearce. "The conversation concerned Ms. Delgado's maternity leave."

A: Can I see that?

Q: [Handing document] Take your time.

A: Okay. Yes. I see what I wrote. But reading this now, I—when I wrote "concerned," I meant it came up. I didn't mean the whole conversation was about that.

Q: What was the conversation about, then?

A: Scheduling, I think. A project timeline. And then her leave came up in that context.

Q: And what did Mr. Whitmore say about her leave?

A: He said something like—this is where I want to be careful—he said it was inconvenient timing.

Q: "Inconvenient timing."

A: Or bad timing. One of those.

Q: Which one?

A: I'm not sure anymore.

Q: In your declaration, you wrote "terrible timing."

A: Did I?

Q: Page 34, line 8.

A: Then I must have remembered it more clearly back then. I wrote that declaration two weeks after it happened. It's been eight months now.

Q: So "terrible timing" is more likely accurate?

A: I suppose so. I don't know why I'd have written it otherwise.

---

topic: A former employee is deposed about discriminatory remarks made by a supervisor
text:
Q: Ms. Trần, let me ask you about the performance review you received in October 2023. You recall that review?

A: I do.

Q: Who conducted the review?

A: It was supposed to be my direct supervisor, Mr. Holt. But Mr. Greer sat in.

Q: Why did Mr. Greer sit in?

A: Nobody told me why.

Q: Did you ask?

A: No.

Q: During that review, were any comments made that you found discriminatory?

A: Mr. Greer said I needed to be "less passive."

Q: "Less passive." How is that discriminatory?

A: It's what he said after.

Q: What did he say after?

A: He said he understood it might be a "cultural thing" but that I needed to speak up more if I wanted to be taken seriously.

Q: Did he specify what culture he was referring to?

A: No.

Q: Did you ask him to clarify?

A: Why would I do that?

Q: I'm simply asking whether you did.

A: No. I didn't.

Q: So when he said "cultural thing," you don't actually know what he meant by that.

A: I know what he meant.

Q: How do you know?

A: Because I was sitting right there. Because of the way he looked at me when he said it. Because he'd never said anything like that to Emily or Marcus, and they're just as quiet as I am. Quieter, actually.

Q: You've observed their performance reviews?

A: I've observed them in meetings. I know how they are.

Q: But you haven't observed their reviews.

A: No. I haven't.

Q: So you don't know what feedback they've received.

A: I know what feedback I received. I know what it meant.

Q: Ms. Trần, I'm trying to understand the basis for your interpretation.

A: And I'm trying to tell you. You're just not hearing it.

topic: A tenant is questioned about property damage they reported to their landlord
text:
Q: Mr. Hernandez, when did you first notice the water damage in the kitchen ceiling?

A: March 14th. I documented it immediately—photographs, written notes, even measured the affected area. I have a system for these things.

Q: A system?

A: I've been renting properties for twelve years. I've learned that landlords respond better when you present them with organized, professional documentation. So yes, a system.

Q: And what did your documentation show?

A: The discoloration covered approximately eighteen inches in diameter initially. I photographed it at 7:42 a.m. that morning, then again at 2:15 p.m. when I noticed expansion. By evening, it had grown to roughly twenty-six inches.

Q: You measured it multiple times in one day?

A: Of course. How else would I establish a timeline of the landlord's failure to respond?

Q: Did you report this to Mr. Patterson that same day?
