A: Within the hour of first discovery. Email, followed by a phone call, followed by a certified letter. I believe in redundancy when dealing with property management.

Q: That seems thorough.

A: It's what any responsible tenant should do. Most people don't understand how to protect themselves. I do.

Q: And you kept copies of all these communications?

A: Naturally. Would you like to see the binder? I organized it chronologically with tabs for each category of correspondence.

Q: That won't be necessary right now. What was Mr. Patterson's initial response?

A: Inadequate. But that's in the record. As I documented.

topic: A tenant is questioned about property damage they reported to their landlord
text:
Q: Ms. Chen, I want to direct your attention to the photographs you submitted to the property management company. You took these yourself?

A: Yes.

Q: All of them?

A: Every single one.

Q: Now, I've reviewed hundreds of tenant damage reports in my career, and I have to say—these are remarkably well-composed. The lighting, the angles, the detail captured. Tell me about your process.

A: I just took pictures of the damage.

Q: With what device?

A: My phone.

Q: These look almost professional. Did someone assist you?

A: No. I worked as a real estate photographer for three years before my current job. It's not complicated—you learn to document spaces accurately.

Q: So you brought professional expertise to documenting this damage?

A: I brought basic competence. Anyone could do it if they paid attention.

Q: But not everyone would think to capture the water staining at that particular angle, showing how it spread from the window frame. That took some forethought?

A: It took looking at the wall and understanding what I was seeing.

Q: You're being modest, Ms. Chen. These photographs essentially built your case.

A: I'm being accurate. The photographs documented what existed. The damage built the case.

Q: Fair enough. Now, the written report you submitted alongside these photos—

A: Also accurate. Also thorough. Also something anyone should be capable of producing when their living space is being damaged by negligence.

topic: A tenant is questioned about property damage they reported to their landlord
text:
Q: When you called maintenance on November 3rd, what exactly did you tell them?

A: That the baseboard heating unit in the bedroom was malfunctioning and I could smell something burning.

Q: Those were your exact words?

A: Close enough. I might have said "electrical smell" rather than "burning." I was precise.

Q: You were precise.

A: I'm always precise when it matters.

Q: And what happened after that call?

A: Nothing. For four days.

Q: Did you follow up?

A: I followed up seven times across those four days. I have the call log.

Q: Seven times seems—

A: It seems like exactly what was necessary when a landlord ignores a potential fire hazard in a tenant's bedroom.

Q: I wasn't criticizing you, Mr. Okonkwo.

A: I didn't assume you were.

Q: Let me rephrase. What was the property manager's explanation for the delay?

A: They claimed they had no record of my initial call. Which is why I had already begun documenting every interaction in writing after the third attempt.

Q: So you anticipated they might deny receiving your complaints?

A: I anticipated the need for evidence. There's a difference.

Q: Is that something you typically do—anticipate problems with landlords?

A: It's something I learned to do after watching other tenants get dismissed. I don't intend to be dismissed.

topic: A tenant is questioned about property damage they reported to their landlord
text:
Q: The mold inspection report dated June 22nd—you arranged for this independently?

A: Yes.

Q: Without consulting your landlord first?

A: I notified them of visible mold growth twice. They sent someone to paint over it. So yes, I arranged my own inspection.

Q: And you paid for this out of pocket?

A: $340.

Q: That's a significant expense.

A: Living with toxic mold is a more significant expense.

Q: The inspector—how did you select them?

A: I researched certified environmental inspectors in the area. Checked credentials, read reviews, confirmed they had no relationship with any property management companies locally.

Q: You were concerned about bias?

A: I was concerned about thoroughness. The inspector I chose had twenty years of experience and had served as an expert witness in eleven mold-related cases.

Q: You verified all of this before hiring them?

A: Is there another way to select an expert?

Q: Some people just search online and pick the first name that appears.

A: Some people also accept landlords painting over active mold growth. I'm not some people.

Q: The report found elevated spore counts in three rooms?

A: Four rooms. The bathroom, both bedrooms, and the hallway closet. It's in the summary. First page.

Q: Yes, I see that now. Thank you.

A: You're welcome. Would you like me to explain what the spore count numbers indicate? I've done considerable reading on the subject.

topic: A tenant is questioned about property damage they reported to their landlord
text:
Q: Ms. Reyes, your repair request mentioned a "persistent sewage odor." How long had you noticed this smell before reporting it?

A: Maybe a day.

Q: Just one day?

A: I don't ignore problems in my home.

Q: That's commendable. And when you reported it, what exactly did you say?

A: I described the smell, identified that it seemed to be coming from the area around the toilet base, and noted that I had checked and the wax ring appeared to be failing.

Q: You diagnosed the problem yourself?

A: I observed what was visible. The wax ring was visibly deteriorated.

Q: Do you have a background in plumbing?

A: I have a background in being a capable adult who understands how basic fixtures work.

Q: I didn't mean to suggest otherwise.

A: My father was a building superintendent. I spent my childhood learning how things break and why landlords pretend not to notice.

Q: So you came into this tenancy with certain... expectations?

A: I came into this tenancy with knowledge. There's nothing wrong with knowing things.

Q: Of course not. When the repair person finally arrived, did they confirm your assessment?

A: They replaced the wax ring exactly as I had recommended, yes.

Q: Did they say anything about your diagnosis?

A: He asked if I was a plumber. I told him no. He said I should be.

Q: And that was the extent of the repair?

A: That was the extent of what should have taken two days, not two weeks.

topic: A witness is questioned about a fire they discovered in a neighboring unit
text:
Q: Please state your name for the record.

A: Maria Costello.

Q: Ms. Costello, I understand you were the first person to discover the fire on the evening of March 14th. Before we get into the details, I want you to know you can take your time with these questions. There's no rush here.

A: Thank you. I appreciate that.

Q: Can you tell me, in your own words, what you first noticed that evening?

A: I was coming home from my shift—I work nights at the hospital—and I smelled smoke in the hallway. At first I thought someone had just burned something on the stove, you know, the way it happens. But it got stronger as I walked toward my door.

Q: What did you do when you realized it was more serious?

A: I knocked on Mrs. Patterson's door. Unit 4B. She's eighty-three years old and she lives alone, and I just—I needed to make sure she was okay. That was the first thing I thought of. Not the fire, really. Her.

Q: That must have been a frightening moment.

A: It was. She moves slowly, you know. She has trouble with her hip. And I kept knocking and calling her name, and there was no answer, and the smoke was getting thicker.

Q: Take a moment if you need to.

A: I'm okay. I just—I think about what could have happened if I'd gotten home ten minutes later.

Q: Did Mrs. Patterson eventually come to the door?

A: She did. She'd been asleep. She didn't even know anything was wrong. I had to help her down the stairs because the elevator—they tell you not to use it during a fire.

Q: You helped her evacuate?

A: I carried her bag. She kept saying she needed her medications, so I went back in and got them. Probably shouldn't have done that, but I couldn't just leave her without them.

Q: I understand. After you got Mrs. Patterson outside, what happened next?

A: The fire department was already there. Someone else must have called. I just sat with her on the bench across the street until her daughter came. She was shaking. I don't think it was cold. I think she was scared.

Q: Is there anything else you remember from that night that you think is important?

A: Just that she held my hand the whole time we waited. I don't think she wanted to be alone.

---

topic: A witness is questioned about a fire they discovered in a neighboring unit
text:
Q: You've stated you live in Unit 6A of the Briarwood Apartments, correct?

A: That's correct.

Q: And the fire originated in Unit 5A, directly below you?

A: That's what they told me afterward, yes.

Q: Mr. Chen, walk me through the sequence of events as you experienced them on the night of the fire.

A: I was watching television. Around nine, maybe nine-fifteen. My dog started acting strange—pacing, whining at the door. He's never like that.

Q: What did you do?

A: I opened my door to see if something was going on in the hallway. That's when I saw the smoke coming up through the floor vents.

Q: The smoke was entering your unit through the ventilation system?

A: Yes. And I could hear—this is hard to talk about—I could hear someone coughing downstairs. Really struggling. That wet, painful kind of cough.

Q: Did you attempt to go downstairs?

A: I did. I grabbed a towel, wet it, put it over my face. I know they say you shouldn't do that, but I could hear him. Mr. Reeves. He's a veteran, lives alone. I couldn't just—I'm sorry, give me a second.

Q: Of course. Take whatever time you need.

A: He was on the floor when I found him. Just inside his door. The smoke was so thick I almost missed him.

Q: You found Mr. Reeves incapacitated inside Unit 5A?

A: He was conscious, but barely. He kept trying to tell me to leave, to save myself. Even then, he was worried about me. That's the kind of man he is.

Q: How did you get him out of the unit?

A: I pulled him. Dragged him, really. He's a big guy, and I'm not—I'm not strong. But you don't think about that. You just do it.

Q: Did you sustain any injuries during this?

A: Some smoke inhalation. Burns on my hands from the door handle. Nothing compared to what could have happened to him.

Q: Mr. Chen, I have to ask—did you at any point see how the fire started?

A: No. I didn't care about that. I just wanted to get him out alive.

---

topic: A witness is questioned about a fire they discovered in a neighboring unit
text:
Q: State your full name.

A: Denise Marlowe.

Q: Ms. Marlowe, you were present in the building the night of the fire?

A: I was.

Q: And you personally witnessed the fire in Unit 2C?

A: I discovered it. Yes.

Q: Discovered it how?

A: I was bringing a casserole to the Okonkwos. They'd just had a baby three weeks prior, and I know how hard those first weeks are. Nobody sleeps. Nobody has time to cook.

Q: So you were approaching their unit with food?

A: With food, yes. And I noticed their door was open. Not all the way—cracked. And there was this orange light flickering from inside that didn't look right.

Q: What did you do?

A: I pushed the door open. The curtains in the living room were on fire. The whole window was just—it was engulfed. And I could hear the baby crying from the back bedroom.

Q: The family was still inside?

A: Adaeze—Mrs. Okonkwo—she was in the bedroom with the baby. She didn't even know. She'd been trying to get the baby to sleep and she had one of those white noise machines going. She didn't hear it, didn't smell it yet.

Q: How did you alert her?

A: I screamed. I just screamed her name as loud as I could. And then I ran to the kitchen to see if there was a fire extinguisher, but I couldn't find one, and the flames were spreading to the couch.

Q: Did Mrs. Okonkwo evacuate with the baby?

A: She came running out with him wrapped in a blanket. Her face—I'll never forget her face. The terror of realizing what could have happened.

Q: Where was Mr. Okonkwo during this?

A: At work. Night shift at the hospital. He didn't know until Adaeze called him from outside.

Q: Ms. Marlowe, do you need a moment?

A: No, I'm fine. I just keep thinking—if I hadn't decided to bring that casserole over that night. If I'd waited until morning like I almost did.

Q: You potentially saved their lives.

A: I just brought a casserole. That's all I did. The rest was just—being in the right place.

---

topic: A witness is questioned about a fire they discovered in a neighboring unit
text:
Q: For the record, please state your name.

A: Thomas Whitfield.

Q: Mr. Whitfield, you're the building superintendent at Maple Creek Condominiums?

A: Going on twelve years now.

Q: So you know the residents well?

A: Most of them, yes. It's a small building. Twenty-two units. People come and go, but some have been here as long as I have.

Q: Tell me about discovering the fire in Unit 14.

A: I was doing my evening rounds. Checking the boiler, making sure the back door was locked. Standard things. And I noticed the smoke detector going off on the third floor. The panel in my office shows which unit.

Q: What did you do?

A: I went up immediately. Unit 14 is—was—Mrs. Yates. Evelyn Yates. Lovely woman. Husband passed two years ago. She makes cookies for me every Christmas.

Q: You knew her personally.

A: I know everyone personally. That's my job. And it's also just—it's how I am.

Q: What did you find when you reached Unit 14?

A: Smoke pouring from under the door. I have a master key, so I went in. The kitchen was fully involved. Something on the stove, I think. A pot.

Q: Was Mrs. Yates inside?

A: She was sitting in her chair in the living room. She has dementia—I don't know if you knew that. Early stages, but it's progressed this past year. She didn't seem to understand what was happening. She asked me if I was there to fix the radiator.

Q: That must have been difficult to witness.

A: I just picked her up. She weighs almost nothing these days. I carried her out and down the stairs and I called 911 from the lobby.

Q: Did you attempt to extinguish the fire yourself?

A: No. I'm trained not to. My priority was Evelyn. The building can be fixed. She can't be replaced.

Q: Mr. Whitfield, do you know if Mrs. Yates has family who looks after her?

A: A son in Portland. He calls every Sunday. I've been meaning to call him myself, actually. Just to let him know she's okay. That someone was looking out for her.

Q: I'm sure he'd appreciate that.

A: It's the least I can do.

---

topic: A witness is questioned about a fire they discovered in a neighboring unit
text:
Q: Can you state your name and unit number?

A: James Delacroix. Unit 8.

Q: Mr. Delacroix, you were one of the first people to respond to the fire in Unit 7?

A: Respond. That's a word for it.

Q: Can you describe what happened in your own words?

A: I heard glass breaking. My bedroom shares a wall with their kitchen—Unit 7, I mean. The Harrisons. So I heard the window blow out, and then I smelled the smoke.

Q: What time was this?

A: Around two in the morning. I wasn't sleeping well that night anyway. My wife passed six months ago, and I still reach for her side of the bed.

Q: I'm sorry for your loss.

A: Thank you. That's kind of you to say.

Q: Can you continue with what happened after you heard the glass break?

A: I went into the hallway. Kevin Harrison—he's maybe thirty, thirty-two—he was already out there in his boxers, banging on my door. His wife and daughter were still inside. He was panicked. Completely panicked. Couldn't form words properly.

Q: What was he trying to communicate?

A: That Sophie—their daughter, she's four—was in her bedroom near the back of the unit. The fire was between him and her room. He couldn't get to her.

Q: What did you do?

A: My unit has a balcony that connects to theirs. There's a divider, but you can climb over it. I've never done it before, but I knew it was there.

Q: You accessed their unit through the balcony?

A: I'm sixty-seven years old. I don't climb anything anymore. But that little girl—I could hear her calling for her daddy. You don't think about your knees when you hear that.

Q: You reached Sophie?

A: I got to her room from the balcony door. She was standing in her crib, crying. I picked her up and I just held her and told her it was going to be okay, that I was going to bring her to her daddy.

Q: And you brought her out safely?

A: Through my unit. Carried her right through my living room and out into the hallway where Kevin was waiting. He fell to his knees when he saw her. Just collapsed right there holding her.

Q: Mr. Delacroix, is there anything else you'd like to add to the record?

A: Only that I've lived alone in that unit since Margaret died. And I've been asking myself what I'm still doing here. That night gave me an answer.

topic: A store manager is questioned about a customer slip-and-fall on their premises
text:
Q: Mr. Donovan, you stated earlier that the floor was inspected at 2:15 p.m. Is that correct?

A: That's what the log shows, yes.

Q: And the incident occurred at approximately 2:45 p.m.?

A: According to the report, yes.

Q: So in your view, thirty minutes is a reasonable inspection interval for a high-traffic area?

A: I didn't say that was my view. I said that's what the log shows. Corporate sets the inspection protocols.

Q: I see. And you follow those protocols exactly as written?

A: We follow them, yes.

Q: Every time? Without exception?

A: I'm not sure what you're asking. We follow the protocols.

Q: Let me be more specific. On March 14th, the day of the incident, did anyone deviate from the inspection schedule?

A: Not that I'm aware of.

Q: Not that you're aware of. Were you in the store that day?

A: I was in the back office for part of the afternoon. I can't account for every minute of every employee's shift.

Q: So it's possible an inspection was missed?

A: Anything's possible, counselor. I can only tell you what the documentation reflects.

Q: And the documentation is always accurate?

A: I wouldn't have any reason to believe otherwise.

topic: A store manager is questioned about a customer slip-and-fall on their premises
text:
Q: Ms. Chen, walk me through what you personally observed after the fall.

A: I heard someone yell, and I came out from behind the register. Mrs. Patterson was on the ground near the produce section.

Q: What was on the floor?

A: There was some water. A small amount.

Q: A small amount. Can you quantify that?

A: I don't know, maybe a few tablespoons? It wasn't a puddle or anything.

Q: A few tablespoons of water caused a customer to fall?

A: I didn't say it caused anything. You asked what was on the floor.

Q: Fair enough. Where did this water come from?

A: I have no idea.

Q: You have no idea.

A: No.

Q: The produce section has misters, doesn't it?

A: It does.

Q: And those misters were operational that day?

A: As far as I know.

Q: But you didn't check?

A: I was focused on the customer on the ground, not investigating the misters.

Q: At any point did you photograph the area?

A: No. We called for assistance and helped her to a chair.

Q: Whose decision was it not to photograph the scene?

A: It wasn't a decision. It just—nobody thought to do it in the moment. We were concerned about the woman who fell.

topic: A store manager is questioned about a customer slip-and-fall on their premises
text:
Q: Mr. Reeves, how long have you been store manager at this location?

A: Eleven years this October.

Q: And in those eleven years, how many slip-and-fall incidents have occurred?

A: I'd have to check the records to give you an exact number.

Q: Approximately.

A: Maybe five or six? It's a grocery store. These things happen occasionally.

Q: These things happen.

A: Yes.

Q: So this is just routine to you?

A: I didn't say that. I said incidents occur from time to time in any retail environment. That's not the same as saying they're routine or that we don't take them seriously.

Q: Tell me about your wet floor signage policy.

A: When a spill is identified, we put out signs and address it immediately.

Q: Were signs out before Mrs. Okafor fell?

A: No.

Q: Why not?

A: Because no one had identified a spill in that area.

Q: So there was no spill?

A: I didn't say that either. I said no one had identified one. There's a difference.

Q: Help me understand the difference, Mr. Reeves.

A: The difference is that a spill can exist without someone having seen it yet. We can't put up signs for something we don't know about.

Q: How often do your employees walk that aisle?

A: Frequently. But not constantly. We have twenty-two thousand square feet and six employees on a weekday afternoon.

topic: A store manager is questioned about a customer slip-and-fall on their premises
text:
Q: You mentioned you reviewed the security footage after the incident?

A: I did.

Q: What did you observe?

A: I saw the customer walking through the aisle, and then she went down.

Q: She went down.

A: She fell. Yes.

Q: Could you see what caused her to fall?

A: The footage isn't high resolution. I couldn't see anything specific on the floor.

Q: But you could see her fall clearly?

A: I could see that she fell, yes.

Q: Did she appear to slip, or trip, or lose her balance?

A: I'm not qualified to characterize her body mechanics from a grainy video.

Q: I'm asking for your observation, Ms. Thornton, not a medical opinion.

A: And my observation is that I saw her walking, and then she was on the ground. I don't want to speculate about what happened in between.

Q: Where is that footage now?

A: It's been preserved per our retention policy.

Q: Your retention policy. How long does that footage get retained?

A: Ninety days typically, but once there's an incident report, we flag it for indefinite retention.

Q: Was it flagged immediately?

A: It was flagged within twenty-four hours. Per policy.

Q: Per policy. Who made that decision?

A: I did, after consulting with our district manager.

topic: A store manager is questioned about a customer slip-and-fall on their premises
text:
Q: Mr. Hawkins, the incident report says the floor was dry when you arrived at the scene. You wrote that?

A: I did.

Q: How did you determine the floor was dry?

A: I looked at it. I touched it with my hand.

Q: You touched it.

A: Yes. I crouched down and felt the floor with my palm.

Q: And this was how long after Mrs. Delgado fell?

A: Maybe four, five minutes.

Q: In those four or five minutes, is it possible any liquid could have been absorbed or spread by foot traffic?

A: I suppose anything's possible.

Q: But you still wrote "floor was dry."

A: Because when I checked it, it was dry. I reported what I found.

Q: Did you check Mrs. Delgado's shoes?

A: Excuse me?

Q: Her shoes. Did you examine them for moisture?

A: No.

Q: Her clothing?

A: No.

Q: So you didn't actually investigate whether she had encountered liquid—you just checked one spot on the floor several minutes later?

A: I checked the area where she fell. That's standard procedure.

Q: Whose standard procedure?

A: Ours. The company's.

Q: And the company trained you to conclude a floor was dry based on a single touch test five minutes after an incident?

A: The company trained me to assess the scene and document what I observe. Which is what I did.

topic: A witness is questioned about events at a party where an assault allegedly occurred
text:
Q: Mr. Hernandez, let me take you back to the evening of March 14th. You were at the residence on Oakmont Drive, correct?

A: Yes.

Q: And approximately what time did you arrive at the party?

A: I don't know. Nine, maybe. Somewhere around nine.

Q: You don't recall the specific time?

A: I said around nine. I wasn't checking my watch every five minutes.

Q: Fair enough. Now, when you arrived, who was already present?

A: Look, there were... I don't know, maybe twenty people? I didn't take attendance.

Q: I'm not asking for a complete roster. Did you see the defendant, Marcus Webb, when you arrived?

A: Yes.

Q: Where was he?

A: Kitchen. Near the kitchen. One of those.

Q: Which was it, Mr. Hernandez? In the kitchen or near the kitchen?

A: Does it matter? He was in that general area. I walked in, I saw him, I got a drink. That's what I remember.

Q: And the complainant, Jessica Torres—did you see her at that time?

A: Not right then. Later.

Q: How much later?

A: I don't know. Some amount of time. I really couldn't tell you.

Q: An hour? Two hours?

A: Maybe an hour. Maybe less. I wasn't keeping track of any of this. I was just at a party.

topic: A witness is questioned about events at a party where an assault allegedly occurred
text:
Q: Ms. Chen, you indicated in your initial statement that you witnessed a confrontation between two individuals. Is that correct?

A: Yes, that's correct.

Q: Okay. And... let me find this here. You said the confrontation occurred in the backyard. Is that your testimony today?

A: It is.

Q: Alright. So. The backyard. Can you describe... um, can you describe the lighting conditions in the backyard at that time?

A: There were string lights along the fence. Some light coming from inside the house through the sliding doors. A porch light, I think.

Q: So you could see clearly?

A: I could see well enough to observe what happened, yes.

Q: Right. And you were positioned where, exactly?

A: By the fire pit. There were chairs set up around it.

Q: How far from the... from where the confrontation took place?

A: Maybe fifteen feet. Possibly twenty.

Q: Fifteen or twenty. And from that distance, in that lighting, you observed what exactly?

A: I saw a man grab another man by the collar and push him against the fence.

Q: You saw that clearly.

A: I did.

Q: ...Alright. Let's move on. Did you hear what was said between them?

A: Some of it.

Q: Some of it. Which parts did you hear, Ms. Chen?

A: The man doing the pushing said something like "stay away from her." I heard that clearly.

topic: A witness is questioned about events at a party where an assault allegedly occurred
text:
Q: Tell me what you observed when you entered the living room.

A: There was broken glass on the floor. A woman was crying. Several people were standing around looking shocked.

Q: What kind of glass?

A: I think it was from a beer bottle, but I'm not completely certain. It could have been a glass. A drinking glass, I mean. It was in pieces, so it was difficult to determine the original vessel with any real certainty.

Q: Did you see how the glass came to be broken?

A: No, I was in another room when it happened. I only came in after I heard the crash. Though I should clarify that when I say "crash," I mean I heard a sound that I interpreted as something breaking. I didn't actually see the moment of impact.

Q: Who was in the room when you entered?

A: The woman who was crying—I later learned her name was Danielle. There was a man standing near the window. Two other women by the couch. And someone was leaving through the doorway to the kitchen as I entered, though I only caught a partial glimpse of that person.

Q: The man by the window—can you describe him?

A: Tall. Taller than me, and I'm five-ten, so I'd estimate he was somewhere between six feet and six-two, though that's an approximation based on my perception at the time, which may have been affected by the distance between us and my own position in the room.

Q: Was he the defendant?

A: I... I believe so, yes. Though I want to be careful. I'm basing that identification on subsequent photographs I was shown, and I want to be accurate in distinguishing between what I observed that night and what I learned afterward.

Q: I understand. What was this man doing when you entered?

A: Standing there. His hands were at his sides. He appeared... still. Very still. Just standing there.

topic: A witness is questioned about events at a party where an assault allegedly occurred
text:
Q: You were in the hallway when you heard shouting?

A: Yeah.

Q: What did you do?

A: Went toward it.

Q: Toward the shouting.

A: That's what I said.

Q: And where did that lead you?

A: The back bedroom.

Q: What did you see there?

A: Two guys. One had the other one against the wall.

Q: Can you describe them?

A: One was wearing a red shirt. The other one, I don't remember what he was wearing.

Q: Which one was against the wall?

A: Red shirt.

Q: Did you recognize either of them?

A: The one doing the pushing. I'd seen him earlier.

Q: Where had you seen him?

A: Out front. When I got there. He was smoking on the porch.

Q: Did you know his name?

A: No.

Q: Have you since learned his name?

A: Yeah.

Q: What is it?

A: They told me it was Derek Paulson.

topic: A witness is questioned about events at a party where an assault allegedly occurred
text:
Q: I want to be very precise about the sequence of events, Mr. Okonkwo. You've testified that you saw Ms. Reyes leave the kitchen. What happened immediately after that?

A: She walked toward the front of the house.

Q: Did you follow her?

A: No.

Q: Did anyone follow her?

A: I wasn't watching to see if anyone followed her. I was having a conversation.

Q: With whom?

A: I don't remember the person's name. Someone's girlfriend. We were talking about... I don't know, restaurants or something.

Q: So your attention was on this conversation.

A: I just said that.

Q: Then how did you come to witness the alleged assault if your attention was elsewhere?

A: Because it happened later. I already explained this. There was a gap in time.

Q: How much of a gap?

A: I've answered this question. Twice now.

Q: I'm asking you to answer it again for clarity.

A: Twenty minutes. Maybe thirty. I don't know. Somewhere in there.

Q: And what drew your attention to the altercation?

A: I heard yelling. Everyone heard yelling. That's generally how yelling works.

Q: What specifically did you hear?

A: A woman's voice. Then a man's voice. Then what sounded like something falling or someone falling. I went to see what happened. Can we move on?

Q: We'll move on when I've completed this line of questioning, Mr. Okonkwo. What did you see when you went to investigate?

A: Ms. Reyes was on the ground. A man was standing over her. People were pulling him back. That's what I saw.

topic: A supervisor is deposed about performance reviews given to an employee who was later fired
text:
Q: Mr. Patterson, I'm showing you what's been marked as Exhibit 14. Do you recognize this document?

A: Yes, that's a performance review.

Q: And this is the performance review you prepared for Danielle Webber in March of 2022?

A: It appears to be, yes.

Q: You gave Ms. Webber an overall rating of "Meets Expectations" on this review, correct?

A: That's what it says.

Q: And yet six weeks later, you recommended her termination. Help me understand that.

A: I'm sorry, what exactly are you asking me?

Q: I'm asking how an employee goes from "Meets Expectations" to terminated in six weeks.

A: Well, I mean—there are different factors. The review covers a specific period. Things can change.

Q: What things changed?

A: Her performance. Her attitude. Multiple things.

Q: Her attitude wasn't mentioned anywhere in this review. Not once.

A: The review focuses on measurable metrics. Attitude is—it's harder to quantify.

Q: So you're saying there were attitude problems before March 2022 that you simply chose not to document?

A: No, that's not—I didn't say that. I said the review focuses on certain things. I'm not sure what you're getting at here.

Q: I'm getting at the fact that you gave her a satisfactory review and then fired her almost immediately after.

A: Six weeks isn't immediately. And I didn't fire her. I made a recommendation. HR makes the final call.

topic: A supervisor is deposed about performance reviews given to an employee who was later fired
text:
Q: Who else had input into Mr. Okonkwo's performance reviews besides yourself?

A: Input? What do you mean by input?

Q: Did anyone else contribute to the evaluation?

A: Contribute how? Like, did someone else write sections? Or are you asking if I talked to other people?

Q: Let's start with whether you talked to other people.

A: I mean, yes, of course. His team lead. Sometimes project managers if there was a relevant project.

Q: And did their feedback make it into the written review?

A: Some of it. If it was relevant.

Q: Who decides what's relevant?

A: I do. It's my review.

Q: So when his team lead told you about the client complaint in October, you decided that wasn't relevant?

A: I don't—which client complaint?

Q: The Morrison account.

A: I genuinely don't know what you're referring to. There were issues with Morrison, but I don't recall Marcus being involved in that.

Q: You don't recall, or it didn't happen?

A: I don't recall. I can't confirm something I have no memory of.

Q: Would it refresh your recollection to see an email from team lead Sandra Chen dated October 14th?

A: It might. I'd have to see it.

topic: A supervisor is deposed about performance reviews given to an employee who was later fired
text:
Q: Let's talk about the rating scale your company uses. There are five levels, correct?

A: Correct.

Q: And they are—

A: Exceptional, Exceeds Expectations, Meets Expectations, Needs Improvement, and Unsatisfactory.

Q: Thank you. Now, in three years of supervising Ms. Trahan, you never gave her anything below Meets Expectations?

A: I'd have to review all the documents to confirm that, but I don't believe I did, no.

Q: Does that strike you as inconsistent with recommending termination?

A: No.

Q: No?

A: No. People get terminated for all kinds of reasons. Not just performance ratings.

Q: What other reasons?

A: Restructuring. Redundancy. Fit. Insubordination. Lots of things.

Q: Which of those applied to Ms. Trahan?

A: I'd say fit. And some performance concerns that developed toward the end.

Q: But you just told me her performance ratings were never below Meets Expectations.

A: The formal ratings, yes. But the day-to-day reality can be different.

Q: Why wouldn't the day-to-day reality show up in the formal ratings?

A: Because—look, the reviews happen once a year. They're a snapshot. They don't capture everything.

Q: Whose job is it to make sure they capture the relevant information?

A: Mine. But I'm also balancing multiple employees, multiple priorities. The process isn't perfect.

Q: The process, or your execution of it?

A: I'm not sure what answer you're looking for here.

topic: A supervisor is deposed about performance reviews given to an employee who was later fired
text:
Q: Did you ever place Mr. Huang on a performance improvement plan?

A: No.

Q: Why not?

A: It wasn't warranted.

Q: But you've testified that his performance was declining.

A: I testified that there were concerns. That's not the same as saying a PIP was necessary.

Q: What would make a PIP necessary?

A: Sustained underperformance. A pattern. Documentation supporting that a formal intervention was needed.

Q: And you didn't have documentation?

A: I had some. Not enough for a PIP.

Q: Not enough, or not the right kind?

A: I don't—what's the distinction you're making?

Q: I'm asking whether the issue was quantity of documentation or the nature of what was documented.

A: I suppose both? A PIP is a serious step. You need a solid foundation.

Q: Termination is also a serious step.

A: Yes.

Q: But that didn't require a PIP first?

A: It depends on the circumstances.

Q: What were the circumstances here?

A: The decision was made at a higher level. I provided my input. I wasn't the final decision-maker.

Q: Your input was to terminate without a PIP?

A: My input was that—I outlined the concerns. The decision about process wasn't mine alone.

Q: Do you have any documentation of that input?

A: I believe I sent an email. I'd have to check the dates.

topic: A supervisor is deposed about performance reviews given to an employee who was later fired
text:
Q: I want to make sure I understand the timeline. Ms. Reeves received a positive review in January?

A: Define positive.

Q: Meets Expectations or above.

A: Then yes.

Q: And in February, you had a conversation with her about attendance issues?

A: I don't remember it being specifically about attendance.

Q: What was it about?

A: General check-in. We talked about several things.

Q: Did attendance come up?

A: It may have.

Q: Did you document that conversation?

A: No.

Q: Any reason why not?

A: It was informal. Not every conversation gets documented.

Q: And then in March, there was a written warning?

A: Yes.

Q: For attendance?

A: Partially.

Q: What else?

A: There were comments made that were inappropriate.

Q: Comments to whom?

A: To a colleague.

Q: Which colleague?

A: I don't think I should name them without—is that necessary?

Q: We can come back to that. The written warning in March—that was the first formal documentation of any problem?

A: Formal, yes.

Q: Eight weeks after a positive review?

A: Like I said, the review is a snapshot. Things evolve.

topic: A building inspector is deposed about a structural assessment they signed off on
text:
Q: Mr. Delacroix, you conducted the structural assessment of the Meridian Tower parking garage on March 14th, 2022, correct?

A: I did.

Q: And you signed off on that assessment, indicating the structure was sound?

A: I signed the assessment, yes.

Q: The assessment you signed contained no recommendations for remediation, isn't that right?

A: That's what the document says.

Q: I'm asking what you determined, Mr. Delacroix. Did you determine that no remediation was needed?

A: Counsel, I've been doing this work for twenty-three years. When I sign an assessment, it reflects my professional judgment at the time based on the conditions I observed. So yes. That was my determination.

Q: Based on the conditions you observed. Were there conditions you didn't observe?

A: I can't observe what I can't see. I'm not sure what you're asking me.

Q: Let me be more specific. Did you observe the underside of the third-level deck?

A: I observed portions of it.

Q: Portions. Which portions?

A: The portions that were accessible. As I've explained in my written report. Which I assume you have.

Q: I have it right here. Can you show me where in the report you documented which portions were inaccessible?

A: Page four. Second paragraph. "Visual inspection limited in areas of mechanical obstruction." It's right there.

Q: "Mechanical obstruction." That's a water heater, correct?

A: It was building equipment, yes.

Q: Did you ask to have the equipment moved?

A: That wasn't my role.

Q: Whose role was it?

A: I conducted the inspection I was contracted to conduct. If you have questions about scope, you should be deposing the property management company.

---

topic: A building inspector is deposed about a structural assessment they signed off on
text:
Q: Ms. Yuen, I want to direct your attention to the support columns on the building's east side. You inspected those?

A: Yes.

Q: All of them?

A: All of the columns that were part of the assessment scope, yes.

Q: How many columns is that?

A: I'd have to check my notes for the exact number. I don't have that memorized.

Q: Would twelve sound right?

A: It might. I said I'd have to check.

Q: Fine. Let's say approximately twelve. You examined each one?

A: I conducted a visual inspection of each one, yes.

Q: And you found no deficiencies?

A: I found no deficiencies that required immediate remediation.

Q: That required immediate remediation. So you did find deficiencies?

A: Minor surface spalling on two columns. Cosmetic. I noted it in my report.

Q: Cosmetic. You're certain of that?

A: I was certain enough to document it as such, yes.

Q: Ms. Yuen, are you aware that three months after your inspection, column E-7 exhibited cracking that extended to the rebar?

A: I'm aware that's been alleged.

Q: It's not alleged. I have photographs.

A: Then you have photographs. I can only tell you what I observed on March 14th.

Q: And you observed cosmetic spalling.

A: That's what I observed.

Q: On column E-7 specifically?

A: I don't recall which specific columns exhibited the spalling. My report would indicate that.

Q: Your report says columns E-4 and E-9.

A: Then those were the columns.

Q: Not E-7.

A: Apparently not.

---

topic: A building inspector is deposed about a structural assessment they signed off on
text:
Q: Mr. Okonkwo, let's talk about timing. How long did you spend on site for this inspection?

A: Approximately four hours.

Q: Four hours for an eleven-story building with underground parking. Is that typical?

A: It depends on the building. It depends on the scope. It depends on access.

Q: I'm asking about this building. Was four hours adequate?

A: I completed the inspection.

Q: That's not what I asked.

A: I'm not sure what you want me to say, Counsel. Four hours was what it took. I finished. I documented my findings.

Q: Did you feel rushed?

A: No.

Q: You didn't feel any pressure to complete the inspection quickly?

A: I felt the pressure I always feel, which is to do my job competently.

Q: From whom?

A: From myself.

Q: Not from the building owner?

A: The building owner wasn't standing over my shoulder with a stopwatch.

Q: But the building owner did request a fast turnaround on the report, didn't they?

A: They wanted the report promptly. Everyone wants reports promptly.

Q: Within forty-eight hours, correct?

A: I believe so.

Q: And you delivered within that window?

A: I delivered a thorough, accurate report within that window, yes.

Q: In your twenty-three years of experience, is a forty-eight-hour turnaround typical?

A: It's on the shorter end.

Q: On the shorter end.

A: Yes.

Q: Did the shorter timeline affect the thoroughness of your inspection?

A: No. And I'd appreciate it if you'd stop implying otherwise.

---

topic: A building inspector is deposed about a structural assessment they signed off on
text:
Q: Let's discuss your qualifications for a moment.

A: I've already provided my CV.

Q: Humor me. You've been a licensed building inspector for how long?

A: Since 2011.

Q: And before that?

A: I worked in construction management.

Q: For how long?

A: Counsel, this is all in my CV. Eight years.

Q: I'm asking you directly.

A: And I'm answering you. Eight years.

Q: Have you ever had a certification suspended or revoked?

A: No.

Q: Have you ever been the subject of a complaint to the licensing board?

A: There was one complaint in 2019. It was dismissed.

Q: Dismissed. By whom?

A: By the licensing board. After investigation.

Q: What was the nature of the complaint?

A: A property owner disagreed with my assessment.

Q: Disagreed how?

A: He felt I was too conservative. He wanted me to approve renovations I didn't believe were structurally sound.

Q: So you were too cautious in that instance.

A: I was appropriately cautious.

Q: But with the Meridian Tower garage, you found no cause for caution?

A: I found no cause for the specific concerns that have apparently been raised after the fact, no.

Q: After the fact.

A: Yes. After the fact. When it's very easy to second-guess.

Q: I'm not second-guessing, Mr. Tran. I'm trying to understand your methodology.

A: Then ask me about my methodology.

---

topic: A building inspector is deposed about a structural assessment they signed off on
text:
Q: Dr. Reeves, you noted in your assessment that the foundation showed "normal settling consistent with building age." Do you recall writing that?

A: I recall the language, yes.

Q: What does "normal settling" mean to you?

A: It means settling within expected parameters for a structure of that age and construction type.

Q: Expected parameters. Can you quantify that?

A: It's not a single number. It's a range based on multiple factors.

Q: Give me the range.

A: Counsel, I'm not going to invent a number for you on the spot. The assessment process is more nuanced than that.

Q: I'm not asking you to invent anything. I'm asking what parameters you applied.

A: I applied my professional judgment based on training, experience, and observed conditions.

Q: That's not a parameter. That's a non-answer.

A: Then perhaps you should rephrase your question.

Q: Let me try again. Did you measure the settling?

A: I observed indicators of settling.

Q: Did you take measurements?

A: I took photographs and documented visible indicators.

Q: Dr. Reeves, I'm asking a simple question. Did you use any instrument to measure the degree of settling in the foundation?

A: No.

Q: No.

A: Correct. That was not within the scope of the assessment I was contracted to perform.

Q: So when you wrote "normal settling," you had no quantitative basis for that conclusion?

A: I had a qualitative basis. Which is standard practice for a Level One assessment.

Q: Standard practice is to guess?

A: Standard practice is to apply professional expertise. Which is what I did. Which is what I always do.

topic: An employee is deposed about a coworker's termination they believe was retaliatory
text:
Q: Mr. Okonkwo, you were present in the office on March 14th when Ms. Delgado was escorted out, correct?

A: I was at my desk, yes.

Q: And what did you observe?

A: I observed two security guards walk her to the elevator. She had a box.

Q: Did anyone explain to you why she was being terminated?

A: No one explained anything to me. No one explains anything to anyone at that company.

Q: Let me rephrase. Did you have any conversations with supervisors about Ms. Delgado's termination?

A: You can rephrase it however you want. The answer is the same. No.

Q: Were you aware that Ms. Delgado had filed an internal complaint two weeks prior?

A: Yes.

Q: How did you become aware of that?

A: She told me. She told several of us. She wasn't hiding it.

Q: And what was the nature of her complaint, as you understood it?

A: She reported that Mr. Hensley was falsifying time records. She had documentation.

Q: Did you believe her complaint had merit?

A: I saw the same spreadsheets she saw. I worked with those numbers every month. So yes. Obviously.

Q: After she filed the complaint, did you notice any change in how management treated her?

A: Did I notice. Yes. I noticed that suddenly her work was being audited daily when no one else's was. I noticed she got written up for being three minutes late when people waltz in at 9:30 without a word. I noticed her parking spot got reassigned. Do you want me to keep going?

Q: That won't be necessary. Did you ever express these observations to anyone in HR?

A: I did. I sent an email on March 10th. I have a copy if your client conveniently lost theirs.

topic: An employee is deposed about a coworker's termination they believe was retaliatory
text:
Q: Ms. Tierney, how long did you work alongside David Chen?

A: Just over four years.

Q: Would you describe him as a competent employee?

A: David was one of the best analysts in the department. I'm not sure why we're even questioning that.

Q: I'm simply trying to establish his work history. Was he ever disciplined prior to his termination?

A: Not that I'm aware of.

Q: You're not aware, or it didn't happen?

A: I said what I said. I'm not aware. I didn't have access to his personnel file.

Q: Fair enough. Now, were you aware that Mr. Chen had raised concerns about workplace safety violations?

A: I was.

Q: When did you first learn about those concerns?

A: He mentioned it to me in January. Maybe late January.

Q: What specifically did he tell you?

A: That he'd found issues with the ventilation system in Building C and that he'd reported it to facilities and been ignored.

Q: Ignored by whom?

A: By facilities. I just said that.

Q: Did he escalate his concerns beyond facilities?

A: Yes.

Q: To whom?

A: To OSHA.

Q: And when did he contact OSHA?

A: I don't know the exact date. February sometime.

Q: Would it refresh your recollection if I told you the complaint was filed February 12th?

A: If you already know when it was filed, why are you asking me?

Q: I'm asking what you knew and when you knew it, Ms. Tierney.

A: Then ask that.

topic: An employee is deposed about a coworker's termination they believe was retaliatory
text:
Q: Let's go back to the meeting on April 3rd. You said earlier that you were in attendance?

A: I was, yes.

Q: Who else was present?

A: Um, there was... let me think. Sandra Whitmore, James Patel, the whole compliance team, and I believe Robert Strauss called in remotely.

Q: Was Ms. Vance present?

A: No. She'd already been terminated by then.

Q: Right. And during this meeting, was Ms. Vance's departure discussed?

A: Briefly. Very briefly.

Q: What was said?

A: Sandra said that Monica was no longer with the company and that we should direct her ongoing projects to James.

Q: Was any reason given for her departure?

A: No.

Q: Did anyone ask?

A: ...Yes.

Q: Who asked?

A: I did.

Q: And what response did you receive?

A: Sandra said it was a personnel matter and couldn't be discussed.

Q: How did you interpret that response?

A: I'm sorry, how did I interpret it?

Q: Yes. What did you understand that to mean?

A: I understood it to mean that Sandra didn't want to tell us the truth. Monica had just filed a harassment complaint against Robert Strauss, and then suddenly she's gone and we can't talk about it? I interpreted it the way anyone would.

Q: Move to strike as speculative.

A: You asked how I interpreted it. That's how I interpreted it.

topic: An employee is deposed about a coworker's termination they believe was retaliatory
text:
Q: Mr. Perkins, I want to be very precise here. You stated that you overheard a conversation between Ms. Hammond and the HR director. Is that correct?

A: That's what I said.

Q: And this was on or about February 20th?

A: Around that time, yes.

Q: Around that time, or on that date?

A: I don't carry a calendar in my head, counselor. It was late February.

Q: Where did this conversation take place?

A: In the hallway outside the break room.

Q: Were they aware you could hear them?

A: I don't think so. I was around the corner, getting coffee.

Q: So you were eavesdropping?

A: I was getting coffee. They were speaking loudly enough for me to hear.

Q: What did you hear Ms. Hammond say?

A: She said, quote, "We need to find a reason to let her go before this gets out of hand."

Q: And you're certain those were her exact words?

A: I wrote them down immediately after.

Q: You wrote them down. Where?

A: In my phone. In the notes app.

Q: Do you still have that note?

A: I do.

Q: Did you bring it with you today?

A: No one asked me to bring it.

Q: I'm asking you now whether you have access to it.

A: It's on my phone. Which I was told to leave outside.

Q: We can take a brief recess if you'd like to retrieve it.

A: That would have been helpful to know before we spent twenty minutes on this.

topic: An employee is deposed about a coworker's termination they believe was retaliatory
text:
Q: Ms. Reeves, did Mr. Donovan ever discuss his concerns about billing practices with you directly?

A: Yes, he did.

Q: On how many occasions?

A: Several. I couldn't give you an exact number.

Q: More than five?

A: Probably.

Q: And what did he tell you?

A: He told me he'd found evidence that the company was overbilling clients, padding invoices with hours that were never worked.

Q: Did you see this evidence yourself?

A: Some of it. He showed me some of the invoices.

Q: And what did you do with that information?

A: I didn't do anything. It wasn't my place.

Q: You didn't think overbilling clients was something that should be reported?

A: I didn't say that. I said it wasn't my place. Marcus was handling it.

Q: And how was he handling it?

A: He went to Patricia Simmons. Our supervisor.

Q: When was that?

A: Mid-October, I think.

Q: What happened after he reported his concerns to Ms. Simmons?

A: Nothing. Nothing happened for about two weeks. And then suddenly Marcus is on a performance improvement plan.

Q: Had he received any negative performance reviews prior to that?

A: No. He had excellent reviews. I saw his last evaluation—he showed it to me. All fours and fives.

Q: But he was placed on a performance improvement plan after raising concerns about billing?

A: That's what happened, yes.

Q: And he was terminated approximately three weeks later?

A: Three weeks to the day. I counted.

topic: A warehouse supervisor is deposed about safety protocols that were allegedly ignored
text:
Q: Mr. Delano, you were the shift supervisor on the night of the accident, is that correct?

A: Yes, I was.

Q: And part of your responsibility was ensuring that all safety protocols were followed?

A: That's right.

Q: I'd like to ask you about the forklift inspection logs. Were those completed that evening?

A: They were supposed to be. I... look, can I explain something here?

Q: Of course. Take your time.

A: Marcus—the operator—he was covering for two other guys that night. We were short-staffed. He'd been there since six in the morning. Fourteen hours by the time... by the time it happened.

Q: I understand. Let me ask you this: did you personally review the inspection log before his final run?

A: No. And I've thought about that every single day since.

Q: Mr. Delano, I'm not trying to assign blame here. I just need to understand what happened. Can you tell me what the protocol required?

A: Protocol says the operator signs off before each shift and again if there's a break longer than two hours. Marcus should have done a second check. I should have made sure he did.

Q: Was there anything preventing him from doing that check?

A: We were behind on a shipment. Client was threatening to pull the contract. Management was... there was pressure. A lot of pressure.

Q: Did anyone instruct you to skip the safety checks?

A: Not in those words. But when someone's telling you the trucks need to roll and there's no one else to drive them... you understand what they're really saying.

Q: I do. Was Marcus the kind of worker who would cut corners on his own?

A: Never. That man was careful. He had three kids at home. He wanted to get home to them safe every night. He just... he trusted that the equipment was good because I told him we were on schedule. That's on me.

Q: Mr. Delano, we can take a break if you need one.

A: No. No, I want to finish. Somebody needs to hear what actually happened to him.

topic: A warehouse supervisor is deposed about safety protocols that were allegedly ignored
text:
Q: Ms. Thornton, how long have you worked as a supervisor at the Greenfield distribution center?

A: A little over seven years now.

Q: In that time, how many safety incidents have you personally witnessed?

A: Witnessed myself? Maybe four or five serious ones.

Q: And would you say the company's safety culture has improved, stayed the same, or declined over that period?

A: That's... that's a complicated question.

Q: I'm sure it is. Why don't you explain what makes it complicated.

A: When I started, we had a dedicated safety coordinator. Full-time position. She knew everyone's name, walked the floor twice a day. Three years ago, they eliminated that role. Said supervisors could absorb the duties.

Q: And could you? Absorb those duties, I mean?

A: We tried. But I've got forty-two people under me on a busy shift. I can't watch everyone and also manage logistics and also handle equipment maintenance requests. Something always falls through.

Q: Did you ever raise these concerns with management?

A: Multiple times. I have emails.

Q: We'll get to those. For now, I want to understand—when you raised these concerns, how did management respond?

A: The first few times, they said they'd look into it. Later, they stopped responding at all. Then I got a note from HR asking if I was "comfortable in my current role." I got the message.

Q: That must have put you in a difficult position.

A: I have two kids in college. I couldn't afford to lose this job. But I also couldn't keep watching people work in conditions that... I'm sorry, I need a moment.

Q: Of course. We're not in a rush. Would you like some water?

A: Thank you. I'm okay. I just... the woman who got hurt, Diane, she'd worked with me for five years. I'd trained her myself. She trusted that I'd keep that floor safe.

Q: And you feel you weren't given the resources to do that.

A: I know I wasn't.

topic: A warehouse supervisor is deposed about safety protocols that were allegedly ignored
text:
Q: Mr. Okafor, I want to direct your attention to the ventilation system in warehouse section C. Were you aware of complaints about air quality prior to May 15th?

A: There were comments here and there.

Q: Comments. Can you be more specific?

A: Workers saying it was stuffy. Harder to breathe on hot days.

Q: Did anyone report these issues formally?

A: Some of them filled out concern cards. That's the process we have.

Q: And what happens to those concern cards?

A: They go to me, I review them, and I forward anything serious to facilities management.

Q: Did you forward the air quality complaints?

A: I did, yes.

Q: All of them?

A: I forwarded... I forwarded the ones that seemed most urgent.

Q: How did you determine urgency?

A: If someone said they felt dizzy or sick, that went straight up. If they just said it was warm, I'd note it but sometimes wait to see if others reported the same thing.

Q: Mr. Okafor, I want to be very clear—I'm not looking to blame anyone who was trying to do their job with limited support. I'm trying to understand the system. Did facilities management respond to your forwards?

A: Sometimes.

Q: When they didn't respond, what did you do?

A: I followed up when I could. But I was also managing inventory, scheduling, dealing with equipment problems. The ventilation thing kept getting pushed down my list.

Q: Did you know that Carmen Reyes had asthma?

A: I knew she had some breathing issues. She mentioned it when she was hired.

Q: Did that affect where you assigned her to work?

A: I tried to keep her in section A when I could. The airflow is better there. But when we were short-handed, sometimes I had to move people around.

Q: And on May 15th?

A: She was in section C. We had a deadline. I didn't have anyone else. And I've had to live with that.

topic: A warehouse supervisor is deposed about safety protocols that were allegedly ignored
text:
Q: Ms. Vance, you conducted the internal investigation after the incident, correct?

A: I participated in it, yes. I wasn't the lead.

Q: But you interviewed Mr. Hartwell, the warehouse supervisor?

A: I did.

Q: How did he seem during that interview?

A: What do you mean, how did he seem?

Q: His demeanor. Was he cooperative? Defensive?

A: Neither of those words really captures it.

Q: Then help me understand.

A: He was... broken. That's the only word for it. He kept saying he'd told them the racking was unstable. Kept saying he'd put in work orders.

Q: Did you verify those work orders existed?

A: We found three of them. Dated over an eight-month period.

Q: And none of them were addressed?

A: One was marked "pending review." The other two had no response logged.

Q: When you found this, what did you do?

A: I included it in my preliminary findings.

Q: And what happened to those findings?

A: Legal asked me to revise certain sections before the final report was issued.

Q: Which sections?

A: The ones about the work orders. They wanted me to say the documentation was "inconclusive."

Q: Was it inconclusive?

A: No.

Q: Ms. Vance, I want you to know that I understand the position this puts you in. You're being asked to contradict your employer's official report. That takes courage.

A: I'm not doing this to be courageous. I'm doing this because a twenty-three-year-old kid lost the use of his legs, and his supervisor tried to prevent it, and nobody listened.

Q: Did Mr. Hartwell know you found the work orders?

A: I told him. Off the record. I thought he deserved to know someone believed him.

topic: A warehouse supervisor is deposed about safety protocols that were allegedly ignored
text:
Q: Mr. Kim, let's talk about the lockout/tagout procedures. You're familiar with those?

A: Very familiar. I've been enforcing them for twelve years.

Q: Good. On the date in question, was a lockout/tagout performed before the conveyor maintenance?

A: According to the log, yes.

Q: According to the log. Does that mean you have doubts?

A: The log says it was done at 2:15 p.m. The injury occurred at 2:22 p.m.

Q: Seven minutes later.

A: That's what the records show.

Q: Is seven minutes enough time for someone to complete the maintenance that was being performed?

A: Not typically. That work usually takes at least twenty minutes.

Q: So either the timestamp is wrong, or—

A: Or someone started before the lockout was actually complete. Yes.

Q: Do you know who performed the lockout that day?

A: It was supposed to be James. But James was out sick.

Q: Who covered for him?

A: That's what I've been trying to find out.

Q: The company hasn't told you?

A: The company has asked me not to look into it further. They said legal would handle the investigation.

Q: Mr. Kim, I want to ask this carefully. How has this incident affected your team?

A: My team is scared. Not just of getting hurt—scared of speaking up. Scared they'll be blamed for something that happened because we were stretched too thin.

Q: And how are you handling that?

A: I've been meeting with them one by one. Off the clock. Just listening. Some of them have worked for me for years. They needed someone to tell them this wasn't their fault.

Q: That's not a small thing, what you're doing.

A: It's the only thing I can do right now. Because I can't change what happened, and I can't make the company admit what went wrong. But I can make sure my people know I'm still in their corner.

Q: Has anyone else from management reached out to the workers?

A: No. No one.

topic: A business partner is deposed about financial records they were responsible for maintaining

Q: Mr. Harrington, you were responsible for maintaining the quarterly revenue reports for Vertex Solutions, correct?

Q: I'm asking specifically about the quarterly revenue reports.

A: And I'm giving you the complete picture. The quarterly reports were one component of a comprehensive system I built over seven years. You can't understand one piece without understanding the architecture.

Q: Let's focus on Q3 of 2022. Did you prepare that report?

A: I prepared every quarterly report from 2016 through 2023. Q3 2022 was no exception. I can walk you through the methodology if that would help you understand what you're looking at.

Q: That won't be necessary. Were there any discrepancies in the Q3 2022 report?

A: There were no discrepancies. I ran a triple-verification process that I developed specifically to eliminate discrepancies. In fact, our external auditors commented that our error rate was the lowest they'd seen in a mid-size firm.

Q: I'm showing you Exhibit 14. Do you recognize this document?

A: Of course I recognize it. I created the template, the formulas, the cross-referencing system. This is my Q3 2022 summary sheet. Notice the color-coding system in the margin—that was my innovation. Made the audit process forty percent faster.

Q: There's a handwritten note in the corner. Is that your writing?

A: It is. I annotated every summary sheet personally. Most people in my position would delegate that, but I believed in maintaining direct oversight of every figure that left my desk.

Q: What does this note say?

A: It says "verified against bank statements 9/14." I can tell you exactly what I was doing that day if you'd like. I have detailed logs going back to 2016.

Q: That won't be necessary. Mr. Harrington, did anyone else have access to these records?

A: Access, technically, yes. But no one else touched them. I made that clear from the beginning. When you build a system that works this well, you don't let other people introduce variables.

topic: A business partner is deposed about financial records they were responsible for maintaining

Q: Ms. Cho, how long did you serve as the bookkeeper for Redline Distributing?

A: I wouldn't know what the investigators found valuable. They took everything.

A: Mr. Dawes thought the handwritten logs were excessive. Once. Then we had the system outage in 2020 and he never mentioned it again.

A: Because my backup records meant there was nothing to reconstruct.

topic: A business partner is deposed about financial records they were responsible for maintaining
text:
Q: Mr. Tanaka, I want to understand the chain of custody for these financial documents.

A: I proposed it, designed it, and oversaw its implementation. The other partners adopted it because it worked.

Q: And this four-tier system was in place when the discrepancy in the equipment depreciation schedule occurred?

A: The system caught that discrepancy. That's how we know about it. Under the old process, it would have gone unnoticed for another fiscal year at minimum.

Q: So your system caught an error?

A: My system caught an error that would have compounded into a significant misstatement. You're welcome.

Q: I'm sorry?

A: I said you're welcome. You're here asking about a discrepancy that was identified, documented, and corrected—because of protocols I put in place. The question you should be asking is what we would have missed without them.

Q: Mr. Tanaka, I'll ask the questions I deem relevant.

A: Of course. I'm just providing context. Financial oversight isn't just about finding errors. It's about building systems that make errors findable.

topic: A business partner is deposed about financial records they were responsible for maintaining

topic: A business partner is deposed about financial records they were responsible for maintaining

topic: A paramedic is questioned about the response time and treatment at an accident scene
text:
Q: Let's talk about the timeline. What time did you arrive at the accident scene?

A: I remember looking at the clock when we pulled up. It said 14:47.

Q: And what time was the call dispatched?

A: 14:38.

Q: Nine minutes. Is that typical for that route?

A: It can vary.

Q: I'm asking if nine minutes is typical.

A: Depending on traffic, yes.

Q: Was there traffic that day?

A: Some.

Q: Some. Can you describe what "some" means?

A: There were vehicles on the road. We used lights and sirens. People moved.

Q: So if people moved, and you had lights and sirens, why nine minutes for a route that Google Maps shows as four minutes?

A: I wouldn't know what Google Maps shows.

Q: Would it surprise you to learn it's four minutes?

A: Google Maps doesn't account for a vehicle our size, intersection protocols, or the fact that not everyone pulls over immediately when they should.

Q: So you're saying every second of those nine minutes is accounted for by those factors?

A: I'm saying we responded as quickly as we safely could.

topic: A paramedic is questioned about the response time and treatment at an accident scene
text:
Q: When you first assessed the victim, what was her condition?

A: Cervical stabilization, then began primary survey.

Q: How long did that take?

A: The primary survey? Three, maybe four minutes.

Q: And then?

A: Secondary survey. Started an IV line. Monitored vitals.

Q: At what point did you call for air transport?

A: We didn't call for air transport.

Q: You didn't. Why not?

A: It wasn't indicated. Ground transport to Regional was twelve minutes. Helicopter would've taken longer to arrive and land.

Q: Who made that determination?

A: I did.

Q: Just you?

A: I was the senior paramedic on scene. That's my call to make.

Q: Did you consult with anyone? Medical control?

A: I didn't need to consult with medical control for a transport decision within protocol.

Q: So no one else weighed in on whether this woman—who later required emergency surgery—should have been airlifted?

A: The protocols exist for a reason, Counselor. I followed them. If you're suggesting I should have ignored my training and called a helicopter that would've delayed transport, I'd like to understand the basis for that.

topic: A paramedic is questioned about the response time and treatment at an accident scene

topic: An employee is deposed about a coworker's termination they believe was retaliatory

A: Performance issues. That's interesting phrasing.

Q: I'm asking what you knew, Mr. Hernandez.

Q: Were you aware of any other concerns management had about Ms. Whitfield?

topic: An employee is deposed about a coworker's termination they believe was retaliatory

topic: An employee is deposed about a coworker's termination they believe was retaliatory

topic: An employee is deposed about a coworker's termination they believe was retaliatory
text:
Q: Dr. Patel, you mentioned earlier that you considered Angela Morrison a strong researcher.

A: I did. She was.

Q: Yet her termination was characterized as being due to poor research outcomes. How do you reconcile those two things?

A: I don't reconcile them. They don't fit together.

Q: Let me approach this differently. Were you consulted before Ms. Morrison was terminated?

A: No.

A: One would think.

Q: But you weren't.

A: I was informed the morning of. After the decision had been made.

Q: Who informed you?

A: Richard Estes, in a four-minute phone call.

Q: Four minutes specifically?

A: I checked afterward. Four minutes, twelve seconds.

Q: Why did you check the call duration?

A: Because I wanted to see how long it took to undo three years of someone's career. Four minutes, apparently.

Q: What did Mr. Estes tell you in that call?

A: That the decision had been made. That it was related to "alignment issues." That I shouldn't discuss it with other team members.

Q: Alignment issues. Did he explain what that meant?

A: He did not.

Q: Did you ask?

A: I asked several questions. I received no answers.

Q: Dr. Patel, you're aware that Ms. Morrison had recently raised concerns about the Hartley trial data?

A: I'm aware she raised concerns, yes. Concerns that I happened to share.

Q: Did Mr. Estes know you shared those concerns?

A: I don't know what Mr. Estes knew. I know I put my concerns in writing two weeks before Angela was terminated. And I know that memo went to Richard Estes, among others.

Q: Did you receive a response to that memo?

A: I did not. But I did notice that Angela was gone within fourteen days of its circulation.

Q: You're drawing a connection between those events?

A: I'm stating facts, counselor. If connections emerge, that's not my doing.

topic: A building inspector is deposed about a structural assessment they signed off on
text:
Q: Mr. Harmon, you conducted the structural assessment of 4200 Riverside Drive on March 15th of last year, correct?

A: I conducted an inspection on that date, yes. Whether you want to call it a "structural assessment" depends on what you mean by that term.

Q: What would you call it?

A: A routine compliance inspection. That's what the permit application required. That's what I was there to do.

Q: And you signed off on the building as structurally sound?

A: I signed off on the inspection checklist indicating the building met code requirements for the items I was there to inspect. That's not the same thing as certifying a building is "structurally sound." I'm not sure who told you it was.

Q: The checklist included structural elements, did it not?

A: It included visible structural elements accessible during a routine inspection, yes.

Q: So you inspected structural elements and indicated they passed?

A: I indicated they showed no visible deficiencies that would constitute a code violation. There's a difference.

Q: Help me understand the difference.

A: I'm not an engineer. I don't perform engineering analyses. I look at what's visible, I compare it to code requirements, and I document what I observe. I've been doing this for nineteen years. I know exactly what my job is and what it isn't.

Q: Did your job that day include looking at the east-facing support columns?

A: If they were on my checklist and accessible, then yes.

Q: Were they?

A: I'd have to see the checklist to answer that. I don't memorize every inspection I've done in the last fourteen months.

Q: I'm handing you what's been marked as Exhibit 14. Take your time.

A: Thank you. I will.

topic: A building inspector is deposed about a structural assessment they signed off on
text:
Q: Ms. Delgado, how many building inspections would you estimate you've conducted in your career?

A: Thousands. I couldn't give you an exact number.

Q: And in those thousands of inspections, have you ever made a mistake?

A: Define "mistake."

Q: Have you ever missed something you should have caught?

A: I'm human. But I follow procedure. Every time.

Q: Every single time?

A: Yes.

Q: Let's talk about the Greenway Commons building specifically. You were there on August 8th?

A: According to my records, yes.

Q: How long did that inspection take?

A: I don't recall the exact duration.

Q: Would your records reflect that?

A: They might. They might not. Time in and time out isn't always documented.

Q: So you have no idea if you were there for fifteen minutes or three hours?

A: I have an idea. I said I don't recall the exact duration. Those aren't the same thing.

Q: What's your idea, then?

A: An inspection of that type, for a building of that size, typically takes between ninety minutes and two hours if there are no access issues.

Q: Were there access issues?

A: I don't recall any.

Q: So roughly two hours. And in that time, you examined the basement foundation?

A: If it was required by the inspection type, which I believe it was, then yes.

topic: A building inspector is deposed about a structural assessment they signed off on
text:
Q: Mr. Chen, I want to make sure I understand your testimony. You're saying the cracks you observed in the foundation were within acceptable limits?

A: That's what I documented, yes.

Q: Based on what standard?

A: Based on the municipal building code, Section 4.7.2, which specifies tolerances for hairline cracking in poured concrete foundations.

Q: Did you measure the cracks?

A: I made visual assessments.

Q: That's not what I asked. Did you measure them?

A: Visual assessment is the standard protocol for routine inspections.

Q: Mr. Chen, it's a yes or no question. Did you take any measurements of the cracks?

A: No. I did not take measurements with a measuring device.

Q: So when you say they were within acceptable limits, you're estimating?

A: I'm applying nineteen years of professional experience to a visual observation.

Q: But you didn't measure.

A: Counsel, I've already answered that question.

Q: You also didn't photograph the cracks, did you?

A: Photography wasn't required under the inspection protocol.

Q: That's not what I asked.

A: No, I did not photograph them. Because it wasn't required. Because they didn't present as a concern.

Q: So we have no objective record of what you saw that day?

A: You have my professional assessment, signed and dated. That is the record.

Q: A record of your opinion.

A: A record of my findings. There's a difference.

topic: A building inspector is deposed about a structural assessment they signed off on
text:
Q: Walk me through what you actually did when you arrived at the site on October 3rd.

A: I checked in with the site supervisor, reviewed the permit documentation, and began the inspection according to the standard checklist.

Q: Who was the site supervisor?

A: I don't remember his name. It would be in my notes.

Q: Did you find that unusual? That you don't remember?

A: No. I meet a lot of people. I don't remember most of their names.

Q: Fair enough. What happened after you reviewed the permit documentation?

A: I proceeded to inspect the areas indicated on the checklist. Started with the exterior, moved to the interior, then the mechanical systems.

Q: How did you access the roof?

A: I... I'm not certain there was a roof inspection that day.

Q: Your report indicates you inspected the rooftop HVAC mounting points.

A: Then I must have accessed the roof.

Q: You don't remember?

A: It was a year ago. I remember the inspection in general terms. I don't remember every step I took.

Q: Do you remember whether there was a ladder or a stairwell access?

A: Typically those buildings have interior stairwell access to the roof.

Q: Typically. But you don't specifically remember this building.

A: No. I don't specifically remember how I got to the roof of that particular building on that particular day.

Q: But you're certain you were on the roof.

A: If my report says I inspected rooftop elements, then I was on the roof. I don't falsify reports.

topic: A building inspector is deposed about a structural assessment they signed off on
text:
Q: Ms. Torres, did anyone from Meridian Development contact you before the inspection?

A: Define "contact."

Q: Did anyone from that company communicate with you in any way before you arrived at the site?

A: Not that I recall.

Q: Would you have documented it if they had?

Q: Has anyone ever asked you to expedite an inspection?

A: People ask for all kinds of things.

Q: That's not an answer, Ms. Torres.

A: Yes, people have asked. No, I don't accommodate those requests.

Q: And you're certain no one from Meridian made such a request regarding this particular property?

A: I said I don't recall any communication. If you have evidence otherwise, I'd be happy to look at it.

Q: I'm asking about your recollection.

A: And I've given it to you. Three times now.

Q: Let me ask it differently. Did anyone pressure you—from any source—regarding the inspection of 557 Industrial Parkway?

A: No.

topic: A witness is asked about a car accident they saw from their front porch
text:
Q: State your name for the record.

A: Margaret Ellen Holloway. I already gave this to the other attorney.

Q: Mrs. Holloway, you understand you need to answer my questions today regardless of what you've told anyone else?

A: I understand how a deposition works, counselor.

Q: Good. Where were you on the morning of March 15th at approximately 8:45 a.m.?

A: On my porch. Drinking coffee. Same as every morning for the last thirty-two years.

Q: And from your porch, you claim you witnessed a collision?

A: I don't "claim" anything. I saw what I saw.

Q: Tell me what you saw.

A: The blue truck ran the stop sign and hit the sedan. That's it. That's the whole story.

Q: How fast would you estimate the truck was traveling?

A: Fast enough to blow through a stop sign and total someone's car.

Q: I'm asking for a number, Mrs. Holloway.

A: And I'm telling you I'm not a speedometer. It was fast. Recklessly fast.

Q: Would you say thirty miles per hour? Forty?

A: I would say fast enough to kill someone, and your client is lucky he didn't.

Q: Mrs. Holloway, I'll remind you to answer only what's asked.

A: Then ask better questions.

---

topic: A witness is asked about a car accident they saw from their front porch
text:
Q: You were seated on your porch when the accident occurred, correct?

A: I was wearing my glasses.
