Q: I'm reading directly from—

A: You're reading something, and you're trying to make it sound like I'm blind. I'm not blind. I saw a truck run a stop sign.

Q: Let me finish my question.

A: Then finish it.

Q: Did you have any obstructions to your view? Trees, parked cars?

A: No.

Q: None at all.

A: I said no. That means none.

topic: A witness is asked about a car accident they saw from their front porch
text:
Q: What were you doing when you first noticed the vehicles?

A: I was reading the newspaper. I heard brakes, looked up.

Q: So you didn't actually see the moments before the collision?

A: I saw enough.

Q: That's not what I asked. Did you see the moments before impact, yes or no?

A: I saw the truck in the intersection when it should have been stopped.

Q: Sir, I need you to answer my question directly.

A: I am answering directly. You don't like the answer.

Q: Did you see the truck approach the stop sign?

A: No.

Q: Did you see whether the truck slowed down at any point?

A: I heard the brakes screech. There was no slowing before that.

Q: But you just said you were reading. You weren't watching.

A: I wasn't watching until I was watching. Then I watched a truck plow into a car.

Q: So your testimony about speed is based on sound, not sight?

A: It's based on the fact that a two-ton vehicle doesn't sail through an intersection at five miles an hour.

Q: Move to strike as nonresponsive.

A: Strike whatever you want. Doesn't change what happened.

topic: A witness is asked about a car accident they saw from their front porch
text:
Q: Mr. Tate, let's go through this carefully. You were on your front porch?

topic: A witness is asked about a car accident they saw from their front porch
text:

topic: A financial advisor is deposed about investment decisions made on a client's behalf
text:
Q: Mr. Hartley, I'd like to ask you about the Medina account. You were Mrs. Medina's advisor for how long?

A: Eleven years. From when her husband passed until she moved to the care facility last spring.

Q: And in those eleven years, you made the investment decisions for her portfolio?

A: I made recommendations. She signed off on everything. But yes, I guided her. She trusted me to guide her.

Q: I'm asking about the decision in March of 2022 to move sixty percent of her holdings into high-yield bonds. Can you walk me through that?

A: I can. I want to, actually. Mrs. Medina—Elena—she came to me in February. She'd just gotten the diagnosis. Early-onset Alzheimer's. She was scared. Not for herself, she said. For her daughter. Maria has Down syndrome. She's thirty-four. Elena wanted to make sure Maria would be provided for. That was the only thing she cared about.

Q: So the shift to high-yield bonds was her idea?

A: It was my recommendation, but it came from what she needed. She needed income. Reliable, monthly income that would flow into the special needs trust. The equities weren't doing that. I explained the risks. I documented that I explained the risks. She understood.

Q: The portfolio lost eleven percent over the following six months.

A: It did. The market moved against us. Against her.

Q: Did you consider more conservative options? Treasury bonds, for instance?

A: I did. I walked her through all of it. The yields on Treasuries at that time—they wouldn't have generated enough. Not for Maria's care costs. Elena made a choice. I helped her make an informed choice. That's what I was there for.

Q: Do you regret that recommendation?

A: I regret that she got sick. I regret that the market did what it did. But I don't regret trying to help her take care of her daughter. I'd make the same recommendation again.

Q: Even knowing the outcome?

A: Even knowing. Because I knew Elena. I knew what she was trying to do. And I still believe it was the right path for what she needed.

---

topic: A financial advisor is deposed about investment decisions made on a client's behalf
text:
Q: Ms. Torres, you've been a financial advisor for how many years?

A: Seventeen.

Q: And the Okonkwo account came to you in 2019?

A: Correct. Dr. Okonkwo was referred by another client.

Q: Take your time with this. I know these accounts involve real people, not just numbers.

A: Thank you. I appreciate that.

Q: Dr. Okonkwo was seventy-three when he opened the account?

A: Seventy-two. He turned seventy-three that June.

Q: And what were his stated investment goals at that time?

A: He wanted to preserve capital. He'd retired from his medical practice, and he had—he had some health concerns. He wanted to make sure his wife would be secure. That was the word he used. Secure.

Q: I understand. Given those goals, can you help me understand the allocation to emerging market equities?

A: It was a small allocation. Eight percent. He asked about growth opportunities because his wife is younger—she's sixty-one now—and he wanted part of the portfolio to keep pace with inflation over a longer horizon. For her.

Q: He specifically asked for that?

A: He did. I have the notes from our meeting. He was very clear-minded about it. He'd done his own research. He came in with articles printed out.

Q: And when those positions declined in early 2020?

A: We spoke on the phone. March fifteenth, I think. I remember because my own mother was in the hospital at the time—different reasons—and I was thinking about what it means to worry about someone you love. He wasn't panicked. He asked questions. We talked about holding versus selling. He chose to hold.

Q: Did you recommend holding?

A: I presented both options. I told him selling would lock in losses. I told him holding carried risk. He made the decision. I supported his decision.

Q: I appreciate your thoroughness here, Ms. Torres. We're almost done with this line of questions.

---

topic: A financial advisor is deposed about investment decisions made on a client's behalf
text:
Q: Let's discuss the Brennan account.

A: Okay.

Q: You were Mr. Brennan's advisor from 2018 to 2021?

A: That's right.

Q: Three years. And in that time, the account's value decreased by roughly forty percent.

A: That's the number, yes.

Q: I'm not trying to assign blame here, Mr. Reeves. I'm trying to understand what happened.

A: What happened is that Kevin—Mr. Brennan—had very specific ideas about what he wanted. He came to me convinced that cryptocurrency was the future. I pushed back. I documented my concerns. He insisted.

Q: You documented your concerns how?

A: Emails. Meeting notes. I have copies of all of it. I told him the volatility was extreme. I told him he was risking his retirement.

Q: And he proceeded anyway.

A: He did. He was—look, he was going through a divorce. His wife had been the cautious one in the marriage. He was trying to prove something. To himself, I think. I don't know. But I could see he was in pain, and he was making decisions from that pain.

Q: Did you consider refusing to execute the trades?

A: I considered it. Seriously considered it.

Q: But you didn't.

A: No. I talked to him. Multiple times. I asked him to wait thirty days before any major moves. He agreed to that, actually. We built that waiting period into our process. But after thirty days, he still wanted to move forward. At a certain point, it's his money. It's his life.

Q: That must have been difficult.

A: It was. It still is. I think about Kevin. I hope he's doing okay.

---

topic: A financial advisor is deposed about investment decisions made on a client's behalf
text:
Q: Mr. Whitfield, you managed the Patterson family trust?

A: I was the investment advisor to the trust, yes.

Q: From 2017 until when?

A: Until the family terminated the relationship in December 2022.

Q: The trust lost significant value during that period.

A: The trust's value decreased, yes. Particularly in 2022.

Q: I want to focus on the decision to maintain equity exposure through the downturn. Whose decision was that?

A: Mine.

Q: Exclusively yours?

A: I made the recommendation. The trustees approved it.

Q: The trustees being?

A: Linda Patterson and her brother, Marcus.

Q: Did they understand the risks?

A: I explained the risks in every quarterly meeting. I sent written summaries. But—

Q: But?

A: Linda and Marcus were dealing with their mother's estate. Their mother had just passed. The trust was her legacy. They were grieving. I tried to shield them from some of the complexity. Maybe I shielded them too much.

Q: What do you mean by that?

A: I mean I saw two people who had lost their mother, who were arguing with each other about things that had nothing to do with money, and I thought—I'll handle this part for them. I'll keep this part simple. I'll protect them from having to make hard decisions during a hard time.

Q: And in retrospect?

A: In retrospect, I should have made them engage more. Even if it was painful. Because now they've lost money and they feel blindsided, and I contributed to that.

Q: That's a candid answer.

A: It's the true answer.

---

topic: A financial advisor is deposed about investment decisions made on a client's behalf
text:
Q: Dr. Chen came to you in January 2020?

A: Yes.

Q: And she was investing an inheritance?

A: Correct. Her grandmother had passed away. Left her approximately four hundred thousand dollars.

Q: That's a significant sum. How did you approach the initial consultation?

A: Carefully. Dr. Chen was—she was conflicted about the money. She told me she almost didn't want it. It felt like it came from loss.

Q: Did that affect your recommendations?

A: It affected how I presented the recommendations. I tried to frame things in terms of what her grandmother might have wanted for her. Security. Opportunity. I thought it might help her feel less guilty about investing it.

Q: Was that your role? To help her feel less guilty?

A: My role was to advise her on investments. But she's a person. She was sitting across from me, and she was sad. I couldn't pretend not to see that.

Q: The portfolio you recommended was moderately aggressive. Why?

A: Because she was thirty-one. Because she had a stable income from her medical practice. Because she had decades of growth ahead of her. And because—she told me her grandmother had been bold. Had come to this country with nothing. She wanted to honor that somehow.

Q: So you factored emotional considerations into a financial recommendation?

A: I factored in my client's values and goals. Yes. That's what I do.

Q: And when the portfolio declined in March 2020?

A: I called her before she could call me. I knew she'd be frightened. I walked her through what was happening, what the options were. We talked for an hour. Maybe longer.

Q: You spent an hour on the phone with one client?

A: I spent an hour on the phone with someone who needed to understand what was happening to her grandmother's legacy. Yes. I'd do it again.

topic: A daycare worker is deposed about an injury a child sustained while in their care
text:
Q: Ms. Hernandez, let's go back to the moment you first noticed Lily was injured. Where were you standing?

A: It could be. I didn't measure it.

A: It's an estimate. Based on being in that room every day for three years.

A: I heard her cry. I turned and she was on the mat.

Q: That wasn't my question. Did you see her fall?

Q: I want you to answer my questions, Ms. Hernandez. Did any other child touch Lily before she fell?

A: Not that I saw. But as I just said, I didn't see the fall itself.

Q: Right. Because you were fifteen—or twenty—feet away. By the cubbies.

A: Yes. Doing my job. Supervising twelve children.

topic: A daycare worker is deposed about an injury a child sustained while in their care
text:

topic: A daycare worker is deposed about an injury a child sustained while in their care
text:
Q: Ms. Patterson, after you noticed the bite mark on Dylan's arm, what did you do?

Q: Ms. Patterson—

topic: A daycare worker is deposed about an injury a child sustained while in their care
text:

topic: A doctor is deposed about informed consent procedures before a surgery
text:

Q: And on March 14th, with Mrs. Delgado, how long did your consent discussion last?

A: I don't recall the exact duration.

Q: You don't recall.

A: No. I see many patients. I don't time each conversation.

Q: Would it surprise you to learn that Mrs. Delgado was in the pre-operative area for only eleven minutes total before being taken to the OR?

A: I wouldn't know what happened in the pre-operative area. That's nursing's domain.

Q: So you're saying your consent discussion happened elsewhere?

A: I'm saying I don't track timestamps. I conduct my consultations thoroughly, wherever they occur.

Q: Dr. Holloway, is it your testimony that you discussed the risk of bile duct injury with Mrs. Delgado?

A: I discuss that risk with all my cholecystectomy patients. It's standard.

Q: That wasn't my question. Did you discuss it with *her*?

A: I follow my standard practice. So yes.

Q: Do you have any documentation of that specific discussion?

A: The signed consent form indicates she was informed of the risks.

Q: The consent form lists "risks of surgery" generally. It doesn't mention bile duct injury specifically, does it?

A: The form is a summary. The conversation is more detailed.

topic: A doctor is deposed about informed consent procedures before a surgery
text:
Q: Dr. Okonkwo, you performed a cervical disc replacement on Alan Mercer on September 8th, correct?

A: That's correct.

Q: Before surgery, did you discuss alternative treatment options with Mr. Mercer?

A: Absolutely. We discussed physical therapy, epidural injections, anterior cervical discectomy and fusion, and the artificial disc replacement, which he ultimately chose.

Q: Did you tell him that fusion was the more established procedure?

A: I told him that fusion has a longer track record, yes. I also explained that disc replacement preserves motion at the segment and may reduce adjacent segment disease over time. I was thorough. I'm always thorough.

Q: I'm just asking what you told him, Doctor.

A: And I'm telling you. Completely.

Q: Did you inform Mr. Mercer that you had performed only three cervical disc replacements prior to his surgery?

A: I don't believe the exact number came up in those terms.

Q: In what terms did it come up?

A: He asked if I was experienced with the procedure. I told him I was trained and credentialed to perform it.

Q: That's not the same as telling him your case volume, is it?

A: Patients don't typically ask for a specific number. They ask if you're qualified.

Q: So if he had asked for the number, you would have told him?

A: If he had asked, I would have answered honestly.

Q: But he didn't ask the right question, so you didn't volunteer it.

A: That's not—I answered what he asked. That's what informed consent is. A dialogue.

Q: A dialogue where you control what information enters the conversation?

A: Counsel, I resent the implication. I gave Mr. Mercer everything he needed to make his decision.

topic: A doctor is deposed about informed consent procedures before a surgery
text:
Q: Let's talk about the consent form itself, Dr. Patel. Who prepared it?

A: The surgical coordinator prepares the form based on the scheduled procedure.

Q: And when do you first see it?

A: Typically when I'm with the patient, reviewing it before signature.

Q: So you don't review it in advance to ensure it's accurate?

A: I trust my staff to prepare it correctly. But yes, I review it with the patient.

Q: On October 3rd, the consent form for Mr. Huang listed "lumbar discectomy L4-L5." Do you see that?

A: I see it.

Q: But you performed the discectomy at L5-S1, didn't you?

A: The MRI findings at L5-S1 were more significant. I made an intraoperative judgment.

Q: An intraoperative judgment. So you changed the surgical plan during the procedure?

A: I adjusted based on what I observed. This happens.

Q: Did you discuss the possibility of operating at L5-S1 with Mr. Huang before surgery?

A: We discussed his disc herniations. He had pathology at multiple levels.

Q: Doctor, I'm asking specifically: did you tell him you might operate at L5-S1?

A: I... I believe the conversation covered the affected levels generally.

Q: You believe.

A: It was over a year ago, counsel.

Q: The consent form says L4-L5. His signature is under L4-L5. Did you obtain consent for L5-S1 or not?

A: The consent was for treatment of his lumbar disc disease. The specific level—

Q: Yes or no, Doctor.

A: The form reflects the primary plan. Surgeons must adapt. That's the nature of surgery.

topic: A doctor is deposed about informed consent procedures before a surgery
text:
Q: Dr. Yamamoto, how do you typically document your informed consent discussions?

A: I make a note in the patient's chart summarizing our conversation, and the consent form is signed and witnessed.

Q: Every time?

A: Every time. Without exception.

Q: I'm showing you Exhibit 14, the chart for Rebecca Stillman. Can you find your consent discussion note?

A: I'm looking. One moment.

Q: Take your time.

A: The pre-operative note is here. It documents the planned procedure and the patient's agreement to proceed.

Q: That's your pre-operative assessment. I'm asking about documentation of the consent discussion itself. The risks you described, the alternatives you presented.

A: The consent discussion is inherent in the pre-operative process.

Q: Inherent.

A: Yes.

Q: So it's your testimony that "patient agrees to proceed" constitutes documentation of informed consent?

A: Combined with the signed consent form, yes.

Q: Dr. Yamamoto, the consent form is a one-page document listing the procedure name and a checkbox for "risks and benefits discussed." That's the totality of your documentation?

A: The documentation reflects that the process occurred. The substance of the conversation exists in my memory and the patient's memory.

Q: The patient is deceased, Doctor.

A: I'm aware of that.

Q: So your memory is all that remains.

A: That's unfortunately the case, yes.

Q: Convenient.

A: Excuse me?

Q: Withdrawn. Let me ask you this: do you have any way to prove what you told Mrs. Stillman about the risk of anesthesia complications?

A: I know what I told her because I know what I always tell my patients.

topic: A doctor is deposed about informed consent procedures before a surgery
text:
Q: When did you first meet Theodore Baxter, Dr. Chen?

A: The day before his surgery. June 11th.

Q: Not before that?

A: No. He was referred by his cardiologist. I reviewed his records and met him for the pre-surgical consultation.

Q: So you had one meeting before performing a triple bypass on him.

A: One in-person meeting, yes. I also spoke with his cardiologist extensively.

Q: During that one meeting, you covered the informed consent?

A: Yes.

Q: What risks did you disclose?

A: The standard risks for CABG. Bleeding, infection, stroke, heart attack, death, reaction to anesthesia, need for reoperation. I also discussed his specific risk factors given his diabetes and age.

Q: Did you tell him his mortality risk was elevated?

A: I told him the surgery carried serious risks and that his comorbidities increased those risks.

Q: Did you give him a percentage?

A: I gave him a range based on STS risk scores.

Q: What range?

A: I believe it was in the four to six percent range for mortality.

Q: The STS calculator—and I have the printout here, Exhibit 22—shows a predicted mortality of 8.4 percent for Mr. Baxter. Not four to six.

A: May I see that?

Q: Of course.

A: This... I don't know when this printout was generated. I would have to check what data was entered.

Q: Are you suggesting the data is incorrect?

A: I'm suggesting I'd like to verify it before accepting your characterization.

Q: Fair enough. But sitting here today, you're not certain what mortality risk you actually quoted to Mr. Baxter, are you?

A: I am certain I gave him an accurate assessment based on the information I had at the time.

Q: That's not the same thing, Doctor.

A: It's my answer.

topic: An employee is deposed about a coworker's termination they believe was retaliatory
text:
Q: Ms. Hartwell, you were employed in the same department as Marcus Chen at the time of his termination, correct?

A: Yes.

Q: And you sat in the cubicle directly adjacent to his?

A: I sat in the cubicle to the east of his, yes. Not directly adjacent. There was a filing station between us.

Q: Fine. Near him. You were near him.

A: I was in proximity to him, yes.

Q: Did you ever hear Mr. Chen express concerns about the company's billing practices?

A: I heard him say things, sure.

Q: What things?

A: Things about billing.

Q: Ms. Hartwell, I'm going to need you to be more specific. What exactly did you hear Mr. Chen say about the company's billing practices?

A: He said he thought some of the line items on the Kramer account were questionable. He said it in the break room. I was getting coffee.

Q: When was this?

A: Sometime in February. I don't remember the exact date. I didn't realize I'd need to keep a calendar of other people's conversations.

Q: Did he say who he planned to report these concerns to?

A: He mentioned Janet. Janet Okonkwo. She was the compliance officer.

Q: Did you ever learn whether he actually made that report?

A: I'm not a mind reader. I know what I heard. I heard him say he was going to talk to Janet. Whether he did or didn't, you'd have to ask him. Or Janet.

Q: Ms. Hartwell, I'm asking what you know.

A: And I'm telling you what I know. Which is what I heard. In the break room. While I was getting coffee.

topic: An employee is deposed about a coworker's termination they believe was retaliatory
text:
Q: You were Mr. Chen's friend, weren't you?

A: We were friendly. I'd say we were work friends.

Q: You socialized outside of work?

A: A few times. Happy hours, that kind of thing.

Q: So you had insight into his state of mind during his employment?

A: I wouldn't say insight. I knew him. We talked.

Q: Let me ask you this directly. In the weeks before his termination, did Marcus Chen tell you he believed he was being retaliated against?

A: He said he felt like he was being watched more closely after he went to Janet.

Q: Being watched. What do you mean by that?

A: I mean what he said. He felt like management was paying more attention to him. To his schedule, his work output. He said it felt different.

Q: Different how?

A: I just said how. More scrutiny.

Q: Did you observe this increased scrutiny yourself?

A: I saw Greg standing by Marcus's desk more than usual. I saw emails getting CC'd to people who didn't need to be on them.

Q: Did you find that unusual?

A: I found it noticeable.

Q: That's not what I asked. Did you find it unusual?

A: Yes. I found it unusual. I've been there four years and I've never seen anyone's badge swipes get audited except Marcus.

Q: How do you know his badge swipes were audited?

A: Because Greg asked me if I knew what time Marcus usually arrived in the morning. I thought that was a strange question to ask a coworker instead of just checking the system yourself. Unless you were building a file.

topic: An employee is deposed about a coworker's termination they believe was retaliatory
text:
Q: Mr. Tran, let's go back to the meeting on March 3rd. You were present?

topic: An employee is deposed about a coworker's termination they believe was retaliatory
text:
Q: Did Mr. Chen ever complain to you about retaliation?

topic: An employee is deposed about a coworker's termination they believe was retaliatory
text:
Q: Ms. Yuen, we've been at this for two hours now. I want to make sure we're clear on the timeline.

topic: A doctor is deposed about informed consent procedures before a surgery
text:
Q: Dr. Hensley, let's talk about what happened on the morning of March 14th, before Mrs. Patterson's surgery. You met with her that morning?

topic: A doctor is deposed about informed consent procedures before a surgery
text:
Q: Dr. Muñoz, I want to understand your standard practice. When you obtain informed consent, do you follow a checklist?

topic: A doctor is deposed about informed consent procedures before a surgery
text:
Q: Let me ask you about the consent form itself, Dr. Pratt. Who prepared this document?

A: It is.

A: I see it.

A: That's what it says.

Q: Did you explain to Mr. Reeves what "changes in cognitive function" might mean in practical terms?

A: I explained that there are risks with any surgery involving anesthesia, including the possibility of confusion afterward, memory issues. It's not common, but it happens.

Q: Did you tell him there was a risk he might not recognize his own children?

A: I... no. I didn't phrase it that way.

Q: Would that have been accurate? That it was possible?

A: In extremely rare cases, yes. But you're asking me to predict the unpredictable.

Q: I'm asking what you told your patient.

A: I told him the truth. I told him there were risks. I told him we'd take every precaution. I told him what I believed was necessary for him to make a decision.

Q: Alright. Let's move on. The anesthesiologist—did he have a separate consent conversation with Mr. Reeves?

A: He should have. That's protocol.

Q: Should have?

topic: A doctor is deposed about informed consent procedures before a surgery
text:
Q: Dr. Yuen, you've been sued before over informed consent. Correct?

A: I did.

Q: And this note, from three years after that change, doesn't mention alternatives.

A: It doesn't. You're correct. I can see that.

Q: So either you discussed alternatives and didn't document it—

Q: —or your documentation practices aren't as thorough as you indicated.

I'm a surgeon. I had three surgeries that day. I did my job. I talked to her. I explained her options. She chose surgery. That's what happened.

Q: Let's take a short break.

A: Fine.

topic: A doctor is deposed about informed consent procedures before a surgery
text:
Q: Dr. Okonkwo, I've been at this a while, so I'll just ask directly—did you tell Mr. Salazar that the device you planned to implant had been on the market for less than two years?

A: I don't believe that came up specifically.

Q: It didn't come up, or you don't recall?

A: I don't recall discussing the device's market history with him, no.

A: I think Mr. Salazar wanted to stop living in pain. That's what I think.

Q: Did you give him the opportunity to ask questions?

A: I always do.

A: I'd have to look at the schedule to be certain. Fifteen minutes, perhaps twenty.

A: The manufacturer's brochure was available. I believe my staff provided it.
