topic: A building inspector is deposed about a structural assessment they signed off on
text:
Q: Mr. Harmon, let's turn to the inspection you conducted on March 14th of last year. You were at the Westfield Commons site that day, correct?

A: I was there March 14th, yes. Arrived at 7:15 in the morning, completed my walkthrough by 11:40, and submitted my report by 3 p.m. that same day.

Q: That's a fairly quick turnaround for a building of that size, wouldn't you say?

A: No, I wouldn't say that. A 12,000 square foot commercial structure with standard steel framing—four hours on site is appropriate. I've done hundreds of these.

Q: Hundreds.

A: Four hundred and thirty-seven structural assessments in my eighteen years with the county. You can verify that with our records department.

Q: I'm not disputing your experience, Mr. Harmon. I'm asking about this particular inspection.

A: And I'm telling you this particular inspection was conducted exactly as it should have been. What specifically would you like to know?

Q: Did you personally examine the load-bearing columns on the second floor?

A: Every single one. There were fourteen. I documented visible conditions, checked for deflection, looked for cracking at the base plates. My notes are in exhibit seven if you'd like to walk through them column by column.

Q: That won't be necessary at this time.

A: I'm happy to do it. I have nothing to hide in that report.

Q: Let's move on. The foundation—

A: Before we move on, I want to be clear about something. The columns were sound. They remain sound today, as far as I'm aware. Whatever theory you're building here, you won't find negligence in my inspection.

Q: I haven't alleged negligence, Mr. Harmon.

A: Then we understand each other.

topic: A building inspector is deposed about a structural assessment they signed off on
text:
Q: Ms. Castellano, you signed the structural assessment for 440 Industrial Parkway on June 3rd, is that right?

A: That's correct.

Q: And your signature indicates the building met code requirements for occupancy?

A: It indicates the building met the applicable structural requirements under the 2018 International Building Code as adopted by the state, yes.

Q: Now, I'm going to hand you what's been marked as Exhibit 12. Do you recognize this document?

A: This is my inspection checklist from that date.

Q: I'd like to direct your attention to item 14—the notation regarding the roof trusses.

A: I see it.

Q: You wrote, and I quote, "Minor deflection observed, within acceptable parameters." Do you see that?

A: I do.

Q: Ms. Castellano, isn't it true that deflection in roof trusses can indicate serious structural compromise?

A: It can. It can also indicate nothing of concern whatsoever. Deflection within parameters is exactly what those words say—within parameters. The engineering specifications for those trusses permitted up to three-quarters of an inch. I measured less than half that.

Q: You measured.

A: With a laser level and a tape measure, yes. Would you like me to explain the methodology?

Q: That's not—

A: Because I'm happy to walk you through exactly how deflection measurements are taken and why half an inch on a forty-foot span is unremarkable.

Q: Let's stay focused on the document.

A: I am focused on the document. The document reflects accurate measurements and a sound professional judgment.

Q: Moving to item 17—

A: Before you do, I'd like to add that I photographed those trusses as well. Sixteen photographs. They should be in your discovery materials.

topic: A building inspector is deposed about a structural assessment they signed off on
text:
Q: Mr. Okonkwo, how long have you held your certification as a structural inspector?

A: Um, let me think—it would be eleven years this past February.

Q: And in those eleven years, have you ever had a certification challenged or suspended?

A: No. No, I haven't.

Q: Good. Now, I want to walk you through something very carefully. On the date of your inspection at the Riverside Lofts project, what tools did you bring with you?

A: My standard kit—moisture meter, laser level, flashlight, inspection mirror, camera.

Q: A crack monitor?

A: I... yes, I believe so. I typically carry one.

Q: You believe so, or you did?

A: I did. Yes, I did bring one that day.

Q: And you used it?

A: On the basement foundation walls, yes.

Q: Let me be very specific, Mr. Okonkwo. I'm going to show you exactly where this is going, so there are no surprises. Exhibit 4 shows a hairline fracture in the eastern foundation wall. Your report makes no mention of it. I want to know why.

A: Can I see the exhibit?

Q: Of course. Take your time.

A: Okay. I see the photograph. This fracture—this is a shrinkage crack. This is completely normal in poured concrete of this age.

Q: You're certain it's a shrinkage crack?

A: I am.

Q: Despite not documenting it?

A: I don't document every cosmetic imperfection, counsel. If I did, my reports would be three hundred pages. A shrinkage crack in a thirty-year-old foundation is not a structural concern. It wasn't then, and the fact that someone photographed it later doesn't change that.

topic: A building inspector is deposed about a structural assessment they signed off on
text:
Q: Tell me what you observed when you first entered the building.

A: Which building are we talking about now?

Q: The Cranston warehouse. Your inspection of September 9th.

A: Oh, the Cranston property. All right. When I entered, I observed a single-story steel-frame warehouse, approximately 8,000 square feet, with a concrete slab foundation.

Q: Any immediate concerns?

A: No.

Q: None at all?

A: None that rose to a structural concern. There was debris in the northwest corner. Some water staining on the ceiling tiles. But structurally, no.

Q: Water staining didn't concern you?

A: Water staining concerns me when it indicates active leakage affecting structural members. Stained ceiling tiles in a warehouse are not unusual. I noted it. I looked for the source. I didn't find active moisture or damage to the roof deck.

Q: So you documented it?

A: In my notes, yes.

Q: But not in the final report.

A: The final report addresses structural adequacy. Cosmetic observations go in my field notes. That's standard practice.

Q: Standard practice according to whom?

A: According to the county inspection protocol, which I helped draft in 2019. Would you like me to cite the specific section?

Q: I'd like you to answer my questions directly.

A: I am answering directly. You're asking me about documentation standards, and I'm telling you I follow the standards I helped create. If you have a copy of the protocol, we can review it together.

Q: Let's move on to the roof inspection.

A: Certainly.

topic: A building inspector is deposed about a structural assessment they signed off on
text:
Q: Ms. Tran, did you discuss your findings with anyone before submitting the final assessment?

A: I discussed them with my supervisor, as required.

Q: Who is your supervisor?

A: David Kowalski. He's the chief building official for the county.

Q: And what did Mr. Kowalski say when you presented your findings?

A: He reviewed the report, asked a few clarifying questions, and approved it for submission.

Q: What kind of clarifying questions?

A: He asked about the age of the HVAC supports on the roof. Whether I'd checked the anchor bolts.

Q: Had you?

A: Had I what?

Q: Checked the anchor bolts.

A: Of course I had.

Q: All of them?

A: There were six rooftop units with four anchor bolts each. Twenty-four bolts total. I inspected each one visually and checked torque on a random sample of eight.

Q: Why only eight?

A: Because random sampling is an accepted methodology when visual inspection reveals no anomalies. I had no anomalies. The bolts were properly seated with no visible corrosion or loosening.

Q: Ms. Tran, you understand that one of those HVAC units later shifted during a windstorm?

A: I understand that's what's been alleged.

Q: Do you believe your inspection was adequate to identify any risk of that occurring?

A: My inspection was thorough, methodical, and consistent with professional standards. Those anchor bolts were secure on the day I inspected them. What happened eight months later, in weather conditions I wasn't asked to predict, doesn't change what I observed and documented.

Q: You stand by your assessment?

A: Completely.

topic: A pharmacist is deposed about a prescription that was filled with the wrong dosage
text:
Q: Please state your name and current position for the record.

A: David Chen. Pharmacist-in-charge at Westbrook Pharmacy. I've held that position for eleven years, if that matters to you.

Q: Mr. Chen, I'm going to direct your attention to February 14th of this year. You were working that day, correct?

A: I was.

Q: And you filled a prescription for methotrexate for the plaintiff, Margaret Holloway?

A: I filled numerous prescriptions that day. If you're asking whether my initials appear on that particular label, then yes, they do.

Q: The prescription called for 2.5 milligram tablets. What dosage was actually dispensed?

A: You have the documentation in front of you. You already know the answer.

Q: I'm asking you to state it for the record.

A: Twenty-five milligram tablets were dispensed.

Q: So ten times the prescribed dosage.

A: That's arithmetic, counselor. I'm capable of basic math.

Q: How did this happen?

A: How did what happen? You'll need to be more specific.

Q: How did your pharmacy dispense ten times the prescribed dosage to an elderly patient?

A: I don't accept the premise of that question. I'm one part of a system. The prescriber's handwriting was illegible, the software flagged nothing, and the technician pulled what she believed was correct.

Q: But you performed the final verification, did you not?

A: I did, and I've already acknowledged that the wrong medication went out. What I won't do is sit here and pretend that I'm the only link in this chain you should be examining.

Q: I'm not asking about other links right now. I'm asking about you.

A: Then ask better questions.

topic: A pharmacist is deposed about a prescription that was filled with the wrong dosage
text:
Q: Ms. Patel, how long have you been a licensed pharmacist?

A: Seven years this September.

Q: And your training included coursework on dosage verification?

A: Of course it did.

Q: Walk me through what that training taught you about verifying dosages before dispensing.

A: I'm sorry, do you want me to recite my entire pharmacy school curriculum? Because we'll be here for several days.

Q: I'm asking generally. What are the steps?

A: You compare the prescription to the label. You verify the drug name, strength, quantity, and directions match. You check for interactions. You use professional judgment.

Q: Professional judgment. And on March 3rd, when you filled Mr. Okonkwo's prescription for lisinopril, what did your professional judgment tell you?

A: That I was filling a prescription for lisinopril 10 milligrams, thirty tablets, once daily.

Q: But that's not what the prescription said, was it?

A: The prescription said what it said. I read it as 10 milligrams.

Q: When in fact it said 40 milligrams.

A: I'm aware of what's being alleged.

Q: It's not an allegation. I have the prescription right here. Would you like to look at it?

A: I've seen it dozens of times. I don't need you to wave it at me.

Q: The "4" is quite clear, isn't it?

A: It's clear to you, sitting in a conference room with perfect lighting and unlimited time. It was less clear at hour nine of a twelve-hour shift with sixty prescriptions in the queue.

Q: So you're saying the work conditions caused the error?

A: I'm saying you weren't there. You don't know what it's like. And I'm finished speculating about what I should have seen on a piece of paper four months ago.

topic: A pharmacist is deposed about a prescription that was filled with the wrong dosage
text:
Q: Let's talk about your pharmacy's quality control procedures. You do have written procedures, correct?

A: Yes.

Q: And those procedures require a pharmacist to personally verify every prescription before it leaves the pharmacy?

A: They do.

Q: Every single one?

A: I just said yes.

Q: Did you personally verify the prescription at issue in this case?

A: According to our records, yes.

Q: According to your records. Do you have an independent recollection?

A: I fill two hundred prescriptions on a busy day. Do you remember every document you reviewed four months ago?

Q: I'm not the one being deposed, Mr. Franklin.

A: No, you're the one asking me to perform impossible feats of memory and then acting surprised when I can't.

Q: Let's try this differently. The prescription was for oxycodone, 5 milligrams, correct?

A: Correct.

Q: And oxycodone 15 milligrams was dispensed.

A: That's what the incident report reflects.

Q: Three times the dosage. For a controlled substance.

A: I'm aware of what oxycodone is.

Q: Doesn't that warrant extra scrutiny?

A: It warrants exactly the scrutiny our procedures require, which I followed.

Q: You followed your procedures and still dispensed three times the prescribed dosage?

A: Procedures aren't magic, counselor. They reduce errors. They don't eliminate human fallibility. If you've found a system that does, the entire healthcare industry would love to hear about it.

topic: A pharmacist is deposed about a prescription that was filled with the wrong dosage
text:
Q: Dr. Hassan, I want to understand something. The pharmacy's own records show a dosage discrepancy was flagged by your software system. Is that accurate?

A: There was a soft alert, yes.

Q: A soft alert. What does that mean?

A: It means the system generated a notification that could be overridden with a click.

Q: And someone clicked override?

A: Obviously.

Q: You say obviously. Was it you?

A: The system doesn't track individual users for overrides. It's a known limitation.

Q: That seems like a significant gap.

A: I didn't design the software.

Q: But you work with it daily. Have you raised concerns about this gap?

A: I've raised concerns about many things. Would you like a list? Because I have emails going back three years that corporate has ignored.

Q: I'm asking specifically about override tracking.

A: Yes. I've raised it. Multiple times. In writing.

Q: And nothing was done?

A: You'd have to ask corporate. I'm just the person on the ground trying to do my job with inadequate tools and inadequate staffing while lawyers and executives sit in offices deciding how much risk is acceptable.

Q: Dr. Hassan, I'm simply trying to establish—

A: You're trying to establish that I made a mistake so your client can recover damages. I understand litigation. What I don't understand is why I'm the one sitting here instead of the people who decided that one pharmacist and one technician could safely handle three hundred prescriptions a day.

Q: Let's move on.

A: By all means.

topic: A pharmacist is deposed about a prescription that was filled with the wrong dosage
text:
Q: The label on the bottle indicated 100 milligrams of sertraline, correct?

A: Yes.

Q: But the prescription from Dr. Yamamoto specified 25 milligrams?

A: That's correct.

Q: Four times the intended dose.

A: I can do the math.

Q: And you verified this prescription?

A: My initials are on the label.

Q: Ms. Reyes, do you understand the severity of what happened here?

A: I'm sorry, is that a question for the deposition or are you delivering a lecture?

Q: It's a question.

A: Then yes, I understand. I've understood since the moment we discovered the error. I've lost sleep over it. I've questioned every decision I've made in my career. Does that satisfy you?

Q: I'm not looking for satisfaction. I'm looking for facts.

A: No, you're looking for someone to blame. That's what this is. You want me to say I was careless or incompetent so you can wrap this up neatly.

Q: Were you careless?

A: I was human. I made an error that our systems should have caught and didn't. An error that our staffing levels made more likely. An error I will carry with me regardless of what happens in this lawsuit.

Q: So you acknowledge the error was yours?

A: I acknowledge that I was the last person who could have caught it, and I didn't. That's not the same thing as saying I was the cause, and I won't let you twist my words into something they're not.

Q: I'm not twisting anything.

A: Then we're finished with this line of questioning.

topic: An employee is deposed about a coworker's termination they believe was retaliatory
text:
Q: Please state your name for the record.

A: Marcus Webb.

Q: Mr. Webb, how long have you worked at Cornerstone Logistics?

A: Seven years.

Q: And you worked directly with Janet Reeves?

A: Yes.

Q: In what capacity?

A: Same team. Shipping coordination.

Q: Were you present on March 14th when Ms. Reeves met with HR?

A: I was in the building, yes.

Q: Did you observe anything unusual that day?

A: Look, I already told your colleague all of this during the interview. Janet went to HR at 9 a.m., came back to her desk at 9:45, and by 2 p.m. she was packing a box. That's what I saw.

Q: I understand you may have discussed this before, but I need your testimony on the record. Did Ms. Reeves say anything to you about the meeting?

A: She said they told her the position was being eliminated. Three weeks after she filed that safety complaint. You do the math.

Q: Mr. Webb, I'm asking what she said, not your interpretation—

A: That is what she said. I'm giving you exactly what she said.

Q: Did she use the word "retaliation"?

A: She didn't have to.

Q: That's not what I asked. Did Janet Reeves specifically use the word "retaliation" in your presence?

A: No. She said, "They're punishing me." Direct quote. Are we done with this part?

topic: An employee is deposed about a coworker's termination they believe was retaliatory
text:
Q: Ms. Thornton, you've testified you were friends with the plaintiff outside of work, correct?

A: We got coffee sometimes. I wouldn't say we were close friends.

Q: Fair enough. Did Mr. Patterson ever discuss his concerns about the warehouse temperature controls with you?

A: He mentioned it once or twice.

Q: Once or twice. Which is it?

A: I don't have a logbook, counselor. It was more than zero times and less than ten. Is that specific enough?

Q: I need your best recollection.

A: Fine. Twice that I remember clearly. Maybe a third time but I'm not certain.

Q: And when were these conversations?

A: The first one was in November, around Thanksgiving. The second was January, maybe the second week.

Q: What specifically did he say in the November conversation?

A: That the coolers weren't holding temperature and he'd reported it twice and nothing happened.

Q: Did he say who he reported it to?

A: Diane Marsh. His supervisor. Who, by the way, is the same person who signed his termination paperwork two months later.

Q: I'm going to ask you to just answer the questions I pose rather than—

A: I am answering. You asked who he reported to. I told you. I added relevant context.

Q: Let me decide what's relevant. Did Mr. Patterson ever say he feared losing his job?

A: Yes. He said exactly that. The week before they fired him.

topic: An employee is deposed about a coworker's termination they believe was retaliatory
text:
Q: State your position at Meridian Healthcare.

A: I'm a billing specialist. I've been there four years.

Q: And you knew Danielle Foster?

A: I knew her, yes. We worked in the same department.

Q: When did you first become aware that Ms. Foster had raised concerns about billing practices?

A: Um, I'm not sure exactly. Maybe... late August?

Q: Late August of last year?

A: I think so. Yes.

Q: How did you become aware?

A: I... she told me. In the break room.

Q: What did she tell you?

A: That she'd found some irregularities. Duplicate charges. She was worried about it.

Q: Did she say she was going to report it? I need a yes or no.

A: I—it's not a yes or no situation, really.

Q: Did she indicate she was going to report it? Yes or no.

A: She indicated she was thinking about it.

Q: That's not what I asked. Did she or did she not say she was going to report the irregularities?

A: Could you... I mean, are you asking if she said the exact words "I am going to report this"? Because I don't remember her exact words.

Q: I'm asking whether she communicated an intent to report. This isn't complicated.

A: Then... yes. I believe she intended to report it.

Q: When was she terminated?

A: September 12th.

Q: How many days after your break room conversation?

A: I don't know. Two weeks? Maybe three?

Q: You said late August. September 12th is less than three weeks from August 31st. So which is it?

A: I said I wasn't sure of the exact date.

topic: An employee is deposed about a coworker's termination they believe was retaliatory
text:
Q: Good morning. You are Terrence Williams?

A: That's correct.

Q: How are you acquainted with the plaintiff, David Chen?

A: We were both project managers at Bellweather Construction.

Q: You worked on the same projects?

A: Adjacent ones. We shared resources sometimes, attended the same status meetings.

Q: Mr. Williams, were you aware that Mr. Chen had filed a complaint with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission?

A: Not at the time.

Q: When did you become aware?

A: After he was let go.

Q: Let me back up. Before Mr. Chen was terminated, did you ever hear anyone in management express frustration with him? Anyone at all?

A: Not with him specifically.

Q: What does that mean, not specifically?

A: It means there was general frustration about the OSHA situation, but nobody said David's name.

Q: What OSHA situation?

A: Someone had filed a complaint about the Riverside job site. Management was upset about the inspection.

Q: Did anyone suggest they knew who filed it?

A: Carl Jessup said—and I'm quoting—"I know exactly who's behind this."

Q: Did he say who?

A: No.

Q: But Mr. Chen was terminated two weeks later?

A: Eleven days, actually. I counted.

Q: Why did you count?

A: Because it was obvious, counselor. I have eyes. I can see when something's rotten.

Q: I'm asking about facts, Mr. Williams, not your conclusions.

A: Those are the facts. Complaint, statement, eleven days, termination. Fact, fact, fact, fact.

topic: An employee is deposed about a coworker's termination they believe was retaliatory
text:
Q: You supervised Rachel Kim directly, is that correct?

A: For about eight months, yes.

Q: During that time, did she ever raise concerns about workplace safety?

A: She raised a lot of concerns about a lot of things. Rachel was very... vocal.

Q: I'm asking specifically about safety. Did she raise safety concerns?

A: Yes.

Q: More than once?

A: I'd have to check my records to give you an exact—

Q: Your best estimate.

A: Four, maybe five times.

Q: And did you act on those concerns?

A: When they were valid, yes.

Q: When they were valid. So you're saying some weren't valid?

A: I'm saying I evaluated each one on its merits.

Q: Let's talk about the concern she raised on February 3rd regarding the chemical storage protocols. Did you consider that one valid?

A: That matter is still under review by—

Q: I didn't ask about review status. Did you personally consider it valid when she raised it?

A: It had merit.

Q: And yet nothing changed?

A: Changes take time. There are procedures.

Q: How much time? It's been six months.

A: I don't control the timeline.

Q: But you did control whether Ms. Kim kept her job, didn't you?

A: Her termination was a departmental decision based on restructuring.

Q: Restructuring. How many other positions were eliminated in this restructuring?

A: Her role was unique.

Q: How many, Mr. Donovan?

A: One. But that's because—

Q: Just one. Thank you. No further questions on this topic.

topic: A driver is deposed about the events leading up to a multi-vehicle collision
text:
Q: Mr. Hernandez, let's talk about what you were doing in the five minutes before the collision. Where were you coming from?

A: Work.

Q: And where is your workplace located?

A: 4200 Industrial Boulevard.

Q: What time did you leave work that day?

A: Around 5:15.

Q: Around 5:15. So you don't know the exact time?

A: I said around 5:15 because it was around 5:15. I don't punch a clock on my way out the door.

Q: Were you in a hurry to get somewhere?

A: No.

Q: No appointments, no dinner reservations, nothing like that?

A: I just answered that.

Q: I'm asking if there was any reason you might have been driving faster than usual.

A: And I said no. I wasn't in a hurry. I was driving home like I do every single day.

Q: What route do you typically take from Industrial Boulevard to your home?

A: I take Industrial to Maple, Maple to the highway, highway to my exit. Same route for three years.

Q: Did you deviate from that route on the day of the accident?

A: No.

Q: So you were on Maple Street when the collision occurred?

A: Yes. Which you already know from the police report.

Q: Mr. Hernandez, I'm asking you questions so we have your testimony on the record. Do you understand that?

A: I understand how a deposition works.

---

topic: A driver is deposed about the events leading up to a multi-vehicle collision
text:
Q: Ms. Thornton, I want to direct your attention to the traffic conditions that afternoon. How would you describe them?

A: Heavy. It was rush hour, so, you know, everyone was trying to get home.

Q: When you say heavy, were vehicles moving or at a standstill?

A: Stop and go. Mostly stop, honestly. We'd creep forward a few feet, then stop again.

Q: For how long had you been in that stop-and-go traffic?

A: Maybe ten minutes? Fifteen? It felt like forever, but probably ten or fifteen minutes.

Q: Were you feeling impatient?

A: I don't know if impatient is the word. I was just... sitting there. Everyone was sitting there.

Q: Let me ask it differently. Did the traffic conditions affect your mood at all?

A: I mean, nobody loves sitting in traffic, but I wasn't, like, road-raging or anything.

Q: I didn't ask about road rage. I asked if the traffic affected your mood.

A: Fine. Sure. I would have preferred to be moving. Is that what you're looking for?

Q: I'm looking for your honest recollection, Ms. Thornton.

A: That is my honest recollection. I was sitting in traffic. I was tired from work. I wanted to get home and take my shoes off. That's the whole story.

Q: Did that desire to get home cause you to take any actions you wouldn't normally take?

A: No. I was boxed in by cars on all sides. There was nowhere to go and nothing to do but wait.

Q: And yet somehow a collision occurred.

A: A collision that I did not cause, which I've explained multiple times now.

---

topic: A driver is deposed about the events leading up to a multi-vehicle collision
text:
Q: Mr. Warren, when did you first notice the vehicle in front of you braking?

A: Probably a second or two before impact. Maybe less. It happened fast.

Q: A second or two. Let's slow that down. You're driving along, and at some point you perceive brake lights ahead of you. What do you do?

A: I hit my brakes.

Q: Immediately?

A: Yes, immediately. What else would I do?

Q: I'm asking you, Mr. Warren. What did you do?

A: I just told you. I hit my brakes.

Q: Did you brake hard or gradually?

A: Hard. I slammed them.

Q: And what happened to your vehicle when you slammed the brakes?

A: It skidded. The road was wet. I couldn't stop in time.

Q: The road was wet. Was it raining at that moment?

A: It had been raining earlier. The road was still wet.

Q: Had you adjusted your following distance because of the wet road conditions?

A: I thought I had, yes.

Q: You thought you had. But you rear-ended the car in front of you.

A: Because they stopped dead in the middle of the road with no warning.

Q: So it's your testimony that the vehicle ahead of you stopped suddenly and without warning?

A: That is exactly what happened. I don't know how many different ways I can say it.

---

topic: A driver is deposed about the events leading up to a multi-vehicle collision
text:
Q: Dr. Patel, let me make sure I understand your testimony. You're saying you checked your mirrors before changing lanes?

A: Yes.

Q: Both mirrors?

A: My side mirror, yes. And I glanced over my shoulder.

Q: Which shoulder?

A: My left shoulder. I was merging left.

Q: How long did that glance take?

A: I don't know. A second?

Q: A second. And in that one second, you were able to confirm the lane was clear?

A: It appeared clear, yes.

Q: It appeared clear. But there was a motorcycle in that lane, wasn't there?

A: Apparently there was, yes.

Q: Apparently. You didn't see it?

A: If I had seen it, I wouldn't have merged.

Q: So your glance over your shoulder—this one-second check—failed to reveal a motorcycle traveling in the lane you were entering?

A: The motorcycle must have been in my blind spot, or it came up very quickly after I checked. I don't know which. I only know I checked before I merged.

Q: You don't know which. Do you have any explanation for how a motorcycle in broad daylight escaped your attention?

A: I've given you my explanation. I checked. I didn't see it. That's all I can tell you.

Q: Let's try this again. You're traveling at approximately what speed before you initiated the lane change?

A: We've covered this. Approximately fifty-five miles per hour. Posted speed is sixty. I've answered this question.

---

topic: A driver is deposed about the events leading up to a multi-vehicle collision
text:
Q: Tell me what you observed about the white SUV before the collision.

A: I noticed it weaving a little. Drifting in the lane, maybe crossing the line once or twice.

Q: When you say drifting, can you be more specific?

A: It would sort of ease toward the shoulder, then correct back. Then ease toward the center line.

Q: Did you form any impression about why the SUV was driving that way?

A: I assumed the driver was distracted. Or tired. I don't know.

Q: Did you consider passing the SUV?

A: Not really. We were in the right lane, and I didn't want to get close to it.

Q: So you maintained your position behind the SUV?

A: For a little while, yes.

Q: How far behind?

A: I don't know exactly. Several car lengths.

Q: More than five car lengths? Less?

A: I really couldn't say with precision. Several.

Q: You couldn't say. You noticed this vehicle was driving erratically, you made a decision to stay behind it, but you can't tell me how far behind?

A: I noticed it. I stayed back. I'm not a human measuring tape. I kept what I thought was a safe distance.

Q: And at some point the SUV's driving led to the collision. What did you see happen?

A: It drifted hard to the left, like the driver overcorrected, and then it clipped the sedan in the next lane. After that, everything just... cascaded.

Q: Cascaded how?

A: The sedan spun. Another car hit it. I braked, the truck behind me didn't stop in time. You have the police report. It's all documented.

Q: I'm asking what you saw, Ms. Delaney.

A: And I've told you. Repeatedly. The SUV hit the sedan, and everything fell apart from there.

topic: A witness is asked about a car accident they saw from their front porch
text:
Q: Good morning. You were present at your residence on March 14th of this year, correct?

A: I was.

Q: And where exactly were you when the accident occurred?

A: On my porch.

Q: The front porch?

A: Yes.

Q: Were you seated or standing?

A: Seated.

Q: Can you describe what you observed?

A: A car hit another car.

Q: Can you be more specific about what you saw?

A: One car was going down Maple, the other pulled out from the side street. They collided.

Q: Which vehicle struck which?

A: I couldn't tell you which one hit which. They just came together.

Q: Did you see the moment of impact?

A: I saw it, sure.

Q: And what happened after the collision?

A: People got out. Someone called 911, I assume. There were sirens eventually.

Q: Did you go to offer assistance?

A: No.

Q: Why not?

A: Wasn't my business. Other people were already there.

topic: A witness is asked about a car accident they saw from their front porch
text:
Q: State your name for the record.

A: PatriciaWendell.

Q: Ms. Wendell, you've indicated you witnessed an automobile accident on the afternoon of June 3rd?

A: That's what I'm here about, so yes.

Q: Alright. What were you doing on your front porch that afternoon?

A: Drinking iced tea, watching the street. It was hot. Not much else to do.

Q: And what did you see happen?

A: The red truck ran the stop sign. The sedan was coming through the intersection and the truck just plowed right into the driver's side. Glass everywhere. Loud. The sedan spun maybe a quarter turn and ended up on the Hendersons' lawn.

Q: You said the truck ran the stop sign. You're certain of that?

A: I've lived on that corner for nineteen years. I know who stops and who doesn't. That truck didn't even tap the brakes.

Q: Okay. Moving on. Did you see the drivers afterward?

A: The truck driver got out. He was walking around, seemed fine. The other one, the woman in the sedan, she stayed in the car for a while.

Q: Did she appear injured?

A: I couldn't say from where I was sitting.

Q: Did you approach the scene at any point?

A: I walked to the edge of my yard.

Q: And then?

A: And then I went back inside. There were enough people standing around.

topic: A witness is asked about a car accident they saw from their front porch
text:
Q: You told the officer at the scene that you witnessed the collision, is that right?

A: I told him I saw some of it.

Q: Some of it. What parts did you see?

A: I heard the noise first. Then I looked up and the cars were already—you know, they were already crashed.

Q: So you didn't see the actual moment of impact?

A: I saw them right after. Like, immediately after. Still moving from the hit.

Q: But the collision itself—the instant they made contact—you didn't observe that?

A: I guess not. I was reading.

Q: Reading what?

A: Does it matter? A magazine.

Q: Sure. Now, after you looked up, what did you observe?

A: The blue car was sort of pushed up onto the curb. The other one, the white SUV, it was stopped in the middle of the road. Steam or smoke coming from under the hood.

Q: Which vehicle's hood?

A: The SUV. Maybe both. I wasn't really paying that close attention.

Q: Did you see anyone exit the vehicles?

A: Eventually.

Q: Eventually. How long after the collision?

A: I don't know. A minute? Two minutes? I wasn't timing it.

Q: Fair enough. Did you notice anything about the drivers' behavior?

A: Not particularly.

topic: A witness is asked about a car accident they saw from their front porch
text:
Q: Let's talk about the lighting conditions. This accident occurred at what time?

A: Around five-thirty, maybe closer to six. Evening.

Q: Was the sun still up?

A: It was getting low. That golden hour kind of light, I guess you'd call it.

Q: Any glare affecting your ability to see the roadway?

A: No.

Q: No glare at all?

A: The sun was behind my house. I was in shade on the porch. I had a clear view.

Q: Perfect. Now, the vehicles involved—describe them for me.

A: A dark-colored sedan, maybe charcoal or black, and a lighter truck. Tan or beige. Something like that.

Q: Makes? Models?

A: I don't really follow cars. The sedan was one of those generic four-door types. The truck was a pickup. Domestic, probably.

Q: You don't know the makes.

A: I don't know the makes.

Q: Okay. What about speed? How fast would you estimate the vehicles were traveling?

A: The sedan was going normal speed. Maybe thirty. The truck was faster.

Q: Faster. Can you quantify that?

A: Forty? Forty-five? I'm not a speed gun.

Q: I'm just asking for your best estimate.

A: And I gave you one.

Q: Let's move on. After the collision, did either driver appear impaired to you?

A: I wouldn't know what that looks like from sixty feet away.

topic: A witness is asked about a car accident they saw from their front porch
text:
Q: Mr. Huang, how long have you lived at 4412 Birchwood Lane?

A: Since 2019, so about five years now.

Q: And you're familiar with the traffic patterns on that street?

A: Sure. It's my street.

Q: On the morning of October 8th, what drew your attention to the accident?

A: I heard the crash. Wasn't really watching the road before that.

Q: What were you doing?

A: Just sitting. Having coffee. Checking my phone, probably.

Q: When you heard the crash, what did you do?

A: Looked up. Saw the cars. Called 911.

Q: You called 911?

A: Someone had to.

Q: That was good of you. Now—

A: Can we speed this along? I have a thing at noon.

Q: We'll try to be efficient. When you looked up, where were the vehicles positioned?

A: Middle of the intersection. The hatchback was T-boned. The other car, the one that hit it, was still sort of attached, if that makes sense. Pushed up against the side.

Q: Could you tell which direction each vehicle had been traveling?

A: The hatchback was going east. The other one came from the north, I think.

Q: You think?

A: I think. Yes. I wasn't studying the whole thing. I just saw what I saw and made the call.

Q: Did you stay on the porch after calling 911?

A: For a few minutes. Then I went back inside to get ready for work.

topic: A business partner is deposed about financial records they were responsible for maintaining
text:
Q: Mr. Hartwell, you were the partner responsible for maintaining the accounts receivable ledger, is that correct?

A: Yes.

Q: And you maintained that ledger from 2019 through the end of 2022?

A: I did. Every entry. Every single one.

Q: I'm showing you what's been marked as Exhibit 14. Do you recognize this document?

A: It's... yes. That's my ledger. The one I kept.

Q: Can you explain why there's a gap in entries between March and June of 2021?

A: I was going to fix it. I had notes, I had everything written down separately, I just... I never transferred them over. I meant to.

Q: You meant to?

A: Thomas was sick. My son. He was very sick that spring, and I was at the hospital more than I was at the office. I thought I'd have time to catch up. I thought there would be more time.

Q: So the missing entries—

A: I wrote them down. I have them somewhere. I kept everything, I just didn't... I didn't put them where they belonged. I'm sorry. I know that doesn't help now.

Q: Mr. Hartwell, I'm just trying to establish what records exist.

A: I know. I know what you're trying to do. I kept good records for three years. Three years, everything balanced to the penny. And then three months... three months, and it all...

Q: Take your time.

A: I'm fine. What's your next question?

Q: Did anyone else have access to the accounts receivable ledger during your absence?

A: No. It was mine. That was my responsibility. Just mine.

topic: A business partner is deposed about financial records they were responsible for maintaining
text:
Q: Ms. Okonkwo, how long did you serve as the financial manager for Ridley Partners?

A: Seven years. Almost eight.

Q: And during that time, who else had signatory authority on the operating accounts?

A: David Ridley. Only David.

Q: Not you?

A: No. I prepared everything, reconciled everything, flagged everything. But I couldn't sign. That was David's role.

Q: I'm going to hand you Exhibit 22. Can you identify this document?

A: It's a wire transfer authorization. From September 2023.

Q: And whose signature appears at the bottom?

A: David's.

Q: You prepared this authorization, didn't you?

A: I prepared all of them.

Q: Ms. Okonkwo, do you know where David Ridley is today?

A: I... no. I don't know where he is.

Q: When did you last speak with him?

A: October. Last October. He called to say he was taking some time away. That's the word he used. "Away."

Q: Did he say where he was going?

A: He didn't say. I asked. He just said he needed to go, and that I'd understand eventually.

Q: Did you understand?

A: I thought I did. I thought he was tired. We were all tired. I didn't think he meant... I didn't think it would be like this.

Q: Like what?

A: Like I'd be sitting here. Answering for things I prepared but couldn't control. For someone who isn't here to answer for himself.

Q: Ms. Okonkwo—

A: I'm answering your questions. I'm doing what he should be doing. Ask me the next one.

topic: A business partner is deposed about financial records they were responsible for maintaining
text:
Q: Let's turn to the quarterly reconciliation process. You performed those reconciliations personally?

A: For the first two years, yes.

Q: And after that?

A: I trained Rebecca to take over. Rebecca Morse.

Q: Why did you stop performing them yourself?

A: The company grew. I had other responsibilities. Rebecca was capable.

Q: Was she?

A: Excuse me?

Q: I'm asking if Rebecca Morse was, in fact, capable of performing accurate reconciliations.

A: She was young. She was learning. Everyone makes mistakes when they're learning.

Q: The discrepancy we're discussing today—$340,000—you would characterize that as a learning mistake?

A: I would characterize it as something I should have caught.

Q: But you didn't.

A: No.

Q: Because you weren't reviewing her work?

A: I was supposed to review it. That was the process. I just... I got busy. I assumed.

Q: You assumed.

Q: Mr. Hendricks, you conducted the 2022 annual performance review for Daniel Okafor, correct?

Q: And what rating did you give Mr. Okafor in that review?

A: I gave him a "meets expectations" rating, which, I should note, places him squarely in the middle tier. Not a failing grade by any means, but it reflected areas where improvement was needed.

Q: What areas specifically?

A: Time management, primarily. Meeting deadlines. I documented this thoroughly—I have a system I developed myself for tracking deliverables, and his numbers were consistently running about fifteen percent behind the team average. I can walk you through the methodology if that would be helpful.

Q: That won't be necessary. Did you discuss this rating with Mr. Okafor?

A: Extensively. I believe in transparency. I sat with him for nearly two hours—far longer than most supervisors spend, I might add—and went through every metric, every data point. I wanted him to understand exactly where he stood and what he needed to do to improve.

Q: How did he respond?

A: He was disappointed, naturally. But I explained to him that my reviews are consistent across the board. I hold everyone to the same standard—I've terminated high performers when their conduct warranted it, and I've championed underperformers who showed genuine growth. Results speak for themselves.

Q: Did you offer him any kind of performance improvement plan at that time?

A: I created a customized thirty-day action plan. Developed it myself, actually. It's a framework I've refined over the years—other supervisors in the company have started using it. I outlined specific, measurable goals and scheduled weekly check-ins.

Q: And did those check-ins occur?

A: Every single one. I kept detailed notes, time-stamped, with Mr. Okafor's acknowledgment signatures on each. I can produce those records. My documentation practices have been cited in internal audits as exemplary.

Q: Let me ask you this—did anyone review your performance evaluation of Mr. Okafor before it was finalized?

A: HR signs off on all reviews, yes. But they've never once modified one of my evaluations. Not in eleven years. I know how to conduct a fair, defensible review.

A: I have.

Q: You've seen employees struggle and improve?

A: Yes.

Q: Employees who seemed promising but didn't work out?

A: Unfortunately, yes.

Q: Now, this brings us to Claire Nakamura. Your documentation shows you conducted three performance reviews for her over a two-year period. The first one, in 2021, you rated her as "exceptional." That's the highest rating available, correct?

A: It is. And she earned it. Her work on the Kerrigan study was genuinely excellent. I don't give that rating lightly—I've given it perhaps a dozen times in nearly two decades.

Q: Exceptional work. And then in 2022, you dropped her to "meets expectations."

A: That's correct.

I explained to her—and I've explained this to many researchers over the years—that at a certain level, you need to develop your own framework for approaching problems. You can't always wait for someone to tell you what to do.

Q: Did she disagree with that assessment?

A: She pushed back, yes. She felt I wasn't giving her adequate support.

Q: And what was your response?

A: I told her that I'd supported dozens of researchers through transitions like this, and that the ones who succeeded were the ones who embraced the ambiguity. I offered that perspective based on my experience.

Q: Did she embrace the ambiguity?

A: Evidently not.

topic: A daycare worker is deposed about an injury a child sustained while in their care
text:
Q: Please state your name and your position at Little Sprouts Daycare.

A: Certainly. My name is Margaret Chen, and I am the Lead Early Childhood Educator at Little Sprouts. I've held that position for eleven years now, and I also serve as our curriculum coordinator and mentor for new staff members.

Q: Were you working on March 14th of this year?

A: I was, yes. I was supervising the Butterfly Room that day—that's our three-to-four-year-old classroom. I should mention I personally designed the activity stations in that room based on Montessori principles I studied during my advanced certification.

Q: Let's talk about the incident involving Lily Patterson. Can you describe what happened?

A: Of course. I want to be clear that our classroom operates under a supervision protocol I developed myself, one that's actually been adopted by two other facilities in the district. On that particular day, Lily was at the sensory table—a station I created specifically to promote fine motor development—when she slipped.

Q: How did she slip?

A: There was a small amount of water on the floor near the table. Now, our safety checklist—which I authored and update quarterly—requires floor checks every fifteen minutes. I had completed one just twelve minutes prior.

Q: So water appeared within twelve minutes?

A: Children explore. They experiment. That's actually a sign of healthy cognitive development, which I've written about in our parent newsletter. The water likely came from a child transferring materials between stations.

Q: Was anyone watching Lily at the moment she fell?

A: I was overseeing the entire room. I should note that my supervision techniques were specifically praised during our state inspection last fall. The inspector told our director she'd never seen such organized classroom management.

Q: But you didn't see the water on the floor?

A: I maintain visual contact with all fourteen children simultaneously through a positioning system I developed. It's impossible to observe every square inch of flooring while engaging meaningfully with children's developmental progress.

Q: What happened after Lily fell?

A: I responded within seconds—three seconds, perhaps four. I'm trained in pediatric first aid, actually. I recertified just two months ago with a perfect score. I assessed her injury, comforted her, and followed our incident protocol, which I helped write.

Q: Did you fill out an incident report?

A: I did. And I'd like the record to reflect that our incident reports are considered models in the early childhood education community. The format was featured in a regional training seminar last year. I filled it out completely and accurately.

Q: Thank you, Ms. Chen.

A: You're welcome. I take documentation very seriously. It's one of the reasons I've been asked to train other facilities on proper reporting procedures.

---

A: We've worked hard to build something special, yes.

Q: Tell me about your safety protocols.

A: Our safety protocols exceed state requirements in every category. We conduct monthly drills, quarterly equipment inspections, and annual comprehensive safety audits. I personally review every incident report within twenty-four hours.

Q: Every incident report. So you reviewed the report from May 17th regarding Ethan Carr?

A: I did.

Q: Walk me through what you learned from that report.

A: Ethan was in our outdoor play area during afternoon free time. He was running near the sandbox when he tripped over an exposed tree root and fell, striking his head on the sandbox frame.

Q: An exposed tree root?

A: That's correct.

Q: In the play area of a facility that conducts quarterly equipment inspections?

A: The root had become exposed recently due to erosion from spring rains. Our last inspection was in March.

Q: Two months earlier.

A: Yes.

Q: And no one noticed this root in two months?

A: The play area is checked daily for obvious hazards. The root was at the far edge of the yard, partially obscured by grass.

Q: But Ethan found it.

A: Children move through spaces differently than adults. They run, they don't watch their feet.

Q: So the root that your staff missed for two months was obvious enough for a five-year-old to trip over.

A: I've already acknowledged this was a failure. I'm not here to pretend otherwise.

Q: What have you done since?

A: We've implemented weekly ground-level inspections. Staff now physically walk every inch of outdoor space on their hands and knees, checking for any ground-level hazards.

Q: On their hands and knees?

A: That's correct. I do it myself every Monday morning before the children arrive.

Q: You personally?

A: I don't ask my staff to do anything I won't do. I designed this protocol. I implemented it. And I will continue to refine it until it's perfect.

Q: Until it's perfect.

A: We owe these families nothing less.

topic: A driver is deposed about the events leading up to a multi-vehicle collision
text:
Q: Mr. Hartley, I want to direct your attention to the afternoon of September 14th. You were driving a 2019 Honda Accord, correct?

A: Yes.

Q: What was the weather like that afternoon?

A: It was— it was clear. Sunny. No rain or anything like that.

Q: How long had you been driving before the collision occurred?

A: Maybe forty-five minutes? Could have been an hour. I'm not— I don't want to say exactly because I'm not certain.

Q: That's fine. Approximately forty-five minutes to an hour. Were you coming from work?

A: Yes.

Q: And where is your workplace located?

A: It's in— sorry, could you clarify what you're asking? The street address, or the town, or—

Q: The town is fine.

A: Millbrook. The office is in Millbrook.

Q: At any point during that drive, did you use your cell phone?

A: I need to be careful here. I don't— I may have glanced at it. At a red light. I think. But I wasn't— I wasn't using it while I was actually driving. I want to be clear about that.

Q: When you say you "glanced at it," what do you mean?

A: Just— to check the time, maybe? Or to see if I had a notification. I don't remember specifically. I'm trying to be accurate.

Q: I understand. Did you send any text messages during the drive?

A: No. No, I don't believe so. I mean, I'd have to check my phone records, but I don't think I did. I really don't think so.

topic: A driver is deposed about the events leading up to a multi-vehicle collision
text:
Q: Ms. Delgado, let me ask you about the moments just before impact. You said the traffic ahead of you slowed suddenly?

A: Yes.

Q: How suddenly? Help me understand what you saw.

A: The brake lights came on. All at once. It was like a chain reaction going forward.

Q: And how far were you from the vehicle directly in front of you when you first saw those brake lights?

A: I don't know. A few car lengths.

Q: A few car lengths. Two? Three? Five?

A: Maybe three.

Q: You're saying maybe. I need something more concrete. Was it two car lengths or was it five?

A: I said three. Approximately three.

Q: Fine. Three car lengths. And what was your speed at that moment?

A: Around forty.

Q: Forty miles per hour, three car lengths back. Did you apply your brakes immediately?

A: Yes.

Q: Immediately. No hesitation?

A: I saw the lights and I braked. That's what happened.

Q: Let me ask it differently. How much time elapsed between seeing the brake lights and pressing your brake pedal?

A: I don't— a second? Less than a second?

Q: Less than a second. You're certain?

A: I'm telling you what I remember.

Q: Ms. Delgado, I'm going to ask you one more time. Did you brake immediately, or was there a delay?

A: I already answered that.

Q: Then answer it again.

A: I braked when I saw the lights. I don't know what else you want me to say.

topic: A driver is deposed about the events leading up to a multi-vehicle collision
text:
Q: Walk me through what happened after you merged onto the highway.

Q: Did you signal?

A: Yes.

Q: Did you check your mirrors?

A: Yes. Side mirror, rearview. I always do.

Q: You always do. Every single time?

A: I mean— yes, it's habit. I've been driving for twenty years.

Q: I'm not questioning your experience. I'm asking whether, on this specific occasion, you checked your mirrors before changing lanes.

A: Yes. I did.

Q: Both mirrors?

A: Yes. I just said that. Side and rearview. Both.

Q: Did you turn your head to check your blind spot?

A: I— yes. I believe so.

Q: You believe so, or you did?

A: I did. That's part of how I drive. I'm not going to sit here and let you suggest I was being careless.

topic: A driver is deposed about the events leading up to a multi-vehicle collision
text:
Q: Mr. Okonkwo, how many hours of sleep did you get the night before the accident?

topic: A driver is deposed about the events leading up to a multi-vehicle collision
text:
Q: Let's go back to the intersection. You were stopped at the red light at Oak and Merchant?

A: Yes.

A: Yes.

A: It's not an assumption. That's how traffic lights work.

Q: Mr. Patterson, I'm asking what you observed, not what you've concluded. Did you see their light?

A: No. I already said no.

topic: A supervisor is deposed about performance reviews given to an employee who was later fired
text:
Q: Mr. Patterson, you conducted Marcus Williams' annual review in March 2022, correct?

A: I did, yes.

Q: And you gave him an overall rating of "meets expectations"?

A: That's what the form says, yes. But I want to be clear about the context, if I may.

Q: Go ahead.

A: Marcus was going through a difficult period. His mother had been diagnosed with cancer that January. He told me about it, and I could see it was affecting him. He was still showing up, still trying. The "meets expectations" rating—I gave him that because I believed he was doing the best he could under circumstances that would have broken a lot of people.

Q: So you're saying the rating didn't reflect his actual performance?

A: I'm saying it reflected who he was as a whole person during that period. His numbers were down, yes. But I've supervised a lot of people, counsel. I've learned that employees aren't machines. They go through things.

Q: Did you document his mother's illness in the review?

A: I did, actually. In the comments section. I wrote that he was managing personal hardships with professionalism.

Q: Did anyone from HR tell you that was inappropriate?

A: No one used the word "inappropriate." Someone mentioned I should focus on metrics. I understood their position. I just didn't agree with it.

Q: Why not?

A: Because metrics don't tell you whether someone's going to get through a hard time and come back stronger. And I believed Marcus would.

Q: Did he?

A: He never got the chance to show us. We terminated him four months later.

Q: Do you think that termination was justified?

A: I think... I think there were other ways we could have handled it. That's what I think.

topic: A supervisor is deposed about performance reviews given to an employee who was later fired
text:
Q: Ms. Okonkwo, I want to ask you about the performance improvement plan you placed David Reeves on in September 2021.

A: Okay.

Q: Whose decision was that?

A: It was a joint decision between myself and HR.

Q: But you initiated it?

A: I did.

Q: Take your time with this next question. When you initiated that PIP, did you believe David Reeves was capable of meeting its requirements?

A: That's—yes, I did. I wouldn't have put him on a plan I thought was impossible. That's not why we do PIPs.

Q: Why do you do them?

A: To give someone a clear path. To say, here's what we need from you, here's how long you have, here's what support we'll provide. It's supposed to be a lifeline, not a trap.

Q: Did you provide that support?

A: I tried. I checked in with him weekly. I offered to adjust his workload. I asked him multiple times if there was anything going on that I should know about.

Q: What did he say?

A: He said he was fine. He said he could handle it.

Q: Did you believe him?

A: I believed he wanted to believe it himself.

Q: That's not what I asked.

A: No, I suppose it isn't. I had concerns. He seemed tired. Withdrawn. But he didn't open up to me, and I didn't want to push too hard and make him feel surveilled.

Q: Looking back, do you wish you had pushed harder?

A: Looking back, I wish a lot of things.

Q: Such as?

A: I wish I'd found a way to reach him before it got to the point it did.

topic: A supervisor is deposed about performance reviews given to an employee who was later fired
text:
Q: Mr. Torres, how long did you supervise Jennifer Markham?

A: About two years.

Q: And in that time, how many performance reviews did you conduct for her?

A: Two annual reviews and one mid-year check-in.

Q: Let's talk about the check-in. That was in June 2023?

A: That sounds right.

Q: What do you remember about that meeting?

A: I remember it was hard. For both of us.

Q: Why was it hard?

A: Because I had to tell her that her work wasn't meeting standards, and I knew—I could see—that she was already struggling. She looked exhausted. She'd lost weight. I don't think she was sleeping.

Q: Did you ask her about that?

A: I asked if everything was okay outside of work.

Q: What did she say?

A: She said she was handling it.

Q: Mr. Torres, I want to be direct with you. This is a wrongful termination case. Did you believe Ms. Markham was being treated fairly by the company?

A: Counsel, I'm here to answer questions about what happened.

Q: That is what I'm asking you.

A: I believed—I believe—that Jennifer deserved more patience than she received. I told that to HR. I have emails documenting that.

Q: And what was HR's response?

A: They said they appreciated my input.

Q: Did they follow it?

A: She was terminated six weeks later. So I suppose that's your answer.

Q: I understand. Thank you for your candor.

A: I just wish it had mattered when it could have made a difference.

topic: A supervisor is deposed about performance reviews given to an employee who was later fired
text:
Q: Ms. Chen, you gave Robert Holloway a rating of "needs improvement" in November 2022?

A: I did.

Q: How did that conversation go?

A: It's—can I ask what you mean by "go"?

Q: Sure. Walk me through the meeting. What was said, what was his reaction?

A: All right. I sat him down in my office. I told him that his numbers had fallen below expectations for the second quarter in a row. I told him I'd been getting complaints from the Atlanta office about missed deadlines.

Q: How did he respond?

A: He got quiet. Then he apologized. Said he knew he'd been dropping the ball.

Q: Did he offer an explanation?

A: Not initially. But I could tell something was wrong. So I waited. I didn't push.

Q: And?

A: Eventually he told me his wife had moved out. He was trying to handle everything with his kids on his own. He hadn't told anyone at work because he was embarrassed.

Q: What did you do with that information?

A: I asked him what he needed. I asked if he wanted to take some leave, if he needed a modified schedule. I told him we could figure something out.

Q: Did he take you up on that?

A: He said he'd think about it. Then the next week, I got an email from the VP saying they'd decided to move forward with separation.

Q: Did you know that was coming?

A: No. I did not.

Q: How did you feel about it?

A: Counsel, I don't know that my feelings are relevant to this proceeding.

Q: They're relevant to me.

A: Then I'll tell you I lost sleep over it. I still do, sometimes.

topic: A supervisor is deposed about performance reviews given to an employee who was later fired
text:
Q: Ms. DeLuca, I want to understand the timeline here. You gave Amir Patel a positive review in January, and then he was terminated in April?

A: That's correct.

Q: Help me understand how that happens.

A: I can try. But I want to say first that I've asked myself that question many times.

Q: What answer have you come to?

A: That decisions get made above my head, and I don't always agree with them.

Q: Did you agree with this one?

A: No.

Q: Did you tell anyone that?

A: I told my manager that I thought Amir was a valuable employee who was improving. I said I thought termination was premature.

Q: What was the response?

A: She said the decision had already been made.

Q: How was Amir notified?

A: HR handled it. I wasn't in the room.

Q: Did you speak with him afterward?

A: I called him that evening. On my personal phone.

Q: What did you say?

A: I told him I was sorry. I told him the review I wrote was genuine and that I'd be happy to serve as a reference.

Q: Is that typical—supervisors calling terminated employees personally?

A: I don't know what's typical. I know what felt right.

Q: Did he say anything to you?

A: He thanked me. He said he knew I'd tried. And then he said he hoped this wouldn't affect my standing at the company.

Q: He was worried about you?

A: Yes. That's the kind of person Amir is. Was. That's who we let go.

topic: A witness is questioned about a conversation they overheard in a company hallway
text:
Q: Mr. Delacroix, I want to direct your attention to March 15th of last year. Were you present at the Westfield corporate office that day?

A: Yes.

A: I overheard a lot of conversations. It's a hallway. People talk in hallways.

A: Then you should ask about that specifically.

Q: I'm asking now. Did you overhear a conversation between Sandra Mitchell and David Reeves on March 15th?

A: Yes.

Q: Where exactly were you when this conversation occurred?

A: I was in the copy room. The door was open. The copy room is adjacent to the hallway. I'm sure you have the floor plan.

Q: What did you hear Ms. Mitchell say?

A: She said something about the quarterly numbers. I don't remember the exact words because, unlike some people apparently, I wasn't recording it.

Q: Mr. Delacroix, I'm simply asking what you remember. Did she mention anything about adjusting figures?

A: She might have used the word "adjust." She might have used "revise." She might have used "update." I was making copies. I wasn't taking dictation.

Q: Did Mr. Reeves respond to her?

A: He did.

Q: What did he say?

A: He said—and I'm paraphrasing here since you seem to want me to perform a transcript from memory—something like "that's not how we do things."

Q: Did he say anything else?

A: He said they should talk in his office. And then they walked away. And then I finished my copies. Anything else you'd like to know about my copy job that day?

---

topic: A witness is questioned about a conversation they overheard in a company hallway
text:
Q: Ms. Patterson, you've testified that you were in the third-floor hallway on October 8th. Correct?

A: That's correct.

A: I did, yes.

A: I heard him say something similar to that.

Q: Similar. What do you mean by similar?

A: I mean I'm not certain those were his exact words. It was something to that effect.

Q: Ms. Patterson, this is important. I need you to tell me what you actually heard.

A: And I'm trying to do that. I heard him say something about keeping it quiet or burying it. I don't have a photographic memory for conversations I wasn't part of.

Q: Let's slow down. Let's slow down. Were you walking or standing still when you heard this?

A: I was walking toward the elevator.

Q: So you were moving. You heard a fragment of a conversation.

A: It wasn't a fragment. I heard several sentences. I just don't have them memorized word for word.

Q: Why do you remember that part clearly?

A: Because it struck me as odd. That's why it stuck.

Q: Did you report this conversation to anyone?

A: Not at the time, no.

Q: Why not?

A: Because I didn't think it was my place to report a conversation I'd overheard in a hallway. I still had to work there.

---

topic: A witness is questioned about a conversation they overheard in a company hallway
text:
Q: You were near the executive wing that afternoon?

topic: A witness is questioned about a conversation they overheard in a company hallway
text:
Q: Ms. Yuen, you've stated you overheard a conversation between Richard Calder and an unidentified woman near the break room. Is that right?

A: Near the hallway by the break room, yes.

Q: I'm going to ask you a series of questions about that conversation, and I'd like you to answer as specifically as you can. Understood?

A: Of course.

Q: What time of day was this?

A: Mid-afternoon. Around 2:30, maybe 3:00.

Q: What were you doing in that area?

A: I was getting coffee.

Q: And you stopped to listen?

A: I didn't stop to listen. I was waiting for the coffee to brew. They were speaking in the hallway. I couldn't help but hear.

Q: Right. What did you hear first?

Q: Did the woman respond?

Q: And Mr. Calder's response?

A: He laughed. Sort of a short laugh. And he said, "Because Helen wanted it done."

Q: Helen being Helen Markowitz?

A: I assume so. She's the only Helen in senior leadership.

Q: Did the conversation continue?

A: Not that I heard. The coffee finished. I went back to my desk.

Q: Did you tell anyone what you'd heard?

A: I mentioned it to a colleague. Just in passing.

Q: Who was that colleague?

A: Do I have to answer that?

Q: You do, Ms. Yuen.

A: Because we were friendly. Because it seemed strange. I don't know. People talk.

---

topic: A witness is questioned about a conversation they overheard in a company hallway
text:
Q: Tell me about the conversation you heard on the fourth floor.

A: Can you be more specific? What aspect of it?

Q: Start from the beginning, Mr. Reinholt. What did you hear?

A: I heard two voices coming from around the corner. One was Patricia Engel. The other I didn't recognize.

Q: Male or female, the one you didn't recognize?

A: Male.

Q: What were they discussing?

A: They were discussing—look, I came around the corner, I heard maybe thirty seconds of a conversation, and then they stopped talking when they saw me.

Q: What did you hear in those thirty seconds?

A: Ms. Engel said something about the safety report being "incomplete." The man said they didn't have time to redo it. She said—I think—"then we file what we have."

Q: "We file what we have." You're certain?

A: I'm certain that's what she said, yes.

Q: Did she say anything about the consequences of filing an incomplete report?

A: No.

Q: Did the man?

A: No. They stopped talking. Because I walked into view. I already told you that.

Q: And then what happened?

A: They nodded at me. I nodded at them. I kept walking. It was a hallway interaction. It lasted seconds.

Q: Did you think about reporting what you heard?

A: Reporting it to whom? And saying what? That I heard two people having a work conversation about a report?

Q: You didn't think it was significant at the time?

A: I didn't know what I was hearing. I still don't, entirely. That's why I'm just telling you what I heard and not what it means.

A: I don't remember. Probably. We work on the same floor.

Q: Did you ever discuss what you overheard with her?

A: No. Why would I?

topic: A witness is asked about a car accident they saw from their front porch
text:
Q: Please state your name for the record.

A: Linda Moravec. M-O-R-A-V-E-C.

Q: Ms. Moravec, you were at home on the afternoon of September 14th?

A: Yes.

Q: And where specifically were you when the accident occurred?

A: On my front porch. I already told the police this. I told the insurance investigator. I've told multiple people.

Q: I understand. But I need you to tell me. Were you sitting or standing?

A: Sitting. In the rocking chair. The green one, if that matters.

Q: What were you doing at the time?

A: Drinking iced tea and watching the street. Is that detailed enough, or do you need to know what kind of tea?

Q: That won't be necessary. What did you observe?

A: I observed a silver sedan run the stop sign and hit a blue pickup truck.

Q: How can you be certain the sedan ran the stop sign?

A: Because I've lived at that house for twenty-three years and I know what it looks like when someone stops at that sign and what it looks like when they don't. This one didn't.

Q: Did the sedan slow down at all before entering the intersection?

A: I just said they ran the sign.

Q: I'm asking if you observed any reduction in speed.

A: No. None. They went through like the sign wasn't there. Is there another way you'd like me to say it?

Q: Let's move on. After the collision—

A: The silver car spun sideways and the truck ended up on Mrs. Patterson's lawn. I already drew a diagram for someone. Do you have that?

Q: I'm not asking about a diagram. I'm asking what you personally witnessed.

A: That's what I witnessed.

---

topic: A witness is asked about a car accident they saw from their front porch
text:
Q: Mr. Doyle, approximately what time did this accident occur?

A: Around four, four-fifteen. Somewhere in there.

Q: Can you be more specific?

A: I wasn't checking my watch.

A: No.

A: No.

Q: So somewhere between four o'clock and four-fifteen, give or take?

A: That's what I said the first time.

Q: I'm just trying to establish—

A: And I'm trying to answer. I said around four. That's my answer. I can't give you a timestamp down to the second.

A: East. Toward downtown.

Q: And the pickup?

A: South. Coming from the Hendricks subdivision, probably.

Q: That won't be necessary. What happened when the two vehicles met at the intersection?

A: They collided. That's generally what happens when two cars try to occupy the same space.
