---

topic: A witness is asked about a car accident they saw from their front porch
text:
Q: Now, Mrs. Chen, you've testified you were on your porch. How far is your porch from the intersection?

A: I'm not sure exactly. Maybe a hundred feet?

Q: Could it be further than that?

A: It could be. I've never measured it.

Q: Would you say it's closer to one hundred feet or two hundred feet?

A: I really couldn't say with certainty.

Q: Let me ask it this way. Could you clearly see the stop sign from your porch?

A: Yes.

Q: Could you read the word "stop" on the sign?

A: I... yes, I believe so.

Q: You believe so, or you could?

A: I could. Yes.

Q: Mrs. Chen, had you been drinking any alcohol that afternoon?

A: What? No.

Q: Not even a glass of wine?

A: No, I don't— no.

Q: Do you wear corrective lenses?

A: Yes, I wear glasses.

Q: Were you wearing them at the time of the accident?

A: I... I usually wear them.

Q: Usually isn't my question. Were you wearing them at that specific time?

A: I think so. Yes.

Q: You think so. Let me ask again. As you sit here today, under oath, can you state with certainty that you were wearing your prescription glasses at the moment of the collision?

A: Yes. I was wearing them.

Q: Thank you. Now, you claim the silver vehicle failed to stop—

A: I don't "claim" anything. I saw it happen.

Q: Let me rephrase. You have testified that the silver vehicle failed to stop. Is that based on what you actually saw, or what you assumed happened after hearing the crash?

A: I saw the car go through the intersection without stopping. I was looking right at it.

---

topic: A witness is asked about a car accident they saw from their front porch
text:
Q: You said in your written statement that the pickup truck had the right of way. Do you recall writing that?

A: Yes.

Q: What made you conclude that the pickup had the right of way?

A: The pickup was on Maple. There's no stop sign on Maple. There's a stop sign on Thornwood. The sedan was on Thornwood.

Q: So your conclusion is based on the placement of traffic signs.

A: It's based on basic traffic law.

Q: Are you a traffic engineer, Mr. Bassett?

A: No.

Q: A police officer?

A: No.

Q: Have you received any professional training in accident reconstruction?

A: No, but I have a driver's license. I know how stop signs work. Most adults do.

Q: Let's talk about what you actually observed, not your interpretation. Did you see the sedan approach the intersection?

A: Yes.

Q: From how far away?

A: I don't know. A few houses down.

Q: Could you estimate in feet?

A: I already said I don't know. A hundred feet, maybe more.

Q: And you watched it continuously from that point until the impact?

A: Yes.

Q: You didn't look away? Not even for a second?

A: I was watching the street. I watched the car come down the road and I watched it go into the intersection and hit the truck. I didn't look away.

Q: What color was the driver's shirt?

A: I have no idea.

Q: But you were watching continuously.

A: I was watching the car. I wasn't studying the driver's wardrobe.

---

topic: A witness is asked about a car accident they saw from their front porch
text:
Q: Let's go back to the moment of impact. You said the sedan was traveling— and I want to make sure I have this right— at approximately thirty-five miles per hour?

A: I said it looked like it was going about thirty-five. I can't be exact.

Q: How did you arrive at that estimate?

A: I've driven on that street for years. I know what thirty-five looks like.

Q: So this is based on your personal sense of speed.

A: Yes.

Q: Not on any measurement.

A: Obviously not. I don't have a radar gun.

Q: Could the sedan have been traveling at twenty-five miles per hour?

A: I don't think so.

Q: Is it possible?

A: Anything's possible. But I'm telling you what I saw.

Q: What you believed you saw.

A: What I saw. I'm not— I saw it. I was there. Were you?

Q: Mr. Hammonds, I'm just trying to understand the basis for your testimony.

A: And I've explained it. Three times now.

Q: After the collision, did you go to the scene?

A: Yes. I walked over.

Q: Immediately?

A: Within a minute or two. I had to put on shoes.

Q: Did you speak to either driver?

A: I spoke to the truck driver. He was still in his vehicle. The sedan driver was on the phone.

Q: What did the truck driver say to you?

A: He asked if I saw what happened. I said yes.

Q: Did he say anything else?

A: He said the other car came out of nowhere.

Q: Those were his exact words? "Came out of nowhere"?

A: Yes.

Q: But you've testified the sedan was visible approaching for a hundred feet.

A: That's what the man said. I'm telling you what he said. Do you want me to tell you what he said or not?

topic: An HR director is questioned about a harassment complaint that was filed and closed
text:
Q: Ms. Holloway, I understand you were the HR director at Benton & Associates when the complaint involving Marcus Chen was filed?

A: Yes, that's right. I'd been in that role for about six years at that point, and I remember the situation well.

Q: Can you walk me through what happened when you first received the complaint?

A: Of course. Dina Alvarez came to my office on a Tuesday afternoon—I remember because I'd just come back from a meeting. She was clearly nervous, and I wanted to make sure she felt comfortable, so we talked for a bit before she even got into the details. I offered her water, closed the door, made sure she knew this was a safe space.

Q: And what did she tell you?

A: She described several incidents where Marcus had made comments about her appearance, touched her shoulder repeatedly despite her asking him to stop, and sent her text messages outside of work hours that she felt were inappropriate. She was upset, and I took detailed notes so she wouldn't have to repeat herself more than necessary.

Q: How did you proceed after that initial conversation?

A: I thanked her for trusting me with this—I know how hard it is to come forward—and I explained our process step by step. I wanted her to feel informed and supported throughout. I told her I'd be interviewing witnesses and reviewing any documentation she could provide.

Q: Did you conduct those interviews?

A: I did. I spoke with three coworkers Ms. Alvarez identified, and I also interviewed Marcus. I tried to approach everyone with an open mind, because I think that's what fairness requires.

Q: What was your impression of the witness statements?

A: They were mixed, honestly. Two people corroborated some of what Dina described—the comments, the hovering. One person said she hadn't noticed anything unusual. I made sure to document everything carefully because I wanted the record to reflect the full picture.

Q: And what was the outcome of the investigation?

A: After reviewing everything, I recommended a formal warning for Marcus and mandatory training. I also suggested some workspace adjustments so Dina wouldn't have to interact with him directly unless necessary.

Q: Was the complaint then closed?

A: It was, yes. But I followed up with Dina twice afterward—once after a week, once after a month—just to check in and make sure she felt the situation had improved. I wanted her to know that filing the complaint wasn't the end of my involvement if she still needed support.

Q: Did she express satisfaction with the outcome?

A: She said she appreciated that I'd listened and taken her seriously. I think that meant a lot to her, and frankly, it meant a lot to me too.

topic: An HR director is questioned about a harassment complaint that was filed and closed
text:
Q: Mr. Tate, you closed the harassment complaint filed by James Oren in March of last year, correct?

A: That's correct.

Q: I'd like to understand the investigation process. Take your time with your answers—I know these matters can be sensitive.

A: I appreciate that. Yes, it was a difficult situation for everyone involved.

Q: When did Mr. Oren first bring his concerns to you?

A: He emailed me on March 3rd asking if we could speak privately. I made time for him that same day because I could tell from his message that it was weighing on him.

Q: What did he describe?

A: He said his supervisor, Rachel Nguyen, had been making comments about his personal life—his dating life, specifically—in front of other team members. He felt humiliated and said it had been going on for several months.

Q: That must have been difficult for him to share.

A: It was. He actually teared up at one point, and I just let him take a moment. I didn't want to rush him.

Q: How did you approach the investigation?

A: Carefully. I interviewed four members of the team individually, and I reviewed some Slack messages Mr. Oren provided. I wanted to be thorough because I knew this was affecting his wellbeing.

Q: What did the Slack messages show?

A: Some joking comments from Ms. Nguyen about James needing to "find a nice girl" and references to his weekend plans. Taken individually, they might seem minor, but in context, I could see a pattern.

Q: What was your finding?

A: I determined that while Ms. Nguyen likely didn't intend harm, her comments had created an uncomfortable environment for Mr. Oren. I spoke with her about it, and she was genuinely remorseful. She apologized to James directly.

Q: Did Mr. Oren feel the matter was resolved?

A: He told me he did. He thanked me for believing him, which honestly stayed with me. I think he'd expected to be dismissed.

topic: An HR director is questioned about a harassment complaint that was filed and closed
text:
Q: Ms. Cartwright, the complaint we're discussing today was filed by your employee, Derek Simmons, against a client representative. Is that right?

A: Yes. Derek came to me because he didn't know where else to turn, and I wanted to help him figure out his options.

Q: That's an unusual situation—a complaint against someone outside the company.

A: It is, and I'll be honest, I wasn't sure at first how to handle it procedurally. But Derek was clearly distressed, and I felt it was important to take it seriously regardless of who the complaint was against.

Q: What did Mr. Simmons allege?

A: He said that during a site visit, the client representative—a woman named Lorraine Voss—had made repeated sexual comments to him and, on one occasion, touched his thigh under a conference table. He was embarrassed and felt he couldn't say anything at the time because of the client relationship.

Q: How did you respond?

A: I told him I was glad he came to me and that he shouldn't have to tolerate that from anyone, client or not. We talked through his options together.

Q: What were those options?

A: He could file a formal internal complaint, which would be documented. We could also raise the issue with the client company's HR department. Or he could request to be removed from that account without a formal complaint.

Q: What did he choose?

A: He wanted it documented internally, but he asked that we not contact the client. He was worried about professional repercussions.

Q: Did you honor that request?

A: I did, though I explained that it limited what corrective action we could take. I reassigned him to a different account and made sure his file reflected that the reassignment was at his request and not performance-related.

Q: Did you follow up with him?

A: Several times. I checked in after a few weeks, and then again a couple months later. I wanted him to know the door was always open if anything changed or if he experienced anything else.

Q: How did he seem when you last spoke?

A: Relieved, I think. He said he felt like someone had actually listened to him for once.

topic: An HR director is questioned about a harassment complaint that was filed and closed
text:
Q: Let's discuss the timeline of the Santos complaint, Ms. Whitfield. I want to make sure I understand each step you took.

A: Absolutely. I'm happy to walk through it.

Q: When did you first learn of Gabriela Santos's concerns?

A: She stopped by my office on October 14th. She seemed hesitant at first, like she wasn't sure if what she'd experienced was "bad enough" to report.

Q: What did you tell her?

A: I told her that my door was open and that she didn't need to have everything figured out before talking to me. I said we could just have a conversation and go from there.

Q: And she opened up?

A: She did. She told me that a coworker, Brian Holt, had been sending her messages on the company chat system that made her uncomfortable—compliments that felt too personal, questions about whether she was single, that sort of thing.

Q: Did she show you these messages?

A: She did, and I could see why she was unsettled. Some of them were innocuous on their own, but the frequency and tone were concerning.

Q: What steps did you take?

A: I documented everything she shared, and I spoke with Brian. I tried to approach him without accusations—I wanted to understand his perspective too.

Q: How did that conversation go?

A: He was surprised, actually. He said he'd just been trying to be friendly and hadn't realized he'd crossed a line. He seemed genuinely upset that he'd made Gabriela uncomfortable.

Q: What was the resolution?

A: I counseled him on appropriate workplace communication and documented the conversation. I also spoke with Gabriela afterward to let her know what had happened and to make sure she felt safe.

Q: Did she?

A: She said she did. She thanked me for handling it quietly and for not making her feel like she'd overreacted. That was important to me—I never want someone to regret coming forward.

topic: An HR director is questioned about a harassment complaint that was filed and closed
text:
Q: Mr. Desmond, I'd like to ask about the Faulkner complaint, but I want to start by acknowledging that these investigations can be personally taxing for the people who conduct them. How was this one for you?

A: I appreciate you saying that. This one was hard, actually. Both people involved were good employees, and I genuinely liked them both.

Q: Tell me about the complaint.

A: Natalie Faulkner came to me in January. She said that her team lead, Oscar Medina, had been making comments about her body—specifically about her weight loss—that made her extremely uncomfortable.

Q: How did she describe these comments?

A: She said he would comment almost daily. Things like "You're looking so good now" or "Whatever you're doing, keep doing it." She felt like he was always watching her, and it was affecting her ability to focus at work.

Q: That sounds difficult.

A: It was. She was anxious just telling me about it. I made sure to let her know that her feelings were valid and that I would handle this with care.

Q: What did your investigation involve?

A: I interviewed Natalie in detail, spoke with Oscar, and talked to two other team members who had witnessed some of the comments. I also reviewed whether there were any prior complaints about Oscar, which there weren't.

Q: What did Oscar say when you spoke with him?

A: He was mortified, honestly. He said he'd thought he was being supportive—he'd lost weight himself a few years ago and knew how hard it was. He hadn't realized the comments were unwelcome.

Q: Did that change your assessment?

A: It helped me understand his intent, but I explained to him that impact matters more than intent in these situations. He understood, and he apologized to Natalie in writing.

Q: How did Natalie feel about that resolution?

A: She told me she felt heard. She said that was all she really wanted—for someone to acknowledge that her discomfort was legitimate. I told her that it was, and that I was glad she trusted me enough to come forward.

topic: A nurse is questioned about a patient fall that occurred during her shift
text:
Q: Please state your name and credentials for the record.

A: Rebecca Torres, RN, BSN. I've been a registered nurse for eleven years, eight of those at Mercy General, and I hold certifications in medical-surgical nursing and fall prevention. I completed the hospital's advanced patient safety training in 2022.

Q: You were working the night shift on March 15th when Mrs. Patterson fell?

A: I was, yes. I was the charge nurse that evening, responsible for overseeing the east wing of the third floor.

Q: Walk me through your assessment of Mrs. Patterson when you came on shift.

A: Gladly. At 1903, I conducted my initial rounds. Mrs. Patterson was alert and oriented times four. I reviewed her fall risk score—she'd been assessed at a 14 on the Morse scale, which placed her in the high-risk category. I confirmed her bed alarm was active, verified the yellow fall-risk bracelet was on her wrist, and ensured her call light was within reach. I documented all of this in the electronic medical record at 1917.

Q: Did you take any additional precautions given her high-risk status?

A: I did. I placed non-slip socks at her bedside, lowered the bed to its lowest position, and moved her IV pole to the far side so it wouldn't obstruct her path to the bathroom. I also spoke with her directly about calling for assistance before attempting to get up. She acknowledged understanding.

Q: And what time did the fall occur?

A: The fall was reported at 2214. I was at the nurses' station completing medication reconciliation when her bed alarm activated.

Q: How quickly did you respond?

A: I was at her doorway within eighteen seconds. We track response times on our unit, and the alarm system logs confirmed this.

Q: What did you find when you arrived?

A: Mrs. Patterson was on the floor beside her bed. She had attempted to reach her water pitcher, which had been moved to the far nightstand by a family member who'd visited earlier in the evening—something I was not aware of until that moment.

Q: So you're saying this fall was caused by a family member?

A: I'm saying that I followed every protocol required of me, documented every intervention, and responded within the expected timeframe. The pitcher's relocation was an intervening factor that occurred outside my observation.

Q: Do you believe you could have done anything differently?

A: I've reviewed my actions carefully, counsel. I followed the standard of care precisely as trained. Every box was checked, every precaution taken. The documentation supports this completely.

topic: A nurse is questioned about a patient fall that occurred during her shift
text:
Q: Nurse Okafor, you've reviewed the incident report from September 3rd?

A: Yes.

Q: The report indicates Mr. Bellamy fell at approximately 0330. Where were you at that time?

A: Conducting rounds on the opposite end of the hallway.

Q: How many patients were you responsible for that night?

A: Seven.

Q: Is that typical?

A: It's within the range we're given.

Q: That's not what I asked. Is seven patients typical for a night shift nurse in your unit?

A: Some nights it's six. Some nights it's eight. Seven is common enough.

Q: Mr. Bellamy was recovering from hip surgery. Were you aware he'd been given pain medication ninety minutes before the fall?

A: I administered it myself.

Q: Hydromorphone?

A: Correct.

Q: Did you reassess his fall risk after administering a narcotic pain medication?

A: The standing orders didn't require reassessment for routine pain management doses.

Q: I didn't ask about standing orders. Did you reassess him?

A: No.

Q: Now, the fall occurred when Mr. Bellamy attempted to use the bathroom. Was he on any toileting schedule?

A: He was offered assistance at 0200. He declined.

Q: But no one checked on him between 0200 and 0330—ninety minutes?

A: Rounds were every two hours per protocol. I was due at his room at 0400.

Q: So your position is that everything was done correctly?

A: My position is that I followed the protocols in place at the time. If you want to discuss whether those protocols were adequate, that's a question for hospital administration, not for me.

topic: A nurse is questioned about a patient fall that occurred during her shift
text:
Q: You mentioned earlier that you've testified in depositions before, correct?

A: This is my third.

Q: Then you understand the importance of precision. Let's talk about the bed alarm. You're certain it was activated when you left Mr. Yates's room at 2100?

A: Absolutely certain.

Q: How can you be so sure?

A: Because I have a personal checklist I run through every time I leave a high-fall-risk patient's room. Bed alarm is item number three. I've done it so many times it's automatic, but I still consciously verify.

Q: Yet the nursing assistant who found Mr. Yates on the floor at 2147 states the alarm was not sounding.

A: That's correct. It wasn't sounding when she arrived.

Q: Which would suggest it wasn't activated.

A: Or it would suggest the alarm malfunctioned, which is exactly what the biomedical engineering report concluded two days later. The sensor pad had a defective connection. It had been flagged for replacement but hadn't been swapped out yet.

Q: You're aware of that report?

A: I requested a copy the day it was issued.

Q: Were you informed the sensor pad was on the replacement list before the incident?

A: I was not. That information wasn't communicated to floor nurses.

Q: Do you find that problematic?

A: Very much so. I raised it at our unit safety meeting. We've since implemented a tagging system so nurses know when equipment is pending service.

Q: That change came from your recommendation?

A: It did. The policy was adopted hospital-wide last month.

Q: Let's move on. When you found Mr. Yates—

A: I didn't find him. CNA Martinez found him. I arrived approximately forty-five seconds later and took over the assessment.

Q: Fair enough. When you arrived at Mr. Yates's room—

A: He was alert, denying pain initially, though he had a small laceration above his left eyebrow. I followed our post-fall protocol, including neurological checks every fifteen minutes for the first hour. He recovered without complication.

topic: A nurse is questioned about a patient fall that occurred during her shift
text:
Q: Nurse Chen, I want to understand the timeline. You clocked in at what time?

A: 1845.

Q: And received report from the day shift nurse?

A: Yes, at approximately 1900. We do bedside handoff.

Q: During that handoff, was Mrs. Franklin's fall risk discussed?

A: It was mentioned, yes.

Q: Mentioned?

A: Her Morse score was included in the verbal report.

Q: What was the score?

A: I don't recall the exact number.

Q: You don't recall?

A: It was six months ago. I remember she was categorized as moderate risk.

Q: The record shows her score was 55. Does that refresh your recollection?

A: If that's what the record shows.

Q: A score of 55 places her in the high-risk category, not moderate.

A: Then I misspoke. High risk.

Q: That's a significant difference, wouldn't you agree?

A: The category informs the interventions. The interventions were in place regardless of my recollection today.

Q: What interventions specifically?

A: Bed in low position, call light in reach, room close to the nurses' station.

Q: No bed alarm?

A: I... I would need to check the documentation.

Q: I have the documentation here. There's no indication a bed alarm was activated for Mrs. Franklin until after her fall.

A: If that's what it shows.

Q: I'm asking you, as the nurse responsible for her care, whether you activated a bed alarm.

A: I don't specifically remember activating one for her, no.

Q: Even though she was high risk?

A: I had seven patients that night. I followed the protocols as best I could.

Q: As best you could. That's your answer?

A: That's my answer.

topic: A nurse is questioned about a patient fall that occurred during her shift
text:
Q: Good morning, Nurse Patel. This shouldn't take too long—I just have a few questions about the incident on April 12th.

A: Good morning.

Q: You were assigned to Mr. Drummond that evening?

A: I was.

Q: He was admitted for pneumonia, correct?

A: Community-acquired pneumonia, yes. He was on day three of IV antibiotics.

Q: And he fell at some point during your shift?

A: He did. Around 0215.

Q: Can you tell me what happened?

A: Certainly. Mr. Drummond woke up disoriented—we later determined he had developed hospital-acquired delirium, which is not uncommon in elderly patients. He attempted to leave his bed to find the bathroom despite being on continuous telemetry and having instructions to call for assistance.

Q: Was anyone with him when this happened?

A: No. He was alone in his room.

Q: You weren't concerned about leaving a confused patient alone?

A: At 2300 rounds, he was oriented and sleeping comfortably. The confusion developed acutely sometime between then and the fall.

Q: How do you know it developed acutely?

A: Because I assessed him myself at 2300. He answered questions appropriately, knew where he was, recognized me from earlier in the evening.

Q: But you didn't check on him again until after the fall?

A: Rounds were every four hours for stable patients. He was categorized as stable.

Q: In retrospect, should he have been checked more frequently?

A: In retrospect, knowing he would develop delirium, yes. But nursing requires us to make decisions based on the information available at the time, not information we learn afterward.

Q: That's a fair point.

A: I documented my assessments thoroughly. The record reflects a patient who showed no signs of confusion at my last encounter with him. What happened after was unforeseeable.

Q: I think that covers what I needed. Thank you for your time, Nurse Patel.

A: You're welcome.

topic: A former employee is deposed about discriminatory remarks made by a supervisor
text:
Q: Ms. Delgado, thank you for being here today. I want to ask you about your time at Hartwell Industries. How long were you employed there?

A: Three years, four months, and—actually, let me be exact—three years, four months, and twelve days. I kept track because I knew this day would come. I kept everything.

Q: You kept everything?

A: Every email, every text, every note I wrote to myself after meetings. I have a whole binder at home. I can tell you dates, times, who was in the room. I was ready for this.

Q: Let's talk about your supervisor, Marcus Webb. Did you ever hear him make remarks about employees' national origins?

A: Oh, absolutely. Where do you want me to start? Because I have examples. Plural. Many of them.

Q: Why don't you start with the first incident you recall?

A: September 14th, 2022. Staff meeting in Conference Room B. There were seven of us present. Marcus pointed at the new org chart and said, and I quote, "We're going to have to do something about the UN situation in this department." Then he looked right at me and Priya Sharma.

Q: What did you understand that to mean?

A: I understood exactly what it meant. He meant too many immigrants. Too many people with accents. He'd made comments before about "understanding people," but this was the first time he said it in front of the whole team. I wrote it down within the hour.

Q: You wrote it down?

A: In my black notebook. I still have it. I brought a copy today, actually, in case you wanted to see it. Do you want to see it?

Q: We'll mark that as an exhibit shortly. Were there other incidents?

A: There were at least a dozen more. Do you want them chronologically or by severity? I can do either.

Q: Let's continue chronologically for now.

A: Perfect. So the next one was October 3rd, same year. Marcus called me into his office and asked me where I was "really from." When I said California, he laughed and said, "No, I mean originally." I told him my parents were from Mexico, and he nodded like that explained something and said, "That's what I thought. You people have a different work style."

Q: Did anyone else witness that conversation?

A: No, but I sent myself an email right afterward documenting it. Time-stamped 4:47 PM. I can pull it up on my phone right now if you need it.

Q: That won't be necessary at this moment. Did you report any of these incidents to Human Resources?

A: I reported three separate incidents. I have the HR ticket numbers memorized if you want them. They did nothing. Well, that's not true—they did something. They put a note in Marcus's file, which I only know because I requested my personnel records later and saw a reference to it. Then they promoted him six months later.

topic: A former employee is deposed about discriminatory remarks made by a supervisor
text:
Q: Mr. Patterson, I represent Hartwell Industries in this matter. I'd like to ask you some questions about conversations you may have witnessed involving your former supervisor, Linda Chen.

A: Sure.

A: I don't recall.

A: I don't recall.

Q: Mr. Patterson, isn't it true that you submitted a written complaint to HR on March 3rd, 2023, specifically describing comments Ms. Chen made about older employees?

A: If you have the document, then I guess I did.

Q: I'm asking what you remember.

A: I remember submitting something.

A: It was a while ago.

topic: A former employee is deposed about discriminatory remarks made by a supervisor
text:
Q: Dr. Okonkwo, you worked in the research division at Hartwell, is that right?

A: That's correct.

Q: And your supervisor was Dr. Richard Ames?

A: For approximately two years, yes.

Q: I want to ask you about a specific meeting—the quarterly review on August 8th, 2023. Do you remember that meeting?

A: I do.

Q: Tell me what happened.

A: Dr. Ames was presenting budget allocations. When he got to my team's funding, he said our numbers were "surprisingly good, considering."

Q: Considering what?

A: He didn't finish the sentence. But he looked at me when he said it. I was the only Black person at the table.

Q: Now, let's be careful here—isn't it possible he meant something else entirely? Perhaps the budget constraints your team faced?

A: Counsel, I have a PhD in biochemistry from Stanford. I've been in corporate research for fifteen years. I know when someone is implying something about my competence based on my race.

Q: But you can't read minds, can you, Dr. Okonkwo?

A: I don't need to read minds when the pattern is consistent.

Q: What pattern?

A: The pattern where Dr. Ames questioned every decision I made while accepting identical decisions from my white colleagues without comment. The pattern where he called my presentation style "aggressive" and Dr. Mueller's identical style "passionate." The pattern where he—

Q: I didn't ask about Dr. Mueller—

A: You asked about the pattern. Dr. Mueller is part of the pattern.

Q: Let's move on. Did Dr. Ames ever explicitly mention race in your presence?

A: He said I was a "diversity hire" to my face on November 12th, 2023. Is that explicit enough for you?

Q: Were there witnesses to that statement?

A: Three. Dr. Sarah Lindstrom, James Carey, and Maria Vance. I have their contact information if you need it.

Q: We'll obtain that through proper channels.

A: I'm sure you will.

topic: A former employee is deposed about discriminatory remarks made by a supervisor
text:
Q: Ms. Thornton, I'm going to jump right in because I think you have some incredibly important testimony to share with us today. You witnessed the exchange between Kevin Rodriguez and his supervisor, Diane Mercer, on January 15th, correct?

A: Yes.

Q: Wonderful! Walk me through exactly what you saw.

A: I was at my desk, which is near the break room. I heard raised voices.

Q: Raised voices! And then what?

A: I looked over and saw Diane and Kevin by the coffee machine.

Q: This is exactly what we need. What were they saying?

A: I couldn't hear everything. But I heard Diane say something about Kevin's "people."

Q: His "people"—and Kevin is Hispanic, isn't he?

Opposing Counsel: Objection, leading.

Q: I'll rephrase. What is Kevin Rodriguez's ethnic background, to your knowledge?

A: I think he's Mexican-American. Or maybe his family is from somewhere else in Central America. I'm not sure.

Q: That's fine, that's fine. Now, when Diane said "your people," what was her tone?

A: She sounded annoyed.

Q: Annoyed! Hostile, even?

Opposing Counsel: Objection, leading.

Q: Was her tone hostile?

A: I don't know if I'd say hostile. She was definitely upset about something.

Q: And after she said "your people," what happened next?

A: Kevin walked away. He looked embarrassed, I think.

Q: Of course he was embarrassed—he was being publicly humiliated based on his ethnicity!

Opposing Counsel: Objection. Counsel is testifying.

Q: Withdrawn. Ms. Thornton, how did the phrase "your people" strike you when you heard it?

A: It made me uncomfortable.

Q: Because it was discriminatory?

A: Because it felt like she was singling him out for something he couldn't control.

Q: Perfect. Now, had you witnessed any other incidents involving Diane Mercer?

A: Not exactly witnessed, but I heard things.

Q: Tell me everything you heard!

topic: A former employee is deposed about discriminatory remarks made by a supervisor
text:
Q: Mr. Kowalski, how long did you work under Thomas Grant?

A: About eighteen months.

Q: During that time, did you observe Mr. Grant interact with female employees?

A: Of course. We all worked together.

Q: How would you characterize those interactions?

A: I'm not sure what you're asking.

Q: Did Mr. Grant treat male and female employees differently?

A: Looking back, yes. I think he did.

Q: In what way?

A: He was more casual with the men. More... careful with the women.

Q: Careful?

A: Or maybe critical is a better word. He held the women to a different standard.

Q: Can you give me an example?

A: There was this one time—actually, I remember this clearly because it bothered me at the time—Jennifer Walsh made the same mistake I had made the week before. I got a correction in private. She got called out in front of the whole team.

Q: Did Mr. Grant ever make explicit comments about women in the workplace?

A: He used to say things about how women were "more emotional" in meetings.

Q: Did he say this once or multiple times?

A: Multiple times. It was kind of a running thing with him. Like a joke he kept making.

Q: Was it funny?

A: Not to me. And definitely not to the women on the team.

Q: Did anyone ever push back?

A: Carla Reyes did once. She asked him straight out if he thought women were less capable than men.

Q: What did he say?

A: He said he didn't think they were less capable, just "wired differently." Then he laughed and said something about his wife being the real boss at home, like that made it okay.

Q: How did Ms. Reyes respond?

A: She didn't say anything else. But she put in for a transfer the next week. I think she saw the writing on the wall.

topic: A tenant is questioned about property damage they reported to their landlord
text:
Q: Ms. Hernandez, I understand you reported water damage to the bedroom ceiling in Unit 4B. Can you walk me through what you first noticed?

A: It was a Tuesday morning, I remember because my daughter had just left for school. I heard this dripping sound, and when I looked up, there was this brown stain spreading across the ceiling, right above where my mother sleeps.

Q: Your mother lives with you in the unit?

A: Yes, she moved in after her stroke last year. She can't live alone anymore, and I couldn't afford—well, she needed somewhere to go.

Q: I see. Take your time. When you noticed the stain, what did you do next?

A: I moved her bed first. She was still in it, actually, and she was confused about what was happening. I had to calm her down before I could even call anyone. Then I called the emergency maintenance line.

Q: And what time was that call, approximately?

A: Maybe eight-thirty? I wasn't watching the clock. I was more worried about getting her settled in the living room. She doesn't do well with changes to her routine.

Q: That's completely understandable. Did you speak with someone directly, or did you leave a message?

A: I left a message. No one answered. I called twice more before noon.

Q: And when did someone from the management company return your call?

A: Not until the next day. By then, the ceiling had started to sag. I put a bucket under it, but I was terrified it would come down on us during the night.

Q: Did you feel you had to stay awake to monitor it?

A: I tried to. I kept checking on my mother every hour. She didn't understand why she couldn't sleep in her own bed.

Q: I can only imagine how difficult that night must have been. When maintenance finally arrived, what did they say?

A: The man who came—he was kind about it, actually. He said it was a pipe problem from the unit above, and that it should have been addressed sooner. He looked at my mother in her wheelchair and said he was sorry.

Q: Did he document the damage at that time?

A: He took some photos on his phone. I don't know if those went into any official file. He mostly just seemed concerned about getting us somewhere dry.

topic: A tenant is questioned about property damage they reported to their landlord
text:
Q: Mr. Patterson, you submitted a repair request on March 3rd regarding the kitchen floor. Is that correct?

A: That's right.

Q: Can you describe the condition of the floor when you made that request?

A: The linoleum was buckling near the sink. Not just a little—I mean, you could trip on it. My wife almost did, twice.

Q: Was your wife injured either of those times?

A: No. Thank God, no. But she has balance issues already, and I kept thinking what if. You know? What if she fell and I wasn't home.

Q: How long had you noticed the buckling before you reported it?

A: Maybe a week. I tried to fix it myself at first. I pushed it down, put some heavy boxes on it overnight. But it kept coming back up.

Q: Why didn't you report it immediately?

A: Honestly? I didn't want to be a bother. The landlord's got a lot of units, a lot of people asking for things. I figured I could handle it myself.

Q: But eventually you decided to make the report.

A: My daughter came to visit. She saw it and got upset with me. She said, "Dad, this is dangerous, you have to say something." She was right.

Q: What happened after you submitted the request?

A: Mr. Okonkwo—the landlord—he came by himself the next week. Didn't send someone else. Came himself.

Q: And what did he do?

A: He got down on his knees and looked at it. Really looked. Then he asked about my wife, how she was doing with her MS. I hadn't expected that.

Q: Did he make repairs at that time?

A: He said he'd need to pull up the whole section, that it was worse underneath than it looked. He scheduled someone for that Saturday and asked if that timing worked for us, with my wife's medical appointments and all.

Q: Did the repair take place as scheduled?

A: It did. And he called afterward to check that we were satisfied. That meant something to me.

topic: A tenant is questioned about property damage they reported to their landlord
text:
Q: You testified earlier that you discovered mold in the bathroom on or about January 15th. How did you first become aware of it?

A: I smelled it before I saw it. This musty smell that wouldn't go away no matter how much I cleaned.

Q: And when you located the source?

A: It was behind the toilet. Black spots all along the baseboard, creeping up the wall.

Q: What was your reaction?

A: I panicked, honestly. My son has asthma. He's only seven. I kept thinking about what he'd been breathing in.

Q: Did you contact the landlord that same day?

A: Within the hour.

Q: Tell me about that conversation.

A: I was upset. Probably more upset than I should've been on the phone. But Mr. Tran, the property manager, he just let me talk. He didn't interrupt or get defensive.

Q: What did he say when you finished?

A: He said, "I hear you. Let's get someone out there today." And he meant it. He had a guy there by four o'clock.

Q: The same day you called?

A: The same day.

Q: What did the inspection reveal?

A: A slow leak from the pipe behind the wall. The mold had been growing for a while, apparently. Longer than I'd been smelling it.

Q: How did that make you feel, learning it had been there longer?

A: Sick. Guilty. Like I should've caught it sooner. I kept apologizing to my son, which probably confused him.

Q: Did Mr. Tran say anything about the timeline of the damage?

A: He told me not to blame myself. He said these things hide, and I'd done the right thing by calling as soon as I noticed. He said his own kid has asthma too, so he understood.

Q: Was the mold remediated?

A: Fully. They put us up in a hotel for three nights while they did the work. Mr. Tran checked in each day to make sure we were okay.

topic: A tenant is questioned about property damage they reported to their landlord
text:
Q: Ms. Oyelaran, let's turn to the incident you reported on September 8th involving the front door lock. You stated in your written complaint that the lock was "non-functional." Can you be more specific?

A: The deadbolt wouldn't engage. You could turn the key, but nothing would catch. The door would just... swing open.

Q: How long had the lock been in that condition before you reported it?

A: It started sticking about a month before. Then one night it just stopped working entirely.

Q: You waited a month?

A: I didn't wait. I managed. I put a chair under the doorknob at night. I told myself it was temporary.

Q: Were you living alone at the time?

A: Yes.

Q: I ask because your complaint mentioned feeling unsafe. Can you describe that feeling for the record?

A: I didn't sleep well. I'd hear sounds in the hallway—normal sounds, probably—and I'd lie there with my heart pounding. I work early shifts. I need my rest. But I couldn't rest.

Q: That must have been exhausting.

A: It was.

Q: When you finally made the formal complaint, what prompted that decision?

A: My neighbor, Mrs. Chen, she noticed I looked tired and asked what was wrong. When I told her, she got upset on my behalf. She walked me down to the management office herself.

Q: And what was the response from management?

A: The woman at the desk, I think her name was Linda, she stopped what she was doing and really listened. She asked me how many nights I'd gone without proper sleep, and when I said almost two weeks, she shook her head like it pained her.

Q: Did she expedite the repair?

A: She had a locksmith there by that evening. She also gave me her direct number and said to call if anything else came up, day or night.

Q: Did you feel your concern was taken seriously?

A: I did. For the first time in a while, I felt like someone cared whether I was safe.

topic: A tenant is questioned about property damage they reported to their landlord
text:
Q: Mr. Brennan, your deposition concerns the broken window in the living room of Unit 12. When did you first notice the crack?

A: November 2nd. The day after that big windstorm.

Q: Can you describe the damage?

A: A crack running diagonal across the whole pane. Maybe two feet long. And cold air just pouring through.

Q: Did you report it right away?

A: I did. I called that morning.

Q: What was the response?

A: They said they'd add it to the list. I understood—the storm had done damage all over the complex. Everyone needed something fixed.

Q: So you were patient with the delay?

A: I tried to be. But after a week, it was hard. The temperature kept dropping, and I've got arthritis in my hands. The cold makes it worse.

Q: Did you communicate that to the management company?

A: I didn't want to complain again. Other people had it worse, I figured. Mrs. Delgado in 14 had a tree branch through her kitchen window. I saw them working on her place.

Q: But eventually you did follow up?

A: My nephew came to visit and saw me wearing gloves inside my own apartment. He called on my behalf. I was embarrassed, but he wouldn't let it go.

Q: What happened after his call?

A: The next day, a woman from the office came by. Not a repair person—someone from management. She brought a space heater and said the window would be fixed by end of week, but she didn't want me suffering until then.

Q: Did she say anything else?

A: She apologized. She said I'd been too kind by waiting, and that I should've pushed harder. She asked if I needed anything else, medication picked up, groceries. I told her I was fine.

Q: Was the window repaired as promised?

A: It was. And she came back afterward to check that the new pane was sealed properly. She brought me soup. Said the cold had been hard on everyone.

topic: A warehouse supervisor is deposed about safety protocols that were allegedly ignored
text:
Q: Mr. Hernandez, I'm going to ask you about the forklift inspection logs for October of last year. Those exist, correct?

A: They exist.

Q: And you were responsible for ensuring those logs were completed daily?

A: That was one of my responsibilities, yes.

Q: One of them. Let's look at Exhibit 14. Can you tell me how many days in October show a completed inspection?

A: I can count them if you'd like.

Q: Please do.

A: Eleven.

Q: Eleven out of thirty-one days. Mr. Hernandez, where are the other twenty inspections?

A: I don't know.

Q: You don't know. You were the supervisor. You just told me it was your responsibility. And you don't know?

A: I said it was one of my responsibilities. I had fourteen direct reports, three shifts to coordinate, and a facility manager who pulled me into meetings every other day. You want to know where the inspections went? Ask the people who kept cutting my staffing while telling me to do more with less.

Q: I'm asking you.

A: And I'm telling you I don't have a simple answer because it wasn't a simple situation.

Q: Did you report the inspection gaps to anyone?

A: I reported staffing concerns multiple times.

Q: That's not what I asked. Did you report that forklift inspections were not being completed?

A: No. I did not file a formal report stating that specific thing. Is that what you wanted to hear?

Q: I want to hear the truth, Mr. Hernandez.

A: That is the truth. Whether you like the shape of it is not my problem.

topic: A warehouse supervisor is deposed about safety protocols that were allegedly ignored
text:
Q: You received safety training when you were promoted to supervisor, correct?

A: Yes.

Q: And that training covered lockout-tagout procedures?

A: Yes.

Q: How long was that training?

A: I believe it was a half-day session.

Q: A half day. Four hours?

A: Approximately.

Q: And in those four hours, you learned everything you needed to know to supervise lockout-tagout compliance for an entire warehouse?

A: I learned the basics. Experience fills in the rest.

Q: Experience. So when Mr. Donovan's arm was caught in the conveyor mechanism, was that part of the experience filling in the rest?

A: Objection—

Q: You can answer.

A: That's a disgusting way to phrase that question.

Q: Is it? A man lost his arm, Mr. Whitfield.

A: I know what he lost. I was there. I rode in the ambulance. I visited him in the hospital three times. So don't sit there and act like I don't understand what happened.

Q: Then help me understand why lockout wasn't performed that morning.

A: Because Jenkins was told to clear the jam quickly. Because we were behind on shipments. Because someone above me decided speed mattered more than procedure.

Q: Someone above you. Who?

A: I'm not going to name names so you can twist this into something it wasn't.

Q: Mr. Whitfield, you're under oath.

A: I'm aware of that. Ask the question properly and I'll answer it properly.

topic: A warehouse supervisor is deposed about safety protocols that were allegedly ignored
text:
Q: Ms. Tran, I want to be very precise here. The safety harness policy—when was it implemented?

A: March of 2022.

Q: And it required harnesses for any work above eight feet?

A: Correct.

Q: Who was responsible for enforcing that policy on the floor?

A: Shift supervisors.

Q: And you were a shift supervisor?

A: I was.

Q: So you were responsible for enforcing it.

A: On my shift, yes.

Q: Was Marcus Webb working your shift on June 15th?

A: You already know he was.

Q: I'm asking you to confirm it.

A: Yes.

Q: And was he wearing a harness when he fell?

A: No.

Q: Why not?

A: I don't know. I wasn't standing next to him.

Q: You were his supervisor.

A: I was supervising nineteen people across forty thousand square feet. I am not physically capable of watching all of them simultaneously.

Q: Did you check whether he had a harness before he went up?

A: I did not personally check, no.

Q: Did anyone?

A: That I don't know.

Q: So the policy existed, but no one was actually checking compliance?

A: I didn't say that.

Q: Then what are you saying?

A: I'm saying I cannot account for every second of every worker's day, and if your implication is that I should have been able to, then you don't understand how a warehouse operates.

topic: A warehouse supervisor is deposed about safety protocols that were allegedly ignored
text:
Q: Mr. Chen, you were aware that aisle seven had a drainage issue?

A: I was aware there had been some water accumulation, yes.

Q: Some water accumulation. How much water are we talking about?

A: It varied.

Q: On November 3rd, how much water?

A: I don't recall exactly.

Q: Would you say it was a puddle, or something more substantial?

A: It was... more than a puddle.

Q: Inches deep?

A: Possibly an inch in some areas.

Q: An inch of water in a warehouse aisle where forklifts operate. Did you report this?

A: I reported it to maintenance.

Q: When?

A: The week before.

Q: And what did maintenance do?

A: They said they'd look into it.

Q: Did they look into it?

A: Not that I'm aware.

Q: Did you follow up?

A: I had other things to deal with.

Q: Other things. More important than standing water in a forklift aisle?

A: I didn't say more important. I said I had other things. I filed the report. It's documented. What maintenance did or didn't do after that isn't my department.

Q: Mr. Chen, a forklift skidded in that water and struck Mrs. Okonkwo. You understand that?

A: Yes, I understand that. Do you understand that I told them about the water and nothing was done? Do you understand that I put it in writing and nobody responded? Because I'm sitting here answering these questions like I made the water appear.

topic: A warehouse supervisor is deposed about safety protocols that were allegedly ignored
text:
Q: Let's talk about the chemical storage area.

A: Fine.

Q: The OSHA guidelines require secondary containment for all flammable liquids. You're familiar with that requirement?

A: I am.

Q: Was secondary containment in place in December of last year?

A: There were containment pallets.

Q: Were they adequate?

A: They met the specifications I was given.

Q: The specifications you were given. By whom?

A: By the regional safety coordinator.

Q: That would be Mr. Jeffries?

A: Yes.

Q: Mr. Jeffries says he never provided specifications for that storage area.

A: Then Mr. Jeffries has a convenient memory.

Q: Are you saying he's lying?

A: I'm saying what I'm saying. I received an email in August with guidelines attached. I followed those guidelines.

Q: Do you have that email?

A: I had it on my work computer. Which, as I understand it, was wiped when I was terminated.

Q: Terminated. You were terminated after the fire?

A: Three days after. For cause, supposedly.

Q: And what cause was given?

A: Failure to maintain safety protocols. Which is interesting, because I was maintaining exactly what I was told to maintain.

Q: So your position is that you were set up?

A: My position is that I did my job, and when something went wrong, they needed someone to blame. I'm not going to sit here and pretend that isn't what happened.

Q: Mr. Palmer—

A: No. You asked me to come here and answer questions. I'm answering them. If the answers don't fit whatever story you're building, that's not my concern.

topic: A witness is questioned about a workplace injury they observed but did not report
text:
Q: Ms. Delgado, I'd like to turn your attention to the morning of March 14th. You were working your regular shift that day?

A: Yes, I was. I clocked in at 6:15, about fifteen minutes early like I usually do.

Q: And at some point that morning, did you observe anything unusual in the warehouse?

A: I did. Around 9:30 or so, I saw Marcus—Marcus Webb—fall from the loading platform.

Q: Can you describe what you saw?

A: He was stacking pallets on the upper platform, and I saw him step backward and lose his footing. He fell maybe five or six feet onto the concrete floor below.

Q: What happened after he fell?

A: He got up pretty quickly. He was holding his shoulder, and I could tell he was in pain. He walked over to the break area and sat down for a while.

Q: Did you approach him?

A: I did. I asked if he was okay, and he said he'd be fine, just tweaked something.

Q: Did you report what you'd seen to a supervisor?

A: No, I didn't.

Q: Why not?

A: Marcus asked me not to. He said he didn't want to make a big deal out of it, and I respected that. Looking back, I understand that might not have been the right call, but at the time, it seemed like his decision to make.

Q: Did anyone else witness the fall?

A: Not that I'm aware of. That section of the warehouse was pretty empty that morning. It was just the two of us over there.

Q: Did you ever see Marcus favor that shoulder in the days that followed?

A: I did notice him moving a little differently, yes. But he never brought it up again, so neither did I.

---

topic: A witness is questioned about a workplace injury they observed but did not report
text:
Q: Mr. Okonkwo, you've been employed at Ridgeline Manufacturing for how long?

A: Going on eleven years this September.

Q: In your eleven years, have you received training on workplace safety reporting procedures?

A: We do the annual training, yes.

Q: So you're familiar with the requirement to report observed injuries?

A: I am.

Q: Let's talk about what you observed on June 2nd. You saw an incident involving a coworker?

A: I saw Diane catch her hand in the conveyor housing.

Q: Tell me what you saw.

A: She was clearing a jam, and the belt restarted while her hand was still inside. She pulled it out fast. There was blood on her glove.

Q: What did you do?

A: I went over and asked if she needed help. She said no, she had it handled.

Q: Did she seek medical attention?

A: She went to the first aid station and wrapped it up herself.

Q: Did you observe her injury?

A: I saw the cut. It was across her palm, maybe two inches.

Q: And you didn't report this to management?

A: No.

Q: Help me understand why.

A: Diane's been there longer than me. She's a team lead. She told me she'd handle it, and I took her at her word. It wasn't my place to go over her head.

Q: Do you see it differently now?

A: I've had time to think about it. The policy doesn't make exceptions for seniority. I should have filed something.

---

topic: A witness is questioned about a workplace injury they observed but did not report
text:
Q: State your name for the record.

topic: A witness is questioned about a workplace injury they observed but did not report
text:
Q: Good morning, Ms. Tran. Thank you for being here.

A: Of course.

Q: I want to ask you about something you may have witnessed at the Carver Street job site last August. Does that timeframe ring a bell?

A: It does. I was on that project for about six weeks.

Q: During that time, did you observe any injuries to workers on site?

A: I saw one, yes.

Q: Tell me about it.

A: One of the electricians—I think his name was Ray—was up on a ladder running conduit. The ladder shifted, and he came down hard. Landed on his side.

A: I don't know. I went back to my work area after I saw him get up. I assumed someone would take care of it.

topic: A witness is questioned about a workplace injury they observed but did not report
text:
Q: Mr. Salazar, you were working at Beacon Industries on April 4th of this year, correct?

A: Correct.

Q: Walk me through your shift that day.

A: I came in at 7, worked the press line until lunch, then switched over to quality inspection for the afternoon.

Q: At any point during that shift, did you witness an injury to a coworker?

A: I did. Around 10 or 10:15, I saw Anita Mosley get her arm caught between two rollers on the press line.

Q: What happened exactly?

A: She was reaching across to clear some scrap material, and the rollers caught her sleeve and pulled her arm in partway. She managed to hit the stop, but not before it got her pretty good.

Q: What do you mean by "pretty good"?

A: Deep bruising on her forearm. I could see it swelling up right away.

Q: What did she do after the machine stopped?

A: She pulled her arm out, looked at it, and flexed her fingers a few times. Then she went back to work.

Q: She didn't seek medical attention?

A: Not that I saw.

Q: Did you say anything to her?

A: I asked if she was okay. She said it looked worse than it was.

Q: Did you report this to your supervisor?

A: I didn't.

Q: Why not?

A: I've thought about this a lot since then. Honestly, it happened fast, she seemed to have it under control, and I didn't want to create a problem for her if she didn't want one. That's the truth of it.

Q: Do you recognize now that the injury should have been documented?

A: I do. I should have said something regardless of what she wanted.

topic: A pharmacist is deposed about a prescription that was filled with the wrong dosage
text:
Q: Please state your name and current position for the record.

A: Dr. Rebecca Chen, and I'm the staff pharmacist at Greenwood Family Pharmacy—actually, I should say I'm the lead pharmacist now. I was promoted about six months after the incident we're discussing today, which I mention only because it's relevant to understanding my responsibilities at the time versus now.

Q: Thank you. On March 15th of last year, were you working at Greenwood Family Pharmacy?

A: I was, yes. I was on the morning shift, which runs from 7 AM to 3 PM, and I specifically remember that day because we were implementing a new inventory tracking system, which is actually something I had advocated for, and it meant we were all paying extra attention to our procedures.

Q: Do you recall filling a prescription for metoprolol that day?

A: I filled several prescriptions for metoprolol that day—it's one of our most common cardiac medications—but I know exactly which one you're referring to. The Hendricks prescription. I've reviewed my notes extensively in preparation for today.

Q: What dosage was indicated on the original prescription from Dr. Patel?

A: Twenty-five milligrams, twice daily. I can tell you that the prescription came in electronically at 9:47 AM, and I processed it at 10:12 AM. The e-prescribing system we use timestamps everything, which is one of the reasons I pushed for the upgrade two years ago.

Q: And what dosage was actually dispensed?

A: This is what I want to explain, because it's important to understand the full context. The bottle that went home with Mrs. Hendricks contained 100-milligram tablets. But the system flagged it—I want to be clear about that—the system did generate an alert.

Q: You're saying there was an alert?

A: Yes! This is actually crucial. Our system has a dose-range checking feature, and it flagged the discrepancy. I remember seeing the alert. What happened was—and I've thought about this so many times—we were getting frequent alerts that day because of the new inventory system integration, and there was what we call "alert fatigue." I've since written a white paper on this exact phenomenon for our regional pharmacy association.

Q: So you overrode the alert?

A: I did, and I want to take full responsibility for that while also explaining that this is a systemic issue across the entire pharmacy industry. I've actually been invited to speak at a conference next month about improving alert systems. The reality is that pharmacists override alerts dozens of times per day because the systems are oversensitive.

Q: Did you perform any independent verification of the dosage before dispensing?

A: Under our standard protocol, yes, I would have checked the original prescription against the filled bottle. And this is where I have to be honest—I don't have a specific memory of that particular verification, though I do have a memory of the day being unusually hectic. What I can tell you is that I've since developed a checklist system that I've shared with every pharmacy in our network.

Q: Has that system been adopted?

A: Twelve pharmacies so far, and I'm presenting it to corporate next month. If there's any silver lining to this terrible situation, it's that we're going to prevent this from happening to other patients. I genuinely believe that.

topic: A pharmacist is deposed about a prescription that was filled with the wrong dosage

topic: A pharmacist is deposed about a prescription that was filled with the wrong dosage
text:
Q: You've been a pharmacist for how long?

A: Twenty-two years, and I have to say, I've never seen a case quite like this one. The circumstances were truly unusual.

Q: Unusual how?

A: Well, if you'll let me explain—the prescription in question, for Mr. Davis, came through with what appeared to be a legitimate override code from his physician. Now, in twenty-two years, I've seen perhaps a handful of legitimate overrides, usually for cancer patients or other exceptional circumstances, but this one had all the hallmarks of authenticity.

Q: What is an override code?

A: Oh, it's a wonderful question, and it gets to the heart of how the prescribing system works. An override allows a physician to prescribe outside normal parameters—say, a higher dose than typical—when there's clinical justification. The code essentially tells us, "Yes, I know this looks unusual, I have my reasons, proceed."

Q: And you saw such a code on this prescription?

A: I did! And I verified it through our standard channels. I called the prescriber's office—I have the call log—and spoke with someone who confirmed the override. Now, as we later learned, that person was not actually authorized to make such confirmations, but how was I to know that?

Q: What dosage did the override authorize?

A: The prescription with the override indicated 80 milligrams of oxycodone, when the patient's previous prescriptions had all been for 20 milligrams. Now, that's a significant jump, which is exactly why I called to verify. I did my due diligence.

Q: Did the system generate any alerts?

A: It did, and this is what makes the situation so interesting from a systems-design perspective. The override code suppressed the standard dose-range alert, which is exactly what it's designed to do. So I received no warning that would have prompted additional scrutiny beyond what I already performed.

Q: You called the doctor's office, you said. Tell me about that call.

A: Gladly! I called at 2:15 PM—I have the exact time in my records—and I asked specifically about the dosage increase. The person I spoke with, who identified herself as a medical assistant named "Jennifer," said that Dr. Morrison had adjusted the dose due to the patient's increased pain levels and tolerance. She was professional, she knew the patient's name, she had details that seemed credible.

Q: Was there a "Jennifer" working at Dr. Morrison's office?

A: As it turns out, no. And this is where the case becomes genuinely fascinating—someone had apparently obtained enough information about the practice to convincingly impersonate staff. I've since consulted with three different pharmacy organizations about improving verification protocols, and they've all found this case instructive.

topic: A pharmacist is deposed about a prescription that was filled with the wrong dosage
text:

A: 5 milligrams.

Q: That's a significant difference.

A: Very significant.

A: With warfarin, yes.

Q: You're aware Mrs. Kendrick was hospitalized?

A: I am.

Q: Internal bleeding?

A: That's my understanding.

Q: Because of the dosage error?

A: I can't speak to causation—I'm not a physician.

Q: Fair enough. Let's talk about the error itself.

A: Okay.

Q: How did it happen?

A: The "2" on the handwritten prescription looked like a "5."

Q: So this was a handwritten prescription?

A: Yes.

Q: Not electronic?

A: Dr. Hernandez still uses paper scripts for controlled substances and a few other categories. It's not uncommon.

Q: Did the handwriting concern you?

A: Looking back, I should have called. At the time, "5 milligrams" seemed plausible.

Q: Did you have any hesitation?

A: I don't recall hesitation, no.

Q: Any system alerts?

A: No. Five milligrams is within the standard dosing range for warfarin.

Q: So nothing flagged it?

A: Nothing.

Q: Who else handled this prescription?

A: Just me. It was near closing, we were short-staffed.

Q: No second verification?

A: Our protocol requires it for certain high-risk medications. I failed to follow that protocol.

topic: A pharmacist is deposed about a prescription that was filled with the wrong dosage
text:
Q: Let's talk about training. When did you complete your pharmacy degree?

A: 2019. University of Michigan.

Q: And since then, continuing education?

A: Oh, absolutely—yes, I complete well above the minimum required hours every year. I actually just finished a course on medication error prevention that I found incredibly valuable. It used case studies, simulations, the whole thing. I could talk about it for hours.

Q: Let's focus on the incident at Careway Pharmacy.

A: Of course, sorry. I just—I want you to understand that I take this seriously. Education, I mean. Learning from mistakes.

Q: On February 8th, you filled a prescription for Thomas Green.

A: I did, yes.

Q: For Synthroid?

A: Levothyroxine, yes. Synthroid is the brand name. I dispensed the generic, which is standard practice and perfectly equivalent therapeutically.

Q: What dosage was prescribed?

A: 50 micrograms.

Q: What did you dispense?

A: 150 micrograms.

Q: How did that happen?

A: This is actually something I've analyzed extensively since then, and I think I understand the exact sequence of events, if you'd like to hear it.

Q: Please.

A: So the prescription came in electronically, 50 mcg, straightforward. I acknowledged it, went to pull the medication. Now, here's what I believe happened—we had just received a shipment that morning, and the 150-mcg bottles had been shelved in a slightly different location than usual. Not wrong, exactly, but shifted. I reached for where my muscle memory expected 50 mcg to be, and I grabbed 150 mcg instead. And because the bottles are similar—same manufacturer, similar label design—I didn't catch it.

Q: Did you check the bottle against the prescription?

A: I thought I did. But clearly, I didn't do it effectively. And this is where the training I mentioned becomes relevant, actually—the course I took discussed "inattentional blindness," where you can look directly at something and not see it because you're expecting something else. I think that's exactly what happened.

Q: The labels are different colors, aren't they?

A: They are, yes, but—and this is important—the difference is subtle. The 50-mcg is white with blue text, and the 150-mcg is white with green text. In pharmacy lighting, moving quickly, the distinction is not as obvious as you might think.

Q: Did anyone else verify the prescription?

A: We're a small pharmacy. That day, I was the only pharmacist on duty. Our protocol says a technician can serve as a second check for non-controlled substances, but my technician was on lunch when Mr. Green came to pick up.

Q: So no second check occurred?

A: No, and I've since changed my own personal practice to never let a high-alert medication leave without verification, even if it means asking the patient to wait. I actually presented this as a case study to my colleagues. It's something I'm passionate about now—preventing this from happening to anyone else.
