A: Vaguely.

Q: Vaguely?

A: I knew there was something in the agreement about it. I didn't memorize the terms.

Q: Did anyone follow up with you about whether backups were being made?

A: No.

Q: So no one checked?

A: Apparently not.

Q: And you didn't raise the issue yourself?

A: Why would I? No one asked.

topic: A tenant is questioned about property damage they reported to their landlord
text:
Q: Ms. Patterson, you submitted a maintenance request on March 15th of this year, is that correct?

A: Yes.

Q: And in that request, you described water damage to the ceiling in your bedroom?

A: I described what I saw, yes.

Q: What exactly did you see?

A: A stain. Brown. About the size of a dinner plate, maybe a little bigger. It was wet when I first noticed it.

Q: When did you first notice it?

A: The night before I submitted the request. March 14th.

Q: And you're certain it wasn't there before March 14th?

A: I can't tell you what I didn't see. I noticed it on the 14th. Whether it was there before and I missed it, I don't know. I suppose anything's possible.

Q: Did you take any photographs?

A: I did.

Q: How many?

A: Three or four. I don't remember exactly. I can check my phone if that matters.

Q: We'll get to the photographs. Did you notice any other damage that night?

A: The carpet was damp near the wall. Under where the stain was.

Q: Did you report that as well?

A: I thought I did. If it's not in the request, then I guess I didn't. I don't know what else to tell you.

Q: Did you do anything to address the water damage yourself before the landlord responded?

A: I put a bucket down. And a towel. I didn't know what else I was supposed to do.

topic: A tenant is questioned about property damage they reported to their landlord
text:
Q: Mr. Chen, how long have you lived at 4521 Briarwood Lane?

A: Coming up on three years in August.

Q: And during those three years, how many maintenance requests have you submitted?

A: I'd have to count. Several. Maybe eight or nine.

Q: The request we're discussing today, dated November 3rd, concerned damage to the kitchen floor?

A: That's right.

Q: Describe the damage for me.

A: Look, I've described it three times already in writing. The linoleum was buckling near the dishwasher. There was discoloration underneath when I lifted the corner. It smelled like mildew.

Q: I understand you've described it before. I'm asking you to describe it now, for the record.

A: Fine. The linoleum was buckling. Near the dishwasher. Discoloration underneath. Mildew smell.

Q: When did you first observe this buckling?

A: Late October. I don't have the exact date written down anywhere.

Q: But you waited until November 3rd to report it?

A: I waited until I was sure it wasn't something I could fix myself.

Q: What did you try?

A: I looked under the sink for leaks. I ran the dishwasher and watched. I didn't find anything obvious.

Q: So you attempted repairs?

A: I attempted to identify the source. I didn't repair anything. There's a difference.

Q: Fair enough. Did you speak to anyone else about this damage before submitting the request?

A: My wife. That's it.

Q: Not the landlord?

A: No. What would have been the point? I knew it would end up like this anyway.

topic: A tenant is questioned about property damage they reported to their landlord
text:
Q: Let's talk about the broken window, Ms. Okonkwo. You reported this on January 8th?

A: I believe so, yes.

Q: The report states the window in the living room was cracked. How did that happen?

A: I don't know.

Q: You don't know?

A: No, I don't. I came home from work and it was cracked. I didn't see it happen.

Q: Had anyone else been in the apartment that day?

A: Not that I'm aware of.

Q: No guests? No maintenance workers?

A: No.

Q: So the window simply... cracked on its own?

A: I'm telling you what I know. I left in the morning, the window was fine. I came back, it was cracked. I'm not going to make something up just to give you a better answer.

Q: I'm not asking you to make anything up. I'm trying to understand what happened.

A: Then we're in the same position, aren't we?

Q: Let me ask it differently. Was there any evidence of forced entry? Anything disturbed in the apartment?

A: No. Nothing was taken. Nothing was moved.

Q: Did you contact the police?

A: No.

Q: Why not?

A: Because nothing was stolen. Because it was just a crack, not a shattered window. Because I've called about things before and nothing ever comes of it. I just reported it to the landlord and moved on with my life.

topic: A tenant is questioned about property damage they reported to their landlord
text:
Q: Mr. Reeves, I want to direct your attention to the email you sent to Greenfield Property Management on September 22nd.

A: Okay.

Q: Do you have a copy in front of you?

A: I do.

Q: In this email, you describe—let me find the exact language—"extensive mold growth in the bathroom." Do you see that?

A: I see it.

Q: Was that an accurate description?

A: It was accurate to what I was looking at, yes.

Q: When you say "extensive," what do you mean by that?

A: It covered most of the ceiling above the shower. It was spreading to the wall. It had been there a while, clearly.

Q: How do you know it had been there a while?

A: Because mold doesn't grow overnight. Because the discoloration was deep. I'm not an expert, counsel. I'm just describing what was obvious.

Q: Had you noticed the mold before September?

A: Probably. I don't know. There's always been some discoloration in that bathroom.

Q: So this wasn't a new problem?

A: I think you already know the answer to that.

Q: I'm asking what you know, Mr. Reeves.

A: It wasn't new. It got worse. I reported it when it got bad enough that I was worried about my health.

Q: Why didn't you report it earlier?

A: I did report it earlier. Two years ago. Nothing happened. So I stopped expecting anything to happen.

Q: Are you saying Greenfield ignored a prior complaint?

A: I'm saying I submitted a request and the mold is still there. You can draw whatever conclusion you want from that.

topic: A tenant is questioned about property damage they reported to their landlord
text:
Q: Ms. Hartwell, the maintenance log shows you called the emergency line on February 2nd at approximately 11 p.m. Is that accurate?

A: If that's what the log shows.

Q: Do you recall making that call?

A: I recall making a call. I don't remember the exact time.

Q: What prompted the call?

A: The radiator in my daughter's bedroom was leaking. Badly.

Q: Define "badly."

A: Water was pooling on the floor. It was hot. I was worried she'd burn herself.

Q: What did you do before calling?

A: I moved her to the living room. I put towels down. I turned off the valve—or tried to. It was stuck.

Q: Were you able to stop the leak?

A: Eventually. After about an hour.

Q: How?

A: I used a wrench. Got the valve to turn most of the way. It slowed down enough that I could manage it.

Q: So you resolved the issue yourself?

A: For that night. Yes.

Q: Did anyone from the property management company respond to your call?

A: Someone called back the next morning. Around nine or ten.

Q: And what happened then?

A: They said they'd send someone out. Someone came three days later. Looked at the radiator, said it needed to be replaced, and left.

Q: Has it been replaced?

A: What do you think?

Q: I need you to answer for the record, Ms. Hartwell.

A: No. It hasn't been replaced. It's February 2nd, then someone comes February 5th, and here we are in June, and my daughter still sleeps in the living room when it gets cold because I don't trust that radiator. So no. It has not been replaced.

topic: A nurse is questioned about a patient fall that occurred during her shift
text:
Q: Ms. Delgado, you were the charge nurse on the third floor the night of October 14th, correct?

A: Yes.

Q: And Mr. Patterson was assigned to your unit?

A: He was one of twenty-three patients on the floor that night, yes.

Q: I'm asking specifically about Mr. Patterson.

A: And I answered your question. Yes, he was on my unit.

Q: What time did you last check on Mr. Patterson before the fall?

A: I documented a check at 2:15 a.m.

Q: And what time was the fall reported?

A: 3:47 a.m.

Q: So over ninety minutes passed between your check and when he fell?

A: If you're asking whether I personally stood in his doorway every fifteen minutes for an hour and a half while also managing a code blue in room 312 and two new admissions from the ER, then no. I did not.

Q: Ms. Delgado, I'm simply asking about the timeline.

A: And I'm giving you the context that the timeline requires.

Q: Was Mr. Patterson identified as a fall risk?

A: Yes. He had a yellow bracelet, a bed alarm, and non-slip socks. All of which were in place.

Q: The bed alarm was functioning?

A: I checked it myself at the start of my shift.

Q: Then why didn't it alert staff when he got out of bed?

A: You'd have to ask whoever examined it after the fact. I can only tell you it was working at 7 p.m. when I tested it.

Q: You're saying the alarm malfunctioned?

A: I'm saying I don't know. What I know is that I set it, I tested it, and it worked. What happened at 3:47 in the morning, I cannot explain sitting here today.

---

topic: A nurse is questioned about a patient fall that occurred during her shift
text:
Q: Nurse Thompson, walk me through the hospital's fall prevention protocol.

A: Every patient gets assessed on admission using the Morse Fall Scale. Based on their score, we implement interventions—bed alarms, gait belts, closer monitoring, things like that.

Q: And Mrs. Okonkwo scored how on that scale?

A: I believe she was a 55.

Q: You believe, or you know?

A: I'd have to look at the chart to give you the exact number.

Q: We've provided you the chart. It's in front of you.

A: Then give me a moment, please.

Q: Take your time.

A: ... She scored 55.

Q: Which puts her in what category?

A: High risk.

Q: High risk. And what interventions were implemented for this high-risk patient?

A: Bed alarm, non-slip footwear, and she was on a q2 rounding schedule.

Q: Every two hours?

A: That's what q2 means, yes.

Q: I'm clarifying for the record.

A: Fine.

Q: Your documentation shows rounds at 10 p.m. and then not again until 2 a.m. That's four hours.

A: I'm aware of what the documentation shows.

Q: Can you explain the gap?

A: We were short-staffed. I had twelve patients. I did what I could.

Q: "What you could" didn't include checking on a high-risk fall patient for four hours?

A: Counsel, I'm not sure what answer you're looking for. I've told you we were short-staffed. I've told you I did what I could. I can't manufacture time I didn't have.

---

topic: A nurse is questioned about a patient fall that occurred during her shift
text:
Q: Let's talk about what you observed when you entered Mr. Huang's room after the fall.

A: He was on the floor, on his left side, near the bathroom door.

Q: Was he conscious?

A: Yes.

Q: Was he speaking?

A: He was moaning. Not forming words.

Q: What did you do first?

A: I called for assistance and began assessing him. Checked his pupils, asked him questions, looked for obvious injuries.

Q: You didn't move him?

A: No. Absolutely not. Not until we'd assessed for spinal injury.

Q: How long did that assessment take?

A: I don't know exactly. Several minutes.

Q: Several meaning what? Two? Ten?

A: I wasn't watching the clock, counsel. I was watching my patient.

Q: I understand, but—

A: Do you? Because I had an eighty-year-old man on the floor who might have broken his neck, and you're asking me to recall whether the assessment took six minutes or eight minutes. I don't know. It took as long as it needed to take.

Q: Let me rephrase. After you called for assistance, who responded?

A: Dr. Patel and another nurse, Maria something. I don't remember her last name.

Q: And they helped you move him?

A: After we cleared his spine, yes. We used a transfer board.

Q: Was the family notified?

A: Not by me. That would have been the charge nurse or the physician.

---

topic: A nurse is questioned about a patient fall that occurred during her shift
text:
Q: Ms. Reyes, you've been a nurse for how long?

A: Fourteen years.

Q: And in those fourteen years, have you received training on bed alarm systems?

A: Of course.

Q: Of course. So you'd consider yourself competent in setting these alarms?

A: Yes.

Q: Then help me understand something. The bed alarm in Mr. Foster's room—you set it that evening?

A: Yes.

Q: And you're certain it was activated?

A: Yes.

Q: The incident report indicates the alarm was found in the "off" position after Mr. Foster's fall.

A: I've read the incident report.

Q: Does that concern you?

A: It concerns me that someone apparently turned it off.

Q: Someone. Who would that someone be?

A: I have no idea.

Q: Could it have been you?

A: No.

Q: Could you have thought you activated it but didn't?

A: No.

Q: You're certain?

A: I've answered that question three times now. Yes, I am certain.

Q: Could Mr. Foster have turned it off himself?

A: He had advanced dementia. He didn't know what day it was. I doubt he figured out the alarm panel.

Q: So in your view, who turned off the alarm?

A: I don't know. But it wasn't me, and it wasn't the patient. So you tell me who else was in that room.

Q: I'm not the one answering questions today, Ms. Reyes.

A: Apparently not.

---

topic: A nurse is questioned about a patient fall that occurred during her shift
text:
Q: I want to make sure I understand the sequence of events. Mr. Bradley requested to use the restroom at approximately 1 a.m.?

A: Somewhere around then, yes.

Q: And you assisted him?

A: I did.

Q: Walked him to the bathroom?

A: Yes.

Q: Stayed with him?

A: I stayed outside the door. He wanted privacy.

Q: He wanted privacy. Did you explain to him that he was a fall risk?

A: He was well aware. We'd discussed it multiple times.

Q: But he still insisted on privacy?

A: Patients have rights, counsel. They can refuse assistance.

Q: Even when that refusal puts them in danger?

A: I'm not going to physically force myself into a bathroom with a patient. That's not how this works.

Q: I'm not suggesting you should have forced anything.

A: Then what exactly are you suggesting?

Q: I'm trying to understand—

A: Because it sounds like you're suggesting I should have done something that would have violated his autonomy, his dignity, and about four different hospital policies.

Q: Ms. Warren, I'm simply trying to establish what happened.

A: What happened is that I followed protocol. I offered to stay. He declined. I waited outside the door. I heard him fall. I went in immediately. That is what happened.

Q: How long were you outside the door before you heard him fall?

A: Less than a minute.

Q: Less than a minute. And in that time—

A: In that time, I did not develop the ability to see through walls, no.

topic: A witness is questioned about a fire they discovered in a neighboring unit
text:
Q: Mr. Delgado, you were the first person to see the fire on the evening of March 14th, is that correct?

A: I was, yes. I was actually just finishing up some work on my patio when I noticed it. The timing worked out because I'd normally be inside by that hour, but I happened to stay out a bit later than usual.

Q: And what exactly did you observe?

A: Smoke first, coming from the vents on the east side of Unit 7B. Then within maybe thirty, forty seconds, I could see an orange glow through the kitchen window. I remember thinking the color was distinctive—more amber than what you'd expect from, say, cooking smoke.

Q: You seem quite certain about these details.

A: I am. I actually took notes that same night, right after the fire department arrived. I wanted to make sure I had everything down while it was fresh. Would you like me to walk you through the timeline I documented?

Q: That won't be necessary at this moment. Did you attempt to alert anyone?

A: Immediately. I called 911 first—the call was placed at 8:47 PM, I have the phone record—and then I went to Unit 7B and knocked, but no one answered. Then I pulled the building's fire alarm at 8:49. I timed everything carefully.

Q: And the occupants of Unit 7B, the Chens—did you see them at any point?

A: Not until they came around from the parking garage about ten minutes later. Mrs. Chen was carrying groceries. I was actually relieved to see them safe, and I was able to tell them exactly what I'd witnessed and when.

Q: You mentioned taking notes. Is this something you typically do?

A: When something significant happens, yes. I find it helpful to have an accurate record. In this case, I thought it might be useful later, and apparently I was right about that.

Q: Do you have those notes with you today?

A: I do. I brought copies as well, in case your team needed them for the record.

topic: A witness is questioned about a fire they discovered in a neighboring unit
text:
Q: Ms. Patterson, let's turn to what you saw on the night in question. You discovered the fire at approximately what time?

A: I think around nine? Maybe a little after?

Q: You think, or you know?

A: I didn't check my phone right away, so I can't be exact.

Q: That's fine. We're just trying to establish a general timeframe. What were you doing when you first noticed something was wrong?

A: I was in my living room, and I started smelling something burning. At first I thought it was my own stove, so I checked, but everything was off.

Q: And then?

A: I opened my front door to see if it was coming from outside.

Q: Good. And what did you see when you opened that door?

A: Smoke in the hallway. A lot of it, actually. Coming from under the door of 4C.

Q: You're certain it was 4C specifically?

A: Yes, I could see it pooling out from under the door frame.

Q: Excellent. That's very helpful. What did you do next?

A: I banged on the door and yelled to see if anyone was inside.

Q: Did anyone respond?

A: No. So I ran back inside and called 911.

Q: Perfect. And the fire department arrived how long after your call?

A: I'm not sure exactly. It felt fast, though. Maybe five or six minutes?

Q: You've been very clear about the sequence of events. Just a few more questions, and I think we'll have everything we need from you today.

topic: A witness is questioned about a fire they discovered in a neighboring unit
text:
Q: Mr. Whitmore, you've testified that you saw flames coming from the window of Unit 12. Is that accurate?

A: It's accurate that I saw flames, yes.

Q: From Unit 12 specifically.

A: From a window on that side of the building. Whether it was Unit 12 or 11, I couldn't say with certainty. The angles are tricky from where I was standing.

Q: Where were you standing?

A: In the parking lot, near my car. Third row back.

Q: And you're telling me you couldn't distinguish between two units from that distance?

A: I'm telling you I won't guess under oath. The windows are identical. The units share a wall. I know what I saw, but I'm not going to claim precision I don't have.

Q: Fair enough. Let me ask you this—

A: I'd also point out that I was the one who stayed on scene and directed the fire trucks to the correct building entrance. So while I may not be able to pinpoint the exact unit number from eighty feet away, I was apparently reliable enough for the first responders.

Q: I'm not questioning your reliability, Mr. Whitmore.

A: It sounded like you might be headed in that direction.

Q: I'm simply trying to establish the facts.

A: And I'm giving them to you as accurately as I can. I saw flames. I called 911. I stayed until the situation was under control. What I won't do is manufacture details I'm not certain about.

Q: Let's move on. Did you see anyone exit the building?

A: Several people, yes. I can describe them if you'd like.

topic: A witness is questioned about a fire they discovered in a neighboring unit
text:
Q: Ms. Reyes, how long have you lived at the Parkview complex?

A: Coming up on four years now.

Q: And you're familiar with the layout of the buildings?

A: Very familiar, yes.

Q: On the evening of January 8th, you reported a fire to building management before calling 911. Is that correct?

A: I called management first because their office is on-site and I thought they could respond faster. Then I called 911 immediately after.

Q: Why not call 911 first?

A: In hindsight, maybe I should have. But the management office is literally a two-minute walk from where the fire was. I thought they'd have a fire extinguisher, could do something immediate.

Q: Did they?

A: They did, actually. Tom from the office got there with an extinguisher before the fire department arrived. It was already too far gone by then, but he tried.

Q: So your instinct to call management first may have actually been useful.

A: I'd like to think so.

Q: Let's talk about what you observed. Where exactly was the fire when you first saw it?

A: In the storage area attached to Unit 3A. The one that faces the courtyard.

Q: How did you happen to notice it?

A: I was taking my dog out for his evening walk. We always go through the courtyard, and I saw light flickering where there shouldn't be any light.

Q: What time was this?

A: Just after 10 PM. I remember because I'd just finished watching the news.

Q: And your dog's name?

A: Biscuit.

Q: Biscuit. For the record, then, you and Biscuit discovered the fire at approximately 10 PM.

A: That's right. He actually started pulling toward it before I saw anything. Good instincts, that dog.

topic: A witness is questioned about a fire they discovered in a neighboring unit
text:
Q: Dr. Okonkwo, you've stated that you were in your unit when you became aware of the fire in the adjacent apartment.

A: That's correct.

Q: What was the first indication something was wrong?

A: My smoke detector activated.

Q: Your own smoke detector?

A: Yes. Which I found odd, because I wasn't cooking or doing anything that would trigger it.

Q: What did you do?

A: I walked through my apartment checking each room. When I got to the bedroom that shares a wall with Unit 6F, the wall was warm to the touch.

Q: Warm.

A: Noticeably so. Enough that I immediately left the apartment and called emergency services from the hallway.

Q: Did you attempt to alert your neighbors in 6F?

A: I knocked several times, but there was no answer. I later learned the unit was unoccupied that evening.

Q: Dr. Okonkwo, I want to make sure I understand. You felt heat through the wall itself?

A: Through the drywall, yes. It was alarming.

Q: That must have been frightening.

A: It was concerning enough that I grabbed my laptop and my passport before leaving. Those were my priorities.

Q: Did you see any smoke at that point?

A: Not in my unit, no. But when I opened my front door, there was a haze in the corridor.

Q: How would you describe the haze?

A: Thin. Gray. The smell was more pronounced than the visual.

Q: What did it smell like?

A: Electrical, mostly. With something chemical underneath. Not like wood burning or food burning. Something synthetic.

Q: That's a useful distinction. Thank you, Dr. Okonkwo. I think that establishes the timeline clearly.

topic: A neighbor is questioned about noise complaints and a confrontation they witnessed
text:
Q: State your name for the record, please.

A: Linda Whitmore.

Q: Ms. Whitmore, you live at 4412 Cedarbrook Lane, is that correct?

A: That's what I said in my written statement. Yes.

Q: And you've lived there for how long?

A: Eleven years. Eleven years without a single problem until these people moved in.

Q: When you say "these people," you're referring to the Defendants, the Harmon family?

A: I'm referring to the family at 4408 who decided that three in the morning is an appropriate time to run a table saw in their garage.

Q: Let's slow down. I'm asking about the night of September 14th specifically. Were you home that evening?

A: I was home every evening because I couldn't leave without wondering what fresh nightmare I'd come back to.

Q: Ms. Whitmore, I need you to answer the question I'm asking. Were you home on September 14th, yes or no?

A: Yes. Obviously yes.

Q: What time did you first notice any disturbance that night?

A: 11:47 p.m. I know because I looked at the clock when the bass started vibrating my bedroom wall. Again.

Q: And what did you do?

A: What I always did. I waited. I gave it twenty minutes like the HOA suggested, and then I walked over there because apparently I'm the only adult in this situation.

Q: Did you knock on the Harmons' door?

A: I pounded on it. Yes. Because no one could hear a knock over that noise.

Q: What happened when someone answered?

A: Greg Harmon opened the door with a beer in his hand and told me to—may I say what he said?

Q: Please do.

A: He told me to "get the hell off his property before he made me."

topic: A neighbor is questioned about noise complaints and a confrontation they witnessed
text:
Q: Good morning. You are David Chen, correct?

A: Correct.

Q: And you reside at 7720 Millbrook Drive?

A: Yes.

Q: How long have you lived at that address?

A: About three years now.

Q: Do you know the Plaintiff, Sandra Okonkwo?

A: She lives two doors down. We've spoken.

Q: Mr. Chen, let me direct your attention to July 8th of last year. You were interviewed by Officer Daniels that night, weren't you?

A: I was, yes.

Q: And you told Officer Daniels you witnessed a confrontation between Ms. Okonkwo and my client, Richard Brewer. Is that accurate?

A: I saw something. I wouldn't call it—I mean, I saw part of something.

Q: Part of something. Let's be precise, Mr. Chen. You told Officer Daniels—and I'm reading from the police report—"I saw him grab her arm and yank her backward." Those were your words?

A: I said something like that.

Q: Something like that, or exactly that?

A: I don't remember my exact phrasing from a year ago.

Q: But you remember what you saw clearly enough to have said it?

A: I remember what I thought I saw.

Q: What you thought you saw. That's interesting. At what point did your certainty change, Mr. Chen?

A: I'm not saying it changed. I'm saying I was across the street. It was dark.

Q: It was 8:15 p.m. in July. The sun hadn't set.

A: There were shadows. There was a hedge partially blocking my view.

Q: A hedge. That hedge wasn't in your statement to Officer Daniels, was it?

A: He didn't ask about hedges.

Q: I bet he didn't.

A: What is that supposed to mean?

topic: A neighbor is questioned about noise complaints and a confrontation they witnessed
text:
Q: Please state your full name.

A: Margaret Anne Holloway.

Q: Ms. Holloway, you submitted a written complaint to the Riverside Homeowners Association on March 3rd, correct?

A: I did.

Q: That complaint concerned noise from the property at 1847 Riverside Court?

A: It concerned a lot more than noise, but yes, noise was part of it.

Q: What else did it concern?

A: The complaint speaks for itself. It's in your file.

Q: I'd like to hear it in your words.

A: It concerned dogs barking at all hours. It concerned music so loud my china rattled in the cabinet. It concerned complete and total disregard for anyone else in the neighborhood.

Q: When you say "all hours," what hours specifically?

A: I kept a log. I have dates and times going back to January.

Q: Did you bring that log today?

A: No one told me to bring it.

Q: We requested all relevant documents in our subpoena.

A: The subpoena said documents related to the March 15th incident. My log covers months of harassment.

Q: Let's focus on March 15th, then. You witnessed the altercation between Mr. and Mrs. Patterson?

A: I witnessed James Patterson screaming at his wife in their driveway. I wouldn't call that an altercation. I'd call it abuse.

Q: Did you see Mr. Patterson strike his wife?

A: I saw him raise his hand.

Q: That's not what I asked.

A: I saw enough.

Q: Ms. Holloway, did you see Mr. Patterson make physical contact with his wife, yes or no?

A: ...She flinched. She stepped back. She was afraid.

Q: I'll ask one more time. Did you see him strike her?

A: I saw a woman who was terrified. Maybe that should be enough.

topic: A neighbor is questioned about noise complaints and a confrontation they witnessed
text:
Q: You are Marcus Webb, residing at 2201 Thornton Street?

A: Yeah, that's me.

Q: Mr. Webb, I represent Katherine Sorrell, your neighbor at 2205 Thornton Street.

A: I know who you represent.

Q: Then you know why we're here. You made several calls to the police about Ms. Sorrell between January and April, didn't you?

A: I made calls about noise violations. Whether that's "about Ms. Sorrell" is a matter of interpretation.

Q: Seven calls in four months. That's nearly two per month.

A: Okay.

Q: You don't think that's excessive?

A: I think it reflects the number of times I was woken up at 2 a.m.

Q: Ms. Sorrell is a hospice nurse who works night shifts. Were you aware of that?

A: I don't keep track of her schedule.

Q: But you kept track of every time a door closed too loud or a car started in her driveway?

A: Objection—argumentative.

Q: I'll rephrase. Did you ever speak to Ms. Sorrell directly about your concerns?

A: I tried. Once.

Q: Once. And what happened?

A: She told me she needed to get to work and closed the door.

Q: And that was enough for you to begin a campaign of police complaints?

topic: A daycare worker is deposed about an injury a child sustained while in their care
text:

A: Four years. Four years and two months, actually. I started in March of 2020.

Q: And you were working on September 14th of last year?

A: Yes.

Q: Were you the assigned caregiver for the Toddler Room that day?

A: I was one of them. There were two of us. I want to be clear about that. There were two of us assigned to that room.

Q: Who was the other caregiver?

A: Jessica Morin.

Q: At approximately 10:15 a.m., where were you physically located?

A: I was—okay, so the Toddler Room has different areas, and I was near the sensory table, which is by the window, the east window, and I was supervising the children at the sensory table. There were four children there. With me. At the sensory table.

Q: Could you see the climbing structure from that position?

A: I could see—parts of it. The room isn't that large, but there's a bookshelf, a low bookshelf, and it partially—I mean, I could see most of the climbing structure. Not all of it. The back side, no.

Q: Were you watching the climbing structure?

A: I was watching my area. That was my assigned area. Jessica was supposed to be—we divide the room. That's protocol. We divide supervision zones.

Q: I'm asking what you personally observed.

A: I understand. I'm trying to answer accurately. I observed the children at my station, and I had peripheral awareness of the rest of the room. I didn't see the fall itself. I heard it. I heard Oliver cry out, and then I turned, and I saw him on the mat.

Q: You heard it before you saw it?

A: Yes. That's what I said. I heard it first.

topic: A daycare worker is deposed about an injury a child sustained while in their care
text:

Q: Did you move him?

A: No, I didn't move him.

A: I don't know exactly. It felt fast. Everything happened fast.

Q: Give me your best estimate.

A: I didn't say five minutes for certain. I said maybe. I wasn't watching a clock. I was trying to keep him calm. He was scared, and I was talking to him and keeping the other children back and waiting for Sandra to come because Jessica went to get Sandra and—it was a lot happening at once.

Q: Who made the decision to call 911?

A: Sandra. The director. She took one look and said to call.

Q: Did you suggest calling 911?

A: I don't remember if I specifically said those words.

Q: Did it occur to you to call 911?

A: Everything occurred to me. I was trying to do the right thing.

Q: I want to ask you about the upstairs hallway. When did you go upstairs?

A: Sometime around eleven. Maybe eleven-fifteen.

Q: Why did you go upstairs?

A: To use the bathroom. The one downstairs had a line.

Q: And when you reached the top of the stairs, what did you see?

A: Nothing at first. The hallway was—it was dim. A couple of people were talking near one of the bedroom doors.

Q: Did you recognize these people?

A: One of them was Jenna. I don't know her last name. The other one I didn't recognize.

Q: Was one of these individuals the plaintiff, Sierra Marsh?

A: No.

Q: Where did you next see Sierra Marsh that evening?

A: I—I'm trying to remember the exact sequence. Can you give me a moment?

Q: Take your time.

A: Okay. So I went to the bathroom. And when I came out, that's when I heard—there was a commotion further down the hall.

Q: What do you mean by commotion?

A: A door opened. Someone was talking loudly. Not yelling, but—loud.

Q: Male or female voice?

A: Male. I think. It was muffled.

Q: What did you do when you heard this?

A: I walked toward it. Not—not aggressively, I just, I moved in that direction to see what was happening.

Q: And what was happening?

A: The door to the last bedroom was open. I could see Sierra standing just inside the doorway.

Q: Could you see her face?

A: Yes.

Q: Can you describe her demeanor?

A: She looked—her eyes were wide. She was holding her arm. Her left arm, I think. Holding it against her body.

topic: A witness is questioned about events at a party where an assault allegedly occurred
text:
Q: Mr. Brennan, were you drinking alcohol that night?

A: Yes.

Q: How much would you say you consumed?

A: A few beers over the course of several hours. I wasn't drunk, if that's what you're implying.

Q: I'm not implying anything. I'm asking questions. How many beers is "a few"?

A: Three. Maybe four. Over four or five hours.

Q: Three or four?

A: I didn't count them. Three or four is my best recollection.

Q: Now, you've testified that you saw my client, Daniel Vance, arguing with the plaintiff near the garage door. Yes?

A: That's correct.

Q: How far were you from this argument?

A: I was on the driveway. So maybe twenty feet. Twenty-five.

Q: You're certain about that distance?

A: Approximately, yes.

Q: And you'd had three or four beers by this point?

A: I already answered that question. I wasn't impaired.

Q: Mr. Brennan, I'm trying to establish what you could and couldn't perceive. Do you wear corrective lenses?

A: I wear contacts. I was wearing them that night.

Q: Good. And this was at what time?

A: Around midnight. Shortly before or after.

Q: The lighting near the garage—describe it for me.

A: There's a light above the garage door. It was on. And the driveway has those solar lights along the edge.

Q: So you could clearly see faces from twenty to twenty-five feet away?

A: Yes. I could see that it was Daniel. I could see that it was Amir. And I could see Daniel grab Amir by the collar.

topic: A witness is questioned about events at a party where an assault allegedly occurred
text:
Q: Let's go back to something you said earlier. You mentioned you were standing near the fireplace when the altercation began?

A: In that general area, yes.

Q: The fireplace in the main living room?

A: Yes, the main—yes.

Q: And you had an unobstructed view?

A: Mostly. I mean, no, wait—there was a couch between me and where it happened. But I could see over it.

Q: You could see over the couch. Were you standing the entire time?

A: Yes.

Q: You never sat down?

A: No. I'd been sitting earlier but I stood up to talk to someone.

Q: Who were you talking to?

A: I don't see how that's relevant.

Q: Ms. Okonkwo, I'll determine what's relevant. Who were you talking to when you stood up?

A: Brian something. I don't know his last name.

Q: What were you and Brian discussing?

A: Nothing important. Just talking.

Q: Fine. Now, you're standing, talking to Brian, and then what happened?

A: I heard a crash. Like glass breaking. And I turned and saw Kevin—Kevin Marsh—he was on the ground near the coffee table.

Q: What position was he in?

A: On his side. Or his back. He was on the ground.

Q: Did you see how he got to the ground?

A: I turned when I heard the glass. So I saw him falling. The last part of the fall.

Q: You didn't see what caused the fall?

A: No. I only saw him going down.

Q: Did you see anyone else near him at that moment?

A: There were several people. I couldn't—I didn't process who they all were.

Q: Was the defendant, Marcus Webb, one of those people?

A: He might have been. I honestly—everything happened very fast. I don't want to say something I'm not sure about.

topic: A store manager is questioned about a customer slip-and-fall on their premises
text:
Q: Mr. Hendricks, you were the manager on duty the morning of February 12th, correct?

A: I was, yes.

Q: And can you describe the store's policy for floor inspections?

A: Absolutely. We conduct hourly walkthrough inspections of all aisles, and any spill or hazard gets documented in our incident log with a timestamp. We've been doing this for six years now, ever since I took over as manager.

Q: And on February 12th, were those inspections performed?

A: Every single one. I can tell you that at 9:15 a.m., my associate Marcus completed the floor check. At 10:15, I did it myself. The incident occurred at 10:47, so we were well within our window.

Q: You seem very certain about those times.

A: I am. Because I pulled the logs the same day, made copies, and secured them. I know how these things go.

Q: The plaintiff claims there was a puddle of liquid near the freezer section for at least twenty minutes before she fell.

A: That's simply not consistent with our records. I walked that exact aisle at 10:15. There was no liquid on the floor.

Q: Is it possible you missed it?

A: No.

Q: No?

A: No. The aisle is twelve feet wide, well-lit, and I walk it slowly, looking at the floor. That's the whole point of the inspection. There was nothing there at 10:15.

Q: Let's move on. Who responded to the incident first?

A: I did. I was at the service desk when I heard someone call out, and I was there within thirty seconds. We followed every protocol exactly as trained.

topic: A store manager is questioned about a customer slip-and-fall on their premises
text:
Q: Ms. Patterson, how long have you worked at Franklin's Grocery?

A: Coming up on four years.

Q: And you were working the morning the plaintiff fell?

A: I was stocking dairy, yes.

Q: Did you see the fall occur?

A: No, I heard it. Heard her cry out.

Q: What did you do when you heard that?

A: I came around the end of the aisle and saw her on the ground. I called for the manager on my radio.

Q: Did you see any liquid on the floor at that time?

A: There was... some liquid, yes. Near her.

Q: Can you describe it?

A: Clear. Not a lot. Maybe like someone spilled part of a water bottle.

Q: Now, I want to be very clear here. You saw liquid on the floor near where the plaintiff had fallen, correct?

A: Correct.

Q: Thank you. That's all I needed on that point. Now, prior to the incident, had you walked through that section of the store?

A: Earlier, yes. When I first got to dairy.

Q: And what time was that?

A: Maybe 10:00? 10:05?

Q: Did you notice any liquid then?

A: No, the floor was dry.

Q: Excellent. So between 10:05 and the time of the fall—which we've established was approximately 10:47—something was spilled in that area.

A: That would seem to be the case.

Q: Perfect. That's very helpful, Ms. Patterson.

topic: A store manager is questioned about a customer slip-and-fall on their premises
text:
Q: Mr. Chen, who is responsible for cleaning up spills at your store?

A: Any available associate. Whoever sees it first is supposed to stay with it and call for cleanup, or clean it themselves if they're able.

Q: And how are associates trained on this?

A: There's a module they complete during onboarding. Computer-based. Takes about twenty minutes.

Q: Do you verify they've completed it?

A: The system tracks it. They can't finish orientation without completing all required modules.

Q: Did the plaintiff ever make any statements to you about how the fall occurred?

A: She said she slipped. That her feet went out from under her.

Q: Did she say what she slipped on?

A: She said she didn't know. She said she didn't see anything.

Q: She told you she didn't see anything on the floor?

A: That's what she said at the time, yes.

Q: I want to make sure I understand. Immediately after the fall, the plaintiff stated to you that she did not see what caused her to slip?

A: Correct.

Q: Did she appear to be looking for something on the floor?

A: She was sitting there, and she did look around, yes. She seemed confused about what happened. Her exact words were, "I don't know what I slipped on."

Q: Thank you, Mr. Chen. I appreciate you being so precise about that.

A: Of course.

Q: Just one more thing. Did you document her statement in your incident report?

A: Word for word. I always do.

topic: A store manager is questioned about a customer slip-and-fall on their premises
text:
Q: Let's talk about the wet floor signs your store uses. What color are they?

A: Yellow. Bright yellow.

Q: How many does the store own?

A: I'd have to check inventory, but at least a dozen.

Q: At least a dozen. And where are they stored?

A: Various places. There's some in the back stockroom, some near the entrance, some by the cleaning supplies in aisle four.

Q: On February 12th, were any of those signs deployed in the freezer section prior to the plaintiff's fall?

A: No.

Q: None at all?

A: No, because there was no identified hazard requiring one.

Q: But there was liquid on the floor.

A: That was not identified until after the fall occurred.

Q: So your testimony is that no employee saw this liquid before the plaintiff slipped in it?

A: That's what I'm saying.

Q: Mr. Okonkwo, you have a dozen wet floor signs at your disposal. You have employees throughout the store. You conduct hourly inspections. And yet, somehow, no one noticed this hazard.

A: Counselor, we're not omniscient. We have procedures. We follow them. If a spill happens at 10:40 and someone falls at 10:47, there is a very small window in which anyone could have seen it. We're a grocery store, not a surveillance state.

Q: I'm simply trying to understand how your systems failed.

A: I don't accept that they failed. Something spilled. Within minutes, an accident happened. That's not a failure of our systems. That's reality.

Q: We'll let the jury decide that.

A: I'm sure they will.

topic: A store manager is questioned about a customer slip-and-fall on their premises
text:
Q: Ms. Vance, did anyone witness the spill itself occurring?

A: Not that I'm aware of.

Q: So you don't know who spilled the liquid?

A: No.

Q: You don't know what the liquid was?

A: It appeared to be water or a clear sports drink. We couldn't determine the exact source.

Q: You don't know how long it was on the floor?

A: Based on our inspection logs, it could not have been more than thirty-two minutes. Likely much less.

Q: That's a pretty specific number.

A: I've reviewed the timeline carefully.

Q: I'm sure you have. Now, the plaintiff sustained a fractured wrist in this fall. Were you aware of that?

A: I was informed of it later, yes.

Q: Does that concern you?

A: Of course I'm sorry she was hurt. Any time a customer is injured in my store, I take it seriously.

Q: Do you take any responsibility for her injury?

A: I take responsibility for ensuring my store follows proper safety procedures, which it did.

Q: That's not what I asked.

A: I think it is, actually. You're asking if the store is at fault. We followed every procedure. We inspected the floors. We trained our employees. A spill occurred and an accident happened before anyone could address it. That's unfortunate, but it's not negligence.

Q: You seem very confident about that.

A: I've been a retail manager for fifteen years. I know what negligence looks like, and this isn't it.

Q: I think we're done here.

A: I'll be here if you have more questions.

topic: A former employee is deposed about discriminatory remarks made by a supervisor
text:
Q: Ms. Patterson, I want to direct your attention to the morning of March 14th, 2023. You were present in the break room, correct?

A: Yes.

Q: And who else was present?

A: I'd have to think. There were several people. David Chen was there. I believe Maria was there. And Mr. Hargrove came in at some point.

Q: By Mr. Hargrove, you're referring to your direct supervisor, Thomas Hargrove?

A: Yes. That's correct. Thomas Hargrove. My supervisor. Former supervisor, I should say, since I no longer work there.

Q: What happened when Mr. Hargrove entered the break room?

A: He—can you be more specific? A lot of things happened. He walked in. He got coffee. He spoke to people.

Q: What did he say?

A: I don't remember every word. I don't want to mischaracterize anything.

Q: I'm not asking for every word. What do you remember him saying?

A: He made a comment. About Maria. About her being—he said something about her accent, about how he couldn't understand her on calls, and that maybe she should go back to wherever she learned English. Or something close to that. I'm paraphrasing. I want to be clear I'm paraphrasing.

Q: What were his exact words, to the best of your recollection?

A: I just told you what I remember. I said I was paraphrasing. I don't want to put words in his mouth that weren't exactly his words, but that was the substance of it. The substance. Do you want me to guess at exact words? Because I don't think that would be helpful to anyone.

Q: Did anyone respond to Mr. Hargrove's comment?

A: No. No one said anything. We just—no.

Q: Why not?

A: Why not? Because he was the supervisor. Because that's how it was. I don't know what kind of answer you're looking for.

Q: I'm just asking what you observed.

A: I observed people being quiet. I observed Maria looking at the floor. I observed myself not saying anything either, if that's what you're getting at. Is that what you want me to say?

topic: A former employee is deposed about discriminatory remarks made by a supervisor
text:
Q: Mr. Franklin, how long did you work in the distribution center?

A: Four years, two months. Started June 2019, ended August 2023.

Q: During that time, who was your shift supervisor?

A: Denise Webber for the first year, then Carl Ostrowski after she transferred.

Q: I want to ask you about Mr. Ostrowski. Did he ever make comments about employees' religious practices?

A: Yes.

Q: Can you describe those comments?

A: He made fun of people. People who prayed. People who needed schedule accommodations for religious observance.

Q: Let's slow down. You said he made fun of people who prayed. What specifically did he say?

A: Once—and I'm trying to remember this right—he saw Ahmed going to do his midday prayer during break and said, "There goes Ahmed, off to talk to his invisible friend." Laughed about it.

Q: When was this?

A: I don't know the exact date.

Q: Month? Year?

A: Sometime in 2022. Maybe spring. Maybe not. I'm not certain.

Q: You're not certain.

A: No. I said I'm not certain. It was over a year ago.

Q: Were there other incidents?

A: Yes. Several.

Q: Can you tell me about another one?

A: He denied Priya's request to swap shifts for Diwali. Told her—and this I remember clearly—"We're not rearranging the whole schedule every time someone wants to light candles for their gods."

Q: Did you report any of these incidents?

A: No.

Q: Why not?

A: Because—look, I needed that job. I had two kids. I saw what happened to people who complained. They got shifted to worse routes, worse hours. I wasn't going to paint a target on myself.

Q: What happened to people who complained?

A: I just told you. Worse routes. Worse hours. Suddenly their performance reviews had problems that didn't exist before.

topic: A former employee is deposed about discriminatory remarks made by a supervisor
text:
Q: Let's move to the team meeting on September 8th. You were there?

A: I was there.

Q: Who else attended?

A: The whole analytics team. So that's me, Jennifer Park, DeShawn Williams, both Michaels—Michael Reeves and Michael Torres—and Lisa Thornton was running it.

Q: Lisa Thornton was your manager?

A: Director. She was director of analytics.

Q: What was discussed at this meeting?

A: We were going over Q3 targets. Assignments for the Henderson project.

Q: Did Ms. Thornton make any comments about team members during this meeting?

A: She made a lot of comments. It was a meeting.

Q: I'll rephrase. Did she make any comments that struck you as inappropriate?

A: Define inappropriate.

Q: Comments related to a protected characteristic—race, gender, national origin.

A: She made a comment about Jennifer. About the Henderson client.

Q: What did she say?

A: She said—and I want to get this right because it matters—she said Jennifer probably shouldn't be on the Henderson calls because the client was "old school" and might not be comfortable with—and then she gestured at Jennifer.

Q: She gestured?

A: At Jennifer's face. At Jennifer, generally.

Q: What did you understand that gesture to mean?

A: That Jennifer is Asian. That the client might have a problem with that. That's what I understood it to mean.

Q: Did anyone object to this comment?

A: Michael Reeves said something like, "That's not really fair to Jennifer." And Lisa said she was just being realistic about client management and moved on.

Q: How did Jennifer react?

A: She didn't say anything. She just—her face went very still. She didn't say anything for the rest of the meeting, actually.

topic: A former employee is deposed about discriminatory remarks made by a supervisor
text:
Q: You mentioned in your declaration that you witnessed discriminatory conduct on multiple occasions. I want to go through each one. Let's start with the first incident you can recall.

A: Okay.

Q: When was it?

A: I think it was maybe October 2022? Could have been November.

Q: Which was it, October or November?

A: I said I'm not sure. It was fall. Late fall.

Q: Where did this occur?

A: The parking garage. B level.

Q: Who was involved?

A: Mr. Garrett and Rosa Mendez.

Q: What happened?

A: Rosa was walking to her car. Mr. Garrett was there, he'd parked near her I guess. He said something to her.

Q: What did he say?

A: I couldn't hear all of it. I was across the garage.

Q: What could you hear?

A: I heard him say something about her people, and something about anchor babies.

Q: "Her people" and "anchor babies." That's what you heard?

A: Parts of it. There was more but I couldn't make it out.

Q: So you're testifying about a conversation you couldn't fully hear?

A: I'm testifying about what I heard and what I saw, which was Rosa crying afterward. Which was her coming to me shaking. Which was her telling me what he said.

Q: I'm asking about what you personally witnessed, not what Ms. Mendez told you.

A: I personally witnessed my coworker in tears. I personally witnessed her shaking. I personally heard some of what he said. Is that not enough for you? Is that not—

Q: Ms. Okonkwo, I'm just trying to establish what you directly observed.

A: And I'm telling you.

Q: Let's move on. You mentioned multiple occasions. What's the next incident you recall?

A: I need a minute.

Q: Take your time.

A: [Pause] The next one was in December. The holiday party.

topic: A former employee is deposed about discriminatory remarks made by a supervisor
text:
Q: Dr. Reeves, in your role as department chair, you supervised Dr. Margaret Holloway, correct?

A: I did, yes.

Q: From what dates?

A: From when I assumed the chair position in 2020 through her departure in 2023.

Q: You're aware that Dr. Holloway has alleged that you made discriminatory remarks regarding her age?

A: I'm aware of the allegations, yes.

Q: Did you ever make comments about Dr. Holloway's age?

A: I may have referenced her experience level, which—

Q: I'm asking specifically about her age.

A: I don't believe I ever said anything inappropriate about her age, no.

Q: Did you ever suggest she might want to consider retirement?

A: I might have mentioned it as an option. As it is for all faculty of a certain seniority.

Q: How many other faculty did you suggest retirement to?

A: I don't have that number in front of me.

Q: Approximately?

A: I'd have to review my records.

Q: Was it more than five?

A: I said I'd have to review my records.

Q: Dr. Reeves, did you tell Dr. Holloway that the department needed, quote, "fresh blood"?

A: I may have used that phrase in the context of discussing new hires. Not specifically about her.

Q: So you did use the phrase "fresh blood"?

A: I don't recall the specific context. I'm saying it's possible I used that phrase at some point, in some meeting, not directed at Dr. Holloway personally.

Q: Did you tell Professor Chen that Dr. Holloway was, quote, "past her expiration date"?

A: Absolutely not.

Q: You're certain?

A: I am certain I never said that.

Q: Professor Chen has provided a sworn declaration stating that you did.

A: Then Professor Chen is mistaken or is misremembering or—I don't know what Professor Chen's motivations are, but I did not say that.

topic: A project manager is questioned about deadlines they missed on a software contract
text:
Q: Good morning. Before we dive into the timeline questions, how are you holding up? I know these can be long days.

A: I appreciate that. I'm doing fine, thank you. Ready to help clarify whatever I can.

Q: Let's start with the integration milestone that was originally scheduled for March 15th. Can you walk me through what happened there?

A: Of course. So the integration milestone—we'd scoped it based on the API documentation Nexus provided in January. When we actually got into the work, we discovered the documentation was about eighteen months out of date. I know that sounds like an excuse, and I want to be clear I'm not trying to shift blame entirely, but it did require us to essentially re-architect our approach.

Q: That sounds frustrating. How much time did that re-architecture add?

A: About three weeks initially. We brought it to Nexus right away, same day we discovered the discrepancy, and I have to say their team was incredibly responsive. We worked through it together.

Q: So the delay wasn't a surprise to either party?

A: No, not at all. I sent an email on February 3rd—I can get you the exact time if that's helpful—documenting what we'd found and proposing a revised timeline. Their project lead, Sarah Chen, responded within two hours agreeing to the adjustment.

Q: And you felt that communication was sufficient?

A: I did. I genuinely did. Looking back now, I wonder if I should have escalated it higher on their side, but at the time it felt like we were all on the same page.

Q: I appreciate your candor on that. Let's move to the April milestone.

A: Of course. Whatever helps.

topic: A project manager is questioned about deadlines they missed on a software contract
text:
Q: Ms. Okonkwo, you were the project manager of record for the Bellwether implementation, correct?

A: That's right.

Q: And you reported to Daniel Marsh?

A: Yes, Daniel was our VP of delivery.

Q: When you first realized the June 1st deadline was in jeopardy, what did you do?

A: I brought it to Daniel immediately. Same afternoon. I remember because we ended up talking until almost seven o'clock that night, just working through options. He was great about it, actually—really focused on solutions rather than finger-pointing.

Q: What options did you discuss?

A: We looked at bringing in additional developers, we looked at descoping some of the lower-priority features, and we looked at requesting a formal extension. Daniel was the one who suggested we be completely transparent with Bellwether. He said—and I remember this clearly—he said trust is worth more than looking good in the short term.

Q: It sounds like you and Mr. Marsh worked well together.

A: We did. I've been doing this for twelve years and he's one of the best leaders I've worked with. He never once made me feel like I'd failed, even when things got difficult.

Q: Did Bellwether agree to the extension?

A: They did. Their program manager, Tom Huang, he was understanding about it. I think because we came to them early and with a clear plan, it felt collaborative rather than adversarial.

Q: How much of an extension?

A: Three weeks. And we actually delivered two days early within that revised window. I was proud of the team for that.

Q: I can see why you would be.

A: Thank you. I just want to make sure the record reflects that people worked incredibly hard on this project. Whatever the legal outcome here, that matters to me.

topic: A project manager is questioned about deadlines they missed on a software contract
text:
Q: Let's discuss the testing phase delays. Who made the decision to skip the second round of QA?

A: I need to push back on that characterization. We didn't skip it. We consolidated it with UAT based on a joint decision with the client.

Q: Fair enough. Who proposed that consolidation?

A: I did, but I want to explain the context if that's alright.

Q: Please.

A: Thank you. So by that point, we were looking at a choice between two imperfect options. We could either run sequential testing phases and miss the go-live window entirely, or we could run a more intensive combined phase. I laid out both options for the client with all the risks clearly documented.

Q: And they chose the consolidated approach?

A: They did. And honestly? I think it was the right call given the circumstances. Their IT director, Marcus Webb, he really understood the tradeoffs. We had a good working relationship by that point.

Q: You seem to have positive feelings about the client team.

A: I do. This litigation is between the companies, and I understand why it's happening, but on a human level, those were good people trying to do good work. Same as us.

Q: Did Mr. Webb express any concerns about the consolidated testing?

A: He asked good questions, which I appreciated. He wanted to know what additional safeguards we'd put in place. We added daily status calls during that phase, and I assigned a dedicated QA lead just to manage the overlap.

Q: And you felt those safeguards were adequate?

A: I did then, and I still do now. The issues that came up later weren't related to testing coverage.

topic: A project manager is questioned about deadlines they missed on a software contract
text:
Q: Mr. Patel, I want to make sure I understand your role correctly. You weren't just managing the timeline—you were also the primary client contact?

A: That's right. It was a smaller engagement, so I wore both hats.

Q: That's a lot of responsibility.

A: It was, but I enjoyed it. The client was Meridian Healthcare, and their team was—I don't want to sound overly sentimental in a legal proceeding, but they were a pleasure to work with.

Q: No need to apologize. Tell me about the first missed deadline.

A: So the data migration was supposed to complete by August 10th. We hit an issue with their legacy system that nobody had anticipated—not us, not them, not the vendor who'd originally built it twenty years ago.

Q: What kind of issue?

A: The date formats were inconsistent across different modules. Some records used two-digit years, some used four-digit years, and there was one subsystem that used a completely proprietary format we'd never seen before.

Q: That sounds like a nightmare.

A: It was challenging, but honestly, solving problems like that is why I got into this field. My team was fantastic. We had people staying late not because I asked them to, but because they wanted to get it right for Meridian.

Q: How did Meridian respond to the delay?

A: With grace, really. Their CTO, Dr. Amelia Foster, she sent my team a catering delivery when she heard we were working through a weekend. That meant a lot to people.

Q: That's not typical in my experience.

A: No, it isn't. It made the eventual breakdown in the relationship all the more painful, honestly. I think everyone wanted this to succeed.

topic: A project manager is questioned about deadlines they missed on a software contract
text:
Q: You mentioned in your earlier testimony that you raised resource concerns in January. Who did you raise them with?

A: My direct supervisor, Christine Holloway, and also our resource manager, Keith Yamamoto.

Q: What was their response?

A: They listened. They really did. Christine was dealing with competing priorities across four other projects, but she carved out time to go through my concerns point by point.

Q: But ultimately you didn't get additional resources?

A: Not immediately, no. But I want to be fair to Christine here—she advocated for me internally. She went to leadership twice that I know of. The constraints were above her level.

Q: Did that frustrate you?

A: At the time? A little, yes. But I understood the position she was in. And when things got critical in March, she found a way to get me two additional developers, even though I know it created problems elsewhere.

Q: Let's talk about March then. What changed?

A: The client—Redwood Financial—they added a compliance requirement that hadn't been in the original scope. Christine and I sat down together to figure out how to handle it.

Q: Together?

A: Yes. She didn't just hand it back to me and say figure it out. We spent—I think it was about four hours one afternoon—just mapping out the options together. That meant a lot.

Q: What did you ultimately decide?

A: We proposed a scope change with an associated timeline extension. Redwood accepted. It wasn't contentious at that point.

Q: At that point?

A: Right. Things got more difficult later, in May. But in March, everyone was still working in good faith. I genuinely believe that.

topic: An HR director is questioned about a harassment complaint that was filed and closed
text:
Q: Ms. Chen, you were the HR director at Pemberton Manufacturing in March of 2022, correct?

A: I was.

Q: And you received a harassment complaint from an employee named Danielle Foster on March 14th of that year?

A: I received a complaint, yes. I'd have to check the exact date.

Q: Would it refresh your recollection if I showed you the intake form?

A: If you have it, sure.

Q: I'm handing you what's been marked as Exhibit 14. Is that your signature at the bottom?

A: It is.

Q: And the date next to your signature?

A: March 14th.

Q: So you did receive the complaint on March 14th, 2022?

A: That's what the document says.

Q: Ms. Chen, I'm asking what you know, not what the document says.

A: And I'm telling you that I processed dozens of complaints that year. I don't have the dates memorized. The document confirms it was March 14th. So yes, March 14th.

Q: How many days passed between receiving that complaint and closing the investigation?

A: I'd need to see the closing documentation.

Q: Would it surprise you to learn it was four days?

A: I don't know what you mean by "surprise." We had procedures. We followed them.

Q: Four days seems like a thorough investigation to you?

A: It seems like the investigation took the time it took. I'm not going to sit here and characterize it as too long or too short based on a number you're giving me without context.

---

topic: An HR director is questioned about a harassment complaint that was filed and closed
text:
Q: Mr. Okonkwo, let's talk about the interview process for the Foster complaint. You conducted interviews, correct?

A: I did.

Q: How many people did you interview?

A: Three.

Q: Who were they?

A: Ms. Foster, the complainant. Mr. Raines, the accused. And one witness Ms. Foster identified.

Q: Just one witness?

A: Correct.

Q: Ms. Foster's complaint named three witnesses. I'm looking at Exhibit 14, page two. Do you see where she lists Marcus Webb, Terri Solis, and James Huang?

A: I see that.

Q: But you only interviewed one of them?

A: I interviewed the one who was relevant.

Q: How did you determine the other two weren't relevant?

A: Mr. Webb was on leave. Ms. Solis had transferred departments six months prior.

Q: And Mr. Huang?

A: Mr. Huang was the one I interviewed.

Q: So your testimony is that Mr. Webb being on leave made him impossible to interview?

A: I didn't say impossible. I said he wasn't available during the investigation window.

Q: Did you attempt to contact him?

A: I don't recall specifically.

Q: You don't recall whether you tried to reach a named witness?

A: Counsel, I'm telling you what I recall. I conducted dozens of these investigations. I followed our protocols. If there's a document showing I contacted him or didn't, I'm happy to review it.

Q: I'm asking about your memory.

A: And I've given you my answer.

---

topic: An HR director is questioned about a harassment complaint that was filed and closed
text:
Q: Ms. Chen, the investigation concluded that the complaint was "unsubstantiated." Is that accurate?

A: That was the finding, yes.

Q: What does "unsubstantiated" mean in the context of your HR policies?

A: It means we couldn't confirm the allegations based on the evidence gathered.

Q: It doesn't mean the harassment didn't happen?

A: No, it doesn't mean that.

Q: It just means you couldn't prove it?

A: It means the evidence was insufficient to reach a conclusion either way. That's the definition.

Q: Whose decision was it to close the investigation with that finding?

A: Mine.

Q: Yours alone?

A: I made the recommendation. Legal signed off.

Q: Let me ask you this. Did anyone suggest the investigation should continue?

A: I don't recall anyone suggesting that.

Q: Did Ms. Foster request additional interviews?

A: She may have.

Q: She may have? You don't remember?

A: Counsel, I'm trying to be accurate. I believe she expressed some concerns about the process, but I don't remember specifically whether she requested additional interviews or something else.

Q: Did you document her concerns?

A: If I did, it would be in the file.

Q: I've reviewed the file. I don't see any documentation of concerns she raised.

A: Then I suppose I didn't document them.

Q: You suppose?

A: I didn't. Is that clearer?

---

topic: An HR director is questioned about a harassment complaint that was filed and closed
text:
Q: Mr. Okonkwo, I want to understand the timeline here. You received the complaint on a Monday, correct?

A: If March 14th was a Monday, then yes.

Q: It was. You interviewed Ms. Foster on Tuesday?

A: I believe so.

Q: You interviewed Mr. Raines on Wednesday?

A: That sounds right.

Q: And the investigation was closed on Friday?

A: I'd need to verify that.

Q: Exhibit 19, the closure memo. Dated March 18th, which was a Friday.

A: Okay.

Q: Four days.

A: You've said that.

Q: I'm just establishing the timeline.

A: And I've confirmed it. Several times now.

A: I reviewed documents. Emails. I believe I spoke with Mr. Huang.

A: I reviewed the relevant policies to assess whether the conduct described, if it occurred, would constitute a violation.

A: He disputed Ms. Foster's characterization of events.

topic: An HR director is questioned about a harassment complaint that was filed and closed
text:
Q: Ms. Chen, were you aware that Mr. Raines had two prior complaints filed against him?

A: I was aware of his personnel history, yes.

Q: Two prior harassment complaints?

A: I believe one was a harassment complaint. One was characterized differently.

Q: How was it characterized?

A: I'd need to review the files.

Q: You don't remember?

A: I remember there were prior matters. I don't remember the precise categorization.

Q: Did the existence of prior complaints factor into your investigation of Ms. Foster's complaint?

A: We consider relevant history, yes.

Q: How did it factor in here?

A: I'm not sure I understand the question.

Q: What weight did you give to the fact that Mr. Raines had been complained about before?

A: We don't prejudge based on prior complaints. Each matter is evaluated on its own merits.

Q: So it was given no weight?

A: I didn't say that. I said we don't prejudge. Prior history is context, not conclusion.

Q: Ms. Chen, both of Mr. Raines's prior complaints were also closed as unsubstantiated. Were you aware of that?

A: I was.

Q: Three unsubstantiated complaints against the same individual. Did that strike you as significant?

Q: I'm asking whether a pattern concerned you.

A: And I'm telling you that I don't conduct investigations based on patterns. I conduct them based on evidence.

topic: An employee is deposed about a coworker's termination they believe was retaliatory
text:
Q: Please state your name for the record.

A: Marcus Chen. And I want to say right off the bat that I've been waiting for someone to actually ask about this, because what happened to Denise was completely wrong and I have a lot to say about it.

Q: Mr. Chen, I'll be asking the questions today. How long have you worked at Thornton Industries?

A: Seven years, but honestly, the last six months have felt like a different company entirely. Ever since Denise filed that safety complaint, management changed. The whole atmosphere changed.

Q: Let's slow down. I'm asking about your tenure first.

A: Seven years. But you're going to want to hear about what I saw, because I documented everything. I have dates, I have names, I have—

Q: Mr. Chen, we'll get there. What is your current position?

A: Production floor supervisor, same as Denise was. We worked side by side for four years. Same shift, same responsibilities, same performance reviews—until she spoke up about the ventilation problems. Then suddenly her reviews tanked. You want to explain that coincidence? Because I can't.

Q: I'm asking the questions, Mr. Chen. Did you directly observe Ms. Patterson's termination meeting?

A: No, but I saw Randy Hollister—that's the plant manager—I saw him come out of that conference room with this look on his face, and when I asked him what happened, he said, and I'm quoting directly here, "That's what happens when people can't keep their mouths shut."

Q: You're certain those were his exact words?

A: Absolutely certain. I wrote it down immediately. Check my phone notes—November 14th, 2:47 PM. I knew right then this was retaliation, and I knew someone would eventually ask, so I made sure I had it right.

Q: Did Mr. Hollister say anything else?

A: He didn't have to. That sentence told me everything. Denise had been there nine years with spotless reviews, then she reports a safety violation to OSHA and three months later she's terminated for "performance issues"? Come on. Anyone paying attention could see what was happening.

Q: Did you ever discuss the OSHA complaint with Ms. Patterson directly?

A: Multiple times. She came to me before she even filed it because she was worried about exactly this. And I told her—I said, "Denise, do the right thing, they can't legally retaliate." I was wrong. I was completely wrong, and I feel terrible about that, and that's part of why I'm here telling you everything I know.

topic: An employee is deposed about a coworker's termination they believe was retaliatory
text:
Q: Ms. Okonkwo, let's cut right to it—you were present when Mr. Reeves received his final written warning, correct?

A: I was in the office, yes.

Q: And this was approximately two weeks before his termination?

A: That sounds right.

Q: The warning cited attendance issues—did you find that characterization accurate?

A: No.

Q: No? Tell me more. Help me understand why not.

A: James had the same attendance record as everyone else. Maybe better, actually.

Q: So you're saying the warning was pretextual?

A: I'm saying it didn't match what I observed.

Q: What did you observe? Specifically. Give me the details.

A: James was reliable. On time. Stayed late when needed.

Q: But something changed after his complaint to HR, didn't it? Walk me through that. What did you start seeing?

A: Management started tracking his breaks.

Q: Just his breaks? Nobody else's?

A: Just his.

Q: Isn't that remarkable? One employee, singled out, right after he raises concerns about overtime violations. Who authorized this tracking?

A: I don't know who authorized it.

Q: But you noticed it. You found it unusual enough to remember it now.

A: Yes.

Q: Did you say anything to anyone about this disparate treatment?

A: I mentioned it to my supervisor.

Q: And what was the response? What did they tell you?

A: She said it wasn't my concern.

Q: Not your concern. Even though you'd worked beside Mr. Reeves for how long?

A: Three years.

Q: Three years, and suddenly his break times are being monitored like he's a problem employee. Did that seem fair to you?

A: No.

Q: I didn't think so. Nothing further on this line.

topic: An employee is deposed about a coworker's termination they believe was retaliatory
text:
Q: Mr. Petrov, how would you describe the general workplace atmosphere prior to Ms. Yamamoto's internal complaint?

A: It was fine. Collegial, I suppose. People got along. Tomoko—Ms. Yamamoto—she was well-liked. Really well-liked, actually. She organized the holiday party two years running and everyone looked forward to it. She had this way of remembering everyone's birthdays, even in a department of forty people. She'd leave cards on your desk with inside jokes. Little things, but it mattered.

Q: And after her complaint about discriminatory promotion practices?

A: Night and day. But let me be specific, because I want you to understand exactly what happened. First, they moved her desk. She'd been near the window, near the team she worked with, and they relocated her to this back corner by the supply closet. No explanation. Then the meeting invitations stopped. She'd been on every project call, and suddenly she was "accidentally" left off distribution lists.

Q: Were these actions documented?

A: Not officially, but I started keeping track myself because I could see what was happening and I thought someone should have a record. I have emails I forwarded to my personal account—not confidential ones, just ones where you can see her suddenly dropped from chains she'd been on for years.

Q: Why did you feel the need to keep personal records?

A: Because I've seen this before at a previous job. The slow freeze-out. The paper trail that gets built to justify what they've already decided to do. And I thought, if Tomoko ever needs a witness, I want to be able to actually help, not just say "yeah, it seemed bad but I don't remember specifics."

Q: Did you discuss your record-keeping with Ms. Yamamoto?

A: No, I didn't want to worry her more than she already was. She was stressed enough. She started eating lunch alone in her car. Someone who used to sit at the big table and make everyone laugh was hiding in the parking lot.

Q: What ultimately precipitated her termination, in your understanding?

A: They claimed budget cuts, but they hired her replacement two weeks later under a different title. Same job, same responsibilities, different name. I know because I trained him.

topic: An employee is deposed about a coworker's termination they believe was retaliatory
text:
Q: State your role in the IT department.

A: Network administrator.

Q: How long in that role?

A: Eleven years.

Q: You worked with Kevin Marsh?

A: Yes.

Q: Closely?

A: We shared an office.

Q: For how long?

A: Six years.

Q: So you knew him well.

A: Better than most.

Q: Tell me about his termination.

A: What specifically?

Q: Start with what you observed in the weeks prior.

A: Things got tense.

Q: Tense how?

A: After Kevin reported the data privacy issue, his projects started getting reassigned.

Q: Who reassigned them?

A: Director Simmons.

Q: Did Simmons give reasons?

A: He said Kevin needed to "focus."

Q: Focus on what?

A: That was never clear.

Q: Did Kevin ask?

A: Several times.

Q: And?

A: He was told it was a "management decision."

Q: Did you find that explanation sufficient?

A: I found it suspicious, honestly. Kevin had the highest project completion rate in our department. He'd just gotten an excellence award in Q2. Then suddenly he can't handle his workload? That didn't add up for me, and I told him so.

topic: An employee is deposed about a coworker's termination they believe was retaliatory
text:
Q: Ms. Thornton, you've stated you attended the department meeting on March 3rd.

A: That's correct.

Q: Was Mr. Delgado present?

A: He was, but I need to give you context, because what happened at that meeting—

Q: I'm just establishing who was present first.

A: Yes, Rafael was present, but the meeting was clearly designed to humiliate him. I'm sorry, but I can't just answer yes or no when what I witnessed was so blatant.

Q: Let me ask the questions. Who else attended?

A: Our whole department—twelve people—plus Director Hayes, who never attended our regular meetings before. Never once in three years. But suddenly, two weeks after Rafael files a wage complaint, Hayes shows up to "observe."

Q: Did Director Hayes speak during the meeting?

A: He called on Rafael specifically, repeatedly, asking him to justify his project timelines in front of everyone. Nobody else was questioned like that. It was like watching an interrogation, not a department meeting.

Q: How did Mr. Delgado respond?

A: Professionally. Calmly. He answered every question even though they were clearly designed to make him look incompetent.

Q: That's your interpretation?

A: That's what I saw with my own eyes. And I wasn't the only one. After the meeting, three of us talked about how wrong it was. Andrea Fischer said it was "like watching a public execution."

Q: Did anyone raise concerns with HR?

A: I did, actually. I filed a formal complaint the next day saying Rafael was being targeted.

Q: What was the response?

A: I was told they'd "look into it." Three days later, Rafael was terminated. So you tell me how seriously they took my concerns.

Q: I'm not here to offer opinions, Ms. Thornton.

A: Well, I am. That's why I'm under oath, isn't it? To tell the truth about what I saw? Because what I saw was a man getting punished for asking to be paid correctly.

topic: A witness is questioned about a workplace injury they observed but did not report
text:
Q: You were working on the loading dock the morning of September 14th, correct?

A: I was in that general area, yes.

Q: In that general area. Can you be more specific about where exactly you were positioned?

A: I was moving between the dock and the staging area. Back and forth. It's hard to pin down an exact location because I wasn't stationary.

Q: At any point that morning, did you see Marcus Williams?

A: I saw a lot of people that morning.

Q: I'm asking specifically about Marcus Williams.

A: Yes. I saw him.

Q: And did you see him fall?

A: I saw him on the ground.

Q: That's not what I asked. Did you see him fall?

A: I heard something and turned around and he was on the ground. So I didn't see the actual moment, no.

Q: You heard something. What did you hear?

A: A sound. Like something heavy. Metal, maybe, or—I don't know. It was loud.

Q: And you turned around. How quickly?

A: Immediately.

Q: So you turned immediately, and Marcus Williams was already on the ground. Not falling. Already down.

A: That's what I said.

Q: Yet you didn't report what you saw to anyone.

A: I wasn't the only one there. Other people were closer. I assumed someone else would handle it.

Q: You assumed. Did you see anyone else report it?

A: I went back to work. I don't know what other people did or didn't do.

topic: A witness is questioned about a workplace injury they observed but did not report
text:
