Q: How long have you worked at Redfield Manufacturing?

A: Seven years this past June.

Q: In those seven years, have you received safety training regarding incident reporting?

A: We do the online modules every year. Everyone does.

Q: So you're familiar with the company's policy on reporting workplace injuries?

A: I know there's a policy, yes.

Q: Can you describe it for me?

A: If you see something, you're supposed to report it to your supervisor. That's the gist of it.

Q: The gist of it. Is there anything more to it than that?

A: There's probably more detail in the handbook. I don't have it memorized word for word.

Q: Fair enough. On January 8th, you witnessed Danielle Okonkwo injure her hand, correct?

A: I saw her react like she'd hurt herself. I didn't see the actual injury happen.

Q: What do you mean by "react"?

A: She pulled her hand back fast. She was holding it. She looked like she was in pain.

Q: Did she say anything?

A: Not that I heard. It's loud in there.

Q: How far away from her were you?

A: Maybe fifteen feet. Maybe twenty.

Q: Close enough to see her holding her hand and appearing to be in pain.

A: Yes.

Q: But you didn't report this to your supervisor.

A: No.

Q: Why not?

A: I figured if it was serious, she'd report it herself. It wasn't my place to make a thing out of it if she didn't want to.

Q: Wasn't your place. Even though the policy you just described says if you see something, you report it.

A: The policy says a lot of things.

topic: A witness is questioned about a workplace injury they observed but did not report
text:
Q: Let's talk about what you saw on March 3rd. You were on the second floor of Building C?

A: Correct.

Q: What were you doing there?

A: Checking inventory in the overflow storage room.

Q: Is that part of your normal duties?

A: Sometimes. When we're short-staffed or when there's a rush order.

Q: Were you short-staffed that day?

A: Why does that matter?

Q: I'm just trying to understand why you were in that location.

A: I was doing my job. That's why I was there.

Q: Okay. While you were in the overflow storage room, did you witness an injury to an employee named Thomas Brennan?

A: I saw Tom. I don't know that I'd call what I saw an "injury."

Q: What would you call it?

A: He slipped. Caught himself on a shelf. Seemed fine after a second.

Q: He slipped on what?

A: I don't know. The floor. There might have been something wet. I wasn't looking at the floor.

Q: You were looking at Tom.

A: I was looking in his direction when it happened, yes.

Q: Did he seem fine, or was he fine? Those are different things.

A: He got up. He kept working. That's all I know.

Q: Did he say anything to you about what happened?

A: No. We don't really talk much.

Q: Did you say anything to him?

A: I asked if he was okay. He said yeah. That was it.

Q: And you didn't think this was worth mentioning to a supervisor.

A: He said he was okay. What was I supposed to do, call him a liar?

topic: A witness is questioned about a workplace injury they observed but did not report
text:
Q: I want to be very precise about the timeline here. You clocked in at 6:00 a.m.?

A: 6:00 a.m. on the dot.

Q: And the incident involving Patricia Reyes occurred at approximately what time?

A: I couldn't give you an exact time.

Q: An approximate time.

A: Mid-morning. Maybe 9:30, 10:00. Somewhere in there.

Q: So you'd been on shift for three and a half to four hours at that point.

A: If you say so. I wasn't watching the clock.

Q: Where were you when you first became aware something had happened to Ms. Reyes?

A: I was at my station. Line four.

Q: Can you see the forklift area from line four?

A: Parts of it. Not all of it.

Q: Which parts can you see?

A: The aisle closest to the loading bay. If someone's further back, no, I can't see that.

Q: Where was Ms. Reyes when you saw her?

A: She was in the aisle I can see.

Q: Convenient.

A: Excuse me?

Q: I said convenient. That she happened to be in your line of sight.

A: I don't know what you're implying, but I'm telling you what I saw.

Q: I'm not implying anything. I'm establishing facts. What exactly did you see happen to Ms. Reyes?

A: The forklift clipped a stack of pallets. The pallets shifted. She got knocked down. That's what I saw.

Q: Did you leave your station to help her?

A: No.

Q: Did you call for help?

A: Other people were already responding.

Q: Other people. Can you name them?

A: I don't remember who specifically. There were people moving toward her.

Q: But you remember the incident clearly enough to describe it in detail.

A: I remember what I saw. I don't remember every person who was standing around.

topic: A witness is questioned about a workplace injury they observed but did not report
text:
Q: You testified earlier that you considered the injury minor. I want to revisit that.

A: All right.

Q: What made you characterize it as minor?

A: He didn't seem that hurt. He was walking around. He didn't go to the hospital or anything.

Q: How do you know he didn't go to the hospital?

A: I saw him the next day at work.

Q: People go to the hospital and return to work the next day all the time.

A: Okay. Then I don't know for certain he didn't go.

Q: So when you said he didn't go to the hospital, that was an assumption.

A: I suppose it was.

Q: What else in your testimony today has been an assumption?

A: I've been telling you what I saw and what I thought at the time. That's what you asked me to do.

Q: I asked you to tell me facts. Are you able to distinguish between facts and assumptions?

A: Yes.

Q: Let's try again, then. Fact: you saw Derek Loomis sustain an injury.

A: I saw him get hurt, yes.

Q: Fact: you did not report this to your supervisor.

A: Correct.

Q: Fact or assumption: you believed the injury was minor.

A: That was my assessment at the time based on what I observed.

Q: An assessment isn't a fact, is it?

A: No. I guess it isn't.

Q: Is it possible your assessment was wrong?

A: It's possible.

Q: Is it possible you chose not to report it for reasons other than your assessment of its severity?

A: I don't know what you're getting at.

Q: I'm asking a simple question.

A: And I'm telling you I didn't report it because I didn't think it was serious. That's the only reason.

topic: A paramedic is questioned about the response time and treatment at an accident scene
text:
Q: Let's talk about the timeline that night. What time did your unit receive the dispatch call?

A: 10:47 PM.

Q: And what time did you arrive at the scene?

A: 11:02 PM.

Q: So fifteen minutes from dispatch to arrival, correct?

A: That's the math, yes.

Q: Is fifteen minutes a typical response time for your unit?

A: It depends.

Q: On what?

A: On about a dozen different variables. Traffic. Weather. Distance. Road conditions. Whether we're coming from the station or returning from another call. Whether there's construction. Whether—

Q: I understand there are variables. I'm asking whether fifteen minutes is typical.

A: And I'm telling you that "typical" isn't a meaningful word without context.

Q: Let me put it differently. Was there anything that night that delayed your response?

A: We responded as fast as conditions allowed.

Q: That's not what I asked. Was there a specific delay?

A: There was construction on Miller Road. We had to reroute.

Q: How much time did that add?

A: I don't have a stopwatch running while I'm trying to save someone's life, Counselor.

Q: Your best estimate.

A: Three to four minutes. Maybe.

Q: So without the construction, you would have arrived in approximately eleven minutes?

A: Hypothetically. Sure. If that helps you.

topic: A paramedic is questioned about the response time and treatment at an accident scene
text:
Q: When you arrived at the scene, who was already present?

A: Fire and rescue had a unit there. Two officers from county. A few bystanders.

Q: Did you speak with any of the officers before beginning treatment?

A: Briefly. One of them pointed us toward the vehicle.

Q: What did you observe when you approached the vehicle?

A: The driver was still in the seat, unconscious. Significant trauma to the head and chest. The passenger had already been moved to the grass.

Q: Who moved the passenger?

A: I don't know.

Q: You didn't ask?

A: I was focused on the patients.

Q: Would it have been relevant to your treatment to know whether the passenger had been moved properly?

A: Relevant how?

Q: Whether spinal precautions were taken, for instance.

A: We assume they weren't. We always assume they weren't. That's protocol.

Q: So you treated the passenger as a potential spinal injury?

A: Yes.

Q: Even though you didn't know the circumstances of how she was moved?

A: That's what I just said.

Q: I'm trying to understand your process.

A: And I'm explaining it. We don't have the luxury of getting a full history before we start treatment. Someone's bleeding, we stop the bleeding. Someone might have a spinal injury, we immobilize. That's how it works.

Q: I appreciate that. Let me ask—

A: Do you? Because these questions suggest otherwise.

Q: Mr. Torres, I'm just trying to establish what happened.

A: Then let me do that without the implication that we did something wrong.

topic: A paramedic is questioned about the response time and treatment at an accident scene
text:
Q: You indicated in your report that you administered epinephrine at the scene. Is that correct?

A: Yes.

Q: What dosage?

A: One milligram, IV push.

Q: And that's the standard dose for cardiac arrest?

A: It's within the standard range, yes.

Q: Within the range. What is the range?

A: One milligram is the standard adult dose per ACLS protocol.

Q: So it's not a range, it's a specific dose.

A: I said it's within the standard range because there are circumstances where dosing may vary. But one milligram is standard.

Q: What circumstances would cause you to vary the dose?

A: Pediatric patients. Certain pre-existing conditions. Anaphylaxis versus cardiac arrest.

Q: This was a cardiac arrest situation?

A: Yes.

Q: So one milligram was appropriate?

A: Yes. Which is why I administered one milligram.

Q: How long after arriving on scene did you administer the epinephrine?

A: I'd have to check the report for the exact time.

Q: Approximately.

A: I don't like to approximate medical timelines.

Q: Your best recollection.

A: Four to five minutes after arrival.

Q: Is that within the expected timeframe?

A: We had to establish an airway first. So yes.

Q: You had to establish an airway before administering epinephrine?

A: I'm not going to push epi into someone who isn't being ventilated. That would be pointless.

topic: A paramedic is questioned about the response time and treatment at an accident scene
text:
Q: I want to make sure I understand the sequence of events. You arrived at 11:02?

A: Correct.

Q: And the patient was pronounced at 11:41?

A: At the hospital, yes. We transported.

Q: So you worked on the patient for approximately how long at the scene?

A: Around twenty minutes before transport.

Q: Twenty minutes. And during that time, what interventions did you perform?

A: CPR. Intubation. Two rounds of epinephrine. Defibrillation. Fluid resuscitation.

Q: That's a significant number of interventions.

A: That's our job.

Q: At what point did you make the decision to transport?

A: After we achieved a shockable rhythm but couldn't maintain it.

Q: Couldn't maintain it. What does that mean?

A: It means exactly what it sounds like. We got the heart into a rhythm we could work with, and then it deteriorated again.

Q: So you transported despite an unstable rhythm?

A: We transported because of an unstable rhythm. The patient needed surgical intervention we couldn't provide in a field setting.

Q: Was the patient stable enough for transport?

A: Define stable.

Q: I'm asking for your medical judgment.

A: My medical judgment was that staying on scene would result in death and transport gave him a chance. That's the calculation.

Q: Some might say transporting an unstable patient is risky.

A: Some might not have been there.

Q: Excuse me?

A: I said some people who weren't there might have opinions about decisions they didn't have to make.

topic: A paramedic is questioned about the response time and treatment at an accident scene
text:
Q: Let's go back to something you said earlier. You mentioned that bystanders had attempted CPR before you arrived.

A: That's what I was told.

Q: By whom?

A: One of the firefighters on scene.

Q: Did you observe the quality of the CPR being performed?

A: It had stopped by the time I got there.

Q: So you have no firsthand knowledge of whether it was effective?

A: No.

Q: Did you note in your report that bystander CPR had been attempted?

A: I believe so.

Q: You believe so, or you know so?

A: I'd have to look at the report.

Q: I'm showing you what's been marked as Exhibit 14. Is this your report?

A: Yes.

Q: Can you point to where you documented the bystander CPR?

A: ...I don't see it in the narrative section.

Q: So it wasn't documented?

A: It appears not.

Q: Is that an oversight?

A: It's not—look. We're working on someone who's dying. We're documenting what we do, what we administer, what we observe. I was told secondhand that someone had done CPR. I didn't witness it. It wasn't something I could verify, so I didn't include it.

Q: Wouldn't that information be relevant to the patient's outcome?

A: Everything is relevant to someone after the fact.

Q: I'm asking whether—

A: And I'm telling you that in the moment, my priority was keeping that man alive, not creating a paper trail for a lawsuit that might happen two years later. I'm sorry if that's inconvenient.

topic: A supervisor is deposed about performance reviews given to an employee who was later fired
text:
Q: Mr. Okonkwo, you were Ms. Patel's direct supervisor from 2019 through 2022, is that correct?

A: That's correct.

Q: And in that capacity, you were responsible for conducting her annual performance reviews?

A: Yes, I conducted all annual reviews for employees in my department.

Q: Let's start with the 2020 review. I'm handing you what's been marked as Exhibit 14. Do you recognize this document?

A: I do. This is the performance review I completed for Ms. Patel covering the 2020 calendar year.

Q: And if you look at page two, you rated her as "meets expectations" in all six categories. Is that accurate?

A: That's what the document reflects, yes.

Q: Was that rating consistent with your actual assessment of her work at the time?

A: It was. Ms. Patel was performing her job duties adequately in 2020. She completed her assignments, met her deadlines, and worked reasonably well with her colleagues.

Q: Did you have any concerns about her performance in 2020 that aren't reflected in this document?

A: No. If I had concerns, I would have documented them. That's the purpose of the review process.

Q: Moving to 2021, did your assessment of Ms. Patel's performance change?

A: Somewhat, yes. She continued to meet the basic requirements of her position, but I noted some areas where improvement would be beneficial.

Q: And those areas are documented in Exhibit 15, the 2021 review?

A: They are. I specifically noted communication with clients and time management on complex projects.

Q: Did you discuss these concerns with Ms. Patel directly?

A: I did, during the review meeting and in several informal conversations throughout the year. She was receptive to the feedback.

---

topic: A supervisor is deposed about performance reviews given to an employee who was later fired
text:
Q: When you gave Ms. Thornton her 2021 performance review, did she sign the acknowledgment page?

A: She did.

Q: Did she raise any objections at that time to the ratings you gave her?

A: She asked a few questions about the methodology, which I answered. She didn't file a formal objection.

Q: What do you mean by "methodology"?

A: She wanted to understand how I weighted different factors—client retention, billable hours, that sort of thing. I explained the rubric the company uses.

Q: And after that explanation, she signed?

A: Yes.

Q: Now, one of the ratings on that review was a two out of five for "teamwork and collaboration." Do you see that?

A: I do.

Q: Can you explain what specific behaviors led to that rating?

A: Certainly. Over the course of 2021, I received feedback from three different team members that Ms. Thornton was difficult to work with on joint projects. She missed two team meetings without notice, and there was an incident in September where she refused to share client files with a colleague who needed them.

Q: Did you investigate these complaints before including them in the review?

A: I spoke with each person who raised concerns. I also spoke with Ms. Thornton to get her perspective.

Q: What did she say?

A: She said the complaints were exaggerated and that the file-sharing issue was a misunderstanding about confidentiality protocols.

Q: Did you find her explanation credible?

A: I found it partially credible. The confidentiality issue may have been a genuine confusion. The pattern of missed meetings and the feedback from multiple colleagues, though, suggested a real problem with collaboration.

Q: So you included it in the review despite her explanation?

A: I included an accurate account of what occurred and what was reported. That's my job.

---

topic: A supervisor is deposed about performance reviews given to an employee who was later fired
text:
Q: Ms. Rivera, I want to ask you about a phrase that appears in Mr. Dawson's 2022 performance review. On page four, you wrote that he "requires significant oversight." What did you mean by that?

A: I meant that compared to other employees at his level, Mr. Dawson needed more check-ins and guidance to complete his work.

Q: How many check-ins are we talking about?

A: I'd say I was meeting with him two to three times per week on matters that other employees would handle independently.

Q: Were those meetings at his request or yours?

A: A mix. Sometimes he came to me with questions. Other times I initiated because I noticed work wasn't progressing as expected.

Q: Did you ever tell him directly that you felt he required more oversight than his peers?

A: I did. In the mid-year check-in, I told him I wanted to see him take more ownership of projects without waiting for me to follow up.

Q: How did he respond?

A: He thanked me for the feedback and said he'd work on it.

Q: Did you see improvement after that conversation?

A: Some improvement, yes. He started sending me status updates proactively, which reduced the need for me to check in. But on more complex matters, the pattern continued.

Q: Did you document that mid-year conversation?

A: I made a note in my files, yes.

Q: Is that note part of the official personnel file?

A: No, it was in my personal supervisor notes. Those aren't typically added to the HR file unless there's a formal write-up.

Q: But the phrase "requires significant oversight" made it into the formal review?

A: It did, because that was my honest assessment at year-end.

---

topic: A supervisor is deposed about performance reviews given to an employee who was later fired
text:
Q: Let me ask you about the timing of these reviews. The 2021 review is dated March 15, 2022. Is that when it was completed?

A: That's when I finalized it and submitted it to HR.

Q: When did you meet with Mr. Chen to discuss it?

A: March 22nd.

Q: So the review was already finalized before you met with him?

A: The written document was complete, yes. But the meeting is part of the process—that's when the employee has a chance to respond.

Q: Can the employee's response change the ratings?

A: In theory, yes. If an employee raises something I wasn't aware of, I could submit an amendment.

Q: Has that ever happened with any employee you've supervised?

A: Once, yes. An employee pointed out that I'd attributed a project delay to her when it was actually caused by a vendor issue. I corrected the record.

Q: Did Mr. Chen raise anything in his March 22nd meeting that caused you to reconsider any of your ratings?

A: He disagreed with several of the ratings, but he didn't present new information I hadn't already considered.

Q: What did he disagree with specifically?

A: He felt the "needs improvement" rating on initiative was unfair. He also questioned the productivity metrics I used.

Q: Did you explain your reasoning?

A: I did. I walked him through each rating and the documentation supporting it.

Q: How long did that meeting last?

A: Approximately forty-five minutes.

Q: And at the end, he signed the acknowledgment?

A: He did, though he wrote "signing under protest" next to his signature, which is his right.

---

topic: A supervisor is deposed about performance reviews given to an employee who was later fired
text:
Q: You've testified that you gave Ms. Franklin a verbal warning in October 2022. Was that warning documented anywhere?

A: I sent a follow-up email summarizing our conversation.

Q: To Ms. Franklin?

A: Yes, and I copied HR.

Q: Do you have a copy of that email?

A: I believe it's in the materials I provided to counsel.

Q: I'm showing you Exhibit 23. Is this the email you're referring to?

A: Yes, this is it.

Q: The email states that Ms. Franklin was late to three client meetings in September. Do you see that?

A: I do.

Q: Did Ms. Franklin dispute that characterization?

A: She replied to the email. You can see her response on the second page.

Q: I see it. She writes that one of the meetings was rescheduled without her knowledge. Did you look into that?

A: I did. I spoke with the project coordinator, who confirmed the meeting time had been moved but said the update was sent to the full team, including Ms. Franklin.

Q: So you concluded she had received notice?

A: I concluded she should have received notice. Whether she actually saw the email, I can't say.

Q: Did that affect how you weighed that particular incident?

A: I gave her the benefit of the doubt on that one meeting. That's why the warning addressed a pattern of lateness rather than that single incident.

Q: But all three meetings are listed in the email.

A: For completeness, yes. I wanted the record to reflect what had occurred. My focus in the conversation was on the pattern, not on assigning blame for each individual instance.

Q: Did Ms. Franklin's performance improve after this warning?

A: It did, for a time. November and December were better. The issues resurfaced in January.

topic: A witness is questioned about a workplace injury they observed but did not report
text:
Q: Please state your name for the record.

A: Marcus Delano Webb. Happy to be here, happy to help however I can.

Q: Mr. Webb, you were working at the Greenfield distribution center on March 14th of this year?

A: I was, yes. Third shift, which I've been on for—actually, let me think—going on four years now. Started in 2020, right before everything went crazy with COVID, so I've seen a lot of changes in that facility, a lot of different safety protocols come and go.

Q: Did you witness an incident involving a forklift that evening?

A: Oh, absolutely. I had a front-row seat, unfortunately. I was restocking pallets in aisle seven—the narrow aisle, the one everyone always complains about—and I heard this sound, this really distinctive metal-on-metal scraping, and I turned around just in time to see the whole thing happen.

Q: Describe what you saw.

A: So Danny—Daniel Ruiz, he operates the Toyota forklift, the older one with the squeaky backup alarm—he was making a turn at the end of aisle six, and his load shifted. Cases of automotive parts, pretty heavy stuff. And one of the cases caught the edge of the racking, and the whole stack came down on his left side. Caught his arm and shoulder. I remember thinking it looked like slow motion, you know how they say that happens?

Q: What did you do immediately after?

A: Well, first I ran over. I wanted to make sure he was okay. He was conscious, thank God, but his arm was pinned under two cases, and he was making this face—not screaming, just this tight grimace. I helped pull the cases off. They weren't as heavy as I expected, maybe forty pounds each.

Q: Did you report this incident to a supervisor?

A: No, I didn't. And I want to explain that, if I can—

Q: Just answer the question for now.

A: Right, no, I didn't report it. But I want to be clear, Danny told me not to, and there's a whole context there that I think matters.

Q: You said Mr. Ruiz told you not to report it?

A: He did. He was worried about his performance review coming up. He'd already had one incident on his record from November, completely minor, but you know how these things stack up. He begged me, really. Said he'd handle it himself, ice it up, take some Advil.

Q: And you agreed to that?

A: I did. I know now that was wrong, and I've actually been wanting to get this all on record because I think it points to a bigger problem with how our facility handles injury reporting. People are scared, you know? There's this culture of—can I talk about the culture?

Q: We'll get to that. Did you see Mr. Ruiz receive any medical attention that night?

A: Not professional medical attention, no. But I did see him wrap his arm with an ACE bandage from the first aid kit. I actually walked him over there myself. The kit was pretty picked over, I noticed—we were out of the instant cold packs, which I thought was a problem.

Q: Did anyone else witness this incident?

A: You know, I've been thinking about that a lot since I got the subpoena. There might have been someone in aisle eight—I think I saw a shadow, someone moving around—but I can't say for certain who it was. I could speculate, but I'm guessing you want me to stick to what I actually know.

topic: A witness is questioned about a workplace injury they observed but did not report
text:
Q: Good morning. You understand you're under oath?

A: Yes.

Q: Wonderful. Let's dive right in. You were present at Hartley Manufacturing on October 3rd, correct?

A: Correct.

Q: And you saw—with your own two eyes—the accident involving the hydraulic press?

A: I saw something happen, yes.

Q: Something happen. Let's unpack that. A man lost two fingers, didn't he?

A: I learned that later.

Q: But you were there. You were standing—what, fifteen feet away?

A: Maybe twenty.

Q: Twenty feet away when Thomas Kendrick's hand went into that press?

A: I didn't see his hand go in. I heard him yell.

Q: You heard him yell. That must have been alarming. What did you do?

A: I looked over.

Q: And what did you see when you looked over?

A: Tom was holding his hand. There was blood.

Q: There was blood. Was there a lot of blood?

A: I couldn't say.

Q: You couldn't say. You were twenty feet away from a man who just lost two fingers and you couldn't tell if there was a lot of blood?

A: I didn't examine him. Other people rushed over.

Q: Ah, other people rushed over. But not you?

A: I stayed at my station.

Q: Why is that?

A: We're supposed to stay at our stations during incidents. That's protocol.

Q: Fascinating. And did protocol also tell you not to report what you witnessed?

A: I assumed someone else reported it.

Q: You assumed. Did you ask?

A: No.

Q: Did you fill out an incident witness form?

A: No.

Q: Did you mention it to your supervisor, in passing, at any point that day?

A: I don't recall.

Q: You don't recall. A man loses two fingers twenty feet from where you're standing, and you don't recall if you mentioned it to anyone?

A: It was a busy day.

topic: A witness is questioned about a workplace injury they observed but did not report
text:
Q: How long have you worked at Cedarbrook Nursing Facility?

A: Eleven years this coming February. Started as a floor aide, worked my way up to shift supervisor.

Q: So you're familiar with the safety reporting procedures?

A: Very familiar. I helped write the current version of the handbook, actually. Section four through six, the incident response protocols.

Q: Then you'd know better than most when an injury should be reported?

A: I would.

Q: Let's talk about January 19th. You observed Nurse Practitioner Simmons injure her back while transferring a patient?

A: I observed her wince and grab her lower back during a transfer. I wouldn't characterize it as an injury without medical documentation.

Q: She winced and grabbed her back.

A: Correct.

Q: Did she say anything?

A: She said, quote, "That didn't feel right."

Q: "That didn't feel right." And what did you take that to mean?

A: I asked her if she was okay. She said she was fine.

Q: And you accepted that?

A: I asked her twice more during the shift. Both times she said she was managing.

Q: But you didn't file a report.

A: The reporting threshold, per section 4.2 of the handbook—which I helped author—requires either a request for medical attention, visible injury, or loss of function. She exhibited none of those criteria during my shift.

Q: She's now on permanent disability.

A: So I've heard.

Q: Does that change your assessment?

A: It changes the outcome. It doesn't change what I observed on January 19th.

Q: You helped write the handbook.

A: Sections four through six.

Q: Do you think the handbook failed Ms. Simmons?

A: I think the handbook reflects the standards we were given by corporate. If you're asking whether I personally failed her—

Q: I'm asking about the handbook.

A: Then no. The handbook was followed correctly.

Q: By you.

A: By me.

Q: While a woman who said "that didn't feel right" ended up on permanent disability.

A: I'm not a medical professional. I followed procedure.

topic: A witness is questioned about a workplace injury they observed but did not report
text:
Q: State your position at Ridgeway Construction.

A: Journeyman electrician.

Q: Were you on the Maple Street project last August?

A: I was.

Q: Tell me about the scaffolding collapse on August 12th.

A: What do you want to know?

Q: Everything. Start from the beginning. Take your time.

A: Alright. Well. It was a Tuesday. Hot. Really hot, actually, which matters because we'd been pushing to finish the exterior work before a cold front came in. Everyone was tired. I was running conduit on the second floor when I heard— it's hard to describe.

Q: Try.

A: Like a groan? The scaffolding groaned. Then there was shouting, and then this crash. Not as loud as you'd think, actually. More of a crumple.

Q: What did you do?

A: I ran to the window.

Q: And?

A: And I saw Ricky— Ricardo Garza— on the ground. The scaffolding was on top of him. Part of it.

Q: Was he moving?

A: He was... twitching. His leg was at a bad angle.

Q: Who else saw this?

A: Everyone came running. It was chaos for a few minutes.

Q: But you didn't file a witness report.

A: I wasn't asked to.

Q: You need to be asked?

A: I mean... there were site managers everywhere. OSHA showed up that afternoon. I figured they had it handled.

Q: Did anyone interview you?

A: Not formally.

Q: Informally?

A: My foreman asked if I saw anything. I said I heard it happen and saw the aftermath. He said okay.

Q: That was the extent of it?

A: That was it.

Q: Do you wish you'd said more?

A: I wish someone had asked.

topic: A witness is questioned about a workplace injury they observed but did not report
text:
Q: You work in the meatpacking section?

A: Eleven months now.

Q: And you were trained on the industrial slicer?

A: Two-day training, yeah.

Q: Describe the incident with Ms. Okonkwo.

A: Linda was clearing a jam. She does it a certain way—everyone does, actually—where you reach in while the blade's cycling down instead of waiting for full stop.

Q: That's against protocol?

A: Technically, yes. But if you waited for full stop every time, you'd lose maybe six, seven minutes per jam. Management tracks our throughput.

Q: So everyone does it the unsafe way?

A: I'm just saying it's common.

Q: What happened when Ms. Okonkwo reached in?

A: The blade caught her glove. Pulled her hand in about two inches before she yanked it out.

Q: Was she cut?

A: Yeah. Three fingers, across the palm.

Q: Deep?

A: Deep enough that she was bleeding through her glove in about ten seconds.

Q: Did she receive medical attention?

A: She went to the bathroom to wash it out. Came back with paper towels wrapped around her hand.

Q: And she kept working?

A: We were behind quota.

Q: Did you say anything to her?

A: I asked if she needed the nurse. She said the nurse would write it up and she'd get flagged.

Q: Flagged?

A: Three write-ups and you're on probation. She already had two.

Q: For injuries?

A: For "safety incidents." That's what they call them.

Q: So you watched her work the rest of the shift with an open wound?

A: I gave her my backup glove. The thick one.

Q: But you didn't report it.

A: She asked me not to.

Q: And that was enough for you?

A: At the time? Yeah. At the time, I thought I was helping her.

topic: A witness is questioned about a conversation they overheard in a company hallway
text:
Q: Ms. Peralta, I'd like to direct your attention to the afternoon of March 14th. Were you present on the fourth floor of the Bridgewater building that day?

A: I was.

Q: And at approximately 3:30 p.m., where specifically were you located?

A: In the hallway. Near the water cooler.

Q: Did you overhear a conversation between two individuals at that time?

A: I heard people talking, yes.

Q: Who was speaking?

A: I'm not going to guess at identities I wasn't certain of.

Q: Ms. Peralta, I'm asking what you observed. Did you recognize the voices?

A: I recognized one voice. Maybe.

Q: Whose voice did you recognize?

A: It sounded like Mr. Hartwell. I said "maybe" for a reason.

Q: And the other speaker?

A: I don't know.

Q: You don't know, or you won't say?

A: I don't know. There's no difference. I didn't see the person's face and I'm not going to manufacture testimony for you.

Q: What did you hear Mr. Hartwell say?

A: Something about shipment dates. I wasn't standing there taking notes.

Q: Can you be more specific?

A: No. I can't. I've told you what I remember, and I remember it was about shipment dates. If you want me to invent details, I won't do that.

topic: A witness is questioned about a conversation they overheard in a company hallway
text:
Q: You were in the east corridor on the ninth floor on June 2nd, correct?

A: That's correct.

Q: And you testified earlier that you heard raised voices coming from near the conference room. Is that accurate?

A: Yes.

Q: Let's slow down here. I want to be very precise. You heard raised voices. Whose voices?

A: Linda Chen and a man.

Q: A man. You don't know which man?

A: I didn't say that. I said "a man."

Q: Then let me ask directly. Do you know which man?

A: It was David Okonkwo.

Q: How certain are you?

A: Completely certain.

Q: And you waited until I asked twice to provide his name. Why is that?

A: Because you asked imprecise questions. I answered what you asked.

Q: Fair enough. What were Ms. Chen and Mr. Okonkwo discussing?

A: The quarterly numbers. Linda was upset about something being excluded.

Q: Excluded from what?

A: From the report. She said, and I'm quoting, "You can't just bury this."

Q: What was "this"?

A: I don't know. I only heard fragments.

Q: But you heard enough to quote her verbatim.

A: I heard that sentence clearly. I didn't hear everything clearly. Those are two different things.

topic: A witness is questioned about a conversation they overheard in a company hallway
text:
Q: Mr. Byrne, you've worked at Crestfield for eleven years, haven't you?

A: Twelve in September.

Q: Twelve years. Long time. You know the players pretty well.

A: I know the people I work with.

Q: On October 10th, you were on the third floor near the supply room. Yes?

A: Yes.

Q: You overheard a conversation between two executives. Tell me what you heard.

A: I heard a conversation. I don't know that they were executives.

Q: You don't know who they were?

A: I didn't say that either. I said I don't know they were executives. One of them was Sandra Milstein. She's a senior manager, not an executive. Words matter in depositions, don't they, counselor?

Q: They do. Who was the other person?

A: Tom Reeves.

Q: What did you hear them say?

A: Sandra was concerned about the timeline for the product recall. Tom told her to stop putting things in writing.

Q: "Stop putting things in writing." Those were his exact words?

A: Yes.

Q: You're certain?

A: I just said yes. Would you like me to say it a third time?

Q: What did Ms. Milstein say in response?

A: She didn't say anything. She walked away.

topic: A witness is questioned about a conversation they overheard in a company hallway
text:
Q: I'm going to ask you about the conversation one more time.

A: You've asked me about it four times already.

Q: And I'll ask as many times as necessary to get a complete answer. Now. You were standing outside Mr. Tennant's office on February 8th.

A: I was walking past his office. I wasn't standing there eavesdropping, if that's what you're implying.

Q: I'm not implying anything. I'm establishing where you were. You walked past his office. The door was open?

A: Partially open.

Q: And you heard a conversation.

A: I heard voices. Briefly. As I walked past. Which is what happens when people are talking and you have functional hearing.

Q: Who was speaking?

A: Mr. Tennant and someone else.

Q: Someone else. Man or woman?

A: Woman.

Q: Did you recognize the woman's voice?

A: No.

Q: You didn't recognize it, or you didn't hear it well enough to identify it?

A: Both. It was a woman's voice. I didn't stop to analyze it.

Q: What did you hear Mr. Tennant say?

A: He said something about "handling" the situation before the board meeting.

Q: Before which board meeting?

A: I don't know. He just said "the board meeting." I wasn't given a calendar invite.

topic: A witness is questioned about a conversation they overheard in a company hallway
text:
Q: Ms. Yuen, let me take you back to what you heard on April 3rd.

A: Alright.

Q: You stated previously that you heard Mr. Caruso speaking with another individual in the hallway near the elevators.

A: I did state that, yes.

Q: I want to understand the substance of what was said. You indicated it related to personnel decisions.

A: I indicated it touched on personnel matters. "Decisions" is your word.

Q: Fine. Personnel matters. What specifically did you hear?

A: I heard Mr. Caruso say they needed to "clean house" before the audit.

Q: "Clean house." Meaning terminate employees?

A: I don't know what he meant. I know what he said.

Q: What's your interpretation of "clean house"?

A: My interpretation isn't testimony. You're asking me to speculate.

Q: I'm asking for your understanding based on context.

A: And I'm telling you I won't guess. He said "clean house." The other person laughed. That's what I heard.

Q: The other person laughed. Who was that?

A: I couldn't see them. They were around the corner.

Q: But you could hear them laugh.

A: Yes. Laughter carries. Faces don't.

topic: An employee is deposed about a coworker's termination they believe was retaliatory
text:
Q: Ms. Hartwell, you were present at the staff meeting on March 14th, correct?

A: I was in the room, yes.

Q: And during that meeting, did you observe any interaction between Mr. Reeves and the department head, Sandra Colton?

A: I observed them speaking, if that's what you're asking.

Q: What was the nature of that conversation?

A: The nature. Well, Marcus asked a question about the new overtime policy. Sandra answered it.

Q: Was there anything notable about how Ms. Colton responded?

A: Notable how?

Q: In her tone, her demeanor, anything that struck you as unusual?

A: She seemed irritated. But Sandra seemed irritated a lot of the time, so I'm not sure that qualifies as unusual.

Q: Did Mr. Reeves say anything else during that meeting?

A: He asked a follow-up question about whether the policy had been reviewed by legal.

Q: And what was Ms. Colton's response to that follow-up?

A: She said it had been handled and moved on.

Q: Did she answer his question?

A: I suppose that depends on your definition of answering a question.

Q: In your view, did she provide the information Mr. Reeves was asking for?

A: No. She did not.

Q: Was Mr. Reeves terminated within a week of this meeting?

A: Six days later, yes.

Q: And you're aware that the stated reason for his termination was performance-related?

A: I'm aware that's what the paperwork said.

---

topic: An employee is deposed about a coworker's termination they believe was retaliatory
text:
Q: You worked directly with James Reeves for how long?

A: About three years. A little over.

Q: And in that time, did you ever have concerns about his job performance?

A: Never.

Q: Never once in three years?

A: That's what I said.

Q: No missed deadlines, no errors in his work product?

A: Everyone makes minor mistakes. If you're asking whether James was a problem employee, the answer is no.

Q: I'm just trying to understand the basis for your assessment. You said never, and I want to make sure that's accurate.

A: It's accurate.

Q: Were you aware that Mr. Reeves had filed an internal complaint about safety violations two weeks before his termination?

A: I was aware of it, yes.

Q: How did you become aware?

A: He told me.

Q: Did he tell you the substance of the complaint?

A: He said he'd reported the ventilation issues in Building C to HR.

Q: And what happened after he filed that complaint?

A: What happened is he got fired.

Q: You're saying those two events are connected?

A: I'm saying one happened, and then the other happened. You can draw whatever conclusion you want from the timeline.

Q: I'm asking what you believe.

A: I believe James was a good employee who got terminated six days after reporting a safety violation. I believe that's worth looking at.

---

topic: An employee is deposed about a coworker's termination they believe was retaliatory
text:
Q: Let me direct your attention to the email chain marked as Exhibit 14. Do you recognize this document?

A: Yes.

Q: And you're copied on this email, correct?

A: I am.

Q: In this email, Ms. Colton writes that Mr. Reeves has been, quote, "consistently underperforming relative to team standards." Did you agree with that assessment at the time?

A: At the time.

Q: Yes. When you received this email.

A: I don't recall having a strong opinion about it when I received it.

Q: Do you have an opinion about it now?

A: I think the word "consistently" is doing a lot of work in that sentence.

Q: What do you mean by that?

A: I mean I don't know what she was basing that on. I worked with James daily. I didn't see consistent underperformance.

Q: Is it possible there were aspects of his performance you weren't privy to?

A: Anything's possible.

Q: So you can't say definitively that Ms. Colton's assessment was wrong?

A: I can say definitively that I never saw what she's describing. Whether that makes her wrong or me blind, I suppose that's the question.

Q: Did you ever raise concerns about Mr. Reeves' termination with HR?

A: I did.

Q: And what response did you receive?

A: I was told the decision had been made at the appropriate level and that my feedback was noted.

Q: Noted.

A: That was the word they used, yes.

---

topic: An employee is deposed about a coworker's termination they believe was retaliatory
text:
Q: Mr. Okonkwo, how would you describe your relationship with James Reeves?

A: We were coworkers. Friendly. We got lunch sometimes.

Q: Would you say you were close?

A: I'd say we were work friends. I don't know if that counts as close.

Q: Fair enough. Were you surprised when Mr. Reeves was terminated?

A: Very.

Q: Why is that?

A: Because it didn't make sense. He'd just gotten a positive quarterly review. I saw it on his desk.

Q: You saw his performance review?

A: He showed it to me. He was happy about it.

Q: When was this?

A: Maybe three weeks before they let him go.

Q: So you're telling me that three weeks before his termination for performance issues, he received a positive review?

A: That's exactly what I'm telling you.

Q: Do you know who conducted that review?

A: His direct supervisor. Tom Henley.

Q: And Mr. Henley gave him a positive evaluation?

A: Yes.

Q: But it was Ms. Colton who made the termination decision, correct?

A: That's my understanding.

Q: Did Ms. Colton supervise Mr. Reeves directly?

A: No. She was two levels up.

Q: Do you have any knowledge of why she would have overridden Mr. Henley's assessment?

A: I have a theory.

Q: I'm not asking for theories. I'm asking what you know.

A: Then no. I don't know why. I just know that it happened.

---

topic: An employee is deposed about a coworker's termination they believe was retaliatory
text:
Q: You mentioned earlier that there was a shift in how Mr. Reeves was treated after he raised concerns about the project timeline. Can you describe that shift?

A: It was subtle at first. He stopped getting invited to certain meetings.

Q: Which meetings?

A: The planning sessions for the Henderson rollout. He'd been on all of them, and then suddenly he wasn't.

Q: Did anyone explain why?

A: Not to him. Not that he told me, anyway.

Q: Did you ask anyone about it?

A: I asked Tom Henley. He said it was a scheduling thing.

Q: Did you believe that?

A: I didn't have a reason not to at the time.

Q: And now?

A: Now I think there was more to it.

Q: Let's be precise here. Are you saying you have evidence of something, or are you speculating based on how things unfolded?

A: I'm saying I watched a pattern develop. I'm saying James raised a concern about an unrealistic deadline, and two weeks later he was being frozen out of meetings, and a month after that he was gone. I'm saying I sat in that office for four years and I never saw anything like that happen to anyone who kept their head down.

Q: That's not quite an answer to my question.

A: I think it is. I think you just don't like the shape of it.

Q: Let's move on. Were you interviewed by HR during their internal review of Mr. Reeves' termination?

A: I was.

Q: And did you share these observations with them?

A: I shared what I could. They didn't ask many follow-up questions.

Q: What do you mean by that?

A: I mean the interview lasted about twelve minutes, and most of the questions were yes or no.

topic: A driver is deposed about the events leading up to a multi-vehicle collision
text:
Q: Mr. Harmon, I'd like to take you back to the morning of October 14th. What time did you leave your residence?

A: It was right around 7:15. I remember because I checked my watch before I walked out the door.

Q: And what was your destination that morning?

A: I was heading to my office on Crane Street, downtown. Same route I take most days.

Q: Can you describe the weather conditions as you drove?

A: It had rained earlier, maybe stopped about an hour before I left. The roads were still wet in spots, some puddles here and there, but visibility was fine. Overcast, but no fog or anything like that.

Q: How would you describe traffic that morning?

A: Moderate. Normal for that time of day. Nothing unusual.

Q: As you approached the intersection of Crane and Fifth, what lane were you traveling in?

A: The center lane. I'd moved over about two blocks earlier because I knew I'd need to turn left eventually.

Q: And what was your approximate speed as you approached that intersection?

A: I'd estimate around thirty, maybe thirty-two miles per hour. The limit there is thirty-five.

Q: What's the first thing you observed that seemed out of the ordinary?

A: The pickup truck ahead of me—two cars ahead, actually—its brake lights came on hard. Very sudden.

Q: What did you do when you saw those brake lights?

A: I applied my brakes and checked my mirrors to see what was behind me.

Q: Did you have time to come to a complete stop?

A: I did, yes. I stopped with maybe eight or ten feet between me and the car directly ahead. That part I'm certain about.

Q: What happened next?

A: About two seconds later, I felt the impact from behind.

---

topic: A driver is deposed about the events leading up to a multi-vehicle collision
text:
Q: Ms. Vaughn, I want to ask you about your familiarity with that stretch of Highway 9. How often would you say you drive that road?

A: Oh, probably four or five times a week. It's my main route to my daughter's school.

Q: So you're quite familiar with the curves and the grade changes along that section?

A: Yes, I'd say so.

Q: On the day of the accident, did you notice anything different about the road conditions?

A: There was some loose gravel on the shoulder near mile marker 12. I remember noticing that.

Q: Did that gravel affect your driving in any way?

A: No, I stayed in my lane. I just made a mental note of it.

Q: Let's talk about the vehicle that you first noticed in your rearview mirror. When did you become aware of it?

A: Maybe a mile before the accident site. It was a white SUV, moving faster than the rest of traffic.

Q: When you say faster, can you give me an estimate?

A: I was doing about fifty-five, which is the limit there. The SUV was gaining on everyone, so I'd guess maybe sixty-five, seventy. It's hard to say exactly.

Q: Did you observe the SUV change lanes?

A: Several times. It was weaving, trying to get ahead.

Q: How did you react to that?

A: I kept my speed steady and stayed aware of where it was. I didn't want to make any sudden moves with a driver like that nearby.

Q: At any point did the SUV come into your lane?

A: Yes, it cut in front of me right before the curve near marker 14. I had to ease off the gas to give it room.

Q: And then what did you observe?

A: The SUV's rear end started to slide. Then it overcorrected and went across the center line.

---

topic: A driver is deposed about the events leading up to a multi-vehicle collision
text:
Q: Mr. Desmond, had you consumed any alcohol in the twelve hours before the collision?

A: No.

Q: Any medications, prescription or otherwise?

A: I take a blood pressure pill in the mornings. I'd taken it that day, same as always.

Q: Does that medication cause drowsiness or affect your ability to drive?

A: No, I've been on it for six years. Never had any issue.

Q: Let me ask you about the moments just before impact. You've testified you were in the right lane. Correct?

A: Correct.

Q: And the sedan that struck you came from which direction?

A: From my left. It crossed over from the center lane into mine.

Q: Did you see it coming?

A: Not until the last second. Maybe half a second before contact.

Q: Was there anything obstructing your view to the left?

A: A delivery truck was in the center lane, slightly ahead of me. It blocked my sightline.

Q: So your first awareness of the sedan was when it emerged from behind that truck?

A: That's right.

Q: Did you have time to take any evasive action?

A: I turned the wheel to the right and tried to accelerate out of the way. There just wasn't enough time.

Q: Your vehicle then struck the guardrail, is that correct?

A: Yes. The sedan hit my rear quarter panel, which pushed me into the rail.

Q: Were you injured in that impact?

A: Bruised ribs, some whiplash. I was wearing my seatbelt.

---

topic: A driver is deposed about the events leading up to a multi-vehicle collision
text:
Q: I'd like you to think carefully before answering this next question, Mr. Okonkwo. Take your time.

A: All right.

Q: At any point before the collision, did you use your cell phone?

A: No.

Q: You're certain of that?

A: I'm certain. My phone was in my bag on the back seat. I don't use it while driving.

Q: The reason I ask is that records indicate a text message was sent from your phone at 8:47 a.m. The collision occurred at approximately 8:49 a.m. Can you explain that?

A: I can. I sent that message before I started the car. I was still in my driveway.

Q: You're saying you sent the message, then placed the phone in your bag, and then began driving?

A: That's exactly what happened, yes.

Q: How long was your drive from your driveway to the location of the collision?

A: Usually about twelve to fifteen minutes, depending on lights.

Q: So if you left shortly after 8:47, arriving at the scene at 8:49 would be inconsistent with your typical drive time?

A: I left at 8:32. I remember because I was running a few minutes behind. The text at 8:47 must have been delayed in sending—that happens sometimes when service is spotty at my house.

Q: I see. Let's move on. You mentioned you were running behind. Were you driving faster than usual?

A: No. Being a few minutes late to a staff meeting isn't worth risking an accident.

Q: Fair enough. Let's talk about what you observed at the intersection.

A: Of course.

---

topic: A driver is deposed about the events leading up to a multi-vehicle collision
text:
Q: Ms. Tran, you've stated that the light was green when you entered the intersection.

A: Yes, it was green.

Q: How long had it been green, to your estimation?

A: I couldn't say exactly. I was approaching and it was already green. I didn't see it change.

Q: Did you consider that it might be about to turn yellow?

A: I suppose that's always a possibility, but it was green, so I proceeded.

Q: At what speed?

A: About thirty miles per hour.

Q: And the vehicle that struck you—where did it come from?

A: It came through the intersection from my right. From Ashford Avenue.

Q: That would mean that vehicle had a red light, if yours was green?

A: That's correct.

Q: Did you see that vehicle before it entered the intersection?

A: No. There's a building on that corner, a dry cleaner, and it blocks the view until you're in the intersection itself.

Q: So your first sight of the other vehicle was when it was already crossing into your path?

A: Yes. I saw a flash of dark color and then the impact happened.

Q: Did you brake or swerve?

A: I don't remember consciously doing either. It happened very fast. My body may have reacted but I couldn't tell you specifically what I did.

Q: That's understandable. After the collision, were you able to exit your vehicle on your own?

A: Yes, after a minute or two. I was shaken, and my door was jammed, so I climbed out the passenger side.

Q: Did you speak with the other driver at the scene?

A: Briefly. He asked if I was okay. I said I thought so. Then the paramedics arrived.

topic: A witness is questioned about a workplace injury they observed but did not report
text:
Q: Mr. Delgado, you were working on the loading dock the morning of September 14th, correct?

A: That's right. I was there from about six until we broke for lunch.

Q: And at some point that morning, you observed an incident involving Marcus Webb?

A: I did. I saw the whole thing happen, actually. I was maybe fifteen feet away, sorting pallets, and I had a clear line of sight to where Marcus was working.

Q: Tell me what you saw.

A: Marcus was pulling a pallet jack—one of the manual ones—and the wheel caught on something. A crack in the concrete, I think. The handle swung around fast and caught him right in the ribs. He went down hard.

Q: What did Mr. Webb do after he fell?

A: He stayed down for a minute, maybe two. Then he got up slow, holding his side. I could tell he was hurting. He walked it off for a bit, then went back to work.

Q: Did you approach him?

A: I did. I walked over and asked if he was okay. He said he was fine, just got the wind knocked out of him. Told me not to make a big deal out of it.

Q: And you honored that request.

A: I did. Marcus has been there longer than me. If he said he was fine, I figured he knew his own body.

Q: You didn't report the incident to a supervisor?

A: No. And I want to be clear about why—it wasn't because I didn't care. It was because Marcus specifically asked me not to. He said he didn't want the paperwork, didn't want to deal with it. I respected his wishes.

Q: Did anyone else witness this incident?

A: Terry Okonkwo was on the dock too, but I don't know if he saw it happen. He might have. You'd have to ask him.

Q: Thank you, Mr. Delgado. That's very helpful.

A: Of course. I want to make sure you have the full picture. Marcus is a good guy, and I want to help however I can.

topic: A witness is questioned about a workplace injury they observed but did not report
text:
Q: Ms. Patterson, how long have you worked in the fabrication department?

A: Seven years this coming March.

Q: So you know the safety protocols well.

A: Inside and out.

Q: On January 8th, you were present when Jessica Hartman injured her hand?

A: I was.

Q: Walk me through it.

A: Jess was operating the punch press. Standard job, something she'd done hundreds of times. But her sleeve got caught—just barely—and her hand went toward the die. She pulled back fast enough to avoid the worst of it, but she still got a pretty deep gash across her palm.

Q: What happened immediately after?

A: She wrapped it in a shop rag and went to the bathroom to clean it up.

Q: Did she return to work?

A: She did. About ten minutes later. She had it bandaged up.

Q: Did you ask her about it?

A: I did. She said it looked worse than it was. Said she'd take care of it at home.

Q: And you accepted that.

A: I did.

Q: Despite the fact that safety protocols require immediate reporting of any injury involving blood?

A: Yes.

Q: You're aware that's a violation.

A: I'm aware now that you've pointed it out so clearly, counselor.

Q: I'm simply establishing the facts.

A: No, you're establishing that I should have done something differently. That's fine. I understand that's your job. But at the time, Jess was a grown woman who told me she was handling it herself. I wasn't going to override her on that.

Q: Fair enough. Did you discuss this incident with anyone else that day?

A: No. It didn't seem like a discussion kind of thing. It seemed like something that happened and was over.

topic: A witness is questioned about a workplace injury they observed but did not report
text:
Q: Mr. Chen, you've testified that you were in the warehouse when Mr. Okafor fell from the ladder.

A: Yes.

Q: How far away were you?

A: Twenty feet, maybe. Close enough.

Q: Close enough for what?

A: Close enough to see what happened.

Q: Describe it for me.

A: He was up on one of the rolling ladders, reaching for something on the top shelf. The ladder shifted—it wasn't locked properly—and he lost his balance. He fell about eight feet and landed on his back.

Q: Did he get up immediately?

A: No. He laid there for probably thirty seconds. Then he got up slowly.

Q: Did he appear to be in pain?

A: He was moving stiff. I assumed he was sore.

Q: Did you go to him?

A: I started to, but he waved me off. Said he was embarrassed more than hurt.

Q: Embarrassed.

A: That's what he said.

Q: And you didn't think a fall from eight feet warranted medical attention?

A: Counselor, I'm not a doctor. The man told me he was fine.

Q: So you took him at his word.

A: I did. And let me add something—in twenty-two years at that warehouse, I've seen dozens of falls. Most of them, people dust themselves off and get back to work. That's the culture. I'm not saying it's right, but that's how it was. When Kofi said he was fine, I had no reason to doubt him.

Q: That's exactly what I was hoping you'd tell me.

A: Well, good. Then we're on the same page.

topic: A witness is questioned about a workplace injury they observed but did not report
text:
Q: Ms. Bright, let me be direct with you. You saw Angela Torres get hurt, you didn't report it, and I need to understand why.

A: I appreciate the directness.

Q: Good. Then we'll get along fine. What exactly did you see?

A: Angie was cleaning one of the fryers—this was after the lunch rush—and she reached in before it had cooled enough. Burned her forearm pretty bad.

Q: Define "pretty bad."

A: Red, blistering within a few minutes. Maybe four inches of burned skin.

Q: That sounds serious.

A: It looked serious.

Q: Yet no report was filed.

A: Correct.

Q: Why not?

A: Because Angie asked me not to.

Q: She asked you not to.

A: That's what I said.

Q: Did she explain why?

A: She said she'd already had two incidents on her record and was worried about getting written up again. She said she'd treat it at home.

Q: And you went along with this.

A: I did. Angie was my friend. She was scared for her job. I made a judgment call.

Q: A judgment call that violated company policy.

A: Yes.

Q: Do you regret it?

A: Do you want me to?

Q: I want you to answer honestly.

A: Then honestly? I regret that Angie got hurt. I regret that she felt she couldn't report it without fearing for her job. Do I regret not ratting her out? No. I'd do the same thing again.

Q: That's quite an answer.

A: It's the truth.

topic: A witness is questioned about a workplace injury they observed but did not report
text:
Q: Mr. Holloway, you were on the night shift on March 3rd?

A: I was.

Q: And you observed what happened to Daniel Reeves?

A: Observed might be too strong. I saw the aftermath.

Q: Explain the distinction.

A: I didn't see the moment of injury. I came around the corner and Danny was already on the ground, holding his ankle. The forklift was stopped a few feet away.

Q: What did you do?

A: I asked him what happened. He said he'd stepped wrong getting off the forklift and twisted his ankle bad.

Q: His words? "Twisted it bad"?

A: His exact words were stronger than that, but yes, that was the gist.

Q: Could he walk?

A: Barely. He was limping heavily.

Q: Did he seek medical attention?

A: Not that night.

Q: Not that night. Meaning he did later?

A: I don't know what he did later. I only know what happened on my shift.

Q: Fair enough. You didn't report this to a supervisor.

A: No.

Q: Help me understand why.

A: There wasn't much to report. A guy stepped wrong and twisted his ankle. It happens.

Q: Except now Mr. Reeves is claiming a more significant injury.

A: That's what I've been told.

Q: Does that change your recollection of what you saw?

A: My recollection is exactly what I described. Danny was hurt, he said it was an ankle twist, and that's what I believed at the time.

Q: That's all I needed to hear, Mr. Holloway.

A: Then I'm glad I could help clarify things.

Q: You've been very helpful.

A: Just telling you what I saw.

topic: A tenant is questioned about property damage they reported to their landlord
text:
Q: Mr. Hernandez, when did you first notice the water stain on the ceiling?

A: March 14th.

Q: And what did you do when you noticed it?

A: I reported it.

Q: To whom?

A: The landlord. Who else would I report it to?

Q: I'm asking the questions here, Mr. Hernandez. How did you report it?

A: Email.

Q: Do you have a copy of that email?

A: I assume my attorney provided it. It's in the records.

Q: I'm asking if you personally have a copy.

A: Somewhere, yes.

Q: Did you take photographs of the water stain on March 14th?

A: Yes.

Q: How many photographs?

A: I don't know. Several.

Q: Several meaning two? Ten? Twenty?

A: I didn't count them. Maybe four or five. I was documenting damage, not conducting a photography session.

topic: A tenant is questioned about property damage they reported to their landlord
text:
Q: Ms. Patterson, let's talk about the broken window in the second bedroom. When did you first discover it was broken?

A: It was the morning of January 8th. I remember because I had just gotten back from visiting my sister in Delaware for the holidays, and I walked into the bedroom to put my suitcase away, and there it was—this huge crack running diagonally across the entire pane. I couldn't believe it. The room was freezing.

Q: Did you touch the window?

A: No, I didn't touch it. I didn't want to make it worse or cut myself. I'm not— I know better than to handle broken glass.

Q: I wasn't suggesting otherwise. What did you do next?

A: Well, I took pictures first, obviously. Then I went through my lease to find the emergency maintenance number because I wasn't sure if this counted as an emergency, but it was January and there was cold air just pouring in, so I thought it probably qualified.

Q: Did you call the emergency number?

A: I did, yes. I called, and I got a recording, and I left a message explaining the whole situation, and then I also sent an email to Mr. Donnelly because I wanted everything in writing. I've learned that lesson before with landlords, no offense.

Q: What time did you make that call?

A: Around nine in the morning. Maybe nine-fifteen. I hadn't even had coffee yet.

Q: Did anyone return your call?

A: Not that day, no. I got a call back on January 10th, which—well, I had already bought plastic sheeting by then to cover it myself.

topic: A tenant is questioned about property damage they reported to their landlord
text:
Q: The incident report says you found mold in the bathroom. Is that accurate?

A: It says I "found" mold, but that makes it sound like I went looking for it. It was growing visibly on the wall. Anyone would have seen it.

Q: Fine. You observed mold growing on the bathroom wall.

A: Yes.

Q: When?

A: Late September.

Q: Can you be more specific?

A: The 26th. Or the 27th. One of those two days.

Q: Which one?

A: I don't remember exactly. It was one or the other.

Q: You're not sure?

A: I said the 26th or 27th. I'm sure it was one of those days. I'm not sure which. There's a difference.

Q: Let's move on. What color was the mold?

A: Excuse me?

Q: The color. Was it black? Green? White?

A: It was dark. Blackish-green. Why does the color matter?

Q: I'll ask the questions, Ms. Thornton. Did you attempt to clean the mold yourself?

A: No. I know you're not supposed to disturb black mold. I'm not an idiot.

topic: A tenant is questioned about property damage they reported to their landlord
text:
Q: Mr. Okafor, I want to make sure I understand the timeline here. You're saying the heat stopped working on November 2nd?

A: Correct.

Q: And you reported it that same day?

A: That same evening, yes.

Q: Walk me through that evening for me.

A: I got home from work around six. The apartment was cold. I checked the thermostat, turned it up, nothing happened. Waited about twenty minutes. Still nothing. So I called the property management office.

Q: What happened when you called?

A: I got voicemail. Office was closed.

Q: Did you leave a message?

A: Yes.

Q: And then?

A: And then I put on a sweater and went to bed cold.

Q: Did you try anything else that night to address the heating issue?

A: Like what? Build a fire in the living room?

Q: I'm simply asking—

A: I checked the pilot light. It was on. I checked the vents to make sure they weren't blocked. They weren't. There wasn't anything else for me to do.

Q: Did you contact anyone else that night besides the property management office?

A: No.

Q: No text to the building superintendent?

A: We don't have a building superintendent. It's property management or nothing.

Q: I see. When did you hear back from property management?

A: November 5th.

Q: Three days later.

A: Yes. Three days later. As I've already explained in my written complaint.

topic: A tenant is questioned about property damage they reported to their landlord
text:
Q: Let's discuss the garage door. You submitted a maintenance request about it, correct?

A: I did.

Q: Tell me about the problem with the garage door.

A: The spring broke. It wouldn't open.

Q: It wouldn't open at all?

A: Well, it would open if you lifted it manually, but the automatic opener didn't work. The spring mechanism was broken.

Q: So to be clear, the door could be opened, just not automatically?

A: Technically, yes, but—

Q: Okay. Did you try to open it manually?

A: Once. It was extremely heavy. That's the whole point of the spring—it counterbalances the weight.

Q: But it was functional.

A: Are we really going to argue about what "functional" means?

Q: I'm trying to establish the facts, Ms. Chen.

A: The fact is that a 150-pound garage door with a broken spring is a safety hazard. It could have come down on my car. On me. On my daughter.

Q: Did it come down on anyone?

A: No.

Q: Did it damage your car?

A: No, because I stopped using the garage. I parked on the street for three weeks.

Q: You chose to park on the street.

A: I chose not to risk a garage door falling on my head, yes. That was my choice.

Q: When was the spring ultimately repaired?

A: December 3rd. Twenty-two days after I reported it. Not that anyone was counting.

topic: A supervisor is deposed about performance reviews given to an employee who was later fired
text:
Q: Mr. Harmon, you conducted the 2022 annual review for Jessica Traylor, correct?

A: Yes.

Q: And you gave her an overall rating of "meets expectations"?

A: That's what the form says, yes.

Q: I'm asking if that's the rating you gave her.

A: Yes. I gave her that rating.

Q: Had you ever given her a lower rating in previous years?

A: I'd have to look at the documents to be sure. I don't want to misstate anything.

Q: You reviewed her for three consecutive years, didn't you?

A: If that's what the records show.

Q: Mr. Harmon, I'm asking what you remember.

A: I remember reviewing her. I don't remember the exact number of years without looking at the paperwork. I'm trying to be accurate here.

Q: Fair enough. In any of those reviews, did you document concerns about her attendance?

A: I may have. I'd need to see the specific documents.

Q: You don't recall whether attendance was ever an issue?

A: I recall some discussions. I don't recall exactly what was written down versus what was just discussed verbally. There's a difference.

Q: What do you recall discussing verbally?

A: I— look, there were a lot of employees. I had twelve direct reports at that time. I'm not trying to be difficult, but I want to make sure I'm giving you accurate information.

Q: I understand. Let me show you what's been marked as Exhibit 14.

A: Okay. Thank you.

---

topic: A supervisor is deposed about performance reviews given to an employee who was later fired
text:
Q: Who made the final decision to terminate Mr. Okonkwo?

A: That was a joint decision involving HR and senior leadership.

Q: Were you part of that decision?

A: I provided input.

Q: That's not what I asked. Were you part of the decision?

A: I was consulted.

Q: Ms. Vance, yes or no—did you participate in the decision to fire Mr. Okonkwo?

A: I don't know what you mean by "participate." I didn't have the authority to fire anyone unilaterally. I gave my assessment when asked.

Q: And what was your assessment?

A: That his performance had declined significantly over the previous two quarters.

Q: But his written reviews don't reflect that, do they?

A: The written reviews reflect a point in time. Things changed.

Q: Things changed. When exactly did things change?

A: I don't have specific dates memorized.

Q: Approximately.

A: After the Q2 review, maybe. Around August. Can I ask—are you going to show me the documents, or are we just going to keep doing this?

Q: I'll show you whatever documents are relevant, Ms. Vance. Right now I'm asking about your memory.

A: My memory is that his performance declined. That's what I remember.

Q: And you never documented this decline in writing before his termination?

Q: Did you inform Martin Delacroix about the crew situation?

A: I told him we had a scheduling conflict. I didn't... I didn't want to worry him. He had a lot going on with his father's health.

Q: So you did not disclose that your framing crew had walked off the job?

A: No.

Q: Why not?

topic: A contractor is questioned about delays that caused a construction project to fail

Q: Ms. Chen, I want to understand the timeline of the HVAC installation. Your company was subcontracted for that work, correct?

Q: I'm asking about the HVAC installation timeline.

A: And I'm telling you we did everything we could. We worked nights. Weekends. My guys missed Thanksgiving with their families trying to make up for lost time. We all wanted to get that house finished.

A: No. We didn't.

topic: A contractor is questioned about delays that caused a construction project to fail

topic: A witness is questioned about events at a party where an assault allegedly occurred

A: I'm telling you what I observed and what I didn't observe. I didn't observe any interaction between them.

topic: A witness is questioned about events at a party where an assault allegedly occurred
