topic: A paramedic is questioned about the response time and treatment at an accident scene
text:
Q: Let's talk about what time you arrived at the scene. What time was that?

A: I already provided that information to investigators. It's in the run report.

Q: I'm asking you now, under oath. What time did you arrive?

A: 14:47.

Q: And what time was the call dispatched?

A: 14:31.

Q: So sixteen minutes from dispatch to arrival. Is that correct?

A: If that's the math you want to do, sure.

Q: I'm asking if it's accurate, not if it's the math I want to do.

A: It's accurate that those are the two times. Whether that constitutes "response time" as you seem to be implying depends on how you define it, which I'm sure you'll tell me.

Q: What's the average response time for your unit?

A: There is no single "average." It depends on traffic, location, weather, whether we're returning from another call—

Q: Ballpark, Mr. Hendricks.

A: Eight to twelve minutes under normal conditions.

Q: And this was sixteen. Were conditions abnormal that day?

A: We were returning from a transfer at St. Joseph's, which added to our route. That's documented.

Q: But you were the closest available unit?

A: I don't make those decisions. Dispatch does.

Q: You didn't answer my question.

A: I answered what I can answer. Ask dispatch what I was or wasn't.

topic: A paramedic is questioned about the response time and treatment at an accident scene
text:
Q: When you arrived at the scene, where was the patient located?

A: She was still in the driver's seat of the vehicle, partially pinned.

Q: Partially pinned. Can you describe that?

A: The dashboard had compressed into her lower extremities. Her legs were trapped below the knee.

Q: And what did you do first?

A: I conducted a primary assessment while my partner retrieved the extrication equipment and coordinated with fire.

Q: You didn't wait for fire to arrive before beginning treatment?

A: No. She was conscious and in respiratory distress. I wasn't going to stand there with my hands in my pockets.

Q: I didn't suggest you should have. I asked a simple question.

A: And I gave you a simple answer. With context.

Q: Did you administer any medication at that point?

A: I established an IV line and administered morphine for pain management per protocol.

Q: Before she was extricated?

A: Yes.

Q: Is that standard?

A: It's within protocol when a patient is experiencing severe pain and is hemodynamically stable enough to tolerate it. Which she was. At that time.

Q: At that time. What changed?

A: Her pressure dropped during extrication. Which happens. Which is why we monitor continuously.

Q: Did the morphine contribute to that drop?

A: I'm not going to speculate about hypotheticals for your benefit, counselor.

Q: I'm asking for your medical opinion.

A: My medical opinion is that crush syndrome contributed to her decline. Not the pain management that kept her from going into shock from agony.

topic: A paramedic is questioned about the response time and treatment at an accident scene
text:
Q: You've been a paramedic for how long?

A: Eleven years.

Q: And in those eleven years, you've responded to how many motor vehicle accidents, approximately?

A: I don't keep a tally. Hundreds.

Q: Hundreds. So you'd consider yourself experienced in this type of emergency?

A: I would.

Q: Good. Then you should be able to answer this clearly. Why did you wait four minutes to begin CPR?

A: I didn't wait four minutes.

Q: The fire captain's report indicates CPR was initiated at 9:47. Your arrival was logged at 9:43.

A: Arrival at the scene isn't the same as arrival at the patient.

Q: Explain.

A: The vehicle was down an embankment. It took time to reach it safely with equipment. I wasn't going to tumble down a ravine and become a second patient.

Q: So you're saying you reached the patient at what time?

A: Approximately 9:45, 9:46.

Q: Approximately.

A: I wasn't looking at my watch while climbing down a muddy slope with a jump bag, counselor. My apologies for not documenting my every footstep.

Q: And when you reached the patient, what was his condition?

A: Unresponsive, no pulse, no spontaneous respiration.

Q: Yet you waited another minute or two to begin CPR?

A: I assessed. That's what you do. You don't just start compressions on someone who might have a pulse you missed.

Q: Did he have a pulse you missed?

A: No. Which is why I started CPR.

topic: A paramedic is questioned about the response time and treatment at an accident scene
text:
Q: Walk me through the treatment you provided, step by step.

A: We've been through this.

Q: We're going through it again.

A: Fine. Arrived on scene. Patient was supine on the roadway, bystander was applying pressure to a laceration on the left thigh. I took over direct pressure and assessed the wound while my partner checked vitals.

Q: What were the vitals?

A: Pulse 120, BP 90 over 60, respiration 24.

Q: Indicating?

A: Early hypovolemic shock.

Q: What did you do about it?

A: Applied a tourniquet above the wound, established large-bore IV access, started a fluid bolus.

Q: A single tourniquet?

A: Initially, yes.

Q: Did that control the bleeding?

A: It reduced it significantly.

Q: But didn't stop it.

A: Tourniquets don't always achieve complete occlusion on the first application.

Q: So what did you do?

A: Applied a second tourniquet proximal to the first.

Q: How much time elapsed between the first and second tourniquet?

A: I don't have an exact number.

Q: Estimate.

A: A minute. Maybe two.

Q: A minute or two where the patient continued to bleed.

A: A minute or two where I was managing multiple interventions simultaneously, counselor, not standing around enjoying the scenery.

topic: A paramedic is questioned about the response time and treatment at an accident scene
text:
Q: I want to ask about your documentation.

A: Go ahead.

Q: Your run report indicates you administered epinephrine at 11:23. Is that accurate?

A: If that's what the report says, that's what happened.

Q: You don't have an independent recollection?

A: I respond to three, four, five calls a shift. This was two years ago. I remember the call. I don't remember the exact minute I pushed every drug.

Q: So you rely on the documentation.

A: That's what documentation is for.

Q: The hospital's intake records show the patient arrived at 11:41 with no epinephrine noted in her system.

A: Then the hospital's records are incomplete, or the epi had metabolized, or their tox screen wasn't looking for it.

Q: Or you didn't administer it.

A: I administered it.

Q: You're certain, despite just telling me you have no independent recollection of the exact time.

A: I remember giving epi. I don't remember whether it was 11:23 or 11:24. There's a difference.

Q: Is there?

A: Don't do that.

Q: Do what?

A: Play games with me. I've been doing this job for a long time. I know what I did that day, and I documented what I did, accurately, the way I always do.

Q: Then you can explain the discrepancy.

A: I just did. You don't like the explanation. That's not my problem.

topic: A paramedic is questioned about the response time and treatment at an accident scene
text:
Q: Please state your name and occupation for the record.

A: Michael Torres, paramedic with County Fire and Rescue, twelve years now.

Q: Mr. Torres, I'd like to walk through the events of September 14th. What time did your unit receive the dispatch call?

A: 2:47 PM. I remember because I'd just checked my watch after finishing lunch.

Q: And what time did you arrive at the scene?

A: 2:54 PM. Seven minutes from dispatch to arrival.

Q: Seven minutes. Is that consistent with your typical response times in that area?

A: Actually, it's better than typical. That stretch of Route 9 usually runs eight to ten minutes depending on traffic. We caught a break with the lights.

Q: When you arrived, can you describe what you observed?

A: Two-vehicle collision, sedan and pickup truck. The sedan had significant front-end damage, driver still seated, conscious but disoriented. The pickup driver was already out of his vehicle, appeared ambulatory with minor lacerations.

Q: Walk me through your initial assessment of the sedan driver.

A: Absolutely. I approached the driver's side, identified myself, began verbal assessment. Patient was responsive but confused about the date—knew his name, didn't know what day it was. Pupils were reactive but sluggish on the left side. I suspected a concussion at minimum, possible more serious head trauma.

Q: What treatment did you administer on scene?

A: Cervical collar first, standard protocol for any head trauma with unknown spinal involvement. Established an IV line, administered a saline drip. Monitored vitals continuously—BP was elevated at 150 over 95, heart rate 88. We had him stabilized and loaded within eleven minutes of arrival.

Q: Eleven minutes. Is that within your standard protocols?

A: Well within. Our target for a trauma load-and-go is under fifteen. We were efficient that day, and I'm proud of how my partner and I worked together on that call.

Q: Thank you, Mr. Torres. No further questions at this time.

A: Happy to help.

---

topic: A paramedic is questioned about the response time and treatment at an accident scene
text:
Q: Paramedic Jensen, how long have you been certified in advanced cardiac life support?

A: Going on eight years.

Q: On the morning of March 3rd, what was your initial assessment of Mrs. Patterson's condition when you arrived?

A: She was unresponsive, not breathing, no pulse detected. Her husband was attempting CPR when we got there.

Q: What time did you arrive on scene?

A: 6:23 AM.

Q: And dispatch was at what time?

A: 6:17.

Q: Six minutes. Now, the defendant's expert has suggested that a four-minute response time could have altered the outcome. What's your response to that?

A: I'd need to see the basis for that opinion, but I can tell you that six minutes is an excellent response time for that neighborhood. We're talking about a residential area three miles from the station, early morning, and we still beat the national average by a wide margin.

Q: Let's discuss the treatment you provided. You initiated ACLS protocols?

A: Immediately. My partner took over compressions while I prepared the defibrillator. First shock was delivered at 6:25. We continued cycles of CPR and defibrillation, administered epinephrine at the three-minute mark, then again at the six-minute mark.

Q: How long did you continue resuscitation efforts?

A: Twenty-two minutes on scene before we transported. We worked that code hard—never stopped, never gave up on her.

Q: The hospital records indicate Mrs. Patterson was pronounced at 7:14 AM. Looking back, is there anything you would have done differently?

A: Counsel, I've gone over that call a hundred times. We did everything right. Sometimes the outcome isn't what we want, but that's not because we failed her.

Q: I appreciate your candor. That's all I have.

A: Thank you.

topic: A paramedic is questioned about the response time and treatment at an accident scene
text:
Q: You mentioned earlier that traffic was a factor in your response time. Can you elaborate on that?

A: I can try, but I want to be precise. Traffic wasn't a factor in our response time. Traffic was present, but we navigated it effectively.

Q: So you're saying traffic did not delay your arrival?

A: Correct. We used sirens and lights, vehicles yielded appropriately, and we maintained a steady pace. Arrival was within normal parameters.

Q: Within normal parameters. What exactly does that mean?

A: For that district, a response time of nine minutes or under is considered optimal. We arrived in eight minutes, forty seconds.

Q: I see. Now, when you reached Mr. Okonkwo, he was pinned in the vehicle, correct?

A: His left leg was trapped beneath the dashboard. Upper body was accessible.

Q: Did that complicate your treatment?

A: It required coordination with fire rescue for extrication, but it didn't prevent us from providing care. I was able to assess his condition, establish IV access, and manage his pain while the extraction team worked.

Q: How long did extraction take?

A: Fourteen minutes from our arrival to having him free and on the stretcher.

Q: And during those fourteen minutes, what was Mr. Okonkwo's condition?

A: Stable. He was conscious, oriented, in significant pain from what turned out to be a compound fracture of the left tibia, but his vitals remained steady throughout. We kept him calm, kept him informed, and kept him stable.

Q: You sound confident in the care you provided.

A: I am. We trained for exactly this kind of scenario, and we executed well.

Q: Very well. Let's move on to the transport.

A: In my assessment, the helmet did its job. That young man is alive because he was wearing it.

topic: A paramedic is questioned about the response time and treatment at an accident scene
text:
Q: Paramedic Reeves, let's discuss the oxygen administration. At what point did you place the patient on supplemental oxygen?

A: Within the first two minutes of contact.

Q: Why so quickly?

A: Her oxygen saturation was reading 89 percent. Anything below 94 warrants supplemental oxygen, and with the mechanism of injury—chest impact against the steering wheel—I was concerned about underlying pulmonary contusion.

Q: Was she having difficulty breathing when you arrived?

A: She was breathing, but shallow. Complained of chest pain with inspiration. Classic presentation for blunt chest trauma.

Q: What level of oxygen did you provide?

A: Started her on 15 liters via non-rebreather mask. Her sats came up to 96 within four minutes.

Q: Good. Now, I understand there was some delay at the hospital. Can you speak to what happened during transport?

A: There was no delay during transport. We were en route at 3:41 PM and arrived at Memorial at 3:58 PM. Seventeen minutes, which is standard for that distance.

Q: I apologize, I misspoke. I meant to ask about the handoff at the hospital.

A: The handoff was smooth. I gave report to the trauma team, they took over care, and we were cleared by 4:10.

Q: So from your perspective, everything proceeded according to protocol?

A: From my perspective and from the documentation, yes. We moved efficiently, communicated clearly, and the patient received continuous care from the moment we arrived on scene until we transferred her. That's exactly what's supposed to happen.

Q: I appreciate the thoroughness of your answers, Paramedic Reeves.

A: I believe in being thorough. It's how we do this job right.

A: Of course I do. I kept detailed notes on every adjustment over $10,000. That was my personal policy.

Q: Why that threshold?

A: Because large adjustments require explanation. I wasn't going to rely on my memory three years later when someone asked questions—which is exactly what's happening now.

Q: Do you have those notes with you?

A: I provided everything I had to my attorney during document collection. If it wasn't produced, you'd have to ask about that process.

Q: Were there adjustments you made that weren't documented?

A: No. I documented everything.

Q: Everything?

A: Everything that went through my hands. What my partners did with the accounts I didn't have access to, I couldn't say.

Q: Which accounts didn't you have access to?

A: The investment accounts were managed directly by Mr. Fenton. I never saw statements, never reconciled them, never touched them.

Q: Did you ask to see them?

A: Once. I was told it wasn't necessary for my role.

Q: Who told you that?

A: Mr. Fenton.

topic: A business partner is deposed about financial records they were responsible for maintaining
text:
Q: Mr. Baines, let's discuss the petty cash fund.

A: All right.

Q: How large was this fund?

A: We kept $5,000 in the safe at any given time.

Q: Who had access to the safe?

A: Myself and the office manager, Patricia Noon.

Q: How were withdrawals documented?

A: There was a log. You write the date, the amount, and the purpose.

Q: Were all withdrawals logged?

A: They were supposed to be.

Q: Were they?

A: I can only speak for myself. I logged every withdrawal I made.

Q: I'm showing you Exhibit 19. This is the petty cash log for August 2022. There are three entries in your handwriting—August 4th, August 15th, and August 22nd.

A: Yes.

Q: The fund was replenished on August 1st with $5,000. Your three entries total $1,200. But the ending balance recorded on August 31st was $1,400.

A: Okay.

Q: That's a discrepancy of $2,400.

A: Is that a question?

Q: Where did that $2,400 go, Mr. Baines?

A: I have no idea.

Q: You were responsible for this fund.

A: I was one of two people with access. And the log speaks for itself—my withdrawals are documented. If there's a discrepancy, it didn't come from my entries.

Q: Are you saying Patricia Noon took the money?

A: I'm saying my entries are documented and accounted for. Draw whatever conclusions you want from that.

Q: Did you ever confront Ms. Noon about discrepancies in the fund?

A: I raised concerns with my partner, David Welsh, on more than one occasion.

Q: What did Mr. Welsh do about those concerns?

A: He said he'd handle it.

Q: Did he?

A: The discrepancies continued. So you tell me.

topic: A paramedic is questioned about the response time and treatment at an accident scene
text:
Q: State your name and occupation for the record.

A: Michael Torres. Paramedic with County Fire and Rescue, twelve years.

Q: Mr. Torres, I want to direct your attention to the evening of March 15th. What time did the dispatch call come in?

A: 7:42 PM.

Q: And what time did your unit arrive on scene?

A: 7:58 PM.

Q: Sixteen minutes. Is that consistent with your usual response times?

A: It's within the range, yes.

Q: Within the range. Can you be more specific?

A: It depends on traffic, distance, road conditions. Sixteen minutes isn't unusual for that part of the county.

Q: I'm asking whether sixteen minutes is fast, slow, or average for your unit specifically.

A: Average. Maybe slightly longer than average.

Q: Which is it?

A: I don't have the statistics memorized. I said it's within the acceptable range.

Q: Let's move on. When you arrived, what was the plaintiff's condition?

A: She was conscious, complaining of neck pain, had visible lacerations on her forehead and left arm.

Q: Did you immobilize her spine?

A: Yes. Standard protocol for vehicle accidents with potential spinal involvement.

Q: How long after arrival did you begin transport?

A: Approximately eleven minutes.

Q: Eleven minutes seems like a long time for someone with potential spinal injuries, doesn't it?

A: No. We had to stabilize her, assess vitals, secure the scene. Eleven minutes is appropriate.

Q: I didn't ask if it was appropriate. I asked if it seemed long.

A: And I'm telling you it wasn't.

---

topic: A paramedic is questioned about the response time and treatment at an accident scene
text:
Q: You were the lead paramedic on the unit that responded to the accident on Route 9, correct?

A: That's correct.

Q: Tell me what you observed when you first approached the vehicle.

A: Single-car accident. The vehicle had struck a utility pole on the driver's side. The driver—your client—was slumped against the steering wheel. Airbag had deployed. There was significant intrusion into the driver compartment.

Q: Significant intrusion. What do you mean by that?

A: The door was pushed inward, maybe eight to ten inches. Made extraction more complicated.

Q: More complicated how?

A: We couldn't simply open the door and remove him. We had to coordinate with fire for extrication equipment.

Q: How long did that coordination take?

A: Look, I've already been through this with your colleague last month. The fire crew was on scene within four minutes of our arrival. Extrication took another twelve. None of that is in my control.

Q: I understand, Mr. Reeves. I'm just trying to establish a timeline.

A: The timeline is in my report. Page three.

Q: I've read your report. I'm asking you to walk me through it verbally.

A: Fine. We arrived at 9:17. Fire arrived at 9:21. Patient was extracted by 9:33. We began transport at 9:41.

Q: Why the eight-minute gap between extraction and transport?

A: Assessment. IV access. Spinal immobilization. Oxygen administration. The basics.

Q: Would you characterize the patient's condition as critical at that point?

A: He was serious. Not critical.

Q: What's the distinction?

A: Critical means imminent risk of death. Serious means significant injury requiring immediate care. There's a difference.

---

topic: A paramedic is questioned about the response time and treatment at an accident scene
text:
Q: Ms. Okonkwo, you've been a paramedic for how long?

A: Seven years this October.

Q: And you responded to the accident involving my client on January 8th?

A: Yes.

Q: What was your unit's response time that day?

A: I believe it was around fourteen minutes.

Q: You believe, or you know?

A: I'd have to check the exact log, but approximately fourteen minutes.

Q: Fourteen minutes. Now, the accident occurred less than four miles from your station, correct?

A: Yes.

Q: Four miles in fourteen minutes. That's—let me do the math—roughly seventeen miles per hour. Can you explain that?

A: There was construction on Miller Road. We had to detour.

Q: Did you document that detour?

A: It would be in the GPS log.

Q: I'm asking if you personally documented it.

A: I noted road conditions in my report.

Q: Let me read from your report. Quote: "Arrived on scene without delay." Does that sound accurate to you now?

A: We arrived as quickly as conditions allowed. That's what I meant.

Q: That's not what those words say, is it?

A: I'm not going to argue semantics with you.

Q: I'm not asking you to argue. I'm asking whether "without delay" accurately describes a fourteen-minute response to a scene four miles away.

A: Given the circumstances, yes.

Q: Let's talk about what you found when you arrived. The plaintiff was outside the vehicle?

A: She had self-extricated, yes. She was sitting on the guardrail.

Q: Did that concern you?

A: Of course it concerned me. Movement after an accident can exacerbate spinal injuries.

Q: Did you tell her that?

A: I told her not to move any further. I told her we'd take it from there.

---

topic: A paramedic is questioned about the response time and treatment at an accident scene
text:
Q: Mr. Aldridge, I want to understand the sequence of events. You arrive on scene at 4:47 PM. What's the first thing you do?

A: Scene safety assessment.

Q: Which takes how long?

A: Thirty seconds, maybe.

Q: Then?

A: Approach the vehicle, assess the patient.

Q: And?

A: He was unresponsive. I checked for pulse and breathing.

Q: And?

A: Pulse was weak and rapid. Breathing was shallow.

Q: Then?

A: My partner retrieved the stretcher while I maintained c-spine stabilization.

Q: Mr. Aldridge, I'm going to need more than one-sentence answers. This is a deposition, not a quiz show. Can you describe in detail what interventions you performed?

A: I stabilized his cervical spine manually. My partner applied a collar. We log-rolled him onto a backboard. I established an IV line, started a saline drip. We administered oxygen via non-rebreather mask. We loaded him into the ambulance and initiated transport.

Q: How long from your arrival to transport?

A: Nine minutes.

Q: Is that typical?

A: For a trauma case, yes.

Q: Your report says the patient's blood pressure was 80 over 50. Is that dangerous?

A: It's hypotensive, yes.

Q: So he was in shock.

A: He was showing signs consistent with hypovolemic shock.

Q: And you waited nine minutes before transporting someone in shock?

A: We didn't wait. We worked. There's a difference.

---

topic: A paramedic is questioned about the response time and treatment at an accident scene
text:
Q: Let me ask you again. At the time you arrived, was the plaintiff conscious?

A: I've answered that. She was semi-conscious. Responsive to pain, not to verbal commands.

Q: When did she become fully conscious?

A: During transport. Maybe five minutes into the ride.

Q: Did she say anything at that point?

A: She asked what happened. She asked about her daughter.

Q: Her daughter was in the vehicle?

A: I've been over this three times already.

Q: I'm asking you to confirm for the record.

A: Yes. Her daughter was in the back seat.

Q: And the daughter's condition?

A: Minor injuries. Treated on scene by my partner.

Q: Why wasn't the daughter transported?

A: Parents declined transport. Signed a refusal.

Q: The mother signed a refusal while semi-conscious?

A: No. The father arrived on scene. He signed.

Q: When did the father arrive?

A: I don't know exactly. Before we transported.

Q: Before you transported. So within your nine-minute window on scene?

A: Apparently.

Q: You don't remember?

A: I remember treating two patients simultaneously while managing a chaotic scene with bystanders and traffic. I don't remember the exact minute someone's husband showed up.

Q: Fair enough. Let's talk about the mother's treatment. You said she was responsive to pain. How did you assess that?

A: Sternal rub.

Q: And her response?

A: She grimaced and pulled away.

Q: Is that documented?

A: Yes. Page two of my report.

Q: I see it now. Thank you. Did you perform any neurological assessment beyond the sternal rub?

A: Pupil response. Both reactive. I noted it.

topic: A daycare worker is deposed about an injury a child sustained while in their care
text:
Q: Ms. Hernandez, you were the only staff member in the toddler room when Marcus fell, correct?

A: I was the only one physically in the room at that exact second, yes.

Q: That's a yes?

A: I just said yes.

Q: How many children were in the room at that time?

A: Eight.

Q: And the ratio requirement is one adult to four toddlers, isn't that right?

A: The ratio requirement is one to four, and I had already radioed for Dina to come back from her break because I knew—

Q: I didn't ask what you radioed. I asked about the ratio.

A: And I'm trying to explain the context.

Q: Ma'am, there will be time for context. Right now I need you to answer the question I'm asking. Were you in compliance with the ratio requirement at the moment Marcus fell?

A: Technically, no. For about ninety seconds.

Q: Ninety seconds. And during those ninety seconds, a two-year-old fell off a changing table and fractured his arm.

A: Is that a question?

Q: Did Marcus fall during those ninety seconds when you were out of ratio compliance?

A: Yes. Obviously. You already know that.

Q: Where were you standing when he fell?

A: I was three feet away, dealing with another child who had bitten someone.

Q: Three feet away, but you didn't catch him.

A: I had my hands on a child who was actively biting another child's face. I'm not an octopus.

Q: No one suggested you were.

A: Then stop asking questions like you expect me to be in four places at once.

topic: A daycare worker is deposed about an injury a child sustained while in their care
text:
Q: Let's talk about the incident report you filled out that afternoon.

A: Okay.

Q: You wrote that Emma "tripped on a toy and struck her head on the bookshelf." Do you see that?

A: I see it.

Q: Is that accurate?

A: That's what I observed, yes.

Q: What toy did she trip on?

A: I... I don't remember the specific toy.

Q: You don't remember.

A: It was seven months ago. There are toys everywhere in that room. It could have been a block, a truck—I didn't catalog it.

Q: But you were watching her when she fell?

A: I was in the room.

Q: That's not what I asked. Were you watching Emma at the moment she fell?

A: I was supervising the entire room.

Q: Ms. Okonkwo, I'm going to ask you again. Were your eyes on Emma at the moment she tripped?

A: No.

Q: So you didn't actually see what she tripped on.

A: I saw her on the ground next to toys. I made a reasonable conclusion.

Q: A reasonable conclusion. You put a guess in an official incident report?

A: I put what I believed happened based on what I saw immediately after.

Q: Let me ask you this: is it possible Emma didn't trip at all?

A: What are you suggesting?

Q: I'm asking if it's possible.

A: Anything is possible. I wasn't staring at her like a surveillance camera. I had eleven other kids.

topic: A daycare worker is deposed about an injury a child sustained while in their care
text:
Q: Good morning, Mr. Franklin. You understand you're under oath?

A: I do.

Q: How long have you worked at Sunny Days Learning Center?

A: Six years.

Q: And in those six years, have you received training on how to document injuries?

A: Yes.

Q: Multiple trainings?

A: Yearly. Sometimes more.

Q: So you knew, on April 14th, that any injury—no matter how minor—needed to be documented before the child left for the day?

A: I knew that.

Q: Then why wasn't Olivia Patterson's bruise documented until three days later?

A: Because I didn't see any bruise when her mother picked her up.

Q: You didn't see it, or it wasn't there?

A: I didn't see it. I can't speak to whether it was there.

Q: Her mother testified she saw it that night during bath time. A bruise the size of a golf ball on her daughter's thigh.

A: I understand that's what she said.

Q: You sound skeptical.

A: I'm not skeptical. I'm telling you I didn't observe it.

Q: Olivia was in your care for nine hours that day. You're telling this jury you never once saw a golf-ball-sized bruise on her leg?

A: The children wear clothes, counselor. I don't inspect their thighs.

Q: Do you think this is funny, Mr. Franklin?

A: I think you're trying to make me responsible for something I never saw.

topic: A daycare worker is deposed about an injury a child sustained while in their care
text:
Q: Ms. Tran, walk me through the morning routine on September 8th.

A: Children arrive between seven and eight-thirty. We do breakfast, free play, then circle time around nine.

Q: And where does playground time fall in that schedule?

A: Usually after circle time. Around nine-thirty or nine-forty-five.

Q: Was it after circle time on September 8th?

A: Yes.

Q: You took the children outside yourself?

A: Myself and Jennifer.

Q: Jennifer Mosley?

A: Yes.

Q: Now, the playground has a gate, correct?

A: Correct.

Q: Was the gate latched when you went outside?

A: I... I believe so. I don't specifically remember checking it.

Q: You don't specifically remember.

A: I check it every day. It's automatic at this point.

Q: But you can't tell me, under oath, that you checked it on September 8th.

A: I can tell you it's part of my routine.

Q: Routine isn't memory, Ms. Tran.

A: I'm aware of that.

Q: Tyler Chen was found outside that gate, on the sidewalk, thirty feet from the playground. You're aware of that?

A: Yes. It was the worst moment of my career.

Q: How do you think he got there?

A: I don't know. The gate must not have latched properly.

Q: Or someone didn't check it.

A: Or the latch is faulty. Which I've reported multiple times, by the way.

Q: We'll get to those reports. Right now I'm asking about your actions.

A: And I've told you what I know.

topic: A daycare worker is deposed about an injury a child sustained while in their care
text:
Q: You were Jaylen's primary caregiver that day?

A: One of them, yes.

Q: Who else?

A: Rebecca was in the room too.

Q: But you were assigned to Jaylen specifically?

A: We don't assign workers to specific children. We supervise the whole group.

Q: Let me rephrase. You were the one who changed Jaylen's diaper that afternoon?

A: Yes.

Q: You were the one who put him down for his nap?

A: Yes.

Q: And you were the one who found him with the cord wrapped around his arm?

A: Yes.

Q: Tell me about the cord.

A: It was from the blinds. The window blinds.

Q: How did Jaylen reach the blinds from his crib?

A: The crib was positioned near the window.

Q: Whose decision was that?

A: It's where the crib has always been.

Q: That's not what I asked. Who decided to put the crib there?

A: I don't know. It was there when I started.

Q: You never thought to move it? Never thought a cord hanging near a crib might be dangerous?

A: The cords are supposed to be tied up. They were tied up.

Q: Clearly not well enough.

A: I'm not the one who ties them. Maintenance does that.

Q: So this is maintenance's fault?

A: I didn't say that.

Q: Then whose fault is it, Ms. Baylor?

A: I don't know whose fault it is. I just know it isn't mine.

topic: A building inspector is deposed about a structural assessment they signed off on
text:
Q: Mr. Delgado, you conducted the structural assessment on the Meridian Tower project, correct?

A: I conducted an assessment, yes.

Q: And you signed off on that assessment on March 14th of last year?

A: I'd need to see the document to confirm the exact date.

Q: I'm handing you what's been marked as Exhibit 7. Is that your signature?

A: It appears to be.

Q: It "appears to be"?

A: It's my signature.

Q: Now, the assessment indicates the load-bearing walls on floors twelve through fifteen met code requirements. Do you recall physically inspecting those floors?

A: I inspected the building according to standard protocol.

Q: That wasn't my question. Do you recall physically inspecting floors twelve through fifteen?

A: I don't have independent recollection of every floor I've ever walked through, counselor. I inspect dozens of buildings.

Q: So you don't remember?

A: I'm saying I followed protocol. Protocol requires inspection of all structural elements.

Q: Mr. Delgado, isn't it true that the elevator serving floors ten through twenty was out of service during the week of your inspection?

A: I wouldn't know about that.

Q: You wouldn't know if the elevator was working?

A: I don't recall. There are stairwells.

Q: Did you take the stairs to floor fifteen?

A: I don't recall the specific route I took through the building. I conducted my inspection.

topic: A building inspector is deposed about a structural assessment they signed off on
text:
Q: Ms. Thornton, how long have you worked as a building inspector for the city?

A: Eleven years this coming September.

Q: And in those eleven years, have you ever amended a structural assessment after filing it?

A: Why would I need to amend an assessment?

Q: I'm asking if you ever have.

A: If there were a material change in circumstances, an amendment might be appropriate. But I don't file incomplete work.

Q: Let me ask you about the Greenway Commons project specifically. You filed your assessment on October 3rd. Does that sound right?

A: I'll accept that date.

Q: Three weeks later, a supplemental report was filed. Same property. Also bearing your signature. Can you explain that?

A: A supplemental report is not an amendment. It's additional documentation.

Q: What prompted the need for additional documentation?

A: I'd have to review the file to give you a complete answer.

Q: Generally speaking, what circumstances lead to a supplemental filing?

A: New construction. Modifications. Additional testing results.

Q: Was there new construction at Greenway Commons between October 3rd and October 24th?

A: I don't believe so.

Q: Additional testing?

A: I'd need to review my notes.

Q: Ms. Thornton, did anyone contact you between those dates asking you to take another look at Greenway Commons?

A: People contact me about projects all the time. That's my job.

Q: Did someone ask you to revisit this particular assessment?

A: I don't recall being asked to do anything improper, if that's what you're implying.

topic: A building inspector is deposed about a structural assessment they signed off on
text:
Q: Mr. Okonkwo, I want to understand your process. When you arrive at a site, what's the first thing you do?

A: Review my documentation. Check the permit file. Familiarize myself with what I'm looking at.

Q: Then you enter the building?

A: Typically.

Q: On the Ashford Residences project, you noted in your report that you observed quote "no visible signs of structural compromise." Do you recall writing that?

A: If it's in my report, I wrote it.

Q: What would visible signs of structural compromise look like?

A: Cracking in load-bearing elements. Deflection. Water damage to key supports. Spalling. Exposed rebar. Depends on the structure.

Q: Did you observe any cracking at Ashford Residences?

A: Minor surface cracking in non-structural elements. Cosmetic. Not reportable.

Q: How do you determine whether cracking is cosmetic versus structural?

A: Training. Experience. Measurement. Pattern analysis.

Q: Did you measure the cracks you observed?

A: I don't recall whether I took specific measurements of cracks I deemed cosmetic.

Q: Your report doesn't mention any cracking at all.

A: Because it wasn't structural. I just explained that.

Q: So you observed cracking, determined it was cosmetic, and chose not to document it?

A: That's standard practice. We don't document every nail hole.

Q: We're not talking about nail holes though, are we, Mr. Okonkwo?

A: No, counselor, we're talking about cracks I assessed as cosmetic. Which they were.

topic: A building inspector is deposed about a structural assessment they signed off on
text:
Q: Tell me about your relationship with Harmon Development.

A: What do you mean by "relationship"?

Q: Have you worked on their projects before?

A: I've inspected buildings they've developed. That's not a relationship.

Q: How many of their buildings have you inspected in the past three years?

A: I'd have to check my records.

Q: Ballpark.

A: Maybe eight or ten.

Q: Is that typical? To inspect that many buildings for one developer?

A: They build a lot.

Q: Do other inspectors in your office also handle Harmon projects?

A: You'd have to ask them.

Q: I'm asking about your understanding. Is the work distributed, or do you handle most of Harmon's inspections?

A: I handle what I'm assigned.

Q: Who makes the assignments?

A: My supervisor.

Q: Have you ever socialized with anyone from Harmon Development?

A: Socialized?

Q: Dinner. Drinks. Golf. That sort of thing.

A: I've attended industry events where Harmon employees were present. So have a hundred other people.

Q: What about outside of industry events?

A: No.

Q: Never?

A: Asked and answered, counselor.

topic: A building inspector is deposed about a structural assessment they signed off on
text:
Q: Mr. Fitzgerald, your assessment indicated that the foundation at 400 Larkspur Lane was, in your words, "structurally sound and suitable for the proposed construction." Correct?

A: That's what my assessment concluded, yes.

Q: You seem to be drawing a distinction. Between what the assessment concluded and what?

A: I'm not drawing a distinction. You asked if that's what my assessment said. It is.

Q: Did you personally believe the foundation was structurally sound?

A: My professional opinion is reflected in the assessment.

Q: That's not quite what I asked.

A: It's the answer I'm giving.

Q: Fair enough. Let me ask you this: did anyone else review the foundation before you signed off?

A: There was a geotechnical report in the file.

Q: Did you rely on that report?

A: I considered it as part of my review.

Q: The geotechnical report flagged concerns about soil stability in the northeast quadrant. Did you address those concerns?

A: The concerns were noted. They were within acceptable parameters.

Q: Acceptable according to whom?

A: According to code. According to engineering standards.

Q: Did you consult with the geotechnical engineer who authored that report?

A: I don't recall whether I spoke with that individual directly.

Q: Would there be a record if you had?

A: There might be.

Q: But you don't recall?

A: I review hundreds of reports. I don't remember every conversation. What I remember is doing my job.

topic: A doctor is deposed about informed consent procedures before a surgery
text:
Q: Dr. Patel, I'd like to direct your attention to the informed consent process for Mrs. Gallagher's surgery on March 15th.

A: Okay.

Q: Can you describe your standard practice for obtaining informed consent?

A: I talk to the patient. They sign the form.

Q: Could you elaborate on what you discuss with the patient during that conversation?

A: Risks, benefits, alternatives. The usual.

Q: The usual. And what specific risks did you discuss with Mrs. Gallagher?

A: I don't recall the specifics. It was eighteen months ago.

Q: Do you have any notes that might refresh your recollection?

A: There's a consent form in the chart. It lists the risks.

Q: I'm asking about your conversation with her, not the form.

A: I understand what you're asking. I don't have independent recollection.

Q: Is it your testimony that you have no memory of speaking with Mrs. Gallagher about her surgery?

A: I'm sure I spoke with her. I always do. I just don't remember what was said.

Q: Do you remember how long that conversation lasted?

A: No.

Q: Five minutes? Thirty minutes?

A: I couldn't say.

Q: Dr. Patel, do you consider informed consent to be an important part of patient care?

A: Sure.

topic: A doctor is deposed about informed consent procedures before a surgery
text:
Q: Doctor, let's talk about the consent form itself. Who prepared the form that Mr. Dawson signed?

A: It's a standard hospital form. I didn't prepare it personally.

Q: Did you review it before presenting it to Mr. Dawson?

A: I'm sure I glanced at it.

Q: You glanced at it. So you didn't read it carefully?

A: I've seen that form hundreds of times, Counsel. I know what it says.

Q: Fair enough. Moving on. The form lists nerve damage as a potential complication.

A: If you say so.

Q: I'm showing you Exhibit 14. Do you see where nerve damage is listed?

A: Yes, I see it. Third item down.

Q: Did you verbally explain to Mr. Dawson what nerve damage might mean for his daily life?

A: I explained the risks in terms a patient could understand.

Q: That wasn't my question. Did you explain the practical implications of nerve damage specifically?

A: I covered it. Whether I used those exact words, I can't tell you.

Q: Next question. Did Mr. Dawson ask you any questions about the procedure?

A: I don't recall him asking anything unusual.

Q: What would constitute an unusual question?

A: I don't know. Something I'd remember, I suppose.

topic: A doctor is deposed about informed consent procedures before a surgery
text:
Q: Dr. Warren, how long have you been performing this particular procedure?

A: About twelve years now. Maybe thirteen.

Q: And in that time, how many times would you estimate you've obtained informed consent for it?

A: I really couldn't give you a number. Hundreds, certainly. It's become somewhat automatic at this point—not the surgery itself, but the process around it. You develop a rhythm after the first few years.

Q: A rhythm. Could you describe that rhythm for me?

A: I meet with the patient, usually the day before or the morning of. I go through the procedure step by step—what we'll do, why we're doing it, what could go wrong. I ask if they have questions. Most don't, honestly. They've already decided they want the surgery by the time they're in that room. Then they sign.

Q: Most don't have questions. Did Ms. Thornton have questions?

A: She asked about scarring, I believe. That's fairly common with the female patients. I explained what to expect.

Q: Anything else?

A: Not that I recall. She seemed satisfied with my answers. Ready to proceed.

Q: Did you discuss the risk of post-operative infection?

A: Yes. That's standard.

Q: Did you discuss the specific infection rate for this procedure at your facility?

A: No. We don't typically get into facility-specific statistics.

Q: Why not?

A: It's not part of the standard disclosure. If she'd asked, I would have told her.

topic: A doctor is deposed about informed consent procedures before a surgery
text:
Q: Dr. Okonkwo, I want to understand the timeline here. When exactly did you first meet Mr. Reyes?

A: The morning of surgery.

Q: That was the first time?

A: Yes. Dr. Hartman had been managing his care. I was brought in to perform the procedure.

Q: So the informed consent conversation happened that same morning?

A: Correct.

Q: How much time elapsed between that conversation and when Mr. Reyes was taken to the operating room?

A: Perhaps forty-five minutes. Maybe an hour.

Q: Did that concern you at all?

A: Did what concern me?

Q: Meeting a patient for the first time and obtaining consent less than an hour before cutting into him.

A: That's how it works sometimes. Schedules are complicated. Patients are referred.

Q: I'm asking whether it concerned you.

A: No, Counsel, it did not concern me. The consent was obtained. The form was signed.

Q: Was Mr. Reyes alert during your conversation?

A: He was pre-medicated but responsive.

Q: Pre-medicated. With what?

A: I'd have to check the chart. Probably Versed, maybe something for anxiety.

Q: Do you think a patient on Versed is in an optimal state to understand surgical risks?

A: He understood well enough to sign his name. That's the legal standard, isn't it?

topic: A doctor is deposed about informed consent procedures before a surgery
text:
Q: Let's talk about alternatives, Doctor. Did you discuss any alternatives to surgery with Mrs. Chen?

Q: What does conservative management mean in this context?

A: Physical therapy. Pain management. Lifestyle modifications. Waiting to see if symptoms improved on their own.

Q: Did you recommend any of those alternatives?

A: No. Surgery was the appropriate choice given her condition.

Q: In your opinion.

A: Yes, in my medical opinion. That's what I'm paid to have.

Q: Did you tell Mrs. Chen that other physicians might recommend trying conservative management first?

A: Other physicians weren't treating her. I was.

Q: I understand that. My question is whether you informed her that reasonable physicians might disagree about the best course of treatment.

A: I told her surgery was the best option. I stand by that.

Q: Doctor, informed consent requires disclosure of reasonable alternatives. Do you agree with that statement?

A: Sure.

Q: And you don't consider it relevant to mention that some physicians would take a different approach?

A: I mentioned conservative management. She chose surgery. We're going in circles here.

Q: Did she choose surgery, or did you choose it for her?

A: She signed the form. That's a choice.

topic: A doctor is deposed about informed consent procedures before a surgery
text:
Q: Dr. Hartwell, let's turn to the consent process for Mrs. Patterson's thyroidectomy. Did you personally discuss the risks with her?

A: I did. Every time. That's my standard practice, and I don't deviate from it.

Q: When you say "every time," what do you mean?

A: I mean I met with Mrs. Patterson on three separate occasions before surgery. Once at the initial consultation, once at the pre-op appointment, and once the morning of the procedure. Each time, we discussed the surgery and its risks.

Q: What specific risks did you cover?

A: Damage to the recurrent laryngeal nerve, hypoparathyroidism, bleeding, infection, scarring, the possibility of needing lifelong thyroid hormone replacement, and anesthesia risks. I also discussed the risk of incomplete removal and the potential need for revision surgery.

Q: Did you document these conversations?

A: Absolutely. You'll find detailed notes in the chart for each encounter. I dictate my notes immediately after seeing patients for exactly this reason.

Q: The consent form Mrs. Patterson signed—did she have time to read it?

A: She had it for eleven days. I gave it to her at the pre-op appointment and told her to take it home, read it, write down questions, and bring it back. She did exactly that.

Q: Did she have questions when she returned?

A: Two questions. She asked about the likelihood of voice changes, and she asked how long she'd be on medication. I answered both, and she initialed next to those sections on the form.

Q: How can you be certain she understood what she was signing?

A: Because I asked her to explain it back to me. I do that with every surgical patient. She repeated the major risks in her own words. She understood.

Q: Do you recall her exact words?

A: She said, "So the main things are my voice could be affected, my calcium could drop, and I'll probably need pills for the rest of my life." Those were her words. I wrote them in the chart.

Q: Is it your testimony that informed consent was properly obtained?

A: It is. Without qualification.

---

topic: A doctor is deposed about informed consent procedures before a surgery
text:
Q: Dr. Nasser, who is responsible for obtaining informed consent at your hospital?

A: The operating surgeon.

Q: That would have been you, correct?

A: That's correct.

Q: Walk me through what you told Mr. Dominguez before his spinal fusion.

A: I explained the nature of the procedure, the anticipated benefits, the material risks, and the alternatives including non-surgical management.

Q: Let's slow down. What material risks?

A: Infection, blood loss requiring transfusion, nerve injury, dural tear, hardware failure, adjacent segment disease, failure to fuse, and continued pain.

Q: Did you tell him paralysis was possible?

A: I did.

Q: You're certain?

A: I am. I have this conversation with every spinal surgery patient. It's not something I would forget to mention.

Q: The consent form doesn't specifically list paralysis. Can you explain that?

A: The form lists "nerve damage, including permanent neurological deficit." Paralysis is a form of permanent neurological deficit. I explained that verbally in clear terms, and the written form captures the category.

Q: Did Mr. Dominguez ask you any questions about paralysis risk?

A: He asked me how often it happens. I told him less than one percent in my experience, but it's never zero.

Q: What did he say?

A: He nodded and said he understood. He said his pain was bad enough that he wanted to proceed.

Q: Did you document that exchange?

A: I documented that risks were discussed and that the patient verbalized understanding and wished to proceed.

Q: Why didn't you document his specific question about paralysis?

A: Because I document the substance of the conversation, not a word-for-word transcript. The substance is there. He was informed. He consented.

---

topic: A doctor is deposed about informed consent procedures before a surgery
text:
Q: Let me direct your attention to the morning of December 14th. You saw Ms. Yuen before surgery?

topic: A doctor is deposed about informed consent procedures before a surgery
text:
Q: Dr. Okonkwo, you perform roughly how many laparoscopic cholecystectomies per year?

A: Between eighty and a hundred.

Q: And for each one, you personally conduct the informed consent discussion?

A: Personally? No. My physician assistant conducts the initial discussion. I follow up.

Q: So you're delegating informed consent to a PA?

A: I'm utilizing a PA as part of a team-based approach, which is standard practice and entirely appropriate.

Q: Is it appropriate under hospital policy?

A: It is.

Q: Is it appropriate under the standard of care?

A: It is.

Q: In Mr. Tran's case, did you personally speak with him about the risks of surgery?

A: I did.

Q: When?

A: At the pre-operative appointment, after my PA had gone through the consent form with him, and again the morning of surgery.

Q: What did you tell him at the pre-operative appointment?

A: I asked if he had questions. I reviewed the major risks, including bile duct injury, bleeding, infection, and conversion to open surgery. He said he understood.

Q: Did you explain bile duct injury could be life-altering?

A: I explained it could require additional surgery and long-term management. Whether that's "life-altering" depends on the individual.

Q: It's a yes or no question, Doctor.

A: Then my answer is yes. I conveyed the seriousness of that complication. The exact words I used, I can't reproduce verbatim, but the substance was clear.

Q: The morning of surgery—did you discuss anything new with Mr. Tran?

A: I confirmed he had no new questions, that he hadn't eaten or drunk since midnight, and that he was ready to proceed.

Q: That's a fairly brief exchange.

A: It's an appropriate exchange when the detailed discussion has already occurred.

---

topic: A doctor is deposed about informed consent procedures before a surgery
text:
Q: Doctor, you testified earlier that your consent process is thorough. Let me test that.

A: Go ahead.

Q: Mrs. Franklin was sixty-seven years old with multiple comorbidities. Did you discuss how her age affected her surgical risk?

A: Of course.

Q: What did you say?

A: I told her that her age and her diabetes increased her risk of complications, including delayed healing and infection.

Q: What about her cardiac history?

A: I discussed that as well. I told her the anesthesia team would evaluate her and that there were cardiac risks any time someone with her history undergoes general anesthesia.

Q: Did you quantify those risks?

A: I don't give patients percentages they won't understand. I told her the risks were real and we were taking precautions.

Q: Patients won't understand percentages?

A: I said percentages they won't understand. Telling a patient she has a 2.3% risk of a cardiac event means nothing without context. I provide context.

Q: What context did you provide?

A: I told her we'd have cardiology clear her, that we'd monitor her closely, and that despite the risks, I believed the surgery was in her best interest given her condition. I told her she could decline if she wasn't comfortable.

Q: Did she express any hesitation?

A: She asked if I thought she should do it. I told her I wouldn't have recommended it if I didn't think the benefits outweighed the risks.

Q: And that was enough for her?

A: She said she trusted my judgment and wanted to proceed. That's what I documented, and that's what happened.

Q: You documented that she trusted your judgment?

A: I documented that the patient expressed understanding of the risks and wished to proceed. The phrase "trusted my judgment" was her words to me. The substance is in the chart.

Q: Thank you, Doctor.

A: You're welcome.

topic: A business partner is deposed about financial records they were responsible for maintaining

topic: A business partner is deposed about financial records they were responsible for maintaining
text:
Q: Mr. Patterson, I want to understand the reconciliation process you used at the end of each quarter.

topic: A driver is deposed about the events leading up to a multi-vehicle collision
text:
Q: Could you state your name for the record?

A: Michael Torres. And just so you know, I've been driving professionally for eighteen years now, so I know exactly what happened out there.

Q: I appreciate that, Mr. Torres. Let's talk about the morning of March 14th. What time did you leave your residence?

A: 6:47 a.m. I remember because I always check my watch before I pull out. It's a habit. Good habit, actually. Saved me more than once in situations like this where people want to know the exact details.

Q: And where were you headed?

A: Downtown distribution center on Fifth and Kramer. I've made that run probably two thousand times, no exaggeration. I could drive it with my eyes closed—not that I would, obviously, but you understand what I mean.

Q: Describe the weather conditions that morning.

A: Clear skies, maybe forty-two degrees, roads were dry, visibility was excellent—I'd say at least a mile, probably more. Perfect driving conditions. Textbook, really.

Q: What route did you take?

A: Oh, the best route. I took Morrison Boulevard to the 95 interchange, then merged onto the expressway heading south. It's three minutes faster than the alternative if you time it right, which I always do.

Q: At what speed were you traveling on the expressway?

A: Sixty-two miles per hour. Speed limit's sixty-five, but I like to keep a small buffer. That's something they don't teach you in driving school—you learn it from experience, from actually being out there.

Q: Tell me what you observed in the moments before the collision.

A: Everything. I saw everything. The white sedan two cars ahead started drifting left, the brake lights on the pickup in front of me came on, and I immediately began my defensive response. I want to walk you through exactly what I did, step by step, because it's actually a really good example of proper technique.

Q: Please do.

A: First, I checked my mirrors—both of them—in under a second. Then I began controlled deceleration while simultaneously scanning for an escape route. The shoulder was clear, so I had options. I want to be clear that I was completely in control of my vehicle the entire time.

topic: A driver is deposed about the events leading up to a multi-vehicle collision
text:
Q: Ms. Patterson, you were traveling northbound on Highway 12, correct?

Q: Fantastic. Now, I want to take you through this minute by minute, because the details here are absolutely critical. What lane were you in?

Q: The middle lane—perfect. And this is a three-lane highway at that stretch, isn't that right? Three lanes going north, three lanes going south, with a concrete divider?

A: I think so. Yes.

A: It was a dark truck. Maybe blue or black.

A: I don't know. A few car lengths.

Q: A few car lengths. Would you say three? Four? More than that?

A: Maybe three.

Q: Three car lengths at highway speed—now, you were doing about sixty-five, seventy miles per hour, would that be accurate?

A: Around there.

Q: So at seventy miles per hour, three car lengths—that's roughly what, forty-five feet? Does that sound right to you? Forty-five feet between you and this dark truck?

A: I guess. I wasn't measuring.

Q: Of course not, of course not. But this is exactly the kind of detail that helps us reconstruct what happened. Now—and this is where it gets really interesting—what's the first thing you noticed that told you something was wrong?

A: The truck's brake lights.

Q: The brake lights came on. And then what did you do?

A: I hit my brakes.

topic: A driver is deposed about the events leading up to a multi-vehicle collision
text:
Q: How long have you held a commercial driver's license?

A: Twelve years.

Q: In those twelve years, have you been involved in any prior accidents?

A: No.

Q: None at all?

A: Well—one. But that wasn't my fault either, and I want to explain that one too because it's actually relevant here.

Q: Let's stay focused on March 14th for now.

A: Sure, but the situations are really similar, and I think if you understood what happened in 2019, you'd see the pattern. Other drivers not paying attention, me doing everything right—

Q: Mr. Kendall, I need to direct you to the incident at hand.

A: I'm trying to give you context. You want the truth, right? The whole picture?

Q: I want to understand what happened on March 14th.

A: And I'm telling you! Look, I was in the right lane, traveling at an appropriate speed, maintaining proper following distance—I always maintain proper following distance, which is more than most people can say. The Camry came out of nowhere.

Q: When you say "out of nowhere"—

A: From my left. She cut across two lanes without signaling. I have dashcam footage, by the way. Have you seen it? Because it shows everything. It shows exactly what I'm describing.

Q: We'll get to the dashcam footage.

A: You should look at it now. Seriously. It would save us a lot of time because you'd see I'm not exaggerating.

Q: Describe what happened after the Camry entered your lane.

A: I took evasive action. Textbook evasive action. Checked my mirror, steered right toward the shoulder, applied steady brake pressure—not slamming, steady pressure, the way you're supposed to. I did everything right.

Q: Did your vehicle make contact with the Camry?

A: Barely. Because of what I did. If I hadn't reacted so fast, this would have been much, much worse. You should be taking notes on this.

topic: A driver is deposed about the events leading up to a multi-vehicle collision
text:
Q: State your name, please.

A: Denise Armitage.

Q: Ms. Armitage, were you the driver of the Honda Accord involved in the March 14th collision?

A: I was.

Q: Where were you coming from that morning?

A: My daughter's house. In Cedarville.

Q: How long is that drive typically?

A: About forty minutes if traffic's normal.

Q: And was traffic normal that morning?

A: It was heavier than usual, actually.

Q: Heavier. More vehicles on the road?

A: Yes.

Q: Now, as you approached the intersection of Route 9 and Millbrook Road, did you observe the traffic signal?

A: I did.

Q: What color was it?

A: Green.

Q: You're certain it was green?

A: I am. I've thought about it many times since then.

Q: Of course. Understandably. Now, here's what I'm trying to piece together, and I think your perspective is going to be really valuable—did you see the other vehicles before the impact occurred?

A: I saw the SUV run the red light.

Q: You saw the SUV enter the intersection against the light! That's exactly what I needed to understand. From which direction?

A: From my right. It came through very fast.

Q: Very fast—would you say it was exceeding the speed limit?

A: I couldn't say exactly.

Q: But your impression was that it was moving quickly?

A: Yes. Too quickly to stop.

Q: Too quickly to stop. And what happened in your mind at that moment? Walk me through your thought process, because I think this is crucial.

A: There wasn't much thought. I just reacted. I tried to brake and turn left.

topic: A driver is deposed about the events leading up to a multi-vehicle collision
text:
Q: Mr. Okafor, prior to the collision, had you consumed any alcohol?

A: No.

Q: Any medications?

A: No.

Q: Had you slept adequately the night before?

A: I slept fine. Seven hours, maybe more. I want to be clear about something—I was completely alert. Completely focused. This wasn't a fatigue situation.

Q: I haven't suggested it was.

A: I know, but people assume things. I've been dealing with that since this happened. Everyone wants to find something wrong with the driver, and there wasn't anything wrong. Not with me.

Q: Tell me about the moment you first perceived a hazard.

A: I saw brake lights ahead. Several cars. And I thought, okay, traffic's slowing, so I began to slow down too. Normal. Routine.

Q: Then what?

A: Then the car in front of me stopped much faster than I expected. Much faster. Almost like he slammed his brakes for no reason.

Q: What did you do?

A: I braked. Hard. And I almost stopped in time—almost—but then I was hit from behind, which pushed me into him.

Q: You were struck from behind before your vehicle made contact with the vehicle ahead?

A: Yes! Exactly. Finally. Yes. That's what happened, and nobody seems to understand that. I was stopped—practically stopped—and then bam, from behind. The guy behind me caused this. He caused all of this.

Q: Did you see the vehicle behind you before the impact?

A: I saw headlights in my mirror. Close. Too close. He was tailgating me.

Q: For how long?

A: At least a mile. Maybe more. I remember thinking, this guy is going to cause an accident. And then he did.

topic: A paramedic is questioned about the response time and treatment at an accident scene
text:

A: Cervical stabilization. Standard protocol.

topic: A financial advisor is deposed about investment decisions made on a client's behalf
text:
Q: Mr. Harrington, I'd like to discuss the Westfield municipal bond allocation you made in Mrs. Patterson's portfolio in March of 2021. Do you recall that transaction?

A: I do, yes. The Westfield Infrastructure Series B bonds. We allocated approximately $340,000 of Mrs. Patterson's fixed-income holdings to that position.

Q: And what was your rationale for selecting those particular bonds?

A: Well, Mrs. Patterson had expressed a clear preference for tax-advantaged income given her retirement status. The Westfield bonds carried a AA- rating at the time, offered a 4.2% yield, and the municipality had an excellent debt service coverage ratio—I believe it was around 2.3x. The maturity schedule also aligned well with her projected income needs through 2035.

Q: You mentioned the rating. Did you conduct any independent analysis beyond the rating agency's assessment?

A: Absolutely. I reviewed three years of the municipality's audited financials, examined their pension obligations, looked at the regional economic indicators, and spoke with two analysts who covered that sector. I have all of that documented in my recommendation memorandum, which I believe has been produced in discovery.

Q: It has. Let's move on to the timing. Why March specifically?

A: The bonds came to market on March 8th, and I had been monitoring the issuance calendar for approximately six weeks waiting for them. We were able to participate in the initial offering, which meant we avoided any secondary market premium.

Q: So you were actively seeking this particular investment?

A: This type of investment, yes. When the Westfield issuance was announced, it fit the parameters I had established for Mrs. Patterson's portfolio almost exactly.

Q: Did you discuss this purchase with Mrs. Patterson before executing it?

A: I did. We spoke by phone on March 5th, I sent her a written summary of my analysis that evening, and she confirmed her approval via email the following morning. I'm happy to walk you through the email chain if that would be helpful.

Q: That won't be necessary at this time. The bonds have since matured, correct?

A: The first tranche matured in September of last year, yes. Principal returned in full, all coupon payments received on schedule. The remaining tranches are performing as expected.

Q: I have nothing further on this transaction.

A: Of course.

---

topic: A financial advisor is deposed about investment decisions made on a client's behalf
text:
Q: Mr. Okonkwo, I want to be very precise here. You're telling me that you rebalanced the Hendricks Family Trust portfolio in February 2022 without explicit written authorization?

A: No, that's not what I said. I said the rebalancing was conducted pursuant to the discretionary authority granted in the investment management agreement.

Q: But you didn't obtain specific approval for the February trades?

A: Specific approval wasn't required. The IMA grants me discretionary authority to rebalance within the established asset allocation bands. The February trades were within those parameters.

Q: Let's look at the IMA then. I'm showing you Exhibit 14.

A: I'm familiar with it.

Q: Section 4.2 states that discretionary authority applies to, quote, "routine rebalancing transactions not to exceed 5% of total portfolio value in any calendar quarter." Did the February trades exceed that threshold?

A: They did not.

Q: What was the total value of the February transactions?

A: Approximately $1.2 million, against a portfolio valued at roughly $31 million at that time. That's less than 4%.

Q: Fine. Now, the rebalancing reduced equity exposure by approximately 8 percentage points, correct?

A: Correct. We moved from 64% to 56% equity allocation.

Q: That's a significant shift.

A: It was a shift within the allowable band of 50% to 70% equity exposure, as specified in the investment policy statement. Section 2.1, if you'd like to reference it.

Q: I'm aware of the IPS. My question is whether such a significant reduction warranted consultation with the trustees regardless of your technical authority.

A: I spoke with Eleanor Hendricks, the primary trustee, on February 3rd. She was aware of my concerns about equity valuations and supported the defensive posture. I have notes from that call.

Q: But no written authorization.

A: None was required. None was requested. The conversation was informational, not a request for permission.

Q: The market declined substantially in the weeks following your rebalancing, did it not?

A: It did.

topic: A financial advisor is deposed about investment decisions made on a client's behalf

Mr. Morrison initialed each page of that summary.

topic: A financial advisor is deposed about investment decisions made on a client's behalf
text:
Q: Dr. Anand-Patel, you mentioned earlier that you viewed the Chen account as requiring a conservative approach. Tell me what that meant in practice.

Q: And yet, in June of 2020, you allocated 8% of the Chen portfolio to growth equities. How do you reconcile that?

A: Approximately 10%, which represents both the appreciation of those holdings and a small additional allocation we made in early 2023.

Q: At her request?

A: At her request, yes. She asked whether we might add a bit more. Her words.

Q: One final question on this account. Any regrets about your recommendations?

A: None.

Q: None at all?

A: None at all.

topic: A driver is deposed about the events leading up to a multi-vehicle collision
text:
Q: Please state your name for the record.

Q: Mr. Reeves, you were driving the silver Honda Accord on the morning of March 15th, correct?

A: That's correct.

Q: And what time did you leave your residence that morning?

A: 7:42 a.m. I checked my phone before pulling out of the driveway.

Q: You checked your phone while in the vehicle?

A: While parked, yes. I looked at the time, put the phone in the center console, and then I drove. I don't use my phone while driving.

Q: Fair enough. Now, as you approached the intersection of Miller Road and Highway 9, what lane were you traveling in?

A: The right lane. I was planning to turn right onto the highway on-ramp about a quarter mile past that intersection.

Q: And what was your speed at that point?

A: Between 35 and 40 miles per hour. The speed limit there is 45, so I was actually under it.

Q: How do you know your exact speed?

A: I glanced at my speedometer. I do it regularly. It's a habit.

Q: Did you observe the traffic light at that intersection?

A: I did. It was green when I entered the intersection and green when I was in the middle of it.

Q: You're certain it was green?

A: I'm certain. I watched it turn green from yellow about 200 feet before I reached it. I remember thinking I wouldn't have to brake.

Q: What happened next?

A: The pickup truck ran the red light coming from my left and struck the minivan in front of me. The minivan spun, and I couldn't avoid it.

---

topic: A driver is deposed about the events leading up to a multi-vehicle collision
text:

topic: A driver is deposed about the events leading up to a multi-vehicle collision
text:
Q: Mr. Dominguez, I want to be very precise about timing here. You've testified that you saw the white sedan run the stop sign.

A: Yes.

A: I don't know exactly. A few seconds. I'm not a stopwatch.

A: I did try to stop.

topic: A driver is deposed about the events leading up to a multi-vehicle collision
text:
Q: State your name, please.

A: David Robert Thornton.

Q: Mr. Thornton, you were the driver of the delivery truck, correct?

A: The Hendricks Plumbing Supply truck, yes sir.

Q: How long have you been a commercial driver?

A: Nineteen years this past February. Started when I was 23.

Q: And in those 19 years, how many accidents have you been involved in?

A: Before this one? Zero. Not a single at-fault accident in 19 years.

Q: That's an impressive record.

A: I take my job seriously.

Q: Let's discuss March 15th. What was your cargo that day?

A: Copper piping, PVC fittings, and two commercial water heaters. I have the manifest if you need it.

Q: That won't be necessary at this time. How did the weight of that cargo affect your stopping distance?

A: It increases it. That's basic physics. A loaded truck doesn't stop like an empty one.

Q: So you were aware that your stopping distance was extended.

A: Of course I was aware. That's why I was keeping a six-second following distance instead of the standard four.

Q: How do you know it was six seconds?

A: Because I count. I've counted following distance every day for 19 years. I pick a fixed point, and I count. One-one-thousand, two-one-thousand. Six seconds that morning.

Q: And yet you still struck the vehicle in front of you.

A: After two other vehicles collided and came to a dead stop in front of me, yes. I reduced a 45-mile-per-hour impact to maybe 8 or 9 miles per hour. I did that. My training did that.

topic: A driver is deposed about the events leading up to a multi-vehicle collision
text:
Q: Walk me through what you did after you first saw the brake lights ahead of you.

A: It covered it, yes. They explained how it works and what to do if it engages.

Q: Did you attempt to steer around the obstacle?

A: I started to, but there was a car to my left and a guardrail to my right. I had nowhere to go.

Q: So you made a judgment call to stay in your lane and brake.

A: I made the only call I could make. And I'd make the same one again.

topic: A pharmacist is deposed about a prescription that was filled with the wrong dosage
