topic: A pharmacist is deposed about a prescription that was filled with the wrong dosage
text:
Q: Good morning. Please state your full name for the record.

A: Linda Chen.

Q: And you're the pharmacist-in-charge at MedFirst Pharmacy on Delancey Street?

A: I am.

Q: How long have you held that position?

A: Seven years this September.

Q: Let me direct your attention to the prescription for Dorothy Walsh, filled on or about January 8th. Do you recall that prescription?

A: Yes, I'm familiar with it.

Q: You're familiar with it because of this lawsuit?

A: I'm familiar with it because a patient was harmed and I take that seriously.

Q: Let's talk about what happened. The prescription was for metoprolol 25 milligrams twice daily, correct?

A: Correct.

Q: And Mrs. Walsh received metoprolol 100 milligrams?

A: That's correct.

Q: Four times the prescribed dose.

A: I can do arithmetic, counsel.

Q: I'm just establishing the facts. Four times the dose?

A: Yes. Four times.

Q: And she was eighty-three years old?

A: She was.

Q: With a documented history of bradycardia?

A: Which I was not aware of at the time of filling, because her prescriber did not include that information and her insurance profile didn't flag it.

Q: Are you saying this is the prescriber's fault?

A: I'm saying I answered your question about her medical history. Would you like to ask another one?

---

topic: A pharmacist is deposed about a prescription that was filled with the wrong dosage
text:
Q: Let's go back to the label printing process. You said the label is generated automatically?

A: Yes.

Q: By the computer system?

A: Yes, by the dispensing software.

Q: And you trust that system?

A: I—trust isn't really the right word. I verify against the system.

Q: But you didn't catch the error on November 2nd, did you?

A: No.

Q: So the verification failed?

A: On that occasion, yes.

Q: On that occasion. How many other occasions?

A: I'm not aware of any others.

Q: In your entire career?

A: In my career at this location, involving this type of error, I'm not aware of any others.

Q: That's a lot of qualifiers, Mr. Brooks.

A: I'm trying to be precise. I thought that's what you wanted.

Q: What I want is a straight answer. Have you ever dispensed the wrong dosage before?

A: Not that resulted in patient harm.

Q: So you have dispensed wrong dosages before?

A: If we're including near-misses that were caught at the counter, then statistically, over fifteen years, yes, there have been catches. That's why we have a verification process.

Q: The process that failed.

A: The process that failed once. Yes.

Q: That you know of.

A: That I know of.

---

topic: A pharmacist is deposed about a prescription that was filled with the wrong dosage
text:
Q: I'm going to show you what's been marked as Exhibit 14. Do you recognize this document?

A: Yes.

Q: What is it?

A: It's a printout from our pharmacy management system showing the prescription entry for Mr. Okonkwo.

Q: And the dosage field—what does it show?

A: It shows 50 milligrams.

Q: But the physician's order was for 5 milligrams, wasn't it?

A: Apparently, yes.

Q: Apparently? You've seen the original prescription?

A: I have.

Q: And it clearly says 5 milligrams, doesn't it?

A: The handwriting is not—look, it says 5. I accept that it says 5.

Q: So someone entered 50 instead of 5?

A: Someone entered 50. That's what the system shows.

Q: Who?

A: The entry log shows my credentials.

Q: Your credentials?

A: Yes.

Q: So you entered it?

A: My credentials were used. I don't—I'm not going to sit here and tell you I remember typing those specific keystrokes six months ago.

Q: But you're not denying it was you?

A: I'm not denying my credentials were used. No, I'm not denying that.

Q: Is there anyone else who had access to your credentials?

A: No. That would be a violation of policy.

Q: So it was you.

A: It was my login. Yes.

---

topic: A pharmacist is deposed about a prescription that was filled with the wrong dosage
text:
Q: Ms. Yamamoto, is it your testimony that you followed all standard protocols on the day in question?

A: To the best of my recollection, yes.

Q: All of them?

A: Yes, all of them.

Q: Including the triple-check verification?

A: Yes.

Q: Let me read from your pharmacy's own policy manual, page 47: "The pharmacist shall visually compare the original prescription against the label and the medication in the vial before releasing to the patient." Did you do that?

A: I did.

Q: You visually compared all three?

A: I did.

Q: And somehow you didn't notice that the bottle said 200 milligrams when the prescription said 20?

A: I—the bottles are similar. The labels—

Q: I'm sorry, the bottles are similar?

A: The manufacturer uses nearly identical packaging for the 20 and the 200. It's a known issue in the industry.

Q: A known issue. Did you report it?

A: I have now.

Q: After the lawsuit was filed?

A: Yes.

Q: But not before?

A: I didn't think—it wasn't—no. Not before.

Q: So this known issue in the industry, you knew about it, and you didn't flag it, and you didn't catch it?

A: That's what happened.

Q: You seem to be placing a lot of responsibility on the packaging.

A: I'm explaining a contributing factor. I'm not placing responsibility anywhere. I made an error. I've said that. I don't know what else you want me to say.

topic: A witness is asked about a car accident they saw from their front porch
text:
Q: Good afternoon. Could you please state your name for the record?

A: Margaret Ellen Holloway.

Q: Ms. Holloway, I understand you were home on the afternoon of September 14th. Is that correct?

A: Yes, I was home all day. I'd taken the day off to wait for a furniture delivery that never came, actually, but that's neither here nor there.

Q: And where were you in your home around 3:15 that afternoon?

A: On my front porch. I have a swing out there, and I like to sit with my coffee and watch the birds at the feeder. I'd been there maybe twenty minutes by that point.

Q: Can you describe what you observed from that position?

A: Well, the blue sedan—I believe it was a Honda, maybe an Accord—was traveling westbound on Maple. The pickup truck was coming from the opposite direction. The sedan drifted over the center line, and the truck tried to swerve but couldn't avoid it. They collided near the front driver's side of the truck.

Q: When you say the sedan drifted, can you elaborate on what you mean?

A: It was gradual. Not a sudden jerk. Like the driver wasn't paying attention, or maybe was reaching for something. The car just eased over, almost lazy-like, if that makes sense.

Q: Did you observe the driver of the sedan before the collision?

A: I couldn't see through the windshield clearly from my angle. The glare was pretty strong that time of day.

Q: What did you do after the collision occurred?

A: I set my coffee down, went inside to get my phone, and called 911. Then I walked down to the street to see if anyone needed help.

Q: Approximately how long did that take?

A: Oh, maybe two minutes total. I'm not as quick on my feet as I used to be, but I didn't dawdle.

Q: Thank you. When you reached the vehicles, what did you observe?

A: The man in the truck was already out, standing by his door. He seemed shaken but upright. The woman in the sedan was still in her seat. She was conscious, talking, but her airbag had deployed and she looked disoriented.

Q: Did you speak with either driver?

A: Briefly. I told them help was on the way and asked if they were hurt. The woman said her chest hurt. The man just kept saying he didn't see her coming over.

---

topic: A witness is asked about a car accident they saw from their front porch
text:
Q: Please state your full name.

A: David Robert Chen.

Q: Mr. Chen, directing your attention to March 3rd of this year, were you present at your residence at 4847 Birchwood Lane?

A: I was.

Q: What were you doing at approximately 4:40 in the afternoon?

A: Sitting on my porch, having a cigarette. My wife doesn't let me smoke inside.

Q: And from your porch, do you have a view of the intersection of Birchwood and Crescent?

A: Clear view. Maybe sixty feet away.

Q: Tell me what you saw.

A: Gray minivan ran the stop sign. Black SUV was already in the intersection. SUV hit the minivan on the passenger side.

Q: You said the minivan ran the stop sign. Did you actually see the minivan approach the sign?

A: Yes.

Q: Did the minivan slow at all?

A: Didn't appear to.

Q: Did it stop?

A: No.

Q: How fast would you estimate the minivan was traveling?

A: I'm not good with speeds. Faster than you'd go if you were planning to stop.

Q: Would you say it was traveling at the posted speed limit?

A: I couldn't say for certain. It was moving with purpose.

Q: What about the SUV? Did you observe its approach?

A: I saw it come through the intersection. It had the right of way. No stop sign on Crescent.

Q: Did the SUV appear to brake before impact?

A: I heard brakes. Saw the nose dip. But there wasn't much time.

Q: After the collision, what happened?

A: Both vehicles came to rest in the middle of the intersection. I went inside to tell my wife to call 911.

---

topic: A witness is asked about a car accident they saw from their front porch
text:
Q: State your name, please.

A: Rosalind Vance.

Q: Ms. Vance, I want to ask you about what you witnessed on July 8th. You were on your front porch that evening?

A: That's right.

Q: What time was this?

A: Around seven, seven-fifteen. The sun was getting low.

Q: Was there anything obstructing your view of the street?

A: No. I have a straight shot to the road. My hedges are only about two feet high.

Q: Tell me what you saw.

A: I saw two cars collide.

Q: Can you be more specific?

A: A white car—some kind of sports car, I think—was going too fast down the street. A dark-colored sedan pulled out of a driveway. The white car hit it.

Q: Which driveway did the sedan pull out of?

A: The Pattersons'. Three houses down from me, on the same side of the street.

Q: You said the white car was going too fast. How did you determine that?

A: Because I could hear it before I saw it. The engine was loud. And when it passed my house, I remember thinking that's too fast for a residential street.

Q: Do you have any training in estimating vehicle speed?

A: No. I'm just someone who's lived on that street for eighteen years.

Q: Fair enough. Did the sedan stop before pulling into the road?

A: I don't know. I wasn't watching the driveway. I only noticed the sedan when it was already in the street.

Q: So you can't say whether the driver of the sedan looked for oncoming traffic?

A: No, I can't say that.

Q: What happened immediately after the collision?

A: The white car spun and ended up on the Nguyens' lawn. The sedan stayed in the road.

Q: Did you approach the vehicles?

A: Not right away. I waited to see if anyone got out first.

---

topic: A witness is asked about a car accident they saw from their front porch
text:
Q: For the record, please state your name.

A: Thomas Andrew Whitfield.

Q: Mr. Whitfield, you've been identified as a witness to an accident that occurred on October 12th on Sycamore Drive. Is that accurate?

A: That's accurate, yes.

Q: Where exactly were you when this accident occurred?

A: On my porch. I have a rocking chair out there. I was reading.

Q: Reading what, if you recall?

A: A biography of Theodore Roosevelt. Not that it's relevant.

Q: Just establishing the scene. What drew your attention away from your book?

A: The sound of tires. That high-pitched squeal.

Q: And when you looked up, what did you see?

A: I saw a red pickup truck skidding, trying to stop. There was a motorcycle in front of it.

Q: Can you describe the motorcycle?

A: Smaller bike. Not a Harley type. More like what the younger folks ride. Dark color—black or navy.

Q: What happened next?

A: The truck couldn't stop in time. It struck the rear of the motorcycle. The rider went down.

Q: Did you see what caused the truck to brake so suddenly?

A: The motorcycle had stopped short. There was a dog in the road—I saw it run off after the collision.

Q: A dog?

A: Yes. Medium-sized, brown and white. Ran off toward the Hendersons' yard.

Q: Did the motorcycle have any opportunity to avoid stopping?

A: I wouldn't know. I only looked up when I heard the tires.

Q: Did you see how closely the truck had been following the motorcycle before the braking began?

A: No. Like I said, I was reading. I only saw the last few seconds.

Q: After the rider went down, what did you do?

A: I set my book on the rail, walked to the street, and asked if he was alright. He was conscious but not moving much. I told someone to call for an ambulance.

---

topic: A witness is asked about a car accident they saw from their front porch
text:
Q: Your name for the record?

A: Patricia Simmons.

Q: Ms. Simmons, you live at 2201 Harker Avenue, correct?

A: Correct.

Q: And your porch faces the street?

A: It does. Faces east.

Q: On the morning of April 5th, you were outside on that porch?

A: I was. Having my tea and watching the neighborhood wake up. That's my routine.

Q: What time was this?

A: Just before eight. I remember because I was thinking about going inside to watch the morning news.

Q: Describe what you observed.

A: There was a school bus stopped on the street, about four houses down. Red lights flashing. A car came up behind it and tried to go around.

Q: When you say tried to go around, what do you mean?

A: The car pulled into the oncoming lane to pass the bus.

Q: And what happened?

A: A delivery truck was coming from the other direction. The car swerved back, clipped the rear of the bus, and then went onto the sidewalk.

Q: Was there any contact between the car and the delivery truck?

A: I don't believe so. The car swerved in time to avoid the truck, but that's what sent it into the bus and then onto the sidewalk.

Q: Were there children outside the bus at that time?

A: No. Thank goodness. The bus had just stopped. No one had gotten off yet.

Q: Could you see the driver of the car at any point?

A: Not clearly. I could see a figure, a man I think, but I couldn't make out features.

Q: After the car went onto the sidewalk, what did you observe?

A: It came to a stop against a tree in front of the Dooleys' house. The driver got out, looked at the damage, and then just stood there with his hands on his head.

Q: Did you hear him say anything?

A: From that distance? No. But his body language said plenty.

Q: Did you remain on your porch?

A: For a bit. Then I walked down to make sure everyone on the bus was alright. The driver was already on her radio. No one seemed hurt.

topic: A witness is questioned about a conversation they overheard in a company hallway
text:
Q: Let's turn to the afternoon of March 14th. You were in the east hallway on the third floor, correct?

A: I was.

Q: And you overheard a conversation between two individuals?

A: I've already said that, yes.

Q: I'm asking you again for the record. Did you overhear a conversation?

A: Yes.

Q: Who was speaking?

A: Mr. Hendricks and someone else. A woman.

Q: You don't know who the woman was?

A: I didn't see her face. I was at the water fountain. I heard voices around the corner.

Q: But you're certain it was Mr. Hendricks?

A: I worked with the man for six years. I know his voice.

Q: What did you hear Mr. Hendricks say?

A: Something about the quarterly numbers. That they needed to "handle it" before the board meeting.

Q: "Handle it." Those were his exact words?

A: That's what I heard. I'm not a tape recorder, counsel. I'm telling you what I remember.

Q: I'm not suggesting you're a tape recorder. I'm asking if you're certain about the phrasing.

A: I'm certain enough.

topic: A witness is questioned about a conversation they overheard in a company hallway
text:
Q: You stated in your written statement that you were present in the hallway near Conference Room B on the afternoon in question. Is that accurate?

A: That's what I wrote, yes.

Q: What were you doing there?

A: Waiting for a meeting. The room was occupied, so I was standing outside.

Q: For how long?

A: I don't know, maybe five minutes. Maybe a little longer. I wasn't timing myself.

Q: During those five minutes, did you observe anyone exit the conference room?

A: No.

Q: Did you hear anything from inside the room?

A: The door was closed.

Q: That's not what I asked. Did you hear anything?

A: I heard muffled voices. I couldn't make out words.

Q: So when you wrote in your statement that you heard Mr. Tran say—and I'm quoting—"We need to bury this before compliance finds out," you couldn't actually hear the words clearly?

A: That was in the hallway. After. He came out with Ms. Patel and they were talking as they walked past me.

Q: So they were walking. Moving away from you?

A: They passed right by me. I was three feet away.

Q: And they didn't lower their voices? Didn't stop talking when they saw you?

A: I don't think they noticed me.

Q: You don't think?

A: They didn't notice me. I was looking at my phone. People don't pay attention to someone staring at their phone.

topic: A witness is questioned about a conversation they overheard in a company hallway
text:
Q: Ms. Cortez, how long have you worked at Denning & Associates?

A: Fourteen years this October. If we're still counting.

Q: What do you mean by that?

A: I mean I've been on administrative leave for two months now, so I'm not sure what counts anymore.

Q: I see. Let's focus on February 22nd. You were on the fourth floor that day?

A: I worked on the fourth floor every day.

Q: Around 2 p.m., did you observe anything unusual in the hallway near the elevators?

A: Depends on your definition of unusual.

Q: I'm asking you, Ms. Cortez. In your judgment.

A: Fine. I saw David Okonkwo and Raj Mehta having what looked like a heated discussion.

Q: "Heated." What made it appear heated?

A: Mr. Okonkwo was pointing his finger. His voice was raised. Mr. Mehta had his arms crossed and kept shaking his head.

Q: Did you hear what they were discussing?

A: Parts of it.

Q: What parts?

A: Mr. Okonkwo said something about how "this is exactly what the auditors are going to find." Mr. Mehta said they needed to talk somewhere private.

Q: Then what happened?

A: Then Mr. Mehta looked over and saw me standing there, and they both stopped talking and walked toward the stairwell. So I don't know what else you want me to tell you.

topic: A witness is questioned about a conversation they overheard in a company hallway
text:
Q: Where exactly were you standing when this conversation took place?

A: Near the supply closet. Across from the break room.

Q: How far from the individuals speaking?

A: I don't know. Fifteen feet? Twenty?

Q: Fifteen or twenty?

A: I didn't measure it.

Q: I'm asking for your best estimate.

A: And I gave you a range. Fifteen to twenty feet.

Q: Was there anything obstructing your line of sight?

A: No.

Q: Any ambient noise? Machinery, other conversations?

A: There might have been some background noise. The copier was running, I think. Or the printer. One of them.

Q: Could that have affected your ability to hear clearly?

A: I heard what I heard.

Q: Let me ask it differently. Is it possible you misheard portions of the conversation?

A: Anything's possible.

Q: That's not a responsive answer.

A: It's the only answer I have. I'm telling you what I heard. I'm not going to sit here and say I'm 100 percent certain of every syllable because that would be a lie. But I heard them talking about moving money between accounts before the end of the fiscal year. That I'm sure of.

Q: Who said that specifically?

A: Mr. Warren. He said they needed to "clean this up" before anyone noticed.

Q: And the other person?

A: Just nodded. Didn't say much.

topic: A witness is questioned about a conversation they overheard in a company hallway
text:
Q: You've testified that you were walking toward your office when you heard voices. Let's slow down. What time was this?

A: Late afternoon. Maybe 4:30.

Q: Maybe?

A: Somewhere around 4:30. I wasn't checking my watch.

Q: Was anyone else in the hallway?

A: Not that I saw.

Q: You were alone?

A: Yes.

Q: And the voices you heard—where were they coming from?

A: The alcove near the emergency exit. Where the vending machines are.

Q: Could you see who was speaking?

A: Not initially. I came around the corner and then I could see them.

Q: Who did you see?

A: Brenda Walsh and Tom Schiller.

Q: What were they doing?

A: Standing close together. Talking quietly.

Q: Did they see you?

A: I don't know. I didn't stop. I kept walking.

Q: But you heard part of their conversation as you passed?

A: A few words.

Q: What words?

A: Ms. Walsh said something like "they can't prove anything if the emails are gone."

Q: You're sure she said "emails"?

A: I know what I heard, counsel.

Q: I'm simply asking—

A: And I've simply answered. Three times now. She said emails. She said "if the emails are gone." Do you need me to say it again, or can we move on?

topic: A paramedic is questioned about the response time and treatment at an accident scene
text:
Q: Let's talk about the timeline. What time did you arrive at the scene?

A: 14:47.

Q: And what time was the call dispatched?

A: 14:31.

Q: So sixteen minutes from dispatch to arrival?

A: That's the math, yes.

Q: Is sixteen minutes a typical response time for your unit?

A: It depends on the circumstances.

Q: What circumstances?

A: Traffic. Distance. Road conditions. Weather. Whether we're coming from the station or from another call. Do you want me to keep going?

Q: I'm simply trying to understand whether sixteen minutes was reasonable.

A: And I'm telling you it depends on the circumstances.

Q: Fine. What were the circumstances that day?

A: We were returning from a call on the west side. The accident was on Route 9, which is approximately seven miles from our location at the time of dispatch. There was construction on Miller Road, which is the most direct route, so we had to reroute.

Q: Did you consider using your lights and sirens to move through the construction zone?

A: We had lights and sirens active the entire time. Construction doesn't disappear because you turn on a siren.

Q: So you're saying there was nothing you could have done to arrive sooner?

A: I'm saying we arrived as quickly as we could given the actual conditions that existed in the actual world on that actual day.

Q: Is that your professional opinion?

A: That's a fact.

topic: A paramedic is questioned about the response time and treatment at an accident scene
text:
Q: When you first assessed Mr. Thornton at the scene, what did you observe?

A: He was conscious, alert, complaining of neck pain and pain in his left leg. There was visible deformity to the left tibia. Abrasions on his face and arms consistent with contact with broken glass.

Q: Did you immobilize his spine?

A: Yes.

Q: Immediately?

A: Yes, immediately. That's standard protocol for any patient presenting with neck pain after a motor vehicle collision.

Q: I'm not questioning protocol. I'm asking what you did.

A: And I answered. We immobilized his spine.

Q: Using what equipment?

A: Cervical collar and a long spine board.

Q: Now, the leg injury—did you splint it at the scene?

A: We did.

Q: How long did that take?

A: I don't have an exact number. Several minutes.

Q: Several meaning what? Two? Ten?

A: I didn't have a stopwatch running. We were treating a patient.

Q: But you would agree that splinting took time that could have been spent transporting him to the hospital?

A: No, I wouldn't agree with that.

Q: You wouldn't?

A: Moving a patient with an unstabilized fracture can cause additional injury. We splint before transport. That's not a delay. That's proper treatment.

Q: I see. So in your view, everything you did was textbook.

A: I didn't say textbook. I said proper.

topic: A paramedic is questioned about the response time and treatment at an accident scene
text:
Q: You mentioned earlier that your partner administered oxygen to the patient. Is that correct?

A: That's correct.

Q: At what point during your treatment did that occur?

A: Within the first minute or two of contact.

Q: Before or after you assessed her airway?

A: After. Obviously.

Q: Why obviously?

A: Because you assess the airway before you administer supplemental oxygen. That's basic emergency medicine.

Q: I'm just trying to establish the sequence, Mr. Reeves. I don't have your medical training.

A: It's the ABCs. Airway, breathing, circulation. It's taught in every first aid course in the country.

Q: Let's move on. What was the patient's oxygen saturation when you first measured it?

A: 94 percent.

Q: And is that concerning?

A: It's on the lower end of normal. We monitor it and provide supplemental oxygen as a precaution.

Q: Did her saturation improve?

A: It did.

Q: To what level?

A: 98 percent by the time we loaded her into the ambulance.

Q: And you attribute that improvement to the oxygen you administered?

A: I attribute it to appropriate medical intervention, yes.

Q: Not to the passage of time?

A: I'm not going to speculate about what would have happened if we hadn't treated her. That's not how medicine works. You treat the patient in front of you.

topic: A paramedic is questioned about the response time and treatment at an accident scene
text:
Q: Mr. Hastings, walk me through the first sixty seconds after you arrived on scene.

A: We pulled up, I grabbed the jump bag, my partner grabbed the monitor and backboard. We approached the vehicle. The driver was slumped against the steering wheel. Passenger was conscious, yelling for help.

Q: Which patient did you attend to first?

A: The driver.

Q: Because he appeared more seriously injured?

A: Because he was unresponsive.

Q: Let me ask it this way. Did you make a triage decision?

A: Every call involves triage decisions.

Q: I understand that. I'm asking whether you consciously chose—

A: Yes. I consciously chose to assess the unresponsive patient before the conscious one. Is that what you're looking for?

Q: I'm looking for accurate testimony about what happened that day.

A: And I'm giving it to you.

Q: Let's slow down. When you reached the driver, what was his condition?

A: Unresponsive to verbal stimuli. Shallow breathing. Pulse present but weak.

Q: Did you attempt to remove him from the vehicle?

A: Not immediately. We needed to assess for spinal injury and ensure the scene was safe. There was fluid leaking from the engine compartment.

Q: What kind of fluid?

A: I'm a paramedic, not a mechanic. It was a fluid. It could have been flammable. We made sure fire was en route before we extricated.

Q: How long did that delay your treatment?

A: It didn't delay treatment. Assessment is treatment. Ensuring the scene is safe is treatment. We don't just yank people out of cars.

topic: A paramedic is questioned about the response time and treatment at an accident scene
text:
Q: The dispatch notes indicate the call was coded as a priority two. Do you see that?

A: I see what the notes say.

Q: What does priority two mean?

A: It means the call was categorized as urgent but not immediately life-threatening based on the information available to dispatch at the time.

Q: So not the highest priority.

A: Correct.

Q: If it had been coded priority one, would you have responded differently?

A: Our lights and sirens were already activated. We were already responding as quickly as conditions allowed.

Q: That's not what I asked. I asked if you would have responded differently.

A: And I'm explaining that there was no different way to respond. We were already at maximum response.

Q: So the coding made no difference whatsoever.

A: In terms of our response? No.

Q: Then why have coding at all?

A: You'd have to ask dispatch. I don't design the system.

Q: But you work within it.

A: Yes. And on that day, within that system, we responded appropriately.

Q: Let me ask this differently. If you had been told a patient was in cardiac arrest—

A: But we weren't told that.

Q: I'm asking a hypothetical.

A: I don't answer hypotheticals about calls that didn't happen. I can tell you what we did on the call that did happen. We responded in four minutes, arrived on scene, and treated the patient. That's what the record shows, and that's what occurred.

topic: A daycare worker is deposed about an injury a child sustained while in their care
text:
Q: Ms. Hernandez, you were working in the Sunshine Room on March 14th, correct?

A: Yes.

Q: And that's the room for children ages two to three?

A: Two to four, actually.

Q: I apologize. Two to four. Now, at approximately 2:15 p.m., you were the only staff member present in that room, weren't you?

A: I was the only one in the room at that exact moment, yes, but I need to clarify that—

Q: I'm just asking about that moment right now. One staff member, twelve children?

A: It was eleven children. Mia Chen had been picked up early.

Q: Eleven children, one staff member. Is that within your facility's ratio guidelines?

A: It's within state guidelines, yes.

Q: I asked about your facility's guidelines.

A: I'd have to look at the handbook to give you the exact number. I don't want to guess.

Q: You've worked there for six years and you don't know the staff-to-child ratio?

A: I know the state ratio. I follow the state ratio. If you want the specific number from our handbook, I can tell you it meets or exceeds state requirements.

Q: Let's talk about when Oliver fell. You were across the room?

A: I was approximately eight feet away, maybe ten. I was helping another child.

A: It really is. They become like family, honestly. Every single one of them.

Q: I'd like to ask you about November 14th, specifically about a child named Oliver Chen.

A: Oliver. Yes. I think about that day a lot, if I'm being honest with you.

Q: Take your time. Can you describe what happened that morning?

A: We were doing free play—that's usually around 9:30. Oliver was at the block station. He loved blocks. He'd build these towers, and the way his face would light up when they got really tall—anyway. He was building, and then he turned to show me, and his foot caught the edge of the play mat.

Q: What happened when his foot caught the mat?

A: He fell forward. His chin hit the corner of the wooden shelf. I was maybe six feet away, and I just—I got to him as fast as I could. I keep thinking if I'd been closer, maybe I could have caught him.

Q: You were six feet away. Is that consistent with your supervision protocols?

A: It is. We're supposed to maintain visual supervision and be within reasonable proximity. I was watching him. I saw the whole thing happen, which almost makes it worse, you know?

Q: What did you do immediately after he fell?

A: I scooped him up—gently, supporting his head—and I talked to him the whole time. I said, "It's okay, sweetheart, Miss Maria's got you." I could see the cut right away. There was blood, and he was crying, but I kept my voice calm for him.

Q: Then what happened?

A: I called for my co-teacher, Angela, to take over the room, and I carried Oliver to the director's office. We have a first aid station there. I held gauze to his chin and just kept telling him he was so brave, he was doing so good.

Q: Did you contact his parents at that point?

A: Mrs. Chen—his mom—yes. I called her myself. I wanted her to hear it from me, not just from the director reading an incident report. She deserved that.

Q: What did you tell her?

A: The truth. That her little boy got hurt and that I was so sorry. That we were taking care of him and he was being so brave. I could hear her panic, and I just—I wanted her to know he wasn't alone. That someone who loved him was right there with him.

A: We were outside for recess. Sophia was on the climbing structure with two other kids. I was stationed at the swings—that was my assigned zone. I heard her scream before I saw anything.

Q: What did you see when you turned toward the sound?

A: She was on the ground. On her back. The other kids were standing on the platform looking down at her.

Q: What was your reaction?

A: I ran to her. Faster than I've ever run, I think. I kept saying her name—"Sophia, Sophia, can you hear me?"—and she was crying, which was actually a relief because it meant she was conscious.

Q: Did you move her?

A: No. No, I didn't move her. I knelt down next to her and I held her hand and told her to stay very still, that she was going to be okay, that I was right there.

Q: Why didn't you move her?

A: Because I didn't know if she'd hurt her neck or her back. You're not supposed to move someone if there's a chance of spinal injury. So I just stayed with her. I kept my hand on hers and I kept talking to her—about her dog, actually. She talks about her dog all the time, Biscuit. I asked her to tell me about Biscuit.

Q: Did that help?

A: I think so. She stopped screaming. She was still crying, but she started talking about how Biscuit sleeps at the foot of her bed. It gave her something else to focus on.

Q: What happened next?

A: My co-teacher, Janet, called 911. And I stayed right there on the ground with Sophia until the paramedics arrived. I didn't leave her side. I wouldn't.

A: I was at her side before she even started crying. That's the thing about little ones—there's that pause, that moment of shock before the tears come. I used that moment to pick her up, cradle her against my chest, and start moving toward the first aid kit.

Q: You picked her up immediately?

A: She wasn't unconscious. She was looking at me with these big scared eyes. She needed to be held. That was what she needed right then.

A: I followed what Emma needed and what our protocols required. Those things don't have to be in conflict. I applied pressure to the wound. I kept my voice soft and steady. I said, "You're okay, sweetheart. That was a big bump, but you're so brave. I've got you."

A: I mean she was terrified. And children look to adults to know how to feel. If I had panicked, she would have panicked more. So I made a choice to be the calm she needed, even though my heart was pounding.

A: I sat in the rocking chair with her while my supervisor called her parents. I rocked her and sang—quietly, so I wouldn't wake the other kids. "You Are My Sunshine." She asked me to keep singing it, so I did. Until her dad got there.

A: I recall it was morning. Mid-morning. I don't have the exact time in my memory.

Q: During your 8:00 a.m. inspection, did you walk through aisle seven?

A: The inspection covers all aisles.

Q: That's not what I asked. Did you personally walk through aisle seven?

A: Yes. That would be—yes.

Q: And you observed no hazards?

A: I didn't note any.

topic: A store manager is questioned about a customer slip-and-fall on their premises
text:
Q: Mr. Reeves, I want to understand the timeline here. The incident occurred at 8:47 a.m.?

A: Approximately, yes.

Q: When were you first notified?

A: I heard someone—a customer, I think—call out. I was in the back office.

Q: How long did it take you to reach Mrs. Patterson?

A: I moved quickly. Maybe a minute.

Q: Maybe a minute. Could it have been longer?

A: I don't—it could have been ninety seconds? I was hurrying.

Q: And what did you observe when you arrived?

A: Mrs. Patterson was on the ground. She was—she seemed to be in pain. Her leg was—she was holding her leg.

Q: Was anyone else present?

A: Derek was there. He was kneeling next to her.

Q: Derek Hollins?

A: Yes.

Q: What was Mr. Hollins doing?

A: He was asking if she was okay. Trying to help.

Q: Did you have a conversation with Mr. Hollins about what happened?

A: Briefly. At some point that morning.

Q: What did he tell you?

A: He said—I don't want to misquote him.

Q: Just your best recollection.

A: He said he had been mopping in that area earlier.

Q: Earlier meaning when?

A: I don't know exactly. Before.

Q: Did he say whether he'd put up a wet floor sign?

A: He said he had.

Q: He said he put up a sign?

A: That's what he told me.

Q: But you testified earlier that you didn't see a sign when you arrived.

A: I didn't see one. That's correct. I'm just telling you what Derek said.

Q: Did you ask him where the sign was?

A: I don't remember if I specifically—I may have. I don't remember his answer.

topic: A store manager is questioned about a customer slip-and-fall on their premises
text:
Q: Let's move on. Are you aware that Mrs. Patterson suffered a fractured hip?

A: I—yes. I understand she was injured.

Q: A fractured hip requiring surgery. Were you aware of that?

A: I don't know the medical details.

Q: Have you ever had any other slip-and-fall incidents at your store?

A: Incidents happen in retail.

Q: That's not responsive. Have there been other slip-and-fall incidents at your location? Yes or no.

A: Yes.

Q: How many in the past three years?

A: I don't have that number.

Q: More than five?

A: I'd have to review the records.

Q: More than ten?

A: I genuinely don't know. I'm not trying to be difficult. We document incidents, and I would need to look at the documentation.

Q: Who maintains those records?

A: Corporate receives copies. I keep copies at the store.

Q: And you didn't bring those records today?

A: I wasn't asked to bring—I brought what I was asked to bring.

Q: Were you asked to bring incident reports?

A: The subpoena referenced the March 14th incident specifically.

Q: Mr. Reeves, have you had conversations with anyone about limiting your testimony today?

A: I spoke with corporate counsel about the deposition.

Q: And what were you told?

A: To answer truthfully.

Q: Anything else?

A: To answer the questions asked.

Q: Nothing else?

A: No. Just—no.

topic: A store manager is questioned about a customer slip-and-fall on their premises
text:
Q: Okay. Mr. Reeves. Let's go back to something. You mentioned a mopping protocol.

A: I mentioned that we have protocols, yes.

Q: What is the protocol when an employee mops a floor?

A: Put up signage, use the proper solution, let it dry adequately before removing the sign.

Q: What signage specifically?

A: The yellow wet floor signs. We have several.

Q: Several. How many?

A: I think—four? Maybe five in the store.

Q: Where are they kept?

A: Utility closet in the back. And there might be one near the front registers.

Q: On March 14th, were all of those signs accounted for?

A: I didn't count them.

Q: After the incident—did you check?

A: I don't recall specifically checking the inventory of signs.

Q: Would that have been a reasonable step to take?

A: I suppose—I was focused on the customer. On making sure she received medical attention.

Q: Of course. And after that?

A: After that, there were reports to file. Calls to make.

Q: But at no point did you verify whether a sign had been deployed?

A: I—no. I took Derek at his word.

Q: You took the word of the employee who had just mopped the floor where a customer fell?

A: Derek is a reliable employee.

Q: That wasn't my question.

A: Could you repeat the question?

Q: You took the word of the employee who mopped that floor, rather than independently verifying whether he'd put up a warning sign. Is that correct?

A: In retrospect—yes. That's what happened.

topic: A supervisor is deposed about performance reviews given to an employee who was later fired
text:
Q: Mr. Harmon, you conducted the 2022 annual performance review for Jessica Tillman, correct?

A: That's what the document says.

Q: I'm asking if you personally conducted it.

A: If my signature's on it, then yes.

Q: Do you recall the substance of that review?

A: Not particularly.

Q: She received a rating of "meets expectations" in all categories. Does that refresh your recollection?

A: Sure.

Q: What does "meets expectations" mean in your department?

A: It means what it sounds like. The employee is doing their job.

Q: Is that a positive assessment?

A: It's a neutral assessment. They're not exceeding, they're not failing. They're meeting.

Q: Six months later, Ms. Tillman was terminated for performance issues. How do you reconcile that with a "meets expectations" rating?

A: I don't reconcile anything. I fill out the forms they give me. HR makes termination decisions.

Q: You had no input into her termination?

A: I was consulted. I gave my opinion. They did what they did.

Q: What opinion did you give?

A: I don't remember the exact words. Probably that she was fine. Average.

topic: A supervisor is deposed about performance reviews given to an employee who was later fired
text:
Q: Let's talk about the performance improvement plan that was issued in March 2023.

A: Okay.

Q: You drafted that document?

A: I contributed to it. HR has templates.

Q: What specific deficiencies did you identify in Mr. Okonkwo's performance?

A: There were some issues with timeliness. Missing deadlines. I think there was something about communication with clients.

Q: You think, or you know?

A: It was over a year ago. I've supervised a lot of employees since then.

Q: This is a termination that resulted in litigation, Mr. Castillo. I'd expect you to remember.

A: Well, I don't remember every detail. I remember there were problems.

Q: Let me show you Exhibit 14. This is the PIP. Does this refresh your recollection?

A: Sure. Timeliness, client communication, attention to detail. That's what it says.

Q: Did Mr. Okonkwo's performance improve after this PIP was issued?

A: Somewhat.

Q: Somewhat. Can you quantify that?

A: No.

Q: Did you document any improvement or lack thereof?

A: I may have sent some emails. I don't know.

Q: You don't know if you documented an employee's progress on a formal improvement plan?

A: I'm sure I did something. I just don't have it memorized.

topic: A supervisor is deposed about performance reviews given to an employee who was later fired
text:
Q: Ms. Vance, how long did you supervise Darnell Washington?

A: A little over two years.

Q: And in that time, you completed two annual reviews for him?

A: That's right.

Q: The first review, in 2021, rated him as "exceeds expectations" in three of five categories.

A: If that's what the document shows.

Q: It does. I'm asking if you agreed with that assessment at the time.

A: I wrote it, so presumably I agreed with it.

Q: Presumably?

A: I agreed with it. Yes.

Q: The following year, his ratings dropped to "needs improvement" in two categories. What changed?

A: His performance changed.

Q: In what way?

A: He became less reliable. Started missing things.

Q: Missing things. Can you be more specific?

A: Deadlines. Details in reports. That sort of thing.

Q: Did anything happen in his personal life that you were aware of that might have affected his work?

A: I don't keep track of employees' personal lives.

Q: He didn't mention anything to you?

A: He may have. I don't recall.

Q: You don't recall if an employee who went from exceeding expectations to needing improvement explained why?

A: People's performance fluctuates. I documented what I observed. That's my job.

topic: A supervisor is deposed about performance reviews given to an employee who was later fired
text:
Q: Mr. Petersen, I want to understand your review process. Walk me through how you evaluate an employee.

A: There's a form. I fill it out once a year.

Q: Do you keep contemporaneous notes?

A: I might have.

A: I don't think so. I usually throw that stuff out after the review is done.

Q: Right. Moving on. You gave Ms. Chen a rating of "below expectations" in teamwork. What behaviors led to that rating?

Q: With whom?

A: With the team generally.

Q: Can you give me an example?

A: Not off the top of my head.

Q: Not a single example?

A: It was a general impression. She kept to herself. Didn't contribute in meetings.

Q: Did you ever discuss this concern with her directly?

A: I put it in the review. She saw the review.

A: I don't typically do that. The review is when we discuss performance.

topic: A supervisor is deposed about performance reviews given to an employee who was later fired
text:
Q: You mentioned earlier that Kevin Marsh had "potential." What did you mean by that?

A: He was smart. Quick learner. Had the raw ability to do well.

Q: But his reviews suggest otherwise. He received "needs improvement" in his final two review cycles.

A: Potential and performance aren't the same thing.

Q: Fair enough. What was preventing him from reaching that potential?

A: Various things.

Q: Such as?

A: Focus, probably. Follow-through.

Q: Did you try to help him improve in those areas?

A: I gave him feedback.

Q: What kind of feedback?

A: The usual. Told him what he needed to work on.

Q: How did he respond?

A: He said he understood.

Q: But his performance didn't improve?

A: Apparently not enough.

Q: Did you advocate for him to keep his job?

A: I don't remember if I was asked.

Q: If you had been asked, would you have?

A: Objection, calls for speculation.

Q: I'll rephrase. Did you believe Mr. Marsh should have been terminated?

A: I believed the company would make whatever decision it made. I provided my documentation. That's my role.

topic: A building inspector is deposed about a structural assessment they signed off on
text:
Q: Mr. Hendricks, you conducted the structural assessment of the Riverside Commons building on March 14th, 2022, correct?

A: I did, yes.

Q: And you signed off on that assessment as passing all required structural integrity standards?

A: That's correct. The building met every criterion under the municipal code, and frankly, it exceeded several of them. The load-bearing calculations were well within tolerance—better than most buildings I inspect in that district.

Q: What specific tests did you perform that day?

A: I conducted a visual inspection of all accessible structural members, performed deflection measurements on the primary floor joists, examined the foundation walls for cracking or moisture intrusion, and reviewed the original engineering documents against current conditions. I also took core samples from two of the concrete support columns, which I sent to Meridian Labs for compression testing.

Q: And the lab results?

A: Came back at 4,200 PSI. Code minimum is 3,000. So we were sitting at 140% of the required strength. I actually made a note of that in my report because it's not something you see every day with a building of that age.

Q: You made a note specifically because the results were favorable?

A: I made a note because they were notable. When something stands out—good or bad—I document it. That's thorough inspection work.

Q: How long did the entire inspection take?

A: Just under four hours on-site, plus another two hours for report preparation and documentation review.

Q: Is that typical for a building of that size?

A: It's actually longer than typical. I wanted to be comprehensive. There had been some water damage reported the previous year, so I paid extra attention to any areas that might have been affected. Found no structural compromise whatsoever.

Q: Let's move on to the basement level—

A: Happy to. That was actually the strongest part of the building, structurally speaking.

topic: A building inspector is deposed about a structural assessment they signed off on
text:
Q: State your name for the record.

A: Patricia Okonkwo.

Q: Ms. Okonkwo, how long have you been a licensed building inspector in this state?

A: Seventeen years.

Q: And in those seventeen years, approximately how many structural assessments have you conducted?

A: I'd estimate somewhere between eight hundred and a thousand.

Q: You inspected the Garfield Street property on or about June 3rd, 2023?

A: I did.

Q: What was the purpose of that inspection?

A: Pre-sale structural assessment requested by the buyer's mortgage lender.

Q: What did you find?

A: Significant deterioration in the rear support beam. Termite damage that had compromised roughly 40% of the beam's cross-section.

Q: And yet you signed off on the assessment.

A: I signed off on the assessment with conditions. The report clearly stated that the sale could proceed contingent on repair of the identified deficiency within 60 days.

Q: So the building did not pass in its current condition?

A: The building passed with a conditional notation, which is a standard designation. I've used it perhaps two hundred times in my career. It means the structure is safe for continued occupancy but requires specific remediation before final clearance.

Q: Who was responsible for ensuring that remediation occurred?

A: The report specified that a follow-up inspection would be required, to be conducted by my office or another licensed inspector, with documentation submitted to the lender.

Q: Did you conduct that follow-up?

A: I did, on August 12th. Repairs had been completed by Morrison Contracting. New beam installed, proper sistering technique, full termite treatment. I have the photographs in my file if you'd like to see them.

Q: That won't be necessary at this time.

A: The file is quite thorough.

topic: A building inspector is deposed about a structural assessment they signed off on
text:
Q: Mr. Castellano, I want to direct your attention to page 47 of your report.

A: I have it in front of me.

Q: You wrote, and I quote, "Foundation settling observed within normal parameters." Do you see that?

A: I do.

Q: What does "normal parameters" mean to you?

A: It means... look, every building settles. It's a function of soil composition, load distribution, time. The question isn't whether settling has occurred, it's whether the settling indicates ongoing structural compromise.

Q: And in this case?

A: In this case, no.

Q: How did you reach that conclusion?

A: I measured the differential settlement at multiple points along the foundation wall. The maximum variance was three-sixteenths of an inch over a span of forty feet.

Q: Is that significant?

A: It's not.

Q: How do you know it's not significant?

A: Because the engineering standards I'm trained to apply set the threshold for concern at three-quarters of an inch over the same span. We were at less than a quarter of that.

Q: Did you consult with a structural engineer before reaching this conclusion?

A: I am qualified to make this determination independently. It's within the scope of my certification.

Q: That wasn't my question. Did you consult with a structural engineer?

A: No. There was no need.

Q: In your professional judgment.

A: In my professional judgment, which is what I was hired to provide.

Q: Let's move on. The east wall—

A: Before we do, I want to clarify something about the foundation measurements.

Q: We can come back to that.

A: I'd prefer to address it now while it's fresh. The three-sixteenths variance I mentioned was the maximum. Most measurement points showed less than one-eighth inch. I want the record to reflect that.

Q: Noted.

topic: A building inspector is deposed about a structural assessment they signed off on
text:
Q: Good morning, Ms. Yamamoto. Let's start with some background. You were the inspector of record for the Belmont Towers project?

A: I was one of three inspectors assigned to that project over its construction period.

Q: But you conducted the final structural assessment?

A: Correct.

Q: When was that?

A: November 8th, 2021.

Q: And this was a new construction inspection?

A: Certificate of occupancy inspection, yes.

Q: Walk me through your process that day.

A: Certainly. I arrived at approximately 8 AM. I reviewed the construction documents on file, including all prior inspection reports from my colleagues. Then I conducted a systematic walkthrough of each floor—there are twelve residential floors plus ground-level commercial space.

Q: How long did the walkthrough take?

A: The better part of the day. I finished my on-site work around 4:30.

Q: What were you looking for specifically?

A: Compliance with approved plans, quality of structural connections, proper installation of fire-stopping materials, adequate clearances, appropriate fastening—the full scope of items on the CO checklist.

Q: Did you find any deficiencies?

A: Minor punch-list items only. A handful of electrical cover plates that hadn't been installed yet, some finish work in the stairwells. Nothing structural.

Q: Nothing structural whatsoever?

A: Nothing structural whatsoever. The general contractor on that project—Hendricks & Moy—they run a tight operation. I've inspected perhaps a dozen of their buildings over the years and they consistently deliver quality work.

Q: So you expected to find the building in good condition before you arrived?

A: I expected to conduct a thorough and impartial inspection, which is exactly what I did. The results reflected the contractor's workmanship, not my expectations.

topic: A building inspector is deposed about a structural assessment they signed off on
text:
Q: Mr. Oduya, you've testified that you spent approximately ninety minutes inspecting the warehouse facility.

A: That's right.

Q: Ninety minutes for a 40,000 square foot industrial building.

A: Yes.

Q: Does that seem adequate to you?

A: It was adequate for the scope of the assessment I was asked to perform.

Q: And what scope was that?

A: Limited structural review focused on the roof truss system. The client's insurance carrier had specific concerns about snow load capacity following the previous winter.

Q: So you didn't inspect the entire building?

A: I inspected what I was engaged to inspect. My report clearly states the scope and limitations on the first page.

Q: I see. And within that limited scope, what did you find?

A: The roof truss system was sound. Original construction from 1987, steel web trusses at eight-foot centers, no signs of deformation, corrosion, or connection failure.

Q: No concerns at all?

A: None within the scope of my review.

Q: You keep qualifying your answers with "within the scope."

A: Because precision matters in my field, counselor. If you ask me whether this building will stand for another fifty years, I can't answer that—I didn't inspect everything. If you ask me whether the roof truss system met the requirements for the insurance carrier's snow load concerns, the answer is yes, definitively, and I'd sign that report again today.

Q: Would you?

A: Without hesitation.

Q: Let me ask you about the connection plates on the western span.

A: Go ahead.

Q: Any issues there?

A: None. Standard gusset plate connections, properly welded, no visible cracking or fatigue. I photographed each one. Would you like me to walk you through the images?

topic: A witness is asked about a car accident they saw from their front porch
text:
Q: Could you please state your name for the record?

A: Margaret Holloway.

Q: Ms. Holloway, you were home on the afternoon of March 14th, is that correct?

A: Yes.

Q: And where were you at approximately 2:30 p.m.?

A: On my porch. The front one.

Q: What were you doing there?

A: Just... sitting. I sit out there most afternoons.

Q: Did you witness a collision that afternoon?

A: I did.

Q: Can you describe what you saw?

A: A truck hit a sedan. The sedan was turning.

Q: Which direction was the sedan turning?

A: Left, I think. Into the—the subdivision. Maple Creek, the entrance there.

Q: You said you think. Are you uncertain?

A: No, it was left. I'm certain. It was left.

Q: And the truck—what color was it?

A: I don't... it was dark. Blue, maybe. Or black. I'm not sure anymore.

Q: Did you see the truck before the collision occurred?

A: I saw it coming down the road.

Q: How fast would you estimate it was traveling?

A: I really couldn't say. It was moving. That's all I know.

topic: A witness is asked about a car accident they saw from their front porch
text:
Q: Mr. Reeves, I want to walk you through the sequence of events one more time.

A: We've been through this twice already.

Q: I understand. The sedan—you said it was in the intersection when the light turned yellow?

A: That's what I said, yes.

Q: And the pickup truck entered the intersection after the light changed?

A: It was yellow when the truck went in. Turned red maybe a second later. Maybe less. I don't know exactly.

Q: So the light was yellow, not red, when the truck entered?

A: I just said that.

Q: Did you see the driver of the sedan attempt to brake?

A: I saw brake lights. Whether she was attempting to brake or had already braked or whatever distinction you're looking for—I saw brake lights.

Q: How long were the brake lights illuminated before impact?

A: A second. Less than a second. I don't have a stopwatch on my porch, counselor.

Q: I'm asking for your best estimate.

A: And I gave it.

Q: Fair enough. After the collision, did either vehicle move from the point of impact?

A: The sedan spun. Ended up facing the wrong direction. The truck stopped where it was, more or less.

Q: Did you approach either vehicle?

A: No. I called 911 from inside and then went back out to watch for the ambulance.

topic: A witness is asked about a car accident they saw from their front porch
text:
Q: Ms. Patterson, what is your address?

A: 4712 Greenbriar Lane.

Q: And your front porch faces Greenbriar Lane directly?

A: It does.

Q: On August 8th, were you on your porch at around six in the evening?

A: I was, yes.

A: The sound. The screeching, then the crash.

Q: So you heard it before you saw it?

A: That's correct.

topic: A witness is asked about a car accident they saw from their front porch
text:
Q: You mentioned you were drinking iced tea on your porch. Is that right?

A: That's right.

Q: And this was around 4 p.m.?

A: Around then. Maybe 4:15.

Q: Walk me through what you observed.

A: The silver car was coming from the east—that's my left when I'm facing the road. The SUV was coming from the other direction.

A: Yes.

A: Yes. Can we wrap this up soon? I've told you everything I remember.

topic: A witness is asked about a car accident they saw from their front porch
text:
Q: State your name.

topic: A warehouse supervisor is deposed about safety protocols that were allegedly ignored
text:
Q: Mr. Delgado, you were the warehouse supervisor on the night of September 14th, correct?

A: That's correct.

Q: And part of your responsibilities included ensuring compliance with safety protocols?

A: Yes, that was part of my job.

Q: Now, I want to direct your attention to the forklift inspection logs for that week. You're familiar with those?

A: Very familiar. I maintained them myself.

Q: Good. Can you tell me how many inspections were documented between September 10th and September 14th?

A: All five. One per day, as required. I can tell you the exact times if you'd like—7:15 AM on the 10th, 7:22 AM on the 11th, 7:08 AM on the 12th, 7:19 AM on the 13th, and 7:11 AM on the 14th.

Q: You have those memorized?

A: I reviewed my records thoroughly before today. I take documentation seriously, Counselor.

Q: And each of those inspections was performed by you personally?

A: Every single one. I initialed them, dated them, and noted any deficiencies. There were none that week, which I also documented.

Q: No deficiencies at all?

Q: That won't be necessary at this time.

A: I brought copies anyway. I assumed you'd want to be thorough.

Q: Let's move on. Were you aware of any complaints from employees about equipment that week?

A: Not a single one. And I'll add that I hold a weekly safety meeting every Monday morning. Attendance is mandatory. I have the sign-in sheet from September 11th showing all twelve warehouse employees present.

Q: Mr. Delgado, I'm asking the questions here.

A: Of course. I just want to make sure the record is complete.

topic: A warehouse supervisor is deposed about safety protocols that were allegedly ignored
text:
Q: Ms. Thornton, how long did you serve as night shift supervisor at the Henderson Road facility?

A: Just under three years.

Q: And during that time, who was responsible for conducting the weekly safety audits?

A: That would have been me.

Q: Would have been?

A: Was. It was me.

Q: I see. Now, I'm looking at the audit schedule for July of last year. Do you see any gaps in that schedule?

A: I... I'd need to look at the document.

Q: Of course. I'm handing you what's been marked as Exhibit 14. Take your time.

A: Okay. Yes. I see there are two weeks without entries.

Q: Two consecutive weeks, correct?

A: Yes.

Q: And can you explain why those audits weren't conducted?

A: I was told—I mean, I understood that we were short-staffed and that Mr. Brennan had authorized a temporary suspension of non-essential checks.

Q: Non-essential. That's interesting. Did Mr. Brennan put that authorization in writing?

A: Not that I'm aware of.

Q: So you have no documentation of this authorization?

A: No.

Q: And the safety audits—those were classified as non-essential in your view?

A: That's what I was told.

Q: By Mr. Brennan?

A: Yes.

Q: Directly?

A: In a team meeting. There were others present.

Q: Perfect. We'll get to those others. Now, during those two weeks, were any incident reports filed?

A: I'd have to check the—

topic: A building inspector is deposed about a structural assessment they signed off on
text:
Q: Mr. Patterson, thank you for being here today. I know these depositions can be long, so just let me know if you need a break at any point.

A: I appreciate that. I'm fine for now, but thank you for offering.

Q: You've been a building inspector for how long now?

A: Twenty-three years this coming April. Started right out of the Army Corps of Engineers, actually. Best decision I ever made.

Q: That's quite a career. And during those twenty-three years, roughly how many structural assessments would you say you've completed?

A: Oh, goodness. Thousands, certainly. I'd have to check my records for an exact number, but I kept meticulous notes over the years. I could get that for you if it would help.

Q: That won't be necessary for now, but I appreciate the offer. Let's talk about the Meridian Heights building specifically. Do you recall your inspection on March 15th of last year?

A: I do, yes. It was actually a memorable one for me because it was my first inspection after my daughter's wedding. I was in good spirits that week.

Q: Congratulations on that, by the way.

A: Thank you kindly.

Q: Can you walk me through what you observed during that inspection?

A: Of course. I arrived around 8:30 in the morning—I always prefer morning inspections when the light is good. Started with the foundation, as I always do. Checked the load-bearing walls on the first three floors. Everything appeared sound to my eye at that time.

Q: When you say "appeared sound," were there any concerns at all?

A: You know, I want to be completely honest with you. There was some minor cracking in the east stairwell that I noted. It was within acceptable parameters, but I documented it anyway because I believe in erring on the side of caution. I've seen too many inspectors cut corners, and that's just not how I operate.

Q: I can see that from your file. Your documentation is quite thorough.

A: Well, these buildings—they're people's homes, their workplaces. They deserve someone who takes this seriously. I hope I've done that over the years.

Q: Mr. Patterson, did you have any communication with the building's owner before or after this inspection?

A: I did. Mr. Hensley called me afterwards to thank me for the quick turnaround. Seemed like a decent fellow, genuinely concerned about his tenants' safety.

Q: And that was the extent of your communication?

A: That was it. Just a brief, courteous call. Nothing more to it than that.

topic: A building inspector is deposed about a structural assessment they signed off on
text:
Q: Ms. Delgado, I'm going to show you what's been marked as Exhibit 14. Take your time looking it over.

A: It was a Tuesday. I remember because my granddaughter has dance class on Tuesdays, and I was hoping to finish in time to pick her up. She's seven now, doing ballet.

A: She's a gem, truly. Cares about that building like it's her own home.
