topic: A building inspector is deposed about a structural assessment they signed off on
text:
Q: Mr. Kim, I understand you've inspected several properties in the downtown corridor over the past five years.

A: That's correct.

Q: The Broadmore Building at 445 Commerce Street—you signed off on that assessment in January 2022?

A: I did, yes.

Q: Take me through your methodology for that particular inspection.

A: Certainly. I started with a review of the previous inspection reports, which I always think is important context. The building had a good history—no major structural concerns noted in the past decade.

Q: And you found that history reassuring?

A: Reassuring is a strong word. I found it informative. Every inspection starts fresh for me. The history tells me where to look, but it doesn't tell me what I'll find.

Q: Fair enough. I like that approach.

A: Well, I've learned over the years that buildings change. Owners cut corners, tenants make modifications without permits, water finds new paths. You have to see what's in front of you, not what used to be there.

Q: Speaking of water, did you find any moisture-related concerns at Broadmore?

A: There was some evidence of past water intrusion in the basement level. Staining patterns, mostly. The building manager—a young fellow, very eager—told me they'd addressed a drainage issue the previous summer. The repairs looked sound.

Q: Did you verify those repairs?

A: I examined them visually and checked for any ongoing moisture. Everything was dry, properly sealed. I documented my observations with photographs. I can walk you through those if you'd like.

Q: Let's do that. I appreciate your thoroughness.

A: Of course. I actually take more photos than required because I've found it helpful when questions come up later. Like now.

Q: That's genuinely helpful for everyone involved.

A: I hope so. I just want to make sure we get to the truth of what happened—or didn't happen—at that building.

Q: Mr. Kim, did you have any conversations with the property owners about your assessment?

A: I did. They were a couple, the Hendersons. Retired teachers. They inherited the building from her father and were doing their best to maintain it properly. Good people who asked thoughtful questions.

Q: What kind of questions?

A: About maintenance schedules, mostly. What they should prioritize, where to allocate their limited budget. I gave them my honest recommendations. That's all I can do.

topic: A building inspector is deposed about a structural assessment they signed off on
text:
Q: State your name for the record.

A: Thomas Reeves.

Q: Mr. Reeves, you've been doing this work for a while now.

A: Fourteen years.

Q: And in those fourteen years, have you ever had an assessment questioned like this before?

A: Once. A property in Eastwood. Turned out the owner had falsified some maintenance records. I cooperated fully with the investigation then, and I'm cooperating fully now.

Q: I can see that. The documents you've provided have been very complete.

A: I keep everything. Notebooks, photographs, correspondence. My wife jokes that I'm a hoarder, but this job—you need records. Memory isn't enough.

Q: Let's talk about the Avalon Ridge apartment complex. What prompted the inspection in the first place?

A: It was a standard five-year assessment. Required by code. The property management company scheduled it through normal channels.

Q: Nothing unusual about the request?

A: Nothing at all. Just routine.

Q: When you arrived, what was your first impression of the building's condition?

A: Honestly? Better than I expected for a building that age. The exterior had been recently painted, landscaping was maintained. First impressions can be deceiving, but this one looked cared for.

Q: You mentioned first impressions can be deceiving. Did your opinion change as you inspected further?

A: It deepened, I'd say. The care I saw outside was reflected inside. The mechanical systems were well-maintained. The hallways were clean. Little things, but they tell a story about how a building is run.

Q: Did you interact with any residents during your inspection?

A: A few, yes. One elderly gentleman—Mr. Pearson, I believe—insisted on showing me a crack in his bathroom ceiling. Turned out to be cosmetic, but I appreciated that he cared enough to mention it. Good tenants watch out for their buildings.

Q: And you documented that interaction?

A: I did. I note everything. It's just how I operate.

Q: Mr. Reeves, I want you to know that nothing you've told me today raises any concerns about your conduct.

A: I appreciate that. I've lost some sleep over this, wondering if I missed something. It helps to hear you say that.

topic: A building inspector is deposed about a structural assessment they signed off on
text:
Q: Good morning, Ms. Okonkwo. Thank you for coming in today.

A: Good morning. Of course—I want to help clarify things however I can.

Q: I've reviewed your credentials, and I have to say, your background is impressive. Structural engineering degree before you moved into inspection work?

A: That's right. I worked design for about eight years before transitioning. I found I liked being out in the field more than sitting at a computer.

Q: That experience must inform your inspections.

A: It does. I see buildings differently than someone who came up through the trades, I think. Neither approach is better—they're just different lenses.

Q: Let's discuss the Sentinel Place property at 890 Industrial Way.

A: Yes, I inspected that facility in November of last year.

Q: What type of facility is it?

A: It's a light manufacturing warehouse. About 45,000 square feet. The company makes automotive parts, I believe.

Q: Heavy equipment on site?

A: Yes, and that was actually a focus of my inspection. Floor loading is crucial in those environments. I spent extra time on the slab integrity.

Q: And what did you conclude?

A: The slab was in good condition. Some surface wear, which is normal, but the structural integrity was sound. The original engineering was quite good—overbuilt by today's standards, actually, which I always appreciate seeing.

Q: When you say "overbuilt," you mean that as a positive?

A: Absolutely. Buildings constructed in the sixties and seventies often have more robust construction than what code minimally requires today. It's like finding extra insurance built right in.

Q: Did you examine the roof structure as well?

A: I did. The original timber trusses had been supplemented with steel reinforcement at some point—looked like maybe the nineties based on the materials. A previous owner had been proactive about maintenance.

Q: Ms. Okonkwo, in your professional opinion, was there anything about Sentinel Place that concerned you?

A: I noted some recommendations for improvement—there always are—but nothing that rose to the level of concern. I gave it a sound assessment because that's what it merited. I wouldn't have signed my name to it otherwise.

Q: I believe that about you.

A: Thank you. My name is the only thing I have in this business, really. I protect it.

topic: A contractor is questioned about delays that caused a construction project to fail
text:
Q: Mr. Harmon, you were the general contractor on the Riverside Commons project, correct?

A: I was the general contractor, yes. Harmon Construction held that contract from day one through termination.

Q: And the project was terminated approximately fourteen months after groundbreaking?

A: Fourteen months and six days, to be exact. March 22nd of last year.

Q: The owner claims the delays were caused by your company's mismanagement. What's your response to that?

A: My response is that the owner is wrong. I've been doing this for twenty-three years. I know what mismanagement looks like, and this wasn't it.

Q: So in your view, what caused the delays?

A: The owner's own changes caused the delays. We received forty-seven change orders in the first eight months. Forty-seven. You want to pour a foundation when someone keeps moving the walls?

Q: Aren't change orders a normal part of construction?

A: A handful, sure. Forty-seven is not normal. Forty-seven is a client who doesn't know what they want and expects you to read their mind.

Q: Did you communicate these concerns to the owner at the time?

A: In writing. Every single time. I have copies of every letter, every email, every meeting minute. Would you like me to walk you through them?

Q: That won't be necessary at this time.

A: I'm happy to do it. It's all documented.

Q: Let's move on. Were there any issues with your subcontractors?

A: None that weren't directly traceable to the change orders I just mentioned. My subs are people I've worked with for a decade or more. They know how to do their jobs.

Q: The electrical subcontractor was replaced midway through the project, wasn't he?

A: He was. At the owner's insistence, not mine. They wanted their cousin's company brought in. I advised against it in writing. That's documented too.

---

topic: A contractor is questioned about delays that caused a construction project to fail
text:
Q: Can you describe your understanding of the original project timeline?

A: The original completion date was set for November 15th. We had an eighteen-month schedule, which was aggressive but achievable under normal circumstances.

Q: And what were the circumstances that made it not achievable?

A: Well, there were several factors—

Q: Let's start with the most significant one.

A: The permit delays from the city. We lost eleven weeks waiting on the revised structural permits after the design changes.

Q: Whose responsibility was it to obtain those permits?

A: Technically mine, but you can't pull a permit on plans that keep changing. The architect was still issuing revisions in week fourteen.

Q: Did you flag this as a concern?

A: I... yes, I raised it at the progress meetings.

Q: You hesitated. Were there meetings where you didn't raise it?

A: I may not have raised it at every single meeting, no.

Q: So there were opportunities to escalate the issue that you didn't take?

A: I raised it when it was appropriate to raise it. You have to understand how these meetings work—

Q: I'm just asking whether you raised the concern at every available opportunity.

A: No. Not every single meeting. But I raised it enough.

Q: Enough by whose standard?

A: By any reasonable standard. Look, I've been through this before. I know what's expected. The owner knew about the permit situation because I told them about the permit situation. Multiple times.

Q: In writing?

A: Yes, in writing. And verbally. And in meetings. I did my job.

---

topic: A contractor is questioned about delays that caused a construction project to fail
text:
Q: Mr. Harmon, I want to ask you about the concrete delivery issues in months four and five.

A: Go ahead.

Q: Your supplier, Lakeside Concrete, failed to deliver on three separate occasions. Is that accurate?

A: They were late twice. One delivery was rescheduled at our request due to weather.

Q: I have invoices showing three missed delivery windows.

A: Then your invoices are incomplete. The August 14th delivery was rescheduled by us because we had two inches of rain that morning. You can check the weather records.

Q: I will. What about the other two?

A: Lakeside had some equipment problems. It happens.

Q: It happens?

A: In construction, yes, it happens. You build contingency into your schedule for exactly this reason.

Q: Did your schedule have sufficient contingency?

A: It did until the contingency got eaten up by client changes.

Q: So you're saying the Lakeside delays wouldn't have mattered if not for the change orders?

A: That's exactly what I'm saying.

Q: That seems convenient.

A: It's not convenient, it's arithmetic. I can show you the schedule analysis if you'd like. My project manager put together a delay allocation that accounts for every single day.

Q: We'll get to that document.

A: Good. I think you'll find it informative.

Q: Let's talk about your project manager. She left the project in month nine?

A: She took another position, yes.

Q: In the middle of a troubled project?

A: In the middle of a project the owner was making impossible. I didn't blame her for leaving. I considered it myself.

---

topic: A contractor is questioned about delays that caused a construction project to fail
text:
Q: I'd like to discuss the framing phase of construction.

A: All right.

Q: The framing was completed approximately six weeks behind the original schedule?

A: I'd have to check the exact figure, but that sounds approximately right.

Q: What caused that delay?

A: Primarily the foundation issues we had to address.

Q: What foundation issues?

A: We encountered soil conditions that didn't match the geotechnical report. Required additional engineering and reinforcement.

Q: Wasn't the geotechnical survey your responsibility?

A: The survey was conducted by a firm the owner selected. I objected to using them at the time.

Q: Why did you object?

A: I'd had problems with their work before. On the Millbrook project in 2019.

Q: But you proceeded anyway?

A: The owner insisted. It was their prerogative.

Q: Did you document your objection?

A: I did.

Q: In writing?

A: In an email to the owner's representative dated March 3rd. I can give you the exact text if you want. I remember it clearly.

Q: That won't be necessary right now. So when the soil conditions proved problematic—

A: When the survey proved wrong, you mean.

Q: When the conditions didn't match expectations, what did you do?

A: I brought in my own geotechnical engineer, had the site reevaluated, developed a remediation plan, and executed it. Added four weeks to the foundation phase but gave us a structure that wasn't going to crack.

Q: Did the owner approve this remediation?

A: They approved it because they had no choice. I wasn't going to build on a compromised foundation. That's not how I operate.

---

topic: A contractor is questioned about delays that caused a construction project to fail
text:
Q: Were you aware that the project lender had expressed concerns about the timeline as early as month six?

A: I heard something about that, yes.

Q: From whom?

A: I believe the owner mentioned it at a meeting.

Q: What was your reaction?

A: I told them what I'd been telling them all along—that the timeline was being impacted by their own decisions.

Q: Did you take any steps to address the lender's concerns?

A: That wasn't my role. The lender's relationship was with the owner, not with me.

Q: But you understood that lender concerns could affect the project's viability?

A: Sure, in theory. But I had a job to do, and I was doing it.

Q: Were you doing it on schedule?

A: I was doing it on a schedule that reflected the reality of the project as the owner had shaped it.

Q: That's not what I asked.

A: It's the only answer that makes sense. You can't ask me if I was on the original schedule when the original schedule became meaningless after the twentieth change order.

Q: Fair enough. Let me rephrase. Were you tracking to any schedule at that point?

A: We maintained a rolling three-week lookahead, which is standard practice. We hit those targets consistently.

Q: But the overall completion date kept moving?

A: Because the scope kept moving. That's how it works. I don't know what else to tell you.

Q: You seem frustrated, Mr. Harmon.

A: I'm not frustrated. I just want to make sure the record reflects what actually happened on this project, not what the owner wishes had happened.

topic: A nurse is questioned about a patient fall that occurred during her shift
text:
Q: Nurse Delgado, let's go back to the night of March 14th. You were assigned to the east wing, correct?

A: Yes.

Q: And Mr. Patterson was one of your patients that night?

A: He was.

Q: How many times did you check on Mr. Patterson between 10 p.m. and midnight?

A: I rounded on all my patients every hour, so twice during that window.

Q: Twice. And during those checks, did you assess whether Mr. Patterson was a fall risk?

A: He was already documented as a fall risk. That assessment was done at admission.

Q: I'm asking about your checks that night, Nurse Delgado. Did you personally assess his fall risk during your rounds?

A: I observed him. I noted his condition. I followed the protocol that was in place.

Q: That's not what I asked. Did you perform a fall risk assessment?

A: The fall risk assessment is done at admission and updated when there's a change in condition. There was no change in condition. So no, I did not redo an assessment that had already been completed.

Q: The bed alarm—was it activated when you checked on him at 11 p.m.?

A: I don't specifically recall checking the bed alarm at that exact moment.

Q: You don't recall. So it's possible it wasn't activated?

A: I said I don't specifically recall. That doesn't mean it wasn't activated. It means I'm not going to guess about something I don't have a clear memory of.

Q: Fair enough. What do you recall about the 11 p.m. check?

A: I recall that he was in bed, the side rails were up, and he was resting comfortably.

Q: And the next time you saw him?

A: Was when I responded to the sound of the fall.

topic: A nurse is questioned about a patient fall that occurred during her shift
text:
Q: Walk me through the staffing situation on the night in question.

A: We were short. Two nurses for twenty-three patients.

Q: Is that typical?

A: It's become typical. Whether it should be is a different question.

Q: I'm just asking about that night.

A: And I'm telling you. Two nurses, twenty-three patients.

Q: Were you feeling rushed that evening?

A: I was doing my job.

Q: That's not what I asked, Nurse Thompson.

A: I'm aware of what you asked. I'm telling you I was doing my job. Whether I felt rushed is—I don't really know how to quantify that for you.

Q: Let's try. Did you feel you had adequate time to spend with each patient?

A: I spent the time that was necessary with each patient.

Q: Necessary. Who determines what's necessary?

A: Clinical judgment. Training. Experience.

Q: Your clinical judgment told you Mr. Okonkwo didn't need more supervision?

A: My clinical judgment told me he was stable, oriented, and had been ambulatory with assistance all day without incident. So yes.

Q: And yet he fell.

A: Yes. He fell. Patients fall. Even with perfect care, patients fall. That's a medical reality.

Q: I'm not asking about medical realities in the abstract. I'm asking about this patient, this night.

A: And I've answered you. Multiple times now.

topic: A nurse is questioned about a patient fall that occurred during her shift
text:
Q: The incident report says the fall occurred at approximately 2:15 a.m. Do you agree with that time?

A: That's what I documented, yes.

Q: How did you determine that time?

A: I looked at the clock when I entered the room.

Q: After you heard what, exactly?

A: A thud. From his room.

Q: You were at the nurses' station?

A: I was in the hallway, returning from another patient's room.

Q: Which patient?

A: Mrs. Bernstein. Room 408.

Q: And what were you doing in Mrs. Bernstein's room?

A: Administering medication.

Q: For how long?

A: I don't know. A few minutes.

Q: Five minutes? Ten?

A: I said I don't know. I wasn't timing myself.

Q: Nurse Chen, I'm trying to establish a timeline here.

A: And I'm trying to give you accurate information. If I had to guess, maybe five minutes. But it's a guess. I don't want my guess in a legal record as though it's fact.

Q: Understood. Let's say approximately five minutes. So you left Mrs. Bernstein's room, you're in the hallway, and you hear a thud.

A: Correct.

Q: Did you run to Mr. Davis's room?

A: I walked quickly.

Q: You didn't run?

A: Running in a hospital hallway isn't—we don't run unless there's a code. I moved with urgency.

topic: A nurse is questioned about a patient fall that occurred during her shift
text:
Q: Nurse Patel, are you familiar with the hospital's fall prevention protocol?

A: Of course.

Q: Can you summarize it for me?

A: It's a forty-page document. Which part would you like summarized?

Q: The parts relevant to patients like Mrs. Hartley—elderly, post-surgical, on pain medication.

A: Bed alarm activation. Hourly rounding. Non-slip footwear. Rails up. Call light within reach. Clear path to bathroom. That's the baseline.

Q: And you followed all of those with Mrs. Hartley?

A: Yes.

Q: The bed alarm was on?

A: Yes.

Q: Then why didn't it alert you when she got out of bed?

A: I don't know. I've asked myself that question.

Q: You've asked yourself. Have you asked anyone else? Maintenance? Biomedical engineering?

A: That's not my department.

Q: But you reported the malfunction?

A: I documented that the alarm did not sound. What happened after that with the equipment is beyond my scope.

Q: So you documented it and moved on.

A: I documented it and continued caring for my other patients, yes. I had eleven other patients that night. What would you have had me do?

Q: I'm asking the questions here, Nurse Patel.

A: Then maybe ask ones I can actually answer.

topic: A nurse is questioned about a patient fall that occurred during her shift
text:
Q: Let's talk about the call light. Was it within Mrs. Freeman's reach?

A: Yes, it was clipped to her pillow.

Q: You're certain?

A: I'm certain that's where I placed it.

Q: Did you observe her using it that night?

A: She used it once, around nine o'clock.

Q: What for?

A: She needed help to the bathroom.

Q: Did you assist her?

A: I did.

Q: Personally?

A: Personally, yes.

Q: And after that bathroom trip, did you reassess her mobility?

A: She walked to the bathroom and back with my assistance without difficulty.

Q: Without difficulty. Those are your words?

A: Those are the accurate words, yes.

Q: She didn't seem unsteady?

A: I just said she walked without difficulty. If she'd seemed unsteady, I would have noted it.

Q: Would you have? Because there's no note in the chart about that bathroom trip.

A: The chart documents that she was ambulatory with assistance. It doesn't require a narrative entry for every bathroom trip.

Q: Doesn't require it, or you just didn't do it?

A: Both. It's not required, and I didn't do it, because it's not required. If you're suggesting I should have written a novel every time a patient used the toilet, I'd have had time for nothing else.

Q: I'm not suggesting anything, Nurse Washington. I'm asking questions.

A: Then I've answered them.

topic: A witness is questioned about a workplace injury they observed but did not report
text:
Q: Mr. Delgado, you were working on the afternoon of September 14th, correct?

A: Yes.

Q: And you were in the warehouse during the second shift?

A: Yes, I was there.

Q: At approximately 3:45 p.m., where exactly were you standing?

A: I don't—I mean, I was near the loading area. Somewhere around there.

Q: Somewhere around there. Can you be more specific?

A: It's a big space. I was doing my job. I don't remember the exact spot.

Q: Were you within sight of the forklift operating area?

A: I could see parts of it. Some of it. Depending on where I was moving.

Q: Did you see Marcus Webb that afternoon?

A: I saw a lot of people that afternoon.

Q: That's not what I asked. Did you see Marcus Webb?

A: Yes. At some point, yes.

Q: Did you see him get injured?

A: I—can you define what you mean by "see"?

Q: Did you witness, with your eyes, Marcus Webb sustain an injury on September 14th?

A: I saw something happen. I didn't see everything. I wasn't—I was working. I had my own responsibilities.

Q: What did you see happen?

A: I heard a sound. I looked over. He was on the ground. That's what I saw. That's all I saw.

Q: And what did you do after you saw him on the ground?

A: I went back to work. Other people were already there. They were handling it.

topic: A witness is questioned about a workplace injury they observed but did not report
text:
Q: Ms. Okonkwo, let's go back to the incident with the conveyor belt. You've stated you were present?

A: I was in the facility, yes.

Q: In the facility. How far from the conveyor system where Mr. Huang was working?

A: Maybe thirty feet. Maybe more. I'm not good with distances.

Q: But you could see the conveyor from where you were?

A: Parts of it.

Q: Which parts?

A: The—look, the section near the sorting bins. That general area.

Q: Did you see Mr. Huang's hand make contact with the conveyor mechanism?

A: I saw him pull his hand back. I saw him react to something.

Q: Did you see blood?

A: I don't—there might have been—I didn't get a clear look.

Q: You didn't get a clear look, but you were thirty feet away with a line of sight to the sorting bins?

A: Things were moving. Product was moving. People were moving. It's not like I was standing there watching him.

Q: After you saw him react, what did you do?

A: Nothing. I mean, I kept working. It wasn't—I assumed if it was serious, someone closer would handle it.

Q: Did anyone closer handle it?

A: I don't know. I didn't watch what happened after.

Q: You didn't watch. Did you report what you saw to a supervisor?

A: No.

Q: Why not?

A: Because I didn't—I wasn't sure what I saw. And it wasn't my place. I'm not his supervisor. I'm not safety. I just work there.

topic: A witness is questioned about a workplace injury they observed but did not report
text:
Q: Mr. Patterson, I'm going to ask you again. When did you first become aware that Janet Moreno had fallen?

A: And I'll tell you again—I heard someone say something about it maybe twenty minutes after it happened.

Q: Someone. Who?

A: I don't remember exactly who.

Q: You don't remember who told you a coworker had fallen down a flight of stairs?

A: People talk. It wasn't a formal announcement. Someone mentioned it.

Q: Let me rephrase. Before someone mentioned it—before you heard about it secondhand—did you personally observe anything related to Ms. Moreno's fall?

A: What do you mean by "related to"?

Q: Did you see her fall?

A: No.

Q: Did you hear her fall?

A: I heard something. I didn't know what it was at the time.

Q: What did you hear?

A: A thud. Could have been anything. Could have been someone dropping a box.

Q: But it wasn't someone dropping a box, was it?

A: I didn't know that then.

Q: When did you know?

A: When someone told me.

Q: And between the thud and someone telling you—what did you do?

A: My job. I kept doing my job. What was I supposed to do, investigate every noise?

Q: Did you walk toward the stairwell at any point?

A: I might have walked past it.

Q: Did you see Ms. Moreno on the ground?

A: I—no. I don't think so. I don't remember seeing her specifically.

topic: A witness is questioned about a workplace injury they observed but did not report
text:
Q: Let's move on to the chemical exposure incident. December 3rd. You were working the morning shift?

A: Yes.

Q: In the mixing area?

A: Adjacent to it. My station is adjacent.

Q: When the spill occurred, what was your first indication that something had gone wrong?

topic: A witness is questioned about a workplace injury they observed but did not report
text:
Q: Ms. Chen, you've been with the company how long?

A: Six years in March.

Q: And in six years, have you received training on incident reporting procedures?

A: We do training modules. Yes.

Q: So you're aware that employees who witness workplace injuries are required to report them?

A: I'm aware of the policy.

Q: Good. Now—on the date in question, you were working on the production floor?

A: Yes.

Q: Near station seven?

A: Relatively near.

Q: Can you explain why you didn't follow the procedure you just confirmed you were trained on?

topic: A neighbor is questioned about noise complaints and a confrontation they witnessed
text:
Q: Good afternoon. You live at 4215 Maple Court, is that correct?

A: Yes.

Q: And how long have you resided at that address?

A: Seven years. Seven years and... actually, it'll be eight in November. Seven years and about four months, I guess, if you need it exact.

Q: That's fine. Now, the property at 4217 Maple Court is immediately adjacent to yours?

A: It shares a fence line, yes. The east side of my property.

Q: On the night of March 15th of this year, did you hear any unusual sounds coming from that property?

A: I heard sounds. Whether they were unusual—I mean, I'd heard loud sounds before from over there, so in that sense it wasn't unusual, but it was loud, if that's what you're asking.

Q: What specifically did you hear?

A: Music. Bass, mostly. And then later there was shouting. I wrote it down actually, the time—I started keeping a log because—well, I just started keeping one. It was 11:47 when the shouting started.

Q: You kept a log of noise incidents?

A: I did. I do. I have it at home if you need it. I didn't know if I should bring it. Nobody told me to bring it.

Q: We may request that. The shouting you heard—could you make out any words?

A: Some. I don't want to say something wrong. I heard someone yell "get out," I'm certain of that. And there was a woman's voice, but I couldn't—the music was still going, so it was hard to separate everything.

Q: Did you witness any physical confrontation?

A: I saw—okay, I went to my window. The bedroom window faces their driveway. I saw two people, and one of them—look, I don't want to say "shoved" if it was more of a push, or—can you ask me something more specific?

Q: Did you see one person make physical contact with another?

A: Yes. I saw that.

Q: Who made contact with whom?

A: The man pushed the woman. Or—his hands went toward her and she moved backward. I was looking through a window, at night, with their porch light on, so I'm telling you what it looked like from where I was standing.

topic: A neighbor is questioned about noise complaints and a confrontation they witnessed
text:
Q: You called the police on April 3rd regarding a disturbance at your neighbor's residence, correct?

A: That's correct.

Q: What time did you place that call?

A: Around 2 a.m., I think. Maybe a little after.

Q: And what prompted that call?

A: The noise. There was a party or something, I don't know, but it had been going on for hours and I have work at six in the morning.

Q: Had you spoken to your neighbor about the noise before calling police?

A: I'm not going over there at 2 a.m.

Q: That wasn't my question. Had you, prior to that night, ever spoken to your neighbor about noise?

A: Yes.

Q: How many times?

A: I don't know. A few.

Q: More than five times?

A: I really don't know. Maybe. Probably.

Q: So this was an ongoing issue.

A: You could say that.

Q: I'm asking if you would say that.

A: Fine. Yes. It was ongoing.

Q: When you called the police, what did you tell the dispatcher?

A: That there was loud music, that it had been going on since around 10 or 11, that I'd asked them to keep it down before and nothing changed.

Q: Did you mention any confrontation?

A: There wasn't a confrontation yet. That happened after the police came and left.

Q: Tell me about that.

A: After the cops left, maybe twenty minutes later, someone started pounding on my door. It was the neighbor—Mr. Hartley—and he was screaming that I needed to mind my own business.

Q: What did you do?

A: I didn't open the door. I told him through the door to leave or I'd call the police again.

Q: Did he leave?

A: Eventually.

topic: A neighbor is questioned about noise complaints and a confrontation they witnessed
text:
Q: Let's talk about what you observed on the evening of June 22nd.

A: Okay.

Q: Where were you at approximately 9 p.m. that evening?

A: In my backyard.

Q: Doing what?

A: Just sitting. Having a drink. It was a nice night.

Q: And what drew your attention to the neighboring property?

A: Yelling.

Q: From the Kowalski residence?

A: Yes.

Q: What did you hear?

A: A man and a woman arguing.

Q: Could you hear what they were arguing about?

A: Something about money, I think. And someone named "Dana." I wasn't trying to listen.

Q: But you could hear them clearly enough to make out those details?

A: They were loud. I wasn't eavesdropping—I was just there.

Q: I'm not suggesting you were eavesdropping.

A: It sounded like you were.

Q: I'm simply trying to establish what you could and couldn't hear. Did you see either party during this argument?

A: I saw them come outside onto their back deck at one point.

Q: Both of them?

A: The man came out first. Then the woman followed.

Q: Were they still arguing at that point?

A: Yes. She was—her arms were moving a lot. Gesturing.

Q: And him?

A: He was more—he had his hands up, like this, like he was trying to calm her down. Or defend himself, I don't know. I'm not a body language expert.

Q: Did you see any physical contact between them?

A: She threw something at him. A glass or a cup, I couldn't tell.

Q: Did it hit him?

A: I think it hit the railing. I heard it break.

topic: A neighbor is questioned about noise complaints and a confrontation they witnessed
text:
Q: Ms. Thornton, I want to be very clear about the timeline here. You're telling me you heard shouting at 10 p.m.?

A: Around 10, yes.

Q: Around 10. Not at 10.

A: I didn't have a stopwatch. It was around 10 o'clock.

Q: And yet in your written statement to police, you said—and I'm quoting—"approximately 10:30 p.m."

A: Then it was 10:30. I'm not trying to mislead anyone.

Q: Which is it?

A: It was somewhere between 10 and 10:30. I'm doing my best here.

Q: Fine. Let's move on. You stated you saw Mr. Brennan in his driveway.

A: Yes.

Q: Was anyone with him?

A: His wife came out at some point.

Q: At some point. Before or after the shouting?

A: During, I think. Look, everything happened quickly. I wasn't taking notes.

Q: You seem to have a lot of uncertainty about the details.

A: Because you're asking me to remember exact minutes and sequences from something that happened four months ago while I was half-asleep on my couch.

Q: Were you half-asleep?

A: I was tired. I'd had a long day.

Q: So your recollection might be impaired.

A: My recollection is fine. I know what I saw. I saw them arguing in the driveway, I saw her go back inside, and I saw him kick over the trash cans. That I remember clearly.

Q: But the timeline is fuzzy.

A: The timeline is approximate because I'm a human being, not a security camera.

topic: A neighbor is questioned about noise complaints and a confrontation they witnessed
text:
Q: How would you describe your relationship with the Delgados prior to the incident?

A: We were friendly. We'd wave, say hello. Normal neighbor stuff.

Q: Did you socialize with them?

A: We had them over for a barbecue once. Maybe twice.

Q: And after the incident?

A: We don't really talk anymore.

Q: Why is that?

A: I think they know I'm the one who gave a statement.

Q: Did they say something to you about it?

A: Not directly. But Mrs. Delgado—she doesn't wave anymore. She looks away when she sees me.

Q: Let's focus on what you witnessed. May 8th, sometime in the evening.

A: Yes.

Q: Tell me what you saw.

A: I was walking my dog. We go around the block every night around 8:30. When I passed their house, I heard raised voices from inside.

Q: Did you stop?

A: For a second. The dog stopped, actually—he doesn't like loud noises.

Q: What did you hear?

A: A man's voice, very loud. And then a crash. Like something breaking.

Q: What did you do?

A: I stood there for a moment. I didn't know if I should—I wasn't sure what to do.

Q: Did you call the police?

A: Not then. I kept walking. But when I got home, I thought about it, and I called the non-emergency line. I didn't know if it was—I just thought someone should know.

Q: What did you tell them?

A: What I heard. That there was shouting and something breaking. I gave them the address. They asked if I wanted to leave my name and I did.

Q: And that's the extent of your involvement?

A: I wasn't trying to get involved. I was just walking my dog.

topic: A witness is questioned about events at a party where an assault allegedly occurred
text:
Q: Ms. Thornton, I want to direct your attention to the evening of March 14th. You were present at the party at 445 Oakwood Drive, correct?

A: Yes.

Q: And approximately how long were you at this party?

A: I don't know exactly. Maybe three hours? Could have been less. I wasn't really watching the clock.

Q: That's fine. At some point during the evening, did you observe an altercation between two individuals?

A: I saw something, yes.

Q: What did you see?

A: I saw—okay, I was in the kitchen, and I heard yelling from the living room, and when I came out, I saw two people, two men, and one of them was on the ground.

Q: Which man was on the ground?

A: I don't—I didn't know everyone there. The one in the blue shirt. I think someone said his name was Derek? Or Darren?

Q: Did you see how he ended up on the ground?

A: No. No, I only saw after. I already said I was in the kitchen.

Q: I understand. What happened next?

A: People were shouting. Someone pulled the other guy back. The one who was standing.

Q: Did you see the standing man strike the man on the ground at any point?

A: I didn't see the beginning. I keep telling you that. I only saw him on the ground already.

Q: I'm asking what you observed after you entered the room. Did you see any physical contact between these two men?

A: He—the standing one—he sort of lunged forward again, but someone grabbed him. I don't know if he made contact. There were people in the way.

Q: You said he "lunged." Can you describe that motion?

A: Like he moved toward him fast. With his arms. I don't know how else to describe it. It happened very quickly and I was across the room and honestly I wish I had never walked out of that kitchen.

---

topic: A witness is questioned about events at a party where an assault allegedly occurred
text:
Q: Mr. Reeves, you told police that night that you saw the defendant punch Mr. Holloway. Do you recall making that statement?

A: He went down.

Q: Mr. Reeves, have you spoken with anyone about your testimony before today?

topic: A witness is questioned about events at a party where an assault allegedly occurred
text:
Q: Let's talk about what happened before the altercation. You said there was an argument.

topic: A witness is questioned about events at a party where an assault allegedly occurred
text:
Q: Tell me exactly where you were standing when the physical contact occurred.

A: By the sliding glass door. The one that goes to the backyard.

Q: How far is that from where the two men were?

A: Maybe fifteen feet. I'm not great with distances.

Q: Give me your best estimate.

A: Fifteen feet. Maybe twenty.

Q: And your view was unobstructed?

A: Mostly.

Q: Mostly?

A: There were people at the party. Some of them were between me and where it happened, but I could see—I saw enough.

Q: What do you mean by "enough"?

A: I saw the fight.

Q: I need you to be more specific. What specifically did you see?

A: I saw Marcus shove Patrick. Then Patrick shoved back. Then Marcus hit him.

A: I couldn't tell from where I was.

A: Jason stepped in. Jason Mercado.

Q: After the hit.

A: Yes.

Q: Not before.

A: It happened fast. Nobody expected it to escalate like that. We were all just—people freeze. When something like that happens right in front of you, you don't always react the way you think you would. You just don't.

topic: A witness is questioned about a workplace injury they observed but did not report
text:
Q: Mr. Delgado, you were working on the loading dock the morning of September 14th, correct?

A: Yes.

Q: And you observed the incident involving Marcus Thompson?

A: I saw something happen. I don't know that I'd call it an "incident" the way you're using that word.

Q: Fine. You saw something happen. What did you see?

Q: Did you see what caused him to grab his shoulder?

A: I wasn't watching him the whole time. I was doing my own work. I looked up when I heard him make a noise.

Q: What kind of noise?

A: I don't know how to describe it. A sound. Like when someone hurts themselves.

Q: A yell? A grunt? A scream?

A: Somewhere between a yell and a grunt, I guess. I'm not a sound engineer.

Q: Mr. Delgado, I'm just trying to understand what you witnessed.

A: And I'm trying to tell you. I heard a sound, I looked up, I saw him holding his shoulder. That's what I witnessed.

Q: Did you approach him?

A: I walked over, yes.

Q: What did he say to you?

A: He said he was fine. He said it was nothing.

Q: And you believed him?

A: I believed that's what he told me. Whether I believed he was actually fine—that's a different question, and you didn't ask that one.

topic: A witness is questioned about a workplace injury they observed but did not report
text:
Q: Ms. Yoon, how long have you worked in the fulfillment center?

A: I observed a lot of things. Can you be more specific?

Q: Did you observe a coworker get injured?

A: I observed someone fall.

topic: A witness is questioned about a workplace injury they observed but did not report
text:

topic: A witness is questioned about a workplace injury they observed but did not report
text:
Q: Tell me what you remember about the afternoon of July 19th.

topic: A witness is questioned about a workplace injury they observed but did not report
text:
Q: I want to go back to the chemical spill for a moment.

topic: A daycare worker is deposed about an injury a child sustained while in their care
text:
Q: Could you state your full name for the record, please?

A: Margaret Ellen Cho.

Q: And Ms. Cho, how long have you been employed at Sunshine Days Learning Center?

A: It will be seven years this coming March.

Q: I'd like to direct your attention to the afternoon of September 14th. You were working that day?

A: I was, yes. I was assigned to the Butterfly Room, which is our three-year-old classroom.

Q: How many children were present in the Butterfly Room that afternoon?

A: Twelve. We had two absences that day—one for a doctor's appointment, one for a family trip.

Q: And how many staff members?

A: Two. Myself and DeShawn Harris. Our ratio requirement is one to six for that age group, so we were in compliance.

Q: Tell me what you observed regarding Lily Brennan that afternoon.

A: Lily was having a good day, actually. She'd eaten well at lunch, participated in circle time. During free play, she was at the block station with two other children—I believe Marcus and Sophia.

Q: What time did free play begin?

A: We transitioned to free play at approximately 2:15. I noted the time because I had just finished updating the daily logs.

Q: And where were you positioned during free play?

A: I was circulating. I moved between the art table, the dramatic play area, and the reading corner. DeShawn was stationed near the gross motor equipment and the blocks.

Q: At what point did you become aware that Lily had been injured?

A: I heard her cry out. A sharp cry, not the usual fussing. I looked over and saw she was on the ground near the block shelf.

Q: What did you do next?

A: I went to her immediately. DeShawn was already kneeling beside her. We followed our injury assessment protocol—checked her responsiveness, looked for visible injury, asked her where it hurt.

Q: And what did that assessment reveal?

A: Her left wrist was swelling. She was holding it against her chest and crying. We applied a cold pack, kept her still, and I called the front office to notify her parents and request they come immediately.

topic: A daycare worker is deposed about an injury a child sustained while in their care
text:
Q: Mr. Patterson, you mentioned you were outside on the playground when the incident occurred. Is that right?

A: That's right.

Q: Describe the playground layout for me.

A: Sure. There's a large climbing structure in the center—it's got slides, a bridge, some monkey bars. Around the perimeter we have a sandbox, a tricycle track, and a small garden area the kids help maintain.

Q: What surface is under the climbing structure?

A: Rubber mulch. It's inspected monthly for depth. We rake it every morning.

Q: Who inspected it on the morning of October 3rd?

A: I did. It's part of the opening checklist. I documented it in the playground log at 7:45 a.m.

Q: And you found it satisfactory?

A: I found it met our twelve-inch depth requirement in all areas beneath the equipment, yes.

Q: Now, you were supervising the four-year-old group that morning?

A: Correct. Eleven children.

Q: Where were you standing when Aiden fell?

A: I was near the sandbox, maybe fifteen feet from the climbing structure. I had clear sightlines to all the equipment.

Q: Did you see Aiden climb onto the structure?

A: I did. He went up the ladder on the east side, crossed the bridge, and was heading toward the slide.

Q: Did you observe anything unusual about his movements?

A: No. He was moving at a normal pace. He wasn't running or roughhousing.

Q: What happened next?

A: He reached for the slide rail, and his foot slipped off the platform edge. He fell to the side rather than going down the slide.

Q: How far did he fall, approximately?

A: The platform is thirty-two inches high. So roughly that distance.

Q: What was your response?

A: I was at his side within seconds. I called to my co-teacher to maintain supervision of the other children while I assessed Aiden.

topic: A daycare worker is deposed about an injury a child sustained while in their care
text:
Q: Let's talk about the sign-in procedures at Little Explorers Academy.

A: Okay.

Q: Walk me through what happens when a parent drops off a child in the morning.

A: Parent comes in, signs the child in on the tablet at the front desk—that timestamps the entry—and then walks the child to their classroom. The classroom teacher does a visual check and initials the attendance sheet.

Q: Visual check meaning what?

A: We look at the child. Are they alert? Any visible injuries? Any signs of illness? If something looks off, we note it and speak with the parent before they leave.

Q: Did you perform this visual check on Emma Vasquez the morning of November 12th?

A: I did.

Q: What did you observe?

A: Emma appeared healthy and in good spirits. No visible marks or injuries. Her mother mentioned she'd slept well and had breakfast at home.

Q: Did you initial the attendance sheet?

A: I did.

Q: I'm showing you what's been marked as Exhibit 7. Do you recognize this document?

A: Yes. That's the attendance sheet for November 12th. Those are my initials next to Emma's name.

Q: Now, the incident report indicates Emma sustained a bruise to her forehead at approximately 11:30 a.m. You prepared that report?

A: I did.

Q: In your own words, what happened?

A: Emma was walking from the sink back to the lunch table—we have them wash hands before meals. Another child, who was already seated, pushed his chair back suddenly as she was passing. The chair struck her forehead.

Q: Was the other child being supervised?

A: We had two teachers in the room with fourteen children. Everyone was being supervised. Sometimes things happen very quickly.

topic: A daycare worker is deposed about an injury a child sustained while in their care
text:
Q: Ms. Reeves, I want to understand the training you received regarding incident documentation. When did you complete that training?

A: During my initial onboarding, so that would have been August of 2021. And we do annual refreshers every January.

Q: What does the training cover?

A: How to fill out an incident report completely and accurately. When to complete it—within the hour, while details are fresh. What information is required. Who needs to sign it.

Q: Who needs to sign it?

A: The staff member who witnessed the incident, a supervisor or director, and the parent at pickup.

Q: Turning to the incident report for February 8th, involving the Martinez child. Did you prepare this report?

A: I did.

Q: I notice the time of the incident is listed as "approximately 3:00 p.m." Why approximately?

A: Because I didn't look at a clock at the exact moment. I was focused on the child. When I sat down to write the report fifteen minutes later, I estimated based on where we were in our afternoon routine.

Q: That's reasonable. Now, in the description section, you wrote that Oliver "tripped over a toy truck and struck his chin on the edge of a shelf." Did you witness this happen?

A: I did.

Q: Where were you in relation to Oliver?

A: About six feet away. I was helping another child with a puzzle.

Q: Was the toy truck supposed to be on the floor?

A: Toys end up on the floor during play. That's developmentally appropriate. We do regular tidying throughout the day, but we can't prevent every object from ever being on the ground.

Q: I'm not suggesting you could. I'm asking whether the truck's presence there violated any policy.

A: No. It did not.

Q: What happened after Oliver fell?

A: I went to him immediately, assessed the injury. He had a small laceration on his chin, some blood but not excessive. I applied pressure with a clean cloth, notified my supervisor, and we contacted his parents.

topic: A daycare worker is deposed about an injury a child sustained while in their care
text:
Q: You've been at Happy Hearts for three years now?

A: Three and a half.

Q: And in that time, approximately how many incident reports have you been involved with, either as a witness or preparer?

A: I couldn't give you an exact number. Maybe fifteen to twenty? Children fall, bump into things. It's part of childhood.

Q: Sure. I'm focusing today on the incident involving Jayden Williams on April 22nd. You were his primary caregiver that day?

A: I was one of two teachers in the toddler room. We don't designate primary caregivers for individual children during the day—we both care for all of them.

Q: Fair enough. Tell me about nap time that day.

A: Nap time starts at 12:30. We dim the lights, put on soft music. The children go to their assigned cots.

Q: Where was Jayden's cot located?

A: Against the east wall, second from the window. Same spot every day.

Q: And where were you during nap time?

A: I was at the small desk near the door, doing paperwork. My co-teacher, Amanda, was doing a slow walk through the room, checking on children, adjusting blankets.

Q: Do children always sleep during nap time?

A: No. Some rest quietly. We don't force sleep, but we do require that they stay on their cots and keep their bodies still so others can sleep.

Q: Did Jayden sleep that day?

A: He did, for about forty minutes. Then he woke up and was resting quietly.

Q: What happened next?

A: At approximately 2:15, he got up from his cot—which he's not supposed to do without asking—and walked toward the cubbies. He tripped over another child's cot and fell forward onto the tile floor.

Q: Who saw this happen?

A: Amanda did. She was about ten feet away. I heard the sound and looked up immediately after.

Q: What sound?

A: The impact. And then Jayden crying.

topic: A project manager is questioned about deadlines they missed on a software contract
text:
Q: Mr. Dalton, the contract specified a delivery date of March 15th for the authentication module. Do you recall that date?

A: I recall the contract, yes.

Q: Was the module delivered on March 15th?

A: No.

Q: When was it delivered?

A: April 3rd.

Q: So nineteen days late. Who was responsible for managing that deliverable?

A: I was the project manager, if that's what you're asking.

Q: I'm asking who was responsible.

A: And I'm telling you I was the project manager. That was my role. Whether "responsible" means what you want it to mean is a different question.

Q: Let me rephrase. Did the authentication module fall under your supervision?

A: Yes.

A: I've testified it was delivered April 3rd. You did the math.

Q: Mr. Dalton, I'm going to ask you to answer the questions I'm actually posing. Did you, at any point before March 15th, inform Nextera Systems that the deadline would not be met?

A: Seven days, yes.

topic: A project manager is questioned about deadlines they missed on a software contract
text:
Q: Ms. Okonkwo, let's talk about the milestone schedule attached as Exhibit 4. Do you recognize this document?

topic: A project manager is questioned about deadlines they missed on a software contract
text:
Q: Mr. Pearce, how many status meetings did you hold with the client during the development phase?

topic: A project manager is questioned about deadlines they missed on a software contract
text:
Q: Let me ask you about the payment processing integration. When did your team begin work on that component?

A: February, I believe. Early February.

Q: And the deadline for that component was April 30th?

A: Yes.

Q: Was it delivered April 30th?

A: No, it was delivered May 22nd.

Q: Why?

A: Because the third-party API documentation we were given was incomplete, the sandbox environment wasn't provisioned until March, and we had to rebuild the authentication layer twice when the client changed their security requirements mid-stream.

Q: So you're saying the delay wasn't your team's fault.

A: I'm saying the delay had multiple causes.

Q: But you were the project manager.

A: I was.

Q: Wasn't it your job to anticipate these issues?

A: It was my job to manage them. I can't anticipate that a client will change their security requirements six weeks into development.

Q: Did you build buffer time into your schedule?

A: Two weeks.

Q: And you still missed by twenty-two days.

A: Because, as I've now explained, circumstances beyond our control consumed that buffer and more.

Q: "Beyond your control." That's your testimony?

A: That's the reality.

A: Then maybe you could ask questions like it's a deposition instead of like I'm on trial for something.

topic: A daycare worker is deposed about an injury a child sustained while in their care
text:
Q: Ms. Patterson, the state requires a ratio of one caregiver to every four infants, correct?

A: Correct.

Q: On February 2nd, how many infants were in the nursery?

A: I believe there were nine.

Q: And how many caregivers?

A: Two.

Q: Two caregivers for nine infants. That's a violation of state ratios, isn't it?

A: We were waiting for a third person to arrive. She was running late.

Q: How late?

A: About twenty minutes.

Q: So for twenty minutes, you were out of compliance.

A: I... yes. Technically.

Q: And during those twenty minutes, baby Olivia was injured.

A: Yes.

Q: Ms. Patterson, I'm going to ask you something directly. Did you report the ratio violation to your supervisor?

A: I don't—I'm not sure what you mean by report.

Q: Did you tell anyone that you were understaffed when this injury occurred?

A: My supervisor was aware that Jenna was late.

Q: That's not what I asked. Did you specifically connect the staffing shortage to Olivia's injury in any written or verbal report?

A: No.

Q: Why not?

A: Because I didn't think—I mean, we were doing the best we could. It wasn't like—

Q: Take your time.

A: I didn't write it down because I didn't want it to look like we were negligent. We weren't negligent. We were short-staffed for twenty minutes because someone's car wouldn't start.

Q: But you chose not to document that.

A: I chose to focus on what happened to the baby and how we responded. That's what mattered.

Q: What mattered to whom, Ms. Patterson?

A: To Olivia. To her parents. To doing the right thing.

Q: And documenting a staffing violation wasn't part of doing the right thing?

A: I'm not going to answer that the way you want me to.

topic: A daycare worker is deposed about an injury a child sustained while in their care
text:
Q: When did you first notice that Marcus had a mark on his arm?

A: When I was changing him for nap time. Around 12:30.

Q: Describe the mark.

A: It was red. Oval-shaped. On his upper left arm.

Q: Did it look like a bite mark to you?

A: I'm not a medical professional.

Q: I'm asking for your observation, Ms. Keller. You've worked with children for six years. Did it look like a bite mark?

A: It could have been.

Q: Did you document it as a possible bite?

A: I documented it as a red mark of unknown origin.

Q: Unknown origin. Even though you had, what, twelve children in that room who all have teeth?

A: I didn't see it happen. I'm not going to write down that a child bit another child when I don't know that for a fact.

Q: So you wrote "unknown origin" to protect yourself.

A: No. I wrote "unknown origin" because that was the truth.

Q: Or because you didn't want to admit you had no idea what was happening in your own classroom.

A: Objection—

Q: I'll rephrase. Ms. Keller, isn't it true that you have no idea how Marcus got that mark?

A: That's correct. I don't know exactly how it happened.

Q: And you were his primary caregiver that morning.

A: I was one of two caregivers.

Q: Who was responsible for him specifically?

A: We don't assign specific children to specific adults. We work as a team.

Q: A team where no one saw a child get injured badly enough to leave a mark.

A: Children get marks. They bump into things. They fall. Sometimes other children are involved. It happens faster than you can blink, and I'm sorry if that doesn't fit your neat little narrative, but that's the reality of caring for toddlers.

topic: A daycare worker is deposed about an injury a child sustained while in their care
text:
Q: Ms. Tran, I want to understand the timeline. You said Lily was playing with blocks at 2:15.

topic: An accountant is deposed about transactions they processed on behalf of a client

topic: An accountant is deposed about transactions they processed on behalf of a client
text:

topic: A neighbor is questioned about noise complaints and a confrontation they witnessed
text:
Q: Mr. Deluca, you live at 4412 Pinewood Lane, is that correct?

A: That's right. Twelve years now. I know that street better than anyone.

Q: And the property at 4408 Pinewood Lane is directly adjacent to yours?

A: Shares my eastern fence line, yes. I can see their backyard from my kitchen window, my living room, even the upstairs bathroom if I'm being honest.

Q: Let's talk about the evening of March 14th. You called the police that night?

A: I did. Third time that month, actually. I kept a log. Started keeping one in January when it became clear this wasn't going to stop on its own.

Q: What prompted that particular call?

A: Well, it was a Saturday, around 11:15 p.m.—I noted the time specifically—and they had what I can only describe as a full outdoor gathering. Music loud enough that my windows were vibrating. I timed it. Forty-five minutes of bass I could feel in my chest before I picked up the phone.

Q: Did you observe anything else that night?

A: I observed plenty. I saw Mr. Hensley in his backyard with approximately fifteen to twenty guests. I saw someone urinate against my fence. I saw beer cans thrown over into my yard—I collected four of them the next morning and photographed them with timestamps.

Q: You photographed them?

A: I photograph everything now. Dates, times, conditions. I have a folder on my computer with over two hundred images since November.

Q: Did you speak with Mr. Hensley directly that evening?

A: I walked over around 10:30, before I called the police. Asked politely if they could lower the music. He laughed, Counselor. Laughed and told me to go back inside and close my windows.

Q: What happened after the police arrived?

A: They spoke with him for maybe ten minutes. Music went down for about an hour. Then right back up again at 12:45 a.m. I documented that too.

Q: Do you have that documentation with you today?

A: I brought copies for everyone. Organized by date.

topic: A neighbor is questioned about noise complaints and a confrontation they witnessed
text:
Q: Ms. Brennan, how long have you lived on Cedarbrook Drive?

topic: A neighbor is questioned about noise complaints and a confrontation they witnessed

topic: A neighbor is questioned about noise complaints and a confrontation they witnessed
text:
Q: Dr. Okonkwo, you've lived at the Meridian Condominiums for how long?

topic: A neighbor is questioned about noise complaints and a confrontation they witnessed
text:
Q: You were present for the incident on July 4th, is that right?

topic: A contractor is questioned about delays that caused a construction project to fail
text:
Q: Mr. Hardin, I'd like to turn your attention to the foundation work at the Riverside Commons project. When did your crew begin that phase?

A: We mobilized for foundation work on March 3rd, 2022. Actual excavation started March 7th after we completed the site survey verification.

Q: And what was the contractual deadline for completing the foundation?

A: April 15th, 2022.

Q: When was it actually completed?

A: We poured the final section on June 2nd.

Q: So approximately seven weeks behind schedule, is that fair?

A: That's the arithmetic, yes. Though I'd note that "completed" has a specific meaning in the contract that includes curing time and inspection sign-off, which occurred June 9th.

Q: I appreciate the clarification. Let's talk about what happened during those seven weeks. What caused the initial delay?

A: The soil composition differed significantly from what was represented in the geotechnical report provided during bidding. We encountered clay deposits at fourteen feet that weren't documented.

Q: Did you notify the owner of this discovery?

A: I sent written notice to the project manager, Ellen Vasquez, on March 12th. I have the email and the certified letter, both timestamped.

Q: What response did you receive?

A: Ms. Vasquez acknowledged receipt on March 14th and indicated she would consult with the project engineer. I received revised specifications on March 28th.

Q: Sixteen days later.

A: That's correct.

Q: Did your crew continue working during those sixteen days?

A: We performed work on other preparatory tasks where we could. We couldn't proceed with excavation below twelve feet without engineering guidance on the clay deposits. That would have been improper and potentially unsafe.

Q: And you documented this waiting period?

A: Daily logs, yes. I can provide those if they haven't already been produced.

topic: A contractor is questioned about delays that caused a construction project to fail
text:
Q: Tell me about the lumber shipment that was scheduled for September 14th.

A: Which one? There were three separate orders scheduled that week.

Q: Let's start with the framing lumber from Pacific Northwest Supply.

A: That shipment arrived on the 14th as scheduled.

Q: No issues with that delivery?

A: The delivery itself was on time. The material was wrong.

Q: Wrong how?

A: We ordered Douglas fir, construction grade. They delivered hem-fir, and about thirty percent of it was stamped utility grade. Wasn't suitable for structural framing.

Q: What did you do when you discovered this?

A: I refused the shipment. Driver wasn't happy about it. I called our purchasing coordinator and had her contact Pacific Northwest directly while I documented the load with photographs.

Q: Did refusing that shipment delay the project?

A: Delayed the framing phase, yes. We couldn't proceed without appropriate materials. I wasn't going to install substandard lumber and create a liability for everyone involved, including the owner.

Q: How long until you received correct materials?

A: Eleven days. The replacement shipment arrived September 25th.

Q: Could you have sourced materials elsewhere more quickly?

A: Possibly. But the contract specified Pacific Northwest Supply as the approved vendor. Switching vendors required owner approval, and when I requested that approval on September 15th, I was told to wait for the replacement shipment.

Q: Who told you that?

A: Tom Reeves, the owner's representative.

Q: Did you document that conversation?

A: I followed up the phone call with an email summarizing what we discussed. Mr. Reeves replied confirming the direction to wait. I have both.

---

topic: A contractor is questioned about delays that caused a construction project to fail
text:
Q: I want to ask you about change orders on this project. How many were submitted?

A: Seventeen total.

Q: Over what time period?

A: The project ran from January 2021 through what was supposed to be December 2021, then extended through August 2022. So roughly twenty months.

Q: Were all seventeen approved?

A: Eventually, yes.

Q: What do you mean by "eventually"?

A: Some were approved within a reasonable timeframe. Others sat for weeks without response. Change order number nine, for example, was submitted April 3rd, 2021 and wasn't approved until June 1st.

Q: Did you proceed with work covered by that change order before approval?

A: No.

Q: Why not?

A: Because the contract requires written approval before proceeding with changed work. If I proceed without approval, I'm accepting the risk that I won't be compensated. I wasn't willing to take that risk on a forty-thousand-dollar change.

Q: So you waited.

A: I waited. I also sent reminder notices on April 15th, April 28th, and May 12th. I kept working on everything else I could, but that particular scope sat idle.

Q: Was that typical of how change orders were handled on this project?

A: More typical than it should have been. Average approval time was around nineteen days. Industry standard is closer to seven to ten.

Q: Did you raise this as a concern during the project?

A: Multiple times, yes. At the monthly progress meetings in March, April, June, and August of 2021. It's in the meeting minutes.

---

topic: A contractor is questioned about delays that caused a construction project to fail
text:
Q: Let's discuss the HVAC installation. Were you the subcontractor responsible for that work?

Q: Did you consider replacing Meridian?

A: Not that I'm aware of. But I wasn't privy to all their communications.

topic: A contractor is questioned about delays that caused a construction project to fail
text:
Q: Mr. Hardin, you've been doing this work for how long?

A: Thirty-one years as a licensed contractor. Forty-two if you count the years I worked under my father's license.

Q: In your experience, what's a reasonable amount of weather delay to anticipate on a project of this type in this region?

A: For a fourteen-month project in the Pacific Northwest, I'd budget fifteen to twenty weather days, depending on the specific months.

Q: How many weather delay days did you record on the Riverside project?

A: Forty-three.

Q: More than double your estimate.

A: More than double a reasonable estimate, yes. The winter of 2021-2022 set records for precipitation. That's not something that could have been anticipated.

Q: Did the contract have a provision for weather delays?

A: It did. Section 8.3 provided for time extensions due to unusually severe weather, defined as weather conditions that exceed historical averages by more than twenty percent.

Q: Did you submit claims under that provision?

A: I submitted five weather delay claims between November 2021 and February 2022.

Q: Were they approved?

A: Three were approved. Two were denied.

Q: On what basis were they denied?

A: The owner's representative took the position that some of the days I claimed could have been worked through with additional protective measures. I disagreed with that assessment.

Q: Did you appeal those denials?

A: I submitted written objections preserving my rights under the dispute resolution clause. The matter was never resolved during the project.

Q: Is it still pending?

A: As far as I understand it, yes. It's part of why we're all sitting here.

topic: A pharmacist is deposed about a prescription that was filled with the wrong dosage
text:
Q: Dr. Huang, I'm going to direct your attention to August 14th of last year. Were you working at the Walton Street pharmacy that day?

A: Yes, I was. I was the pharmacist on duty. The only pharmacist, I should say, because we were short-staffed that day, which I had reported to management multiple times before this incident, just to be clear about that.

Q: I'm just asking if you were working that day.

A: Yes. I was working. I just want to make sure the record reflects the circumstances.

Q: We'll get to the circumstances. The prescription at issue was for methotrexate, correct?

A: That's correct. Methotrexate, yes.

Q: And the prescribed dosage was 2.5 milligrams once weekly?

A: That's what the prescription said, yes. I have reviewed the original prescription since then, and that is what it said.

Q: But the patient received tablets of a different strength?

A: The patient received—yes, there was a discrepancy. The tablets dispensed were 10 milligram tablets instead of 2.5 milligram tablets. I want to be very clear that the label on the bottle was correct. The label said 2.5 milligrams. It was the tablets themselves that were incorrect.

Q: So the label was right but the pills were wrong?

A: That is—yes, that's accurate. That's what happened.

Q: How does something like that happen, Dr. Huang?

A: I mean, there are—it can happen in several ways. The stock bottles are similar in appearance. Methotrexate comes in multiple strengths and the bottles are—they're not identical, but they're similar. The lighting in the dispensing area isn't ideal. I've made requests about that too, actually. And we were, as I said, we were extremely busy that day.

Q: Are you saying the pharmacy's lighting caused this error?

A: No, I'm not—I'm not saying it caused it. I'm explaining the contributing factors. There were multiple contributing factors.

Q: Who pulled the medication from the shelf that day?

A: I did. I pulled it. The technician was at lunch and there was a line and I pulled it myself.

Q: And who was responsible for verifying the medication before it went to the patient?

A: I was. That's the pharmacist's responsibility. I'm not—I understand that. I'm the one who is responsible for final verification.

Q: And you verified it?

A: I thought I had. Obviously I—there was an error. But I followed the verification procedure. I followed our standard procedure.

Q: The standard procedure that resulted in a patient receiving four times the prescribed dose?

A: That's—yes. I mean, the procedure was followed but the error still occurred. I understand how that sounds.

topic: A pharmacist is deposed about a prescription that was filled with the wrong dosage
text:
Q: Ms. Vance, let's talk about your training. Where did you complete your PharmD?

Q: And the original order in this case specified lisinopril 10 milligrams?

A: It did.

A: Yes.

Q: Walk me through—actually, let me ask it this way. When a prescription comes in electronically, what's your verification process?

A: Okay. So. The prescription comes in through our system. A technician does initial data entry. They pull the medication. Then I verify the entry against the original order, verify the medication that was pulled, check for interactions, check the patient profile. Then it's ready for pickup.

Q: That's the process you followed on March 3rd?

A: That's the process I follow every day.

Q: So somewhere in that process, 10 became 40?

A: I... yes, somewhere there was an error.

Q: Where?

A: I don't know exactly.

Q: You don't know?

A: The investigation suggested it was a data entry error that I failed to catch during verification.

Q: Let me make sure I understand. The technician entered the wrong number, and you—whose job it is to catch errors—didn't catch it?

A: That appears to be what happened.

Q: Appears to be?

A: That's what happened.

Q: Thank you. Now—

A: I just want to say—may I say something?

Q: You can answer my questions.

A: I've filled over forty thousand prescriptions. This is the only one—this has never happened before.

Q: Ms. Vance, I didn't ask you a question.

A: I understand.

topic: A neighbor is questioned about noise complaints and a confrontation they witnessed
text:
Q: Mr. Delano, how long have you lived at 4512 Birchwood Lane?

A: Eleven years. Eleven years and four months, if you want to be precise about it.

Q: And the property at 4508 Birchwood, that's immediately to your east?

A: Yes.

Q: You can see that property from your home?

A: I can see parts of it. The driveway. Some of the backyard if I'm on my deck.

Q: On the night of June 14th, did you hear anything unusual coming from 4508?

A: Look, I've already been through this with the police twice. Yes. I heard noise.

Q: What kind of noise?

A: Music. Loud music. Bass that I could feel through my walls at eleven-thirty at night.

Q: Did you take any action in response?

A: I went over there. Which I shouldn't have had to do, by the way. I shouldn't have to walk across my lawn in my bathrobe at nearly midnight because someone can't figure out how a volume knob works.

Q: What happened when you went over?

A: I knocked. I knocked three times. Nobody answered. So I knocked again, harder.

Q: And then?

A: Then Mr. Reeves finally opened the door, and we had a conversation.

Q: Can you describe that conversation?

A: I told him his music was too loud. He told me to mind my own business. I told him my sleep is my business. He said some things I won't repeat. I said some things back. Then his wife came to the door and he went inside.

Q: When you say he said things you won't repeat—

A: I won't repeat them. That's what that means.

topic: A neighbor is questioned about noise complaints and a confrontation they witnessed
text:
Q: Mrs. Okonkwo, you were home on the evening of March 3rd?

A: I was.

Q: And your residence is directly across the street from the Hartwell property?

A: Directly across, yes.

Q: Okay. Now, at approximately what time did you first become aware of any disturbance?

A: I don't know about approximately. I know it was eight forty-seven because I looked at the clock on my microwave.

Q: Eight forty-seven. And what did you observe at eight forty-seven?

A: I heard shouting.

Q: From where?

A: From across the street. The Hartwell driveway.

Q: Could you hear words, or just the sound of raised voices?

A: Both.

Q: What words did you hear?

A: I heard Mr. Hartwell say—and this is exactly what he said—"Get off my property before I make you get off."

Q: Who was he speaking to?

A: The young man who lives two doors down from him. I don't know his name.

Q: Did you see any physical contact between them?

A: Not at that point.

Q: At that point. So you saw physical contact later?

A: I saw what I saw.

Q: Mrs. Okonkwo, I need you to describe what you observed.

A: And I'm trying to, but you keep interrupting me before I can finish a thought.

Q: I apologize. Please continue.

A: Thank you. The young man stepped forward. Mr. Hartwell put his hands up. Then the young man—he pushed Mr. Hartwell. One push. Open palms. Mr. Hartwell stumbled but didn't fall. That's what I saw.

Q: What happened after the push?

A: Mr. Hartwell's wife came outside and everyone started talking over each other. I closed my window. I'd seen enough.

topic: A neighbor is questioned about noise complaints and a confrontation they witnessed

A: What else was I supposed to do? Sit there and take it?

Q: Mr. Huang, I'm just trying to establish the timeline—

topic: A neighbor is questioned about noise complaints and a confrontation they witnessed

topic: A neighbor is questioned about noise complaints and a confrontation they witnessed

topic: A financial advisor is deposed about investment decisions made on a client's behalf
text:
Q: Mr. Harrington, let's talk about the Meridian Growth Fund. You placed Mrs. Chen into that fund in March of 2021, correct?

A: I recommended the fund. She made the decision.

Q: You recommended it. Fine. What due diligence did you perform before making that recommendation?

A: The standard due diligence we perform on all funds.

Q: Which consists of what, exactly?

A: Review of the prospectus, historical performance data, risk metrics, expense ratios, manager track record. The same process I've followed for eighteen years without a single complaint until your client decided—

Q: I'm going to stop you there. I asked about your process, not your complaint history.

A: And I'm telling you my process has been consistent and thorough. For eighteen years.

Q: The Meridian Growth Fund lost forty-three percent of its value in eleven months. Were you aware the fund was concentrated in a single sector?

A: It was a growth fund. Growth funds carry sector concentration. That's not hidden information. It's in the name.

Q: Did you explain that concentration to Mrs. Chen?

A: I explained the risk profile of the fund, yes.

Q: Did you explain that seventy percent of the fund was in cryptocurrency-adjacent equities?

A: I explained it was a technology-focused growth fund.

Q: That's not what I asked. Seventy percent. Cryptocurrency-adjacent. Did those words leave your mouth?

A: I don't have a transcript of every conversation, counselor. Do you?

Q: I have Mrs. Chen's testimony that you told her it was, quote, "diversified across emerging sectors." Did you say that?

A: I may have used similar language. Because it was accurate. At the time.

Q: At the time. So your position is that "diversified" was accurate for a fund with seventy percent concentration in a single speculative sector?

A: My position is that I provided appropriate guidance based on the information available, and I'm not going to sit here and be interrogated like I committed a crime when your client signed every disclosure document we put in front of her.

---

topic: A financial advisor is deposed about investment decisions made on a client's behalf
text:
Q: Good morning, Ms. Delacroix. I want to discuss the account rebalancing you performed in October 2022.
