text:
Q: Please state your name.

A: David Chen.

Q: Mr. Chen, where do you live?

A: 4512 Vine Street.

Q: And you were home on the afternoon of March 3rd?

A: Yes.

Q: Where in your home were you at approximately 3:45 p.m.?

A: Front porch.

Q: Okay. Let's talk about what you saw. You witnessed a collision?

A: I saw a fender bender.

Q: Can you describe it?

A: Blue car rear-ended a white SUV.

Q: What were the circumstances leading up to the collision?

A: The SUV stopped short. The blue car didn't stop in time.

Q: Why did the SUV stop?

A: A kid ran into the street chasing a ball. The SUV did exactly what anyone would do.

Q: So the SUV driver wasn't at fault, in your view?

A: I'm not here to assign fault. You asked what I saw.

Q: Fair enough. How fast would you estimate the blue car was traveling?

A: Fast enough that they couldn't stop. Maybe twenty-five, thirty.

Q: Were you able to see the driver of the blue car?

A: I saw someone behind the wheel. Couldn't make out features.

Q: What about the driver of the SUV?

A: A woman. She got out right away to check on the kid. That's what I remember.

Q: This is very helpful, Mr. Chen. Very clear. Exactly what we needed. The distance from your porch to the point of impact—would you say that's about fifty feet?

A: That sounds about right.

Q: Perfect. I think we have what we need here.

---

topic: A witness is asked about a car accident they saw from their front porch
text:
Q: State your name, please.

A: Rosa Gutierrez-Mendez.

Q: Ms. Gutierrez-Mendez, you've indicated you witnessed a vehicle accident on June 8th. Before we discuss what you saw, I want to establish your vantage point. Where exactly were you?

A: On my porch. The covered part, in my rocking chair.

Q: And the accident occurred where in relation to your home?

A: Right in front. Maybe forty feet from where I was sitting. The whole thing happened in front of my eyes.

Q: What time was this?

A: A little after noon. I'd just finished lunch and brought my iced tea outside.

Q: Describe the accident for me.

A: Two cars. A red sports car—looked like a Mustang—and a gray minivan. The Mustang was speeding down the street, weaving a little, you know, like the driver was showing off. The minivan was pulling out of the Petersons' driveway, and the Mustang swerved but clipped the back end of the van. Spun the van around almost completely.

Q: When you say speeding, can you estimate a speed?

A: Fifty, at least. This is a residential street. The limit is twenty-five.

Q: You sound very certain.

A: I raised four children on this street. I know what fifty looks like when it's coming at you.

Q: Was anyone injured?

A: Mrs. Kim—she was driving the minivan—she hit her head on the window. There was blood. I ran inside for towels.

Q: You rendered assistance?

A: Of course I did. What else would I do?

Q: And the driver of the Mustang?

A: Young man. Got out, looked at his car, looked at the van, got back in his car and sat there. Didn't check on Mrs. Kim once.

Q: That's a very complete account. Very thorough. Thank you, Ms. Gutierrez-Mendez. Just a few more questions if you don't mind—this is exactly the kind of detail that helps.

A: Ask whatever you need. I know what I saw, and I'm happy to tell it.

---

topic: A witness is asked about a car accident they saw from their front porch
text:
Q: Your name?

A: Thomas Wright.

Q: You live at 78 Maple Avenue?

A: That's correct.

Q: And on August 22nd, you observed an accident from your property?

A: I did.

Q: Tell me what you saw.

A: I was on my porch, reading the paper. I heard brakes, looked up, and saw a black SUV sliding into the intersection. A delivery truck was coming through on the cross street—had the green light—and the SUV hit the truck's rear quarter panel.

Q: The SUV ran a red light?

A: The SUV entered the intersection against the light, yes. I watched the light cycle. It was red for Maple, green for Vine.

Q: You're certain about the light?

A: Absolutely. I looked at it specifically because I heard the brakes. I wanted to see what was happening.

Q: Now, Mr. Wright, some witnesses have suggested the light may have been yellow when the SUV entered.

A: Then those witnesses weren't paying attention the way I was.

Q: You're very confident.

A: I am. The light was red. The SUV ran it. That's not a matter of opinion.

Q: Alright. What happened after the impact?

A: The delivery driver got out and checked his truck. The SUV driver stayed in the vehicle for a minute, then got out and started taking pictures.

Q: Of the damage?

A: Of everything. The vehicles, the intersection, the traffic light. He was documenting.

Q: Did you speak with either driver?

A: The delivery driver came over and asked if I'd seen what happened. I told him I had. I gave him my phone number in case anyone needed a witness.

Q: You volunteered that?

A: I did. When you see something happen, you ought to say so. That's how I was raised.

Q: And here you are today, doing exactly that.

A: Here I am.

---

topic: A witness is asked about a car accident they saw from their front porch
text:
Q: Please state and spell your name.

A: Patricia Okonkwo. P-A-T-R-I-C-I-A, O-K-O-N-K-W-O.

Q: Ms. Okonkwo, I'm going to ask you about the accident you witnessed on December 12th. But first—had you been drinking any alcohol that morning?

A: No.

Q: Taking any medications that might affect your perception?

A: No.

Q: Any issues with your vision?

A: I wear reading glasses. For distance, my vision is fine. I just had an eye exam in November.

Q: Good. Now, you were on your front porch. Why were you outside in December?

A: Waiting for a package. The delivery trucks come down my street around ten, so I was watching for them.

Q: And instead you saw an accident.

A: I saw a collision, yes. A green sedan and a white pickup.

Q: Describe what happened.

A: The pickup was heading north on my street. The sedan pulled out from a side street—I think the driver didn't see the truck, or misjudged the distance. The truck swerved but couldn't avoid it. Hit the sedan on the driver's side door.

Q: Did either driver appear to be speeding?

A: The truck wasn't. Normal speed for the street. The sedan—it's hard to say. They pulled out too fast, but I couldn't tell you the exact speed.

Q: That's fair. That's an honest answer. What happened after the collision?

A: Both drivers got out. The woman from the sedan was holding her side, seemed hurt. The truck driver called for help—I could see him on his phone.

Q: Did you approach them?

A: I walked to the edge of my property and asked if they needed me to call anyone. The truck driver said he'd already called 911. So I stayed where I was in case they needed anything else.

Q: And did you give a statement to police?

A: I did. When the officers arrived, I flagged one down and told him I'd seen the whole thing.

Q: Very thorough of you. That's precisely the kind of civic engagement we hope for.

A: I just did what anyone should do. Tell the truth about what you saw.

Q: That's all we need today. Thank you.

topic: A witness is asked about a car accident they saw from their front porch
text:
Q: Please state your name for the record.

A: Margaret Elaine Whitfield.

Q: Ms. Whitfield, you've indicated you witnessed a car accident on the afternoon of September 14th, is that correct?

A: I saw what I saw.

Q: I'm asking whether you witnessed an accident on that date.

A: And I'm telling you I saw what I saw. Whether you want to call it an accident or a collision or whatever term your client prefers, that's your business.

Q: Let's try this again. Were you on your front porch on September 14th at approximately 3:15 p.m.?

A: I was on my porch. I don't wear a watch.

Q: But it was afternoon?

A: The sun was out. It wasn't dark. Draw your own conclusions.

Q: Did you see two vehicles make contact with each other?

A: I saw a blue truck run a stop sign and plow into a sedan. If that's what you mean by "make contact," then sure.

Q: You say the truck ran a stop sign. Are you certain it didn't stop first?

A: I've lived on that corner for thirty-one years. I know what a rolling stop looks like. I know what a full stop looks like. And I know what not even pretending to stop looks like. That truck didn't pretend.

Q: Is it possible your view was obstructed?

A: By what? My hydrangeas? No.

Q: You seem very certain of your recollection.

A: That's not a question.

Q: Let me rephrase. Are you certain your recollection is accurate?

A: More certain than you'd like me to be, apparently.

---

topic: A witness is asked about a car accident they saw from their front porch
text:
Q: Good morning. Can you describe where you were sitting when you observed the accident?

A: On my porch. The wooden rocker, the one closest to the steps.

Q: And how far is that from the intersection?

A: Maybe forty feet. Close enough.

Q: Close enough for what, exactly?

A: Close enough to see everything clearly. That's what you're getting at, isn't it?

Q: I'm simply trying to establish distances. Now, which direction were you facing?

A: Toward the street. Obviously.

Q: Were you wearing your glasses?

A: I was.

Q: You're wearing glasses now. Are those the same ones?

A: Same prescription. Different frames.

Q: So they're not the same glasses.

A: The lenses are what matter. You want to debate fashion choices, or do you want to know what I saw?

Q: What did you see?

A: The white car—your client's car—was going at least forty in a twenty-five zone. The other car had the right of way. Your client hit them.

Q: How do you know the speed was forty miles per hour?

A: I've watched cars on that road my whole life. I know fast when I see it.

Q: But you didn't have a radar gun.

A: And you didn't have a witness who saw it differently. So here we are.

---

topic: A witness is asked about a car accident they saw from their front porch
text:
Q: Mr. Delaney, let's be very precise here. You said the Honda entered the intersection first?

A: That's what I said.

Q: And you're basing this on what you observed from approximately sixty feet away, correct?

A: Fifty feet, but sure, let's round up if it helps you.

Q: I'm using the measurement from the accident reconstruction report.

A: Then the report's wrong.

Q: You're disputing the official measurement?

A: I'm telling you I know how far my porch is from that intersection. I've walked it. Have you?

Q: Mr. Delaney, I'm not the one giving testimony today.

A: Could've fooled me with all the statements you're making.

Q: Let me ask this differently. At the moment of impact, where were your eyes focused?

A: On the cars.

Q: Both cars?

A: On the collision. You tend to look at the thing that's happening.

Q: So you can't say with certainty which driver's face you were observing?

A: I wasn't watching faces. I was watching a truck barrel through an intersection like the rules didn't apply.

Q: That's a characterization, Mr. Delaney.

A: That's what happened, Counselor.

---

topic: A witness is asked about a car accident they saw from their front porch
text:
Q: I want to return to the timeline. You said you'd been outside for approximately ten minutes before the accident?

A: Give or take.

Q: And in that time, had you observed any other vehicles pass through the intersection?

A: A few.

Q: How many is a few?

A: I wasn't counting.

Q: More than two?

A: Probably.

Q: More than five?

A: I said I wasn't counting. You can ask the same question different ways all afternoon if you want.

Q: I'm trying to establish how much traffic you observed.

A: Light traffic. It's a residential street. Is that sufficient for your purposes?

Q: Did any of those other vehicles stop at the stop sign?

A: The ones going that direction did, yes.

Q: Every single one?

A: Every single one that I noticed.

Q: But you just said you weren't paying close attention.

A: I said I wasn't counting. Noticing and counting are two different things. You're an attorney; I'd think you'd appreciate the distinction.

Q: Were you distracted by anything before the collision occurred?

A: I was drinking my coffee and watching the street. That's not distraction. That's my afternoon.

Q: Fair enough. Now, after the impact—

A: The impact that your client caused by failing to yield.

Q: Ms. Patterson, please let me finish my questions.

A: Then please stop implying I wasn't paying attention.

---

topic: A witness is asked about a car accident they saw from their front porch
text:
Q: You testified earlier that the accident happened quickly. Is that accurate?

A: Accidents tend to.

Q: So you'd agree it was difficult to observe all the details?

A: No, I wouldn't agree to that.

Q: But you just said it happened quickly.

A: Quick doesn't mean unclear. A camera takes a picture in a fraction of a second. Doesn't mean the photo is blurry.

Q: That's an interesting analogy, Mr. Torres.

A: It's an accurate one.

Q: Let me ask you this. Did you see the traffic signal at the time of the collision?

A: There's no traffic signal at that intersection. It's a four-way stop.

Q: I apologize, the stop signs then. Did you see whether both drivers approached stop signs?

A: Yes. Both directions have stop signs.

Q: And did you observe both vehicles come to a complete stop?

A: I observed one vehicle stop completely. The other vehicle—the silver SUV—rolled through without stopping.

Q: You're certain of that?

A: I am.

Q: No hesitation whatsoever?

A: You've asked me four different ways now. My answer isn't going to change because you don't like it.

Q: I'm simply being thorough.

A: And I'm simply being honest. One of us is going to run out of patience first, and I've got nowhere else to be today.

topic: A witness is questioned about a conversation they overheard in a company hallway
text:
Q: Mr. Tanaka, I'd like to direct your attention to March 14th of last year. Were you present at the Westfield office that day?

A: Yes.

Q: And at some point during that day, did you happen to overhear a conversation in the hallway?

A: I heard people talking, yes.

Q: Who was talking?

A: Linda Marsh and someone from accounting. I don't know his name.

Q: You don't know his name. How long have you worked at Westfield?

A: Seven years.

Q: Seven years, and you don't know the name of someone from accounting?

A: There are forty-three people in accounting. I don't know all of them. Should I?

Q: I'm asking the questions, Mr. Tanaka. What did you hear Ms. Marsh say?

A: She said something about the quarterly numbers.

Q: Something. Can you be more specific?

A: She said the quarterly numbers were "adjusted." Her word, not mine.

Q: What else?

A: That's what I heard.

Q: That's all you heard? You were standing right there and that's all you heard?

A: I was walking past. I wasn't standing there taking notes.

Q: Did Ms. Marsh see you?

A: I have no idea what Ms. Marsh saw or didn't see. You'd have to ask her.

Q: I'm asking what you observed, Mr. Tanaka.

A: And I'm telling you. I walked past. I heard one sentence. I kept walking. That's it.

topic: A witness is questioned about a conversation they overheard in a company hallway
text:
Q: Ms. Chen, can you describe where you were standing when this conversation took place?

A: I was near the water cooler, which is in an alcove off the main hallway on the third floor, approximately fifteen feet from the elevator bank, if that level of detail is helpful to you.

Q: It is. Thank you. Who did you observe in the hallway?

A: I observed David Proctor, the regional sales manager, speaking with a woman I later learned was his assistant, though at the time I didn't know her name, her title, or her relationship to Mr. Proctor.

Q: What were they discussing?

A: I couldn't hear the beginning of the conversation, so I don't want to speculate about the overall topic, but the portion I heard—and I want to be clear this was fragmentary—concerned a client named Meridian.

Q: What specifically did you hear about Meridian?

A: Mr. Proctor said—and I'm paraphrasing because I don't have a perfect memory—something to the effect that "Meridian doesn't need to know" about something. I didn't hear what the something was. I want that on the record.

Q: Did the assistant respond?

A: She did.

Q: What did she say?

A: She said, "Are you sure?" or possibly "Are you certain?"—one of those two phrases. I couldn't tell you which with absolute confidence.

Q: How did Mr. Proctor respond to that?

A: He laughed. Though I should note it could have been a chuckle or even a scoff—I'm not an expert in categorizing vocalizations.

Q: Did you hear anything else?

A: The elevator arrived. They got in. The doors closed. That concluded what I was able to hear.

topic: A witness is questioned about a conversation they overheard in a company hallway
text:
Q: You were in the hallway on June 8th, correct?

A: Correct.

Q: You heard a conversation?

A: Correct.

Q: Between whom?

A: Between Thomas Whitmore and James Okafor.

Q: Where exactly were they standing?

A: Outside the conference room.

Q: Which conference room? There are four on that floor.

A: The one closest to the stairwell. I don't know what you call it.

Q: Conference Room C?

A: If that's closest to the stairwell, then yes.

Q: I'm asking you.

A: And I'm telling you I don't memorize conference room names.

Q: Fine. What did you hear Mr. Whitmore say?

A: He said the safety report was "taken care of."

Q: Taken care of. Did he elaborate?

A: Not that I heard.

Q: What did Mr. Okafor say in response?

A: He asked if "legal" knew.

Q: And?

A: And what?

Q: What was the answer?

A: Mr. Whitmore said, "Legal doesn't need to know everything."

Q: Were those his exact words?

A: To the best of my recollection, yes.

topic: A witness is questioned about a conversation they overheard in a company hallway
text:
Q: Tell me about the hallway conversation, please.

A: Which aspect of it?

Q: Let's start with when it occurred.

A: October. Mid-October. I don't remember the exact date—I didn't realize I'd be questioned about it eight months later.

Q: Fair enough. Mid-October. Who was present?

A: Rachel Emory and someone on the phone. She was on speaker.

Q: She was on speakerphone in a hallway?

A: Yes.

Q: Doesn't that strike you as unusual?

A: I don't set the standards for phone etiquette at my workplace.

Q: What did you hear Ms. Emory say?

A: Look, I was coming back from the restroom. I heard maybe twenty seconds of this call. She was talking about contract terms—something about changing the delivery schedule.

Q: Go on.

A: The person on the phone—I don't know who it was—said something like "the client won't agree to that."

Q: And Ms. Emory's response?

A: She laughed and said, "The client doesn't get a vote."

Q: Did that concern you?

A: I'm not here to share my concerns. You asked what I heard.

Q: Did you report this conversation to anyone?

A: No.

Q: Why not?

A: Because it wasn't my business, and frankly, I had work to do.

topic: A witness is questioned about a conversation they overheard in a company hallway
text:
Q: Good afternoon. You've previously stated you overheard a conversation between Gary Stein and Paula Navarro, is that right?

A: That's right.

Q: Where were you at the time?

A: I was in the copy room, which has an open doorway to the hall.

Q: Could you see them?

A: Partially. I could see Mr. Stein. Ms. Navarro was to his left, mostly out of my line of sight.

Q: What was the nature of what you overheard?

A: They were talking about a vendor. Summit Industrial, I think.

Q: You think?

A: I'm ninety percent sure it was Summit. It might have been Summit Industries. The names are similar.

Q: Were they discussing payments to this vendor?

A: They were discussing—wait, I want to be careful here. They mentioned payments, yes.

Q: What specifically did they say about payments?

A: Mr. Stein said something about payments being "rerouted."

Q: Rerouted. That's an interesting word. Did he say where they were being rerouted?

A: He didn't finish the sentence. Ms. Navarro interrupted him.

Q: What did she say?

A: She said, "Not here."

Q: Did Mr. Stein say anything else?

A: He lowered his voice. I couldn't hear after that.

Q: Convenient.

A: Excuse me?

Q: I said that's convenient timing. That your hearing failed at that exact moment.

A: My hearing didn't fail. He started whispering. There's a difference, Counselor.

Q: No further questions on this topic.

A: I'm sure there aren't.

topic: A paramedic is questioned about the response time and treatment at an accident scene
text:
Q: State your name and occupation for the record.

A: Michael Torres. Paramedic. Fourteen years.

Q: Mr. Torres, I'd like to direct your attention to the evening of March 15th. You responded to a motor vehicle accident on Route 9, correct?

A: Yes.

Q: What time did you arrive on scene?

A: The log says 8:47 p.m.

Q: And what time was the call dispatched?

A: 8:31.

Q: So sixteen minutes from dispatch to arrival?

A: If that's what the math says.

Q: Is sixteen minutes consistent with your department's standard response time for that area?

A: It's within range. Route 9 has limited access points. There was construction. I've already explained this in my written statement.

Q: I'm asking you now, under oath. Was there any delay that night that you would characterize as unusual?

A: No.

Q: Did you take the most direct route available?

A: I took the route I always take. The one that gets me there.

Q: That's not what I asked.

A: Then ask it differently.

Q: Let me rephrase. Were there alternative routes that might have been faster?

A: I don't know. I wasn't running simulations. I was driving to a crash.

Q: Fair enough. When you arrived, what was the condition of the plaintiff?

A: Conscious. Complaining of neck pain. Some laceration on the forehead. Look, it's all in my report. Page three.

---

topic: A paramedic is questioned about the response time and treatment at an accident scene
text:
Q: You've been a paramedic for how long?

A: Going on eleven years now. Eleven in September, I think. Maybe October. It's been a long week. Eleven years, roughly.

Q: And you were working the night shift on April 2nd of last year?

A: That's correct. Started at seven, off at seven. Twelve-hour rotation.

Q: How many calls had you responded to before the accident in question?

A: That night? I'd have to check the log, but... four, I think. Maybe five. There was the chest pain call on Elmwood, the slip-and-fall at the grocery store, a possible overdose that turned out to be a panic attack, and... I'm losing one. There was another. I'm sorry, I'm not trying to be evasive, it's just blending together.

Q: Take your time.

A: No, I've got it. Diabetic emergency. That was the fourth one. Then the MVA.

Q: So the accident involving my client was your fifth call of the shift?

A: Sounds right. Fifth, yes.

Q: When you arrived at the scene, walk me through your initial assessment.

A: We pulled up, my partner grabbed the jump bag, I went to the vehicle. Driver's side. The door was... it was already open, I think someone had opened it. A bystander maybe. And I just started going through the checklist. Airway, breathing, circulation. The basics. It's automatic at this point. You just do it.

Q: You said it's automatic. Does that mean you might not recall specific details?

A: No, I... I remember. I'm just saying the training takes over. You don't think, you do. Then you think later. Like now. Now I'm thinking about it.

---

topic: A paramedic is questioned about the response time and treatment at an accident scene
text:
Q: Paramedic Chen, let's move this along. You arrived at 9:15 p.m., correct?

A: According to the dispatch record, yes.

Q: And the patient was unresponsive when you reached her?

A: She was responsive but altered. GCS of 12.

Q: Fine. GCS of 12. What treatment did you administer first?

A: Cervical collar, then we started a line.

Q: IV access?

A: Yes.

Q: How long did that take?

A: Counsel, I don't have a stopwatch running when I'm—

Q: Approximately.

A: Two minutes. Maybe three.

Q: And then?

A: Loaded her. Transported.

Q: Let's talk about the loading. Did you use a backboard?

A: Yes.

Q: Was there any difficulty securing the patient?

A: I don't... what do you mean by difficulty?

Q: Did anything go wrong?

A: No. Nothing went wrong. We secured her and we transported her. That's what we do.

Q: I'm just trying to understand what happened.

A: And I'm trying to answer. But if you could ask one question at a time instead of four, that would help.

Q: Understood. Let me ask this: at any point during transport, did the patient's condition change?

A: Her pressure dropped slightly. We adjusted the IV rate. It stabilized. That's in my report too. Page two, I believe. Bottom half.

---

topic: A paramedic is questioned about the response time and treatment at an accident scene
text:
Q: Good afternoon. You're Steven Okafor, paramedic with County Fire and Rescue?

A: I am.

Q: How are you holding up? I know we've been at this for a while.

A: I'm here.

Q: Let's see if we can get through this section. On the night of the accident, you and your partner were dispatched at what time?

A: 11:42 p.m.

Q: And that was for a single-vehicle collision on Miller Road?

A: Yes.

Q: When you arrived, who was already on scene?

A: Sheriff's deputy. I don't remember which one. And some people standing around. Family, I think, from one of the nearby houses.

Q: Was fire and rescue there?

A: We are fire and rescue.

Q: I'm sorry, I meant... the fire engine. Heavy rescue.

A: No, they weren't needed. It wasn't an extrication.

Q: Okay. When you approached the vehicle, was the driver still inside?

A: He was. Seatbelt on. Airbag deployed.

Q: What did you observe about his condition?

A: He was conscious. Talking. Some confusion, but that's normal with airbag deployment. He had abrasions on his forearms, some bruising starting to show on his chest from the belt.

Q: Did he complain of any pain?

A: Everywhere, he said. Just... everywhere.

Q: I see. Did you ask him to be more specific?

A: Counsel, when someone's just been in an accident and they say everything hurts, you don't interrogate them. You treat them.

Q: I understand. I'm just trying to get a full picture here.

A: Then the picture is: he hurt everywhere, we treated him for what we could see and what he could tell us, and we got him to the hospital.

---

topic: A paramedic is questioned about the response time and treatment at an accident scene
text:
Q: Ms. Franklin, I want to ask you about the equipment you had available that night.

A: Go ahead.

Q: Your ambulance was stocked with... let me see... a cardiac monitor, correct?

A: Yes.

Q: And that monitor was functioning?

A: It was.

Q: Did you use it on the plaintiff?

A: We did. We put him on the monitor during transport.

Q: What did it show?

A: Sinus rhythm. Rate in the nineties, if I recall.

Q: And blood pressure?

A: 140 over... I'd have to check the run sheet. I don't remember the exact diastolic.

Q: That's fine. Let me ask about... I'm sorry, let me find my notes here. One moment.

A: Take your time.

Q: Here we go. The oxygen administration. Did you provide supplemental oxygen?

A: We did. Nasal cannula, two liters.

Q: Is that standard for this type of injury?

A: It depends on the patient. His O2 sat was fine, but we provide it as a precaution with any trauma.

Q: Okay. And... let's see. Was there any medication administered?

A: No.

Q: None at all?

A: No medications were indicated.

Q: What about pain management?

A: He didn't request any, and we were eight minutes from the ER. We don't typically... look, we don't just give medications because someone's uncomfortable. There's protocols. He didn't meet the threshold.

Q: I'm not suggesting you did anything wrong.

A: I know. I'm just explaining.

Q: Appreciated. Let me see if I have anything else here... I think that's all I have on equipment. Let's move to transport.

topic: A pharmacist is deposed about a prescription that was filled with the wrong dosage
text:
Q: Dr. Pham, walk me through the verification process you completed on March 14th for the Hendricks prescription.

A: Gladly. The prescription came in electronically at 9:47 a.m. I pulled it up, confirmed the patient's date of birth and allergy profile, checked the prescribing physician's DEA number, and then reviewed the dosage against our clinical decision support system.

Q: And what did that system flag, if anything?

A: Nothing. It flagged nothing because the prescription as written was within normal parameters. The issue arose later, during the filling process, which is a separate step handled by the technician before my final verification.

Q: So you're saying the error occurred after your initial review?

A: I'm saying the electronic prescription I received called for 10 milligrams. The bottle that left this pharmacy contained 100 milligram tablets. That discrepancy originated at the filling stage.

Q: You seem quite certain about that timeline.

A: I am certain. I printed the original e-prescription that morning, and I have it here in the file your office subpoenaed. Would you like me to direct you to the relevant timestamp?

Q: That won't be necessary at this moment.

A: The timestamp is on page fourteen, third line from the top.

Q: Dr. Pham, who was the technician working that shift?

A: Marcus Delano. He's been with us for six years. Excellent employee, but he was also covering two stations that morning due to a staffing shortage I had flagged to management three weeks prior.

Q: Did you document that staffing concern?

A: Email dated February 21st, copied to regional operations. I can provide that as well if it's not already in your materials. It should be.

Q: Let's move on to the final verification step.

A: Of course. I'm happy to explain exactly how the system failed Mr. Hendricks—and where the responsibility actually lies.

topic: A pharmacist is deposed about a prescription that was filled with the wrong dosage
text:
Q: When did you first realize an error had been made?

A: When the patient's wife called the pharmacy, upset, saying her husband had been hospitalized.

Q: What did she tell you specifically?

A: She said he'd taken three doses and started experiencing tremors and confusion. She asked if we'd given him the right medication.

Q: And what did you do?

A: I pulled his file immediately.

Q: What did you find?

A: That the label read metoprolol 25 milligrams, but we'd dispensed 100 milligram tablets.

Q: So a fourfold increase in dosage.

A: Yes.

Q: Did you report this to anyone?

A: I filed an incident report within the hour and contacted my district manager.

Q: Did you contact the prescribing physician?

A: Yes, Dr. Sutton. I called her office and spoke with her directly.

Q: Now, you mentioned pulling the file "immediately." How long did that actually take?

A: Under two minutes. I was already at the dispensing station.

Q: And the conversation with Mrs. Okafor—how long did that last?

A: Perhaps four minutes. She was understandably distraught. I let her speak.

Q: Did you apologize to her?

A: I expressed that I was deeply sorry her husband was in the hospital and that I would do everything in my power to determine what happened.

Q: But you didn't admit fault.

A: I told her the truth: that I didn't yet know where the error occurred, but I would find out.

topic: A pharmacist is deposed about a prescription that was filled with the wrong dosage
text:
Q: Is it your testimony that you followed every protocol that day?

A: No.

Q: No?

A: I said no. I did not follow every protocol.

Q: Which protocols did you fail to follow?

A: I failed to perform a visual verification of the tablet imprint against the NDC code on the stock bottle. That's step seven in our standard dispensing checklist.

Q: Why did you skip that step?

A: I didn't skip it intentionally. I was interrupted by a phone call from a patient with an urgent insurance question. When I returned to the station, I resumed at step eight.

Q: And you didn't realize you'd missed a step?

A: Not until after the incident. Then I reviewed everything.

Q: So you've done your own investigation.

A: I have. I went through that day minute by minute. I know exactly where I made my mistake.

Q: Does your employer know you've conducted this review?

A: I provided them a written summary the day after Mr. Hendricks was hospitalized.

Q: On your own initiative?

A: On my own initiative. It seemed like the right thing to do.

Q: That's helpful. Very helpful.

A: I would hope so. I'm not here to hide anything, Counselor. I made an error. A man was harmed. I'd like to understand how to prevent it from happening again.

topic: A pharmacist is deposed about a prescription that was filled with the wrong dosage
text:
Q: You've been a licensed pharmacist for how long?

A: Nineteen years.

Q: And in those nineteen years, how many prescriptions would you estimate you've filled?

A: Hundreds of thousands. I couldn't give you a precise number.

Q: Have you ever made a dispensing error before March 14th?

A: Define "dispensing error."

Q: A situation where the medication or dosage given to a patient differed from what was prescribed.

A: Once, in 2016. A quantity error—patient received a 30-day supply instead of 90. It was caught before she left the pharmacy.

Q: So in nineteen years, two errors. That's your testimony.

A: Two that I'm aware of, yes.

Q: The 2016 error—was there an incident report?

A: There was.

Q: Who filed it?

A: I did.

Q: And the error on March 14th—who filed that incident report?

A: I did.

Q: You self-reported both times.

A: That's correct. That's what you do.

Q: Some pharmacists might not be so forthcoming.

A: I wouldn't know about that. I know what my license requires and what my conscience requires. They happen to align.

Q: Fair enough. Let's talk about the specific workflow that morning.

A: Please. I'd welcome the opportunity to walk you through it in detail.

topic: A pharmacist is deposed about a prescription that was filled with the wrong dosage
text:
Q: Did you count the tablets yourself?

A: No.

Q: Who counted them?

A: The pharmacy technician on duty.

Q: That would be Mr. Delano?

A: No, actually. That would be Priya Nair. Marcus had stepped away for his break.

Q: So the technician who filled the prescription was different from the one you initially mentioned?

A: I mentioned Marcus because he opened the workflow. Priya completed the fill.

Q: I see. Does your system track which technician performs each step?

A: Yes. Every scan, every action is logged with a timestamp and user ID.

Q: And you've reviewed those logs?

A: Extensively.

Q: What did they show?

A: They showed that Priya scanned the correct NDC code for metoprolol 25 milligrams at 10:14 a.m. But the physical tablets in the vial—when I examined the remaining stock later—came from a bottle of 100 milligrams that had been misshelved.

Q: Misshelved.

A: Placed in the wrong bin. The bottles look nearly identical. Same manufacturer, same color label, different strength.

Q: Whose responsibility is it to ensure proper shelving?

A: That rotates. I'd have to check the schedule.

Q: But you could check it.

A: I could. I already have. I'm simply verifying whether you want me to state it for the record.

Q: Please.

A: It was my responsibility that week. I shelved that bottle incorrectly.

topic: An employee is deposed about a coworker's termination they believe was retaliatory
text:
Q: Ms. Patel, how long did you work alongside David Chen before his termination?

A: Three years. A little over three years.

Q: And during that time, would you say you were aware of his job performance?

A: I sat eight feet from him. I heard every phone call he made. I saw him stay late. I saw him come in early. Yes. I was aware.

Q: Did you ever hear management express concerns about his performance prior to his filing the safety complaint?

A: No.

Q: Not once in three years?

A: Not once. He got the quarterly recognition award twice. You probably have that in your documents somewhere.

Q: I'm asking what you observed, Ms. Patel.

A: And I'm telling you. He was a good employee. Everyone knew it. Then he filed the complaint, and three weeks later he's being written up for things nobody ever mentioned before.

Q: What kinds of things?

A: Tardiness. Attitude. Vague things. The kind of things you write down when you need something on paper.

Q: That's your interpretation?

A: That's what I watched happen. You can call it whatever you want.

Q: Did anyone in management discuss these write-ups with you?

A: No. Why would they?

Q: Did you discuss them with David?

A: He showed them to me. He didn't understand what was happening. I did.

Q: What do you mean you did?

A: I mean I've worked there eleven years. I've seen how it goes. You learn to recognize the pattern.

Q: And you believe you saw that pattern with Mr. Chen?

A: I know what I saw. Whether it matters to anyone at this point, I couldn't tell you.

---

topic: An employee is deposed about a coworker's termination they believe was retaliatory
text:
Q: Mr. Okonkwo, I want to ask you about the weeks leading up to Ms. Brennan's termination.

A: Alright.

Q: Did you notice any change in how management interacted with her after she reported the harassment?

A: Yes.

Q: Can you describe that change?

A: She used to be included in things. Meetings, project discussions. After she made the report, that stopped.

Q: Stopped entirely?

A: I don't know if I can say entirely. But I can say I noticed her sitting at her desk more, being left out of conversations she would have been part of before.

Q: Did anyone explain why?

A: No one explained anything. That's not how it works.

Q: How what works, Mr. Okonkwo?

A: How these things work. People don't announce what they're doing. They just do it, and you either see it or you don't.

Q: Let me ask it differently. Did you ever hear anyone say Ms. Brennan was being excluded because of her complaint?

A: No.

Q: So you're drawing an inference.

A: I'm describing what I observed and when I observed it. The timing is the timing. I'm not going to pretend I didn't notice.

Q: Fair enough. Did Ms. Brennan ever discuss with you how she was feeling during this period?

A: Once or twice. She said she felt like she was being pushed out. I told her I saw it too.

Q: What did she say to that?

A: She didn't say anything. She just nodded. There wasn't much to say.

Q: Did you report your observations to anyone in HR or management?

A: No.

Q: Why not?

A: Because I've been there long enough to know what good that would do.

---

topic: An employee is deposed about a coworker's termination they believe was retaliatory
text:
Q: Let's move on to the termination meeting itself. You were present?

A: I was asked to be there, yes. As a witness for the company.

Q: And who else was in the room?

A: Sandra Mejia, who's HR. Tom Aldrich, who was Kevin's direct supervisor. And Kevin.

Q: What was said at the beginning of the meeting?

A: Sandra read from a script. Or a document. Something prepared. About performance deficiencies and failure to meet expectations.

Q: Did Mr. Aldrich say anything?

A: Not much. He looked at the table mostly.

Q: What about Kevin—Mr. Marsh? How did he respond?

A: He asked what specific deficiencies they were talking about. Sandra listed some things. He asked for examples. She said they were documented in his file.

Q: Did he dispute the characterizations?

A: He tried. He brought up his numbers, his client feedback. Sandra just kept saying the decision had been made.

Q: How did the meeting end?

A: Kevin asked if this had anything to do with the complaint he'd filed about the overtime violations. Sandra said it didn't. Then he was asked to collect his things.

Q: What was your reaction, sitting in that room?

A: I don't know that my reaction is relevant.

Q: I'm asking what you observed about your own response.

A: I observed that I sat there and didn't say anything. That's what I observed.

Q: Did you believe what Sandra was saying about the performance issues?

A: I think Sandra believed what she was told to believe.

Q: That's not what I asked.

A: I know. But it's the answer I have.

---

topic: An employee is deposed about a coworker's termination they believe was retaliatory
text:
Q: Ms. Torres, I'll be brief. I know we've been at this for a while.

A: It's fine. I understand you have questions.

Q: I want to focus on one specific conversation. You mentioned in your written statement that you overheard Mr. Dunlap say something about Rachel Vance shortly after she filed her EEOC charge.

A: I did.

Q: What did he say?

A: He said, "She's not going to be a problem much longer."

Q: Those were his exact words?

A: That's what I remember him saying. I can't swear to the exact phrasing after this much time, but that was the substance of it.

Q: Who was he speaking to?

A: Carla Finch. They were in the hallway outside the break room. I don't think they knew I was there.

Q: Did you report this conversation to anyone?

A: No.

Q: Why not?

A: To who? Mr. Dunlap was the department head. Carla was HR.

Q: You could have gone above them.

A: I could have. I didn't.

Q: Do you wish you had?

A: I don't know what good it would have done. Rachel was terminated two weeks later regardless.

Q: You say regardless. Regardless of what?

A: Regardless of anything. These situations, they play out the way they play out. One person in the hallway overhearing something—that doesn't change the ending.

Q: You sound certain of that.

A: I've worked in enough places to know what I've seen.

---

topic: An employee is deposed about a coworker's termination they believe was retaliatory
text:
Q: I want to understand the timeline clearly. Mr. Huang filed his whistleblower complaint on March 3rd, correct?

A: If that's what the documents say. I don't remember exact dates.

Q: And you testified earlier that you first heard about alleged performance issues with Mr. Huang sometime in mid-March?

A: Around then, yes.

Q: Who raised those issues?

A: Linda Ashford mentioned something to me in passing. Said there were concerns.

Q: What kind of concerns?

A: She didn't get specific. Just that there were concerns about Peter's fit with the team going forward.

Q: His fit?

A: Her word.

Q: Had you ever heard anyone question Mr. Huang's fit before March?

A: No.

Q: In the two years he'd worked there?

A: No. He was well-liked. Competent. People respected him.

Q: So this was new.

A: Yes.

Q: What did you make of that?

A: I made of it what anyone would make of it.

Q: Which is?

A: Which is that once someone becomes inconvenient, suddenly there are concerns about their fit. It's not complicated.

Q: Did you share that view with anyone at the time?

A: I mentioned it to my wife. At home. That's about it.

Q: Not to anyone at the company?

A: What would be the point? The decision-makers had already decided. My opinion wasn't going to change anything.

Q: You seem sure of that.

A: I've been doing this a long time. You learn what battles are worth fighting. This one was already over before any of us knew it started.

topic: A business partner is deposed about financial records they were responsible for maintaining
text:
Q: Mr. Tanaka, you were responsible for maintaining the accounts receivable ledger for the partnership, correct?

A: Yes.

Q: And that ledger would reflect all incoming payments from clients?

A: That's what an accounts receivable ledger does, yes.

Q: I'm asking whether yours did.

A: It did.

Q: Were there instances where payments came in that weren't recorded same-day?

A: I'm sure there were. We're talking about a five-year period. Sometimes things got entered the next morning.

Q: The next morning. What about longer delays?

A: Define "longer."

Q: More than 48 hours.

A: Probably. I didn't sit there with a stopwatch.

Q: Mr. Tanaka, I'm not asking you to guess. Did you or did you not have a practice of delaying entries?

A: No, I did not have a "practice" of delaying entries. Sometimes entries were late. That's not a practice. That's reality.

Q: Let's look at Exhibit 14. You see the entry dated March 3rd for Greenfield Industries?

A: I see it.

Q: The check was dated February 19th. That's twelve days.

A: Then I suppose it was entered twelve days late. I don't know what you want me to say.

Q: I want you to explain how that happened.

A: I don't remember. It was three years ago. Maybe it sat on someone's desk. Maybe I was out sick. I don't have a specific memory of every deposit.

topic: A business partner is deposed about financial records they were responsible for maintaining
text:
Q: Ms. Vaughn, how often did you reconcile the partnership's bank statements?

A: Monthly.

A: I believe so, yes.

A: Counsel, I reconciled the accounts monthly. I've been doing this for eighteen years. It's not something I skip.

A: And I'm telling you now, under oath. The same thing I told her then.

Q: Did you ever identify discrepancies during these reconciliations?

A: Small ones, occasionally. A transposed digit here and there.

Q: How small?

A: Usually under a hundred dollars. Rounding errors. Human error. Always corrected.

topic: A business partner is deposed about financial records they were responsible for maintaining
text:
Q: Mr. Okonkwo, I'm going to hand you Exhibit 22. Take your time and let me know when you've reviewed it.

topic: A business partner is deposed about financial records they were responsible for maintaining
text:
Q: Let's talk about the petty cash fund.

topic: A business partner is deposed about financial records they were responsible for maintaining
text:
Q: Ms. Chen, the partnership agreement required annual audits, correct?

A: It required annual financial reviews. Not full audits. There's a distinction.

Q: Explain the distinction.

A: An audit is a comprehensive examination with formal attestation. A review is less extensive. It's an intermediate level of assurance.

Q: Fine. Were those reviews conducted?

A: Yes.

Q: Every year?

A: Every year that I was managing the finances, yes.

Q: Which firm performed them?

A: Henderson & Associates.

Q: That's your brother-in-law's firm, isn't it?

A: It's a firm where my brother-in-law is one of several partners.

Q: Did you disclose the family relationship?

A: Of course I disclosed it. I mentioned it in the very meeting where I made the recommendation. This is all in the partnership minutes.

A: Obviously not, or we wouldn't have used them.

Q: Did Henderson & Associates ever identify any irregularities in the financial records you maintained?

A: Minor procedural recommendations. Nothing substantive.

Q: You're certain?

A: I have the reports. Would you like me to read them to you? Because I'm happy to do that if it would save us another thirty minutes of questions you already know the answers to.

topic: A financial advisor is deposed about investment decisions made on a client's behalf
text:
Q: Mr. Hartwell, let's discuss the Meridian Growth Fund. When did you first recommend that investment to Mrs. Patterson?

topic: A financial advisor is deposed about investment decisions made on a client's behalf
text:
Q: You've testified that you met with Mr. Okonkwo quarterly. What was the purpose of those meetings?

topic: A financial advisor is deposed about investment decisions made on a client's behalf
text:
Q: Ms. Vaughn, I want to understand your process for selecting the Bellweather Capital Fund. Walk me through it.

A: Certainly. We have an investment committee that evaluates funds based on multiple criteria—historical performance, management stability, fee structures, risk-adjusted returns, alignment with client objectives. Bellweather met our thresholds across those categories.

Q: When you say "met your thresholds," what specifically were those thresholds for risk-adjusted returns?

A: We generally look for funds that have outperformed their benchmark on a Sharpe ratio basis over trailing three- and five-year periods.

Q: And Bellweather satisfied that?

A: At the time of selection, yes.

Q: Did you personally review the fund's performance data?

A: I reviewed the committee's summary materials, which included performance data.

Q: So you didn't independently verify the underlying data?

A: That's not my role. The committee has analysts who handle verification.

Q: What is your role, then?

A: I implement committee-approved recommendations for my clients based on their individual circumstances.

Q: You implement. So you're more of a... conduit?

A: I wouldn't use that term. I exercise professional judgment in matching approved investments to client needs.

Q: Did you exercise professional judgment when placing $400,000 of the Delgados' retirement savings into Bellweather?

A: Yes.

Q: What judgment did you exercise?

A: That the fund was appropriate given their stated objectives and timeline.

Q: Their stated objectives. Whose words were those objectives written in—theirs or yours?

A: The objectives were developed collaboratively and documented with their signed acknowledgment.

topic: A financial advisor is deposed about investment decisions made on a client's behalf
text:
Q: Let's talk about the period between January and March 2023. The Nakamura account lost approximately thirty-one percent of its value during that period. Were you aware of that?

A: I was aware the account experienced losses during a period of market volatility, yes.

topic: A financial advisor is deposed about investment decisions made on a client's behalf
text:
Q: Tell me about the due diligence process your firm uses for alternative investments.

A: It was noted in the report. Whether I focused on that particular item at the time, I couldn't say.

Q: You couldn't say. Is that because you don't remember, or because you didn't focus on it?

A: I reviewed a lot of materials. I can't reconstruct my mental state from three years ago.

topic: A driver is deposed about the events leading up to a multi-vehicle collision
text:
Q: Mr. Hernandez, let's talk about what you observed in the moments before the collision. You were traveling northbound on Route 9, correct?

A: That's what I've already stated, yes.

Q: And at some point, you noticed the white pickup truck in your rearview mirror?

A: I noticed a vehicle, yes. I couldn't tell you the exact make or model from my mirror.

Q: But you testified earlier that it was a white pickup truck.

A: I testified that after the accident, I saw it was a white pickup. That's different from saying I identified it as such while it was behind me.

Q: I see. So when you first noticed this vehicle—whatever it was—how far back would you estimate it was?

A: I'm not going to guess at distances. I don't know how far back it was.

Q: You can't give any estimate at all?

A: I could give you a number, but it wouldn't be accurate. I wasn't measuring. I was driving.

Q: Were there any other vehicles between you and this vehicle you noticed?

A: At what point?

Q: When you first noticed it.

A: There may have been. I wasn't cataloging every car on the road.

Q: Mr. Hernandez, I'm just asking what you remember.

A: And I'm telling you what I actually remember, not what would be convenient.

Q: Did you at any point feel that the vehicle behind you was following too closely?

A: Define "too closely."

Q: In your judgment.

A: In my judgment, a lot of people follow too closely. That doesn't mean anything unusual was happening.

topic: A driver is deposed about the events leading up to a multi-vehicle collision
text:
Q: Ms. Okonkwo, you've stated that you had a clear view of the intersection when you entered it.

A: Yes.

Q: And the light was green for your direction of travel?

A: Yes, it was green.

Q: How long had it been green when you entered the intersection?

A: I don't know exactly. It was already green when I approached.

A: It could have been, sure.

Q: Could it have been about to turn yellow?

A: I suppose anything's possible. But it was green. Solid green.

Q: You seem very certain about that.

A: Because I am certain. I wouldn't have entered on a yellow.

Q: Never?

A: Excuse me?

Q: You've never in your life entered an intersection on a yellow light?

Q: How fast were you going when you entered the intersection?

A: Around thirty, thirty-five.

Q: Around. So you don't know exactly.

A: I know approximately. Most people don't stare at their speedometer while driving through an intersection.

Q: Let's move on. After you entered the intersection, what did you see?

topic: A driver is deposed about the events leading up to a multi-vehicle collision

topic: A driver is deposed about the events leading up to a multi-vehicle collision

topic: A witness is questioned about a conversation they overheard in a company hallway
text:
Q: Please state your name for the record.

A: David Chen.

Q: Mr. Chen, you were employed at Westbrook Industries in March of this year?

A: I was, yes. Still am.

Q: And on March 14th, you were present on the fourth floor of the Westbrook building?

A: I was in the hallway outside the executive conference room at approximately 2:15 in the afternoon. I remember the time because I had just left a 2 o'clock meeting that ran short.

Q: Did you overhear a conversation that day?

A: I did. Between Sandra Hoffman and Richard Tate. They were standing near the water cooler alcove, about fifteen feet from where I was walking.

Q: How do you know it was Ms. Hoffman and Mr. Tate?

A: I've worked with both of them for six years. I know their voices. I also saw them as I passed.

Q: What did you hear?

A: Ms. Hoffman said, and I'm quoting as closely as I can remember, "The audit numbers don't match what we submitted to the board." Mr. Tate responded, "Then we make them match."

Q: You're certain those were the exact words?

A: Those were the exact words. I stopped walking when I heard it. It struck me as significant, so I made a point to remember.

Q: Did they see you?

A: Mr. Tate glanced in my direction, yes. He didn't acknowledge me, but he lowered his voice after that.

Q: Did you hear anything else?

A: Ms. Hoffman said something about "the Patterson account" and then they moved into the stairwell. I didn't follow them.

Q: Why not?

A: Because I'm not in the habit of chasing down executives to eavesdrop, counselor. I heard what I heard. That was enough.

Q: Did you report this conversation to anyone?

A: I reported it to the ethics hotline the following Monday. I have the confirmation number if you'd like it.

---

topic: A contractor is questioned about delays that caused a construction project to fail
text:

Q: That won't be necessary. So you continued pouring foundation despite knowing the specifications had changed?

A: I continued pouring foundation because I was directed to continue. I'm a contractor. I build what I'm told to build, when I'm told to build it, by the people paying me to build it.

Q: And you didn't think to raise concerns?

A: I raised concerns. Multiple times. In writing. I'm starting to wonder if anyone on your side actually read the project file before scheduling this deposition.

Q: Mr. Hendricks—

topic: A contractor is questioned about delays that caused a construction project to fail

topic: A contractor is questioned about delays that caused a construction project to fail

topic: A contractor is questioned about delays that caused a construction project to fail
