topic: An HR director is questioned about a harassment complaint that was filed and closed
text:
Q: Ms. Brennan, you were the HR director at Lakeview Financial in March of 2022, correct?

A: I was, and I still am.

Q: And you received a harassment complaint from an employee named David Chen on March 14th of that year?

A: I did. I received it, reviewed it, and initiated our standard intake process that same day.

Q: Let's slow down. I only asked if you received it.

A: I understood your question. I'm providing you with the complete picture of what occurred.

Q: What did Mr. Chen allege in his complaint?

A: He alleged that his supervisor, Brenda Walsh, made repeated comments about his appearance that made him uncomfortable. He also alleged she touched his shoulder on two occasions without his consent.

Q: And what was your determination after investigating?

A: That the complaint did not rise to the level of harassment under our policy or under applicable law.

Q: How long did that investigation take?

A: Eleven business days from intake to closing memo.

Q: That seems fast for a harassment investigation.

A: It's actually within our standard window. Our policy provides for fourteen business days, and we completed it in eleven. I can walk you through each step if that would be helpful.

Q: Did you interview Ms. Walsh?

A: Of course. She was the accused party. Interviewing her was mandatory under our protocol, and I conducted that interview myself on March 18th.

Q: Did you find her credible?

A: I found her account to be consistent with the documentary evidence and with the statements of three other witnesses who were present during the alleged incidents.

Q: So you simply believed her over Mr. Chen?

A: That's not what I said. I weighed the evidence. The evidence supported closing the complaint. That's what I did.

topic: An HR director is questioned about a harassment complaint that was filed and closed
text:
Q: You closed this complaint in April, is that right?

A: April 9th, yes.

Q: And Mr. Chen was terminated in May.

A: He was separated from the company on May 22nd, that's correct.

Q: Separated. You mean fired.

A: I mean separated. There are different categories of separation, and his was a reduction in force.

Q: A reduction in force that only affected him?

A: It affected his position. His position was eliminated as part of a restructuring of the client services team.

Q: Who made that decision?

A: The decision was made by the VP of Operations in consultation with finance.

Q: Not you?

A: Not me. I was informed of the decision and processed the paperwork. That's HR's role in a RIF situation.

Q: You didn't think the timing was suspicious? Complaint in March, closed in April, fired in May?

A: I don't engage in speculation about timing, counsel. I process documentation according to policy. The RIF was documented, justified, and approved through proper channels.

Q: Did anyone ask you whether Mr. Chen had filed a complaint before approving the RIF?

A: No.

Q: You're certain?

A: I am certain. That question was never posed to me by anyone involved in the decision.

Q: Would you have told them if they had asked?

A: That's a hypothetical. But complaint records are confidential under our policy, so no, I would not have disclosed that information without a legitimate business need.

topic: An HR director is questioned about a harassment complaint that was filed and closed
text:
Q: Walk me through your investigation process, if you would.

A: Sure. When we receive a complaint, we open a file and assign an investigator. In this case, I assigned myself because of the seniority of the individuals involved.

Q: Is that typical?

A: For complaints involving a department head? Yes, I handle those personally.

Q: What's the first step once you've assigned yourself?

A: Interview the complainant. Get the full account in their own words. I did that on March 15th with Mr. Chen.

Q: Did he seem... how would you describe his demeanor?

A: I don't document demeanor. I document facts.

Q: Fair enough. What facts did he provide?

A: He described four specific incidents. Two involved comments about his physical appearance, specifically his arms and his smile. Two involved Ms. Walsh placing her hand on his shoulder during conversations.

Q: And you investigated each of these?

A: Each one, yes. I interviewed witnesses who were present. I reviewed calendar records and seating arrangements. I spoke with Ms. Walsh.

Q: What did Ms. Walsh say?

A: She acknowledged making comments she described as complimentary. She denied any physical contact beyond normal workplace interaction.

Q: Normal workplace interaction. Those are her words?

A: Those are her words. I'm quoting from my notes.

Q: Did you find that characterization accurate?

A: I found that the physical contact, as described by both parties and by witnesses, did not constitute harassment under our policy. Our policy requires conduct that is severe or pervasive. Two instances of shoulder-touching over a six-month period does not meet that threshold.

topic: An HR director is questioned about a harassment complaint that was filed and closed
text:
Q: Let me ask you something directly, Ms. Brennan. Did you want this complaint to go away?

A: No.

Q: No?

A: No. I investigated it thoroughly and reached a conclusion based on the evidence. If the evidence had supported a finding of harassment, I would have made that finding.

Q: Have you ever made a finding of harassment against a department head?

A: Twice. In 2019 against the director of marketing, and in 2021 against a senior project manager.

Q: What happened to them?

A: The marketing director was terminated. The project manager received a written warning and mandatory training after a single substantiated incident.

Q: So you do terminate people for harassment.

A: When warranted, absolutely.

Q: But it wasn't warranted here.

A: The evidence did not support it here.

Q: The evidence being Ms. Walsh's denial?

A: The evidence being witness statements, contemporaneous records, the nature of the conduct as described, and yes, Ms. Walsh's account. All of it together.

Q: Do you think Mr. Chen was lying?

A: I don't think he was lying. I think he experienced discomfort. I think that discomfort was genuine. But discomfort, standing alone, does not constitute harassment under our policy or under the law.

Q: That's a fine distinction.

A: It's an important one. And it's my job to make it.

topic: An HR director is questioned about a harassment complaint that was filed and closed
text:
Q: Now, you mentioned earlier that you closed the Chen complaint. Let's talk about what happened after that.

A: After the closing memo was issued?

Q: Yes.

A: Mr. Chen was notified of the outcome. He was informed of his right to appeal. He did not appeal.

Q: Did you speak with him personally?

A: I did. I sat with him for approximately thirty minutes on April 10th.

Q: How did that conversation go?

A: He was disappointed. He expressed frustration. I listened, I explained our findings, and I answered his questions.

Q: Did he threaten to sue?

A: He did not use the word "sue." He said he might need to explore other options.

Q: And what did you say to that?

A: I told him that was his right.

Q: Were you concerned?

A: I'm never concerned when an employee exercises their legal rights. I documented the conversation, as I do with all sensitive discussions, and I filed the documentation appropriately.

Q: Did you tell anyone about his statement? Legal, perhaps?

A: I informed our general counsel as a matter of routine. Any indication of potential litigation gets flagged.

Q: And what did legal say?

A: Legal reviewed the file and concurred with my findings.

Q: They concurred.

A: They did. Within forty-eight hours of receiving the file, they confirmed the investigation was thorough and the conclusion was supported by the evidence.

Q: Convenient.

A: Accurate.

topic: A pharmacist is deposed about a prescription that was filled with the wrong dosage
text:
Q: Dr. Patel, I'm showing you what's been marked as Exhibit 14. Do you recognize this document?

A: Yes, that's a prescription label from our pharmacy.

Q: And this label indicates a dosage of 200 milligrams of metformin, correct?

A: That's what it says, yes.

Q: Is 200 milligrams a standard dosage for metformin?

A: I'm sorry, can you clarify what you mean by "standard"?

Q: Is it a dosage you would commonly dispense?

A: Well, metformin comes in various strengths. 500, 850, 1000 milligrams are typical. 200 milligrams would be... I mean, that's not a commercially available tablet strength that I'm aware of.

Q: So if this label says 200 milligrams—

A: I'm looking at this and I genuinely don't understand how that number would appear. We don't stock 200 milligram metformin. It doesn't exist as a product we carry.

Q: But this is your pharmacy's label, yes?

A: It appears to be, but the label is generated from our system, and our system pulls from our inventory, which doesn't include a 200 milligram option for metformin. So I'm... I don't know how to explain what I'm looking at.

Q: Could someone have manually entered that dosage?

A: Manual entry? That would require override permissions. I suppose theoretically, but why would anyone—I'm not following the logic of how this would happen.

Q: I'm simply asking if it's possible.

A: Possible in what sense? Technically possible if someone bypassed multiple safety protocols? I suppose. But I've never seen it done. I've been doing this for eleven years and I've never seen a label like this.

Q: Dr. Patel, did you personally fill this prescription?

A: According to the initials, yes, those are mine. But I have no memory of this, and frankly, I cannot reconcile what this document shows with anything I would have done.

topic: A pharmacist is deposed about a prescription that was filled with the wrong dosage
text:
Q: Walk me through your standard verification process when filling a prescription.

A: Certainly. The prescription comes in, either electronic or paper. A technician enters the information into the system. I verify the entry against the original prescription. Then I verify the medication pulled matches the label. Then it's bagged for pickup.

Q: And you verified this particular prescription?

A: According to the records, yes.

Q: The records indicate the patient was prescribed 10 milligrams of lisinopril daily, but received 100 milligrams. How does that happen under the process you just described?

A: It shouldn't.

Q: But it did.

A: I understand that's the allegation.

Q: It's not an allegation, Dr. Reeves. The pills were tested. They were 100 milligram tablets.

A: Okay.

Q: So I'm asking you—how does that happen?

A: And I'm telling you I don't have an answer that will satisfy you. The process has multiple checkpoints.

Q: Which you performed?

A: Which I performed, yes.

Q: So did you verify the wrong medication, or did you not actually verify it?

A: I—those aren't—I need you to understand that I'm not trying to be difficult. I verified what was in front of me. If the wrong pills were in the bottle, I would have caught a discrepancy between the pill appearance and what the system said should be there.

Q: Unless you didn't look.

A: I looked.

Q: Then how do you explain the 100 milligram tablets?

A: I can't. I've been sitting here trying to reconstruct this in my head and I cannot figure out where the breakdown occurred.

Q: That's your testimony? You can't figure it out?

A: That's my testimony.

topic: A pharmacist is deposed about a prescription that was filled with the wrong dosage
text:
Q: Were you working alone on the evening of March 15th?

A: No, there were two technicians on shift with me.

Q: Who were they?

A: Maria Gonzalez and a newer employee, I believe his name was Tyler something. I'd have to check the schedule.

Q: Tyler Brennan?

A: That sounds right.

Q: How new was Mr. Brennan?

A: Maybe three weeks? A month?

Q: And he was working the fill station that night?

A: I don't specifically recall the task assignments for that particular evening.

Q: But it's possible he pulled the medication for Mrs. Chen's prescription?

A: It's possible. I'd need to see the workflow logs.

Q: Let me ask it differently. Under your supervision, a new technician with three weeks of experience may have been responsible for pulling a controlled medication?

A: I'm not following your question. Hydrocodone is a controlled substance, yes, and technicians can pull it from inventory, but I verify everything before it goes out.

Q: So even if Mr. Brennan pulled the wrong strength—

A: I would catch it.

Q: You would catch it.

A: Yes.

Q: But the patient received 10 milligram tablets instead of 5 milligram tablets.

A: So I've been told.

Q: Which means either Mr. Brennan made an error and you missed it, or—

A: Or the patient is mistaken, or the tablets were switched after leaving the pharmacy, or the medical examiner's report has an error, or—

Q: You're suggesting the medical examiner made an error?

A: I'm suggesting I don't understand how we arrived at the conclusion we're apparently working from, and I'm trying to identify alternative explanations because the one you're proposing doesn't align with what I know about my own processes.

topic: A pharmacist is deposed about a prescription that was filled with the wrong dosage
text:
Q: Let's talk about the prescription as written. You have Exhibit 7 in front of you?

A: I do.

Q: Can you read the dosage indicated by Dr. Morrison?

A: It says... it appears to say 1.5 milligrams.

Q: Appears to say?

A: The handwriting is not entirely clear.

Q: What else might it say?

A: It could potentially be read as 15 milligrams.

Q: And what did you dispense?

A: We dispensed 15 milligrams.

Q: So you interpreted the prescription as 15 milligrams?

A: At the time, apparently, yes.

Q: Is 15 milligrams of Xanax a typical prescribed dose?

A: No.

Q: What is a typical dose?

A: 0.25 to 0.5 milligrams, up to three times daily. Maximum would rarely exceed 4 milligrams per day.

Q: So 15 milligrams would be—

A: Significantly above normal range, yes.

Q: Did that not raise a red flag?

A: It should have.

Q: But it didn't?

A: Counsel, I'm looking at this prescription right now, and I can see the ambiguity. I don't know what I was seeing that day. I don't know if I was rushed, if I was distracted, if the original was clearer before being photocopied—I don't know.

Q: You have no explanation?

A: I have no explanation that makes sense to me, no.

Q: Do you wish you had called Dr. Morrison to clarify?

A: Of course I wish that now.

Q: Why didn't you then?

A: I... I don't know. I should have. I clearly should have.

topic: A pharmacist is deposed about a prescription that was filled with the wrong dosage
text:
Q: You testified earlier that your pharmacy uses a barcode scanning system.

A: Correct.

Q: Explain how that system is supposed to prevent dispensing errors.

A: When we scan the medication bottle, the system cross-references the NDC code with the prescription on file. If there's a mismatch, we get an alert. Red screen, audible beep.

Q: Did you receive an alert when filling Mr. Patterson's prescription?

A: I did not.

Q: You're certain?

A: I would remember a red screen.

Q: But Mr. Patterson received atorvastatin 80 milligrams instead of the prescribed 20 milligrams.

A: That's what I've been told.

Q: Those have different NDC codes.

A: They do.

Q: So the system should have flagged it.

A: It should have, yes.

Q: But you're saying it didn't.

A: I'm saying I don't recall an alert.

Q: Is it possible you overrode the alert?

A: Override requires a reason code and a second authorization.

Q: That's not what I asked. Is it possible you overrode it?

A: I... suppose it's technically possible.

Q: Do you have any record of an override?

A: I haven't seen one. But I also haven't seen system logs that would show whether an alert was generated in the first place.

Q: Has anyone pulled those logs?

A: I've asked. I was told they're still being retrieved.

Q: By whom?

A: By corporate IT. I've asked three times now.

Q: So as we sit here today, you cannot tell me whether your own safety system functioned properly?

A: No. And believe me, I want to see those logs more than anyone in this room.

topic: A tenant is questioned about property damage they reported to their landlord
text:
Q: Let's talk about the water damage you reported on March 15th. When did you first notice it?

A: I noticed it when I noticed it. March 12th.

Q: And you waited three days to report it?

A: I reported it the same day I had time to call during your client's so-called "office hours," which are apparently designed to make sure no working person can ever reach anyone.

Q: I'm asking about the timeline, not the office hours. Did you take any photographs on March 12th?

A: Yes.

Q: How many?

A: Enough.

Q: I need a number.

A: Fourteen. Would you like me to describe each one, or can we move this along?

Q: Did you attempt any repairs yourself before reporting?

A: I'm not a plumber. I'm also not responsible for a pipe that was already corroded when I moved in, which I documented in my move-in inspection that your client apparently lost.

Q: I didn't ask about the move-in inspection.

A: No, you didn't. But you should have.

Q: Let me ask the questions. Did you place any containers under the leak?

A: I placed a bucket. I placed towels. I placed a formal complaint with the housing authority. Anything else you want to know about what I placed?

Q: Just answer what's asked.

A: I am. Precisely.

topic: A tenant is questioned about property damage they reported to their landlord
text:
Q: You submitted a maintenance request on October 3rd regarding mold in the bathroom, correct?

A: That's correct.

Q: Had you noticed the mold before October 3rd?

A: I'd noticed some discoloration, yes. I wasn't certain it was mold until I looked closer.

Q: How much closer?

A: I'm sorry, are you asking me to quantify the distance between my face and the wall?

Q: I'm asking when you became certain it was mold.

A: October 3rd. When I submitted the request. As I said.

Q: The report mentions the mold was "extensive." Your word?

A: The property manager's word. I said it was spreading.

Q: You didn't say extensive?

A: I know what words I used.

Q: What words did you use?

A: "Spreading." "Getting worse." "Been there for a while based on the pattern." I have the email if you'd like to see it, since apparently your client didn't provide you with complete records.

Q: We have the records.

A: Then you have my exact words.

Q: Did you ever fail to run the bathroom exhaust fan?

A: The bathroom doesn't have an exhaust fan. It has a window painted shut. I documented that in my first month.

Q: Move to strike the editorial comment.

A: It's not editorial. It's structural.

topic: A tenant is questioned about property damage they reported to their landlord
text:
Q: Mr. Okonkwo, I want to be very clear about the damage to the bedroom ceiling. You reported it on January 8th?

A: Yes.

Q: Tell me exactly what you observed.

A: A section of drywall, approximately two feet by three feet, had become saturated and was bulging downward.

Q: Bulging.

A: Yes.

Q: Not collapsed?

A: Not at the time of my report, no.

Q: But it later collapsed?

A: Six days later. After no one came to repair it.

Q: I'm going to ask you to just answer the question I ask.

A: I did answer it. You asked if it collapsed. I told you when.

Q: Let's back up. On January 8th, did you hear any water running above you?

A: I heard dripping. I'd been hearing dripping for approximately two weeks.

Q: Two weeks.

A: Yes. I reported the dripping on December 26th. I have the confirmation number if you need it. I have all of them, actually.

Q: Why didn't you mention the two weeks of dripping in your January 8th report?

A: Because I'd already reported it. I assumed someone at the management company could connect two reports about the same ceiling. Perhaps that was optimistic of me.

Q: That's not responsive.

A: It's entirely responsive. You asked why. I told you why.

topic: A tenant is questioned about property damage they reported to their landlord
text:
Q: The broken window in the living room—you reported that on July 19th?

A: Correct.

Q: How did the window break?

A: I don't know. I came home and it was broken.

Q: You don't know.

A: That's what I said.

Q: You have no theory about how a window breaks on its own?

A: I didn't say it broke on its own. I said I don't know how it broke because I wasn't there.

Q: Was anyone else in the apartment that day?

A: Not to my knowledge.

Q: Do you have frequent guests?

A: Define frequent.

Q: More than once a week.

A: No.

Q: Once a week?

A: Sometimes. I don't keep a log. Should I?

Q: I'm just trying to establish who had access.

A: Management has access. Maintenance has access. The previous tenant probably still has a key for all I know—the locks were never changed despite my request.

Q: We're not here to discuss the locks.

A: You asked about access.

Q: Did you break the window?

A: No.

Q: Do you know who did?

A: No. I reported it, I documented it, I covered it with plastic to prevent further damage. That's what a responsible tenant does. Would you like to question that too?

topic: A tenant is questioned about property damage they reported to their landlord
text:
Q: Ms. Vance, let's discuss the pest infestation you reported.

A: All right.

Q: When did you first see evidence of rodents in the unit?

A: August. Early August.

Q: Can you be more specific?

A: The first or second. I'd have to check my calendar.

Q: Please do that now.

A: I don't have my calendar with me. I was told to bring documents related to the property damage, not my personal schedule.

Q: You don't recall the specific date?

A: I recall it was early August. That's what I said.

Q: You reported it on August 20th. That's nearly three weeks later.

A: Yes.

Q: Why the delay?

A: Because I tried to handle it myself first. Traps. Sealing gaps. Then I realized the entry points were in the walls—in the infrastructure—and that's not my responsibility.

Q: You waited three weeks to determine that?

A: I waited until I had enough evidence to prove this wasn't about crumbs on my counter. Which is exactly what your client accused me of when I did report it.

Q: I'm not asking about what my client—

A: You're asking why I waited. I'm telling you. I waited because I knew exactly how this conversation would go, and I wanted documentation.

Q: And you have that documentation?

A: Every photograph. Every date-stamped video. Every ignored email. Yes.

topic: A paramedic is questioned about the response time and treatment at an accident scene
text:
Q: Please state your name and occupation for the record.

A: Marcus Webb, paramedic with County Fire and Rescue, Unit 7. Eleven years on the job. I've logged over four thousand emergency responses in that time.

Q: Thank you. Now, regarding the accident on Route 12 on March 15th, what time did you receive the dispatch call?

A: 14:32. We were wheels rolling by 14:34. Two minutes. That's faster than the national standard, by the way.

Q: I didn't ask about national standards, Mr. Webb. What time did you arrive on scene?

A: 14:41. Nine minutes from dispatch to arrival. On a rural highway with one access road. You can check the GPS logs if you'd like—they'll confirm exactly what I'm telling you.

Q: And when you arrived, what did you observe?

A: Single-vehicle rollover, driver entrapped, significant deformation to the passenger compartment. I assessed the scene, established a perimeter, and had my partner begin extrication protocols while I initiated patient contact. We were working that scene like a Swiss watch.

Q: Was the plaintiff conscious when you made contact?

A: Semi-conscious. GCS of 11. I stabilized her cervical spine manually while talking her through what we were doing. Kept her calm. That matters more than people realize—patient anxiety can complicate everything from blood pressure to cooperation.

Q: Did you administer any medication at the scene?

A: I established an IV line with normal saline and administered 4 milligrams of morphine for pain management at 14:58. Textbook dosing, appropriate for her presentation, documented in real-time on my tablet.

Q: Some might say twenty-five minutes before pain medication is a long time for someone in distress.

A: Some might say that if they've never worked a rollover extrication. You can't push narcotics into someone you're still cutting out of a vehicle. We had her packaged, on the stretcher, and medicated within seventeen minutes of gaining full access. I'd put that timeline up against any crew in the state.

Q: I'm just trying to establish the facts, Mr. Webb.

A: And I'm giving them to you. Thoroughly.

topic: A paramedic is questioned about the response time and treatment at an accident scene
text:
Q: Paramedic Okonkwo, you were the lead responder on the night of January 8th, correct?

A: Yes.

Q: Walk me through the initial moments after you arrived at the intersection of Maple and Third.

A: We arrived at 21:17. Two-vehicle collision, T-bone impact. I triaged both drivers. The plaintiff had visible head trauma and was unresponsive. The other driver was ambulatory with minor lacerations.

Q: You made the decision to prioritize the plaintiff?

A: That's correct.

Q: Based on what specific criteria?

A: Mechanism of injury, level of consciousness, visible trauma. Standard triage protocol. I've made that call hundreds of times.

Q: Now, I want to understand something. The hospital records indicate the plaintiff arrived with a blood pressure of 80 over 50. That's quite low, isn't it?

A: It is.

Q: Dangerously low?

A: Concerning, yes.

Q: And yet your field notes don't reflect any intervention for hypotension until—let me check—twelve minutes into transport. Can you explain that gap?

A: I can. Because there was no gap. I initiated a fluid bolus at 21:24, which was six minutes after we loaded her. My notes reflect when I documented it, not when I did it. I was a little busy keeping her alive.

Q: So your documentation was delayed?

A: My documentation was completed when it was safe to complete it. My interventions were immediate. There's a difference, and it's an important one.

Q: I see. And you're confident in that sequence of events?

A: I am. Absolutely.

Q: Even though we only have your word for it?

A: You have my word, my training, my eleven years of experience, and the fact that she survived a crash that should have killed her. So yes. I'm confident.

topic: A paramedic is questioned about the response time and treatment at an accident scene
text:
Q: Let's talk about the decision to call for air transport. Whose call was that?

A: Mine.

Q: And you made that call at what time?

A: Approximately 10:15 AM.

Q: The helicopter didn't arrive until 10:47. Over thirty minutes. That must have been frustrating.

A: It wasn't frustrating. It was the reality of the situation. The nearest trauma center was forty-two miles away. Ground transport would have taken longer. I made the right call.

Q: I wasn't suggesting otherwise.

A: Good.

Q: During that thirty-minute window, what was the plaintiff's condition?

A: He had sustained multiple fractures to his lower extremities and was showing signs of internal bleeding. I maintained spinal immobilization, monitored his vitals every two minutes, and kept him as stable as humanly possible given the circumstances.

Q: Every two minutes seems frequent.

A: For a patient with suspected internal hemorrhage and declining pressure? That's exactly the frequency indicated. I've trained for this. I've drilled this. When the flight crew landed, they told me my handoff was one of the cleanest they'd received. Their words, not mine.

Q: Did they document that?

A: You'd have to ask them.

Q: Fair enough. Let's talk about the tourniquet application—

A: Applied at 10:08, right leg, above the knee. The wound was arterial. Without it, he would have bled out before the helicopter was even airborne.

Q: I hadn't asked my question yet.

A: I know where you're going. I'm saving us both time.

Q: I appreciate your... efficiency. Was the tourniquet applied according to protocol?

A: According to protocol, according to best practices, according to common sense. It stopped the bleeding. That's what it's supposed to do.

topic: A paramedic is questioned about the response time and treatment at an accident scene
text:
Q: Ms. Reyes, how long have you been a paramedic?

A: Three years.

Q: So relatively new to the field.

A: I suppose that depends on your definition.

Q: Well, compared to someone with, say, fifteen or twenty years of experience—

A: I have over a thousand emergency responses, ongoing training certifications, and the same medical protocols as any paramedic in this county. But sure. Three years.

Q: I meant no offense. Let me ask about February 22nd. You responded to the accident on Interstate 40. What do you recall about the scene?

A: It was a clear day, moderate traffic. A pickup had crossed the median and struck a sedan. One victim, the driver of the sedan, was unresponsive.

Q: What was your initial assessment?

A: Blunt force trauma to the chest. No spontaneous breathing. I began CPR within ninety seconds of patient contact.

Q: And the outcome?

A: We achieved return of spontaneous circulation at minute eleven. He was transported to St. Mary's and, to my knowledge, survived.

Q: That must have been—

A: It's the job.

Q: I was going to say significant. Bringing someone back.

A: Every call is significant.

Q: Of course. Now, there's been some question about whether the vehicle was fully stabilized before you entered—

A: It was.

Q: How can you be certain?

A: Because I made sure of it. I had my partner chock the wheels and confirm the ignition was off before I made entry. I don't take shortcuts. Ever.

Q: That's commendable.

A: It's standard.

Q: Perhaps. But not everyone adheres to standards under pressure, do they?

A: I do.

topic: A paramedic is questioned about the response time and treatment at an accident scene
text:
Q: Tell me about your training on spinal immobilization.

A: I've completed the standard curriculum, plus advanced trauma life support certification, which I renew every two years.

Q: And you applied spinal immobilization to Mr. Hernandez at the scene?

A: I did.

Q: Now, the emergency room physician noted some concern about the positioning of the cervical collar. Are you aware of that?

A: I am.

Q: What's your response?

A: The collar was applied correctly in the field. What happens during a thirty-minute transport on uneven roads—that's physics. I can't control every variable, but I can tell you the application was sound.

Q: You seem quite certain.

A: I am.

Q: The physician's note suggests the collar may have been one size too large.

A: With respect, I measured the patient's neck before selecting the collar. The measurement indicated a no-neck size. That's what I used.

Q: Is it possible you made an error?

A: It's possible the physician made an assumption without knowing the patient's condition in the field. Swelling changes things. A collar that looks too large at the ER might have fit perfectly at the scene.

Q: That's an interesting point. Did you document the neck measurement?

A: I documented the collar size used, which is standard practice. The measurement is implied by the selection. But I'll tell you this—I've immobilized patients in rainstorms, in overturned vehicles, in situations you wouldn't believe. I know how to size a collar.

Q: I don't doubt your experience, Ms. Chen.

A: Then we understand each other.

Q: Let me ask this differently. Is there anything you would have done differently that day?

A: No. Mr. Hernandez arrived at the trauma center alive, neurologically intact, with his spine protected. That's the outcome. That's what matters.

Q: Nothing at all?

A: Nothing at all.

topic: An accountant is deposed about transactions they processed on behalf of a client
text:
Q: Mr. Hartwell, you prepared the quarterly reconciliation reports for Meridian Holdings, correct?

A: I did, yes. Every quarter for six years without exception.

Q: And in preparing those reports, you would review all incoming wire transfers?

A: Absolutely. Every single one. I maintained a verification log, cross-referenced against the bank statements, and flagged anything that deviated from expected patterns. It was a thorough process.

A: From the Cayman account, yes. I remember that one clearly.

Q: You do?

A: I do. It was flagged in my system because the originating bank was new to us. I pulled the supporting documentation, verified the authorization chain, and confirmed it with Mr. Davenport directly before processing.

topic: A tenant is questioned about property damage they reported to their landlord
text:
Q: Ms. Hernandez, I want to direct your attention to the water damage you reported on September 14th. Can you describe what you observed that morning?

A: Absolutely. I woke up around 6:15, maybe 6:20, and I noticed the carpet near the bedroom window was damp. When I walked closer, I could see water actively dripping from the ceiling—there was a steady stream, really, about every two or three seconds a new drop would fall. The drywall had already started to buckle, maybe about a six-inch section, and there was discoloration spreading outward from the center of the leak.

Q: And you documented this?

A: I did. I took seventeen photographs that morning, timestamped, and I also recorded two videos showing the active leak. I saved the original files on my phone and backed them up to cloud storage that same day. I can provide exact file names if that would help.

Q: That won't be necessary at this time. When did you first contact the landlord?

A: I called at 6:47 a.m. No answer. I called again at 7:15. Still no answer. Then I sent a text message at 7:22 with three of the photographs attached, followed by an email at 8:01 a.m. to the property management address listed in my lease. I have records of all of those communications.

Q: What was the response?

A: Mr. Feldman returned my call at approximately 11:30 that morning. He said he'd send someone out "when he could." I asked him to clarify the timeline, and he said maybe that afternoon, maybe the next day.

Q: Did someone come that afternoon?

A: No. No one came until September 16th. Two full days later. By then, the damage had spread to approximately a four-foot radius on the ceiling, and I'd had to move my dresser and several boxes of belongings to prevent further damage to my personal property.

Q: You moved those items yourself?

A: I did. I also placed three buckets to catch the water and emptied them roughly every four hours. I kept a log of each time I emptied them, actually—I thought it might be relevant.

Q: Let's move on. The repair that was eventually made—

A: Of course. I'm happy to walk you through exactly what they did and what they didn't do.

---

topic: A tenant is questioned about property damage they reported to their landlord
text:

topic: A tenant is questioned about property damage they reported to their landlord
text:
Q: Mr. Patterson, I'm going to ask you about the plumbing issues you experienced in Unit 4B. You lived there from when to when?

A: January 2022 through August 2023.

Q: And the plumbing problems—when did those begin?

A: Honestly? Almost immediately. Within the first month, I noticed the kitchen sink was draining slowly.

Q: Did you report that?

A: I mentioned it to the super when I saw him in the hallway. He said old buildings are like that, give it a few days.

Q: Did it improve?

A: It got worse.

Q: Tell me about that.

A: By February, the sink would back up completely when I ran the dishwasher. By March, I was getting sewage smell from the bathroom drain. By April, I had standing water in my bathtub that wouldn't drain for hours after I showered.

Q: That's a significant escalation.

A: I thought so too.

Q: What did you do?

A: I submitted a formal maintenance request on April 3rd. Got a response saying someone would come out within 48 hours.

Q: Did they?

A: They did not.

Q: When did someone eventually address the plumbing?

A: June 15th.

Q: June 15th. More than two months after your April request?

A: Correct. And only after I sent a letter citing the relevant habitability statutes and mentioning the possibility of rent escrow.

Q: Ah. And how quickly did they respond after that letter?

A: Two days.

Q: How about that. What did the repair involve?

A: They found a collapsed section of pipe in the wall. The plumber told me—and I thought this was interesting—that the corrosion indicated it had been deteriorating for at least two years.

Q: Did he put that in writing?

A: He did. I made sure of that.

topic: A supervisor is deposed about performance reviews given to an employee who was later fired
text:
Q: Mr. Hernandez, you conducted the April 2022 performance review for Jessica Thornton, correct?

A: I did, yes, and I have to say, that review was one of the most detailed I've ever put together. I spent nearly three weeks on it because I wanted to make sure everything was documented properly.

Q: And what was your overall assessment of Ms. Thornton's performance?

A: Exceeded expectations. Across the board. She was hitting targets nobody else on the team could touch—I'm talking 147% of quota in Q1 alone. I actually had to double-check the numbers because I thought there might be an error.

Q: Did you recommend her for promotion in that review?

A: Absolutely. I wrote a full page justification for it. I outlined her client retention rates, her mentorship of the junior staff, her initiative on the Westbrook account—that was a $2.3 million save, by the way, that she handled almost entirely on her own.

Q: What happened to that promotion recommendation?

A: That's what I'd like to know! It went up to HR and then to regional, and I never heard another word about it. I followed up three times. Three times.

Q: Did anyone explain why it wasn't approved?

A: Nobody would give me a straight answer. I got a lot of "we're still reviewing" and "budget considerations," but Jessica was generating revenue, not costing it.

Q: Let's move to the October 2022 review. Did your assessment change?

A: Not one bit. If anything, she'd gotten better. She closed the Morrison deal in October, which—I don't think people understand how difficult that client was. I'd been trying to land them for two years before Jessica took over.

Q: Yet she was terminated in January 2023.

A: And I still don't understand it. Nobody consulted me. Nobody asked for my input. I found out the same day she did.

Q: Did you express your concerns to anyone after the termination?

A: I sent an email to HR that same afternoon, and I have to tell you, I laid it all out—her numbers, her reviews, the fact that this made no sense from a performance standpoint. I kept a copy because I knew someone was going to have questions eventually.

topic: A supervisor is deposed about performance reviews given to an employee who was later fired
text:
Q: You supervised Marcus Webb from 2021 to 2023?

A: That's correct.

Q: And you conducted his annual performance reviews during that time?

A: Yes.

Q: Let's talk about the 2022 review. How would you characterize his performance that year?

A: Satisfactory. He met the basic requirements of his position.

Q: Just satisfactory? Nothing more?

A: I stand by that assessment.

Q: Mr. Webb's sales numbers show he was in the top quartile of his division. Doesn't that warrant more than "satisfactory"?

A: Numbers don't tell the whole story.

Q: Then tell me the whole story! What was missing?

A: There were... interpersonal issues.

Q: What kind of interpersonal issues?

A: I'd prefer not to speculate about—

Q: I'm not asking you to speculate. I'm asking what you observed. What interpersonal issues?

A: He could be difficult in meetings.

Q: Difficult how? Give me an example. One concrete example.

A: He pushed back on directives sometimes.

Q: Pushed back on directives. You mean he asked questions? He offered alternative viewpoints?

A: It was more than that.

Q: Was he ever written up for insubordination?

A: No.

Q: Was he ever formally counseled about these interpersonal issues?

A: Not formally, no.

Q: So we have a top-quartile performer with no formal disciplinary record, and you gave him "satisfactory." Is that your testimony?

A: That is my testimony, yes.

topic: A supervisor is deposed about performance reviews given to an employee who was later fired
text:
Q: Ms. Okafor, how long have you been a supervisor at Ridgeline Industries?

A: Eleven years this coming March. I started as a line worker myself, actually, worked my way up through quality control, then shift lead, and I've been supervising for the last six. It's been quite a journey.

Q: You reviewed Danielle Morrison's performance in 2022?

A: I did, yes.

Q: What were your findings?

A: She needed improvement in several areas. I documented everything very carefully—I always do, I believe strongly in giving employees a clear roadmap.

Q: What areas specifically?

A: Attendance was the main one. I pulled her punch records going back six months, created a spreadsheet tracking every late arrival, every early departure. I think there were seventeen instances total.

Q: Were there extenuating circumstances for any of those instances?

A: She mentioned some things, yes.

Q: What things?

A: Childcare issues, I believe. Transportation problems once or twice.

Q: Did you document those explanations in her review?

A: I... I focused on the pattern. The pattern was what mattered.

Q: Did anyone else on your team have attendance issues?

A: Most people have an occasional issue here and there.

Q: Did you track their punch records the same way? With spreadsheets?

A: I—well, Danielle's situation required closer monitoring.

Q: Why?

A: Because of the pattern.

Q: The pattern you created the spreadsheet to find?

A: I think that mischaracterizes my process.

Q: Help me understand your process, then.

A: I was being thorough. That's my job.

topic: A supervisor is deposed about performance reviews given to an employee who was later fired
text:
Q: Mr. Parekh, the 2021 review you wrote for Samuel Chen—I'd like to understand your methodology.

A: Of course.

Q: How did you determine his performance ratings?

A: I used a combination of metrics. Quantitative output, peer feedback, self-assessment, my own observations. I actually developed a weighted scoring system specifically for my team because I felt the standard company form didn't capture enough nuance.

Q: Can you explain this scoring system?

A: Gladly. So I break it down into five categories, each worth up to twenty points. Technical proficiency, collaboration, initiative, reliability, and growth potential. Then within each category, I have subcriteria—

Q: Let me stop you there. Did HR approve this custom scoring system?

A: I shared it with them. They didn't object.

Q: Did they approve it?

A: They didn't say not to use it.

Q: What score did Mr. Chen receive under your system?

A: Eighty-three out of a hundred. That's actually quite good—it put him in the "strong performer" tier.

Q: Yet the standard company form you submitted rated him "needs improvement."

A: Because I had to translate my scores into their categories. Their form only has four options.

Q: An eighty-three translates to "needs improvement"?

A: In their system, given the category constraints—

Q: Mr. Parekh, did an eighty-three, a "strong performer" in your own words, translate to "needs improvement"?

A: The forms aren't really designed to capture—

Q: Please answer my question.

A: When I look at it now, I can see how there might be some inconsistency.

topic: A supervisor is deposed about performance reviews given to an employee who was later fired
text:
Q: You were Ms. Foster's direct supervisor for how long?

topic: An HR director is questioned about a harassment complaint that was filed and closed
text:
Q: Ms. Hernandez, you were the HR director at Westfield Manufacturing in 2022, correct?

A: I was, yes.

Q: And you received a harassment complaint from an employee named Danielle Porter?

A: I did.

Q: Can you tell me what happened after you received that complaint?

A: I... I opened a file. I documented her concerns. I followed the procedures we had in place at the time.

Q: What were those procedures?

A: We would gather statements, interview relevant parties, review any documentation, and then make a determination.

Q: Did you interview Ms. Porter?

A: I did. Twice, actually.

Q: Twice. And what did she tell you?

A: She described... she described a pattern of comments from her supervisor. Comments about her appearance. About her personal life. She said it had been going on for months before she came to me.

Q: Months.

A: Yes.

Q: And what determination did you ultimately make?

A: The complaint was closed as unsubstantiated.

Q: Unsubstantiated. Can you explain how you reached that conclusion?

A: There were no witnesses to the specific incidents she described. The supervisor denied everything. I didn't have... I didn't have enough.

Q: Did you believe her, Ms. Hernandez?

A: That's not... the question was whether I could prove it. That's what the procedure required.

Q: That wasn't my question. Did you believe Danielle Porter?

A: I think she was telling me what happened to her. Yes.

topic: An HR director is questioned about a harassment complaint that was filed and closed
text:
Q: Mr. Okafor, how long have you served as HR director for Pinnacle Logistics?

A: Seven years this past March.

Q: In that time, approximately how many harassment complaints have you processed?

A: I couldn't give you an exact number. Dozens. Perhaps more.

A: I remember Mr. Webb, yes.

A: He alleged that a coworker had made repeated racial comments to him. Slurs. He said it happened in the break room, in the parking lot. Multiple occasions.

Q: And you investigated this complaint?

A: I did.

Q: What was the outcome?

A: The complaint was closed.

Q: On what basis?

A: The accused employee had already resigned by the time I completed my interviews. He left the company. There was no one to discipline.

Q: So the complaint was closed because the perpetrator quit?

A: The matter was resolved through his departure. That's how it was characterized in my report.

Q: Did anyone follow up with Mr. Webb after that?

A: I... I don't believe so. No.

Q: You don't believe so, or no?

A: No. No one followed up with him.

Q: He filed a complaint about racial slurs, and when the investigation ended, no one called him? No one checked on him?

A: That's correct.

Q: Does that strike you as adequate, Mr. Okafor? Looking back?

A: I've thought about it many times since then. Many times.

topic: An HR director is questioned about a harassment complaint that was filed and closed
text:
Q: Let's turn to the complaint filed by Jennifer Stein on March 3, 2023.

A: All right.

Q: You're familiar with that complaint?

A: I am.

A: And I wrote what I wrote in the report.

Q: Ms. Stein left the company two weeks after the complaint was closed. Were you aware of that?

A: I was.

Q: Did you speak with her before she left?

A: She didn't want to speak with me.

Q: She didn't want to speak with you.

A: No. She said... she said she'd already told me everything, and it hadn't mattered.

Q: What did you say to that?

A: Nothing. There wasn't anything I could say.

topic: An HR director is questioned about a harassment complaint that was filed and closed
text:
Q: I want to ask you about the complaint filed by Thomas Reilly.

A: Okay.

Q: Mr. Reilly alleged that his supervisor made sexually explicit comments to him over a period of several months. Correct?

A: That's what he alleged.

A: Thank you.

Q: What do you recall about Mr. Reilly when he came to you with this complaint?

A: Yes.

A: Yes.

A: Mr. Reilly filed a second complaint four months later.

A: Yes.

Q: Did he get the transfer?

A: He did.

Q: Ms. Park, do you have children?

topic: An HR director is questioned about a harassment complaint that was filed and closed
text:
Q: The complaint from Rachel Morrison—that was filed in January 2022?

A: January 14th, yes.

Q: You have the exact date memorized?

A: I looked at the file before today. To prepare.

Q: What did you find when you looked at it?

A: I found my notes. My interviews. The determination letter.

Q: And what did the determination letter say?

A: It said the complaint was closed due to insufficient evidence to support a policy violation.

Q: Insufficient evidence. What evidence did you have?

A: Ms. Morrison's statement. A text message she provided. That was all.

Q: What did the text message say?

A: It was from her supervisor. It said, "I can't stop thinking about last night. We need to talk about this."

Q: And that wasn't sufficient evidence?

A: The supervisor said it referred to a work project. A deadline they'd been working on.

Q: Did you believe that explanation?

A: I... I noted it in the file.

Q: Ms. Hartley, do you still work at Crestwood Industries?

A: I resigned last month.

Q: After how many years?

A: Eleven years.

Q: Why did you resign?

A: I don't see how that's relevant to this deposition.

Q: You're right. I apologize. Let me rephrase—

A: I couldn't do it anymore. Is that what you want to know? I couldn't keep writing those letters. Telling people like Rachel Morrison that what happened to them didn't meet our evidentiary threshold. I couldn't do it anymore.

Q: I understand.

A: Do you?

topic: A daycare worker is deposed about an injury a child sustained while in their care
text:
Q: Ms. Hernandez, how long had you been working at Sunny Days Childcare before the incident on March 15th?

A: Four years. Four years and two months, actually.

Q: And in that time, had you ever had a child sustain an injury while under your direct supervision?

A: No. Never.

Q: I'd like to turn your attention to the morning of March 15th. Can you describe Lily's demeanor when she arrived?

A: She was... she was happy. She ran in. She always ran in. Her mom would barely get her coat off before she'd run to the block corner.

Q: The block corner?

A: It's where we keep the building blocks. Lily loved building. She'd build these towers, these tall towers, and she'd talk to herself the whole time. Little stories about who lived in them.

Q: Ms. Hernandez, I need to ask you about the moment of the fall. Where were you standing?

A: I was... I was by the sink. Six feet away. Maybe seven.

Q: And what did you see?

A: I've gone over it so many times. She was on the climbing structure. She was fine. And then she wasn't. Her foot slipped, or she reached for something, I don't... I don't know exactly. I've tried to remember exactly.

Q: You've tried to remember?

A: Every night. What I could have done. If I'd been closer. If I'd told her to come down. She liked to go high, and I let her because she was careful. She was always so careful.

Q: What happened immediately after she fell?

A: I was there. I was holding her. I don't remember crossing the room.

Q: Did she lose consciousness?

A: No. She looked at me. She looked at me and she said, "Miss Ana, my arm feels funny." That's what she said. Those words. "My arm feels funny."

Q: Take your time, Ms. Hernandez.

A: I'm fine. I'd like to finish. I'd like to answer your questions.

topic: A daycare worker is deposed about an injury a child sustained while in their care
text:
Q: Mr. Okonkwo, you were the lead teacher in the toddler room on June 3rd, correct?

A: Correct.

Q: How many children were present that day?

A: Eleven.

Q: And how many staff?

A: Two. Myself and Priya Sharma.

Q: Is that ratio in compliance with state regulations?

A: Yes.

Q: I'm going to show you what's been marked as Exhibit 4. Do you recognize this document?

A: It's the incident report I filled out.

A: That's what I wrote.

A: No.

Q: Where were you?

A: Changing another child.

Q: And Ms. Sharma?

A: Handling a situation by the water table.

Q: A situation?

A: Two children were having a disagreement over a toy.

Q: So neither of you saw what happened to Marcus?

A: No.

Q: Mr. Okonkwo, I have to ask these questions. I understand this is difficult.

A: I know you have to ask them.

Q: When you found Marcus, what did you observe?

A: Blood. On his forehead, on his hands. He was sitting by the bookshelf, not crying, just... sitting there. Looking at his hands.

Q: He wasn't crying?

A: Some children don't. When it's bad enough. They just go quiet.

topic: A daycare worker is deposed about an injury a child sustained while in their care
text:
Q: Let's talk about the supervision policy at Little Explorers. You're familiar with it?

A: Of course.

Q: It requires "active supervision" at all times, doesn't it?

A: Yes.

Q: Define that for me.

A: Positioning yourself to see all children, scanning regularly, being aware of high-risk areas.

Q: High-risk areas like the outdoor play structure?

A: Yes.

Q: The one where Ethan fell?

A: Yes.

Q: Were you actively supervising when Ethan fell eleven feet onto the rubber matting?

A: I was supervising eight children.

Q: That's not what I asked.

A: I was watching. I was doing my job.

Q: Then how did a four-year-old climb to a height of eleven feet without intervention?

A: He climbed fast. Kids climb fast.

Q: Ms. Patterson, I'm not trying to—

A: You are, though. You're trying to find the moment I failed. The exact second. So you can point to it.

Q: I'm trying to understand what happened.

A: He climbed. He fell. I ran to him. His leg was bent wrong. I held his hand and told him he was brave while we waited for the ambulance. That's what happened.

Q: How long was the ambulance response time?

A: Seven minutes. It felt longer.

Q: Did Ethan say anything while you waited?

A: He asked if his mom was coming. He kept asking. I told him yes. I told him she was coming as fast as she could.

topic: A daycare worker is deposed about an injury a child sustained while in their care
text:
Q: Ms. Chen, you mentioned you heard the sound before you saw what happened?

A: Yes.

Q: Describe the sound.

A: Do I have to?

Q: I'm asking you to, yes.

A: It was... a crack. And then nothing for a second. Then screaming.

Q: Whose screaming?

A: Sofia's. And then the other children.

Q: What did you do when you heard it?

A: I turned. She was on the ground by the rocking horse. It had tipped.

Q: The rocking horse had tipped over?

A: It's bolted down. It's supposed to be bolted down. But the bolt was loose. I didn't know. I checked the equipment that morning, I always check, but I didn't—I didn't notice.

Q: You check the equipment every morning?

A: Every morning. It's on my checklist. I have the checklists. I saved them all.

Q: I've seen them. Your initials are on the March 8th checklist.

A: Then you know I checked.

Q: I know you initialed a box.

A: I checked. I did check. But a bolt can be loose and still look... it can look fine. It can look fine until it isn't.

Q: Ms. Chen, do you need a moment?

A: No. No moment. What else do you need to know? I'll tell you whatever you need to know. I just need you to understand I checked. Every morning. Every single morning. I was careful with them. They mattered to me. Sofia mattered to me.

topic: A daycare worker is deposed about an injury a child sustained while in their care
text:
Q: How would you describe your training in first aid, Mr. Warren?

A: I'm certified in pediatric first aid and CPR. I renew every two years.

Q: And that training was current on August 22nd?

A: Yes.

Q: When you reached Emma, was she responsive?

A: She was breathing. She was conscious. She wasn't moving her neck, and I didn't move her.

Q: Why not?

A: Because that's what you do. When there might be a spinal injury. You don't move them.

Q: How long did you stay with her before the paramedics arrived?

A: I don't know exactly.

Q: Estimate.

A: Twelve minutes. Fifteen. I don't know. I was talking to her.

Q: What were you saying?

A: Just... things. That she was going to be okay. That her mom and dad loved her so much. That she was the bravest girl.

Q: Did she respond?

A: She held my finger. She's three. Her whole hand wrapped around my one finger, and she just... held on.

Q: Mr. Warren, I want to acknowledge—

A: I'd rather you just ask your questions.

Q: Alright. Did you see how she fell from the window?

A: The latch was faulty. We'd reported it. I have the emails.

Q: We'll get to those.

A: I want you to see them. I want you to see that we told them. We told the building management. We told them something was wrong with that window.

Q: Who is "we"?

A: Me. The director. We both sent emails. Multiple emails. She's three years old. She held my finger and didn't make a sound. Someone should have fixed that window.

topic: An accountant is deposed about transactions they processed on behalf of a client
text:
Q: Mr. Feldman, let's talk about the wire transfers from the Meridian Holdings account in October 2022. You processed those, correct?

A: I did, yes, and I have to say, those were some of the most meticulously documented transfers I've ever handled. Every single one had full supporting documentation, board resolutions, the works.

Q: I'm just asking if you processed them.

A: Right, yes, I processed them. But I want to make sure you understand the context here—these weren't just routine wires. We're talking about a sophisticated restructuring of intercompany obligations that took months to plan.

Q: How many wire transfers total in October?

A: Fourteen. Fourteen separate transactions, each one timed to coincide with specific contractual milestones. It was actually quite elegant from an accounting perspective.

Q: And the total dollar amount?

A: $4.2 million, give or take. I'd have to check the exact figure, but what's really interesting is how we structured the timing to optimize the client's cash position across three different jurisdictions.

Q: I didn't ask about the structure.

A: No, I know, but it's relevant! You can't understand these transactions in isolation. The whole point was the coordination between them.

Q: Let's focus on the $4.2 million figure. Where did those funds originate?

A: Operating accounts, primarily. But here's the thing—we had established a pooling arrangement six months earlier specifically to facilitate this kind of movement. I actually helped design that system.

Q: You designed it?

A: Co-designed. With the CFO. It was one of the more creative solutions I've worked on in my career, honestly.

Q: Did anyone outside the company review these transactions before they were executed?

A: Our external auditors were informed, yes. They were impressed, actually—said it was one of the cleaner implementations they'd seen.

Q: "Impressed" is what they said?

A: Words to that effect. Look, I've been doing this for twenty-three years. I know when something is done right, and this was done right.

topic: An accountant is deposed about transactions they processed on behalf of a client
text:
Q: Ms. Chen, walk me through what happened when you first received the Baxter invoice.

A: I received it by email on March 3rd. I logged it into our system.

Q: And then—let me ask you this—did you recognize immediately that this was different from previous Baxter invoices?

A: I don't know what you mean by "different."

Q: The amount! The amount was triple the usual retainer, wasn't it?

A: It was higher than previous invoices, yes.

A: I noticed the amount was larger.

Q: What did you do when you noticed?

A: I followed standard procedure. I flagged it for review.

Q: Perfect! Exactly right. And who reviewed it?

A: Mr. Davidson.

Q: And he approved it that same day, didn't he? Same day!

A: I believe so.

Q: You believe so, or you know so? This is important, Ms. Chen.

A: I would need to check the timestamp on the approval, but my recollection is that it was approved quickly.

Q: Within hours. I have the records right here. Approved at 4:47 PM, same day it was submitted. Does that refresh your recollection?

A: If that's what the record shows.

Q: It is what the record shows. Now, here's what I really want to understand—did Mr. Davidson give any explanation for why he approved such an unusually large invoice so quickly?

A: He didn't share his reasoning with me.

Q: But you must have had some reaction. Some thought about it.

A: I processed the payment as instructed.

topic: An accountant is deposed about transactions they processed on behalf of a client
text:
Q: Tell me about the quarterly reconciliation process for the Thornton account.

A: Sure. So every quarter, we would pull all the transaction records from the various sub-accounts—and there were seven of them by the end—and we'd reconcile them against the master ledger. It was a three-day process minimum.

Q: Seven sub-accounts seems like a lot.

A: It was! It was a lot! But Mr. Thornton had very specific ideas about how he wanted his funds segregated. Real estate in one, securities in another, the foundation money completely separate. I actually built a custom spreadsheet system just to track it all.

Q: You built it yourself?

A: From scratch. Took me two weekends, but it cut our reconciliation time in half. I'm pretty proud of it, honestly. Still use a version of it for other clients.

Q: Let's focus on Q3 2021 specifically.

A: Oh, that was a fascinating quarter. We had the property sale closing, the foundation's annual disbursement, and Mr. Thornton decided to restructure his securities holdings all at once.

Q: A lot happening.

A: A tremendous amount. I think I logged sixty hours that month just on Thornton alone. But everything balanced to the penny. Every single account.

Q: Were there any discrepancies during that reconciliation?

A: One small one—a $340 timing difference on a wire that crossed quarter-end. Completely normal, completely explainable.

Q: How did you resolve it?

A: Documented it in the reconciliation notes, carried it forward, and it cleared in the first week of Q4. Textbook handling, really.

Q: Did anyone else review your reconciliation work?

A: Patricia Ng, our senior manager. She signed off on everything. Actually complimented the documentation—said it was the cleanest Thornton file she'd ever seen.

Q: Did she have any questions about the Q3 transactions?

A: Not a single one. Because there was nothing to question. That's what thorough looks like.

topic: An accountant is deposed about transactions they processed on behalf of a client
text:
Q: Mr. Okonkwo, I want to ask you about the vendor payments processed through the Cypress account in 2020.

A: Okay.

Q: You handled those payments, correct?

A: I was one of several people involved, yes.

Q: How many vendors were being paid through that account?

A: I'd have to review the records to give you an exact number.

Q: Ballpark.

A: Maybe fifteen to twenty regular vendors. But I want to be accurate, so I'd prefer to check.

Q: That's fine. Let me show you Exhibit 14. Do you recognize this document?

A: Yes. It's a payment authorization form.

Q: Now this is interesting—look at the approval signature. Whose signature is that?

A: That appears to be Mr. Harmon's signature.

Q: Appears to be, or is?

topic: An accountant is deposed about transactions they processed on behalf of a client
text:
Q: Ms. Reeves, the Castellan transactions. You remember those?

A: Vaguely.

Q: Vaguely?

A: It was four years ago. I've handled thousands of transactions since then.

Q: These were unusual transactions, wouldn't you agree?

A: In what sense?

Q: Well, let's think about this together—you had round-dollar amounts, offshore destinations, no clear business purpose documented. That's unusual, isn't it?

A: Round-dollar amounts aren't inherently unusual.

Q: But $500,000 exactly? Then $500,000 exactly again? Then $500,000 a third time?

A: Some clients prefer round numbers for budgeting purposes.

Q: For budgeting purposes! And you just accepted that explanation?

A: I didn't say anyone gave me that explanation. I said it's a possible reason.

Q: What explanation were you given?

A: I don't recall a specific explanation.

Q: Now, the destination accounts—and this is what really caught my attention when I reviewed these records—they were all in the Cayman Islands. Every single one!

A: Many legitimate businesses have Cayman accounts.

Q: Did you verify that these were legitimate businesses?

Q: But you have professional obligations, don't you? As a CPA?

A: I followed all applicable professional standards.

Q: You're certain of that?

A: I am.

Q: Because three identical payments to offshore accounts with no documented purpose—wouldn't that raise a red flag for any competent accountant?

A: The transactions were authorized by the appropriate parties within the client organization.

Q: That's your answer.

A: That's my answer.

topic: A supervisor is deposed about performance reviews given to an employee who was later fired

topic: An HR director is questioned about a harassment complaint that was filed and closed

topic: A store manager is questioned about a customer slip-and-fall on their premises
text:
Q: Good morning. Could you state your name and position for the record?

A: Of course. I'm Daniel Reeves, and I've been the store manager at the Greenfield location for about six years now. Happy to be here to help sort this out.

Q: Thank you, Mr. Reeves. I appreciate you taking the time. Can you tell me, in your own words, what you remember about the day of the incident?

A: Absolutely. It was a Tuesday—October 15th—and we'd had some rain that morning. I remember because I'd asked our maintenance team to be extra vigilant about the entryway. We have a protocol for wet weather days, and I wanted to make sure we were following it.

Q: That's helpful context. When did you first become aware that a customer had fallen?

A: One of my cashiers, Maria, came to find me. She said a woman had slipped near the produce section and was sitting on the floor. I went over immediately—probably within thirty seconds of being told.

Q: And what did you observe when you arrived?

A: The customer—Mrs. Patterson, I learned later—was sitting near the banana display. She seemed shaken, holding her wrist. There was a small puddle of water on the floor, maybe from condensation dripping from the produce misters. I knelt down and asked if she was okay, if she wanted me to call an ambulance.

Q: Take your time with this next question. Did you have any conversation with Mrs. Patterson at that moment?

A: I did. I told her to stay still, that we'd take care of everything. I asked if there was anyone I could call for her. She mentioned her daughter, so I had Maria get the number and make the call personally. I stayed with her until the paramedics arrived.

Q: That was good of you. Were there any witnesses to the actual fall?

A: I believe one of our stockers, Jerome, saw it happen. He was the one who stayed with her before Maria came to get me. I made sure to have him write down what he saw that same day, while it was fresh.

Q: And that written statement—is that something you preserved?

A: Yes, it should be in the incident file. I can make sure your office gets a copy if that would be helpful.

Q: That would be very helpful, thank you. One last question for now—did you personally inspect the area where she fell?

A: I did, after the paramedics took her. I wanted to understand what happened so we could prevent it in the future. I noticed the mister timing might have been causing excess water to pool. We adjusted the settings the next day.

topic: A store manager is questioned about a customer slip-and-fall on their premises
text:
Q: State your name.

A: Rebecca Thornton.

Q: You're the manager at ShopMart on Delaware Avenue, correct?

A: That's right.

Q: Ms. Thornton, I want to ask you about your inspection logs for December 3rd. Do you recall that date?

A: I do. That's when Mr. Hendricks fell.

Q: The logs indicate an inspection at 9:00 a.m. and then not again until 1:15 p.m. Is that accurate?

A: That's what the log shows, yes. But I want to explain something, if I may—

Q: Please, go ahead. I want to understand the full picture here.

A: Thank you. We had two callouts that morning. I was covering the service desk myself for part of the shift, which meant I couldn't do the walkthrough I normally would have done around eleven. I take responsibility for that gap.

Q: I appreciate your candor. So the 1:15 inspection—that was after the fall?

A: Yes, about twenty minutes after. I did it myself once things had calmed down.

Q: And what did you find during that inspection?

A: There was a broken jar of pasta sauce in aisle seven. That's where he fell. It had been there—I honestly don't know how long. Maybe thirty minutes, maybe an hour. I can't say for certain, and I won't guess.

Q: I understand. Was there any signage or barrier around the spill before Mr. Hendricks fell?

A: No. And that's on us. If one of my team saw it and didn't address it, or if no one saw it at all—either way, our system failed that day.

Q: That must have been difficult to come to terms with.

A: It was. I've been in retail management for fifteen years. You never want someone to get hurt in your store. I called Mr. Hendricks at home that evening to check on him, just person to person.

Q: Did he take your call?

A: He did. We talked for about ten minutes. He was gracious about it, honestly. More gracious than I deserved.

Q: Thank you for sharing that, Ms. Thornton.

topic: A store manager is questioned about a customer slip-and-fall on their premises
text:
Q: How long have you worked at the Maple Street location?

A: Eight years this March.

Q: And you were the manager on duty when Ms. Carlisle fell?

A: Yes.

Q: Tell me about your floor maintenance procedures.

A: We mop every morning before open, spot-clean throughout the day as needed, and do a full cleaning after close.

Q: Who's responsible for spot-cleaning during business hours?

A: Whoever sees a spill is supposed to address it or call for someone who can.

Q: Is that documented anywhere? A written policy?

A: It's in our employee handbook. Page twelve or thirteen, I think.

Q: Did you personally witness Ms. Carlisle's fall?

A: No. I was in the back office doing a vendor call.

Q: How did you learn about it?

A: My assistant manager, Paul, radioed me. I came out right away.

Q: What was Ms. Carlisle's condition when you reached her?

A: She was sitting in a chair—Paul had helped her up. She was holding her hip and looked like she was in a lot of pain. My first thought was just, how can I help this woman.

Q: Did you offer her any assistance?

A: I offered to call an ambulance. She said no at first, that she'd be fine. But I could tell she was hurting, so I got her some water and sat with her for a while. I told her there was no rush, that she should take all the time she needed.

Q: Did you discuss how the fall happened?

A: She said she slipped on something wet. I didn't press her for details right then—it didn't seem like the time.

Q: Why not?

A: Because she was in pain and she was embarrassed. I wanted her to feel like a person, not like a problem to be managed. The details could wait.

Q: Did you eventually document her account?

A: I did, later that afternoon, after her son came to pick her up. I wrote down everything I could remember from our conversation, plus what Paul had told me.

topic: A store manager is questioned about a customer slip-and-fall on their premises
text:
Q: Mr. Okonkwo, how would you describe the lighting in the area where the plaintiff fell?

A: The lighting in that section is adequate. We have overhead fluorescents on a standard grid.

Q: "Adequate" is a subjective term. Can you be more specific?

A: I can tell you the fixtures are inspected monthly. I've never received a complaint about visibility in that part of the store.

Q: Were all the lights functioning on the day in question?

A: To my knowledge, yes.

Q: To your knowledge. Did you personally verify that?

A: Not before the incident, no. But I checked afterward, and all bulbs were operational.

Q: Let me ask you about the floor surface. What material is it?

A: Polished concrete with a seal coat. It's standard for retail.

Q: Does that surface become slippery when wet?

A: Any surface can become slippery when wet. That's why we have protocols for addressing spills promptly.

Q: Fair enough. Were those protocols followed that day?

A: I believe so, but clearly something went wrong, or we wouldn't be here. I've gone over it many times in my head.

Q: That sounds frustrating.

A: It is. I don't like that someone got hurt. Mrs. Delgado is a regular—I've seen her in the store dozens of times. She always stops to chat with the staff. Knowing she was injured in my store... it stays with you.

Q: Have you spoken with her since the incident?

A: I wanted to, but I was advised not to because of the legal situation. I did send flowers to her home, though. I hope that wasn't out of line.

Q: I don't think anyone would fault you for that, Mr. Okonkwo.

A: Thank you. I just wanted her to know we cared.

topic: A store manager is questioned about a customer slip-and-fall on their premises
text:
Q: Were you trained on incident reporting procedures?

A: Yes.

Q: When?

A: When I was promoted to manager, about three years ago.

Q: Describe that training.

A: It was a half-day seminar at the regional office. We covered documentation, witness statements, how to preserve the scene, when to contact corporate.

Q: Did you follow those procedures after Mr. Liu's fall?

A: I did my best.

Q: Your best. Walk me through what you did.

A: I took photographs of the area. I got contact information from two witnesses. I filled out the incident report and submitted it to corporate within the hour.

Q: The photographs—what did they show?

A: The floor near the freezer section. There was a patch of condensation, maybe two feet by three feet. You could see the wet mark clearly in the pictures.

Q: Was there a floor mat in that area?

A: No.

Q: Should there have been?

A: In hindsight, probably yes. That freezer has always had a condensation issue. I'd put in a maintenance request about it twice before.

Q: Twice before. And nothing was done?

A: They sent someone out once to look at it. He said it was within normal parameters. I disagreed, but I'm not a refrigeration technician.

Q: So you flagged the problem, and it wasn't addressed to your satisfaction.

A: That's right. I should have pushed harder. I think about that a lot now.

Q: It sounds like you did what you could within the system you were working in.

A: I appreciate you saying that, but I was the manager. The buck stopped with me. I could have put a mat down myself. I could have roped off the area. I had options, and I didn't take them.

Q: Thank you for your honesty, Ms. Yates.

A: Mr. Liu deserves honesty. He's a kind man who came in to buy groceries, and he left in an ambulance. That's not something I can just set aside.

topic: A daycare worker is deposed about an injury a child sustained while in their care

topic: A daycare worker is deposed about an injury a child sustained while in their care

topic: A daycare worker is deposed about an injury a child sustained while in their care

topic: A business partner is deposed about financial records they were responsible for maintaining
text:
Q: Mr. Tanaka, you were the partner responsible for maintaining the accounts receivable ledger for Meridian Consulting, correct?

topic: A driver is deposed about the events leading up to a multi-vehicle collision
text:
Q: Tell me what you saw immediately before the collision.

topic: A nurse is questioned about a patient fall that occurred during her shift
text:
Q: Can you state your full name for the record?

A: Around 2:15 in the morning. I heard the call light alarm and then... then one of the aides called out.

Q: What did you do when you heard the aide call out?

A: I went to the room. I went right away.

Q: Can you describe what you saw when you entered Room 412?

A: She was on the floor. On her side, near the bed. The bed rail was down on that side. She was... she wasn't moving at first. Then she started to moan.

A: No. No, she was alone.

Q: The bed rail being down — was that consistent with the care plan?

A: ...No.

Q: Who was responsible for ensuring the bed rails were up?

A: I was. I had been in there at midnight. I should have... I checked them. I thought I checked them.

Q: You thought you checked them?

A: I did check them. I don't know how it was down. I don't know.

Q: Mrs. Patterson suffered a hip fracture from this fall, correct?

A: Yes.

Q: She was 84 years old?

A: She was. She reminded me of my grandmother, actually. She used to call me "dear." Every time I came in the room.

topic: A nurse is questioned about a patient fall that occurred during her shift

topic: A nurse is questioned about a patient fall that occurred during her shift
text:
Q: I want to understand the sequence of events. Mr. Chen was admitted at what time?

[PAUSE IN RECORDING]

Q: Back on the record. Nurse Thompson, I apologize for the interruption. My mother... she passed in a hospital last year. Fall. I want to make sure I ask these questions properly.

topic: A nurse is questioned about a patient fall that occurred during her shift

A: Okay.

topic: A nurse is questioned about a patient fall that occurred during her shift
text:
Q: Nurse Delgado, you've been an RN for how long?

A: Fourteen years.

Q: And in those fourteen years, have you ever had a patient fall during your shift?

A: Once before this.

Q: Tell me about Mr. Abrams' fall.

A: He was post-operative. Hip replacement. He was supposed to call for assistance before getting up.

Q: But he didn't?

A: He did call. The light was on when I got there. But I didn't get there fast enough.

Q: Why not?

A: I was charting. In the medication room. Catching up on documentation because we'd been short-staffed and I was behind.

Q: How far behind?

A: Three hours. More.

Q: So you were charting instead of answering call lights?

A: I was charting because if I don't chart, I lose my license. And if I answer every call light immediately, I never chart, and then I lose my license. So.

Q: That sounds like an impossible situation.

A: It is. It's exactly that.

Q: Mr. Abrams — he broke his wrist in the fall.

A: He did. He was a pianist. Retired, but he still played at his church every Sunday.

Q: Did you speak with him afterward?

A: I went to his room the next morning. Before my shift. He wouldn't look at me.

Q: What did you say to him?

A: I told him I was sorry. And he just... he nodded. That was all. He just nodded and looked out the window.

Q: And did the noise level increase as the evening went on?

A: Of course it did. That's what happens at parties.

Q: At what point did the noise become disruptive to you personally?

A: Disruptive how? I couldn't hear my television. My dog wouldn't stop barking. I couldn't have a phone conversation without stepping into my bathroom and closing the door.

Q: So the noise was significant.

A: I just gave you three examples.

Q: Did you approach anyone at the Henderson residence to complain?

A: I walked over around 9 o'clock.

Q: And what happened?

A: Mr. Henderson told me it was a holiday and I should, quote, lighten up.
