Q: Those were his exact words?

A: His exact words included a profanity I'd rather not repeat in this setting, but yes, "lighten up" was the gist.

Q: What did you do after that?

A: I went home. I closed my windows. I waited for it to end.

---

topic: A neighbor is questioned about noise complaints and a confrontation they witnessed
text:
Q: Mr. Yates, you've testified that you saw Ms. Corbin approach the defendant's front door.

A: That's correct.

Q: What time was this?

A: Sometime around 10 p.m.

Q: Can you be more specific?

A: I wasn't checking my watch. It was dark. It was after dinner. That's as specific as I can be.

Q: You were watching from your window?

A: I was standing at my window, yes.

Q: Why were you standing at your window at 10 p.m.?

A: Because there had been noise coming from that house all evening and I was curious whether something was going to come of it.

Q: What kind of noise?

A: Loud voices. Sounds like things being thrown. A door slammed so hard my wife asked if it was thunder.

Q: So you positioned yourself to observe?

A: I positioned myself because I live thirty feet away and I was wondering if I needed to call someone.

Q: Did Ms. Corbin knock on the door?

A: She pounded on it.

Q: Pounded?

A: That's the word I used. That's the word I meant.

Q: How many times?

A: I didn't count. Several.

Q: And then what happened?

A: The door opened. There was shouting. More shouting, I should say. Then the door closed and Ms. Corbin stood there for a minute before walking back to her car.

Q: Did she appear upset?

A: Counselor, everyone involved in this situation appeared upset. That's the whole point, isn't it?

topic: A contractor is questioned about delays that caused a construction project to fail
text:
Q: Mr. Hardin, you were the general contractor on the Riverside Office Complex project, correct?

A: That's what the contract says.

Q: And the project was originally scheduled for completion in March of 2023?

A: March 15th, specifically.

Q: But the building wasn't actually completed until November of that year, was it?

A: Sounds about right.

Q: That's an eight-month delay, Mr. Hardin.

A: If you say so.

Q: Do you dispute that calculation?

A: No. I just don't see why you need me to confirm basic arithmetic.

Q: Let me ask you about the steel delivery issues. Your project logs indicate that structural steel arrived eleven weeks late. Did you take any steps to expedite that delivery?

A: We made some calls.

Q: Some calls. Can you be more specific?

A: Called the supplier a few times. They said it would get there when it got there.

Q: Did you consider sourcing from an alternative supplier?

A: Considered it.

Q: And?

A: Decided against it.

Q: Why?

A: Would've cost more. Nobody was offering to pay for that.

topic: A contractor is questioned about delays that caused a construction project to fail
text:
Q: Ms. Trent, how long have you been working in commercial construction?

A: Twenty-two years, give or take.

Q: And in your experience, is it unusual for a project of this scope to experience weather-related delays?

A: Weather happens. You plan for it.

Q: Did you plan for it on the Meridian Heights project?

A: We had contingency days built into the schedule, yes.

Q: How many contingency days?

A: Twelve.

Q: The project experienced thirty-one days of weather delays according to your own daily reports. Does that sound accurate?

A: Could be.

Q: So you exceeded your contingency by nearly three weeks.

A: Math checks out.

Q: What steps did you take to recover that lost time?

A: Added some weekend shifts when we could get guys to show up.

Q: Okay. And when that wasn't sufficient, what else did you do?

A: Look, we did what we could. The weather was what it was. I'm not sure what you want me to tell you here.

Q: I want you to tell me what actions you took.

A: I just did.

Q: Fine. Let's move on. Were you aware that the owner was incurring penalty fees on their existing lease due to the delays?

A: I heard something about that.

Q: Did that affect your approach to the project timeline?

A: Not particularly. That's their business problem, not mine.

topic: A contractor is questioned about delays that caused a construction project to fail
text:
Q: Mr. Okonkwo, I'd like to direct your attention to the subcontractor issues that arose in July of 2022.

A: Sure.

Q: Your electrical subcontractor, Benning Electric, walked off the job on July 14th. Is that correct?

A: They terminated their contract, yes. I wouldn't characterize it as walking off.

Q: They stopped showing up.

A: After providing written notice pursuant to their contractual rights, yes.

Q: Why did they terminate?

A: You'd have to ask them.

Q: I'm asking you.

A: Payment dispute. They claimed we owed them for change order work that hadn't been approved.

Q: Did you owe them for that work?

A: The change orders hadn't been approved. So no.

Q: How long did it take you to bring in a replacement electrical contractor?

A: I don't recall exactly.

Q: Your records indicate it was six weeks.

A: Then it was six weeks.

Q: Alright. Moving on. The mechanical subcontractor also filed a lien against the property in August. Were you aware of that?

A: I was informed, yes.

Q: What was your response?

A: Noted it. Kept working.

Q: Did you attempt to resolve the lien?

A: That was between them and the owner at that point.

topic: A contractor is questioned about delays that caused a construction project to fail
text:
Q: Let's talk about the permitting delays.

A: Okay.

Q: The fire suppression system permit was rejected twice before approval. Do you recall that?

A: I recall there were some issues with the fire marshal's office.

Q: What caused the initial rejection?

A: They wanted changes to the sprinkler head spacing in the basement level.

Q: And the second rejection?

A: Same issue, different inspector. They couldn't get their story straight over there.

Q: Did you or anyone from your team meet with the fire marshal's office to resolve the discrepancy?

A: We sent over revised drawings.

Q: That's not what I asked. Did you meet with them?

A: No.

Q: Any particular reason?

A: We were busy. The drawings spoke for themselves.

Q: The permit delays alone added seven weeks to the project timeline.

A: Okay.

Q: Does that concern you?

A: It's not ideal, but permitting authorities operate on their own schedule. Everyone in this business knows that.

Q: Did you inform the project owner about these delays in a timely manner?

A: They got copies of the same rejection letters we did.

Q: So that's a yes?

A: That's a "they had the same information we had."

topic: A contractor is questioned about delays that caused a construction project to fail
text:
Q: Mr. Castellan, I want to understand your communication with the project owner during the delay period.

A: What would you like to know?

Q: How frequently did you provide progress updates?

A: Weekly written reports. Sometimes more often if something significant came up.

Q: I have here a series of emails from the owner's project manager asking for status updates in September and October of 2022. Do you recall receiving these?

A: I received a lot of emails during this project.

Q: Let me show you what's been marked as Exhibit 14. This email from September 22nd asks, and I quote, "Please advise immediately on current timeline and recovery plan." Do you see that?

A: I see it.

Q: Did you respond to this email?

A: I don't recall.

Q: We have no record of a response, Mr. Castellan.

A: Then maybe I didn't respond. Things were hectic.

Q: The owner claims they were kept in the dark about the severity of the delays. How do you respond to that?

A: I'd say they had access to the same jobsite we did. They could've visited anytime.

Q: Is it your testimony that the owner should have figured it out themselves?

A: I'm saying the information was available.

Q: But you didn't provide it.

A: I provided what I provided. We were trying to build a building, not write novels.

topic: A business partner is deposed about financial records they were responsible for maintaining
text:
Q: Mr. Harmon, you were responsible for maintaining the accounts receivable ledger for Centennial Properties, correct?

A: That was one of my responsibilities, yes.

Q: One of them. What were the others?

A: I handled general bookkeeping, bank reconciliations, vendor payments. The usual things you'd expect from someone managing the financial side of a small partnership.

Q: Let's focus on the accounts receivable ledger. How often did you update it?

A: It depended. Weekly, sometimes more frequently if there was a lot of activity.

Q: Sometimes more frequently. Sometimes less frequently?

A: I said weekly. I don't know why you're—weekly was the standard.

Q: I'm just trying to understand your practices, Mr. Harmon. Were there periods when the ledger went more than a week without being updated?

A: There may have been. I can't recall every single week over a three-year period. That's not a reasonable thing to ask someone to remember.

Q: I'm not asking about every week. I'm asking whether it happened.

A: Fine. Yes. Probably. During busy periods or if I was traveling, there might have been a lag. A few days. Nothing that would affect the accuracy of the records.

Q: How would you know it didn't affect accuracy if you weren't updating it?

A: Because I reconciled everything when I caught up. That's how bookkeeping works. You reconcile.

Q: Did you document those reconciliations?

A: I—yes. The reconciliations would be reflected in the ledger itself.

Q: So there's no separate record of when you performed a reconciliation versus when a transaction actually occurred?

A: The dates are in the ledger. I don't know what else you want me to say.

Q: I want you to answer the question. Is there a separate record?

A: No. There is not a separate record.

topic: A business partner is deposed about financial records they were responsible for maintaining
text:
Q: Ms. Tan, I'm going to hand you what's been marked as Exhibit 14. Do you recognize this document?

A: Yes.

Q: What is it?

A: It's a quarterly financial summary for Bridgewater Consulting. Q3 2021.

Q: And who prepared this summary?

A: I did.

Q: The revenue figure on page two lists $847,000 for the quarter. Do you see that?

A: I see it.

Q: Where did that number come from?

A: From the underlying transaction records. Invoices, payment receipts, the usual sources.

Q: Do you still have those underlying records?

A: Some of them.

Q: Some of them. Which ones don't you have?

A: I'd have to check. I don't have them memorized.

Q: You prepared this summary, correct?

A: Yes.

Q: And you're telling me you don't know what records you used?

A: I'm telling you it was three years ago and I would need to review my files to give you an accurate answer. I'm trying to be precise here.

Q: I appreciate that. Let me ask it differently. Is it possible that some of the underlying records for this $847,000 figure no longer exist?

A: I suppose it's possible. I don't—I would really need to look.

Q: When did you last look?

A: I don't remember exactly. Maybe six months ago when this lawsuit started.

Q: And at that time, were all the records present?

A: I think so. I believe so. I didn't do a complete audit, I just pulled what was requested.

Q: So you don't actually know.

A: I know what I looked at. I can't testify about things I didn't specifically examine.

topic: A business partner is deposed about financial records they were responsible for maintaining
text:
Q: Mr. Okonkwo, let's talk about the petty cash fund.

A: Okay.

Q: How much was typically kept in that fund?

A: It varied.

Q: Give me a range.

A: Maybe two thousand. Sometimes up to five if we had a lot of small vendor payments coming up.

Q: Who had access to this fund?

A: Myself, David Pritchard, and our office manager Linda.

Q: And how were withdrawals documented?

A: There was a log. A physical logbook. You'd write down the date, amount, and purpose.

Q: I'm going to ask you to slow down, Mr. Okonkwo.

A: I'm sorry?

Q: You're speaking very quickly. I want to make sure the court reporter gets everything.

A: Oh. Okay. Sorry.

Q: The logbook—where is it now?

A: I assume it's still at the office. I haven't been there since January, so I don't—I wouldn't know for certain.

Q: Did you ever take money from the petty cash fund without logging it?

A: No.

Q: Never?

A: No. Never.

Q: Did you ever observe anyone else taking money without logging it?

A: I... no. I don't think so.

Q: You hesitated.

A: I was thinking. The answer is no.

Q: You were thinking about what?

A: Whether I had ever seen anything like that. And I haven't. The answer is no.

Q: Mr. Okonkwo, I'll remind you that you're under oath.

A: I'm aware of that. I said no.

topic: A business partner is deposed about financial records they were responsible for maintaining
text:
Q: Let's move to the invoicing system.

A: Fine.

Q: Who designed the invoicing system that Harper & Leigh used?

A: It wasn't really designed. We used QuickBooks and customized it over time.

Q: Who did the customizing?

A: I did, mostly.

Q: Mostly. Who else?

A: Our accountant made some suggestions. I implemented them.

Q: Did you ever create invoices for services that weren't actually rendered?

A: Excuse me?

Q: It's a straightforward question, Ms. Reyes.

A: I understood the question. I'm just—no. Absolutely not. I have never done that.

Q: Then let me show you Exhibit 22.

A: Okay.

Q: This is an invoice dated March 15, 2022, billing Northgate Industries for "consulting services—phase two implementation." Do you see that?

A: Yes.

Q: Phase two was never implemented, was it?

A: It was started.

Q: But not completed.

A: No, it was not completed.

Q: So why does this invoice exist?

A: Because—we billed for work performed. Not for project completion. We billed hourly and for deliverables. Phase two was started, work was done, and we billed for that work.

Q: The invoice says "phase two implementation." Not "partial work toward phase two."

A: That's the naming convention we used. It doesn't mean the entire phase was complete. It means work on that phase.

Q: Is that documented anywhere?

A: It would be understood from the contract terms.

Q: Is it documented anywhere, Ms. Reyes?

A: I would have to review the engagement letter.

Q: We'll get to that.

A: Fine.

topic: A business partner is deposed about financial records they were responsible for maintaining
text:
Q: Mr. Castellano, who maintained the partnership's bank statements?

A: I did.

Q: For how long?

A: The entire duration of the partnership. Seven years.

Q: Where are those statements now?

A: I have them. Most of them. There was a period where the bank switched to electronic-only statements and I didn't always download them right away, so there might be some gaps. From 2019, I think. Maybe a few months.

Q: A few months of missing bank statements.

A: I said gaps. I didn't say missing. They might be recoverable from the bank.

Q: Have you tried to recover them?

A: Not yet.

Q: Why not?

A: Because no one asked me to until now. I didn't realize it would be—I just hadn't done it yet.

Q: Mr. Castellano, this lawsuit was filed eight months ago.

A: I understand that.

Q: And you're telling me you haven't attempted to obtain complete financial records?

A: I've been gathering documents as they've been requested. I have most of what you need. The 2019 statements are a small piece of—look, I can contact the bank this week.

Q: I'm not asking you to contact the bank. I'm asking why you haven't already.

A: I don't know what you want me to say. I haven't. I can. I will.

Q: Let's move on. Did you ever transfer partnership funds to a personal account?

A: Distribution checks went to personal accounts. That was how distributions worked.

Q: Outside of distributions.

A: No.

Q: Never?

A: No. Never.

Q: We'll come back to that.

A: I look forward to it.

topic: A witness is questioned about a conversation they overheard in a company hallway
text:
Q: I'd like to turn your attention to March 14th of this year. Were you present at the Rayburn Technologies office that day?

A: Yes, I was.

Q: And at some point during that day, did you happen to overhear a conversation in the hallway near the executive suite?

A: I did, yes. I was coming back from the break room.

Q: Take your time with this. Can you describe what you observed?

A: There were two people standing near the corner by the supply closet. Mr. Hendricks and someone I later learned was from HR. Ms. Delgado, I think her name was.

Q: What, if anything, did you hear them say?

A: Mr. Hendricks was... he was upset. His voice was low but I could tell. He said something like, "She's been here twelve years, there has to be another way."

Q: Did you hear Ms. Delgado respond?

A: She said the decision had already been made. That it came from above her.

Q: How did Mr. Hendricks react to that?

A: He just stood there for a moment. Then he said, "At least let me be the one to tell her. She deserves that much."

Q: Did you hear anything else?

A: Ms. Delgado said she understood. That she'd give him until end of day.

Q: What happened next?

A: I walked past them. Mr. Hendricks nodded at me, and I kept going. I didn't want to intrude on whatever was happening.

Q: Did Mr. Hendricks appear to notice that you might have overheard?

A: I don't think so. Or if he did, he didn't let on. He just looked... tired. Like he was carrying something heavy.

Q: Thank you. I know that wasn't easy to recount.

A: I just hope whatever happened, it worked out for whoever they were talking about.

topic: A witness is questioned about a conversation they overheard in a company hallway
text:
Q: You were employed at Crestwood Financial in November of last year, correct?

A: That's correct.

Q: On November 8th, did you overhear a conversation in the hallway outside Conference Room B?

A: I heard voices, yes.

Q: Whose voices?

A: I recognized David Chen's voice. The other person I wasn't sure about at first.

Q: Were you able to identify the second person later?

A: I believe it was Mr. Okonkwo. From compliance.

Q: What did you hear Mr. Chen say?

A: He was talking about a client. He said, "The guy just lost his wife, Marcus. Three months ago. And we're going to audit his accounts right now?"

Q: What was Mr. Okonkwo's response?

A: He said something about protocols. That they had to follow the timeline regardless of circumstances.

Q: Did Mr. Chen say anything further?

A: Yes. He said, "Then flag me as the one requesting the extension. I'll take the heat. Just give the man sixty days."

Q: How would you describe Mr. Chen's tone during this exchange?

A: He wasn't angry. He was... firm. But there was something underneath it. Like he genuinely couldn't stomach doing it any other way.

Q: Did you hear how the conversation concluded?

A: Mr. Okonkwo said he'd see what he could do. That was the last I heard before I moved on.

Q: Did you have any further interaction with either of them that day?

A: No. But I remember thinking Mr. Chen was taking a risk. Not everyone would've pushed back like that.

topic: A witness is questioned about a conversation they overheard in a company hallway
text:
Q: Ms. Varma, you were working late on the evening of July 22nd?

A: Yes. I was finishing up a project proposal.

Q: And you've indicated you overheard a conversation in the hallway near your office?

A: That's right.

Q: Who was involved in this conversation?

A: Karen Mitchell and someone on the phone. She had it on speaker, I think, because I could hear both sides.

Q: What did you hear?

A: The person on the phone was upset. Crying, actually. It sounded like a younger woman.

Q: Could you make out what was being said?

A: The woman on the phone said something about not knowing how she was going to afford her medication. That she couldn't keep up with the payment plan.

Q: What did Ms. Mitchell say in response?

A: She said—and I remember this clearly—she said, "Okay, stop, stop. Don't worry about the payment plan right now. We're going to figure this out together."

Q: Did she say anything else?

A: She asked if the woman had eaten that day. When the woman said no, Ms. Mitchell said she was going to have groceries sent over and that they'd talk about the rest tomorrow.

Q: How long did this conversation continue?

A: A few more minutes. Ms. Mitchell was speaking very quietly, very calmly. Almost like she was talking to a frightened child.

Q: Were you surprised by what you heard?

A: Honestly? A little. I'd only seen Ms. Mitchell in meetings before. She's always so... professional. Reserved. But that night, she sounded like a completely different person.

Q: Thank you for sharing that, Ms. Varma.

A: Of course. I think it's important that people know what she did.

topic: A witness is questioned about a conversation they overheard in a company hallway
text:
Q: Mr. Patterson, I want to ask you about something you witnessed on February 3rd. Are you prepared to discuss that?

A: I'll do my best.

Q: I understand. Just answer what you can. Were you in the east corridor near the loading dock that afternoon?

A: Yes, I was grabbing a dolly from storage.

Q: Did you observe anyone else in that area?

A: Janet Reeves was there. She was talking to one of the temporary workers. Young guy, couldn't have been more than nineteen or twenty.

Q: Could you hear what they were discussing?

A: Parts of it. The kid had messed something up with a shipment. Mixed up labels or something. He looked terrified.

Q: What did Ms. Reeves say to him?

A: That's the thing—she wasn't yelling. She said, "Look at me. Look at me. It's a mistake. It's not the end of the world."

Q: Did she say anything else?

A: She told him that everyone screws up their first month. She said she once sent an entire pallet to the wrong state when she started.

Q: How did the young man respond?

A: He relaxed a little. His shoulders dropped. He said he thought he was going to be fired.

Q: And Ms. Reeves?

A: She laughed—not at him, more like to put him at ease. She said, "You're not getting fired over labels. Come on, let's fix it together."

Q: Did you see what happened after that?

A: They walked off toward the shipping office. She had her hand on his shoulder. Steadying him, you know?

Q: I appreciate you walking me through this.

A: That kid needed someone in his corner. I'm glad she was there.

topic: A witness is questioned about a conversation they overheard in a company hallway
text:
Q: Dr. Anand, you were in the administrative wing on September 9th?

A: Yes, I had just finished a meeting with the department chair.

Q: And you overheard a conversation between two individuals?

A: I did. It was in the hallway just past the elevators.

Q: Who was speaking?

A: Dean Morrison and Professor Castellano.

Q: What did you hear?

A: Professor Castellano was talking about one of her graduate students. She said the student had missed several deadlines and that there were grounds for academic probation.

Q: What was Dean Morrison's response?

A: He asked if anyone had actually spoken to the student. Not officially—just as a person.

Q: How did Professor Castellano react to that question?

A: She paused. I remember that. Then she said she'd sent emails.

Q: Did Dean Morrison respond?

A: He said—and I'm paraphrasing—"Elena, her father died eight weeks ago. I pulled her file. She's been drowning and nobody's thrown her a line."

Q: What happened next?

A: Professor Castellano didn't say anything for a moment. Then she said, "I didn't know."

Q: Did the conversation continue?

A: Dean Morrison said he wasn't trying to make her feel guilty. He said, "Let's just figure out what she actually needs. Not what the handbook says."

Q: Did you hear anything further?

A: No, I moved on. But I could see Professor Castellano's face as I passed. She looked shaken. Like someone had just reminded her why she got into teaching in the first place.

topic: A tenant is questioned about property damage they reported to their landlord
text:
Q: Good morning, Ms. Delgado. I understand you've been living at the Maple Street property for some time now?

A: Yes, almost four years this coming March. It's been a good place for me, honestly. My daughter learned to ride her bike in that driveway.

Q: That's a nice memory. Now, I'd like to ask you about the water damage you reported. Can you tell me, in your own words, what you first noticed?

A: Of course. It was a Tuesday morning—I remember because I always do laundry on Tuesdays—and I saw this dark patch spreading across the ceiling in the hallway. At first I thought maybe I was imagining it, but by that evening it had grown to maybe two feet across.

Q: And what did you do when you saw it spreading?

A: I called Mr. Patterson right away. I didn't want to wait, you know, because water damage can get so much worse if you leave it. I've seen what can happen. My aunt had a similar situation years ago and it ended up being a whole ordeal with the mold.

Q: How did Mr. Patterson respond when you reached him?

A: Oh, he was wonderful about it, really. He picked up on the second ring and said he'd send someone out first thing the next morning. And he did. He kept his word.

Q: Take your time with this next question. Did you notice any signs of water damage before that Tuesday?

A: That's a fair question. I've thought about it a lot, actually. There might have been a faint discoloration near the light fixture a week or so before, but I genuinely thought it was just a shadow. I wish I'd paid closer attention, but I didn't think anything of it at the time.

Q: No one's suggesting you should have. Did you take any photographs?

A: I did, yes. I took several with my phone that first evening and then more over the next few days. I wanted to document everything properly—I figured it would help Mr. Patterson with the insurance, and I wanted to be useful.

Q: That was thoughtful of you. Were there any belongings of yours that were damaged?

A: A few things, yes. Some books I'd stored on a shelf in the hallway got water-stained. Nothing irreplaceable, thankfully. I was more worried about the house itself, to be honest. I know Mr. Patterson takes a lot of pride in that property.

Q: I appreciate your candor, Ms. Delgado. We may have a few more questions later, but that's all for now.

A: Of course. Whatever helps get this sorted out.

---

topic: A tenant is questioned about property damage they reported to their landlord
text:
Q: Mr. Okonkwo, you submitted a maintenance request on September 14th regarding damage to the kitchen floor. Is that correct?

A: That's correct.

Q: Can you describe what you observed?

A: The linoleum near the sink had started buckling. There were these ripples forming, maybe six inches out from the base of the cabinet.

Q: And had you noticed any water leaks in that area prior to the buckling?

A: Not leaks exactly. The faucet had been dripping for a while. I'd mentioned it to the property manager back in July, I think. Maybe late June.

Q: I see. And when you mentioned the dripping faucet, what response did you receive?

A: Someone came out and tightened something. It helped for a few weeks, then started up again.

Q: Did you report it a second time?

A: No, I didn't. I probably should have. I figured it was just a drip, you know? I put a bowl under it and emptied it when I remembered.

Q: That's understandable. These things don't always seem urgent in the moment. How long would you say you used the bowl method?

A: Maybe five or six weeks? I wasn't keeping close track. It just became part of the routine.

Q: Of course. And when the buckling appeared, did you connect it to the dripping faucet?

A: Eventually, yes. I didn't at first. But once I really looked at where the damage was spreading from, it made sense.

Q: Looking back, is there anything you wish you'd done differently?

A: Reported the drip again. Definitely. I feel bad about it, honestly. I wasn't trying to let things get worse. I just didn't realize how much water was getting under there.

Q: I understand completely. These situations have a way of creeping up. One last question—did you notice any odor or discoloration before the buckling became visible?

A: There was a slight smell. Musty. I thought it was just the garbage disposal needing to be cleaned. I ran some lemon peels through it.

Q: Thank you, Mr. Okonkwo. Your honesty is genuinely helpful here.

A: I just want to make sure everything's accurate. I know these details matter.

---

topic: A tenant is questioned about property damage they reported to their landlord
text:
Q: State your name for the record.

A: David Chen.

Q: Mr. Chen, how long have you resided at 4521 Birchwood Lane?

A: Eleven months.

Q: I'd like to discuss the incident you reported on March 3rd. You described damage to the bathroom ceiling?

A: Yes.

Q: Tell me what happened.

A: Part of the ceiling fell in. Drywall, insulation. It came down while I was at work.

Q: That must have been alarming to come home to.

A: It was. I didn't know what to do at first. I just stood there looking at it.

Q: Take your time. What did you do next?

A: I called the emergency maintenance line. Then I took pictures. Then I called my mom, actually. She always knows what to do in a crisis.

Q: Good thinking on all counts. Was there any warning before the collapse? Cracks, sagging, anything like that?

A: There were some cracks. I'd noticed them maybe two weeks before. Hairline cracks, nothing that seemed serious.

Q: Had you reported those cracks?

A: No. I didn't think they were anything. Old buildings have cracks, you know?

Q: They do. It's easy to overlook. Was there any water damage visible when the ceiling came down?

A: Yes. The insulation was soaked. And there was this brown staining on the drywall pieces.

Q: Did the maintenance team identify the source?

A: They said there was a slow leak from the unit above me. The tenant up there had a dripping shower valve, apparently.

Q: Were you injured at all? Any belongings damaged?

A: No injuries, thank goodness. Some towels got ruined, and my bathmat. Small stuff.

Q: I'm glad you weren't hurt. Is there anything else about that day you think we should know?

A: Just that the maintenance crew was really kind. They helped me clean up, even though I don't think they had to. It meant a lot.

---

topic: A tenant is questioned about property damage they reported to their landlord
text:
Q: Ms. Tran, you filed a report on October 8th concerning mold in your bedroom closet. Let's talk about that.

A: Okay.

Q: When did you first notice the mold?

A: Early October. Maybe the 5th or 6th.

Q: What drew your attention to it?

A: The smell. My clothes were starting to smell musty. I thought maybe I'd left something damp in there, but when I checked, I found the spots on the wall.

Q: What did the spots look like?

A: Dark greenish-black. Clustered in the corner, near the floor. Maybe covering an area the size of a dinner plate.

Q: That sounds concerning. What did you do when you found it?

A: I didn't touch it. I'd read that you're not supposed to disturb mold because of the spores. So I closed the closet door and called the landlord that same evening.

Q: Smart approach. How did the landlord respond?

A: She was great, actually. She came by herself the next morning to look at it. She seemed genuinely worried. She kept asking if I was feeling okay, if I'd had any respiratory issues.

Q: Had you experienced any health effects?

A: Maybe some extra sneezing? I have allergies anyway, so it's hard to say what was the mold and what was just October being October.

Q: That's fair. Did the landlord take any immediate action?

A: She set up a fan and a dehumidifier that same day. Then she had a remediation company come out within the week. She even offered to put me up in a hotel while they worked, but I stayed with my sister instead.

Q: It sounds like she handled it responsibly.

A: She really did. I know these depositions are supposed to be about finding fault or whatever, but I don't have anything bad to say about how she dealt with it. She treated me like a person, not just a tenant.

Q: That's noted. Thank you for being so forthcoming, Ms. Tran.

A: Of course. I just want to tell the truth about what happened.

---

topic: A tenant is questioned about property damage they reported to their landlord
text:
Q: Mr. Babic, you've been deposed before?

A: Once. Car accident, years ago.

Q: Then you know how this works. I'm going to ask you questions about the property damage you reported. Just answer truthfully, to the best of your recollection.

A: Understood.

Q: On July 22nd, you notified the property management company about damage to your living room wall. Can you describe what you saw?

A: There was a crack running from the ceiling down to about eye level. And the paint was bubbling in a few spots around it.

Q: When did you first notice this?

A: That same day. I'd been out of town for two weeks, and it wasn't there when I left.

Q: That must have been unsettling to return to.

A: It was. I kept my dog at a friend's place while I was gone, and my first thought was, "Thank God he wasn't here alone with this happening."

Q: I can imagine. Did you have any idea what might have caused it?

A: At first, no. But I'd heard the neighbors mention there'd been a pretty bad thunderstorm while I was away. Lightning struck a tree in the courtyard, apparently.

Q: Did you observe any damage to the tree yourself?

A: Yeah, one of the main branches was split. They'd already cordoned it off by the time I got back.

Q: Did anyone from management explain whether the tree damage and your wall damage were connected?

A: The property manager—Diane—she came by personally to check on things. She said they were still investigating, but she thought the vibration or impact might have stressed the wall. She was really transparent about not knowing everything yet.

Q: How did you feel about that response?

A: Good, honestly. I appreciated that she didn't just make something up to placate me. She said she'd keep me in the loop, and she did. She called me twice that week with updates.

Q: Did you feel your concerns were being taken seriously?

A: Absolutely. Diane made me feel like I wasn't alone with this. That matters when you're dealing with damage to your home.

Q: Thank you, Mr. Babic. I think we have a clear picture of events.

A: Happy to help. I hope it all gets sorted out fairly for everyone involved.

topic: A witness is questioned about a workplace injury they observed but did not report
text:
Q: You were working on the second floor on March 14th, correct?

A: If that's what the schedule says.

Q: I'm asking what you remember.

A: Then yeah, probably. I was usually on two.

Q: And at some point that day, did you witness an incident involving Marcus Webb?

A: I saw him fall, if that's what you mean.

Q: Can you describe what you saw?

A: He was on the ladder, then he wasn't. He hit the ground. People came over.

Q: What did you do when you saw him fall?

A: I looked. Then I went back to what I was doing.

Q: You didn't go over to help?

A: Other people were already there.

Q: Did you report the incident to anyone?

A: No.

Q: Why not?

A: Wasn't my job. I figured someone else would handle it.

Q: Did it concern you that Mr. Webb might have been seriously injured?

A: I mean, he was moving around. He seemed fine enough.

Q: Fine enough. Did you see him get up?

A: I didn't really watch the whole thing. I had work to do.

---

topic: A witness is questioned about a workplace injury they observed but did not report
text:
Q: Let's talk about the safety protocols at the distribution center. Were you trained on incident reporting procedures?

A: Yeah, at orientation. They showed us a video, gave us some forms.

Q: So you understood that employees were expected to report workplace injuries they witnessed?

A: I understood that was the policy, sure.

Q: And you witnessed Jennifer Okafor injure her hand on the conveyor belt on October 3rd?

A: I saw her hand get caught, yes.

Q: What happened after her hand got caught?

A: She pulled it out. There was some blood. She wrapped it up with something, I don't remember what.

Q: Okay. Did she seek medical attention?

A: Not that I saw.

Q: Did you offer to help her?

A: She said she was fine.

Q: Did you ask if she needed help, or did she volunteer that information?

A: Does it matter?

Q: I'm asking what happened.

A: I think I asked. She said she was fine. That was it.

Q: And you didn't file an incident report.

A: No.

Q: Even though you'd been trained to do so.

A: Look, people got little injuries all the time there. You'd be filling out paperwork all day if you reported every cut and scrape.

---

topic: A witness is questioned about a workplace injury they observed but did not report
text:
Q: Mr. Patterson, I want to move through this efficiently so we can get you out of here. You saw the plaintiff fall on November 8th, yes or no?

A: Yes.

Q: Where were you standing when it happened?

A: By the tool cage, maybe thirty feet away.

Q: Did you see what caused him to fall?

A: I saw him slip. I don't know what caused it.

Q: Was there anything on the floor? Water, oil, debris?

A: I didn't inspect the floor.

Q: I'm asking what you observed.

A: I observed him slip and fall. That's it.

Q: Okay. Did anyone call for a supervisor?

A: I assume so. Someone usually does.

Q: You assume so. Did you see anyone call for a supervisor?

A: I wasn't really paying attention after the first few seconds.

Q: What were you paying attention to?

A: My own work. I had a quota to hit.

Q: After the fall, did anyone ask you what you saw?

A: Not until now.

---

topic: A witness is questioned about a workplace injury they observed but did not report
text:
Q: Ms. Vance, I'd like to understand the timeline here. What time did your shift begin on the day in question?

A: Six a.m.

Q: And the incident with Mr. Hernandez occurred at approximately what time?

A: I don't know exactly. Maybe nine? Nine-thirty?

Q: You'd been working for about three hours at that point.

A: If you say so. I don't track time that precisely.

Q: What were you doing when you first noticed something was wrong?

A: I was sorting packages. I heard someone yell.

Q: What did you hear them yell?

A: I don't remember the exact words. Something like "whoa" or "watch out." Something like that.

Q: And then what did you see?

A: I turned around and saw Mr. Hernandez on the ground near the forklift.

Q: Was the forklift moving?

A: No. It was stopped by then.

Q: Do you know if the forklift struck Mr. Hernandez?

A: I didn't see it happen. I just saw him on the ground.

Q: Did you go over to where he was?

A: No. I stayed where I was.

Q: Any particular reason?

A: There were already people around him. And honestly, I didn't think it was that serious. People fall sometimes.

---

topic: A witness is questioned about a workplace injury they observed but did not report
text:
Q: You've testified that you saw blood on the floor near the loading dock.

A: That's right.

Q: And you saw this before or after the paramedics arrived?

A: Before. I saw it when I walked by.

Q: Did you know at that point that someone had been injured?

A: I figured something happened, yeah.

Q: What did you do with that information?

A: What do you mean, what did I do?

Q: Did you tell anyone? Did you ask what happened?

A: I asked Danny what was going on. He said Ray cut his leg. That was about it.

Q: Did you see Ray after he was injured?

A: I saw him sitting on a crate, holding his leg. Someone had given him a rag or something.

Q: Did he appear to be in pain?

A: I guess. I don't know. He was sitting there.

Q: You mentioned you didn't report this incident. Is that accurate?

A: I didn't file anything official, no.

Q: Did it occur to you to do so?

A: Not really. Ray was a grown man. He could report it himself if he wanted to.

Q: Were you aware that he didn't report it?

A: That's his business, not mine.

topic: A witness is questioned about a fire they discovered in a neighboring unit
text:
Q: Mr. Delacroix, you testified earlier that you first noticed the fire at approximately 10:15 p.m. Is that correct?

A: That's when I called 911. I noticed it maybe a minute or two before that.

Q: And where exactly were you when you first noticed the fire?

A: On my balcony. Having a cigarette.

Q: You smoke on your balcony regularly?

A: Most nights, yes.

Q: What drew your attention to unit 4B?

A: The smell. Then I saw the glow through their sliding door.

Q: The glow. Can you describe that more precisely?

A: Orange. Flickering. What fire looks like.

Q: Was anyone else on your balcony with you?

A: No.

Q: Had you seen anyone enter or exit unit 4B that evening?

A: I wasn't watching unit 4B that evening. I was having a cigarette.

Q: That's not what I asked, Mr. Delacroix. Did you see anyone enter or exit unit 4B?

A: And I'm telling you I wasn't paying attention to their door. So no. I didn't see anyone.

Q: You seem quite certain about the time, though. 10:15 p.m. Do you often check the time before calling emergency services?

A: My phone shows the time when you unlock it. I unlocked it to dial. I noticed the time. That's how memory works.

Q: Of course. Now, you mentioned a smell. What kind of smell?

A: Chemical. Sharp. Not like wood burning.

Q: Had you ever smelled anything similar coming from that unit before?

A: I don't make a habit of cataloging my neighbors' smells.

topic: A witness is questioned about a fire they discovered in a neighboring unit
text:
Q: Please state your name for the record.

A: Teresa Womack.

Q: Ms. Womack, you live at 742 Ridgeline Drive, unit 6, is that correct?

A: Yes, that's correct.

Q: And unit 6 shares a wall with unit 5, where the fire originated?

A: Yes. The bedroom wall.

Q: Tell me what you observed on the night of March 3rd.

A: Well, I was in bed, probably around eleven, maybe eleven-thirty. I heard what I thought was—I don't know—a popping sound? And then about twenty minutes later, my smoke detector went off.

Q: A popping sound. You're certain it was twenty minutes before your smoke detector activated?

A: Roughly. I'm not—I wasn't looking at a clock. It felt like twenty minutes.

Q: Did you investigate the popping sound?

A: No. I thought maybe it was the TV next door. Mr. Harmon watches—watched—action movies pretty loud sometimes.

Q: Pretty loud. Did that bother you?

A: Sometimes.

Q: Had you ever complained about the noise?

A: I—once. Maybe twice. To building management. What does that have to do with anything?

Q: I'm just trying to understand the relationship between the units. Did Mr. Harmon know you had complained?

A: I have no idea what Mr. Harmon knew.

Q: You never spoke to him directly about it?

A: We weren't—we said hello in the hallway. That's all.

Q: When your smoke detector went off, what did you do?

A: I went to my front door, and I could smell smoke in the hallway. I grabbed my purse and my cat and I left. I called 911 from the parking lot.

Q: Did you see Mr. Harmon in the parking lot?

A: No. I didn't see anyone from unit 5.

topic: A witness is questioned about a fire they discovered in a neighboring unit
text:
Q: How long have you lived in the Briarwood complex, Mr. Osei?

A: Eleven years this August.

Q: So you were familiar with the residents of unit 12?

A: The Castellanos, yes. Good people. Known them since they moved in.

Q: When did they move in?

A: 2019, I believe. Maybe late 2018.

Q: Were you aware of anyone who might have had a dispute with the Castellanos?

A: A dispute?

Q: A disagreement. A conflict of any kind.

A: They were quiet people. Kept to themselves mostly.

Q: That's not quite what I asked.

A: I know what you asked. I'm telling you they didn't have problems with people.

Q: Mr. Osei, I'm going to ask you directly. Did you ever witness anyone behaving in a concerning manner around unit 12?

A: Define concerning.

Q: Unusual. Out of place. Something that struck you as wrong.

A: There was a man.

Q: Go on.

A: Maybe three weeks before the fire. I saw a man I didn't recognize standing near their door. Just standing there. Not knocking.

Q: Did you report this to anyone?

A: No. He left after a minute. I thought maybe he had the wrong unit.

Q: Can you describe him?

A: White, maybe forty, forty-five. Dark jacket. Baseball cap.

Q: Did you see his face?

A: Not clearly. He was looking at their door, not at me.

Q: Have you seen this man since the fire?

A: No.

topic: A witness is questioned about a fire they discovered in a neighboring unit
text:
Q: Mrs. Yuen, I understand this is difficult, and I appreciate your time today.

A: It's fine. I want to help if I can.

Q: You discovered the fire in unit 3A at approximately 6:00 a.m.?

A: Yes. I wake up early. I was getting my newspaper from the hallway.

Q: And what did you observe?

A: Smoke. Coming from under their door. A lot of smoke, actually, for—well, it surprised me how much there was.

Q: For what? You started to say something.

A: I just meant—there was a lot of smoke for how early it must have been. The fire, I mean. The investigators said it had only been burning for maybe fifteen, twenty minutes.

Q: How do you know what the investigators said?

A: They interviewed me. Right after.

Q: I see. Did you hear anything before you opened your door that morning?

A: I don't think so. Maybe—I thought I heard a door close. But that could have been anyone.

Q: What time was that?

A: I don't know exactly. Maybe ten minutes before I found the smoke? I was still in bed.

Q: A door closing. Could you tell which direction?

A: No. Sound carries strangely in that building.

Q: Mrs. Yuen, was unit 3A occupied at the time of the fire?

A: The Patels were on vacation. Everyone knew that.

Q: Everyone knew?

A: I mean—I knew. I assume others did too. Mrs. Patel mentioned it to me before they left. Asked me to water their plants.

Q: Did you water their plants?

A: I—no. I was going to do it that morning, actually. But then the fire.

topic: A witness is questioned about a fire they discovered in a neighboring unit
text:
Q: Let's talk about what you saw when you first approached the building that night.

A: Okay.

Q: You were returning from where?

A: From my sister's house. She lives about fifteen minutes away.

Q: What time did you leave your sister's house?

A: Around 9:00, 9:15. I wasn't really paying attention.

Q: And you arrived at Maple Grove apartments at what time?

A: Maybe 9:30. 9:35.

Q: That's a fairly quick drive.

A: There's no traffic that time of night.

Q: When you pulled into the parking lot, what did you notice?

A: I saw flames. Second floor, east side of the building.

Q: You could see actual flames?

A: Through the window, yes.

Q: What did you do?

A: I called 911 immediately. Then I ran inside to make sure people were getting out.

Q: You ran toward a burning building?

A: People could have been trapped.

Q: That's very brave. Or very reckless, depending on your perspective.

A: I'm not sure what you want me to say to that.

Q: Let me ask you this—did you know who lived in the unit that was on fire?

A: I knew it was Marcus Wheeler's unit.

Q: How did you know that from the parking lot?

A: I know which unit is which. I've lived there four years.

Q: And you and Mr. Wheeler, you were acquainted?

A: We knew each other.

Q: Could you characterize that relationship?

A: I said we knew each other. He was a neighbor.

Q: Did you see Mr. Wheeler that night?

A: Not until later. At the hospital. He'd inhaled a lot of smoke.

Q: But you didn't see him before the fire? Or during?

A: No.

Q: Nowhere near the building?

A: I answered the question.

topic: A paramedic is questioned about the response time and treatment at an accident scene
text:
Q: Please state your name and occupation for the record.

A: Michael Reeves. I'm a paramedic with County EMS, Unit 7.

Q: How long have you been a paramedic, Mr. Reeves?

A: Eleven years. Eleven years this past March.

Q: And you responded to the accident on Route 12 on the evening of September 14th?

A: Yes.

Q: What time did you arrive on scene?

A: We... the dispatch log says 7:47 p.m.

Q: The log says. What do you recall?

A: I recall it was dark. The sun had just gone down. There was a lot of debris on the road.

Q: Mr. Reeves, I'm asking about the time.

A: I know what you're asking. The log says 7:47. I don't have any reason to dispute that.

Q: The call came in at 7:31 p.m. Does that sound right?

A: If that's what the record shows.

Q: Sixteen minutes, then. From call to arrival.

A: The Hendricks Road bridge was out. We had to take the long way around through Miller's Crossing. I've explained this.

Q: To whom have you explained it?

A: To... to my supervisor. During the review.

Q: Was sixteen minutes an acceptable response time, in your professional opinion?

A: It was the best we could do that night. It was the best we could do.

Q: That wasn't my question.

A: No. No, it wasn't acceptable. None of it was acceptable. But that's not the same as saying we could have done it differently.

Q: When you arrived, what was the condition of the driver?

A: She was... she was still conscious. She asked me if her daughter was okay. Those were her first words to me.

topic: A paramedic is questioned about the response time and treatment at an accident scene
text:
Q: You were the lead paramedic on the call, correct?

A: Correct.

Q: Walk me through the treatment you provided to the juvenile victim.

A: We extracted her from the rear passenger seat. She was unresponsive. No visible bleeding but her breathing was shallow, irregular. We initiated oxygen, started an IV line, immobilized her spine.

Q: How long did extraction take?

A: I'd estimate four to five minutes.

Q: You'd estimate.

A: The fire crew had to cut the door. I wasn't watching a clock. I was watching her.

Q: Fair enough. After extraction, what was your next step?

A: We got her on the stretcher, continued monitoring vitals, and transported.

Q: Did you perform CPR at any point on scene?

A: Not on scene. In the ambulance, yes. Approximately two minutes into transport.

Q: Her heart stopped.

A: Her heart stopped. Yes.

Q: Take me through that moment, if you would.

A: I... my partner was driving. I was in back with her. The monitor alarmed. I started compressions immediately.

Q: Were you able to restore a heartbeat?

A: Temporarily. We got a rhythm back, then lost it again at the hospital.

Q: How old was she? The child.

A: Seven. She was seven years old.

Q: I'm going to ask you something, and I want you to take your time if you need to. In your professional judgment, would an earlier arrival have changed the outcome?

A: I've asked myself that question every day since September. I don't have an answer for you. I wish I did.

topic: A paramedic is questioned about the response time and treatment at an accident scene
text:
Q: Let's talk about the adult male victim, the passenger in the front seat.

A: Mr. Donnelly.

Q: You remember his name.

A: I remember all their names.

Q: What was his condition when you reached him?

A: He was alert, talking, but he had significant chest trauma. Steering column impact, we suspected. Difficulty breathing. He was in a lot of pain.

Q: What treatment did you provide?

A: We stabilized his chest, administered pain management, started a line. He was second priority for transport after the child.

Q: Second priority. Who made that determination?

A: I did.

Q: On what basis?

A: Pediatric patients take priority when resources are limited. That's standard protocol. It's how we're trained.

Q: Was Mr. Donnelly conscious when you made that decision?

A: He was.

Q: Did he say anything to you about it?

A: He told me to help his granddaughter first. He said... he said she was the only thing that mattered.

Q: And you honored that request.

A: I followed protocol. His request aligned with protocol.

Q: I see. Did Mr. Donnelly survive his injuries?

A: I don't... I believe he did, yes. He was in the ICU for some time.

Q: You believe he did. You don't know?

A: We don't always get follow-up. We drop them at the ER and then there's another call. There's always another call. But I checked on this one. He made it.

Q: You checked on this one.

A: I check on all of them. When I can.

topic: A paramedic is questioned about the response time and treatment at an accident scene
text:
Q: I want to direct your attention to the protocols for multi-casualty incidents. You're familiar with those?

A: Of course.

Q: In your eleven years, how many multi-casualty incidents have you responded to?

A: Dozens. Maybe more. I haven't kept count.

Q: Does the protocol require triage assessment before treatment begins?

A: Yes.

Q: And you performed triage assessment on September 14th?

A: I did.

Q: How long did that assessment take?

A: Two, maybe three minutes. We had three victims. We needed to prioritize.

Q: Who performed the assessment? You personally?

A: Yes.

Q: Not your partner?

A: My partner was getting equipment from the rig. I did the initial assessment.

Q: So you alone made the decision about who received treatment first.

A: That's correct.

Q: That's a significant responsibility.

A: It is.

Q: Does it ever weigh on you? That responsibility?

A: Counselor, I don't understand the relevance of that question.

Q: I'll rephrase. Did you feel any hesitation during the triage process that night?

A: No. There's no room for hesitation. You assess, you decide, you act. Hesitation costs lives.

Q: And yet, despite acting without hesitation, a seven-year-old girl died.

A: Yes.

Q: I don't have any further questions on this topic.

A: I... may I say something?

Q: Go ahead.

A: I did everything I was trained to do. My partner did everything he was trained to do. Sometimes that's not enough. Sometimes it's just not enough.

topic: A paramedic is questioned about the response time and treatment at an accident scene
text:
Q: When you arrived at the scene, how many other emergency vehicles were present?

A: Just the sheriff's deputy. Fire was about three minutes behind us.

Q: Deputy Morrison?

A: I don't recall his name. Young guy. He looked pretty shaken.

Q: Did he provide any assistance before you arrived?

A: He was holding pressure on the driver's leg wound. He'd used his belt as a tourniquet. Did a good job, actually. Probably saved her leg.

Q: Did you speak with him?

A: Briefly. He told me there were three victims, one was a child, and the child wasn't responding to him.

Q: Not responding. Meaning unconscious?

A: Meaning she wasn't talking, wasn't moving. He wasn't sure if she was breathing. That's when I went to her first.

Q: What did you find?

A: She was breathing. Barely. Her eyes were open but she wasn't... she wasn't tracking. She wasn't seeing anything.

Q: Can you describe her injuries?

A: Internal, mostly. She didn't have a scratch on her face. She looked like she was sleeping, except for her eyes. I remember thinking... I remember thinking how unfair that was. That she didn't have a mark on her.

Q: Unfair.

A: That's not a medical term. I apologize.

Q: No need to apologize. What happened next?

A: I called for my partner. We started working. We worked on her the entire time.

Q: Mr. Reeves, do you need a moment?

A: No. No, I'm fine. What's your next question?

Q: I think we can take a short break.

A: I said I'm fine. Let's continue. Please.

topic: A witness is questioned about a conversation they overheard in a company hallway
text:
Q: Good morning. I understand you've been with Meridian Technologies for about six years now?

A: Yes, that's right. Six years this coming April, actually. Started in the facilities department and worked my way into operations. It's been a good run.

Q: That's wonderful. And you mentioned in your initial statement that you happened to be in the third-floor hallway on the afternoon of March 15th?

A: I was, yes. I remember it clearly because I was coming back from getting coffee for myself and Linda—she's our receptionist, lovely woman—and I always take the long way around because the view from that hallway is really something.

Q: Take your time with this. Can you tell me, in your own words, what you observed?

A: Of course. So I came around the corner by the supply closet, and I could hear Mr. Brennan and someone else—turned out to be Ms. Alvarez—having a conversation near the window alcove. They weren't exactly whispering, but they weren't being loud either.

Q: And what was the nature of that conversation, as you understood it?

A: Well, I don't want to overstate what I heard, but it seemed like they were discussing the quarterly projections. Mr. Brennan was saying something about the numbers needing to be "adjusted" before the board meeting. His exact word—adjusted.

Q: I appreciate your precision there. Did Ms. Alvarez respond to that?

A: She did. She seemed a bit hesitant, if I'm being honest. She asked him something like, "Are you sure that's the right approach?" And he kind of put his hand on her shoulder—in a reassuring way, nothing inappropriate—and said they'd discuss it further in his office.

Q: You're doing great. Did either of them notice you were there?

A: Oh, I don't think so. I kind of hung back by the supply closet. I wasn't trying to eavesdrop, you understand—I just didn't want to interrupt what seemed like an important conversation.

Q: Of course. That's completely understandable. Did you hear anything else before you moved on?

A: Just one more thing. As I was walking away, I heard Mr. Brennan say something about "keeping this between us for now." That stuck with me.

Q: Thank you for sharing that. I know this isn't easy, recounting conversations about colleagues.

A: I appreciate you saying that. These are good people, you know? I just want to tell the truth about what I heard.

topic: A witness is questioned about a conversation they overheard in a company hallway
text:
Q: State your name for the record.

A: Derek Okonkwo.

Q: Mr. Okonkwo, you work in the IT department at Hargrove Financial?

A: I do. Network security, specifically.

Q: And on October 3rd of last year, you were on the fourth floor?

A: Yes.

Q: Why were you there?

A: Routine maintenance on the server closet. We check those systems weekly.

Q: While you were there, did you overhear a conversation?

A: I did. Look, I want to help here. I know this is important, and I've been thinking about it a lot since you first reached out.

Q: I can tell you've given this thought. What did you hear?

A: There were two people in the hallway—I couldn't see them at first because I was inside the closet, but the door was propped open. One of them was definitely Mr. Trent. I'd know his voice anywhere; he has this very distinctive way of speaking.

Q: And the other person?

A: I'm pretty sure it was someone from legal. A woman's voice. She kept referencing "liability exposure" and "disclosure obligations." The way she phrased things—it sounded like someone who deals with that kind of language every day.

Q: What was Mr. Trent saying?

A: He was pushing back. Not aggressively, but firmly. He said something like, "We can't let this derail the merger. There has to be another way." And she—whoever she was—said they needed to loop in outside counsel.

Q: Did Mr. Trent agree to that?

A: Not exactly. He said he wanted to "handle it internally first." Those were his words.

Q: Mr. Okonkwo, I want you to know that your recollection here is very helpful.

A: Thank you. I've been worried about getting involved, honestly. But I figure the truth matters more than my discomfort.

Q: It does. And we appreciate you being here today.

A: Of course. Whatever else you need, just ask.

topic: A witness is questioned about a conversation they overheard in a company hallway
text:
Q: Ms. Ferreira, how long have you worked at Crestwood Manufacturing?

A: Twelve years.

Q: In what capacity?

A: Executive assistant to the CFO.

Q: So you're familiar with the executive floor?

A: Very.

Q: On January 8th, did you have occasion to be in the hallway near the conference rooms?

A: I did.

Q: What were you doing there?

A: Retrieving documents from the printer station. It's down the hall from my desk.

Q: And while you were there, did you hear a conversation?

A: Yes. Between Mr. Holloway and Mr. Chen.

Q: Tell me about it.

A: They were speaking quietly, but I have good hearing. Mr. Holloway was talking about some kind of arrangement with a vendor. He mentioned a name—Spectra Logistics, I think.

Q: What about Spectra Logistics?

A: Something about payments that weren't going through the normal channels. Mr. Chen seemed uncomfortable. He kept saying, "I don't know about this, Richard."

Q: What did Mr. Holloway say to that?

A: He laughed—not meanly, just kind of dismissively—and said Mr. Chen worried too much. That "these things are done all the time."

Q: How did that make you feel, hearing that?

A: Honestly? Conflicted. I've known Mr. Holloway for years. He's always been kind to me. Remembered my daughter's graduation, sent flowers when my mother passed. So hearing something like that... it was hard.

Q: I understand. That's a difficult position to be in.

A: It is. But I care about this company too. I've given it twelve years of my life. If something's wrong, it should be addressed.

Q: That's an admirable perspective.

A: Thank you. I just hope this all works out for everyone involved.

topic: A witness is questioned about a conversation they overheard in a company hallway
text:
Q: You are Sandra Liu?

A: That's correct.

Q: You work in human resources at Belmont Group?

A: I do.

Q: Ms. Liu, I want to make sure you're comfortable. Would you like some water before we continue?

A: No, I'm fine, thank you.

Q: Let me know if that changes. Now, on August 22nd, you were in the east corridor on the second floor?

A: Yes, I was walking to the break room.

Q: What time was this?

A: Around 2:30, maybe 2:45 in the afternoon.

Q: And you overheard something there?

A: I did. Ms. Hartley was speaking with someone I didn't recognize—a man in a gray suit.

Q: What were they discussing?

A: Employee records. Specifically, someone's personnel file. Ms. Hartley said something about needing to "clean up" the documentation before an audit.

Q: Did she say whose file?

A: She mentioned a name—Patterson, I think. Or Paterson with one T. I'm not certain.

Q: That's okay. You're doing just fine. What did the man say?

A: He asked if there was anything "problematic" in the file. Ms. Hartley said there were some complaints that "shouldn't have been recorded that way."

Q: Did she elaborate?

A: Not while I was there. I kept walking because I didn't want them to see me lingering.

Q: I understand. Did anything else about the conversation stand out to you?

A: Just the tone. Ms. Hartley seemed stressed but determined. Like she'd made up her mind about something.

Q: Thank you, Ms. Liu. You've been very patient with these questions.

A: I just want to be helpful. This has been weighing on me since it happened.

topic: A witness is questioned about a conversation they overheard in a company hallway
text:
Q: How are you doing today?

A: Fine, thanks.

Q: Good, good. Before we start, I want to say—I've reviewed your employment history, and your dedication to Pacific Dynamics is really evident.

A: Well, I do my best.

Q: Twenty-three years is impressive. You must have seen a lot of changes.

A: I have. The company's grown quite a bit since I started.

Q: I imagine that gives you a unique perspective. Now, about what you heard on November 14th—you were in the main hallway near the executive suites?

A: That's right. I was dropping off some quarterly reports to Ms. Jennings' office.

Q: And you overheard a conversation between whom?

A: Mr. Park and Mr. Davidson. They were standing outside Mr. Park's office.

Q: What did you hear?

A: Mr. Davidson was asking about some contracts. He wanted to know if certain terms had been changed after signing.

Q: What did Mr. Park say?

A: He said the amendments were "standard practice." But Mr. Davidson didn't seem convinced. He kept asking questions—politely, but persistently.

Q: Did Mr. Park explain further?

A: He said something about verbal agreements superseding the written terms in some cases. That struck me as odd, honestly.

Q: Why odd?

A: Because in my experience, everything at Pacific goes through legal. Everything gets documented. So hearing about verbal agreements... it just didn't fit.

Q: That's a thoughtful observation. Did the conversation continue?

A: Mr. Park noticed me then and sort of nodded in my direction. They both went quiet.

Q: Did either of them say anything to you?

A: Mr. Park just smiled and said hello. Mr. Davidson gave me a little wave. They've both always been friendly to me.

Q: It sounds like you have a good relationship with many people there.

A: I do. That's what makes this hard, honestly. These are people I've worked alongside for years. Good people, most of them. I don't take lightly what I'm saying here.

topic: A witness is asked about a car accident they saw from their front porch
text:
Q: Please state your name for the record.

A: Margaret Ellison.

Q: Ms. Ellison, you've indicated you witnessed a car accident on the afternoon of September 14th, is that correct?

A: I saw something, yes.

Q: Something. Can you describe what you saw?

A: Two cars collided at the intersection of Maple and Vine. I was on my porch.

Q: And from your porch, you had a clear view of the intersection?

A: I've lived in that house for thirty-one years. I know that intersection better than anyone.

Q: That wasn't my question. I asked whether you had a clear view.

A: There's a magnolia tree. It blocks part of the stop sign on the south side. But I could see the cars just fine.

Q: Just fine. So no obstructions to your view of the actual collision?

A: I said the tree blocks part of the stop sign. I didn't say it blocked the cars.

Q: What color was the vehicle that you say ran the stop sign?

A: I didn't say anyone ran the stop sign. You're putting words in my mouth.

Q: Let me rephrase. Which vehicle entered the intersection first?

A: The blue sedan. It was already in the intersection when the pickup came through.

Q: And you're certain it was a blue sedan?

A: It was blue. It might have been more of a hatchback, now that I think about it. But it was definitely blue. I'm not guessing about that.

Q: You're not guessing about the color, but you're uncertain about the type of vehicle?

A: I'm being precise. You should appreciate that.

---

topic: A witness is asked about a car accident they saw from their front porch
text:
Q: Good morning. Could you tell us where you were on March 3rd at approximately 4:15 p.m.?

A: On my front porch, like I already told the police and the insurance investigator and now you.

Q: I understand you've answered these questions before. I need your testimony under oath today.

A: Fine. I was on my porch. Drinking iced tea. Reading the paper.

Q: And you heard the accident before you saw it?

A: Yes. A loud crash. I looked up.

Q: How much time passed between the sound and when you looked up?

A: I don't know. A second? Two seconds?

Q: So the collision had already occurred by the time you actually looked?

A: Yes.

Q: Then you didn't actually witness the collision itself.

A: I saw the cars. I saw where they ended up. I saw the white SUV spinning.

Q: But you didn't see the moment of impact.

A: No one said I did.

Q: Your statement to police says, and I quote, "I saw the whole thing."

A: I saw the whole aftermath. I saw the driver of the SUV get out. I saw him stumble. I saw the other driver screaming.

Q: But the "whole thing" would suggest—

A: I know what I meant. Maybe the officer wrote it down wrong.

Q: Are you suggesting the police report is inaccurate?

A: I'm suggesting I know what I saw, and I know what I said.

---

topic: A witness is asked about a car accident they saw from their front porch
text:
Q: Mr. Brennan, how far is your front porch from the intersection where this accident occurred?

A: About a hundred feet, give or take.

Q: A hundred feet. That's roughly the length of three school buses parked end to end, would you agree?

A: I wouldn't know. I don't spend much time measuring school buses.

Q: Fair enough. At that distance, you were able to see the license plate of the red truck?

A: I didn't say I saw the license plate.

Q: You told the investigating officer the plate started with "7K."

A: Because after the accident, the truck was facing my direction. It ended up much closer. Maybe forty feet.

Q: So your identification of the plate came after the collision, not before.

A: That's right.

Q: What were the lighting conditions at the time?

A: Late afternoon. Sun was getting low but it wasn't dark yet.

Q: Was the sun in your eyes?

A: No. It was behind my house. I face east.

Q: You're certain about the compass direction?

A: I know which way my own house faces, counselor.

Q: And yet you initially told police the accident happened around 6:30, but the 911 call was logged at 5:47.

A: I wasn't wearing a watch. I estimated.

Q: You estimated wrong by over forty minutes.

A: I got the important parts right.

---

topic: A witness is asked about a car accident they saw from their front porch
text:
Q: Ms. Torres, I'd like to understand exactly what you observed. Take your time.

A: Okay.

Q: Where were you seated on your porch?

A: The rocking chair. It's on the left side if you're facing the house.

Q: And you were doing what, prior to the accident?

A: Just sitting. It was a nice evening.

Q: Were you looking at your phone? Reading? Anything like that?

A: No. Just watching the street. The kids across the way were playing basketball.

Q: So your attention was on the children playing basketball?

A: Partly. I was just... looking around. People do that.

Q: Of course. Now, when the two vehicles approached the intersection, which one did you notice first?

A: The motorcycle. Because of the sound.

Q: The sound. It was loud?

A: It was. Revving. Like he was accelerating.

Q: "Like he was accelerating." You're not certain he was accelerating?

A: I'm not a mechanic. It sounded like acceleration to me.

Q: Did you actually see the motorcycle accelerate, or are you inferring that from the sound?

A: I... I saw it moving fast. And it was getting louder. So yes, I think he was speeding up.

Q: You think.

A: I'm telling you what I observed. I'm not going to pretend I had a radar gun.

Q: No one's asking you to pretend anything, Ms. Torres. I'm just trying to understand the basis for your observations.

A: And I'm giving it to you. As best I can.

---

topic: A witness is asked about a car accident they saw from their front porch
text:
Q: Sir, you've testified you were approximately sixty feet from the intersection.

A: Closer to fifty, I'd say now.

Q: Now? Has your estimate changed since your written statement?

A: I walked it off yesterday. Wanted to be accurate for today.

Q: You walked it off yesterday. Did anyone ask you to do that?

A: No. I just figured you'd want to know.

Q: And you measured fifty feet.

A: Forty-seven steps. My stride's about a foot, foot and a half.

Q: So somewhere between forty-seven and seventy feet, depending on your stride.

A: I suppose, if you want to do the math that way.

Q: Let's move on. You claim the silver car was traveling above the speed limit.

A: I don't claim it. I observed it.

Q: How fast was the silver car traveling, in your estimation?

A: Fast. Maybe forty. The limit there is twenty-five.

Q: Have you ever been trained in estimating vehicle speed?

A: No.

Q: Have you ever been wrong about how fast a car was going?

A: Probably. Everyone has.

Q: But you're confident about this particular estimate.

A: I've watched cars on that street for nine years. I know when one's going too fast.

Q: Is it possible the car was traveling at thirty miles per hour?

A: It's possible. But it didn't look like thirty to me.

Q: What does thirty look like, as opposed to forty?

A: It looks slower. I don't know how else to explain it.

topic: A project manager is questioned about deadlines they missed on a software contract
text:
Q: Mr. Harmon, I'd like to direct your attention to the Meridian software contract. You were the project manager on that engagement, correct?

A: That's correct. I was assigned as project manager in March of 2022 and remained in that role through the contract's completion.

Q: And the original delivery date for Phase Two was September 15th, 2022?

A: Yes, that was the date specified in the initial statement of work.

Q: But Phase Two wasn't delivered on September 15th, was it?

A: No, it was not. We delivered on October 3rd.

Q: So you missed the deadline by approximately eighteen days.

A: Eighteen days, yes. Though I'd note that the client had approved a revised timeline on September 8th, so from our operational perspective, we delivered within the adjusted parameters.

Q: Let's set aside the revised timeline for a moment. The original contract specified September 15th. You did not meet that date.

A: That's accurate. We did not meet the original date.

Q: What was the primary cause of that delay?

A: There were several contributing factors. The most significant was a change in the API specifications from the client's payment processor, which occurred in late July. That required us to substantially rework the integration module.

Q: When did you first communicate to Meridian that September 15th was at risk?

A: I sent a formal status update on August 12th identifying the risk, and I had a call with their project lead, Sandra Chen, on August 14th to discuss mitigation options.

Q: And between August 14th and September 8th, when you say the timeline was revised, what steps did you take?

A: We added two developers to the integration team, extended working hours, and I provided weekly progress updates to Sandra. We also proposed the revised timeline with three delivery scenarios, and Meridian selected the October 3rd option.

Q: Did you document those weekly updates in writing?

A: Every one of them. I can provide email records with timestamps if that would be helpful to this proceeding.

Q: We'll get to document production. For now, I'm simply establishing the sequence of events.

A: Understood. I'm happy to continue.

topic: A project manager is questioned about deadlines they missed on a software contract
text:
Q: Ms. Tierney, how long have you worked in software project management?

A: Going on fourteen years now.

Q: And in those fourteen years, have you ever missed a contractual deadline?

A: I'd need you to define what you mean by "missed." If you're asking whether a project I've managed has ever delivered after an originally scheduled date, the answer is yes, that's happened. If you're asking whether I've ever failed to deliver within a contractually agreed timeframe, accounting for amendments, the answer is no.

Q: Fair enough. Let's talk about the Beacon Analytics project specifically. The contract called for a beta release by June 1st, 2023.

A: Correct.

Q: When was the beta actually released?

A: June 22nd.

Q: Three weeks late.

A: Three weeks after the original date, yes.

Q: Why?

A: Beacon requested a significant scope addition in April—they wanted real-time dashboard functionality that wasn't in the original requirements. We advised them that adding it would impact the timeline. They chose to proceed.

Q: Did you put that in writing?

A: I did.

Q: And they acknowledged the timeline impact in writing?

A: Their VP of Product, Daniel Reeves, responded to my email on April 19th stating—and I'm paraphrasing here—that they understood the tradeoff and prioritized the feature.

Q: Do you recall the exact language?

A: Not verbatim, no. I'd want to refer to the document to give you precise wording.

Q: Let me ask it differently. Did Mr. Reeves explicitly approve a new deadline?

A: He acknowledged that the June 1st date would slip. We formalized the revised date of June 22nd in a change order signed by both parties on April 26th.

Q: Who drafted that change order?

A: I did, with input from our legal team.

Q: And Beacon signed it without objection?

A: That's correct. Mr. Reeves signed it the same day I sent it over.

topic: A project manager is questioned about deadlines they missed on a software contract
text:
Q: Tell me about the staffing levels on the Greenfield project during the summer of 2023.

A: We started with a core team of six developers, one QA lead, and myself as project manager. In July, we scaled up to nine developers based on the milestone schedule.

Q: And was that staffing level adequate to meet the August deadline?

A: At the time we established the plan, yes, we believed it was adequate.

Q: But it wasn't, was it?

A: In hindsight, we underestimated the complexity of the legacy system migration. So no, it wasn't sufficient for what the work actually required.

Q: Whose responsibility was it to assess that complexity?

A: Mine, ultimately. I relied on estimates from my technical lead, but the final staffing decisions went through me.

Q: So you made an error in judgment?

A: I made an assessment based on the information available. It proved to be optimistic. Whether you call that an error in judgment—I suppose that's a reasonable characterization.

Q: I'm not trying to put words in your mouth. I'm asking whether you, sitting here today, believe you made a mistake.

A: I think I would make a different decision with what I know now. At the time, I thought we had adequate resources. We did not.

Q: Did you communicate the resource shortage to anyone before the deadline passed?

A: On July 28th, I flagged to my director that we were tracking behind and requested additional headcount.

Q: What was the response?

A: She approved one additional senior developer, who started on August 5th.

Q: And the deadline was August 15th.

A: Correct.

Q: Ten days wasn't much runway.

A: No. It wasn't.

Q: Did you tell your director that ten days wasn't enough?

A: I told her it would help but that we were still at risk. She understood. The headcount she approved was what was available.

topic: A project manager is questioned about deadlines they missed on a software contract
text:
Q: Let's walk through the timeline one more time, Mr. Okafor. When did you first learn that the authentication module was behind schedule?

A: I don't recall the exact date. It would have been sometime in mid-March.

Q: Mid-March. And the final deliverable was due when?

A: April 30th.

Q: So you had approximately six weeks' notice that a component was behind.

A: For that particular module, yes. The overall project had other components that were on track.

Q: But the authentication module was on the critical path, wasn't it?

A: It was.

Q: So if that module slipped, the entire delivery would slip.

A: In theory, yes. In practice, we had some flexibility because we'd built buffer into the integration phase.

Q: How much buffer?

A: About a week.

Q: A week. And how far behind was the authentication module in mid-March?

A: At that point, roughly two weeks behind where we wanted to be.

Q: So you had a week of buffer and two weeks of delay.

A: That's the arithmetic, yes.

Q: What did you do with that information?

A: I met with the development lead to understand the root cause.
