We identified that the third-party identity provider had changed their documentation, and our developers had been working from outdated specs. We corrected course, put two additional people on the integration, and I reset expectations with the client.

Q: When did you reset expectations with the client?

A: March 20th. I have the meeting invite if you need the specific time.

Q: And what did you tell them?

A: I told them we were at risk for April 30th, that we were taking steps to recover, and that I would provide a revised date by end of month if recovery efforts fell short.

Q: Did they express concern?

A: They expressed concern, yes. They weren't happy. But they appreciated the transparency, and we worked together from there.

topic: A project manager is questioned about deadlines they missed on a software contract
text:
Q: Ms. Castellanos, you've managed how many software projects of this scale?

A: Similar scale and complexity? Probably eight or nine.

Q: And of those eight or nine, how many have delivered on time?

A: On the original contract date? I'd say five, maybe six. On the operative deadline after any amendments? All of them.

Q: Let's focus on original dates. Why do you think nearly half of your projects have required timeline amendments?

A: Because software development involves uncertainty. Requirements evolve. Dependencies shift. Clients change their minds about priorities. A good project manager plans for variability and communicates proactively when adjustments are needed.

Q: So in your view, missing a deadline isn't a problem as long as you communicate about it?

A: I didn't say that. I said variability is inherent to the work. Managing it responsibly is part of the job.

Q: On the Northfield contract specifically, when did you first realize the January 15th deadline was at risk?

A: Late November. The 22nd or 23rd.

Q: What triggered that realization?

A: Our lead architect identified a performance bottleneck in the reporting engine. The fix wasn't trivial—it required rethinking some core data structures.

Q: And you communicated that to Northfield when?

A: December 1st. I called their program manager, Lisa Huang, and followed up the same day with a written summary.

Q: What options did you present?

A: I gave her three paths. Deliver on January 15th with reduced functionality. Deliver full functionality by February 1st. Or bring in a specialized contractor to attempt acceleration, which would add cost.

Q: Which option did Northfield select?

A: They chose February 1st. They wanted the full feature set.

Q: And you delivered on February 1st?

A: We delivered on January 29th.

Q: Ahead of the revised schedule.

A: By two days, yes. We like to build in margin when we can.

topic: An HR director is questioned about a harassment complaint that was filed and closed
text:
Q: Ms. Thornton, you were the HR director responsible for handling the complaint filed by Jessica Mendez, correct?

A: I was the HR director. Whether I was "responsible" for it depends on what you mean by responsible.

Q: You reviewed the complaint?

A: I reviewed it.

Q: And you made the decision to close it?

A: I made a recommendation. The decision involved multiple parties.

Q: Who else was involved in that decision?

A: I'm not going to name individuals who aren't parties to this litigation when their involvement was routine and procedural.

Q: I'm asking you a straightforward question. Who else decided to close this complaint?

A: And I'm giving you a straightforward answer. The closure followed standard protocol, which involves HR review, legal consultation, and executive sign-off. That's documented. You have the documents.

Q: Did you personally believe the complaint had merit?

A: My personal beliefs aren't relevant to how complaints are processed.

Q: I'm asking what you believed.

A: And I'm telling you that what I believed doesn't change what the investigation found.

Q: What did the investigation find?

A: Insufficient evidence to sustain the allegations. Which, again, is in the documents your office already has.

Q: Did you interview the complainant yourself?

A: I did.

Q: How long was that interview?

A: Long enough.

Q: Can you give me a number? Minutes? Hours?

A: Approximately forty-five minutes. Maybe closer to an hour. I didn't bring a stopwatch.

---

topic: An HR director is questioned about a harassment complaint that was filed and closed
text:
Q: Mr. Okonkwo, let's be very clear about the timeline here. The complaint was filed on March 3rd. When did you first learn of it?

A: March 3rd or 4th.

Q: Which was it?

A: I don't recall the exact date. It was one of those two days.

Q: And when was the complaint closed?

A: March 17th.

Q: Fourteen days. That's a fast turnaround for a harassment investigation, wouldn't you agree?

A: No, I wouldn't agree.

Q: You wouldn't.

A: No.

Q: How many witnesses were interviewed?

A: Three, including the complainant.

Q: Three people in fourteen days. And you're comfortable that was thorough?

A: Counsel, I've been doing this work for eleven years. I know what thorough looks like.

Q: I didn't ask about your resume. I asked if three interviews in two weeks constitutes a thorough investigation into workplace harassment.

A: And I'm telling you it does. The allegations were specific. The witnesses were the relevant parties. There was no need to interview the entire department to check a box for your benefit.

Q: Were there any witnesses suggested by the complainant that you did not interview?

A: She suggested one additional person who had no firsthand knowledge. We made a judgment call.

Q: You made that call?

A: We made that call. HR. As is our function.

Q: So you decided her suggested witness wasn't worth talking to.

A: I decided that interviewing someone who wasn't present for any of the alleged incidents would not advance the investigation. Yes.

---

topic: An HR director is questioned about a harassment complaint that was filed and closed
text:
Q: Let's talk about the documentation. You closed this complaint with a one-page summary. Does that strike you as adequate?

A: It was a summary.

Q: A summary of a harassment complaint that a woman says derailed her career.

A: Objection to the characterization. But I'll answer. The summary reflected the findings. Findings don't require a certain page count.

Q: Were there notes from your interviews?

A: Yes.

Q: Where are they?

A: I assume they were produced in discovery. You'd have to ask your own team.

Q: I'm asking you where you kept them.

A: In the HR files, where we keep everything.

Q: I'm looking at what was produced, Mr. Pratt, and I don't see interview notes.

A: Then you should take that up with whoever handled your production requests. I can't account for what your office did or didn't receive.

Q: You're not concerned that notes from a harassment investigation might be missing?

A: I'm not stipulating that anything is missing. I'm telling you where I kept them.

Q: When was the last time you saw those notes?

A: I don't recall.

Q: Before or after litigation was filed?

A: I don't recall.

Q: Convenient.

A: I'm sorry, was that a question?

Q: Let me rephrase. You have no memory of when you last accessed notes from an investigation that's now the subject of a federal lawsuit?

A: I have no specific memory, no. I handle dozens of complaints. I don't keep a mental log of every time I open a file.

---

topic: An HR director is questioned about a harassment complaint that was filed and closed
text:
Q: Ms. Chen, did you ever tell the complainant, in words or in substance, that she should "think carefully" before pursuing her complaint?

A: No.

Q: You never said that.

A: I never said that.

Q: Did you tell her that complaints "have a way of following people"?

A: Absolutely not.

Q: You're certain?

A: I'm certain. And frankly, I'm troubled by where these questions are coming from, because that's not language I would use.

Q: I'm asking the questions here, Ms. Chen.

A: And I'm answering them. But I'm also going to note for the record that you're putting fabricated statements to me.

Q: I'm reading from your complainant's declaration.

A: Then she's mistaken. Or worse.

Q: Or worse? What does that mean?

A: It means what it means.

Q: Did you have any off-the-record conversations with the complainant about this complaint?

A: All my conversations were appropriate. Every single one.

Q: That's not what I asked. Were any of them off the record?

A: I don't know what you mean by "off the record." There's no recording device in my office. But nothing I said was hidden or improper.

Q: Did you take notes of all your conversations with her?

A: I took notes when notes were warranted.

Q: And who decided when notes were warranted?

A: I did. That's my job.

---

topic: An HR director is questioned about a harassment complaint that was filed and closed
text:
Q: I want to understand the standard you applied here. What does it take to sustain a harassment complaint at your company?

A: There has to be credible evidence that policy was violated.

Q: Credible evidence.

A: Yes.

Q: And you didn't find that here?

A: The investigation didn't find that.

Q: You were the investigation, weren't you?

A: I conducted it.

Q: So you didn't find it.

A: The process didn't find it. I don't personalize these outcomes.

Q: The complainant provided emails. She provided text messages. She provided the name of a witness who saw one of the incidents. What more would she have needed?

A: Counsel, I'm not going to re-litigate the investigation in this deposition.

Q: I'm asking you to explain your reasoning.

A: My reasoning is documented.

Q: Your one-page summary?

A: My documentation. Yes.

Q: Did you find the complainant credible?

A: I found her sincere in her beliefs.

Q: That's not what I asked.

A: That's my answer.

Q: Did you believe her account of what happened?

topic: A doctor is deposed about informed consent procedures before a surgery
text:
Q: Dr. Patel, I'd like to turn your attention to the informed consent process for Mrs. Donovan's procedure. Can you describe your standard practice?

A: My standard practice. Yes. Well, I meet with patients prior to any surgical intervention to discuss the procedure, the risks, the benefits, and alternatives. That's what I do. That's what I've always done.

Q: And you did this with Mrs. Donovan?

A: I did, yes. I met with her on—let me think—it would have been November 14th, two days before the surgery.

Q: What specifically did you discuss during that meeting?

A: I discussed the nature of the cholecystectomy, the laparoscopic approach we intended to use, the possibility of conversion to open surgery if necessary, the risks of bleeding, infection, bile duct injury—I covered all of it. I'm very thorough. I want to be clear about that.

Q: You mentioned bile duct injury. Did you use those specific words with Mrs. Donovan?

A: I—yes. I believe so. I would have. That's part of my standard discussion.

Q: You believe so, or you did?

A: I did. I'm certain I did. I always discuss bile duct injury with gallbladder patients. It's a known risk. It would be—I mean, it would be irresponsible not to.

Q: Did you document this conversation in the medical record?

A: The consent form was signed. That's documentation.

Q: I'm asking about notes from your conversation. A narrative description of what was discussed.

A: I don't—I don't typically write out a narrative of every single thing I say to patients. The consent form exists for a reason. It lists the risks. She signed it. She had an opportunity to ask questions.

Q: Did she ask questions?

A: I don't recall specific questions, no. But I would have answered them if she had. I always do. I always encourage patients to ask questions. That's—that's part of the process.

Q: Dr. Patel, is it possible you didn't specifically mention bile duct injury?

A: No. No, that's not possible. I've been doing this for seventeen years. I know what I discuss with patients. I know my own practice.

A: A few minutes.

Q: A few minutes to read four pages of dense medical and legal terminology?

A: Counselor, I'm not her reading tutor. I provide the document. I offer to answer questions. I give patients time. What they do with that time is their choice.

Q: So you have no way of knowing whether she actually understood what she was signing?

A: I know that I explained the procedure and the risks in plain language before I ever handed her the form.

Q: Did you assess her comprehension in any way?

A: I asked if she had questions. She said she didn't.

Q: That's your assessment of comprehension? Whether she had questions?

A: That's a reasonable assessment, yes. Along with my clinical judgment of the patient's capacity.

Q: What clinical observations did you make about her capacity?

A: She was alert, oriented, engaged in conversation, responded appropriately to questions. She wasn't impaired.

Q: Did you document any of those observations?

A: It's implicit in the fact that I proceeded with obtaining consent.

Q: Implicit. But not explicitly written anywhere.

A: Correct.

topic: A doctor is deposed about informed consent procedures before a surgery
text:
Q: Dr. Chen, I want to ask you about your standard practice regarding informed consent. You do have a standard practice, correct?

A: Yes, I do.

Q: Tell me what that is.

A: Well, it depends somewhat on the procedure, the patient, the clinical context—there are a lot of variables.

Q: I understand there are variables. I'm asking about your standard practice.

A: And I'm trying to explain that "standard" doesn't mean "identical in every case." I tailor the conversation to the patient.

Q: Let me try this differently. Do you have a checklist you follow?

A: Not a written checklist, no.

Q: A mental checklist?

A: I suppose you could call it that.

Q: What's on this mental checklist?

A: The nature of the procedure. The expected benefits. The material risks. Alternatives to surgery. The risks of not proceeding. Whether the patient has questions.

Q: Do you always cover all of those items?

A: Yes. Though not always in that order, and not always in those exact words.

Q: With Mr. Franklin specifically—this was an elective procedure, correct?

A: It was.

Q: And with elective procedures, would you agree there's more time for the consent conversation?

A: Generally, yes.

Q: How much time did you spend with Mr. Franklin on consent?

A: I met with him twice before surgery. The first consultation was probably forty-five minutes. The second was shorter, maybe twenty minutes, focused on final questions.

Q: And you documented both conversations?

A: I documented the clinical notes from each visit. The consent discussion is part of that.

Q: Show me where in your notes you document the specific risks you discussed.

A: It's— let me see the exhibit. It's in here. "Risks and benefits discussed, patient verbalized understanding."

Q: That's the extent of it? One sentence?

A: That's the documentation, yes. The conversation was considerably longer than one sentence.

topic: A doctor is deposed about informed consent procedures before a surgery
text:
Q: Dr. Yamamoto, have you ever had a patient decline surgery after you explained the risks to them?

A: Yes, occasionally.

Q: More than once?

A: Yes.

Q: More than five times in your career?

A: I'd have to think about it. Yes, probably more than five times.

Q: And when a patient declines after the consent discussion, what do you do?

A: I document their decision and we discuss alternatives, if there are any.

Q: You don't try to persuade them to proceed?

A: I make sure they understand the consequences of declining. But no, I don't pressure patients into surgery.

Q: Let's talk about Ms. Archer. Did she express any hesitation during your consent discussion?

A: Not that I recall.

Q: She didn't ask to think about it?

A: She may have wanted some time to consider. That's normal.

Q: How much time did she take?

A: Between our initial consultation and the surgery was about two weeks.

Q: Did you speak with her during those two weeks?

A: My office followed up to schedule the procedure.

Q: But you personally didn't speak with her?

A: Not until the day of surgery.

Q: And on the day of surgery, you had another consent conversation?

A: A brief one. I confirmed she still wanted to proceed, asked if she had any new questions.

Q: How brief?

A: Five minutes, perhaps.

Q: Five minutes. And this was in pre-op, correct? She was already in a hospital gown, IV placed?

A: That's the standard setting for pre-operative confirmation, yes.

Q: Do you think a patient is in the best position to change her mind about surgery when she's already gowned, IV in her arm, lying in a hospital bed?

A: Patients can change their mind at any time. I've had patients decline on the table.

Q: That wasn't my question, Doctor. I asked whether you think that's the best position—

A: And I'm telling you it doesn't matter what I think is "best." Patients have the right to decide at any point. I honor that right.

topic: A tenant is questioned about property damage they reported to their landlord
text:
Q: Mr. Delgado, when did you first notice the water damage in the unit?

A: November 3rd.

Q: And what specifically did you observe on that date?

A: Water stains on the ceiling. Bubbling paint. Exactly what I wrote in the maintenance request.

Q: I'm asking what you observed, not what you wrote.

A: Those are the same things. Water stains. Bubbling paint. On the ceiling of the bedroom.

Q: Was there any water actively dripping at that time?

A: No.

Q: So the damage you observed was limited to staining and paint damage?

A: At that time, yes. At that time.

Q: Did you take any photographs on November 3rd?

A: I did.

Q: How many?

A: Four. Maybe five. I can check if you need the exact number.

Q: And you submitted these photographs with your maintenance request?

A: I submitted the maintenance request through the portal. The portal has an upload function. I used the upload function. So yes.

Q: Mr. Delgado, I'm simply trying to establish what documentation you provided. Did the photographs accompany the written request?

A: I just answered that.

Q: Let me rephrase. Were the photographs attached to the same submission as your written description of the damage?

A: Yes. Same submission. Same date. Same portal. November 3rd.

topic: A tenant is questioned about property damage they reported to their landlord
text:
Q: Ms. Thornton, let's talk about the mold you reported in March. Where in the apartment did you first see it?

A: The bathroom. Along the grout lines near the tub, and then later I noticed it spreading up toward the ceiling vent.

Q: When you say "spreading," over what period of time?

A: I mean, it's hard to say exactly. I first noticed it around March 8th, and by the time someone finally came out—which was April 2nd, I should add—it had gotten significantly worse.

Q: I'll get to the response timeline in a moment. Right now I'm asking about your observations.

A: My observations include the fact that it took almost a month for anyone to show up.

Q: Ms. Thornton—

A: I'm answering your question. I observed mold. I observed it getting worse. I observed no one doing anything about it.

Q: Did you attempt to clean the mold yourself before reporting it?

A: I wiped down the grout with bathroom cleaner, yes. Like any normal person would.

Q: So you did disturb the affected area before maintenance inspected it?

A: I cleaned my bathroom. I didn't "disturb" anything. It's a bathroom. I live there.

Q: I'm not suggesting anything improper. I'm establishing what condition the area was in when maintenance arrived.

A: The condition was moldy. Still moldy. Worse than before, actually, despite my apparently controversial decision to clean my own bathroom.

Q: Did maintenance provide you with any documentation of their findings?

A: They gave me a copy of the work order. Which I've already provided to my attorney, so I assume you have it.

topic: A tenant is questioned about property damage they reported to their landlord
text:
Q: You reported a broken window to building management on January 15th, correct?

A: That's correct.

Q: Tell me how the window came to be broken.

A: I don't know how it broke. I came home from work and found it that way.

Q: You have no idea how a window in your own apartment was broken?

A: I wasn't there when it happened, so no, I don't have firsthand knowledge of the cause.

Q: Was there glass inside the apartment or outside?

A: Inside, mostly. On the floor below the window.

Q: Which suggests the window was broken from the outside, would you agree?

A: I'm not a glass forensics expert, counselor.

Q: I'm asking for your lay observation.

A: My lay observation is that there was glass on my floor and cold air coming through a hole in my window in the middle of January.

Q: Did you report this to the police?

A: No.

Q: Why not?

A: Because I didn't know if it was a break-in attempt or just some random act. Nothing was taken. I reported it to the landlord because it was a building issue.

Q: So you made an assumption that no crime had occurred?

A: I made a decision about what was worth my time. Calling management to fix the window seemed like the priority.

Q: Let's move on to the repair itself. How long did it take before the window was replaced?

A: Eleven days. Not that I was counting or anything.

topic: A tenant is questioned about property damage they reported to their landlord
text:
Q: Mr. Okafor, I want to ask you about the HVAC issues you documented last summer.

A: All right.

Q: According to your complaint, the air conditioning stopped working on July 19th?

A: It stopped cooling effectively, yes. The unit was running but not producing cold air.

Q: And the temperature inside your apartment—do you know what it was?

A: I had a thermometer. It read 94 degrees in the living room on the afternoon of July 20th.

Q: Did you—94 degrees?

A: Yes.

Q: Inside the apartment.

A: That's what the thermometer said. I have a photograph of it, which your client also has, since I sent it with my third request for service.

Q: Your third request. So you made multiple requests?

A: July 19th, July 21st, and July 23rd. I also called the emergency maintenance line twice.

Q: Let's slow down and take these one at a time. The first request on July 19th—

A: I've already provided written documentation of all three requests with dates and timestamps. Do you want me to just read them into the record?

Q: I'm entitled to ask you questions about them, Mr. Okafor.

A: And I'm entitled to have working air conditioning in July, but here we are.

Q: Let's stay focused. On July 19th, what did you write in your maintenance request?

A: I wrote that the AC unit was running constantly but not cooling the apartment below 85 degrees. I requested urgent repair due to the heat advisory that was in effect.

Q: Were you aware that the building was experiencing system-wide HVAC issues that week?

A: I became aware of that excuse after the fact, yes.

topic: A tenant is questioned about property damage they reported to their landlord
text:
Q: The incident report mentions a ceiling collapse. Is that an accurate characterization?

A: Part of the ceiling in the hallway came down. About a two-foot section.

Q: When did this occur?

A: December 12th. Around 2 in the afternoon.

Q: Were you home at the time?

A: Yes.

Q: Did you witness the ceiling actually fall?

A: I heard it. I was in the kitchen. There was a loud cracking sound and then a crash.

Q: Were you injured?

A: No.

Q: Was anyone else present in the apartment?

A: My daughter was in her room. She wasn't hurt either, thank God, but that's not really the point, is it?

Q: I'm trying to establish the basic facts, Ms. Reyes.

A: The basic facts are that my ceiling fell in. In the middle of the afternoon. While my nine-year-old was twenty feet away.

Q: I understand this was frightening—

A: Do you? Because these questions don't really suggest that.

Q: Ms. Reyes, I have to ask these questions. Had you previously reported any issues with the ceiling in that hallway?

A: I reported water stains on October 30th. Discoloration and what looked like sagging on November 15th. Both times I was told someone would "look into it."

Q: Did anyone come to inspect the ceiling after those reports?

A: Someone came out after the November report. Looked at it for maybe two minutes. Said it was "probably cosmetic."

Q: And after that inspection, did you make any additional reports before December 12th?

A: No. I was told it was cosmetic. I believed, foolishly, that the person who inspected it knew what he was talking about.

topic: A neighbor is questioned about noise complaints and a confrontation they witnessed
text:
Q: Please state your name for the record.

A: Margaret Chen. And I have to say, I've been waiting to talk about this because I saw everything—I mean everything—from start to finish.

Q: Ms. Chen, we'll get to what you observed. First, how long have you lived at 4512 Maple Drive?

A: Eleven years, three months. I moved in right after my divorce was finalized, which was September 2013, so yes, eleven years and three months as of this deposition. I know that street better than anyone.

Q: And the defendant, Mr. Kowalski, lives where in relation to you?

A: Directly across the street! 4511 Maple. I can see his front porch from my living room window, his driveway from my kitchen, and his backyard if I'm in my upstairs guest room—which is where I happened to be that night.

Q: Let's talk about the night of August 14th. What time did you first notice any disturbance?

A: 10:47 PM. I know because I had just checked my phone—I was texting my daughter about her cat's vet appointment—and then I heard the music start. Bass so heavy my windows were vibrating. Vibrating! In a house built in 1987 with double-pane glass!

Q: What did you do when you heard the music?

A: Well, first I went to every window on that side of the house to see what was happening. Mr. Kowalski had at least—and I counted—at least fourteen cars parked up and down the street, some of them blocking Mrs. Patterson's driveway, which she would have been furious about if she hadn't been visiting her sister in Tampa.

Q: Did you observe the confrontation between Mr. Kowalski and the plaintiff, Mr. Reeves?

A: Did I observe it? I had a front-row seat! I pulled my reading chair right up to the guest room window. Mr. Reeves walked over at 11:23—I noted the time—and I watched the whole thing unfold.

Q: Please describe what you saw.

A: Mr. Reeves walked up the driveway—he was wearing his green bathrobe, the one with the coffee stain on the pocket—and he approached Mr. Kowalski who was standing by the coolers near the garage. They talked for maybe thirty seconds, and then Mr. Kowalski started pointing his finger and stepping forward, and Mr. Reeves stepped back, and then—this is the important part—Mr. Kowalski shoved him with both hands right in the chest!

Q: You're certain it was a shove with both hands?

A: Both hands, open palms, center of the chest. I know what I saw. I've been describing it to everyone who'll listen for months now.

Q: What happened after the shove?

A: Mr. Reeves stumbled backward—he nearly fell over that little garden border Mr. Kowalski has, the decorative brick one—and then two of the party guests came over and sort of formed a wall between them. That's when I called 911. I still have the call log on my phone if you want to see it!

Q: That won't be necessary at this time. Did you hear what was said during the confrontation?

A: The music was too loud for exact words, but I could tell from the body language—and I've taken two community college courses in nonverbal communication—that Mr. Kowalski was the aggressor. His posture was forward, dominant, shoulders squared. Textbook intimidation.

Q: Did police arrive that evening?

A: Yes! Two officers, about fifteen minutes after my call. I was going to go outside and give a statement, but they left before I could get my shoes on. I've been ready to tell this story to anyone official ever since.

topic: A neighbor is questioned about noise complaints and a confrontation they witnessed
text:
Q: Mr. Donovan, you've lived at 782 Crescent Avenue for how long?

A: Six years.

Q: And you're familiar with both parties in this matter?

A: I know who they are, yeah.

Q: Excellent. Now, I want to take you right to the heart of this—the night of March 3rd. You were home that evening, correct?

A: I was.

Q: Fantastic. And isn't it true that you heard the dispute between Mr. and Mrs. Ashford and their neighbor, the plaintiff, Mr. Vance?

A: I heard some yelling.

Q: Some yelling! Can you tell me—and please, take your time with this because the details matter—exactly where you were when this yelling began?

A: In my garage. Working on my car.

Q: What kind of car? Actually, never mind—let's focus on what matters. The garage door was open?

A: Yeah.

Q: Perfect. So you had a clear line of sight to the Ashford property?

A: I could see part of their side yard.

Q: And that's where the confrontation occurred, isn't it? Right there in that side yard you could see?

A: Part of it happened there, I guess.

Q: Tell me everything. What did you see first?

A: Mr. Vance was standing near the property line. The Ashfords came outside.

Q: Both of them? Husband and wife?

A: Yeah.

Q: And then what? Walk me through it moment by moment.

A: They were arguing about the dog. Mr. Vance's dog had gotten into their yard again, apparently.

Q: The dog—yes! This is important. Had you witnessed previous incidents involving this dog?

A: A couple times.

Q: A couple times. So this was an ongoing issue, a pattern of conflict between these neighbors, would you say?

A: I don't know if I'd say pattern.

Q: But you just said it happened multiple times. More than once is a pattern, wouldn't you agree? Legally speaking, that's significant.

A: I'm not a lawyer.

Q: Fair enough, fair enough. Let's get back to March 3rd. The Ashfords came outside, there was arguing about the dog—did it escalate?

A: Voices got louder.

Q: Louder! And did you see anyone make physical contact?

A: Mr. Ashford stepped toward Mr. Vance.

Q: Stepped toward him aggressively?

A: I don't know about aggressively. He stepped toward him.

Q: But you'd agree the situation felt tense, confrontational, potentially dangerous?

A: It was a loud argument. I went back to working on my car.

topic: A neighbor is questioned about noise complaints and a confrontation they witnessed
text:
Q: State your name, please.

A: David Okonkwo.

Q: Mr. Okonkwo, where do you reside?

A: 1445 Birchwood Lane, Unit C.

Q: How long have you lived there?

A: About two years.

Q: Are you familiar with the plaintiff in this matter, Sandra Holloway?

A: She lives in Unit A. Same building.

Q: And the defendant, Marcus Webb?

A: Unit B. He's between us.

Q: I'd like to ask you about the incident on November 19th of last year. Were you home that evening?

A: Yes.

Q: Did you hear or observe any kind of disturbance?

A: There was an argument in the hallway. Loud enough that I opened my door to see what was going on.

Q: Tell me what you observed when you opened your door.

A: Ms. Holloway and Mr. Webb were standing in the hallway between their units. Ms. Holloway was holding her phone up like she was recording. Mr. Webb had his arms crossed.

Q: Could you hear what they were saying?

A: Ms. Holloway was telling him she'd documented every noise violation—her words—for the past six months. She said she had recordings, time stamps, everything.

Q: What was Mr. Webb's response?

A: He said—and this is close to verbatim because it stuck with me—he said, "You've made my life hell with these complaints, and now you want to record me? You're unbelievable."

Q: Did his tone seem threatening to you?

A: His tone seemed like someone who was frustrated and fed up. I didn't feel like violence was about to happen, if that's what you're asking.

Q: What happened next?

A: Ms. Holloway said she was calling the police. Mr. Webb laughed—not a mean laugh, more like an exhausted laugh—and said, "Of course you are." Then he went back into his unit.

Q: Did he slam the door?

A: He closed it harder than normal. I wouldn't call it a slam.

Q: Did you observe any physical contact between the parties?

A: No. They stayed about four feet apart the whole time. I was paying attention to that specifically because I wasn't sure if I'd need to intervene.

Q: Prior to November 19th, had you witnessed other disputes between these neighbors?

A: I'd heard arguments through the walls maybe three or four times. And Ms. Holloway had come to my door twice asking if I'd sign something about the noise.

Q: Did you sign it?

A: No. I told her I work night shifts, so I'm not usually home when she said the noise was happening. I couldn't verify what I hadn't heard myself.

topic: A neighbor is questioned about noise complaints and a confrontation they witnessed
text:
Q: Please state your full name.

A: Teresa Marie Volkov.

Q: Ms. Volkov, you submitted a written statement to police on June 8th regarding an incident between your neighbors. Do you recall that?

A: I do.

Q: I'd like to explore some details from that statement. You wrote that you heard—I'm quoting here—"screaming and sounds of a struggle" coming from the Brennan residence. Is that accurate?

A: That's what I wrote, yes. But I should clarify something.

Q: Go ahead.

A: When I wrote "struggle," I meant I heard loud noises—banging, thumping. I couldn't actually see what was happening. So I don't know if it was a physical struggle or someone slamming cabinets or what. I was being, maybe, dramatic in my word choice because I was shaken up.

Q: I appreciate that clarification. So you heard loud voices and loud noises, but you didn't visually witness any physical altercation?

A: That's right. I was inside my house the whole time. I could hear through the walls—they're thin, these townhouses—but I didn't see anything.

Q: The voices you heard—could you identify who was speaking?

A: I recognized Mrs. Brennan's voice. I'm less sure about the other voice. I assumed it was her husband, Mr. Brennan, because who else would be there? But I couldn't swear to it under oath. Which, I guess I am under oath. So no, I can't positively identify the second voice.

Q: Did you hear any specific words or phrases?

A: Mrs. Brennan said "get out" at least twice. I heard that clearly. The other person's words were more muffled. Lower voice, couldn't make out specifics.

Q: How long did this disturbance last?

A: Ten minutes? Fifteen? It felt longer in the moment, but probably somewhere in that range.

Q: Did you take any action?

A: I called my husband first—he was at work—because I didn't know if I was overreacting. He said to call the non-emergency police line if I was worried. So I did that. Then maybe twenty minutes later, I saw a police car pull up, and I went back to what I was doing.

Q: Did you speak with police that night?

A: No. They went to the Brennan house. I watched from my window for a bit, but it seemed like everything calmed down, so I didn't insert myself into the situation.

Q: Looking back, is there anything in your written statement you'd want to change or clarify beyond what you've already told me?

A: Just what I said—the word "struggle" was probably too strong. I heard conflict. I heard distress in Mrs. Brennan's voice. But I can't tell you exactly what happened in that house. I reported what I heard, and I tried to be a responsible neighbor. That's all.

topic: A neighbor is questioned about noise complaints and a confrontation they witnessed
text:
Q: Good morning. Please state your name.

A: Raymond Price.

Q: Mr. Price, you live at 29 Sycamore Court?

A: That's right. Corner lot. I can see basically the whole cul-de-sac from my front porch—which, let me tell you, has given me a front-row seat to more drama than I ever wanted!

Q: Let's talk about the ongoing issues between the Delgados and Mr. Harriman. When did you first become aware of problems between them?

A: Oh, it started almost the minute Mr. Harriman moved in—so that would be, what, spring of 2022? He's got this workshop in his garage, runs power tools at all hours. The Delgados have a baby. You can imagine how well that went over!

Q: Were you present for any direct confrontations?

A: Multiple! But the big one was July 4th weekend. That's the one you're asking about, right?

Q: Let's discuss that incident.

A: Okay, so it's the Saturday before the 4th, maybe 9 PM, and Mr. Harriman decides to test his table saw—on a holiday weekend! Carlos Delgado goes over there and I'm thinking, "Here we go."

Q: Where were you at this time?

A: On my porch with a beer. Perfect vantage point. My wife came out too because she heard the shouting start.

Q: Describe the shouting.

A: Carlos was gesturing toward the Harriman garage, saying something about the baby, about sleep schedules. Mr. Harriman—and this is the part that got me—Mr. Harriman pulls out his phone and starts recording Carlos. Just holds it up right in his face!

Q: What was Mr. Delgado's reaction?

A: He didn't like it! He said something like, "Are you kidding me right now?" and Mr. Harriman goes, "I'm documenting your harassment." Harassment! The man runs power tools at 9 PM and he's claiming harassment!

Q: Did the confrontation become physical?

A: Carlos knocked the phone out of Mr. Harriman's hand. Swatted it, really. And then Mr. Harriman—you're not going to believe this—Mr. Harriman yells, "Assault! That's assault!" And he picks up his phone and calls 911 right there in the driveway.

Q: What did Mr. Delgado do?

A: He threw his hands up like, "I'm done," and walked back home. Maria—Mrs. Delgado—was standing on their porch holding the baby the whole time. She looked exhausted.

Q: Did police respond?

A: They did. Took about twenty minutes. And here's the thing that really gets me—when the officers showed up, Mr. Harriman was back in his garage, sawing away again! Like nothing happened! The officer had to yell over the noise to talk to him.

Q: Did you provide a statement to police that night?

A: They didn't ask me, which I thought was a missed opportunity frankly. I had the whole picture. But I'm happy to be here now, giving you everything I've got.

topic: A driver is deposed about the events leading up to a multi-vehicle collision
text:
Q: Mr. Hendricks, I want to direct your attention to the moments just before the collision. You were traveling northbound on Route 9, correct?

A: Yes.

Q: And what was your speed at that time?

A: I don't—I was going the speed limit. Around the speed limit.

Q: Around the speed limit. What is the speed limit on that stretch of Route 9?

A: Forty-five, I believe. Forty-five miles per hour.

Q: You believe, or you know?

A: I know it's forty-five. I drive that road every day.

Q: So you were traveling at forty-five miles per hour?

A: I said around the speed limit. Maybe forty-three, forty-seven. I wasn't staring at my speedometer. I was watching the road.

Q: Were you watching the road when the Honda Civic entered the intersection?

A: I—yes. Yes, I was.

Q: Then you saw it enter?

A: I saw it, but it happened fast. Very fast. You have to understand, it just—it came out of nowhere, from my perspective.

Q: From your perspective. But you just testified you were watching the road.

A: I was watching the road. That doesn't mean I can see through buildings. There's a strip mall on that corner. You can't see the cross street until you're practically on top of it.

Q: Mr. Hendricks, I'm not asking about the strip mall. I'm asking what you saw.

A: And I'm trying to explain it to you.

topic: A driver is deposed about the events leading up to a multi-vehicle collision
text:
Q: Ms. Okonkwo, let's be very precise here. You testified that you checked your mirrors before changing lanes. Which mirrors?

A: The rearview mirror. And the side mirror.

Q: Which side mirror?

A: The left side mirror. Because I was merging left.

Q: Fine. And after checking those mirrors, what did you do?

A: I signaled and began to merge.

Q: How long did you signal before you began to merge?

A: I don't know exactly. A few seconds.

Q: A few seconds. One? Two? Five?

A: I don't—maybe three seconds? I don't count.

Q: You don't count. So you don't actually know whether you signaled for a sufficient amount of time before merging, do you?

A: I signaled. I checked my mirrors. I did everything I was supposed to do.

Q: That wasn't my question. My question was whether you know—with certainty—how long you signaled.

A: No. I do not know with certainty how many seconds passed. But I know I signaled. I know I looked. And I know the other car was not there when I looked, and then it was, and then everything happened very fast.

Q: When you say "everything happened very fast"—

A: I mean the collision. The collision happened.

Q: You're saying the other vehicle appeared out of nowhere?

A: I'm saying it wasn't in my mirror when I checked, and then it was beside me. That's what I'm saying. I can only tell you what I saw.

topic: A driver is deposed about the events leading up to a multi-vehicle collision
text:
Q: You were on your cell phone at the time of the accident, weren't you?

A: No.

Q: No? Mr. Castellan, I'm going to show you what's been marked as Exhibit 14. Do you recognize this document?

A: It looks like phone records.

Q: Your phone records, correct?

A: If you say so.

Q: I'm asking you.

A: I haven't reviewed them in detail.

Q: Then let me help you. There's a call logged at 4:47 p.m. The accident occurred at 4:48 p.m. That's your phone number at the top of the page, isn't it?

A: Yes.

Q: So there was a call on your phone one minute before the collision. Who were you talking to?

A: I don't remember.

Q: You don't remember who you were speaking with one minute before a collision that sent two people to the hospital?

A: I make a lot of calls for work. I don't—I don't keep track of every single one.

Q: Were you holding the phone to your ear?

A: No. No. I use Bluetooth. Hands-free. It's all hands-free.

Q: So you were on a call, but your hands were on the wheel.

A: My hands were on the wheel. I was paying attention to the road. The call doesn't—it's not relevant. I wasn't distracted.

topic: A driver is deposed about the events leading up to a multi-vehicle collision
text:
Q: I want to ask you about the weather that evening.

A: Okay.

Q: It was raining, wasn't it?

A: It was. Light rain.

Q: Light rain. How would you characterize visibility?

A: Fine. Visibility was fine. I had my headlights on, my wipers were going.

Q: What speed were your wipers set to?

A: I don't understand the question.

Q: Intermittent? Low? High?

A: I think low. Maybe intermittent. I don't remember which setting exactly.

Q: You don't remember.

A: It was raining lightly. I didn't need them going full speed. Is that—I'm sorry, is this really important?

Q: I'll ask the questions, Ms. Tran. You had your wipers on a low or intermittent setting. Did you reduce your speed because of the rain?

A: I was driving appropriately for the conditions.

Q: That's not what I asked. Did you reduce your speed from what you would normally drive in dry conditions?

A: I—probably. Yes. Somewhat.

Q: Somewhat. Five miles per hour? Ten?

A: I don't have a number for you. I'm sorry. I just drove the way I normally drive when it's wet out. More carefully.

Q: More carefully. But you still rear-ended the vehicle in front of you.

A: Because they stopped. They stopped suddenly, with no warning, in the middle of the road.

topic: A driver is deposed about the events leading up to a multi-vehicle collision
text:
Q: Mr. Bashir, you've stated that you saw the pickup truck run the red light.

A: That's correct.

Q: And you're certain the light was red?

A: Yes. Completely certain.

Q: How long had it been red when the truck entered the intersection?

A: I couldn't say exactly. But it was red. It had been red.

Q: Had been red for how long? A second? Ten seconds?

A: I wasn't counting. I was waiting to make my turn. The light was red for the cross traffic. That's all I know for certain. That's the relevant fact.

Q: I'll decide what's relevant. Did you see the light change from yellow to red?

A: I don't specifically recall seeing it change. I recall that it was red when the truck came through.

Q: So it's possible the light had just turned red?

A: Possible, I suppose, but—

Q: Yes or no, Mr. Bashir.

A: Don't—please don't interrupt me. I'm trying to answer your question accurately.

Q: Then answer it. Is it possible the light had just turned red when the truck entered the intersection?

A: In the strictest sense, yes. It's possible. But the truck did not slow down. It did not attempt to stop. It went through at full speed. That's what I saw.

Q: What you saw. From what position?

A: From—I was stopped at the light. First in line, left turn lane.

Q: And your attention was on the truck?

A: My attention was on the intersection. Because I was about to enter it.

topic: A tenant is questioned about property damage they reported to their landlord
text:
Q: Could you please state your name and current address for the record?

A: Yes. My name is David Okonkwo, and I reside at 2847 Maple Ridge Drive, Apartment 4B.

Q: And how long have you lived at that address, Mr. Okonkwo?

A: It will be three years in February. I moved in February 2022.

Q: I'd like to direct your attention to a maintenance request you submitted on September 14th of this year. Do you recall that request?

A: I do.

Q: In your own words, could you describe what prompted you to submit that request?

A: Certainly. I noticed water staining on the ceiling in my bedroom, in the northeast corner. The stain was roughly circular, about eight inches in diameter when I first observed it. I documented it with photographs and submitted the request through the tenant portal that same evening.

Q: When you say you documented it with photographs, how many photographs did you take?

A: Three initially. I took one wide shot showing the location relative to the window, and two closer images showing the discoloration and texture of the stain.

Q: Did you observe any active water intrusion at that time?

A: No, not at that time. The stain appeared to be from a prior event. The ceiling was dry to the touch when I checked.

Q: How did you check whether the ceiling was dry?

A: I stood on a step stool and pressed my palm against the area for several seconds. It felt cool but not damp.

Q: What happened after you submitted the maintenance request?

A: I received an automated confirmation within a few minutes, and then a follow-up call from the property manager two days later, on September 16th.

Q: Did anyone from the property management company inspect the ceiling?

A: Yes. A maintenance technician visited on September 18th. He examined the area and said he would report his findings to management.

topic: A tenant is questioned about property damage they reported to their landlord
text:
Q: Ms. Brennan, you reported a broken window to your landlord on March 3rd. Is that correct?

A: That's correct.

Q: Which window was broken?

A: The window in my living room, the one facing the courtyard.

Q: Can you describe the damage?

A: There was a crack running diagonally across the lower pane. It started near the bottom left corner and extended up toward the center.

Q: Do you know what caused the crack?

A: I don't know for certain.

Q: Do you have any belief or suspicion about what caused it?

A: I'd rather not speculate.

Q: Fair enough. When did you first notice the crack?

A: The morning of March 3rd, when I opened the blinds.

Q: Had you noticed anything unusual the night before?

A: No.

Q: No sounds, no disturbances?

A: Nothing that I recall.

Q: How did you report the damage to your landlord?

A: I called the main office and spoke with someone at the front desk. Then I followed up with an email that included a photograph.

Q: Did you receive a response to that email?

A: I did. Ms. Patterson replied the same afternoon and said someone would be out to assess it.

Q: And did someone come to assess it?

A: Yes, two days later. A gentleman from a glass company came and took measurements.

topic: A tenant is questioned about property damage they reported to their landlord
text:
Q: Let's talk about the incident you reported on July 22nd. You stated there was damage to your bathroom floor?

A: That's right.

Q: What kind of damage?

A: The vinyl flooring had begun to lift and bubble near the base of the toilet.

Q: Had you noticed any problems with the flooring before July 22nd?

A: I'd noticed a small area that seemed slightly raised maybe a week earlier. It wasn't significant enough to report at that point.

Q: Why not?

A: Because I wasn't sure if it was actually a problem or just a minor imperfection. I wanted to monitor it before making a formal complaint.

Q: That seems like a reasonable approach. So what changed between that initial observation and July 22nd?

A: The raised area expanded noticeably, and I could feel moisture underneath when I pressed on it.

Q: You could feel moisture through the vinyl?

A: When I pressed down on the bubbled section, I could feel it give in a way that suggested liquid beneath the surface. And there was a slight dampness at the edge where the vinyl had started to separate from the subfloor.

Q: Did you investigate further to determine where the moisture was coming from?

A: I checked the visible areas around the toilet base and the supply line. I didn't see any obvious leaks, but I'm not a plumber.

Q: Of course. Did you communicate that observation to your landlord?

A: Yes. I included it in my written report.

Q: How did your landlord respond?

A: They sent a plumber within forty-eight hours, which I appreciated.

topic: A tenant is questioned about property damage they reported to their landlord
text:
Q: Mr. Yates, I want to ask you about a report you made concerning your kitchen appliances. This would have been sometime in November?

A: November 9th.

Q: Thank you. What appliance was involved?

A: The refrigerator.

Q: What was wrong with it?

A: It stopped maintaining temperature. The freezer section was barely cold, and items in the refrigerator compartment were spoiling.

Q: When did you first notice the temperature issue?

A: November 8th, in the evening. I noticed some items felt warmer than they should.

Q: Did you take any steps to verify there was actually a malfunction?

A: I placed a thermometer inside. The refrigerator section was reading around 52 degrees, and the freezer was at 28.

Q: Is it possible you had inadvertently adjusted the temperature settings?

A: I checked that. The settings were where I always keep them.

Q: And where is that?

A: Middle position for the refrigerator, one notch above middle for the freezer.

Q: What did you do after confirming the temperature readings?

A: I submitted a maintenance request online and also called the emergency line, since food safety was a concern.

Q: Did anyone respond to the emergency line?

A: Yes. The on-call maintenance person called me back within an hour. He couldn't come out that night but arranged for a technician the next morning.

Q: Were you satisfied with that response time?

A: Given the circumstances, yes. They handled it appropriately.

topic: A tenant is questioned about property damage they reported to their landlord
text:
Q: You submitted a written complaint about your heating system last January. Do you remember the specific date?

A: January 15th.

Q: What was the nature of the complaint?

A: The heating unit in my apartment wasn't producing warm air. It would run, but the air coming from the vents was room temperature at best.

Q: How cold was it in your apartment?

A: I measured it at 58 degrees that morning.

Q: 58 degrees. And the outdoor temperature?

A: I believe it was in the low twenties.

Q: That must have been uncomfortable.

A: It was certainly not ideal.

Q: Had you experienced any heating issues prior to January 15th?

A: There had been some inconsistency. Some days the unit seemed to work harder than others to maintain temperature. But January 15th was the first time it failed to produce heat entirely.

Q: Did you report those earlier inconsistencies?

A: I did not.

Q: Why not?

A: Because the apartment remained at an acceptable temperature. The unit seemed to compensate on its own. I only reported when it became an actual problem.

Q: Walk me through how you reported the issue on January 15th.

A: I called the property management office when they opened at nine. I explained the situation, and they said they would dispatch someone that day.

Q: Did they?

A: They did. A technician arrived around two in the afternoon, diagnosed a faulty igniter, and replaced it.

Q: And that resolved the issue?

A: It did. The system has functioned normally since then.

topic: A witness is questioned about a workplace injury they observed but did not report
text:
Q: Mr. Hernandez, you were working the floor on October 14th, correct?

A: Yes.

Q: And at approximately 2:15 p.m., you witnessed an incident involving Marcus Thompson?

A: I saw something happen, yes.

Q: Can you describe what you saw?

A: He was... Marcus was working the press. The one near the back. And his hand got caught. The guard wasn't—it wasn't where it should have been.

Q: What did you do when you saw this happen?

A: I went over to him.

Q: And then?

A: I helped him. I helped him get his hand free.

Q: Did you call for a supervisor?

A: No.

Q: Did you file an incident report?

A: No. I didn't.

Q: Why not, Mr. Hernandez?

A: Marcus asked me not to. He was worried about... he'd only been there four months. He was still in his probation period. He said he couldn't lose this job.

Q: So you honored that request?

A: I did what he asked me to do.

Q: And now Mr. Thompson has permanent nerve damage in three fingers. Were you aware of that?

A: ...Yes. I know.

Q: Is there anything you'd like to add to your answer about why you didn't report it?

A: I think about it. Every day I think about whether I did the right thing. That's what I'd like to add.

topic: A witness is questioned about a workplace injury they observed but did not report
text:
Q: Ms. Patterson, I want to take this slowly because I understand you worked closely with the injured party.

A: Linda and I shared a station for two years.

Q: I appreciate that. And I appreciate you being here today.

A: I don't know that I have much to offer.

Q: Let's just take it one step at a time. On the morning of March 3rd, where were you positioned in the warehouse?

A: Same place I always was. Station 7, next to Linda.

Q: And you observed her injury occur?

A: I was standing right there. Not three feet away.

Q: What did you see?

A: The shelving unit. The one they'd been saying for months was unstable. It came down on her.

Q: "They'd been saying for months"—who is "they"?

A: All of us. Everyone on the floor. We'd written it up twice.

Q: But after the incident itself, you didn't file a report?

A: No.

Q: Help me understand that.

A: When the ambulance came, they told us to go back to work. They said management would handle the paperwork. I thought... I assumed someone was taking care of it.

Q: No one asked you to provide a statement?

A: No. No one asked me anything. Not until now.

Q: Ms. Patterson, if someone had asked you then what you'd observed—

A: I would have told them everything. I would have told them we knew that shelf was going to fall on somebody eventually.

Q: I'm sorry. I know this is difficult.

A: It shouldn't have been Linda. That's all.

topic: A witness is questioned about a workplace injury they observed but did not report
text:
Q: You testified earlier that you saw Mr. Okonkwo slip on the wet floor.

A: That's right.

Q: And you saw him fall?

A: Yes.

Q: And you saw him struggle to get up?

A: I saw all of it, counselor. I was there.

Q: Then why is your name absent from every single document related to this incident?

A: Because I didn't put it there.

Q: You didn't think to come forward?

A: I didn't think it was my place.

Q: A man falls, injures his back, and it's not your place to say you witnessed it?

A: There were other people around. Plenty of people saw what happened.

Q: But you're the one who was standing closest to him when he fell, isn't that true?

A: Maybe I was.

Q: Not maybe. You were within arm's reach.

A: Then yes. Fine. I was close.

Q: Did you help him up?

A: ...He told me not to touch him. He said he couldn't feel his legs right.

Q: He couldn't feel his legs.

A: That's what he said.

Q: And you walked away?

A: I went to get the shift supervisor. And when I came back, they were already putting him on a stretcher.

Q: But you never filed a report.

A: The supervisor said he had it. He said he'd take care of everything.

Q: And you believed him?

A: I wanted to believe him. I wanted it to be someone else's responsibility.

topic: A witness is questioned about a workplace injury they observed but did not report
text:
Q: Let me direct your attention to the afternoon of July 19th.

A: Okay.

Q: You were present in the kitchen at approximately 4:30 p.m.?

A: Yes.

Q: And you observed an incident involving hot oil?

A: I observed Destinee get burned, if that's what you're asking.

Q: Tell me what you saw.

A: The fryer. The oil. It splashed up when she was draining it. Got her on the arm, part of her neck.

Q: What was your reaction?

A: I ran cold water. I got towels. I stayed with her until the manager came.

Q: The manager came. And then?

A: And then he took her to the back office.

Q: Did you accompany them?

A: No. I was told to stay on the line.

Q: Were you asked to provide any written account of what you'd witnessed?

A: No.

Q: Did you volunteer one?

A: No. I figured... the manager saw how bad it was. I figured they'd do right by her.

Q: Did they?

A: Objection, calls for speculation.

Q: I'll rephrase. Are you aware of what happened to Destinee after that day?

A: She never came back. That's what I'm aware of. Eighteen years old, and she never came back to work.

Q: Do you know why?

A: I heard things. I heard her burns got infected. I heard she didn't have insurance because they kept her under thirty hours.

Q: And you never made any formal statement about what you saw?

A: Nobody asked. And I thought—I kept thinking someone would ask. Someone would want to know. But nobody ever did.

topic: A witness is questioned about a workplace injury they observed but did not report
text:
Q: Mr. Chen, you've been with the company for eleven years, is that correct?

A: Eleven years in August.

Q: And in that time, you've seen your share of workplace incidents?

A: More than my share.

Q: But you've never filed a witness report. Not once in eleven years.

A: That's not—that's not accurate. I filled out a report in 2019 when—

Q: Let me rephrase. You never filed a report regarding the incident involving Daniel Reeves on September 8th.

A: No.

Q: Daniel Reeves, who worked alongside you for six years?

A: I know who Daniel is.

Q: Who was struck by a forklift while you watched?

A: I didn't watch. I didn't just stand there and watch, that's not—

Q: What did you do?

A: I yelled at him to move. I was yelling before it happened, I could see it coming, and I yelled—

Q: But you didn't file a report.

A: No.

Q: Why not?

A: Because I couldn't. I couldn't sit in an office and write down the sound it made when—

Q: Mr. Chen—

A: You want to know why? Because I go home at night and I see it. I see him looking up at me after he went down and I had to tell him not to move, don't try to move, Danny, just stay still—

Q: We can take a break if you need one.

A: I don't need a break. I need you to understand that not filing a piece of paper doesn't mean I forgot. It doesn't mean I don't remember every second of it.

Q: I understand.

A: Do you?

topic: A daycare worker is deposed about an injury a child sustained while in their care
text:
Q: Ms. Hernandez, let's go back to the morning of March 14th. What time did you first see Olivia Chen that day?

A: I already answered this in my written statement. It was around 7:45 when her mother dropped her off.

Q: I'm asking you now, under oath. Was it 7:45 exactly?

A: I didn't have a stopwatch running. It was around that time. Between 7:40 and 7:50.

Q: And between 7:45 and the time of the incident, how many times did you personally check on Olivia?

A: I was with the whole group. I was always checking on all of them.

Q: That's not what I asked. How many times did you specifically observe Olivia?

A: I don't know. I don't count. That's not how this works. You have fifteen children, you're watching all of them, you're not tallying each one individually.

Q: So your testimony is you have no idea whether you looked at Olivia once, twice, ten times?

A: My testimony is that I was doing my job, which is supervising the room, which includes Olivia.

Q: Were you supervising the room when she fell from the play structure?

A: I was in the room, yes.

Q: Were you watching the play structure?

A: I was watching the room.

Q: Ms. Hernandez, it's a yes or no question. Were your eyes on the play structure when Olivia fell?

A: No. They weren't. Because I have two eyes and fifteen children, and I cannot physically watch everything at once. Is there anything else you'd like me to explain about basic geometry?

Q: Let's move on.

A: Fine.

---

topic: A daycare worker is deposed about an injury a child sustained while in their care
text:
Q: Mr. Patterson, can you describe the layout of the outdoor play area?

A: Sure. It's a fenced rectangle, maybe forty by sixty feet. There's a sandbox on the north side, swings on the south, and a climbing structure in the middle.

Q: What's the surface material under the climbing structure?

A: Rubber mulch. The soft kind, specifically for playgrounds.

Q: How deep is that mulch?

A: I believe it's supposed to be about six inches. Maintenance handles that.

Q: You believe? Do you know?

A: I'm not the one who measures it. I've been told it's six inches. I assume that's accurate.

Q: Did you ever measure it yourself?

A: No.

Q: Did you ever notice whether it seemed thin in certain areas? Packed down?

A: I'm a childcare provider. I watch children. I'm not a grounds inspector.

Q: I'll rephrase. In your time working at the facility, did you ever observe the mulch looking compressed or insufficient in any area?

A: Not that I specifically recall, no.

Q: When the Jameson boy fell, where exactly did he land?

A: At the base of the climbing structure. Near the ladder.

Q: And after he landed, did you examine the mulch in that spot?

A: I was focused on the child. He was screaming. I picked him up and brought him inside.

Q: So you didn't look at the ground at all?

A: I looked at the injured four-year-old.

---

topic: A daycare worker is deposed about an injury a child sustained while in their care
text:
Q: State your name for the record.

A: Denise Crawford.

Q: How long have you worked at Little Sprouts Daycare?

A: Seven years.

Q: In those seven years, how many injuries have you personally witnessed?

A: I don't have an exact number.

Q: Estimate.

A: Maybe... fifteen? Twenty? Kids fall. They bump heads. It happens.

Q: And prior to September 9th, had any child in your care required hospitalization?

A: No.

Q: So September 9th was the first time?

A: Yes.

Q: Tell me what happened that day. What did you see?

A: I've gone over this so many times.

Q: I need you to go over it again.

A: Fine. Aiden was playing with blocks. Another child, Marcus, wanted a block Aiden had. They struggled. Aiden fell backward and hit his head on the corner of the bookshelf.

Q: How far were you from them when this happened?

A: Maybe eight feet.

Q: And you didn't intervene before Aiden fell?

A: It happened in two seconds. Maybe less.

Q: You were eight feet away and watching?

A: I was eight feet away. I was also monitoring four other children in my immediate area. When I saw Marcus grab for the block, I started moving toward them. I didn't get there fast enough.

Q: Next question. Had Marcus shown aggressive behavior before that day?

A: He's three. They all grab things.

---

topic: A daycare worker is deposed about an injury a child sustained while in their care
text:
Q: Let's talk about the incident report you filed. I'm showing you what's been marked as Exhibit 7. Do you recognize this document?

A: Yes.

Q: You prepared this?

A: Yes.

Q: The time stamp says 2:47 PM. The incident occurred when?

A: Around 2:15.

Q: So roughly thirty minutes passed before you documented what happened?

A: I was dealing with the situation. Comforting Sophie. Calling her parents. Getting ice.

Q: But you found time to write this report within thirty minutes?

A: As soon as things were under control, yes.

Q: I notice this report is only four sentences long.

A: It covers what happened.

Q: Does it? Let me read it back to you. "Sophie M. fell while running in the classroom and struck her chin on a table. Ice was applied. Parents were notified. No visible bleeding."

A: That's accurate.

Q: Why was Sophie running in the classroom?

A: I don't know. Kids run.

Q: Were you watching her when she started running?

A: I was in the room.

Q: That's not—

A: I was supervising twelve children. I cannot tell you why any individual child decides to start running at any given moment.

Q: Did you tell her to stop?

A: I started to. Then she fell.

Q: So you saw her running before she fell?

A: For maybe a second, yes.

Q: Why isn't that in the report?

A: Because the report is about what happened to Sophie, not a play-by-play of every second before it.

Q: I'd argue the seconds before are highly relevant.

A: Then you can argue that.

---

topic: A daycare worker is deposed about an injury a child sustained while in their care
text:
Q: Ms. Okonkwo, were you the only staff member in Room 3 at the time of the incident?

A: Yes.

Q: How many children were in Room 3?

A: Eleven.

Q: Is that within ratio requirements?

A: Yes. The ratio for that age group is one to twelve.

Q: So you were at near-maximum capacity, alone?

A: I was within the legal ratio. That's what I'm required to maintain.

Q: I didn't ask about legal requirements. I asked if you were alone with eleven children.

A: Yes. I was. Which is permitted.

Q: Had you requested additional support that day?

A: No.

Q: Why not?

A: Because I didn't need it. Eleven children is manageable.

Q: Even during nap time transitions?

A: Yes.

Q: Describe what happens during a nap time transition.

A: Children finish lunch, wash hands, use the bathroom, get their mats, lie down.

Q: And you supervise all of that simultaneously? Alone?

A: Yes.

Q: Where was Emma when she was injured?

A: In the bathroom area.

Q: Were you in the bathroom area?

A: No, I was helping another child with his mat.

Q: So Emma was unsupervised in the bathroom?

A: The bathroom is four feet from where I was standing. The door was open. I could hear everything.

Q: But you couldn't see her.

A: Not at that exact second, no.

Q: How long was she out of your sight?

A: Seconds. Ten, maybe fifteen seconds.

Q: That's when she slipped?

A: Yes.

Q: Do you think eleven children is still manageable, Ms. Okonkwo?

A: I'm not going to answer that the way you want me to. I followed every protocol. The floor was wet because a child had just washed her hands. It was an accident.

topic: A former employee is deposed about discriminatory remarks made by a supervisor
text:
Q: Ms. Thornton, I'd like to ask you about your time working under David Reeves in the accounting department. How long did you work directly with him?

A: About two and a half years. From when I started in March 2021 until I transferred out in September 2023.

Q: And during that time, did you ever hear Mr. Reeves make comments about other employees' national origins?

A: I did. Yes.

Q: Can you describe one of those occasions for me?

A: There was a morning meeting—I think it was maybe June or July of 2022. Priya Sharma had just presented her quarterly projections, and after she left the room, David said something about how he couldn't understand why we kept hiring people who "barely speak English." Priya was born in Ohio. Her English is perfect. She just... she has a slight accent from her parents, I think.

Q: Take your time if you need it. What happened after Mr. Reeves made that comment?

A: A few people laughed. Nervously, I think. I didn't say anything. I wish I had.

Q: I understand. Were there other employees present who heard this?

A: Yes. Mark Donnelly, Susan Chen, and I believe Thomas Wright. Maybe others. It was a full team meeting before Priya stepped out.

Q: And how did this comment affect your view of the workplace?

A: I started noticing things more after that. Who got praised, who got interrupted. I'm not sure if things changed or if I just finally saw what was already there.

Q: Did you ever speak with Priya about what Mr. Reeves said?

A: No. I've thought about that a lot. I didn't want to hurt her, but maybe she deserved to know. I don't know what the right thing was.

Q: You mentioned you transferred out of the department. Was this incident part of that decision?

A: Part of it. Not all of it. But I didn't want to be someone who just sat there anymore.

Q: Is there anything else about that meeting you think is important for us to understand?

A: Just that Priya worked harder than anyone on that team. She deserved better. We all knew it was wrong, and none of us said a word.

topic: A former employee is deposed about discriminatory remarks made by a supervisor
text:
Q: Mr. Franklin, you've stated you witnessed discriminatory remarks by your supervisor, Carolyn Meyers. I want to understand the context. What was your relationship with Ms. Meyers like generally?

A: Professional. Cordial, I suppose. She wasn't someone I'd call warm, but she wasn't hostile to me personally.

Q: Not hostile to you personally. Was she hostile to others?

A: To some people, yes.

Q: Who specifically?

A: Darnell Washington. James Okonkwo. A few others.

Q: What did those individuals have in common?

A: They were Black. I'm stating what I observed.

Q: I'm not challenging you. I'm just trying to understand what you saw. Can you describe a specific incident involving Mr. Washington?

A: There was a day—I remember because it was right before Thanksgiving 2022—when Darnell suggested a process change in our team huddle. Carolyn cut him off and said, "Let's hear from someone who understands how things work here." Darnell had been with the company two years longer than her.

Q: How did Mr. Washington respond?

A: He didn't. He just went quiet. I've never seen someone shrink like that before. It's hard to describe.

Q: You don't have to rush. Did anyone else react?

A: A few people exchanged looks. Nobody spoke up. I didn't speak up.

Q: What was going through your mind at that moment?

A: That I was a coward. That Darnell was my friend and I sat there like everyone else.

Q: Did you ever discuss this incident with Mr. Washington afterward?

A: About a week later. I told him I was sorry I didn't say anything. He said, "I know. It's okay." But I could tell it wasn't.

Q: When you say you could tell—what do you mean?

A: He stopped eating lunch with the group after that. He'd take his food to his car. You could see something in him had just... closed off.

Q: Thank you, Mr. Franklin. I know this isn't easy to talk about.

A: It shouldn't be easy. That's the point, isn't it?

topic: A former employee is deposed about discriminatory remarks made by a supervisor
text:
Q: Dr. Navarro, you've indicated you heard remarks from Dr. Patterson that concerned you. Before we discuss those, I want to make sure—are you comfortable proceeding?

A: Yes. I agreed to be here. I want to help if I can.

Q: I appreciate that. Let's start with the October 2023 staff meeting. What do you remember?

A: Dr. Patterson was discussing candidates for the fellowship position. When Dr. Yusuf's application came up, he made a comment about whether someone "from that part of the world" would fit the department culture.

Q: Those were his exact words—"from that part of the world"?

A: Yes. I wrote it down afterward because I wanted to remember it precisely.

Q: Why did you feel the need to document it?

A: Because I knew no one would believe it otherwise. These things get softened in memory. People convince themselves they misheard.

Q: Did anyone respond to Dr. Patterson's comment in the meeting?

A: Dr. Chen said Dr. Yusuf's qualifications were exceptional. Dr. Patterson said qualifications weren't everything.

Q: What did you understand him to mean?

A: I understood him to mean exactly what he said. That being from—wherever he imagined Dr. Yusuf was from—disqualified him despite his credentials.

Q: Was Dr. Yusuf offered the fellowship?

A: No. The position went to a candidate with fewer publications and less clinical experience.

Q: Do you know how Dr. Yusuf learned of the decision?

A: He received a form letter. I know because he showed it to me. He asked if I knew what he'd done wrong.

Q: What did you tell him?

A: I told him he hadn't done anything wrong. I wanted to tell him more, but I didn't know how without making things worse for him.

Q: That must have been a difficult position.

A: It was. He trusted the process. I didn't have the heart to tell him the process had already decided against him before he applied.

topic: A former employee is deposed about discriminatory remarks made by a supervisor
text:
Q: Ms. Fitzgerald, you worked as an executive assistant on the fourteenth floor from 2019 to 2023, correct?

A: Correct.

Q: During that time, did you ever hear Richard Sloane make comments about employees' religious practices?

A: Yes.

Q: Describe what you heard.

A: On multiple occasions, he made remarks about Fatima Al-Hassan taking breaks to pray. He called it "constantly disappearing" and once asked me if I thought she was "actually working or just performing."

Q: What did you say when he asked you that?

A: I said I thought she was one of the most efficient people on the floor. Because she was.

Q: How did he respond?

A: He laughed and said I was "too nice."

Q: Did his comments about Ms. Al-Hassan continue after that exchange?

A: They did. He started CC'ing me on emails questioning her productivity. I think he wanted an ally.

Q: Did you become an ally?

A: No. I started keeping records instead.

Q: What kind of records?

A: Dates, times, what was said, who was present. I have them on a personal drive if you need them.

Q: We may request those. Why did you decide to keep records?

A: Because Fatima was too afraid to. She had a family depending on her job. She couldn't risk being seen as difficult. Someone had to pay attention.

Q: Did Ms. Al-Hassan know you were documenting these incidents?

A: Not at first. I told her eventually, maybe six months before I left. She cried. She said she thought she was imagining things.

Q: What did you say to her?

A: I told her she wasn't imagining anything. I told her she was brave for staying as long as she did.

Q: Was there a reason you ultimately left the company?

A: Several reasons. But watching what happened to Fatima and feeling like I couldn't stop it—that was part of it. I couldn't keep pretending everything was normal.

topic: A former employee is deposed about discriminatory remarks made by a supervisor
text:
Q: Mr. Huang, I want to turn to the April 2022 incident you mentioned in your written statement. You said Carlos Mendez was passed over for promotion. Is that right?

A: That's right.

Q: And you believe this was connected to remarks made by the regional director, Beth Sinclair?

A: I don't believe it. I know it. She said—in front of four of us—that Carlos was "a little too spicy" for client-facing work.

Q: Too spicy.

A: Her word. She laughed when she said it, like it was clever.

Q: Who else heard this comment?

A: Jennifer Walsh, Derek Thompson, and Amy Liu.

Q: Have you spoken with any of them about testifying?

A: I haven't. I don't want to pressure anyone. This is hard enough without feeling obligated.

Q: That's understandable. Let me ask—how did Carlos take the news about the promotion?

A: He didn't know why he was passed over. He thought he'd done something wrong in his interview. He asked me to review his presentation materials.

Q: Did you review them?

A: I did. They were excellent. He'd prepared for weeks.

Q: Did you tell him what Ms. Sinclair had said?

A: Eventually. About two months later, when he was thinking about reapplying. I thought he should know what he was up against.

Q: How did he react?

A: He got very quiet. Then he thanked me. He said at least now he understood.

Q: Did he reapply for the position?

A: No. He left the company three months later. Started his own consulting business.

Q: Do you know if he's doing well?

A: I check in on him sometimes. He's doing better than well, actually. But that's not really the point, is it? He shouldn't have had to leave to succeed.

topic: A nurse is questioned about a patient fall that occurred during her shift
text:
Q: Ms. Delgado, you were the charge nurse on the third floor the night Mr. Patterson fell, correct?

A: I was the charge nurse, yes.

Q: And as charge nurse, you would have been responsible for ensuring adequate staffing levels?

A: I was responsible for a lot of things. Staffing is determined by administration based on census.

Q: But you had the authority to call in additional staff if you felt it was needed?

A: In theory.

Q: In theory. Did you attempt to call in additional staff that night?

A: No.

Q: Why not?

A: Because at the start of the shift, I had no indication we would need additional staff. We were at standard ratios.

Q: Standard ratios. And yet Mr. Patterson fell.

A: Patients fall. It happens even on fully staffed units. I'm not sure what you're suggesting.

Q: I'm asking questions, Ms. Delgado. I'm not suggesting anything. How many patients were assigned to the nurse caring for Mr. Patterson?

A: Six.

Q: Is six patients typical for a night shift on your unit?

A: It's within the range that administration considers acceptable. Whether I personally consider it ideal is a different question, and I don't think that's what you're asking me.

Q: What would you personally consider ideal?

A: Four to five, depending on acuity. But I don't set the budget.

Q: So you were working with staffing levels you yourself would not consider ideal on the night a patient fell and fractured his hip?

A: I was working with the staffing levels I was given. As I do every shift.

---

topic: A nurse is questioned about a patient fall that occurred during her shift
text:
Q: Walk me through the fall risk assessment you conducted on Mr. Patterson when he was admitted.

A: I used the Morse Fall Scale, which is our standard protocol. I assessed his history of falling, secondary diagnoses, use of ambulatory aids, IV access, gait, and mental status.

Q: And what score did you arrive at?

A: Fifty-five.

Q: What does a fifty-five indicate?

A: High fall risk.

Q: High fall risk. And what interventions did you implement based on that score?

A: Bed alarm, yellow socks, yellow wristband, fall risk sign on the door, and I documented the need for assistance with ambulation.
