Q: Did you implement hourly rounding?

A: We do purposeful rounding every two hours on night shift.

Q: Every two hours. Not hourly?

A: That's correct.

Q: For a high fall risk patient?

A: That's our protocol.

Q: I'm not asking about your protocol. I'm asking whether, in your professional judgment, hourly rounding would have been appropriate for this patient.

A: My professional judgment is informed by evidence-based protocols.

Q: That's not an answer to my question.

A: I think it is. You're asking me to second-guess a protocol that's based on research and approved by our clinical leadership.

Q: I'm asking whether you, as a registered nurse with—how many years of experience?

A: Twelve.

Q: Twelve years of experience—whether you believed two-hour rounding was sufficient for Mr. Patterson.

A: I believed I was providing appropriate care according to our standards. That's what I believed then, and that's what I believe now.

---

topic: A nurse is questioned about a patient fall that occurred during her shift
text:
Q: The incident report states that Mr. Patterson was found on the floor at approximately 2:40 a.m. Is that accurate?

A: That's what the report says.

Q: Is it accurate?

A: To the best of my recollection, yes.

Q: When had you last checked on Mr. Patterson before he was found on the floor?

A: I personally checked on him at around 1:15.

Q: So approximately an hour and twenty-five minutes before he was found?

A: If your math is correct, yes.

Q: Was anyone else supposed to check on him during that window?

A: The nursing assistant rounds at the top of each hour.

Q: Did the nursing assistant check on him at 2:00 a.m.?

A: You would have to ask her. I don't stand over my staff and watch them complete every task.

Q: But you reviewed the documentation?

A: I reviewed what was documented after the incident.

Q: And was a 2:00 a.m. check documented?

A: There was no entry at 2:00 a.m.

Q: So either it wasn't done or it wasn't documented.

A: Those are the two possibilities, yes.

Q: Which do you believe occurred?

A: I'm not going to speculate about what someone else did or didn't do. That's not fair to her and it wouldn't be accurate testimony from me.

Q: Fair enough. Let me ask you this—after the incident, did you speak with the nursing assistant about whether she had checked on Mr. Patterson at 2:00 a.m.?

A: I did.

Q: What did she tell you?

A: She said she checked on him but forgot to document it.

Q: And you believed her?

A: I documented what she told me. What I believed isn't in the chart.

---

topic: A nurse is questioned about a patient fall that occurred during her shift
text:
Q: You mentioned the bed alarm was activated. Help me understand how that works.

A: When the patient shifts their weight off the sensor pad, it triggers an alarm at the nursing station and outside the room.

Q: How quickly does the alarm sound once the patient begins to move?

A: It's essentially immediate. Within a second or two of the weight shift.

Q: And the alarm was functioning properly that night?

A: It was tested at the beginning of the shift. It was functioning.

Q: Tested by whom?

A: By me.

Q: You personally tested it?

A: Yes.

Q: How?

A: I pressed on the pad and released to trigger the alarm, then silenced it. Standard check.

Q: Did you document that you tested it?

A: I don't recall if I made a specific note about it. It's part of the routine bed check.

Q: So there may be no documentation that you tested this alarm that you say was functioning properly?

A: I said I don't recall. The documentation would show one way or the other.

Q: I've reviewed the documentation. I don't see any record of an alarm test.

A: Then perhaps I didn't document it. That doesn't mean I didn't do it.

Q: I understand. Now, when the alarm went off at 2:40 a.m., how long did it take for someone to respond?

A: I couldn't say exactly.

Q: The incident report says the patient was found by a nursing assistant who heard the alarm. How long between the alarm and her arrival in the room?

A: I wasn't there. I don't know.

Q: You didn't ask?

A: I asked if she responded promptly. She said she did.

Q: What does "promptly" mean?

A: I suppose that depends on who you ask.

---

topic: A nurse is questioned about a patient fall that occurred during her shift
text:
Q: Ms. Delgado, I want to be very precise about the timeline. You said you checked on Mr. Patterson at 1:15 a.m.

A: Approximately 1:15, yes.

Q: The chart shows a nursing note timed at 1:47 a.m. Can you explain that discrepancy?

A: There's no discrepancy. I assessed him around 1:15 and charted my assessment at 1:47.

Q: Thirty-two minutes later?

A: I don't chart at the bedside. I assess multiple patients, then I chart.

Q: Is that consistent with your training?

A: It's consistent with reality. We don't have computers in every room, and we don't have time to run back to the station after every patient.

Q: So you're asking me to accept that your recollection of a 1:15 assessment is accurate, even though you didn't document it until 1:47?

A: I'm not asking you to accept anything. I'm telling you what happened.

Q: How can you be certain it was 1:15 and not, say, 1:45?

A: Because I remember my workflow that night. I started on the east end of the hall at 1:00 and worked my way down. Mr. Patterson was in room 312. I know when I saw him.

Q: You have a very clear memory of that night.

A: I have a clear memory because a patient was injured on my shift. That tends to sharpen the recollection.

Q: I'm sure it does. Let me ask you about the medication Mr. Patterson received that evening.

A: Go ahead.

Q: He received Ambien at 10:00 p.m., correct?

A: According to the MAR, yes.

Q: Were you aware that Ambien can increase fall risk in elderly patients?

A: Of course I'm aware of that.

Q: Did that affect your care planning for Mr. Patterson?

A: It was already factored into his fall risk score. That's why he was rated high risk. That's why we had interventions in place.

Q: Interventions that didn't prevent the fall.

A: No intervention prevents every fall. If you're looking for someone to tell you we can guarantee a patient won't fall, you're not going to find that person in nursing.

topic: A witness is questioned about events at a party where an assault allegedly occurred
text:
Q: Please state your name for the record.

A: Marcus Webb. That's M-A-R-C-U-S, W-E-B-B. I've actually been looking forward to this because I want to make sure you have the full picture of what happened that night.

Q: You attended the party at 445 Riverside Drive on June 14th?

A: I did, yes. Arrived around 9:15, maybe 9:20. I remember because I'd just gotten off a shift at the restaurant where I work—I'm a line cook at Barolo's downtown—and I texted my girlfriend from the parking lot. I can tell you exactly what that text said if it helps.

Q: That won't be necessary at this time. How many people were present when you arrived?

A: Oh, let me think—I actually counted at one point because the apartment felt packed. When I first walked in, I'd say thirty to thirty-five people. By eleven, it had to be pushing fifty. The living room alone had maybe twenty people dancing. The kitchen had another cluster. And people kept spilling onto the balcony.

Q: Did you know the host?

A: Derek Simmons, absolutely. We played rugby together for three years at State. I know him well. Great guy, actually—always the first to help someone move, you know the type. That's part of why I want to be thorough here, because I know the kind of person he is.

Q: Let's focus on what you observed. Did you see the defendant, Ryan Coates, at the party?

A: I did. Multiple times throughout the night, actually. First time was near the kitchen island—he was mixing drinks, doing this whole bartender routine. Second time was on the balcony around 10:30. Third time—and this is the important one—was in the hallway near the bathroom at approximately 11:45.

Q: What did you observe at 11:45 in the hallway?

A: Okay, so I was walking toward the bathroom, and Ryan was standing very close to this woman—I later learned her name was Jessica—and his hand was on her shoulder. She was pressed against the wall. Her body language was completely closed off. Arms crossed, leaning away from him.

Q: Did you hear what was said?

A: I heard him say something like "come on, just five minutes." And she said "no" at least twice. I remember thinking I should intervene, and I actually took a step toward them, but then Derek appeared from the bedroom and Ryan backed off immediately.

Q: Did you see any physical contact beyond the hand on the shoulder?

A: At that moment, no. But—and I think this is relevant—about twenty minutes later, I saw Ryan grab her wrist near the front door. That's when the shouting started.

Q: We'll get to that. Let's stay with the hallway for now.

A: Of course, absolutely. I just want to make sure you have the complete timeline because I think the pattern matters.

Q: After Derek appeared, where did Mr. Coates go?

A: Back toward the living room. He grabbed a beer from a cooler by the couch—I noticed because he nearly knocked it over—and started talking to a group by the TV like nothing had happened. But he kept looking back toward the hallway. I counted at least four times in the next ten minutes.

topic: A witness is questioned about events at a party where an assault allegedly occurred
text:
Q: You were in the backyard when the altercation occurred, correct?

A: I was in the backyard, yes.

Q: And you had a clear line of sight to the patio door?

A: Partially. There was a group of people between me and the door.

Q: Walk me through exactly what you saw. Take your time. Every detail you can remember.

A: I heard raised voices first. Then I saw two figures through the glass—

Q: Male? Female?

A: Two males. One was larger, wearing something dark. The other was in a light-colored shirt.

Q: Excellent. Now, this is important—what happened next? Paint the picture for me.

A: The larger one—the one in dark clothing—he shoved the other one. Hard. The guy in the light shirt stumbled backward into a table.

Q: Fantastic, you're doing great. Was there a lamp on that table? A glass table?

A: I... I'm not sure about a lamp. It might have been glass.

Q: Think carefully now. Did you hear glass breaking? That distinctive sound?

A: I heard something break, yes. Could have been glass.

Q: Perfect. Now here's the critical moment—after the shove, after the breaking glass, did you see the larger man throw a punch?

A: I think so. His arm moved in a punching motion.

Q: His arm moved in a punching motion. Connected with the other man's face?

A: I couldn't see exactly where it connected. The people in front of me shifted and blocked my view.

Q: But you're confident there was a punching motion. You saw the arm extend with force?

A: Yes.

Q: And this was definitely the larger man, the one in dark clothing, who threw this punch?

A: Yes, that's what I saw.

Q: Outstanding. Now, what did the man in the light shirt do after being struck?

A: He fell. Or dropped, maybe. Went down.

Q: He went down. Completely? To the floor?

A: I think to his knees, at least. Then people rushed over and I couldn't see anymore.

topic: A witness is questioned about events at a party where an assault allegedly occurred
text:
Q: What time did you arrive at the residence?

A: I'm not really sure.

Q: Approximately.

A: Maybe around ten?

Q: Were you intoxicated when you arrived?

A: No.

Q: Had you consumed any alcohol prior to arriving?

A: One beer at home.

Q: Just one?

A: Yes. One beer. I was driving.

Q: Fine. Now I need you to think very carefully about what you're about to tell me. When did you first see the complainant, Jessica Reeves?

A: Um. Maybe an hour after I got there?

Q: So approximately 11 PM?

A: I guess. I wasn't watching the clock.

Q: Where was she when you first noticed her?

A: In the living room.

Q: What was she doing?

A: Talking to people.

Q: Which people?

A: I don't know their names.

Q: Describe them.

A: I don't really remember.

Q: You don't remember anything about the people she was talking to?

A: It was crowded. I just saw her in a group.

Q: Was the defendant in that group?

A: I didn't notice.

Q: You didn't notice whether Ryan Coates—a man you've known for six years, according to prior testimony—was standing three feet from you?

A: I didn't say he was three feet from me.

Q: How far was this group from where you were standing?

A: I don't know. Across the room.

Q: So you could see Ms. Reeves clearly enough to identify her later, but not clearly enough to see who she was speaking with?

A: I recognized her face. I wasn't studying the whole group.

Q: Let's try this another way. At any point that night, did you see the defendant and Ms. Reeves together?

A: I'm not sure.

Q: You're not sure. You were at a party for approximately three hours, in a confined space, and you're not sure whether two people were ever near each other?

A: People moved around a lot.

topic: A witness is questioned about events at a party where an assault allegedly occurred
text:
Q: State your name.

A: Danielle Ortiz.

Q: Ms. Ortiz, you were working as a bartender at the party?

A: I was, yes! Derek hired me through an app—I do private events on weekends—and honestly, I'm so glad I was there because I probably have the best vantage point of anyone you could talk to. I was stationed right at the kitchen island all night, which had a direct sightline to both the living room and the hallway.

Q: How many drinks would you estimate you served?

A: Oh God, I kept a mental tally for my own amusement—somewhere around 180 to 200 individual drinks over four hours. I was slammed but I loved it. Great tippers, that crowd.

Q: Did you serve alcohol to the defendant?

A: Ryan? Multiple times. He was one of my regulars that night—came back probably six or seven times. Started with whiskey sours, switched to straight bourbon around 11. I remember because he made a whole thing about it, said he was "done with the sweet stuff."

Q: Did he appear intoxicated?

A: Toward the end, absolutely. By midnight, he was slurring a little, and he kept leaning on the counter in that way people do when they're trying to look casual but actually need the support.

Q: Did you cut him off?

A: I probably should have. That's actually something I've thought about a lot since this happened. But here's the thing—and I want to be really clear about this because I think it's important for understanding the timeline—

Q: Just answer the question. Did you refuse to serve him at any point?

A: No. I kept serving him.

Q: Did you observe any interaction between the defendant and Jessica Reeves?

A: Oh, yes. Several. The first one was actually really interesting because—

Q: Describe the first interaction.

A: Right, so she came up to the bar around 10:30, ordered a vodka cranberry. Super polite, seemed sober. Ryan sort of materialized next to her—that's the only way I can describe it, he just appeared—and started talking to her. She was giving one-word answers. Classic "I'm not interested" body language. And I'm watching this thinking, "buddy, read the room."

Q: Did they leave the bar area together?

A: No, she left first. Walked toward the balcony. He stayed and ordered another bourbon, then about five minutes later, wandered off in the same direction she'd gone.

Q: Did you see them interact again?

A: Yes! Around 11:15, they were in the hallway—I could see it from my station—and he had her kind of cornered, for lack of a better word. That's when I started getting a bad feeling.

topic: A witness is questioned about events at a party where an assault allegedly occurred
text:
Q: You testified earlier that you saw the defendant push Ms. Reeves.

A: No. That's not what I said.

Q: Let me rephrase. You saw physical contact between them.

A: I saw him grab her arm.

Q: Grab her arm. Was this a gentle touch?

A: It didn't look gentle.

Q: Describe "not gentle."

A: His fingers were wrapped around her forearm. She tried to pull away and couldn't immediately.

Q: How long did this contact last?

A: A few seconds, maybe. Then she yanked her arm free.

Q: What happened next?

A: She said something to him—I couldn't hear what—and walked toward the front door.

Q: Did he follow her?

A: Yes. That's when Derek stepped in.

Q: Tell me about Derek's intervention.

A: He put himself between Ryan and Jessica. Said something like "that's enough" or "cool it." Something like that.

Q: How did the defendant respond?

A: He laughed. Kind of a mean laugh? And said Derek should mind his own business.

Q: Then what?

A: Then Ryan tried to go around Derek, and Derek put a hand on his chest to stop him.

Q: Derek initiated physical contact with the defendant?

A: If you want to call it that. He was trying to protect Jessica.

Q: I'm asking what you observed, not your interpretation. Derek placed his hand on Ryan's chest?

A: Yes.

Q: And what did Ryan do?

A: He shoved Derek's hand away. Then shoved Derek. That's when it became a fight.

Q: Who threw the first punch?

A: Depends what you mean by first. Ryan escalated it physically when he shoved Derek.

Q: Who threw the first closed-fist punch?

A: I didn't see. Too many people crowded in at that point.

topic: A doctor is deposed about informed consent procedures before a surgery
text:
Q: Dr. Patel, let's talk about your standard informed consent process. What does that typically involve?

A: A discussion with the patient about the procedure, the risks, the benefits, the alternatives. That's the standard approach.

Q: How long does this discussion usually take?

A: It depends on the patient and the procedure.

Q: For this procedure specifically—the laparoscopic cholecystectomy on Mrs. Fontaine—how long would you estimate?

A: I don't time my consultations with a stopwatch, counsel.

Q: A rough estimate, Doctor.

A: Ten to fifteen minutes. Perhaps longer if there are questions.

Q: And you documented this conversation where?

A: In the operative note and the consent form itself.

Q: The consent form that Mrs. Fontaine signed?

A: Yes. Obviously.

Q: Did you discuss the specific risk of bile duct injury with her?

A: I discussed the risks of the procedure. Bile duct injury is a known risk.

Q: That wasn't my question. Did you specifically mention bile duct injury to Mrs. Fontaine?

A: I covered the material risks. I've already said that.

Q: Doctor, I need a yes or no. Did the words "bile duct injury" come out of your mouth during that conversation?

A: I don't have a transcript of a conversation from fourteen months ago. I followed my standard practice, which includes discussing significant complications.

Q: So you don't actually remember whether you told her?

A: I remember having a thorough informed consent discussion. That's what I remember.

topic: A doctor is deposed about informed consent procedures before a surgery
text:
Q: Dr. Simmons, who in your practice is responsible for obtaining informed consent?

A: For surgical procedures, the operating surgeon. That would be me.

Q: Always you personally?

A: For my patients, yes.

Q: Do nurses ever participate in that process?

A: They witness the signature. They don't conduct the consent discussion.

Q: Let's move to Mr. Okonkwo's surgery on March 3rd. Did you obtain his informed consent?

A: I did.

Q: When?

A: The day before surgery, during his pre-operative appointment.

Q: What risks did you discuss?

A: The standard risks—bleeding, infection, nerve damage, the possibility of incomplete relief of his symptoms.

Q: Nerve damage. Can you be more specific about what you told him?

A: I explained that the procedure carried a small risk of nerve injury that could result in numbness or weakness.

Q: Did you tell him the nerve damage could be permanent?

A: Yes.

Q: Did you tell him it could affect his ability to walk?

A: I—counsel, I explained the general nature of the risk. I don't give patients a medical school lecture.

Q: I'm asking what you told this patient, Doctor.

A: And I'm telling you I discussed nerve damage as a risk. Thoroughly. Whether I used those exact words—

Q: Did you use those exact words?

A: I'm not finished. Whether I used those exact words, I can't say with certainty, but the substance was communicated.

topic: A doctor is deposed about informed consent procedures before a surgery
text:
Q: Good morning, Dr. Weiss. We're here to discuss the informed consent process for Ms. Delacroix's cardiac catheterization. You performed that procedure?

A: Good morning. Yes, I did.

Q: Tell me about your conversation with Ms. Delacroix before the procedure.

A: Certainly. I met with her the morning of the procedure, reviewed the diagnostic findings, explained what the catheterization would involve, discussed the risks including bleeding, infection, arterial damage, stroke, heart attack, and death, explained the alternatives including medical management, and answered her questions.

Q: How long did that take?

A: Approximately twenty minutes.

Q: She had questions?

A: She did. She asked about recovery time and when she could return to work. She asked about the likelihood of needing a stent.

Q: What did you tell her about stroke risk specifically?

A: I told her it was a small but real possibility, less than one percent in most studies.

Q: Did you tell her about the specific risk factors that might increase her odds?

A: I discussed her individual risk profile, yes. Her diabetes, her age, her peripheral vascular disease.

Q: Did you tell her those factors increased her stroke risk during the procedure?

A: I explained that her overall risk profile was higher than average, yes.

Q: Those are different statements, Doctor. Did you connect her risk factors to procedural stroke risk, specifically?

A: I believe I did. Yes.

Q: You believe you did, or you did?

A: I did.

topic: A doctor is deposed about informed consent procedures before a surgery
text:
Q: Dr. Hassan, I want to understand the timeline. You met with Mr. Briggs on January 10th?

A: Correct.

Q: Surgery was January 11th?

A: Correct.

Q: So you had one conversation with him before operating on his spine?

A: One formal pre-operative consultation, yes. We also spoke briefly on the morning of surgery.

Q: One consultation. For a three-level spinal fusion. Okay. Moving on—who else was present during the January 10th meeting?

A: Just myself and Mr. Briggs.

Q: Not his wife?

A: She may have been in the waiting room. She wasn't in the exam room.

Q: Mr. Briggs was seventy-three years old at the time?

A: I'd have to check the chart for his exact age.

Q: He was seventy-three. Did you consider having a family member present for a complex surgical consent discussion with a seventy-three-year-old patient?

A: Mr. Briggs was cognitively intact. He didn't require a chaperone.

Q: I didn't say chaperone. I asked whether you considered having family present.

A: It wasn't necessary. Mr. Briggs understood everything I told him.

Q: How do you know he understood?

A: Because I asked him if he had questions, and he demonstrated understanding.

Q: What questions did he ask?

A: I don't recall specifically.

Q: You don't recall what he asked, but you're certain he understood?

A: He signed the consent form. He told me he understood. I had no reason to doubt him.

topic: A doctor is deposed about informed consent procedures before a surgery
text:
Q: Dr. Castellano, you've testified that you discussed alternatives to surgery with Ms. Park. What alternatives did you present?

A: Physical therapy, corticosteroid injections, and continued conservative management.

Q: Did you discuss the success rates of those alternatives?

A: In general terms, yes.

Q: What does "in general terms" mean?

A: It means I explained that physical therapy helps some patients, injections provide temporary relief for others, and conservative management is appropriate when symptoms are manageable.

Q: Did you give her any numbers? Percentages?

A: I don't typically quote statistics because they vary widely depending on the study.

Q: So no percentages.

A: That's what I said.

Q: Did you recommend surgery, or did you present it as one option among equals?

A: I recommended surgery. Her imaging showed significant pathology, and she had failed conservative treatment.

Q: Define "failed."

A: Six months of physical therapy with no meaningful improvement.

Q: Meaningful improvement according to whom?

A: According to her reported symptoms and my clinical assessment.

Q: Did she tell you she wanted to try injections before surgery?

A: We discussed injections. She understood they would provide temporary relief at best.

Q: That's not what I asked. Did Ms. Park tell you she wanted to try injections first?

A: She may have expressed interest. I explained why I didn't think that was the best approach.

Q: And then she agreed to surgery?

A: She consented to surgery, yes. After a full discussion of her options.

topic: A former employee is deposed about discriminatory remarks made by a supervisor
text:
Q: Ms. Thornton, you were employed at Ridgeway Financial from 2019 to 2023, correct?

A: I was.

Q: And during that time, your direct supervisor was Marcus Webb?

A: That's who they assigned me to, yes.

Q: I'm asking if he was your supervisor.

A: And I'm telling you he was the person they put in charge of me. Whether he actually supervised anything is a different question.

Q: Let's talk about the meeting on March 15, 2022. You were present?

A: I was present. I remember every word.

Q: Can you describe what Mr. Webb said during that meeting?

A: He said, and I quote, "We need someone who fits the client profile better. Someone the old boys' club will actually listen to." Then he looked directly at me and said, "No offense, but they're not going to take a young Black woman seriously."

Q: Did anyone else hear this?

A: Four other people were in that room. You have their names.

Q: I'm asking what you observed.

A: I observed four people look down at their notebooks like their lives depended on it. I observed nobody say a word. And I observed myself sitting there being told my race and gender made me unsuitable for my own account.

Q: Did you report this comment to Human Resources?

A: I reported it the same day. In writing. I have the email timestamped at 4:47 PM if you'd like me to recite the contents from memory.

Q: That won't be necessary—

A: I also have the response I received six weeks later telling me they'd "addressed the matter internally," which apparently meant doing absolutely nothing.

Q: Ms. Thornton, I just need you to answer the questions I ask.

A: Then ask better questions.

topic: A former employee is deposed about discriminatory remarks made by a supervisor
text:
Q: Mr. Delgado, you worked in the Houston office for approximately seven years?

A: Seven years and three months.

Q: During that time, did you ever hear Mr. Patterson make comments about employees' national origins?

A: Could you define what you mean by "comments"?

Q: Remarks. Statements. Things he said.

A: I heard him say many things over seven years. You'll need to be more specific.

Q: Comments relating to where employees were born or their ethnic background.

A: Yes.

Q: Can you give me an example?

A: He called the cleaning staff "the illegals" even though most of them were born in Texas. He asked me once if I needed extra time off for "siesta." He told Jenny Nguyen her "people" were good at math so she should double-check the quarterly reports.

Q: Let's focus on the comment about "siesta." When did that occur?

A: Which time?

Q: He said this more than once?

A: I stopped counting after the fourth or fifth time. It was a running joke to him. "Delgado, you look tired, need a siesta?" Big laugh. Every time.

Q: How did you respond?

A: The first few times I didn't respond. Then I told him I found it offensive. Then he told me to "lighten up" because "it's a compliment, your culture knows how to relax."

Q: Did you document these incidents?

A: I documented everything after my first HR complaint went nowhere.

Q: You filed an HR complaint?

A: June 2021. I have the case number memorized. Would you like it?

Q: That's not necessary at this time.

A: 2021-HR-0847. For the record.

Q: Mr. Delgado, I'll ask the questions.

A: And I'll make sure the answers are complete.

topic: A former employee is deposed about discriminatory remarks made by a supervisor
text:
Q: You testified earlier that you overheard a conversation between Ms. Hartley and another employee. Let's go back to that.

A: Okay.

Q: Who was the other employee?

A: I don't know his name. He was from the third floor.

Q: But you're certain Ms. Hartley was one of the speakers?

A: Yes.

Q: How can you be certain?

A: Because I've worked with her for three years and I know what she sounds like.

Q: Is it possible you were mistaken?

A: No.

Q: People make mistakes in recollection all the time, don't they?

A: I'm not mistaken.

Q: You're telling me there's no possibility—

A: I'm telling you I was ten feet away, the door was open, and she said, "We can't promote him, he's too old and he'll just retire in a few years anyway." I heard her clearly. I am not mistaken.

Q: Did you see her face when she said this?

A: I saw her through the glass partition.

Q: But you didn't have a direct line of sight to her mouth?

A: I don't need to read lips to recognize a voice I've heard in meetings for three years.

Q: I'm establishing what you actually observed—

A: And I'm telling you what I observed. Would you like me to repeat it a third time?

Q: That won't be necessary. Did you report this conversation to anyone?

A: I reported it to my own supervisor, who told me to "stay out of it."

Q: Those were his exact words?

A: Her exact words. My supervisor was Linda Chen. She said, and I quote, "That's above your pay grade, stay out of it."

topic: A former employee is deposed about discriminatory remarks made by a supervisor
text:
Q: Dr. Okonkwo, I want to ask you about the departmental review process that took place in fall of 2022.

A: Go ahead.

Q: Were you part of the committee that reviewed candidates for the senior research position?

A: I was.

Q: And Dr. Michaels was also on that committee?

A: He chaired it.

Q: During committee deliberations, did Dr. Michaels express any views about the candidates?

A: He expressed many views. That was the purpose of the deliberations.

Q: Did he express any views that you found inappropriate?

A: I'm not sure "inappropriate" captures it.

Q: Then how would you characterize them?

A: Discriminatory. He said Dr. Ananya Sharma was "probably going to leave to have babies anyway" so we shouldn't waste the position on her. He said it in front of the entire committee.

Q: What was the reaction?

A: Silence.

Q: No one objected?

A: One person did.

Q: Who?

A: Me. I told him that was a sexist assumption and had no place in our evaluation. He told me I was being "oversensitive" and that he was just being "realistic about retention."

Q: How did the conversation proceed after that?

A: It didn't. He moved on to the next candidate and never acknowledged what he'd said.

Q: Did you take any further action?

A: I submitted a formal complaint to the Dean's office. I have the response letter if you need it. It thanks me for my "commitment to inclusive excellence" and assures me that "all committee members have been reminded of university values."

Q: Was any disciplinary action taken against Dr. Michaels?

A: He received the Faculty Excellence Award three months later. Does that answer your question?

topic: A former employee is deposed about discriminatory remarks made by a supervisor
text:
Q: Let's be very precise here, Ms. Franklin. You claim Mr. Torres made a discriminatory statement on November 8th, 2023.

A: I don't claim it. It happened.

Q: You understand the difference between a claim and an established fact?

A: I understand you're trying to suggest I'm lying.

Q: I'm not suggesting anything. I'm asking questions.

A: Then I'll answer them. Yes, on November 8th, Mr. Torres told me that clients "don't want to deal with someone in a wheelchair" and that I should "stick to back-office work."

Q: Were those his exact words?

A: Those were his exact words.

Q: You're certain?

A: I wrote them down immediately afterward because I knew—I knew—that one day I'd be sitting in a room like this with someone asking me if I was certain.

Q: Who else was present?

A: No one. He made sure of that.

Q: So there are no other witnesses to this alleged statement.

A: There are no other witnesses to this statement that happened.

Q: You understand that makes verification difficult.

A: I understand that's convenient for your client.

Q: Ms. Franklin—

A: I understand that he waited until we were alone because he knew exactly what he was doing. I understand I reported it anyway. I understand I was transferred to a different department two weeks later while he kept his position. And I understand I'm sitting here being asked if I'm certain, as if my memory and my integrity are on trial instead of his conduct.

Q: Are you finished?

A: Are you?

topic: A warehouse supervisor is deposed about safety protocols that were allegedly ignored
text:
Q: Mr. Harmon, you were the warehouse supervisor on the date of the incident, correct?

A: I was the shift supervisor, yes. Not the warehouse supervisor. There's a difference.

Q: Fine. As shift supervisor, you were responsible for ensuring safety protocols were followed?

A: I was responsible for a lot of things. Safety was one of them.

Q: Let me rephrase. Did your job duties include enforcing safety protocols?

A: My job duties included making sure the shift ran smoothly, that we met our quotas, and that employees followed company guidelines—which, yes, included safety protocols.

Q: Were you aware that forklift operators were required to wear high-visibility vests at all times?

A: I'm aware of the policy, yes.

Q: Were all forklift operators wearing high-visibility vests on March 14th?

A: You're asking me to remember what every single person on a forty-person shift was wearing on a specific day eight months ago.

Q: I'm asking if you can recall whether the policy was being followed.

A: The policy was always communicated. Whether every single employee followed it every single second of every single shift—no one can guarantee that. Not me, not the plant manager, not anyone.

Q: So the answer is you don't know?

A: The answer is I did my job. I communicated the policy, I enforced it when I saw violations, and I documented what I was required to document.

Q: Did you document any vest violations on March 14th?

A: If there's no documentation, then I didn't observe any violations that day.

Q: That wasn't my question.

A: That's my answer.

topic: A warehouse supervisor is deposed about safety protocols that were allegedly ignored
text:
Q: Ms. Tran, how long have you worked at Kellerman Distribution?

A: Seven years. Started on the floor, worked my way up.

Q: And you're proud of that.

A: Is that a question?

Q: Let me ask you about the lockout-tagout procedures. You're familiar with them?

A: Of course.

Q: Did you receive formal training on those procedures?

A: Yes.

Q: When?

A: When I was promoted to supervisor. And then annually after that, like everyone else.

Q: So you knew that any machine undergoing maintenance had to be locked out before work began?

A: I knew the policy. Every supervisor knew the policy.

Q: Then why was the conveyor belt still operational when Mr. Desmond began his repair work?

A: I don't accept the premise of your question.

Q: Excuse me?

A: You're asking me "why" something happened as if it's established fact. I don't agree that the conveyor was operational when he started.

Q: We have testimony that it was.

A: You have testimony from someone. I have seven years of doing this job correctly.

Q: Are you saying the other witness is lying?

A: I'm saying I know what I saw, and I know what I did. And I did my job.

Q: So you locked out the conveyor yourself?

A: I verified that lockout procedures were initiated. That was my role.

Q: Initiated. Not completed?

A: Initiated. As in, begun, in process, underway. Do you need more synonyms?

topic: A warehouse supervisor is deposed about safety protocols that were allegedly ignored
text:
Q: Let's talk about the training records, Mr. Okonkwo.

A: Let's.

Q: You seem eager.

A: I've got nothing to hide. Ask your questions.

Q: The records show that six employees on your shift had not completed their annual safety recertification. Were you aware of that?

A: I was aware that there were scheduling issues with the training sessions, yes.

Q: Scheduling issues.

A: That's what I said.

Q: Did you flag this to anyone?

A: I flagged it to HR. I flagged it to operations. I flagged it in writing, I flagged it in person, and I flagged it in three separate shift-lead meetings.

Q: And what was the response?

A: The response was that we were short-staffed and that training would be rescheduled when coverage allowed.

Q: So you were told to keep those employees working.

A: I was told the company would handle it. I did what I was supposed to do.

Q: Did you follow up?

A: Did I follow up? I followed up until I was told to stop following up because it was "being handled."

Q: Who told you that?

A: Regional operations. Derek Statham. You want his phone number, or do your clients already have it?

Q: Mr. Okonkwo—

A: No, I'm serious. Because I'm sitting here answering questions about policies I tried to enforce, and the people who actually made the decisions aren't in this room.

topic: A warehouse supervisor is deposed about safety protocols that were allegedly ignored
text:
Q: Mr. Aldridge, you understand you're under oath?

A: I do.

Q: Good. I want to be very precise here. On the morning of the accident, did you conduct a safety walkthrough?

A: Yes.

Q: What time?

A: Approximately 6:15 a.m.

Q: Approximately. You don't know exactly?

A: I didn't check my watch to the second. It was around 6:15.

Q: Your shift started at 6:00 a.m., correct?

A: Correct.

Q: So within fifteen minutes, you had already completed a full safety walkthrough?

A: I didn't say I completed it. I said I conducted it. I started it at 6:15.

Q: When did you finish?

A: I don't recall exactly.

Q: More than ten minutes? Twenty?

A: I really couldn't say.

Q: You really couldn't say. Mr. Aldridge, isn't it true that you rushed through that walkthrough—or skipped it entirely—to meet the 7:00 a.m. loading deadline?

A: No.

Q: No?

A: No. I did the walkthrough. I've done it every shift for three years. I didn't skip it, I didn't rush it, and I'm not going to sit here and let you suggest otherwise.

Q: I'm not suggesting anything. I'm asking questions.

A: Then ask better ones.

topic: A warehouse supervisor is deposed about safety protocols that were allegedly ignored
text:
Q: Ms. Cahill, did you ever observe forklifts operating in pedestrian zones without spotters?

A: Define "observe."

Q: Did you see it happen?

A: I supervised a warehouse with sixty employees across 200,000 square feet. I didn't see everything that happened every minute of every day.

Q: That's not what I asked.

A: It's the context you need to understand my answer.

Q: Let me try again. At any point during your tenure as supervisor, did you witness a forklift operating in a pedestrian zone without a spotter present?

A: If I had witnessed a safety violation, I would have addressed it immediately. That's what supervisors do.

Q: So your answer is no?

A: My answer is that I addressed every violation I observed. If you're asking me to speculate about things I didn't see—

Q: I'm asking about what you did see.

A: And I'm telling you that I did my job. Every day. Every shift.

Q: Your job included ensuring spotters were present?

A: My job included a hundred things. Spotters, vests, clearance zones, load limits, training compliance, equipment checks—you want me to keep going?

Q: I want you to answer the question.

A: I have answered it. Three times now. Maybe four.

Q: Then let's move on. Did you ever report a spotter violation to upper management?

A: I reported what needed to be reported when it needed to be reported. Check the records.

Q: I'm asking you.

A: And I'm telling you—check the records. They'll show exactly what I did.

topic: An employee is deposed about a coworker's termination they believe was retaliatory
text:
Q: Good morning. I understand you worked in the same department as Ms. Thornton?

A: Yes, that's right. For about four years. She sat two desks over from me, actually. We worked on a lot of the same projects together.

Q: I appreciate you being here today. I know these situations can be uncomfortable.

A: I just want to help however I can. Rebecca didn't deserve what happened to her.

Q: Let's talk about what you observed. Were you aware that Ms. Thornton had filed a complaint with HR in March?

A: Yes. She told me about it the day after she filed. She was nervous, you know, about how it would be received. I told her she was doing the right thing. The way Marcus was treating people—someone had to say something.

Q: How would you describe Ms. Thornton's work performance prior to her termination?

A: Excellent. Genuinely excellent. She was the kind of person who'd stay late to help someone else meet a deadline, not because she had to, but because that's who she was. I've been there eleven years, and she was one of the best colleagues I've ever had.

Q: Did you notice any changes in how management treated her after the complaint was filed?

A: It was like a switch flipped. Suddenly she was getting criticized in meetings for things that would've been fine a month earlier. Little things. The tone of her emails, the way she formatted reports. It felt—I'm sorry, I don't want to editorialize.

Q: Please, go ahead. Your observations are exactly what we're here for.

A: It felt targeted. Like they were building a case against her, one write-up at a time. And I watched her try so hard to meet every new standard they set. She kept asking me, "Am I crazy? Is my work actually slipping?" And it wasn't. It just wasn't.

Q: That must have been difficult to witness.

A: It was. She's a good person. She has two kids, and she was so worried about providing for them. I'm sorry—I know that's not really relevant to the facts.

Q: It's quite all right. Take your time.

A: Thank you. I just hope telling the truth here actually makes a difference for her.

---

topic: An employee is deposed about a coworker's termination they believe was retaliatory
text:
Q: State your name for the record.

A: Daniel Okonkwo.

Q: Mr. Okonkwo, how long have you been employed at Ridgeline Manufacturing?

A: Seven years this October.

Q: And you're here today under subpoena, is that correct?

A: Yes.

Q: I want to be clear from the start—you're not in any trouble. We're simply trying to understand what happened with Mr. Castillo's termination. Does that make sense?

A: It does. And honestly, I'm relieved someone's finally asking questions. I've been carrying this around for months.

Q: Then let's give you a chance to set it down. Did you witness the interaction between Mr. Castillo and the plant manager on April 12th?

A: I was about fifteen feet away. Close enough to hear most of it.

Q: In your own words, what did you observe?

A: Javier—Mr. Castillo—he was calm. Professional. He was explaining why the safety protocol hadn't been followed, and that it wasn't his team's fault because we never received the updated guidelines. That's true, by the way. None of us got that memo.

Q: How did the plant manager respond?

A: He got in Javier's face. Told him he was "done making excuses" and that maybe he should've thought twice before "running to OSHA like a snitch." His words.

Q: He specifically referenced the OSHA report?

A: Yes. And everyone heard it. There were at least six of us on the floor. We all just kind of froze.

Q: What happened to Mr. Castillo after that?

A: He was terminated two days later. The official reason was "insubordination," but—look, Javier wasn't insubordinate. He was the most respectful person on our shift. He just wouldn't pretend things were safe when they weren't.

Q: It sounds like you respected him.

A: I did. I do. He looked out for all of us. And I think that's exactly why they wanted him gone.

---

topic: An employee is deposed about a coworker's termination they believe was retaliatory
text:
Q: You were Ms. Patterson's direct supervisor, correct?

A: For about eighteen months, yes.

Q: And in that role, you would have conducted her performance reviews?

A: I conducted two of them. Both were positive. I gave her exceeds expectations in almost every category.

Q: Almost?

A: She met expectations in "timeliness of deliverables." Not because she was slow, but because she was thorough. She'd rather turn something in a day late and have it be right than rush it out with errors. I respected that about her.

Q: The termination letter states she was dismissed for "ongoing performance deficiencies." Does that align with your observations?

A: No. It doesn't. And I told HR that at the time.

Q: You raised concerns?

A: I did. I said I thought the timing was suspicious—that this was coming just six weeks after she testified in the Rodriguez grievance hearing. I was told my concerns were "noted."

Q: What did you understand that to mean?

A: That they'd already made their decision and didn't want to hear otherwise.

Q: How did that make you feel?

A: Frustrated. Disappointed. I hired Sarah. I trained her. I watched her grow into someone the whole team relied on. And then I had to sit there while they handed me talking points for why she was suddenly inadequate.

Q: Did you deliver the termination?

A: They asked me to. I refused. I told them if they wanted her gone, someone else would have to do it, because I wasn't going to pretend this was about performance.

Q: That was a risk for you to take.

A: Maybe. But some things matter more than playing it safe. Sarah trusted me. The least I could do was not be the one to betray that trust.

---

topic: An employee is deposed about a coworker's termination they believe was retaliatory
text:
Q: Ms. Huang, did you have occasion to speak with Mr. DeMarco on the day of his termination?

A: I did. He came to my office around 2:30 in the afternoon.

Q: What was his demeanor?

A: He was shaken. I'd never seen him like that. He's usually so steady, you know? But that day his hands were trembling.

Q: What did he tell you?

A: He said they'd just walked him out. Gave him fifteen minutes to collect his things. After nine years.

Q: Did he say why he believed he'd been terminated?

A: He said—and I'm paraphrasing—that it was because he wouldn't stop asking questions about the billing discrepancies. He'd been raising concerns for months. To his manager, to compliance, to anyone who would listen.

Q: Were you aware of these concerns before that conversation?

A: Yes. He'd mentioned them to me a few times. He was worried about some of the invoices he was seeing. He thought clients were being overcharged, and he felt like no one wanted to hear it.

Q: What did you say to him that day?

A: I told him I was sorry. I told him this wasn't right, and that I believed him. I don't know if it helped, but I wanted him to know he wasn't alone.

Q: Did you ever consider raising your own concerns about the situation?

A: I thought about it. A lot. I'm still thinking about it. It's part of why I agreed to testify today.

Q: Even though no one compelled you to?

A: No one compelled me. But David was a good man who tried to do the right thing, and they punished him for it. Staying silent felt like being complicit.

Q: Thank you for that, Ms. Huang.

A: I just hope it counts for something.

---

topic: An employee is deposed about a coworker's termination they believe was retaliatory
text:
Q: For the record, can you describe your working relationship with the plaintiff?

A: We weren't close personally, but professionally, I'd say we had a lot of mutual respect. We collaborated on the Henderson account for about eight months.

Q: How would you characterize his work during that period?

A: Meticulous. Maybe too meticulous for some people's taste—he'd push back if he thought a shortcut was going to cause problems down the line. Some managers didn't love that.

Q: Did you observe any friction between him and senior leadership?

A: After he raised the issue about the falsified inspection reports, yes. There was a definite shift.

Q: What kind of shift?

A: He started getting excluded from meetings he'd normally be in. His emails would go unanswered for days. People who used to stop by his desk just... stopped.

Q: Did anyone say anything to you directly about him?

A: Linda Chen—she was the operations director—she pulled me aside once and told me I should "be careful" about being associated with him. Her words.

Q: What did you take that to mean?

A: That they were going to make an example of him, and anyone standing too close might get caught in it.

Q: Did that warning change your behavior toward him?

A: No. If anything, I made a point of having lunch with him more often. I know that sounds small, but when someone's being frozen out, sometimes just showing up matters.

Q: You didn't worry about consequences for yourself?

A: I worried. But I've been in situations before where I watched someone get mistreated and said nothing. I didn't like who I was in those moments. I decided I wasn't going to do that again.

Q: Even at personal risk?

A: Even then. Some people are worth standing up for. Marcus was one of them.

topic: A witness is asked about a car accident they saw from their front porch
text:
Q: Please state your name for the record.

A: David Margolis.

Q: Mr. Margolis, where were you on the afternoon of September 14th at approximately 3:15 p.m.?

A: On my front porch. I was sitting in my rocking chair, drinking iced tea, same as I do every afternoon when the weather's nice.

Q: And from that location, did you observe a vehicle collision?

A: I did. Watched the whole thing happen right in front of me, maybe forty feet from my property line.

Q: Can you describe what you saw?

A: The silver Honda was traveling eastbound on Maple, going the speed limit or close to it. The black pickup ran the stop sign on Crescent without even tapping the brakes and hit the Honda broadside on the driver's door.

Q: How can you be certain the pickup didn't brake?

A: Because I was looking right at it. No nose dip, no brake lights, no tire squeal. That truck went through that intersection like the sign wasn't there.

Q: Were there any obstructions to your view?

A: None. My porch sits elevated about three feet, and there's nothing between my house and that intersection but my front lawn.

Q: What about the tree in your yard?

A: That tree is fifteen feet to the south of my sightline to the intersection. It wasn't blocking anything.

Q: You seem very certain of these details.

A: I know what I saw.

Q: Is it possible the pickup did stop and you simply didn't notice?

A: No. That's not possible. I was watching that truck from the moment it came down Crescent. It did not stop.

Q: What happened immediately after the collision?

A: The Honda spun about ninety degrees and came to rest against the curb. The pickup ended up in the Hendersons' yard across the street. I went inside, told my wife to call 911, then went out to check on the drivers.

Q: Did you speak to either driver?

A: I spoke to the woman in the Honda. She was conscious but hurt. The man in the pickup was already out of his vehicle, walking around, didn't appear injured.

---

topic: A witness is asked about a car accident they saw from their front porch
text:
Q: Good morning. You are Patricia Vance?

A: Yes.

Q: Ms. Vance, I understand you witnessed the accident that occurred on October 3rd on Birchwood Lane?

A: I saw part of it, yes.

Q: Only part of it?

A: I mean, I didn't see the cars before they were close to the intersection. I heard tires and looked up.

Q: So you heard tires screeching before you looked?

A: I heard a sound. I'm not sure it was screeching exactly.

Q: What did you see when you looked up?

A: Two cars, one was a red SUV, the other was a white sedan. They were already—it happened very fast.

Q: Which vehicle struck the other?

A: The SUV hit the sedan. I think. The SUV was coming from my left.

Q: You think, or you know?

A: The SUV hit the sedan.

Q: Let's slow down. What direction was the white sedan traveling?

A: Toward downtown. So that would be... north, I guess.

Q: And the red SUV?

A: Coming from Oakdale Road, so west to east.

Q: Was the sedan in the intersection when the SUV entered it?

A: I believe so. Yes. The sedan was already there.

Q: Did you see any traffic signals or signs from your vantage point?

A: There's a stop sign for Oakdale traffic. Not for Birchwood.

Q: Did you see whether the SUV stopped at that sign?

A: I didn't see it stop. But like I said, I wasn't watching until I heard the noise.

Q: I understand. Let me ask you this: when you first looked up, where exactly was the SUV positioned?

A: It was entering the intersection. Moving fast.

---

topic: A witness is asked about a car accident they saw from their front porch
text:
Q: Mr. Okonkwo, how long have you lived at 414 Spruce Street?

A: Thirty-one years this November.

Q: In that time, how many accidents have you witnessed at the intersection of Spruce and Miller?

A: This was the fourth.

Q: So you're familiar with how traffic moves through that intersection.

A: Very familiar.

Q: Tell me what you observed on the morning of March 8th.

A: I was on my porch around 7:40 a.m., waiting for my daughter to pick me up for a doctor's appointment. A blue minivan was heading south on Spruce. A gray coupe was heading west on Miller. The coupe had the right of way because there's a yield sign for southbound Spruce traffic. The minivan didn't yield. It pulled into the intersection and the coupe struck it on the passenger side.

Q: Are you certain about which vehicle had the right of way?

A: The yield sign has been there since 1996. I watched them install it after the second accident I witnessed at that corner.

Q: Did the minivan slow down at all before entering the intersection?

A: It slowed, but it didn't yield. There's a difference. Slowing down isn't the same as giving the right of way to crossing traffic.

Q: How fast would you estimate the coupe was traveling?

A: I'm not going to guess at miles per hour. I can tell you it wasn't speeding, it wasn't crawling. It was moving at a normal pace for that road.

Q: Fair enough. What about the minivan?

A: Same. Normal speed. The problem wasn't speed. The problem was the minivan driver didn't look, or didn't look carefully enough.

Q: Did you see the driver of either vehicle before the collision?

A: I saw a woman driving the minivan. She was looking down at something, maybe her phone, maybe something in the passenger seat. I couldn't tell you which.

Q: You could see that clearly from your porch?

A: My eyesight is fine, counselor. I had cataract surgery two years ago and my vision is 20/25 with my glasses, which I was wearing.

---

topic: A witness is asked about a car accident they saw from their front porch
text:
Q: State your name, please.

A: Reginald Foster.

Q: Mr. Foster, were you present at your residence on July 22nd when an accident occurred nearby?

A: I was.

Q: Where specifically were you?

A: Front porch.

Q: Did you see the accident?

A: Part of it.

Q: What part?

A: The impact. The aftermath.

Q: What did you see leading up to the impact?

A: Not much.

Q: Can you elaborate?

A: I was reading. Heard a horn, looked up, saw two cars collide.

Q: Which cars?

A: A dark-colored sedan and a light-colored truck.

Q: Can you be more specific about the colors?

A: The sedan was dark blue or black. The truck was white or cream.

Q: Who honked the horn?

A: I don't know.

Q: Which vehicle do you believe was at fault?

A: Objection, calls for a legal conclusion.

Q: Let me rephrase. Based on what you saw, which vehicle entered the intersection first?

A: I didn't see them enter. I only looked up when I heard the horn.

Q: What did you observe about the point of impact?

A: The truck hit the driver's side of the sedan.

Q: So the truck struck the sedan?

A: That's what I said.

Q: How fast was the truck moving at impact?

A: I couldn't tell you. I'm not able to estimate that.

Q: Faster than a walking pace?

A: Obviously faster than a walking pace. It was a car accident, not a fender bump in a parking lot.

Q: Was the sedan moving at the moment of impact?

A: It was in the intersection, so it had been moving. Whether it was still moving at the exact moment the truck hit it, I couldn't say for certain.

---

topic: A witness is asked about a car accident they saw from their front porch
text:
Q: Ms. Yamamoto, I want to be very precise about the timeline here. You said you were on your porch at 5:45 p.m.

A: That's correct.

Q: How do you know the exact time?

A: I had just checked my phone. My husband texted that he was leaving work, and I looked at the time to calculate when he'd be home.

Q: And how long after you checked your phone did the accident occur?

A: Less than a minute. I hadn't even put the phone down yet.

Q: Walk me through exactly what you saw. Take your time.

A: A motorcycle was heading east on Linden. A black sedan was coming out of the CVS parking lot, making a left turn onto Linden, which would be heading west. The sedan pulled out directly into the path of the motorcycle.

Q: Did the motorcycle have time to stop?

A: No. The sedan pulled out too close. The motorcycle braked—I saw the rear end rise up—but there wasn't enough distance.

Q: You saw the rear end of the motorcycle rise up?

A: Yes.

Q: That's a very specific observation.

A: The sun was behind me. I had a clear, well-lit view of everything. The motorcycle was maybe sixty feet from me at that point.

Q: Did the sedan stop before pulling out, or did it roll through?

A: It stopped. Then it pulled out. The driver just didn't see the motorcycle, or misjudged how fast it was coming.

Q: How fast was the motorcycle traveling, in your estimation?

A: Under the speed limit. The limit there is thirty-five. The motorcycle wasn't going faster than traffic normally goes on that road.

Q: And you're basing that on what?

A: Living on that street for eleven years and watching traffic every single day. I know what thirty-five looks like on Linden Avenue.

Q: What happened after the collision?

A: The motorcyclist went over the hood of the sedan and landed in the road. The sedan stopped. I ran inside, grabbed my phone, called 911 while I was heading down to help.

Q: Did you speak to the driver of the sedan?

A: Briefly. She was hysterical. Kept saying she didn't see him. I told her to stay calm, that help was coming.

topic: A project manager is questioned about deadlines they missed on a software contract
text:
Q: Mr. Harmon, I want to direct your attention to the Phase Two milestone. When was that originally due?

A: March 15th.

Q: And when was it actually delivered?

A: April 3rd.

Q: So approximately nineteen days late, correct?

A: If you want to characterize it that way, yes.

Q: I'm asking if that's mathematically accurate, Mr. Harmon.

A: Yes. Nineteen days.

Q: What caused the delay?

A: Several factors.

Q: Can you identify them?

A: Resource allocation issues. Scope changes. Technical debt from Phase One that hadn't been addressed.

Q: Let's take those one at a time. What resource allocation issues?

A: We lost two senior developers in February. One quit, one went on medical leave.

Q: Did you inform Nexgen Technologies about these departures?

A: I don't specifically recall.

Q: You don't recall whether you told your client that you'd lost a quarter of your development team?

A: I'm sure it came up in some form. I don't recall the specific communication.

Q: Would it refresh your recollection to see an email chain from that period?

A: It might.

Q: We'll mark this as Exhibit 14. Take a moment to review it.

A: ...Okay.

Q: Does that refresh your recollection?

A: This is an internal email. I was asking about backfill options. I don't see anything here about client notification.

topic: A project manager is questioned about deadlines they missed on a software contract
text:
Q: Ms. Castellano, how long had you been project manager on the Ridgeline implementation at the time the problems began?

A: Could you define "problems"?

Q: The missed deadlines.

A: I'd been on the project from the start. About fourteen months at that point.

Q: Fourteen months. And in those fourteen months, how many milestone deadlines were met on time?

A: I'd have to look at the project documentation to give you an exact number.

Q: Approximately.

A: I really couldn't say without the documentation in front of me. I don't want to guess and have it be wrong.

Q: Fair enough. Let me ask it differently. Were you aware, as of June 2022, that the project was behind schedule?

A: Yes.

Q: Significantly behind schedule?

A: That's subjective.

Q: Were you concerned about the schedule?

A: I was monitoring it closely.

Q: That's not what I asked. Were you concerned?

A: I... yes. I had concerns.

Q: What specifically concerned you?

A: The authentication module was proving more complex than originally scoped. We kept finding edge cases. Every time we thought we'd addressed the requirements, something else would surface. It was... it became difficult to project completion dates with any confidence.

Q: Did you communicate these concerns to anyone at Ridgeline?

A: I believe so.

Q: You believe so, or you did?

A: I did. I'm certain I did. I just don't remember the exact date or format right now.

topic: A project manager is questioned about deadlines they missed on a software contract
text:
Q: Let's talk about the weekly status reports. You prepared those, correct?

A: Correct.

Q: Every week without exception?

A: As far as I recall.

Q: I'm going to hand you what's been marked as Exhibit 7. Can you identify this?

A: It's a status report dated August 12th.

Q: Who prepared it?

A: I did.

Q: Please turn to page two. Under "Schedule Status," what does it say?

A: "On track with minor variances."

Q: "On track with minor variances."

A: That's what it says.

Q: Mr. Okonkwo, isn't it true that by August 12th, the project was already three weeks behind the contracted delivery date?

A: The contracted delivery date had been... there had been discussions about adjusting the timeline.

Q: I'm asking about the original contracted date. August 12th. Three weeks past due. Yes or no?

A: Based on the original contract, yes.

Q: Then why does this report say "on track"?

A: Because we were on track relative to the revised internal timeline that had been discussed with stakeholders.

Q: Discussed but not formally agreed to?

A: The approval process was still—it was ongoing.

Q: So when you wrote "on track," you meant on track with a timeline that hadn't been approved?

A: I meant we were making progress consistent with realistic expectations given the circumstances. Look, I can explain the context if you want, or we can keep going in circles. It's your deposition.

Q: Let's move on. Exhibit 8, please.

topic: A project manager is questioned about deadlines they missed on a software contract
text:
Q: Ms. Yuen. Can you describe your role in managing the Terraform integration deadline?

A: I was the project manager responsible for coordinating between our development team and Terraform's technical leads.

Q: What was the original deadline for that integration?

A: October 1st.

Q: What was the actual completion date?

A: We delivered a functional build on November 19th.

Q: Almost seven weeks late.

A: The final build, yes. We had delivered interim builds before that.

Q: But the contractually required deliverable—that was November 19th?

A: Yes.

Q: I want to understand the decision-making process here. At what point did you know October 1st wasn't achievable?

A: Probably... mid-September. Maybe earlier. It's hard to pinpoint.

Q: What did you do when you reached that conclusion?

A: I escalated to my director. We had several meetings. We explored options—additional resources, scope reduction, parallel workstreams.

Q: And what was decided?

A: We brought in two contractors and moved some non-critical features to a later phase.

Q: Did that help?

A: Somewhat. Not enough, obviously.

Q: Not enough.

A: No.

Q: Looking back, is there anything you would have done differently?

A: I've thought about that a lot.

Q: And?

A: There were signs earlier. In August. I should have raised the flag then instead of trying to make it work. I kept thinking we could recover. You always think you can recover.

topic: A project manager is questioned about deadlines they missed on a software contract
text:
Q: Mr. Petrov, you've already testified that you were aware of the deadline. I want to ask you about something else. The deployment environment—whose responsibility was that?

A: Could you... sorry, could you repeat that?

Q: The deployment environment. Who was responsible for having it ready?

A: That was a shared responsibility between our infrastructure team and the client's IT department.

Q: Shared. Can you explain what that means in practice?

A: We were responsible for the application configuration. They were responsible for server provisioning and network access.

Q: And did both sides meet their obligations?

A: We did.

Q: The client didn't?

A: There were delays on their end with the firewall rules and the VPN configuration.

Q: How significant were those delays?

A: I don't have the exact... I mean, we documented it at the time. It's in the project files somewhere.

Q: Days? Weeks?

A: A few weeks, I think. My recollection is a few weeks.

Q: Mr. Petrov, did those delays impact your ability to meet the final deadline?

A: They contributed, yes. Along with other factors.

Q: What other factors?

A: I've been over this several times now, in this deposition and before. The change requests, the resource issues, the technical complexity. It's all documented. I'm not sure what else I can add at this point.

Q: I'm just trying to understand—

A: And I'm trying to answer. But I've given you the same information multiple ways now. The documents will show what happened. That's what documents are for.

Q: Let's take a short break.

A: Fine.

topic: A paramedic is questioned about the response time and treatment at an accident scene
text:
Q: Please state your name and occupation for the record.

A: Marcus Webb, and I've been a paramedic with County Fire and Rescue for eleven years now—eleven years this past April, actually. Best job I've ever had.

Q: Mr. Webb, I'd like to discuss the response on the evening of March 14th. What time did you receive the dispatch call?

A: 7:42 PM, exactly. I remember because I had just checked my watch—we'd been talking about how quiet the evening was, and then boom, the call comes in. That's how it always goes, right?

Q: And what were you told about the nature of the emergency?

A: Two-vehicle collision on Route 9, possible entrapment, multiple injuries. The dispatcher—Sarah, she's great, really clear communicator—she gave us the mile marker and said witnesses reported one vehicle had rolled.

Q: What was your response time to the scene?

A: Eight minutes flat. I'm actually proud of that because Route 9 has those tricky curves past the fairgrounds, and we still made excellent time. My partner Danny was driving, and he knows that road like the back of his hand.

Q: Eight minutes. Is that consistent with your department's protocols?

A: Absolutely, yes. Our target is under ten minutes for priority-one calls in that zone, so we beat it by two full minutes. The rig was in perfect shape that night—we'd just done our morning checks, everything was stocked, ready to go.

Q: When you arrived, what did you observe?

A: Oh, it was a scene, let me tell you. The sedan was on its roof in the ditch—completely inverted—and the pickup had spun out about forty feet past it. Debris everywhere. But here's the thing, and I think this is important: there was already a civilian applying pressure to the plaintiff's head wound. Good Samaritan, probably saved that man's life. I always love seeing that, people stepping up.

Q: What was your initial assessment of the plaintiff's condition?

A: GCS of 12, which told me he was conscious but altered. Visible head laceration, maybe three inches, bleeding controlled by the time we got there thanks to that civilian. Suspected rib fractures on the left side based on his breathing pattern and the bruising I could see. I started my assessment immediately—airway, breathing, circulation, just like we train, just like I've done hundreds of times.

Q: Did you administer any medication at the scene?

A: I did. Four milligrams of morphine IV for pain management, and I started a saline drip because his pressure was borderline. The morphine was the right call—you could see the relief on his face. That's the part of the job that really gets me, you know? Being able to actually help someone in their worst moment.

topic: A paramedic is questioned about the response time and treatment at an accident scene
text:
Q: State your name for the record.

A: Jennifer Okafor.

Q: And your profession?

A: Paramedic.

Q: Ms. Okafor, let's get right to it. The dispatch log shows you arrived at the accident scene at 9:47 PM. Does that match your recollection?

A: I'd have to see the log to confirm.

Q: I'm showing you Exhibit 7. Take a look at the highlighted entry.

A: Yes. 9:47.

Q: The call came in at 9:31. That's sixteen minutes. Sixteen minutes for a critical response. Can you explain that?

A: There was construction on Miller Avenue. We had to reroute.

Q: Construction. At 9:30 at night?

A: The barriers were still up. The road was closed.

Q: So you're saying you couldn't use Miller Avenue at all?

A: That's correct.

Q: And what alternate route did you take?

A: South on Parker, then east on Industrial.

Q: That's quite a detour. Did you radio dispatch about the delay?

A: Yes. Standard protocol.

Q: Now this is fascinating to me—I pulled the dispatch recordings, and I have to say, I was genuinely surprised. There's no record of any such communication. None. How do you account for that?

A: I don't know what to tell you. I radioed it in.

Q: You're certain?

A: Yes.

Q: Let me ask you this—and I find this really interesting—is it possible you simply didn't radio and you're misremembering?

A: No.

Q: Sixteen minutes is a long time when someone is bleeding, wouldn't you agree? I mean, every second counts in your line of work, correct?

A: I'm aware of that.

Q: I'm sure you are. I'm absolutely sure you are. So help me understand—if you knew every second mattered, why didn't you find another way? Why didn't you push harder to get there faster?

A: We took the fastest available route given the road closure.

Q: The fastest available route. But not the fastest route, correct?

A: The fastest route was closed.

topic: A paramedic is questioned about the response time and treatment at an accident scene
text:
Q: How long have you been a paramedic?

A: Six years with Metro EMS.

Q: And you were the lead responder on February 2nd?

A: I was.

Q: Tell me about the patient's condition when you first made contact.

A: She was conscious, alert, complaining of neck pain and difficulty breathing. Visible abrasions on her forearms and face.

Q: What did you do first?

A: Cervical stabilization. I had my partner hold manual inline stabilization while I assessed her airway.

Q: Good, good. And the airway was compromised?

A: Not compromised, but she was having some difficulty. Shallow breaths. I was concerned about potential chest trauma.

Q: So what did you do about that?

A: Applied oxygen via non-rebreather mask at fifteen liters per minute and continued my assessment.

Q: Excellent. Now, walk me through your full assessment—I want to understand exactly what you found and what you did about each finding. Take your time. This is important.

A: Sure. After securing the airway and starting oxygen, I did a rapid trauma assessment. Head—abrasions but no deformity, pupils equal and reactive. Neck—tenderness at C5, C6, so we maintained stabilization. Chest—diminished breath sounds on the right side, which concerned me. Abdomen was soft, non-tender. Pelvis stable. Extremities—she had good pulses, no obvious fractures, but the abrasions I mentioned.

Q: The diminished breath sounds on the right—tell me more about that. What were you thinking at that moment?

A: Possible pneumothorax or hemothorax. I made the call to expedite transport rather than spend more time on scene.

Q: Smart. Really smart decision. How long were you on scene total?

A: Approximately nine minutes.

Q: Nine minutes from arrival to departure?

A: That's correct. We packaged her quickly—long spine board, head blocks, straps—and we were moving.

Q: And the transport time to Memorial?

A: Eleven minutes. I radioed ahead so the trauma team was waiting.

Q: Perfect. That's exactly what I was hoping to hear. The hospital records indicate she went straight to imaging upon arrival. Your communication made that possible, didn't it?

A: I'd like to think so, yes.

topic: A paramedic is questioned about the response time and treatment at an accident scene
text:
Q: Mr. Reeves, what do you recall about the scene when you arrived?

A: Single vehicle into a tree. Driver entrapped, front end completely crumpled.

Q: What was the time of your arrival?

A: 3:15 AM per my report.

Q: You seem very certain.

A: I am. I documented it contemporaneously.

Q: Did you document everything contemporaneously?

A: Yes.

Q: Then let me ask you about the intubation—

A: I didn't intubate. I performed a cricothyrotomy.

Q: I'm sorry, let me rephrase. The surgical airway. When did you make the decision to perform that procedure?

A: As soon as I assessed the patient's airway. There was significant facial trauma—mandible fracture, blood in the oropharynx. Traditional intubation wasn't viable.

Q: Had you performed a cricothyrotomy before?

A: Yes. Twice in the field, multiple times in training simulations.

Q: Twice. In six years.

A: It's a rare procedure. That's why we train extensively—so when the moment comes, you're ready. And I was ready.

Q: Tell me about performing it that night.

A: I palpated the cricothyroid membrane, made a horizontal incision, inserted a 6.0 tracheostomy tube, confirmed placement with capnography and bilateral breath sounds. The whole procedure took maybe ninety seconds.

Q: Ninety seconds to cut into someone's throat.

A: Ninety seconds to establish an airway in a patient who would have died without one. I don't mean to be combative, counselor, but I want to be very clear about what we're discussing here. That man had blood pouring into his airway. He was going to suffocate. I gave him a way to breathe.

Q: No one is questioning your intentions—

A: Good. Because my intentions were to save his life, and I did. He's alive. He's walking around today because of what I did in those ninety seconds on the side of the road at three in the morning.

Q: Mr. Reeves, I need to ask—did you consider any alternatives before performing the cricothyrotomy?

A: I considered and rejected bag-valve mask, nasal airway, and oral intubation within about fifteen seconds of assessment. None of them would have worked. The surgical airway was the only option.

Q: And you're confident about that.

A: Completely confident. I'd make the same call again in a heartbeat. That's not arrogance—that's experience. That's training. That's knowing what to do when someone's life is in your hands.

topic: A paramedic is questioned about the response time and treatment at an accident scene
text:
Q: Please describe the accident scene.

A: Intersection collision, T-bone configuration. SUV struck a compact car on the driver's side.

Q: Were there multiple patients?

A: Three total. The SUV driver was ambulatory with minor complaints. The compact had a driver and front-seat passenger, both with significant injuries.

Q: Who did you treat?

A: The driver of the compact. My partner took the passenger.

Q: What were the driver's injuries?

A: Left arm fracture—open fracture, bone visible through the skin. Multiple lacerations. Signs of internal bleeding based on his vitals.

Q: What were his vitals?

A: Blood pressure 88 over 60, heart rate 124, respiratory rate 22.

Q: What do those numbers tell you?

A: Hypovolemic shock. He was bleeding internally, probably spleen or liver given the mechanism of injury.

Q: What did you do?

A: Two large-bore IVs, started aggressive fluid resuscitation, applied a tourniquet above the open fracture to control the external bleeding.

Q: A tourniquet on the arm.

A: Yes.

Q: Did you consider other options for hemorrhage control?

A: Direct pressure wasn't adequate given the location and severity. The tourniquet was the right call.

Q: The patient's family has suggested the tourniquet caused additional damage.

A: I understand families want answers. But that tourniquet kept him from bleeding out in the back of my rig. Without it, we're having a very different conversation right now.

Q: How long was the tourniquet in place?

A: From application at the scene to arrival at the trauma center—approximately fourteen minutes.

Q: Is that within acceptable parameters?

A: Absolutely. Current guidelines support tourniquet use for up to two hours before significant tissue damage becomes a concern. Fourteen minutes is nothing. And I documented the time of application clearly so the surgeons knew exactly what they were working with.

Q: When you arrived at the hospital, what was the patient's condition?

A: Stabilized. Blood pressure had improved to 94 over 68 with the fluids. Still tachycardic but better. He was conscious, which honestly—given how he looked when I first got to that car—was remarkable. Cases like that are why I do this job.

topic: A tenant is questioned about property damage they reported to their landlord
text:
Q: Mr. Valdez, you submitted a maintenance request on October 3rd regarding water damage in your unit. Is that correct?

A: October 3rd, yes. That's when I submitted the formal written request. I'd already called twice before that.

Q: Let's focus on the written request for now. You described water staining on the ceiling of your bedroom?

A: Water staining, yes, but also active dripping. The request specifically noted both. I have a copy if you'd like to compare it to whatever version you're working from.

Q: That won't be necessary at this time. How long had you observed the staining before submitting the request?

A: Approximately eleven days. I noticed it on September 22nd when I returned from a work trip. I photographed it that same evening with a timestamp.

Q: And you waited eleven days to report it?

A: No, I called the management office on September 23rd and again on September 27th. I submitted the written request on October 3rd because no one had responded to my calls. I documented each attempt.

Q: Do you have records of those phone calls?

A: I have my phone log showing outgoing calls to the management office number on both dates, the duration of each call, and the notes I made immediately afterward.
