Q: What did your notes say?

A: September 23rd: spoke to someone who identified herself as Maria, told me maintenance would call back within 48 hours. September 27th: left voicemail, no callback. October 3rd: submitted written request via the tenant portal and kept the confirmation email.

Q: Did you take any steps to mitigate the water damage yourself?

A: I placed a bucket under the drip and moved my belongings away from the affected area. I'm a tenant, not a roofer.

Q: Fair enough. Did the dripping worsen between September 22nd and October 3rd?

A: It did. I have photographs from four separate dates showing the progression. Would you like me to describe them, or will you be requesting the actual images?

---

topic: A tenant is questioned about property damage they reported to their landlord
text:
Q: Ms. Thornton, when did you first notice the mold in your bathroom?

A: It was—I believe it was early March. Maybe the 4th or 5th?

Q: You're not certain of the exact date?

A: I didn't write it down at the time. It wasn't much at first. Just some dark spots near the grout.

Q: And when did you report it to your landlord?

A: March 19th. I sent an email.

Q: So you waited approximately two weeks before reporting a potential mold issue?

A: I wasn't sure it was mold at first. I cleaned the grout with bathroom cleaner and it seemed to help, but then it came back worse.

Q: What made you decide it was worth reporting on March 19th specifically?

A: The spots had spread to the ceiling above the shower. I could see the discoloration spreading.

Q: Now, in your email, you wrote that the mold was, quote, "everywhere in the bathroom." Was that accurate?

A: It felt that way when I was looking at it. I was concerned. Maybe "everywhere" was—I was describing how it felt to me.

Q: So that was an exaggeration?

A: I was trying to convey that it was serious. It was on the ceiling, the walls near the shower, and the grout. Three separate areas.

Q: Three areas. Not "everywhere."

A: I suppose if you want to be literal about it, no. Not the floor. Not the vanity. But it was more than a small problem.

Q: Did you have the mold tested?

A: No, I asked the landlord to arrange testing. That's in the same email.

Q: And did they?

A: Not that I'm aware of. They sent someone to paint over it.

---

topic: A tenant is questioned about property damage they reported to their landlord
text:
Q: Let's talk about the broken window, Mr. Patterson. You reported this on June 14th?

A: June 14th, correct.

Q: Tell me exactly what happened to the window.

A: A crack appeared in the lower pane of the living room window. Ran diagonally from the bottom left corner upward, roughly eighteen inches.

Q: A crack just "appeared"?

A: That's what I said, yes.

Q: Windows don't typically crack on their own, Mr. Patterson.

A: This one did. I'm familiar with how thermal stress cracks present. The window faces west, receives direct afternoon sun, and the frame showed signs of age-related settling. The crack pattern was consistent with thermal stress, not impact.

Q: Are you a window expert?

A: I spent twelve years as a general contractor before I retired. I've replaced more windows than I could count.

Q: So in your expert opinion—

A: In my professional experience, that crack wasn't caused by anything I did. It was a material failure.

Q: Did you provide this theory to your landlord when you reported it?

A: I explained exactly what I observed and what I believed caused it. They sent someone who took a photograph and left.

Q: No repair was made?

A: Not until after I sent a letter citing the relevant habitability code. Then someone came within three days.

Q: You sent a letter citing building codes?

A: I know my rights as a tenant, counselor. I also know what thermal stress looks like.

Q: Let's move on. Were there any other issues with the windows in your unit?

A: The bedroom window had a failed seal. I reported that on July 2nd. Same lack of response until I put it in writing with the code citation.

---

topic: A tenant is questioned about property damage they reported to their landlord
text:
Q: Ms. Chen, I want to ask you about the flooding incident you reported on January 8th.

A: Of course.

Q: In your own words, what happened that day?

A: I came home from work around 6:15 p.m. and found standing water in my kitchen. It was coming from under the sink.

Q: How much water are we talking about?

A: It had spread across most of the kitchen floor and into the edge of the living room carpet. I'd estimate—maybe a quarter inch deep in the kitchen itself?

Q: What did you do when you discovered this?

A: I turned off the water valve under the sink, then I called the emergency maintenance line. While I waited, I used towels to start sopping up water.

Q: The emergency line. Did someone answer?

A: Yes, after about—I'd say four or five rings. I explained the situation.

Q: What were you told?

A: That someone would be dispatched within the hour.

Q: And were they?

A: A maintenance person arrived at 7:40. So, roughly an hour and twenty-five minutes after my call.

Q: What did they determine was the cause?

A: A supply line connection under the sink had failed. The coupling had corroded.

Q: Had you noticed any problems with that sink before January 8th?

A: There had been a small leak I reported in November. Maintenance came and tightened something. They said it was fixed.

Q: Do you believe the November leak and the January flood were related?

A: I'm not a plumber, so I can't say for certain. But the location was the same—under the sink, same general area.

Q: That's not a yes or no answer, Ms. Chen.

topic: A tenant is questioned about property damage they reported to their landlord
text:
Q: Mr. Okafor, your complaint mentions a pest infestation. Let's discuss that.

A: Happy to.

Q: What type of pests are we talking about?

A: Roaches. German cockroaches specifically.

Q: How do you know they were German cockroaches?

A: I looked it up when I first saw them. Smaller than American cockroaches, light brown with two dark stripes behind the head. That's what I was seeing.

Q: When did you first notice them?

A: August, last year. Mid-August.

Q: Where in the unit?

A: Kitchen first. Then I started seeing them in the bathroom and near the water heater closet.

Q: How many would you say you observed?

A: At first, one or two at night. By the time I reported it formally, I was seeing five or six daily.

Q: You say "formally." Had you mentioned it informally before that?

A: I mentioned it to the building super in the hallway. He said he'd "look into it." Nothing happened.

Q: When was that hallway conversation?

A: Late August. Maybe the 25th or 26th.

Q: And your formal written complaint was dated?

A: September 15th.

Q: Why did you wait three weeks?

A: I was giving them time to "look into it" like the super said. When nothing happened and the problem got worse, I put it in writing.

Q: Did you attempt any pest control on your own?

A: I bought roach bait stations and kept my kitchen immaculate. I wasn't going to live with roaches while waiting for management to act. But bait stations in one unit don't solve a building-wide problem.

Q: How do you know it was building-wide?

A: I spoke with my neighbor in 4C. Same issue. Same timeline. She'd reported it too.

Q: Did management eventually respond to your written complaint?

A: They sent an exterminator on September 28th. Thirteen days after my written complaint.

Q: And did that resolve the issue?

A: For about two weeks. Then they were back. Because you can't treat one unit and expect results when the infestation is in the walls.

topic: A witness is questioned about a fire they discovered in a neighboring unit
text:
Q: Please state your name for the record.

A: Michael Reeves. That's R-E-E-V-E-S.

Q: Mr. Reeves, you were the first person to discover the fire at 4721 Maple Drive, Unit B, is that correct?

A: I was. I want to be clear about that—I was the first to discover it, the first to call 911, and the first to alert the other residents. All of that was me.

Q: Let's start with the discovery. What time did you first notice something was wrong?

A: 2:47 in the morning. I know that precisely because I checked my phone when the smell woke me up. I have a very acute sense of smell—always have—and I knew immediately that wasn't normal smoke, like from a fireplace or someone grilling. This was electrical. Acrid. I can distinguish between combustion sources.

Q: What did you do after you smelled the smoke?

A: I didn't waste time second-guessing myself, which I think is important. A lot of people would have rolled over, gone back to sleep. Not me. I got up immediately, put on my robe and shoes—proper shoes, not slippers, because I knew I might need to move quickly—and I went to investigate.

Q: Did you call 911 before or after you located the source?

A: Before. And I want to explain why, because it shows proper emergency protocol. I called while I was moving toward the source. Multitasking. The dispatcher even commented that I was very calm and gave excellent information. She said most callers are hysterical.

Q: What information did you provide to the dispatcher?

A: Address, unit number, nature of the emergency, number of occupied units in the building, and I confirmed there were no known mobility-impaired residents. All within the first forty-five seconds of the call. I actually timed it later when I reviewed my call log.

Q: After the call, what did you observe?

A: Smoke coming from under the door of Unit B. Thick, gray smoke—not black yet, which told me it hadn't reached full involvement. I've done some reading on fire behavior. I knew we had a window, but not a large one.

Q: Did you attempt to enter Unit B?

A: Absolutely not. That would have been reckless and contrary to basic fire safety. What I did was begin systematic evacuation of the other units. I went door to door—Units A, C, and D—waking residents, ensuring everyone got out. I had all seven residents assembled at the designated meeting point before the fire department arrived. Seven for seven.

Q: The designated meeting point—was that something you had established?

A: I had suggested it at a building meeting about eight months prior. Not everyone took it seriously at the time. They took it seriously that night.

topic: A witness is questioned about a fire they discovered in a neighboring unit
text:
Q: Ms. Okonkwo, you live at 558 Birchwood Lane, Unit 3?

A: Yes.

Q: And Unit 4, where the fire originated, shares a wall with your unit?

A: A wall and part of the ceiling, yes. It's an older building with some unusual layouts.

Q: Tell me about the night of March 15th.

A: I was up late finishing a work project. Around one in the morning, I heard a popping sound. Could have been anything, but then I heard it again.

Q: What did you do?

A: I stopped typing and listened. Then I smelled it—something burning that shouldn't be burning.

Q: Now, I want to establish the timeline precisely. You've indicated you heard popping sounds at approximately one a.m.?

A: Approximately, yes. I wasn't watching the clock.

Q: But you were able to respond quickly despite the late hour?

A: I responded appropriately given what I observed.

Q: Ms. Okonkwo, I'm going to suggest that your quick thinking that night prevented what could have been a much more serious incident. Would you agree?

A: I'm not here to characterize my own actions. I'm here to tell you what happened.

Q: Fair enough. What happened after you smelled the burning?

A: I checked my own unit first—stove, outlets, anything that could be a source. Everything was fine. Then I went into the hallway.

Q: And in the hallway?

A: Smoke was seeping from under Mrs. Patterson's door. Unit 4. I knocked loudly, called her name. No answer.

Q: At what point did you contact emergency services?

A: After knocking three times with no response. I called 911, gave them the address and situation, then I got the other residents out while staying on the line with the dispatcher.

Q: The fire marshal's report credits an early alert with saving the structure. Did you read that report?

A: I did.

Q: Any reaction to it?

A: My reaction isn't relevant. The facts are what they are.

topic: A witness is questioned about a fire they discovered in a neighboring unit
text:
Q: Let's turn to your actions immediately following your discovery of the fire.

A: Okay.

Q: You've testified that you saw flames through the window of Unit 12.

A: Through the sliding glass door, yes. Not a window. The sliding glass door that leads to their patio.

Q: Through the sliding glass door. What did you do next?

A: Called 911. Then I ran back inside and grabbed my fire extinguisher.

Q: Your personal fire extinguisher?

A: Yes. I keep one in my kitchen and one in my garage. The one in the garage is larger—ten pounds, ABC rated. That's the one I grabbed.

Q: Mr. Stanton, you went toward a fire with a personal extinguisher?

A: I did.

Q: Why?

A: Because I saw Mrs. Levine's cat in the window. The unit was her mother's—she'd passed recently—and Mrs. Levine had been checking on the cat daily. The cat was in there. I wasn't going to just watch.

Q: Did you attempt to extinguish the fire yourself?

A: I contained it. There's a difference. The fire was concentrated near an outlet on the far wall. I broke the patio door with a paving stone, went in low under the smoke—you want to stay below the thermal layer—and I discharged the extinguisher at the base of the flames. By the time fire department arrived, I had it about eighty percent knocked down.

Q: You broke into the unit.

A: I made entry to prevent loss of life and property. Yes.

Q: And the cat?

A: She's fine. Her name is Mochi. Mrs. Levine brings her by to visit me now.

Q: The fire department report indicates that your intervention prevented the fire from spreading to adjacent units.

A: I've read the report.

Q: Do you have any training in firefighting, Mr. Stanton?

A: Twenty-two years as an aircraft rescue firefighter before I retired. ARFF certified, hazmat certified, technical rescue certified. I've worked plane crashes, fuel fires, structural collapses. So yes. Some training.

Q: I see.

A: That fire was nothing. But I knew what I was doing.

topic: A witness is questioned about a fire they discovered in a neighboring unit
text:
Q: Dr. Pham, you've described smelling smoke at approximately 9:15 p.m.

A: Yes.

Q: What was your first action?

A: I paused the movie I was watching and got up to investigate.

Q: You didn't immediately call 911?

A: No. That would have been premature. I needed to assess the situation first.

Q: Some might argue that in a potential fire situation, calling emergency services immediately is the safest course of action.

A: Some might argue that, yes.

Q: But you chose to investigate first.

A: I chose to gather information before making a report. I'm a scientist. That's what I do.

Q: So you went to investigate. What did you find?

A: Smoke in the hallway, increasing in density as I moved toward Unit F. I felt the door with the back of my hand—that's important, you use the back of your hand because if there's a heat differential, you won't instinctively grab the handle—and it was warm but not hot.

Q: Then what?

A: I knocked. No answer. The smoke was getting thicker, so at that point I called 911.

Q: The record indicates you also evacuated several residents.

A: I assisted in the evacuation, yes. Others were helping as well by that point.

Q: The Morales family—they have a young child?

A: Twin boys, yes. Four years old.

Q: And you helped them evacuate?

A: I carried one of the boys down the stairs because his mother had the other one and couldn't manage both. It wasn't heroic. It was practical.

Q: I didn't suggest it was heroic.

A: No, but your tone suggested you were building toward that characterization, and I want to be clear: I did what made sense given the circumstances. Nothing more.

Q: Dr. Pham, is it fair to say you handled the situation effectively?

A: It's fair to say everyone got out safely, which was the goal.

topic: A witness is questioned about a fire they discovered in a neighboring unit
text:
Q: When did you first realize there was a fire?

A: When I saw the flames.

Q: Just like that? No warning signs before?

A: Maybe there were warning signs. I wasn't looking for them.

Q: But you were the one who reported the fire, correct?

A: Yeah. I was coming back from walking my dog, and I saw the flames shooting out of the second-floor window. I called 911.

Q: What did you tell the dispatcher?

A: I said there was a fire at the Greenview Apartments, building C, second floor. I gave the address. I said it looked bad.

Q: You said it looked bad?

A: It did.

Q: And then what did you do?

A: I started yelling. Fire, fire, get out—like that. Running along the building, banging on doors.

Q: How many doors did you bang on?

A: I don't know, all of them. Five, six, however many there are on the ground floor. I was just going down the line.

Q: Did people respond?

A: Some did. Some opened their doors looking confused, and I told them to get out. One guy argued with me.

Q: Argued?

A: Said I was overreacting. I pointed at the flames coming out of the building, and then he stopped arguing.

Q: The responding firefighters noted in their report that most residents were already outside when they arrived.

A: Yeah. We didn't wait around.

Q: Because of your warning?

A: I don't know who got people out. I got some of them out. Other people were yelling too by that point. Does it matter who did what?

Q: I'm just trying to establish the sequence of events.

A: The sequence is: I saw fire, I called 911, I yelled, people got out, firefighters came. That's the sequence.

topic: A witness is questioned about a workplace injury they observed but did not report
text:
Q: Mr. Delgado, you were working in Warehouse C on the afternoon of September 14th, correct?

A: I was assigned there, yes.

Q: And at some point that afternoon, you observed an incident involving Marcus Webb?

A: I saw... I saw something happen, yes.

Q: What did you see?

A: Marcus was up on the racking system. The third level, I think. Maybe the second. And then he wasn't.

Q: He wasn't?

A: He was on the ground.

Q: Did you see him fall?

A: I saw him up there and then I saw him down. I don't know if I saw the actual—I mean, I must have, right? I was looking in that direction.

Q: I'm asking what you observed, Mr. Delgado.

A: I know. I'm trying to tell you. It happened fast. There was a sound, a kind of crash, and Marcus was on the concrete. Whether I actually watched him go down or just turned when I heard—I honestly couldn't swear to it either way.

Q: What did you do after Mr. Webb was on the ground?

A: I went over to him. A few of us did.

Q: And then?

A: And then... we helped him. Someone helped him.

Q: Did you report the incident to a supervisor?

A: I thought—see, this is where I'm not sure what you're asking exactly. Report it how? Like formally?

Q: Did you tell anyone in a supervisory role that Marcus Webb had fallen?

A: Dave Ostrowski came over. He saw Marcus on the ground same as the rest of us.

Q: So your answer is no, you did not report it?

A: My answer is that Dave was standing right there. I didn't think there was anything to report that he didn't already see with his own eyes.

topic: A witness is questioned about a workplace injury they observed but did not report
text:
Q: Ms. Thornton, how long have you worked at Prestige Manufacturing?

A: Seven years in April.

Q: And you were present on the production floor on March 3rd of this year?

A: I was.

Q: Tell me what you witnessed that day involving Darnell Price.

A: I saw Darnell get his hand caught.

Q: Caught in what?

A: The stamping press. The one at station twelve.

Q: Walk me through exactly what happened.

Q: What happened next?

Q: Now—and I want to be very precise here—did anyone call a supervisor?

A: Someone must have.

Q: Did you?

A: I was dealing with Darnell.

Q: So that's a no?

A: I was trying to stop the bleeding.

Q: Ms. Thornton, I understand you were helping Mr. Price. My question is whether you personally reported this incident to management.

A: I don't—I'm not following what you mean by "reported." We weren't hiding anything. Half the floor saw it happen.

Q: Did you fill out an incident report?

A: No.

Q: Did you tell a supervisor verbally?

A: I told you, I was with Darnell.

Q: At any point that day, did you communicate to anyone in management that an injury had occurred?

A: I assumed—I mean, with everyone standing around, with Darnell screaming—are you suggesting I was supposed to do something different?

Q: I'm simply asking what you did.

A: Then no. I guess no.

topic: A witness is questioned about a workplace injury they observed but did not report
text:
Q: You testified earlier that you saw the plaintiff slip on the loading dock.

A: That's right.

Q: What time was this?

A: Around two, two-fifteen.

Q: In the afternoon?

A: Yes.

Q: And this was during your shift?

A: Obviously, yes.

Q: Was there anything on the ground that caused him to slip?

A: There was water. Or some kind of liquid.

Q: You're not sure if it was water?

A: It was wet. The dock was wet.

Q: From what source?

A: I don't know. It had been raining earlier? Or maybe the sprinkler system, the one for the landscaping? I'm not—I didn't investigate it.

Q: Fair enough. Now, after Mr. Hendricks fell, what did you do?

A: I asked if he was okay.

Q: What did he say?

A: He said his back hurt.

Q: Did you help him up?

A: I offered. He got up on his own.

Q: And then?

A: And then we got back to work.

Q: You got back to work.

A: Yes.

Q: Mr. Hendricks told you his back hurt, and you both returned to work?

A: He said it hurt. He didn't say he couldn't work. I'm not a doctor. I don't—what was I supposed to do, carry him to the hospital?

Q: Did you consider that the wet surface might cause someone else to fall?

A: I... well, yes, I suppose I might have thought about it.

Q: Did you alert anyone to the hazard?

A: I thought Jerome would say something. It was more his area.

topic: A witness is questioned about a workplace injury they observed but did not report
text:
Q: Let's talk about what you saw on January 9th.

A: Okay.

Q: You were in the break room?

A: Yes.

Q: What happened there?

A: Linda came in holding her arm.

Q: Linda Vasquez, the plaintiff?

A: That's right.

Q: What was wrong with her arm?

A: It was burned. She said the steam line had burst.

Q: She told you a steam line burst?

A: Yes.

Q: Where?

A: In the kitchen. The main kitchen, where she worked.

Q: What did her burn look like?

A: Red. Blistered in one spot. It looked painful.

Q: What did you do?

A: I got her some ice from the freezer.

Q: Anything else?

A: I sat with her for a bit.

Q: Did you report this to anyone?

A: I—no.

Q: You didn't tell anyone that a steam line had burst and injured an employee?

A: Linda said she was going to tell Chef Morrison.

Q: Did you confirm that she did?

A: No.

Q: Did you follow up in any way?

A: Follow up how?

Q: Did you check whether the steam line was repaired? Whether management was aware?

A: That's not really my—I work in accounting. I don't have anything to do with kitchen equipment.

Q: But you knew there was a dangerous condition that had injured someone.

A: I knew Linda got hurt. I didn't—I mean, she said she would handle it. I took her at her word. Was I supposed to go over her head? I'm trying to understand what you're asking me.

Q: I'm asking whether you took any action to report what you learned.

A: And I'm telling you Linda said she would talk to Morrison. I didn't think it was my place.

topic: A witness is questioned about a workplace injury they observed but did not report
text:
Q: You witnessed the incident with Mr. Okonkwo?

A: Part of it.

Q: What part?

A: The aftermath, I guess you'd call it.

Q: Meaning what?

Q: Was the forklift running?

A: I don't remember.

Q: You don't remember if a forklift was running ten feet from where you stood?

A: I was looking at Emeka. I wasn't taking inventory of the equipment.

Q: Was anyone else present?

Q: Did he appear to be in pain?

A: He wasn't smiling about it.

A: Ray said he was going to get the first aid kit.

Q: What about calling a supervisor or safety officer?

A: I would have thought Ray—I mean, he's been there longer. He would know the procedure.

Q: Did you see him contact anyone?

A: He went to get the first aid kit. I don't know who he talked to on the way.

Q: Did you personally report what you saw?

A: I stayed with Emeka.

Q: That's not an answer to my question.

A: Then I guess—no, I didn't go report it.

Q: Why not?

topic: A financial advisor is deposed about investment decisions made on a client's behalf
text:
Q: Mr. Hartwell, let's talk about the Meridian Growth Fund. When did you first recommend that investment to Mrs. Patterson?

A: I'd have to check my notes for the exact date.

Q: Approximately.

A: Sometime in early 2021. January or February.

Q: And what was your basis for that recommendation?

A: The fund had strong historical returns, low expense ratios, and aligned with her stated risk tolerance.

Q: Her stated risk tolerance. Did you document that risk tolerance anywhere?

A: Yes. In the client intake forms and the investment policy statement.

Q: The investment policy statement you prepared?

A: That I prepared with her input, yes.

Q: Mr. Hartwell, I'm asking who prepared the document.

A: I prepared it. Based on information she provided. As I just said.

Q: And in that document, what risk category did you assign to Mrs. Patterson?

A: Moderate growth.

Q: Moderate growth. Yet the Meridian Fund was classified as aggressive growth, wasn't it?

A: It was classified that way by Morningstar. Our internal classification was different.

Q: So you had your own classification system that differed from industry standards?

A: We had a classification system that accounted for factors Morningstar doesn't weigh. That's not unusual. That's called doing our job.

Q: I didn't ask whether it was unusual, Mr. Hartwell.

A: Then perhaps you could ask what you actually want to know.

---

topic: A financial advisor is deposed about investment decisions made on a client's behalf

topic: A financial advisor is deposed about investment decisions made on a client's behalf

Q: Mr. Torres, were you aware that Greenleaf Capital was under SEC investigation when you recommended it to your clients?

topic: A paramedic is questioned about the response time and treatment at an accident scene
text:
Q: Could you please state your name and occupation for the record?

A: Michael Torres. I'm a paramedic with County Emergency Medical Services. Been there eleven years this August.

Q: Thank you. Mr. Torres, I'd like to ask you about the events of March 14th of this year. Were you on duty that evening?

A: I was. I was working the twelve-hour shift, started at seven p.m.

Q: And at some point that evening, you responded to a motor vehicle accident on Route 9?

A: That's correct. The call came in at approximately 9:47 p.m.

Q: Can you walk me through what happened after you received that call?

A: Sure. My partner and I were stationed at the Route 4 substation. We received the dispatch, acknowledged it, and proceeded to the scene. We arrived at 9:58 p.m.

Q: Eleven minutes from dispatch to arrival. Is that consistent with your usual response times for that area?

A: It is. Route 9 is about six miles from our station, and there's a stretch with limited shoulder access. Eleven minutes is well within our target window for that zone.

Q: What did you observe when you arrived?

A: Single vehicle, sedan, had left the roadway and struck a tree on the passenger side. The driver was conscious, still in the vehicle. A bystander was standing near the car. Fire department arrived maybe two minutes after we did.

Q: And the driver—that would be the plaintiff, Mrs. Kendall?

A: Yes. I learned her name later from her license, but yes.

Q: What was her condition when you first made contact?

A: She was alert and responsive. She was experiencing pain in her left shoulder and complained of dizziness. There was no visible bleeding, but given the mechanism of injury, we treated her as a potential spinal case until we could rule it out.

Q: You mentioned a bystander. Did that person provide any information?

A: He said he'd called 911 and had been talking to her through the window. He didn't move her, which was the right call. We thanked him and asked him to step back while we worked.

Q: At any point, did Mrs. Kendall ask why it took so long for you to arrive?

A: She did, actually. She asked something like, "What took you guys so long?" I explained the distance and that we'd arrived within our standard response time. She seemed to understand.

Q: How would you characterize her demeanor at that moment?

A: She was in pain and understandably shaken. But she was cooperative throughout.

topic: A paramedic is questioned about the response time and treatment at an accident scene
text:
Q: Paramedic Davis, you've reviewed the run report from May 3rd prior to today's deposition?

A: Yes, I reviewed it yesterday with counsel.

Q: Good. The dispatch log indicates the call was received at 2:14 p.m. Does that match your recollection?

A: It matches the report. I don't have an independent memory of the exact minute, but I have no reason to dispute the log.

Q: Fair enough. The report also shows arrival at 2:31 p.m. That's seventeen minutes. Can you explain what accounts for that time?

A: I can. We were returning from a prior call when the dispatch came through. We were not at our station; we were approximately nine miles from the accident location. Additionally, there was construction on Miller Road that required a detour.

Q: Did you document the construction detour anywhere?

A: It's noted in the narrative section of my report. I can point you to it if you'd like.

Q: That won't be necessary right now. When you arrived at the scene, what did you find?

A: Two-vehicle collision at the intersection. One vehicle had significant front-end damage. The other had rear-end damage. Two patients total. My partner took the driver of the first vehicle; I assessed the driver of the second.

Q: That would be Mr. Okonkwo?

A: Correct.

Q: What was his condition?

A: He was ambulatory when I approached but complained of neck pain and had visible bruising from the seatbelt across his chest. Standard protocol—I had him sit down, stabilized his neck, and began assessment.

Q: Did he express any concerns about the response time?

A: Not to me directly. He was focused on his vehicle and kept asking about the other driver.

Q: Did anyone at the scene express concerns about response time?

A: A woman who identified herself as a witness said something to the effect of, "I thought you'd never get here." I explained we'd come as quickly as we could given the circumstances.

Q: And how did she respond?

A: She didn't say anything else about it. She gave her information to the police officer and left.

topic: A paramedic is questioned about the response time and treatment at an accident scene
text:
Q: Let's talk about the treatment you provided. You've indicated you applied a cervical collar to the patient. At what point in your assessment did you make that decision?

A: Almost immediately. The mechanism of injury—a rollover—automatically triggers spinal precautions in our protocol. So the collar went on within the first two minutes of contact.

Q: Within the first two minutes. You're certain of that?

A: I am. It's one of the first things we do in that scenario.

Q: The plaintiff's expert has suggested that the collar was not applied until after the patient was moved to the stretcher. Do you have a response to that?

A: I would respectfully disagree with that characterization. The collar was applied while the patient was still seated in the vehicle. My partner can corroborate that, and it's consistent with our training.

Q: You seem quite sure.

A: I am sure. I've done this hundreds of times. The sequence is consistent.

Q: Let's move on. The patient was transported to Memorial Hospital, correct?

A: Correct.

Q: And the transport time was approximately twelve minutes?

A: That sounds right. Memorial was the closest Level II trauma center.

Q: During transport, what was the patient's status?

A: Stable. She remained conscious and responsive. Her vitals were within normal ranges. She continued to report neck pain, rated it a six out of ten.

Q: Did she say anything during transport that you recall?

A: She asked if she was going to be okay. I told her she was in good hands and that the hospital would take excellent care of her. She seemed reassured.

Q: Did you observe any change in her neurological status during transport?

A: No. She was moving all extremities, responding appropriately to questions. No deficits noted.

Q: When you transferred care to the hospital, did you communicate any concerns to the receiving team?

A: I gave a full report—mechanism of injury, vitals, treatment provided, patient complaints. Standard handoff. I didn't have concerns beyond what you'd expect from that type of accident.

topic: A paramedic is questioned about the response time and treatment at an accident scene
text:
Q: I want to go back to something you said earlier. You mentioned that when you arrived, there were already two bystanders performing CPR?

A: That's right.

Q: And how would you assess the quality of the CPR they were providing?

A: It was adequate. The compressions were a little shallow, but they had the right idea. They were alternating, which was smart. They'd been at it for maybe four or five minutes before we got there, based on what they told us.

Q: Did you take over immediately?

A: We did. I took over compressions while my partner prepared the AED and got the airway kit ready.

Q: Walk me through the next few minutes.

A: We continued CPR, applied the AED—it advised a shock—we delivered the shock, resumed compressions. After the second cycle, we had a pulse. Weak, but present.

Q: How long from your arrival until you detected that pulse?

A: Approximately six minutes. It's documented in the report.

Q: The family has raised questions about the twelve-minute response time. Do you have any thoughts on that?

A: I understand their concern. Twelve minutes can feel like a lifetime when someone you love is in distress. From a protocol standpoint, twelve minutes for a rural call with a cardiac arrest is within expected parameters. We came as fast as we safely could.

Q: Is there anything you would have done differently?

A: No. I've thought about it. The bystanders did their part, we did ours, and the patient survived. That's the outcome we work toward.

Q: The patient did survive, but with significant deficits. Do you believe earlier arrival would have changed that outcome?

A: I'm not a physician, so I can't speak to the medical prognosis. What I can say is that we followed protocol, and the chain of survival was maintained from the bystanders to us to the hospital.

Q: Fair enough. I have no further questions on this topic.

A: Understood.

topic: A paramedic is questioned about the response time and treatment at an accident scene
text:
Q: Paramedic Chen, when you arrived at the scene, the patient was trapped in the vehicle. Is that accurate?

A: Partially trapped. Her legs were pinned under the dashboard, but her upper body was accessible.

Q: And fire rescue was already on scene?

A: They arrived about a minute before we did. They were assessing the best approach for extrication when we pulled up.

Q: What was your role during the extrication?

A: I positioned myself at the driver's side window to monitor the patient and provide medical support while the firefighters worked on cutting the door.

Q: How long did the extrication take?

A: From the time we arrived to the time she was fully out of the vehicle, approximately fourteen minutes.

Q: During that time, what was the patient's status?

A: She was conscious for most of it. She was in significant pain—she told me her legs felt like they were on fire. I started an IV and administered pain medication per protocol. I talked to her throughout to keep her focused and to monitor her mental status.

Q: What did you talk to her about?

A: Anything to keep her engaged. I asked about her family, her job. She told me she was a teacher, third grade. She asked me if I thought she'd lose her legs. I told her we were going to do everything we could, and that she was being very brave.

Q: That must have been difficult.

A: It's part of the job. You stay focused on the patient and the task.

Q: Once she was extricated, what happened next?

A: We moved her to a backboard, loaded her into the ambulance, and transported to University Medical Center. They have the best trauma unit in the region for this type of injury.

Q: And her legs?

A: I don't have information about her long-term outcome. I know she was alive when we transferred her to the trauma team. Beyond that, I wasn't involved in her care.

Q: Thank you for your time today, Paramedic Chen.

A: Of course.

topic: A paramedic is questioned about the response time and treatment at an accident scene
text:
Q: Could you walk me through what you observed when you first arrived at the accident scene on March 14th?

A: Of course. We pulled up at approximately 2:47 PM, and I immediately saw a two-vehicle collision in the intersection. The sedan—a blue Honda—had significant front-end damage, and there was a pickup truck that had been pushed onto the curb. I grabbed my kit and headed straight for the Honda because I could see someone slumped against the steering wheel.

Q: And what did you find when you reached that vehicle?

A: The driver was a woman, maybe early thirties. She was conscious but disoriented—kept asking what happened, where her phone was. She had a laceration above her left eyebrow, blood running down her face, but she was breathing steadily. I talked to her the whole time, just trying to keep her calm while I assessed her injuries.

Q: You mentioned you talked to her. What kinds of things were you saying?

A: Oh, just reassurance mostly. Told her my name was Marcus, that I was there to help, that she was going to be okay. I find that helps—people are scared, you know? They need to hear a human voice telling them it's going to be alright.

Q: That's understandable. Now, regarding your response time—dispatch records show the call came in at 2:41 PM. Does a six-minute response time sound accurate to you?

A: That sounds about right, yes. We were actually finishing up a transport back to the station when the call came in, so we were maybe a mile and a half away. Got there as fast as we safely could.

Q: Would you say that was an unusually quick response for your unit?

A: I'd say we got lucky with positioning that day. Average in our district is probably eight to ten minutes, depending on traffic and distance. So yes, we were fortunate to be close by.

Q: I appreciate you explaining that context. Once you'd stabilized the woman in the Honda, what was your next step?

A: My partner Delia had already checked on the truck driver—he was shaken up but walking around, no visible injuries. We got the woman onto a stretcher, maintained cervical spine precautions just in case, and transported her to Riverside Memorial. Delia stayed with the truck driver until another unit could clear him.

Q: It sounds like you and your partner work well together.

A: Twelve years now. She's the best partner I've ever had. We don't even have to talk sometimes—just know what the other one's going to do.

Q: One last question for now: in your professional opinion, did the six-minute response time have any impact on the outcome for the Honda driver?

A: Honestly? I think every minute matters, but her injuries weren't life-threatening. The laceration needed stitches, she had a mild concussion. If we'd taken fifteen, twenty minutes, she still would've been okay. But I'm glad we got there when we did. She was scared, and nobody should have to sit in a wrecked car, bleeding, feeling alone.

---

topic: A paramedic is questioned about the response time and treatment at an accident scene
text:
Q: State your name and occupation for the record.

A: Teresa Vang, paramedic with County Fire and Rescue, Station 12.

Q: Ms. Vang, you responded to a motorcycle accident on Highway 9 on the evening of October 3rd, correct?

A: That's correct.

Q: What time did you arrive on scene?

A: 7:23 PM.

Q: And what time was the 911 call placed?

A: I believe it was 7:09.

Q: So fourteen minutes elapsed between the call and your arrival.

A: If those are the times, then yes.

Q: Does fourteen minutes strike you as an acceptable response time for a serious accident?

A: It depends on the circumstances.

Q: What circumstances would make fourteen minutes acceptable?

A: Distance, traffic conditions, weather, whether other units were already committed to other calls. That evening we were responding from across the district. There was also construction on Miller Road that forced us to reroute.

Q: I see. Let's talk about the construction. Did you report that delay to anyone?

A: It's documented in my incident report.

Q: You documented it because you knew the delay might be questioned later?

A: I documented it because that's my job. I document everything relevant to the response.

Q: Fair enough. Now, when you arrived, what was the condition of the motorcyclist?

A: He was lying on the shoulder, approximately twenty feet from his bike. A bystander had placed a jacket under his head. He was conscious, complaining of severe pain in his right leg and hip. There was visible deformity in the right femur.

Q: What did you do first?

A: I introduced myself, told him we were going to take care of him. Then I began my primary assessment while my partner retrieved the stretcher and splinting equipment.

Q: Did he say anything to you during that initial contact?

A: He asked if his leg was broken. I told him it looked like it, but we'd get him to the hospital and they'd take good care of him. He grabbed my hand and just held on for a minute. People do that sometimes. They just need something to hold onto.

Q: And you let him?

A: Of course I did. I wasn't going anywhere.

---

topic: A paramedic is questioned about the response time and treatment at an accident scene
text:
Q: Let's move to the treatment you provided in the ambulance. You started an IV, correct?

A: Correct.

Q: And administered morphine for pain?

A: Yes, 4 milligrams IV push, at approximately 3:15 PM.

Q: Was the patient in significant pain prior to that?

A: She was experiencing substantial discomfort, yes. She'd been in that vehicle for almost forty minutes before we could safely extricate her.

Q: Forty minutes is a long time to be trapped.

A: It is. The fire department had to cut through the B-pillar to get the door open. She was incredibly patient through the whole thing—just kept asking about her dog, whether someone had gotten her dog out of the back seat.

Q: Had someone?

A: First thing we did. My partner handed the dog off to a police officer before we even started the extrication. Little terrier mix, completely unharmed, just scared.

Q: Did you tell the patient her dog was safe?

A: Multiple times. I think it helped her stay calm more than anything else I could have done medically.

Q: Let's go back to the morphine. Who made the decision to administer it?

A: I did, in consultation with online medical control. Her blood pressure was stable, she wasn't showing signs of head trauma, and her pain level was—well, she was trying not to cry, but I could see it in her face.

Q: You could see what, exactly?

A: The way she was clenching her jaw, how she'd squeeze her eyes shut every time we hit a bump in the road. Some patients scream, some go quiet. She was the quiet type. But that doesn't mean they're hurting any less.

Q: Did the morphine help?

A: Within about five minutes, her whole body relaxed. She looked at me and said, "Oh, thank God." I told her we were about eight minutes out from the hospital and she was doing great.

Q: Is that something you typically tell patients? That they're doing great?

A: If they are, yes. And she was. She was doing everything right—staying still, staying calm, trusting us to get her through it.

Q: I notice you seem to remember this call quite vividly.

A: I remember most of my calls. But yes—she stayed with me. Some patients do.

---

topic: A paramedic is questioned about the response time and treatment at an accident scene
text:
Q: Mr. Okonkwo, you've been a paramedic for how long?

A: Seventeen years this coming April.

Q: And in those seventeen years, approximately how many accident scenes have you responded to?

A: I couldn't give you an exact number. Hundreds, certainly.

Q: Hundreds. So the accident on Birch Street in February—would that stand out to you, or was it routine?

A: No accident is routine to the people involved. But I understand what you're asking. It was a relatively straightforward response, yes.

Q: Walk me through what made it straightforward.

A: We arrived on scene within seven minutes of dispatch. Single-vehicle accident, driver had lost control and struck a telephone pole. Driver was outside the vehicle when we arrived, sitting on the curb. He had lacerations on his forearms from the airbag deployment—you see that sometimes with older airbag systems—but was otherwise alert and oriented.

Q: Did he require transport to the hospital?

A: We recommended it. The lacerations needed proper cleaning and possibly sutures, and I wanted him evaluated for any internal injuries that weren't immediately apparent.

Q: Did he agree to transport?

A: Not at first. He was worried about the cost, kept saying he felt fine, just wanted to go home.

Q: How did you handle that?

A: I sat down next to him on the curb. Not standing over him, not holding a clipboard—just sat down so we could talk at the same level. I told him I understood his concerns, that medical bills are a real worry for a lot of people. But I also told him that some of the most serious injuries don't show symptoms right away, and I'd feel a lot better if a doctor could look him over properly.

Q: That's not standard protocol, is it? Sitting on a curb with a patient?

A: I don't know that there's a protocol against it. I've found that people respond better when you come to them, rather than standing over them with a checklist.

Q: Did he ultimately agree to transport?

A: He did. And it turned out he had a small pneumothorax—partial collapsed lung from the impact. Nothing life-threatening at that moment, but it could have become serious if it had gone untreated.

Q: So your instinct was correct.

A: I'd say my training was correct. But I'm glad he listened.

Q: I imagine he is too.

A: Last I heard, he made a full recovery. Sent a card to the station a few weeks later. That doesn't happen often, but it means a lot when it does.

---

topic: A paramedic is questioned about the response time and treatment at an accident scene
text:
Q: You noted in your report that you arrived on scene at 11:42 PM.

A: That's correct.

Q: And the estimated time of the accident was approximately 11:15 PM?

A: That's what witnesses reported, yes.

Q: So nearly half an hour passed between the accident and your arrival.

A: I understand that sounds like a long time.

Q: Does it not concern you?

A: It concerns me greatly. But I want to explain the circumstances, if I may.

Q: Please.

A: The accident occurred on a rural stretch of County Road 7, about twelve miles from our station. The 911 call didn't come in until 11:31 because the accident wasn't witnessed immediately—a passing driver saw the vehicle in the ditch and stopped to investigate. We were dispatched at 11:32 and arrived in just under eleven minutes, which is actually faster than our average response to that area.

Q: So the delay was in reporting, not responding.

A: Exactly. And believe me, those are the calls that stay with me—wondering what might have been different if someone had seen it happen, if the call had come in sooner.

Q: What condition was the driver in when you arrived?

A: She was unconscious, still in the vehicle, with significant head trauma. We initiated rapid extrication and began treatment immediately. My partner managed the airway while I started bilateral IVs. We had her en route to the trauma center within eight minutes of arrival.

Q: Did she survive?

A: She did. Three weeks in the ICU, multiple surgeries, but she pulled through. I visited her once, after she was moved to a regular room.

Q: You visited her?

A: I don't usually do that—boundaries, you know. But her mother had called the station asking to thank whoever had responded that night. So I stopped by on my day off. Just for a few minutes.

Q: What did you talk about?

A: Honestly? She didn't remember any of it—the accident, the ambulance, nothing. But she held my hand and thanked me anyway. Her mother cried. I may have teared up a bit myself.

Q: That must have been meaningful to you.

A: This job takes a lot out of you. But moments like that—they give something back.

topic: A warehouse supervisor is deposed about safety protocols that were allegedly ignored
text:
Q: Mr. Dawson, how long have you been the warehouse supervisor at the Ridgeline facility?

A: Seventeen years. Seventeen years and four months, to be exact. Started as a forklift operator in 2007, worked my way up through every position in that building.

Q: And in your role as supervisor, you're responsible for implementing safety protocols?

A: I'm responsible for a lot more than just implementing them. I designed half the protocols we use. When I took over in 2015, our incident rate was one of the highest in the region. I brought it down to near zero within eighteen months. Built that safety program from the ground up.

Q: I'm asking specifically about the fall protection requirements for the mezzanine storage area.

A: Which I personally rewrote in 2019 after OSHA updated their guidelines. I didn't wait for corporate to hand down new procedures. I got ahead of it. Had our team trained before most facilities in the state even knew the regulations had changed.

Q: On March 14th of this year, were those fall protection requirements being followed?

A: Every single day I'm on that floor, I do a walkthrough. Every single day. I check harness stations, I check anchor points, I check signage. March 14th was no different.

Q: That wasn't my question. Were the requirements being followed on March 14th?

A: I just told you—I conducted my inspection that morning. Logged it at 6:47 AM, same as always. You can check the records. My records are impeccable.

Q: Did you observe Mr. Hernandez working on the mezzanine that morning?

A: I observe everyone. That's my job. That's what I do better than anyone who came before me in that position.

Q: Did you see whether Mr. Hernandez was wearing fall protection?

A: I saw him arrive for his shift. I saw him check in. I have systems in place—systems I created—to ensure compliance. If there was a lapse, it happened after my inspection window.

Q: So you didn't personally witness whether he was harnessed when he was working at height?

A: What I can tell you is that in seventeen years, I have never had a fatality in my warehouse. Never. Not until corporate started cutting my training budget.

Q: Mr. Dawson, I need you to answer the question I'm asking.

A: And I need you to understand the context. You don't build the kind of safety record I built by accident. You build it through dedication, through expertise, through years of doing things the right way when nobody's watching.

topic: A warehouse supervisor is deposed about safety protocols that were allegedly ignored
text:
Q: Ms. Trenton, you supervised the night shift at the Colby Road warehouse, correct?

A: That's correct.

Q: How many workers reported to you on a typical shift?

A: Between twelve and fifteen, depending on the season.

Q: Let's talk about the chemical storage procedures. Did you receive training on proper handling of hazardous materials?

A: I did. I also trained others. For three years, I was the one management brought in when new supervisors needed to learn the protocols. They'd pull me off my regular shifts to run those sessions.

Q: Who developed the training materials you used?

A: Corporate provided a baseline, but I'll be honest with you—it was inadequate. I supplemented it with my own documentation. Diagrams, checklists, scenario walkthroughs. I have copies if you'd like to see them.

Q: That won't be necessary at this time. On the night of the incident, November 8th, where were the chlorine tablets stored?

A: In the designated chemical storage area, Section C-7, per the protocol.

Q: Were they stored adjacent to any other chemicals?

A: Not adjacent. Separated by the required distance as specified in the SDS documentation. I know because I personally reorganized that section six months prior when I noticed the previous arrangement was technically compliant but not optimal.

Q: What do you mean by "not optimal"?

A: I mean the previous supervisor had done the bare minimum. Met the letter of the regulation but not the spirit. I believe in exceeding requirements, not just meeting them. So I restructured the entire chemical storage layout. Added secondary containment where it wasn't strictly required. Color-coded the shelving.

Q: Did anyone ask you to do that?

A: No. I did it because it was the right thing to do. Because I take my responsibilities seriously.

Q: On November 8th, were the ammonia-based cleaning supplies stored in Section C-7 as well?

A: Absolutely not. I kept those in the janitorial closet on the opposite side of the building. Specifically to prevent any possibility of cross-contamination.

Q: Our records indicate that ammonia supplies were found in Section C-7 the morning after the incident.

A: Then someone moved them after my shift ended. I can tell you with complete certainty they weren't there when I did my final walkthrough at 11:15 PM.

Q: How can you be certain?

A: Because I don't miss things like that. I've caught errors that three levels of management overlooked. You can ask anyone who's worked under me.

topic: A warehouse supervisor is deposed about safety protocols that were allegedly ignored

topic: A warehouse supervisor is deposed about safety protocols that were allegedly ignored
text:
