topic: A financial advisor is deposed about investment decisions made on a client's behalf
text:
Q: Good morning, Mr. Hartwell. I understand you've been managing the Peterson family accounts for quite some time now?

A: Good morning. Yes, it's been almost fifteen years. Arthur Peterson and I actually met through our kids' soccer league, if you can believe it. He trusted me with their retirement planning from the very beginning.

Q: That's a long relationship. Can you walk me through how you typically communicated with Mr. Peterson about investment decisions?

A: Of course. Arthur preferred phone calls—he's old school that way, didn't like email much. We'd talk at least once a month, sometimes more if markets were volatile. I always made sure he understood what I was recommending and why. He'd ask good questions too. Sharp man.

Q: And in those conversations, did you discuss the Meridian Energy Fund specifically?

A: We did, yes. I remember that conversation clearly because Arthur was excited about it. His grandson had just started an internship at a solar company, and Arthur wanted to support clean energy investments. It felt meaningful to him.

Q: So the investment aligned with his stated interests?

A: Absolutely. And I want to be clear—I also believed it was financially sound. I wouldn't have recommended it otherwise, regardless of the personal connection. Arthur trusted me to look out for his family's future, and I took that seriously.

Q: Did you explain the risks associated with the fund?

A: I did. We talked about sector concentration, the regulatory uncertainties in renewable energy at the time, all of it. Arthur asked specifically about downside scenarios—like I said, he was sharp. I told him my honest assessment.

Q: And what was that assessment?

A: That the risk-reward profile was favorable over a five-year horizon, but there could be bumps along the way. He understood that. He'd been through market cycles before.

Q: After the fund declined, did Mr. Peterson express any concerns to you?

A: He called me, yes. He was disappointed, of course. But Arthur—he didn't blame me. He said, "We made the decision together, and I still believe in what we were trying to do." That meant a lot to me.

Q: Did you offer to adjust the portfolio at that point?

A: I did. We discussed several options. Arthur decided to hold the position, which I supported. He wasn't someone who panicked at paper losses. I admired that about him, honestly.

topic: A financial advisor is deposed about investment decisions made on a client's behalf
text:
Q: Ms. Reyes, I want to ask you about the Chen account. When did you first become their advisor?

A: March of 2019.

Q: And how would you describe your relationship with Dr. and Mrs. Chen?

A: Professional.

Q: Just professional?

A: I'm not sure what you're asking.

Q: Let me rephrase. Did you have regular contact with them outside of formal meetings?

A: We had quarterly reviews. Sometimes they'd call between meetings if they had questions. That's standard.

Q: Did Mrs. Chen ever express concerns about the aggressive allocation you recommended?

A: She asked questions, yes. That's appropriate.

Q: Questions or concerns?

A: Questions. She wanted to understand the strategy. I explained it. She was satisfied.

Q: Take your time if you need to think about this—I'm not trying to rush you. Did she ever specifically mention worry about losing principal?

A: I appreciate that. Let me think. She mentioned once that her mother had lost money in the market during the 2008 crisis. She wanted to make sure they were protected.

Q: And how did you respond to that?

A: I listened. I took her concern seriously. We adjusted the bond allocation by about ten percent to give her more peace of mind. That's documented in the file.

Q: That sounds like a thoughtful response. Was Dr. Chen involved in that decision?

A: He deferred to his wife on most financial matters, actually. He was busy with his practice. But yes, I made sure they both signed off on any changes. I wanted them both comfortable.

Q: I appreciate your thoroughness. One more question—did you ever recommend investments that weren't in their stated risk tolerance?

A: No. Never. I cared about getting this right for them.

topic: A financial advisor is deposed about investment decisions made on a client's behalf
text:
Q: State your name for the record.

A: Thomas Brennan.

Q: Mr. Brennan, you managed the Okonkwo trust, correct?

A: I did. For six years, until Mrs. Okonkwo passed.

Q: I'm sorry—I know this may involve some difficult memories. We can take breaks if needed.

A: Thank you. I'm alright. Grace was a remarkable woman. I'd like to help clarify whatever I can.

Q: Can you tell me about the investment philosophy you developed for her trust?

A: Grace had very clear wishes. The trust was primarily for her grandchildren's education. She wanted growth, but she was adamant—no investments in tobacco, firearms, or private prisons. Those were her words exactly.

Q: And you honored those restrictions?

A: To the letter. I actually created a custom screen for her account. It was extra work, but it mattered to her, so it mattered to me.

Q: The family has raised questions about the Apex Global Fund. Can you address that?

A: I understand their concern, and I'm glad to clear it up. Apex passed our initial screen. Six months later, they acquired a subsidiary with defense contracts. The moment I found out—and I found out within days—I contacted Grace.

Q: What did she say?

A: She said, "Thomas, get me out of it." So I did. There was a small redemption fee, which I paid out of my own commission. She never asked me to do that.

Q: Why did you do that?

A: Because it was the right thing. Grace trusted me to protect what she cared about. A few hundred dollars wasn't worth compromising that.

Q: Did you document this conversation?

A: I did. I sent her a follow-up letter summarizing our call and the steps I'd taken. I have a copy if you'd like to see it.

Q: That would be helpful, thank you. How did Mrs. Okonkwo respond to your handling of this situation?

A: She sent me a handwritten note. I still have it. She said I'd restored her faith in the financial industry. That's probably the proudest moment of my career.

topic: A financial advisor is deposed about investment decisions made on a client's behalf
text:
Q: Mr. Castellano, how long have you been a financial advisor?

A: Twenty-two years next month.

Q: You've seen a lot of market cycles then.

A: More than I'd like, honestly. Each one teaches you something.

Q: Let's talk about the Whitfield account. You recommended a significant position in emerging market bonds in early 2021?

A: I did. Around eighteen percent of their portfolio.

Q: That's a substantial allocation. Walk me through your reasoning.

A: The Whitfields had a ten-year horizon, solid income, and they'd specifically told me they wanted to diversify internationally. Emerging market bonds offered attractive yields with manageable duration risk, given their timeline.

Q: Did you consider that they were approaching retirement?

A: They weren't approaching retirement—James was fifty-one, Linda was forty-eight. They both planned to work until at least sixty-five. Ten to fifteen years is a long runway.

Q: Fair point. I appreciate the correction. When the bonds declined in value, how did you handle that conversation?

A: I called them before they even saw the statements. I believe in getting ahead of bad news, not hiding from it.

Q: That must have been a difficult call.

A: It was. But James actually thanked me for calling directly. He said too many advisors disappear when things go south.

Q: What did you recommend at that point?

A: We talked through three options—hold, reduce, or eliminate the position. I gave them my honest view, which was that the fundamentals hadn't changed, but I also said I'd support whatever decision helped them sleep at night.

Q: And their decision?

A: They held. Linda was nervous, but James felt strongly about staying the course. They made that decision together, and I documented it carefully.

Q: Looking back, do you stand by the original recommendation?

A: I do. I genuinely believed it was right for them, and I still believe the process was sound. Markets don't always cooperate with good analysis, but that doesn't mean the analysis was wrong.

topic: A financial advisor is deposed about investment decisions made on a client's behalf
text:
Q: Ms. Franklin, you've been very patient today. I just have a few more questions about the Morrison account.

A: Of course. Take whatever time you need.

Q: The Morrisons claim they were never informed about the fee structure for the alternative investments. How do you respond to that?

A: I understand why they might feel that way now, but I have a different recollection. I walked them through the fee schedule in our second meeting. I even highlighted the management fees and carried interest on the document. Richard initialed next to those sections.

Q: Do you have that document?

A: I do. I keep very thorough records. It's something my first mentor taught me—"document like someone's watching," she used to say. She was right.

Q: That's good practice. The Morrisons seem to feel they didn't fully understand what they were signing.

A: That troubles me to hear. I always encouraged questions. I told them—and I tell all my clients—there's no such thing as a stupid question when it comes to your money. I meant that sincerely.

Q: Did Mrs. Morrison ask many questions during your meetings?

A: She did, actually. She was very engaged. She asked about liquidity specifically, and I explained the lock-up period in detail. She seemed comfortable with it at the time.

Q: Is it possible she was uncomfortable but didn't express it?

A: I suppose anything's possible. But I tried to create an environment where they felt safe raising concerns. I'm not a salesperson—I'm an advisor. There's a difference, and it matters to me.

Q: If you could go back and do anything differently with this account, would you?

A: I've thought about that. I might have followed up with a written summary after that meeting, just to give them something to review at home. I do that with all clients now.

Q: That sounds like a reasonable adjustment.

A: We learn from every relationship. Even the difficult ones. Especially the difficult ones.

Q: Thank you for your candor, Ms. Franklin.

A: Thank you for being fair in your questions. I know we're on different sides here, but I appreciate how you've conducted this.

topic: A contractor is questioned about delays that caused a construction project to fail
text:
Q: Mr. Castellano, you were the general contractor for the Riverside Commons project, correct?

A: I was. And I did my job.

Q: I didn't ask whether you did your job. I asked whether you were the general contractor.

A: And I answered. Yes.

Q: The project was scheduled for completion in March of 2023, wasn't it?

A: That was the original date, which changed multiple times, as everyone involved knew perfectly well.

Q: I'm asking about the original contracted date. March 2023. Yes or no?

A: Yes. March 2023. The date your client agreed to and then made impossible.

Q: Mr. Castellano, I'm going to ask you to answer only the question posed.

A: I am answering the question. You want context removed so you can build whatever story you're building. I'm not going to help you do that.

Q: Did construction begin on schedule in April 2022?

A: We broke ground April 4th. Right on time. My crews were ready. The site was not.

Q: What do you mean the site was not ready?

A: I mean your client hadn't finished remediation. We had crews standing around for eleven days waiting for clearance. You want to talk about delays? Start there.

Q: So your testimony is that the owner caused the initial delay?

A: My testimony is the truth. Make of it what you will.

Q: Were you ever informed in writing that remediation was incomplete?

A: I didn't need it in writing. I had eyes. I had soil reports. I had a crew that couldn't dig because the ground was contaminated.

Q: That's not what I asked. Were you informed in writing?

A: No. Because your client didn't want a paper trail.

topic: A contractor is questioned about delays that caused a construction project to fail
text:
Q: Ms. Thornton, how long have you been working in commercial construction?

A: Twenty-two years.

Q: And in those twenty-two years, have you ever had a project fail to reach completion?

A: Define "fail."

Q: Abandoned. Terminated. Left unfinished.

A: Once. This one.

Q: Let's talk about the timeline. When did you first realize the project was in trouble?

A: September 2022. Maybe late August.

Q: What indicated to you that there were problems?

A: Payments stopped.

Q: Payments from whom?

A: From the developer. Hartfield Properties. They owed us for August draws. Nothing came.

Q: Did you inquire about the missing payments?

A: Of course I did. I called Marcus Webb every day for two weeks.

Q: And what did Mr. Webb tell you?

A: First it was "processing delays." Then it was "cash flow timing." Then he stopped taking my calls.

Q: So you continued working without payment?

A: For a while. I had subcontractors who needed to feed their families. I floated what I could.

Q: At what point did you stop work?

A: October 14th. When I'd burned through my reserves and had nothing left to float.

Q: And you believe the project failed because of payment issues, not construction delays?

A: I know it did. I've got three filing cabinets of documentation. You want to see them, counselor, or would you rather keep pretending this was my fault?

topic: A contractor is questioned about delays that caused a construction project to fail
text:
Q: Mr. Okonkwo, let me direct your attention to the change order dated June 15th.

A: Which one? There were four change orders that week alone.

Q: Exhibit 14. The structural modifications to the east wing.

A: All right. I see it.

Q: This change order added approximately six weeks to the project timeline, didn't it?

A: It added time. I don't recall the exact figure.

Q: The document in front of you states six weeks. Is that incorrect?

A: If that's what it says.

Q: I'm asking if it's accurate, Mr. Okonkwo. You signed this document.

A: I signed a lot of documents. Your client's architect kept redesigning mid-construction. I signed whatever was put in front of me to keep the project moving.

Q: So you're saying you signed documents without reviewing them carefully?

A: No, counselor. I'm saying when you have an architect who changes his mind every week and an owner who can't make a decision, you spend less time reviewing paperwork and more time trying to keep your crews employed.

Q: Let's focus on this specific change order—

A: Let's. Six weeks for structural modifications because the architect decided load-bearing walls were in the wrong place. That wasn't my call. That wasn't my delay.

Q: I haven't accused you of anything, Mr. Okonkwo.

A: You've been accusing me since we sat down. You're just being polite about it.

topic: A contractor is questioned about delays that caused a construction project to fail
text:
Q: I want to understand your relationship with the subcontractors on this project.

A: What about it?

Q: You hired Brennan Electric, correct?

A: Correct.

Q: And Brennan Electric walked off the job in November 2022?

A: They did.

Q: Why?

A: Because they weren't getting paid. Same as everyone else.

Q: Were you responsible for paying the subcontractors?

A: I was responsible for paying them with money I received from the owner. Money I did not receive.

Q: So you're testifying that Hartfield Properties failed to provide funds?

A: I'm testifying to what happened. Draw your own conclusions.

Q: Mr. Vance, I'm asking you directly.

A: And I'm answering you directly. I can't pay people with money I don't have.

Q: Did you notify the owner that subcontractors were leaving?

A: Multiple times. In writing. I have copies of every letter and email.

Q: And what was the response?

A: The response was silence. Then, three months later, the response was this lawsuit blaming me for everything.

Q: You sound frustrated, Mr. Vance.

A: Do I? Imagine that.

Q: I'm simply observing—

A: Observe whatever you want. Are we going to discuss the actual facts of what happened, or are we going to keep dancing around your client's failures?

topic: A contractor is questioned about delays that caused a construction project to fail
text:
Q: Let's go back to the permit delays. You mentioned those in your earlier answer.

A: I mentioned them because they're relevant.

Q: The city held up permits for the foundation work, is that right?

A: For three months, yes.

Q: And during that time, what was your crew doing?

A: Waiting. Sitting on their hands. Losing money.

Q: Did you attempt to expedite the permit process?

A: What do you think?

Q: I'm asking what you did, Mr. Lucero.

A: I made seventeen calls to the building department. I went down there in person four times. I filed every form they asked for, some of them twice because they kept losing paperwork.

Q: And the delay was still three months?

A: It was. And you know why? Because the owner submitted incomplete site plans. Because the engineer your client hired made errors that had to be corrected. Because I was cleaning up someone else's mess while the clock ran.

Q: Are you saying the permit delays were entirely the owner's fault?

A: I'm saying I don't control the city. I don't control your client's engineers. I control my crews, my materials, and my schedule. All three were ready. We waited because other people weren't.

Q: Mr. Lucero, we're going to be here for a while. I'd appreciate more cooperative answers.

A: I'd appreciate questions that aren't designed to make me the scapegoat. We all have our disappointments.

topic: A witness is questioned about a fire they discovered in a neighboring unit
text:
Q: Please state your name for the record.

A: Michael Tran. T-R-A-N.

Q: Mr. Tran, on the evening of March 14th, you were home in your apartment at 4215 Crane Street, Unit B, correct?

A: Yes.

Q: What time did you first become aware something was wrong?

A: I think—I want to say around 9:15? It might have been 9:20. I remember looking at the microwave clock but I'm not certain I'm remembering it right. Somewhere in that range.

Q: That's fine. What drew your attention?

A: The smell. I smelled something. Burning. Like electrical, maybe? Or plastic? I don't know exactly what it was, I'm not—I couldn't tell you the chemical composition or anything, I just knew something was burning.

Q: What did you do when you smelled the burning?

A: I walked around my apartment first. Checked the kitchen, checked the outlets. I have a power strip by my desk and sometimes—well, it's old, I thought maybe—but it wasn't that.

Q: Then what?

A: Then I went to my front door. I opened it. And I could see the smoke. It was coming from under their door. Unit A.

Q: The Petersons' unit?

A: Yes. I mean, I assume—I don't know whose name is on the lease, but that's who lives there. Lived there.

Q: What did the smoke look like?

A: Gray. Dark gray, getting darker. It was—there was a lot of it. More than I expected. I don't know what I expected.

Q: Did you approach their door?

A: I knocked. I knocked and I yelled. I don't remember exactly what I yelled. "Fire," probably. "Get out." Something like that. Then I called 911. I should have called first, maybe. I don't know the right order for something like that.

Q: Did anyone answer when you knocked?

A: No. Nobody answered. I kept knocking until the smoke got too thick and then I—I left. I went outside. I'm sorry, is that what you needed to know? I'm trying to remember it correctly.

Q: You're doing fine, Mr. Tran. Did you see any flames at that point?

A: Not then. Not until later, when I was outside. Then I saw them in the window. But by then the fire department was almost there, I think. I'm not sure of the exact timing anymore.

---

topic: A witness is questioned about a fire they discovered in a neighboring unit
text:
Q: You discovered the fire at approximately what time?

A: Just after 11 PM.

Q: Let's slow down. I need you to be precise. How do you know it was just after 11?

A: I had just turned off the television. The news had ended.

Q: The news ends at 11 or 11:30 in your market?

A: Eleven.

Q: Fine. So the news ended. What happened next?

A: I heard glass breaking.

Q: From where?

A: Next door. Unit 7.

Q: You're certain it came from Unit 7 and not outside, not from the parking lot?

A: It came from the wall. My wall.

Q: The shared wall between your unit and Unit 7?

A: Yes.

Q: What did you do?

A: I went to check. I went out to the hallway.

Q: Immediately?

A: Yes.

Q: You didn't wait, didn't hesitate?

A: No. I heard glass break, I went to check. That's what happened.

Q: When you reached the hallway, what did you observe?

A: Smoke under their door. Orange light in the peephole when I looked. I could see it flickering.

Q: You looked through their peephole?

A: No, I could see the light around the door frame. Through the crack at the bottom.

Q: So you didn't actually look through the peephole?

A: I just said I didn't.

Q: I want to make sure the record is clear, Ms. Delgado.

A: The record is clear. I saw light under the door. Orange, flickering. Fire.

Q: Did you attempt to enter Unit 7?

A: No.

Q: Did you knock? Call out?

A: I knocked. I yelled. Nobody came.

Q: How many times did you knock?

A: I don't know. Several. Does it matter? There was a fire.

---

topic: A witness is questioned about a fire they discovered in a neighboring unit
text:
Q: Good morning. Could you describe your relationship with the occupants of Unit 12?

A: We were neighbors. Friendly enough. We'd say hello in the hallway.

Q: Did you know them by name?

A: Sandra. I knew her name was Sandra. The husband, I'm not sure—Jim? James? Something like that.

Q: That's fine. Now, I want to direct your attention to the night of the fire. May 3rd.

A: Okay.

Q: You were the one who called 911, correct?

A: I was.

Q: Before you called, what did you observe?

A: I—well, let me think. I want to make sure I tell you this right. I was in my bathroom. I heard what I thought was—it was a popping sound. Several of them. Pop, pop, pop. And I thought, that's strange, because it was late, almost midnight.

Q: What did you do?

A: I finished what I was doing and I came out and that's when I noticed the smell.

Q: What kind of smell?

A: Smoke. Definitely smoke. And something else, something chemical. Sharp.

Q: Did you investigate the source?

A: I opened my front door. The hallway was—there was a haze. Not thick yet, but visible. And it was coming from their end. From 12.

Q: What did you do then?

A: I went down there. To their door.

Q: You approached their door?

A: Yes. I knocked. Loudly. I said, "Sandra? Sandra, are you in there?" No answer.

Q: Did you try the door handle?

A: I—yes. It was hot.

Q: Hot to the touch?

A: Very. I pulled my hand back. That's when I knew it was serious. That's when I called 911.

Q: How long did you stay in the hallway?

A: Not long. Maybe a minute after the call? The smoke was getting worse. I went back to my unit and then outside to wait for the fire department. I kept thinking I should have knocked longer. I don't know if it would have mattered.

---

topic: A witness is questioned about a fire they discovered in a neighboring unit
text:
Q: I want to get the timeline exactly right here. You said you first noticed the smoke at 7:45 PM?

A: Around then, yes.

Q: Around then. Can you be more specific?

A: I don't know the exact minute. I wasn't looking at a clock.

Q: But it was before 8 PM?

A: Yes. Definitely before 8.

Q: How can you be certain?

A: Because my show starts at 8 and I hadn't turned on the TV yet.

Q: Alright. Good. Now, the smoke—where was it coming from?

A: The vent. The bathroom vent.

Q: Smoke was coming through your bathroom vent?

A: That's what I said.

Q: And that vent connects to the neighboring unit's system?

A: I assume so. I'm not an engineer. I don't know how the building is designed.

Q: But you believed the smoke was coming from next door?

A: Where else would it come from?

Q: I'm asking what you believed at the time, Mr. Okonkwo.

A: Yes. I believed it was coming from next door.

Q: What did you do?

A: I went over there. Apartment 4C. I knocked.

Q: Did someone answer?

A: No. I knocked again. I could hear something—a crackling sound.

Q: Crackling?

A: Yes. Like—you know what fire sounds like. That sound.

Q: What did you do then?

A: I tried the door. It was locked. I called out, I said, "Is anyone in there? There's smoke, you need to get out." Nothing. So I called 911 and I got the other neighbors out.

Q: You evacuated the other units?

A: Someone had to. The alarm wasn't going off yet. People didn't know.

---

topic: A witness is questioned about a fire they discovered in a neighboring unit
text:
Q: Ms. Chen, I understand this is difficult. Take your time.

A: Thank you.

Q: When did you first realize there was a fire in the adjacent unit?

A: It was—I don't know exactly. I was asleep.

Q: Something woke you?

A: The dog. My dog was barking.

Q: What time was this?

A: Three, three-thirty in the morning. I looked at my phone.

Q: And the dog's barking woke you. What happened next?

A: I got up to quiet her down. She was by the door, by the front door, and she wouldn't stop. She was—she doesn't bark like that normally.

Q: Did you notice anything unusual at that point?

A: The floor was warm.

Q: The floor?

A: Near the door. The floor was warm. And I could smell—it's hard to describe. It was acrid. Burning.

Q: What did you do?

A: I opened the door. Just a crack. And there was smoke in the hallway. A lot of smoke.

Q: Could you see the source?

A: It was coming from 2B. Right next to me. The door had smoke pouring out from the top, from around the edges.

Q: Did you see flames?

A: Not then. Just smoke. Black smoke.

Q: What did you do?

A: I grabbed the dog and I—I should have knocked, I know I should have knocked on their door, but the smoke was so thick and I couldn't—I just ran. I went down the stairs and outside.

Q: Did you call for help?

A: I called 911 from the parking lot. I was—my hands were shaking. I could barely dial.

Q: Did you see anyone exit the building?

A: Some people came out after me. The Nguyens from downstairs. But I didn't see anyone from 2B. I kept watching for them but they never came out. I should have knocked. I know I should have knocked.

Q: You were describing what you observed, Ms. Chen. That's what we need.

A: I know. I know. I'm sorry. I just keep thinking about it.

topic: A building inspector is deposed about a structural assessment they signed off on
text:
Q: Mr. Harmon, you conducted the structural assessment of the Ridgeline Apartments on March 14th, 2022, correct?

A: I did, yes, and I have to say, that building was one of the more interesting inspections I'd done that quarter. The original construction was 1967, post-tensioned concrete, which you don't see as often in residential—

Q: Mr. Harmon, I just need a yes or no on that.

A: Yes. Absolutely yes.

Q: And you signed off on the assessment indicating the structure was sound?

A: I did, and I stand by that completely. The load-bearing walls, the foundation, the lateral support systems—everything was exactly where it needed to be. Better than a lot of buildings half its age, frankly.

Q: Did you examine the parking structure as part of that assessment?

A: Oh, extensively. That was actually the highlight, if I can call it that. The parking structure had this really well-designed drainage system that prevented the kind of water infiltration you typically see degrading rebar in coastal environments. Whoever designed that in '67 knew what they were doing.

Q: So you found no issues with the parking structure?

A: None worth noting. Minor surface spalling on the northwest corner, which I documented, but structurally? Solid as a rock. I actually took extra photos because I wanted to use it as an example for some of the newer inspectors on my team.

Q: You train other inspectors?

A: When I can, yes. Thirty-two years in this field, you accumulate knowledge that deserves to be passed on. The Ridgeline parking structure is a perfect teaching case for how proper waterproofing extends structural life.

Q: Let's focus on the assessment itself. How long were you on site?

A: Four hours and—let me check my notes—four hours and twenty minutes. Longer than typical, but I was thorough. I always am, but this building deserved the extra attention.

Q: Did anyone accompany you during the inspection?

A: The building manager, Patricia Vance, for the first hour. Wonderful woman, very knowledgeable about the building's history. After that, I continued alone. I prefer it that way, actually—lets me focus entirely on the structural elements without distraction.

Q: And your final report contained no recommendations for remediation?

A: Just routine maintenance items. Seal that minor spalling I mentioned, inspect the expansion joints annually—standard best practices. The building was in excellent condition. I remember telling Patricia that the owners should be proud of how well it had been maintained.

topic: A building inspector is deposed about a structural assessment they signed off on
text:
Q: Ms. Delacroix, I want to walk through your inspection methodology step by step. Are you ready to do that?

A: If you'd like.

Q: Excellent! Let's start with the foundation. What tools did you use to assess the foundation at 445 Commerce Street?

A: A visual inspection. Moisture meter. Standard practice.

Q: Just those two? No ground-penetrating radar, no core sampling?

A: Those aren't required under the municipal code.

Q: But they're available to you, aren't they? Your firm owns that equipment?

A: We do.

Q: And yet for a building that's now showing significant settling, you chose not to deploy more advanced diagnostic tools. Fascinating choice, wouldn't you say?

A: I followed protocol.

Q: Protocol! Let's talk about protocol. Section 4.2.3 of your own firm's inspection manual—I have it right here, I was so pleased to find this—states that ground-penetrating radar "should be considered" for buildings over fifty years old. 445 Commerce was built in 1968. Help me understand your thinking.

A: "Should be considered" is discretionary language.

Q: So you considered it and rejected it?

A: I made a professional judgment based on what I observed.

Q: What did you observe that made you comfortable skipping that step?

A: No visible cracking. No water damage. No signs of differential settlement at that time.

Q: At that time. But now there's two inches of differential settlement on the east side. Does that surprise you, Ms. Delacroix?

A: I can't speak to current conditions.

Q: Oh, but I think you can! You inspected this building. You signed your name to it. Let me show you Exhibit 14—these are the current engineering reports. Take your time. I want you to really look at these numbers.

A: I see them.

Q: Two inches. In eighteen months. Your assessment gave this building a clean bill of health. How do you reconcile that?

A: Conditions change.

topic: A building inspector is deposed about a structural assessment they signed off on
text:
Q: Mr. Okonkwo, how many structural assessments have you conducted in your career?

A: I'd have to estimate, but somewhere in the range of two thousand. Give or take.

Q: And of those two thousand, how many have later been called into question?

A: This is the first.

Q: The first. That's a strong track record.

A: I take my work seriously. Every inspection, I approach it like it's the only one that matters. Because to the people living or working in that building, it is the only one that matters.

Q: That's a commendable philosophy.

A: It's just the truth. When I walk into a structure, I'm thinking about the family on the third floor, the business owner on the ground level. Real people depending on me to get it right. That's not something I take lightly.

Q: Let's apply that philosophy to the Westbrook Office Complex. You inspected it in August 2021?

A: August 17th, yes. Beautiful building, actually. Mid-century modern design with some really thoughtful engineering choices. The cantilevered sections were impressive for the era.

Q: You noted in your report that the building was structurally sound.

A: Because it was. I spent six hours there, Mr. Ashworth. I walked every floor. I examined every load-bearing element I could access. I reviewed the original blueprints, which the management company was kind enough to provide. That building was solid.

Q: So when the fourth-floor ceiling collapsed nine months later—

A: That was a water damage issue from a roof failure, not a structural deficiency. Two different things entirely.

Q: Help me understand the distinction.

A: Gladly! A structural assessment evaluates the integrity of the building's skeleton—the bones, if you will. Foundation, framing, load paths. What happened at Westbrook was a roofing membrane failure that allowed water infiltration over time, which then degraded ceiling materials. That's a maintenance failure, not a structural one. My assessment was accurate on the day I conducted it.

Q: You seem confident about that distinction.

A: I am. Because I understand what I was hired to evaluate and what falls outside that scope. Roofing conditions weren't part of my engagement. I actually recommended they have a roofing specialist take a look—it's in my report, page seven.

topic: A building inspector is deposed about a structural assessment they signed off on
text:
Q: State your full name for the record.

A: David Chen-Ramirez.

Q: And your occupation?

A: Licensed building inspector. Commercial and residential.

Q: Mr. Chen-Ramirez, I'm going to show you what's been marked as Exhibit 7. Do you recognize this document?

A: Yes.

Q: What is it?

A: My structural assessment report for the Millbrook Heights development.

Q: Dated when?

A: November 3rd, 2022.

Q: On page four, you note that the building's lateral bracing system meets code requirements. Do you see that?

A: I see it.

Q: Now I'm going to show you Exhibit 8. This is a report from Dr. Sandra Oyelaran, a structural engineer retained by my client. She concludes that the lateral bracing was undersized by approximately fifteen percent. How do you respond to that?

A: I'd need to review her methodology.

Q: She used the same code provisions you cite in your report.

A: Then I'd want to see her calculations. Different engineers can reach different conclusions depending on assumptions about load factors, occupancy classifications—

Q: So you're saying Dr. Oyelaran might be wrong?

A: I'm saying I'd need to see her work before I could comment.

Q: Fair enough! I love that. Let's look at her work together, then. Turn to page twelve of Exhibit 8. She walks through her calculations right there. Take your time.

A: I see it.

Q: What do you notice?

A: Her assumptions about wind load appear to use a higher exposure category than I used.

Q: Why would that be?

A: Possibly because—I'd have to look at the surrounding terrain data she relied on.

Q: She's using the same terrain data your firm uses. We confirmed that.

A: Then I don't have an immediate explanation.

Q: Would you like more time to review this? I'm happy to wait. This is important stuff.

A: That might be helpful, yes.

Q: Take all the time you need. Really. I want you to be comfortable with your answer.

topic: A building inspector is deposed about a structural assessment they signed off on
text:
Q: Mr. Patterson, did you personally inspect the basement level of 200 Industrial Parkway?

A: Every square foot of it. Got my boots muddy doing it too—there was about an inch of standing water in the mechanical room, which I documented.

Q: You found standing water and still passed the structure?

A: Standing water isn't automatically a structural concern. It can be plumbing, it can be drainage, it can be groundwater intrusion. I noted it in my report and recommended they bring in a waterproofing specialist. My job was structural integrity, and structurally, that basement was sound.

Q: How did you assess the foundation walls with standing water present?

A: Same way I always do. I looked for cracking patterns, efflorescence, bowing, any signs of hydrostatic pressure damage. The walls were poured concrete, twelve inches thick, with proper footing drains. The water was coming from a failed sump pump, not foundation failure.

Q: You determined the source of the water during a structural inspection?

A: I determined the likely source, yes. Twenty-six years of experience, you develop an eye for these things. But I also put it in writing that they needed further evaluation from the appropriate specialist. I'm thorough, but I know my lane.

Q: Let's talk about the east wall specifically.

A: Oh, the east wall was actually in remarkable condition for a building that age. 1954 construction, and the original waterproofing was still doing its job along that elevation. I remember thinking someone made smart choices during the original build.

Q: My client alleges that wall has since shown significant deterioration.

A: I can only speak to what I observed on October 9th, 2021. On that date, that wall showed no signs of structural compromise.

Q: None whatsoever?

A: Minor cosmetic cracking consistent with normal curing shrinkage. Nothing that would concern me. I have photographs, if you'd like to see them.

Q: We'll get to those. You took photographs of the east wall specifically?

A: I take photographs of everything. Minimum of two hundred per inspection. I learned early in my career that documentation protects everyone—the client, the building owner, and me. That east wall? I probably have fifteen or twenty shots of it from different angles. Happy to walk you through every single one.

topic: A supervisor is deposed about performance reviews given to an employee who was later fired
text:
Q: Mr. Hartley, you conducted performance reviews for Ms. Chen during the period she reported to you, correct?

Q: I'm asking specifically about Ms. Chen.

A: And I'm telling you, yes, she was one of my direct reports, so yes, I reviewed her. Along with eleven other people.

Q: Let's look at her 2022 annual review. You gave her a rating of "meets expectations." Do you see that?

Q: Were you surprised when you learned she'd been terminated?

A: Surprised isn't the word I'd use.

Q: What word would you use?

A: I wasn't consulted. So I didn't have an opinion one way or the other.

A: I'm telling you what I'm telling you. You can write it down however you want.

Q: Did you believe Ms. Chen was a poor performer in 2022?

A: My review speaks for itself. "Meets expectations." That's what I wrote because that's what I observed.

Q: So the answer is no?

A: The answer is what I already said. Read the document.

topic: A supervisor is deposed about performance reviews given to an employee who was later fired

topic: A contractor is questioned about delays that caused a construction project to fail

topic: A witness is asked about a car accident they saw from their front porch
text:
Q: Please state your name for the record.

A: Margaret Ellen Cho.

Q: Ms. Cho, you've indicated you witnessed a car accident on the afternoon of September 14th. Where were you at the time?

A: On my front porch. I was... I had my coffee. I sit there most afternoons.

Q: And what did you see?

A: The white sedan—it came through the intersection. And then the other car, the blue one, it just... it didn't stop. It didn't stop at all.

Q: When you say "didn't stop," do you mean—

A: I mean the driver never even tried. No brake lights. Nothing. Just... straight into the side of that sedan.

Q: Could you see the occupants of either vehicle?

A: There was a woman in the white car. The sedan.

Q: Did you see anyone else?

A: There was a car seat. In the back. I could see it through the window after—after everything stopped moving.

Q: Ms. Cho, I need to ask you specifically what you observed about—

A: I know what you need. I've been sitting with this for three months. There was a car seat. It was rear-facing. Yellow fabric. I don't know if anyone was in it. I don't know. I've gone over it so many times and I don't know.

Q: Did you approach the vehicle after the collision?

A: I called 911 first. My hands were... it took me three tries to dial.

Q: And then?

A: And then I went to the white car. The woman was conscious. She kept trying to turn around, to look in the backseat, but she couldn't move. She just kept saying "my baby, my baby." Over and over.

Q: What did you do?

A: I held her hand. I told her help was coming. That's all I could do. I just held her hand until the sirens came.

Q: Did you observe the driver of the blue vehicle at any point?

A: He was walking around. After. Just walking in circles in the middle of the street like he didn't know where he was. Like none of it was real.

Q: Ms. Cho, I understand this is difficult—

A: I still sit on that porch every afternoon. I still drink my coffee there. But I can't stop watching that intersection. Every single car that goes through.

topic: A witness is asked about a car accident they saw from their front porch
text:
Q: Mr. Brennan, how far is your porch from the intersection where the accident occurred?

A: Forty feet, maybe fifty. Close enough.

Q: And you had a clear line of sight?

A: Crystal clear. Nothing blocking my view.

Q: Tell me what you observed.

A: Silver pickup ran the red, struck a motorcycle. Motorcycle went down.

Q: Can you describe the motorcyclist?

A: Young guy. Early twenties, maybe. He was wearing a helmet, thank God.

Q: What happened immediately after impact?

A: The bike slid maybe thirty feet. Sparks everywhere. The rider... he separated from the motorcycle about halfway through.

Q: Did the pickup stop?

A: Eventually. Took its sweet time.

Q: What do you mean by that?

A: I mean the driver sat there for a good ten, fifteen seconds before pulling over. Like he was thinking about whether to stay or go.

Q: Did you see the driver exit the vehicle?

A: I did.

Q: Can you describe his demeanor?

A: He looked annoyed. That's what got me. This kid is lying in the street not moving, and this guy gets out looking like he's late for something.

Q: Did you approach the scene?

A: I went straight to the kid on the ground.

Q: Was he conscious?

A: In and out. He kept asking if his bike was okay. That's all he wanted to know about—his bike. It was his dad's, he kept saying. His dad's bike.

Q: What was the condition of the motorcycle?

A: Destroyed. Completely destroyed. But I didn't tell him that. I just said it was fine, help was on the way.

Q: Did you interact with the pickup driver at any point?

A: He came over. Asked if the kid was alive. I said yes. He said "good," and walked back to his truck to make a phone call. Didn't check on him again. Not once.

topic: A witness is asked about a car accident they saw from their front porch
text:
Q: Let's go through the sequence of events one more time, Mrs. Patterson.

A: We've been through it twice already.

Q: I understand. But I need to clarify the timing.

A: Fine.

Q: You said you first noticed the vehicles approximately three seconds before impact?

A: Approximately. Yes.

Q: And in those three seconds, what did you observe?

A: The red SUV was already in the intersection. The compact car—the gray one—entered from the north.

Q: Did either vehicle appear to be speeding?

A: The gray car was going too fast. Much too fast.

Q: How would you estimate its speed?

A: I wouldn't. I'm not an expert.

Q: Based on your observation—

A: Based on my observation, it was going too fast to stop. That's all I can say.

Q: Fair enough. Now, the driver of the gray vehicle—did you see them before impact?

A: I saw a shape. A person.

Q: Could you determine age or gender?

A: It was a girl. Young. I found out later she was seventeen.

Q: How did you find that out?

A: It was in the newspaper.

Q: Mrs. Patterson, after the collision—

A: She had just gotten her license. Two months prior. That was in the paper too.

Q: I see.

A: Her mother came to my door a week later. She wanted to know exactly what I saw. She wanted to understand how it happened.

Q: What did you tell her?

A: The truth. That her daughter never braked. That it happened so fast nobody could have done anything.

Q: How did she respond?

A: She thanked me. Then she stood on my porch and looked at that intersection for a long time. I offered her coffee. She didn't want any. She just wanted to see what her daughter saw.

topic: A witness is asked about a car accident they saw from their front porch
text:
Q: State your occupation, please.

A: Retired. Thirty-two years with the fire department.

Q: So you've seen accidents before.

A: More than I can count.

Q: Does that experience inform what you witnessed on October 3rd?

A: It means I know what I'm looking at. It means I don't get confused by the chaos.

Q: Tell me what you observed.

A: Two-vehicle collision, T-bone configuration. Minivan versus sedan. Sedan had the right of way.

Q: How do you know the sedan had the right of way?

A: I watched the light cycle from my porch. Sedan had green. Minivan ran the red by at least two full seconds.

Q: What happened after impact?

A: Minivan spun about ninety degrees. Sedan pushed into the light pole on the southeast corner.

Q: Did you render assistance?

A: Immediately. Checked the sedan first—driver was unconscious, passenger was alert but pinned.

Q: And the minivan?

A: Driver was conscious. Kept asking about the other car. Kept saying he didn't see the light, he didn't see it change.

Q: Was anyone else in the minivan?

A: No.

Q: You're certain?

A: I checked. It was empty except for the driver.

Q: Mr. Okonkwo, did you recognize either driver?

A: The man in the sedan. David Marsh. He lives—lived—four houses down from me.

Q: You said "lived."

A: He passed away. Nine days after the accident. I visited him in the hospital twice. He never woke up.

Q: I see. I'm... let me just check my notes here.

A: Take your time.

Q: Did Mr. Marsh have any family?

A: A wife. Two grown kids out of state. Margaret—his wife—she sat by his bed the whole time. I brought her food because she wouldn't leave to eat.

Q: ...Let's move on to the road conditions that day.

A: Dry. Clear. Perfect visibility. There was no reason for any of it.

topic: A witness is asked about a car accident they saw from their front porch

A: Yes. Right away.

A: He was a regular. Walked that route every morning. We'd wave sometimes.

Q: Did you speak to him that morning before the accident?

A: I waved. He waved back. He had a nice smile.

Q: Ms. Vega—

A: He had a nice smile and I waved at him and ninety seconds later he was lying in the street. So yes, I remember exactly what I saw. I remember all of it.

Q: We can take a break if—

A: I don't need a break. Ask your next question.

topic: A contractor is questioned about delays that caused a construction project to fail
text:
Q: Good morning, Mr. Delacroix. Before we get started, can I get you anything? Water, coffee?

A: I'm fine, thank you. And good morning to you as well.

Q: I understand you've been doing this work for quite some time—over twenty years in commercial construction, is that right?

A: Twenty-three years this past March, yes. Started as a framing carpenter, worked my way up. It's been a good career, all things considered.

Q: That's admirable. Truly. Now, I'd like to talk about the Riverside Commons project, if you're comfortable diving in.

A: Of course. I figured that's why we're here.

Q: The project was initially scheduled for completion in September of 2022. Can you walk me through what the timeline looked like from your perspective?

A: Sure, happy to. We broke ground in February of 2021. The first six months went smoothly—foundation work, structural framing, all on schedule. I was proud of the crew. They were putting in solid work.

Q: It sounds like you had a good team.

A: I did. I really did. Most of them had been with me for years. That's why what happened later was so hard, honestly.

Q: What changed after those first six months?

A: The steel deliveries started slipping. First it was a week, then two weeks. By October, we were sitting idle for almost three weeks waiting on structural beams. I've got a whole file of emails documenting it, if that helps.

Q: We may look at those. When you say "sitting idle," how did that affect your crew?

A: It was tough. I tried to keep everyone busy with what we could do, but there's only so much you can work around. Some of my guys had to pick up other jobs to make ends meet. I understood, but it hurt to see the team fragment like that.

Q: Did you communicate these concerns to the project owner?

A: Every step of the way. I believe in transparency—always have. I sent weekly updates, called when things changed. I wanted everyone working together to solve the problem, not pointing fingers later.

topic: A contractor is questioned about delays that caused a construction project to fail
text:
Q: State your name for the record.

A: Rebecca Chen.

Q: Ms. Chen, you served as the general contractor for the Millbrook Office Complex project, correct?

A: That's correct.

Q: The project was terminated by the owner in March 2023. Do you understand why we're here today?

A: I understand you're looking for answers about the delays. I'm here to provide whatever clarity I can.

Q: Let's start with the subcontractor selection. Who chose Hendricks Electrical for the project?

A: I did. And I'd like to explain that choice, if I may, because I think context matters here.

Q: Please.

A: Tom Hendricks and I had worked together on four previous projects without a single issue. His bids were competitive, his work was reliable. When he submitted for Millbrook, there was no reason to doubt him. I vouched for him because I believed in him.

Q: And when did you first notice problems with his performance?

A: Around month three. He started missing inspections. At first, I thought it was scheduling confusion—these things happen on complex builds. I sat down with him personally to work through it.

Q: How did that conversation go?

A: He was struggling. I could see it. His wife had been diagnosed with something serious, and he was stretched thin. I wanted to help him, not replace him. So I offered to bring in additional support, cover some costs myself to keep things moving.

Q: That's an unusual accommodation.

A: Maybe. But we're not just contractors, counsel. We're people. I've known Tom for fifteen years. I wasn't going to abandon him at the first sign of trouble.

Q: Did the accommodation work?

A: For a while. We got back on track for about six weeks. Then the material shortages hit everyone, and that's when things really unraveled. But I want to be clear—I don't regret trying to help him. I'd do it again.

topic: A contractor is questioned about delays that caused a construction project to fail
text:
Q: Mr. Okonkwo, I'm going to ask you about a meeting that took place on June 14th, 2022. Do you recall that meeting?

A: I do. It was at the Hartwell site trailer, around two in the afternoon.

Q: Who was present?

A: Myself, David Hartwell—the owner—his project manager Linda something, and our structural engineer, Pete Marsden.

Q: What was the purpose of the meeting?

A: David wanted to understand why we were behind schedule. He was frustrated, and honestly, I didn't blame him. If I'd been in his shoes, I'd have wanted answers too.

Q: How would you describe the tone of that meeting?

A: Tense at first. David came in ready for a fight, I think. But we laid everything out—the permit delays from the city, the soil issues we'd discovered, all of it. By the end, I think he understood we weren't making excuses.

Q: Did Mr. Hartwell express anger toward you personally?

A: He did, early on. Called the whole thing "amateur hour." That stung, I won't lie. But I've learned over the years that when clients lash out, it's usually fear talking. He had investors breathing down his neck. I tried to remember that.

Q: How did you respond to the "amateur hour" comment?

A: I took a breath and said, "David, I know this isn't what you wanted to hear. Let me show you what we're dealing with." Then I walked him through the soil reports myself. Showed him the photos of what we found when we dug.

Q: Did his demeanor change?

A: It did. By the end of the meeting, he shook my hand and apologized for the comment. I told him no apology was necessary—we were all under pressure. I meant it.

Q: Did you continue working with Mr. Hartwell after that?

A: We did. Finished the project five months late, but we finished it. He hired me again last year for a smaller build. I consider him a friend now, strange as that might sound.

topic: A contractor is questioned about delays that caused a construction project to fail
text:
Q: Let's discuss the weather delays you referenced in your earlier answers.

A: Of course.

Q: Your logs show seventeen days lost to weather between November 2021 and February 2022. Does that sound accurate?

A: It does. That was an unusually harsh winter. I've been building in this region for two decades, and I hadn't seen anything like it since maybe 2009.

Q: Some might say a contractor should anticipate weather delays in their scheduling.

A: And I did. We built in twelve contingency days. But counsel, there's only so much you can plan for. When you get ice storms back to back for three weeks, concrete won't cure, cranes can't operate safely, and I'm not going to put my people in danger to meet a deadline.

Q: So you made the decision to halt work during those periods?

A: I did. Every time. And I'd make the same decision again. I've got people who've worked for me for fifteen years. They've got families. I can explain a delay to an owner. I can't explain to someone's wife why her husband fell off scaffolding because I pushed too hard.

Q: I appreciate you sharing that perspective.

A: Thank you for hearing it. I know we're here because the project failed, and I take responsibility for my part. But I won't apologize for keeping people safe.

Q: Let's turn to the subcontractor invoices from that period. Do you have those records available?

A: I brought everything you requested, organized by month. I want to make this as easy as possible for everyone. The sooner we understand what happened, the sooner we can all move forward.

Q: That's very helpful. Let's start with November 2021.

A: Absolutely. That was actually a month I remember well—we'd just finished the second-floor framing and the crew was in good spirits. Let me walk you through it.

topic: A contractor is questioned about delays that caused a construction project to fail
text:
Q: Ms. Tran, you mentioned earlier that you had concerns about the foundation work. When did those concerns first arise?

A: Early. Maybe three weeks into the pour. Something felt off to me—the consistency of the concrete, the way it was setting. I've been doing this long enough to trust my instincts.

Q: Did you raise those concerns with anyone?

A: I raised them with everyone. The project manager, the concrete supplier, even the owner's rep. I wasn't trying to cause problems—I was trying to prevent them.

Q: How were those concerns received?

A: Mixed. The project manager, Steve Halston, he listened. Really listened. Came out to the site himself to look at what I was seeing. That meant a lot, actually.

Q: And the others?

A: The supplier got defensive. Told me I was imagining things, that their mix was fine. But Steve backed me up. He ordered independent testing even though it slowed us down.

Q: What did the testing reveal?

A: The supplier had substituted materials without telling us. Lower grade aggregate. Steve and I sat down together when we got those results, and I remember he just sighed and said, "Thank God you caught this."

Q: That must have been validating.

A: It was. But more than that, it reminded me why I do this work. When people actually listen to each other, trust each other, things work out. The delays we had later—they weren't because of that foundation. That foundation is solid because we worked together.

Q: The project still failed, though. How do you reconcile that?

A: It failed for a lot of reasons, counsel. Financing fell through, the owner's priorities shifted. But I'll tell you this—the work we did, the parts we built, they're still standing. That matters to me. I hope it matters to someone.

Q: I think it does, Ms. Tran.

A: Thank you for saying so.

Q: Where did this conversation take place?

A: Her office. The door was open.

Q: Who else was present?

A: Just me.

Q: So this was a private conversation between you and Ms. Felton?

A: I wouldn't call it a conversation. She was venting. I was there.

Q: Did you respond to her comment about Mr. Patel?

A: I didn't say anything.

Q: You didn't agree or disagree?

A: I didn't say anything. There's a difference between not responding and agreeing.

Q: I didn't suggest you agreed, Mr. Okonkwo. I'm trying to understand the full exchange.

A: And I'm telling you there wasn't much of an exchange. She talked. I listened. That was the dynamic.

Q: Did Ms. Felton make similar comments about other employees?

A: She made comments about a lot of people. Whether they were "similar"—that's a characterization I'd leave to you.

Q: Let me rephrase. Did she make other comments that referenced employees' backgrounds, heritage, or national origin?

A: Yes. More than once.

topic: A former employee is deposed about discriminatory remarks made by a supervisor
text:
Q: You mentioned earlier that you reported Mr. Branson's comments to Human Resources.

A: She thanked me for coming forward and said she'd look into it.

Q: What did she tell you at that time?

Q: Did she elaborate on what that meant?

A: No.

Q: Did you ask?

A: I asked. She said she wasn't at liberty to discuss personnel matters with me.

Q: Were you satisfied with that response?

A: Does it matter if I was satisfied?

Q: I'm asking whether you took any further action after that conversation.

A: I didn't. I'd said what I had to say. The ball was in their court.

Q: So as far as you know, no disciplinary action was taken against Mr. Branson?

A: As far as I know. Which isn't very far, apparently.

topic: A former employee is deposed about discriminatory remarks made by a supervisor

topic: A former employee is deposed about discriminatory remarks made by a supervisor
text:

topic: An HR director is questioned about a harassment complaint that was filed and closed
text:
Q: Ms. Thornton, you were the HR director at Westfield Manufacturing when the complaint against David Mercer was filed, correct?

A: March 14th.

A: That's what the stamp says.

A: I oversaw the process. Several people were involved.

A: I did.

A: I did.

topic: An HR director is questioned about a harassment complaint that was filed and closed
text:
Q: Mr. Okonkwo, how long after receiving the harassment complaint did you close the investigation?

A: I'd need to review the file to give you an exact timeline.

Q: Would it refresh your recollection if I told you it was eleven days?

A: If that's what the records show.

Q: Does eleven days strike you as sufficient time to investigate a complaint alleging months of workplace harassment?

A: Every investigation is different.

Q: That's not an answer.

A: It is an answer. You asked if it struck me as sufficient, and I'm telling you that sufficiency depends on the circumstances.

Q: What circumstances made eleven days sufficient here?

A: The allegations were specific. The witnesses were available. The documentary evidence was limited. We conducted the interviews, reviewed what was relevant, and reached a conclusion.

Q: You reached a conclusion. Let's talk about that. You found the complaint "unsubstantiated," correct?

A: Correct.

Q: Based on what?

A: Based on the totality of the evidence.

Q: Which was what, specifically?

A: Counsel, I'm not going to recite an entire investigative file from memory. I reviewed statements, I reviewed emails, I considered credibility—

Q: Whose credibility did you consider?

A: Everyone's.

Q: And you found Mr. Patterson more credible than the complainant?

A: I found that the evidence did not substantiate the allegations as presented.

Q: That's a careful way of putting it.

A: It's an accurate way of putting it.

topic: An HR director is questioned about a harassment complaint that was filed and closed
text:
Q: Dr. Reeves, did you personally interview anyone as part of this investigation?

topic: An HR director is questioned about a harassment complaint that was filed and closed
text:
Q: Ms. Chen, I'm going to ask you about the closure memo you drafted. Do you have Exhibit 12 in front of you?

topic: A driver is deposed about the events leading up to a multi-vehicle collision
text:
Q: Mr. Haskell, how long have you been driving commercial vehicles?

A: Twenty-three years this October. Started when I was nineteen, drove for Consolidated Freight out of Memphis, worked my way up through regional carriers, and I've been with my current company for the last eleven years. Never had a single at-fault accident in that entire time.

Q: I'm just asking about your experience for now—

A: I understand. I'm giving you context. Twenty-three years, over two million miles logged. I think that's relevant context.

Q: Fair enough. On the morning of March 15th, what time did you begin your shift?

A: 5:47 a.m. I logged in at 5:47 precisely. I always start my pre-trip inspection at least forty-five minutes before my first pickup, which was scheduled for 7:15 that morning.

Q: Can you describe that pre-trip inspection?

A: Thoroughly. I checked all eighteen wheels, tire pressure and tread depth. I checked all marker lights, brake lights, turn signals. I walked the trailer twice. I checked the fifth wheel coupling, the glad hands, the brake lines. I tested the brakes at idle and at pressure. I checked my mirrors, my horn, my wipers. Took me thirty-eight minutes. I documented it in my logbook, which I'm sure you have.

Q: We do have it. Moving to the collision itself—

A: The incident, yes.

Q: The collision occurred at approximately 2:15 p.m.?

A: 2:17. My dashcam timestamps everything.

Q: When did you first observe the white sedan?

A: I observed the white sedan approximately eight seconds before impact. It entered my lane without signaling while traveling at a speed I estimated at forty-five in a sixty-five zone. I immediately checked my mirrors, confirmed my escape route was blocked by the vehicle in my left blind spot, applied steady brake pressure to avoid jackknifing, and activated my hazards. Textbook defensive response.

Q: Did you consider moving to the shoulder?

A: There was no shoulder at that point. Concrete barrier. I'm surprised you don't have that in your accident reconstruction. I noticed it immediately because I always note my surroundings. That's what twenty-three years teaches you.

Q: So your testimony is that you had no options available?

A: My testimony is that I executed every available option correctly. The sedan driver created an unavoidable situation. I minimized the damage. If I hadn't reacted the way I did, with the training and instincts I've developed, we'd be talking about fatalities instead of fender damage.

topic: A driver is deposed about the events leading up to a multi-vehicle collision
text:
Q: Ms. Chen, I want to walk through the moments just before the collision. You were in the center lane, correct?

A: Yes.

Q: And the pickup truck was where?

A: To my left. One car length ahead, maybe.

Q: Did you observe anything unusual about how that truck was being driven?

A: He was weaving. Slightly. I noticed it maybe a minute before everything happened.

Q: When you say weaving—

A: Drifting. Touching the lane markers, then correcting. I thought maybe he was on his phone.

Q: What did you do when you noticed this?

A: I slowed down. I wanted distance between us. I checked my rearview, saw I had room, and eased off the gas.

Q: That was your instinct? To create space?

A: That's what you're supposed to do. I took a defensive driving course three years ago. My company requires it. I actually teach a portion of it now for new hires.

Q: You teach defensive driving?

A: The awareness module. Recognizing hazards before they develop. It's something I've put a lot of time into.

Q: So when you slowed down, how much distance did you create?

A: Probably three car lengths. Enough that when he swerved, I had time to brake and check my right side before making my own lane change.

Q: You were able to avoid contact entirely?

A: I was. The SUV behind me wasn't as fortunate. But I was already clear by then.

Q: Would you say your training helped you in that moment?

A: I would say that when you prepare for something, when you take it seriously and actually internalize it, it becomes automatic. I didn't have to think. I just responded correctly.

Q: Some might call that lucky.

A: Some people don't understand the difference between luck and preparation.

topic: A driver is deposed about the events leading up to a multi-vehicle collision
text:
Q: Mr. Okonkwo, you stated earlier that you braked hard when you saw the collision beginning ahead of you.

A: That's correct.

Q: And your vehicle came to a stop without striking any other cars?

A: Correct.

Q: I want to understand how that was possible given the testimony we've heard about the chain reaction. Seven vehicles were involved.

A: Seven vehicles driven by people who weren't paying attention, yes.

Q: You were paying attention?

A: I'm always paying attention.

Q: Counselor, let me ask this more directly. What specifically were you doing differently than those seven other drivers?

A: Following distance. I maintain a four-second gap at highway speeds. Not two, not three. Four.

Q: That's more than recommended.

A: The recommendation is a minimum. I prefer margins.

Q: Did you learn that somewhere specific?

A: I learned it from watching my father drive for thirty years without a single accident. He drove a cab in Lagos, then here in Houston. Forty years total. He taught me that the road doesn't care about your excuses.

Q: So when the collision began—

A: I had time. I had time because I gave myself time. I checked my mirror, braked firmly, and stopped. The person behind me nearly hit me because they were following too close. That's their failing, not mine.

Q: The vehicle behind you did make contact, according to the police report.

A: A tap. Her bumper touched mine at maybe two miles per hour because I had already stopped. If she'd been maintaining proper distance, even that wouldn't have happened. But I cannot control other drivers. I can only control myself, and I controlled myself correctly.

Q: You seem very certain about that.

A: I have no reason not to be.

topic: A driver is deposed about the events leading up to a multi-vehicle collision
text:
Q: Let's establish your position on the roadway. You were in the far right lane?

A: Yes.

Q: Traveling at what speed?

A: Sixty-two.

Q: The speed limit is sixty-five.

A: I'm aware. I drive three under. It gives me reaction time and saves fuel.

Q: Every time you drive?

A: Without exception.

Q: Mr. Davenport, walk me through what you observed in your mirrors prior to the collision.

A: Counsel, I have to tell you—my mirror discipline is something I've worked on for years. I was checking every five seconds, rotating between rearview, left, right, rearview. I saw the situation developing before most people would have recognized there was a situation.

Q: What did you see?

A: The black SUV three cars back was accelerating aggressively, changing lanes without signaling. I saw it cut off the silver sedan, saw the sedan brake hard, saw the sedan get rear-ended by the delivery truck.

Q: And you had time to observe all of this?

A: Because I was watching. Because I'm always watching.

Q: What action did you take?

A: I accelerated slightly to clear the impact zone and moved to the shoulder. I was out of the lane before the chain reaction reached my position.

Q: So you sped up?

A: I made a tactical decision to remove myself from danger. Yes.

Q: Above the speed limit?

A: For approximately four seconds, yes. Then I was on the shoulder, stationary, calling 911. Would you prefer I had stayed in the lane and become the eighth vehicle in the pileup?

Q: I'm not expressing a preference. I'm establishing facts.

A: Then the fact is I responded correctly. The fact is I was the only driver in that entire stretch who saw it coming and acted effectively. That's not opinion. That's what happened.

topic: A driver is deposed about the events leading up to a multi-vehicle collision
text:
Q: You've described seeing the motorcycle split lanes just before the collision.

A: Yes. He came up between me and the car to my right.

Q: And this was in slow traffic?

A: Traffic was moving, but slowly. Maybe twenty-five miles per hour. He was doing at least forty.

Q: Did that concern you?

A: Of course it did. I grew up around motorcycles. My father raced them. I rode for eight years before I had kids. I know what reckless riding looks like, and that was reckless riding.

Q: What did you do?

A: I held my line. Steady hands. Didn't flinch, didn't jerk the wheel, didn't brake suddenly. You cannot react unpredictably around a motorcycle—you'll kill someone.

Q: That's a very specific response.

A: It's the correct response. Most drivers see a motorcycle and panic. They swerve into the next lane, they slam their brakes, they make everything worse. I didn't do any of that.

Q: The collision occurred ahead of you?

A: Correct. He clipped the mirror of the sedan two cars up, lost control, went down, and the cars behind him couldn't stop in time.

Q: But you stopped in time.

A: I stopped in time because I was already prepared. I had my foot over the brake, I was watching his trajectory, and when he went down, I was braking before the car in front of me was.

Q: How can you be sure of that timing?

A: Because I stopped with two car lengths to spare and the SUV behind me stopped with his bumper six inches from my tailgate. He was reacting. I was anticipating.

Q: You feel you performed well in this situation?

A: I feel I performed exactly as someone with my experience and training should perform. If every driver on that road had done what I did, there would have been one man with road rash instead of a twelve-car pileup.

topic: A financial advisor is deposed about investment decisions made on a client's behalf
text:
Q: Mr. Harrington, how long have you been a licensed financial advisor?

A: Eighteen years this coming September.

Q: And during that time, approximately how many client accounts have you personally managed?

A: I'd estimate somewhere in the range of three hundred to three hundred fifty, though that number fluctuates as clients come and go. Would you like me to provide a more precise figure from our records?

Q: That won't be necessary at this time. Let's turn to the Meridian Growth Fund. When did you first recommend this fund to Mrs. Patterson?

A: That would have been during our quarterly review meeting on March 14th, 2022. I have the notes from that meeting if it would be helpful.

Q: We'll get to those. What was your basis for recommending that particular fund?

A: Several factors. Mrs. Patterson had expressed interest in increasing her exposure to mid-cap equities. Her risk tolerance assessment, which we update annually, indicated she was comfortable with moderate volatility. The Meridian fund had a strong five-year track record and reasonable expense ratios compared to similar offerings.

Q: Did you disclose to Mrs. Patterson that your firm receives higher commissions on Meridian funds compared to comparable alternatives?

A: Yes. That disclosure is part of our standard documentation, and I also discussed it verbally with her during that March meeting. It's on page three of the meeting summary I mentioned.

Q: Do you recall her specific reaction to that disclosure?

A: She asked what the difference amounted to in dollar terms. I calculated it for her—it was approximately forty dollars annually on her anticipated investment amount. She said that seemed reasonable given the fund's performance history.

Q: And you documented that exchange?

A: I did. I make it a practice to document substantive client conversations regarding fees and disclosures.

Q: Mr. Harrington, in your eighteen years, have you ever recommended an investment primarily because of the commission structure rather than client suitability?

A: No, I have not.

Q: Not once?

A: Not once. My reputation and my license depend on putting clients first. The commission differences between comparable products are frankly not significant enough to be worth compromising that.

topic: A financial advisor is deposed about investment decisions made on a client's behalf
text:
Q: Let's talk about the timeline here. You made the initial trade on October 3rd, correct?

A: Correct.

Q: And by October 17th, the position had lost roughly thirty-two percent of its value.

A: That's accurate, yes.

Q: Did you contact Mr. Yamamoto during those two weeks?

A: I did. I called him on October 10th when the position was down approximately eighteen percent.

Q: What did you tell him?

A: I explained that the sector was experiencing volatility related to the Fed announcement. I recommended he consider whether he wanted to hold through the turbulence or reduce his exposure.

Q: What was his response?

A: He asked for my professional opinion.

Q: And what did you tell him?

A: I told him that historically, this type of sector correction tends to recover within six to nine months, but that there were no guarantees. I said if he needed the funds within the next year, we should consider trimming the position. If his timeline was longer, holding was a reasonable strategy.

Q: Did he indicate his timeline to you?

A: He said he didn't anticipate needing the money for at least three years. He decided to hold.

Q: You're certain he said three years?

A: I am. I noted it in my file.

Q: Did you follow up again before the October 17th date?

A: I sent him a brief email on October 15th with a market update. I have a copy of that email in my records.

Q: Did he respond?

A: He replied the same day. He wrote, and I'm paraphrasing, that he appreciated the update and was comfortable staying the course.

topic: A financial advisor is deposed about investment decisions made on a client's behalf
text:
Q: Ms. Thornton, I want to understand your process. When a new client comes to you, walk me through the first meeting.

A: Of course. We begin with what I call a discovery conversation. I ask about their financial goals, their current assets and liabilities, their income and expenses, their family situation, their risk tolerance—

Q: Let me stop you there. How do you assess risk tolerance?

A: We use a standardized questionnaire that's been validated by our compliance department. It's twelve questions. Based on the responses, clients are categorized into one of five risk profiles.

Q: And those profiles are?

A: Conservative, moderately conservative, moderate, moderately aggressive, and aggressive.

Q: Where did Dr. Okonkwo fall on that scale?

A: He scored as moderately aggressive.

Q: When was that assessment completed?

A: At our initial meeting on June 8th, 2021.

Q: Did you ever reassess his risk tolerance after that date?

A: We did. We readminister the questionnaire annually, and also whenever there's a significant life change.

Q: What were the results of subsequent assessments?

A: In June 2022, he again scored as moderately aggressive. In June 2023, after his divorce was finalized, he shifted to moderate.

Q: Did you adjust his portfolio allocations after that 2023 reassessment?

A: Yes. We reduced his equity exposure from seventy-two percent to fifty-eight percent and increased his fixed income allocation accordingly. I have the rebalancing documentation available.

Q: I'd like to see that. We'll mark it as an exhibit.

A: Certainly.

topic: A financial advisor is deposed about investment decisions made on a client's behalf
text:
Q: The allegation, as you understand it, is that you churned Mr. Bellamy's account. Correct?

A: That is my understanding of the allegation.

Q: And your response to that allegation?

A: It's without merit.

Q: You deny it.

A: I do.

Q: There were forty-seven trades in Mr. Bellamy's account between January and June of last year.

A: I don't have that number in front of me, but I'll accept it for purposes of this discussion.

Q: Does that seem like a high number to you?

A: It depends entirely on the investment strategy and the client's instructions.

Q: Explain what you mean.

A: Mr. Bellamy specifically requested an active trading approach. He was interested in short-term momentum plays, particularly in the technology sector. He was engaged, informed, and initiated many of those trades himself through conversations with me.

Q: He initiated them?

A: Yes. He would call me, sometimes several times a week, with ideas he'd read about or stocks he wanted to discuss. A significant portion of those forty-seven trades were his suggestions that I then executed after confirming they were suitable.

Q: What portion?

A: I would estimate roughly half, perhaps slightly more. My records distinguish between client-initiated and advisor-initiated trades.

Q: You kept those records?

A: Yes. It's my standard practice to note the origin of each trade recommendation in my files.

Q: We'll want to see those records.

A: I assumed you would. I've already provided them to my counsel.

topic: A financial advisor is deposed about investment decisions made on a client's behalf
text:
Q: The concentration in Vertex Pharmaceuticals. Take me through how that developed.

A: Vertex was a position Mr. Reeves held before he became my client.

Q: How large was the position when you took over the account?

A: Approximately four hundred thousand dollars, which represented about thirty-one percent of his total portfolio at that time.

Q: That's a significant concentration in a single stock.

A: It is.

Q: Did you recommend reducing that concentration?

A: I raised the topic at our very first meeting. I explained the risks of having such a large percentage in one equity, particularly in the pharmaceutical sector where regulatory and pipeline risks can create significant volatility.

Q: What was his response?

A: He was reluctant to sell. The position had significant unrealized gains, and he was concerned about the tax implications.

Q: Did you document that conversation?

A: I did. I also followed up with a written summary that outlined the diversification benefits of reducing the position, along with a preliminary tax impact analysis.

Q: Do you have that document?

A: Yes.
