Q: You mentioned you were outside when the confrontation began. Where exactly were you standing?

A: I was at my mailbox. It's at the curb, maybe forty feet from where they were.

Q: Forty feet. You're certain of that distance?

A: I've walked it since then. It's thirty-eight feet from my mailbox to the edge of the Delgados' driveway. So yes, roughly forty feet.

Q: That's quite precise. Did you measure it specifically because of this incident?

A: I measured it because I assumed someone would ask.

Q: Fair enough. At forty feet, could you hear what was being said?

A: Some of it. When voices were raised, yes. When they spoke at normal volume, I caught fragments.

Q: Let's focus on what you heard clearly. What were the first words you could make out?

A: The first clear phrase I heard was "This is the third time this week." That was the man I didn't recognize—the one in the dark jacket.

Q: What was Mr. Delgado's response?

A: I didn't catch all of it. Something about "not my responsibility" and then a word I couldn't make out.

Q: Did the tone of the conversation escalate from that point?

A: It went up and down. There'd be a moment where the jacket man would get louder, and then Mr. Delgado would say something and it would drop back down again.

Q: Did you consider intervening?

A: I considered it. I stood there a moment longer than I needed to. But neither of them looked at me or seemed to want a third party involved.

Q: So you returned to your house?

A: I finished getting my mail and went inside. I watched from the window after that.

Q: How long did the confrontation continue after you went inside?

A: Another ten minutes, maybe. I wasn't timing it precisely.

---

topic: A neighbor is questioned about noise complaints and a confrontation they witnessed
text:
Q: Ms. Yamamoto, do you recall what date you first contacted the police about noise from the property?

A: July 8th of last year.

Q: And what prompted that call?

A: There was a party. Live music—someone had set up amplifiers in the backyard. It started around four in the afternoon and was still going strong at eleven.

Q: Had you attempted to address the issue directly before calling the police?

A: I had not. I didn't know the residents at that point. They'd only moved in a few months earlier, and we hadn't introduced ourselves.

Q: So your first interaction with them was through law enforcement?

A: In a sense. I didn't interact with them that night. The police came, the music stopped, and that was that.

Q: Did you ever have a direct conversation with the residents after that incident?

A: I did. About a week later, the woman—I learned her name was Sandra—knocked on my door. She apologized for the noise and said it had been a housewarming party that got out of hand.

Q: How would you describe that conversation?

A: It was polite. She seemed embarrassed. I told her I appreciated her coming by and that I hoped we could just be good neighbors going forward.

Q: Did the noise issues continue after that conversation?

A: They did, though not at that level. It was more intermittent—a loud evening here and there, not weekly parties.

Q: Did you contact the police again?

A: Twice more. Once in September, once in February.

Q: On those occasions, did you first attempt to speak with the residents?

A: In September, yes. I went over and knocked, but no one answered the door, even though I could see people inside. In February, I didn't try. I just called.

Q: Why didn't you try in February?

A: By that point, I felt I'd made enough good-faith efforts. The pattern was clear.

---

topic: A neighbor is questioned about noise complaints and a confrontation they witnessed
text:
Q: You've testified that you saw Mr. Harmon approach Mr. Delgado's property. What time was this?

A: Shortly after eight-thirty. I know because I'd just let the dogs out and checked my phone for the time.

Q: Where did Mr. Harmon approach from?

A: He came from the direction of his house, which is two doors down on the same side. He was walking with purpose—not rushing, but not strolling either.

Q: Did he go to the front door?

A: No. He stopped at the edge of the driveway and called out. I heard him say, "Michael, can we talk?"

Q: Did Mr. Delgado respond?

A: The garage door was open, and Mr. Delgado came out from inside. He was holding something—a rag, maybe, like he'd been working on something.

Q: What happened next?

A: They talked. At first it seemed conversational, like neighbors. I wasn't paying close attention because it seemed routine.

Q: When did your attention return to them?

A: When I heard Mr. Harmon's voice get sharper. He said something about "basic respect" and "people have to work in the morning."

Q: What was Mr. Delgado's demeanor at that point?

A: He'd set down whatever he was holding. His arms were at his sides. He didn't match Mr. Harmon's energy—he just let him talk.

Q: Did Mr. Delgado say anything in response?

A: He did, eventually. I heard him say, "I hear you, and I'll keep it in mind." Something like that.

Q: How did Mr. Harmon react to that?

A: He stood there for a moment, like he was deciding whether to say more. Then he nodded once and walked back toward his house.

Q: Did either man appear agitated after the conversation ended?

A: Mr. Harmon walked faster going back than he had coming over. Mr. Delgado just picked up his rag and went back into the garage.

topic: A witness is asked about a car accident they saw from their front porch
text:
Q: State your name for the record, please.

A: Margaret Tilson.

Q: Ms. Tilson, you were on your front porch on the afternoon of September 14th, correct?

A: I already told the police everything. Yes. I was on my porch.

Q: And from your porch, you witnessed a collision between two vehicles?

A: I saw what I saw.

Q: What exactly did you see?

A: A red truck ran the stop sign and hit a silver sedan. The sedan spun and ended up on my lawn. Is there something unclear about that?

Q: I'm just trying to establish the facts, ma'am. How far is your porch from the intersection?

A: Maybe forty feet. Close enough.

Q: Close enough for what?

A: Close enough to see a man run a stop sign and nearly kill someone. What else would I mean?

Q: That wasn't my question. Could you see the stop sign at the moment of impact?

A: I could see that truck blow right past it without so much as tapping his brakes. So yes. I could see it.

A: No.

Q: No trees, no parked cars?

topic: A witness is asked about a car accident they saw from their front porch
text:
Q: Good morning. Could you describe what you were doing on the afternoon in question?

A: I was sitting on my porch. Reading a book.

Q: What book?

A: I don't remember the title. It wasn't memorable.

Q: You were reading a book you can't remember, and you expect us to believe you remember details of an accident?

A: I didn't say I couldn't remember the accident.

Q: Let's talk about what you claim to have seen. You say the blue vehicle was speeding?

Q: Estimate.

A: I said I don't know exactly.

Q: You don't know. But you told the police the blue car was "flying down the street." Those were your words?

A: It was moving fast.

Q: So you exaggerated to the police?

A: No. I described what I saw.

Q: Which is it, Ms. Patterson? Was it "flying" or was it just "moving fast"? Because those are very different things.

A: You're twisting what I said.

Q: I'm reading your own statement back to you. Did the blue vehicle come to a complete stop before entering the intersection?

A: I... I think so. It slowed down significantly.

Q: You think so. A moment ago you were certain about everything. Now you think so?

A: I'm telling you what I remember.

---

topic: A witness is asked about a car accident they saw from their front porch
text:
Q: Mr. Dawes, I'll try to keep this brief. You witnessed the accident from your residence?

topic: A witness is asked about a car accident they saw from their front porch
text:
Q: Let's be very clear about the timeline. You were on your porch at approximately 4:15 PM?

A: Around then, yes.

Q: Around then. Not exactly 4:15?

A: I wasn't checking my watch.

A: Waiting for my daughter. She was picking me up.

topic: A witness is asked about a car accident they saw from their front porch
text:
Q: You've testified you were on your porch. Were you seated or standing?

A: Seated. In the rocking chair.

Q: Which direction does your porch face?

A: East.

Q: And the intersection is to your... ?

A: Southeast. Slightly to my right.

Q: So you would have had to turn your head to see it?

A: I suppose, yes. A little.

Q: How far did you have to turn? Show me.

A: Like this. Maybe twenty degrees.

Q: Let the record reflect the witness turned her head slightly to the right. Now, when you heard the collision, where were your eyes focused?

A: I was looking at the intersection by then.

Q: By then. What made you look?

A: I heard an engine revving. It sounded wrong.

Q: Wrong how?

A: Like someone was going too fast. Like they weren't going to stop.

Q: That's quite an interpretation from just an engine sound.

A: I've lived on that corner for eighteen years. I know what cars sound like when they're going to stop and when they're not.

Q: Do you have mechanical training?

A: Do I need mechanical training to hear a car speeding?

Q: I'm asking if you have any expertise that qualifies you to assess engine sounds.

A: Common sense. Is that allowed?

Q: Ms. Huang, I'd ask you to simply answer the questions put to you.

A: And I'd ask you to stop implying I don't know what I heard.

topic: A warehouse supervisor is deposed about safety protocols that were allegedly ignored
text:
Q: Mr. Deluca, can you tell me about the safety training program you implemented in 2021?

A: Oh, absolutely. So what we did—and I'm really proud of this—we completely overhauled the entire orientation process. Before, new hires would get maybe an hour of safety review, tops. I pushed for a full three-day program. Three full days before anyone touches a forklift or goes near the loading dock.

Q: And this was your initiative?

A: Mine and my assistant supervisor's, Rachel Torres. We sat down together, looked at incident reports from the previous two years, identified every single failure point, and built the curriculum around those actual problems. Real-world scenarios, not just checkbox compliance stuff.

Q: What did that curriculum include specifically?

A: Forklift certification—real certification, not the joke version some warehouses do. Hazard identification walkthroughs. Emergency evacuation drills. We even brought in a physical therapist to teach proper lifting mechanics. That was my idea, actually. I'd seen too many back injuries.

Q: How was this program received by management?

A: They were skeptical at first about the cost—three days of paid training before productive work, right? But I put together a presentation showing projected reduction in workers' comp claims. Walked them through the numbers myself.

Q: Did you track outcomes?

A: Religiously. I kept spreadsheets going back to my first month. Incident rates dropped thirty-one percent in the first year after implementation. Thirty-one percent. I still have those spreadsheets if you want them.

Q: The plaintiff alleges that on March 14th, 2023, no safety supervisor was present on the floor during the overnight shift. How do you respond to that?

A: That's—well, that's incorrect. We always had coverage. I built the schedule myself to ensure overlapping shifts. There was never a gap.

Q: Do you have documentation of who was on duty that night?

A: I can get that for you. I kept meticulous records. Every shift, every supervisor, every walk-through logged with timestamps. I actually created the logging system we use because the old one was inadequate.

Q: Mr. Deluca, I appreciate your thoroughness—

A: I just want to be clear about what we built there. It wasn't a perfect system, nothing is, but it was a good system. A really good system.

Q: Understood. Let's move to the specific incident report from that night.

A: Of course. Whatever you need.

topic: A warehouse supervisor is deposed about safety protocols that were allegedly ignored
text:
Q: Ms. Okonkwo, I want to ask you about the lockout/tagout procedures at the Riverside facility.

A: Okay.

Q: Can you describe those procedures for me?

A: When equipment is being serviced, you lock it out and tag it so it can't be activated.

Q: That's the general concept. Walk me through the specific steps as practiced at your facility.

A: Technician notifies the floor supervisor. Supervisor verifies the equipment is powered down. Lock goes on the main breaker with a tag identifying who placed it and when. Same person has to remove it.

Q: And this procedure was followed consistently?

A: Yes.

Q: Every single time?

A: Yes.

Q: Let me show you what's been marked as Exhibit 14. This is an internal memo dated February 3rd, 2023, with your signature. Do you recognize it?

A: I do.

Q: And can you read the highlighted portion for the record?

A: "Lockout compliance remains below target at 73% based on spot audits."

Q: Below target. So not every single time, then.

A: The audit methodology—look, I need to explain this. The 73% figure reflects documentation compliance, not procedural compliance. Locks were being placed. Tags were going on. But technicians weren't always completing the paper log within the required timeframe.

Q: So your testimony is that the physical safety measures were being followed even when not documented?

A: That's exactly what I'm saying, yes.

Q: How would you know that if it wasn't documented?

A: Because I was out on that floor every day. I watched these procedures happen. The documentation gap was a training issue about paperwork, not a safety issue about actual lockout.

Q: But you'd agree documentation exists for a reason?

A: Absolutely. Which is why I wrote that memo. To fix the problem.

topic: A warehouse supervisor is deposed about safety protocols that were allegedly ignored
text:
Q: Mr. Yates, let's talk about the conveyor belt incident.

A: Alright.

Q: Tell me what happened on the morning of June 7th.

topic: A warehouse supervisor is deposed about safety protocols that were allegedly ignored
text:
Q: Let's get right to it. The emergency exit on the east side of Building C—blocked or unblocked on November 12th?

A: Unblocked.

Q: You're certain?

topic: A warehouse supervisor is deposed about safety protocols that were allegedly ignored
text:
Q: Ms. Tran, I've been looking forward to this part of our conversation. You developed the hazard reporting app that employees use, correct?

A: The in-house app, yes. I developed it with IT support over about six months.

Q: Tell me about it. How does it work?

A: Employees can submit hazard reports directly from their phones. Photos, GPS tagging, dropdown categories for hazard type. Goes straight to a dashboard I monitor.

Q: And response times—how quickly do reports get addressed?

A: I set a policy of four-hour acknowledgment for all reports, twenty-four-hour resolution for anything not immediately dangerous, and immediate response for critical hazards.

Q: I'd love to see those. Now, the plaintiff submitted a report through this system on October 3rd, didn't she?

A: I'd have to check the records. We get dozens of reports daily.

Q: Let me refresh your memory. Exhibit 31. A hazard report flagging loose racking bolts in Aisle 7.

A: Okay. Yes, I see this report now.

topic: A store manager is questioned about a customer slip-and-fall on their premises
text:
Q: Mr. Hendricks, how long have you been the store manager at this location?

A: Four years, seven months.

Q: And in those four years and seven months, you've received training on safety protocols, correct?

A: Yes.

Q: Including protocols for wet floors?

A: Yes.

Q: Including protocols for inspecting the premises during business hours?

A: I said yes. We get trained on all of it.

Q: I'm just trying to establish the record, Mr. Hendricks. On the morning of March 14th, did you personally inspect the produce section before opening?

A: I inspect the entire store before opening. That's my job. I've done it every single day for four years and seven months, since you seem interested in that number.

Q: What time did you complete that inspection on March 14th?

A: Around 7:45.

Q: "Around" 7:45. Could it have been 7:30?

A: It was around 7:45. I don't stand there with a stopwatch.

Q: The store opens at 8:00 a.m., correct?

A: You know it does.

Q: Mr. Hendricks, I'm asking questions for the record. The store opens at 8:00 a.m.?

A: Yes. Eight o'clock. A.M. In the morning.

Q: And between 7:45 and Mrs. Patterson's fall at approximately 9:20 a.m., how many times was the produce section checked for hazards?

A: I don't have that information memorized. I'd have to look at the floor walk logs.

Q: You don't recall?

A: I recall that we follow our procedures. Every procedure. Every day.

---

topic: A store manager is questioned about a customer slip-and-fall on their premises
text:
Q: Let's talk about the incident report you prepared. You wrote that the floor was—and I'm quoting—"slightly damp." Do you see that?

A: I see it.

Q: What does "slightly damp" mean to you?

A: It means what it says. Not soaked. Not dry. Slightly damp.

Q: Was there standing water?

A: No.

Q: Was there a visible puddle?

A: I just said no standing water.

Q: I'm asking about a puddle specifically, Mr. Hendricks.

A: A puddle is standing water. No, there was no puddle.

Q: Then where did the dampness come from?

A: I don't know. Could have been anything. Condensation from the misters. A customer's wet shoes. A child with a drink. I wasn't there when it happened.

Q: But you were there afterward, weren't you?

A: Obviously.

Q: And you didn't investigate where the moisture came from?

A: I secured the area, I helped the customer, I called for first aid, and I filled out the report. That's the protocol.

Q: So the answer is no? You didn't investigate?

A: The answer is I followed the protocol that your client's lawyers have a copy of.

Q: My client is the woman who fell, Mr. Hendricks.

A: Then her lawyers. Whatever. You know what I mean.

Q: Let's move on. Did you take any photographs of the floor?

A: No.

Q: Why not?

A: Because the protocol doesn't require photographs. Are we going to keep doing this, or do you have real questions?

---

topic: A store manager is questioned about a customer slip-and-fall on their premises
text:
Q: Who was working the produce section that morning?

A: I'd have to check the schedule.

Q: You don't remember?

A: It was eight months ago.

Q: Fair enough. Do you remember how many employees were on shift that morning?

A: Roughly six, maybe seven. Again, I'd have to check.

Q: Do you remember speaking with any employees about the wet floor before Mrs. Patterson fell?

A: No.

Q: No, you don't remember, or no, you didn't speak with anyone?

A: No, I did not speak with anyone about a wet floor before the fall because I was not aware of any wet floor before the fall.

Q: So no one reported it to you?

A: Correct.

Q: Is there a system for employees to report hazards?

A: Yes.

Q: What is that system?

A: They radio it in or tell a manager directly.

Q: And no one did that on March 14th?

A: Not that I'm aware of.

Q: Wouldn't you be aware, as the manager?

A: I would be aware if someone told me. No one told me. What are you suggesting?

Q: I'm not suggesting anything. I'm asking questions.

A: It sounds like you're suggesting my employees failed to do their jobs.

Q: Did they?

A: No.

---

topic: A store manager is questioned about a customer slip-and-fall on their premises
text:
Q: You mentioned earlier that you have floor walk logs. Were those produced in discovery?

A: You'd have to ask the lawyers about that.

Q: I'm asking you if they exist.

A: They exist.

Q: For March 14th?

A: Yes.

Q: Did you review them before this deposition?

A: Briefly.

Q: And what did they show for the produce section between 8:00 and 9:20 a.m.?

A: I don't recall the specific times.

Q: You reviewed them briefly but don't recall?

A: I reviewed eight months of logs briefly. I don't have a photographic memory. I'm sorry if that's inconvenient.

Q: Were there any notations about moisture, spills, or wet conditions?

A: Not that I recall.

Q: So either there were no wet conditions, or no one documented them. Which is it?

A: I'm not going to speculate about things I don't remember.

Q: Is it possible your employees missed it?

A: Anything is possible. Is it possible your client wasn't paying attention to where she was walking?

Q: Mr. Hendricks—

A: I'm just asking. Since we're speculating.

Q: I'd ask you to just answer the questions.

A: I'd like to. When you ask fair ones.

---

topic: A store manager is questioned about a customer slip-and-fall on their premises
text:
Q: Tell me about the footwear Mrs. Patterson was wearing when she fell.

A: I don't recall specifically.

Q: You don't recall at all?

A: I was focused on whether she was injured. I wasn't cataloging her outfit.

Q: Did you notice if her shoes were wet when you approached her?

A: I didn't inspect her shoes.

Q: Did you notice anything about the soles? Whether they were worn?

A: No. I didn't flip her feet over and examine them. She was on the ground. She was upset.

Q: Did anyone examine her shoes?

A: Not that I'm aware of.

Q: Wouldn't that be relevant to understanding how she fell?

A: I'm a store manager, not an accident reconstructionist.

Q: You seem to have opinions about what caused this fall.

A: I have facts. The floor was barely damp. We followed every protocol. I don't know why she fell. I know it wasn't because we did anything wrong.

Q: That's your testimony?

A: That's the truth.

Q: You're aware she suffered a fractured wrist?

A: I'm aware. And I'm sorry that happened. But being sorry doesn't mean we're liable.

Q: I didn't ask if you were sorry.

A: No. You didn't.

topic: A paramedic is questioned about the response time and treatment at an accident scene
text:
Q: Please state your name and occupation for the record.

A: Michael Torres. I'm a paramedic with County Emergency Medical Services. Have been for eleven years.

Q: Mr. Torres, you responded to the accident on Route 12 on the evening of March 14th, correct?

A: Yes.

Q: What time did your unit arrive on scene?

A: According to our log, 7:47 PM.

Q: And what time was the 911 call placed?

A: I don't have that information in front of me. You'd need to ask dispatch.

Q: Let me refresh your recollection. The call came in at 7:23 PM. Does that sound right?

A: If that's what the record says, then yes.

Q: So that's a twenty-four minute response time. Is that consistent with your protocols?

A: Look, I don't set the protocols. I respond to calls. We had two other units tied up on a multi-vehicle accident on the interstate. We were the next available.

Q: I'm simply asking whether twenty-four minutes falls within acceptable response times.

A: It depends. Every situation is different. Traffic, weather, distance from the station, other calls—there are a lot of factors you're not accounting for.

Q: I'm asking about this situation specifically.

A: And I'm telling you it's not a simple yes or no. We responded as fast as we could given the circumstances. I don't know what else you want me to say.

Q: Were you aware that the victim had sustained a cervical spine injury?

A: Not until we assessed him on scene, no.

Q: And by that point, how much time had passed since the accident occurred?

A: I couldn't tell you exactly. I'm not a witness to when the accident happened. I only know when we arrived.

---

topic: A paramedic is questioned about the response time and treatment at an accident scene
text:
Q: Walk me through your initial assessment when you arrived at the scene.

A: The patient was a female, approximately thirty-five years old, found unresponsive in the driver's seat. Airbag had deployed. There was visible trauma to her forehead and she was bleeding from a laceration above her left eye.

Q: What did you do first?

A: My partner and I stabilized her neck with a cervical collar while we checked for responsiveness. She was breathing but shallow. Pulse was weak. We called for additional support and began preparing for extraction.

Q: How long did extraction take?

A: Approximately—I want to say twelve minutes. Maybe fourteen. The door was jammed and fire rescue had to use the Jaws of Life.

Q: During those twelve to fourteen minutes, what treatment were you able to provide?

A: We maintained cervical stabilization, monitored her vitals, started an IV line through the window, and kept talking to her when she showed signs of regaining consciousness.

Q: Did she regain consciousness?

A: Briefly. She was in and out.

Q: Did she say anything?

A: She asked about her son. Whether he was okay.

Q: Was there a child in the vehicle?

A: No. No, there wasn't anyone else. We checked thoroughly. She was alone.

Q: What did you tell her?

A: I told her to stay calm and that we were taking care of her. That's—that's what you say. You keep them calm.

Q: Mr. Torres, are you all right to continue?

A: I'm fine. Yes. What's your next question.

Q: After extraction, you transported her to Memorial Hospital?

A: That's correct. We arrived at the ER at 8:34 PM.

---

topic: A paramedic is questioned about the response time and treatment at an accident scene
text:
Q: You mentioned the patient was complaining of chest pain. When did that begin?

A: He reported it almost immediately after we arrived. Said it felt like pressure.

Q: And what did you do in response to that complaint?

A: We followed protocol. Administered aspirin, got him on oxygen, ran a twelve-lead ECG.

Q: Did the ECG indicate a cardiac event?

A: The reading was—it was inconclusive. There were some irregularities but nothing that definitively indicated an MI at that moment.

Q: So you didn't administer nitroglycerin?

A: No.

Q: Why not?

A: Because his blood pressure was borderline low. Nitro can drop BP further. It was a judgment call.

Q: Whose judgment?

A: Mine. And my partner agreed.

Q: Your partner agreed, or your partner deferred to you?

A: I don't understand the distinction you're trying to make.

Q: I'm asking whether your partner independently assessed the situation or simply went along with your decision.

A: We discussed it. Briefly. In the field, you don't have the luxury of a committee meeting. You make a call and you act.

Q: And you made the call not to give nitroglycerin.

A: Yes. Based on his vitals at the time, yes.

Q: The hospital records indicate he went into cardiac arrest approximately forty minutes after arriving at the ER.

A: I'm aware of what happened.

Q: Do you believe—

A: I believe we made the best decision we could with the information we had. That's what I believe. I can't predict the future, counselor. I can only respond to what's in front of me.

---

topic: A paramedic is questioned about the response time and treatment at an accident scene
text:
Q: I want to be very precise here, so please listen carefully. At what time did you first establish physical contact with the patient?

A: Approximately 9:15 PM.

Q: Approximately?

A: I didn't check my watch at that exact second. I was focused on the patient.

Q: Your unit's log shows you arrived at 9:12 PM. Are you saying it took three minutes before you reached the victim?

A: The vehicle had gone down an embankment. It wasn't directly accessible from the road. We had to get our equipment and make our way down on foot.

Q: Three minutes seems like a long time.

A: Have you ever climbed down a muddy embankment in the dark carrying forty pounds of gear?

Q: I'm not the one being deposed, Mr. Hernandez.

A: I understand that. I'm providing context.

Q: Let's move on. What was the patient's condition when you reached her?

A: She was conscious but confused. Complaining of pain in her left leg and abdomen. There was significant deformity to the lower left leg—obvious fracture. We were concerned about internal bleeding given the abdominal pain.

Q: What steps did you take to address the potential internal bleeding?

A: There's nothing we can do in the field for internal bleeding except transport quickly. We stabilized the leg fracture, got her on a backboard, and moved her to the ambulance as fast as safely possible.

Q: How long did that take?

A: I don't have an exact number. It was difficult terrain and we had to be careful not to cause additional injury.

Q: More than ten minutes?

A: Possibly. Probably. I don't know exactly. We weren't moving slowly, if that's what you're implying.

Q: I'm not implying anything. I'm asking questions.

A: Fine. Then ask your next question.

---

topic: A paramedic is questioned about the response time and treatment at an accident scene
text:
Q: Let's discuss the treatment you provided at the scene.

A: All right.

Q: The patient had a penetrating wound to the upper right chest, correct?

A: That's correct. Appeared to be caused by debris from the collision.

Q: How did you treat that wound?

A: We applied an occlusive dressing and monitored for signs of tension pneumothorax during transport.

Q: Did you observe any such signs?

A: His breathing became increasingly labored about eight minutes into transport. We suspected the lung was collapsing.

Q: What did you do at that point?

A: I made the decision to perform a needle decompression.

Q: In the ambulance? While moving?

A: Yes.

Q: Is that standard practice?

A: When someone can't breathe, you don't wait for ideal conditions. You act.

Q: I'm asking whether performing that procedure in a moving vehicle is something you're trained to do.

A: Yes. It's within our scope of practice for paramedics in this state. I've performed it before. It's not—it's not something we do lightly, okay? But the alternative was watching him suffocate.

Q: Did the procedure succeed?

A: There was immediate improvement in his breathing. His oxygen saturation came back up. He was alive when we reached the trauma center.

Q: But he didn't survive.

A: No. He didn't.

Q: Do you believe the outcome would have been different if you'd reached him sooner?

A: I can't answer that. I'm not—I don't have a crystal ball. I did everything I could from the moment I arrived. Everything.

Q: I understand.

A: Do you?

topic: A supervisor is deposed about performance reviews given to an employee who was later fired
text:
Q: Mr. Harrison, you conducted the annual performance review for Claire Mendez in March of 2022, is that correct?

A: Yes.

Q: And what was your overall assessment of her work at that time?

A: She was... she was doing fine. She was meeting expectations in most areas.

Q: Most areas. Were there areas where she wasn't meeting expectations?

A: There were some notes. Some areas for development. That's normal. Everyone has those.

Q: What were the specific areas for development you noted for Ms. Mendez?

A: I'd have to look at the document. I don't want to misstate anything.

Q: I'm showing you what's been marked as Exhibit 14. Does this refresh your recollection?

A: Yes. I wrote that she could improve her time management on complex projects. And that she should speak up more in client meetings.

Q: And these were areas you believed she could improve?

A: I believed she would improve. That was... that was my belief at the time. I thought she had time.

Q: You thought she had time?

A: To grow. To develop. She'd only been with us eighteen months.

Q: Did you communicate to Ms. Mendez that you believed she had time to develop?

A: I told her she was on the right track. I told her to keep doing what she was doing.

Q: And seven months later, she was terminated. Is that correct?

A: That's correct.

Q: Mr. Harrison, did anything change between March and October that altered your assessment of Ms. Mendez's trajectory?

A: I wasn't... I wasn't the one who made that decision. I want to be clear about that. I wasn't the one.

---

topic: A supervisor is deposed about performance reviews given to an employee who was later fired
text:
Q: Ms. Okonkwo, how many direct reports did you have in 2021?

A: Eight.

Q: And David Restrepo was one of those eight?

A: He was.

Q: Tell me about David's first performance review under your supervision.

A: It was positive. Very positive, actually. He had a strong first year.

Q: What made it strong?

A: He hit every metric. He was early to every meeting. He volunteered for the difficult assignments nobody else wanted. He stayed late. He cared about the work.

Q: You're speaking in past tense.

A: Well, he doesn't work there anymore, so yes.

Q: Fair enough. The second performance review—that would have been in 2022?

A: February 2022, yes.

Q: Was that review also positive?

A: It was... it was more mixed.

Q: More mixed. What changed?

A: I don't know that anything changed with David. I think the expectations changed. The company wanted different things.

Q: What different things?

A: More output. Faster turnaround. Less... less of what David was good at.

Q: And you communicated these new expectations to him?

A: I did. I sat with him for over an hour. I explained everything. I told him exactly what they were looking for.

Q: How did he respond?

A: He said he understood. He thanked me. He said he'd try his best. And then three months later, he was gone, and I didn't even get to... I wasn't informed until after.

Q: You weren't informed until after the termination decision was made?

A: That's correct. I found out the same day he did.

---

topic: A supervisor is deposed about performance reviews given to an employee who was later fired
text:
Q: Let's talk about the rating scale used in these reviews. Can you explain it?

A: It's one through five. One is unacceptable. Five is exceptional. Three is meeting expectations.

Q: And what rating did you give Mr. Vogel in his 2023 review?

A: I gave him a three.

Q: Across all categories?

A: Mostly threes. A few fours. One two.

Q: What was the two in?

A: Collaboration.

Q: You gave him a two in collaboration. Can you tell me what that means, practically speaking?

A: It means there was room for significant improvement.

Q: Can you be more specific?

A: He had difficulty working with certain team members.

Q: Which team members?

A: I'd rather not—I don't think it's appropriate to name them.

Q: Mr. Kessler, this is a deposition. I need you to answer the question.

A: Sarah Chen. And Marcus Williams. Those were the two who filed complaints.

Q: Complaints about what?

A: About Theo being difficult. About him not responding to emails. About him taking credit.

Q: Did you investigate these complaints?

A: I asked him about them. I asked him directly.

Q: And what did he say?

A: He said he didn't realize. He said he'd do better. He was trying so hard at that point. He really was.

Q: But you still gave him the two?

A: I had to. The complaints were documented. I didn't have a choice.

Q: Did you want to give him a higher rating?

A: I wanted a lot of things for Theo. None of them happened.

---

topic: A supervisor is deposed about performance reviews given to an employee who was later fired
text:
Q: Dr. Patel, when you wrote in the performance review that Ms. Lindgren had "potential for leadership," what did you mean by that?

A: Exactly what it says. She had potential.

Q: Did you believe she would eventually be promoted?

A: I believed it was possible, yes.

Q: More than possible? Did you believe it was likely?

A: I thought if she stayed, if she kept improving, yes. It was likely.

Q: You thought if she stayed. Did you have reason to believe she might not stay?

A: No. Not at that time.

Q: But something changed?

A: Counselor, I'm trying to answer your questions accurately. Can you tell me what specifically you want to know?

Q: I want to know whether, between the time you wrote that review and the time Ms. Lindgren was terminated, your opinion of her leadership potential changed.

A: My opinion didn't change.

Q: Then help me understand something. If your opinion didn't change, how did she go from "potential for leadership" to terminated in eleven months?

A: Because it wasn't my decision.

Q: Whose decision was it?

A: HR. Executive team. I was consulted, but I was not the decision-maker.

Q: Were you in favor of the termination?

A: No. I was not.

Q: Did you tell anyone you were not in favor?

A: I told my supervisor. I told Rachel in HR. I made my position clear.

Q: And what happened?

A: They thanked me for my input.

---

topic: A supervisor is deposed about performance reviews given to an employee who was later fired
text:
Q: I want to make sure I understand the timeline. You conducted Mr. Huang's mid-year review in June?

A: That's correct.

Q: And at that time, were you aware that his position was being considered for elimination?

A: No.

Q: When did you first become aware?

A: August. Early August.

Q: So you conducted a performance review for an employee in June, and two months later you learned his position might be eliminated?

A: Yes.

Q: Did you feel that was appropriate?

A: I'm not sure what you're asking.

Q: Did you feel it was appropriate that you were not informed about the potential elimination before conducting his review?

A: It wasn't my place to feel anything about it. That's above my pay grade.

Q: I'm asking what you actually felt, Mr. Dennison.

A: I felt like I'd wasted his time. And mine. I sat there with him for forty-five minutes talking about his goals for the next quarter. His development plan. What skills he wanted to build. And none of it... none of it was going to matter.

Q: Did you tell him that?

A: Of course not. I didn't know yet.

Q: When you did find out, did you tell him then?

A: I wasn't permitted to. I was told to let HR handle the communication.

Q: So you never spoke to Mr. Huang about it directly?

A: The last real conversation I had with James was that review. Where I told him he was doing a good job. Where I told him he had a future with the company.

Q: And then?

A: And then I didn't see him again. They let him go on a Friday. I was traveling. I didn't even get to say goodbye.

topic: A store manager is questioned about a customer slip-and-fall on their premises
text:
Q: Mr. Hendricks, you were the store manager on duty the morning of October 14th, correct?

A: Yes.

Q: And you personally responded to the incident involving Mrs. Delgado?

A: I was notified and I went to the location, yes.

Q: How long after the fall did you arrive at the scene?

A: I don't know exactly. A few minutes.

Q: More than five minutes? Less than five?

A: I said I don't know exactly.

Q: Who notified you?

A: One of the associates. I don't remember which one.

Q: You don't remember which employee told you a customer had fallen in your store?

A: We have forty-two employees. I was in the back office. Someone came and got me. I didn't write down their name.

Q: What did you observe when you arrived?

A: The customer was on the ground near the produce section. A few people were standing around.

Q: Was the floor wet?

A: There was some moisture, yes.

Q: Some moisture. Can you describe what you mean by "some moisture"?

A: A small amount of liquid on the floor. I'm not a scientist. I don't have a measurement for you.

Q: Did you document the presence of this liquid?

A: An incident report was completed, yes.

Q: By you?

A: By the shift supervisor under my direction.

---

topic: A store manager is questioned about a customer slip-and-fall on their premises
text:
Q: Ms. Tran, how long have you been the manager at this location?

A: A little over three years.

Q: And in those three years, how many slip-and-fall incidents have occurred in the store?

A: I'd have to check the records to give you an accurate number.

Q: Approximately?

A: I really wouldn't want to guess. I could be wrong, and I don't want to mislead anyone.

Q: More than ten?

A: Again, I'd need to see the documentation.

Q: Let me ask it this way. Are slip-and-fall incidents common at your store?

A: Define common.

Q: Do they happen regularly?

A: Things happen in retail. I wouldn't say regularly. I wouldn't say never.

Q: Fair enough. Now, your store has a policy for floor inspections, correct?

A: Yes, absolutely. Every hour, a designated associate walks the floor and logs any hazards.

Q: Every hour without exception?

A: That's the policy, yes.

Q: And on February 3rd, the day Mr. Okonkwo fell, were those inspections completed?

A: I believe so.

Q: You believe so, or you know so?

A: I reviewed the logs afterward. They appeared to be in order.

---

topic: A store manager is questioned about a customer slip-and-fall on their premises
text:
Q: Mr. Feldman, you mentioned earlier that a spill occurred near Aisle 7. Who caused that spill?

A: I have no idea.

Q: No idea at all?

A: No. Could've been anyone. A customer, a stocker, someone's kid. I wasn't there when it happened.

Q: But you were there when Mrs. Patterson fell?

A: No, I was not there at that exact moment either. I arrived after.

Q: So when did you first learn about the spill itself?

A: When I responded to the fall.

Q: Not before?

A: Not before.

Q: I'm simply asking what you know, Mr. Feldman.

---

topic: A store manager is questioned about a customer slip-and-fall on their premises
text:
Q: Walk me through your store's procedure when a customer reports an injury.

A: Sure. We secure the area, assist the customer, call for medical if needed, and complete an incident report.

A: The manager on duty. Or a supervisor if the manager isn't available.

Q: You were the manager on duty on March 18th?

A: I was.

Q: So you completed the incident report for Mr. Yates?

A: I did.

Q: I'm looking at the report now. It says the fall occurred at 2:15 p.m. How did you determine that time?

A: That's when it was reported to me.

Q: The report also says—and I'm quoting—"floor was dry upon inspection." You wrote that?

A: Yes.

Q: When did you inspect the floor?

A: After I responded to the scene.

Q: How long after the fall?

A: I don't know. Ten minutes, maybe. Maybe less.

---

topic: A store manager is questioned about a customer slip-and-fall on their premises
text:
Q: Ms. Brennan, you stated that the surveillance footage from December 12th is unavailable. Is that correct?

A: That's correct.

Q: Help me understand why.

A: Our system records on a 30-day loop. The footage wasn't preserved in time.

Q: Who makes the decision to preserve footage?

A: Typically the manager on duty or loss prevention.

Q: And who was the manager on duty?

A: I was.

Q: Did anyone ask you to preserve the footage?

A: Not that I recall.

Q: The plaintiff's attorney sent a preservation letter dated December 15th. Three days after the incident. Are you aware of that letter?

A: I'm aware of it now, yes.

Q: But not at the time?

A: Letters go to corporate. I don't handle legal correspondence.

Q: So no one from corporate contacted you about preserving video evidence?

A: Not that I recall.

Q: You seem to have difficulty recalling quite a few things, Ms. Brennan.

A: I recall what I recall, Counselor. I'm not going to invent memories to make your job easier.

Q: I'm not asking you to invent anything. I'm trying to understand how surveillance footage of a slip-and-fall simply vanished.

A: It didn't vanish. It was overwritten. That's how the system works. I didn't design it.

topic: A neighbor is questioned about noise complaints and a confrontation they witnessed
text:
Q: Please state your name and address for the record.

A: Margaret Holloway. 4512 Pinecrest Drive. Same place I've lived for thirty-one years, if that matters to anyone here.

Q: Ms. Holloway, you submitted a noise complaint on the evening of March 14th, correct?

A: I submitted twelve noise complaints over four months. You'll have to be more specific about which one you're interested in.

Q: Let's focus on March 14th.

A: Fine. Yes. March 14th. Another complaint that went nowhere.

Q: Can you describe what you heard that evening?

A: What I heard was the same thing I'd been hearing since November. Music. Bass so loud my windows rattled. Shouting. Laughter. The usual.

Q: Approximately what time did the noise begin?

A: It started around nine. Or maybe it was eight-thirty. I wasn't sitting there with a stopwatch because I didn't realize I'd need to document everything like a court reporter just to be taken seriously.

Q: Did you attempt to address the noise yourself before filing the complaint?

A: Did I attempt— yes. Yes, I did. I walked over there three separate times. I knocked on the door. I left a note. I did everything a person is supposed to do before "escalating," as they like to say.

Q: And what was the response?

A: The response was Mr. Kendrick telling me to mind my own business and go back inside. Direct quote.

Q: Did he use those exact words?

A: Those exact words, counselor. Would you like me to repeat them more slowly?

Q: That won't be necessary. Did you witness any physical altercation that evening?

A: I saw him shove someone. Whether that counts as an "altercation" in your legal terminology, I couldn't say. To me it looked like assault.

Q: Who did you see him shove?

A: A younger man. I don't know his name. He'd been at the party. He ended up on the ground in the driveway, and Mr. Kendrick stood over him yelling something I couldn't make out from my window.

Q: But you didn't go outside at that point?

A: I'd already been told to mind my own business. I called the police instead. Which, as I'm sure you know, accomplished absolutely nothing.

---

topic: A neighbor is questioned about noise complaints and a confrontation they witnessed

topic: A neighbor is questioned about noise complaints and a confrontation they witnessed
text:
Q: Let me direct your attention to the events of September 22nd.

A: All right.

Q: You've previously stated you witnessed a confrontation between David Marsh and Thomas Whelan in the parking lot of your apartment complex.

A: That's right.

Q: Now I want to be very precise here. You were sixty feet away, correct?

A: I was on my balcony. I don't know the exact distance.

Q: Your balcony is on the third floor.

A: Yes.

Q: It was after nine PM. Already dark.

A: There are lights in the parking lot.

Q: But it was dark.

A: It was evening. There was lighting. I could see fine.

Q: You could see "fine" from sixty feet away, three stories up, in the dark.

A: Are you asking me a question or telling me what I saw?

Q: I'm testing the reliability of your account, Mr. Nance.

A: Then test it with questions, not speeches.

Q: Fair enough. Could you see the faces of the two men clearly?

A: I recognized them. I've lived there four years. I know what my neighbors look like.

Q: But could you see their facial expressions?

A: I could see enough.

Q: That's not what I asked.

A: I could see David grab Thomas by the shirt. I could see Thomas stumble backward into a car. I could hear David screaming at him about the noise complaints Thomas had filed. That enough detail for you?

Q: And you're certain it was David Marsh who initiated physical contact?

A: I'm certain of what I saw.

Q: You filed your own noise complaint against Mr. Marsh two weeks before this incident, didn't you?

A: I did.

Q: So you had your own grievance against him.

A: I had a grievance against the noise, counselor. Not the man. I'm telling you what happened because it happened.

---

topic: A neighbor is questioned about noise complaints and a confrontation they witnessed
text:
Q: Mrs. Patterson, you told the police you saw the confrontation from start to finish.

A: That's right.

Q: Walk me through it.

A: I was bringing in groceries. I heard raised voices from the Okonkwo residence. I stopped to listen.

Q: You stopped deliberately to listen?

A: Yes.

Q: Why?

A: Because there had been problems before. I wanted to know what was happening.

Q: What did you hear?

A: I heard a man—I believe it was Mr. Bryant—yelling that he was sick of the noise, that he'd called the city, that he was going to "handle it himself" if nothing changed.

Q: "Handle it himself." Those were his words?

A: Yes.

Q: Did that strike you as threatening?

A: It struck me as frustrated.

Q: I didn't ask if he was frustrated. I asked if you found it threatening.

A: And I'm telling you it didn't strike me that way.

Q: Let me rephrase. Could a reasonable person interpret "handle it himself" as a threat?

A: A reasonable person could interpret anything as anything, counselor. I'm telling you what I observed and what I thought.

Q: You're not here to offer your opinions, Mrs. Patterson.

A: Then stop asking for them.

Q: Did Mr. Okonkwo respond?

A: He told Mr. Bryant to get off his property.

Q: Was he calm when he said this?

A: He was firm.

Q: Was he calm?

A: I don't know what was happening inside his head. His voice was raised. He pointed toward the street. He said "Get off my property" more than once.

Q: How many times?

A: Three, maybe four.

Q: And did Mr. Bryant leave?

A: Eventually.

Q: What happened before he left?

A: They stood about two feet apart. There was more shouting. Then Mr. Bryant turned around and walked away.

Q: No physical contact?

A: None that I saw. And I was watching.

---

topic: A neighbor is questioned about noise complaints and a confrontation they witnessed
text:
Q: Mr. Salazar, I understand you may have concerns about being here today.

topic: A doctor is deposed about informed consent procedures before a surgery
text:
Q: Dr. Hensley, let's talk about what you actually told Mrs. Carmichael before the surgery. You did speak with her, correct?

A: Yes.

Q: And when was that conversation?

A: The morning of the procedure.

Q: The morning of. So just to be clear, the first time you personally discussed the risks of this surgery with your patient was the same day you were going to cut into her spine?

A: I didn't say it was the first time.

Q: When else did you discuss it?

A: I had a consultation with her two weeks prior.

Q: That consultation is documented where, exactly?

A: In my office notes.

Q: I've reviewed your office notes, Doctor. I see a notation that says "discussed surgical options." That's it. Three words. Is that your idea of informed consent documentation?

A: My notes are summary notes. They don't capture every word of a conversation.

Q: I'm not asking for every word. I'm asking for any word about risks. Any word about alternatives. Any word about what could go wrong. Where are those words, Doctor?

A: The conversation happened. I'm telling you it happened.

Q: And I'm looking at a medical record that doesn't reflect it happened. Do you understand the difference?

A: I understand you have a job to do, Counselor. So do I. And my job, on that day, was taking care of a patient—not drafting legal documents to satisfy lawyers who would second-guess me years later.

Q: Is that a yes or a no?

A: Yes. I understand the difference.

topic: A doctor is deposed about informed consent procedures before a surgery
text:
Q: Dr. Okonkwo, walk me through your standard informed consent process for laparoscopic cholecystectomy.

A: Certainly. I meet with the patient in the pre-operative area. I confirm their understanding of the procedure, review the major risks—bleeding, infection, bile duct injury, conversion to open surgery—answer any questions, and then the patient signs the consent form.

Q: And you do this personally, every time?

A: Every time.

Q: Every single time?

A: I just said yes. Every time.

Q: With Mr. Davenport, you're certain you followed this process?

A: Yes.

Q: You specifically remember this patient?

A: I remember following my process.

Q: That's not the same thing, is it, Doctor?

A: I perform this surgery roughly two hundred times a year. I follow the same protocol each time. That's how I know.

Q: So you don't actually remember Mr. Davenport specifically.

A: I remember the surgery. I remember the complication. I remember doing everything correctly.

Q: Doctor, do you remember his face? Do you remember what questions he asked you?

A: I remember he was nervous. Most patients are.

Q: What did he ask you?

A: I don't recall the specific questions.

Q: You don't recall whether he asked about bile duct injury? The very complication that now has him here?

A: I would have discussed it regardless of whether he asked. That's my protocol.

Q: Protocol. You keep using that word like it answers my question.

A: Because it does.

topic: A doctor is deposed about informed consent procedures before a surgery
text:
Q: Dr. Yamamoto, who witnessed the consent form being signed?

A: One of the nurses, I believe.

A: The form should indicate the witness.

Q: I have the form here. The witness signature line is blank.

A: Then it may have been overlooked.

Q: Overlooked.

A: These things happen in busy surgical centers.

Q: Let's slow down. You're the surgeon. You're about to perform an elective cosmetic procedure on a patient's face. And nobody witnessed the consent signature?

A: The patient signed it. That's what matters. She signed it, she understood it, she wanted the procedure.

Q: How do you know she understood it if nobody witnessed the conversation?

A: Because I had the conversation with her.

Q: Where is that documented?

A: It's in my pre-operative note.

Q: Your pre-operative note says, and I'm quoting, "Consent obtained." Two words.

A: That means I obtained consent.

Q: Doctor, I'm trying to understand what you actually said to this woman before you operated on her face and left her with permanent nerve damage. Can you help me with that, or is "consent obtained" the full extent of your recollection?

A: I explained the procedure. I explained that there were risks to nerves and blood vessels. I explained there would be swelling and recovery time. I explained—

Q: Did you explain the specific risk of permanent facial paralysis?

A: I explained nerve damage was a risk.

Q: Nerve damage. Those words?

A: Words to that effect. I'm not going to sit here and pretend I have a transcript of a conversation from three years ago. I don't. Nobody does.

topic: A doctor is deposed about informed consent procedures before a surgery
text:
Q: When did you first become aware that Mr. Stillwell had questions about the surgery?

Q: Would have.

A: Yes.

Q: But you don't actually know.

topic: A doctor is deposed about informed consent procedures before a surgery
text:
Q: Dr. Patel, did you use any visual aids when explaining the procedure to Mrs. Fontaine?

topic: A former employee is deposed about discriminatory remarks made by a supervisor
text:
Q: Please state your name and former position for the record.

A: Diane Okonkwo. I was Senior Quality Assurance Manager at Brennan Logistics for eleven years and four months. I built that department from three people to a team of twenty-two.

Q: Ms. Okonkwo, I'm going to direct your attention to a meeting that took place in March 2023. Were you present at a quarterly review with your supervisor, Thomas Harding?

A: I was. And I should note that I had just completed the ISO certification audit with zero non-conformances—the first time in company history that had happened.

Q: I didn't ask about the audit, Ms. Okonkwo.

A: You asked about the meeting. That context matters because Mr. Harding's comments came directly after I presented those results to the executive team.

Q: What did Mr. Harding say to you after that presentation?

A: He pulled me aside in the hallway and said, "You people always need to make a show of things, don't you?"

Q: What did you understand him to mean by "you people"?

A: I understood exactly what he meant. I've heard variations of that phrase my entire career. I also understood that I had just outperformed every other department head in that room, and that fact was apparently difficult for him.

Q: Did you respond to Mr. Harding?

A: I told him that if presenting factual results constituted "a show," then perhaps the company should expect more shows from other departments.

Q: How did he react to that?

A: He turned red. Walked away. He didn't speak to me directly for two weeks after that.

Q: Did you report this incident to Human Resources?

A: I documented it in an email to myself, which I've preserved. I also want the record to reflect that I continued to lead my department to exceed every metric for the following six months, despite receiving no support from Mr. Harding.

Q: I'm asking specifically whether you reported it to HR.

A: I did not, because I was not going to let his ignorance define my tenure there. My work spoke for itself. It still does.

Q: Let's move on to the incident in July 2023.

A: The incident in July 2023, yes—which occurred one week after I received the Regional Excellence Award from corporate headquarters.

topic: A former employee is deposed about discriminatory remarks made by a supervisor
text:
Q: Good morning. You were employed at Cedarbrook Financial Services, correct?

A: Yes, from 2019 to 2024.

Q: And your supervisor during that time was Martin Schell?

A: For most of it, yes.

Q: I want to ask you about statements Mr. Schell made regarding a colleague of yours, Priya Sharma. Did you ever hear Mr. Schell comment on Ms. Sharma's national origin?

A: I did. On multiple occasions.

Q: Let's start with the first occasion you can recall.

A: It was during a team lunch. Priya had just closed the Hannover account—that was a $4.2 million institutional client, for context. She'd been working on it for eight months.

Q: What did Mr. Schell say?

A: He made a joke. He said something like, "Must be nice having family back home who can work the call centers. Bet that helps with the international clients."

Q: What was the reaction in the room?

A: Silence. Then nervous laughter from a few people. Priya didn't laugh.

Q: Did you say anything?

A: Yes. I said, "Priya closed that account because she built the relationship from nothing and understood their risk tolerance better than anyone else on this team, including you, Martin."

Q: You said that directly to your supervisor?

A: I did. Someone needed to.

Q: What happened after you made that statement?

A: Martin said I was being "sensitive." I told him that accuracy wasn't sensitivity.

Q: Were there any professional repercussions for you?

A: He gave me a mediocre performance review that quarter. I filed a formal objection and had it amended after presenting documentation of my actual numbers.

Q: Did anyone else speak up on Ms. Sharma's behalf during that lunch?

A: No. But I had worked with Priya since her first day. I trained her. When she succeeded, that wasn't luck or call centers. That was preparation meeting opportunity, and I wasn't going to let that be diminished.

Q: Did you ever discuss this incident with Ms. Sharma directly?

A: She thanked me afterward. I told her she had nothing to thank me for. She earned that account.

topic: A former employee is deposed about discriminatory remarks made by a supervisor
text:
Q: How long did you report directly to Janet Cromwell?

A: About two years.

Q: And during those two years, did you become aware of any statements Ms. Cromwell made about employees' religious practices?

A: Aware? I witnessed them personally.

Q: Excellent. Can you describe what you witnessed?

A: I can, yes. I can describe it thoroughly, because I took detailed notes each time it occurred.

Q: You took contemporaneous notes?

A: I've worked in corporate environments for eighteen years, counsel. Documentation isn't optional when you understand how these situations unfold.

Q: Very well. Please describe the first incident you documented.

A: December 2022. Ahmad Farouk requested accommodation for Friday prayers. Standard request. Ms. Cromwell said, in a team meeting, "I don't know why we have to rearrange schedules every time someone's imaginary friend has demands."

Q: Were other employees present?

A: Seven of us. I can provide the names.

Q: How did Mr. Farouk respond?

A: He didn't. He shouldn't have had to. But I followed up with him after the meeting to make sure he knew the request was reasonable and appropriate.

Q: Did you speak to Ms. Cromwell about her statement?

A: I sent her an email—which I've retained—explaining that her characterization was inappropriate and potentially exposed the company to liability. I cc'd my personal email address.

Q: What was her response?

A: She called me "HR adjacent" and told me to stay in my lane.

Q: And what was your reaction to that?

A: I told her that employment law was everyone's lane, and that I'd been navigating it successfully since before she made manager.

Q: Did you escalate this matter?

A: I escalated it through every channel available, documented each step, and maintained copies of everything. My files on this matter are extensive and organized by date.

topic: A former employee is deposed about discriminatory remarks made by a supervisor
text:
Q: Mr. Patterson, I'm going to show you what's been marked as Exhibit 14. Do you recognize this document?

A: Yes.

Q: What is it?

A: An email I sent to Carol Vance on September 3rd, 2023.

Q: Now, this email references a conversation you had with Derek Simmons, your supervisor at the time. Is that correct?

A: That's what the email says, yes.

Q: I'm asking if it's accurate.

A: It's accurate. I wrote it within an hour of the conversation occurring.

Q: In the email, you describe Mr. Simmons using certain language about an employee named Marcus Webb. Can you tell me what Mr. Simmons said?

A: He said—and I'm quoting because I remember it exactly—"I don't know why they keep hiring these people. They're never going to fit the culture here."

Q: Did you ask Mr. Simmons what he meant by "these people"?

A: I didn't need to ask. Marcus is Black. Derek was gesturing toward Marcus's desk when he said it. The meaning was obvious to anyone with functional comprehension.

Q: But you didn't seek clarification?

A: Counsel, I've been in HR-adjacent roles for twelve years. I've seen this pattern dozens of times. When someone says "these people" while pointing at the only Black employee in the department, clarification isn't ambiguous. It's theater.

Q: You seem very certain of your interpretation.

A: I am certain. And I'll note that my certainty is based on professional experience that includes testifying as a witness in two prior discrimination matters, both of which resulted in findings for the plaintiffs.

Q: Let's focus on this case, Mr. Patterson.

A: I am focused. I'm also providing context that's relevant to my credibility as a witness, which is presumably why I'm here.

Q: Did Marcus Webb ever tell you he felt discriminated against?

A: He didn't need to tell me. I could see how he was being treated—the assignments he didn't get, the meetings he wasn't invited to. I documented those patterns as well.

topic: A former employee is deposed about discriminatory remarks made by a supervisor
text:
Q: You've testified that you heard Robert Tran make comments about female employees on more than one occasion.

A: I have.

Q: Let's discuss the incident on February 15th, 2024.

A: That was the day of the Henderson presentation.

Q: What happened that day?

A: Jennifer Moss gave what I can only describe as a flawless presentation to the Henderson Group. Flawless. She'd prepared for three weeks, rehearsed with me twice, anticipated every question they might ask.

Q: And what did Mr. Tran say after this presentation?

A: He said—in front of five people—"Well, at least she's easy on the eyes. That probably helped close the deal."

Q: How did you react?

A: I said, "Actually, what closed the deal was the fact that Jennifer identified a $600,000 cost savings in their supply chain that their own team had missed."

Q: Did Mr. Tran respond?

A: He laughed. He said I was "no fun."

Q: Did anyone else speak up?

A: No. But I wasn't finished. I told him that Jennifer's analysis was the most sophisticated work our department had produced in the last fiscal year, and that his comment said considerably more about his limitations than hers.

Q: That's a direct quote?

A: Yes. I remember my exact words because I meant every one of them.

Q: Were there any consequences for you after making that statement?

A: Robert stopped inviting me to client dinners. I considered that more of a benefit than a consequence.

Q: Did you report this incident formally?

A: I did. I submitted a written complaint that detailed not only this incident but the pattern of similar comments I had witnessed over the preceding fourteen months. The complaint was six pages, single-spaced, with dates and witnesses listed for each incident.

Q: Was any action taken?

A: I was told it would be "addressed." Jennifer was passed over for promotion two months later. I testified at her EEOC hearing. She prevailed.

topic: A driver is deposed about the events leading up to a multi-vehicle collision
text:
Q: Mr. Hernandez, I want to take you back to the morning of October 14th. What time did you leave your residence?

A: Around 6:15. Maybe 6:20.

Q: And what was your intended destination?

A: Work. Same as every day.

Q: Which route did you take?

A: The same route I always take. Down Millbrook, onto the 405, exit at Culver.

Q: Had you taken that route the previous day?

A: Yes.

Q: The day before that?

A: Yes. I've taken it for eleven years. I don't know what else to tell you.

Q: I'm just establishing the facts, Mr. Hernandez. Now, at the time you merged onto the 405, what was the traffic like?

A: It was heavy. It's always heavy. It's Los Angeles at 6:30 in the morning.

Q: Did you observe any brake lights ahead of you as you merged?

A: There are always brake lights. That's how it works.

Q: I'm asking specifically about that morning.

A: Then yes. There were brake lights. There were brake lights in front of me, and behind me, and in every lane. That's the answer.

Q: How fast were you traveling when you completed your merge?

A: I don't know. Thirty, thirty-five. Whatever the car in front of me was doing.

Q: And at any point did you look at your speedometer?

A: No. I was watching the road. I was watching the cars. I was doing what you're supposed to do.

topic: A driver is deposed about the events leading up to a multi-vehicle collision
text:
Q: Ms. Chen, prior to the collision, had you consumed any alcohol that day?

A: No.

Q: Any medications?

A: I take blood pressure medication. I took it that morning like I always do.

Q: What medication specifically?

A: Lisinopril. Ten milligrams.

Q: Does that medication cause drowsiness?

A: It can. It doesn't for me. I've been on it for three years.

Q: But the label warns of possible drowsiness?

A: I suppose it does. Most medications do.

Q: So you were aware of that warning?

A: Counselor, I was not drowsy. I was not impaired. I've answered this. I'll answer it again if you need me to, but the answer isn't going to change.

Q: I'm simply trying to understand your physical state at the time.

A: My physical state was fine. I was alert. I was driving the speed limit. The truck in front of me jackknifed. I don't know what you want me to say about my blood pressure medication that changes any of that.

Q: Let's move on. What do you recall seeing immediately before the truck jackknifed?

A: Rain. Spray from other vehicles. The truck's taillights. That's it. There wasn't anything to see before it happened.

Q: Nothing unusual?

A: If there had been something unusual, I would have mentioned it. There wasn't.

topic: A driver is deposed about the events leading up to a multi-vehicle collision
text:
Q: Mr. Patterson, you stated earlier that you checked your mirrors before changing lanes.

A: That's correct.

Q: You glanced.

A: I looked. I checked. However you want me to phrase it.

Q: I want you to phrase it accurately.

A: I am phrasing it accurately. I checked my mirrors. I've been driving for forty years.

Q: And in those forty years, have you ever failed to see a vehicle in your blind spot?

A: I'm sure I have. Everyone has.

Q: But not on October 14th?

A: Not that I was aware of at the time.

Q: At the time.

A: Look—I've already told your investigator what happened. I've told my insurance company. I've told the police. I checked my mirrors, I signaled, I began to change lanes, and then everything happened at once. I didn't see the motorcycle until it was too late. That's the truth. I wish it were different, but it's not.

Q: When you say everything happened at once—

A: The motorcycle, the sedan behind me, the guardrail. All of it. Seconds. Maybe less.

Q: Let's slow down and take those one at a time.

A: Fine.

topic: A driver is deposed about the events leading up to a multi-vehicle collision
text:
Q: Mrs. Okonkwo, how long had you been driving before the accident occurred?

A: About forty-five minutes.

A: No.

topic: A pharmacist is deposed about a prescription that was filled with the wrong dosage
text:
Q: Dr. Patel, can you walk me through what happened when you first learned about the dosage error?

A: I was finishing up the afternoon shift, and I got a call from the patient's daughter. She was... she was very upset. And rightfully so. I listened to everything she had to say before I even looked at our records.

Q: What did she tell you?

A: That her mother had been taking the medication for three days and was experiencing severe dizziness, confusion. She read me the label on the bottle, and I knew immediately something was wrong.

Q: What did you do next?

A: I pulled the original prescription from Dr. Hensley. It clearly said 25 milligrams. The label on Mrs. Okonkwo's bottle said 250.

Q: A tenfold increase.

A: Yes. I need you to understand—I've been doing this for nineteen years. I have never made an error like this. Not once. And to know that this woman, this 74-year-old woman who trusted us, was harmed because of something that happened in my pharmacy... I'm still not over it. I don't think I will be.

Q: I appreciate you sharing that, Dr. Patel. Let's take a moment if you need one.

A: No, I want to continue. She deserves to have this on record. What happened to her matters.

Q: Understood. Who actually filled the prescription that day?

A: I did. It was my hands, my verification, my failure.

Q: Was there a second verification step in place?

A: There should have been. Marcus, my technician, was home with his sick child that day. I was covering both roles. That's not an excuse—I want to be clear about that—but it's the context.

Q: Were you aware of being short-staffed when you filled this prescription?

A: I was aware. And I made the decision to keep the pharmacy open rather than turn patients away. I thought I could manage. I was wrong, and Mrs. Okonkwo paid for my mistake.

Q: Is there anything you'd like to add before we move on?

A: Just that I've reached out to the family. I know it doesn't fix anything. I know that. But I needed her to hear from me directly that I'm sorry.

topic: A pharmacist is deposed about a prescription that was filled with the wrong dosage
text:
Q: State your name for the record.

A: Michael Chen. I'm the pharmacist of record at Greenway Pharmacy on Delancey Street.

Q: Mr. Chen, on February 14th of this year, did you fill a prescription for metoprolol for a patient named James Whitfield?

A: I did.

Q: And what dosage did you dispense?

A: 100 milligrams.

Q: What dosage was prescribed?

A: 10 milligrams.

Q: So Mr. Whitfield received ten times the prescribed dose.

A: That's correct.

Q: Can you explain how this happened?

A: I've gone over it a hundred times. The prescriber's handwriting was difficult to read. I interpreted a "10" as "100." I should have called to verify. I didn't.

Q: Why didn't you call?

A: We had a line out the door that day. I was rushing. But that's not a reason—it's just what happened.

Q: I'm not asking you to justify it, Mr. Chen. I'm trying to understand the circumstances.

A: I know. I'm sorry. I just... I keep thinking about what could have happened. What almost happened.

Q: Take your time.

A: Mr. Whitfield collapsed at his daughter's wedding. That's something I have to live with. His daughter called 911 while she was still in her wedding dress.

Q: How did you learn about this?

A: His wife came into the pharmacy the next week. I thought she was going to scream at me. I was prepared for that. Instead, she just looked tired. She said, "I thought you should know what your mistake cost us." And then she left.

Q: Did you respond?

A: I tried. I said I was sorry. It felt completely inadequate. Because it was.

Q: Has Greenway Pharmacy changed any procedures since this incident?

A: Yes. We now require verbal confirmation on any dosage that could be ambiguous. And I personally call the prescriber if there's any doubt. Any doubt at all. I don't care how long the line is.

topic: A pharmacist is deposed about a prescription that was filled with the wrong dosage
text:
Q: Ms. Reeves, I want to make sure I understand the verification process at your pharmacy. When a prescription comes in electronically, what happens?

A: I was.

A: Yes.

A: I'm saying the system showed 5 milligrams. But I'm also saying that I should have caught it. Mr. Thornton had been on 2 milligrams for eight years. I filled his prescriptions myself, dozens of times. I knew his dosage. I should have questioned the change.

Q: Why didn't you?

A: Because I trusted the system more than my own memory. And because I was tired. I'd been working doubles for two weeks. None of that matters to Mr. Thornton, though.

Q: What happened to Mr. Thornton?

A: He was hospitalized for internal bleeding. He's recovering, thank God. But he spent eleven days in the ICU.

Q: I have to ask you some difficult questions about the staffing situation. Are you able to continue?

A: Yes. I want to answer. Someone needs to understand how we got here—not just me, but all of us. The whole system.

Q: Were you required to work those double shifts?

A: Required? No. But if I didn't, the pharmacy would close. And people depend on us. People like Mr. Thornton.

Q: That sounds like an impossible position.

A: It felt like one. But I still made the choice to keep going when I was too tired to be safe. That's on me.

topic: A pharmacist is deposed about a prescription that was filled with the wrong dosage
text:
Q: Let's talk about your training procedures, Ms. Okafor. How do new pharmacists learn your dispensing protocols?

A: Shadowing, primarily. They work alongside an experienced pharmacist for their first six weeks.

Q: And in the case of the prescription error involving patient Diane Marsh, who was being shadowed?

A: Dr. Kevin Walsh. He'd been with us for four weeks at that point.

Q: Who was his supervising pharmacist?

A: I was.

Q: So Dr. Walsh filled the prescription, but you verified it?

A: That's correct. The error is mine. I want to be clear about that. Kevin was still learning. The responsibility to catch mistakes—that's why I was there.

Q: Tell me what happened.

A: The prescription was for 0.5 milligrams of Xanax. Kevin entered 5 milligrams. He missed the decimal point.

Q: And you verified it?

A: I did. I looked at the screen, I looked at the bottle, and I approved it. I don't know how I missed it. I've asked myself every day since then.

Q: Has Dr. Walsh spoken to you about this incident?

A: He tried to take the blame. I wouldn't let him. He came to me almost in tears, saying he should have been more careful. I told him—and I'll say it again now—he was learning. That's what training is for. The safeguard was me, and I failed.

Q: How is Mrs. Marsh now?

A: She's... she's working through it. Her husband told me she's afraid to take any medication now. She has anxiety—that's why she was prescribed Xanax in the first place—and now she can't trust the pills meant to help her. I think about that constantly.

Q: What changes have you implemented since?

A: Two-pharmacist verification for all controlled substances. I argued for it for years before this. Corporate finally listened. It shouldn't have taken hurting someone to make them listen, but at least it's in place now.

Q: Do you believe that would have prevented this error?

A: I know it would have. Because someone else would have caught what I missed.
