Q: And what did that review conclude about whether proper lockout procedures were followed?

A: The review concluded that... that there were questions about whether the procedures were followed completely.

Q: "Questions." Let me rephrase. Was there a lock on the breaker?

A: No.

Q: Was there a tag?

A: No.

Q: So the procedures weren't followed at all, were they?

A: Not... not on that occasion, no.

Q: And whose responsibility was it to ensure those procedures were followed?

A: The individual worker is responsible for their own lockout.

Q: Is that your final answer?

A: It's the answer in the handbook. Section 4.2.

topic: A warehouse supervisor is deposed about safety protocols that were allegedly ignored
text:
Q: Tell me about the forklift training program.

A: What do you want to know?

Q: Let's start with frequency. How often do operators receive refresher training?

A: Annually. Plus whenever there's an incident, plus whenever we get new equipment.

Q: And who conducts this training?

A: I do, mostly. Sometimes we bring in the equipment vendor for new models.

Q: You're certified to conduct OSHA-compliant forklift training?

A: Yes. Have been since 2017.

Q: Mr. Patterson, how many forklift operators were working at the facility in September of last year?

A: Fourteen.

Q: How many of those fourteen had completed their annual refresher training by September?

A: I'd have to check the records.

Q: I have the records here. Would you like to look at them?

A: Sure.

Q: Take your time.

A: Okay... looks like we had—eight had completed it by then.

Q: Eight out of fourteen. What about Derek Simmons specifically?

A: Derek... he was scheduled for October.

Q: He was operating a forklift in September without current certification?

A: His certification was still technically valid. The annual refresher is a company policy, not a legal requirement. OSHA requires retraining after incidents or observed unsafe operation, and every three years at minimum. Derek was compliant with OSHA.

Q: I didn't ask about OSHA. I asked about your company's policy.

A: And I'm telling you the context. You're trying to make it sound like Derek was driving around unlicensed. That's not accurate.

Q: I'm asking whether your own policy was followed. Was it?

A: It was being followed. He was scheduled.

Q: Before or after his forklift struck Mr. Yamamoto?

A: Before. He was already on the calendar.

topic: A warehouse supervisor is deposed about safety protocols that were allegedly ignored
text:
Q: How would you describe the general safety culture at the warehouse?

A: I'm not sure what you mean by "safety culture."

Q: Fair enough. Let me ask it differently. Were employees encouraged to report safety concerns?

A: Of course.

Q: How were they encouraged?

A: We have a reporting system. Anonymous tip line, suggestion boxes, they can come to me directly.

Q: How many safety concerns were reported through those channels in 2023?

A: I don't have that number memorized.

Q: Would it surprise you to learn the number was three?

A: For the whole year?

Q: For the whole year.

A: I... I'd want to verify that.

Q: We'll mark this as Exhibit 14. This is the log your company produced in discovery. Take a look at the entries for 2023.

A: Okay.

Q: How many entries do you count?

A: Three.

Q: For a facility with how many workers?

A: About forty-five.

Q: Does that number concern you, Mr. Raines? Three reports from forty-five employees over twelve months?

A: It could mean the system isn't being used. It could also mean there weren't many concerns.

Q: Which do you think it is?

A: Honestly? I think people came to me directly. Not everything goes through the formal system.

Q: And did you document those direct conversations?

A: Not always formally, no.

Q: So there's no record.

A: There's no paper record. That doesn't mean the conversations didn't happen.

topic: A warehouse supervisor is deposed about safety protocols that were allegedly ignored
text:
Q: Ms. Chen, are you familiar with the chemical storage protocols in Warehouse B?

A: Very familiar. I wrote most of them.

Q: You wrote them?

A: Drafted them, I should say. Based on manufacturer specs and OSHA requirements. Regional management approved them, but the substance came from me.

Q: Then you should be the perfect person to explain why oxidizers were stored next to flammable solvents on November 3rd.

A: They weren't.

Q: Excuse me?

A: They weren't stored next to each other. I've seen the incident report and I've seen the photos, and I know exactly what you're going to point to. The oxidizers were in their designated area. The solvents that Mr. Garrett moved that morning were supposed to go to the flammables cabinet. He staged them temporarily on the wrong shelf. That's an employee error, not a protocol failure.

Q: You're saying your protocols were adequate, and Mr. Garrett simply ignored them?

A: I'm saying exactly what happened. Garrett was new, he was rushing to finish before lunch, and he put the drums in the wrong place for twenty minutes. He's admitted this.

Q: Isn't it your job to make sure employees follow protocols?

A: It's my job to create good protocols, train employees on them, and monitor compliance. I can't physically stand behind every employee every second. Garrett was trained. He signed the acknowledgment form. He made a mistake.

Q: A mistake that resulted in a fire.

A: A mistake that resulted in a fire, yes. A terrible mistake. But the protocols themselves were sound. The failure was human.

Q: You don't believe the company bears any responsibility for that?

A: That's a legal question, counselor, and I'm not a lawyer. I'm telling you what happened.

Q: You seem very certain about what happened.

A: I am certain. Because I was there for the investigation, I reviewed every piece of evidence, and I've thought about nothing else for four months.

topic: An HR director is questioned about a harassment complaint that was filed and closed
text:
Q: Ms. Patterson, I want to direct your attention to the complaint filed by Denise Morales in March of 2022. You were the HR director who handled that complaint, correct?

A: I was the HR director, yes. Whether I "handled" it depends on what you mean by that word.

Q: You were the person responsible for investigating the complaint?

A: I was responsible for overseeing the investigation process, yes.

Q: And the complaint was against Marcus Webb, a regional sales manager?

A: That's correct.

Q: Ms. Morales alleged that Mr. Webb made repeated unwelcome comments about her appearance. Is that accurate?

A: She made a complaint. I'm not going to characterize what she alleged without the document in front of me.

Q: I can provide you with the document if you need it.

A: That would be appropriate, yes.

Q: Let me rephrase. Do you recall the general nature of Ms. Morales's complaint?

A: I recall it involved allegations of inappropriate workplace conduct.

Q: Can you be more specific?

A: I've already said I'd prefer to have the document.

Q: Ms. Patterson, you investigated this complaint personally, didn't you?

A: I conducted interviews as part of the investigation, yes. Along with outside counsel.

Q: And you don't recall what the complaint was about?

A: I recall the complaint. I'm declining to paraphrase it from memory when you could simply show me the document and we could discuss what it actually says. That seems like it would be more productive for everyone.

topic: An HR director is questioned about a harassment complaint that was filed and closed
text:
Q: How many harassment complaints did you process in 2022, roughly?

A: I'd have to check the records for an exact number. Approximately fifteen to twenty, I believe.

Q: And the complaint filed by Denise Morales—that was one of them?

A: Yes.

Q: Walk me through your standard process when a complaint comes in.

A: We receive the complaint, document it, assess whether it requires immediate action, assign an investigator, conduct interviews, gather evidence, and make a determination.

Q: That's the standard process. Did you follow that process for the Morales complaint?

A: Yes.

Q: Every step?

A: Yes. Every step.

Q: Who conducted the interviews?

A: I did. Along with outside counsel from Brecker & Associates.

Q: How many witnesses did you interview?

A: I believe it was four, including Ms. Morales and Mr. Webb.

Q: Four people. For a complaint involving repeated harassment over several months. Four people seemed sufficient to you?

A: It was sufficient to reach a determination, yes.

Q: Let me ask it this way—did you interview anyone who worked in the same office as Ms. Morales and Mr. Webb, other than those two?

A: Two others, yes.

Q: Two others. Out of how many people in that office?

A: I don't have that number in front of me.

Q: Roughly?

A: I'm not going to guess.

Q: More than ten?

A: Probably. I don't know. I'd need to look at the organizational chart from that time.

topic: An HR director is questioned about a harassment complaint that was filed and closed
text:
Q: The investigation was closed on April 14, 2022, correct?

A: If that's what the document says.

Q: I'm asking if you recall.

A: I don't recall the specific date. We close a lot of investigations.

Q: The finding was that the complaint was "unsubstantiated." What does that mean in your organization's terminology?

A: It means the investigation did not produce sufficient evidence to conclude that a policy violation occurred.

Q: Does "unsubstantiated" mean the conduct didn't happen?

A: No.

Q: Does it mean Ms. Morales was lying?

A: No. It means what I said. Insufficient evidence to substantiate.

Q: So the conduct could have happened exactly as Ms. Morales described, and you still could have found it "unsubstantiated"?

A: Theoretically, yes. That's how evidentiary standards work.

Q: That doesn't trouble you?

A: Counsel, I'm not sure what you're asking me. Am I troubled by the concept of evidentiary standards?

Q: I'm asking whether it troubles you that your process might have allowed harassment to continue.

A: I'm not going to accept the premise of that question. Our process was thorough and followed established protocols.

Q: Established by whom?

A: By the company, in consultation with legal counsel, in compliance with applicable regulations.

Q: And those protocols—you wrote them?

A: I contributed to them. I didn't write them single-handedly.

Q: But you had input.

A: I had input. Yes. As did legal. As did senior leadership. As did outside consultants. Would you like me to name everyone who's ever touched the employee handbook?

topic: An HR director is questioned about a harassment complaint that was filed and closed
text:
Q: Ms. Patterson, did Ms. Morales ever contact you after the investigation was closed?

A: She did.

Q: When?

A: I don't recall exactly. Within a few weeks, I think.

Q: What did she say?

A: She expressed dissatisfaction with the outcome.

Q: Can you be more specific about what she said?

A: She felt the investigation hadn't been thorough. She disagreed with the finding.

Q: Did she provide any new information at that time?

A: She mentioned some things, yes.

Q: What things?

A: I'd have to review my notes.

Q: You took notes?

A: I always take notes.

Q: But you don't recall what she said?

A: I recall the general nature of the conversation. I don't recall specifics verbatim, no. It was over two years ago.

Q: Did you reopen the investigation based on what she told you?

A: No.

Q: Why not?

A: Because what she provided didn't constitute new evidence that would have changed the outcome.

Q: That was your determination to make?

A: Yes.

Q: Yours alone?

A: I consulted with legal.

Q: Who in legal?

A: I don't recall specifically. Whoever was available.

Q: You don't recall who you consulted with about whether to reopen a harassment investigation?

A: Counsel, I speak with people in legal daily. I don't keep a log of every conversation. I consulted with legal. The decision was made not to reopen. That's what I can tell you.

topic: An HR director is questioned about a harassment complaint that was filed and closed
text:
Q: Did anyone from senior leadership contact you about the Morales complaint?

A: I don't understand the question.

Q: It's straightforward. Did anyone in senior leadership—VP level or above—ever speak to you about the Morales complaint?

A: We provide regular reports to senior leadership about HR matters.

Q: That's not what I asked. Did anyone specifically contact you about this complaint?

A: I may have had conversations. I don't recall specifically.

Q: You don't recall whether a senior executive contacted you about a harassment complaint against one of their regional managers?

A: I receive a lot of inquiries. I don't remember every one.

Q: Let me try to refresh your memory. Did Tom Harding, the VP of Sales, ever call you about the Morales complaint?

A: He may have.

Q: Yes or no, Ms. Patterson.

A: I can't give you a yes or no if I don't specifically remember.

Q: Do you have any recollection of speaking with Tom Harding about Denise Morales?

A: I have a vague recollection that he may have asked about the status of an investigation involving one of his people. I don't know if it was this specific investigation.

Q: When would that conversation have occurred?

A: I have no idea.

Q: Before or after the investigation closed?

A: I said I don't know.

Q: Was it typical for VPs to inquire about investigations involving their direct reports?

A: It happened.

Q: Did it influence your investigations when it happened?

A: Absolutely not.

Q: Never?

A: Never. I don't appreciate the implication.

topic: A tenant is questioned about property damage they reported to their landlord
text:
Q: Ms. Huang, when did you first notice the water damage in the apartment?

A: It was... I remember it was a Tuesday. November 14th. I came home from work and the ceiling in the nursery was—the paint was bubbling. There was water coming through the light fixture.

Q: The nursery?

A: We were—my husband and I were getting the room ready. For the baby.

Q: I see. What did you do when you discovered the leak?

A: I just stood there for a while. I don't know how long. Then I called the emergency maintenance line. I called it four times that night.

Q: Did anyone respond?

A: Not until the next morning. By then the carpet was soaked through. All of it. Everything we had put in there was ruined.

Q: What specifically was damaged?

A: The crib. It was my grandmother's. She had shipped it from Taiwan when she heard—she passed away three weeks later. She never got to... I'm sorry. The crib, a rocking chair, books, the carpet. Clothes we had been given.

Q: Did you document the damage?

A: I took photographs. I have them all. Every single thing.

Q: Ms. Huang, I need to ask—did Mr. Brennan, the landlord, ever come to see the damage himself?

A: He came five days later. He walked in, looked around for maybe two minutes, and told me it wasn't as bad as I'd made it sound.

Q: What did you say to that?

A: I didn't say anything. What was there to say?

Q: Did he offer any remediation?

A: He said he'd send someone to repaint. That was it. Just repaint.

Q: And the personal property? The items you lost?

A: He said that wasn't his responsibility. He said I should have had renter's insurance.

Q: Did you have renter's insurance?

A: No. We were twenty-three years old. We didn't know. We just didn't know.

topic: A tenant is questioned about property damage they reported to their landlord
text:
Q: Mr. Okonkwo, I want to take this slowly. I know this is difficult.

A: I appreciate that.

Q: The fire damage you reported occurred on what date?

A: March 3rd of this year.

Q: And the source of the fire?

A: Faulty wiring in the kitchen. The inspector confirmed it. The wiring in that building—I had complained about it. Multiple times.

Q: Let's get to those complaints. But first—were you home when the fire started?

A: No. I was at work. My neighbor called me.

Q: What did your neighbor tell you?

A: She said there was smoke. She said she couldn't get my dog out.

Q: You had a dog in the apartment?

A: Winston. I'd had him for eleven years.

Q: Take your time, Mr. Okonkwo.

A: I'm fine. Ask your questions.

Q: Did you—I'm sorry, let me rephrase. When you arrived at the property, what did you observe?

A: The kitchen was gone. The living room was mostly smoke damage. Winston was in the bedroom. He didn't—he couldn't get out. The door must have closed behind him.

Q: I'm sorry. I truly am.

A: You're doing your job.

Q: Had you reported the wiring issues to Mr. Castellano prior to this incident?

A: Three times in writing. Twice on the phone. I have the emails.

Q: What was his response?

A: The first time, nothing. The second time, he said he'd "look into it." The third time, he told me I was being paranoid. That the building was up to code.

Q: Was it up to code?

A: No. The fire marshal's report says it wasn't.

topic: A tenant is questioned about property damage they reported to their landlord
text:
Q: You submitted a maintenance request on February 2nd regarding the mold, correct?

A: That's correct.

Q: And what happened after that?

A: Nothing happened.

Q: Nothing at all?

A: They sent someone to look at it. He looked at it. Then nothing.

Q: How long did you wait before following up?

A: I followed up every week for two months. I have a log.

Q: Every week?

A: Every single week. Sometimes more. I sent photos. I sent air quality readings I had done myself. I explained about my daughter's asthma.

Q: Your daughter has asthma?

A: Had. She has permanent lung scarring now. The pulmonologist says the mold exposure—

Q: Let's stay focused on the timeline.

A: The timeline is my daughter can't run anymore. The timeline is she used to play soccer and now she can't finish a flight of stairs without her inhaler. That's the timeline.

Q: Ms. Vasquez, I understand you're upset—

A: I'm not upset. I'm answering your questions. You asked about the timeline. I'm telling you what the timeline cost.

Q: Did the landlord ever remediate the mold?

A: After we moved out. After I broke the lease because I had no choice. Then suddenly they were able to fix it within a week. Suddenly it was possible.

Q: Did they return your security deposit?

A: No. They kept it because I broke the lease.

Q: Did you dispute that?

A: I tried. I was told I had no case because I left voluntarily. Voluntarily.

topic: A tenant is questioned about property damage they reported to their landlord
text:
Q: Tell me about the condition of the heating system when you moved in.

A: It worked. It was old, but it worked.

Q: And when did that change?

A: December of last year. It got cold, really cold, and the heat just—it stopped one night. Completely.

Q: What was the temperature outside?

A: Fourteen degrees. It was that whole cold snap, you might remember it.

Q: What did you do?

A: I called the landlord. I called her directly because I knew the office would be closed.

Q: What did she say?

A: She said she'd send someone in the morning. I told her we couldn't wait until morning. My father lives with me. He's eighty-one.

Q: What was her response to that?

A: She said to use the oven. To leave the oven open.

Q: Did you do that?

A: What choice did I have?

Q: Mr. Petrov, did anyone come the next morning?

A: Two days later. Someone came two days later. We used space heaters. I bought them myself. The outlets in that building—they weren't meant for that kind of load.

Q: Did something happen?

A: One of them shorted. Started a small fire. We put it out, but my father—he fell trying to get away from it. Broke his wrist.

Q: Did you report that to the landlord?

A: I did. She said it was my fault for using space heaters.

Q: Did she ever fix the heating system?

A: Eventually. Three weeks later. By then my father had been in the hospital, and when he came back, he didn't want to stay in the apartment anymore. He was afraid.

Q: Where is your father now?

A: He's in a care facility. I couldn't—the apartment was all I could afford, and after everything, he didn't feel safe there. So I had to find somewhere else for him.

topic: A tenant is questioned about property damage they reported to their landlord
text:
Q: The report says you discovered the structural damage on July 7th. Is that accurate?

A: Yes.

Q: Describe what you found.

A: There was a crack in the wall. In the bedroom. I thought it was just cosmetic at first, but then I noticed the floor was uneven.

Q: Uneven how?

A: Sloping. Toward the window. It got worse over time.

Q: Did you notify the property manager?

A: I did. I sent photographs. I sent a video showing a ball rolling across the floor on its own.

Q: What did they say?

A: They said the building was settling. That it was normal.

Q: Did you accept that explanation?

A: I'm not an engineer, so I didn't know what to think. But it kept getting worse. The crack got longer. The door stopped closing properly.

Q: Did you follow up?

A: Many times. I started keeping a file. Dates, photos, measurements. I measured the slope with a level.

Q: What did those measurements show?

A: That it was getting worse. Week by week. The slope increased by almost an inch over three months.

Q: What happened after three months?

A: The building was condemned. The city came in, did an inspection, and we had forty-eight hours to leave.

Q: Forty-eight hours?

A: They said it wasn't safe. The foundation was failing.

Q: Where did you go?

A: I stayed with my sister at first. Then a motel. Then another motel. I'm still looking.

Q: What about your belongings?

A: We couldn't take everything. They said the structure was unstable, so we could only go in for essentials. The rest—my mother's furniture, my books, things I'd had my whole life—I had to leave them. They demolished the building two weeks later.

Q: Did the property management company offer any assistance?

A: They offered to return my last month's rent. That's all.

Q: How much was that?

A: Eight hundred dollars. Everything I owned was in that building, and they gave me eight hundred dollars.

topic: An accountant is deposed about transactions they processed on behalf of a client
text:
Q: Mr. Davenport, I'm going to show you what's been marked as Exhibit 14. Do you recognize this document?

A: It's a wire transfer confirmation.

Q: A wire transfer confirmation that you processed, correct?

A: That my office processed, yes.

Q: Your office. You're the only accountant at your office, isn't that right?

A: I have administrative staff.

Q: Administrative staff who process international wire transfers for your clients?

A: I processed the wire transfer. Is that what you need me to say?

Q: I need you to answer my questions truthfully, Mr. Davenport. Now, this wire transfer was for $2.3 million to an account in the Cayman Islands, wasn't it?

A: You have the document in front of you.

Q: I'm asking you to confirm it.

A: Yes. $2.3 million. Cayman Islands. November 14th. Account ending in 7842. Anything else you'd like me to read aloud for you?

Q: Did Mr. Hartwell tell you the purpose of this transfer?

A: He told me it was for an investment in a real estate development fund.

Q: And you believed him?

A: I'm an accountant, counselor. I process transactions. I don't interrogate my clients about their business decisions.

topic: An accountant is deposed about transactions they processed on behalf of a client
text:
Q: Ms. Chen, how long have you served as the accountant for Meridian Holdings?

A: Seven years.

Q: And in those seven years, approximately how many transactions have you processed on their behalf?

A: I couldn't give you an exact number.

Q: Ballpark it for me.

A: I'm not comfortable guessing under oath.

Q: You have no idea? Hundreds? Thousands?

A: Thousands. Probably.

Q: Let's talk about the quarterly payments to Ashford Consulting. You're familiar with those?

A: I am.

Q: Those payments averaged around $175,000 per quarter, didn't they?

A: I'd have to review the records to confirm the average.

Q: We've provided you with those records. They're in the binder in front of you.

A: Then you already know the answer.

Q: Ms. Chen, I'm asking you.

A: Fine. Yes. Approximately $175,000 per quarter.

Q: Did you ever verify that Ashford Consulting provided services to justify those payments?

A: That wasn't my role.

Q: Your role was just to write the checks?

A: My role was to execute transactions that were authorized by my client. Which I did. Properly. Every single time.

topic: An accountant is deposed about transactions they processed on behalf of a client
text:
Q: You processed a payment of $50,000 on March 3rd to an individual named Robert Vance, correct?

A: I processed a lot of payments. I'd need to see documentation.

Q: Here's Exhibit 22. Take your time.

A: Yes. I see this.

Q: You processed it?

A: Yes.

Q: What was the purpose?

A: Consulting services.

Q: What kind of consulting services?

A: I wasn't provided with specifics.

Q: $50,000, and you weren't curious what it was for?

A: Curious isn't the same as entitled to know, counselor.

Q: So you just—

A: I just did my job. Which, last time I checked, isn't a crime.

Q: I didn't suggest it was a crime, Mr. Okonkwo.

A: The tone of your questions suggests otherwise.

Q: Let me be clear: I'm trying to understand the nature of these transactions.

A: And I'm trying to answer your questions. But I won't pretend I knew things I didn't know. That would be perjury. I assume you don't want me to commit perjury?

Q: Did you ever meet Robert Vance?

A: No.

Q: Did you ever speak with him?

A: No.

Q: Did you have any reason to believe he was a real person?

A: I had no reason to believe he wasn't.

topic: An accountant is deposed about transactions they processed on behalf of a client
text:
Q: Let's go back to the December transactions one more time.

A: We've been over December three times now.

Q: Then this should be easy. The $400,000 transfer to Lighthouse Ventures—who authorized that?

A: Mr. Brennan.

Q: Verbally or in writing?

A: Email.

Q: Do you have that email?

A: Your office has every email from my files. If you don't have it, I can't help you.

Q: I'm asking if you personally have that email, Ms. Reyes.

A: I don't carry seven years of correspondence in my pocket, counselor.

Q: Did you find anything unusual about the Lighthouse Ventures transfer?

A: No.

Q: $400,000 to a company incorporated three weeks earlier didn't raise any flags?

A: I wasn't aware of the incorporation date.

Q: Wouldn't a prudent accountant check?

A: A prudent accountant follows client instructions and maintains accurate records. Both of which I did.

Q: So in your view, you did nothing wrong?

A: I didn't say that. You're putting words in my mouth.

Q: I'm asking your view.

A: My view is that I performed my professional duties. What you're implying is something else entirely.

topic: An accountant is deposed about transactions they processed on behalf of a client
text:
Q: Mr. Patterson, when did you first become aware that the IRS was investigating your client?

A: Sometime in early February of last year.

Q: And after learning about the investigation, did you continue to process transactions for this client?

A: I continued to do my job, yes.

Q: Including the wire transfers we've discussed?

A: The wire transfers preceded the investigation by several months.

Q: I'm asking about transactions after February.

A: Then you should ask about specific transactions. I'm not going to guess which ones you mean.

Q: Fair enough. Exhibit 31. The $89,000 payment to Coastal Property Management on February 28th. Walk me through that.

A: Rent payment for a commercial property.

Q: A property your client owned?

A: Leased.

Q: Leased from whom?

A: I don't recall offhand.

Q: The lease was with your client's brother-in-law, wasn't it?

A: If you have documentation showing that, I'll take your word for it.

Q: Did you know that at the time you processed the payment?

A: No.

Q: Would it have mattered if you did?

A: Rent is rent, counselor. If my client had a lease obligation, they had a lease obligation. I don't run background checks on landlords.

Q: Even when federal investigators are circling?

A: Especially then. My job is to maintain accurate books, not to panic.

topic: A supervisor is deposed about performance reviews given to an employee who was later fired
text:
Q: Mr. Harmon, you conducted the annual performance review for Danielle Webb in March of 2022, correct?

A: I did.

Q: And you gave her an overall rating of "meets expectations"?

A: That's what the form says, yes.

Q: Is there some reason you're qualifying that answer?

A: I'm not qualifying anything. You asked about the form. The form says "meets expectations."

Q: Did Ms. Webb, in your personal assessment, meet expectations?

A: At the time of that review, based on the metrics we use, she fell within the range that corresponds to that rating.

Q: That's a very careful answer, Mr. Harmon.

A: It's an accurate answer.

Q: Let me ask it differently. Were you satisfied with her performance in March 2022?

A: "Satisfied" isn't really the standard we use. We have specific criteria. She met them.

Q: Did you have concerns about her performance that aren't reflected in the written review?

A: I have concerns about a lot of employees at various times. That's part of managing people.

Q: That's not what I asked.

A: Then maybe you could be more specific about what you're asking.

Q: Did you have concerns about Danielle Webb's performance in March 2022 that you did not document in her review?

A: Nothing that rose to the level of formal documentation, no.

Q: What does that mean, "rose to the level"?

A: It means I use my judgment about what belongs in a permanent personnel file and what gets handled through coaching conversations.

topic: A supervisor is deposed about performance reviews given to an employee who was later fired
text:
Q: Ms. Trujillo, how long had you supervised Kevin Okonkwo before his termination?

A: A little over two years.

Q: And in that time, you completed how many formal performance reviews for him?

A: Two annual reviews and one mid-year check-in.

Q: Let's talk about the first annual review. You rated him as "exceeds expectations" in three out of five categories. Do you recall that?

A: I'd have to see the document to confirm the exact numbers, but that sounds approximately right.

Q: I'm happy to show you the document.

A: Please.

Q: Exhibit 14. Take a moment to review it.

A: All right. Yes, three categories at "exceeds expectations."

Q: So in November 2021, Kevin Okonkwo was exceeding expectations in the majority of his job functions?

A: According to that review, yes.

Q: According to that review? You wrote it, didn't you?

A: I did.

Q: So according to you, he was exceeding expectations?

A: At that time, based on the information I had, yes.

Q: What information did you not have?

A: I'm not saying I was missing information. I'm saying performance is assessed at a point in time.

Q: And at that point in time, he was a strong performer?

A: He was performing well in those specific categories, yes. I wouldn't say I had the complete picture of how things would develop.

Q: Did you have any indication in November 2021 that he would be terminated fourteen months later?

A: No.

topic: A supervisor is deposed about performance reviews given to an employee who was later fired
text:
Q: When you wrote that Mr. Desai "needs improvement in client communication," what specifically were you referring to?

A: There had been a few instances where clients felt he was too abrupt in emails.

Q: A few instances. Can you be more specific?

A: I believe there were two complaints that came to my attention.

Q: Two complaints over what period of time?

A: That review covered the prior twelve months, so within that year.

Q: Two complaints in twelve months. Is that unusual for someone in his role?

A: It's not unheard of.

Q: That's not what I asked. Is two complaints in a year unusual?

A: I'd say it's on the higher end.

Q: Really? How many client-facing employees do you supervise?

A: Currently, eight.

Q: And in the same twelve-month period, how many complaints were lodged against other employees you supervise?

A: I'd have to check the records to give you an exact number.

Q: Give me your best estimate.

A: Maybe... six or seven total across the team.

Q: So out of roughly eight complaints, two were about Mr. Desai?

A: If those numbers are right, yes.

Q: That's twenty-five percent. For one employee out of eight. So roughly proportional, wouldn't you say?

A: I suppose that's one way to look at it.

Q: What's another way to look at it?

A: Context matters. The nature of the complaints matters. Not all complaints are equal.

Q: Were Mr. Desai's complaints more serious than the others?

A: I'd characterize them as... indicative of a pattern.

Q: Two complaints is a pattern?

A: When they're similar in nature, it can suggest one, yes.

topic: A supervisor is deposed about performance reviews given to an employee who was later fired
text:
Q: Did you ever discuss Ms. Fontaine's performance with HR prior to the decision to terminate her?

A: Yes, of course.

Q: How many times?

A: I don't have an exact count. Several.

Q: More than five?

A: Probably around that.

Q: And when did these conversations begin?

A: I'd say late summer of 2022.

Q: August? September?

A: Probably September.

Q: So the conversations with HR about Ms. Fontaine began about three months before her termination?

A: That sounds right.

Q: But her last performance review, in June 2022, rated her as "meets expectations" with no formal improvement plan. Is that correct?

A: Correct.

Q: Help me understand something.

A: I'll try.

Q: How does an employee go from "meets expectations" in June to termination discussions in September?

A: Things can change quickly.

Q: What changed?

A: Her attitude, primarily. Her responsiveness to feedback.

Q: Is attitude something you measure in your performance reviews?

A: Not as a standalone category, no.

Q: So this attitude problem—it wouldn't have appeared anywhere in writing before September?

A: It might have been referenced in the comments sections.

Q: I've reviewed the June review. I don't see any reference to attitude concerns. Would you like to take another look?

A: If you've reviewed it, I'll take your word for it.

Q: I'd rather you look at the document.

A: Fine. May I see it?

topic: A supervisor is deposed about performance reviews given to an employee who was later fired
text:
Q: I want to make sure I understand the timeline. Mr. Briggs received a positive review in January, correct?

A: Correct.

Q: Then a verbal warning in April?

A: Yes.

Q: A written warning in June?

A: Yes.

Q: And termination in August?

A: That's correct.

Q: That's a significant decline over seven months.

A: It is.

Q: What happened?

A: His performance deteriorated.

Q: In what way?

A: Missed deadlines. Quality issues. Failure to follow established procedures.

Q: Were any of these issues present when you gave him the positive review in January?

A: Not to the same degree.

Q: But to some degree?

A: There may have been early signs. In retrospect.

Q: In retrospect. But at the time, you gave him a positive review.

A: At the time, I believed the review was accurate.

Q: You believed it was accurate?

A: It was accurate based on the standards we applied.

Q: Mr. Patterson, I'm noticing you keep adding these qualifiers. "At the time." "Based on the standards." "In retrospect." Is there something about the January review you'd like to clarify?

A: No. I stand by the review as written.

Q: Then why the qualifications?

A: Because you're asking me to explain how someone can go from a positive review to termination, and I'm trying to give you a complete picture. Performance isn't static. People change. Circumstances change.

Q: Did the standards change?

A: No.

Q: Did your expectations of Mr. Briggs change?

A: My expectations remained consistent with his role.

topic: A store manager is questioned about a customer slip-and-fall on their premises
text:
Q: Mr. Daniels, you were the store manager on duty the morning of March 14th, correct?

A: Yes.

Q: And you received training on spill response procedures?

A: Yes, I did.

Q: When did you receive that training?

A: When I was hired. Four years ago.

Q: Any refresher courses since then?

A: I don't recall specifically.

Q: You don't recall, or there weren't any?

A: I said I don't recall. If there were records, you'd have them.

Q: I'm asking what you remember, Mr. Daniels.

A: And I told you. I don't recall.

Q: Fine. Let's move on. Who was responsible for floor inspections that morning?

A: Whoever was assigned. I'd have to check the schedule.

Q: You don't know who was working your own floor that day?

A: It was over a year ago. Do you remember what you had for breakfast last Tuesday?

Q: Mr. Daniels, I'd ask that you simply answer the questions.

A: I am answering. You're just not liking the answers.

Q: Were floor inspections conducted every thirty minutes as required by store policy?

A: That's the policy, yes.

Q: That wasn't my question. Were they actually conducted that morning?

A: I assume so.

topic: A store manager is questioned about a customer slip-and-fall on their premises
text:
Q: Ms. Thornton, how long had the liquid been on the floor before Mrs. Patterson fell?

A: I don't know. I wasn't aware of any liquid until after the incident.

Q: So no one reported it to you?

A: No.

Q: No employee mentioned it?

A: No, counsel, no one mentioned it. As I just said.

Q: Was there a system in place for employees to report hazards?

A: Of course there was.

Q: Can you describe it?

A: They radio it in or tell a manager directly. It's not complicated.

Q: And that system failed that day?

A: I didn't say it failed. No one saw the spill before she fell. That's not a system failure; that's just—it happened quickly.

Q: How quickly?

A: I don't know. I wasn't standing there with a stopwatch.

Q: I understand. I'm asking for your best estimate.

A: I don't have one. Could have been thirty seconds, could have been five minutes. I genuinely don't know.

Q: Let's try this differently. When was the last floor inspection before the fall?

A: According to the log, 9:15 a.m.

Q: And the fall occurred at?

A: 9:47.

Q: Thirty-two minutes. Your policy requires inspections every thirty minutes, correct?

A: Yes.

Q: So the floor was overdue for inspection.

A: By two minutes. Yes. Two minutes.

topic: A store manager is questioned about a customer slip-and-fall on their premises
text:
Q: Tell me about the lighting in aisle seven.

A: What about it?

Q: Was it adequate?

A: It was the same as every other aisle.

Q: That's not what I asked. Was it adequate for customers to see potential hazards on the floor?

A: I'm not a lighting engineer.

Q: You're the store manager.

A: And I'm telling you the lighting met code. Beyond that, I can't give you a technical assessment.

Q: Had anyone complained about lighting in that aisle?

A: Not that I'm aware of.

Q: Would such complaints come to you?

A: Sometimes. Depends.

Q: Depends on what?

A: On whether the employee thought it was worth escalating.

Q: Mr. Reeves, I need you to work with me here. We're going to be at this for a while regardless.

A: I'm working with you. I'm answering every question.

Q: Were there any maintenance requests related to aisle seven in the six months before this incident?

A: I'd have to check the records.

Q: You don't know?

A: I manage forty-two aisles and sixty employees. No, I don't have every maintenance request memorized.

topic: A store manager is questioned about a customer slip-and-fall on their premises
text:
Q: The incident report says the substance was "clear liquid." What was it?

A: We believe it was water.

Q: You believe?

A: It appeared to be water. We didn't run a chemical analysis.

Q: Was there any product nearby that might have leaked?

A: There was a refrigerated display case about fifteen feet away.

Q: Could condensation from that case have caused the spill?

A: It's possible.

Q: Had that case had condensation issues before?

A: I'd need to review maintenance logs.

Q: Generally speaking, Mr. Okonkwo. In your experience.

A: In my experience, those cases sometimes produce condensation, yes.

Q: Sometimes. How often is sometimes?

A: I don't have a percentage for you.

Q: Once a week? Once a month?

A: I really couldn't say.

Q: You've been manager for three years and you can't say how often your refrigeration equipment produces condensation on the floor?

A: Counsel, I can tell you it happens occasionally. I can tell you we address it when we find it. What specific number are you looking for? Because I don't have it, and asking the same question different ways isn't going to change that.

Q: Let's move on. After the fall, what steps did you take—

A: Finally.

Q: Excuse me?

A: Nothing. What steps did I take. Go ahead.

topic: A store manager is questioned about a customer slip-and-fall on their premises
text:
Q: Who cleaned up the spill after Mrs. Donovan's fall?

A: One of our stock clerks. Jason, I think.

Q: You think?

A: Jason Medina. Yes.

Q: How long after the fall was the area cleaned?

A: Within ten minutes. We responded immediately.

Q: Did anyone photograph the spill before cleaning it?

A: I don't believe so.

Q: Why not?

A: Our first priority was making sure the customer was okay and eliminating the hazard.

Q: So no photographic evidence of what she slipped on was preserved.

A: That's correct.

Q: Is that standard protocol?

A: Our protocol is to address the hazard and attend to the injured party.

Q: I'm asking about documentation, Ms. Vance.

A: And I'm telling you our priorities. Look, we had a woman on the ground in pain. We weren't thinking about litigation; we were thinking about her.

Q: I appreciate that. But surely your training covers preserving evidence?

A: My training covers a lot of things. In the moment, you make judgment calls.

Q: Was it a judgment call not to photograph the scene, or did it simply not occur to anyone?

A: Does it matter? Either way, we don't have photographs.

Q: It matters for establishing what procedures were followed.

A: The procedure we followed was helping someone who was hurt. Can we please move on?

topic: A warehouse supervisor is deposed about safety protocols that were allegedly ignored
text:
Q: Mr. Delgado, how long have you been employed at the Branford Distribution Center?

A: Seven years this coming March.

Q: And in your role as warehouse supervisor, you oversee safety compliance?

A: That's one part of my responsibilities, yes. I also manage scheduling, inventory flow, and personnel issues as they come up.

Q: Let's focus on the safety component. Can you describe for me the standard protocol when a forklift operator reports a mechanical issue?

A: Sure. The operator fills out a yellow maintenance request form, tags the vehicle with a red out-of-service tag, and parks it in the designated repair bay near loading dock C. Then the form goes to maintenance, and they handle it from there.

Q: Every time?

A: That's the protocol, yes.

Q: I'm asking whether it happens every time in practice.

A: In my experience, yes. I can't account for every shift I'm not physically present for, but when I'm on the floor, that's how it works.

Q: Were you on the floor on November 14th of last year?

A: I'd have to check the schedule, but I believe so. That was a Tuesday, if I'm remembering right.

Q: It was a Tuesday, yes. Do you recall any forklift being taken out of service that day?

A: Not specifically, no. But I wouldn't necessarily remember every maintenance request from a year ago unless there was something unusual about it.

Q: Would a brake failure be unusual?

A: It would be notable, yes.

Q: But you don't recall one?

A: I don't, no. If there's documentation, I'm happy to review it.

Q: We'll get to the documentation. Thank you, Mr. Delgado.

A: Of course.

---

topic: A warehouse supervisor is deposed about safety protocols that were allegedly ignored
text:
Q: Ms. Chen, I want to ask you about the training records for temporary workers.

A: Okay.

Q: Specifically, the safety orientation that's supposed to happen before they begin work on the warehouse floor.

A: Right.

Q: How long is that orientation?

A: Four hours.

Q: And what does it cover?

A: Equipment operation basics, hazard identification, emergency exits and procedures, PPE requirements. There's a video portion and then a walkthrough with a floor supervisor.

Q: Who conducts the walkthrough?

A: Depends on the shift. Could be me, could be one of the other supervisors. We rotate.

Q: Is there a sign-off sheet when the orientation is complete?

A: There is.

Q: And the temporary worker signs it?

A: Yes.

Q: And the supervisor?

A: Yes.

Q: Do you have any recollection of a temporary worker named Marcus Webb?

A: The name sounds familiar. I'd have to see the paperwork to be sure.

Q: If I told you Mr. Webb began work on September 3rd and was injured on September 5th, would that refresh your memory?

A: I remember an incident in early September, yes. I wasn't certain of the name.

Q: Did Mr. Webb complete the four-hour orientation?

A: If he was on the floor, he would have.

Q: That's not what I asked. Do you know, specifically, whether he completed it?

A: I would need to see the sign-off sheet to answer that with certainty.

---

topic: A warehouse supervisor is deposed about safety protocols that were allegedly ignored
text:
Q: You mentioned earlier that inspections happen weekly.

A: That's right.

Q: Who performs them?

A: Rotating assignment. Supervisors take turns.

Q: Is there a checklist?

A: There is. Thirty-two items covering racking stability, floor conditions, lighting, equipment, signage, that sort of thing.

Q: And when an item fails inspection, what happens?

A: It gets logged, and a work order goes to the appropriate department. Facilities for structural issues, maintenance for equipment.

Q: How quickly are those work orders typically addressed?

A: Depends on the severity. Critical issues same day. Minor things might take a week or two.

Q: Who decides what's critical?

A: The supervisor doing the inspection makes an initial call. If it's borderline, we'd discuss it.

Q: In the six months before the incident, were there any inspection failures related to the racking in aisle 12?

A: I'd have to review the records.

Q: Sitting here today, you don't recall any?

A: I don't recall specifics, no. We have a lot of racking.

Q: If I showed you an inspection from August 8th noting loose anchor bolts in aisle 12, would that surprise you?

A: I'd want to see the document.

Q: That's fair. Let me hand you what's been marked as Exhibit 14.

A: Thank you. Give me a moment to read it.

Q: Take your time.

A: Okay. Yes, I see the notation here.

Q: Does that refresh your recollection?

A: It does. I see my initials on the work order. So this would have gone to facilities.

---

topic: A warehouse supervisor is deposed about safety protocols that were allegedly ignored
text:
Q: How many forklifts are typically in operation during a day shift?

A: Eight to ten, depending on volume.

Q: Are they inspected daily?

A: They're supposed to be.

Q: Supposed to be?

A: The operators do a pre-shift check. Walk around, check the brakes, horn, lights, look for leaks. It takes about five minutes.

Q: And they document this?

A: There's a clipboard in each forklift with a daily log.

Q: Have you reviewed those logs recently?

A: I spot-check them. Maybe once a week I'll grab a few clipboards and look through them.

Q: What do you do if you find gaps?

A: Talk to the operator. Remind them it needs to be done.

Q: Any disciplinary action?

A: For a first offense, no. We document the conversation. If it's a pattern, then we escalate.

Q: Has anyone been terminated for failing to complete pre-shift inspections?

A: Not for that alone.

Q: For that in combination with other things?

A: I believe so, yes. I'd have to check HR records to give you a specific case.

Q: In your opinion, is compliance with pre-shift inspections at an acceptable level?

A: I think there's always room for improvement.

Q: That's diplomatic. Let me ask it differently. On any given day, what percentage of forklifts have complete, accurate pre-shift logs?

A: I'd estimate eighty to eighty-five percent.

Q: So fifteen to twenty percent are operating without documented inspections?

A: Without complete documentation, yes. That doesn't mean the check wasn't done. Sometimes operators forget to log it.

---

topic: A warehouse supervisor is deposed about safety protocols that were allegedly ignored
text:
Q: Mr. Patterson, I'd like to talk about the communication chain when a safety concern is raised by a floor worker.

A: Alright.

Q: What's the procedure?

A: Worker tells their immediate supervisor. Supervisor assesses, and if it's something that needs to go higher, it comes to me.

Q: And then?

A: I make a determination. Either we address it internally or, if it's a regulatory matter, we loop in corporate safety.

Q: How often does something need to go to corporate?

A: Rarely. Most things we can handle at the facility level.

Q: In 2022, how many issues went to corporate safety?

A: I couldn't give you an exact number. A handful, maybe. Three or four.

Q: And in 2023?

A: Similar. Maybe a few more because of the expansion.

Q: The expansion added square footage and personnel, correct?

A: Correct. About thirty percent more capacity.

Q: Did safety staffing increase proportionally?

A: We added one safety coordinator position.

Q: One position for thirty percent more capacity?

A: That was the decision that was made, yes.

Q: By whom?

A: That would have been a corporate decision. Headcount comes from above my level.

Q: Did you request additional safety staffing?

A: I made recommendations in my annual operational review.

Q: Were those recommendations followed?

A: We got the one position.

Q: But you recommended more?

A: I recommended what I thought was appropriate. The final decision wasn't mine to make.

topic: A building inspector is deposed about a structural assessment they signed off on
text:
Q: Mr. Hensley, I want to take you back to the inspection of September 14th, 2021. You were the licensed inspector who signed off on the structural assessment for the Meridian Towers project, correct?

A: Yes, I was.

Q: And at the time of that inspection, you had been with the county for how long?

A: Twenty-three years. I started in 1998.

Q: That's a long career. You must have seen a lot of buildings in that time.

A: I have. More than I could count.

Q: Mr. Hensley, I understand this case involves a building where people were hurt. Before we go further, I want you to know—you can take your time with these questions. If you need a break at any point, just say so.

A: I appreciate that. I do. But I'd rather just... get through it, if that's alright.

Q: Of course. When you arrived at Meridian Towers that morning, what was the first thing you assessed?

A: The foundation. I always start with the foundation. It's—you have to understand, everything else depends on what's underneath.

Q: And what did you observe about the foundation that day?

A: It looked sound. The concrete wasn't showing any significant cracking. The rebar exposure we'd flagged on the earlier visit had been addressed. I documented all of it. I took photographs.

Q: You mentioned an earlier visit. Had there been concerns raised before?

A: There had been. Minor ones. I want to be clear—I flagged them, and I followed up. That's why I was back in September. To confirm the corrections.

Q: And you were satisfied the corrections had been made?

A: I was. At the time, based on everything I could see—yes. I was satisfied.

Q: Mr. Hensley, knowing what you know now, is there anything you wish you had done differently that day?

A: Every day. I think about it every single day. Those families—I think about those families.

Q: I understand. Thank you for your honesty.

A: I just wish thinking about it changed something.

---

topic: A building inspector is deposed about a structural assessment they signed off on
text:
Q: Ms. Reeves, you conducted the structural assessment for 445 Industrial Parkway on March 3rd, 2022, is that correct?

A: That's correct.

Q: How many inspections would you estimate you perform in an average month?

A: It varies. Somewhere between forty and sixty.

Q: That's quite a workload.

A: It is. We're understaffed. Have been for years.

Q: When you say understaffed, can you help me understand what that means practically? For your day-to-day work?

A: It means I'm often rushing. It means I'm driving between sites without a proper lunch break. It means I'm filling out reports in my car at 7 PM so I can get home to my kids at a reasonable hour.

Q: That sounds exhausting.

A: It is. But people depend on us. Building owners, tenants, the city. So you do what you have to do.

Q: When you inspected 445 Industrial Parkway, do you recall how much time you spent on site?

A: I don't recall exactly. Maybe forty-five minutes? An hour at most.

Q: Is that typical for a commercial property of that size?

A: It's on the shorter end. I'll admit that.

Q: Do you feel you had enough time to conduct a thorough assessment?

A: I—look, I followed protocol. I checked everything on my list. Whether I would have preferred more time, whether I would have liked to go slower and look at every weld, every joint... of course I would have. But that's not the reality we work in.

Q: I'm not trying to criticize you, Ms. Reeves. I'm trying to understand the circumstances.

A: I know. I'm sorry. It's just—a man lost his leg in that collapse. I've thought about him. I don't even know his name, but I've thought about him.

Q: That's not lost on me. Let's take this one step at a time.

A: Okay. Thank you.

---

topic: A building inspector is deposed about a structural assessment they signed off on
text:
Q: Mr. Chen, you signed off on the structural integrity of the Bayside Lofts conversion on November 8th, 2020?

A: I did.

Q: Prior to your inspection, had any other inspector examined that property?

A: Yes. Tom Harwell did the initial assessment.

Q: And Mr. Harwell is no longer with the department?

A: Tom passed away. Last spring. Heart attack.

Q: I'm sorry to hear that.

A: He was a good man. A good inspector. One of the best I worked with.

Q: I understand. I'll try to keep my questions focused on what you personally observed, then.

A: I'd appreciate that. I don't want to speak for Tom when he can't speak for himself.

Q: Of course. When you conducted your inspection, were you aware of any concerns Mr. Harwell had raised previously?

A: He'd noted some irregularities in the load-bearing wall modifications. The developer had made changes to the original plans.

Q: And did you examine those modifications yourself?

A: I did. Extensively. I spent almost two hours on the third floor alone because of what Tom had flagged.

Q: What was your conclusion?

A: That the structural engineer's revised calculations were sound. That the modifications, while different from the original plans, were within code.

Q: You trusted the engineer's calculations?

A: I verified what I could. I'm not a structural engineer myself—I'm an inspector. I rely on their expertise, and I use my own judgment and experience to assess whether what I'm seeing matches what's on paper.

Q: Mr. Chen, the families in this case—they've lost a great deal.

A: I know. I know they have. I've read the reports. I've seen the photographs. I'm not here to protect myself. I'm here to tell the truth about what I saw and what I did. That's all I can offer them now.

---

topic: A building inspector is deposed about a structural assessment they signed off on
text:
Q: Let's talk about the roof structure, Mr. Dominguez. Your report indicated no concerns with the truss system. Do you recall making that determination?

A: I do.

Q: Walk me through your assessment of the trusses.

A: I accessed the roof through the interior hatch. I conducted a visual examination of the truss connections, looked for signs of stress, warping, water damage.

Q: Did you physically touch or test any of the trusses?

A: I tested several of the connections by hand. Applied pressure, looked for give or movement.

Q: Several. How many, approximately?

A: Maybe eight or ten.

Q: And how many trusses were there in total?

A: I don't have the number in front of me. A lot. Maybe forty?

Q: So you tested roughly a quarter of them.

A: I tested the ones that were accessible and representative. That's standard practice.

Q: Mr. Dominguez, I'm not suggesting you did anything wrong. I'm trying to understand the limitations of what any inspector can realistically observe.

A: I appreciate you saying that. Because I want you to understand—I didn't cut corners. I did my job the way I was trained to do it. But I'm human. I can't see through wood. I can't see metal fatigue that hasn't manifested yet.

Q: That must be a difficult position to be in—knowing you're making decisions that affect people's safety, but also knowing you can't see everything.

A: It is. You learn to live with it, or you find another line of work.

Q: Did the truss that failed—was it one of the ones you tested?

A: No. It wasn't.

Q: How does that sit with you?

A: How do you think it sits with me? There was a child in that building. A little girl. Eight years old. She's fine, thank God—she wasn't hurt. But she could have been. That sits with me every single night.

---

topic: A building inspector is deposed about a structural assessment they signed off on
text:
Q: Ms. Patel, you've been an inspector for eleven years, correct?

A: Eleven years next month.

Q: In that time, have you ever refused to sign off on a structural assessment?

A: Yes. Several times.

Q: Can you give me an example?

A: There was a warehouse conversion in 2019. The developer wanted to turn it into event space. I found significant foundation settling, cracks in the slab that suggested ongoing movement. I declined to approve it.

Q: What happened after you declined?

A: The developer wasn't happy. He complained to my supervisor. But my supervisor backed me up.

Q: So you've demonstrated that you're willing to stand your ground when you see a problem.

A: I have. That's my job.

Q: Then help me understand—what was different about the Greenfield Commons inspection?

A: I've asked myself that question a hundred times.

Q: Take your time.

A: The signs weren't there. Or if they were, I missed them. I've gone over my notes, my photographs—I've gone over them until I can't see straight. And I don't see what I missed. But something was wrong with that building, and I signed off on it. So I must have missed something.

Q: Ms. Patel, is it possible that the failure was caused by something that occurred after your inspection?

A: It's possible. The engineering report suggests that's likely, actually. But that doesn't... it doesn't make me feel any better. There are people who trusted that my signature meant the building was safe.

Q: You carry that with you.

A: I do. Of course I do. I became an inspector because I wanted to protect people. That's all I ever wanted to do. And now there's a family who can't go home.

Q: I can hear how much that weighs on you.

A: It should weigh on me. If it didn't, I'd have no business doing this job.

topic: A contractor is questioned about delays that caused a construction project to fail
text:
Q: Mr. Delano, you submitted a change order request on March 15th, is that correct?

A: That's what the documents show, yes.

Q: I'm asking if you submitted it.

A: I signed it. Whether I physically handed it to someone or it went through my office manager, I couldn't tell you the precise mechanics of how it traveled from point A to point B.

Q: The change order added eleven days to the timeline. What was the basis for that extension?

A: Soil conditions. We hit clay where the survey indicated sand. You can't pour footings into soup.

Q: The geotechnical report from February didn't mention clay in that section.

A: Then the geotechnical report was wrong.

Q: You didn't request a supplemental survey before submitting the change order?

A: We had shovels in the ground. We could see what was there.

Q: So you made a determination that contradicted a licensed engineer's report based on visual observation?

A: Based on reality, counselor. I've been doing this thirty-two years. I know what clay looks like.

Q: Did you photograph these soil conditions?

A: I'm sure someone did.

Q: You're sure, or you know?

A: I'm sure. My crews document everything. If you're implying otherwise, I'd like to see what basis you have for that.

Q: I'm not implying anything, Mr. Delano. I'm asking questions.

A: And I'm answering them. Accurately.

topic: A contractor is questioned about delays that caused a construction project to fail
text:
Q: When did you first become aware that the steel delivery would be late?

A: Sometime in early April. I'd have to check my records for the exact date.

Q: Your project logs show a note on April 3rd. Does that refresh your recollection?

A: If that's what it says, then April 3rd.

Q: The note says, and I quote, "Morris called re: steel - Loss River having issues." What does that mean?

A: Loss River was our steel supplier. They were having issues.

Q: What kind of issues?

A: I don't recall specifically.

Q: You don't recall what caused a delay that set your project back three weeks?

A: I recall it wasn't anything we caused. Beyond that, you'd have to ask Morris or Loss River.

Q: Who is Morris?

A: Tom Morris. He handled procurement.

Q: Is Mr. Morris still with your company?

A: No.

Q: When did he leave?

A: I don't have that date memorized.

Q: Was it before or after the project was terminated?

A: After.

Q: How long after?

A: I'd have to check.

Q: Approximately.

A: A few months. Maybe more. I don't keep track of former employees' departure dates in my head, counselor.

topic: A contractor is questioned about delays that caused a construction project to fail
text:
Q: Let's talk about the subcontractor situation. You had three electrical subs quit the project?

A: Two quit. One we terminated.

Q: Why did the two quit?

A: You'd have to ask them.

Q: You never discussed it with them?

A: They gave notice. We moved on.

Q: No exit interviews, no conversations about why they were walking off an active job?

A: Subs come and go. It's not unusual.

Q: On the same project? Within six weeks of each other?

A: It happens.

Q: And the one you terminated—what was the reason?

A: Performance issues.

Q: Can you be more specific?

A: They weren't performing to our standards.

Q: Which standards specifically?

A: Workmanship. Timeliness. The usual.

Q: Was this documented?

A: I assume so.

Q: You assume your company documented the termination of a subcontractor on a twelve-million-dollar project?

A: I know we follow proper procedures. I don't personally review every piece of paper that gets filed.

Q: Who would have handled that documentation?

A: Project manager. Maybe site super.

Q: Would that be the same project manager who's now employed by Hartwell Development?

A: I don't keep tabs on where people go after they leave.

Q: That wasn't my question.

A: Then rephrase it.

topic: A contractor is questioned about delays that caused a construction project to fail
text:
Q: I want to ask about a meeting on May 9th.

A: Okay.

Q: You were there?

A: I was at a lot of meetings.

Q: This one was at the Marriott on Commerce. Conference room B. Ring any bells?

A: It might.

Q: Your calendar shows it blocked for two hours with the notation "RC - discuss options."

A: Okay.

Q: Who is RC?

A: Probably Bob Castellan. We called him RC sometimes.

Q: Robert Castellan from Pacific Mutual Insurance?

A: That's him.

Q: What options were you discussing?

A: I'd have to think about that. We talked about a lot of things over the course of the project.

Q: This was two weeks before you filed the force majeure claim.

A: Was it?

Q: Yes, Mr. Delano. It was.

A: Then we probably discussed the weather delays. That was the main issue at the time.

Q: The claim mentions supply chain disruptions, not weather.

A: It mentions both.

Q: Paragraph four specifically references material shortages as the primary cause.

A: Then I guess it does.

Q: Did Mr. Castellan help you draft that language?

A: That would be attorney-client privilege.

Q: Mr. Castellan isn't an attorney.

A: Then I'll need to consult with my counsel before answering that.

topic: A contractor is questioned about delays that caused a construction project to fail
text:
Q: You mentioned earlier that crew scheduling was tight. Can you elaborate?

A: We had the people we needed when we needed them. Mostly.

Q: Mostly?

A: Construction isn't a factory. You adjust.

Q: The daily logs from June show crew sizes dropping from fourteen to eight over a two-week period.

A: That sounds about right for that phase.

Q: Your original staffing plan called for twelve minimum through the end of framing.

A: Plans change.

Q: Why did this one change?

A: Budget realities. Weather setbacks. Reallocation of resources.

Q: Reallocation to where?

A: Other projects.

Q: Which projects?

A: I'd have to look at the schedule from that period.

Q: Would one of those projects be the Meridian Commons development?

A: Possibly.

Q: The one where you had a completion bonus tied to a July 15th deadline?

A: I don't recall the specific terms of that contract.

Q: But you recall pulling workers from this project to send somewhere else.

A: I recall making normal business decisions about resource allocation.

Q: And this project missed its deadline by forty-three days.

A: Lots of factors contributed to that.

Q: But the crew reduction wasn't one of them?

A: I didn't say that. I said lots of factors.

topic: A project manager is questioned about deadlines they missed on a software contract
text:
Q: Mr. Delgado, you were the project manager for the Vertex software implementation, correct?

A: I was the lead project manager, yes. One of two assigned to that contract.

Q: And the original delivery date was March 15th of last year?

A: That was the date in the initial scope document, yes.

Q: Was the software delivered on March 15th?

A: No.

Q: When was it delivered?

A: The final deployment was completed on June 3rd.

Q: So roughly eleven weeks late?

A: I'd need to check the exact calendar count, but that sounds approximately right. Though I'd point out that "delivered" is doing a lot of work in that question.

Q: What do you mean by that?

A: I mean we had functional modules in the client's hands starting in early April. The June date reflects full integration testing sign-off. Those are different things.

Q: But June 3rd was the date the contract was considered fulfilled?

A: According to one interpretation, yes.

Q: Was there another interpretation?

A: There were ongoing discussions about what constituted delivery milestones. I assumed you'd reviewed the amendment documents.

Q: I'm asking what you understood at the time, Mr. Delgado.

A: At the time, I understood that we were working within a scope that had changed at least three times at the client's request.

Q: So is it your testimony that the client caused the delay?

A: I'm testifying that the situation was more complicated than "you were late." If you want a simple yes or no, you're going to get an incomplete picture.

topic: A project manager is questioned about deadlines they missed on a software contract
text:
Q: Ms. Okonkwo, how many projects had you managed before the DataStream contract?

A: At Ridley Tech specifically, or in my career overall?

Q: At Ridley Tech.

A: DataStream was my third.

Q: And how did those earlier projects perform relative to deadline?

A: Both were completed on schedule.

Q: So what happened with DataStream?

A: Could you be more specific? A lot of things happened over eighteen months.

Q: Let me rephrase. Why was DataStream delivered late when your other projects were not?

A: The scope was significantly larger. The client's legacy systems presented integration challenges we didn't anticipate. We lost two senior developers mid-project.

Q: You lost them how?

A: They left the company.

Q: For what reason?

A: I wasn't privy to their personal career decisions.

Q: You had no conversations with them about why they were leaving?

A: I had conversations, yes.

Q: And what did they tell you?

A: One mentioned compensation concerns. The other didn't give me a specific reason.

Q: Did either of them mention problems with project management?

A: Not to me, no.

Q: Would they have told you if they had concerns about your management?

A: I really couldn't speculate about what someone might or might not have said in a hypothetical conversation.

topic: A project manager is questioned about deadlines they missed on a software contract
text:
Q: Walk me through the timeline of the deadline extensions.

A: The original deadline was August 1st. That was extended to September 15th, then to October 30th, then finally to December 12th.

Q: Who requested these extensions?

A: I submitted the formal requests through our internal change management process.

Q: So you requested them.

A: I submitted them. The requests reflected assessments made by the technical team.

Q: But your name is on the extension requests?

A: Yes, as project manager, I sign off on timeline documents.

Q: Mr. Yates, is it your testimony that you were simply passing along what others told you?

A: That's not what I said. I said the assessments came from the technical team. I evaluated those assessments and made the decision to submit the requests. I'm not disclaiming responsibility.

Q: Good. So you took ownership of the decision to extend.

A: I took ownership of the process. The underlying technical realities weren't invented by me.

Q: Were the technical realities ever verified by anyone outside your team?

A: We brought in a consultant in October.

Q: What did the consultant conclude?

A: That the December timeline was achievable with additional resources.

Q: And was December achieved?

A: December 19th.

Q: So that's a no.

A: That's a seven-day variance on a project that had been replanned three times. I'd call that a success given the circumstances.

topic: A project manager is questioned about deadlines they missed on a software contract
text:
Q: You mentioned in your earlier testimony that you raised concerns about the deadline. When did you first raise those concerns?

A: To whom?

Q: To anyone.

A: I raised concerns internally as early as January, maybe late December of the prior year.

Q: December of 2022?

A: That's right.

Q: And the contracted deadline was April 2023?

A: Yes.

Q: So four months before the deadline, you already had concerns?

A: I had questions about resource allocation. Concerns might be too strong a word for that stage.

Q: What word would you use?

A: I was flagging potential risks. That's standard practice.

Q: Did you flag these risks in writing?

A: I believe there are emails, yes.

Q: You believe, or you know?

A: I know I sent emails. I don't have them memorized.

Q: Ms. Chen, we've produced your emails in discovery. Would you like to see them?

A: If it would help clarify something specific, sure.

Q: I'm showing you Exhibit 14. Is this your email dated December 28th, 2022?

A: It appears to be.

Q: Please read the highlighted portion.

A: "I'm confident we can hit April if we stay focused and don't lose anyone from the core team."

Q: Does that sound like flagging potential risks to you?

A: It sounds like me doing my job, which was to maintain realistic optimism while documenting dependencies.

Q: Where in that email do you document the dependencies?

A: The next paragraph discusses the core team assumption.

topic: A project manager is questioned about deadlines they missed on a software contract
text:
Q: Let's talk about the status reports you submitted to the client.

A: Okay.

Q: How often were those submitted?

A: Weekly.

Q: Who prepared them?

A: I did, with input from the team leads.

Q: Did those reports accurately reflect the project's status?

A: Yes.

Q: Every time?

A: To the best of my knowledge at the time they were written, yes.

Q: Mr. Franklin, I'm looking at the report from February 10th. It says the project is "on track for April delivery." Do you see that?

A: I see that language, yes.

Q: And the report from February 17th says the same thing.

A: If you say so. I don't have it in front of me.

Q: I'm handing it to you now. Same language?

A: Similar, yes. "On track with noted risks."

Q: When did the reports stop saying "on track"?

A: I'd have to review them sequentially.

Q: Would it surprise you to learn that the first report acknowledging a delay was dated March 28th, three days before the deadline?

A: That doesn't sound right.

Q: Would you like to review Exhibit 22?

A: Yes, actually, I would.

Q: Take your time.

A: This report references the amended timeline. We had already communicated the extension to the client verbally by this point. The formal documentation followed the conversation.

Q: So your testimony is that the client knew before March 28th?

A: That's my clear recollection, yes.

topic: A financial advisor is deposed about investment decisions made on a client's behalf
text:
Q: Mr. Harrington, you've been a licensed financial advisor for how long?

A: Eighteen years this coming September.

Q: And in those eighteen years, how many times have you placed a client's retirement funds into a single concentrated stock position?

A: I'd have to review my records to give you an exact number.

Q: Ballpark it for me.

A: I don't ballpark when we're talking about people's financial futures, counselor. That's precisely the kind of thinking I avoid.

Q: Fair enough. Let's talk about Mrs. Delacroix specifically. You placed sixty-two percent of her retirement portfolio into Nexion Pharmaceuticals, correct?

A: I recommended that allocation, yes. She approved it.

Q: You recommended it. Did you also recommend she understand that Nexion was under SEC investigation at the time?

A: There was no public SEC investigation when I made that recommendation.

Q: When did you first learn of the investigation?

A: When it became public. Same as everyone else.

Q: So you had no advance knowledge?

A: I just said that.

Q: You did. I'm just making sure I understand your testimony. You're telling this court you had zero indication—none—that Nexion had regulatory problems before you moved Mrs. Delacroix's money?

A: I'm telling you what I knew and when I knew it. If you're asking me to speculate about things I didn't know, I won't do that.

Q: I'm not asking you to speculate, Mr. Harrington. I'm asking if you conducted any due diligence on Nexion's regulatory standing before recommending it as a majority position.

A: I conducted appropriate due diligence consistent with industry standards.

Q: And that due diligence revealed nothing?

A: It revealed what was publicly available. Which, at that time, raised no red flags.

topic: A financial advisor is deposed about investment decisions made on a client's behalf
text:
Q: Let's talk about the Meridian Capital Fund. You placed the Okonkwo account into that fund in March of 2021?

A: That's correct.

Q: What was your basis for that recommendation?

A: Strong historical returns, diversified holdings, experienced management team. It fit the client's risk profile.

Q: Strong historical returns. Over what period?

A: The previous seven years showed consistent growth above benchmark.

Q: And did you examine the fund's performance during market downturns specifically?

A: Of course.

Q: Of course. What did that examination reveal?

A: That the fund had weathered the 2020 correction reasonably well.

Q: Define reasonably well.

A: Losses consistent with or slightly below sector average.

Q: Slightly below. You mean the fund lost less money, or more money?

A: Less. Slightly less than comparable funds.

Q: Now, the Meridian fund had a fee structure, correct?

A: All funds have fee structures.

Q: I'm aware. What was this particular fee structure?

A: There was a management fee of one point eight percent and performance fees tied to returns above a certain threshold.

Q: One point eight percent. Was that disclosed to Mr. Okonkwo?

A: It was in the prospectus he received.

Q: Did you walk him through the prospectus?

A: I provided it to him and made myself available for questions.

Q: That's not what I asked. Did you walk him through it?

A: I explained the fund's general characteristics. I didn't read the prospectus aloud line by line, if that's what you're asking.

Q: Did you tell him, in plain language, that one point eight percent of his investment would go to fees annually regardless of whether the fund made money?

A: I believe the disclosure documents were clear.

topic: A financial advisor is deposed about investment decisions made on a client's behalf
text:
Q: Ms. Vance, I want to understand your decision-making process. When you recommended the Terraform Energy position to Mr. Schultz, what materials did you rely on?

A: Analyst reports, company filings, sector trends, my own research.

Q: Your own research. What did that entail?

A: Reviewing financial statements, listening to earnings calls, reading industry publications.

Q: Did any of your research raise concerns about Terraform's debt load?

A: Their debt-to-equity ratio was elevated, yes.

Q: Elevated. Can you be more specific?

A: Around three to one at the time of my recommendation.

Q: Three to one. Is that typical for the energy sector?

A: It's on the higher end.

Q: And you still recommended it despite being on the higher end?

A: I weighed multiple factors. Debt was one consideration among many.

Q: Help me understand what outweighed a three-to-one debt ratio.

A: Growth projections. Their pipeline of contracts. The broader energy market conditions at the time.

Q: You trusted their growth projections?

A: I evaluated them against industry data and found them reasonable.

Q: Terraform missed those projections by forty percent the following year. Were they still reasonable?

A: Hindsight allows for different conclusions than foresight.

Q: I'm not asking about hindsight. I'm asking whether your evaluation at the time was adequate.

A: My evaluation was thorough and professionally sound. Markets involve uncertainty. That's not a failure of process.

Q: So your testimony is that losing Mr. Schultz three hundred thousand dollars reflects a professionally sound process?

A: My testimony is that I followed appropriate protocols. Outcomes and process are not the same thing.

topic: A financial advisor is deposed about investment decisions made on a client's behalf
text:
Q: You met with Dr. Patel on January fourteenth, correct?

A: I'd have to check my records.

Q: I'm showing you what's been marked as Exhibit 14. Is that your signature on this meeting summary?

A: Yes.

A: I don't believe so.
