A: I advised her of an option that fit her stated goals. She made the decision.

topic: A financial advisor is deposed about investment decisions made on a client's behalf
text:
Q: Mr. Torres, let's slow down for a moment. You've testified that your recommendation of the Blackwell REIT was based on your assessment of the real estate market at that time.

A: Correct.

Q: And you made that assessment yourself?

A: With the tools and data available to me, yes.

Q: What tools and data?

A: Market reports. Interest rate projections. Regional vacancy rates. Comparable REIT performance.

Q: Did you consult with anyone else at your firm about this recommendation?

A: I may have discussed it informally.

Q: You may have. Did you or didn't you?

A: I don't recall a specific conversation, but it's possible.

Q: Is it standard practice at your firm to consult colleagues before making major allocation recommendations?

A: It's encouraged but not required.

Q: So you could have made this recommendation entirely on your own judgment?

A: Yes.

Q: And if your judgment was wrong, there was no check on that?

A: There are compliance reviews.

Q: After the fact.

A: Compliance reviews occur at various stages.

Q: Did compliance review this particular recommendation before you presented it to the Weston family?

A: I don't believe so.

Q: You don't believe so, or no?

A: No. Not before.

Q: So the Westons relied entirely on your individual judgment when they moved four hundred thousand dollars into a fund that lost sixty percent of its value in eleven months?

A: They relied on my professional judgment, yes. Which is what they hired me to provide.

topic: A witness is questioned about a conversation they overheard in a company hallway
text:
Q: Mr. Delacroix, I want to direct your attention to March 14th of last year. Were you at the Westfield office that day?

A: I was, yes. Arrived around 8:15, maybe 8:20.

Q: And at some point that morning, did you find yourself in the third-floor hallway near the executive conference room?

A: I did. I was on my way to IT to pick up a replacement laptop charger.

Q: Tell me what you observed.

A: Well, I heard voices as I came around the corner by the water fountains. Mr. Henning and Ms. Castellano were standing outside Conference Room C, and they were having what I'd call a heated discussion.

Q: A heated discussion. What made it heated?

A: Mr. Henning's face was red. Genuinely red. And Ms. Castellano had her arms crossed, and she kept saying "That's not what we agreed to, David. That's not what we agreed to."

Q: She repeated that phrase?

A: At least twice while I was within earshot. Maybe three times.

Q: What else did you hear Mr. Henning say?

A: He said—and I remember this clearly because it struck me—he said, "The board doesn't need to know every line item. That's not how this works."

Q: Those were his exact words?

A: Those were his exact words. "The board doesn't need to know every line item."

Q: What happened next?

A: Ms. Castellano noticed me. She sort of straightened up and said good morning, very professional, and Mr. Henning just walked into the conference room without acknowledging me.

Q: Did you discuss this conversation with anyone afterward?

A: I mentioned it to my supervisor, Rachel Okonkwo, that same afternoon. I thought it was strange enough to note.

Q: Thank you, Mr. Delacroix. Let's move on.

A: Of course.

---

topic: A witness is questioned about a conversation they overheard in a company hallway
text:
Q: You were in the hallway on the fourth floor on or about June 7th, correct?

A: I was waiting for the elevator.

topic: A witness is questioned about a conversation they overheard in a company hallway
text:
Q: Ms. Thornberg, I'd like to ask you about an incident in September of last year.

topic: A witness is questioned about a conversation they overheard in a company hallway
text:
Q: Good afternoon, Mr. Wasserman. Let's talk about February 3rd.

topic: A witness is questioned about a conversation they overheard in a company hallway
text:
Q: State your name for the record.

A: Elena Marchetti.

Q: Ms. Marchetti, you worked in Human Resources at Beacon Financial from 2019 to 2023, correct?

A: Correct.

Q: On October 10th, 2022, were you present on the first floor of the downtown office?

A: I was, yes.

Q: And did you overhear a conversation in the hallway outside the HR suite?

A: I did.

Q: Who was involved in that conversation?

A: Craig Bellamy from Compliance and a woman I didn't recognize.

A: Mr. Bellamy said, "If anyone asks, the policy was always interpreted this way."

Q: Did the woman respond?

A: Those were his words. I wrote them down as soon as I got back to my desk.

Q: You wrote them down.

A: I did.

Q: Why?

A: Because I knew—I knew right then that something was wrong. And I thought someday someone might need to know exactly what he said.

Q: Do you still have those notes?

A: I do. I kept them.

A: You're welcome.

topic: A project manager is questioned about deadlines they missed on a software contract
text:
Q: Mr. Hendricks, let's turn to the API integration module. When was that originally due?

A: March 15th, 2023.

Q: And when was it actually delivered?

A: June 2nd.

Q: So roughly eleven weeks late. Who was responsible for that timeline?

A: I was the project manager, so the timeline was my responsibility. I'll own that completely.

Q: You'll own it. That's refreshing. Can you tell me why it was eleven weeks late?

A: Certainly. The client's legacy database schema was undocumented. We discovered on February 28th that their system used a proprietary encoding format from 1997 that wasn't in any of the materials they'd provided during scoping.

Q: And you have documentation of this discovery?

A: I do. I have the email chain, the Jira tickets, the Slack messages, and the recorded call where their own IT director admitted he didn't know the encoding existed. I brought copies, actually, if you'd like them marked as exhibits.

Q: That won't be necessary at this moment. Did you communicate this issue to Vertex Solutions?

A: Within four hours of discovery. I have the timestamp.

Q: And their response?

A: They thanked us for identifying a problem their own team had missed for six years. I believe the exact words were "you've done us a favor." I can pull up that email too.

topic: A project manager is questioned about deadlines they missed on a software contract
text:

topic: A project manager is questioned about deadlines they missed on a software contract

Q: Let me make sure I understand the timeline correctly, Mr. Reeves. The inventory tracking system was delivered on December 3rd.

topic: A project manager is questioned about deadlines they missed on a software contract

topic: A project manager is questioned about deadlines they missed on a software contract
text:
Q: Ms. Tanaka, let me ask you about the final delivery date. April 30th, 2024.

topic: An accountant is deposed about transactions they processed on behalf of a client
text:
Q: Good morning. Would you please state your name and professional title for the record?

Q: I'd like to direct your attention to a wire transfer dated November 15, 2022, in the amount of $340,000. Do you recall that transaction?

A: I do. It was a transfer to a vendor account in the Cayman Islands.

Q: Walk me through the authorization process you followed for that transfer.

A: Certainly. For any transfer over $50,000, I required dual authorization from company officers. In this case, I received signed authorization forms from both the CFO, Mr. Hartley, and the CEO, Ms. Vance. I verified their signatures against the samples we keep on file, confirmed the receiving account details matched our vendor records, and then initiated the transfer through our banking portal.

Q: Did you ever inquire about the nature of the services being provided by that vendor?

A: Of course.

topic: A warehouse supervisor is deposed about safety protocols that were allegedly ignored
text:
Q: Mr. Hendricks, I'd like to start by asking about your role at the warehouse. How long have you been a supervisor there?

A: Going on twelve years now. Started as a forklift operator, worked my way up. I've seen a lot of changes in that building, most of them good.

Q: That's quite a tenure. You must know the place inside and out.

A: I'd like to think so. The people especially. That's what matters most to me—the folks on the floor.

Q: Speaking of the people on the floor, can you tell me about the safety training protocols that were in place last August?

A: Sure, I'd be happy to. We had monthly refreshers, toolbox talks every Monday morning, and I personally walked the floor twice a day checking on things. I know some supervisors do it from their office, but that's not how I operate.

Q: The toolbox talks—who attended those?

A: Everyone on shift. And I mean everyone. I'd bring donuts, make it worth their while to show up on time. You get better participation when people feel like you actually want them there, you know?

Q: That's a thoughtful approach. Were these talks documented?

A: Every single one. I kept binders—old school, I know—but I wanted to be able to look anyone in the eye and show them exactly what we covered and when.

Q: Mr. Hendricks, I have to ask about August 14th specifically. The incident report suggests certain lockout-tagout procedures weren't followed. Can you walk me through what you observed that day?

A: I can, and I want to be clear about something first. That young man, Derek, he's a good worker. What happened wasn't about anyone being careless or lazy. Sometimes things move fast, and I wonder every day if I could've done something different.

Q: Take your time. What did you observe?

A: I was doing my afternoon walkthrough, and I saw the conveyor running while Derek was reaching in to clear a jam. I shouted, hit the emergency stop myself. But by then—well, you've seen the medical reports.

Q: You hit the emergency stop. How far away were you?

A: Maybe forty feet. I moved as fast as these old knees would let me. I still hear myself yelling his name when I close my eyes at night.

Q: Mr. Hendricks, in your twelve years, had you ever seen someone bypass lockout-tagout before?

A: I'd be lying if I said never. But we always caught it, always corrected it. I thought we'd built something—a culture where people looked out for each other. I still believe we did. One terrible moment doesn't erase that.

topic: A warehouse supervisor is deposed about safety protocols that were allegedly ignored
text:
Q: State your name for the record.

A: Patricia Vance.

Q: Ms. Vance, you were the night shift supervisor at the Cedar Road facility, correct?

A: That's correct.

Q: How many people reported to you?

A: Twenty-three on a full crew. Sometimes fewer depending on call-outs.

Q: I'd like to ask you about the safety equipment inspections. How often were those conducted?

A: Weekly, per company policy.

Q: And who performed them?

A: I did them myself, every Sunday night before the shift started. I didn't delegate that.

Q: Why not?

A: Because if something's wrong with a harness or a guard rail, I want to be the one who catches it. These aren't strangers to me—I've been to their kids' birthday parties. Maria's daughter calls me Aunt Patty.

Q: That's a significant level of personal investment.

A: It's just how it is when you work nights together for years. You become family.

Q: Ms. Vance, the plaintiff's complaint alleges that a faulty guardrail on the mezzanine level was reported multiple times before the incident. Do you have any knowledge of those reports?

A: I submitted three work orders myself. I've got the emails.

Q: Three work orders. What responses did you receive?

A: The first two, nothing. The third one, I got a reply saying it was "in the queue."

Q: How did you handle the situation while waiting for repairs?

A: I put up caution tape, told my crew verbally to stay clear, and I stood there myself during loading operations to make sure nobody leaned on it. Every single night until—

Q: Until?

A: Until I wasn't there. I had two days off. When I came back, the tape was down and Ronnie was in the hospital.

Q: Who removed the tape?

A: I don't know. I've asked myself that a hundred times. But I should've done more. I should've refused to run operations up there entirely.

Q: Ms. Vance, I can see this is difficult.

A: Ronnie's a good man. He trusted me to keep that floor safe. I'm here today because he deserves the truth on the record, whatever that means for me.

topic: A warehouse supervisor is deposed about safety protocols that were allegedly ignored
text:
Q: Let's talk about the incident report dated March 3rd. You wrote this, correct?

A: I did.

Q: In the narrative section, you wrote, "Employee failed to utilize required PPE." Can you elaborate on that?

A: Yes. Anthony wasn't wearing his safety glasses when he was operating the grinder.

Q: And that's what caused the injury?

A: A metal fragment hit him in the eye. So yes.

Q: Mr. Deluca, I notice you also wrote, "Supervisor intervention occurred prior to incident." What does that mean?

A: It means I had spoken to him about the glasses maybe ten minutes before.

Q: Can you tell me more about that conversation?

A: I saw him without them, I reminded him, he put them on. I watched him do it. Then I went to check on something else, and when I came back—look, Anthony's twenty-two years old. He's got a baby at home. I keep thinking if I'd just stayed there another five minutes.

Q: You're not responsible for another adult's choices, Mr. Deluca.

A: Counselor, with respect, that's kind of you to say, but when you're the supervisor, it doesn't feel that way.

Q: I understand. Let's talk about what happened immediately after the injury.

A: I called 911, administered the eyewash, kept him calm. The kid was terrified. I held his hand until the paramedics got there—I don't care if that sounds unprofessional.

Q: Did anyone else witness this?

A: Half the floor. But they were keeping their distance, giving us space. Good people, all of them.

Q: Has Anthony returned to work?

A: He has. Partial vision in that eye now. But he's back, and he asked to stay on my shift specifically. That meant something to me.

Q: Do you two talk about the incident?

A: Not directly. But last week he brought me a coffee—said his daughter had started smiling and he wanted to show me a picture. I think that was his way of saying we're okay.

topic: A warehouse supervisor is deposed about safety protocols that were allegedly ignored
text:
Q: Mr. Okonkwo, I'll be asking you questions today about the safety protocols at the Riverside distribution center. Do you understand?

A: Yes, I understand.

Q: You've been a supervisor there for how long?

A: Four years.

Q: In those four years, how would you characterize management's attitude toward safety compliance?

A: That's a broad question.

Q: Take it however you'd like.

A: I think there were people who cared and people who cared about numbers. I tried to be one of the ones who cared.

Q: Can you give me an example of how you demonstrated that?

A: When we got new hires, I didn't just hand them a manual. I walked the floor with them personally. Showed them every pinch point, every place where someone could get hurt. I told them stories—not to scare them, but so they'd understand that these rules exist because someone got hurt before them.

Q: That's more than the standard onboarding requires.

A: The standard onboarding takes thirty minutes. Mine took half a day. I got pushback from operations about productivity, but I told them I'd rather be slow than sorry.

Q: Did they accept that?

A: They tolerated it. Probably because my shift had the lowest incident rate in the building.

Q: Let's discuss the loading dock specifically. Were there protocols for severe weather operations?

A: Yes. High winds, we close the bay doors. Lightning, everyone comes inside. Ice, we salt before and during.

Q: On January 15th, there was freezing rain. What happened?

A: The salt spreader was broken. I requisitioned a new one in November, never got it. So I sent two of my guys to buy bags of salt from the hardware store with petty cash.

Q: That was your solution?

A: That was the only solution available to me. We spread it by hand, all of us, including me. My back hurt for a week, but nobody slipped.

Q: Nobody slipped on your shift. But first shift—

A: First shift didn't do what we did. I heard about the fall when I came in that night. I wish I'd left a note, told them what we'd done. Maybe that would've helped.

Q: You feel some responsibility for that?

A: I feel like I'm part of a system that should've worked better. We all are.

topic: A warehouse supervisor is deposed about safety protocols that were allegedly ignored
text:
Q: Ms. Thornton, let's cut to the chase. You were the supervisor on duty when Mr. Reeves was injured, correct?

A: I was.

Q: The forklift that struck him—who was operating it?

A: Danny Mullins.

Q: Was Mr. Mullins certified to operate that equipment?

A: He was certified, yes.

A: But he'd been on the job for two weeks. Certification and experience aren't the same thing.

Q: Did you express any concerns about assigning him to that area?

A: I did.

A: My operations manager, Tom Briggs.

Q: What did Mr. Briggs say?

A: I tried. I didn't try hard enough, apparently.

Q: Do you blame yourself for what happened to Mr. Reeves?

A: I blame a lot of things. Myself included. But I also blame a system that puts supervisors in impossible positions and then acts surprised when something goes wrong.

Q: You sound frustrated.

And now I'm sitting here answering questions while Marcus is in physical therapy learning to walk again. So yes, I'm frustrated. But more than that, I'm heartbroken.

topic: A pharmacist is deposed about a prescription that was filled with the wrong dosage
text:
Q: Good morning. Would you please state your name and current position for the record?

A: Good morning. My name is David Chen, and I am a staff pharmacist at Greenwood Pharmacy on Elm Street. I've held that position for approximately eleven years.

Q: Thank you. And you were working on March 14th of this year, is that correct?

A: Yes, I was. I worked the morning shift that day, from 7 a.m. until 3 p.m.

Q: I'd like to direct your attention to a prescription for a patient named Margaret Holloway. Do you recall filling that prescription?

A: I do recall it, yes. I've had the opportunity to review the records in preparation for today, and I remember the transaction.

Q: What medication was prescribed for Mrs. Holloway?

A: The prescription was for metoprolol succinate, which is a beta-blocker commonly used to treat high blood pressure and certain heart conditions.

Q: And what dosage was indicated on the prescription from the physician?

A: The prescription from Dr. Anand specified 25 milligrams, to be taken once daily.

Q: What dosage was actually dispensed to Mrs. Holloway?

A: The bottle that was dispensed contained 100-milligram tablets. That was an error on my part.

Q: Can you walk me through your standard verification process when filling a prescription?

A: Certainly. We receive the prescription, either electronically or on paper. I enter the information into our system, which pulls up the medication. I then physically retrieve the medication from the shelf, scan the barcode, and the system is supposed to flag any discrepancies. After that, I count the tablets, label the bottle, and perform a final visual check before it goes to the pickup area.

Q: And on March 14th, with Mrs. Holloway's prescription, did you follow each of those steps?

A: I believed I did at the time. Looking back, I can see that something went wrong during the retrieval step. The 25-milligram and 100-milligram bottles are stored adjacent to one another, and I selected the wrong one.

Q: Did the barcode scan not alert you to the discrepancy?

A: It should have. I've reviewed the system logs, and I honestly cannot explain why it didn't flag the error that day. That's something I've thought about quite a bit since this happened.

Q: Is there anything else you'd like to add regarding that day?

A: Only that I take full responsibility for my part in this. Mrs. Holloway trusted us, and I failed to meet the standard of care she deserved.

---

topic: A pharmacist is deposed about a prescription that was filled with the wrong dosage
text:
Q: Let's start with your training. Where did you complete your pharmacy degree?

A: University of Wisconsin-Madison. I graduated in 2015.

Q: And since then, how many prescriptions would you estimate you've filled?

A: Tens of thousands. Possibly more. I haven't kept a count.

Q: Fair enough. Now, on the date in question, September 8th, were you the only pharmacist on duty?

A: No. There were two of us. Myself and a pharmacy intern, though she was not yet licensed to perform final verification.

Q: So you performed all final verifications that day?

A: That's correct.

Q: How many prescriptions did you fill that day, approximately?

A: I'd estimate somewhere between 180 and 220. It was a busy day.

Q: That's a high volume.

A: It is, yes. Not unusual for a retail pharmacy, though.

Q: The prescription at issue was for lisinopril, correct?

A: Correct.

Q: What was the prescribed dosage?

A: 5 milligrams.

Q: And what was dispensed?

A: 40 milligrams.

Q: That's eight times the intended dose.

A: Yes, I'm aware of the math.

Q: How do you account for that error?

A: I've gone over it many times in my mind. The most likely explanation is that I was working from muscle memory. The 40-milligram is our most commonly dispensed strength for lisinopril. I believe I reached for it automatically without fully processing the prescription details.

Q: Does your pharmacy have any protocols to prevent that kind of automatic behavior?

A: We have the scan verification system, and we're trained to read the label three times—when we pull it, when we pour it, and when we shelve it. Clearly, those safeguards failed that day, and that failure is mine.

---

topic: A pharmacist is deposed about a prescription that was filled with the wrong dosage
text:
Q: Ms. Okonkwo, how long have you been a licensed pharmacist?

A: Seven years this coming April.

Q: And during that time, have you ever made a dispensing error before?

A: I'd prefer to answer that carefully, if I may.

Q: Please do.

A: To my knowledge, I have not made an error that resulted in patient harm prior to this incident. Whether I have ever made a minor error that was caught before dispensing—it's possible. We catch things in verification all the time. That's what the process is for.

Q: That's a thoughtful distinction. Thank you. Now, regarding the prescription for Mr. Theodore Grant—

A: Yes.

Q: What did Mr. Grant receive?

A: He received 5-milligram tablets.

Q: When did you become aware of the error?

A: Three days after dispensing, when Mr. Grant's daughter called the pharmacy. She said her father's pills looked different from his previous prescription.

Q: What did you do at that point?

A: I pulled the original prescription, compared it against our dispensing record, and confirmed the discrepancy. I then contacted Mr. Grant's physician immediately and documented everything per our protocol.

Q: How did you feel when you realized what had happened?

A: I'm not sure that's relevant to the facts, but I'll answer. I felt the weight of it. I still do.

topic: A pharmacist is deposed about a prescription that was filled with the wrong dosage
text:
Q: I'd like to understand the physical layout of your pharmacy. Can you describe where medications are stored?

A: Of course. Behind the counter, we have floor-to-ceiling shelving arranged alphabetically by generic name. Each shelf is subdivided by dosage strength, with the lowest strength on the left and the highest on the right.

Q: And where would atorvastatin be located?

A: In the A section, second row from the top. We keep all strengths together—10, 20, 40, and 80 milligrams.

Q: On November 2nd, when you filled the prescription for James Whitfield, which strength were you supposed to dispense?

A: The prescription called for 10 milligrams.

Q: Which strength did you dispense?

A: I dispensed the 80-milligram tablets.

Q: The bottles were adjacent to each other?

A: They were on the same shelf, yes. About six inches apart.

Q: Are the bottles similar in appearance?

A: The manufacturer uses the same bottle size and label format. The dosage is printed on the label, but the bottles are otherwise quite similar.

Q: Has that ever caused confusion before, to your knowledge?

A: I can't speak to other pharmacists' experiences. For myself, this was the first time I made this particular error.

Q: Have you recommended any changes to how medications are stored since this incident?

A: I have, yes. I suggested to our pharmacy manager that we use color-coded shelf tags to differentiate dosage strengths. That recommendation is under review.

Q: That seems like a reasonable suggestion.

A: I hope it helps prevent something like this from happening again.

---

topic: A pharmacist is deposed about a prescription that was filled with the wrong dosage
text:
Q: Let's talk about the afternoon of January 19th. Do you remember how busy the pharmacy was?

A: Moderately busy. Not our peak, but steady.

Q: Were there any staffing issues that day?

A: Our pharmacy technician called in sick, so I was working with reduced support.

Q: Did that affect your workflow?

A: It meant I was handling tasks I wouldn't normally handle—answering phones, running the register, things like that—in addition to filling prescriptions.

Q: The prescription at issue was for a child, correct?

A: Yes. A seven-year-old boy named Marcus Webb.

Q: What was he prescribed?

A: Amoxicillin suspension, 250 milligrams per 5 milliliters, to be taken three times daily.

Q: What was actually dispensed?

A: The bottle I dispensed was the 400-milligram concentration.

Q: Nearly double the strength.

A: Yes.

Q: Who caught the error?

A: The child's mother. She noticed the concentration listed on the label didn't match what she remembered from previous prescriptions.

Q: How did she notify you?

A: She called the pharmacy the next morning. I took the call myself.

Q: Walk me through that conversation.

A: She was understandably concerned. I asked her to read me the label, and as soon as she said 400 milligrams, I knew what had happened. I apologized, asked her not to administer any more doses, and arranged for her to come in for the correct medication immediately.

Q: Did the child experience any adverse effects?

A: He had received two doses before the error was caught. His mother reported some stomach upset, but thankfully nothing more serious.

Q: Looking back, is there anything you would have done differently that day?

A: I would have asked for additional staffing support, or slowed down my pace, even if it meant longer wait times for customers. A delay is inconvenient. An error like this is unacceptable.
