Q: The adjusting entries to the consulting expense accounts.

A: Alright.

Q: You made four adjusting entries totaling $156,000. Do you recall that?

A: I made adjusting entries at year-end, yes. I don't have the specific figures memorized.

Q: Would you agree that $156,000 in adjustments is a significant sum?

A: Significant is relative.

Q: Relative to what?

A: Relative to the size of the accounts. Relative to the overall revenue. Relative to what's being adjusted and why.

Q: So tell me why.

A: I'd need to see the workpapers.

Q: You don't recall why you made $156,000 in year-end adjustments?

A: I make a lot of adjustments, counsel. It's my job. If you show me the workpapers, I can walk you through the reasoning. If you want me to guess from memory, I'm not going to do that in a deposition.

Q: Fair enough. Exhibit 22. Take your time.

A: ...Okay. These were reclassifications. Expenses that had been coded to the wrong line items during the year.

Q: All four of them just happened to be coding errors?

A: All four of them were coding errors, yes. That's what the documentation shows.

Q: That's convenient.

A: I don't know what you want me to say to that. It's what happened.

---

topic: An accountant is deposed about transactions they processed on behalf of a client
text:
Q: Ms. Okonkwo, you were the primary accountant on the Heller Group engagement?

A: One of them. Janet Morrison was also on the account.

Q: But you handled the day-to-day transactions?

A: For the most part.

Q: Including the payments to subcontractors?

A: Yes.

Q: I want to ask you about a subcontractor called PrimeTech Solutions.

A: Okay.

Q: You processed invoices from PrimeTech totaling over $400,000 in 2022 alone, correct?

A: If that's what the records show. I don't have the total memorized.

Q: Did you ever meet anyone from PrimeTech?

A: Meet them? No.

Q: Speak to anyone there?

A: I don't believe so.

Q: Receive any deliverables from them?

A: I received invoices.

Q: That's not what I asked. Did you receive any deliverables? Work product? Reports? Anything indicating that PrimeTech actually performed services?

A: That wasn't my role.

Q: What was your role?

A: To process properly authorized invoices for payment.

Q: And you never wondered what $400,000 was buying?

A: Counsel, I process hundreds of invoices. I don't investigate whether every vendor is actually doing their job. That's management's responsibility.

Q: So if someone handed you an invoice from a company that didn't exist, for work that was never performed—

A: Objection, that's hypothetical and argumentative.

Q: I'll rephrase. Did you have any reason to believe PrimeTech was a legitimate company?

A: I had no reason to believe it wasn't.

topic: A witness is questioned about a workplace injury they observed but did not report
text:
Q: Mr. Patterson, you were working on the loading dock the morning of September 14th, correct?

A: I was in that general area, yes.

Q: And you had a clear line of sight to bay three where the incident occurred?

A: I could see bay three from where I was standing, sure.

Q: So you saw Marcus Williams fall from the forklift?

A: I saw him on the ground afterward. Whether I saw the actual fall—I mean, I don't know that I could say I watched it happen, moment by moment.

Q: You were looking in that direction, weren't you?

A: I was looking in that direction at various points, yes. But I was also doing my job. I wasn't standing there staring at Marcus Williams.

Q: What exactly did you see?

A: I heard a noise, I turned, and Marcus was on the ground near the forklift. That's what I saw.

Q: A noise. What kind of noise?

A: A sort of crash. Metal on concrete, maybe. And a yell. I think.

Q: You think?

A: It was a loud environment, counselor. Forklifts, trucks backing up, people shouting. I'm not going to sit here and tell you I can isolate exactly which sound came from where.

Q: But you knew something had happened?

A: I knew something had happened, yes.

Q: And you didn't report it.

A: Other people were already there. Supervisors. What was I supposed to report that they didn't already know?

Q: I'm asking whether you personally made a report.

A: No. I did not personally file a report. I answered that.

topic: A witness is questioned about a workplace injury they observed but did not report
text:
Q: Ms. Chen, how long have you worked at Graystone Manufacturing?

A: Eleven years this past March.

Q: In those eleven years, you've received safety training, correct?

A: Every year. Sometimes twice a year.

Q: And that training covers the reporting of workplace accidents?

A: It does.

Q: So you know that employees are required to report accidents they witness?

A: I know what the training says, yes.

Q: Is that different from what actually happens?

A: I didn't say that.

Q: I'm asking.

A: I'm not going to speak for what other people do.

Q: I'm asking about you. You witnessed Mr. Benton's hand get caught in the press, didn't you?

A: I saw him holding his hand afterward. I saw blood on the machine.

Q: But not the moment of injury?

A: The moment? No. It happened fast. I heard him scream.

Q: And after the scream, after you saw the blood—what did you do?

A: I went over to help. Someone had already called for the medic.

Q: Did you fill out an incident witness form?

A: No.

Q: Why not?

A: Because Tom—the floor supervisor—was already writing everything down. He saw me there. He knew I was a witness. Nobody handed me a form.

Q: Nobody handed you a form, so you didn't fill one out.

A: That's right.

Q: Did you ask for one?

A: Why would I ask for one if Tom was already handling it?

Q: You tell me, Ms. Chen. You've had eleven years of safety training.

A: And in eleven years, I've never once been asked to fill out a witness form when a supervisor was present and documenting everything himself. Is there something unusual about this particular incident that I should know about?

topic: A witness is questioned about a workplace injury they observed but did not report
text:
Q: Walk me through your movements between 2:00 and 2:30 p.m. on the day in question.

A: I was on break until about 2:15. Came back to the floor, clocked back in, went to my station.

Q: Your station being where?

A: Station seven. Finishing line.

Q: And station seven has a view of the catwalk above the main floor?

A: Partial view. If you're looking up.

Q: Were you looking up that afternoon?

A: Not particularly.

Q: Not particularly, or not at all?

A: I glanced up at some point, I think.

Q: You think. When you glanced up, did you see anyone on the catwalk?

A: There might have been someone. I don't recall specifically.

Q: Mr. Okonkwo, the incident report states that James Harlan fell from the catwalk at approximately 2:22 p.m.

A: Okay.

Q: You were at your station. You had a partial view. You're telling me you don't recall seeing him fall?

A: I'm telling you what I recall, which is not much. It was a normal afternoon until suddenly it wasn't.

Q: What changed?

A: People started running. Someone was yelling for help. That's when I knew something happened.

Q: Did you go to help?

A: I stayed where I was. I'm not trained in first aid. I would have been in the way.

Q: Did you report what you saw—or didn't see—to anyone?

A: What would I have reported? That I didn't see anything useful?

Q: That's not an answer to my question.

A: No. I didn't make a report. There's your answer.

topic: A witness is questioned about a workplace injury they observed but did not report
text:
Q: You've stated you were in the warehouse when the shelving unit collapsed.

A: That's correct.

Q: And you were approximately—what?—thirty feet away?

A: I didn't measure the distance.

Q: Estimate for me.

A: Maybe thirty feet. Maybe forty. I don't know.

Q: Close enough to see what happened?

A: Close enough to see shelves falling and hear the noise. Yes.

Q: Did you see what caused them to fall?

A: The forklift driver hit the support beam. I assume you already know that.

Q: I want to hear what you observed.

A: I observed the forklift making contact with the beam, and then the shelves came down.

Q: You observed this directly?

A: Yes.

Q: With your own eyes, in real time?

A: Is there another way to observe something directly?

Q: I want to be clear for the record.

A: I'm being clear. I saw the forklift hit the beam. I saw the unit collapse. I saw Rodriguez underneath it afterward.

Q: And you didn't think that warranted a report?

A: I thought it warranted getting Rodriguez out from under a thousand pounds of metal. Which is what I did.

Q: But afterward—

A: Afterward, half the management team was there. OSHA was called. There were investigators everywhere. What exactly was I supposed to add?

Q: Your account.

A: You have my account right now. Ask me what you want to know.

Q: Why do you think no one asked you at the time?

A: You'd have to ask them. Maybe they assumed I'd be available if needed. Maybe they were busy with the guy who had a broken pelvis. I don't presume to know what management is thinking at any given moment, and I don't think you should either.

topic: A witness is questioned about a workplace injury they observed but did not report
text:
Q: Ms. Franklin, you were in the break room when the chemical spill occurred, is that right?

A: I was in the break room when I heard about the chemical spill, yes.

Q: You didn't witness the spill itself?

A: No.

Q: But you went to the area afterward?

A: I walked toward it, yes. Someone said there was an accident. I wanted to see if I could help.

Q: What did you see when you arrived?

A: Yellow tape. People in hazmat suits. They were already containing it.

Q: So you didn't see the injured employee?

A: I saw the ambulance leaving.

Q: Did you see who was injured?

A: Not at that moment. I found out later it was David.

Q: David Moreno?

A: David Moreno, yes.

Q: Were you and David close?

A: We worked together. We talked sometimes. I wouldn't say close.

Q: Did anyone ask you what you knew about the incident?

A: No.

Q: Did you volunteer any information?

A: I didn't have any information to volunteer.

Q: You didn't see anything that led up to the spill? No warning signs, no problems with the equipment?

A: Are you asking if I knew ahead of time that something was going to happen?

Q: I'm asking if you observed anything in the days or hours before that might have been relevant.

A: Relevant to what? The containers looked the same as always. The procedures looked the same. If there was something wrong with the equipment, I wasn't trained to recognize it.

Q: So nothing stood out to you?

A: Nothing stood out to me. I'm sorry I can't give you more than that. I genuinely don't know what you're looking for me to say.

topic: A witness is questioned about a fire they discovered in a neighboring unit
text:
Q: Ms. Hernandez, I'd like to take you back to the evening of March 14th. You discovered the fire in Unit 4B, is that correct?

A: Yes.

Q: Can you tell me what time that was?

A: It was... I think around 9:15. Maybe 9:20. I'm not certain of the exact minute.

Q: That's fine. What were you doing when you first became aware of something was wrong?

A: I was reading. In my living room. And I heard the smoke detector going off through the wall.

Q: The wall adjoining Unit 4B?

A: Yes. The wall we shared with the Carsons.

Q: What did you do when you heard the alarm?

A: I went to the hallway. I knocked on their door.

Q: Did anyone answer?

A: No. No one came to the door.

Q: How many times did you knock?

A: I don't... I knocked several times. I was calling out. I was saying their names.

Q: The Carsons' names?

A: Linda. I was calling for Linda. She was usually home in the evenings.

Q: And when there was no response, what did you do next?

A: I called 911. And I kept knocking. I could smell it by then. The smoke. It was coming from under the door.

Q: Ms. Hernandez, take your time if you need to. Did you at any point attempt to enter the unit yourself?

A: I tried the handle. It was... it was too hot to touch. So I just waited. I just stood there in the hallway until the fire department came.

topic: A witness is questioned about a fire they discovered in a neighboring unit
text:
Q: Mr. Okonkwo, you've testified that you were the first person to call emergency services regarding the fire at 2847 Ridgewood Lane, Unit 12. Is that your understanding?

A: That's what I was told afterward, yes.

Q: I want to be very careful with the timeline here. Very precise. When you first smelled smoke, where exactly were you standing?

A: I was in my kitchen.

Q: Your kitchen shares a wall with Unit 12?

A: No, it's across the hall. But I had my door open. I was airing out—I'd burned something on the stove earlier.

Q: So your front door was open?

A: Just partway. A few inches.

Q: And the smoke you detected—you're certain it wasn't from your own cooking?

A: I know what my burned toast smells like, counselor. This was different.

Q: I'm not suggesting otherwise. I'm simply trying to establish the facts. What did this smoke smell like?

A: It smelled like something was really wrong.

Q: Mr. Okonkwo, I understand this is difficult to revisit. Can you describe the smell in more specific terms?

A: It was... thick. Chemical, almost. And there was something else underneath it. I don't want to say what I thought it was.

Q: I'm going to need you to tell me.

A: It smelled like something that shouldn't burn was burning.

Q: Did you know the occupant of Unit 12? A Mr. David Weiss?

A: I knew him. We'd talk in the mailroom sometimes. He had a dog—a little terrier. He'd let my daughter pet it when we saw him.

Q: Mr. Okonkwo, I have just a few more questions. Are you able to continue?

A: Yes. I can continue.

topic: A witness is questioned about a fire they discovered in a neighboring unit
text:
Q: You've stated you were returning from a night shift when you observed smoke coming from the building. What time was this?

A: About 6:40 in the morning.

Q: And you're a nurse at St. Anthony's, correct?

A: Correct.

Q: So you'd been working all night?

A: Twelve-hour shift. I was tired. But I know what I saw.

Q: I'm not questioning what you saw, Ms. Tadesse. I'm just establishing context. You were fatigued.

A: I was alert enough to call 911 before anyone else on the street even woke up.

Q: Fair enough. Tell me what you observed as you approached the building.

A: There was smoke coming from a window on the second floor. The corner unit.

Q: Could you see flames at that point?

A: No. Just smoke. Gray smoke, pouring out steady.

Q: What did you do?

A: I pulled over and called emergency services. Then I went to the front entrance and started buzzing apartments.

Q: Which apartments did you buzz?

A: All of them. Everyone I could. The ones that answered, I told them to get out.

Q: Did you attempt to reach the unit where the fire originated?

A: I tried. I went up the stairs. But the smoke—it was too thick on the second floor landing. I couldn't get through.

Q: So you turned back?

A: I had to. I could hear someone's television still playing through one of the doors. I banged on it. I shouted. But I couldn't stay up there.

Q: Ms. Tadesse, you did what you could under the circumstances.

A: That's what people keep telling me.

topic: A witness is questioned about a fire they discovered in a neighboring unit
text:
Q: Let's discuss the events of November 3rd. You were home that afternoon?

A: I was.

Q: And your unit is directly below Unit 7C, where the fire started?

A: That's right. I'm in 6C.

Q: When did you first realize something was wrong?

A: When water started coming through my ceiling.

Q: Water from the sprinkler system?

A: I assume so. It was brown, dirty water. It came through the light fixture in my hallway.

Q: What did you do?

A: I went upstairs to see what was happening. I thought maybe a pipe burst, or someone left a bathtub running.

Q: Did you know the resident of 7C?

A: Mrs. Huang. Yes, I knew her.

Q: How would you describe your relationship with Mrs. Huang?

A: We were neighborly. She'd bring me soup sometimes when she made too much. I'd collect her packages when she was visiting her grandchildren.

Q: So you went up to check on her?

A: I went up. And the door to her unit was open. The firefighters were already there. There was water everywhere, and smoke, and they were bringing out—they were carrying—

Q: Take your time, Mr. Reeves.

A: They were carrying her out on a stretcher.

Q: Did you speak with emergency personnel at that time?

A: Someone asked me to step back. So I stepped back. I stood in the hallway and I watched them take her away. That's what I did. I stood there.

topic: A witness is questioned about a fire they discovered in a neighboring unit
text:
Q: Dr. Patterson, you've indicated you were in the parking garage when you first became aware of the fire. Is that accurate?

A: Yes. I was getting groceries out of my car.

Q: What drew your attention to the situation?

A: The alarms. I heard the building's fire alarm go off.

Q: Did you proceed into the building at that point?

A: No, I went around to the front to see what was happening. Other residents were coming out the main entrance.

Q: Did you recognize any of these residents?

A: Some of them. The family from 2A—the Nguyens, I think. A few others.

Q: Was there any indication at that time of the fire's severity?

A: I could see smoke on the fourth floor. The windows on the east side of the building.

Q: That would be near Unit 4E?

A: I believe so, yes.

Q: Did you know the tenant of 4E?

A: Tom. Tom Brennan. He'd lived there for years. Since before I moved in.

Q: Were you friends?

A: We were friendly. He was a quiet man. Kept to himself mostly. But he always remembered my son's name. Asked about him whenever we talked.

Q: Dr. Patterson, I need to ask—did you see Mr. Brennan exit the building that evening?

A: No.

Q: Did you see him at any point during or after the evacuation?

A: No. I didn't.

Q: Were you aware that Mr. Brennan was home that evening?

A: I didn't know for certain. But he was almost always home. He didn't go out much anymore. Not since his wife passed.

Q: I see. Were you present when emergency services made entry into the fourth floor units?

A: No. They kept us back by the street. We just waited there. All of us, just standing on the sidewalk. Watching the smoke.

topic: A store manager is questioned about a customer slip-and-fall on their premises
text:
Q: Please state your name and position for the record.

A: Margaret Chen. I'm the store manager at the Riverside location. I've been there eleven years now.

Q: You were working on March 14th of this year?

A: Yes.

Q: And you were present when Mrs. Patterson fell?

A: I... yes. I was in the back office when it happened, but I came out right after. Someone called for me over the intercom.

Q: What did you see when you arrived?

A: She was on the floor. Near aisle seven. She was trying to get up, but her leg... she couldn't put weight on it. One of my employees, Danny, he was kneeling next to her, telling her not to move.

Q: Was there anything on the floor near where she fell?

A: There was liquid. Some kind of... it looked like it might have been from a broken jar. Pickle juice, we think. We found glass fragments nearby.

Q: How long had that liquid been on the floor before the fall?

A: I don't know. I wish I did.

Q: You don't have any estimate?

A: No. I've gone over it so many times. We do hourly sweeps. The last one was logged at 2:15. She fell at 2:47. So somewhere in that window, but I can't... I can't tell you exactly when it happened.

Q: Did anyone report the spill before Mrs. Patterson's fall?

A: No. No one came to me. No one told Danny or any of the other floor staff. At least not that I've been able to determine.

Q: Have you spoken with Mrs. Patterson since the incident?

A: I tried to visit her in the hospital. I brought flowers. She was... her daughter asked me to leave.

Q: Why did her daughter ask you to leave?

A: I think she felt I should have done more. Prevented it somehow. I understand that.

topic: A store manager is questioned about a customer slip-and-fall on their premises
text:
Q: Mr. Okonkwo, how long have you been the manager at the Franklin Street store?

A: Three years in January.

Q: You're familiar with the incident involving Gerald Hutchins on September 3rd?

A: Yes.

Q: Tell me about your store's policy regarding wet floor signage.

A: We have yellow signs. The folding kind. When there's a spill or when the floors are mopped, we put them out.

Q: Was there a sign out on September 3rd?

A: Not when I got to Mr. Hutchins.

Q: So no warning was present?

A: There was no sign, no.

Q: Mr. Okonkwo, I'm trying to understand something. An elderly man fell in your store and broke his wrist. Doesn't that concern you?

A: Of course it concerns me.

Q: Then help me understand how this happened.

A: I'm trying to. You keep asking the same questions.

Q: Because I'm not getting clear answers.

A: I don't have every answer you want. I wasn't standing in that aisle watching it happen. I came when I heard him cry out.

Q: What did that sound like?

A: What?

Q: The cry. What did it sound like?

A: I don't... it was a sound of pain. Of surprise. I don't know how to describe it beyond that. I heard it, and I went.

Q: When you reached him, what was his condition?

A: He was holding his wrist against his chest. His face was very pale. He kept saying "I'm fine, I'm fine," but he wasn't. Anyone could see he wasn't.

topic: A store manager is questioned about a customer slip-and-fall on their premises
text:
Q: Let's talk about the maintenance schedule at your location.

A: Okay.

Q: How often are the floors inspected during business hours?

A: Every hour, on the hour. That's the policy.

Q: And on the day in question, November 12th, was that policy followed?

A: To my knowledge, yes.

Q: To your knowledge?

A: I've reviewed the logs. They were signed.

Q: Signed by whom?

A: Different employees throughout the day.

Q: Was the 4 p.m. inspection completed?

A: It was signed.

Q: That's not what I asked. Was it actually completed?

A: I can only tell you what the log shows.

Q: Do you have reason to believe the inspection wasn't performed?

A: ...

Q: Mr. Harmon?

A: I've asked myself that question many times.

Q: What's your answer?

A: I don't know. I want to believe my staff did their jobs. But a woman fell, so something failed somewhere.

Q: Who signed the 4 p.m. log?

A: A young man named Tyler. He's nineteen. It was his second week.

Q: Have you spoken with Tyler about whether he actually performed the inspection?

A: He says he did. He says he walked the whole floor. He didn't see anything.

Q: Do you believe him?

A: He couldn't look at me when he said it. He kept staring at his shoes. I've managed people for fifteen years. I know what guilt looks like.

topic: A store manager is questioned about a customer slip-and-fall on their premises
text:
Q: Ms. Vance, you mentioned earlier that you have children?

A: I don't see what that has to do with—

Q: Bear with me. Do you have children?

A: Yes. Two.

Q: And the plaintiff, Mrs. Delgado, she has a seven-year-old daughter. Were you aware of that?

A: I learned that later, yes.

Q: Mrs. Delgado's daughter was with her when she fell. Did you know that?

A: Yes.

Q: Did you see the child?

A: I saw her.

Q: What was she doing?

A: She was standing next to her mother. Very still. Not crying. Just... watching.

Q: Watching what?

A: Watching us try to help. Watching her mother on the ground.

Q: Did you speak to the child?

A: I tried to. I bent down and asked if she was okay. She didn't answer. She just kept looking at her mother's face.

Q: What was Mrs. Delgado's condition at that point?

A: She was conscious. In pain. She kept saying, "Mija, I'm okay, Mommy's okay." Over and over.

Q: Ms. Vance, do you need a moment?

A: No. I'm fine. What's your next question?

Q: Were paramedics called?

A: Yes. I called them myself. It took eleven minutes for them to arrive. It felt much longer than that.

Q: Did the child stay with her mother the entire time?

A: She held her mother's hand. She never let go. Not once.

topic: A store manager is questioned about a customer slip-and-fall on their premises
text:
Q: How would you describe the lighting in the area where Mr. Foster fell?

A: It's adequate. We have overhead fluorescents throughout the store.

Q: Were any of those lights malfunctioning on January 8th?

A: One of the tubes in that section had been flickering for a few days.

Q: Flickering?

A: Going on and off intermittently.

Q: And you were aware of this before Mr. Foster's fall?

A: Yes.

Q: Had you taken steps to repair it?

A: We had a work order in.

Q: When was that work order submitted?

A: January 3rd.

Q: So five days before the incident?

A: Yes.

Q: And in those five days, the light was never repaired?

A: Our maintenance contractor had a backlog. We were told it would be handled by the 10th.

Q: Mr. Foster fell on the 8th.

A: I know.

Q: Did you consider closing off that section of the store until the lighting was repaired?

A: It was the main grocery aisle. I didn't think... I weighed the options and made a judgment call.

Q: Do you stand by that judgment call?

A: I made the decision I thought was right at the time.

Q: That's not what I asked.

A: I know what you asked. I've been asking myself the same thing for three months. Every morning I walk past that aisle, and I think about a man who can't see properly out of his left eye anymore because I decided a flickering light wasn't urgent enough.

topic: A witness is questioned about events at a party where an assault allegedly occurred
text:
Q: Ms. Thornton, you arrived at the residence on Maple Street at what time?

A: Around ten, ten-thirty. Somewhere in there.

Q: Which is it? Ten or ten-thirty?

A: I didn't check my watch and sign a logbook. It was around ten.

Q: Fine. And when you arrived, who was already present?

A: A lot of people. It was a party.

Q: I need names, Ms. Thornton.

A: Derek was there. The host. Lisa Brennan. Some guy named Chris or maybe Craig. A bunch of people I didn't know.

Q: You didn't know most of the attendees?

A: I knew some. I didn't know all. That's how parties work.

Q: Let's talk about the backyard. You went outside at some point?

A: Yes.

Q: When?

A: After I'd been there a while.

Q: An hour? Two hours?

A: I don't know, maybe an hour. Maybe forty-five minutes. I wasn't keeping a schedule.

Q: And who was in the backyard when you went outside?

A: Look, I've already been over this with the police twice. Derek was out there. The guy who got hit was out there. A few others.

Q: The guy who got hit—you're referring to Mr. Alvarez?

A: If that's his name, yes.

topic: A witness is questioned about events at a party where an assault allegedly occurred
text:
Q: Mr. Chen, did you observe any altercation that evening?

A: I saw some pushing near the kitchen, yes.

Q: Pushing. Between whom?

A: Between Marcus and another individual. I don't know the other person's name.

Q: Can you describe what you saw?

A: Marcus had his hands on the other man's chest and was pushing him backward toward the counter.

Q: What happened next?

A: The other man pushed back. They were both shouting.

Q: What were they shouting?

A: I couldn't make out specific words. The music was loud.

Q: You were how far away?

A: Perhaps fifteen feet. Maybe a bit more.

Q: Fifteen feet. And you couldn't hear anything they said?

A: I said I couldn't make out specific words. I could hear that they were yelling.

Q: There's a difference between not hearing and not making out words, Mr. Chen. Which is it?

A: I just told you which it is. I could hear yelling. I could not distinguish the specific words being spoken. Is there something unclear about that?

Q: Did anyone intervene?

A: Yes. A woman stepped between them.

Q: Do you know this woman?

A: No.

Q: Can you describe her?

A: Blonde hair, shorter than both men, wearing something dark. A dress, I think. That's all I remember.

topic: A witness is questioned about events at a party where an assault allegedly occurred
text:
Q: You testified earlier that you were in the living room when you heard a commotion.

A: That's right.

Q: What did you do when you heard it?

A: I walked toward the sound.

Q: Which direction was that?

A: Toward the back of the house. The den area.

Q: How long did it take you to reach the den?

A: Seconds. It wasn't far.

Q: Five seconds? Ten?

A: I didn't count. Seconds.

Q: What did you see when you got there?

A: A man on the ground and another man standing over him.

Q: Did you recognize either man?

A: The one standing was Tommy Briggs. I've known him for years.

Q: And the man on the ground?

A: I'd seen him earlier at the party but I didn't know his name.

Q: Had you spoken to him earlier?

A: Briefly. He asked me where the bathroom was.

Q: What was Mr. Briggs doing when you observed him standing over this man? Was he speaking? Moving? Just standing there? Help me out here.

A: He was just standing there. Breathing heavy. His fists were still clenched.

Q: Did he say anything at that point?

A: Not right then. A few seconds later he said something like "He swung first" or "He started it." Something along those lines.

Q: Which was it? "He swung first" or "He started it"? Those mean different things.

A: I'm telling you what I remember. It was one of those or something similar. I'm not going to manufacture a quote I'm not certain about.

topic: A witness is questioned about events at a party where an assault allegedly occurred
text:
Q: Ms. Doyle, I want to direct your attention to the moment Mr. Harrison entered the party. Did you see him arrive?

A: Yes.

Q: What time was that?

A: Late. After eleven.

Q: Was he alone?

A: No, he came with two other people.

Q: Who were they?

A: I only knew one of them. Brittany something. I don't remember her last name.

Q: And the third person?

A: A man. Tall. I'd never seen him before.

Q: Okay. Now—

A: Can I ask how much longer this is going to take? I've been here for two hours and we keep going over the same ground.

Q: Ms. Doyle, I understand this is time-consuming, but I need to ask these questions. When Mr. Harrison came in, what was his demeanor?

A: He seemed fine. Normal.

Q: Was he intoxicated?

A: I'm not a breathalyzer.

Q: In your observation.

A: He didn't seem drunk to me at that point.

Q: At that point. Did that change?

A: Over the next hour or so, yes, he seemed to get more intoxicated.

Q: How could you tell?

A: Louder. Slurring a little. The usual signs. Can we move on to the actual incident? I have to pick up my son at four.

Q: We'll get there, Ms. Doyle. Did you interact with Mr. Harrison directly at any point before the incident?

A: Once. He bumped into me and apologized. That was it.

topic: A witness is questioned about events at a party where an assault allegedly occurred
text:
Q: Let me ask you again, Mr. Wallace. You're claiming you didn't see who threw the first punch?

A: I'm not claiming anything. I'm telling you what I saw and didn't see.

Q: You were standing right there.

A: I was standing in the vicinity. There were people between me and them.

Q: How many people?

A: Two, maybe three.

Q: And these two or three people completely blocked your view?

A: They blocked my view of the initial contact, yes.

Q: But you saw what happened after?

A: I saw Nathan on the ground holding his face. I saw the other man—the defendant—shaking out his hand like he'd just hit something.

Q: So you did see him strike Mr. Vance?

A: No. I saw the aftermath. I already said this. Twice now.

Q: Mr. Wallace, I'm trying to establish—

A: You're trying to get me to say I saw him throw a punch. I didn't. I saw the result. Those are two different things, and I'm not going to conflate them because you keep asking the same question different ways.

Q: Fair enough. What happened next?

A: Someone yelled to call 911. A few people pulled the defendant away. Nathan stayed on the ground.

Q: Did the defendant say anything?

A: He was yelling something. I couldn't tell you what.

Q: You couldn't hear him?

A: I could hear that he was yelling. Everyone was yelling. It was chaos. I don't have a transcript of what everyone said.

Q: Did you see any weapons?

A: No.

Q: No knives, bottles, anything like that?

A: I said no.

topic: A financial advisor is deposed about investment decisions made on a client's behalf
text:
Q: Mr. Harmon, you were the primary advisor on the Delacroix account from 2019 to 2022, correct?

A: Yes.

Q: And during that period, you made investment decisions on behalf of Eleanor Delacroix?

A: On her behalf, yes. With her authorization.

Q: I want to focus on the allocation decisions made in March of 2021. You moved approximately forty percent of her portfolio into high-yield bonds. Is that accurate?

A: It was... it was thirty-seven percent. Approximately.

Q: Thirty-seven percent. And Mrs. Delacroix was seventy-four years old at that time?

A: She was. Yes.

Q: Did you discuss the risk profile of those bonds with her before making that allocation?

A: I... we had conversations. Several conversations.

Q: That wasn't my question, Mr. Harmon. Did you specifically discuss the risk profile of those high-yield bonds before you moved thirty-seven percent of her retirement savings into them?

A: I explained... I thought I explained it clearly. I believed I did.

Q: You believed you did.

A: Yes.

Q: Mrs. Delacroix passed away in November of last year. Were you aware of that?

A: I was. I attended the service.

Q: Her estate lost approximately $340,000 as a result of the bond defaults. That money was intended for her grandchildren's education, wasn't it?

A: That's what she told me. When we first met. She showed me their photographs.

Q: I'm sorry?

A: Nothing. Yes. That was her intention for those funds.

topic: A financial advisor is deposed about investment decisions made on a client's behalf
text:
Q: Let's talk about the Meridian Tech investment specifically. When did you first recommend this stock to Mr. Okonkwo?

A: July of 2020. I remember because it was just after the quarterly review.

Q: And what was your basis for recommending a company that had never turned a profit?

A: The growth metrics were strong. The sector was performing. I had every reason to believe—

Q: I'm asking what your basis was. Not what you believed.

A: The analyst reports. Internal research. Market trends.

Q: Did you personally review Meridian Tech's financial statements?

A: I reviewed the summaries.

Q: The summaries.

A: Yes.

Q: Not the actual statements filed with the SEC?

A: That wasn't standard practice. We relied on our research team.

Q: Mr. Okonkwo trusted you with his savings. Forty years of work. Did you know that when you recommended this stock?

A: He told me he'd been saving since he was twenty-three. He told me a lot of things about his life. I listened to him.

Q: Did that factor into your risk assessment?

A: ...Yes. It should have factored in more.

Q: How much of his portfolio was in Meridian Tech when it collapsed?

A: Twenty-two percent. I think about it often, counselor. If that's what you're asking.

Q: I'm asking about the percentage.

A: Twenty-two percent.

topic: A financial advisor is deposed about investment decisions made on a client's behalf
text:
Q: Ms. Vance, I want to understand the timeline here. When did you first notice irregularities in the Chen portfolio?

A: Irregularities is your word. I noticed a deviation from the projected returns in September.

Q: A deviation. Meaning losses.

A: Meaning the returns weren't tracking the model. Yes. There were losses.

Q: And yet the Chens weren't informed until December. Three months later.

A: The market corrects. We were waiting to see if—

Q: Three months, Ms. Vance.

A: I'm aware of the timeline.

Q: During those three months, did you continue to collect management fees on the account?

A: That's how advisory fees work. Yes.

Q: Mrs. Chen submitted a written complaint to your firm stating that she and her husband had to postpone his cancer treatment because of the losses in this account. Did you see that complaint?

A: ...I did.

Q: Take your time.

A: I've already answered.

Q: She wrote that they had waited their whole lives to retire. That this was supposed to be their safety net.

A: I read the complaint, counselor. I don't need you to read it to me.

Q: I'm just trying to understand whether you appreciated the human impact of those three months.

A: I appreciated it. I appreciate it now. Can we move on?

topic: A financial advisor is deposed about investment decisions made on a client's behalf
text:
Q: Mr. Foster, how long have you been a financial advisor?

A: Seventeen years this past March.

Q: And in those seventeen years, have you ever had a client lose their entire investment in a single position?

A: Once. This case.

Q: The Patterson account.

A: Yes.

Q: Tell me about David Patterson.

A: What would you like to know?

Q: How did he come to be your client?

A: He was referred by his daughter. She was already a client. She thought I could help him with his pension rollover. He'd just retired from the school district.

Q: A teacher?

A: Thirty-one years. High school chemistry.

Q: And you recommended the leveraged ETF strategy for his pension?

A: I recommended a diversified approach that included some leveraged positions. In hindsight—

Q: I'm not asking about hindsight yet. I'm asking about the moment you made the recommendation.

A: I thought it was sound. I ran the projections. I showed him the models.

Q: Did you show him what would happen in a sustained downturn?

A: ...We discussed volatility in general terms.

Q: In general terms.

A: He trusted me. He said his daughter trusted me, so he trusted me. Those were his words.

Q: Is the daughter still your client?

A: No. She is not.

topic: A financial advisor is deposed about investment decisions made on a client's behalf
text:
Q: I'd like to return to the conversation you had with Mrs. Whitmore on January 14th. You testified earlier that you called her. What was the purpose of that call?

A: To inform her that the annuity product she'd purchased was underperforming.

Q: Underperforming.

A: Yes.

Q: By how much?

A: At that point, approximately eighteen percent below projected returns.

Q: And what was her response when you told her this?

A: She asked if she should be worried.

Q: What did you say?

A: I told her we would monitor the situation.

Q: Did you tell her that you had received internal memos suggesting the product might collapse entirely?

A: I didn't have confirmation of that at the time.

Q: You had the memos, Mr. Torres.

A: I had memos with speculation. Not confirmation.

Q: Mrs. Whitmore's husband had died three months before that call. Did you know that?

A: I knew. I'd sent flowers.

Q: She was relying on this annuity to supplement her Social Security. The only income she had left.

A: I know what she was relying on. I know exactly what she was relying on.

Q: Then why didn't you tell her about the memos?

A: Because I wanted to believe they were wrong. I wanted to believe I hadn't put a widow's future into something that was going to disappear.

Q: But it did disappear.

A: It did. Yes. It did.

topic: A witness is questioned about events at a party where an assault allegedly occurred
text:
Q: Ms. Thornton, you were present at the residence on March 15th, correct?

A: I was there. Yes.

Q: And approximately how long had you been at the party before the incident occurred?

A: Maybe two hours. I don't... I'm not entirely sure. It could have been longer.

Q: During those two hours, did you observe the defendant interacting with anyone?

A: He talked to a lot of people. Everyone was talking to everyone.

Q: Did you observe him speaking with the complainant specifically?

A: Yes.

Q: Can you describe what you saw?

A: They were by the kitchen. Near the island. She was leaning against it and he was... he was just standing there talking to her. It looked normal. It looked like any conversation.

Q: How far away were you when you observed this?

A: I was in the living room. So maybe fifteen feet. Maybe twenty.

Q: Could you hear what they were saying?

A: No. There was music. People talking. I couldn't hear anything specific.

Q: What happened next, as far as you observed?

A: I looked away. I was talking to someone else. And then... then I heard her. I heard Emma.

Q: What did you hear?

A: She was... it wasn't a scream exactly. It was more like... I don't know how to describe it. Like she was trying to say something but couldn't.

Q: And what did you do when you heard that?

A: Nothing. I didn't do anything fast enough. By the time I turned around, by the time I got there, it was... other people had already... I should have been paying attention. I was right there and I wasn't paying attention.

topic: A witness is questioned about events at a party where an assault allegedly occurred
text:
Q: Mr. Donovan, I want to take you back to the moment you first noticed something was wrong.

A: Okay.

Q: Take your time. What first drew your attention to the altercation?

A: I heard glass break. A bottle, I think.

Q: Where were you standing when you heard the glass break?

A: The back porch. I'd stepped out for air.

Q: Were you alone on the porch?

A: Yes.

Q: And when you heard the glass break, what did you do?

A: I went inside. Quickly.

Q: What did you see when you entered?

A: People had moved back. There was a circle, almost. Like everyone had stepped away from the center of the room.

Q: Who was in the center?

A: Marcus. And Delia. She was on the floor.

Q: Can you describe her position?

A: She was... she was trying to get up. She had her hand on the coffee table, trying to pull herself up. Her other hand was on her face.

Q: Did you approach her?

A: I did. I went to help her.

Q: What did she say to you, if anything?

A: She didn't say anything at first. She just looked at me. She looked at me like she didn't recognize where she was.

Q: Mr. Donovan, did there come a time when she did speak to you?

A: Later. In the kitchen. I brought her ice wrapped in a towel.

Q: What did she say?

A: She said, "I thought he was different." That's all. She just kept saying that.

topic: A witness is questioned about events at a party where an assault allegedly occurred
text:
Q: You testified that you and Mr. Reeves arrived at the party together?

A: That's correct.

Q: And you'd known Mr. Reeves for how long at that point?

A: Eleven years. Since freshman orientation.

Q: So you'd characterize yourselves as close friends?

A: Yes. I would have, yes.

Q: Would have?

A: I don't... I'm sorry, what's the question?

Q: You used the past tense. "Would have."

A: I'm just here to answer questions about that night.

Q: Fair enough. Let me ask you this—in the eleven years you'd known Mr. Reeves, had you ever seen him become physical with anyone?

A: No.

Q: Never?

A: I said no.

Q: Had you ever seen him lose his temper?

A: Everyone loses their temper sometimes.

Q: That's not what I asked, Mr. Hale.

A: No. I never saw anything like what happened that night. I never saw anything that would have made me think he was capable of... no. The answer is no.

Q: When you saw him strike Ms. Patterson, what did you do?

A: I pulled him off. I grabbed him by the shoulders and I pulled him away from her.

Q: Did he say anything to you?

A: He said he didn't mean to. He kept saying it over and over. "I didn't mean to, I didn't mean to."

Q: What did you say in response?

A: I didn't say anything. I just... I couldn't look at him. I took her outside and I called 911 and I didn't say anything to him.

topic: A witness is questioned about events at a party where an assault allegedly occurred
text:
Q: Ms. Chen, how many people would you estimate were present at this party?

A: I don't know. Thirty? Forty?

Q: And you knew most of these people?

A: Some. It was a mixed group.

Q: Did you know the complainant prior to that evening?

A: Rachel? Yes. We work together.

Q: Had you spoken with her earlier in the evening, before the incident?

A: Briefly. We said hello when I got there.

Q: How did she seem to you at that time?

A: Fine. She seemed fine.

Q: Did you speak with her again at any point before the assault allegedly occurred?

A: No.

Q: Why not?

A: I... I don't know. I got caught up talking to other people. I meant to find her later, but I didn't.

Q: Ms. Chen, are you alright to continue?

A: Yes. I'm fine. I apologize.

Q: Take whatever time you need.

A: I just keep thinking I should have checked on her. She texted me earlier that day and said she was nervous about seeing him there, and I told her it would be fine, and then I didn't even... I'm sorry. I'm ready to continue.

Q: She texted you that she was nervous about seeing the defendant?

A: Yes.

Q: Did she say why?

A: She said things had ended badly between them. I didn't ask for details. I should have asked.

Q: What did you say in response to her text?

A: I said, "It'll be fine, there'll be tons of people there." That's what I said. "It'll be fine."

topic: A witness is questioned about events at a party where an assault allegedly occurred
text:
Q: You mentioned the defendant was your roommate at the time?

A: For about eight months, yeah.

Q: In those eight months, did he ever discuss his relationship with Ms. Torres?

A: Sometimes.

Q: What did he tell you?

A: Just normal stuff. That they'd been on a date, that he liked her. That kind of thing.

Q: Did he ever express frustration with her?

A: I don't really remember.

Q: Mr. Walsh, I need you to answer to the best of your recollection.

A: I'm trying to.

Q: I understand. Let me rephrase. Did there come a time when he indicated to you that he was unhappy with how things were going with Ms. Torres?

A: Yeah. About a week before the party. He said she'd been distant.

Q: What were his exact words, if you recall?

A: He said she was pulling away and he didn't understand why.

Q: Did he seem angry when he said this?

A: I... no. He didn't seem angry. He seemed confused. Lost, almost.

Q: Lost.

A: Like he didn't understand what was happening. Like he thought everything was fine and then suddenly it wasn't.

Q: And then a week later, he struck her in front of forty people.

A: Is that a question?

Q: Let me withdraw that. Mr. Walsh, after the incident, did you continue living with the defendant?

A: I moved out the next week. I couldn't... the apartment felt different. Everything felt different after that.

topic: An HR director is questioned about a harassment complaint that was filed and closed
text:
Q: Ms. Thornton, you were the HR director at Velocity Partners in March of 2022, correct?

A: I was, yes.

Q: And you received a formal harassment complaint from an employee named David Chen on March 14th of that year?

A: I received a complaint, yes. I'd have to check the exact date.

Q: The complaint alleged verbal harassment by his direct supervisor, Marcus Webb. Is that right?

A: That's what the complaint alleged, yes.

Q: And you closed that investigation within six days. Correct?

A: I'd need to see the file to confirm the timeline.

Q: I'm showing you Exhibit 14. Does that refresh your recollection?

A: It does. Yes, the matter was resolved within that timeframe.

Q: "Resolved." You mean closed?

A: I mean resolved. We took appropriate action and the matter was addressed.

Q: What witnesses did you interview during those six days?

A: I spoke with the relevant parties.

Q: That's not what I asked. What witnesses—specifically—did you interview?

A: I interviewed Mr. Chen. I interviewed Mr. Webb. I believe I also spoke with one other team member whose name I don't recall sitting here today.

Q: One other team member. In a department of eleven people.

A: I interviewed the individuals I determined were relevant to the inquiry.

Q: And you made that determination yourself?

A: That's my job, yes.

topic: An HR director is questioned about a harassment complaint that was filed and closed
text:
Q: Mr. Reeves, how many harassment complaints did your department handle in 2021?

A: Ballpark? Probably somewhere between fifteen and twenty.

Q: And of those fifteen to twenty, how many resulted in disciplinary action against the accused?

A: I don't have that figure memorized.

Q: Would it surprise you if I told you the number was one?

A: I'd want to see how you're defining "disciplinary action."

Q: Written reprimand, suspension, termination, demotion. Any formal consequence documented in the personnel file.

A: Then I'd say that number sounds low, but I can't confirm or deny it without reviewing the files.

Q: Let's talk about the complaint filed by Jessica Morales.

A: All right.

Q: You closed that complaint as "unsubstantiated" on August 3rd, 2021. Do you recall that?

A: I recall the Morales matter, yes.

Q: She alleged that her manager made repeated comments about her body. Correct?

A: She made certain allegations, yes. I don't remember the specific language she used.

Q: You don't remember whether she said her manager commented on her body?

A: Counselor, I've handled dozens of these. I remember the case. I don't have every detail committed to memory two years later.

Q: Fair enough. Do you remember what evidence you gathered before closing it as unsubstantiated?

A: I followed our standard protocol.

Q: Which is what?

A: Interview the complainant, interview the accused, review any documentation, interview witnesses if applicable.

Q: If applicable. Who decides if it's applicable?

A: I do. Based on the circumstances of each case.

topic: An HR director is questioned about a harassment complaint that was filed and closed
text:
Q: Ms. Patterson, you testified earlier that you take every complaint seriously.

A: I do.

Q: Every single one.

A: Yes.

Q: Let me ask you about the complaint filed by Terrence Williams in September 2023.

A: Okay.

Q: Mr. Williams alleged that his supervisor, Dana Kristoff, had created a hostile work environment. You're familiar with this complaint?

A: I am.

Q: You closed the investigation in eleven days and found the complaint to be—I'm reading from your summary—"without merit." Correct?

A: Correct, but I'd add some context if you'll allow me.

Q: I'm asking the questions, Ms. Patterson. You'll have a chance to explain. My question is: did you or did you not close the investigation with a finding of "without merit"?

A: I did.

Q: Now, were you aware that Mr. Williams had previously reported concerns about Ms. Kristoff to his previous HR representative?

A: I was not aware of that at the time, no.

Q: You didn't review his personnel file?

A: I reviewed portions of it. Apparently not the portion you're referencing.

Q: Apparently not. Were you aware that three other employees had made informal complaints about Ms. Kristoff in the eighteen months before Mr. Williams filed his formal complaint?

A: Define "informal complaints."

Q: Verbal reports to HR staff that were not reduced to writing.

A: If they weren't reduced to writing, I wouldn't necessarily have access to them.

Q: Is that a no?

A: It's an explanation of why the answer might be no.

Q: Ms. Patterson. Were you aware of those complaints or not?

A: No. I was not.

topic: An HR director is questioned about a harassment complaint that was filed and closed
text:
Q: You've been in HR for nineteen years, is that right?

A: Closer to twenty now, yes.

Q: So you've handled a significant number of workplace harassment investigations.

A: I have.

Q: Hundreds?

A: Over twenty years? Yes, certainly.

Q: In your professional opinion, what constitutes a thorough investigation?

A: It depends entirely on the nature and scope of the allegations.

Q: Let's make it concrete. The Sandra Oyelaran complaint. April 2022. What steps did you take?

A: I interviewed Ms. Oyelaran. I interviewed the respondent, Keith Donovan. I reviewed emails that Ms. Oyelaran provided. I made a determination based on the totality of the information.

Q: Did you interview anyone else?

A: I did not.

Q: Why not?

A: Because the allegations concerned private interactions between two people. There were no witnesses to interview.

Q: Ms. Oyelaran identified three coworkers who she said had observed Mr. Donovan's behavior toward her. Did she not?

A: She mentioned some names, yes.

Q: And you chose not to contact them.

A: I made a judgment that their observations would be peripheral at best.

Q: You made a judgment.

A: Yes.

Q: Before speaking with them.

A: Based on Ms. Oyelaran's own description of what they might have seen.

Q: So you relied on Ms. Oyelaran's characterization to decide her own witnesses weren't worth interviewing?

A: I relied on my professional judgment.

Q: I see. And how long after your "professional judgment" was Mr. Donovan promoted?

A: I don't recall the timing.

Q: Would four months sound about right?

A: I said I don't recall.

topic: An HR director is questioned about a harassment complaint that was filed and closed
text:
Q: Ms. Choi, I want to make sure I understand the process. When an employee files a harassment complaint, it goes directly to you?

A: Not necessarily directly to me. It goes to the HR department, and it's assigned based on workload and the nature of the complaint.

Q: But the Brennan complaint—that one was assigned to you.

A: It was.

Q: And you conducted the entire investigation yourself?

A: I did.

Q: No oversight? No second reviewer?

A: That wasn't our protocol at the time.

Q: At the time. Has the protocol changed?

A: We've made some adjustments since then, yes.

Q: What prompted those adjustments?

A: I'm not sure that's relevant to the matter at hand.

Q: I'll decide what's relevant. What prompted the adjustments?

A: Leadership decided to implement additional review procedures. I wasn't privy to all the reasons behind that decision.

Q: This happened after the Brennan complaint was closed, didn't it?

A: I believe so, yes.

Q: Ms. Brennan alleged that a senior vice president had propositioned her on multiple occasions. Correct?

A: That was her allegation.

Q: "Her allegation." Did you find it credible?

A: I found that there was insufficient evidence to substantiate the claims.

Q: That's not what I asked. Did you personally find her account credible?

A: My personal beliefs aren't the standard. The standard is whether the evidence supports a finding.

Q: Ms. Choi, did you believe her?

A: I documented my findings in the report.

Q: You're not going to answer my question?

A: I've answered it the way I'm able to answer it.

topic: A daycare worker is deposed about an injury a child sustained while in their care
text:
Q: Ms. Hernandez, how long have you worked at Sunshine Days Daycare?

A: Four years and three months.

Q: And in that time, have you received any disciplinary actions?

A: No. Not one.

Q: Let's talk about March 14th. You were working in the toddler room that day, correct?

A: I was assigned there, yes.

Q: And Lily Chen was in your care?

A: Lily was in the toddler room. There were two of us working that room.

Q: I'm asking if she was in your care.

A: And I'm telling you there were two caregivers. We shared responsibility. That's how it works.

Q: Fine. Were you present when Lily fell?

A: I was in the room.

Q: Did you see her fall?

A: I saw her on the ground afterward.

Q: So you didn't actually witness the fall itself?

A: I had twelve children in that room. Twelve. I was helping another child at the changing station. So no, I did not have my eyes on all twelve children at the exact same second.

Q: The changing station—how far is that from where Lily fell?

A: Maybe fifteen feet. You can look at the room layout yourselves. You have the diagrams.

Q: I'm asking you.

A: And I'm answering. Fifteen feet. Approximately.

Q: Is it your testimony that you were providing adequate supervision?

A: It's my testimony that I was doing my job exactly as I was trained to do it, exactly as I've done it for four years without a single incident, and exactly as the state ratio requirements allow.

---

topic: A daycare worker is deposed about an injury a child sustained while in their care
text:
Q: Mr. Porter, walk me through the standard protocol when a child is injured at the facility.

A: You assess the injury, administer first aid if needed, notify the director, and call the parents.

Q: In that order?

A: Generally.

Q: Did you follow that protocol on June 7th when Marcus Williams was injured?

A: Yes.

Q: Let me be more specific. Did you call his mother immediately?

A: I called her after we assessed the injury.

Q: How long after?

A: I don't know. A few minutes.

Q: Five minutes? Ten? Twenty?

A: I didn't have a stopwatch running.

Q: Mr. Porter, I'm trying to establish a timeline.

A: And I'm trying to give you an accurate answer instead of making something up.

Q: Mrs. Williams testified she didn't receive a call until forty-five minutes after the incident. Does that sound accurate?

A: I don't know what sounds accurate to you. I know we called her.

Q: Forty-five minutes is "a few minutes"?

A: I said I don't know the exact time. We had a child who was hurt. Our priority was the child, not the clock.

Q: Was anyone timing the response?

A: No.

Q: So you have no records of when the call was made?

A: I have records that a call was made. I have records that we followed protocol. What I don't have is a minute-by-minute log because we were taking care of a scared three-year-old with a cut on his forehead.

---

topic: A daycare worker is deposed about an injury a child sustained while in their care
text:
Q: Ms. Okonkwo, you've reviewed the incident report?

A: I have.

Q: That's your signature at the bottom?

A: Yes.

Q: You wrote that Dylan "tripped over his own feet." Those are your words?

A: Those are my words.

Q: You're certain he wasn't pushed?

A: Yes.

Q: How can you be certain?

A: Because I was standing right there.

Q: Other children were nearby, correct?

A: Yes.

Q: And you're telling this jury—

A: There's no jury here. This is a deposition.

Q: You're telling me, under oath, that no other child made contact with Dylan before he fell?

A: That is exactly what I'm telling you.

Q: Ms. Okonkwo, isn't it true that another parent complained that same week about children being too rough?

A: I don't know what other parents complained about. That would go to the director.

Q: You never heard about it?

A: I hear a lot of things. I don't track every complaint that comes through.

Q: Would it surprise you to learn the complaint specifically mentioned pushing?

A: Nothing in this process surprises me anymore.

Q: I'll ask you to answer the question.

A: Would it surprise me? No. Parents complain. That's what parents do. It doesn't change what I saw with my own eyes.

---

topic: A daycare worker is deposed about an injury a child sustained while in their care
text:
Q: You mentioned the climbing structure. Describe it for me.

A: It's a plastic play structure. Age-appropriate. About four feet high at the tallest point. Has a slide, some steps, a small platform.

Q: Four feet high. And Emma Parker is how tall?

A: I don't know her exact height.

Q: Approximately.

A: Small. She's three.

Q: So if she fell from the top—

A: She didn't fall from the top.

Q: Let me finish my question.

A: Your question assumes something that didn't happen.

Q: Ms. Reeves, I'm entitled to ask hypotheticals.

A: Then ask them. But don't expect me to agree with the premise.

Q: If a three-year-old fell from a height of four feet onto a hard surface, that could cause serious injury, couldn't it?

A: The surface under the structure is rubber matting. Not hard.

Q: Answer my question.

A: I am answering it. You said hard surface. The surface is rubber. That's a fact.

Q: Fine. Rubber matting. Could a fall still cause a fracture?

A: I'm not a doctor.

Q: You've worked with children for how long?

A: Eight years.

Q: In eight years, have you seen children get hurt from falls?

A: I've seen children get hurt doing all kinds of things. They're children. But Emma didn't fall from four feet. She slipped on the second step. Maybe eight inches off the ground. Maybe ten.

---

topic: A daycare worker is deposed about an injury a child sustained while in their care
text:
Q: Let's go back to what you told the director that afternoon.

A: Okay.

Q: You said—and I'm reading from her notes—"I only looked away for a second."

A: If that's what she wrote.

Q: Is that what you said?

A: I may have said something like that. People say that. It's an expression.

Q: An expression.

A: Yes.

Q: So you didn't actually look away?

A: I didn't say that.

Q: Then you did look away.

A: I'm saying "a second" is a figure of speech. I wasn't literally counting.

Q: Mr. Tate, this is important. How long were you not watching Aiden?

A: I was supervising eight children in an outdoor play area. I was watching all of them.

Q: But not Aiden specifically.

A: Not every single child every single moment. That's not physically possible.

Q: Whose job is it to make sure it's possible?

A: Are you asking me to criticize my employer's staffing decisions?

Q: I'm asking who's responsible for child safety.

A: We all are. Every single one of us takes that seriously. I've given five years to that daycare. I know those kids' names, their allergies, their favorite songs. Don't sit there and suggest I don't care about their safety.

Q: I haven't suggested anything, Mr. Tate.

A: You've been suggesting it for the last hour.

topic: A witness is questioned about a conversation they overheard in a company hallway
text:
Q: Ms. Thornton, you've testified that you were in the third-floor hallway on the afternoon of September 14th. How long were you standing there before you heard the conversation?

A: I wasn't standing there. I was walking toward the supply room.

Q: Walking toward the supply room. And at what point did you stop walking?

A: When I heard voices coming from the conference room alcove.

Q: So you did stop.

A: I slowed down. There's a difference.

Q: How much did you slow down, Ms. Thornton?

A: Enough to not interrupt what sounded like a private conversation.

Q: Enough to hear the content of that private conversation, though.

A: I didn't seek it out. Sound carries in that hallway.

Q: Does it? Have you tested that acoustically, or is that just your impression?

A: It's a hallway with hard floors and no carpeting. I'm not an acoustics expert. I'm telling you what I heard.

Q: And you're certain—absolutely certain—that you recognized both voices?

A: I've worked with David Chen for four years and reported to Sandra Mullins for two. Yes. I know their voices.

Q: Yet you didn't see either of them.

A: I didn't need to see them.

Q: That wasn't my question. Did you see them, Ms. Thornton?

A: No.

topic: A witness is questioned about a conversation they overheard in a company hallway
text:
Q: Tell me what you remember about the conversation you overheard.

A: Mr. Reeves was saying something about the quarterly numbers. That they needed to be "cleaned up" before the board meeting.

Q: "Cleaned up." Those were his exact words?

A: That's what I remember, yes.

Q: You remember those two specific words from a conversation that happened seven months ago.

A: I do.

Q: What else do you remember with that level of precision?

A: The other person—I believe it was Ms. Hartley—said something like, "Tom won't sign off on that."

Q: "I believe it was Ms. Hartley." So you're not certain.

A: The voice sounded like hers. I can't be one hundred percent certain without having seen her face.

Q: But you are one hundred percent certain about "cleaned up."

A: Yes.

Q: Help me understand that, Mr. Vasquez. You're uncertain about who was speaking but certain about what was said?

A: The words stuck with me. The phrase was... it caught my attention.

Q: Why did it catch your attention?

A: It just did.

Q: That's not an answer.

A: It's the answer I have.

Q: Were you already listening for something like that? Had someone asked you to keep your ears open?

A: No. No one asked me anything. I was getting coffee from the break room.

Q: The break room that's forty feet from where this conversation allegedly took place.

A: Sound carries. And I have good hearing.

topic: A witness is questioned about a conversation they overheard in a company hallway
text:
Q: Where exactly were you standing when you heard this exchange?

A: Outside Margaret Liu's office. Her door was open, but she wasn't in.

Q: Why were you at her office if she wasn't in?

A: I was dropping off a report she'd requested.

Q: So you put the report somewhere?

A: On her desk.

Q: And then you lingered.

A: I didn't linger. I was adjusting the papers so they wouldn't fall off the stack.

Q: How long does that take?

A: A few seconds.

Q: A few seconds. And in those few seconds, you happened to hear a conversation occurring where?

A: Down the hall. Near the elevator bank.

Q: With the door open.

A: Yes, the door was open. I already said that.

Q: You did. I'm just making sure I understand the layout. You're inside an office, and you can hear a conversation happening at the elevator bank.

A: It wasn't a whispered conversation. They were speaking at normal volume.

Q: Who is "they"?

A: I don't know. I only recognized one voice.

Q: Whose voice did you recognize?

A: Mr. Alderman's.

Q: The CFO.

A: Yes.

Q: And you're certain it was him.

A: I've sat through dozens of his presentations. I know what he sounds like.

topic: A witness is questioned about a conversation they overheard in a company hallway
text:
Q: Ms. Park, you've told us you were in the hallway. Can you describe what you were doing there?

A: Walking to the restroom.

Q: At approximately what time?

A: Around 2:15. Maybe 2:20.

Q: And as you walked to the restroom, you passed the executive wing.

A: Yes.

Q: That's not the most direct route to the restroom from your desk, is it?

A: It's the route I take. I don't like the restroom near accounting. It's always crowded.

Q: So you walked an extra—what—sixty feet?

A: I don't know the exact distance.

Q: Roughly.

A: Maybe. Sure. Sixty feet sounds right.

Q: And it just so happens that on this particular day, taking this particular route, you overheard a conversation between Mr. Franklin and Ms. Cho.

A: Yes.

Q: What were they discussing?

A: The Meridian contract. Whether to proceed or pull out.

Q: And what specifically did you hear about that decision?

A: Mr. Franklin said—and I'm paraphrasing—that they should proceed even though the engineering assessment was "incomplete."

Q: Paraphrasing.

A: Yes.

Q: So those weren't his exact words.

A: "Incomplete" was his word. The rest I'm summarizing.

Q: You have a very good memory for certain words and not for others.

A: I remember what stood out.

Q: What stood out to you about "incomplete"?

A: It seemed like it mattered.

topic: A witness is questioned about a conversation they overheard in a company hallway
text:
Q: Let's go through this one more time. You were in the hallway outside Conference Room B.

A: Yes.

Q: The door was closed.

A: Yes, but not latched. It was—there was a gap. Maybe an inch.

Q: You measured this gap.

A: I'm estimating.

Q: An inch. And through this one-inch gap, you heard the entire conversation.

A: Not the entire conversation. I heard a portion of it.

Q: What portion?

A: The part where Mr. Sato told someone—I don't know who—that the safety report had been "adjusted."

Q: "Adjusted."

A: That's what he said.

Q: And you're certain he said "adjusted" and not "updated" or "revised" or—

A: He said adjusted.

Q: Did you write this down at the time?

A: No.

Q: Did you tell anyone about it at the time?

A: I mentioned it to my husband that evening.

Q: But no one at the company.

A: No.

Q: Why not?

A: I wasn't sure what it meant. I didn't want to cause problems if I'd misunderstood.

Q: But now you're sure.

A: I know what I heard.

Q: You know what you heard seven inches from a closed door, through a gap you estimated at one inch, in a conversation you didn't report for nine months.

A: Yes.

topic: A business partner is deposed about financial records they were responsible for maintaining
text:
Q: Mr. Hartwell, you were responsible for maintaining the partnership's accounts receivable ledger, correct?

A: I maintained records, yes. Whether you want to call it "the ledger" is your characterization.

Q: What would you call it?

A: I kept track of what clients owed us. I did my job.

Q: And part of that job included recording payments as they came in?

A: Obviously.

Q: I'm going to show you what's been marked as Exhibit 14. Do you recognize this document?

A: It's a spreadsheet.

Q: A spreadsheet you created?

A: One I worked on. I didn't create the template. Someone else did that before I came on.

Q: But the entries from January through August 2022 — those are yours?

A: If you're asking whether I typed numbers into cells during that period, yes. If you're asking whether I personally verified every single invoice that generated those numbers, that wasn't my role, and you know it.

Q: I'm simply asking who entered the data, Mr. Hartwell.

A: And I'm simply telling you the answer isn't as simple as you'd like it to be.

Q: Let me rephrase. Did your fingers type these entries into this spreadsheet?

A: Yes.

Q: Thank you. Now, directing your attention to the entry dated March 15, 2022—

A: I see it.

Q: —the payment from Orion Industries is listed as $42,000. Does that match your recollection?

A: It matches what's written there. Whether it matches my recollection of a single transaction from three years ago, no, I don't have photographic memory, counsel.

---

topic: A business partner is deposed about financial records they were responsible for maintaining
text:
Q: Ms. Yuen, how long have you served as the financial record keeper for Blackstone Partners?

A: Five years, four months.

Q: And during that time, who had access to the operating account statements?

A: Myself. Daniel Reeves. Initially, Carla Montoya before she left.

Q: Anyone else?

A: Our external accountant received copies quarterly.

Q: Let's talk about the period between July and October 2023. Were you aware of any irregular withdrawals from the operating account?

A: Define "irregular."

Q: Withdrawals that were not connected to documented business expenses.

A: Every withdrawal I processed was connected to something.

Q: Connected to what, exactly?

A: Business operations. That's what operating accounts are for.

Q: Ms. Yuen, I'm going to ask you directly. Were there cash withdrawals totaling $85,000 during that period that you cannot tie to a specific vendor invoice or documented expense?

A: I can tie every withdrawal to an authorization.

Q: That's not what I asked.

A: It's the answer I'm giving you, because your question assumes I was running some kind of shadow operation. I wasn't. I followed authorizations.

Q: Whose authorizations?

A: Daniel's. Always Daniel's.

Q: Did you ever question those authorizations?

A: That wasn't my role. I processed what I was told to process.

Q: So you never raised concerns?

A: I documented everything. Everything. If someone had bothered to look at my records before throwing accusations around, we wouldn't be sitting here.

---

topic: A business partner is deposed about financial records they were responsible for maintaining
text:
Q: I want to understand the reconciliation process you used. Walk me through it.

A: At the end of each month, I compared bank statements against our internal ledger. I flagged discrepancies. I reported them to Marcus.

Q: Every month?

A: Every single month for seven years. Without fail.

Q: And what happened to the discrepancies you flagged?

A: You'd have to ask Marcus.

Q: I'm asking you.

A: And I'm telling you I don't know, because once I handed off my reports, they left my desk. What happened after that was above my pay grade.

Q: Didn't you find that frustrating?

A: Is that relevant?

Q: I'm asking whether you followed up on the discrepancies you identified.

A: I identified them. I reported them. I documented that I reported them. Do you want me to do Marcus's job too? Should I have been running the whole company while I was at it?

Q: Mr. Chin, I'm simply trying to understand—

A: No, you're trying to pin something on me because I'm the one who touched the numbers. I kept meticulous records. Meticulous. If there's money missing, it didn't disappear on my watch.

Q: Let's move on. The report from September 2022—

A: I have it memorized if you'd like to save time.

Q: —reflects a discrepancy of $23,400. What was the nature of that discrepancy?

A: Wire transfer that cleared the bank but hadn't been logged by the project manager. I noted it. I flagged it. I moved on. That's the job.

---

topic: A business partner is deposed about financial records they were responsible for maintaining
text:
Q: When you took over the books in 2019, what condition were they in?

A: Disorganized.

Q: Can you elaborate?

A: Missing receipts. Duplicate entries. Three different spreadsheets tracking the same accounts with different numbers. It was a mess.

Q: Did you report this to anyone?

A: I reported it to both partners. In writing.

Q: And what was their response?

A: They told me to fix it.

Q: Did they give you additional resources to do so?

A: No.

Q: Did they extend your deadlines?

A: No.

Q: Did they acknowledge the scope of the problem?

A: They acknowledged they wanted clean books by the end of Q1.

Q: Ms. Fernandez, isn't it true that during this cleanup period, certain records were destroyed?

A: Old duplicates were consolidated. That's not destruction.

Q: Paper records were shredded, correct?

A: Redundant paper records were disposed of according to the retention policy I was given.

Q: Who gave you that policy?

A: It was in place when I arrived.

Q: So you didn't verify whether it complied with legal requirements?

A: I was hired to organize their finances, not audit their compliance procedures. If their policy was inadequate, that predates me by years.

Q: But you implemented it.

A: I followed it. There's a difference. And if you want to hold someone responsible for that policy, I suggest you depose whoever wrote it.

---

topic: A business partner is deposed about financial records they were responsible for maintaining
text:
Q: Let's go back to the quarterly reports.

A: We've covered the quarterly reports.

Q: We're going to cover them again.

A: Fine.

Q: The Q3 2021 report shows revenue of $1.2 million. Where did that figure come from?

A: The same place every revenue figure came from. I compiled it from the sales data I was given.

Q: Given by whom?

A: The sales team submitted their numbers. I entered them.

Q: Did you verify those numbers?

A: Against what? I wasn't in the field. I didn't sit in on client meetings. I worked with what came across my desk.

Q: So you're saying you had no way of knowing whether the sales figures were accurate?

A: I'm saying that verifying the accuracy of sales data was not part of my job description, and suggesting otherwise is either ignorant of how this company operated or deliberately misleading.

Q: Mr. Okonkwo—

A: I'm not finished. For three years, I raised concerns about the lack of documentation from sales. I have emails. I have meeting notes. I have a paper trail a mile long showing that I tried to implement better verification processes and was told, repeatedly, that it wasn't necessary. So if you want to question someone's accuracy, question theirs.

Q: Are you finished?

A: That depends on whether you're going to ask me a real question or keep implying I falsified records.

Q: Did you falsify records?

A: No. Absolutely not. And I resent the suggestion.

Q: Let's move to Q4.

A: Let's.
